label: Goal
body:
We just need four answers that explain why a higher proportion of workers are getting injured.
  - perhaps the jobs that remain are the more dangerous ones / the jobs we lost were the safer ones
  - perhaps the employees that remain with jobs are the more injury-prone ones / the employees that got fired were the safer ones

label: Evaluate
body:
This isn't quite a paradox in the sense that the background information doesn't really make the surprising claim more or less likely. It should just be an irrelevant factor.
  All other things being equal, whether you have more jobs or fewer jobs, the percent of workers injured would stay the same.

label: Surprising Claim
body: The percentage of workers injured on the job has gone down.

label: Background
body: Since there have been declines in employment (fewer jobs) around the globe, the number of workers injured has gone down.

label: Goal
body:
We just need to find four answers that either suggest
  - something ELSE that explains why the vandalism problem went away
  or
  - something that makes it seem less likely that our buddy actually went with that perimeter lighting plan we'd heard him considering.

label: Evaluate
body:
This is a very reasonable speculation. We know our friend has a problem (ongoing vandalism). We hear them mention a possible solution (bright lighting around perimeter). When we eventually learn that the problem has been solved, we assume they solved it with the means we had heard them discussing.
  This argument can be thought of in the usual Curious Fact / Explanation framework:
  Curious Fact - Why did the vandalism stop?
  Author's Story - My buddy must've installed that perimeter lighting he was talking about.
  Weaken by
  1. suggesting some Other Way to explain [ why the vandalism stopped ]
  or
  2. lowering the plausibility of the Author's Way, [ perimeter lighting stopped the vandalism ]

label: Evidence
body: This guy has a buddy whose store was getting repeatedly vandalized. The buddy mentioned that he'd heard perimeter fencing might be a solution to that problem. A short while later, the problem was solved, so he's assuming his buddy went with the option he knew his buddy was considering.

label: Conclusion
body: Bright lighting has been installed around the perimeter of the store.

label: Goal
body:
It's hard to predict four different disagreements, but we have at least a couple:
  - whether or not heckling is fun for everyone or just the heckler
  - whether clubs should try to stop it
  - whether performers enjoy it or just tolerate it

label: Finding the Disagreement
body:
On this (unusual) question, there will be four points of disagreement. Let's do our usual process of asking, for each one of Person 1's explicit claims, whether Person 2 argued the opposite.
  Did Chapman argue:
  heckling is not a long-standing tradition of stand-up comedy?
  No, he agreed with that. They probably disagree about why it's a long-standing tradition (McKee seems to feel like it's embraced by the performers, whereas Chapman is saying it's only tolerated by the performers but they wish it weren't happening).
  Did Chapman argue:
  performers are not aware that heckling is a tradition,
  or that performers do not learn to respond entertainingly.
  There's no comment on whether performers are aware of the tradition. We could potentially say they disagree when it comes to the entertainment value of heckling.
  McKee thinks that the crowd ends up enjoying the heckling, since the comedian is trained to respond entertainingly. Chapman thinks that heckling is usually only enjoyed by the heckler.
  Did Chapman argue:
  it would be wise for comedy venues to prevent heckling?
  Not explicitly, but he is saying that most of the time heckling is just a distraction, so he would be definitely headed in the direction of "let's prohibit it".

label: Goal
body: Look for an answer helping us to believe that the last 3 months will be average or better.

label: Evaluate
body:
When we do Strengthen questions, we still think about how to object to the argument since so many correct answers are essentially ruling out objections.
  Given that the monthly sales average for the first 9 months of this year have been great, how could it still turn out to be a not-good year in sales?
  It seems like the only way the year could end up bad at this point is if the last 3 months are worse than usual (offsetting the fact that the first 9 months were better than usual).

label: Evidence
body: For the first 9 months of the year, our monthly sales average has been $5 million higher than our monthly sales average for the past 5 years.

label: Conclusion
body: This will be a good year for us in terms of sales.

label: Goal
body: Let's look for "whether or not the govt would save money by hiring contractors to do the work currently done by government employees" or saying "whether or not the people the government currently contracts get paid less than government employees would to do the same work".

label: Javier's 2nd claim
body:
The govt could save money by hiring private contractors to perform services now performed by government employees.
  *Does Mykayla say that the government wouldn't be saving money if they were to hire private contractors to perform services currently done by government employees?*
  Yes, she's making that objection. She's saying, "in terms of the current private contracting the government does, that's not the case". They're paying more for contractors than they would to pay government employees to perform comparable services.

label: Javier's 1st claim
body:
Govt workers are paid higher hourly wages than comparable private sector employees.
  *Does Mykayla say that private sector employees are paid at least as much as govt employees for comparable work?*
  No, not in a sweeping way, although she would say that private sector employees currently being contracted by the government are paid at least as much as government employees would be for that work.

label: Goal
body:
Primarily look for something that increases the plausibility that seabirds managed to take seeds from this Hawaiian tree all the way across the Pacific ocean to an island in the Indian Ocean.
  (Secondarily keep an eye out for an answer that rules out an Alternate Explanation for how the seeds got there.)

label: Evaluate
body:
With this Explain Curious Fact framework, we're always asking the same two questions:
1. could there be some Alternate Explanation for the curious fact?
2. how plausible is the Author's Explanation?
  While the correct answer on Flaw, Weaken, Evaluate, and Necessary Assumption is much more likely to deal with #1, the correct answer on Strengthen is more likely to deal with #2.

label: Hypothesis
body: Seabirds carried A. koa seeds from Hawaii to the Reunion Island in the Indian Ocean.

label: Curious Fact
body: How did A. heterophylla, a descendant of a tree (A. koa) from the Hawaiian islands end up on an island in the Indian Ocean?

label: Goal
body: Find an answer saying "recruiting and retaining better teachers would have more benefit than the slight improvement in student performance we would get from smaller class sizes".

label: Evaluation
body:
This seems to be testing a pretty straightforward assumption that "the author assumes the thing she's recommending is better than the thing she's not recommending".
  However, "better" is too fuzzy. When LSAT is testing this concept, we need to dial in on exactly what "better" means in this argument.
  For example, if I said, "Don't Kathy that watch. If you're trying to impress her parents, you should get that vase instead", then I'm assuming that "vase is better than watch". But what I'm really assuming is "vase more likely to impress Kathy's parents than watch".
  In this argument, the author is saying "better teachers is better than smaller class sizes", for what reason? What advantage does finding/retaining better teachers supposedly have?
  The advantage brought by smaller class size is "only slight improvements in student performance" -- so our author must be assuming that the advantages brought by finding/retaining better teachers is greater than "only slight improvements in student performance".

label: Evidence
body: Smaller class size is know to lead to only slight improvements in student performance.

label: Conclusion
body: Public funds would be better spent on efforts to recruit and retain better teachers than on smaller class size.

label: Goal
body: Let's stay flexible, guard against answers that are Too Strong / Out of Scope, and pick the most provable answer.

label: Evaluate
body:
There's a lot of causal stuff going on here. When it's allergy season, there's more pollen in the air. When large amounts of pollen are inhaled, it triggers allergy symptoms.
  To avoid being triggered in this way, one can stay in indoors on dry, windy days.
  We can infer a Flip the Causal Difference-Maker type idea: "Since staying indoors prevents the allergy symptoms from occurring, it sounds like when you stay indoors you don't inhale large amounts of pollen."

label: Goal
body:
We just want to replicate the meaning of the 2nd sentence. On Main Conclusion, we make sure to import "borrowed language", if there are any pronouns or implied nouns.
  On Enceladus, there is a lake of liquid water between the rocky core layer and the icy surface layer.

label: Evaluate
body:
Whenever we do Main Conclusion (or Role), we prime our brain before we read the paragraph with the reminder that the Conclusion is almost always earlier than the Supporting ideas. In fact, a ton of the time the Conclusion will be the very first claim. We read these listening for the first opinion we hear from the author.
  The word must is being used to convey opinion in the second sentence. It's a weird word, because in conditional logic contexts it means factual necessity. But in "Solve the Mystery / Explain the Curious Fact" contexts, must is used to convey that speculative use of must that we use.
  Pretend you were hosting a party, you left to go to the bathroom, and when you came back you see that two of your friends (a married couple) left without saying goodbye. Your brain would want to Solve the mystery / Explain the Curious Fact.
  You might scratch your temple, confused, and say, "Huh ... they must have gotten a call from their babysitter saying that something was wrong with little Avery."
  That's the speculative "must" being used in the 2nd sentence of this paragraph. We would hear more naturally as announcing the author's causal hypothesis if it occurred at the end of the paragraph:
  We probed Enceladus. We found that there's something in between the ice layer and the rocky layer. It's denser than ice. Liquid water is only plausible thing that could be there that's denser than ice. Thus, there must be a lake between the ice layer and rock layer.
  So one thing assisting our ability to find this conclusion is our knowledge that the Conclusion almost always occurs earlier than the Support (on Main Conclusion and Role questions). Another thing helping us is our awareness that must gets used to convey a speculative causal hypothesis (i.e. an opinion from the author).
  Finally, if the two claims are joined by the word "and", then they are almost always both Supporting ideas. The "and" is showing us that these ideas work together, they blend to let us derive the Conclusion.

label: Evidence (and)
body: The Cassini space probe measured the density of Enceladus: between the rocky core and the icy surface is something denser than ice, and that could only be liquid water.

label: Conclusion (must be)
body: There must be a lake of liquid water between these two layers of Enceladus (the rocky core and the icy surface).

label: Goal
body: Look for an answer saying that "the dire wolves got trapped in the tar pits while scavenging or hunting", or an answer ruling out the possibility that these tar pits were closer to home (where the pups would be).

label: Evaluation
body:
Whenever the conclusion has a new term that isn't discussed in the evidence, that new term will usually be in the correct answer.
  Here, the new term was "scavenging or hunting". What is the author assuming about scavenging or hunting?
  He's explicitly concluding that there would be adults, but wouldn't be pups.
  And his evidence was about fossils found in tarpits where there were adults, but not pups.
  So he must be assuming that "the group of fossils found at the tar pits came from dire wolves who were scavenging / hunting".

label: Evidence
body: We found a ton of dire wolf fossils that got stuck in some tar pits, but none of them were pups under six months old.

label: Conclusion
body: Pups under six months old probably didn't accompany adults as they were hunting or scavenging.

label: Goal
body: Look for an answer descriptively calling out the Necessary vs. Sufficient confusion, an answer descriptively calling out the author's assumption that "water / sun / soil are all you need for a productive garden", or an answer raising the potential objection that "you could have water / sun / soil, but still not have a productive garden".

label: Conclusion
body: Patricia's garden will be productive.

label: Goal
body:
Similarly, if most species aren't rodents, but most individuals are rodents, then there must be more rodents per rodent species than there are non-rodents per non-rodent species.
  (Just like there were more women per female-table than there were men per male-table ... also, my apologies to womankind for making them the rodents in this math metaphor)

label: Information
body:
Since we read Must Be True looking primarily for Conditional, Math-y, or Causal ideas, we would be most attracted to the two Most claims.
  Most NA mammal species are not rodent species, but most individual mammals in NA are rodents.

label: Goal
body: Find something else that's happening with the people who switched that would explain why they experience a strengthening of major leg muscles.

label: Evaluate
body: Given that studies show the shoes themselves don't actually exercise the major leg muscles more, what else could be different about people who switched to toning shoes? Maybe they get more excited to exercise or motivated, since they see themselves wearing athletic gear?

label: Surprising Claim
body: Many people experience a strengthening of their major leg muscles after switching to toning shoes.

label: Background
body: Research shows that the major leg muscles of people walking in toning shoes receive no more exercise than those of people walking in normal walking shoes.

label: Goal
body: Look for an answer saying, "Just because specialists tend to inflate their own importance doesn't mean that we are very justified in being skeptical when geneticists surprise us by saying, 'yes, even personality traits are also genetically determined'."

label: Evaluate
body:
Whenever we're doing Flaw questions, we have a special ear for the 10 famous flaws, in particular the five most common (Necessary vs. Sufficient, Causal, Part vs. Whole, Unproven vs. Proven False, and Ad Hominem).
  This argument feels a bit like Ad Hominem, like we're shooting down someone's claims because of who they are, not what they said. Typically, authors who commit this flaw are saying, "Don't listen to them .... they're biased / they're acting in their own self-interest, or Don't listen to them ... they're past behavior conflicts with what they're now saying."
  This author isn't dismissively saying "don't listen to them", but she is coming pretty close to that by saying, "we are very justified in being skeptical".

label: Evidence
body: Specialists naturally tend to view their own specialties as fundamentally important, and so geneticists (in proclaiming that even these personality traits are genetically determined) are probably just amplifying their sense of their own importance.

label: Conclusion (therefore)
body: We're right to be skeptical when geneticists claim that personality traits, historically thought to not be genetically determined, are genetically determined.

label: Explain / Goal
body:
We need something that changed since the nuclear accident that would promote the growth of wildlife populations.
  Maybe it's as simple as "humans left the area, following the accident". Humans often encroach on habitats, so once they leave the wildlife can thrive?
  Maybe the radiation supercharged some of the local food supplies, so now more food grows there than before.
  Maybe the radiation killed off the top super predators in the region and now all the lower species can proliferate.

label: How can we explain that ..
body: Since that disaster, wildlife populations in the region have expanded rapidly.

label: Given that ...
body: The nuclear accident at Chernobyl left the area contaminated with radiation, such that wild animals there now have very high levels of radiation in their muscles and bones.

label: Goal
body: Look for an answer calling out the author's failure to consider Alternate Explanations for why the profits rose after 1973, or look for an answer to highlight something that would make the author's causal storyline (oil companies/countries colluded) seem less plausible.

label: Evaluate
body:
Given that ... the profits of oil companies and oil-producing countries rose greatly after 1973, How could we argue that ... the oil crisis of 1973 was caused by a real shortage of oil, and wasn't just the result of collusion?
  Well, let's start by supposing there was a shortage of oil. As supply shrinks relative to demand, the price of oil would rise. People used to pay $1 / gallon and now they're paying $3 / gallon, as a reflection of demand outpacing supply.
  Meanwhile, Profit = Revenue - Expenses
  If people are paying higher prices due to short supply, then the revenue per gallon has increased. Have the expenses of the oil producers increased?
  There's not necessarily any reason to think expenses went up, unless it's common sense that when oil is in short supply, oil producers have to spend more money to extract/refine/distribute it.
  So it's reasonable to think that if gas prices rise due to short supply (while expenses of producing gas stay pretty stable), then that would cause the profit margin on gas to go up all on its own.
  Would that explain the profits of oil companies and oil-producing countries going up after 1973? Maybe so, maybe not. Since oil was in short supply, the overall total gas being sold is lower. So even though their profit margin on gas would go up, their overall profits might not go up because of lower volume of sales.
  Still, it's coherent to argue that depending on how much revenue and expenses did / didn't go up, a short supply on its own could explain an increase in profits.
  But we would probably guess that what LSAT really wants to test is the famous Causal reasoning flaw. The author is presenting a Curious Fact premise: "why did profits of oil companies/countries show large increases after 1973?"
  One possible explanation is that the companies/countries were colluding to artificially jack up the price in order to boost profits. But that's not necessarily the only possible explanation, so it's flawed for the author to be so sure of her causal interpretation of these events.

label: Evidence (this is shown by the fact that)
body: After 1973, the profits of oil companies showed large increases, as did the incomes of oil-producing countries.

label: Conclusion
body: The oil crisis of 1973 wasn't due to the shortage of oil but rather the collusion between oil companies and oil-producing countries to restrict supply in order to profit from higher prices.

label: Goal
body: Pick the most provable answer (it might be a safely worded explanation for why the med students are going back to their original diagnosis).

label: Evaluate
body:
This one seems to be like a Solve the Causal Mystery / Identify the Causal Difference-Maker type setup. We have some interesting behavior in that each med student is going back to the disease they were asked about initially.
  Can we say something safely worded like, "When you're asked to rule out a diagnosis, you're more likely to think of that diagnosis?", or "Being asked by an authority figure about a certain topic makes that topic stand out in your mind relative to other similar topics?"

label: Facts
body:
Some med students and a doctor are looking at a sick patient trying to diagnose.
  The doctor says, "Meg, what tests would we order to rule out lupus? Tony, what would we order to rule out emphysema? Karthik, what would we order to rule out diabetes?"
  A week later these same med students and a different doctor are looking at a similar sick patient.
  The new doctor says, "Well, how would we diagnose this patient?"
Meg says, "here's how I would rule out lupus ..."
Tony says, "here's how I would rule out emphysema ... "

label: Goal
body:
Since this is Weaken, we know to prioritize thinking about OTHER STORIES.
  How else could we explain the correlation between caffeinated soda and broken bones? Our customary go-to alternative explanations for correlations are Reverse Causality and Third Factor.
  Could it be that breaking bones came first and caffeinated sodas came next? Maybe. Unlikely, but maybe teens who break their bones become sedentary and sleepier and start drinking caffeinated sodas more to pep themselves up.
  Could there be some Third Factor that really caused the broken bones and just happens to go along with the caffeinated sodas? Sure, there's the whole Mountain Dew X-Games angle. The kids most likely to drink caffeinated sodas are the ones who most frequently engage in physically dangerous activities like skateboarding / snowboarding.
  On a first pass prioritize looking for a different Causal Story, but we could also use an answer that disrupts the plausibility of the author's storyline: first they drank caffeinated soda, then calcium deficiency, then brittle bones.

label: Evaluate
body:
This is the classic Curious Fact / Explanation template we expect on lots of Strengthen / Weaken questions.
  Curious Fact: Why do teenagers who drink caffeinated sodas have a higher incidence of broken bones?
  Author's Story: The caffeinated soda drains their calcium, leading to calcium deficiency, leading to brittle bones, leading to more easily broken bones.
  We always address these with the same two pressure points:
- Is there some OTHER STORY that could explain the Curious Fact?
- How plausible is the AUTHOR'S STORY?

label: Evidence
body: Caffeinated sodas cause people to excrete more calcium. Calcium deficiency can make bones more brittle (presumably making them easier to break).

label: Conclusion
body: Caffeine consumption is the main reason that teenagers who consume caffeinated sodas have a higher incidence of broken bones.

label: Goal
body: We're being asked about the 3rd sentence, which was a premise. If we wanted to get more specific, it was a premise helping to support the Intermediate Conclusion.

label: Evaluate
body:
On Role questions, it's unusual for the last claim of the paragraph to be the Main Conclusion (only about 10% of the time), but we know it's a conclusion from the fact that it's prefaced by Hence.
  On Role questions, it's very common for the first claim of the paragraph to be the Main Conclusion, and the first claim of this paragraph is a conclusion, since we immediately start unpacking / supporting it with the 2nd and 3rd sentences.
  To figure out the relationship between those two conclusions (the first and last claim) we can use the Support Test. Which one would be a supporting idea for the other?
  why should we believe that groups aren't the sort of entity you can praise/blame?
  why should we believe that if we want to praise or blame a group, we have to translate that into a statement about individuals, or else we can't evaluate it properly?
  When we ask the 2nd question, the 1st claim actually sounds like Support.
  Why should we re-cast praise or blame about a group into statements about individuals? Because, groups aren't the sort of entity you can praise or blame.
  This is how we know the first claim is subordinate to the last claim.

label: Evidence
body:
Blaming something requires that the thing has conscience and agency (an ability to decide for themselves).
  Nations don't have consciences. Families are not agents.

label: Intermediate Conclusion
body: Groups are not a type of entity that you can praise or blame.

label: Main Conclusion
body: If you're trying to praise or blame a group, you need to cast that statement in terms of individuals, if we're gonna properly evaluate your claim.

label: Goal
body:
We could point out that the author's thinking, "If two things are both effects of the same cause, one of those thing is causing the other thing."
  We could raise an objection that, "even if X and Y are both symptoms of underlying condition Z, changing X might have no effect on Y."

label: Evaluate
body:
Normally, when we see a causal conclusion, there was a correlation between X and Y in the evidence. The author overconfidently concludes that X causes Y, and we consider alternate explanations such as,
- Reverse Causality (maybe Y causes X?)
- Third Factor (maybe X and Y are both caused by Z?)
  In this argument, though, the evidence also had a causal claim. It's almost as though this argument started by establishing that there is a Third Factor, Z, psychological stress, that causes X and Y (negative emotions and impaired physical health).
  The author bizarrely assumes that X causes Y, out of this love triangle.

label: Evidence
body: Psychological stress is known both to cause negative emotions and to impair physical health.

label: Conclusion
body: Overcoming negative emotions could cause one's health to improve.

label: Goal
body: If we were to try to use what we learned from the first two sentences with what we're told in the last sentence, we would probably be saying something like, "inhibiting the creation of new blood vessels (angiogenesis) prevents obesity in rats".

label: Evaluate
body:
They tell us the causal mechanism by which anticancer drugs work, inhibiting the creation of new blood vessels (angiogenesis), and then they tell us that the same drugs prevent obesity in rodents.
  So it seems like the synthesis we could get here is that the same causal mechanism somehow prevents obesity.

label: Statements
body:
As we search for Causal, Conditional, Comparative, or Pivot type wording, we see two causal claims.
  - causal (work by): Some anticancer drugs work by depriving growing tumors of needed blood vessels.
- causal (work by): These drugs inhibit the process of angiogenesis, which is the creation of new blood vessels.
- causal (prevent): The same drugs prevent obesity.

label: Goal
body:
The conclusion has a signature strength/type we might be able to use for some quick eliminations.
  The conclusion on the correct answer should sound pretty dismissive of a certain strategy "it would be pointless to do X".
  The problem with the strategy needs to feel something like "even if it starts off right, it'll become wrong".

label: Evaluate
body:
Since there was no conditional logic or quantifiers in this argument, it's probably not worth putting into algebra.
  Let's just try to remove the topic and tell the same story:
  - Premise 1: You want to find the perfect match/solution.
- Premise 2: But anything that would initially be perfect would eventually drift and no longer be perfect.
- Conclusion: Thus, it's pointless to spend too much energy trying to find the perfect match/solution.

label: Evidence
body: The color of all paint fades and changes within about a year of being on the wall, so even if you nail the matching shade of paint initially, it will still drift from that shade and eventually not match the old paint.

label: Conclusion
body: It's pointless trying to spend too much time trying to perfectly match your new shade of paint to the old shade (if you're doing touch-ups)

label: Goal
body:
Maybe something like, "If you gear your ads mainly to [the most profitable segment of the market] / [the people who control more personal disposable income than the rest of the population combined], then you'll maximize your clients' profits".
  Naturally, they might disguise the correct answer in contrapositive form, and we should wary of illegal reversals / opposites.

label: Evaluate
body:
If this were anything other than Sufficient Assumption, I would be tempted to start marshaling counterarguments, like "yes, but ... older people's consumer habits are already stuck, so ads don't make as much different", or "most of the money they spend is on behalf of other people, so ads should target those people".
  But Sufficient Assumption just needs a math-y connector that adds on to what we're told in the premise and allows us to derive the conclusion.
  Since there is a New Idea in the Conclusion, (maximizing clients' profits), that idea must be in the correct answer.
  The one thing we know from the Evidence that we can swap out in the conclusion is the detail we're told about "older adults" (they're the overlapping idea).

label: Evidence
body: Older adults control more of this nation's personal disposable income than does the rest of the population combined.

label: Conclusion
body: If ad agencies gear their ads mainly to older adults, they can maximize clients' profits.

label: Goal
body:
If they'd have to fundraise, then electing judges is a bad idea
  or
  If it would mean that they're taking contributions from special interests, then electing judges shouldn't be done
  or (most likely, since this idea was deepest in the chain of Premises)
  If it would produce conflicts of interests for judges, then we shouldn't have them be elected.

label: Evaluate
body:
We want a principle that gets us from something we were told in the Evidence about "electing judges", such as
- they'd have to fundraise
- they'd take contributions from special interests
- they'd presumably run into conflicts of interest
and uses that to get us to Conclusion language like "bad idea / should have judges be elected".

label: Evidence
body: If judges were elected, they'd have to raise funds, which means they'd accept campaign contributions from special interests, which means they'd be likely to run into the same conflicts of interest that politicians run into when they accept contributions.

label: Conclusion
body: It would be a bad idea if all judges were elected rather than appointed.

label: Evaluate
body:
Because this has a conditional (only when) and repeating ideas (makes sound / outlet turned on), it's a good contender for looking at the structure.
  The flaw seems to be a Sampling one. The conditional logic isn't going backwards. It's just that the author is thinking "if it usually makes the sound for me, then it probably usually makes the sound for everyone."

label: Conclusion
body: The electric outlet is usually turned on. (Usually, OTO.)

label: Goal
body:
Look for an answer saying that Binh points out that Kira's evidence, while undeniably true, has no logical force when it comes to supporting the idea that a certain product would be an unwise purchase.
  Binh hasn't said as much, but the common sense gist of his response is, "Sure ... isn't that true of any product?" He's sort of saying, "You're acting like this is some negative property specific to this insurance policy, when it's not distinctive at all. It's a feature of every for-profit product."

label: Evaluate
body:
When Method questions involve one person responding to another, a lot of what LSAT likes to test is the area of disagreement. Did the 2nd person ..
- disagree with the Conclusion?
- disagree with the Evidence? (this almost never happens)
- disagree with an Assumption?
- just raise a further consideration?
  Binh is definitely agreeing with Kira's premise, but he just thinks it's irrelevant when it comes to her conclusion.
  He's presumably saying, "All for-profit businesses are designed the same way: the prices are set so that the business makes money. Are you saying it would be unwise for me to buy anything that a for-profit company is selling? It's unwise for me to buy milk, or eggs, because the farming company is going to profit? It's unwise for me to buy Tylenol because the pharmaceutical company is going to profit?"

label: Binh's response
body: I agree with your evidence (it's designed to make them money), but that doesn't in any way show it's unwise to buy it.

label: Kira's evidence
body: It's designed to make the insurance company money. The prices are set to ensure profits.

label: Kira's conclusion
body: It's unwise for you to buy that insurance policy.

label: Evaluate
body:
How could we argue that an increase in the minimum wage will not lead to a decrease in unemployment?
  - The first thing that probably comes to mind is that raising the minimum wage raises the overhead costs for businesses that depend on minimum wage employees. They might not be able to handle this uptick in wage expense, and they might have to lay people off, which would increase unemployment.
  We should otherwise take each step in the author's causal chain and see if we can push back.
  - Will higher min wage lead to more purchases of consumer goods? Maybe not. Maybe the people who start making more money still won't have enough to buy more stuff. Maybe they'll just pay off debts or bills.
  - Let's say there were more consumer goods purchased. Will that really lead to the hiring of more people to fill needed factory jobs? Maybe not. Maybe those factories are highly automated so if anything it would just mean more robots.

label: Evidence
body: As people make more, they will spend more on consumer goods, which will lead to an increase in factory jobs to increase production.

label: Conclusion
body: The increase in the minimum wage will lead to a decrease in unemployment.

label: Goal
body: We need to eliminate four answers that weaken. They will probably either take issue with the predicted implications the author mentioned concerning an increased minimum wage, or they will just offer a new reason why higher minimum wage could increase unemployment (or not reduce it).

label: Principle
body: The more someone gets the impression that the person who arranged a group of objects succeeded at what he or she was attempting to do, the more aesthetically pleasing that arrangement is.

label: Goal
body: Look for an answer that suggests a different way to explain why the lake stickleback lack armor, or for an answer that undermines the plausibility that stickleback are better off with largeness than with armor, when it comes to fending off the lake's predators.

label: Evaluate

Yikes. This is a tough one to organize. I would use the typical Curious Fact / Explanation template that is so common on Strengthen and Weaken.
  Curious Fact: how come the lake stickleback has no armor, while the ocean stickleback does have armor?
  Author's Story: for the sake of protection against the lake's predators, the stickleback would be better off being large than having armor, and having armor slows a stickleback's growth. So natural selection resulted in larger, armorless stickleback in lakes.
  We should then think our two questions for this template:
1. is there some OTHER WAY we could explain this curious fact?
2. how plausible is the AUTHOR'S WAY of explaining it?
  1. Maybe the armor is made from salt and other minerals that would be found in an ocean but not in a freshwater lake. Perhaps the lake just doesn't have the same raw materials the ocean has that would allow a stickleback to biologically construct the typical armor. Maybe the armor would have been useful for predators, but large size offers some other advantage (better success mating?)
  2. To believe the author's story, I definitely need to assume a difference between the ocean predators and the lake predators. I'm not sure what that difference would be, but it should be where armor is a better defense against the ocean attackers and large size is better against the lake attackers. To weaken the argument, we could hear an answer saying that "the lake stickleback and the ocean stickleback have similar predators".

label: Evaluate
body:
This is a classic, Necessary vs. Sufficient, the most commonly recurring of all the Famous Flaws. It happens when an author presents a conditional rule, such as X → Y and then argues illegally in Backwards or Opposite fashion:
- backwards: A is Y. Thus A is X.
- opposite: A is ~X. Thus A is ~Y
  Here, the author argued in opposite fashion. She gave us a conditional: ~X and ~Y → ~Z
  And then she argued in opposite form: the garden X and Y. Thus, the garden will be Z.
  This, of course, doesn't have to be true. Water/sunlight/rich soil might be necessary conditions, but their presence doesn't guarantee a productive garden.
  A productive garden might require other things as well, such as seeds, non-freezing temperatures, a lack of garden rodents, etc.

label: Evaluate
body:
There are a couple famous inferences we can make with two Most statements, but this example is neither of them. (Here they are, for reference, though)
  - Most A's are B / Most A's are C → infer: Some B's are C
- Most A's are B / Most A's are C → infer: Most B's are ~A / more B's than A's
  However, we can tell that we're supposed to do something mathematical by reconciling those two most claims.
  It's sort of a paradox -- GIVEN THAT most species are not rodent species, HOW CAN IT BE most individuals are rodents?
  Let's pretend we're at a restaurant that forbids co-ed seating. It's either all men eating at a table together or all women eating at a table together.
  What could we infer from this pair of statements? Most of the tables are not female-tables, but most of the individual people eating at the restaurant are females.
  If women are responsible for a minority of tables at the restaurant but a majority of people at the restaurant, then there must be more women sitting per table.
  10 tables with 5 women each = 50 women
12 tables with 4 men each = 48 men
  Out of the 22 tables, most of them aren't female tables (10 of 22), but out of the 98 individuals, most of them are females (50 of 98).

This argument is really hard to understand. We omitted the 2nd sentence from the reasoning core, because it's just providing inessential examples of how different moral orders handle the idea of the good being punished and the bad rewarded (this moral order thinks that cosmic justice is achieved via reincarnation/karma, while that moral order thinks that cosmic justice is achieved via a supreme being in an afterlife).

Because the inventor — by M's own description — would have known the epics by heart already, so they wouldn't need to read them. And per M's setup, no one else even knew the new alphabet, so no one else could read what was written either. So who is the writing for? P is saying: your theory leads to a pointless, silly outcome. How can we defend M's hypothesis, given that the person who would invent the alphabet would be the only person who knew what the alphabet meant and given that they wouldn't have any reason to read a poem they wrote down if they had it memorized in the first place?
  Let's think of each objection
- why write a poem down if you already have it memorized?
  Well ... maybe you're afraid you'll forget it in your old age. Maybe you find something aesthetically beautiful about seeing it in print. Maybe you want to write it down and add your own illustrations. Maybe you want to be able to pass this book on to future generations after you're dead.
  - why write a poem in a language you just invented if you're the only one who would know how to read your alphabet?

The conclusion we're trying to strengthen is that directors of the shelter should **ask for permission** before passing someone's donation on to another recipient.
  After all, the donors thought they were contributing to necessary repairs for Pinecrest. They might not have offered money if they thought it was going to other animal shelters.

label: Goal
body: Let's get rid of four answers that weaken. They can provide an alternate explanation for why most of these workers's comp claims were filed after the factory had closed, or just help us to argue some other way that the claims are legit, not faked.

label: Evaluate
body:
The argument suggests a correlation between the factory closure and the timing of the increased number of injury claims. The author concludes that these claims are frivolous or undeserved, implying that former employees are exploiting their job loss to gain unmerited benefits.
  *Curious Fact*: Why did claims for job-related injury compensation increase sharply after the factory closed?
  *Author's Explanation*: Employees are filing undeserved claims to gain benefits due to job loss.
  To weaken this argument, we would look for alternative explanations for why former employees might justifiably file more claims after losing their jobs.

label: Evidence
body: After Baerton's factory closed, there was a sharp increase in the number of claims filed for job-related injury compensation by the factory's former employees.

label: Conclusion (hence)
body: There is reason to believe that most of those who filed for compensation after the factory closed were just out to gain benefits they did not deserve and filed only to help them weather their job loss.

label: Goal
body: Let's look for an answer that strengthens the plausibility of the story that narrow floorboards were a luxury item that rich people would buy to brag about their wealth, or for an answer that undermines a different explanation for why bigger houses had narrower floorboards.

label: Evaluate
body: The most common argument pattern on Strengthen / Weaken is Explain Curious Fact, so when the first sentence provides a Correlation (ppl with trait 1 were more likely to have trait 2), we're likely to get a causal explanation as our conclusion. CURIOUS FACT: why are these correlated? Bigger houses || narrow floorboards Smaller houses || wider wider floorboards EXPLANATION: Since we know that bigger houses were generally owned by richer people, the author speculates that the rich people sought out the narrow floorboards as a status symbol to flaunt their wealth. As always, with this template, we need to consider 1. alternate explanations for the curious fact maybe bigger houses are just usually built with narrow floorboards for some structural reason 2. how plausible is the author's explanation do narrow floorboards cost more? are they coveted by the lower classes? do rich houseguests comment appreciatively about how narrow the floorboards are?

label: Evidence
body: Bigger houses (built for richer people) had narrower boards; smaller houses (built for poorer people) had wider boards.

label: Conclusion
body: Narrow floorboards in early-19th-century houses were probably a status symbol designed to proclaim wealth.

label: Goal
body: Find an answer ruling out price as the explanation — narrow boards weren't just cheaper.

label: Evidence
body: Rich houses had narrow boards; poor houses had wide boards.

label: Conclusion
body: Narrow floorboards were a status symbol.

label: Goal
body: Find an answer that establishes narrow boards weren't significantly cheaper than wide boards — so the rich weren't just being thrifty.

label: Evaluate
body: For "narrow boards = status symbol" to follow, we'd need narrow boards to be the luxury choice. If narrow boards were actually cheaper than wide boards, then the rich weren't flexing — they just had ordinary practical reasons to use them. The whole status-symbol story depends on narrow boards not being the cheap option.

label: Evidence
body: Big houses (rich people) had narrow boards; small houses (less rich) had wide boards.

label: Conclusion
body: The historians say narrow floorboards in big rich-people houses signaled wealth.

label: Principle
body:
The word "when" (like *if*) is a sufficient indicator, meaning we put that idea on the LEFT side of the arrow, whereas the idea "only when" (like *only if*) is a necessary indicator, meaning we put that idea on the RIGHT side of the arrow.
  If we have "when and only when" then we're getting a bi-conditional, because we're saying that an idea belongs on the left and the right side of the arrow.
  But an even simpler way to think about bi-conditionals is that they're just **either / ors**

label: Goal
body:
Let's look for an answer saying, "even though we aren't willing to pay price X, the ozone layer might still be worth price X".
  Or look for an answer saying, "even though the ozone layer is worth less than astronomically high price X, that doesn't mean we can actually produce any specific monetary value to express the worth of the ozone layer."
  (This is like erroneously arguing, "Since my girlfriend tells me she **doesn't** want sushi for dinner, she must have a specific idea of what she **does** want for dinner")

label: Evaluate
body:
Since there are two conclusions drawn, we should technically consider flaws with both reasoning moves.
  *Given that ...* we wouldn't willingly spend all of the world's economic resources to protect the ozone layer,
  *Does that prove that ...* the ozone layer is demonstrably worth less than the total of all the world's economic resources?
  Not necessarily. Let's say the world has $50 trillion in resources. Yes, we wouldn't willingly spend $50 trillion to protect the ozone layer, but does that prove that the ozone layer is worth less than $50 trillion? Does "willingness" prove "worth"? Maybe I'm not willing to pay for fancy synthetic motor oil when I get an oil change, even though it would be worth doing so (because it will save me money in the long run).
  So we could potentially argue that, "people are sometimes unwilling to pay a certain price for X, even though X is worth that price, because people are too shortsighted or ill-informed about the value of X."
  What about the move from the Intermediate Conclusion to the Main Conclusion?
  *Given that ...*  the ozone layer is worth less the total of all the world's economic resources,
  *Does that prove that ...* the ozone layer has a calculable monetary value?
  Definitely not. Even if the author successfully establishes that "the ozone layer is worth *less than* $50 trillion", that doesn't mean we can calculate its actual value.
  Is it worth $1 million? $1 billion?  $95.4 billion? Who knows?

label: Evidence
body: We wouldn't willingly expend an amount equal to all of the world's economic resources to protect the ozone layer.

label: Intermediate Conclusion (so)
body: The ozone layer is demonstrably worth less than the total of all the world's economic resources.

label: Conclusion (Thus)
body: The ozone layer has a calculable monetary value.

label: Goal
body:
Let's look for something like, "If tax dollars were spent in a way that elected reps were within their rights, then taxpayers have not been treated unjustly".
  Otherwise, look for something that strengthens the idea that it's okay for our tax dollars to get spent on art that we hate.

label: Evaluate
body:
It's hard to call this an argument, because the conclusion comes after a Pivot, not after a Supporting Idea.
  When we ask, "*why should we believe* that taxpayers are not being treated unjustly when tax dollars fund a piece of art they hate?", we don't really find a good answer. The first sentence at least seems like *an* answer.

label: Evidence
body: The elected representatives were within their rights to vote to support the arts with tax dollars.

body: No taxpayers whose tax dollars fund some work of art they find abominable have been treated unfairly.

label: Goal
body: Once we've correctly identified the conclusion, the hard part should be over. We just need to find the best meaning match for the 2nd claim:  "These new findings will promote compassion and tolerance in when we look at people who are mentally *different*".

label: Evaluate
body:
Whenever we do Main Conclusion or Role, we remind ourselves that the Conclusion is **earlier** than the supporting premises 90% of the time.
  Specifically, the conclusion is usually found in these two places:
- the first sentence (if it's the author's opinion)
- attached to a pivot word / rebuttal statement
  In this case, does the first sentence sound like an opinion the author will defend?
  Not really. It sounds more like a factual statement about where we're at in brain science. The author doesn't try to *support* the idea that "we are learning that neurochemical imbalances can cause a wide range of behavior". Supporting that claim would involve citing some of the research that has offered us those takeaways.
  Instead, the author is just announcing those recent science findings as a factual starting point.
  The 2nd claim is an *Opinion*, since it's about the future. Predictions are by definition opinions, and our author is predicting that as more people learn these scientific findings, we will be more compassionate and tolerant in how we think about mental illness or mental quirks.
  We can tell that the author is supporting *this* claim, because it's followed up by a *Support Indicator* (FABS = for, after all, because, **since**).

label: Evidence (since)
body: Being mentally healthy can now being to be seen as simply having the same neurochemical balances as most people.

label: Conclusion
body: Learning that neurochemical imbalances can cause a wide range of behavior will promote compassion and tolerance when looking at a mental illness, quirk, or mere difference between two persons.

label: Goal
body:
Look for an answer that resists the overconfident causal story the author is portraying. She's utterly convinced that this whole computer virus hysteria was a fraudulent marketing ploy, since only 1000 cases of damage occurred.
  We need to suggest that other possible explanations exist, by arguing that it's possible that there was a legitimate global concern even though only 1000 cases of damage were reported.

label: Evaluate
body:
*Given that ...* only about a thousand cases of damage were reported around the world,
  *How could we argue that ...* the companies warning of a destructive virus that would be activated on a certain date were **not** publicizing a fraudulent fear in order to stimulate sales?
  If the companies sincerely believed that the world needed to be concerned about this computer virus, how can we square that with only 1000 cases of damage?
  - maybe those 1000 cases of damage happen to be at the most important facilities (nuclear weapons launch computers / hospital computers / computers that control the water or electric supply), so even though they're small in number, they could still pose lots of trouble for the world because of their importance
  - maybe the antivirus programs that were sold were just super effective at blocking the virus. If the software worked and if most people bought it, then there wouldn't be that many exposed computers for the virus to infect.

label: Evidence
body: Only about a thousand cases of damage were reported around the world. Meanwhile, multitudes of antivirus programs were sold.

label: Intermediate Conclusion
body: The warning that there would be a threatening computer virus activated on a certain date was a fraud.

label: Conclusion (so)
body: The companies' warning was clearly only an effort to stimulate sales.

label: Goal
body:
Unlike other question types, Strengthen correct answers more often come from category 2 than category 1.
  So we'd primarily look for an answer that **adds plausibility** to the Author's Explanation. We want to be further convinced that the reason insects are attracted to *G* webs is that they are attracted to the specific patterns of UV light reflected by the webs.
  The classic formula of Strengthening a causal connection is "No Cause, No Effect". Since the author thinks that the UV reflected patterns cause the insects to be attracted to the webs, a "No Cause, No Effect" answer would sound like this:  *when we blocked the UV light so that it didn't reflect anymore, the insects stopped being attracted to the webs.*
  But, the correct answer could otherwise strengthen by **ruling out** an Alternate Explanation for why the insects are attracted to those webs.

label: Evaluate
body:
The author's conclusion is positing a causal hypothesis:
*Phenomenon X is probably happening **because of**  Y.*
  So we can use our *Explain Curious Fact* mindset.
  *Curious Fact*
These insects are attracted to *G* webs. (Why?)
  *Explanation*
The *G* webs give off specific patterns of UV light, which insects can perceive and which is attracting them to the webs.
  Now we consider the two pressure points of an *Explain Curious Fact* argument.
1. *Alternate Explanations* for the curious fact
2. the *Plausibility* of the Author's Explanation

label: Evidence
body:
Insects can see UV light and can identify potential food sources or mating sites based on the telltale patterns of UV light that those things reflect.
  *Glosomus* webs reflect telltale patterns of UV light.

label: Conclusion (Thus)
body: Insects are probably attracted to *Glosomus* spiderwebs because of the patterns of UV light that the webs reflect.

label: Goal
body: It's hard to predict where this is headed. We would want to give is a comfy second read for deeper comprehension. We might see a couple "hidden" facts in there that could be what the correct answer goes for, but we should stay flexible.

label: Evaluate
body:
This is a messy bowl of facts. There is a *quantifier* ("most") in the first sentence, but there aren't any other quantifiers to pair it up with. There aren't any conditionals. It doesn't end with a pivot. In other words, there's not much to suggest where our thinking should go.
  There's a little bit of causality.
"the fact that Senegalese gold was 92% **allowed** it to be minted into coins without first refining the gold".
  That implies that a gold coin has some minimum gold content. If we acquire gold from a less pure source, and it's only 67% gold, we might have to refine it (i.e. remove the impurities) so that the remaining bits are  a sufficiently high percentage of gold.
  So we can infer that the minimum purity for gold coins was 92% or lower.
  Finally, we might infer something by combining the ideas that
1. Senegalese gold was always 92% and can be recognized as such because of the 92%
  2. Other gold would get refined, and could go even higher than 92%.
  If you can look at a coin and see that it's 92% gold and thus infer that the coin was made with gold mined from the Senegalese area, then that means that other coins were not refined until they landed at 92%. It suggests that only Senegalese gold had 92% purity. We know no other gold started as pure, and it sounds like when that other gold got refined, they didn't stop at a 92% gold composition.
  After all if both unrefined Senegalese and refined crappier-gold were both 92%, then how could we look at a 92% gold coin and be so sure it came from Senegalese gold?

label: Information
body:
Most gold coins in medieval Spain were minted from gold mined in West Africa (the Senegal area).
  This gold was the purest known. It had a gold content of 92%, which allowed coins to be minted without refining the gold.
  Coins minted from this Senegalese gold can be recognized because they have that signature 92% gold content.
  Mints could refine gold to produce coins with gold content higher than 92%, but Senegalese gold was never refined.

label: Evaluate / Goal
body:
We just need an answer that would explain a merchant's preference for Senegalese gold.
  The key differences we know between Senegalese gold vs. other coins?
- Senegalese gold was never refined / other coins were
- Senegalese gold was always 92% gold / other coins may have had purer gold content
  My guess would be that the standardization of gold content was preferable to the variable gold content you might get by dealing with other coins.

label: Why is it that ...
body: Merchants wanted payment in Senegalese gold?

label: Given that ..
body: Other coins had purer gold content (and thus would seemingly be more valuable than a Senegalese coin of the same size).

label: Background
body:
Senegalese gold came out of the mine more pure than any other gold (it was already 92% gold).
  Because the gold content was already so pure, these coins were never refined (i.e. melted down to remove impurities in order to get closer to 100% gold). They just made coins straight up from the 92% gold.

body:
It's hard to guess a correct answer here. There's a lot of looseness in the argument being made, so it's hard to know what the test expects us to be thinking about.

label: Evaluate
body:
This is a pretty brutal argument to understand / engage with. The author seems to be someone who is hopeful that the right political theory could be disseminated and cause change in existing social structures.
  i.e. Society has problematic feature X, but if the right political theory were to spread, it could help change society for the better, fixing X.
  But ... here's the problem. These political theories originate in the university setting, so they end up using nerdy language that is off-putting to people who aren't in the university setting. Those people outside the university are crucial, however, when it comes be being agents of change.

Disseminating political theories has the potential to cause change in existing social structures.

label: Goal
body:
What's the same in both of these scenarios? What's true whether it's the faculty or students (or both) who find this parking policy unpopular?
  We won't be keeping the policy as is (**i.e. it will be modified or replaced by a new one**).

label: Statements
body:
When we read Must Be True, we're primarily looking for Conditional or Math-y ideas, hoping to combine 2 or more ideas to derive something
  "If" = left side
  *policy unpopular with  → should modify it*
  *the faculty*
  *policy unpopular with  → should adopt new*
  *the students*
  Do those chain together? No, because there isn't any overlapping term.
  Can we apply them to the remaining fact?  Kind of.
  FACT
It's bound to be unpopular with the faculty or the students. We could actually put that into a conditional if we wanted to:
~unpop w/ faculty → unpop w/ students
~unpop w/ students → unpop w/ faculty

label: Goal
body:
So let's look for an argument that copies that form:
  - a conclusion saying that a certain idea, "if X, then Y" is absurd / dumb / ridiculous
- a premise just giving us the contrapositive of that idea (but this contrapositive might use some proxy  idea like *subsidy* to stand-in for the idea of *support*)

label: Evaluate
body:
This argument is brutal to understand on the first (and second) read. When we read arguments on Parallel, we're closely attuned to *Repeated Concepts*, because if the argument repeats the same idea multiple times, we might be able to assign that idea a variable and "algebraically keep track" of the argument's structure.
  Are there concepts mentioned in both the first and second claims?
  Yes, both of them talk about [whether or not the government allows a certain artistic endeavor], and if we understand that government subsidies are a proxy for *government support* then both claims talk about [whether or not a government supports an artistic endeavor with subsidies].
  The claim the author is rebutting, the one she thinks is absurd, looks like this:
  *if government refuses  →  then government does*
    *to support art X                not allow art X*
  And the author rephrases it in contrapositive form:
  *if government  → then government supports*
   *allows art X            art X with subsidy*

label: Evidence
body: We can see how absurd that original claim is by rephrasing it in contrapositive form: "No one is allowed to create art without a government subsidy".

label: Conclusion
body:
It's absurd to say that whatever artistic endeavor the government refuses to support it does not allow.
  *rephrased:* The government obviously refuses to support some activities but still *allows* them.
