label: Goal
body:
Once we find the conclusion on Main Conclusion, we've done the hard part. Picking our answer just means finding the closest match to whichever claim we determined was the conclusion.
  So let's look for an answer that means the same thing as:
*for the last 10 years, MC's bridge maintenance budget has been fiscally irresponsible*.

label: Evaluate
body:
Whenever we're doing a Main Conclusion question, we prime our brain (before reading the paragraph) by reminding ourselves that on Main Conclusion we usually find the conclusion either
- in the first sentence, or
- as some form of Rebuttal statement
  That way, as we read this first sentence, we're listening to it like it might be the Conclusion. We're reading it thinking, "Does this sound like my author is expressing an opinion?"
  In this case, yes! The first sentence has the very opinionated claim:  *a prime example of fiscal irresponsibility*.
  Does the rest of the paragraph try to convince us that the maintenance budget is an example of fiscal irresponsibility?
  Yes. It says, "in a *well-run* program, you'd do X. Instead (in this crappy-run program), Metro City is doing Y."
  The idea is that if you spend $15 million a year, then you only have to do about $10 million in repairs. Over ten years that would be $150 + 10 million, or $160 million.
  Instead, they tried to cheap-out (economize), and they've only spent $1 million per year, and now they have a repair bill of $400 million. Over ten years, that's $10 + 400 million, or $410 million.

label: Evidence
body:
In a **well-run** program, they'd spend $15 million a year on maintenance, which would limit deterioration and thus limit money they'd need to reconstruct the bridge to $10 million.
  Instead, because Metro City has only been paying $1 million / year for the last ten years, they now need to do some emergency reconstruction of bridges that will cost $400 million.

label: Conclusion
body: The $1 million / year bridge-maintenance budget has been a prime example of fiscal responsibility.

label: Goal
body: We're always at the mercy of the answers. Our goal is to pick the most provable claim we can find. But maybe we'll see an answer reinforcing the inferences we made, that preparing a tax return is *not* a completely objective process that any professional would do the same way, or that 19 out of 20 of these fools didn't correctly prepare the tax return.

label: Evaluate
body:
On Must Be True and Most Supported (i.e. Inference questions), we're reading the facts and looking to see if we could combine 2 or more of them in order to derive some other truth.
  Generally, that action involves using Conditional, Causal, or Quantitative ideas they've presented. There aren't conditional or causal ideas here, but all three sentences are quantified in some way, so we should think about trying to make some math-y inference.
  20 of them were all given the same records and asked to prepare a tax return.
None of them were the same.
  *What does combining those two ideas tell us*?
  They all had the same records but none of them prepared a tax return the same way? I guess there are a lot of judgment calls to make along the way. If it were more objective, we'd expect them to arrive at the same answer.
  20 of them were all given the same records.
Only one of them was technically correct.
  *What does combining those two ideas tell us*?
  Apparently 19 of them were technically incorrect! Why are we paying these professional tax prep folks our money if 95% of them couldn't get this right?

label: Information
body:
*background fact*
20 pro tax prep pros were given identical records (which unknowingly to them were just made up records compiled by a financial magazine).
  *quantifiers (none, only one)*
*None* of them agreed with each other.
*Only one* was technically correct.

label: Goal
body: Let's find an answer that helps us argue that the plant is NOT safer than most other plants.

label: Evaluate
body:
This argument uses comparative logic to conclude safety based on injury rates. The manager is suggesting that because their injury rate is lower than average, the plant is safer.
  GIVEN THAT the plant's injury rate is way better than the national average for all industrial plants,
  HOW COULD WE ARGUE THAT the plant is **not** safer than most other plants?
  We might consider other aspects of safety that aren't captured by immediate injury rates. We could also question whether the injury reporting is comprehensive or if there are other hidden factors that might misrepresent the true safety conditions.

label: Evidence
body:
The plant's rate of injury is only 3.2 injuries per 200,000 hours of work.
  This rate is less than half the national average for all industrial plants.

label: Conclusion (therefore)
body: The plant is safer than most other plants where employees could work, according to the rate of injuries.

label: Goal
body: Let's look for an answer ruling out our one big objection (what if supply isn't shrinking, because they were nowhere near the old maximum), or any answer that would help us argue that the price of halibut is likely to go up.

label: Evaluate
body:
The author is arguing that new maximums on how much halibut can be caught will affect supply / demand in a way that will increase price.
  We know the two ways that price increases are for demand to rise or supply to shrink. The author must be thinking that setting these new maximums on how much halibut can be caught will cause supply to shrink.
  Is that a definite?
  It doesn't really have to be, if halibut fishers aren't anywhere near the current maximum. Like if Toyota decided that on its new model of Prius's, the top speed would be lowered from 120 mph to 100 mph, does that mean that Prius drivers will be going slower than before?
  No, not necessarily, because maybe no one was ever driving their Prius faster than 100 mph in the first place.

label: Evidence
body: The law of supply and demand dictates prices, and there are new lower ceiling on halibut catches.

label: Conclusion
body: The price of halibut will increase

label: Goal
body: Look for an answer objecting to the Intermediate Conclusion (that since most of these ancient docs are translated, ancient-history scholars can read them) or one objecting to the Main Conclusion (that since they can read translations of most ancient docs, they have no need to learn an ancient language).

label: Evaluate
body:
Since there are two conclusions here, we could potentially scrutinize both reasoning moves.
  *Given that ...* most ancient docs have been translated into modern languages,
*Do we have to accept that ...* ancient-history scholars can read them for their research without learning ancient languages?
  Hmm, not necessarily. Who says that ancient-history scholars have access to these translations? Who says that the modern languages the ancient docs were translated into are a modern language spoken by most ancient-history scholars?
  What about the 2nd move:
  *Given that ..* ancient-history scholars can read translations of most ancient documents without having to learn an ancient language,
*Do we have to accept that ...* people studying to be an ancient-history scholar don't need to learn ancient languages?
  Not necessarily. What if ancient-history scholars often want to study one of those books that *isn't* translated. The fact that **most** are translated could still leave up to 49% of ancient documents that aren't translated.
  Maybe ancient-history scholars need to know an ancient language not for the sake of reading original ancient documents, but for some other reason.

label: Evidence
body: You need to learn ancient languages in order to read *original copies* of ancient documents. But most historical documents have been translated into modern languages.

label: Intermediate Conclusion (so)
body: Ancient-history scholars can read most ancient historical documents without learning ancient languages.

label: Conclusion (Therefore)
body: Aspirants to careers as ancient-history scholars no longer need to take the time to learn ancient languages.

label: Goal
body: Let's look for an answer saying "coffee could be unsafe for some other part of our body, besides the heart", or one saying "this evidence is only talking about *normal amounts* of coffee; what about other amounts?"

label: Evaluate
body:
This argument makes a move from, "Since it doesn't harm your heart, it's safe to drink."
  Is that fair? Could something be harmless to your heart but unsafe for some other reason?
  Probably. Maybe there's something in coffee that harms your kidneys or your reproductive organs.
  The other questionable aspect is that the comprehensive review says only that drinking coffee **in normal amounts** is harmless to the heart. Maybe drinking it in **excessive amounts** is not harmless.
  When the author generalizes in her conclusion, "*coffee drinkers* can relax", she is implicitly referring to all coffee drinkers. and this review of medical studies has not established that coffee is safe to the hearts of coffee drinkers who drink abnormally large amounts of coffee.

label: Evidence
body: A huge review of medical studies found that there's no reason to think that drinking coffee is normal amounts harms the heart.

label: Conclusion
body: Coffee drinkers can relax; it's safe to drink coffee.

label: Goal
body: Let's find the most provable option, probably something that reinforces the idea that "infants prefer bright colors".

label: Evaluate
body:
The **overlapping** ingredient being discussed in the first two sentences is "easy vs. difficult to distinguish a color", so we should pause to synthesize what's going on there.
  Since we all **prefer** *easier to distinguish* colors,
and infants think **bright** are *easier to distinguish*,
then infants **prefer bright** colors.
  We don't know what adults prefer, because we only know that they *might* prefer subtle shades (since they don't find them tough to distinguish).
  The last sentence sounds like a manifestation of our Inference. We had inferred that "infants prefer bright colors", so it makes sense that a bright colored version of Toy X sells better than the subtle colored one.
  Does this mean that the infant got to pick out his/her own toy?
  Not necessarily.

label: Statements
body:
All people prefer easily distinguished colors to tough to distinguish colors.
  Infants can easily distinguish bright colors, but find it tough to distinguish subtle shades.
  Adults do not find it tough to distinguish subtle shades.
  Brightly colored toys for infants sell better than the same toy in subtle shades.

label: Goal
body:
We know we can strengthen an *Explain Curious Fact* argument two ways:
  1. rule out an *Alternate Explanation* for why the group that did aerobics fared better
  2. add to the plausibility that the aerobic exercise helped people in that group quit
  But since our conclusion also goes broader than simply "aerobic exercise helps you quit smoking" and says "replacing smoking with a healthy activity can help you quit", we could also strengthen the argument by providing other examples of healthy activities helping someone quit an unhealthy activity.

label: Evaluate
body:
The conclusion is hard to find and being pretty coy about what it's saying. What are they referring to with "replacing an *unhealthy* activity with a *healthy* one"?
  Well, in the study, people were trying to quit their unhealthy smoking, and people who were in the group that did some aerobic exercise had more success ceasing their smoking.
  So the conclusion is saying, "the key to quitting smoking may be as simple as replacing smoking with a healthy activity like aerobic exercise".
  Since the argument is presenting a *Study*, we'd anticipate that the author is going to make some sort of causal assumption about the study's findings, and so we can use our *Explain Curious Fact* mindset.
  *Curious Fact ...* why did a bigger share of the group that was assigned "program + aerobics" quit smoking, compared to the group that was just assigned "program"?
  *Author's Explanation ...*  the aerobics helped them quit smoking.

label: Evidence
body:
It's hard to quit smoking because it's very stressful and leads to weight gain.
  In a study of people trying to quit smoking, half were assigned to a smoking-cessation program alone, and half were assigned to the same program plus fifteen weeks of aerobic exercise.
  After one month, no one in the first group had quit but 40% of the second group had not smoked.

label: Conclusion (implicit recommendation)
body: The key to quitting smoking may be as simple as replacing an unhealthy activity with a healthy one.

label: Goal
body: Look for an argument assuming something like, "If it's true about the *whole group*, then it's true about *the #1 individual* from the group (or any individual from the group — the correct answer might not be that closely matching, but it will replicate a move from Whole to Part).

label: Evaluate
body:
Conversationally, this is an easy argument to beat. Ms. T doesn't have to have the #1 student, just because she collectively has the #1 class. It's very common for Team A to have more total points in a basketball game (i.e. they won), even though the person with the most point in the game played for Team B.
  Similarly, it might be that none of Ms. T's students were superstars at collecting cans, but they all did solid work and that cumulatively got them the win. Meanwhile, the student with the most cans is some superstar in Mr. X's class, but the rest of those students slacked off.
  However, we need to put this in abstract form. Like many Parallel Flaw questions, this is testing one of the 10 Famous Flaws. Whenever we see a certain trait is being recycled in the premise and the conclusion,
  *e.g.  X collected the most aluminum cans. Therefore, Y collected the most aluminum cans*
  ... we can tell the author is assuming "if it's true about X, then it's true about Y".
  In this argument, "if it's true about Ms. T's *class*, then it's true about Ms. T's *top student*."

label: Evidence
body: The students in Ms. T's class collected a higher total of aluminum cans than did the students in any of the other classes.

label: Conclusion (Therefore)
body: The Milton student who collected the most aluminum cans was in Ms. T's class.

label: Goal
body: Look for an answer saying "unique ≠ best", or one saying "best of the proposed ≠ best anywhere".

label: Evaluate
body:
*Given That*  none of the other proposed candidates have J's unique set of qualifications,
  *How Could We Argue*  that someone else is equally or better qualified to be the new president?
  It seems important that the conclusion is just "who is the most qualified", not necessarily "whom should we hire / who is the best fit". We can't just introduce other considerations that are possible negatives about Jones (she has exorbitant salary demands / she doesn't get along as well with other people).
  So we can only look at qualifications vs. qualifications. Does J's qualifications have some advantage that we can offset with a disadvantage?
  We're stuck with this one, very vague, premise that no one else has J's unique set.
  Okay, does "unique set = best set"?
  No other man has my unique set of facial features, but I definitely do not think I have the best set of facial features.
  The other gap seems to be that we started by comparing Jones to all the other proposed candidates, but the conclusion seems to be saying Jones is best qualified, *out of everyone*.
  So maybe we could object that even if J is best qualified out of the set of proposed candidates, there's someone equally/better qualified that isn't a proposed candidate.

label: Evidence
body: None of the other candidates for president of UW have Jones's unique set of qualifications.

label: Conclusion
body: Jones is best qualified to be the new president of UW.

label: Evaluate / Goal
body:
If we're trying to weaken the argument, we need four ways to argue that "it is *acceptable* to close this recreation center"
  - we're going to build another one?
- no one uses this one?
- this one is falling apart / too dangerous to use?

label: Evidence (since)
body: If closed, we would have no local access to a rec center. We already have the most residents per center, and access to recreational facilities is a necessity for this neighborhood.

label: Conclusion
body: Closing this rec center would be unacceptable.

label: Goal
body:
Some people may have caught on to the **Circular** nature of this argument on the first read, but I think most of us don't see it.
  Nevertheless, we could go to the answers thinking, "How are you so sure of yourself that violent crime is rare? Isn't that just one possibility for why newspapers cover it? Couldn't it also be that newspapers cover it a lot because it happens a lot?"

label: Evaluate
body:
This argument is kind of confusing to unpack. It's saying, "I know people think there's a lot of violent crime, since there are lots of stories about violent crime in the paper, but since violent crime is so rare it's new and interesting and so newspapers are eager to report it."
  In a sense, the author is saying that people think violent crime is common because it's reported on so much, but it's reported on so much because it's rare.
  It sounds like a reasonable argument in the Curious Fact / Explanation realm — if people were asking, "Why are there so many stories on violent crime?", their potential explanation could be, "There must be lots of violent crime".
  Our author is pointing out an Alternate Explanation, saying "no there are lots of stories because violent crime is *rare*, and thus interesting when it happens."
  The problem is that when we point out Alternate Explanations, we're saying "This could *also* explain it, so we can't be sure of *your* explanation."
  This author is coming in with a, "Your explanation is definitely false; mine is correct."

label: Premise
body: Violent crimes are very rare occurrences.

label: Intermediate Conclusion
body: Newspapers are very likely to report on violent crimes

label: Conclusion
body:
The claim that there is a large number of violent crimes in our society is false.
(i.e. there are not a large number of violent crimes in our society)

label: Goal
body: As always, with Principle-Strengthen, we want to be stubborn about getting the Conclusion on the right side of whatever rule we pick. We can be flexible with the trigger language, as long as it sounds applicable, but the principle should help us prove that someone was a "murderer".

label: Evaluate
body:
We're trying to prove that some ordinary people of Q were murderers. We know that the regime did execute many people, and we know that the regime was made up primarily of ordinary people.
  In terms of just connecting the dots between Premise and Conclusion, we'd be looking for something like, "If you executed many people, then you're a murderer".
  One potential objection could be, "Wait a sec --- we know the regime was made up **primarily** of ordinary people seeking paradise. And we know the regime executed many people. But how do we know that the people in the regime who did the executing were any of these *ordinary people seeking paradise*? Maybe the executions were all done by the minority of people in the regime who *weren't* ordinary people seeking paradise."
  So we could also strengthen this argument with some guilt-by-association principle like, "If you were part of a regime that did executing, then you are a murderer".

label: Evidence
body:
The regime of Q was made up primarily of ordinary people enthusiastically seeking paradise.
  The regime executed many people in pursuit of its goal.

label: Conclusion (so)
body: At least some of the ordinary people of Q were in fact murderers.

label: Goal
body:
They're asking us about claim 2, which was definitely Support.
  If we want to get more nuanced, we can say that it directly supports claim 3 (an intermediate conclusion) and indirectly supports claim 1 (the main conclusion.

label: Evaluate
body:
It's a little tricky to figure out the intended argument relationships, unless we know our keywords or unless we know how Role and Main Conclusion typically work.
  Most arguments on Role and Main Conclusion give us the main conclusion **earlier** that its support. These are the two main forms:
  1. Conclusion.            1. Attribution (*some say*)
2. After all, support.    2. (*however*) Conclusion.
                                    3. After all, support.
  This argument has the structure on the left, only it has three claims.
   *Claim 1. (Conclusion)*
      *After all, Claim 2 (Premise)*
          *and thus Claim 3 (Intermediate Conclusion).*
  What keywords would assist us in decoding this structure?
  *Seems to be* = opinion
*Recent figures =* fact
*indicating that* = inference drawn from previous claim
  When it comes to the 2nd sentence, we know that the second half (prefaced by ****indicating that****) is being supported by the first half (prefaced by ****recent figures show****).
  If we're doing Role or Main Conclusion and the first sentence sounds like the Author's Opinion, then 99% of the time that claim will be the main conclusion. Try to hear the rest of the paragraph as though it's meant to be bundled together to collectively support that first claim.

label: Evidence
body: Consumers are buying more durable goods than before.

label: Intermediate Conclusion (indicating that)
body: Consumers expect economic growth in the near future.

label: Conclusion (seems to be)
body: The economy seems to be heading out of recession.

label: Goal
body:
Let's look for an answer rewarding us for making any of these inferences:
  - some people are brilliant, professors, and 18+
- some people are brilliant, legal voters, and 18+
- some people are brilliant, under 18, not professors, and not legal voters

label: Evaluate
body:
Whenever we're given conditional rules, we want to figure out whether they chain together and whether we can apply them to any provided facts.
  Do our two conditionals chain together?
  No, but they have a common trigger. We could say that,
    under 18 → ~Professor  and  ~vote legally
  Do our conditionals apply to any of the provided facts?  (i.e. do the provided facts mention any of the triggers?)
  Sure,
  Some  *brilliant people*  are  ****professors****
   so some brilliant people are 18+
  Some  *brilliant people*  are  ****legal voters****
    so some brilliant people are 18+
  Some  *brilliant people*  are  ****under 18****
     so some brilliant people are not-professors and not legal voters.

label: Statements
body:
*conditionals* (no / no one)
  Professor → 18+
    under 18 →  ~Professor
  under 18 →  ~vote legally
vote legally → 18+
  *quantifiers* (some)
  Some  *brilliant people*  are  ****professors****
Some  *brilliant people*  are  ****legal voters****
Some  *brilliant people*  are  **under 18**

label: Goal
body:
We probably want an answer that means something like the last sentence, although when the question stem says Main Point (rather than the usual Main Conclusion), they don't necessarily go with an explicit claim, and they sometimes package in Conclusion **plus** Evidence.
  But it should essentially sound pessimistic about the worthwhileness of spending money trying to find alien life.

label: Evidence
body:
They've been using ever-increasingly sophisticated equipment (sometimes costing hundreds of millions of dollars) for years to scan the skies in hopes of finding life on other planets, and yet no shred of evidence of life has been found.
  There's no reason to think they will be more successful in the future, no matter how much money they invest.

label: Conclusion
body: The dream of finding alien life is destined to remain a dream.

label: Goal
body:
Let's look for something where the evidence narrows us down to a finite set of options:
  Y only serves decaf. C's decaf is only FR or MJ.
So if Y still gets all his coffee from C's, then Y only has FR or MJ.
  Then look for a premise to rule out all but one of those options, and a conclusion to pick the remaining option.
  Turning this into algebra could be a headache that isn't worth it. There are definitely repeating symbols and conditional indicator words, but there is so much here, that it might be tougher to grapple with then simply looking for the reasoning pattern of, "Arrive at the final conclusion by convincing us we only have a finite set of options and only one is eligible."
  Here's what the (ill-advised) five-variable algebra might look like:
  P1:   X only has two types of A's:  F and M.
P2:   Y only uses A.
P3:   The B that Y used couldn't have been F.
  C:   If Y only uses A from X, then the B that Y used was M.

label: Evaluate
body:
This is a valid argument. It arrives at its conclusion by restricting us to only 2 options (FR and MJ), ruling out one, and concluding the other.
  The conclusion is a *conditional* claim, but technically we would get a similar logical feel if they had just said, as a premise rather than as a conditional trigger, "Y still gets all his coffee from C".

label: Evidence
body:
C has only two decaf coffees: FR and MJ.
  Y only serves decaf, and what he served last night definitely wasn't FR.

label: Conclusion (so)
body: If Y gets all his coffee from C, then last night's was MJ.

label: Goal
body:
We seem to be arguing over whether or not lowering the blood alcohol limit would significantly increase highway safety.
  Steven thinks YES, because social drinkers will be deterred.
Miguel thinks NO, because it won't affect heavy drinkers, and they are the most important part of the drunk driving problem.

label: Steven's 3rd idea
body:
If social drinkers are deterred from drinking and driving, there will be a significant increase in highway safety.
     *Does M disagree?*
  Yes. Miguel is saying it will have little effect on highway safety (since heavy drinkers are the biggest danger and a reduced limit wouldn't have any effect on them).

label: Steven's 2nd idea
body:
With a lowered limit, social drinkers will be deterred from drinking and driving
     *Does M disagree?*
  Not sure. Miguel never comments on social drinkers.

label: Steven's 1st idea
body:
We should cut in half the allowable blood alcohol limit for drivers.
     *Does M disagree?*
  Not sure. Miguel doesn't get into any should / shouldn't language. He's only concerned with what would / wouldn't transpire if we *did* lower blood alcohol level.

label: Main Conclusion
body: Thinking can occur without language.

label: Goal
body:
Look for an answer comparing "North American fish lost in the 1900s to North American fish lost in previous centuries", or for an answer comparing "North American fish to other species".
  On Evaluate, we want to pick an answer choice whose question can be answered in a way that weakens the argument.
  So we'll pick whatever answer choice we could answer in a way that helps us argue "the rate of North American fish extinctions accelerated over the 1900s, the rate of extinction of animal species overall is NOT increasing".

label: Evaluate
body:
In order to argue that the rate of extinction is **accelerating** we need a comparison between the current rate of extinctions and the previous rates of extinctions.
  We know that during the 1900's the rate of extinction among North American fish is accelerating (the last fifty years are worse than the previous fifty years).
  But how many did we lose in the 1800's? More or less than 40? If we lost more than 40 North American fish species in the 1800's and only 40 in the 1900's, then the rate of extinctions is not accelerating for them.
  Furthermore, why are we only talking about North American fish? When we talk about the rate of extinctions of animal species, we're talking about ALL species, not just fish.

label: Evidence
body: 13 species of fish were lost from 1900-1950, while 27 were lost from 1950-2000.

label: Conclusion
body:
They are wrong
*rephrase:  There is some evidence that the rate of extinction of animal species is accelerating.*

label: Goal
body: Hard to have a great guess of where this is going. Maybe it'll be a missing link that connects the Problem and the Solution. Maybe it'll be a Defender answer, where if we negated it, it would sound like the Plan won't achieve its Goal.

label: Evaluate
body: There's a missing link between the Problem identified (a world power might have the burden of enforcing a UN decision it found repugnant) and the Solution (give them veto power). That might sound like, "If you don't want an entity burdened with enforcing a decision they disagree with, they should have veto power over that decision." We might also get more practical and engage our Plan / Goal faculties. The Goal here was to avoid a world power having to enforce a decision it disagreed with, and the Plan is to provide only those five countries with veto power. How could this plan fail to achieve its goal? Could a major power somehow be pressured to not use its veto power, restrained from using its veto power? Could it veto something but still have the burden of enforcing the decision it vetoed?

label: Evidence
body: The maintenance of world peace would rest on the world's major powers, and no nation should be required to enforce a decision it found repugnant.

label: Conclusion
body: The five nations that were major powers at the time of the UN's founding should permanently have sole authority to cast vetoes.

label: Goal
body: Find the assumption that the major-power list won't change — otherwise the rationale would extend to new major powers.

label: Evidence
body: Major powers bear the enforcement burden; no nation should be forced to enforce a repugnant decision.

label: Conclusion
body: The reason supports giving the original five major powers permanent sole vetoes.

label: Goal
body: The right answer establishes that no future nation would join the major-power club. Negate it (some new nation does become a major power) and the reasoning no longer supports permanent sole authority for just the original five.

label: Evaluate
body: Watch the time problem. The reasoning would naturally extend to any nation that becomes a major power — they'd also bear enforcement burden and deserve a veto. But the structure freezes the list at the founding moment. The argument quietly assumes no other nation will later rise to major-power status — otherwise the rationale would justify giving them a veto too, and the "permanent sole authority" arrangement falls apart.

label: Evidence
body: The reasoning: major powers bear the enforcement burden, and no nation should be forced to enforce something it finds repugnant.

label: Conclusion
body: The author treats the rationale as supporting permanent veto authority for the five nations that were major powers when the UN was founded.

label: Goal
body: Look for an answer that combines with what we know to help give us the impression that the government needs to spend more money on these wetlands.

label: Evaluate
body:
*GIVEN THAT* ... the govt spends 3x as much as we used to for an area that is only 2x what it used to be,
*HOW CAN IT BE THAT  ....* the govt isn't spending enough?
  Well, it's possible that the government was spending scandalously low amounts ten years ago. In that case, you could triple the budget and still be woefully underfunding the enterprise.
  There also might be something different between the wetlands we protected ten years ago and the "new" wetlands we're protecting now. It might be that the new wetlands we're trying to preserve are in much worse shape or pose much more costly challenges in terms of preserving them.
  That would explain how the land area we're protecting has only doubled but the price of protecting it has more than doubled (the old land we were protecting was "cheaper to protect").

label: Surprising Claim
body: The government isn't currently spending enough on the preservation of wetlands

label: Background
body:
The government spends six times as much on wetland preservation now as it did 10 years ago, whereas the amount of wetlands to protect is only two times bigger.
  If we take inflation into account, we're spending three times as much to deal with two times as much wetlands.

label: Goal
body:
We're looking for answers to give us different reasons why traffic fatalities have declined (e.g. speed limits are lower / cars are safer / police are cracking down more on reckless driving)
  or we want an answer to make it seem less likely that "more skillful drivers would lead to fewer traffic fatalities" (e.g. the more skilled drivers are, the more dangerous risks they start taking)

label: Evaluate
body:
The author is looking at a **Curious Comparison** and then positing a **Causal Interpretation**, so we can use our Explain a Curious Fact mindset.
  *Curious Fact ...* why have traffic fatalities declined?
*Explanation ...* drivers are more skillful.
  We would **weaken** such an argument one of two ways.
1. (most commonly) suggest an Alternate Explanation for the curious fact
2. undermine the plausibility of the Author's Explanation

label: Evidence
body: Over the last five years, the population that is of driving age has grown larger, but the annual number of traffic fatalities has declined.

label: Conclusion (this leads to conclusion)
body: Overall, the driving-age population of Australia consists of more skillful drivers now than five years ago.

label: Goal
body:
Get rid of four answers that help us argue that "even though every culture is different, there could still be overlapping values shared by two or more cultures".
  (We could also weaken with an answer that just makes it sounds like the anthropological studies are giving us bad data)

label: Evaluate
body:
*Given that ...* each culture has a unique moral code
*How could it be that* ... distinct cultures **could** have shared values?
  Well, just because two moral codes are different doesn't mean they're **entirely** different. They could still have overlapping features.

label: Evidence
body: Distinct cultures differ in their moral codes.

label: Conclusion
body: As long as there are distinct cultures, there are no values shared across cultures.

label: Goal
body:
We want an answer that says
*impossible to enforce → ineffective law*
  But we know on Sufficient Assumption they often present what we're looking for in contrapositive form, so we can mentally prepare as well for
 *effective law → possible to enforce*

label: Evaluate
body:
We might hear the missing link here, but it's been well disguised with filler phrases and qualifiers like "Ethical qualms notwithstanding" (jerks).
  When we're doing Sufficient Assumption, it sometimes benefits us to think of the conclusion as a logic voneyor belt we need to build.
  Proving that "there should be no law against gambling" could look like,
  *Gambling ---------------------------> should be*
                                                          *no law*
  The arrow is intentionally elongated because we're trying to create a space in which we can see what ideas *were* presented, and how the author's train of thought was designed to work. We want to ask ourselves questions about the conclusion:
  - *What were we told (if anything) about gambling?*
  *- what rule were we given (if any) that allows us to derive the idea that there "should not be a legal prohibition".*
  The second to last claim gives us a mechanism for proving that there shouldn't be a law.
  If we can establish that a law ****fails to be effective****, then this rule lets us derive that there shouldn't be a law. So if we knew that gambling laws aren't effective, then that would prove our conclusion.
  Did they tell us that gambling laws are ineffective? No, they told us that gambling laws are unenforceable.
  So we need to get from "unenforceable" to "ineffective". Visually, it looks like this:
  **CONCLUSION**
Gambling -----------------------------> should be
                                                            no law
                            **EVIDENCE**
Gambling --> imposs         fails to      should be
                      to enforce     to be   --> no law
                                           effective
                     **MISSING ASSUMPTION**
  imposs           fails to
                   to enforce  →   to be
                                           effective
  If we could make that internal connection, then we would *have* our desired logical conveyor belt from Gambling to Should Not Be Law.

label: Evidence
body:
If a law fails to be effective, then there should be no law.
  Gambling laws are impossible to enforce.

label: Conclusion
body: There should be no law against gambling.

label: Goal
body: Look for something like, "if all the evidence fits both equally, the simpler theory is the superior one".

label: Evaluate
body:
This paragraph doesn't read too much as an *argument*, but the first sentence *is* an opinion ("superior"). Our usual goal when we're matching a Principle to an argument is to make the conclusion be the outcome of the principle, and a consideration from the evidence to be the trigger of the principle.
  If the conclusion is saying "one system is superior to another", then we want a principle that helps us judge the *superiority* of a theory.
  Why does our author think C's theory was better than P's theory?
  P posited something that C found unlikely. And C ** thought of a simpler theory.
  We obviously know that C's theory is borne out as the correct one, but why did the author find it superior *at the time it was proposed*, even though the available evidence was equally consistent with both theories?
  The superiority must have been its simplicity. That's the famous principle known as Ockham's Razor (the literal phrasing is something like "avoid superfluous entities", but the usage is that "all other things being equal, the simpler explanation is the better one").

label: Evidence
body:
Ptolemy believed that the stars revolved around the earth at great speeds.
  Copernicus correctly thought that a simpler theory is that the earth rotates on its axis.

label: Conclusion
body: Copernicus's system is superior to Ptolemy's, even when it was proposed.

label: Goal
body: Since this is a Principle-Strengthen question, the correct answer might contain this exact assumption. However, the correct answer only needs to strengthen the argument. A principle which states something like, "a person's pay should be directly related to how hard they work" would be good enough. Beware of answers that contain illegal reversals or illegal negations of the assumption we identified above.

label: Evaluate
body:
It's fine to consider the first sentence as part of the evidence, but it's really giving us an idea of how high the average CEO's pay is when compared to the average worker. If anything, we might bake this information into the conclusion:
It is wholly unjustified to pay CEOs many times more than the average worker at their company is paid.
In order for the evidence to fully support this conclusion, we need to assume that, if a CEO does not work many times harder than the average worker at their company, it is wholly unjustified to pay the CEO many times more than the average worker is paid.
We could even diagram this:
~work many times harder → ~pay many times higher

label: Conclusion (Therefore)
body: The high pay of CEOs is wholly unjustified.

label: Evidence
body: It is certain that no CEO works many times harder than the average worker.

label: Goal
body: Thus, we want something like "metaphor was essential to the work Cummings did".

label: Evaluate
body:
Excuse me, waiter? Hi, I believe there's a mistake. I ordered a question 2, but this seems way too hard to read for the 2nd question in an LR section.
Okay, when we're confused we can lean on structural clues. We have to find out Conclusion, and "since" and "and" instruct our eyes that the final two claims are supporting ideas.
The conclusion has a pronoun part of it, "in doing so", so we need to import language from the first sentence in order to grasp the full claim that the Conclusion is making.
When we're confused on Sufficient Assumption, we can lean on a trick I call "Mentioned twice? That'll suffice." The basic idea is that ideas that are mentioned twice (literal language, regimentation, stood against) are pretty much taken care of, in terms of the internal logic of an argument.
Consider this "argument":
If A then B. Thus, if A then D, since B presupposes C.
Without thinking too hard, we can guess that the missing link is between C and D, since they are only mentioned once, whereas A and B are each mentioned twice.
So in this Cummings argument, the stuff only mentioned once is "essential to the work he did" and "metaphor".
To actually understand and predict that link, we should first take advantage of the mini-chain of ideas the Premises are giving us in the final two claims.
Metaphor presupposes literal language. Literal language involves regimentation.
Metaphor → literal language → regimentation
If you're against regimentation, as they say Cummings was, then by contrapositive, you would be against literal language and against metaphor.
The author is saying, "If Cummings stood against metaphor, then Cummings stood against something essential to the work he did."

label: Evidence (since / and)
body:
Metaphor presupposes literal language,
and

label: Evaluate
body:
This argument doesn't contain a clear conclusion indicator word like "thus," or even a clear premise indicator like "since." However, it does seem to follow a common pattern.
The first sentence describes a common belief.
The next sentence begins with a pivot indicator, "but." The statements that follow the pivot indicator refute the common belief presented in the first sentence.
When we see the phrase "and just as" at the beginning of the very last sentence, it indicates that whatever goes in the blank should continue in this direction that the argument is headed: it should continue to refute the idea presented in the first sentence.
The argument compares the current criticism of video games to earlier criticism of novels, movies, and rock music, stating that these were also seen as morally corrupting. The argument claims that it now seems silly to criticize novels this way.
We would expect this argument to conclude that it seems equally silly to suggest that video games are morally corrupting.

label: Given
body:
Video games are commonly criticized as morally corrupting in that they allow people to imagine themselves transgressing conventional morality.
But it is telling that precisely this criticism was leveled against many forms of popular culture in their early stages of development, including novels, movies, and rock music.
It now seems silly to suggest that reading novels is morally corrupting

label: Goal
body:
Assuming we symbolized the rules properly, the hard part is over. Since the Application is saying that PF shouldn't be removed, we can get there by establishing that PF either triggers the first policy or the second.
So we either need to hear that PF
1. isn't badly damaged
2. has been checked out in the past 2 years
or
3. is "locally important" and has been checked out in the past 3 years
Any of those three conditions will do it.

label: Evaluate
body:
When we're given principles, we want to always arrange them so that the Criterion is on the left and the Judgy term (should not be removed) is on the right.
The first rule said
for X to happen, Y and Z must be true
Which contraposes into
if Y false or Z false, X shouldn't happen
The second rule said
Things that are Y or Z can be X only if Z
That one is too complex to have one standard rule to go off of. We're better off thinking, "the default sentiment here is that This group of books can be removed only if they haven't been checked out for over three years"
That look like
checked out within last 3 yrs → can't be removed
Then we just added on to the left side what criteria makes you part of "this group" of books:
written by local author, significant to local history, or both
You could consider fudging the details there and just saying
```
Locally important
and → can't be removed
checked out w/in last 3
```

body: Paper Flowers should not be removed.

label: Policy
body:
```
Not badly damaged            should not be
or → removed from
Checked out w/in            circulation
last two years
Written by local author
or considered locally signif            should not be
and → removed from
Checked out within            circulation
last three years
```

body: Look for an answer saying that even though 1% is a small percentage of the downloading population, that 1% might be prolific music producers who are responsible for lots of the existing music on the Internet.

label: Evaluate
body:
There are a lot of LSAT arguments testing the idea of "how could a small slice make a big impact?", and we're basically supposed to say "maybe that small slice has a disproportionately large effect on the situation".
If only 1% of people who download music publish new music of their own on the Internet, how could we say a ton of music online came about by people downloading music, sampling it into something they made, and then publishing it?
Maybe among those 1% are a lot of avid music producers. 99% of us are just downloading, but the 1% are an army of people like Drake and Post Malone, publishing song after song after song.
To put it a different way, say there are only 100 people. The author is thinking that since only 1 of them (1%) publishes their music online, then only 1% (an insignificant amount) of the music online could be coming in the form of download/sample/publish.
But, if this 1 person creates 50 songs that way, and the other 99 people don't publish any new music of their own, then when it comes to those 100 people, the only music they're contributing to the Internet is those 50 songs that were of the download/sample/publish variety.

label: Evidence
body: 99% of people who download music do not publish new music of their own on the internet.

label: Conclusion
body: It's a myth that a significant amount of music online is the result of people downloading others' music and reworking it into new music of their own. (i.e. there is not a significant amount of music online that came from people downloading something, sampling it in a new creation, and uploading that creation)

label: Goal
body:
Parallel Flaw loves to test these Famous Flaws (Nec vs. Suff / Part vs. Whole / Sampling / Ad Hominem). Since this argument has a Sampling issue (the author is fighting a genera claim based on a just a couple of nonconfirming data points), let's look for an argument relying on a sample that is too small.
The sample might be from personal experience, as was the case here, but using personal experience isn't why this is flawed. It's just because the set of data points yielded by personal experience is so shallow.
Similarly, this argument had a rebuttal structure, so the correct answer might, but the Flaw was assuming that "what was true for this small sample of cases would be true for most cases", so to replicate the flaw we wouldn't necessarily need a rebuttal structure.

label: Evaluate
body:
This argument would be similar to arguing, "A respected epidemiologist claimed that most people will get a pretty mild case of covid unless they are older than 65 or immunocompromised. But this claim is false. After all, I am younger than 65 with a normal immune system and my case of covid nearly hospitalized me!"
We would respond, "Sorry to hear that, dude, but you're just atypical. It's still true that for most non-geriatric people with normal immune systems, they will have a mild case."
We can't fight a generalization with a handful of data points. When we say "most NBA players are taller than average", someone can't argue with us and say, "Nuh-uh ... average height is 6' 1" and several point guards in the NBA are only 6 feet or shorter".
So the flaw in the original argument is thinking that, "Since MY cars didn't have transmission problems, even though I never serviced the transmission, the same would be true for MOST cars."

label: Evidence
body: I've owned both of my cars for over 12 years, never had the transmission services, and never developed a transmission problem.

label: Conclusion (but - rebuttal)
body:
This claim is false.
rephrase: Even if you don't get the transmission serviced at least one every three years, most cars won't develop transmission problems.

label: Evaluate
body:
Usually when we see pivot wording in Most Supported, it creates some tension between statements. The way we resolve that tension is frequently connected to the correct answer.
Here, how can we synthesize the idea of people who have U-W disease, who thereby don't have a working amygdala (which is involved in sensing fear), who still experience fear?
Is there something special about the fear of suffocating (a breath that is very high in carbon dioxide) that doesn't involve the amygdala?

body:
causal (involved in)
The amygdala has some influence on how / whether we sense fear.
causal (destroys)

People with U-W disease generally don't experience fear, but they experience extreme fear if they're given a breath that's high in CO2 (low in oxygen), just as some people with normal amygdala do.

label: Goal
body:
Let's look for an answer making a similar complaint:
Hey, author, isn't there a middle ground between overzealous ticketing and no ticketing at all? You can't say the former is justified because the latter is worse, unless those are our only two options.

label: Evaluate
body:
This is a Straw Man argument, which is a term people use in real life to describe it, but LSAT has never used that wording to describe it. The idea of a Straw Man rebuttal is that you're unfairly representing the position being debated.
If I say, "I think we should extend unemployment benefits another six months, while we recover from the pandemic" and you say, "Well I don't think it's the government's job to make people rich for doing nothing!" ...
... you're not arguing with my position; you're fighting a Straw Man position you designed, because it makes for an easy opponent (a piñata you can knock down).
Extending unemployment benefits (which means paying a jobless person around $1200 / month, which is well below the poverty line) is not making people rich for doing nothing. That's not an intellectually respectful rebuttal to the original position.
In this parking ticket argument, the original position in the critics':
the city is being overzealous in its issuance of parking tickets.
Think about what that means. Give yourself a mental picture, a couple examples. What does it mean for a meter maid to be issuing tickets overzealously?
Maybe the meter runs out for some car at 5:58pm, but the rules for that spot are that you only need to pay until 6pm, after which it's free. Rather than letting it slide, the overzealous meter maid gives you a ticket for those 2 unpaid minutes.
Maybe your car is parked a little too far up, in terms of the parking spot lines or in terms of the red part of the curb where you can't park. Rather than tolerate your front bumper being six inches over the red line, they overzealously give you a ticket for illegal parking.
The author's method of arguing is saying, "You shouldn't criticize the status quo, because the alternative is worse!" You shouldn't criticize this obnoxiously overzealous ticketing by the meter maids, because the alternative, a wold in which no parking regulations are enforced, would be worse.
That's like a parent handing their kid a bowl of lentil soup, and the kid saying, "Ouch, that's too hot", and the parent responding, "You shouldn't criticize. Can you imagine how much worse it would be if it were super cold, with ice cubes in it?"
The kid would properly respond, "Well, that seems like a False Choice. Why does it have to be scalding hot or unappetizingly cold? Isn't there a middle ground?"

label: Evidence
body: Can you imagine how much worse parking would be if parking regulations were not enforced?

label: Conclusion
body:
It is a mistake to criticize the city for being overzealous in its issuance of parking tickets.
translation:
The city's not being overzealous (or if they are, we shouldn't criticize them for it).

label: Goal
body:
On Main Conclusion, if we found the conclusion, we already did the hard part. Picking a correct answer means that we're just making ourselves pick whichever answer choice is closer in meaning to the claim we identified (and possibly highlighted) as the Main Conclusion.
So we want something that says, "It is better that graphic designers not remain anonymous".
Consider what an equivalent rephrasing might sound like, to make your listening ears more nimble: "it would be cool if graphic designers did sign their names" / "having graphic designers remain anonymous is overall not great".

label: Evaluate
body:
When we're doing Main Conclusion and Role, we prime our brain with one big tendency before we start reading the paragraph: the vast majority of the time, the Conclusion will come before the Evidence.
On Main Conclusion, this manifests in two big patterns:
- the very first claim of the paragraph is the Main Conclusion
or
- the author does a little warm-up with Background or Counterpoint ideas, and then pivots into her Conclusion, usually with a "but, yet, however".
This argument followed that second pattern, introducing a Background / Counterpoint idea (graphic designers aren't allowed to sign their works).
Then it pivots with a "nonetheless" into the Conclusion. Then it supports that Conclusion with Evidence.

label: Evidence
body: Anonymity undermines effective graphic design by making it difficult to hold designers accountable for their work.

label: Conclusion
body: It is better that graphic designers not remain anonymous.

label: Goal
body:
With Flaw, we're mainly trying to call out the fact that the author is overconfidently selling us on one possible causal explanation for a curious fact, without ruling out other possible explanations.
So look for an answer to object to the move from a correlation between internships and dropout rates to an assumption that the two are causally related.
Or look for an answer that discusses an alternate explanation for this association between internships and lower dropout rates.

label: Evaluate
body:
The author is looking at a curious fact (an asymmetric comparison) and then making a causal conclusion (X decreases the chance of Y).
Curious Fact ... how come the dropout rate for students in internships is way lower than it is for students overall?
Author's Causal Explanation ... it must be that participating in the internship causes students to be less likely to drop out.
On Flaw (and Weaken and Evaluate and Necessary Assumption), we primarily react to these Explain Curious Fact arguments by thinking, "could there be some Alternate Explanation for the curious fact?"
With correlations, we're programmed like robots to think about potential alternate explanations like Reverse Cause / 3rd Factor:
- Reverse Cause: is it possible that not-dropping out is causing students to have the internship?
- 3rd Factor: could there be some underlying factor (like good grades) that is causing students to stay in school and causing them to be a part of an internship?

label: Evidence
body: Of the high school students who participate in work internships, only 1% drop out (compared to 11% of students overall).

label: Conclusion (Clearly, then)
body: Participation in a work internship decreases the chance that a student will drop out.

label: Goal
body: The correct answer could test the move from "putting money into stock market" to "confident in growth of economy", but it's more likely to address the switch the argument makes from talking about investor confidence to talking about voter confidence, while acting like we're still talking about the same thing.

label: Evaluate
body:
There's a real keyword gumbo going on here: clearly, thus, since. These indicate multiple conclusions, so we theoretically have different reasoning moves to analyze, if we're looking for assumptions.
The logic of all the indicator words works like this:
```
Despite
[counterpoint], opposing idea
claim 1. prem supporting 2
Clearly, claim 2. conc, supported by 1.
Thus, conc, supported by 2.
since claim 3, prem, supporting 4.
claim 4. conc, supp by 2+4
```
I typed that and it looks like crazytalk even to me, but each of those indicator words tells you a story of who's supporting whom or opposed to whom. It's not a replacement for comprehension, but it's a way to understand things when you're not comprehending very well. (sort of like relying on conditional logic indicator words to deal with conditional logic).
Our author's two linking assumptions, therefore, would sound like this
```
If ... Then ...
investors are putting       investors are confident
money into stocks → in economic growth
If ... Then ...
investors are confident
in economic growth       The incumbents
and → will retain power
voter confidence tends
to favor incumbents
```
The first linking assumption was joining claim 1 to claim 2.
The second was joining claims 2 and 3 to claim 4.
More conversationally, this author is expecting the incumbents to win the upcoming election, because when voters are confident in the economy, incumbents usually win.
Okay .... are voters confident in the economy?
The author would say "Sure, why just look at how confident investors are right now!"
Okay ... does investor confidence match voter confidence?

label: Evidence
body: Many investors are putting money into stocks.

label: Intermediate Conclusion (Clearly)
body: Investors are confident the economy will see increased growth.

label: Evidence (since)
body: Voter confidence in the economy tends to favor incumbent political leaders.

label: Conclusion (Thus)
body: It's likely that the party now in power will retain power after the upcoming elections.

body:
Since want to strengthen the evidence, we would want to rule out these objections we just made.
Correct answers could sound like:
- oh, no you can't. You can't make out what any of this stuff is. Too damaged.
- nope, can't learn anything important by doing a chemical analysis of the eroded trash.
- this was the worst kind of erosion

label: Evaluate
body:
This question stem is asking us to strengthen the grounds on which the conclusion is based, so it's specifically asking us to improve the force / relevance of the evidence.
In order for us to figure out what the answer might sound like, we often benefit from thinking about how we'd object to the argument. If we adopt a Weaken mindset, we can get our brain to think of objections, and then those objections become ways to Strengthen the argument (if we rule out or go the opposite direction of those ideas).
given that erosion has had destructive effects on the rubbish within these pits,
how could someone still argue that the rubbish does tell us a lot about the possessions of the people who lived nearby?
I guess we'd just say, "sure it's been damaged, but you can still figure out what most of it is ... or you can learn a lot about their potential possessions based on the types of chemical materials you see in there".

EVID: If X succeeds, something bad happens to us. If X fails, something bad happens to us.

label: Goal
body:
We're being asked about the 2nd sentence. This provides a definition of "culture" as "unique set of customs" so that the author can make her cute mathematical argument.
We could maybe call it a premise, because the author is definitely using it in tandem with the final claim in order to derive the conclusion. But it feels like we could also call it a background claim that the author just scoops up and says, "If this happened to be true, then inference X would be true because premise Y."
The answer will probably sound relational (not as simple as premise / conclusion / background / opposing) and convey the idea that the author is just saying, "by THIS definition, culture definitely preserves culture in a technical, mathematical sense".

label: Evaluate
body:
This author is making a weird, nerdy argument that will make nerdy logicians snap their fingers in nerdy approval.
Anthropologists are debating whether the customs in a culture help to preserve that culture. (i.e. does celebrating Thanksgiving help to preserve American culture?)
The author is not engaging with the substantive truth of whether customs are a way of reinforcing and solidifying cultural identity. Instead, the author is interested in just making an observation about what is technically true, in a vacuous sense.
Suppose you define a culture as "the unique set of customs practiced by that culture".
Culture X does customs A, B, and C.
Culture Y does customs A, B, and D.
Even though they have customs in common, the totality of ABC is different from the totality of ABD, so according to this definition they are each different cultures.
The author's cute observation is that if Culture X were to drop custom C, then they would only do customs A and B. Thus, they would no longer be Culture X, since that culture was defined as the ABC set of customs.
A culture with an AB set of customs is different from a culture with an ABC set of customs. Thus, getting rid of custom C made the group that used to be Culture X no longer be Culture X.
Abandoning that custom destroyed their status as Culture X, so, technically, having custom C preserves Culture X.

label: Evidence (because)
body: Under this definition of culture, if a culture were to abandon any custom, then by definition it would destroy that culture.

label: Conclusion
body: If it's correct to define culture as the totality of customs practiced by those whose culture it is, then the customs of a culture necessarily function to preserve it, even if just in a trivial sense.

label: Goal
body: Look for an answer saying something necessary to the internal logic of the doctor's diagnosis, or look for an answer ruling out the possibility of an alternate diagnosis.

label: Evaluate
body:
Since the doctor is trying to Solve the Causal Mystery of this patient's nerve/back pain, we could use our Curious Fact / Explanation mindset.
The doctor is trying to explain the curious back/leg pain and explains it via pressure on the nerve in question. So we would worry about Alternate Explanations for the back/leg pain and we would worry about the plausibility of the doctor's diagnosis.
The most important moment to notice is when the doctor introduces a conditional claim:
if the nerve was inflamed, cortisone would help.
Cortisone helped. Thus, the nerve was inflamed.
What's wrong with that mini-argument?
Well, that's an illegal reversal of course. Just because cortisone helped doesn't show that the doctor's diagnosis was correct.
Perhaps there are other possible causes for which cortisone would also help. We haven't ruled out any of those possibilities.

label: Evidence
body:
A computer scan suggested there was pressure on a nerve going from the lower vertebra to the leg.
This type of pressure can cause inflammation, which can cause pain.
If the nerve was inflamed, cortisone would reduce the inflammation. We injected cortisone and then the patient experienced pain relief.

label: Conclusion
body: The fines are working! Let us raise them MORE!

label: Conclusion (conclude / therefore)
body: The pressure on the nerve in question was causing this patient's back/leg pain.

label: Goal
body:
Our only job is to find the Conclusion. We did. This paragraph made it particularly hard to do so. It's the first sentence. It sure makes life easier if we know the trick for Main Conclusion questions that the conclusion is earlier than the support, the vast majority of the time.
Let's find an answer that mimics the meaning of the first sentence.

label: Evaluate
body:
Whenever we do Main Conclusion questions, we prime our brain to read the paragraph in that special way you read Main Conclusion and Role paragraphs —
the conclusion will probably be earlier than the support
Normally, in Logical Reasoning, the Conclusion is more likely to come at the end of the paragraph. But that tendency big time flips on Main Conclusion and Role. So you start listening as early as the very first sentence.
You have to ask yourself actively as you read each claim, "Is this the conclusion? Does it sound like the author's opinion? Does the next sentence start off feeling like it's trying to support this claim?"
On this question, the first sentence doesn't quite sound like an opinion, but it does sound like an abstract claim, rather than a specific fact. Does the next sentence sound like it's supporting this initial claim?
Honestly, no. But if we force ourselves to look closer, there is an overlapping element. They're both talking about "the public's tastes" / "the readers' interest".
The first sentence was positing a causal connection:
public's tastes --> undermines public welfare
This second sentence is talking about the public's taste, when it comes to news stories. Does it say that our taste in news stories leads to "undermining public welfare"?
Yes, aloofly. It goes on to complain that serious news stories have been displaced by TMZ and InfoWars type stories (the author is assuming that this switch in emphasis is something that undermines public welfare, but we don't need to worry about assumptions on Main Conclusion).
Incidentally the "Because" being used in the final sentence should probably be interpreted as a causal usage of Because (as in, "Because I fell down, my knee is bleeding"), not a reasoning usage of Because, as a support indicator.

label: Evidence (for example ...)
body: Journalists, because they want to focus on stories that stimulate readers, are increasingly doing gossipy stuff rather than hard news.

label: Conclusion
body: The public's welfare can be undermined by its own tastes.

label: Goal
body: Look for an answer that needs to be true for it to be plausible that human activity is causing these cloudy weekends, or an answer that rules out an alternate explanation for cloudy weekends.

label: Evaluate
body:
This is a Curious Fact / Explanation type template.
Curious Fact ... How come in this study, the weekends were cloudier than the weekdays?
Author's Explanation ... Humans are causing it. (Humans are causing noticeable changes to weather on a large scale)
Since the weekend/weekday thing reminds us of a 7 day workweek, and since they're observing this "weekends are cloudier than weekdays" correlation, the author thinks that humans are causing this.
She considers whether there are any natural explanations for this "weekends are cloudier than weekdays" phenomenon but rules them out because the only 7 day cycles that exist are too puny to affect large scale weather.
We are thinking
- Is there some OTHER WAY to explain the curious fact?
- Is the AUTHOR'S WAY plausible?
The author is definitely assuming a difference:
"humans do have a 7 day cycle that could cause a big scale weather difference"
Necessary Assumption + Curious Fact usually means "ruling out an alternate explanation".
How else could we explain the "cloudy weekends" phenomenon? There are no natural explanations that are 7 day cycles.
Could it be a 14 day cycle, or a 28 day cycle like the lunar cycle?

label: Evidence
body:
A study of 30 urban cities found that weekends were cloudier than weekdays.
There are a few 7 day cycles in nature, but none of them could have this big an effect on weather.

label: Conclusion
body: It's now undeniable that humans have an effect on the weather.

label: Goal
body:
We would expect that the correct answer will either give us the idea that "Most of her abstract works were not oil paintings", or it will be something derivable from the conditional chain we assembled:
Oil → Highly Orig → Late Career
~Late Career → ~Highly Orig → ~Oil

label: Evaluate
body:
Since we see a lot of quantifiers / conditionals, we can probably expect that our job here is to make a Trait Overlap inference and/or to chain together conditionals.
First things first. We always flip negatives to positives:
No A's are B = All A's are ~B
Few A's are B = Most A's are ~B
Not all A's are B = Some A's are ~B
That's why I wrote the two few statements in most language and why I wrote the no statement in all language.
Now that are statements are in their more usable form, our #1 priority becomes the conditionals. We got two of them. Do they chain together? Do they have an overlapping idea?
O → HO       HO → LC
Yes, they both talk about highly original, so we would just get a chain saying
Oil → Highly Orig → Late Career
~Late Career → ~Highly Orig → ~Oil
Now we can look at the other quantified statements and see if any of them are using a trigger from these rules:
Most O are ~CA and ~P
Nope. This statement ends with ~CA and ~P, neither of which are triggers that allow us to extend that claim.
Most A are ~HO
Yes! This ends with ~HO, which is a trigger that leads to ~Oil.
```
Most A are ~HO
+ ~HO → ~O
---------------------
Most A are ~O
```

label: Statements
body:
```
All oil are highly original            O → HO
Most oil are not critically            Most O are ~CA and ~P
acclaimed or popular
All highly are late in            HO → LC
original career
Most abstract are not            Most A are ~HO
highly original
```

body:
This argument springs from a Curious Fact / Explanation template:

- is there some OTHER EXPLANATION for the curious fact?
- how plausible is the AUTHOR'S EXPLANATION that this self-portrait dude did it?
There aren't really any other causal possibilities teased here, so it's hard to think about proposing an alternate person who could have painted it. However, we could certainly come up with other explanations for the similarity between the self-portrait and the guy in the battle scene:

- someone who is friends with the self-portrait dude decided to paint him in the battle scene
How could we make it the author's story sound less plausible?
- we could say that the self-portrait artists was only known for painting portraits (hence painting a battle scene wouldn't likely be in his oeuvre).
- ? ?

label: Goal
body:
Let's look for something like Babson's first claim.
Babson thinks charging $1 / article online will succeed if the quality is high.
Cortez thinks, regardless of quality, that plan does not have much hope (since people aren't accustomed to paying for articles).
Babson, we could say, is assuming that people would be willing to pay for articles.

label: Evaluate
body:
Since Person 2 disagreed with one of Person 1's explicit claims, we have a pretty good angle on what the correct answer will be (it will sound like Person 1's first claim, or its negation). We could go deeper and think about what each party is assuming, but let's cross that bridge if the answer choices for us to.
In the meantime, can we talk about the elephant in the room?

The conclusion we're trying to prove is a weird type of claim. Suppose I said, "Thus, if Shelly has any flowers in her kitchen right now, she has daisies". label: Goal
body:
Look for an answer describing the author's Necessary vs. Sufficient error when it comes to the 2nd conditional (the gnats / wet climate one).
Or look for an answer making the conversational objection of, "Just because there are no gnats doesn't mean it's not a wet climate. There can be wet climates that have no abundant population of gnats".

label: Evaluate
body:
We're doing a Flaw question, and we see conditional logic indicators (any, only). What should we be thinking? We should deeply suspect that this is going to commit the #1 Famous Flaw, Necessary vs. Sufficient, which just means that the author presents a conditional logic premise and then botches using it by making an illegal reversal or negation.
The author draws two conclusions, so we should look at each one.
The first (intermediate) conclusion is that there must not be abundant gnats. Why? Because there are no geckos, and geckos are found in every environment with abundant gnats.
```
~Geckos → ~Lots of Gnats
Here = ~Geckos
Thus, Here = ~Lots of Gnats
```
This mini-argument seems airtight. It just applies a fact (no geckos) that triggers the contrapositive of the conditional in the first sentence (lots of gnats → geckos).
Okay the main conclusion was that the climate is not wet.
We were told that gnats survive only in a wet climate. Only / only if are necessary indicators (the only is sufficient), so the idea of "wet climate" goes on the right of the arrow.
```
Gnats → Wet climate
~Wet climate → ~Gnats
```
The author's move from the 2nd to last claim to the final claim is, "If there is not an abundant population of gnats, then it must not be a wet climate." But that move looks like this:
```
~Gnats → ~Wet climate
```
That's not what the rule said. It said "if yes gnats, then yes wet climate", but the author is trying to argue "if no gnats, then no wet climate". That's an illegal negation.

label: Evidence (because)
body:
There are no geckos here.
```
Anywhere you find lots of gnats, you'll find Geckos.
Lots of gnats → Geckos
Gnats can survive only in wet climates.
Gnats → wet climate
```

label: Intermediate Conclusion (must)
body: There aren't lots of gnats here.

label: Conclusion (consequently)
body: The climate here must not be wet.

label: Goal
body:
Look for something saying, "Just because Costa is guilty of X doesn't mean we should discount Costa when he argues that we are guilty of X".
The answer can also say that the author fails to address the substantive point Costa makes, distracting us instead with irrelevant details about what Costa himself does in his theories.

label: Evaluate
body:
We could get into the details of Costa said, but they are immaterial to recognizing the Famous Flaw that's happening here.
Whenever we're doing Flaw and we see a Rebuttal style argument, we know to look for these two of the 10 Famous Flaws:
1. Ad Hominem — in which an author dismisses the view of person X because person X has some biased interest in the matter or because person X has come conflicting past behavior.
2. Unproven vs. Proven False — in which an author concludes that X is false, since there is a lack of evidence that X is true or since someone's attempt to prove that X is true was a flawed attempt.
The conclusion here isn't saying that Costa is wrong, so we're not dealing with #2. It's saying Costa's view can be discounted / dismissed / disregarded, which is more the style of #1.
Why are we discounting Costa's critique? Because "Costa does the same thing". This is a little like getting busted by Mom for playing with matches and trying to argue that we don't deserve punishment because "Timmy did the same thing!"
Mom will say, "Okay, then both you and Timmy did something wrong."
Similarly, we could say to this professor, "Both you and Costa deserve to be criticized for trying to assign works of art to period styles."
Someone who commits tax fraud should still be listened to when they accuse person X of committing tax fraud. Someone who had their license suspended for a DUI should still be listened to when they tell person X that X has had too much to drink to get behind the wheel.

label: Evidence (since)
body: His own current theories presuppose the same assignment he's criticizing me for.

label: Conclusion
body: Costa's reasoning can be discounted.
