Maybe. Could be that some vandal tampered with the painting during Veronese's lifetime, and Veronese was either uninterested in fixing it or unable to fix it.

label: Goal
body: Since searching for alternate explanations is inherently speculative, we're probably going to see a correct answer that reinforces the idea that either Veronese added the pigment later in life, or the vandalism happened within his lifetime.

label: Conclusion
body: John must have worked in the insurance company on Mon - Thurs last week.

label: Evidence
body:
If it isn't a national holiday and not a vacation week, then John works five days each week.

Last week was neither a holiday nor a vacation week.

He works four days a week at an insurance company. On Friday he works as a blacksmith.

label: Evaluate
body:
The evidence establishes that John worked five days last week. And we know that four of those five days involved working at an insurance company. But there's no reason we need to think those four days were Mon - Thu.

First of all, just because John works as a blacksmith on Fridays, he might **also** work at an insurance company on Friday. Nothing in here says he only works one job per day.

Secondly, even if we accepted that John *only* works as a blacksmith on Friday, that still leaves Saturday, Sunday, Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday, and Thursday as the six remaining options for the four insurance days.

label: Goal
body: The argument is assuming that "if he works as a blacksmith on Friday, he doesn't work at an insurance company on Friday". And it's assuming "John doesn't work on the Sat / Sun".

label: Conclusion
body: These patients whose mental disorders result from chemical imbalances can be effectively treated only with medication that will reduce or correct the imbalance.

label: Evidence
body: In some patients mental disorders result from chemical imbalances affecting the brain.

label: Evaluate
body:
There's not really much of a premise here, is there? The first two sentences are really providing background or counterpoint. The symptoms of mental disorders include behavioral, cognitive, and emotional problems (all of which sound psychological in nature).

And some mental disorders are effectively treated with psychotherapy. But the author seems to think that a chemically-caused case of mental disorder has to be treated chemically (i.e. with drugs / medicines / chemicals).

He must be assuming that the type of cause dictates the type of treatment: *if your MD is caused by X, then it can only be treated by something similar in form to X*.

label: Goal
body:
Look for an answer showing the author's move:
*if it's caused by a chemical imbalance, then it can only be fixed by chemically balancing it.*

Or an answer that rules out some objection about alternative possible treatments:
*Patients with mental disorders from chemical imbalances* **can not** *be effectively treated with psychotherapy as well.*

label: Conclusion
body: The republic's recruitment rates for 18-year-olds depend substantially on recruitment rates for high school dropouts.

label: Evidence
body:
There was a correlation from 1980 and 1986 between an uptick in the % of 18-year-olds recruited by the armed services and an uptick in the % of young people who dropped out of high school.

18-year-olds are generally either high school graduates or high school dropouts.

label: Evaluate
body:
Since the evidence is presenting a *changing statistic*, and the conclusion is assuming a causal explanation for that statistic, we can use our *Explain Curious Fact* mindset:

*Curious Fact ...* why was there an uptick in the % of 18-year-olds recruited into the armed services between 1980-1986? (why was this correlated with an uptick in % of 18-year-olds that were dropouts?)

*Author's Explanation*.... the armed forces try hard to recruit high school dropouts, so during this period when there were more high school dropouts, they were able to recruit more 18-year-olds into the armed services.

We can Weaken an *Explain Curious Fact* argument two ways:
1. (more common) suggest an **Alternate Explanation** for the curious fact
2. hurt the **plausibility** of the **Author's Explanation**

Any time an author presents a correlation between X and Y and then assumes/concludes that X causes Y, we're supposed to reflexively consider these two *Alternate Explanations*:

- could it be **Reverse Cause** (in this case -- could the rise in recruits have come first, and that somehow inspired more 18-year-olds to drop out?)

- could there be some **Third Factor** responsible for both? (maybe a foreign invading army is causing people to drop out of school and sign up for the military)

label: Goal
body:
Look for an alternate way to explain the correlation between more dropouts and more armed service recruits.

Or look for a way to hurt the story that the armed services go after these high school dropouts.

label: Conclusion
body: Humans are no better than apes at investing (they don't attain a better return on their investments than apes do).

label: Evidence
body:
They gave five stock analysts and one chimp $1350 each to invest.

After one month, the chimp won, having increased its net worth by $210. The net worth of the analyst who came in second increased by only $140.

label: Evaluate
body:
*Given that ....* in this game show, the chimp got a better return on its investment than the humans did,

*How could we argue that ....* Humans **are** better than apes at investing (humans **do** attain a better return on their investments)?

Within the experiment itself, it's hard to argue with the fact that the chimp attained a better return than the humans.

So if we're going to fight the conclusion, we'll need to argue that what's going on in this game show experiment is not applicable more broadly to humans and apes.

label: Goal
body: Look for four answers that would help us argue that "even though *in this experiment*, the chimp attained a better return on investments than the humans did, *in general* humans **are** better at investing than apes are."

label: Conclusion (Hence)
body: Depictions of violence among teenagers should be prohibited from movies and television programs, if only in those programs and movies promoted to young audiences.

label: Intermed. Conc. (we have good reason)
body: Depictions of violence cause young people to engage in violent behavior.

label: Evidence
body: TV programs and movies that depict violence among teenagers are extremely popular. These media are influential.

label: Evaluate
body:
The author has established that shows and movies depicting violence are popular and influential, but she hasn't given any solid support for the notion that they're influential in the sense of "seeing these depictions of violence influences kids in a negative way / these depictions make young people more likely to engage in violent behavior".

So one way to strengthen Jane's argument would be to provide some evidence that watching violent shows and movies makes teens more likely to engage in violent behavior, or that "shows that are popular / influential can lead to people imitating the behavior they see on those shows".

The conclusion also makes an interesting caveat, saying that at the very least we should prohibit teen-violence from shows and movies promoted to young audiences.

Jane seems to be assuming that shows and movies promoted to young audiences are more likely to be seen by young audiences.

If we were arguing the anti-conclusion, we might say, "You *shouldn't* prohibit violence, because depicting it has these advantages, which outweigh the disadvantages these depictions may have." We might also say, "What about us mature adults who aren't going to engage in violent behavior but (for whatever reason) want entertainment that involves depictions of teen violence?"

label: Goal
body: Look for anything helping to bolster the connection between teens watching depictions of teen violence and teens engaging in violent behavior, or look for an answer ruling out some potential objection to the idea of prohibiting teen violence from movies and TV aimed at young audiences.

label: Conclusion (However)
body: It's actually quite common for species to change the environment in ways that help their survival.

label: Evidence
body:
The plankton is one example of a non-highly-evolved species that alters the environment for their own benefit.

They cool the earth by releasing a gas that ultimately facilitates cloud cover (and thus more sunlight reflecting back into space).

label: Evaluate
body:
On Method, we're just trying to characterize the type of evidence or type of reasoning move used. There's about 8 of them that the test tends to go back to over and over again: *analogy / (counter)example / implications of logic / ruling out other options / suggest alternate explanation / call out dubious assumption / raise an overlooked consideration*

It seems like this would fall into the category of **example / counterexample**.

The author is trying to support a very general conclusion by means of a specific story about plankton (which is prefaced by "**for example**").

A generalization is usually assumed:
*only the most highly evolved species alter their environment in ways that aid their own survival*

The author is offering a counterexample, a case in which a **not**-highly evolved species (plankton) alters its environment in ways that aid in its own survival.

label: Goal
body: Our standard on Method is simply, "If it matches, it's right." If it's descriptively true, take it. But we might assume we're probably going to hear something like, "discuss a specific example that undermines a general assumption many have".

label: Explanation
body:
GIVEN THAT
Cats spend a lot of time sleeping, waking up only to stretch and yawn.

HOW CAN IT BE THAT
They have strong, agile muscles?

EVALUATE
Essentially, we're wondering how cats are looking so jacked when they just nap. Most animals would have to exercise strenuously to have these strong, agile muscles.

GOAL
Find an answer that explains how cats could have these awesome muscles, even though they mostly sleep.

label: Conclusion (it follows that)
body: Anyone who is accustomed to reading braille can easily adapt to the use of the new thermal electronic screen.

label: Evidence
body:
Braille uses raised dots that are read by touch.

The new technology allows flat computer screens to be heated in patterns identical to braille symbols.

label: Evaluate
body:
This argument follows a comparative reasoning pattern. The key idea is that because the thermal device uses the same braille symbol system, the tactile ability required for reading braille should carry over to reading a heated, flat surface.

In other words, the argument assumes that someone who can discriminate braille’s raised-dot patterns will be equally skilled at interpreting similar patterns produced by heat.

To fight the conclusion, we'd have to say that even though someone might be good at reading raised-dot Braille, they wouldn't find it easy to read on a heated flat surface.

That seems plausible! I mean, feeling for a shape via raised dots seems pretty different than feeling for a shape via its heat imprint on a flat surface. Someone might be good at the former but struggle at the latter.

label: Goal
body: Look for an answer choice that articulates the required connection: namely, that the tactile ability to interpret braille’s raised dots applies to interpreting similar patterns on a flat, heated surface.

label: Statements
body:
Some say the reason there are tons of small goats on islands is a response to evolutionary pressure to ensure a diverse gene pool.
(breeding with something that is very genetically similar to you, f.e. inbreeding, is less healthy than breeding with a member of your species that has a lot of genetic differences).

**However**,

A trait will only become frequent in a population if the trait contributes to reproductive success. So the only kind of reproductive pressure that would make goats smaller is if being a smaller goat resulted in more reproductive success than did being a larger goat.

label: Evaluate
body:
Often, when an Inference paragraph gives us a prominent **Pivot**, then the correct answer ends up being a safe way to synthesize what comes before the pivot with what comes after (**Reconcile the Pivot**).

If we were to relate what comes after the "however" to what came before, it seems like this biologist does not quite agree with the "some people" in the first sentence.

They were saying that there are tons of small goats because having a diverse gene pool would be good for the goat species, and she is saying, "evolutionary pressure doesn't work like that. It's not about what's good for the overall species. It's about traits that lead to more reproductive success (i.e. offspring) becoming more and more frequent. So *smallness* would only be an adaptive evolutionary trait if being smaller led to more offspring."

In short, "the reason for the high frequency of small goats is **not** a response to evolutionary pressure to diversify the gene pool".

In addition to Pivot words, we're also reading Inference paragraphs with an eye for Conditional and Causal words, and the last two claims are both Conditional ideas. They don't chain together. The last one is an application of the first one.

Because of this rule
*doesn't influence → doesn't influence*
*reprod. success freq in population*

the author can derive her final idea
*if we're not saying not an evolutionary*
*that small goats → pressure that could*
*have more reprod. influence frequency*
*success of small goats*

label: Goal
body: We have to be flexible, since we're just looking for the most provable answer, but our instincts might be suggesting an answer that sounds like safely worded version of the biologist's rebuttal takeaway.

label: Evaluate
body:
Often I would go claim-by-claim through the first person's paragraph, trying to figure out whether the second person seemed to disagree. But in this case, the Supervisor's paragraph is pretty explicit about where the disagreement is.

**Supervisor: the latest closed furnaces are extremely fuel-efficient**

So, what comment did the Plant Manager make about "latest closed furnaces" that sounds like, "the latest closed furnaces are **not** extremely fuel-efficient"?

The only negative complaint about the new closed furnaces that relates to fuel-efficiency is this one:

**Plant Manager: the new process costs more to run than the current process**

label: Goal
body: Look for an answer saying, "whether or not the latest closed furnaces are extremely fuel-efficient", or, interchangeably, an answer saying, "whether or not the new closed furnaces cost more to run than the current open ones".

label: Conclusion (So)
body: Overall, adopting the new process will cost much bring the company no profit.

label: Evidence
body: The equipment for the new process is expensive to buy and install. The new process costs more to run than the current process (because the copper has to cool and then be re-heated).

label: Evaluate
body:
Since the author's conclusion is about profit, it's about a *Net Gain / Loss* between expenses and revenue.

The author builds her case that this new process is not profitable by listing two ways in which expenses will rise:
1. new one-time expense of buying and installing equipment
2. new recurring expense of higher processing costs

If we are trying to argue with the conclusion and argue that this new process could still be profitable, we need to point to some other expense that goes down, some revenue that goes up, or both.

All we're told so far is that the new process would greatly reduce the amount of sulfur dioxide released into the atmosphere. Can we turn that into a smaller expense or bigger revenue?

Maybe there's some environmental tax the plant has to pay based on sulfur emissions, and it would save so much money by releasing less sulfur into the atmosphere that it would more than offset the extra money being spent on the equipment / installation / processing.

label: Goal
body: Look for an answer pointing to the possibility that this new process could still be profitable, if it leads to a reduction in some expense or to an increase in revenue (that could offset the higher expenses of installing and running the new process).

label: Conclusion
body: We shouldn't do police lineups of suspects if the eyewitnesses can hear each other's assessments.

label: Evidence
body: There's little correlation between the accuracy of someone's account and the confidence they have in it. And certain factors can affect a witness's confidence without affecting their accuracy.

label: Evaluate
body:
This argument kind of makes a curious jump from the first two sentences to the last idea. What does "confidence and accuracy are two very different things" have to do with "don't let eyewitnesses hear each other at police lineups"?

Since the second sentence is talking about "certain factors" affecting the confidence of eyewitness accounts, I'm presuming that the author is worried that *hearing someone else's* assessment of a police lineup might influence the confidence of that person's own assessment of the police lineup.

I'm not really sure why the author cares if someone's confidence is impacted by hearing another witness's assessment; maybe she thinks that someone who *wouldn't* have sounded confident in their inaccurate pick will now be biased into sounding more confident about their inaccurate pick.

Or vice versa -- the person *would* have sounded confident in their accurate pick, but based on hearing other eyewitnesses, they become less confident about their accurate pick.

label: Goal
body: Find something that feels like it takes us from "witnesses can have their confidence affected by things, and confidence and accuracy are two separate things" and gets us closer to "we shouldn't allow witnesses to hear each other's answers to the police lineup.

label: Conclusion
body: Profit motive is not at fault for the lack of available housing that leads to homelessness.

label: Evidence
body: In general, if the market allows private investors to make a profit, housing will be provided. It's unrealistic to expect investors to take risks if they're not going to get benefit in return.

label: Evaluate
body:
The easiest way to locate the conclusion here is two-fold:
- any time we're reading an argument on Role or Main Conclusion, we should be priming our brain with a reminder that most of these conclusions are an opinionated first sentence or a rebuttal opinion.

The word “should” in the first sentence shows the opinion.

We verify that the first option is the Conclusion by using the Support Test: *why should we believe that profit motive isn't to blame for the lack of affordable housing?*

Because private investors would provide housing if the market allowed them to make a profit doing so, and it's unrealistic (unfair) to expect them to take risks with their property unless they get some benefit in return.

The question stem is asking us for the role of the intro to the first sentence, which was the Main Conclusion. What is the role of the into clause? It sounds like it *qualifies* the conclusion. It allows for the idea that profit motive might be at fault for other aspects of homelessness, but wants to say that profit motive isn't to blame for *lack of affordable housing*.

label: Goal
body: Look for something like, “identifies the specific part of homelessness that the profit motive shouldn't be blamed for”.

label: Ramona's Explicit Claims
body:
1. One of the primary values of college is mental growth from being exposed to wide range of ideas.

2. Too many students miss out on this growth because they pick a technical major that will make them more employable later.

3. Recent pressures to graduate as quickly as possible are worsening this trend.

label: Martin's Position on R's Claims
body:
1. He doesn't indicate what he considers *a primary* value of college, although in a much milder way he seems to agree it is good for students to be exposed to different stuff. He brings up "even tech majors are required to take some liberal arts classes" in a way that suggests, "tech majors are getting some of that (good) wide exposure you're talking about".

2. He somewhat disagrees with this claim by telling us that tech majors are required to take some liberal arts classes. It suggests "tech majors aren't missing out on exposure to a wide range of ideas".

3. He makes no comment on whether recent pressures are doing anything to change anything.

label: Evaluate
body:
As is typical on Agree questions, the 2nd speaker doesn't seem to explicitly agree with any of the 1st speakers claims. So we start looking for background assumptions or beliefs they both seem to share.

In this case, they both seem to recognize some students pick technical majors in order to improve their chances on the job market. Nontechnical majors (such as English major) might have a harder time getting a good job after graduation.

And they both seem to think it would be good for technical majors to be exposed to a wider range of ideas, since Martin defends the status quo by saying, "Don't worry, colleges do force technical majors to take some liberal arts classes."

label: Goal
body: I would have a hard time predicting a specific idea here. We just need to find an answer that feels like it can be supported by each paragraph, even if the support is somewhat gist-y, invisible, or innuendo.

label: Conclusion (this leads to)
body: It seems like there have been spacecraft sighted near Earth that are extraterrestrial in origin.

label: Evidence
body: When the British government gets requests from civilian researchers for information about sightings of UFOs made by military and intelligence agencies, those requests are brushed aside.

label: Evaluate
body:
This author seems to interpret the brushed-aside requests for information as evidence that the British government has something to hide.

Isn't it possible that we could Explain this Curious Fact with some alternate explanation?

Maybe there really is nothing interesting to share with civilians and the British government is just annoyed by the frequent requests. Maybe there is something to hide, but it isn't "we discovered aliens".

label: Goal
body:
Since this author is interpreting the meaning behind a Curious Fact, we can strengthen the argument by finding an answer that either
- **rule out** an alternate explanation for why requests for info are brushed aside
- **boost** the plausibility of the author's explanation, which is that the British government has sighted extraterrestrial spacecraft near Earth and is just unwilling to share info with the public about it.

label: Conclusion (hence)
body: The presence of professional athletes violates the spirit of fairness essential to the games.

label: Intermediate Conclusion
body: It is unlikely that amateurs will ever offer a serious challenge to professionals in Olympic events where they compete against each other.

label: Evidence (since)
body:
Amateurs rarely have the financial or material resources available to professionals.

The ancient Olympics did not include professional athletes.

label: Goal
body:
We don't really need to worry about Michiko's response. We just need a way to accept that amateurs rarely have the resources that professionals have, but argue that amateurs might still offer a serious challenge to professionals and thus it's still a fair competition.

Or we can argue that even though the amateurs won't offer a serious challenge to professionals competing in the same event, the presence of professionals doesn't violate the spirit of fairness.

label: Conclusion (therefore)
body: The current use of plastics actually does less harm to the environment nationwide than that of paper products.

label: Evidence
body:
The environmental damage done by given unit of plastic trash is roughly the same as the damage done by an equal unit of paper trash.

A national survey shows there is currently less plastic trash than paper trash.

label: Evaluate
body:
Usually, like 90% of the time, the conclusion on Main Conclusion questions is **earlier** than the evidence. But in this case it's the final claim, telegraphed with the indicator word "therefore".

The word 'therefore' is definitely signaling that the final sentence is **a** conclusion, but is it just an intermediate conclusion there to fool us?

No. The other two sentences aren't eligible to be conclusions, because they're both facts and there isn't any support offered for either one.

The last sentence is supported by combining the 1st and 2nd sentences.

P1: the harm caused by 1 unit of Plastic trash = 1 unit of Paper trash
P2: nationwide, fewer units of trash are plastic than paper
C: so, nationwide more harm is caused by plastic than paper

label: Goal
body:
We're just looking for the answer whose meaning best matches the final claim, "The current use of plastics actually does less harm to the environment nationwide than that of paper products."

They'll probably invert it or use synonyms, or both: "Paper trash, across the nation as a whole, presently does more harm than plastic trash."

label: Conclusion (thus)
body: To explore cost-effective ways to help people prone to mental disorders, we should increase funding for intervention research.

label: Evidence
body:
Limited research shows therapeutic intervention before the onset of mental disorders can mitigate major contributing factors.

A comprehensive research program is needed to verify and design specific health measures.

label: Evaluate
body:
This argument fits the Plan / Goal pattern.

GOAL: save money helping people prone to mental disorders
PLAN: increase funding for intervention research

We want to know the plan is feasible, that people will cooperate with it, that it won't backfire in some way that undermines the goal, or that it targets the main source of our current issue/problem.

To assess whether increasing funding achieves the goal, consider the differences between the recommendation-world and the current-world. What are the potential advantages and disadvantages?

The argument relies on the premise that therapeutic intervention can mitigate the contributing factors of mental disorders. Thus, if more funding leads to more effective interventions that are relatively inexpensive compared to treatment, then the recommendation would seem beneficial.

label: Goal
body: Let's find an answer that helps us argue that increasing funding for intervention research can lead to more cost-effective help for those prone to mental disorders.

label: Conclusion (conclude)
body: Violent crime is now out of control, and, to be safe from personal attack, one should not leave one's home except for absolute necessities.

label: Evidence
body: Unlike newspapers in the old days, today's newspapers and televised news programs are full of stories about murders and assaults in our city.

label: Evaluate
body:
This argument presents a Curious Difference (an asymmetric comparison) in the evidence. Does the author then assume some causal interpretationof that evidence? Yes!

CURIOUS FACT: How come today's papers and TV news are so much more full of murder/assault stories?

EXPLANATION: Because there's so much more murder and assault these days!

The argument observes that there's an increase in media coverage of violent crime and concludes that violent crime itself is out of control and the city's safety has drastically changed.

The argument assumes that because there's more media coverage of violent crime stories today compared to the past, the actual incidence of violent crime must have increased proportionally.

To weaken this conclusion, we want to consider alternative explanations for the increase in media coverage that do not involve an actual increase in violent crime.

label: Goal
body: Let's find an answer that suggests an alternate reason for the observed change in media content, rather than an actual increase in the amount or rate of violent crimes, or an answer that undermines the plausibility of the author's belief that violent crime has gotten much worse in recent times.

label: Conclusion
body:
The bill to say "using car phone while driving is illegal" should be adopted.
(i.e. it should be illegal to use your car phone while driving)

label: Evidence
body:
Using a car phone distracts the driver, which poses a threat to safe driving.

Meanwhile, if it were illegal to use your car phone while driving, people would be deterred from doing it.

label: Evaluate
body:
On Sufficient Assumption, if there are any New Terms in the conclusion, they need to be in the correct answer. The big one in this conclusion is **should be adopted**.

We need to a construct a rule that sounds like

**if ..... then ....**
the stuff we described in should adopt
the evidence about this bill the bill

So what do we know about this bill?

It would make using your car phone while driving illegal. That would deter people from using their car phone while driving. Using your car phone seriously distracts the driver, which poses a threat to safe driving.

Chunking that all together, this bill would "deter people from doing something that poses a threat to safe driving".

That seems to be the most common sense understanding of the author's rationale for why we should adopt the bill.

label: Goal
body:
So we just need to hear something like

"Any bill that would deter people from doing something that poses a threat to safe driving ... **should be adopted**".

label: Statements
body:
There's a Causal Chain type story presented:

1. buried in the soil all winter
2. churned up to surface when soil is plowed in the spring
3. gets brief exposure to sunlight
4. receptors get stimulated
5. receptors trigger germination

The final idea is a Conditional that says

if not 1 → then 3 doesn't trigger 4

Technically, it's "if there isn't prolonged darkness", then 3 doesn't trigger 4.
Being buried all winter is *one* way to get prolonged darkness, but there are presumably other ways (f.e. watching French films, I'd imagine)

For the last sentence, I would primarily remember it as a Causal Difference-Maker:
*the long exposure to darkness is what makes the receptors sensitive enough to get triggered by brief sunlight*

It's kinda like, "If you don't spend enough time in the dark, your eyes won't adjust to see faint things".

label: Goal
body:
The question stem is about pigweed seeds in the exact situation we just had described to us, so it seems like it's just asking us what we can best prove from the paragraph.

We'd expect them, when plowed, to receive brief sunlight, and if they do, and they've truly been exposed to prolonged darkness over the winter, then we expect them to germinate. Otherwise, we'd expect them not to germinate.

label: Information
body:
*causal* (capacity to neutralize, can increase/stimulate)

CC >> neutralize stomach acids
CC >> increase calcium >> impair kidneys
CC >> more gastrin >> more acid secretion

*recommendation*

Don't take more than 1/2 gram of CC.

label: Evaluate
body:
We know that the #1 focus of *Most Supported* questions is **cause/effect** relationships.

We had a couple causal chains here as well as that initial causal claim about neutralizing stomach acids.

In addition to the obvious overlap where all four claims are about calcium carbonate, we also have two other overlaps:

- multiple claims mention "half a gram" of CC
- multiple claims mention "stomach acids"

If we combine the idea that 1/2 a gram stimulates gastrin and acid secretion with the claim that we *shouldn't* take more than 1/2 a gram, we could probably derive some takeaway like, "Once you're above 1/2 a gram, the benefits of calcium carbonate are outweighed by the harm of stimulating gastrin / stomach acids."

If we combine the idea that CC can neutralize stomach acids with the claim that 1/2 a gram of it can stimulate stomach acid secretion, we'd get some weird idea like "depending on the dose of CC, it might lessen or increase stomach acids?"

label: Goal
body: Look for the most provable claim. It will likely reward us for noticing the cause/effect relationships given.

label: Conclusion (Thus)
body: There is no need to look for a further explanation (beyond using different methods) to explain why the university study and the governmental study had two different estimations of the how the average workweek has changed.

label: Evidence
body: The university study thinks the average workweek has gotten longer. The governmental study think it's gotten shorter. The two studies used different methods of investigation.

label: Evaluate
body:
How could we accept the evidence but argue that **there is** still some need to look further for an explanation of the difference?

There's a curious fact:
*how come the college study says up and the govt. study says down?*

There's a potential explanation:
*the college study and the govt study used different methods.*

The assumption is that different methods could lead to different measurements. Maybe we both measured the temperature of a lake, and I measured near the top and you measured near the bottom and that's why we got different measurements.

But maybe the reason we got different measurements is that we used the same method (measure near the top) but your instrument works fine and my thermometer was busted.

The author is overly confident in assuming that the difference between the college study's results and the govt study's results is that they employed different methods. Maybe something else was the reason.

label: Goal
body: Look for an answer complaining that the author is saying, "As soon as we have one possible explanation, we need look no further. We've cracked the case!" Meanwhile, the author is failing to rule out other possible explanations and failing to convince us that different methods led to the different results

label: Conclusion (concluded)
body: The native ringtail opossum population is endangered not by a scarcity of food, as had been previously thought, but by non-native predator species against which the opossum had not developed natural defenses.

label: Evidence
body:
A number of ringtail opossums that were orphaned and subsequently raised in captivity were monitored after being returned to the wild.

Seventy-five percent of those opossums were killed by foxes, a species not native to Australia.

label: Evaluate
body:
This conclusion has two claims, one of them causal and the other anti-causal. We can reverse engineer from the conclusion what causal mystery they are trying to solve.

*Curious Fact*: Why is the ringtail opossum population endangered?

*Author's Explanation*: It's due to non-native predator species, such as foxes, rather than a scarcity of food.

To strengthen this argument, we can either rule out an alternate explanation (such as food scarcity) or increase the plausibility that non-native predators are indeed a significant threat.

label: Goal
body: Let's find an answer that either undermines the food scarcity theory or strengthens the idea that non-native predators, like foxes, are a significant threat to the ringtail opossum.

label: Conclusion (implied)
body: An opera's stage directions are sometimes reflected in its music.

label: Intermediate Conclusion (Hence)
body: A change of scenery, which is a basic stage direction, can be reflected in the music, so other operatic stage directions can also be reflected.

label: Evidence
body: In some of Mozart's funny operas, there are squeaky violin noises that Mozart clearly meant to echo the sounds that are made while scenery is changing (set pieces are often on rolling wooden frames, so they might squeak ... big backdrops are lowered or raised from the rafters via rope and pully).

label: Evaluate / Goal
body: They're asking us about the Mozart premise, and asking what claim it was offered in support of. We could say that it was directly supporting the intermediate conclusion that "a change of scenery can be reflected in the music", or that it was ultimately supporting the author's rebuttal to the position in the first sentence; our author is saying "an opera's stage directions **are** sometimes reflected in its music".

label: Background
body: Marathons take at least 2 hours to run.

label: Surprising Claim
body: It's better to train for a marathon by doing 90 min runs each day than by doing runs of 2+ hours.

label: Evaluate / Goal
body:
*Given that ...* the race they're training for is 2+ hours

*Why is it that* ... optimal training is only 1.5 hrs?

Maybe you burn yourself out if you practice the full-length thing too much (hint-hint: LSAT students, don't take test after test as your form of practice)

label: Statements
body:
*causal* (can give rise to)

Gene >> new varieties of farm animals
splicing whose genetic makeup not
totally understood

*causal* (can introduce)

Gene >> new genes for whichever
splicing trait is desired

Gene >> new genes relate to making
splicing toxins or carcinogens

It might be hard to discover these new genes related to making toxins or carcinogens.

label: Evaluate
body:
We get a few causal reactions that can come from gene splicing. It sounds like we need to proceed very carefully with gene splicing. The appeal of it is that we can introduce new genes for whichever trait is desired (for example: a cow with a bigger than average milk supply).

But we're also introducing genes that govern production of toxins or carcinogens, and we can't easily detect when we've done so.

So we might successfully make a cow that has a super milk supply, but accidentally also cause the cow to have new toxins or carcinogens in its system.

label: Goal
body: Let's look for a safely worded answer that reinforces the uncertain outcomes of gene splicing.

label: Conclusion (This strongly suggests)
body: Humans hold onto acquired beliefs even in the absence of any credible evidence to support them.

label: Evidence
body: In a study, people read statements that caused them to form new beliefs. Later when they were told that the original statements were false, the subjects maintained those new beliefs.

label: Evaluate
body:
The author's conclusion is extremely broad, speaking for all of humankind, based only on a sample of people in a study (who may not be representative). So it's possible that a Weaken answer would attack this *Sampling* move, where the author reasons, "If it was true for *these* people, it must be true for people in general."

But we can also attack the notion that the conclusion was even true for the people in the study. Were they examples of "humans who continued to hold onto acquired beliefs even in the absence of any credible evidence to support those beliefs"?

If we want to fight that categorization, we either have to find a way to argue that the people in the study:
1. DIDN'T hold onto acquired beliefs, or
2. DID have credible evidence to support those beliefs (or both)

We can't argue that first line of objection, because the evidence explicitly says that most of them persisted in their newly acquired beliefs.

Okay, so is it possible that they *did* have credible evidence to support those beliefs? They probably didn't have credible evidence for those beliefs *prior* to the study, since we know it was reading the statements in the study that caused the people to form these new beliefs.

But in between the time they're reading these statements and forming beliefs and the time, "Later," when they're told the statements were false, could they have gotten credible evidence to support the belief?

Sure, I guess so. You could read a statement like, "Barack Obama plans to invest in a passenger spaceship to Mars" and then form the new belief, "Within the next 50 years, people will be able to take a passenger spaceship to Mars".

Later, we tell you that Obama statement we provided you with was false, but when you got home that day, you Googled "passenger spaceship to Mars" and found out that Elon Musk was actually planning to do this. Your newly acquired belief has some credible evidence, in addition to the statement we provided.

Thus, when we rescind the truth of those statements, it doesn't cause you to jettison that new belief you formed about "within 50 years, passenger travel to Mars". You are **not** an example of someone who is holding onto an acquired belief even though you have no credible evidence to support it.

label: Goal
body:
Look for an answer impugning the Sampling move, by saying that what happened in this study is not a generalizable "human" trait.

Or look for an answer exploiting the wiggle room with "Later, ...". Someone might have found credible evidence to support their new belief in the intervening period. Just because the original reason for the belief turns out to be false, that doesn't mean the belief is false (that's the *Unproven vs. Proven False* distinction).

label: Conclusion
body: Novelists cannot become great as long as they remain in academia.

label: Evidence
body: Schools hone observation and analysis (useful to novelists). But an intuitive grasp of everyday emotions can only be obtained through immersion in everyday life, which being an academic precludes.

label: Evaluate
body: The argument moves from "academics can't get the intuitive grasp of everyday emotions" to "academics can't become great novelists." That step only works if the intuitive grasp of everyday emotions is something *required* for greatness. If it were merely nice to have, the argument would not establish that academics are barred from greatness.

label: Goal
body: The right answer should fill the gap by establishing that an intuitive grasp of everyday emotions is necessary for greatness. Negation test: if it's not necessary, the argument falls apart.

label: Conclusion (thus)
body: There is reason to be skeptical about the conclusion drawn in the magazine's survey.

label: Evidence
body:
The survey question was biased: "Which do you think about more: politics or the joy of earning money?"

The readers of the magazine are a self-selecting sample.

label: Evaluate
body: The statistician is making a case that the results of the magazine's survey are not reliable because the survey question is biased, and the sample is self-selecting, making it unrepresentative. The argument is about questioning the validity and accuracy of the magazine’s conclusion that North Americans care more about finances than politics.

label: Goal
body: Let's get rid of four answers that strengthen the argument. We might see evidence that supports the idea that the survey results are not credible due to these issues. This could include evidence about the bias or unreliability of such surveys or additional data suggesting the survey's conclusion is incorrect.

label: Conclusion
body: The Antarctic ice sheet must temporarily have melted about three million years ago — i.e., Antarctica has not been continuously ice-covered for the last 14 million years.

label: Evidence
body: Three-million-year-old ocean-floor-sediment fossils were found beneath the central Antarctic ice sheet. Either severe climatic warming or volcanic activity could have melted the ice and submerged the continent (which is what would have allowed those fossils to settle into ocean-floor sediments at that location).

label: Evaluate
body: Identify the main conclusion vs. supporting claims. The "either-or" sentence about volcanic activity or climatic warming is offered as *support* for the melting-ice claim ("after all, ..."). The melting-ice claim is the main conclusion the author is arguing for; the previous-belief framing (14M years of ice) sets up the contrast.

label: Goal
body: Find the answer that captures the claim "the ice melted three million years ago" — i.e., the ice sheet has not been continuously present.

label: Conclusion (therefore)
body: About 3 million years ago, the Antarctic ice sheet must have temporarily melted.

label: Evidence (after all)
body:
We recently discovered 3 million year old fossils under the ice sheet covering central America (previously we had only found this type of fossils at the bottom of the ocean).

It's plausible that Antartica could have been submerged under water, since severe climate change or volcanic activity could have melted the ice sheet.

label: Evaluate
body:
Since the author is looking at a puzzling piece of archaeological evidence and speculating what it means / what it tells us, we can use our Curious Fact / Explanation mindset.

*Curious Fact ...* why are we finding these 3 million year old fossils under the ice sheet covering Antartica? (Previously we had only found these fossils in ocean floor sediments)

*Author's Explanation* ... At the time of these fossils, the ice sheet must have been melted, which would raise the water level high enough that Antarctica would be underwater, and so the ocean creature these fossils are from would have been swimming "over" Antarctica, it would have died and sunk to the "ocean floor", which would have been the top of Antarctica, and then later as the water refroze and the continent again rose above sea level, those fossils would be trapped under the ice sheet.

label: Evaluate
body:
Notice how many blanks we had to fill in for the author just to understand her Causal Story! (I'm not even 100% sure I'm interpreting her causal story correctly)

When **Flaw** intersects with Curious Fact / Explanation arguments, the most common type of correct answer just calls out the fact that the author is overconfidently assuming one possible causal interpretation of the evidence, when others exist.

When we simply say "the flaw is that the author *infers a cause from a mere correlation*" we're saying, "Sure, *maybe* this correlation indicates causality, but we can't be as sure as the author is thinking."

Our author's conclusion is way too strong --- the ice sheet **must** have temporarily melted?

There aren't any other explanations? If we assumed that Antarctica did not melt and was still above sea level, can we think of any other possible way that the fossils could have ended up where we found them?

Sure, maybe a bird snatched this fish out of the ocean and was flying over Antarctica and dropped it. Maybe a hurricane or an underwater volcano lifted this fish into the air and flung it over Antarctica. Maybe within the ice sheet there used to be underwater tunnels that this fish could have gone through. Maybe this fish was really an amphibian that was able to scoot across the ice.

label: Goal
body:
When we're doing Flaw and read one of these Curious Fact / Explanation arguments, then we're receptive to three different types of answers:
1. Complain that the author is overly confident in arriving at one *possible* explanation, where others may exist.

2. Suggest that the author may have failed to consider some alternative explanation.

3. Point out something implausible about the author's explanation.

label: Conclusion
body:
This theory may be wrong.
*rephrase:* The reason that women suffer more than men from Alzheimer's might not be because women live longer.

label: Evidence
body: A recent study shows that prescribing estrogen to post-menopausal women can prevent them from developing Alzheimer's. Meanwhile, men have a big supply of testosterone, which the body converts into estrogen.

label: Evaluate
body:
Whenever we do Main Conclusion (and Role) we read the paragraph differently, knowing that 90% of the time the conclusion is the very **first sentence**, or it's some **rebuttal** signified with a pivot word (like "but, yet, however"). In either case, 90% of the time the conclusion is **earlier** than the support, on these two question types.

As we read this first sentence, we ask ourselves whether it's eligible to be a conclusion -- does it sound like an opinion coming from the author? No, it sounds like fact.

But the second sentence contains an attribution (literally). It says "[some people] **attribute** this to women's longer life span". When we see any attribution in the early going of a Main Conclusion paragraph, then we anticipate that our author will probably be rebutting this position.

Sure enough, the second half of the 2nd sentence has one of those signature **pivot** words that we're listening for on Main Conclusion (**but**, yet, however).

So now we think, "Ah! This looks like the conclusion. The author is rebutting the idea that living longer is why women suffer more from Alzheimer's."

Does the author going to go on and try to convince us of that? Yes, because she builds up a case for an Alternate Explanation. This theory that "longer life span" is why women are more afflicted may be wrong, because the real reason that women are more afflicted could be that estrogen is the secret weapon against Alzheimer's and women have less estrogen than men in their old age.

label: Goal
body:
The conclusion was "this theory may be wrong", but since this claim includes a *pronoun* (**this** theory), we need to make sure we insert the specific language that pronoun is referring to:

*It may be wrong to think that longer life span is why women suffer more from Alzheimer's (lack of estrogen may be the real reason that women suffer more from Alzheimer's)*

label: P's Conclusion
body: Computers should be introduced in kindergarten, and computer languages should be required in high school.

label: P's Evidence
body: Children will need computer skills to deal with tomorrow's world.

label: Q's Conclusion
body: [Introducing computers in kindergarten and teaching computer languages in high school] would be pointless.

label: Q's Evidence
body: Tech advances so quickly that the computers / languages that K-12 would be working on would be obsolete by the time these kids became adults.

label: Evaluate
body:
*Given that ...* the computers / languages that kindergarteners and high schoolers would be working on would be obsolete by the time they reached adulthood

*How could we argue ...* it *wouldn't* be pointless -- there is still some value to introducing computers in kindergarten and introducing computer languages in high school?

Maybe using a computer mouse improves hand-eye coordination. Maybe even though the computers the kindergarteners are using will be obsolete, they will still be learning transferable computer **skills** or awareness (like copy / paste / typing / trash, etc.). Maybe some high schoolers will be able to get a part time job coding in the language they're learning (which would not be obsolete at the time they're learning it).

label: Goal
body: We just need some way of saying, "Even though the tech and language would be obsolete, there is still some point in doing this plan to teach computers more in K-12".

label: Conclusion
body:
It is inaccurate to say that a diet high in refined sugar cannot cause adult-onset diabetes.

*rephrase:* a diet high in refined sugar **can** cause adult onset diabetes.

label: Evidence (since)
body: A high-sugar diet can make a person overweight, and being overweight can predispose a person to adult-onset diabetes.

label: Evaluate
body:
The evidence presents a causal chain:
high sugar >> overweight >> adult diabetes

The author has thus shown a causal path from high sugar to adult diabetes.

label: Goal
body:
We want two premises that form a causal chain:
Prem: A can lead to B
Prem: B can lead to C

and then a Conc that connects them (or that denies that they can't be connected)
Conc: A can lead to C
or
Conc: It's wrong to say that A can't lead to C

label: Information
body:
Zoos function both as education and entertainment.

*Causal Chain*
Removing animals from natural habitats to stock the first zoos **reduced** the populations of those species, which then **endangered** the survival of some of those species.

*Contrast*
Modern zoos get most of their animals not by removing them from natural habitats but by breeding new animals in captivity (i.e. at the zoo).

*Causal Difference-Maker*
Maintaining breeding stocks for continued propagation of various species **makes possible** efforts to reestablish endangered species in the wild.

label: Evaluate / Goal
body: This is a pretty varied mix of claims with no obvious momentum for combining facts, so I would head to the answers. We're on guard against language that is Too Strong, makes an Unknown Comparison, goes Against the Passage, or just brings up something Out of Scope.

label: Conclusion
body: People ought to take into account a discipline's blemished origins when assessing the scientific value of that discipline.

label: Evidence
body: Chemistry, for example, had some of its landmark results discovered by alchemists, who believed in crazy stuff like superstitions and magic and helped develop early chemical theory.

label: Evaluate
body:
This is a weird argument Let's think about the Anti-Conclusion client we're representing:
*When we're assessing the value of a scientific discipline, such as chemistry, we do NOT need to take into account its blemished origins.*

Given that early chemical theory sounds like some superstitious / magical non-scientific rubbish, how can we argue that this is irrelevant (does not need to be taken into account) when it comes to assessing what value the discipline of chemistry has.

I guess we would argue that even though it has an embarrassing, scientifically dubious origin story, it's still a really successful scientific theory, and some of our fanciest inventions are based on the correct predictions of chemical reactions, according to the laws of chemistry.

label: Goal
body: Look for an answer saying "chemistry is an unrepresentative sample", or an answer saying that "the bad stuff about chemistry's early days doesn't have impact on how we assess the current value of chemistry".

label: Opponent's Conclusion
body: The projected benefits of drilling new oil wells are not worth the risk of environmental disaster.

label: Evidence
body: The oil currently extracted from these areas provides only 4 percent of our daily oil requirement, and the new wells would add just one-half of 1 percent.

label: Proponent's Reply
body: That's as dumb as saying we shouldn't allow new farms, since no single farm could feed the country even for a day.

label: Evaluate
body:
We need to respond to the proponent. The proponent counters with an analogy, arguing that just because a new oil well contributes a small amount to overall oil supply, it doesn’t mean it should be dismissed, just as new farms, which don't provide the entire food supply, shouldn't be prohibited.

To weaken the drilling proponent's reply, we should look for a flaw in this analogy or a reason why the analogy doesn't hold.

label: Goal
body: Let's find an answer that highlights a dissimilarity between offshore oil drilling and starting new farms, or shows why the proponent's analogy is misleading or flawed.

label: Information
body:
*conditionals* (if = suff, unless = if-not)

Slater --> McG app head
wins of Planning C

Polls are --> Slater
pretty accurate wins

*contrast*

Yerxes is more qualified to head the Planning C than McG is, since she's an architect who's been on Planning C for 15 years.

label: Evaluate
body:
Whenever we see conditionals on Must Be True / Most Supported, we have two immediate questions:

1. Can I chain this conditional up with any other conditionals?
2. Can I apply this conditional (usually via contrapositive) to a fact that was provided?

We had two conditionals (signified by If / Unless), so we should investigate #1. Do they have a common term that would allow them to chain?

Yes, they're both talking about Slater winning. So the chain looks like this:

Polls are → Slater → McG app head
pretty accurate wins of Planning C

We could look for a "first to last" inference like, "If the polls aren't grossly inaccurate, then McG will be appointed head of Planning Committee".

What about the middle sentence? Is that just filler or is it usable?

We know that "If McG is appointed head, then a more qualified person (Yerxes) didn't get the job".

label: Goal
body: Let's look for something rewarding us for chaining the conditionals together and possibly using the middle sentence, like, "If the polls aren't grossly inaccurate, then the person appointed head of the Planning Commission will not be the most qualified candidate".

label: Conclusion (implied)
body: Juicers are a waste of money; just eat the whole fruit or vegetable if you want the juice.

label: Evidence
body: There is no indication that juice separated from the pulp contains any special properties compared to when it is unseparated.

label: Evaluate
body:
GIVEN THAT juice separated from the pulp has no additional benefits over whole fruits and vegetables, HOW CAN WE DEFEND juicers?

To weaken this conclusion, we need to show a benefit or advantage of using a juicer that justifies the expense, regardless of the intrinsic properties of the juice.

label: Goal
body: Identify an answer choice that presents a reason why owning a juicer might still be beneficial or desirable, even though the juice isn't inherently more beneficial than the solid food from which it comes.

label: Conclusion
body: A program concerning scientific issues gives rise to no equal-time obligation.

label: Evidence
body: Equal-time obligations arise for programs on social issues because (1) social issues almost always have important political implications, and (2) social issues seldom can be definitely settled on the basis of available evidence.

label: Evaluate
body:
This is a weird argument, where the author is trying to explain why we DON'T need equal time for science stuff based on why we DO need equal time for social stuff.

If I said, "You don't have to worry about me acting weird around your sister. The other reason I acted weird around your friend was because I have a crush on your friend", that would imply a difference: *it implies that I don't have a crush on your sister*.

We're arguing that these two situations are different because there's some underlying difference that matters.

So this author is also *Assuming a Difference*, thinking that the reasons we need equal time for social issues **don't** apply to science issues.

label: Goal
body:
Let's look for an answer that helps us argue that we DO need an equal time obligation for science issues.

It'll probably attack the assumed differences, so it might say that science issues ALSO have important political implications or that science issues ALSO can rarely be settled on the basis of available evidence.

label: Conclusion (therefore)
body: To minimize crop damage, farmers should water crops only just enough to ensure that there is no substantial threat, from a lack of water, to either the growth or the yield of the crops.

label: Evidence
body:
The leaves of mildly drought-stressed plants are tougher in texture than the leaves of abundantly watered plants.

Insects prefer to feed on the leaves of abundantly watered plants.

label: Evaluate
body:
This argument fits the Recommendation pattern. Peter is suggesting a course of action (water plants minimally) to achieve a goal (minimize crop damage).

To assess this argument, we should consider whether following the recommendation would indeed lead to the intended outcome, with a net gain when compared to the current scenario of abundant watering.

The author thinks insects' preference for softer leaves means that mildly drought-stressed plants will experience less insect damage. The argument assumes that the benefit of reduced insect damage outweighs any negative effects of mild drought stress, so a strong point in favor would be evidence that supports minimizing insect damage as a priority.

label: Goal
body: Let's find an answer that highlights that the potential benefits of reduced insect feeding, thanks to watering crops less, outweigh the risks associated with slight drought stress.

label: Conclusion (this is evidence that)
body: The program to improve the morale of high school students has begun to take effect to reduce dropouts.

label: Evidence
body:
High school students who feel they are not succeeding in school often drop out.

Last year, the city's high school dropout rate was significantly lower than the previous year's rate.

label: Evaluate
body:
This argument falls into the Explain Curious Fact pattern because it identifies a change in situation (a *Curious Fact*) and provides a causal explanation.

*Curious Fact:* Why is the high school dropout rate is lower this year compared to last year?

*Author's Explanation:* The program to improve student morale has caused the reduction in dropout rates.

The argument assumes that the program is the main or only reason the dropout rate has decreased. To weaken this argument, we can look for alternative explanations for the reduced dropout rate, or we could challenge the plausibility that the morale program was indeed responsible for the change.

label: Goal
body: Let's find an answer that suggests an alternative reason for the reduced dropout rate, one that is unconnected to the morale improvement program.

label: Conclusion (must conclude)
body: Henry was widely watched before the move to Wednesday evenings because it followed That's Life and not because people especially liked it.

label: Evidence
body:
The television show Henry was not widely watched until it was scheduled for Tuesday evenings immediately after That's Life, the most popular show on television.

During the year after the move, Henry was consistently one of the ten most-watched shows on television.

Since Henry's recent move to Wednesday evenings, it has been watched by far fewer people.

label: Evaluate
body:
This argument follows the Explain Curious Fact pattern. The author is exploring why *Henry* was widely watched after being moved to a Tuesday slot following *That's Life*, but not before, and why its viewership declined with the move to Wednesday.

*Curious Fact*

Why was Henry widely watched originally only when following That's Life, and then less so after moving to Wednesdays?

*Author's Explanation*

The viewership of Henry was high because it followed the popular show That's Life, not because of its own merits.

To strengthen the argument, we need to enhance the author's explanation by showing that the association with That's Life was a significant factor in Henry's viewership, or rule out some alternate explanation for why Henry is struggling on Wednesday nights (maybe the show fundamentally changed for the worse, or it's competing against some other really popular show on Wed nights).

label: Goal
body: Let's find an answer that increases the plausibility that Henry's high viewership was due to its position immediately after That's Life, or that rules out an alternate explanation for the decline in popularity.

label: Conclusion (to conclude that)
body: VDTs cause headaches.

label: Evidence
body:
Researchers conducted a survey asking office workers to estimate their VDT usage and frequency of headaches over the past year.

The survey showed frequent VDT users suffered headaches more often than other office workers.

label: Evaluate
body:
This argument involves correlational reasoning: it observes a correlation between VDT usage and headache frequency and concludes a causal relationship.

CUROUS FACT: why is VDT usage correlated with headaches?
EXPLANATION: VDT usage causes headaches.

To undermine the argument, we should consider alternative explanations for the observed correlation or demonstrate that the VDT usage doesn't actually cause headaches.

A common pattern to consider is Reverse Causality, where possibly the headaches caused people to think they spent more time using VDTs, or Third Factor, where some other variable causes both headache frequency and VDT usage estimation.

label: Goal
body: Let's find an answer that suggests an alternative explanation for the correlation, such as a factor that could cause both increased VDT usage estimation and headaches or that undermines the plausibility of the idea that using VDT could cause headaches.

label: Advertisement
body: To assess whether female physicians are more sensitive than male physicians to the needs of female patients, we'll ask male and female physicians.

label: Flaw
body:
The people who are best equipped to judge "how sensitive was the doctor to the patient's needs" are the patients!

Meanwhile, this TV show is saying they're going to ask the doctors themselves to self-evaluate how sensitive they were to the patient's needs.

This would be like saying, "Who is better at making Mac & Cheese the way Sammy likes it, Mom or Dad? To get the answer, we'll ask both parents this question."

Shouldn't we ask Sammy? Isn't *he* the arbiter of who make the better Mac & Cheese?

label: Goal
body: Look for an answer saying that it's silly to be asking the physicians who was more sensitive to the patient's needs, when only the patient knows what their needs are and only the patient can tell us which doctor was more sensitive to their needs.

label: Conclusion
body:
The practice of using this therapy to treat the illness cannot be adequately supported by the claim that any therapy for treating the illness is more effective than no therapy at all.

*Rephrase: Effectiveness alone is not enough justification for using this therapy.*

label: Evidence
body: What must also be taken into account is that this therapy is expensive and complicated.

label: Evaluate
body: The conclusion appears in the first sentence and is clarified by the following sentence. This argument fits one of the common patterns, where the conclusion is found in the first sentence and then supported by additional claims or considerations. In this case, the consideration of expense and complication acts as support for the main claim—that effectiveness is not sufficient justification.

label: Goal
body: Find the best available meaning match for *effectiveness alone is not enough justification for using this therapy.*

label: Conclusion of Lydia's Argument
body: Squirrels are attracted to sugar in the sap of sugar maple trees.

label: Rebuttal by Galina
body: The sugar concentration in the sap is too low for squirrels to be attracted to it for sugar.

label: Evaluate
body: Because we're trying to counter someone's objection, we want to defend the idea that squirrels are trying to get sugar from this sap, while addressing the fact that there's so little sugar content that you'd have to drink tons of sap to get much sugar.

label: Goal
body: Given that you'd have to drink tons of sap to get much sugar, how can we still maintain that squirrels are interested in the sap for its sugar content.

label: Conclusion (So)
body: When people express dissatisfaction with their legislative representatives, we can be assured that these representatives are simply doing what they were elected to do.

label: Evidence
body:
Representatives were elected to compete for the government's scarce funds, which requires compromises.

Those compromises give off the impression of ineffectuality, which people express dissatisfaction about.

label: Evaluate
body:
The conclusion is saying that reps are doing what they are elected to do, and it builds that case by defining what they're elected to do (compete for funds), telling us what's required of that (make compromises), and telling us a by-product of that requirement (you look ineffectual to some people).

One of the most helpful observations we can make while reading this one is its *Conditional Conclusion*.

We don't have to symbolize it, but if we did, it would look like this:

*People expressing Reps doing*
*dissatisfaction with - - - - - - - - -> what they were*
*their legislative reps elected to do*

Fighting / Refuting / Rebutting / Contradicting a conditional means saying, "it's possible that the left side is true and the right side is false".

So if we want to fight this conclusion, we need to argue that "it's possible that people are expressing dissatisfaction with their legislative reps, but the reps are **not** doing what they are elected to do".

The evidence only deals with one specific complaint people make. People will complain that their reps are ineffectual, the author ably shows us how apparent ineffectuality is simply the manifestation of them doing something required of their job.

But what about other complaints? What people complain that "their representatives are making personally-enriching deals with foreign leaders"?

Is that the representatives simply doing what they were elected to do?

What if people complain that their representatives are making racist / sexist remarks? Is that the reps simply doing what they were elected to do?

label: Goal
body:
The correct answer will either lock us into the subject matter of the evidence, by giving some *Linking* idea like,

"Whenever people express dissatisfaction with their legislative reps, they are complaining about apparent ineffectuality"

or it will be a *Defender* answer ruling out one of these other reasons,

"People do **not** often complain about their legislative reps making personally-enriching deals with foreign leaders".

label: Conclusion
body: The one-sided facial rash was caused by prolonged contact with telephones.

label: Evidence
body: Several patients had a rash on just one side of their faces, and in each case the rash was on the same side as the patient's telephone use.

label: Evaluate
body:
When we're dealing with a "diagnosis / hypothesis / explanation", we know we're dealing with *Explain Curious Fact*.

CURIOUS FACT:
Why do these patients have a rash on one side of their face?

EXPLANATION:
It's caused by prolonged contact with telephones.

Whenever we're dealing with this template, we know we can strengthen by
1. **ruling out** an Alternate Explanation for the curious fact
2. making the Author's Explanation **more plausible**

label: Goal
body:
We need to get rid of four answers that strengthen. Typically, with EXCEPT questions, three of those four will do it one way and the other one will do it a different way.

So we might get three answers making the phone hypothesis more plausible and one answer ruling out the idea that the rash comes from something else (e.g. the side of their face that lays on their pillow at night).

The correct answer will either weaken or be irrelevant.

label: Conclusion
body: Speed limit reduction can reduce traffic fatalities.

label: Evidence
body: Since we lowered the speed limit a year ago, there have been way fewer highway fatalities than in the previous year.

label: Evaluate
body:
There is a **Curious Comparison** -- why are this year's traffic fatalities so much lower than last year's?

The author assumes a **Causal Explanation** for it -- the new speed limit caused the reduction in fatalities.

What are the two lenses through which we evaluate every Curious Fact / Explanation argument?
- is there some **Other Way** to explain the curious fact?
- how plausible is the **Author's Way**?

How else could one explain a reduction in traffic fatalities?
- fewer drivers
- better road conditions
- more policing, which deters aggressive driving
etc.

How would we assess the plausibility of the author's hypothesis?
- in nearby areas where the speed limit didn't change, were the fatalities still as high as last year?
- are people obeying the new speed limit? i.e., has average driving speed actually decreased?

label: Goal
body: Since this is Necessary Assumption, we would primarily look to **rule out** an **Alternate Explanation** for why fatalities are lower this year, but we'd also consider an answer that states something required for the author's story to be plausible (such as "drivers have started driving differently in response to the new speed limits").

label: Background
body:
After 1950, farmers greatly increased fertilizer use, which led to a doubling of farmland productivity by 1985.

Since 1985, they've been trying to increase productivity even more.

label: Surprising Claim
body: And yet, since 1985, they've started using less fertilizer.

label: Evaluate / Goal
body:
*Given that ...* fertilizer was so effective at increasing productivity from 1950-1985
*Why is it that* ... since 1985, the effort to increase productivity has involved using slightly *less* fertilizer than before?

It seems like the answer will have to say something like, "Fertilizer stopped working to increase productivity" or "Something else was even better / cheaper as a means of increasing productivity".

label: Conclusion (thus)
body: A young child's taste preferences can be affected by the type of food he or she has been exposed to.

label: Evidence
body: One-year-olds usually prefer sweet to salty. But if you feed a one-year-old salty food for a year, by age two they will choose salty over sweet.

label: Evaluate
body:
The "experiment" described does involve exposing 1-year olds to salty foods and does involve their taste preferences changing a year later.

So there doesn't seem to be a Missing Link in terms of what the evidence vs. conclusion are talking about. The only difference is that the conclusion is Causal (*affected by*) and the evidence is just Chronological (*a year later, something has changed*).

Just because the salty food exposure was followed by a change in preference doesn't mean that the salty food exposure *caused* the change in preference.

This is essentially an *Explain Curious Fact* argument where the author is wondering why the kid switches from preferring sweet to preferring salty and chalks it up to that year of exposure to salty foods.

For that type of argument, the author has to assume,
*there isn't some Alternate Explanation for the evidence*
*+ the Author's Explanation is plausible*

label: Goal
body: Look for an answer ruling out an alternate explanation for why the kids prefer salty foods a year later, or look for something required for the author's story (that exposure to salty changed their preference to salty) to be plausible.

label: Information
body:
Some organisms form from endosymbiosis, when organism X engulfs organism Y, and Y becomes a functioning part of X.

We found a weird nucleomorph within a plant called a chlorarachniophyte.

Two versions of a gene were found in the nucleomorph.

If the nucleomorph were not the remains of an engulfed organism's nucleus, then we would expect to find only a single version of the gene.

label: Evaluate
body:
Yikes! This is one of the harder Science-laden stimuli we'll see in LR.

We can get started, though, by focusing on what we typically read Inference paragraphs looking for:

1. overlapping information
2. conditional / causal / math-y wording

Nucleomorphs is mentioned a few times, and engulfed organism shows up twice. The final sentence gives us a conditional rule, signified by **if**.

Inference questions love to provide a conditional and then provide a fact that triggers the contrapositive of the rule, to test us on whether we're shrewd enough to infer the outcome of that contrapositive.

We were told
*N were not remains → find only a*
*of engulfed org's nuc single gene*

Contrapositive
*find more than → N is remains of an*
*a single gene engulfed org's nucleus*

They told us that they *did* find "**two** versions of the gene".

So according to this rule, that nucleomorph is the the remains of an engulfed organism's nucleus. Where in the paragraph did we hear about "engulfed organism" before?

The first sentence said that endosymbiosis is a process in which one organism engulfs another. So is that what's going on with this nucleomorph?

label: Goal
body:
While we can't be certain, it seems like we're being guided towards the suspicion that this nucleomorph (which we know from the final two ideas is the remains of an engulfed organism's nucleus) was involved in some endosymbiosis.

Endosymbiosis involves one organism engulfing another until the latter is part of the former. Since we know that this nucleomorph was part of an organism that was engulfed, and since we know that now it's hanging out inside a plant called a chlorarachniophyte, we could support the idea that the chlora plant engulfed the nucleomorph's former organism.

label: David's Explicit Claims
body:
1. Forbidding companies from hiring permanent replacements for striking employees would be very unfair.

2. Companies who aren't allowed to hire permanent replacements would have little leverage in negotiating with strikers.

label: Lin's Responses
body:
1. UNCLEAR - Lin doesn't quite come out and say "it's fair to forbid companies from hiring permanent replacements". We'd have to infer that belief purely from "No", and that's not a super sound basis.

2. DISAGREES - he says they *would* still have plenty of leverage.

label: Goal
body:
The question stem isn't actually *Agree / Disagree*, so it's not clear whether that's how we should be thinking or not. There is an explicit disagreement, so on the first pass let's look for an answer about whether or not companies who can't hire permanent replacements would have a decent amount of leverage with striking workers.

But since it's just a Most Supported question, we just want the most provable answer.

label: Conclusion (So)
body: Arguing that I violate the laws of conversation would be like arguing that some physicist violates the laws of physics.

label: Evidence
body: I have studied and thoroughly mastered the laws of logic.

label: Evaluate
body:
LSAC loves to clown this haughty logician, by having him (it's gotta be a him, right?) boast about his logic skillz in a Flaw question.

We accept that this logician has thoroughly studied the laws of logic.

How can we reject his conclusion and argue,
*saying that you sometimes violate the laws of logic is* **not** *like arguing that some physicists violate the laws of physics*

When we're evaluating **Comparisons** and we want to think of objections, most commonly we're just trying to think of some salient difference between the two things being compared.

In this case, is "a logician breaking the laws of logic" like "a physicist breaking the laws of physics"?

No, because it's *possible* to break the laws of logic. You can be illogical. You have the freedom to do so. (Cable news *exists* because of that premise.)

Meanwhile, it's not *possible* to break the laws of physics. They govern our universe always and everywhere.

label: Goal
body: Look for an answer complaining about the unfair comparison between being illogical vs. doing something physically impossible.

label: Conclusion (reveals that)
body: Television advertising does not significantly affect children's preferences for breakfast cereals.

label: Evidence
body: The study compared two groups of children: one that watched no television and another that watched average amounts. Both groups showed a strong preference for heavily advertised sugary cereals.

label: Evaluate
body:
This is an Anti-Causal argument, because the conclusion is saying that one thing **doesn't** affect another thing.

GIVEN THAT kids showed a preference for sweet cereals whether they watched TV or not, HOW CAN WE ARGUE THAT tv ads *do* significantly affect kids' preferences for cereal?

label: Goal
body: Identify an answer choice that provides evidence or a causal mechanism indicating that TV advertising does, in fact, influence cereal preferences, contrary to the conclusion.

label: Conclusion
body: The government-owned gas company is within its rights to sell stoves and other gas appliances.

label: Evidence
body: A private gas company would be allowed to sell such appliances without anyone seeing anything wrong with it.

label: Evaluate
