The **big 3** most common moves on Method are Analogies, Faulty Implications, and Alternatives.

This argument seems to involve an Analogy. The author is saying that diverting food crops to produce fuel is analogous to diverting food crops to feed livestock.

It also involves the idea of a **Counterexample**. The opposing claim is that diverting food crops for fuel would be an **unprecedented** move, and the author is trying to argue, "No, there's precedent. Something we're currently doing is essentially the same."

label: Goal
body: Let's pick any answer that is descriptively true. It will probably comment on the analogy or counterexample.

label: Conclusion (Hence)
body: The board's action [selling some works from its collection] will not detract from the quality of the museum's collection.

label: Evidence
body: The curator says that among the collection are several unsuccessful immature works by Renoir and Cezanne that should be sold because they're of inferior quality and so add nothing to the overall quality of the museum's collection.

label: Evaluate
body:
The key issue we're analyzing is whether or not selling some works from the collection would *detract from the quality of the collection*.
  The curator wants to sell some early works by Renoir / Cezanne that are "of inferior quality and **so** add nothing to the overall quality of the museum's collection".
  If they truly add *nothing* to the overall quality of the collection, then it seems logically valid to say getting rid of them doesn't detract from the quality of the collection. So we'd have to fight the argument further upstream.
  That "**so**" from the curator is technically a conclusion that the curator is deriving; we don't necessarily have to go along with that idea. We could try to argue that even though these early works by Renoir / Cezanne are 'unsuccessful', that doesn't mean that they add nothing to the quality of the collection (maybe part of the quality of the collection involves seeing how these eventual masters started off as unsuccessful painters).

label: Goal
body:
We might see a *Linking* answer like, "If it's a successful immature work or if it's of inferior quality, then it adds nothing to the overall quality of the collection".
  More likely, we'll see some *Defender* answer, ruling out a possible objection. If we negate the correct answer, it will weaken the argument, meaning it will help us argue that this action to sell some works from the collection **could** detract from the quality of the collection.

label: Conclusion (Hence)
body: The board's action (selling some works from the collection to raise refurbishing funds) will not detract from the quality of the museum's collection.

label: Intermediate Conclusion (so)
body: The early works of Renoir / Cezanne that would get sold add nothing to the overall quality of the museum's collection.

label: Evidence
body: They are unsuccessful immature works of inferior quality.

label: Evaluate
body:
*Given that ...* the works we'd be selling are immature / unsuccessful / inferior quality works by Renoir and Cezanne,
  *How could we still argue that ...* selling these works **would** detract from the museum's collection / they **do** add something?
  Hmm, how can early crappy paintings add value?
- Maybe they allow the museum to say "we have a complete set", which is something other museum's can't say.
- Maybe Renoir and Cezanne reference these early works or build off them in some way in their later works, so if we didn't have the crappy early ones it would be harder to fully grasp the significance of the later ones.

label: Goal
body: Find some answer that allows us to say "we shouldn't sell these early, crappy Renoir and Cezanne paintings — *for some reason*, they add value to the overall quality of the museum's collection."

label: Conclusion
body: No one should ever follow any recommendations by these so-called experts.

label: Evidence
body: Over the past 12 years, the guests on this TV show (most of whom are successful consultants for big portfolios) recommended a total of 2000 stocks which on average performed less successfully than the market as a whole for this 12 year period.

label: Main Conclusion
body: More of the government's budget should be redirected to preventing spills.

label: Goal
body: Find an answer that contradicts the stated facts plus the deforestation hypothesis — likely one that denies forests existed there.

label: Evaluate
body:
Since the 2000 stocks had a worse performance over the past 12 years than the market as a whole (f.e., *the market grew in value by 8%, but these stocks only averaged a 6% return on investment*), the author is assuming that these so-called experts don't know what they're doing and shouldn't be trusted.
  To fight the argument, we don't have to establish much. Since *their* conclusion is so extreme, our refutation is very weak.
  They say "**no one** should **ever** follow **any** recommendations by these experts".
  We'll prove them wrong by simply establishing that "there is at least one person, who sometimes should follow at least one of the recommendations that one of them made".
  For example, maybe the stock advice they offered would have been bad (read: worse than the market overall) for most people, but it still might have been appropriate advice for an 85 year old investor. So maybe *some people* should follow their recommendations.
  Or, maybe 1900 of the 2000 suggested stocks were poor recommendations, but 100 of them were great, so maybe people should follow *some* of their recommendations.
  Or, maybe most of the experts were bad, but some of them made predictions that performed better than the market. In that case, maybe people should follow the recommendations of *some* of the experts.

label: Goal
body:
Since this is Weaken EXCEPT, there are going to be four different ways to weaken the argument. Our author is being very polemical in saying "NEVER listen to A SINGLE THING that ANY of them say".
  Let's look for ways to accept the evidence that on the whole over the past 12 years this group's recommendations were not great, but find little openings where we can try to argue with the conclusion.
  We either will want the answer to make an excuse for the poor performance of the stocks over the course of the 12 years (so that we can still plausibly argue that they *are* experts), or we'll want to find ways to argue SOME of the experts are good / SOME of the recommendations are good / SOME people would have benefited from this advice / etc.

label: Given that ....
body: Self-pollinating primroses (SPP) have a higher average seed production than non-self-pollinating primroses (~SPP).

label: How can it be that
body: SPP's are rarer than ~SPP's?

label: Evaluate
body:
If you had the same number of self-pollinating and non-pollinating primroses, say 10 each, you get more seeds produced from the self-pollinating primroses.
  Since seeds are what give way to new primroses, we'd think "more seeds = more offspring".
  But the type of primrose that makes more seeds (the self-pollinating kind) is more rare.

label: Goal
body: We need some way of explaining why the self-pollinating primroses are more rare. Do they just grow in fewer habitats? Do they produce more seeds, but the seeds don't ever reach maturity?

label: Statements
body:
*conditionals*
  Cretaceous → southern half of certain region
period              covered entirely by water
  Dinosaur → lived on land
  Dinosaur → didn't live through entire M era
  *facts*
  The C Period was the last 75 million years of the M era, when dinosaurs were alive. Plesiosaurs were not dinosaurs; they were swimming reptiles that lived exclusively during C Period.

label: Evaluate
body:
Correct answers on Must Be False either contradict a conditional that was provided or contradict a Must Be True inference we can make from the info provided.
  The conditionals don't seem to chain together, but we can apply them to some of the facts we got.
  Plesio's lived exclusively during the C period, so we know that for the whole time Plesio's lived, the southern half of a certain region of earth was covered by water. We know that dinosaurs also lived during this time, but they lived only on land.
  So .... Plesio's and Dino's couldn't have hung out much. Plesio's were swimming; they may have been in the underwater part of earth. Dinos were strictly on land.
  How can we use the final sentence, that no Dino lived through the whole M era? I guess we could say that for the whole time dinos were alive, the southern half was covered by water.

label: Goal
body:
There are too many possible inferences here to home in on one likely contender, so we'll have to be flexible.
  We're not looking to pick an answer that represents a bad inference. We don't want **Can't Prove That**. We're looking to pick an answer we can actively contradict. We want **Can Disprove That**.

label: Statements
body:
Wisdom and intelligence are both desirable.
  Being intelligent does not imply that one is wise, nor does being wise imply one is intelligent. (i.e. some people are intelligent but not wise, and some people are wise but not intelligent)
  In my personal experience, people are either wise or intelligent but not both.

label: Evaluate
body:
On **Must Be False** questions, there are two very prevalent patterns to the correct answer:
  1. The correct answer contradicts a conditional we were given.
(if we were given that A → B, then the correct answer will talk about someone who is A but isn't B)
  2. The correct answer contradicts an available inference.
(if we were given that A → B and told that Pam is A, then we can infer Pam is B, and so the correct answer would say *Pam is not B*)
  However, here there were no conditionals and we can't really combine any of these facts to derive an inference. So our normal predictions don't seem to work.

label: Goal
body:
So, if we're going to contradict what we're told, it'll sound something like
- wisdom and intelligence are the same thing
- all who are wise are intelligent
- all who are intelligent are wise
- some people the essayist has met about both wise and intelligent

label: Conclusion
body:
I respectfully disagree.
  *rephrase:* The city should restore city hall.

label: Evidence
body:
The mayor opposes restoration on financial grounds, saying we cannot afford it.
  But the building is the last remaining link to the city's founding, and preserving a sense of municipal history is crucial to maintaining respect for the city government and its authority.

label: Evaluate
body:
The legislator is saying, "Since we gave you funds to hire 500, but you only hired around 400 investigators, we much conclude that you under-hired in order to prevent the full nature of the scandals from being investigated and revealed."
  And the regulator responds by saying, "No, we just couldn't find 500 people willing to accept the job, since the salary you guys were offering was so low".
  There is a bit of an *Explain Curious Fact* vibe going on here:
"How come only 400 investigators were hired?"
  The legislator's explanation is that the regulator was hoping to have fewer people investigating the scandal.
  The regulator's alternate explanation is that the salary for the investigators was too low to even find 500 willing applicants.

label: Economist's Evidence (since)
body: According to your rule, an income tax of 0% would generate the maximum revenue.

label: Evaluate
body:
When we see rebuttal arguments on Flaw, we look out for *Ad Hominem* and *Unproven vs. Proven False*, but neither of those seems to be happening here.
  However, does our author honestly grapple with the mayor's objection? The mayor said we can't afford to do the restoration because it would be expensive and the budget is very tight right now.
  Our author is introducing reasons we'd *want* to restore city hall: it connects us to our founding days and preserves a sense if local history that helps maintain respect for our city government.
  The mayor would probably say, "Sure, I totally agree. I also **want** to restore city hall. I just don't see how it's fiscally **possible**!"
  When the citizen says, "Can we really afford *not* to restore city hall", she's implying "we can't afford *not* to restore city hall".
  Does she mean, "It's not financially possible to not-restore city hall?" No, that's illogical. Not-restoring city hall costs no money. So how would that be financially impossible? She must be saying "we can't afford not to" in some non-monetary way. Like, "we can't accept what it would mean to not restore it".

label: Goal
body:
Since the mayor was saying "can't afford to restore" in the financial sense of budget limitations, whereas the citizen is responding to that by talking about a non-financial sense of "can't afford *not* to restore", we could accuse the author of committing the famous (but rare) Equivocation flaw.
  She is definitely shifting the meaning of a key term in the argument.

label: Conclusion
body: The city should restore city hall.

label: Evidence
body: The building is the last remaining link to the city's founding, and preserving municipal history is crucial.

label: Evaluate
body: The citizen's rebuttal — "Can we afford not to?" — uses "afford" in a different sense (historical loss) than the mayor's "Can we afford to?" (financial cost).

label: Goal
body: Identify that the citizen's argument trades on two senses of "afford."

label: Conclusion
body: The citizen wants the city to restore city hall, even though the mayor says it's too expensive right now.

label: Evidence
body: The citizen's reason: the building is a unique link to the city's past, and losing that link would damage civic identity.

label: Evaluate
body:
Watch the word "afford." When the mayor asks "Can we afford to?" he means: do we have the money? When the citizen flips it to "Can we afford not to?" she means something different: can we live with the historical loss?
  That is like a friend saying "I can't afford a new car right now" and you replying "But can you afford NOT to look successful at work?" Those two "affords" are about totally different things — money vs. image. Answering one doesn't answer the other.
  The citizen's rebuttal sounds clever, but it slides between two meanings of the same word. That's the flaw the question is pointing at.

label: Goal
body: The right answer will call out the slippery use of "afford" — an equivocation.

label: Conclusion (it follows)
body: Only those who appreciate these advances are computer scientists.

label: Evidence
body: Only computer scientists understand the architecture of the PCs, and only those who understand the architecture of PCs can appreciate the advances in tech made in the last deacde.

label: Goal
body:
The most common answers for Method are
  analogies / distinctionsfaulty implications / consequencesalternate explanationsdubious assumptions
  This response would qualify as an alternate explanation, so we could head to the answers with that prephrase, but ultimately we'll pick whatever answer matches.

label: Conclusion
body:
It's a myth that lefties are more prone to cause accidents than are righties.
(i.e. Lefties are not more prone to cause accidents than are righties)

label: Evidence
body: More household accidents are caused by righties than lefties.

label: Intermediate Conclusion
body: It makes little sense that the entire yearly budget for chemical spill prevention is less than the amount spent annually on one typical cleanup site.

label: Evaluate
body:
We're doing Flaw and we see some conditional indicators ("only" x 3), so we immediately get suspicious of illegal negations or reversals (the most famous of all flaws is the **Necessary vs. Sufficient** flaw in which an author performs an illegal negation or reversal).
  The word "only" (and "only if") almost always indicate the *necessary* condition on the Right of the arrow.
  So the first claim looks like this:
  *Understand      →   Computer*
  *architect of PC's        Scientists*
  The second claim looks like this:
  *Appreciate Last        →*  *Understand*
  *Decade's Advances      architect of PC's*
  Whenever we get multiple conditionals, we want to check whether they chain together. These do, since the second half of the 2nd one matches the first half of the 1st one. The whole chain looks like this:
  *Appreciate Last       →*  *Understand*     → *Computer*
*Decade's Advances     architect of PC's     Scientists*
  *The conclusion, meanwhile, is giving us this:*
  *Computer   →   Appreciate Last*
 *Scientists        Decade's Advances*
  So this is indeed an Illegal Reversal. Being a computer scientist is **required** in order to appreciate last decade's advances, but being a computer scientist isn't **sufficient** to prove that you appreciate last decade's advances.
  Conversationally, the original argument said, "Only ppl who get the architecture can appreciate the advances, and only computer scientists get the architecture", so it should be concluding, "Thus, only computer scientists can appreciate the advances".
  Meanwhile, this conclusion is saying "Only people who appreciate the advances are computer scientists".

label: Goal
body: Let's look for an answer describing the formal Necessary vs. Sufficient error, or one saying, "Yo, being a computer scientist is required to appreciate the advances in tech, but no one ever said that appreciating the advances in tech is required to be a computer scientist".

label: Conclusion (therefore)
body: Any person who wants to be as happy as possible would do well to consider not having a pet.

label: Evidence
body: Research shows, contrary to popular opinion, that, all other things being equal, most people who have pets are less happy than most people who do not.

label: Evaluate
body:
The argument presents a Curious Fact (an asymmetric comparison) in the evidence.
  *curious fact:*  Why are people with pets usually less happy than people without?
*explanation:*  The pet made them less happy.
  They usually weaken Explain Curious Fact arguments with an alternate explanation for the curious fact. Since this is a correlation, we can reflexively consider the two alternate explanations we always consider:
  *Reverse Causality* (maybe they here unhappy first, and the unhappiness caused them to get a pet to try to cheer themselves up)
  *Third Factor* (maybe both having pets and being less happy are connected to having children)

label: Goal
body: Find an answer that undermines the idea that the presence of pets decreases happiness, either by suggesting an alternate factor or making it less plausible that owning pets lowers your happiness.

label: Conclusion (so)
body: If we don't take steps to reestablish the spiny cactus population, the dwarf masked owl will not make its home on the Baja peninsula this winter.

label: Evidence
body: Last spring, a blight destroyed all the spiny cacti on the peninsula, and that's the only suitable nesting site for the dwarf masked owl on the peninsula.

label: Evaluate
body:
Because the conclusion is *Conditional*, we might want to think about a Missing Link assumption. The conclusion is trying to achieve this logic path:
  *Don't try to                                                     no owl*
  *reestablish  ------------------------>  on BP this*
*SC population                                                winter*
  The evidence told us that,
*no SC ----> no suitable*
                     *nesting site*
  So the argument the author is trying to make seems to be this:
  *Don't try to          no          no suitable        no owl*
  *reestablish  -->  SC  ---> nesting    --->  on BP this*
*SC population                      site                     winter*
  The author is assuming a link from 1 to 2, and assuming a link from 3 to 4:
  (1 to 2): "If we don't try to reestablish the spiny cactus population, then there won't be spiny cactus this winter". Maybe that's wrong. Maybe the spiny cactus will grow back on its own even if we don't take any steps to reestablish it.
  (3 to 4): "If there's no suitable nesting site for the owl, then the owl won't make it's home on the Baja peninsula." Maybe that's wrong. Maybe the owl will still make its home on the Baja peninsula this winter and just skip laying eggs. Or maybe it will make its home on the BP but find a suitable nesting site a short fly away.

label: Goal
body: Look for an answer establishing either of the missing links, or look for an answer defending against a potential objection (an objection should allow us to argue that even if we don't do anything to reestablish the spiny cactus population, the dwarf masked owl might still make its home on the Baja peninsula this winter).

label: Statements
body:
At night, the crows bunch up into a roost.
By day, they fan out, like radii shooting from the center of a circle, going out about 100km.
Then they come back again to roost.
After a few years, they find a new roosting spot.
It's not that far away from the old one (only about 8km).

label: Evaluate
body:
On Must Be False (or this more softly worded version), the correct answer usually contradicts a conditional idea or contradicts a possible inference.
  There weren't any conditionals in this paragraph, but there does seem to be a bit a math-y inference we can make by considering the two math facts:
- they fan out about 100km in all directions
- they move to a new roosting site within 8km of the previous one
  What can we say by combining those two facts?
  - their scavenging territory hasn't changed much.
- they've moved somewhere within their current scavenging territory
- their new roost was on some crow's old scavenging route

label: Goal
body:
Since we want something to essentially contradict our possible inferences, maybe we'll see a correct answer like
- their scavenging territory has completely changed
- their new roost is somewhere they had never been / in a place none of the flock had been before

label: Conclusion (Therefore)
body:
Implementing the consultant's recommendation would cause us to violate our own policy.
  *rephrase:  Reassigning staff so that all employees are doing both what they like and what they do well would cause us to exploit our workers.*

label: Evidence
body: According to the consultant, following her advice will "increase productivity by fully exploiting our available resources".

label: Evidence
body: If you sell the debt to the collection agency, you only walk away with 15% of what the debt was worth

label: Evaluate
body:
*Given that* ... the consultant says that her plan will allow us to fully exploit our resources,
*and that ...* the policy says "we will not exploit our workers",
  *How could we ague that ...* the consultant's plan will not violate the policy?
  Well, if the plan "will exploit" and the policy says to "not exploit", then we seem stuck. We would have to recognize that these are two different senses of the verb "to exploit".
  When we encourage a bigger basketball player to "exert more force / use your height advantage" over their smaller opponent, we're saying "Exploit your advantage!" This just means "utilize your advantage".
  This is a positive or at least neutral sense of "exploiting".
  But when we talk about "exploitation", that's a negative. That refers to an unfair sense of manipulation caused by some power imbalance. When school systems underpay teachers and don't provide them with enough resources, they know that teachers care so much for their students that they'll work extra hours at home and buy supplies for students out of their own paycheck. That's the negative sense of exploitation.
  The company's policy is pledging that the company won't make unfair use of its employees. It will avoid that negative sense of exploitation.
  The consultant is talking about fully utilizing one's resources. That's a good thing.

label: Goal
body: This is one of the ten famous flaws, Equivocation. This flaw rarely occurs, but it shows up a lot in incorrect answers. But in this case, it's actually happening. The argument is using the same term/concept (exploit) two times as those they are copies of each other, but in reality they're being used with two very different definitions.

label: Conclusion
body: Installing devices in cars that prevent them from exceeding the speed limit would prevent most accidents.

label: Evidence
body: Most accidents involve someone speeding over the limit. A lot drivers routinely speed on the highways.

label: Evaluate
body:
*Given That*
most accidents involve someone speeding,
  *How Could We Argue That*
installing these devices that don't let you speed would **not** prevent most accidents?
  When an author is recommending a Plan, we are always implicitly judging a Comparison between Current World and Plan World.
  In our Current World, people speed and most accidents involve someone speeding.
  In Plan World, nobody would be able to speed. But would these devices create new problems? What if it needs to download a firmware update and shuts me down on a railroad crossing?

label: Goal
body:
The author is assuming a few things:
- Preventing cars from going over the speed limit would prevent most accidents
- These new devices wouldn't end up *creating* new opportunities for accidents (like equipment malfunction, or Slow Rage, when drivers start driving aggressively because they hate the devices the government installed on their cars)

label: Statements
body:
We're reading for Conditional, Causal, Mathematical, or Pivot wording, and we see a lot of Causal wording here. We might want to be assembling a Causal Chain
  *In a recession*
   *less consumer spending (******causes******)*
       *many businesses lay off or close down*
             *workers can't find new job (******resulting***** *in)*
                    *increased number of jobless people*
  Meanwhile, what gets us out of the recession?
  *more consumer spending*
       *expanded business activity (******creates******)*
           *new need for more workers*
               *recovery from recession has begun*
  Finally, in the last sentence, we have a pivot, **But**.
  Most Supported paragraphs frequently provide correct answers that **Reconcile the Pivot**; i.e. the correct answer safely synthesizes the tension the Pivot idea creates with what came before.
  We learn that businesses usually are too scared of a post-recession economy and delay hiring additional workers as long as possible.

label: Evaluate
body: How does this last idea combine with what else we were told? It seems like as we're trying to get out of a recession, we might start spending money, creating more business activity, and creating the potential need to hire new workers, but businesspeople will drag their feet doing so, wanting to make sure they can be confident enough in the economy to invest in hiring new workers.

label: Goal
body: Look for an answer that rewards us for understanding any subset of those Causal Chains, or an answer that gives us a safely worded synthesis of the last idea with the previous sentence about recovery from a recession.

label: Curious Fact
body: How come there's so much ferrous material and so little carbon dioxide in this air bubble from Earth's last ice age?  (why does it seem like the air back then had more Iron and less CO2?)

label: Hypothesis
body: The ferrous material caused an increase in algae (such as diatoms), which suck up the CO2 from the atmosphere.

label: Evaluate
body:
Any time we're evaluating Curious Fact / Explanations, we have two pressure points to consider:
- is there some **other way** to explain the curious fact?
- how plausible is the **author's way** of explaining it?

label: Goal
body:
Since this is Weaken, we either want an answer to
- **provide** some other way to explain why the atmosphere had high ferrous and low CO2
or
- **make it less plausible** that ferrous material from the atmosphere led to more algae, which led to less CO2.

label: Background
body: Adults who work outside the home spend 100 mins less each week preparing dinner.

label: Surprising Claim
body: The meals eaten by adults who work outside vs. inside home don't differ much in terms of nutritional value, variety of menu, or number of courses.

label: Evaluate
body:
Given that the outside-workers have 100 mins less per week, how are they ending up with meals that are comparable in terms of nutrition, variety, complexity?
  - they eat out a couple times more (that accounts for the 100 fewer mins), so the meals they *do* prep at home are made with a similar amount of time
  - outside-workers have more money so they hire personal chefs to help with meals?
  - outside-workers happen to have access to other advantages that allow them to cook just as well with less time

label: Goal
body: We can never predict the exact storyline, so let's just look for any answer that gives us a way to account for that missing 100 mins and end up with comparable meals *eaten* at home.

label: Evidence (Because)
body: Commercial passenger airplanes equipped with this system provides information about the proximity of other airplanes and warns pilots to take evasive action when it thinks there could be a possible collision.

label: Goal
body: Find a statement they clearly disagree on; the obvious target is whether compliance is useful.

label: Evaluate
body:
If we're really on top of our game, we might notice the switch from **Absolute (Number) to Relative (Likelihood)**
  *Given that  ...* more household accidents are caused by righties than lefties,
*How could we still say that* ... lefties are *more prone* to cause accidents?
  One objection could be that the evidence only speaks to household accidents, whereas the conclusion deals with any type of accident.
  Another objection could be to say that there are way more right handed people than left handed people in the world (like an 8:1 ratio), so of course the *raw total* will be higher for right handed people.
  But that's not how you measure "prone" to something. That needs to be a per capita type stat, as in we need to express it as a percent of the population.
  If 13% of lefties have caused an accident whereas only 6% of righties have, then left handed people are more prone to accidents (even though most accidents will be caused by right handed people, since we're taking 6% of a number that's 8 times bigger than the number we're taking 13% of).
  When we lament that in America black people are more prone to by incarcerated for petty drug charges, it doesn't undermine that claim for someone to say, "Oh, yeah?  Well then how come there are *more* white people than black people who are incarcerated for drugs?"
  We need to measure it as a percent of the underlying population. If blacks make up 17% of the population but account for 30% of the drug arrests, whereas whites make up 45% of the population but account for 35% of the drug arrests, that would show that black people are more likely to be incarcerated for drugs.

label: Goal
body: Look for an answer complaining about the switch from household accidents to all accidents, complaining about the switch from evidence about raw numbers to a conclusion about propensity, or objecting that maybe it's unfair to compare the raw number given that there are like 8 times as many right handed people.

label: Conclusion
body: Archeo was probably a tree-dwelling creature.

label: Evidence
body: Archeo's claws had a curvature like that of modern tree-dwelling birds. This curvature enables modern birds to perch in trees. It would have enabled Archeo to perch on tree limbs.

label: Evaluate
body:
Our author is assuming that because this curvature *would* have enabled Archeo to perch on tree limbs that the curvature was used for this purpose.
  When author's look at a Curious Fact like "Why did Archeo have curved claws?" and then arrive at some Causal Interpretation like "they must have evolved them because they were a tree-dwelling creature", we can always weaken with an Alternate Explanation.
  Maybe they didn't live in trees and had curved claws for some other adaptive purpose (food gathering? defense against predators?)

label: Goal
body: Look for an answer that **rules out** an alternate explanation for the curved claws or an answer that provides something that would need to be true for it to be plausible that Archeo was a tree-dwelling creature.

label: Conclusion (Therefore)
body:
The rumors are most likely false.
*rephrased:* The Premier will probably not reshuffle the cabinet this week.

label: Evidence
body:
Every previous reshuffle was preceded by meetings w/ senior cabinet members.
  But no such meetings have occurred or are planned.

label: Evaluate
body:
The author is leaning heavily on historical precedent, as a way to estimate the likelihood of something occurring this week.
  The author thinks if "every previous X has been preceded by Y, and no Y has occurred or is planned to occur soon, then we can be skeptical that X is coming".
  The answer is essentially going to express that form, although it will probably try to condense the two premises into one thought.

label: Goal
body: Look for an answer like "if a certain condition has always preceded a given action, then the absence of that condition implies that the action is unlikely to occur".

label: Carl
body: When researchers operate on animals, they're legally required to fill out pain protocols, but not so for humans. If lawmakers cared as much about humans as they seem to about animals, there would be pain protocols for humans too.

label: Debbie
body: For humans, the doctor just tells you what pain you can expect, and then you get to decide whether or not you want to authorize the operation. So pain protocols aren't necessary for humans.

label: Evaluate
body: Debbie seems to be countering Carl's argument by saying, "Yo, Carl — there's a pretty significant difference between operating on animals and on humans. Humans speak *English*, for example. We need pain protocols for animals because they don't get to make informed consent for the pain we're planning to put them through. Humans can hear us describe the pain, think about it, and consent or not consent."

label: Goal
body: Look for something like, "Showing that two cases are not fair to compare", or "Raising a dissimilarity between two situations to explain why a behavior that is appropriate in one situation might not be appropriate in another situation."

label: Debbie's Conclusion (So)
body: Pain protocols are unnecessary for human beings.

label: Debbie's Evidence (consider this)
body: If a doctor wants to schedule surgery for a person, they can simply tell the patient what pain to expect and the patient can decide whether or not to undergo the operation.

label: Evaluate
body:
*Given that ...* doctors scheduling surgeries for humans can just inform the patient what pain to expect and get the patient's consent,
  *How could we still argue that ...* pain protocols can sometimes be necessary for humans? (i.e. how could there still be times when medical doctors/researchers would need to fill out a form about what pain would be involved in a procedure and what steps would be taken to minimize the pain?)
  Maybe we need to operate on kids or on adults who lack the mental clarity to understand the doctor as they explain what pain to expect.
  Maybe we want to do some procedures on unconscious people, so we can't wake them up to get their consent.
  Maybe insurance companies or medical researchers would benefit enough from having pain protocols filled out for every operation that it's worth requiring them sometimes.

label: Goal
body: We need to think of some situation where a human couldn't just listen to what pain should be expected and consent or decline the surgery, or a situation where even if they can consent, we still want the pain protocol for some other reason.

label: Conclusion
body: Companies with a lot of stale debt should not sell that debt to a collection agency; they should try to pursue collection of that outstanding debt on their own.

label: Evaluate
body:
Let's understand the math involved:  if your company is owed $100k in long overdue unpaid bills, you can try to pursue that debt on your own (investing money into tracking your debtors down and harassing them to pay you back).
  Or you can just offload that chore onto the collection agency. They'll pay $15k for the rights to those bills. (and then they're hoping that they'll be effective enough at harassing debtors that they collect a bigger share than 15% of the unpaid bills)
  If you were trying to make a counterargument and suggest a company *should* go with the collection agency, you'd probably say:
  *look, I know it's depressing to only get back $15k when people collectively owe you $100k, but $15k is better than nothing. Do you think you'd beat $15k if you pursued this debt on your own? And how much effort and resources would that take?'*

label: Goal
body:
Since the argument is comparing two options,
    *pursuing this debt on your own*
         *vs.*
   *selling it to collection agency for 15% its value*
  an author concluding Option 1 is the way to go must think that Option 1 achieves a better outcome. The outcome in Option 2 is 15% the value of the outstanding debt.
  So the author is assuming that a business would end up getting more than 15% of the value of the outstanding debt back if they pursued that debt on their own.

label: Conclusion (So)
body: There is no reason not to try my herb juice.

label: Evidence
body:
Customers report improved physical coordination.
  A few doctors say the herbs are potentially harmful, but doctors are always trying to maintain a monopoly over medical therapies.

label: Evaluate
body:
If we're the other lawyer and we're arguing,
*there IS some reason not to try this herb juice*
what would we say?
  We could start with, "wait — some doctors said the juice was harmful? That would be a reason not to try it."
  And the author will say, "Oh, don't listen to them. Doctors don't want herbs to work. They want a monopoly over medicine, so they talk smack about anything that isn't pharmaceuticals."
  We need a response. We could say, "Sure, I would imagine that Big Pharma is incentivized to diminish non-pharmaceutical treatments. Buuuut, we can't just ignore warnings that something is harmful. What if it's actually harmful? Do you have evidence it's safe?"
  If we know our Famous Flaws, then we'll hopefully recognize this as a classic Ad Hominem. That's when the author dismisses someone's view because they (1) have an ulterior motive / vested interest, or (2) have conflicting past behavior / hypocrisy.
  In this case, the author is trying to immediately disqualify what these doctors are saying just because doctors do have a financial interest in herbal treatments being bad ideas.

label: Goal
body:
Look for an answer addressing the Ad Hominem move where the author fails to seriously address the concerns of the doctors and wipes them away by pointing out their self-interest.
  Or, there might be an answer saying, "even if the herb juice isn't harmful, there still might be some *other* reason not to try it" (e.g. its awful taste, the farts it gives you, etc.)

label: Conclusion
body: Try the herb juice.

label: Evidence
body: Customers report benefits. Doctors say it's harmful, but doctors just want a monopoly.

label: Goal
body: Find the answer naming the ad hominem move — attacking the doctors instead of the claim.

label: Conclusion
body: The herbalist tells customers: there's no reason not to try the herb juice.

label: Evidence
body: Some customers report improved coordination. Doctors warn the herbs are potentially harmful, but the herbalist waves them off — they're just trying to protect their monopoly.

label: Evaluate
body: That's the flaw: instead of dealing with what the doctors actually claim (the herbs are potentially harmful), the herbalist goes after the doctors themselves, accusing them of bad motives. Even if the doctors have ulterior motives, that doesn't address whether their warning is correct. The herbs could still be harmful regardless of why doctors say so.

label: Goal
body: Find the answer that describes attacking the proponents instead of engaging with their claim.

label: Conclusion
body: An effective way to ensure the survival of that species would be periodically trim off the horns of all rhinoceroses.

label: Evidence
body:
Because of the lucrative but illegal trade in rhino horns, a certain rhino species has been hunted nearly to extinction.
  Trimming off the horns would eliminate the motivation for poaching.

label: Evaluate
body:
When an author is selling us on a Plan, we want to think about how we could potentially follow their Plan but **not** achieve their Goal. (This is akin to accepting their Evidence, but thinking about how the Conclusion could fail to be true).
  Can we think of a story in which we trim off the horns, it removes the motivation for poaching, but it *doesn't* ensure the survival of this rhino?
  One angle we could take relates to how overly strong "ensure" is. Even if we remove the threat of poaching. These rhino have already been hunted to near extinction. One bad storm or drought or wildfire or natural calamity could be enough to wipe out the remaining members. So the author is assuming that, "a natural catastrophe will **not** be enough to push this species into extinction".
  Similarly, maybe trimming horns would eliminate poaching, but maybe there are some rich brats who want to hunt rhinos with a crossbow from their private helicopters. Our author is assuming that "the survival of this species is not also threatened by people who hunt for sport".
  LSAT loves when Plans backfire, so is there any unintended consequence of trimming off horns that wouldn't be good?
  Maybe it would make it harder for the rhinos to find food. Maybe it would make it harder for them to defend themselves against attacks.  The author has to assume that trimming the horns doesn't hurt the rhinos survival chances in some way.

label: Goal
body:
Our author is assuming, "Trimming off the horns will **not** result in [something bad happening, which would imperil their survival]."
  She's also assuming, in idea math, that "if we eliminate motivation for poaching, we ensure the survival of the species".

label: Conclusion
body:
Anyone who insists that         *If you believe*
music videos are an art           X *is a type of Y*
form
  should also agree that            *you should believe*
TV gave rise to an art form        *Z gave rise to Y*

label: Evidence
body:
Television gave rise                 *Z gave rise to X*
to music videos.

label: Evidence
body: Some daisies are a kind of chrysanthemum, and there are some palatable chrysanthemums.

label: Evaluate
body:
Because of the repeating symbols (TV / art form / music videos all mentioned twice), it's felicitous to diagram this one.
  The conclusion is an *Implication of Belief* type claim:  "If you believe A, then you should believe B."
  What's the relationship between A and B?
  A:   X is a type of Y
B:   Z gave rise to Y
  What's the premise?
Z gave rise to X.
  The two beliefs being connected have an overlapping ingredient, Y.  (art form)
The premise connects the non-overlapping parts of the two beliefs (TV / music videos)

label: Goal
body:
Look for an argument that concludes a connection between two ideas, based on a premise that links together the non-overlapping ideas from the two beliefs.
  In a looser sense, we might just get an argument representing the same logic, but without the context of it being "if you believe A, you believe B".
  It might feel more like,
Conclusion:  If A is X, then A is Y.
Premise:  X is Y.

label: Conclusion (evidently)
body: Medieval Arab poets didn't have much interest in Aristotle's Poetics.

label: Evidence
body:
When people were interested in a Greek text (such as Aristotle or Homer), it got translated into Arabic.
  If a poet were interested in Aristotle's Poetics, then they would also be interested in reading Homer. But Homer was not translated into Arabic until long after medieval times.

label: Evaluate
body:
This is certainly a very confusing read. It would be especially hard if a student were unaware that Aristotle and Homer are examples of ancient Greek texts.
  The argument seems pretty reasonable. It's going off a couple conditionals:
  *Medieval Arabs    →  text gets translated*
*interested in text        from Greek to Arab*
  If Homer wasn't translated into Arab until modern times, then the conditional does tell us that Medieval Arabs weren't interested in Homer.
  But the author is trying to prove that the Medieval Arab poets weren't interested in Aristotle's Poetics, based on the fact that anyone who read that would have wanted to read Homer, since Aristotle refers to Homer.
  Where is a gap in this argument? It seems like maybe the Arab poets could have been interested in Aristotle's Poetics and just had some other way to understand the parts about Homer (maybe they wouldn't really need Homer's works translated in order to follow the references Aristotle makes).

label: Goal
body: Not really sure what to look for here. We want to be more convinced that medieval Arab poets weren't interested in Aristotle's Poetics. The answer might provide an additional reason for believing that, or it might help us squash out any doubt by making it seem even more like, "if you wanted to read Aristotle's Poetics, you absolutely would have wanted / needed a translation of Homer".

label: Conclusion
body: Sylvia's dinner party is certain to be a success!

label: Evidence
body:
Congenial   Plentiful Supply of  →   Successful
Guests     +  Good Food/Drink       Dinner Party
  Sylvia's got more than enough to eat and drink, and her guests are all congenial people.

label: Evaluate
body:
Man, Sylvia *needs* this party to go well, after the debacle last month with the fondue picnic.
  This argument seems very sound. If you have two things, you have a successful party. Sylvia has those two things:  congenial guests and plenty of food/drink.
  But, wait, didn't the argument say this argument had *flawed* reasoning? What are we missing?
  Have they clearly established Sylvia will have *congenial guests*?
- yes, *her guests are* *****all***** *congenial people*
  Have they clearly established that Sylvia has a plentiful supply of good things to eat and drink?
*-* it said*, she has more than enough to eat and drink*
  Oh, those rascals. It establishes she has a "plentiful supply of things to eat and drink", but the rule demands a plentiful supply of ****good**** things.

label: Goal
body: Look for an answer that has a conditional premise, and then some facts that *almost* trigger it (but some modifier or qualifier is missing from one of them), and then the conclusion will announce that the outcome is true.

label: Conclusion (clearly)
body: The prices settle the issue of whether the museum director deserved criticism for secretly selling some works by major artists.

label: Intermediate Conclusion (since)
body: The prices demonstrate that the critics were right to say that these were first rate pieces and that the director should be condemned for selling them.

label: Evidence
body: Only a few months after the director secretly sold these paintings, they sold in an otherwise stagnant art market at 2-3 times the price the director sold them for.

label: Evaluate
body:
The essence of this argument boils down to this connection:
  *pieces sold for 2-3 times    →   pieces were*
*what director got for them        first-rate*
  I don't really know how the bigger re-sale price indicates that the pieces were first-rate. After all, I might sell you a really crappy bike I have for $5. If a couple months later you sell that same bike to someone else for $10 or $15 (2-3 times as much), does that prove it's a first-rate bike?
  No, it just proves that the original price you paid me was probably less than I could have gotten for it.
  The author is interpreting a Curious Fact (*why did the paintings re-sell at 2-3 times the value of what the director sold them for?)* with one possible interpretation (*these were first-rate pieces by major artists, thus highly coveted, thus commanding a high sales price even in a stagnant art market)*.
  We would push back with alternative explanations, such as the one I just mentioned:
- maybe they are inferior works, but the director just sold them for 1/2 to 1/3 of what she could have sold them for
  - maybe they are inferior works, but the person buying them does not have a good grasp on what the right value of the work is, so they overpaid 2-3 times what they should have simply because they recognized the name of the major artist who painted it

label: Goal
body: Let's look for an answer that allows us to explain the higher re-sale price while still arguing the Anti-Conclusion, that these were ****not**** first-rate pieces and thus the museum director doesn't deserve condemnation.

label: Statements
body:
The US is way worse than Sweden and Canada when it comes to workplace safety.
  However, all three countries have found that joint labor-mgmt committees on workplace safety greatly reduce workplace injuries.
  In the US, only a few companies have these committees (these companies voluntarily created them). In Sweden and some of Canada, these committees are required for any company medium sized or bigger.

label: Evidence
body:
Prevention is far more effective than cleanup.
The government has spent a ton already to clean spill sites, not even one of them is completely cleaned, and the amount spilled each year surpasses the amount cleaned.

label: Evaluate
body:
The information identifies a ****Causal Difference-Maker:****
these labor-mgmt safety committees cause safer workplaces.
  The information describes two ****differences****:
US has fewer of these committees than Sweden / Canada do.
US ranks way behind Sweden / Canada in workplace safety.
  Inference questions love to ****use a difference to explain a difference****.
  It seems like one of the reasons the US ranks way behind Sweden / Canada is because these safety-improving committees are less common in the US than in the other two countries.

label: Goal
body: Look for a safely worded answer that reinforces this idea that having fewer joint labor-mgmt committees in the US is a reason why the US ranks lower in workplace safety.

label: Trisha's Comments
body:
1. Today's family is declining in its ability to carry out its functions of child-rearing and providing stability for adult life.
  2. There must be a return to the traditional values of commitment and responsibility

label: Jerod's Responses (if any)
body:
1. Does Jerod argue that, "Today's family is **not** declining in its ability to carry out its functions of child-rearing" or "**not** declining in its ability to provide stability for adult life"?
  He seems to acknowledge that today's family might be declining in its ability to provide stability. He doesn't seem to address whether it's declining in its ability to carry out child-rearing functions.
  2. Does Jerod argue that, "There **does not** need to be a return to the traditional values of commitment and responsibility"?
  He does. He says "we ought to leave what is good enough alone". Most people don't find today's families to be that bad. Criticisms are exaggerated and potentially harmful.

label: Evaluate
body: We could say they're disagreeing over whether "there must be a return to the traditional values of commitment and responsibility" or more simply over whether "something must be done about today's family".

label: Goal
body:
The question stem has already queued up the beginning of the answer choice. If we have to start this answer with "the institution of the family", then we should look for something like,
  *they're disagreeing over whether*
the institution of the family "needs to be altered / addressed in some way"

label: Conclusion (hence)
body:
The recommendation cannot be satisfied.
  Since this conclusion has referential language, we need to identify what concept it refers back to. The recommendation in question is that regions where Caronian-speakers live be granted autonomy as an independent nation in which they would be a majority.

label: Evidence
body: Caronian-speakers live in several, widely scattered areas that cannot be united within a single continuous boundary while at the same time allowing Caronian-speakers to be the majority population.

label: Evaluate
body:
The conclusion is about an "independent nation" while the evidence is about areas united within a single continuous boundary. This sets us up for a potential missing link assumption: independent nations have to be united within a single continuous geographic boundary.
  If you didn't spot that and this seems like a pretty decent argument to you, it's a great opportunity to deploy the Anti-conclusion technique to generate an objection. How could the evidence be true and the conclusion be false? Well, what if we didn't need a single continuous boundary in order to get an independent nation?

label: Anticipate
body: Predict an answer that addresses the Assumption or Objection above, but be open to other possibilities too because Necessary Assumption questions can be unpredictable.

label: Conclusion
body: The welfare state cannot be successfully implemented.

label: Intermediate Conclusion
body: It rests on the seemingly false assumption that human beings are unselfish.

label: Evidence
body: The welfare state is only feasible if wage earners are prepared to have the money they earn used to help others in greater need, which requires an unselfish attitude. But people innately seek their own well-being, especially if the interest of someone else threatens it.

label: Evaluate
body:
Whenever we do Main Conclusion (and to a lesser extent Role) questions, we prime our brains before reading the paragraph with a crucial reminder:
  - *listen for the Conclusion to arrive* *****before***** *the Evidence!*
  In the vast majority of Main Conclusion questions, the paragraph ends with supporting ideas, not with the main conclusion. The two most common places to find the conclusion on a Main Conclusion question?
  1. some sort of Rebuttal type claim (e.g. "however, they're wrong")
2. the first sentence
  Because the first sentence sounds somewhat like an opinion --- *bah, you'll never be able to pull off the welfare state! --* and because that opinion isn't being attributed to someone else, we start to think, "Hey, I think this *is* the conclusion! In order to confirm that, let me ask myself '*Why should I believe this claim*' and see if what follows seems like support."
  If we read the first sentence, and then ask ourselves "Why should I believe that the welfare state cannot be successfully implemented?", everything that follows sounds like the author's defense of that position.

label: Goal
body:
We want to find a match for the first sentence. It's unclear to me whether they'll just give us the entire first sentence (including the *because* clause that is technically support for the first clause), or whether they'll just give us the first clause, which leads up to the *because*.
  I'm fine with either. They aren't going to offer us both.

label: Information
body:
*Comparison*
early pencil lead: solid graphite (mined in Cumberland)
modern pencil lead: powdered graphite
  *Causality (result of / thus)*
Research sponsored              modern methods
by govt of France in 1790 >>  of powdered graph
  France at war        no access to
with Britain       >>    Cumberland graphite

label: Evaluate
body:
The second sentence contains two causal ideas that could potentially chain together.
  1. France and Britain go to war
2. Thus, the French can't make solid graphite pencils using Cumberland's graphite.
3. Thus, the French government sponsors research into an alternative and comes up with powdered graphite.
4. Those methods are used today.
  So we could potentially say that modern methods of manufacturing pencil leads trace back to the 1790s, when France and Britain were at war.

label: Goal
body: Look for whatever answer we can best support.

label: Conclusion
body: Passengers are safer on airplanes equipped with the system than on comparable airplanes not so equipped, even though the system frequently warns pilots to evade phantom airplanes.

label: Evaluate
body:
The conclusion is making a **Comparison** claim, that passengers will be *safer* flying on a plane that has the system than on a plane that doesn't. So we need to consider all senses in which having this radar system on a plane could make it more safe / less safe.
  The author is assuming that the plane will be more safe, because she assumes that this system will allow planes to evade collisions that they wouldn't evade if they didn't have the system. So the author has to assume things like
  - the warning will be given in time that the pilot still has a chance to make evasive action safely
- the pilot (or someone who can notify the pilot) will notice the radar system when it goes off
- the pilot will react to these warnings with evasive actions, rather than just ignoring them (especially given that we're told the system frequently gives a warning even when there's no danger around)
  This argument resembles those in which we're evaluating a Plan to achieve a Goal. The common issues there are
- feasibility (**Skill**)
- incentive / motivation / cooperation  (**Will**)
- possible backfire
  The Plan is to have this radar system warn us of potential collisions. The Goal is to be safer (to avoid collisions). We have to worry about whether the Plan could feasibly work
(will it warn us in time? will we notice its warning?) as well as whether the people involved can be counted on to behave as we're expecting (will pilots be motivated / willing / incentivized to listen to these warnings?).
  Lastly, we should consider potential ways the Plan could backfire. How could having this radar system make a plane **less** safe? Maybe it beeps a lot and that distracts the pilot. Maybe the radar it sends out makes it harder for the pilot to communicate with airports. Maybe the frequent "false alarm" warnings will create some dangerous flying moves.

label: Goal
body: It's hard to predict specific answers with a Plan / Goal type comparison. We're looking for an answer that sounds like something that would need to be true for the Plan to have a hope of working, or something that is **ruling out** an objection to this argument (i.e. ruling out a potential problem with how this device is intended to work).

label: Conclusion
body: Passengers are safer on airplanes equipped with the collision-avoidance radar system than on comparable airplanes not so equipped.

label: Evidence (because)
body: Collision-avoidance radar systems provide pilots with information about the proximity of other airplanes and warn pilots to take evasive action when a possible collision is indicated.

label: Evaluate
body:
This argument asserts that despite frequent false alarms (phantom warnings), airplanes with the system are safer than those without it. The conclusion relies on the assumption that these false warnings do not negate the safety benefits of having the system.
  There are a couple of ways to strengthen this argument: we can increase the plausibility that the system's benefits (real collision avoidance) outweigh its downsides (phantom warnings) or show that even when responding to false alarms, the system doesn't pose additional risks.
  We could think of this as a Plan / Goal type conversation:
GOAL: make planes safer, by avoiding collisions
PLAN:  system warns pilots take evasive action when a collision is imminent
  The Plan assumes that pilots will hear these warnings, be willing to take evasive action in response to the warning, and be able to safely take evasive action.

label: Goal
body: We want an answer that supports the claim that airplanes with the collision-avoidance radar system are indeed safer, regardless of the frequent phantom warnings.

label: Conclusion
body: People who want to reduce their risk of cancer should reduce their fat intake.

label: Evidence
body: The higher the average fat intake of a country, the higher the incidence of cancer (the lower the intake, the lower the risk).

label: Evaluate
body:
Since the author is looking at a **Curious Comparison** in the evidence and then making a causal assumption to get to his conclusion, we can use our Curious Fact / Explanation mindset.
  *Curious Fact ...* why is there a correlation between fat intake and cancer risk?
*Author's Explanation ....* the fat intake is causing the increased cancer risk.
  Any time we formulate a sentence as "if you want X, you should do Y", we're implying a causal relationship that doing Y leads to X.
  The two pressure points for a causal argument are
- Alternate Explanations for the curious fact
- the plausibility of the Author's Explanation
  Why **else** could it be that fat intake and cancer risk are correlated? With correlations, we always want to consider *Reverse Causality*  (maybe the cancer comes first, and then people end up eating a lot of fat as a result of the cancer diagnosis) or *Third Factor* (maybe the cancer and the fat are both symptoms of some underlying cause, like cigarette smoking. Perhaps smoking cigarettes leads to higher rates of cancer but also causes food cravings for fatty foods).

label: Goal
body: Since this is Weaken, we would primarily look for an answer that provides an Alternate Explanation for why fat and cancer are correlated, but secondarily look for answers that try to undermine the plausibility that fat intake could cause elevated cancer risk.

label: Plan
body: Create a panel of psychologists that can review TV shows before they air and rate their level of violence. High violence would be signified by 4 guns; low violence listed with 1 gun.

label: Goal
body: Parents could be warned about the level of violence in any given program.

label: Evaluate
body:
When we're objecting to Plans, rather than arguments, we're treating the Plan like the Evidence (accept it) and treating the Goal like the Conclusion (fight it).
  So how could we enact this rating system, but parents are **not** forewarned about the level of violence in any given program?
  - maybe the parents never check this listing (it's in the newspaper?!)
- maybe the psychologists have a skewed sense of violence and rank shows very differently from how parents would perceive them
- maybe some shows air live, so the panel wouldn't be able to pre-screen them and rank them
- maybe the silly rating system of "Low violence = 1 gun" would send the wrong message — i.e. parents would assume there's violence in that show (since it's rated with a gun), when that's really meant to mean violence-free

label: Goal
body: Since this is Necessary Assumption, we're looking for an answer that asserts something that must be true for this plan to work, or (probably more likely) an answer that **rules out** a potential objection to this plan that would suggest it won't achieve its goal.

label: Given that ...
body: Ancient kangaroos had grasping tails and long opposable thumbs, which are good for tree-dwelling

label: How can it be that ...
body: Modern tree-dwelling kangaroos now lack these traits?

label: Goal
body:
Essentially we need a story where the ancestor of the modern day tree-dwelling kangaroos could lose some traits that seem like they would be adaptive (provide some benefit to the modern tree-kangaroos' environment).
  Maybe there was an in-between stage when the kangaroos weren't in trees at all, and thus these tree-friendly traits eventually evaporated from the gene pool.

label: Conclusion
body: There is no reason not to grant 17 year old citizens all the privileges of adulthood.

label: Evidence
body:
Society is obligated to grant all the privileges of adulthood upon its members, once they are mature enough to accept the corresponding responsibilities.
  (so this author is assuming that **17 year olds** are mature enough to accept the responsibilities of adulthood?)
  Science has established that physiological development is completed in most people by age 17. This maturing process has been completed by most 17 year olds.

label: Evaluate
body:
Wait, wait, wait.  According to the conditional rule in the first sentence, we need to establish that 17 year olds are "mature enough to accept the corresponding responsibilities that come with the privileges of adulthood".
  And the author is just saying that most 17 year olds have completed the process of physiological development.
  Those are miles apart.

label: Goal
body:
The author is abusing two different sense of the word "mature enough".
  "Mature enough" in the principle is referring to one's intellectual and moral capacities. Are you responsible, wise, smart enough to handle adulthood.
  The "maturing process" the author refers to in the final sentence is just talking about going through puberty physically.
  This is a famous flaw called **Equivocation**, when you use the same term or concept in two very different ways.

label: Conclusion (Therefore)
body: Every new play that ran for more than three months last year was a commercial success.

label: Evidence
body:
Every new play that runs for more than three months is either a commercial or a critical success.
  Last year, all new plays that were critical successes were also commercial successes.

label: Evaluate
body:
Since this argument has some conditional logic (every, all, every) and repeating language in it, we should probably look at the algebraic recipe of the logic. We know that all three ingredients are conditionals, so any answer that doesn't have three conditional ingredients should be wrong.
  P1:  Every new play that runs     A + X → B or C
    3+ mos is comm or crit succ
  P2:  All new plays that were        A + C → B
     crit succ were comm succ
  C:  Every new play that runs    A + X → B
          3+ mos is comm succ
  The algebra here is tricky since all three claims are about "new plays", but a specific subset of "new plays".
  One premise and the conclusion are about "New plays that run for 3+ months". The other premise is about "New plays that are critical successes".
  It might be easier to think about this one conversationally.
  P1:  If you're A, then you're B or C
P2:  But if you're C, then you're also B.
  C:  So if you're A, you're destined to be B.

label: Goal
body: Look for a conditional premise that offers us some "B or C" in the outcome. Then look for a second conditional premise that makes it seem like "one of those two options implies the other". Thus, you're bound to be the implied option either way.

label: Conclusion
body: I have been incorrectly criticized for having made my decision on the power plant issue prematurely.  *rephrased:  I did not make my decision on the power plant issue prematurely*

label: Evidence
body:
I based my decision on the report prepared by the neighborhood association.
  Sure I haven't studied it thoroughly, but I'm sure its info is accurate and I agreed with the neighborhood association's recommendation in the past, when it came to jail relocation.

label: Evaluate
body:
Since this is (the rare) Flaw EXCEPT, we will be finding four answers that we think seem like legit objections to this author.
  On a first read, these are what jump out:
- how can you be sure the info is accurate if you haven't studied it thoroughly?
- just because you agreed with this association in the past, on a different issue, doesn't mean you will agree with them again on this issue.
- how do we know that even if you had read the association's report in detail that this would have sufficed in terms of research on the power plant? should you have also considered other sources of information or opinion on the subject?

label: Goal
body: Get rid of the four answers that seem like flaws. They either call out a sketchy move the author made, or they help us to argue that the commissioner made the decision prematurely.

label: Given that ...
body: The order of the task made a difference for more experienced readers.

label: How can we explain that ...
body: For the beginning readers, the order of the task made no difference (they always made fewer errors when reading the paragraph than when reading the list)?

label: Evaluate / Goal
body:
We seem to want to address two different distinctions:
  - why are beginning readers more likely to make pronunciation errors when reading a **list** than when reading a **paragraph**?
  - how come this reason didn't also apply to the **more experienced** readers?

label: Statements
body:
Violence is an extreme form of aggression.
  Violence ≠ the self-expression sufficient for survival under normal conditions.
  *conditional* (only = Right side, necessary)
  Humans sometimes       conditioned by
 react to unpleasant  →  culture to react
stimuli with violence       this way

label: Evaluate
body:
There are going to be four Must Be True answers that we will eliminate; we probably won't be able to predict all of those, but we can think about what Must Be True inferences we can make to get a head start.
  There *is* a conditional provided. Does anything trigger it, or trigger its contrapositive? Not really.
  We could synthesize claims where we see *Overlapping Info*. The first and second sentence both involve the term *violence,* so we could synthesize them by saying something like,
  *Cultures sometimes condition people to react in a way that is an extreme form of aggression*
  or
  *Cultures sometimes condition people to react in a way that is different from the self-expression sufficient for survival under normal conditions.*

label: Goal
body: We need to find four answers we can derive from the paragraph. The correct answer might be something that goes against the passage, but more than likely it will just be something that isn't 100% derivable from the passage.

label: Conclusion
body:
What Martha's friend told her must be incorrect.
  *rephrase:*  There are some palatable daisies.

label: Evaluate
body:
Our first job was to translate the Rebuttal conclusion "her friend is incorrect" into a specific claim, "There are some palatable daisies".
  We see a lot of symbol repetition in this argument. There are two instances each of 'palatable', 'daisies', and 'chrysanthemum'. Thus this argument is ripe for turning into algebra.
  P1:  Some daisies are a type of chrysanthemum

label: Some A's are B
body: P2: Some chrysanthemums are palatable.

label: Some B's are X
body: C: Some daisies are palatable

label: Some A's are X
body: We can talk about the bad *Quantifier Logic* this argument is employing. A valid argument would say,

label: Thus, Some B's are X
body:
That works because the overlapping idea in the premises ("A") is the *trigger* of the All statement. If Some X's are A, then automatically that means that Some X's are B, since every thing A is B.
  In this argument, by contrast, the premises are just saying *Some*, so no overlap inference can be made. We can never prove from "Some A are B" and "Some B are C" that "Some A are C".
  We could also just conversationally argue with the argument. Just because some daisies belong to a category, some of which is palatable, doesn't mean that daises are palatable.
  Tomatoes belong to the category of fruit, some of which are made into popsicles, but that doesn't mean tomatoes are made into popsicles.
  It's possible that tomatoes are an example of a fruit that **doesn't** get made into popsicles.
  It's possible that daises are an example of a chrysanthemum that **isn't** palatable.

label: Goal
body:
Let's look for something with this type of structure:
P1:  Some A's are B
P2: Some B's are X
C: Some A's are X

label: Conclusion (only reasonable conclusion)
body: Ziegler was insane at the time he fired the shot.

label: Evidence (from the fact that)
body: The accusers have submitted no evidence that he was sane at the time he pulled the trigger, only that he was sane some time after he did so.

label: Evaluate
body:
*Given that ..* there's only evidence that Z was sane *after* the shooting, not during the shooting.
  *How can we argue that ...* Z was **not** insane at the time he fired the shot (i.e. he was sane)?
  Well, what is the evidence he was that we was insane? Z's attorney hasn't presented any evidence to support the contention that Z was insane at the time of the shooting.
  The fact that we don't have evidence Z was sane at the time of the shooting is not therefore evidence that Z was insane. After all, that would work in reverse too. The fact that Z's attorney has provided no evidence that Z was insane at the time of the shooting would, by the same logic, be evidence that Z was sane.
  A lack of evidence for X does not prove or even necessarily suggest that X is false.
  To think this way is to commit one of the 10 famous flaws, *Unproven vs. Proven False.*

label: Goal
body: Look for an answer naming the Unproven vs. Proven False flaw, or one complaining that Z's attorney has presented no evidence that Z was insane at the time of the shooting, or any other objection we could make that would help us argue that Z was sane at the time of the shooting.

label: Conclusion
body: The best way to teach history is to spend most class time recounting the lives of historical figures, and very little time on dates and statistics.

label: Evidence
body: Most students are bored by how history is usually taught, mainly because a large amount of time is spent teaching dates and stats.

label: Evaluate
body:
Well, we have to find four valid assumptions in the answers. Maybe we can think of a few:
- we're assuming that whether or not students are bored is at all relevant to whether or not we're teaching history the best way
  - we're assuming that the solution would work (students would be less bored if we switched to more time on historical figures, less time on dates and stats)
  - we're assuming that Plan B is the "best way" (maybe there's a third option we should consider that's even better than focusing on historical figures)

label: Goal
body: Let's look for answers either connecting language from the Premise to language from the Conclusion, or answers establishing that if we followed the author's plan we would see a positive difference, it wouldn't backfire in some way, or it wouldn't be ignoring a superior option.

label: Conclusion
body: The evidence of the illegal weapon was inadmissible.

label: Evidence
body:
*if evidence is collected  → it's inadmissible*
*during an illegal chase*
  The only cause for the chase was that the suspect ran from the cops upon seeing them, but running from the cops does not create a reasonable suspicion of a criminal act.

label: Evaluate
body:
On Sufficient Assumption and Principle-Strengthen, we're all about looking for rules that prove the wording in the conclusion.
  In this case, the conclusion is trying to prove "inadmissible" and we were provided a rule that lets us derive "inadmissible" (so we need to trigger this rule).
  In order to trigger this rule, we have to establish that this weapon was collected during *an illegal chase*. Does the evidence establish that this was an illegal chase?
  Nope. It suggests it was, but it never uses that wording.
  What we know about this chase is that the only reason the cops chased the suspect is because the suspect ran away, but running away does not create a reasonable suspicion of a criminal act.
  If we synthesized that down, what we know about this chase is that the cops did ****not**** have a reasonable suspicion of a criminal act.

label: Goal
body:
Since we're trying to establish "illegal chase", it looks like the missing link in this argument is something like this:
  *did not have reasonable    →   illegal chase*
  *suspicion of criminal act*

label: Monica's 1st Claim
body:
The sculpture that the town commissioned has been scorned ever since it went up.
     *does Hector disagree*?
  No comment. He doesn't discuss any awareness or skepticism of the scorn the new sculpture has received since it went up.

label: Monica's 2nd claim
body:
The people in our town do not know very much about contemporary art.
      *does Hector disagree?*
  He does not disagree. He indicates that he himself doesn't personally know about this public scorn the sculpture has received, but "*if public opinion of this sculpture is what you say ..."*
  He has no sense of whether it's true or false, so he's definitely not actively disagreeing with it.

label: Premises
body: The southern Levant was abandoned 6,000 years ago; the northern Levant stayed populated despite sharing the same climate.

label: Monica's 4th claim
body:
The sculpture's unpopularity with the public gives no reason for removing the sculpture.
      *does Hector disagree?*
  ****Yes!**** He says that a public sculpture commissioned with public money should benefit the public, and the best way to measure whether the public thinks it's benefiting them is to go by their opinion.
  *If the sculpture is as* *****unpopular***** *as you say, then that* *****is***** *reason to remove the sculpture.*

label: Goal
body: Look for an answer about "whether or not the sculpture's unpopularity is a good reason to remove it."

label: Conclusion (Thus)
body: If [this sculpture has been scorned by the public ever since it went up], the sculpture ought to be removed.

label: Evidence
body: A work of art for a public space ought to benefit the public and popular opinion is the only way to determine what the public feels is to its benefit.

label: Evaluate
body:
When a conclusion is in conditional form, we accept the "if" condition.
  So we could be thinking,
  *Given that ...*
the public has scorned the sculpture ever since it went up,
popular opinion is the only way to determine whether the public benefits,
and a commissioned art such as this ought to benefit the public.
  *How could we still argue that ...*
The sculpture should ****not**** be removed?
  Playing by Hector's rules, we need to argue that the sculpture *is* benefiting the public. We could say that, "even though the sculpture has been scorned, it's still still benefiting the public".
  Maybe some art benefits the public by pointing out something unpleasant about the public. The public might scorn the art, because it's rebuking them, but still benefit from having seen the art because the art lodges this societal criticism in their subconscious.
  Or we argue that scorn is just a short term reaction; in the long term the public would grow to appreciate the benefit the sculpture provides.

label: Goal
body: Look for an answer providing the linking idea, "If the public is scorning it, then the public isn't benefiting", or look for a defending answer saying, "the public will ****not**** eventually grow to love this sculpture" or "the public is ****not**** sometimes benefiting from an artwork it ostensibly doesn't like".

label: Given that ...
body: Average temperatures fell from 900 - 1500 A.D., making Greenland quite cold.

label: How can we explain that ...
body: Norse settlers in Greenland disappeared (seemingly from the cold), while Inuit settlers in Greenland continued to thrive.

label: Evaluate / Goal
body: We're going to need to learn of some *difference* between Norse and Inuit settlers that would make the former leave Greenland and the latter stay.

label: Conclusion
body: The temperature-drop explanation for the disappearance of the Norse settlements cannot be correct.

label: Evidence
