body: Inuit settlers were living in Greenland during the same period as the Norse and continued to thrive long after 1500 — even though average yearly temperatures fell slightly worldwide.

label: Evaluate
body: The opposing view says the temperature drop made Greenland too cold for human habitation, which wiped out the Norse. The author offers a counterexample: the Inuit lived in the same place at the same time and didn't die out. If Greenland really had become too cold for humans, the Inuit should have suffered the same fate — but they didn't. That is a fact directly inconsistent with the opposing explanation.

label: Goal
body: The right answer should describe this move: producing evidence that contradicts the opposing claim.

label: Conclusion
body: The temperature-drop explanation for the Norse disappearance cannot be correct.

label: Evidence
body: The Inuit, who lived in Greenland at the same time, continued to thrive long after 1500.

label: Evaluate
body: The Inuit's survival is inconsistent with the opposing claim that Greenland became too cold for human habitation.

label: Goal
body: Identify the move: producing evidence inconsistent with the opposing explanation.

label: Conclusion
body: The author rejects the popular explanation that cooling temperatures wiped out the Norse settlements in Greenland.

label: Evidence
body: Why? Because another group — the Inuit — was living in the same place at the same time and they did just fine, even after 1500.

label: Evaluate
body:
The opposing claim was: Greenland got too cold for humans. The author's response: well, then how do you explain the Inuit thriving there? If a place is too cold for humans, no humans should be living there. Inuit humans did. That fact is in direct tension with the temperature explanation.
  Think of it like this: someone says "the restaurant closed because the food was inedible," and you respond "but I just ate there last week and it was fine." You've produced a fact that conflicts with the proposed explanation.

label: Goal
body: The right answer should describe this technique — offering evidence that contradicts the opposing position.

label: Conclusion (therefore)
body: The development of synthetic ivory will probably do little to help curb the killing of elephants for their tusks.

label: Evidence
body: Experts have devised a synthetic ivory that has found favor with concert pianists worldwide, but piano makers have never been major consumers of ivory.

label: Evaluate
body:
This is an *Anti-Causal* argument. The author thinks that the new synthetic ivory will do little to reduce elephants' being hunted for their tusks.
  It will reduce demand for ivory from pianists, but the author is saying that's a negligible slice of the ivory market.
  GIVEN THAT  piano makers are just a tiny slice of the ivory market
HOW COULD WE ARGUE THAT  synthetic ivory *will* make a big difference in terms of elephants' being hunted for their tusks?
  It seems very possible that other segments of the ivory market could ALSO find that synthetic ivory is a suitable substitute. Maybe a huge source of ivory demand is for bathroom tile, and tile manufacturers are totally down with using synthetic ivory instead.

label: Goal
body: Let's look for an answer that rules out an objection like "what if other ivory-users also find synthetic ivory a suitable replacement" or that otherwise makes it more likely that even though synthetic ivory is available, most ivory-users will continue to want the real ivory that we get from elephant tusks.

label: Evaluate
body:
When we do Role and Main Conclusion, we read the paragraph with the awareness that on most of these, the Conclusion comes **earlier**, Support comes **after / last**.
  We also know to be more on guard when it comes to possible Intermediate Conclusions.
  The "yet" indicates an Author's Pivot (but, **yet,** however, after all). She starts by complaining about clean-up efforts.
  Then we get the big Opinion Indicator "should" in the 3rd sentence. Since this is a prescriptive recommendation (yes, that was redundant), it feels like our author's main purpose in writing the paragraph.
  Does our author Support this opinion? *Why should more of the government's budget be redirected to preventing spills.*
  Because, the cleanup effort is not even keeping pace with rate of new spills, they currently spend less on prevention each year than they spend on just ONE cleanup site each year, and prevention is far more effective than cleanup.
  The word "Since" (of FABS fame .. for, after all, because, since) indicates that the 1st half of the last sentence is a Premise supporting a Conclusion in the 2nd half.
  But we could only call this an Intermediate Conclusion, since it was still part of the Support for the overall Main Conclusion, "the government should spend more on prevention than cleanup".

label: Goal
body: The claim the question stem is asking us about is that 3rd sentence, which is our Main Conclusion.

label: Conclusion (Therefore)
body: Bringing in predators to eradicate rodents will prevent erosion of the embankments.

label: Evidence
body: Currently, we plant grasses and woody plants on dirt embankments to prevent erosion (the roots of those plants help protect against erosion). But when we mow the grasses, the piles of clippings smother the plants, causing their roots to rot. The clippings also attract rodents, who burrow into the dirt and damage the roots.

label: Evaluate
body: Since this argument is based around a Plan / Recommendation, we want to think about this plan could potentially fail to achieve its goal. The typical issues we consider are things like Feasibility, Motives/Incentives, Potential Backfire, and whether the plan targets Key Source of Problem. How could we ... bring in predators that want to eat rodents, but ... this fails to prevent erosion? What if the predators we brought in aren't able to catch and eat these rodents or don't seem interested in doing so? (feasibility / incentives) What if the predators go after the rodents, but the predators themselves end up causing erosive damage? (backfire) What if the damage to the roots from the rodents isn't nearly as important as the damage from the grass clippings that cause the roots to rot? (key source of problem)

label: Goal
body: Look for some way to object to this plan, to respond in a way that feels like, "Even if ... we bring in predators to eradicate the rodents, we still could have eroding embankments."

label: Conclusion (it follows that)
body: Predicting the future is particularly untrustworthy, when you're dealing with societies where science and tech discoveries are particularly frequent.

label: Evidence
body: Science and tech discoveries have considerable effects on society.

label: Evaluate
body:
The argument is assuming that,
*Predicting the future is particularly untrustworthy, when you're dealing with societies where considerable effects happen frequently.*
  Since *science and tech discoveries* is an **overlapping idea** in both the Premise and the Conclusion, we'd anticipate a Linking assumption bringing together the other two concepts.
  In other words, if we have a premise saying "x = y" and a conclusion saying "x = z", then we'll anticipate a Linking assumption bringing together "y and z".
  How would one object to this argument?
  GIVEN THAT ... Sci & Tech discoveries have considerable effects on society
  HOW COULD WE ARGUE THAT ... frequent Sci & Tech discoveries **do not** make it particularly hard to predict the future condition of societies?
  We could probably say, "Even though these discoveries have considerable effects, the effects are easy to predict, so it doesn't mess up our ability to make predictions".

label: Goal
body: Look for an answer linking "particularly untrustworthy predictions" to "frequent considerable effects", or look for an answer ruling out our objection, like "the effects of these discoveries **are not** easy to predict".

label: Conclusion
body: We are pretty safe in assuming that neither underinflation nor overinflation harms the tread of a tire.

label: Evidence (after all)
body: No one has been able to show that underinflation nor overinflation *do* harm tire tread.

label: Evaluation
body:
This argument is analogous to saying, "We are pretty safe in assuming that there is no God. After all, no one has been able to show that there *is* a God."
  Or, "we are pretty safe in assuming that Hillary Clinton is the mysterious Q from QAnon. After all, no one has been able to show that she *isn't* Q."
  Someone's failure to prove that X is true doesn't prove that X is false. This reasoning move is one of the 10 Famous Flaws, and it's known as **Unproven vs. Proven False**.

label: Goal
body:
Let's look for an answer calling out the abstract form of, "assumes that if no one has been able to show that X is true, then that means that X isn't true".
  Or let's look for a specific objection like, "Even if no one has yet been able to show that over/under-inflating tires is bad for the tread, it's still possible that over/under-inflating tires is bad for the tread. Has anyone ever shown that it *isn't* bad?"

label: Facts
body:
The Levant was heavily populated in prehistoric times.
  Around 6,000 years ago, the southern Levant was abandoned while the northern Levant stayed populated.
  The two areas have the same climate.
  The southern abandonment was caused by an economic collapse driven by deforestation.

label: Evaluate
body:
On Must Be False, the correct answer almost always contradicts a conditional in the stimulus or contradicts some MBT inference we can make by combining claims from the stimulus.
  This stimulus has no conditionals. We can probably infer something though from the fact that these two regions have the same climate, but one of them was abandoned from an economic collapse due to deforestation and the other one stayed populated.
  Can we infer that the norther area, which stayed populated, *didn't* have an economic collapse / didn't have deforestation?
  Can we infer something like, "deforestation can happen in one area but not another, even though they both have the same climate?"

label: Goal
body:
I don't feel great about any definitive must be true inferences we can make, so I'm not sure what we're looking for (no targets in mind for what they'll contradict).
  Let's just keep an open mind and ask ourselves whether stuff we were told would contradict any of these answers.

label: Premises
body: Two regions side by side, same climate. Around 6,000 years ago, the southern half empties out while the northern half keeps going strong. The archaeologists' best guess: the south chopped down its forests, the economy collapsed, and people had to leave.

label: Evaluate
body:
The question asks what *cannot* be true if the facts and the hypothesis are both right. So we're looking for an answer that just doesn't fit with the deforestation story.
  The key thing the deforestation hypothesis quietly requires: there had to *be* forests to begin with. You can't deplete trees that were never there. So any answer that says "actually, there were no trees in the southern Levant before this period" would directly contradict the hypothesis.

label: Goal
body: The right answer should say something logically incompatible with the deforestation explanation — most likely that the forests never existed.

label: Statements
body:
*causal (one of the most important factors)*
How much cholesterol and fat we eat is a big causal factor when it comes to our serum cholesterol.
  *causal (rises proportionally to)*
For a while, the more cholesterol and fat we eat will cause our serum cholesterol to rise proportionally. But at a certain point, eating even tons more cholesterol and fat will barely increase our serum cholesterol.
  *mathematical (1/4)*
This threshold where it switches from rising proportionally to barely rising is 1/4 the consumption level of cholesterol and fat in today's average North American diet.

label: Evaluate
body:
Our job on Inference (Must Be True / Most Supported) is to try to combine at least 2 of the facts we've learned.
  The last two facts have an *Overlapping Concept*, "the threshold".
  If the average North American diet is ****way**** above this threshold where serum cholesterol switches from rising proportionally to barely rising, then we can assume that the majority of North Americans are way above this threshold.
  So we can plausibly infer that most North Americans ****don't**** have proportional responses to eating more/less cholesterol and fat; instead, they're on the side of the threshold where they will see only gradual rises in their serum cholesterol, no matter how much more cholesterol/fat they eat.

label: Goal
body:
Look for the most provable answer (be wary of language that's too strong/specific, switches between Relative and Absolute, or brings in outside ideas).
  It will probably be testing us on the idea that most North Americans aren't in that proportional range; they're in the range where their serum cholesterol changes only slightly even with dramatic increases in consumption.

label: Conclusion
body: Parents who want a strong musical foundation for their children need to ensure those children receive formal instruction.

label: Evidence (since)
body: To provide a strong foundation, parents should provide a good musical education. And formal instruction is often part of a good musical education.

label: Evaluate
body:
We'd be trying to argue that
*parents who want the strong musical foundation **don't** need to ensure their kid gets formal instruction.*
  In other words, "You can get your kid a strong musical foundation **without** formal instruction. It's not necessary."
  The author will say,
"but a strong foundation requires good musical education, and formal instruction is often part of a good musical education".
  We could respond with something like, "Sure it's often part of a good musical education, but it's not *necessary* to a good education. A lot of people get good musical education without any formal instruction."

label: Goal
body: Let's look for an answer that helps us argue that you can get your kid a good musical education without formal instruction, and thus formal instruction is not **needed**.

label: Conclusion
body: Parents wanting a strong musical foundation must ensure their children receive formal instruction.

label: Evidence
body: A good musical education provides the foundation, and formal instruction is *often* part of a good musical education.

label: Evaluate
body: "Often" doesn't mean "always." A good musical education without formal instruction is possible.

label: Goal
body: Point out that formal instruction may not always be part of a good musical education.

label: Conclusion
body: The author tells parents: if you want your kid to have a strong musical foundation, you must make sure they get formal instruction.

label: Evidence
body: The reasoning: a strong foundation comes from a good musical education, and formal instruction is *often* part of that.

label: Evaluate
body:
The word "often" is doing a lot of quiet work here. The argument leaps from "often included" to "must be included." Those aren't the same.
  Think of it like this: "Strong careers usually require a college degree, so anyone wanting a strong career must go to college." But "usually" leaves room for exceptions — entrepreneurs, athletes, artists, tradespeople. Same here. If a good musical education sometimes happens without formal instruction, parents have other options.

label: Goal
body: The right answer should call out the leap from "often part of" to "required."

label: Background
body: For stingrays, it's healthy to not have parasites.

label: Surprising Claim
body: For ecosystems, it's unhealthy for stingrays to not have parasites.

label: Evaluate / Goal
body: I think we know from common sense why it's healthy for an organism **not** to have parasites. So it feels like the burden of the answer choice lies more in explaining why **not** having parasites in stingrays is an indicator of a stressed (unhealthy) ecosystem.

label: Conclusion (clearly)
body:
There have not been decreases in the number of injuries in all categories.
  *rephrase*: there are more knee injuries than before.

label: Evidence (for)
body: Knee injuries used to be 11% of all ski injuries whereas now they represent 16% of all ski injuries.

label: Goal
body:
The author seems to be assuming the *Missing Link* that "if employee morale increases, then production will increase".
  She also is failing to consider ways in which a flextime schedule might impede production (maybe it's harder for workers to be efficient because they need to ask employee X a question, but employee X is now working a different schedule that's more convenient for them).
  So we might see Defender answers like,
"Allowing employees more flexibility in scheduling would not result in work getting stalled out because employees were not all present at the same time".

label: Evaluate
body:
The fact that a percentage goes up (which is what the evidence is saying) doesn't mean that a raw number goes up (which is what the conclusion is saying).
  This is a classic *Percent vs. #* flaw.
  Say there's a room full of 10 people, 5 men and 5 women. Then 2 men leave and so there's 3 men and 5 women.
  The percentage of women increased from **50%** (5/10) to **62.5%** (5/8), but there weren't any women added to the room. The raw number of women stayed the same.
  A percentage can increase without the raw number increasing, if *other things* get smaller. The same raw number is divided by a smaller denominator, and so it looks like a bigger percentage.
  In this argument we actually *know* that the total number of ski injuries (the denominator) has gotten smaller. There's has been a 50% drop in the number of ski injuries. Let's make up a real number to demonstrate this math.
  20 yrs. ago               Now
  total # of               2,000                   1,000
ski injuries
  % of ski injuries    11%                       16%
knee-related
  total # of                 220                    160
knee injuries
  There are actually fewer knee injuries today, because taking 16% of 1,000 is a smaller number than taking 11% of 2,000.

label: Goal
body: Let's look for an answer addressing the author's confusion between an increasing % (knee injuries went from 11% to 16%) and an increasing # (knee injuries actually decreased in number).

label: Facts
body:
~poetry → can be translated well
  ~poets → ~preserve language
  translation provided all → ~learn language
  ~language written in → can't appreciate poem
  Poetry motivates us to learn a new language, since poetry sometimes doesn't translate well, and we can only witness the beauty of a poem in its native language.

label: Evaluate / Goal
body:
It's hard to tell from the question stem whether this is a "soft" Must Be False question, or a Most Supported EXCEPT question.
  If the correct answer is trying to act like a Must Be False, it will probably contradict a conditional. The form of contradicting an inference is "trigger is true, outcome isn't".
  So potential answers could sound like
- Not a poem, but can't be translated well
- Not a poet, but preserves language
- Translation provides everything we need, but we still learn a language
- read a translation of a poem but do still witness all its beauty
  If the four answers we can eliminate are supportable inferences, they will reinforce what we know from the passage. It didn't seem like any of the rules chained together and allowed for inferences by combining facts.

label: Conclusion (as a result)
body: To be successful, commercial computer software cannot require users to memorize unfamiliar commands.

label: Evidence
body: The prime purchases of computer software won't buy a software package if the costs of training staff to use it are high, and the costs of training will be high if the software demands the memorization of unfamiliar commands.

label: Evaluate
body:
On Sufficient Assumption, if the conclusion introduces a new, undefined term (like *Successful* in this example), we know it has to be in the correct answer.
  Specifically, we need our answer to say, "Success requires ___ ", or "you can't be successful without ____ ", or something equivalent.
  Given that this argument has conditional logic (*if*, *require*) and that it has repeating ideas (*memorize unfamiliar commands, training is expensive*), it makes sense to diagram this out if we didn't already perceive the missing ingredient as we read the argument.
  Let's write the Conclusion with an elongated arrow, to represent the logic path we'll be building by combining the Premises with the correct answer.

label: Conclusion
body:
*Successful ---------------------------> doesn't*
*comp soft                                       req mem*
                                                      *new comm's*
                       Or alternatively
*requires                                         won't*
*memorize   ---------------------------> be*
*new comm's                                  successful*
  The second formation seems more useful, because the evidence allows us to build on to "if it requires memorizing new commands"

label: EVIDENCE
body:
*requires          costly               prime*
  *mem       →     to        →  purchasers*
  *new                train             won't buy*
*comm's*
  To complete the logic path the Conclusion is trying to build, it looks like we're missing that last link of
                                  *prime                    won't*
                             *purchasers   →           be*
                               *won't buy            successful*
  If we wanted to avoid conditional logic, we could just ask ourselves, "*Why* does this conclusion think that making people memorize unfamiliar commands will keep software from being *successful*? What idea in the premise seems most connected to the idea of *not successful*? I guess the notion of *prime purchasers won't buy it* sounds a lot like *not successful*. So the argument must be assuming a link between those".
  This is often good enough to get to the correct answer. However, many times there will be an answer with the two ideas that should be linked, but the answer writes the link in Reversed or Negated style so it doesn't actually work.

label: Goal
body:
The two things we know about software that makes you memorize unfamiliar commands are that
1. it's expensive to teach people to use it
2. the companies that are the prime purchasers won't buy it
  So a correct answer will either have to say, "If it's expensive to teach people how to use it, then it won't be successful", or it will (more likely) say, "If prime purchasers won't buy it, then it won't be successful".

label: Statements
body:
*conditional (whenever -* Left side, sufficient)
  Disagree w/ other           acceptable to vote for
candidates on greater →     candidate X, even if
# of important issues         disagree w/ X on one or
                                           more important issues
  *conditional (otherwise -* negate previous trigger)
  **don't** disagree w/ other     **un**acceptable to vote
candidates on greater →      for candidate X, if
# of important issues         disagree w/ X on one or
                                           more important issues
  In upcoming election, there is only one important issue to Kay, and only Medina (of the three candidates) shares her opinion.

label: Evaluate
body:
It looks like in this election, the only acceptable person Kay can vote for is Medina. Kay could otherwise not vote, but were she to vote for Legrand or Norton she'd be breaking her rule.
  She's not allowed to vote for people who don't share her view on an important issue, unless the other candidates mismatch with her view on a greater number of important issues.

label: Conclusion (therefore)
body: Owning a VCR actually stimulates people to go to movie theaters more often than they otherwise would.

label: Evidence
body: Among people who computers at their job, people who owned laptop computers earned 25% more than those who did not.

label: Principle
body:
This one is a BEAST to translate. "Whenever" is the conditional key word in the first part of the principle, and that introduces the condition on the left: **if** Kay disagrees with each of the OTHER candidates on MORE important issues than some particular candidate, **then** it's acceptable to vote for that particular candidate. So, for example, if Kay disagrees with candidate X about 1 important issue and disagrees with the other candidates Y and Z about 2 important issues, it's acceptable for Kay to vote for candidate X.
  The second half of the principle begins after the semicolon: It's otherwise unacceptable to vote for a candidate who disagrees with her on an important issue. This means that **if** Kay DOESN'T disagree with all the other candidates on more important issues than some particular candidate, **then** it's NOT acceptable to vote for that candidate. So, in that same example where Kay disagrees with candidate X about 1 important issue and candidates Y and Z about 2 important issues, it's NEVER acceptable for her to vote for Y and Z, even if she likes them better personally, thinks they'd be a better leader, etc.

label: Facts
body: There is only one issue important to Kay, and of the three options (L, M, and N), only M share's K's position on that 1 important issue.

label: Evaluate
body:
Since L and N disagree with Kay's position on the important issue, and since there's no way for them to agree with Kay on other important issues (because there ARE no other important issues to Kay), that means it's unacceptable for K to vote for them.
  We don't technically have a way to prove that it's acceptable for Kay to vote for M, because the rule provided for "acceptable" involves a trigger that doesn't apply to M.
  The trigger talks about a candidate whose opinions differ on at least one important issue. There's only one important issue to Kay, and M's opinions do not differ. So we can't really apply this rule to M, even though our common sense would tell us it seems acceptable for her to vote for M

label: Goal
body: Look for an answer that reflects that it is unacceptable to vote for L and N, that it's *potentially* acceptable to vote for M, or both.

label: Conclusion
body: People who buy new cars today, on average, spend a larger % of their income on a new car than did people 25 years ago.

label: Evidence
body: Over the past 25 years, the price of a new car has steadily increased in relation to avg individual income.

label: Evaluate
body:
GIVEN THAT the price of a new car has increased relative to avg individual income, HOW CAN WE SAY that people are *not* paying a bigger % of their income on a new car nowadays?
  Hmm, this seems kinda hard to wriggle out of. I thought we were going to say, "yes, they're spending more on their cars, but they also MAKE more money!" But is that kind of ruled out by the fact that the average price of a new car has increased faster than avg income?
  Not necessarily. Say that over the past 25 years, the avg income has gone from $50k to $60k a year, while the avg price of a new car has one from $20k to $25k.  Income went up 1/5, or 20%.  New car prices went up 1/4, or 25%.
  But we would really need to know the income increase of the new-car-buying population. We don't have to assume that everyone in the population buys new cars. Maybe only affluent people buy new cars, and *their* income has gone up 30% over the past 25 years.
  It's possible that the new-car-buying part of the population is an atypical sample whose income has actually increased more than has the price of a new car. In that case, the new car buyers would NOT be spending a higher % of income. It could actually be the same or lower.

label: Goal
body: Look for an answer that gives us more info about who is buying these new cars, because maybe THEIR reality is different from the overall avg increase in income levels.

label: Companies' Conclusion
body: We should charge individual cardholders a late payment fee when they're late on their payments, rather than increasing the cost of all cardholders' policies.

label: Evidence / Principle
body:
**If ...**                               **Then ...**
you expose others     you should pay
 to financial risk           for that risk
  And cardholders who pay late present a greater risk of default than other cardholders.

label: Evaluate
body:
Credit card companies lend out money. If they don't get paid back, if the lender defaults on that loan, what happens to the credit card company?
  They are probably paying for some sort of insurance, so that they wouldn't be totally on the hook for the unpaid debts. Hence, that's increasing their costs. Should they raise the cost of using their card for **all** customers in order to offset that increased cost?
  No, they argue, the extra cost should be paid by the offending parties, not the innocent ones.

label: Goal
body:
It's hard to say what level of coarse / fine grained similarities we'll see, but roughly I'd be looking for
1. A subset of a group is causing a certain thing to occur
2. So, we're going to assess a special treatment (probably negative) on them, and not the others

label: Conclusion
body: Sara definitely doesn't have a strep infection.

label: Evidence
body: Michael definitely doesn't have strep, and Sara probably has the same illness as Michael.

label: Evaluate
body: It seems like the conclusion is too sure of itself. The argument would be valid if it just concluded, "the illness that Sara has is **probably** not strep".

label: Goal
body: Look for an answer saying that the other loses track of the distinction between Probably and Definitely

label: Conclusion
body: To increase production, ABC should implement a flextime schedule.

label: Evidence
body:
Flextime schedules allow individual employees some flexibility in deciding when to begin and end their workday.
  Studies show that working under flextime schedules is associated with increased employee morale.

label: Evaluate
body:
This argument really has more of a Plan / Goal structure to it. The stated goal here is "increasing production", and the plan to get there is "a flextime schedule".
  Well how do we get from "Flextime schedule" to "increasing production"?
  Flextime schedule apparently leads to more employee morale. Does more employee morale lead to increased production?

label: Evidence
body: VCRs enable people to watch movies at home on videotape. People who own VCRs go to movie theaters more often than do people who do not own VCRs.

label: P's Argument
body: Complying with the new regulations is useless since, had they been in effect, they wouldn't have prevented last year's lab fire, nor do they address its underlying causes.

label: Evaluate
body:
This is one of those old-test problems that hasn't aged well. If you're old enough to remember DVD's that's basically the same as VCR's. It was before the age of streaming media.
  Ultimately we can reduce this whole argument down to its classic LSAT formula just by noticing the type of claim made in the Evidence and the Conclusion.
  The evidence is a correlation, signified by the "Ppl who are X are more likely to be Y than people who aren't X" language. People who are VCR owners are more likely to go to movie theaters than are people who are not VCR.
  The conclusion is causal, signified by the causal verb *stimulates*. "Being a VCR owner *stimulates* people to go to the movies".
  When an author presents a correlation between two things,
      X || Y
the author always assumes one causes the other,
      X ⇢ Y
while failing to consider **reverse causality**,
     *it could be that Y ⇢ X*
or to consider that a **3rd factor** accounts for both,
     *it could be that Z ⇢ X and Y*

label: Goal
body:
Let's look for an answer pointing out the illegality of assuming that just because two things (VCR ownership and going to movie theaters) are correlated that a causal relationship exists between them.
  Or look for an answer pointing out that they've failed to consider *Reverse Causality:* maybe people were big movie fans first and *then* they bought a VCR so that they could also watch movies at home.
  Or look for an answer pointing out that they've failed to consider *Third Factor*:  maybe if you're wealthy enough, then you can afford to go to the movies and can afford to buy a VCR and a home movie library.

label: Claim (hence)
body: By the late Bronze Age, these tribes had developed new methods of warfare designed to inflict many casualties.

label: Intermediate Conclusion (indicates that)
body: In late Bronze Age, wars between tribes were frequent / casualty rate was high.

label: Evidence
body: In early Bronze Age, the main weapons were cumbersome spears. This prevented widespread casualties. In late Bronze Age, there was a much higher number of warrior tombs.

label: Evaluate
body:
The author is interpreting the significance of a **Curious Comparison:** why were there way more warrior tombs in late Bronze Age?
  Her **explanation**:  wars were frequent, the casualty rate was high, and tribes had developed new methods of warfare designed to inflict many casualties.

label: Goal
body:
To strengthen a Curious Fact / Explanation argument, we primarily search for an answer that bolsters the **plausibility** of the Author's Story.
  In this case, the question stem is specifically assigning us to support the plausibility of the claim that their were "new methods of warfare designed to inflict many casualties".
  (There's a small chance, though, that the correct answer could **rule out** an Alternate Explanation for why there is a higher number of warrior tombs.)

label: Conclusion (Therefore)
body: If people whose weight falls outside their given range modified their weight to fall within that range, their overall life expectancies would improve.

label: Evidence
body: Life insurance policyholders whose weight fell within the range given for their height lived longer than those whose weight fell outside their given range.

label: Evaluate
body:
The author interprets the correlation in the second sentence to have this causal meaning:  *being inside the standard weight range for your height causes you to live longer*.
  And because of that causal assumption, the author makes the prediction that if you're out of range, then bringing yourself into range would extend your life expectancy.
  If you're underweight for your height, is gaining weight in order to fall within that range going to improve your life expectancy?  (not if you do it through weird, dangerous weight-gaining drugs or do it by overeating crappy food)
  If you're overweight for your height, is losing weight in order to fall within that range going to improve your life expectancy? (not if you do it through weird, dangerous weight-loss drugs or do it by starving yourself)

label: Goal
body:
The correct answer is unlikely to be a *Linking* idea, but if it were, maybe it would sound like, "If being out of your height's standard weight range is correlated with living not as long, then getting yourself in that standard weight range would extend your life expectancy."
  But it's more likely that we'll see a *Defender* idea, an answer that, if negated, would weaken the argument. So look for an answer ruling-out a potential bad thing that could happen if people were to try to modify their weight to fall within that standard range.

label: Conclusion (therefore)
body: In addition to the known planets, there must be at least one planet in our solar system that we have yet to discover.

label: Evidence
body:
Measurements of Uranus show that there is a force tugging it away from the Sun and inner planets.
  But Neptune and Pluto, the two known planets farther than Uranus, don't have enough mass to account for the tugging.

label: Evaluate
body:
Since we're trying to solve a science mystery here, we can use our *Explain Curious Fact* framework.
  *Curious Fact ...* why does it seem like Uranus is being tugged away from the Sun at a force stronger than the gravitational pull of the two farther planets (Neptune and Pluto)?
  *Author's Explanation ...*  there must be at least one planet in our solar system that we have yet to discover (and that planet exists farther from the Sun than Uranus and accounts for the rest of the outward tugging force we're measuring).
  The two pressure points are always
1. Alternate Explanations for the curious fact
2. the plausibility of the author's explanation

label: Goal
body:
On Weaken (and every other question type other than Strengthen), the correct answer is more likely to deal with an alternate explanation.
  So let's primarily look for a different way to explain where this outward tugging force is coming from (a black hole? a planet outside our solar system? an asteroid belt? comets?).
  But we'll keep an open mind for answers that would otherwise be trying to degrade the plausibility that there's another planet in the solar system we've yet to discover.

label: Recommendation
body: Candidates for national office who want to be successful in winning votes should use in their speeches the technique of starting out your argument for X with counterarguments against X.

label: Evidence
body: Showing you recognize the counterpoints to the thing you're arguing makes you seem fair-minded and trustworthy.

label: Evidence
body: After exposure for an hour to superheated steam, this garbage would be far cleaner than food prepared in the cleanest kitchen.

label: Evaluate
body: The columnist conflates individual causation with statistical / population-level evidence.

label: Evaluate
body:
What would *limit the effectiveness* of this recommendation, so, "what would Weaken this recommendation?"
  The author is assuming that one is likely to win votes if one appears fair-minded and trustworthy. So we could write a correct answer that would attack this assumption, like "people tend not to vote for someone that appears fair-minded and trustworthy", but that seems like an unlikely correct answer.
  Normally when we weaken a plan / recommendation, we're saying
- it's not feasible
- people wouldn't react to this the way you're assuming
- this doesn't treat the core issue
- this backfires in some way

label: Goal
body:
Hard to predict. We should just cue up the Anti-Conclusion (or in this case Anti-Recommendation) and hope that the correct answer jumps out as a usable objection.
  "Candidates hoping to win national elections **should not** open up their speeches by presenting counterarguments against their proposals, because ..... [answer choice]."

label: Conclusion
body: No more than 1/4 of the films released in country Z in 1992 were based on books published in Z in 1991.

label: Evidence (since)
body:
100 films were released in country Z in 1992.
25 of the films released in country Z in 1992 were based on novels published in Z in 1991.

label: Evaluate
body:
The conclusion is talking about one-quarter because 25 is one quarter of 100. We could replace the word "one-quarter" with 25 if that helps us think about it.
  Does the evidence prove that no more than 25 out of the 100 films from 1992 were based on books published in 1991.
  Not quite. The evidence establishes that 25 out of the 100 films from 1992 were based on **novels** published in 1991. But the conclusion has made a move from "only 25 were based on 1991 novels" to "only 25 were based on 1991 books".
  It might be that the 100 films of 1992 are broken down like this:
25 - based on 1991 novels
20 - based on 1991 nonfiction books
55 - not based on a book at all
  This would make the author's conclusion wrong, because more than 1/4 (45 out of 100) of the films from 1992 were based on books.

label: Goal
body:
We can think of the job the answer needs to do in a positive or a negative way.
  Positively, we need our answer to be saying "if only 25 were based on novels, then only 25 were based on books".
  Negatively, we can think that our answer needs to **rule out** the objection that "maybe some of the remaining 75 movies were based on books that weren't novels". So it could sound like, "None of the remaining 75 movies were based on books that weren't novels".

label: Statements
body:
As ants leave home to seek food, they leave a trail of pheromones, as a way of guiding themselves back to the nest.
  All pheromones completely evaporate almost immediately when temps rise about 45 Celsius, which commonly happens during the afternoons in hot places like the Sahara.

label: Evaluate
body: We can see the **overlapping** ingredient in these claims is "pheromones". Ants use them to find their way home, and the sun zaps them out of existence when it gets real hot.

label: Goal
body: So combining these ideas we would get that, "If an ant goes out for food when it's over 45 degrees Celsius, they aren't going to be able to use pheromones to get back home."

label: Facts
body:
*conditionals* (if / all / must / never)
  Deceit is rotten → all effective are rotten.
  *rephrase*
Effectiveness requires deceit
    *Effective → Deceit*
  (When it says "they must be deceitful to do the job properly", they are reiterating the same fact that effectiveness/proper job performance requires deceitfulness).
  Scrupulously honest → ~Effective Politician

label: Evaluate
body:
The #1 thing to read for on MBT and MBF is conditional logic.
  We start with a wishy-washy attribution, and then we get into three sentences that each look like conditional ideas. The 2nd and 3rd sentences effectively mean the same thing:  "in order to effectively / properly do their job, politicians must be deceitful".
  And the 4th sentence is really kind of another reiteration of that! It's saying "in order to be an effective politician, you can't be scrupulously honest".

label: Goal
body:
The correct answer to MBF usually contradicts a conditional we're given or contradicts some MBT inference we can make by combining claims.
  We can't really combine any of these claims, since all three rules essentially said the same thing, "In order to be an effective / proper politician, you can't be scrupulously honest / you must be somewhat deceitful."
  So it's likely that the correct answer just contradicts this idea by making it seem like there is some effective politician out there who never lies.

label: Conclusion
body: Two rules: all effective politicians are deceitful; scrupulously honest people are never effective politicians.

label: Evidence
body: The author argues these rules from the demands of the job — deceit is required to do politics properly.

label: Evaluate
body: "Scrupulously honest → not effective." So no scrupulously honest politician can be effective.

label: Goal
body: Pick the answer that asserts a scrupulously honest, effective politician exists — that's the rule violation.

label: Conclusion
body: The author lays out two strict rules. First: every effective politician is deceitful. Second: anyone scrupulously honest about obeying the rules of society will *never* be an effective politician.

label: Evidence
body: The reasoning is that effective politicking requires deceit — so honesty is incompatible with effectiveness.

label: Evaluate
body:
Translate the rules into a logic chain. Effective politician → deceitful. Scrupulously honest → not deceitful → not an effective politician. The two rules together mean: no scrupulously honest person can be an effective politician.
  The question asks what *cannot* be true given these rules. So we need an answer that violates them. The cleanest violation is asserting that a scrupulously honest politician is effective — that's the exact case the rules forbid.
  Watch for trap answers that look concerning but are actually compatible with the rules — for instance, "some politicians are scrupulously honest" doesn't violate anything (the rules don't require all politicians to be dishonest, just all *effective* ones).

label: Goal
body: Pick the answer that asserts the existence of an effective, scrupulously honest politician.

label: Conclusion (argues)
body: The operation of the sterilization plant cannot cause pollution.

label: Intermediate Conclusion (because)
body: The waste would be sterile after processing by the plant.

label: Evaluate
body:
*Given the fact that* ... the waste would be super sterile after processing by the plant,
*How could we still argue that ...* the operation of the plant **could** cause pollution?
  Well, what about everything else going on with the plant other than the waste that comes out of it? Does building the plant cause pollution? Does operating the plant have emissions that cause pollution? Do the employees that run the plant cause pollution?
  The president is only looking at one tiny aspect of building and operating this plant and thinking, "since THAT part doesn't cause pollution, the whole thing won't cause pollution".

label: Goal
body:
Look for a linking answer that says, "If the waste doesn't cause pollution, then the plant overall won't cause pollution",
  or look for a defender answer ruling out some other way (besides waste, after it's been sterilized) that the plant could cause local pollution.

label: Conclusion (Consequently)
body: Offering a manufacturer' rebate on the purchase price of Grow-Again would be unprofitable for the manufacturer.

label: Intermediate Conclusion (Therefore)
body: Offering a manufacturer' rebate on the purchase price of Grow-Again will not increase sales.

label: Evidence
body: Grow-Again is a proven treatment for reversing baldness. Five drops daily is the recommended dose. Exceeding this quantity does not increase the product's effectiveness.

label: Evaluate
body:
This is one of those arguments that is so disconnected/bad that it's hard to even understand what logic the author was going for.
  Why is the author making a jump from "exceeding the recommended dose doesn't increase the product's effectiveness" to "offering a rebate will not increase sales"?
  Those two ideas don't seem to have anything to do with each other. Let's picture someone going through CVS, considering buying some Grow-Again for $40.
  If the package had an offer for a $10 manufacturer's rebate, wouldn't that potentially motivate some people to buy the product, who otherwise would feel like $40 is too much?
  Does the author think that the people buying this product are too rich to care about a rebate? Are the people who buy this product people who know themselves to be someone that will not remember to submit the rebate form? Are they turned off by a company *incentivizing* the purchase via a rebate? (i.e. "If this product really worked, they wouldn't feel the need to offer a rebate)?
  How is any of this connected to the fact that five drops daily is the dose, and exceeding this quantity doesn't add effectiveness?

label: Goal
body: Let's look for an answer that helps us connect some dots here. More than anything, we want to help convince ourselves that offering the rebate won't increase sales.

label: Henry's Conclusion
body: There must be some explanation (besides trying to send the location of food) for the honeybees' dance.

label: Henry's Evidence
body: They don't need a complicated mechanism like a dance to send the location of food; they could just leave a scent trail from the food to the hive.

label: Winnie's Response
body: There doesn't necessarily need to be some other explanation. (i.e. the honeybees' dance may genuinely be to guide other honeybees to a food source.

label: Winnie's Evidence
body: Most animals have multiple ways to accomplish the same task (some bees can navigate using position of Sun or by using memory of landmarks), so even though honeybees can use a scent trail, they can **also** use a dance.

label: Evaluate
body:
Winnie's opener, "*not necessarily"*, is clearly expressing disagreement. What was Henry saying was 'necessarily so'?
  Henry said "there **must** be some *other* explanation for the honeybee dance".
  So, Winnie's "not necessarily" would be saying,
*not necessarily. that could be the only explanation.*
  If we wanted to go farther to the underlying reasoning, Henry thinks
"It's unthinkable that the only purpose of the dance is to communicate the location of food, if the bees already have some other means of communicating food location."
  Winnie thinks
"It's perfectly thinkable that the only purpose of the dance would be a function that is somewhat redundant. It's common for animals to have redundant ways to accomplish a desired end.

label: Goal
body:
Look for something saying they disagree over whether
"if bees can use a scent trail for location of food, then that means that they **don't** use their dance primarily for location of food"

label: Henry's Conclusion
body: There must be some explanation (besides trying to send the location of food) for the honeybees' dance.

label: Henry's Evidence
body: They don't need a complicated mechanism like a dance to send the location of food; they could just leave a scent trail from the food to the hive.

label: Winnie's Response
body: There doesn't necessarily need to be some other explanation. (i.e. the honeybees' dance may genuinely be to guide other honeybees to a food source.

label: Winnie's Evidence
body: Most animals have multiple ways to accomplish the same task (some bees can navigate using position of Sun or by using memory of landmarks), so even though honeybees can use a scent trail, they can **also** use a dance.

label: Evaluate
body:
Why did Winnie mention how bees navigate? It was an example of the claim, "most animals have several ways of accomplishing critical tasks".
  These bee species are animals.
A critical task is navigating.
They have multiple ways: using position of the Sun or the memory of landmarks.

label: Goal
body:
In the context of Winnie's argument, the two different ways that some bees navigate is support for an Intermediate Conclusion (most animals have several ways of accomplishing critical tasks), which is then support for her Main Conclusion that "honeybees might use their dance, in addition to using scent trails, as a way to guide other honeybees to a food source".
  In the context of how it relates to Henry's argument, he was kind of assuming that "if honeybees can send food-directions via scent trail, then they wouldn't also have a 2nd method (like the dance) to send food-directions". So Winnie's two-ways-to-navigate example is undermining one of Henry's assumptions.

label: Politician's Conclusion (So it follows)
body: The lower the rate of income tax, the more revenue the government will generate by that tax.

label: Politician's Evidence
body: A government taxing at a 100% rate will generate no revenue because all economic activity will cease.

label: Economist's Conclusion
body:
Your conclusion can't be correct.
*rephrase:*  It is not the case that the lower the income tax rate, the more revenue the government will generate.

label: Evaluate
body:
Method question tend to test this set of 8 moves, some of which overlap:
- present an analogy
- (counter)example to a general claim
- rule out alternatives
- make a definition / distinction
       (these relate especially to rebuttals)
- raise an overlooked consideration
- call out a faulty assumption
- show bad implications of P1's logic
- suggest an alternate explanation
  The economist is clearly rebutting the politician, and she seems to be showing the bad implications of the politician's logic.
  She's saying, "The logic of your conclusion implies Y, and Y is wrong/absurd." as a way to show that the conclusion is wrong.
  The politician considered an extreme case (maximum income tax rate of 100% would generate no revenue). The economist considers the opposite extreme:  minimum income tax rate of 0% would also generate no revenue.
  This allows her to prove that "the **lower** the rate, the **higher** the revenue" is too extreme a formulation. When you take it to its logical extreme, you get the absurd idea that 0% tax rate would generate the most tax revenue.

label: Goal
body: Look for anything that matches, but it will probably sound like it's saying the economist "shows how the politician's conclusion commits him to an absurd implication".

label: Statements
body:
Sponges attached to the bottom of the ocean let seawater in, filter it, and then eject the water they've just filtered away from where their water intake is.
  *causal* (and thus are)
Tube/vase sponges don't need help from moving water to send that ejected water away, which is why they're adapted to slow-moving quiet waters.
  *causal* (because of their shape)
The tube/vase shape causes strong currents to dislodge them from the ocean floor.
  *conditional* (cannot live)
Strong current → tube/vase sponge can't live
  Tube/vase sponges were widespread during the late Jurassic period.

label: Evaluate
body:
With this many claims, it's impossible to know exactly where the answer might pull support from, but when we see *Conditional / Causal / Mathematical / Pivot* indicator words, that's usually a clue.
  And if we can find any *Overlapping Concepts*, that's also a clue about which claims will be combined.
  There's a pivot (**however**) in the second to last claim as well as a conditional (**cannot**). So that claim sticks out as being spicier.
  When we see *Conditionals* on Inference questions, we always have two specific questions on our mind:
  1. Are there other conditionals that I could chain this one up with?
(not in this case; this was the only conditional)
  2. Is there some fact that I can apply this conditional to (usually via contrapositive)?
  Yes! The contrapositive of the conditional was this:
  **if** tube/vase sponges →  **then**  not strong
    are living                                currents
  We know that both tube and vase sponges were widespread during the late Jurassic, so we can apply that conditional and derive that "not strong currents" were widespread during the late Jurassic.
  The tube/vase sponge overlaps with other claims too. We learn that they are well adapted to slow waters because they don't need help from a fast moving current to eject their post-filtered water. But we also learn that they are poorly adapted to strong currents, because those would dislodge them from the ocean floor.
  So we could see an answer synthesizing those two facts about the pace of the surrounding water ... i.e. "there is more than one reason that tube/vase sponges are found in slow-moving quiet waters".

label: Goal
body:
The most likely suspect would be applying the conditional, via contrapositive, to the final sentence, to derive that "not strong currents were widespread during the late Jurassic period".
  But stay flexible and look for the most provable answer.

label: Given that ...
body: We think the cause of migraines is purely physiological (not psychological).

label: Why is it that ...
body: Several studies find that people who have migraines tend to rank higher on the psychological anxiety score?

label: Evaluate / Goal
body:
If we believed that psychological anxiety caused migraines, then we'd expect people high on the anxiety scale to have more than average migraines.
  We don't believe that psychological anxiety causes migraines (we believe it's purely physiological). But it's still true that people higher on the anxiety scale have a higher than average number of migraines.
  Maybe it's a **reverse cause** situation — knowing your body is prone to migraines makes you be more prone to psychological anxiety.
  Maybe it's connected to a **third factor** — there's a genetic condition that predisposes people to both migraines and anxiety.
  There's also potentially a distinction they're testing between *professionally-treated* for migraines vs. people who have migraines but don't get professional treatment for it.

label: Conclusion
body:
Not all faculty members               *Not all X's are Y*
in Linguistics are full                   *(Some X's are ~Y)*
professors.

label: Evidence
body:
Every faculty member                    *All X's are Z*
in Linguistics has tenure
  Not all tenured faculty                 *Not all Z's are Y*
are full professors                     *(Some Z's are ~Y)*

label: Evaluate
body:
This argument is trying to make a Trait Overlap (or non-overlap) inference, using quantifiers. Generally speaking, if a Parallel Flaw argument has quantifiers, we can find the right answer without thinking about *why* the argument is flawed, as long as we've properly noted its structure.
  The argument tries to                   *All X's are Z*
combine these two ideas     *Some Z's are ~Y*
  in order to derive                  *Some X's are ~Y*
  That's not legal. Consider this similarly flawed argument:
  All former Presidents are men.
Some men have gone to the moon.
Thus, some former Presidents have gone to the moon.

label: Goal
body:
Find an argument combining an All/None premise with a Some/Not All premise, in order to derive a Some/Not All conclusion.
  The trigger of the All/None statement should be one of the two ideas in the conclusion.
  The overlapping term in the two premises should not be in the conclusion.
  Premise 1:         All A's are B
   Premise 2:  Some B's are ~C
 Conclusion:   Some A's are ~C

label: Conclusion
body: The chances that intelligent life will emerge on a planet are low.

label: Evidence
body: Planetary systems are unlikely to have any large planets, and without large planets like Jupiter and Saturn (whose gravity protected Earth from being frequently struck by comets), intelligent life would never have arisen on Earth.

label: Evaluate
body:
Anna's strategy is straightforward: use a past situation as a model to predict what will happen with a current proposal. "Look what happened with cacao — that's what will happen here too."
Whether her prediction is correct is a separate question. The Method question only asks how sheargues, and her tool is comparison to a past case.

label: Evaluate
body:
We start with counterevidence ... when a planetary system forms, the chances it will have a planet capable of supporting life are high. The reason the author concludes pessimism for the change of life emerging is because she's worried that w/o big planets to provide comet-protection services, this life-eligible planet will get pummeled with comets and not be able to have long enough periods of stability during which intelligent life could evolve.
  If we're playing Devil's Advocate and arguing that these life-eligible planets would actually be likely to develop intelligent life, then we need a different means for them to get protection from comets.

label: Goal
body: Look for an answer that would give you a way to say that, "even though planets in these other planetary systems wouldn't have large planets like Jupiter / Saturn, they'd still have some way to be safe from comets".

label: Given that ...
body: Method 1 (contractor gets paid a fixed % of costs) would lead to higher profits for the contractor the higher the costs, whereas Method 2 (contractors gets paid fixed amount on top of costs) would not.

label: Why is it that ...
body: It's more likely that final costs exceed initial estimates with Method 2 more than with Method 1.

label: Evaluate
body:
Since % of costs gives contractors an incentive to add more costs, we would think that they might initially estimate a job would cost $2000 (and their 20% fee would be $400), but then later they'd tell the client, "Sorry, actually we're going to need a platinum-plated wiring for the hallway, so the costs are really going to be $3000 (and thus their fee becomes $600)".
  But instead, it's more likely that a contractor who is going to be paid $500 on top of costs, whatever the costs, will initially estimate $2000 and later tell the client the costs will be more like $3000.

label: Goal
body: We need some difference between these two types of payment plans (what sort of jobs they're used on / what sort of people use them / what sort of clients agree to them) that allows us to explain why the final cost is higher than the estimate more often for the fixed-amount method, than for the fixed-percentage method.

label: Evidence
body:
That wall has several joists.
That wall has a bulge.
The only thing that could have caused the bulge is a broken joist.

label: Conclusion (therefore)
body: Thus, there is at least one broken joist.

label: Evaluate
body:
The main action of the logic here is the conditional, triggered by the fact.
  The conditional (signified by 'the only', which is a sufficient - left side - indicator) looks like this:
  *Wall bulging → broken joist*
  The argument establishes that the wall is bulging and then validly concludes that there is at least one broken joist.

label: Goal
body:
We could itemize the entire argument:
P1: That X has several A's.
P2: That X is Y.
P3:  Y → bad A.
 C: some bad A's.
  But mainly I would be caring that there's a conditional premise, a factual premise that triggers it, and a conclusion that factually declares the outcome of the conditional.

label: Sasha's Conclusion
body: The courts should ban handwriting analysis as evidence of character.

label: Sasha's Evidence
body: Handwriting analysts routinely exaggerate the reliability of their analysis.

label: Greg's Response
body: The current use of handwriting is definitely shady, but it's because there's no licensing board to set professional standards and deter this routine exaggeration of reliability. Once we have a licensing board, handwriting analysis could have a legitimate court presence as evidence of character.

label: Evaluate
body: Greg's response is mainly agreeing with Sasha. He only differs by saying, "I agree with your conclusion *temporarily* but not *permanently*." Greg identifies a causal difference-maker that currently makes handwriting analysis sketchy (lack of licensing board). He argues that if we flipped this causal difference-maker, then we'd be fine.

label: Goal
body: Hard to know what wording to predict. I would think something like, "Greg raises considerations that pinpoint the source of the problem Sasha worries about", or "Greg describes a way that Sasha's concerns could eventually be allayed such that Sasha's conclusion would no longer be valid."

label: Gregory's Conclusion
body: Only the *current* use of handwriting as evidence is problematic.

label: Gregory's Evidence
body: Right now there's no licensing board to set standards and deter frauds. When a board is established, it will be a legitimate courtroom tool.

label: Evaluate
body:
How would Sasha respond to G's claim that it's only the lack of a licensing board that is preventing handwriting analysis from being a legitimate courtroom tool?
  If we were trying to still argue that handwriting analysis as evidence of a person's character should be banned in court, what would we say about that hypothetical licensing board?
  Maybe we would just be pessimistic about whether any licensing board would really be able / willing / likely to carry out its intended job:
- maybe there's no way to set *standards* with something as variable as handwriting
- maybe the board would lack the enforcement power to deter frauds
- maybe the board would quickly become filled with personnel who themselves have fraudulent expertise.

label: Goal
body: Look for an answer saying that the "even a licensing board couldn't solve the problem of using handwriting analysis as a legit piece of evidence indicating a person's character, because .... [ answer choice ] ."

label: Powell's 1st Claim
body:
Private waste-removal companies spend 60% of what public waste-removal companies spend per customer. Does Freeman disagree with this?
No, there's nothing he says that objects to that comparison. In fact, he seems to accept that they spend different amounts, because he's saying private companies choose to serve "less costly" customers, so that the companies don't have to spend as much to serve those customers.

label: Powell's 2nd Claim
body:
Private companies give their customers at least as good service as public companies do.
Does Freeman disagree with this?
No, there's nothing he says that makes it sound like one type of company provides better/worse service than the other type.

label: Goal
body: Find the answer that says: predicts a proposal's outcome by comparing it to a past situation.

body: The desirability of our meals has decreased.
