body: Find evidence that flat-footed kids develop arches just as well without the shoes.

label: Powell's 3rd Claim
body:
Private companies work more efficiently than public ones do.
Does Freeman disagree with this?
Yes. This is Powell's conclusion and Freeman says it's unwarranted. That doesn't mean that Freeman believes theopposite, but it means that Freeman doesn't find Powell's logic convincing.
Freeman thinks that it's possible there's an alternate explanation for why private companies only spend 60% as much as public companies do to provide a comparable quality of service ---the private companies get to cherry-pick doing business with the cheapest customers.
Meanwhile, public utilities have to serve everyone, even those houses way up on the hill or on the outskirts of town (the ones that are more costly to serve).

label: Goal
body: Look for something like, "They disagree over whether the fact that private companies only spend 60% as muchimpliesthat private companies work more efficiently."

label: Statements
body:
math-y comparison
A higher % of smaller birds than larger birds survived the month-long study.
pivot (however)
It's probably wrong to conclude that size is causally affecting chance of survival over a month-long period, because smaller blackbirds are generally younger than larger ones.

label: Evaluate
body:
This has the feel of an Explain Curious Fact argument, even though we're reading it in the context of an Inference question.
It also Ends with a Pivot (however), and the pivot is serving the role of rebutting someone, so we'd expect the correct answer to feel like a safely worded rebuttal.
Curious Fact ... why did a bigger share of smaller birds than larger birds survive over the course of a month?
Yasukawa's Explanation ... the size of the bird affects its chances of survival (being smaller helps you live longer)
The author takes issue with this and suggests an alternative explanation:
Author's Alternate Explanation ... the smaller ones lived longer because they were younger. (being younger makes you more likely to live longer)

label: Goal
body:
This paragraph is a weird mix offacts(the study results / the generalization that smaller birds are usually younger) andopinions(Y's explanation that "small size is helping them live longer" / the author's explanation that "younger age is helping them live longer").
But the question stem does tell us to treat them all the statements as true. There is a statement saying "Y's conclusion is probably mistaken". So we can treat it as true that Y is probably wrong to think that size determines a blackbird's chances of survival.

label: Yasukawa's Research
body:
A higher % of smaller birds than larger birds survived the month-long study.
This must mean that size is a determinant of a blackbird's chances of survival.

label: The Criticism
body: You're ignoring an alternate explanation for why the smaller birds were more likely to survive. It's not because of their small size. It's because of their young age.

label: Evaluate / Goal
body:
This unusual question task wants us to pick an answer that will say, "No, no, no, critic. Your objection isn't valid. You don't seem to realize that [answer choice]."
Let's find something that would potentially respond to the criticism that the data really might just be telling us that theageis the determinant of a blackbird's chances of survival. Maybe Yasukawa controlled for age and found that even within the same age group, smaller ones were more likely to survive.
Maybe the answer will help us say that "age isalsoa determinant, but size is still a determinant of survival likelihood".

label: Conclusion (this surely reflects = opinion)
body: Many Japanese collectors preferred certain aesthetic attributes of 19th century Impressionist paintings.

label: Evidence
body: During the 1980's Japanese collectors were very active in the market for European art, especially buying up 19th century Impressionist paintings.

label: Evaluate
body:
Since the author is interpreting the meaning behind a group of people's behavior, we can use our Explain Curious Fact mindset.
Curious Fact ... Why were these Japanese collectors so interested in buying 19th century Impressionist paintings?
Author's Explanation ... They had a preference for certain aesthetic attributes found in those paintings.
We always analyze this framework by asking the same two questions: 1. Could there be some Alternate Explanation for the curious fact? 2. How plausible is the Author's Explanation?

label: Goal
body:
We can strengthen byruling outan alternate explanation for why Japanese collectors were so interested in buying 19th century Impressionist paintings (theyweren'tbuying them just to turn around and re-sell them at a profit / theyweren'tbuying them just to acquire famous art to enhance their status despite not really liking the paintings aesthetically).
Or we can strengthen byadding plausibilityto the idea that these Japanese collectors really dug certain aesthetic properties of 19th century Impressionist paintings.

label: Conclusion (Anna)
body: Frankie's plan would fail — incentivizing cloudberry use would not raise income for cloudberry gatherers, because farms would supplant wild gatherers.

label: Evidence
body: Cacao was once gathered from wild plants. When demand grew, gatherers couldn't keep up, farms took over, and now all cacao is farmed. Anna projects the same trajectory for cloudberries.

label: Evaluate
body: Anna's technique: take a past case (cacao) and apply its trajectory to a current proposal (cloudberries). She uses the past situation as a model to predict what will happen if Frankie's plan is adopted.

label: Goal
body: The right answer should describe Anna's use of a past case to project the outcome of a current proposal.

label: Conclusion (Anna)
body: Frankie's plan would fail; farmed cloudberries would replace wild gatherers.

label: Evidence
body: Cacao followed exactly that trajectory: when demand rose, farms took over from wild gatherers.

label: Evaluate
body: Anna projects the future of cloudberries by analogy to the past of cacao.

label: Goal
body: Identify Anna's technique: applying a past situation to forecast the outcome of a present proposal.

label: Conclusion (Anna)
body: Anna says Frankie's incentive plan won't actually help cloudberry gatherers.

label: Evidence
body: Her reason: this exact pattern played out before with cacao. Demand went up, gatherers couldn't keep up, farms moved in, and now all the cacao is farmed. Anna says cloudberries will go the same way.

label: Evidence (given that)
body: Looking at individual restaurants, every restaurant that operated last year and two years ago sold a lower number of meals.

label: Evaluate
body:
Given that ... every restaurant that's been open for at least two years reported selling fewer meals this year than last year,
How could we say that ... the desirability of the meals has not decreased?
We could come up with alternate explanations for why all the restaurants sold fewer meals this year than last year, explanations that don't relate to the meals being less desirable.
- Maybe it's "the Starbucks effect" where the restaurant builds so many locations that they steal business from each other (like if you've ever seen two Starbucks that are ridiculously close to each other in the same town, it's pretty much a guarantee that the 2nd location steals some business from the 1st location)
- Maybe this restaurant serves delicious junk food, and there's a local diet craze that means that even though people still desire the food as much as before, they're buying it less often to stay true to their diet
- Maybe this restaurant raised its prices, so even though people desire the meals, they can't afford to eat there as frequently.

label: Goal
body:
When an author is Explaining / Interpreting a Curious Fact, ("the reason individual restaurants are selling fewer meals than before is that consumers desire our meals less than before"), we weaken either with - An Alternate Explanation for the curious fact or by - Undermining the plausibility of the author's explanation
So we need a different reason why fewer meals are being sold at the restaurants that have been open 2+ years, or we need some fact that makes it seem like consumers desire these meals as much or more than before.

label: Conclusion (Therefore)
body: Pesticides are definitely contaminating the river.

label: Evidence
body: A local plant makes pesticides that can cause sterility in small mammals such as otters. Soon after the plant began operating, the incidence of sterility among the otters in a nearby river increased dramatically.

label: Evaluate
body:
The author is trying to Explain a Curious Fact: Why did the incidence of sterility among local otters go up so much?
She takes one possible explanation: Maybe it's because of that new plant that started operating; they produce pesticides that can cause sterility in otters
and overconfidently concludes that thisisthe explanation: The pesticides aredefinitelycontaminating the river

label: Goal
body:
To match this famousCausalflaw, we would want at a minimum a) A curious fact b) A conclusion in which the author overconfidently is sure of one possible explanation for that fact
To match it more closely, the curious fact should be a chronological association:
The supposed effect started happeningsoon afterthe supposed cause started happening

label: Facts
body:
comparison
natural fibers (f.e. cotton): shrink when washed on hot artificial fibers (f.e. polyester): don't shrink when hot-washed
causal connector (the reason for this is)
tightly curled >> shrink when hot-washed in orig state
causal + conditional (cause / all)
Hot wash >> fibers return to orig state

label: Evaluate
body:
We know two things about hot-washing and two things about natural fibers and two things about original state. So there's got to be some inference in these overlapping concepts. 1) hot-washing return to original state 2) hot-washing shrinks natural fibers 3) original state of natural fibers is tightly curled
It sounds like we can infer that when natural fibers go from artificially straightened back to their original tightly curled state, that shrinks the clothes.
If that's the case, then the fact that artificial fibers don't shrink when hot-washed is an indication that their original state is NOT tightly curled.

label: Goal
body: Pick the most provable answer. It'll probably deal with the implied cause effect connection of "going from straight to curled >> shrinks clothes" or the implied difference of "artificial fibers aren't not tightly curled to begin with".

label: Premises
body:
Here's the picture: cotton fibers are naturally curled. To turn them into cloth, manufacturers stretch them straight. When you wash cotton at high heat, the fibers snap back to curled — that's why your shirt shrinks. Polyester clothes don't shrink.
One more important fact: high heat returnsallfibers to their original state, not just natural ones.

label: Evaluate
body:
Now think about polyester. High heat returns it to its original state too — but polyester clothes don't shrink. The fiber doesn't change shape when heated. So whatever its original state is, it must already match its in-cloth state, which is straight.
Putting it together: polyester (and other artificial fibers) must already be straight in their original state.

label: Goal
body: Find the answer that says: artificial fibers are straight in their original state.

label: Conclusion
body: This is not really important. (rephrase: It's not really important that many popular psychological theories are inelegant and do nothing to help dispel the mystery that surrounds our psyche.)

label: Intermediate Conclusion
body: The theories produce the right results

label: Evidence ( ":" )
body: The theories have greater therapeutic success than their more scientific rivals.

label: Evaluate
body:
Whenever we read Role and Main Conclusion paragraphs, we prime ourselves for a Conclusion in the first sentence or a Conclusion that feels like a rebuttal (these two patterns dominate arguments for those two question types).
When the first sentence begins, "Many popular theories are poor theories", thatdoessound like the author's opinion, and she even provides a couple reasons to support that opinion (inelegant / don't dispel mystery).
But then she pivots away from that into a different opinion:this isn't important.
Why? Because the theories produce the right results (more therapeutic success).

label: Goal
body: We're being asked about the final claim, which is a Premise that directly supports the Intermediate Conclusion and indirectly supports the Main Conclusion.

label: Tony's Conclusion (therefore)
body: The special association in the public mind between anarchism and political violence is unwarranted.

label: Tony's Evidence
body: Few anarchists have ever performed violent actions, and these few are vastly outnumbered by the violent adherents of other political ideologies.

label: Keisha's Implied Conclusion
body: The association between anarchism and political violence may be warranted.

label: Keisha's Intermediate Conclusion
body: The proportion of anarchists who are violent is possibly greater than that of other ideologies.

label: Keisha's Premise
body: Anarchists have always been few in number, whereas other ideologies have often spawned mass movements.

label: Evaluate
body:
When we're describing someone's Method of response, it normally takes one of these forms: - Suggests alternate explanation - Raises overlooked consideration - Calls out dubious assumption - Shows undesirable implications of 1st person's logic
In this case, Keisha seems to raise an overlooked consideration that reframes the original evidence.
Yes, violence by other ideologies outnumbers violence by anarchists, if you look atraw numbers. But if you look at percentages / rates, maybe not.
In order words: If there are 100 anarchists, and only 10 engage in violence, that's 10% of anarchists.
Meanwhile: If there are 1,000,000 people in a mass movement of some other ideology, and 10,000 of them engage in violence, that's only 1% of them that are violent.
Keisha's point is that the public perception that anarchists are more associated with violence could be true, in a relative sense (even though it's not true in the absolute sense).

label: Goal
body: Look for any answer with language we can match up with Keisha's argument.

label: Conclusion
body: Sound-change theory in general must be discarded.

label: Intermediate Conclusion (since)
body: The classical account must be discarded.

label: Evidence
body: The classical account's central tenet was that sound change occurs gradually, but recent research shows that sound change isn't gradual; it often emerges suddenly.

label: Evaluate
body:
This question stem looks like Sufficient Assumption because of the "if assumed" but it's only a Strengthen question because it just asks what does the most to justify the conclusion.
We can still use our Sufficient Assumption brain (heavy on conditional logic), but we want to appreciate that the correct answer might come more from the conversational world of Strengthen.
Using our conditional logic brain, we'd think 1. We need to prove "sound-change in general must be discarded" 2. They haven't announced any rule like, "If xyz is true, then must be discarded", so the correct answer will need to give me that rule. 3. The reason for discarding it, in general, is that the classical account must be discarded.
That would lead us to anticipating a missing link answer like: "If the classical account must be discarded, then sound-change theory in general must be discarded".
Using our Strengthen brain, we'd think, "what objections could someone make to this argument? How could one accept that classical account must be discarded but argue that sound-theory in general doesn't need to be?"
An opponent could say, "Why don't we just get rid of the classical account but keep sound-change in general?
If we're trying to strengthen, we want to make that option sound like it's not viable, something like "classical account is basically 90% of sound-change theory in general, so if you get rid of classical, you are getting rid of the majority of sound-change theory".

label: Goal
body:
Let's find an answer that strengthens the connection between the premise and the Intermediate Conclusion (if recent research shows that new sounds often emerge suddenly, then classical's central tenet is ruined and thus classical should be discarded).
Or let's find an answer that strengthens the connection between the Intermediate Conclusion and the Main Conclusion (if we're getting rid of the classical account, we should just get rid of sound-change theory in general).

label: Conclusion
body: The stable functioning of a society depends upon the relatively long-term stability of the goals of its citizens.

label: Evidence (This is clear from the fact that)
body: If a most individuals don't have a predictable or enduring set of aspirations, it will be impossible for a legislature to craft laws that augment their satisfaction, and it should be obvious that a society is stable only if its laws tend to increase the happiness of its citizens.

label: Evaluate
body:
This paragraph is made to be very hard to read. Whenever we do Role and Main Conclusion, though, we know that there's an 80% or better chance that we'll hear the Conclusionbeforewe hear its Supporting idea(s).
So we always read the paragraph on Role and Main Conclusion with a special ear for conclusions in the first sentence. This first sentence doesn't sound like an opinion, so we wouldn't initially know it was the conclusion.
But then the second sentence tells us it was the conclusion, by indicating that now we are trying to support that claim.
This suspect is guilty.This is clear from the fact thathe had a motive and that his fingerprints are on the murder weapon.
The verdict is clear from the facts of the evidence. The conclusion is clear from the facts of the evidence.
The other keyword that's useful here is 'and', which almost always joins two Premises.
So using keywords and knowing the usual tendency of Role and Main Conclusion to put the Conclusionearlierthan the Supporting idea(s) are both very useful when it comes to sorting out this paragraph.
In terms of making it more conversational, the first sentence is saying,
"Society won't be able to function in a stable way if the citizens don't have stable goals in terms of what they want out of life / country."
After all, a government won't be able to write policy in ways that help citizens if most citizens are frequently shifting in terms of what goals they aspire to. And if If a society's laws are helping citizens, then obviously society won't be stable.

label: Goal
body:
They're asking us about the third claim, which is one of the two Premises.
So we'll look for stuff likepremiseevidencepartial support(because there's more than one premise)

label: Curious Fact
body: Why do weightless astronauts frequently get motion sickness?

label: Hypothesis (best explained by)
body: Their brains are getting conflicting information. They see they're moving, but their inner ears indicate they're not moving.

label: Evidence
body: Conflicting received by the brain about the body's motion causes motion sickness.

label: Evaluate
body:
This is an Explain Curious Fact pattern, where the curious phenomenon is that astronauts experience motion sickness in weightless conditions. The author explains this with the hypothesis that conflicting information between visual and inner ear signals causes motion sickness.
Almost always, we strengthen a hypothesis by adding some plausibility to it (usually in "no cause, no effect" form), but occasionally we do so by ruling out an alternate explanation.
"No cause, no effect" in this case would be something like, "when they don't have conflicting sensory information, they don't have motion sickness".

label: Goal
body: Let's find an answer that provides additional support for the hypothesis that conflicting sensory information causes motion sickness (or that rules out an alternate explanation).

body:
On the hunt for Conditional, Causal, Quantitative, or Pivot wording, we find some Causal ideas and a final Pivot.
Causal (can cause)Pollen Release Inflamed nasal tissue, (and ⇢ of ⇢ runny nose, sneezing, others) histamine and congestion
Causal (minimize / by blocking)Antihistamines ⇢ Block ⇢ Minimize action of allergy histamine symptoms
Interestingly, to me, it didn't say that antihistamines stop the histamine from being released from the cells, just that it neutralizes the effects that histamine would normally have.
Pivot (however)Histamine plays no role in how colds produce symptoms.

label: Evaluate / Goal
body:
Since our goal in reading Inference paragraphs is to look for ways to synthesize information (combine 2 or more facts to derive some other statement), the causal chains we checked out involve combining ideas together.
So the correct answer might just be rewarding our understanding of that causal chain, like "certain allergy treatments are able to reduce congestion and sneezing by reducing the effects of a chemical released from nose cells".
But... (pun intended)... it is very common when an Inference paragraph ends with a Pivot (but, yet, however), that the intended synthesis is integrating that last fact with the stuff we were told prior.
So given all we learned about histamine / antihistamine, what truth can we derive from the fact that histamine plays no role in how colds produce their symptoms?
The correct answer will likely be testing what this final fact tells us, in light of all the stuff we heard before it.

label: Evaluation
body:
This is kind of a mess. When we read that novels don't usually exploit the musical characteristics of language (after having just learned that this is one of the definitional qualities of a poem), we could infer that novels are usually not poems. Technically, that looks like we're doing an illegal negation (if you're not the left side, you're not the right side), but in context the first sentence feels to me like a bi-conditional.
Since it's definitional, it seems fair to say that if you fit that definition, you are a poem and if you don't fit that definition you aren't a poem.
We could similarly infer that limericks are not poems, since they don't have the definitional ingredient of being a work of art.

label: Goal
body: Because of how messy the facts are, I would primarily think about the two conditionals we were given. We have the power to prove something is a poem. We have the power to prove something isn't art.

label: Conclusion (should = opinion)
body: Exports of phones and fax machines should be exempted from the ban. Rephrase: We should be allowed to continue exporting phones and fax machines to country S.

label: Evidence
body: We want to pressure country S to become less repressive. And it's impossible for a country to remain repressive when telecommunication equipment is widely available to that country's population.

label: Evaluate
body:
So the manufacturers of phones and fax machines are thinking that even though we're blocking most exports from S, because we're trying to get them to be more open / less repressive, we should still send S phones and fax machines.
This plan is assuming that by sending them phones and fax machines, the population of that country will be better able to communicate and thus will be irrepressible.
Since this is a real-world type plan, it's probably unlikely that we're being tested on a Linking idea and more likely the correct answer will Defend against a potential objection.
Given that ... it's impossible for a country to remain repressive once telecom equipment is widely available to its people,
How can we argue that ... we shouldnotexport phones and fax machines to S?
If the exported phones and fax machines made it so that telecom equipment was widely available, then that would break S's repressive grip of its people (which is desired). So if we're going to fight this plan, we need to argue that we would ship out these phones / fax machines, but itwouldn'tever become the case that the telecom equipment would be widely available to S's population.
Maybe the leaders of S wouldn't distribute the phones and fax machines; they would just sell them to some other country put more money into the corrupt government's coffers.

label: Goal
body: Look for an answer that, if negated, gives us a way to argue that weshould notexport phones and fax machines to country S, or an answer that seems to reflect something the manufacturers are clearly thinking as they sell us on this plan of theirs.

label: Conditionals
body: Bureaucratically controlled → hierarchical organization

label: Facts
body:
PWD is bureaucratically controlled (so, it's hierarchical). It operates very differently from how other bureaucratically controlled (hierarchical) organizations operate.
Some people say, "if you know an organization is hierarchical, then you know everything about how it operates".

label: Evaluation
body:
There were three critical overlapping terms: bureaucratically controlled / hierarchical / how an organization operates.
This paragraph seems to be setting us up to say,Some Peopleare wrong.
They essentially said "all hierarchical organizations operate the same way. Once you know it's a hierarchical organization, you know everything about how it operates."
Not so fast,Some People --the PWD operates very differently from most other hierarchical bureaucracies, so I wouldn't be sure how a hierarchical bureaucracy operates if I weren't sure whether it was in the PWD club or in the "most other" club.

label: Goal

label: Conclusion
body: It's quite likely that Tom is an extreme insomniac.

label: Evidence (since)
body: Tom drinks a lot of coffee, and 90% of extreme insomniacs consume large amounts of coffee.

label: Evaluate
body:
This is not a great way to argue. 90% of prisoners in maximum-security prisons drink coffee every morning. I drink coffee every morning. Does that make it quite likely that I am a prisoner in a maximum-security prison?
Of course not. Just like conditional statements, "most" statements cannot be read backwards.
GIVEN - All Senators speak English. CAN INFER - Bob is a Senator. Thus, he speaks English. CAN'T INFER - Bob speaks English. Thus, he is a Senator. GIVEN - Most Senators are men. CAN INFER - Charlie is a Senator. Thus, Charlie is probably a man. CAN'T INFER - Charlie is a man. Thus, Charlie is probably a Senator.
GIVEN - Most extreme insomniacs drink lots of coffee. CAN INFER - Tom is an extreme insomniac. Thus, it is quite likely that he drinks a lot of coffee. CAN'T INFER - Tom drinks a lot of coffee. Thus, it is quite likely that he is an extreme insomniac.

label: Evidence
body: The tour groups trample most of the small shrubs that are necessary to the survival of any monarch butterflies that fall off the trees.

label: Goal
body: Look for an answer describing the way the author is reading this Most statement in an illegal backwards way. Or look for an answer making the objection that "it's possible that most coffee drinkers aren't extreme insomniacs". In that case, knowing that Tom is a coffee drinker would lead to the conclusion that he likely isn't an extreme insomniac.

label: Conclusion
body: Oral traditions are preferable to written one.

label: Evidence
body:
Oral traditions (which requireexclusivedependence on speech) improve the memory, whereas literate populations (which presumably have written histories) end up with sluggish recall because they can just run to written sources as needed.
Also, writing has no limits (presumably memory / oral traditions do have limits), so it can become so abundant that both writer and reader become confused.
Meanwhile, oral traditions don't suffer from the same accumulation of excess material, because whatever's useless / irrelevant is quickly eradicated.

label: Evaluate
body:
We ascertain that the first sentence is the Main Conclusion because of theopinion indicator"preferable", combined with the fact that the author proceeds to support that opinion with the rest of the paragraph.
There are two main advantages offered in the evidence for why oral history is better than written history:
1. Oral is better for the memory 2. Oral is less likely to lead to an overabundance of material (which can confuse the audience and the speaker)

label: Goal
body:
Since there are two premises, either one might be involved in how the correct answer strengthens. We can pre-phrase what each of those sounds like 1. Whichever tradition is better at improving / maintaining memory ispreferable.
or
2. Whichever tradition is better at pruning away useless, excessive material so that the speaker/reader are clearer on what remains ispreferable.

label: Conclusion (therefore)
body: Personnel managers should not inquire about a candidate's hobbies.

label: Evidence
body:
They inquire because they're hoping that the enthusiasm someone shows for a hobby may well carry over to enthusiasm for a job.
But such enthusiasm may also indicate that the candidate is less concerned with work than with play.

label: Evaluate
body:
So because someone who's enthusiastic about their hobbymaybe more concerned with play than with work, we shouldn't ask people about their hobbies?
It's not even clear this is a significant downside, but even if it is, what if it's outweighed by the positive aspects of asking about hobbies?

label: Goal
body:
Since this is an EXCEPT question, we're less inclined to try to figure out "the" answer ahead of time. After all, there will be four answers that describe a potential objection.
So we move a little more quickly toward the answers, knowing we're not going to anticipate them all, so we might as well get busy.

label: Conclusion
body: It's unreasonable to believe that someone has ESP, just because they've had a few vivid dreams that later came true.

label: Evidence
body: The vast majority of a person's dreams do not come true.

label: Evaluate / Goal
body:
This is sort of saying, "Just because a broken clock is right twice a day, doesn't mean it can tell time."
We want some sort of argument that's like, "If you're wrong the vast majority of the time, you don't get special credit the few times that you're right".

label: Conclusion (therefore)
body: Cable companies will be displaced by the new television services offered by phone companies within a few years.

label: Evidence
body: The average cable company offers 50 channels, but phone companies using fiber-optic lines will be able to offer 100-150 channels at the same price.

label: Evaluate
body:
This author is making the prediction that "because phone companies will be able to offer more channels at the same price as cable, phone companies will beat cable".
This assumes that "more channels" is actually a selling point, so we could Strengthen by saying "consumers want as many channels as they can get", or something to that effect.
In order to Strengthen a case, we need to know its vulnerabilities, so we might also want to think about how someone could make the argument that "even though phone companies will be able to offer 100-150 channels at the same price that cable offers 50, phone companies won't take over within the next few years".
We could say stuff like, - The channels on cable are better (ESPN, Bravo, etc.) than the channels offered on fiber optic (150 channels that all show syndicated TV shows from the 1970s).
- The customer service reps for the cable company are much better to deal with than those at the phone company
- Fiber optic cable won't be available in enough places for that many people to make the switch
- They'll be a disinformation campaign that fiber optic cable (cough: 5G) is a sinister ploy to allow the government to eavesdrop in our homes
- People are committed to a five-year contract with their cable provider, and it's very expensive to break that contract

label: Goal
body:
Let's look for a Linking idea connecting "more channels" with "consumers want that / that would motivate them to switch providers".
Or look for an answer that addresses the broader Net Gain / Loss attached to this decision. Someone might decide to stay with cable because even though they wish they had 100-150 channels, there are other aspects of cable that are better.
So any answer that picks some other aspect besides # of channels and tells us that fiber-optic is at least as good as cable can also strengthen.

body: White-footed mice are strictly nocturnal — they spendalldaytime hours in their underground nests.

label: Evaluate
body: Chain the premises: deer ticks drop off between noon and sunset (daytime). During daytime, white-footed mice are in their nests. Therefore, when a deer tick drops off a white-footed mouse, that mouse is in its underground nest — and so the tick drops off inside the nest.

body: Find the answer that says deer ticks drop off white-footed mice in the mice's nests.

body: Chain: ticks drop off during daytime; mice are in nests during daytime; so ticks drop off in the nests.

Given how strong the word 'necessary' it is, it conveys that if not small shrubs → can't survive
If the tourists are destroying most of the small shrubs, is there any way to say that they're not endangering the monarch population?
We could say, "The tourists are only destroyingmostof the shrubs. The monarchs can still live off the remaining ones." But that's a pretty weak retort. If we're destroying most of the shrubs theyneedto survive, we're definitelyendangeringthem, even if they're able to barely hang on with the remaining shrubs.
So what other wiggle room is there? There's actually a conditional that hasn't been triggered:
"The shrubs are necessary to the survival ofanymonarchs that fall off a tree".

label: Conclusion
body: If you are not well versed in history due to a lack of reading, it will not be easy for you to impress intellectuals.

label: Evidence
body: If you know a lot about history, it will be easy for you to impress intellectuals (history → easy to impress). If you haven't read a lot of history books, you don't know much about history (no reading → no history).

label: Evaluate
body: The argument shows: no reading → no history. Then it leaps to: no history → not easy to impress. But the only premise we have is that history issufficientfor easy impressing — knowing history makes it easy. That doesn't mean history is theonlypath. Maybe other things make impressing intellectuals easy too. The argument treats a sufficient condition as if it were necessary.

label: Goal
body: The right answer should point out other paths to easily impressing intellectuals — i.e., that history isn't the only route.

label: Conclusion
body: If you're not well versed in history because you haven't read, you can't easily impress intellectuals.

label: Evidence
body: History knowledge makes impressing intellectuals easy; reading is required for history knowledge.

label: Evaluate
body: The argument treats history knowledge as the only route to easy impressing — but the premise only said it's sufficient, not required.

label: Goal
body: Identify that there could be other easy ways to impress intellectuals.

label: Conclusion
body: The author tells us: if you haven't read history books, you won't easily impress intellectuals.

label: Evidence
body: Two facts. (1) Knowing history is enough to make impressing intellectuals easy. (2) Reading history books is required to know history.

label: Evaluate
body:
Watch this carefully. The first premise only says historyguaranteeseasy impressing — not that history is theonlyway to impress. But the conclusion needs that stronger claim. The argument quietly converts "history makes it easy" into "only history makes it easy."
Think of it this way: "If you're a millionaire, paying rent is easy. So if you're not a millionaire, paying rent isn't easy." That obviously misses the point — there are plenty of other ways to find rent affordable. Same issue here.

label: Goal
body: The right answer should point out that there are other easy ways to impress intellectuals besides knowing history.

body: It's possible for people to go to Mars and back, using this device.

body:
What was currently preventing a round trip was the weight of the fuel we would need. We couldn't launch something that heavy.
This device will allow us to take half as much fuel, because we can create fuel from the Martian atmosphere for the return trip.

label: Evaluate
body:
Because this is giving off Plan / Goal vibes, I would probably eschew looking for a missing link and try to think of potential Plan objections.
Is it notfeasibleto use this device? (can we launch this spaceship from earth?) Would it fail tocooperateas intended (like could it really make fuel from the atmosphere? how long would that take? what if weird conditions thwarted the process?) Could itbackfire? Could this device somehow make the craft even heavier?

body: The correct answer might link "if can refuel on Mars, then can make round trip", but more likely it'll rule out some objection to the Plan. We'll probably be using the negation test.

label: P's Conclusion
body: Complying with the new safety regulations isuseless.

label: P's Evidence
body: Even if the regulations had been in effect before last year's fire, they wouldn't have prevented it because they don't address its underlying causes.

label: Q's Implicit Conclusion
body: Complying isuseful.

label: Q's Evidence
body: Any regulations that can prevent waste are useful. The new regulations would prevent some accidents, and accidents always waste money.

label: Evaluate
body: We start on Disagree by assessing whether P2 disagrees with any of P1's explicit claims, and in this case Q is definitely pushing back against P's first claim.

label: Goal
body: Let's look for an about whether or not complying with the new safety regulations is useful.

label: P's position
body: Compliance is useless because the regulations wouldn't have prevented last year's fire.

label: Q's position
body: Compliance is useful because preventing accidents prevents wasted money.

label: Evaluate
body: P and Q take opposite stands on the usefulness of compliance.

label: Q's Response
body: If the regulations can potentially prevent money from being wasted, then they're useful. And the new safety regulations will prevent some accidents, which would prevent money from being wasted.

label: Evaluate
body:
Q is attempting to undermined P's conclusion but isn't disputing P's evidence. Nothing Q said is suggesting that the new safety regulations would have prevented last year's fire or would address its underlying causes.
Q seems to implicitly accept those ideas, but they bring up new considerations that argue against P's conclusion.
Q's evidence cites a principle "any regs that prevent wasted money are useful" and then shows how the new regulations satisfy the trigger of that principle.

label: Goal
body: Look for something like, "Raises new considerations, such as a general principle, that fight P's conclusion without challenging P's evidence".

label: Critique
body: It was dangerous to health for nutrition education to promote daily consumption of food from the four food groups, milk / meat / fruit & veggies / breads & cereals.

label: Evaluate / Goal
body: Well, there's really nothing for us to do but head to the answers. We need to get rid of four answers that give us a way to explain how this advice had potentially dangerous results.

label: Summary
body:
It doesn't make a ton of sense to worry about the "argument" here, since the question is very specifically about picking a word that would function in the same way that "absentee" did.
The author started by proposing a general rule:
If it ends in "-ee", then it designates the person affected by someone else.
An employee is employed by someone. A payee is paid by someone. A detainee is detained by someone.
But then the author thinks of an exception:absentee.
An absentee isn'tabsenteedby someone.

label: Goal
body: So we need to find a word that has the same problem as absentee had. It doesn't end up referring to an action that someone else did to you.

label: Conclusion
body: The reason some patients who have not been taking penicillin develop penicillin-resistant bacteria is that they have mercury fillings.

label: Evidence
body:
The genes that give bacteria mercury-resistance are in the same chromosomal spot as the genes that give bacteria resistance to penicillin (so there are probably bacteria that have resistance to both).
The mercury fillings in these patients' teeth are killing off all the bacteria, except the ones that have mercury resistance. But those arealsothe bacteria that have penicillin-resistance. That's why bacteria of the penicillin-resistant variety are emerging in the mouths of these people.

label: Evaluate
body:
The question stem is asking us about the role of an unstated assumption, which is insanely weird. As far as I know, this is the only Role question that's ever asked about the role of anunstatedclaim.
Was the argument assuming that people whodotake penicillindodevelop penicillin-resistant bacteria?
Sure?
This is all so weird. Our outside knowledge is hopefully familiar with the concept of "super bacteria", the ones that have resistance to antibiotics, so the medical community is terrified of them. Doctors are scared to prescribe too many antibiotics, because when you give a patient an antibiotic, it kills off an entire class of bacteria. However, if some bacteria have a cool mutation that allows them to evade this antibacterial massacre, then they are the "last men on Earth", so they re-populate the world in their image.
Thus, the more we use antibacterial stuff, the more we're killing off the type of bacteria that our chemicals work on, and by killing off all that bacteria, we're enabling the scary kind of bacteria that our chemicalsdon'twork on to proliferate more and more and potentially turn into the more dominant strain.
So we know / assume that people who take penicillin (an antibiotic), will kill off all the bacteria that's vulnerable to penicillin, leaving only the bacteria that are resistant to penicillin to survive and "re-populate the environment".
In the first sentence, what wedidn'tunderstand was why penicillin resistance would emerge in someone whowasn'ttaking penicillin, someone whowasn'ttaking a substance that would kill off all bacteria but the penicillin-resistant kind.

label: Goal
body:
I have no idea what we should be looking for, because it's not playing any normal role like Main Conclusion, Support, Opposing, Neutral.
Of those, I would pickNeutral, because the thing they're asking us about is not even really relevant to the paragraph we read, which was about people whoweren'ttaking penicillin.
Let's look for something like, "Weexpect/assumepeople who take penicillin will sometimes develop penicillin-resistant bacteria, but we didn't understand why people who aren't taking penicillin would develop that kind of bacteria as well."

label: Conclusion
body: Some reporter can scoop all of the other reporters ("scoop" means that they can report something first, that the others don't know yet)

label: Evidence
body: Since all the reporters are getting their info solely from the press agent, if the press agent told every reporter everything, then no reporters would know anything special, and thus no press agent could scoop anyone else. But the press agent didn't tell every reporter everything about the accident.

label: Evaluate
body:
Because we see Flaw + Conditional Logic, we should immediately be thinking about the famousNecessary vs. Sufficientflaw, in which the author presents conditional logic in the premises but thinks about some rule or rules in an illegal Backwards or Opposite fashion.
Given: A → B Illegal: B → A (backwards) Illegal: ~A → ~B (opposite)
We had this conditional chain:
Press agent told all reporters no every reporter → know same → reporter everything can scoop
The author is arguing in an illegal opposite fashion, saying:
Press agentdid nottell → some reporter every reporter everythingcanscoop

label: Goal
body:
Look for an answer naming the Necessary vs. Sufficient flaw, or an answer objecting that "even if the press agentdid nottell every reporter everything, it's still possible thatnoreporters can scoop the others".
Maybe the press agent only told 1/2 the story, but she told the same 1/2 to all the reporters. In such a case, the press agent didn't tell every reporter everything, but none of them could scoop any of the others because they're all briefed on the exact same subset of facts.

label: Conclusion
body: Tennyson's line of poetry "nature, red in tooth and claw" is misconstrued by many evolutionists as a reference to Darwin's theory of evolution. This means Tennyson's line of poetry was not meant to refer to Darwin's theory of evolution.

label: Evidence
body: It's possible that the resemblance between his book and those futuristic ones is just that all the others were drawing on the same body of literary conventions that they had been exposed to over the course of their own reading.

label: Evidence
body: The poem in which the line appears was published in 1850, but Darwin kept his theory closely held until publishing it in 1859. In addition, in view of the context provided by the rest of the poem, the line was clearly meant to refer to the dominant biological theory of the early nineteenth century, which was a creationist theory.

label: Evaluate
body: Most arguments on Main Conclusion are Rebuttal style, leveraging opposing descriptors like "misconstrued" to alert us that the author disagrees with the common interpretation. Here, the argument clarifies that Tennyson's line is not a reference to Darwin's theory, providing publication timelines and contextual details from the poem.

label: Goal
body: Identify the best answer that reflects Tennyson’s line of poetry is not a reference to Darwin’s theory of evolution.

label: Conclusion (misconstrued = opinion)
body:
Tennyson's line, "nature, red in tooth and claw" is misconstrued by many evolutionists as a reference to Darwin's theory of evolution.
rephrase: When Tennyson said "nature, red in tooth and claw", he wasnotreferring to Darwin's theory.

label: Evidence
body:
That line appears in a poem published in 1850, but Darwin kept his theory secret until it was published in 1859.
Additionally, you can tell from the rest of the poem that the line is meant to refer to creationist theory that dominated biological theory at the time.

label: Evaluate
body:
Whenever we do Role and Main Conclusion, we remind ourselves that 90% of the time the conclusion will be the First Sentence or a Rebuttal.
Here, the conclusion is both the first sentence and a rebuttal.
The Opinion Indicatormisconstruedallows us to hear the first sentence as the Author's opinion, which she will go on to defend/support.
The "in addition" that joins the 2nd and 3rd sentences tells us that they are both premises, similar to the way in which seeing two claims joined by an "and" tells us that they're both premises (the vast majority of the time).

label: Goal
body:
We're being asked about the role of the 2nd sentence, which was one of the two premises.
So let's look for "support / evidence / premise".

label: Conclusion (Hence)
body: Small retailers that are forced to compete with large discount chains must offer exceptional service in order to retain their level of profitability.

label: Evidence
body:
They can't retain profitability while matching prices with large discount chains (who have an economy-of-scale advantage there).
If they offer exceptional service, they can retain customers.

label: Evaluate
body:
Whenever we're doing a Flaw question and see Conditional Logic, we want to look out for the #1 famous flaw, Necessary vs. Sufficient.
This argument presented a conditional, using the sufficient indicator "if":
If they offer → small companies can exceptional service retain customers and profitability
Does the author proceed to think about this rule in opposite or inverted fashion?
Yes! The author is thinking that
retaining customers offering and profitability -- requires --> exceptional service
Exceptional service is identified as one possible (i.e. sufficient) way to retain customers without losing profits, but the author is acting like it's the only way to do so (i.e. necessary).

label: Goal
body:
Since this question stem ends with "fails to consider that", we shouldn't go looking for the usual abstract description that describes the Necessary vs. Sufficient error.
Fails to consider indicates that we're about to hear potential weakening ideas.
When an author presents X → Y, but then illicitly thinks Y → X, we object that it's possible for Y to happen but X not to happen.
So here we're thinking, "Yo, author --- it's possible to retain customers without sacrificing profitability in other ways besides exceptional service. Yes, we COULD do exceptional service, but we could also host promotional events with local celebrities instead, and use THAT as our means of retaining customers without having to lower our prices."

label: Statements
body:
conditionals
Makes others more virtuous → do it
Makes others less virtuous → don't do it
causal (makes)
Praise makes less virtuous people more virtuous. Praise makes more virtuous people less virtuous.
conditional (none except)
Deserve praise → more virtuous person ~more virtuous person → ~Deserve praise

label: Evaluate
body:
We're given a rule in the first sentence that tells us to do things that make people more virtuous and not do things that make people less virtuous.
And the second sentence has anOverlapping Idea;it talks about making people more/less virtuous.
So from the second sentence we can infer:you should praise people who are less virtuous(because it makes them more virtuous)you should not praise people who are more virtuous(because it makes them less virtuous)
It's a good habit to make inferences as you go (both when reading rules in Logic Games and in reading premises or statements in arguments or Inference stimuli). LSAC is often testing our ability to hear a correct inference, and then relate it to what comes next.
By combining the 1st and 2nd sentences, we have an inference in our heads that "we should praise people who are less virtuous", and then the 3rd sentence says "onlymore virtuouspeople deserve praise".
Huh. Do those contradict each other? They feel like they contradict, but it's just because we get a counterintuitive result:weshouldpraise people who are less virtuous, even though they don't deserve praise.

label: Goal
body: We never know for sure what the answer will be on an Inference question, but we did get some inferences from the 2nd sentence,should praise less virtuousshouldn't praise more virtuousand then we could combine those with the 3rd sentence to get,should praise people who don't deserve itshouldn't praise people who do possibly deserve it

label: Correct (So)
body: Generic drugs are just as effective as their brand-name counterparts, but cost way less.

label: Evidence
body: Generic drugs contain exactly the same active ingredients as their brand-name counterparts, but cost less to develop, produce, and market.

label: Goal
body:
The most likely way they would make this hard is expressing Person 1's position using Person 2's wording, or vice versa. For example:
Person 1's position: Surplus money should not be used for a public works project that would create jobs.
Person 2's position: Surplus money should not be exclusively used to increase government payments to those who are unemployed.
Let's look for any answer where we can infer agreement from one person and disagreement from the other, but it should center around language about "where/how we should or shouldn't spend the budget surplus money".

label: Curious Fact
body: How come the revenue at our town's hotels and restaurants have gone up more than the revenues at our town's tourist attraction?

label: Evaluate
body:
The author seems to be making a move from "If X has the same active ingredients as Y, then X is just as effective as Y."
What could challenge that move? How could things have the same active ingredients, but differ in efficacy?
- It never says they have the same amount of active ingredients. It sounds more like it's just the same type. So maybe generic drugs are less effective because they have a smaller amount of active ingredients.
- What about inactive ingredients? Do those affect efficacy? Maybe generic drugs are less effective because their inactive ingredients aren't as good?
- What about the recipe? I might bake a cake using the same ingredients as you, but if I combine my ingredients in the wrong proportions, it could come out bad.
- What about the delivery system? Maybe they have the same ingredients, but being consumed in capsule vs. gel-cap vs. powder vs. liquid has some effect on efficacy.

label: Goal
body: Look for an answer strengthening the missing link between "same active ingredients --> same efficacy" or look for an answer ruling out any of these objections: "Generic drugs do NOT have less effective inactive ingredients, less effective methods of consumption, less effective recipes of combining those active ingredients."

label: Conclusion
body: Consumers are always obligated to report product defects they discover, while producers are never obligated to reveal them.

label: Evidence
body:
When it comes to both producers and consumers, the only obligation either has is to act in the best interests of their side.
The distribution of information about product defects is in the best interests of the consumer.

label: Evaluate
body:
The author's conclusion is about whether people do or don't have anobligation, and the evidence provides the legal standard by which we'll judge someone'sobligations: acting in the best interests of their own side
Since the author says consumers are obliged to report defects, he's assuming that it's in their best interest to report defects, and his other premise says that "distribution of info about product defects is in the best interests of the consumer".
So there's a tiny missing link there that "if consumers report product defects, it makes it more likely that information about defects will be distributed.
But since the author says that producers arenotobliged to report defects, he must be assuming that it'snotin their best interest (too) to report defects.
There is no premise at all about what is / isn't in the producers' best interests. We can tell that's a huge omission from the argument. The author isAssuming a Difference(it's in the best interest of consumers but not of producers).

label: Goal
body: Look for an answer saying, "it's not in producers' best interests to distribute info about product defects". Or look for an answer that, when negated, would weaken the conclusion.

label: Conclusion
body: Peeling wild potatoes makes them at least as safe to eat as unpeeled domesticated potatoes of the same size.

label: Evidence
body:
All potatoes (wild and domestic) have solanine, which is poisonous in large quantities.
Wild potatoes contain poisonous levels of solanine, while domesticated potatoes contain only very small amounts of solanine.
Most of the solanine in potatoes is concentrated in the skin.

label: Evaluate
body:
We need to prove that peeled wild potatoes areat least as safe to eatas unpeeled domesticated potatoes.
Did the argument ever define some proving mechanism, like "If xyz is true, then it's safe to eat"?
No, so the correct answer would need to do that.
When it comes to wild potatoes' dangerous levels of solanine, most of the solanine is found in the skin, so if you've peeled a wild potato, then you've eliminated most of its solanine.
But is the residual amount of solanine in the peeled wild potato stillless safe to eatthan the small amount of solanine that's in domesticated potatoes?
If domesticated potatoes only have 10g of solanine, whereas wild potatoes have 100g of solanine, peeling a wild potato would mean that there is at most 49g of solanine left, but that could still be more solanine than what's in a domesticated potato, and that could still be a high enough level of solanine to be "dangerous".
Furthermore, who says that "solanine level" is the only metric by which we should be judging whether wild potatoes areat least as safe to eatas domesticated potatoes?
Maybe there are other differences between the two that make wild potatoes less safe to eat.

label: Goal
body:
The correct answer needs rule out all possible ways that wild potatoes could still be more dangerous to eat (even peeled, their residual solanine is too high / there's some other dangerous ingredient they have that domesticated potatoes lack).
Or it needs to provide us with a rule that we know applies to peeled wild potatoes and outputs language like "at least as safe".

label: Goal
body:
Since this question stem is phrased like a Flaw-Weaken hybrid (vulnerable to criticism because it fails to consider), we're not liking to hear the formal description of that flaw.
It's more likely going to just be the conversational objection ... "Yo, author --- you told us that general surgeons will definitely be highly competent. You didn't tell us they were the only ones who would be highly competent. Isn't it possible that other people who could do the surgery (such as even a specialized surgeon or a veterinarian) could also be highly competent?"

label: Conclusion (clearly)
body: If a subsidized art project is successful enough that it allows the artist to repay the public subsidy, the artist is morally obliged to do so.

label: Evidence (since)
body: The public subsidy agency will welcome the repayment, because they can use that money to fund some new up-and-coming artists.

label: Evaluate
body:
For Strengthen-Principle, we're principally (haha, get it?) trying to anticipate a Linking idea, that should sound like "If Premise, then Conclusion".
We want the principle to have a trigger that discusses the Premise, like, "If returning money to someone would be welcome as a source of helping others the way you were helped".
And we want it to have an outcome that sounds like the Conclusion, "then you are morally obliged to return the money".

label: Goal
body:
Let's look for something like
If ... Then ... you're able to repayandmorally the people you're repaying → obligated would welcome that source to pay of opportunity for others

label: Jessica's Claim
body: The only thing the budget surplus should be used for is to increase government payments to the unemployed.

label: Marcie's Response
body: I think it would be better to use the money on a public works project that would create jobs.

label: Evaluate
body: Okay, well this is simpler than usual, in the sense that Jessica only makes one claim, so Marcie has to be disagreeing with that claim.

label: Author's Explanation/Hypothesis
body:
The people visiting the tourist attraction are illicitly selling or sharing the passes with others.
Evaluate
It might take a sec to process what this whole story is describing. It starts with the assumption that if people come to our town and stay at our hotel and eat at our restaurants, they will surely visit our tourist attraction as well, right?
Since the revenue is at the hotels / restaurants is going up more than the revenue at the tourist attraction (and since the people are assuming that anyone going to the former would also go to the latter), they are thinking to themselves, "How are all these people (we assume are) coming to our tourist attraction are not paying?"
And that's how they arrive at the causal explanation that people who visit the tourist attraction are then selling or sharing their passes (which are good for a year) with others.

label: Goal
body:
Since we're trying to find four answers that Weaken, we want them to either suggest an Alternate Explanation for the Curious Fact or we want them to lower the plausibility of the storyline that visitors are sharing / selling their passes.
"Give me a different way to explain why the hotels/restaurants have more revenue uptick than does the tourist attraction" (maybe people don't want to see the tourist attraction that much / maybe locals have started to spend more money at the hotels and restaurants), or "give me a way to make it seem less likely that people are sharing/selling passes" (the passes have a photo on them, so it's hard to get in with someone else's pass).

label: Statements
body:
Manners/etiquette are always social.
Morals are not necessarily social (i.e. at least sometimes morals are not social)
The rules of manners/etiquette do not apply when one is alone.

label: Evaluate
body:
The author has made a distinction and said a couple strong ideas.
Manners/etiquette (same meaning) are always social, so the last sentence is taking that contrapositive and thinking, "If alone (not social), then no rules of manners/etiquette to worry about."
Meanwhile, since morals are not necessarily social in nature, there is at least one moral rule that isn't dependent on other people, and thus at least one moral rule probably still applies even when we're alone.

label: Goal
body: It's hard to know what to predict here, but my guess would be that it will relate to the idea that morality might still apply when we're alone.

label: Conclusion (therefore)
body: In a consumer society, news is primarily entertaining and cannot serve its intended function.

label: Evidence
body:
The intended function of news is to give us information on which to act.
In a consumer society, news becomes a product to be manufactured and dispensed to the consumer.
An enormous industry for the production and consumption of news has evolved.
We ingest news with an insatiable appetite.

label: Evaluate
body:
This argument is following a comparative reasoning pattern, where it's contrasting what news is supposed to do (its intended function) with what it actually ends up doing (becoming primarily entertaining).
The sociologist is assuming there's a necessary conflict between news being entertaining and news providing actionable information. Essentially, the argument contends that if news is primarily entertaining, it fails to deliver the information needed for us to act.
We can try to defend the conclusion by considering if there are any cases where entertainment and actionable information coexist. Alternatively, the argument could be assuming that the qualities of "primarily entertaining" and "providing actionable information" are mutually exclusive or difficult to combine.

label: Goal
body: Let's find an answer that connects being "primarily entertaining" to being unable to provide the information on which we can act. Alternatively, the answer might need to defend against the idea that these two qualities could coexist effectively.

label: Conclusion
body: It's false to say that life began in the ocean and didn't exist on land until half a billion years ago.

label: Evidence
body: We've found carbon 14 on 1.2 billion year old rock in North America, and carbon 14 is extracted by plants and microbes from the atmosphere and released when they die (i.e. it's can be a marker of life).

label: Evaluate
body:
Since we're doing Strengthen EXCEPT, we'll need to find four ways to strengthen the argument. Often, a strengthen answer is really just ruling out a weakening objection, so we're wise to think through some possible objections.
If you were trying to defend the widely held belief that life on land didn't exist until half a billion years ago, how could you explain this carbon 14 on 1.2 billion year old rock?
Maybe we'd say that at the time of its getting smeared with carbon 14, that 1.2 billion year old rock was actually underwater.
Maybe there are other explanations for how carbon 14 gets on a surface (the fact that living things use it and release it doesn't convince us that this is theonlyreason you might ever find carbon 14 somewhere).

label: Goal
body: Look for answers that rule out possible objections or that add some more evidence that life on land may have existed prior to 500 million years ago.

label: Facts
body:
causal (resulted from, reflects)
Dual influence of >> rich and diverse >> nature of Anglo-Sax + French vocabulary English lit contrast / pivot (though)
French doesn't have dual influence. Directly influenced by Latin (barely a trace of Celtic)
French lit is known for simplicity and clarity.

label: Evaluate
body:
The #1 thing we listen for on Most Supported is causal language. The other things we listen for are conditional / pivot / mathy / comparison ideas.
It seems like maybe we're being tested on the causality of "dual influence leads to rich/diverse vocab", or the pivot contrast provided with French's simpler / clearer single origin language.

label: Goal
body: I wouldn't have a good prediction here, so let's just look for the most provable answer. It'll probably relate to the causal difference maker of "multiple languages influencing leads to more complex literature, fewer languages influencing leads to simpler / clearer literature".

label: Premises
body: English literature reflects English's rich, diverse vocabulary, which came from Anglo-Saxon plus French influence.

label: Evaluate
body: Vocabulary came from origins; literature reflects vocabulary. So origins shape literature.

label: Goal
body: Find: the origin of English shaped English literature.

label: Premises
body: The first sentence does most of the work. English literature reflects the rich, diverse vocabulary of English. And English's rich vocabulary came from its origins — Anglo-Saxon plus later French influence.

label: Evaluate
body:
Connect those two ideas:
Origins → vocabulary. Vocabulary → literature. So origins → literature.
The rest of the stimulus (about French literature being simple and clear) is filler that supports the same idea — that the linguistic ancestry of a language helps shape its literature. But the cleanest path is the chain in the first sentence.

label: Goal
body: Find an answer that says, in some form: the origin of English helped shape English literature.

label: Conclusion
body: Both doctrines are mistaken. i.e., The explanation of any historical event doesnotneed to appeal to economic factors.Not allhistorical events can be accounted for psychologically.

label: Evidence
body: Some events were due both to economic forces and to the psychology of the major participants.

label: Evaluate
body:
This is like if we read an argument that said:Luigi thinks that all pasta dishes should have salt in them. Mario says all pasta dishes should have garlic in them. Both of them are wrong, however. Certainly there are some pasta dishes that would benefit from both salt and garlic.
Our objection would be, "Yo, author --- they never said you can't have both salt and garlic. That's not a reason for disagreeing with them. To disagree with Luigi, you need to present evidence of a pasta dish that shouldn't have salt, and to fight Mario's claim, you need to present a pasta dish that shouldn't have garlic."
Similarly, this author was assuming that the two doctrines are mutually exclusive, since he thinks he's proving them wrong by finding a case where they overlap.

label: Goal
body:
It's hard to predict what wording they'll use for the idea of, "he's assuming they're mutually exclusive doctrines".
It might sound like our author is assuming, "If the explanation appeals to economic factors, then it can't appeal to psychological ones" (and vice versa)
or, "Each doctrine is assuming that you can only appeal to one type of factor."

label: Given that
body: 7% of the garments this manufacturer produces are found to be unsalable (some are found to be defective by inspectors, others are just returned by retailers)

label: and that
body: All unsalable garments are recycled as scrap.

label: How can it be that
body: 9% of garments are reported as recycled scrap?

label: Evaluate
body:
What % of recycled scrap should we have been expecting? Why is 9% a surprising fact?
If we think that the only thing that gets recycled as scrap would be unsalable garments, then since 7% of garments are unsalable, we'd expect 7% of garments to end up as recycled scrap.
So if 9% of garments end up as recycled scrap, then there must be something in addition to unsalable garments that ultimately gets recycled as scrap.
It will have to be some form of salable (i.e. sellable) garment, since it can't be in the category of unsalable.

label: Goal
body: So it seems like we're looking for an answer that helps us to understand why some garments that are salable still end up being recycled as scrap. (maybe the manufacturer has a bunch of jeans leftover that they know they could sell at some store, but they want to take "that model" off the shelf so that it can be replaced with "this year's model", which would sell for more?)

label: Conclusion
body: The most reliable way to detect the presence of life on a planet would be to ascertain whether its atmosphere contains methane.

label: Evidence
body: If methane isn't constantly Methane replenished by the biological → disappears processes of living beings

label: Evaluate
body:
When an author argues that, "the best way to achieve X is Y", there will be two big assumptions we could attack - the author assumes that Y is a viable way to achieve X - the author assumes that there isn't some other way of achieving X that is even better than Y
It will be hard for us here to argue that "detecting methane isn't a viable way to detect the presence of life on a planet". By contrapositive logic, the rule that this author has given us says that "If we see methane, we know that it is being constantly replenished by the biological processes of living beings".
So we can't really argue with the author by saying, "Hey, we might see methane but it's not a planet with living beings". The best we could do is say, "we might see methane, but none of the living beings are still present ... we're just seeing the decaying-methane they've left behind".
The other avenue we have is to argue that some other way of detecting the presence of life is even more reliable. (maybe receiving radio communications?)

label: Goal
body: Look for an answer that suggests that the methane method isn't super reliable (i.e. we might detect methane in the atmosphere even though the planet does not have living beings present), or an answer that suggests that there might be a more reliable way of detecting life than the methane way.

label: Conclusion
body: Their decision to reveal their marriage is foolish.

label: Intermediate Conclusion (since)
body: It will mean that one of them has a job offer withdrawn.

label: Evidence (after all)
body:
Evritech has a rule against hiring more than one member of the same family.
They could easily keep their marriage secret initially and then later informing Evritech that they got married; there's no policy of terminating one of two employees who marry each other.

label: Evaluate
body:
Whenever we read Main Conclusion or Role, we look for "upside down arguments", where the conclusion happens before the supporting the evidence, since more than 80% of the arguments on these two question types are structured that way.
In particular, ~65% are a Pivot / Rebuttal claim ~25% are the First Sentence
The first sentence is factual. The second sentence describes someone else's idea or action (they decided to reveal their marriage). Usually, this would be followed by aPivot+ Pushback, and that's exactly what we get when we see, "Their decision is foolish,however".
We would immediately suspect that this claim is the conclusion, and only need verification that it gets supported. It does. The following clause starts with SINCE, which means we're supporting the 'foolish' claim.

label: Goal
body: We just want to find a match for "their decision to reveal their marriage to Evritech is foolish". You could potentially reword that as, "They shouldn't reveal their marriage" or something like that.

label: Conclusion (that is why)
body: You can't be sure that Orwell read the futuristic books that resemble his own 1984.

label: Goal
body:
We would anticipate potential correct answers like,
If unaware of X → not responsible for X
or like
If X is involuntary → not responsible for X

label: Evaluate
body:
Since we're told that the passageillustratesa principle, it means the principle is implicit, and it's our job to name what's going on, in a general way, like when we're doing a Parallel reasoning question.
The author is basically presenting a Curious Fact: why is Orwell's '1984' so similar to these other futuristic books?
She is saying we shouldn't necessarily jump to this Explanation: he read those books (and incorporated similar stuff into his own book)
Why? Because an Alternate Explanation is possible: he and those other futuristic authors were all exposed to the same body of literary conventions (and since they all incorporated that stuff into their books, their books feel similar)

label: Goal
body: Let's look for something like, "Because of the possibility of this Alternate Explanation, we shouldn't jump to this Explanation for the Curious Fact".

label: Hypothesis
body: The skills involved in copying curves must be developed before the skills involved in copying angles can be developed.

label: Evaluate
body: There's really nothing for us to do at this stage, because we don't have any supporting evidence. We might just ask ourselves, "How do you show that somebody has to master X before they can master Y?"

label: Goal
body:
Look for something that increases the idea that you need to be able to copy curves in order to be able to copy angles.
We might get data points showing that "Sally couldn't copy angles, but then she learned to copy curves and all of a sudden she could copy angles!"
Or we might get an answer that sort of describes the Causal Mechanism, like "the brain can't process a hard turn until it's learned to process a soft turn".

label: Conclusion (Hence)
body: It's not forensic evidence in general that should be condemned for this injustice (in the Barker case).

label: Evidence
body: The injustice in the Barker case was due to the fact that some of the forensic scientists believed they owed allegiance only to prosecuting lawyers, and failed to provide evidence impartially to both the defense and the prosecution.

label: Evaluate
body:
In order for us to Strengthen this, we might need to think about how it could be weakened.
Given that ... the injustice in this case came from some forensic scientists, who were hired by the prosecution, being "loyal" to them and not trying to impartially provide testimony to both defense and prosecution,
How could we argue that ... It is forensic evidence in general that should be blamed for this?
We'd probably have to argue that "this kinda thing happens all the time". It's inherent to forensic evidence. It's human nature for forensic witnesses to skew their testimony towards whichever lawyer brought them in.
The author's argument is basically, "These are just a couple bad apples. We don't need to indict the entire field of forensic evidence." It's similar to arguing, "The injustice in this shooting of an unarmed person by the police was due to the failure of the cops on the scene to de-escalate non-violently. Hence, policing in general should not be condemned for this shooting". The counterargument is, "No, it is policing in general. The inability to de-escalate nonviolently is something very widespread within policing. It's inherent. It's baked in."

label: Goal
body:
Since the way we'd object to this argument is to say, "This kinda thing happens all the time. It's very common for forensic witnesses to act too loyally towards one lawyer", that means that we could strengthen the argument by going the other way.
Look for something like, "These were just a couple bad apples. This is an isolated incident. This is not typical for the field of forensic evidence".

label: Statements
body:
conditional (everyone = sufficient condition)
Excessively generous → Not levelheaded Levelheaded → Not excessively generous
conditional (no A's are B = all A's are ~B)
Levelheaded → Not bold Bold → Not levelheaded

label: Evaluate
body:
Whenever we're doing Inference questions and are given any conditional ideas, we think two things: 1. can I chain this conditional up with any others? 2. can I apply this conditional (often via contrapositive) to any facts provided?
In this case, both claims are conditional, so #2 is out.
But #1 is alive and well! The two statements have an overlapping term (whether or not you're levelheaded), which usually means we can chain them. However, here we can't actually chain them. They're just trying to bait us into doing so. We were essentially given this: A → B C → B
Those don't form any A → B → C chain. All we could do would be to say something like, ~B → ~A and ~C

label: Goal
body:
Look for trap answers trying to connect generosity to boldness, which we can't do, since the conditionals did not chain together.
The correct answer might play off the fact that we have "Levelheaded" show up as a trigger twice, so we could say
Levelheaded → ~Extra Generous and ~Bold

label: Conclusion (must)
body: Something must discourage the people who would be the best-liked teachers from entering the profession.

label: Evidence
body: In a study, high school students picked their favorite teacher, and the teachers picked by the most students had a personality trait that's found in 20% of the population, but in only 5% of teachers.

label: Evaluate
body:
We want to really hear the "Thus, something must discourage people from teaching ... " as the author squinting his eyes, stroking his chin, about to solve the case or make the right diagnosis of this causal mystery.
What's the causal mystery?
Curious Fact ... Why is trait X found in 20% of the general population, but in only 5% of teachers (and in 100% of the most-loved teachers in this survey)?
Author's Explanation ... There's something that discourages people with trait X from entering teaching.
We usually weaken these arguments by either, suggesting an Alternate Explanation for the curious fact or by undermining the plausibility of the Author's Explanation
In this case, though, the author doesn't really propose a specific Explanation. It's just, "something must be keeping them from entering the profession".

label: Goal
body:
Since there's no specific causal storyline, it's hard to pick at its plausibility. It seems like the correct answer will just have to offer an Alternate Explanation for why people with Personality X are beloved teachers, 20% of the general population, but only 5% of teachers.
We want a different way to explain that statistic, so that we can argue the Anti-Conclusion, "nothing is discouraging people with personality X from entering the teaching profession".

label: Conclusion
body: If a successful chess-playing computer were invented, the conception of human intelligence would certainly change.

label: Evidence
body: If a successful chess-playing computer were invented, it would either prove that a machine can think or that chess doesn't involve thinking.

label: Evaluate
body:
This argument is saying, "A will either cause B or C. Either way, we'll get Z."
This implies that both B and C would each lead to Z.
