How does that match up with the actual concepts from the argument? The successful chess computer will lead to "a machine can think" or "chess doesn't involve thinking". And the author thinks either one leads to a change in the conception of human intelligence.
Formally:
if we thought a → change conception of machine can think human intelligence
if we thought chess → change conception of didn't involve thinking human intelligence

label: Goal
body:
The author assumes that currently we think "machines can't think" / "chess does involve thinking" (otherwise learning either of those things couldn't possibly change us).
But the author is also assuming a weird connection between whether machines think / whether chess involves thinking and how we think about human intelligence.
Since the author never discussed "our concept of human intelligence" in the evidence but is talking about it in the conclusion, we can expect our answer to have language referring to "our conception of human intelligence".

label: Statements
body:
Conditional (if= sufficient, LEFT of arrow)treating others well more worthy when at least partially → of praise motivated by compassion
(In more conversational terms, this rule says that being nice to others out of some clinical, dispassionate obedience to moral obligation is less praiseworthy than being nice to others with some feelings of compassion on top.)
We give extra praise to those who feel compassion while treating others well, even though one can't choose whether to have feelings (meanwhile, theycanchoose to treat others well in the first place).

label: Evaluate
body:
We typically see two patterns for the correct answer on Must Be False: 1. it contradicts a conditional rule presented 2. it contradicts an available inference we can make by combining claims
The first sentence was a conditional rule.
By combining the first and second sentence, we could infer something like, "sometimes we praise people extra for stuff that's beyond their control".

label: Goal
body:
Look for an answer contradicting the conditional (match the trigger, but don't deliver the outcome):X treats others well, but feels nothing doing so. Y treats others well, in part because Y feels compassion. X deservesat least as muchpraise as Y.
Or look for an answer contradicting our inference, something like, "we only give people extra praise for stuff they can control".

label: Conclusion (Thus)
body: Supertasters experience sharp cheddar as tasting more bitter than mild cheddar, but nontasters experience sharp cheddar as tasting no more bitter than mild cheddar.

label: Evidence
body:
The more bitter a food tastes, the less children like it.
Supertasters strongly prefer mild cheddar to sharp cheddar. Nontasters have no preference.

label: Evaluate
body:
This argument seems to be trying to read a Volume Dial relationship backwards. Given the rule that "the more bitter a food tastes, the less children like it", the author is thinking, "If Johnny likes A less than he likes B, then A must be more bitter than B."
But we can't assume that bitterness is the only thing that affects whether children like something less.
It's possible that supertasters prefer mild cheddar to sharp cheddar not because mild cheddar is less bitter, but for some other reason.

label: Goal
body:
In order to guarantee that the preferences of mild to sharp are related to bitterness, we need to rule out all other possible influences on preference.
We would want to hear something like, "Other than bitterness, mild cheddar and sharp cheddar are identical" or something like, "There is no other factor besides bitterness that affects how supertasters and nontasters judge preference of cheddar cheese".

label: Conclusion
body: If an external force intervenes to give members of a community political self-determination, then that political community will almost surely fail to be truly free.

label: Evidence (since)
body: It is during the people's struggle to become free by their own efforts that the political virtues necessary for maintaining freedom have the best chance of arising.

label: Evaluate
body:
It's easy to see the structure of this paragraph: "Conclusion,sincePremise", but it was very hard for me to compute any of this on a first read. When that happens in RC or LR, I try to use concrete examples to anchor my understanding.
If an external force intervenes to give members of a community political self-determinationOkay, can we think of when an external force would give members of a community political self-determination?
I guess after World War II, the United Nations was an external force that gave members of the Jewish community political self-determination .... Maybe there's some high school where the student government is walked all over by the faculty, until some external force (angry parents) intervene to give that community of students some political self-determination.
... that political community will almost surely fail to be truly freeOkay, so the Jewish state of Israel will almost surely fail to be truly free ... This student government will almost surely fail to be truly free. Why is that? The author is saying the Jewish community and the students will fail to be truly free because ...
it is during the people's struggle to become freeby their ownefforts that the political virtues necessary for maintaining freedom have the best chance of arising.
Okay, the author is essentially saying "you need to fight for your own freedom (and win from your own efforts) in order to really appreciate and master this whole freedom thing".Like Dad saying to Grandpa, "I know you want to buy your granddaughter a car, but if I let you buy her a car, she's not going to treat it well. She needs to earn this car herself in order to really take care of this car."
Our author is saying the same thing about political self-determination and freedom. If you, as some external force, just give the political self-determination, then the recipient will mistreat it and not be truly free. They need to earn it themselves in order to develop the character that will be needed to keep themselves truly free.
Goal
We want to anticipate Principle answers by saying, "If Premise, then Conclusion". The way we were understanding the argument before, that would sound like,
If you don't earn X then you won't bethrough your own efforts able to hold onto X
But is that really what the premise said? The premise actually says this:
don't earn X → won't havebest chanceyourself of developing virtuesnecessary for X
Okay, so the argument's move from premise to conclusion is really this:
If an external force gives you self-determination, rather than you earning it for yourself, then you won't have the best chance of cultivating the virtues you need to hold onto freedom. Thus, you will almost surely fail to be truly free.
The author is making this move:
don't do the thing will almostthat provides best → surely fail tochance of X have X

label: Conclusion
body: These people are mistaken. Rephrase: Midville is generally no more expensive to live in than nearby towns are.

label: Evidence
body: They focus on Midville's relatively high tax rate while ignoring the services paid for by their taxes. Only Midville provides residents with trash removal, rent- and mortgage-assistance programs, and reasonably priced public transportation. In nearby towns, individuals pay for their own trash removal, and housing and transportation costs are high in comparison to Midville.

label: Evaluate
body: The argument follows a Pivot/Rebuttal structure, a common pattern on Main Conclusion questions. The author presents a claim from some residents of Midville and then pivots with "but these people are mistaken," indicating a rebuttal. This is followed by evidence supporting the author's opinion. The conclusion is an opinion from the author, supported by the provided comparisons between Midville and nearby towns.

label: Goal
body: Find the best available meaning match for "Midville is generally no more expensive to live in than nearby towns are."

label: Statements
body: They found a cave you can only access through an underwater tunnel. The inside of the cave is filled with seawater. There are stalagmites, which are pillars of stone that form when water keeps dropping on the same spot for centuries, building up a tower of mineral deposits.

label: Evaluate / Goal
body: There don't seem to be any Conditional, Causal, Mathematical, or Pivot ideas in this paragraph, so it's hard to sense where this would be going. Just head to the answers and look for the most provable claim, being cautious if we see anything that looks Too Strong, looks like an Unsupported Comparison, or looks like it's talking about something Out of Scope.

label: Conclusion
body: The development costs for new vaccines the health department requested should be subsidized by the government.

label: Intermediate Conclusion
body: The marketing of vaccines will be less profitable than the marketing of any other drug.

label: Evidence
body: Sales of vaccines are likely to be lower since each vaccine is only given once, whereas other drugs are administered many times (so that the drug manufacturer has more opportunities to make back their R&D costs)

label: Evaluate
body:
The question stem isn't a typical Weaken stem; it's asking us to Weaken the intermediate conclusion. We can still use our normal Weaken mindset:
Given Thatvaccines are only administered once, whereas other drugs are administered multiple timesHow Can We Argue Thatthe marketing of the vaccinecouldbe as profitable as that of other drugs?
Maybe this is an atypical vaccine (like the coronavirus or flu vaccine, potentially) where people will need to get it every year, or maybe even more frequently than that.
Maybe this vaccine will cost a lot more money for patients / insurance companies than do most vaccines (so that even though the drug company only gets one blip of revenue, it's a big blip!)
Maybe this vaccine is so desperately needed that almost everyone is going to buy it, whereas these other drugs that get administered multiple times are only sought after by a small audience.
A million one-time purchases might be more revenue than 10,000 recurring purchases.

label: Goal
body: Because the author's argument is comparative, in order to break out of her logic, we probably need to highlight a meaningful difference between this vaccine and other vaccines, or between this one-time vaccine and other drugs, which are given multiple times.

label: Conclusion
body: The network should be installed during the day.

label: Evidence (since)
body: The network is designed to increase productivity. Installing it during the day disrupts employees’ work, while a nighttime installation would cost significantly more. Saving money is important.

label: Evaluate
body:
This argument weighs the trade‐offs between a daytime installation (which disrupts work) and a nighttime one (which is more expensive). The manager concludes that because saving money is important, the daytime disruption is acceptable.
To make this conclusion, the argument must assume that the monetary loss due to daytime productivity disruption is lower than the additional cost of a nighttime installation. Essentially, the argument hinges on a cost–benefit comparison: the cost of lost productivity during the day must be less than the premium paid for a nighttime installation.

label: Goal
body: We need an answer that supplies the necessary link by quantifying or comparing the expense of the productivity loss during a daytime installation to the higher cost of installing at night. In other words, the assumption must be that the financial loss from daytime disruption is less than the extra installation cost at night.

label: Conclusion (it can be concluded)
body: The use of marijuana can cause cancer.

label: Evidence
body: An ingredient in marijuana known as THC inactivates herpes viruses. And inactivated herpes viruses can convert healthy cells into cancer cells.

label: Evaluate
body:
The premises give us a bit of a causal chain:
Use⇢ imbibe ⇢ inactivated ⇢ convert healthy MJ THC herpes cells to cancer

label: Goal
body:
It's hard to know how to argue around this, since the conclusion is so weakly worded and the evidence made it sound pretty plausible.
Let's just use our usual Debate Mindset and hope that the correct answer shows us a door.
Given that .... THC (which is in marijuana) can do something that has been found to convert healthy cells into cancer cells,
How can we argue that ... the use of marijuanacannotcause cancer?

label: Conclusion
body: We should reject the corporation's offer to provide funding to restore an archaeological site and make it accessible to the general public.

label: Evidence
body: Many parts of the site contain unexamined evidence.

label: Evaluate
body:
We need to flesh out this premise with a little common sense. Why would it be a problem for the author that this site still has some unexamined evidence?
The author must be thinking that if we were to get money to restore this site and make it readily accessible to the general public, then in the process we would somehow mess up our ability to harness the value of this unexamined evidence.
I'm not sure if the author thinks we'll ruin it while we're doing construction on the site or if the author thinks we'll accidentally wall-off the unexamined evidence and not be able to grab it.

label: Goal
body:
Whatever the author's specific concern is, we could pre-phrase broadly that she is thinking something like this:
If ...there's stillThen ...we shouldn't unexamined evidence do a restoration into at an archaeological site a public attraction

label: Statements
body:
If a female wood duck sees another duck leaving its nest, the female will lay an egg in that nest.
Usually, this doesn't happen too much because the ducks' nests are well hidden.
pivot (however) causal (undercut)
When people put up nesting boxes, it undercuts the ducks' reproductive efforts.
These boxes become so crowded with eggs that few, if any, hatch.

label: Evaluate
body:
This paragraph has the structure of, "Normally, X is true, because of Y. However, when Z occurs, X is not true".
Normally, there aren't too many parasitic eggs put into a duck's nest because the nests are well hidden. However, when people put up a nesting box, there are tons of parasitic eggs in the box.
Often, the test wants us to notice how we've Flipped the Causal Difference-Maker.
Previously, there weren't too many extra eggs in one nest,becausethe nest was well-hidden. If nesting boxes do end up with too many extra eggs, it suggests that nesting boxes are not well hidden. It is much easier for a female duck to see another duck leave its nesting box.

label: Goal
body: Let's look for something safely worded that reinforces this contrast between well hidden nests that don't get extra eggs and more visible nesting boxes that result in too many extra eggs, which then somehow prevents most of the eggs in those boxes from hatching.

label: Curious Fact
body: Why are children especially to develop strong aversions to some foods?

label: Author's Explanation
body: Because if you get sick from a meal, you'll usually develop a strong distaste for the one food in the meal that had the most distinctive flavor.

label: Evaluate
body: This isn't really an argument, so we're not parsing the paragraph into Conclusion / Premise. We just need to justify why the first sentence would beespecially likelyto impact children.

label: Goal
body: Seems like we need to hear that children are more likely to get sick from eating a meal, or that children are more likely than adults to find that one food in the meal has the most distinctive flavor (or both).

label: Conclusion
body: Lives could undoubtedly be saved by banning red cars from the roads altogether.

label: Evidence
body: A greater percentage of red cars are involved in accidents than are cars of any other color.

label: Evaluate
body:
The author conclusion is a conditional, but the trigger is just saying, "If this evidence is true". That's how we treat evidence by default in Logical Reasoning, so we can basically ignore worrying about that.
The author thinks that banning red cars could save lives, which should strike us all as an insane idea. Why are red cars inherently a threat to life?
The author's evidence is a correlation: red cars are more likely to be involved in an accident than are cars of any other color.
Any time an LSAT author presents and considers a correlation between X and Y, she tends to assume that one causes the other.
In this case, we can tell the author is presuming that "being in a red car" is causing people to get into accidents, hence the correlation between red cars and being involved in accidents.
If the author is concluding that lives could be saved by banning red cars, then the author is implicitly thinking that currently lives are being lost because of red cars.

label: Goal
body:
When an LSAT author sees a correlation between two things (red cars / accidents) and overconfidently assumes one causal explanation (red cars ---cause--> accidents), we can talk about the Flaw several different ways:
1. Simply call out this illicit move from a mere correlation between two things to the assertion or assumption of some causal relationship between those things (e.g. "infers a causal relationship from a mere correlation")
2. Debunk the plausibility of the author's causal explanation (e.g. "there's no way that the color of the car makes the car or the driver more dangerous")
3. (most popular)Point out the possibility of some Alternate Explanation for this curious correlation. We want to consider whether the causality could be happening in reverse (could getting into accidents cause someone to drive a red car?), or whether there could be some 3rd factor that explains the other two things (could it just be that flashy, aggressive people both buy red cars and drive like jerks, getting themselves into lots of accidents)

label: Conclusion (therefore)
body: At any given time, customers who purchase merchandise using the bonus points spend less than they would if they purchased the same merchandise in retail stores.

label: Evidence
body: Customers who purchase merchandise using bonus points can buy brand name stuff by mail at prices that are lower than the manufacturers' suggested retail prices.

label: Evaluate
body:
This conclusion is making aComparativeclaim, so we want to think about what is being assumed in this comparison.
The evidence is that "when using points, you spend less than the manufacturers' suggested retail prices".
The conclusion is that "when using points, you spend less than if you bought that same stuff in a retail store".
So the author is assuming that "buying something by mail at less than MSRP is cheaper than buying that same thing in a retail store".
If I were objecting to this conclusion and trying to think of a way to argue that you'renotnecessarily spending less when you buy using points, two thoughts come to mind:
1. What about shipping/handling costs when it comes to mail purchases? Maybe the price tag on the item is lower, but once you add in shipping/handling, you end up spending at least as much as if you had gone to the store.
2. Who says that the price you'd pay at the store is the MSRP? If you've ever gone shopping for a car or a guitar, the dealerships love to show you the (crazy-inflated) MSRP number so that the actual retail price they're selling it at seems like a deal. "Whoa, Guitar Center! This guitar's MSRP is $599 but you're selling it for $299? What a deal!"

label: Goal
body:
Look for an answer naming the missing link "If lower than MSRP, then lower than what you'd spend in retail stores".
Or look for an answer ruling out one of our objections: "the shipping/handling costs of buying it by mail donotend up making it cost at least as much that way"
"retail stores donotusually sell items at lower than the MSRP"

label: Conclusion
body: Colic in infants is probably not caused by the inability of those infants to tolerate the antibodies in cow's milk.

label: Evidence
body: A lot of infants that are fed breast milk exclusively still show symptoms of colic.

label: Evaluate
body:
This is ananti-causalconclusion, so if we're going to object to the author's conclusion, we'll be trying to argue that "Coliciscaused by the inability of some infants to tolerate the antibodies in cow's milk."
We can always frame Weaken questions as GIVEN this evidence HOW CAN I ARGUE the conc is wrong

label: Goal
body: GIVEN THAT some infants who are fed breast milk exclusively still show signs of colic, HOW CAN WE ARGUE that coliciscaused by antibodies in cow's milk?

label: Yolandas Statements
body: 1. Hacking into a computer is kinda like breaking into someone's car and joyriding. 2. Both computer hacking and car jacking / joyriding involve breaking into private property and being reckless with it. 3. Joyriding is more dangerous than computer hacking. 4. Joyriding physically endangers people. 5. Computer hacking only harms intellectual property.

label: Arjuns Statements
body: 1. Some part of that is wrong! 2. Hacking into a medical/hospital computer system could mess up their data and screw up life-or-death patient information. 3. Computer hacking also causes physical harm to people.

label: Conclusion (clearly)
body: Modern aircraft navigation systems are being put at risk by the electronic devices that passengers carry on board, such as cassette players and laptop computers.

label: Evaluate
body:
Which of J's five claims, if any, is A disagreeing with? (If no explicit claims are disagreed with, then we ask ourselves about J's assumptions)
It seems like A's last claim clearly conflicts with J's last claim.

label: Goal
body: So lets look for an answer that's like "whether or not computer hacking only harms intellectual property, or causes physical harm to people too".

label: Arjuns Conclusion
body: Joyriding is not more dangerous than hacking computers.

label: Arjuns Intermediate Conclusion
body: Computer crimes also cause physical harm to people.

label: Arjuns Evidence
body: Hacking into a hospital's medical records could damage life-or-death data systems.

label: Evaluate
body:
Arjun's response seems pretty reasonable to me, so I'm wondering where they want us to go with this one. Theredoesseem to be a leap in strength/certainty, going from "hacking into a hospitalcoulddamage data systems" to "computer crimescausephysical harm to people".
And then there's also the nitpicky issue that the Arjun established that computers indirectly could lead to harm (by damaging data systems which might then lead to incorrect treatment decisions which could then lead to harm).
But his conclusion isn't really capturing that nuance. It sounds like hacking directly causes physical harm to people.

label: Goal
body: Look for answer complaining about the shift from "could damage data systems" to "does cause physical harm", either in terms of the conclusion being stronger than what's warranted to sounding more directly causal than what's warranted.

label: Conclusion (accordingly)
body:
If we find a star with no lithium inside, then it is not one of these coolest brown dwarfs.
(Alternatively) All of these coolest brown dwarfs have some lithium inside them.

label: Evidence
body: Stars when they're first formed contain lots of lithium. All stars but the coolest brown dwarfs are hot enough to burn off the lithium by converting it into helium.

label: Evaluate
body:
This is a tough argument to evaluate. You would only really be able to see a gap or think of an objection if you had outside knowledge that stars go through a life cycle, and some of them end up as brown dwarfs, red dwarfs, red supergiants, supernovae, neutron stars, black holes, etc.
The way the facts are presented here make it seem hard to disagree with the conclusion.
If all stars start off with lithium in them, and the coolest brown dwarfs are not hot enough to burn off lithium by converting it into helium, then it feels like the conclusion is right, that any brown dwarf star would still have lithium in it.
I guess one piece of wiggle room is that the premise doesn't say that "brown dwarfs cannot get rid of lithium", it says that "brown dwarfs can't get rid lithiumby converting it into helium." But maybe they can get rid of lithium by some other means.

label: Goal
body: Let's look for an answer where if we negated it, it would hurt the argument that "all of the coolest brown dwarfs have some lithium in them".

label: Conclusion (Therefore)
body: We can be sure that an Cotoy lost their lawsuit earlier today.

label: Evidence
body:
Whenever a company loses a big product-liability lawsuit, the value of its stocks fall quickly in value within hours after the announcement of the verdict.
Cotoy has been involved in a big product-liability lawsuit, and its stocks fell quickly in value today.

label: Evaluate
body:
If we're going Flaw or Parallel Flaw and we seeconditional logic, we immediately start to suspect that the flaw will be aNecessary vs. Sufficienterror (which just means that the author presents a conditional logic rule, but then uses it in some illegal backwards or inverted fashion to reach his conclusion).
The rule we were given here was signified by "Whenever", which is a Sufficient (left side) indicator.
Sufficient Indicatorsif, when, whenever, whoever, wherever, all, any, each, every, the only
The rule is saying
lose a big lawsuit → stock value drops
The author's argument goes backwards:Since ...Cotoy's stock value dropped today,we can conclude... Cotoy lost a big lawsuit today.

label: Goal
body:
In conversational terms, we can look for a correct answer in which a conditional rule is presented and the author tries to use it in reverse to draw her conclusion.
In more symbolic / algebraic terms, we're looking for something like this:
Prem 1: If X, then Y Prem 2: Y was true for Thing A. Conc: X was true for Thing B.

label: Background
body: Northern Asia is generally cool, but during hotter / more humid stretches, the yields of crops grown there went up a bunch. Soon, global warming will raise the temperatures in Northern Asia so that it's similar to how it is now during hotter / more humid stretches.

label: Surprising Claim
body: Yet scientists predict that yields of most of these crops will decrease in that future world.

label: Evaluate
body:
Given that short term spikes in temp and humidity seem to lead to higher crop yields, why do scientists think that once the temp and humidity settles into that "spiked level", crop yields will go down?
It seems like could resolve the Paradox one of two ways - it's the temperature jump not the temperature that causes more crop yields (i.e. a spike in temperature has a different effect than prolonged warmer temperatures)
- something else will be different in this future global warming world, so even though the temp / humidity is favorable to bigger yields, some other factor will change that compromises crop yields.

label: Goal
body: Look for an answer providing a difference between this world and the warmer world that would harm crop yields, or look for an answer providing a difference between temporary jumps in temp/humidity and permanent increases (that would harm crop yields).

label: Evidence
body:
No one in French department (such as Prof A) can teach more than one intro level class per term.
The only language classes being taught next term are advanced.

label: Conclusion
body: It is not the case that both of Prof A's French classes next term will be intro.

label: Auditor
body: R's family said the funds they donated to the neurology clinic should all be used to minimize patients' suffering. But since 1/5 of those funds has gone to new diagnostic technologies, the clinic has violated those terms.

label: Administrator's Response
body: If we improve our diagnostic technologies, we can diagnose many neurological disorders earlier. And in most cases, treating patients in the early stages of disorders leads to less suffering than when we treat patients only once they've hit advanced stages.

label: Evaluate
body:
Although this argument did have quantifier / conditional terms, there was no overlapping term between the first and second sentence, so this argument probably wouldn't benefit from going symbolic / algebraic.
Do we agree with the logic of the conclusion?
Sure! How could Prof A possibly be teaching two intro French classes next term if the only language classes next term are advanced, and if no one in the French department is allowed to teach more than one intro class per term.
So, it's valid logic. How would we characterize the structure? How do the ingredients combine to get us to the conclusion?
It actually seems like the two premises don't combine; each of one of them on its own would prove that conclusion.

label: Goal
body:
Look for an argument with two premises, each of which is capable of proving the conclusion.
(The first premise makes it possible that Prof A could be teaching one intro French, but it's still impossible for both of his classes to be intro French.)

label: Conclusion (therefore)
body: This new herbal mix is obviously not effective as a remedy for the common cold.

label: Evidence (since)
body: Many people who have colds aren't using the mix.

label: Intermediate Conclusion (it follows)
body: If the mix were effective, almost everyone with a cold would be using it.

label: Evidence (since)
body: Most people with colds wish to recover quickly.

label: Evaluate
body:
Because this argument makes multiple conclusions (signified by "it follows that" / "therefore"), we're allowed to talk about assumptions or flaws that occur in making either move.
What's being assumed in going from "if this mix were an effective cold remedy" to "almost everyone would be using it"?
I guess ideas like, "You're assuming people can afford it / people can obtain it / people have heard of it / it doesn't have bad side effects that would make people avoid it".
What's being assumed in going from "there are many people who have colds but don't use the mix" to "the mix is obviously ineffective"?
Well, seems like the same type of things. The author is assuming they're not using the mix because it's ineffective, so she's assuming there isn't some other reason why they aren't using the mix (too expensive / can't find it / don't know about it / side effects).

label: Goal
body:
Look for four things being assumed. They'll either sound like something the author is clearly thinking or we'll verify they're being assumed by convincing ourselves that when we negate them, they turn into weakening objections.
The correct answer might go against the author's logic, but more likely it will just be stronger than anything the author needs to assume or bring up some concept that's out of scope.

label: Sufferer's Conclusion
body: The herbal mixture is obviously not effective.

label: Sufferer's Evidence
body:
Suppose it were effective -- in that world, almost everybody with a cold would be using it, since most people with colds wish to recover quickly.
But there are many people who have colds but do not use the mixture.

label: Evaluate
body:
There are some serious logic problems with this argument, but who cares, it's a Method question. We're just supposed to describe it accurately.
The signature move the author made here was arguing via a contrapositive (of a counterfactual).
If you were right, then X would be true. But X isn't true. Thus you're not right.

label: Goal
body: Let's look for something that feels like it captures this contrapositive of a counterfactual. "If a claim were true, then X would be happening. But X isn't happening. So the claim must be false."

label: Conclusion
body: Law-abiding people's actions alone are truly responsible for crime.

label: Evidence
body:
Criminal actions, like all actions, are ultimately product of the environment that shaped the agent's characters.
The law-abiding majority, by their actions, do the most to create and maintain this environment.

label: Evaluate
body:
This author was woke before woke was a thing: The onlycrimehere, is the Establishment ... mannnn!
She's saying that we shouldn't hold criminals responsible for their actions, since they are just prisoners of their environment (no pun intended). We should really blame the actions of the law-abiding majority that create this environment.
But wait -- how can the author blameanyonefor their actions, including the law-abiding people?
I thought we said earlier that we can't blame people for their actions, when it's really just the result of the environment that shapes them. Doesn't this also apply to law-abiding people?

label: Goal
body:
Look for an answer pointing out the author'sInternal Contradiction(one of the famous flaws, but one that very rarely shows up as the real problem).
The author is forgiving one groups actions by saying "we're not accountable for our actions", and then going to on to how law-abiding people accountable for their actions.

label: Statements
body:
Causal (usually caused by) Quantifier (most / 1 out of 5)
Most cases of chronic back pain are caused by a bad spinal disk. 1 out 5 people over 30 have a bad spinal disk, but no chronic back pain.
Causal Difference-Maker (brought out by) Quantifier (generally)
When those people who have a bad disk but no chronic back pain eventually DO get chronic pain, it's usually caused by insufficient exercise, allowing the abs and spinal muscles to deteriorate.

label: Evaluate
body:
There aren't any obvious directions to go with combining these facts, but we can be reasonably confident that the correct answer will reinforce the causal difference-maker identified in the last sentence.
There are multiple Most claims, but none of them are talking about the same set of people, so we can't do a Trait Overlap inference there.
We might be able to say something like, "some of the cases of chronic pain are preventable", since the people who start out without pain but later develop it do so as a result of insufficient exercise. If they could/would have exercised, they potentially could have prevented the chronic pain that later developed from their bad disk.

label: Goal
body: Be wary of strong language, out of scope ideas, or unknown comparisons. Expect the correct answer to combine ideas from 2 or more claims.

label: Statements
body:
On the last day of the year, Q tallies up how much total coal supplies they have (mined, but not consumed).
Last day of '91 had much lower supplies than last day of '90.
Q hasn't imported or exported coal since 1970.

label: Evidence
body: The brain and its mental capacities evolved to assist self-preservation.

label: Evaluate
body:
Must Be True questions tend to involve conditional logic or mathematical comparisons. This appears to be the latter.
The last fact, that Q doesn't import or export coal, is seemingly just establishing that Q is a closed system. Any coal they mine, they use. Any coal they use came from their mines.
So if they have less coal in the bank account at the end of '91 than at the end of '90, what can we infer? Why did the coal account go down? Did they start mining less? Did they start using more? Some combo?
The one thing we can say, if our bank account is lower on Dec 31 than it was on Jan 1, is that over the course of the year we spent more money than we earned.

label: Goal
body: So we should be able to say that during 1991, we consumed more coal than we mined.

label: Conclusion
body: The student will probably get a B in this new course.

label: Evidence
body: The student has taken twelve courses so far, and got a B in most of them.

label: Evaluate
body:
"If it was true most of the time before, then it'll probably be true again" is the form of this argument.
To weaken that sort of argument, we would say, "No, no! This time isdifferent." To strengthen that sort of argument, we want to say, "Yes, especially since this time is very similar to those other times."

label: Goal
body: Look for four answers that make this time feel similar to those previous twelve examples (similar difficulty level / interest level / quality of teacher / time of day / etc.)

label: Conclusion (Therefore)
body: In order to keep from depressing the overall level of funding for civilian scientific research, the government should not increase its own funding.

label: Evidence
body:
If the government increases its funding for civilian scientific research, private patrons and industries will believe that such research has become primarily the government's responsibility.
If they believe that research is no longer primarily their responsibility, private patrons and industries will decrease their contributions toward research.

label: Evaluate
body:
Since the two premises are both conditionals (if / when) and have an overlapping term, we should think about whether they chain together. They do, to form this chain:
Govt increases → Private ppl think → Private ppl own funding CS research not will decrease for CS research primarily their contributions responsibility to that research
A valid contrapositive conclusion to draw at this point would be,
"In order to keepprivate patrons and industries from decreasing contributionsto civilian scientific research, the government should not increase its own funding."
The actual pseudo-contrapositive conclusion was,
"In order to keepoverall funding from decreasingfor civilian scientific research, the government should not increase its own funding."

label: Goal
body:
Thus, the author is assuming this Missing Link:
"If private patrons and industries decrease their contributions to CS research, then overall level of funding will decrease".
The author is failing to consider that the increase in government funding might more than offset the decrease in private funding. The net effect could be equal or greater overall funding for CS research.

label: Conclusion (Hence)
body: It's reasonable to believe that no ticket will win the lottery.

label: Evidence
body: For any given ticket in a 1000-ticket lottery, it is reasonable to believe that that ticket will lose.

label: Evaluate
body:
Conversationally, what is our objection?
Given that ... each individual ticket in a 1000-ticket raffle is likely to lose, How can we say that ... is itunreasonable to believe that no ticket will win the lottery?
Well, becauseof coursesome ticket will win the lottery. They'll reach into a bag and pull out ticket #647 and the person who has ticket #647 will win.
Every ticket only has a 1/1000 (0.1%) chance of winning, but there is a 100% chance that there will be a winning ticket, because that's how it works. The winning ticket is whichever ticket gets drawn.
Since both the Premise and the Conclusion are using parallel wording like "it is reasonable to believe that __", we might see this as a Part vs. Whole flaw.
Since it's unreasonable to think each part (each ticket) will be a winner, it's unreasonable to think that the whole (the entire lottery) will have a winner.
That's our author's flawed move.

label: Goal
body: Let's look for an answer where we can make a similar objection: "Sure, each individual entry is unlikely to be X, but for sureoneof the entries will be X".

label: Conclusion (therefore)
body: If the nerves inside the tooth aren't in imminent danger from a cavity, then dentists should not fill a cavity.

label: Evidence
body:
Filling a cavity inevitably damages some of the healthy parts of a tooth.
A cavity is only harmful if the decay reaches the nerves inside the tooth and many cavities left untreated would never get there.

label: Evaluate
body:
This argument feels like it's Weighing Tradeoffs, so we might be less likely to see the typical "If Evidence, then Conclusion" form of most correct Strengthen+Principle answers.
Should we or shouldn't we fill a cavity?
Filling it would provide the positive on reassuring us that we're protecting against the potential harm it could cause if the decay reaches the nerves inside the tooth.
But filling it would provide inevitable harm to some healthy parts of the tooth. And it's possible that the cavity itself would have never caused harm.

label: Goal
body: Look for something like, "If it's possible that X would not cause harm but treating X would definitely cause harm, then don't treat X".

label: Conclusion (therefore)
body: It is unlikely that the increase in the seal population has contributed significantly to the decline in the cod population.

label: Evidence
body: Cod plays a negligible role in the seal's diet.

label: Evaluate
body:
This is an Anti-Causal argument because the author is saying "the increase of seals is NOT what's causing the decrease in cod".
GIVEN THAT seal barely eat any cod HOW CAN WE STILL ARGUE the increase in sealsisa big cause of why the cod population is shrinking?
Maybe they don't eat cod, but the seals scare the cod away, or spread a disease to the cod, or disrupt the cod's habitat or food supply.

label: Goal
body: Let's find an answer that suggests a reason why the increasing seal population might still affect the cod population despite not preying directly on cod.

label: Hudson's response
body: Runs the same logic on himself getting rich and shows it leads to an absurd conclusion.

label: Evaluate
body:
We're debating whether allocating 1/5 of a donation towards researching new diagnostic technologies can qualify as "being used to minimize patients' suffering".
The 1st person is saying, "Of course not --- it's going to research, not flowing directly to patients".
The 2nd person is saying, "It's going to research that hopes to ultimately minimize the suffering of patients."
So if we're describing this response we might say things like - it suggests that the allocation of money does not violate the terms of the donation - it suggests that the allocation of money is still going towards minimizing suffering - it points to future ramifications of this allocation of money in order to justify its adherence to the terms of how the money was meant to be used.

label: Goal
body: Find something that descriptively matches.

label: Conclusion
body: This view is fundamentally mistaken. (i.e. recent policies towards Country X arenotjust appeasement)

label: Evidence (for)
body: Polls show that most people think that recent policies toward Country X are not appeasement.

label: Evaluate
body:
The author is trying to convince us of her conclusion that certain political commentators are wrong.
The only evidence she offers is that according to polls, most people think that these political commentators are wrong.
What's wrong with that?
We have no idea if most people have any idea what they're talking about. Polls may show that most people think that "there are penguins at the North Pole", but that doesn't mean there are penguins at the North Pole (there are not; they live near the South Pole)

label: Goal
body:
Let's look for an answer calling out the fact that an author isn't allowed to assume that just because most people believe A is true, that therefore A is true.
Some people would call this a semi-famous flaw known asOpinion vs. Fact

label: Principle
body:
only when is the same as "only if", which always introduces a necessary (Right side) idea.
So as written, this would say:
nation experiences → consumer confidence economic growth balanced w/ small amt of consumer skepticism
Usually, they like to test us on the contrapositives of Principles, so writing it that way would look like this:
not the case that nation won't consumer confidence → experience balanced w/ small amount economic of consumer skepticism growth

label: Goal
body: Find an answer that conforms to this principle. We only have the power to prove that a nationwon'texperience growth (we can only prove the stuff on the right side of the principle), so we might see some trap answers trying to prove that a nationwillexperience economic growth.

label: Statements
body:
Superlatives Sharks have a higher ratio of cartilage mass to body mass than any other organism. They have a greater resistance to cancer than any other organism. In the past 20 years, no patient responses to therapy have been more positive than the ones that come from eating shark cartilage.
Causal Shark cartilage has a substance that inhibits tumor growth (by not letting new blood networks grow).

label: Evaluate
body:
The correct answer on Must Be False usually contradicts a conditional claim or contradicts some Must Be True inference we can make.
There weren't any conditionals here, but there were three very strong statements.
When it comes to cartilage ratio or cancer resistance, Sharks > all other animals When it comes to therapeutic measures for terminal cancer patients,Eating shark cartilage ≥ all other measures
Note that this one is "greater than or equal to", because saying "no other measure has beenmorepositive" still leaves room for other measures to have beenaspositive.

label: Goal
body:
Look for an answer contradicting one of our facts or contradicting a synthesis we could make from the facts.
For example, a correct answer could say, "the organism with the most cancer resistance has the lowest ratio of cartilage mass to body mass".

label: Statements
body:
Causal (function to attract)
The petals of a poppy flower help to attract pollinating insects.
Conditional/Causal (triggers / causes)
Pollination ⇢ substance released ⇢ petals wilt occurs into flower w/in 2 days
Conditional (If / as long as)
Pollination not occurs and ⇢ substance not ⇢ petals fresh Plant can released into flower for 1+ week nourish petals
Conditional/Causal (triggers)
Cutting ⇢ pollination-substance unpollinated released into flower

label: Evaluate
body:
A lot of causal / conditional stuff to work with there. Do any of the conditionals chain together?
The 2nd and 3rd sentence give opposing rules (what if it IS pollinated / what if it ISN'T), so they don't chain together.
But the 4th sentence gives a rule that seemingly could be extended by the rule in the 2nd sentence:
Cutting an unpollinated poppy triggers that pollination-substance to be released, and that substance causes the petals to wilt, so it sounds like "if you cut an unpollinated poppy, then its petals will wilt within 1 or 2 days".

label: Goal
body: Look for something derivable from any of these facts. It likely won't use all of them, since some of them don't really connect with each other, but it seems like the correct answer will combine sentences 4 and 2.

label: Background
body: Opening a large shopping mall is often expected to boost the local economy and a lot of economic activity does transpire in these malls.

label: Surprising Claim
body: The increase in the local economy is way smaller than the total amount of economic activity that goes on in the mall.

label: Evaluate
body:
It might take a re-read or two to process what this last sentence is saying, but essentially it's saying something like this: Before Mall: local economy was $100 million + New Mall: $5 million of activity in mallyet,Local economy + mall: $101 million
One might have expected that if $5 million of business is being done in the mall, then that would be purely additive to the local economy, bringing us from $100 to $105 million.
But, if the amount of business the mall is doing ($5 million) is more than the boost to the local economy ($1 million), that suggests mathematically that the economic activity in the mall is "stealing" economic activity from elsewhere in the local economy.

label: Goal
body:
Look for an answer saying that a new large shopping mall will "steal" business from other places in the local economy, or an answer that somehow otherwise explains why the money being made in the mall isn't all being added onto the previous total of economic activity in the local economy.
What else could change with the new mall that would make the local economy do worse?

label: Conclusion (But we need to)
body: In considering changes to how science is conducted and regulated, we need to determine whether the changes are warranted, given their cost.

label: Evidence
body:
We could change how we conduct animal research (putting to a halt the testing of animals), but that would cost us opportunities to research certain things or would make researching other things very expensive.
We could change how we regulate DNA usage, by curtailing it drastically.
We could restrict other things too, and even create a system of fraud police, but all this would be costly and would change the character of science.

label: Evaluate
body:
Like most conclusions on Main Conclusion, LSAC is going out of its way to hide it and make it weird. Whenever we do a Main Conclusion, we specifically prime our brain before reading the paragraph to listen / look out for the two main patterns:
- conclusion is in the First Sentence - conclusion sounds like a Rebuttal
By doing that here, it's possibly easier to hear the author'sOpinionshining through in that second sentence (and it starts with a Pivot word likeBut, which would also prime us to wonder, "Is this the Conclusion?").
Once we hear an opinion, if the author seems to be trying to support that opinion then it's probably going to turn out that the first opinion really was the main conclusion.
Our author's 2nd sentence is saying, "as we consider changes, we gotta think about the tradeoffs", and then the author proceeds to give us 4 sentences that unpack that claim, since they all deal with changes, tradeoffs, or both.

label: Goal
body:
If we correctly found the Main Conclusion (the 'highest' Opinion that the author supports), then picking an answer is merely about finding the best language match for that claim.
We're looking for the best meaning match for the 2nd sentence.

label: Conclusion (it follows that)
body: We inhabit a world full of irregular events, in which there are no universal truths.

label: Evidence
body:
The postmodern view involves rejecting modern assumptions about there being order to the universe or universal truths.
The grand theories of the modern era are now sees as limited by the contexts of their time periods.
The belief in order has given way to a belief in the importance of irregularity and chaos.

label: Evaluate
body:
This argument appears to just be acting as though thepostmodern viewisreality.
Why should we accept postmodernism's description of the world? So what if they say the universe doesn't have order or universal truths. What makes them the experts on reality?
Even within the context of this argument, we can see that stuff we happen to believe at one time (such as the grand theories we used to believe) we might later come to doubt.
So who says that it will be any different when it comes to postmodernism? Maybe there will be an intellectual movement after postmodernism that says that the stuff postmodernists were saying was wrong and was just limited by the social and historical context in which it was elaborated?
There's a small pattern of arguments that have a He Said / She Said structure, where the author seems to arbitrarily side with one view over the other, without justifying it.
Grand Theories say that there are universal truths and order (there's an RC passage on these in PT82 that gives examples like Freudians thinking that everything comes back to repressed feelings about our moms, or Marxists thinking that everything comes down to the elites exploiting the working class).
Postmodernists say that there aren't universal truths or order.
The author is acting like we live in the world described by the postmodernists, but who said they're correct?

label: Goal
body: Let's look for an answer saying that the author is treating the Opinion of the postmodern view as though it's Fact. The author is ignoring that belief systems change over time, so there's no reason to think that the current one (postmodernism) is the correct one. And the author is arbitrarily siding with one view over another, without justifying that preference.

label: Statements
body:
Conditional - "if" (left side)prices constanteconomy weak → andunemployment rises
Conditional - "only if" (right side)unemployment → investmentrises decreases
When we're given conditionals, we check to see if they chain together. Is there a common ingredient? Sure, "unemployment rising".
We can chain that together to say:economy → unemployment → investmentweak rises decreases
The other thing we check for with conditionals is to see whether any facts trigger them (or, more commonly, their contrapositives)
The fact that we're told investmentisn'tdecreasing, means that we can derive the contrapositive inferences: - unemployment isnotrising - the economy isnotweak

label: Goal
body:
The correct answer on Must Be False usually contradicts a conditional (trigger happens but outcome doesn't) or contradicts an inference we've made. Look for answer that contradicts this,
economy → unemployment → investmentweak rises decreases
or that contradicts one of these
- unemployment isnotrising - the economy isnotweak

label: Conclusion
body: This claim is false. rephrased: our horoscopes do not completely determine our personalities.

label: Evidence
body: We found two individuals born 40 years ago today on the same day and at the same time (one in Toronto and one in New York), and they have different personalities.

label: Evaluate
body:
In order to prove that "X does not completely determine Y", the author has to show that sometimes X is present and Y happens, but sometimes X is present and Y doesn't happen. Or if we're thinking less in Absolute terms and more in Relative terms ... sometimes X is present and this Y happens, but sometimes X is present and this different Y happens.
If we were trying to prove "which law school you go to does not completely determine your earning power", then we would make our case by saying, "These two both went to school X, but one of them makes way more than the other".
If the author wants to prove that "horoscopes do not completely determine our personalities", then the author needs to show us "Here are two examples of the same horoscope, but they have different personalities".
The author is trying to do just that. Does she establish 1. Same horoscope (no, just that they are born same day / same time) 2. Different personalities (yes, that's the final sentence)

label: Goal
body: The missing idea in this argument is the issue of whether these two individuals have the same horoscope. The author is assuming, "If two people are born on the same day and at the same time, then they have the same horoscope".

label: Evaluate
body:
Why would Engle say that? Only if Engle thinks McKinley is talking about effects thathaven't been confirmed yet— i.e., the drug's therapeutic effects, the very thing the study is designed to test. If McKinley meant already-known side effects, Engle's "you're assuming the outcome" complaint wouldn't apply, because side effects you already know about don't require running the study to discover.
So Engle is reading McKinley as saying "the drug will work in obvious ways during the study." Engle thinks that's premature — we don't know yet whether or how the drug will work.

label: Information
body:
Causal Difference-Maker (under the influence) Because of the modern computer-oriented culture, children's publishing has a flashy new look that emphasizes illustrations and graphic design.
Causal Chain (resulting / leads to)Flashy new look lack of short-lived emphasizing ⇢ substance ⇢ lifespan w/ graphics trendy topics
The last sentence doesn't have any causal connector language attached, so I wouldn't want an answer to try connecting this last sentence to the stuff in the first sentence, but it does offer a few comparative differences with older children's publishing.
We know that today's children's publishing is more likely to have humor, less likely to have complexity, and covers a less wide range of topics.

label: Evaluate / Goal
body:
The correct answer will probably reinforce the causal connections identified in the first sentence.
Computer culture led to a flashier look, which led to a lack of substance, which led to short-lived books that cover trendy (not timeless) subjects.

label: Conclusion
body: One's general disposition is a result of the activity of one's frontal lobe.

label: Evidence
body: In a study, they found a correlation between left frontal lobe activity and your general mood. Happy people had more left lobe activity; sadder people had less left frontal action.

label: Evaluate
body:
Since the author is interpreting a correlation, we could weaken by thinking of other ways to explain this data.
Why else can we say that good-natured people have more left activity and more depressed people have left less left lobe activity?
Given this EKG correlation between left frontal lobe and general mood, is it a safe leap to the idea that "one's disposition isa resultof the frontal lobe"?
No, it seems pretty leap-y. We expand from talking about characteristic mood to talking about general disposition. And instead of saying that frontal lobe has some influence, it goes as far as to say dispositionis the resultof frontal lobe activity.

label: Goal
body:
Any time the author is interpreting data, and we have this Curious Fact / Explanation template, we want toWeakenby either - suggesting an alternate way to explain [why there's a correlation between happy/sad and high/low left frontal lobe activity]
- making the author's way seem less plausible by undermining the idea that disposition is (purely) a result of your frontal lobe.

label: Conclusion
body: What is really aesthetically relevant is not what a painting symbolizes, but what it directly presents to experience.

label: Evidence
body: What is really aesthetically relevant is not its extrinsic properties, but its intrinsic properties (i.e. what it directly presents to experience)

label: Evaluate
body:
With my cleaned up version, where I arrange the Conclusion and Evidence in parallel, it's easier to see that the author seems to be assuming "What a painting symbolizes is in the category of extrinsic properties".
How did we get there?
Both the premises and the conclusion are saying,"Look atthis, notthat"
intrinsic properties extrinsic properties
what it directly what a painting presents to experience symbolizes
aesthetically relevant irrelevant to our aesthetic interactions

label: Goal
body: When we're doing Sufficient Assumption, and there's a New Term in the conclusion (i.e. a term that was never discussed or defined in the Evidence), then that New Termmustbe in the correct answer, in order for us to get a closed circuit of logic.

label: McKinley's Conclusion
body: We will not be able to perform a double-blind study on the new drug.

label: McKinley's Evidence
body: The drug will have various effects on patients' bodies that will make researchers and patients aware of who got the drug versus the placebo.

label: Engle's Critique
body: We could still have a double blind study. You don't know the outcome of the study.

label: Anticipate
body:
Question stems about the 2nd person "interpreting" the 1st person are basically a subtype of Flaw. They're asking us what's wrong with the 2nd person's interpretation. We read the 1st person's statements charitably and carefully so that we're better able to defend them against the 2nd person's confused rebuttal.
Why does Engle think you would need to know the outcome of the study in order to know whether the drug is having various effects that the placebo doesn't have?
Clinical studies of drugs are designed in order to assess whether the drug achieves a certain effect for the patient. When they're testing Ozempic to see if it achieves weight loss for the patient, they have a placebo group who doesn't get Ozempic (they get a fake sugar pill). To firmly establish that Ozempic is what's causing any weight loss, we want to see that the Ozempic group lost more weight than the control group who got the placebo.
Engle is talking about THOSE kinds of effects. You don't know whether Ozempic helps people lose weight, until the study is over and you look at the data, He's thinking, "researchers wouldn't be able to look at people in the study who were losing weight and think that must be an Ozempic subject or someone not losing weight and think that must be a placebo subject because the researchers don't know yet whether Ozempic does anything.
Meanwhile, McKinley might just be saying, "We already know that one of the chemicals in Ozempic makes people have to pee all the time", so he might be saying "we won't be able to stay 'blind' for long, because we'll know that the frequent-urinators received Ozempic."

label: Goal
body: The right answer should describe Engle's read of McKinley: that McKinley meant the desired effect of the drug (e.g. help someone lose weight), not some known side effect (like small bladder syndrome).

label: McKinley's Conclusion
body: A double-blind study can't be performed on this drug.

label: McKinley's Evidence
body: The drug will have effects that reveal who got drug versus placebo.

label: Engle's Critique
body: Engle accuses McKinley of assuming the study's outcome — which only makes sense if Engle is reading "effects" as the therapeutic effects, not known side effects.

label: Goal
body: Identify Engle's interpretation: McKinley means therapeutic effects, not known side effects.

label: McKinley's Argument
body: McKinley says: we can't do a double-blind test on this drug because the drug's effects on patients will give it away.

label: Engle's Pushback
body: Engle replies: hold on, you're jumping ahead — you're assuming you already know what the study would show.

label: Goal
body: Find the answer that says: Engle takes McKinley to be referring to therapeutic effects rather than known side effects.

label: Evidence
body:
Modern navigation systems have low-power circuitry, which is more susceptible to interference than vacuum-tube circuitry found in older planes.
During landing, navigation systems receive radio signals from the airport to guide the plane to the runway.
One plane veered off course during landing and its dials dimmed when a passenger turned on a laptop computer.

label: Evaluate
body:
We're told that new planes are more vulnerable to interference, but we don't know whether the devices that passengers carry on board actually cause interference.
The only evidence for that idea is this one data point where a dude opened his laptop and the plane seemed to experience interference. Do we know for sure the laptop caused it? Maybe it was a coincidence and the dimming dials and veering off course came from some different cause.
The argument is definitely assuming a causal relationship:
Curious Fact: Why did the plane veer off course / why did the dials dim?
Author's Explanation: The opened laptop caused interference.
To strengthen the argument, we would show more evidence that supports this causal relationship. To weaken it, we would suggest alternative causes of the navigational disruptions or show that the electronic devices are not the source of interference.

label: Goal
body: Let's find four answers that help us argue that passenger devices do cause interference for these newer planed.

label: Statements
body:
quantifier (almost all)
Almost all plants have flavonoids.
A specific variety of flavonoid in apples is an antioxidant.
causal(X is a factor in Y)
Antioxidants are known to be a factor in the prevention of heart disease (i.e. antioxidants can help to prevent heart disease).

label: Evaluate
body:
The #1 thing we're reading for on Inference paragraphs isOverlapping Concepts, because usually when two claims have an overlapping concept, we can infer something by combining them.
Claim 1 and 2 both mention "flavonoids". Almost all plants have them, and apples have a specific one that is an antioxidant.
We could infer: "some plants contain antioxidants"
Claim 2 and 3 both mention "antioxidants". Some Apple-flavonoids are antioxidants, and antioxidants can help prevent heart disease.
We could infer: "some apples / some flavonoids can help to prevent heart disease".

label: Goal
body: Look for the safest, most provable claim we can find. It will probably make use of the antioxidant connection between apples/flavonoids and preventing heart disease.

label: Information
body:
causal (doing X protects Y)
raise humidity ⇢ protect furniture, drapes, of the room and computers from damage from dry air
causal (make, helps, alleviates)
raise humidity ⇢ people feel warmer & of the room helps attack viruses & alleviates some rashes

label: Evaluate
body: We were basically told four different things that can result from raising the humidity of the room: 1. Some objects are protected from being damaged by air that's too dry 2. People feel warmer 3. It helps the body defend against viruses 4. it can alleviate some skin rashes

label: Goal
body: Let's find four supportable answers, based on what we were told.

label: Sam's Conclusion
body: Starlight cars are remarkably free from manufacturing defects.

label: Sam's Evidence
body:
If a car has a manufacturing defect in the first year of ownership, people who bought it won't be highly satisfied.
But 95% of Starlight purchases say they are highly satisfied.

label: Tiya's Response
body: Some manufacturing defects don't show up 'til year 3 or later.

label: Evaluate
body:
Sam's 95% "highly satisfied" premise triggers the contrapositive of the conditional he presents.
That conditional outputs the conclusion that 95% of Starlight buyers didn't have a manufacturing defect in their first year of ownership.
However, Sam ventures onward to a further conclusion: Starlight cars are remarkably free from defects.
If 95% of recent Starlight buyers didn't have any manufacturing defects in their first year, does that show that these cars are remarkably free from defects?
Tiya is suggesting that No, that conclusion doesn't necessarily follow. The "jury's still out" on whether these recently purchased Starlight cars are free from defects, since defects sometimes don't surface until year 4 or later.

label: Goal
body: In the vernacular of Method questions, we'd probably be looking for something like, "Tiya raises an additional consideration that suggests that Sam would be premature in drawing a conclusion about being free from defects with incomplete evidence."

label: Statements
body:
Point of View 1 (some environmentalists)
It might not be a good idea for us to exploit features of the environment, because if we exhaust them until they don't exist anymore then we won't be able to get any future benefits from them.
Point of View 2 (many environmentalists)
Nature actually has intrinsic value, so it's wrong to destroy it whether or not it makes economic sense to do so.

label: Evaluate
body: It's hard to take any guess about how to synthesize these two points of view. We could say something like, "There's more than one way to justify not-exploiting the environment", since each point of view gave a different rationale for the same general idea of "don't ruin the environment".

label: Goal
body: Pick the most provable answer we can find.

label: Claim
body: Observational research yields information about consumer behavior that surveys alone cannot provide.

label: Goal
body:
Because we're just strengthening aclaim, not an argument, there isn't really any thinking to do up front.
Let's just find an answer that highlights an advantage or unique insight provided by observational research over surveys.

label: Conclusion
body: You're wrong to say that vexone is only effective against the German cockroach. (it's been used effectively for almost a decade against all the species that infest North America).

label: Evidence
body: We have many documented studies of our product Roach Ender, which contains vexone, that demonstrate this.

label: Evaluate
body:
This question stem looks like a Must Be False EXCEPT. But when we read the stimulus, it sounds like an argument.
The question stem refers to it as a "view", which is an ambiguous term that could allude to an individual belief or to an entire argument.
The stimulus reads like a rebuttal argument. We might notice the Part vs. Whole flaw happening.
Vexone is a part of Roach Ender. Roach Ender, the product, is effective against all the species that infest North America.
Thus, the author concludes,vexoneis effective against all the species that infest North America.

label: Goal
body: It's hard to know what the answers will be offering us, because we never see question stems like, "All of these conflict with this view EXCEPT". We should probably just look for four answers that seem to either weaken the argument or go against one of the claims presented.

label: Party 1
body: Prehistoric birds were cold-blooded (b/c growth rings in their body are thought to only occur in cold-blooded animals)

label: Party 2
body: Prehistoric birds were warm-blooded (b/c dense blood vessels in their bones suggest they were active creatures, and thus warm-blooded)

label: Evaluate
body:
This isn't like a normal Paradox question, because it's not Background Fact vs. Surprising Claim, it's just Point of View 1 vs. Point of View 2.
So we won't try to frame our thinking in the normal way. We'll just recount the evidence in favor of each position so that we can better judge whether each answer choice seems go to with/against 1 or 2.

label: Goal
body:
Maybe we'll support party 2 by saying answering party 1's concern and showing that warm blooded animals ALSO had these weird rings.
Maybe we'll support party 1 by answering party 2's objection, showing that cold-blooded animals sometimes had dense blood vessels in their bones and/or were active creatures.
Or there will just be a new fact that will incline us towards thinking that prehistoric birds were cold vs. warm blooded.

label: Conclusion
body: (implicitly) Citizens should vote.

label: Evidence
body: If citizens don't vote, democratic institutions will crumble and lots of social cohesion will be lost. Yes, one vote isn't going to make a perceptible difference, but you have to think about the act of non-voting on a large scale. If it would be socially damaging for large numbers to not vote, then it would be wrong for an individual to not vote. (Just as if it would be bad for society if large numbers of people engaged in theft, then it's wrong for an individual to engage in theft).

label: Evaluate
body:
Usually, on Main Conclusion questions, the conclusion is found in the first sentence or as part of some "but / yet / however" style rebuttal. Here we kind of have neither. The first sentence isn't a supported idea. "Why would failure to vote lead to the crumbling of institutions or a loss of social cohesion?" The argument doesn't say.
The argument establishes in that first sentence that there are negative consequences if citizens don't vote. Then it presents a discussion that is sort of rebutting the suggested position of, "It doesn't matter if an individual fails to vote".
"Yes it does!", the author thinks. Why does it matter?Here, we get supporting ideas: - if collective omission would damage social cohesion (which we know from the first sentence it would), then individual omission is wrong.

label: Goal
body: Since it's harder to land on one explicit claim to call the Conclusion, I would look for something resembling "Y'all should vote. It's bad if an individual doesn't vote", but ultimately be flexible and test each answer by the standard of ... 1. Does this sound like an opinion the author holds? 2. Did she support this opinion?

label: View
body: Humans, once aware of their superior cognitive faculties, cannot be made happy by anything that does not involve gratification of these faculties.

label: Background
body: Human beings have cognitive faculties that are superior to those of other animals.

label: Evaluate
body:
This is being called a "view", not an argument. There are two claims, so we could potentially attack either one.
Should we try to argue that "humansdon'thave cognitive faculties superior to other animals"? That seems like an uphill battle. We know animals can't take LSAT. :)
Should we try to argue that "even once you're aware of superior faculties like logic, chess, classical music, etc. you can still be made happy by stuff like fast food and cheesy pop music?"
That seems more realistic.

label: Goal
body: Let's find an answer that suggests that humans, even when aware of their cognitive faculties, can find happiness in activities or experiences that do not involve the direct use of these cognitive faculties.

label: Conclusion
body: If we find a trace of mercury in Beethoven's hair, we'll know that venereal disease caused Beethoven's deafness.

label: Evidence
body: In Beethoven's time, mercury was commonly ingested to treat venereal disease.

label: Evaluate
body:
This actually has the structural feel of aNecessary vs. Sufficientflaw. We know that in Beethoven's time that "if you had venereal disease, then you would (commonly) ingest mercury".
The author is thinking, "If Beethoven has mercury in his system, then he had a venereal disease."
We know that venereal disease was one possible reason why you would have mercury in your system, but maybe it's not the only reason. Maybe Beethoven used a mercury-laden shampoo on his hair. Maybe he put mercury on his oatmeal. Maybe mercury was also the treatment for heart disease or lung disease.
Maybe mercury was the cure-all Robitussin of its day (this is an allusion to a Chris Rock comedy routine).

label: Goal
body: The author is assuming there isn't some other explanation for why people would have mercury in their hair, and the author is assuming anything needed to make his explanation plausible (Beethoven would have realized he had a disease, gone to a doctor, been prescribed mercury, taken the prescribed meds, etc.).

label: Background
body: Paper X pays its reporters a much lower average salary than other papers pay their reporters.

label: Justification
body: "Yes, we pay them less, but they receive valuable training via their assignments!"

label: Evaluate
body:
We need to weaken this justification. This is how Paper X justifies paying its reporters lower than average wages, and we need to make this seem like a crappy excuse for the low wages.
This justificationAssumes a Difference-- aren't the reporters at the other papers, where they pay better, also getting valuable training through their assignments?
The executive must be thinking that the training you get at Paper X is a lot more valuable than the training you get elsewhere.

label: Goal
body: Find an answer that makes "the training" seem less valuable or less special than the executive wants to think it is.

label: Conclusion (So)
body: An individual's aesthetic judgments must be evaluated in terms of how much they promote that individual's survival.

label: Intermediate Conclusion (Thus)
body: The capacity to make aesthetic judgments is an adaptation to past environments in which humans lived.

label: Evaluate
body:
There two conclusions drawn, so technically the answer could deal with either reasoning move, but the first reasoning move from claim 1 to claim 2 seems pretty solid (and is already a less likely target, given that it's an intermediate conclusion).
It's essentially assuming that "If something evolved to assist self-preservation, then it's an adaptation to past environments in which humans lived". That's pretty boilerplate natural selection thinking, so the answer probably won't focus there.
The move from Intermediate to Main Conclusion is based on two different claims about aesthetic judgments:
Since they "evolved to" assist self-preservation they "must be evaluated in terms of how well they" assist self-preservation.

label: Goal
body:
On a first pass, be picky about finding normative language in the answer that relates to our conclusion, which is about "how we should evaluate something".
It'll probably sound something like, "If it evolved for purpose of doing X, then we need to evaluate it based on how well it does X."

label: Conclusion
body: Aesthetic judgments must be evaluated by their contribution to individual survival.

label: Evidence
body: Brain evolved for self-preservation; aesthetic capacity is therefore an adaptation.

label: Evaluate
body: The leap "evolved for X → must be judged by X" needs a principle.

label: Goal
body: Find the principle that says: judge things by the function they evolved to serve.

label: Conclusion
body: The author wants to say: aesthetic judgments — like which painting is beautiful — should be evaluated by whether they help you survive.

label: Evidence
body: Why? Because the brain evolved for self-preservation, and aesthetic judgments are part of brain function. So aesthetic judgment is, ultimately, an adaptation for survival.

label: Evaluate
body: The hidden move is the principle: "if a capacity evolved to serve function X, then we evaluate it by how well it serves function X." That's not obviously true — you could evolve a capacity for survival and still evaluate it by other criteria (pleasure, aesthetics, social value). The argument needs the principle to make the leap from "evolved for survival" to "must be judged by survival."

label: Goal
body: Find the answer that supplies that principle.

label: Main Conclusion (it is clear that / thus)
body: It's clear that psychological factors have taken over the role pheromones play (for other animals) in determining sexual behavior.

label: Intermediate Conclusion (So)
body: Pheromones are merely a vestige of our evolutionary past.

label: Evidence
body:
For animals, sexual behaviors are involuntary, which shows they're being controlled by chemicals (pheromones).
For humans, who have free will, behavior is voluntary.

label: Evaluate
body:
This is a bit of a mess. I'm not even 100% willing to stand behind the Main vs. Intermediate conclusion divide.
If we focus on the conclusion that "psychological factors have taken over the role of determining sexual behavior", are we convinced?
It seems like premises are forcing us to believe that psychological factors from free will are kicking in, but I guess I'm wondering if it's clear whether they "take over".
Couldn't human sexual behavior be a product of both psychological factorsandpheromones?
If we focus on the conclusion in the last sentence, we need to think about proving the idea that something is a "vestige of our evolutionary past".
We would create a linking assumption such as, "If something no longer takes over to determine sexual behavior, then it has become a vestige of the evolutionary past".
The idea of "vestige" is sort of like obsolescence. Because we have free will, we don't need/use pheromones.
So, it seems like we could weaken the argument by showing that pheromones still have some current usefulness in human life. Maybe that's by explaining how they assist free will in picking good mates. Maybe pheromones do something for us that isn't related to sexual behavior.

label: Goal
body:
Stay flexible. If we negate it, it should sound like an objection.
The author's main ideas here are that animals and humans are different when it comes to pheromones. Because we have free will, our sexual behavior is voluntary and thus controlled by psychological factors. And if we're not using pheromones for this / if they're not taking over, then they are just a vestige of our evolutionary past.

label: Conclusion
body: Many attributions of 17th century Dutch landscape to major artists are definitely wrong.

label: Evidence
body:
