Of the surviving 17th century Dutch landscapes, there's an equal number attributed to major artists as to minor ones.
But only a handful of major artists painted in this genre, whereas many prolific minor artists made a living cranking these Dutch landscapes out.

label: Evaluate
body:
The author is thinking purely in terms of numbers.
She thinks that during the 17th century, major artists would have produced way fewer Dutch landscapes than minor artists would have (since minor artists were cranking these out prolifically, trying to satisfy the insatiable demands of the market).
So let's say for example that major artists created 100 of these paintings, whereas minor artists created 1000 of them.
The author is thinking, "if the surviving paintings are supposedly 1/2 major, 1/2 minor that's gotta be wrong. After all, the ratio of major to minor wasn't 1:1, it was more like 1 : 10."
We could call this aCurious Comparison-- how could it be that major artists made less than half of the Dutch landscapes in the 17th century but are attributed to half of the surviving ones?
The author's way of explaining this is, "We must be misattributing a bunch of these ones done by minor artists to major artists".
We, of course, are tasked with considering Alternate Explanations .... "Maybe a Dutch landscape painted by amajorartist would be much more likely to survive for several centuries than would one painted by a minor artist."
After all, the ones painted by major artists would be more valuable, presumably, so people would have more incentive to hang onto them. And perhaps they were owned by wealthier people, whose belongings and estates have been better preserved and attended to.
The Dutch landscapes painted by minor artists to satisfy rabid public demand might have been cheap to purchase, painted on cheaper (more degrading) materials, and thus many more of them would have ended up in the garbage eventually.

label: Goal
body: Identify Hudson's tactic: a parallel argument that produces an untenable conclusion.

label: Whittaker's argument
body: Whittaker says you can't count the number of med students who drop out before their second year, because if they drop out, they never reach a second year — so the phrase "before their second year" doesn't apply.

label: Goal
body:
Since this is Strengthen, we need to eitherRule Outan alternate explanation (Dutch landscapes by major artists were no more likely to be carefully preserved over the centuries than were landscapes by minor artists)
or
Increasethe plausibility of the author's explanation (there is reason to believe that a bunch of these 17th century Dutch landscape paintings were erroneously attributed to a major painter)

label: Conclusion (Thus)
body: The size of the interstitial nucleus determines whether or not male cats can contract disease X.

label: Evidence
body: A neurologist performed autopsies on male cats who died from X and found that these male cats had interstitial nuclei that were as large as those generally found in female cats.

label: Evaluate
body:
Since the author is concluding something causal (the size of Y determines whether you can contract X) based off a correlation (male cats with X were more likely to have bigger interstitial nuclei than average male cats), we are in familiar Explain the Curious Fact territory.
Curious Fact ... why did these male cats who died of X have bigger than average interstitial nuclei?
Author's Explanation ... having a big interstitial nucleus makes it possible for a male cat to contract disease X (the ones with regular sized interstitial nuclei cannot contract disease X).

label: Goal
body:
Since this is Weaken, we would want to either 1. suggest anAlternate Explanationfor the Curious Fact why else could it be that the cats who died from X had bigger than average interstitial nuclei? maybe (Reverse Cause) the disease itself causes your interstitial nucleus to enlarge? maybe (Third Factor) there's some genetic condition where a male cat is born with certain female traits, such as the bigger interstitial nucleus, and that genetic condition is ultimately what causes susceptibility to disease X.
or
2. undermine theplausibilityof the Author's Explanationwhat could make it seem less likely that size of interstitial nucleus has any causal bearing on whether male cats can contract X?

label: Conclusion
body: It's irrational to respond to someone who is imploring us to change our behavior by drawing attention to that person's behavior.

label: Evidence
body: Whether or not someone heeds their own advice is irrelevant to whether or not we should heed their advice.

label: Evaluate
body:
This doesn't seem like an argument that will lend itself well to writing an algebraic recipe, but if we tried it might look something like this:
Background: It's common 3when people want us to do X for us to do Y.Premise: But Y is irrelevant to whether or not we should do X.Conclusion: So this response is irrational.
In a more general sense, we could say that the argument is saying "focus on the substance of the criticism, not the source of the criticism".
If the biggest drunk in town is telling you that you drink too much, don't say, "Oh, yeah? Well you drink even more!" Instead, just assess whether it's really true that you drink too much.

label: Goal
body: Let's look for an argument saying that our typical response to X is inappropriate/irrational, because our response is technically irrelevant to how we should respond to X.

label: Conclusion (thus)
body: The current popularity of comedians who display disrespect in their acts is hardly surprising.

label: Evidence
body: When people fail to live up to the very ideals they hold in highest esteem, exaggeration of such failings often forms the basis of successful comedy.

label: Evaluate
body:
The author is arguing, "It's no wonder that comedians who do X are popular. After all, doing Y often forms the basis of successful comedy".
In arguing that way, she's assuming that "doing X is doing Y".

label: Goal
body:
Let's look for something like
"when comedians display disrespect for others in their acts, they are exaggerating the failings of people who have failed to live up to the very ideals they hold in highest esteem".

label: Conclusion (clearly)
body: Triple-trailers are safer than other commercial vehicles.

label: Evidence
body: In areas where triple-trailers are permitted on highways (the western part of the country), the rate of fatalities per mile is lower than the national rate of fatalities per mile for all other commercial vehicles.

label: Evaluate
body:
Since the author is interpreting the causal significance of a statistic (a Curious Comparison), we can use our Curious Fact / Explanation mindset.
Curious Fact .... why do triple-trailers have fewer fatalities per mile than the average rate of other commercial vehicles?
Author's Explanation ... triple-trailers are safer than other commercial vehicles.
We can think about weakening this argument by providing an alternate explanation for why the triple-trailers have a lower fatality rate (maybe there are fewer passengers riding in them, so fewer fatalities per accident ... maybe the drivers are just better, safer drivers, etc.)
Or we can weaken by undermining the plausibility that triple-trailers are safer (they have more blind spots ... their braking distance is much greater ... they're more prone to computer braking malfunctions, etc.)

label: Goal
body:
The more common tendency for Weaken is to provide analternate explanationfor the curious fact, so primarily we'll look for some different way to explain why triple-trailers are getting fewer fatalities per mile.
But we'd also consider any answer that makes it seem like triple-trailers arenotsafer than other commercial vehicles.

label: Whittaker's argument
body: There can be no number of medical school students who drop out before their second year, because if they drop out, they never have a second year.

label: Hudson's response
body: Hudson runs Whittaker's reasoning on a parallel case: by your reasoning, I cannot help becoming rich, since there's no such thing as my dying before my first million is in the bank. The conclusion ("I cannot help but become rich") is obviously absurd, which exposes the reasoning as broken.

label: Evaluate
body: Hudson's technique: build an argument with the same form as Whittaker's, on a different topic, and show that this analogous argument produces an obviously bad conclusion. Since the form leads to absurdity in the parallel case, the same form is suspect in Whittaker's original case.

label: Goal
body: Find the answer that describes Hudson's tactic: showing a relevantly analogous argument leads to an untenable conclusion.

label: Whittaker's argument
body: No number of medical-school dropouts before their second year exists — they never have a second year if they drop out.

label: Hudson's response
body: Hudson plays back the same trick on something obviously wrong: "By your logic, I'll definitely become rich, because there's no such thing as me dying before my first million." Hudson clearly can die before his first million. So the reasoning has to be broken — and if it's broken in the parallel case, it was broken in Whittaker's original case too.

label: Evaluate
body: This is a classic move: take someone's reasoning, run it on a different topic where the conclusion is clearly false, and use the absurd outcome to discredit the original reasoning.

label: Goal
body: Find: shows a relevantly analogous argument leads to an untenable conclusion.

label: Conclusion
body: New bulbs will sell very poorly.

label: Counter-evidence
body: New bulbs are more cost-effective than old bulbs. (costs 3 times more, but lasts 10 times as long)

label: Evaluate
body:
We weren't given any reasons to think that new bulbs will sell poorly (other than their higher upfront cost), so we might see one answer saying, "People don't think about how long a bulb will last; they just look for the cheapest one".
But the other answers that strengthen will just give us reasons to think that these new bulbs will sell poorly.

label: Goal
body: Eliminate four answers that make it seem like new bulbs will sell poorly. Pick the remaining answer (whether it weakens or is just irrelevant).

label: Statements
body:
Since this isMust Be True, we're prioritizing looking for black-and-white claims, so the "possibly caused" in the 1st sentence and "normally" in the 2nd sentence makes them less enticing starting points.
Even the 3rd statement is weak -- "X can be caused by Y".
The last two sentences offer us a conditional and a fact that triggers the contrapositive of that conditional.
conditionalship sinks deep in ocean and → implode ship wasn't fully flooded
contrapositive~implode → ~sink or fully flooded We were told that the Rienzi didn't implode. So it's either true that the R didn't sink, wasn't fully flooded or both.
However, we know that the R sank. So we're left with the idea that the R was fully flooded.
How was it fully flooded? Sabotage? Or maybe the water just entered the ship atypically fast? We can't say that part for sure, so let's not fall for any trap answers speculating about that.

label: Goal
body: Look for an answer saying "the Rienzi was fully flooded when it sank", or something else we could derive from the paragraph.

label: Main Conclusion
body: The decision to restore the cloak's green is fully justified.

label: Intermediate Conclusion (hence)
body: It appears likely that an artist other than Veronese tampered with the painting after its completion.

label: Premises
body: X-ray and chemical tests show the red was appliedafterthe painting was completed, and the red paint wasn't mixed in Veronese's workshop.

label: Evaluate
body:
Whenever we do Main Conclusion and Role, we prep ourselves for the fact that the conclusion is usually Pivot/Rebuttal (60% of them) or First Sentence (25%).
The first sentence is an opinion from the author, "fully justified". If the rest of the paragraph seems to be supporting why we're justified in restoring the cloak from red to green, then this is our main conclusion.
Indeed, the rest of the paragraph defends why it's justified. The final claim is an Intermediate conclusion based on the 2nd sentence.

label: Goal
body: They're asking us about the final claim, so let's look for something like "intermediate conclusion". It's supported by the 2nd sentence and it provides support for the 1st sentence.

label: Main Conclusion
body: The restoration is justified.

label: Intermediate Conclusion
body: A later artist tampered with the painting.

label: Premises
body: Tests show red was applied after completion and not mixed in Veronese's workshop.

label: Goal
body: Identify the tampering claim as a subsidiary conclusion supporting the main conclusion.

label: Judgment on George (should = opinion)
body: George should not have hit his pet for chewing on furniture.

label: Reason (since)
body: Chewing on furniture would not have hurt the bird.

label: Implicit Principle
body: If action X wouldn't hurt your pet, then you shouldn't hit your pet for action X.

label: Judgment on Carla (so)
body: Carla was justified in hitting her pet when it bounded into a busy street.

label: Reason
body: Now the pet enters the street only when accompanied by Carla.

label: Evaluate
body:
When we read this, we might be thinking, "What's up with this double standard, author? Carla's allowed to hit her puppy but George can't hit his parrot?"
The author would have to say that these are two different situations; there's a meaningful difference that makes him shift his pet-hitting policy from "not cool" to "justified".
He never spells it out, but the suggested difference is that in Carla's case, the action she was trying to prevent could have easily hurt the puppy. He probably thinks, "It's worth mildly hurting the puppy by hitting it if that lessens the possibility of the puppy getting terribly hurt by running into traffic".

label: Goal
body: We want a principle that works with the judgments for both actions. Since one act of pet-hitting was justified and the other wasn't, this rule needs to say something like, "Whether or not it's okay to hit your pet (to discipline it against some action) is based on whether or not that action could potentially hurt your pet."

label: Background
body: Mature white pines steal so much sunlight that barely any light reaches the floor, making it impossible for new white pines to grow at the base of those trees. (there's also a deep, dry leaf litter)

label: Setup
body: If we saw a dense forest stand (group of trees) consisting of nothing but mature white pines ...

label: Goal
body:
... there wouldn't be any baby white pines growing on the forest floor? All the trees grew up together? There's a ton of dry litter on the ground?
Look for a safely worded answer that reinforces something we know about white pines.

label: Conclusion (It is obvious from this)
body: Owning a laptop computer led to a higher-paying job.

label: Evaluate
body:
This argument features a classic Correlation to Causation move. Hence, we can use our Explain Curious Fact framework.
The evidence presents a Correlation, the most typical kind of "Curious Fact". The most typical phrasing for a correlation is this: people who are trait A are more likely to be trait B
People who have a laptop are more likely to make 25% more money.
The conclusion is causal, because it uses a causal verb "X led to Y". When LSAT authors look at a correlation, they assume that one half of it caused the other.
This author looks at the correlation betweenowning laptop || making 25% more
and assumes thatowning laptop --led to--> making 25% more
WithExplain Curious Factarguments, we always evaluate 1. could there be someAlternate Explanationfor the curious fact? 2. how plausible is the Author's explanation?
Flaw questions primarily care about #1. When an author assumes that a correlation between X and Y means that X causes Y, we're supposed to consider two alternate explanations:REVERSE CAUSE: Y causes Xmaybe making 25% more came first, and that led to people buying laptops because they could afford them
3RD FACTOR: Z causes X and Ymaybe the sort of jobs that provide their employees with laptops also pay 25% more

label: Goal
body: Look for an answer complaining that the author has assumed a causal relationship from a mere correlation, or look for an answer raising the possibility of alternate explanations, such as Reverse Cause or 3rd Factor.

label: Conclusion (So)
body: Rhonda will not see the movie tomorrow afternoon.

label: Evidence
body: Rhonda will see it tomorrow afternoon only if Paul goes to the afternoon concert. Paul will not go unless Ted goes. But Ted refuses to go.

label: Evaluate
body:
When we're doing Parallel and we see conditional logic, then it's usually beneficial to write up the algebraic recipe of what we're looking for. We can see that the first two sentences / premises are conditionals. The third sentence / premise is a fact. And the the conclusion is a fact.
P1: R movieonly ifP concert Rm → Pc P2: no PcunlessTc Pc → Tc P3: no Tc. ~Tc. C: no R. ~R.
The two premises chain together, Rm → Pc → Tc The contrapositive chain would say ~Tc → ~Pc → ~Rm
The 3rd claim, the factual premise, gives us the trigger of that contrapositive chain: ~Tc.
The conclusion gives us the outcome of that contrapositive chain: ~Rm.

label: Goal
body:
We need two premises that chain together A → B B → C
Then we need a premise saying "not C" and a conclusion saying "not A"

label: Conclusion (So)
body: (assuming government-employed research scientists motivated by their own interests at least as much as by a sense of public duty), the government is likely to lose its most skilled research scientists to private industry.

label: Evidence (since)
body: None of these scientists would have problems finding private-sector jobs. Private industry is trying to attract skilled research scientists by offering them high salaries. Most research scientists employed in private sector jobs earn 50% more than comparably skilled government (public sector) workers.

label: Evaluate
body:
Our author is essentially thinking that if government research scientists are motivated primarily by their own interests, they will leave their government jobs in order to make 50% more at private sector jobs.
So if we were trying to weaken this argument, we might say, "Who said that government researchers are most interested in money?"
Maybe what most interests a certain research scientist is colonizing Mars, and she's more convinced that she can impact that quest via the government's infrastructure and funding than via Elon Musk's private sector attempts.

label: Goal
body: Essentially, the author is assuming that "the higher salaries available in the private sector will be sufficient motivation to lure away many of the most skilled govt research scientists", so she's concurrently assuming, "there isnotsomething besides money that would motivate them to stay".

label: Claim
body: Major improvements in the efficiency with which we use fossil energy (which would be in the interest of both nations and the world) are unlikely unless governments implement rules that eliminate products ranked least efficient in their class.

label: Objection
body: Let's leave energy decisions to the market

label: Evaluate
body:
If we're trying to undermine this objection, we should be thinking of ways to argue that "weshouldn'tleave this energy decision to the market".
Maybe the market incentives run contrary to those of using fossil energy more efficiently. The author would love for the least efficient products or practices to be eliminated.
The Objection is suggesting that the market will naturally take care of that (free market believers think that the free markets and the struggle to obtain competitive advantage result in companies solving for greater efficiencies).
But it might be that a company finds it's more economically efficient to keep its fleet of gas-guzzling trucks and pay some environmental fine for doing so, then it would be to scrap that fleet and buy an all new electric or gas powered fleet.

label: Goal
body: We essentially want an answer to help us argue, "If we left it up to the market, like you're asking us to, it wouldkeepthese least efficient products/practices ... or it willnotsteer towards more efficient use of fossil energy."

label: Conclusion (Therefore)
body: The people who built the ring were not knowledgeable about celestial events.

label: Evidence
body:
Some people thought the ring-builders were knowledgeable because two of the stones form a line that points to the sun at sunrise at the spring equinox.
But given the number of stones in the ring, there's a significant probability that at least one pair of them will form a line that points to something celestially significant.

label: Goal
body: Let's get rid of the four answers that hurt the argument, either by making the author's evidence seem sketchy or by giving us a way to argue that anti-conclusion, that garbage dumps DO harm wildlife.

label: Conclusion (therefore / should)
body: I shouldn't be held responsible for my humming.

label: Intermediate Conclusion
body: My humming is involuntary.

label: Premise (since)
body: I was unaware I was humming.

label: Evaluate
body:
We're trying to support a conclusion that says "should not be held responsible for X", so we'll need an answer choice set up like, "If such-and-such is true, then should not be held responsible".
The author's reason for not thinking she should be held responsible is that she was unaware she was humming and thus the humming was involuntary.

label: Evaluate
body:
As we look at the Support for the claim that the ring-builderswere notknowledgeable about celestial events, we see that it really begins with "People who thought the ring-builderswereknowledgeable were basing that on X."
That's a bad sign, when it comes to this author's logic. You're not allowed to make your case that "X is false" by telling me about the people who believe "X is true".
It looks like a setup for the famousUnproven vs. Proven Falseflaw.
We can't say, "Since these people believed X for a silly reason, then X isn't true."
Maybe I believed that Sally can speak French for a silly reason (she loves croissants). Calling out the stupidity of my assumption that "croissant lovers all speak French" is very different from proving that Sallycan'tspeak French.
That's what this author is doing. She is saying, "It's silly to think the ring-builders are knowledgeable just because two of these rocks happen to point at an interesting celestial phenomenon. After all, given the number of rocks, it was fairly likely that some pair of rocks would point at something celestially significant just by accident."
But even though the historians had a silly reason for believing the ring-builders were knowledgeable, that doesn't prove that the ring-buildersweren'tknowledgeable (there might be a non-silly reason to believe they did have knowledge of celestial events).

label: Goal
body: We either want to find an answer describing this famousUnproven vs. Proven Falseflaw, or we want to otherwise find an answer making the objection that, "Even if the alignment of these rocks doesn't offer strong support for their knowledge of celestial events, there still might be strong support for that elsewhere."

label: Statements
body:
Quantifiers (most / nearly all)
Most correctly addressed arrives w/in 2 mail business days
Most mail arrives three or more business from when it's sent
Conditional (only when = only if = right side)
Takes longer than 2 days for correctly → damaged in transit addressed mail to arrive

label: Evaluate
body:
When we have two Most facts about the same group, we can make a Trait Overlap inference: Most A's are B Most A's are C infer: sometimes B and C overlap
But we didn't have two Most facts aboutthe same group. One was "most mail", the other was "most correctly addressed mail" (a subset). So they're not trying to do the Trait Overlap inference.
There's a conditional. Can we apply it to any facts we were given. The conditional is triggered if we know that "correctly addressed mail took longer than 2 days" or if we know that "mailwasn'tdamaged in transit" (the contrapositive trigger).
We know that "most mail" takes longer than 2 days (it takes 3 or more business days), but we don't know whether any of that is correctly addressed mail.

label: Goal
body:
It seems hard to derive anything conclusive, because we don't know if most mail (the stuff arriving 3 or more days after being sent) is correctly addressed or not.
If it's correctly addressed, then it's being damaged in transit. If it's incorrectly addressed, then we don't know (it still might be damaged in transit, maybe not).

label: Evidence
body:
Report says that within last Source A claims 5 yrs, this program achieved fact Y. a 19% increase in the amt. of arable land.
If that 19% is right, If fact Y is true, the program has been then Z follows. a huge success. (Y → Z)
But the brilliant Senator ARespectedsays the program could notsource B sayshave been a huge success.Z cannot be true

label: Conclusion
body: Thus the figures can't Source A must be be accurate. wrong about Y

label: Evaluate
body:
What's wrong with this argument? It looks like it's offering a conditional statement and triggering the contrapositive in order to derive the conclusion.
I guess the issue is just that the conclusion is overly confident in the trusted source. When we're relying on a trusted source, we should conclude that what they're saying islikelycorrect, not definitely correct.
This seems to even test theFamous FlawofInappropriate Appeal, since it identifies Senator Armand as a brilliant mathematician, but what does that field of expertise have to do with judging whether the land-reclamation program could have successfully increased arable land. You'd have to be an agricultural expert for your opinion to really matter in this domain.

label: Goal
body:
The crucial parts of this argument are these ideas:Premise 1: If Y is true, Z is true.Premise 2: But this trusted source says Z can't be true.Conclusion: Thus Y can't be true.
The conclusion is flawed because it's too sure of itself, and the "trusted source" doesn't seem to be an expert when it comes to the issue at hand. Meanwhile, the source being contradicted is the Interior Ministry, whodoesseem like a relevant expert on this matter.

label: Where's the Disagreement
body:
Does C disagree with W's first claim?Is C saying that "some efforts to identify a gene responsible for manic-depression have succeeded"? No. He says "I do not dispute your evidence".
Does C disagree with W's second claim?Is C saying that "a sizable proportion of researchers still think there is amanic-depressiongene"? No, he's saying that researchers might now be thinking there's a manic-depressionclusterof genes.
Does C disagree with W's final claim?Yes, C says that he disputes W's conclusion. W concluded that "if there is no manic-depression gene, then there is no genetic predisposition to manic-depression." C is saying, "even if there is no manic-depression gene, there still might be a genetic component to manic-depression." And this is because there's a cluster of genes that interact in complex ways to create a vulnerability to manic-depression.

label: Goal
body: The point at issue is whether or not a genetic predisposition to manic-depression would be found in only one gene vs. could be found in the interactions between a set of genes.

label: Anticipate
body:
Chang is saying, "it's true that they haven't found a single gene responsible, but you don't need to have a single gene responsible in order to have a genetic predisposition. It's possible that a set of genes works together to create that predisposition."
Chang is kinda saying, "there's more than one way to skin a cat".

label: Conclusion
body: Garbage dumps do not harm wildlife.

label: Evidence
body: On the Masai-Mara reserve in Kenya, baboons that use garbage dumps mature faster and have more offspring than baboons that do not scavenge on garbage.

label: Evaluate
body:
The author is arguing that garbage dumps aren't harmful to wildlife, but her evidence is only about baboons.
The evidence is a correlation between scavenging on garbage dumps and certain benefits (faster maturity and more offspring) for baboons. The author seems to implicitly assume that garbage dumps are either helping the baboons to mature faster and have more babies, or at least assumes that faster maturity and more babies is a sign that they're NOT being harmed.

label: Conclusion (therefore / should)
body: Marianne should not be held responsible for her humming (i.e. she should not be forced to stop it lest she be disqualified).

label: Intermediate Conclusion
body: The humming is involuntary.

label: Evidence (since)
body: She was unaware of her humming.

label: Evaluate
body:
Since this is a three part argument, Prem → Intermediate Conc → Main Conc we can think about objecting to either of these moves.
Given that ... she was unaware of the humming, How could we argue ... it'snotinvoluntary?
Does being unaware of something automatically make it involuntary? Or could you be unaware of doing something that you nonetheless have voluntary control over?
I might be unaware that I blink more times per minute than most people do, and we would probably agree that my fast blinking is involuntary, but once someone points it out to me, I could potentially exert some voluntary control. I could think about blinking less frequently, and maybe I could even train myself into having a new, slower involuntary blinking rate.
What about the 2nd reasoning move?
Given that ... her blinking was voluntary How could we argue ... she stillshouldbe held responsible for it and be disqualified if she fails to cease humming?
We could probably say, "You're distracting the other contestants. Sorry if it's involuntary, but it's just too debilitating to have you doing it. If you can't stop it, you can't participate."
We might also be able to say, "Sure, you were unaware of it until we brought it to your attention, but we believe you have the power to deal with it. We don't think you're powerless to stop humming. We think you should try to stop humming."

label: Goal
body: Let's look for a way to say that "Sure, you were unaware and maybe it was involuntary the first time, but that doesn't mean that you're stuck humming. You have the power to work on it, and if you can't turn it off then we can't have you in this competition."

label: Given that
body: Smoking in bed has long been the main cause of home fires.

label: and that ..
body: Over the last two decades, there's a significant decline in cigarette smoking.

label: How can it be that
body: There has been no comparable decline in the number of people killed in home fires?

label: Evaluate / Goal
body:
On EXCEPT questions, we have to get rid of four answers that work. However, to make that final down to 2 more confusing, they usually make 3 of those four answers work one way, and 1 of them work a different way.
So we want to be open to different ways to resolve this paradox.
Maybe there's been a decline in smoking, so there's been a decline of smoking in bed, so there's been a decline of house fires caused by smoking, but here has been an increase in house fires that are started some other way.
Or maybe even though there's been a decline in smoking, there hasn't been a decline in bed-smoking or in fires caused by smoking.
That's just a potential example of how 3 answers might resolve it by giving us a "new source of non-smoking fires" but 1 might resolve it by helping us see that there are "just as many smoking fires".
The correct answer, which won't help resolve anything, might be one of those "timeless" facts that doesn't draw any distinction between now and two decades ago.

label: Conclusion (hence)
body: The salaries and the complexity of the duties of these two newest employees should be reduced.

label: Evidence
body: The two newest employees have salaries that are too high for the simple tasks normally assigned to new employees and duties that are too complex for inexperienced workers.

label: Evaluate
body:
The author is concerned about these new employees, for two reasons that seem to almost contradict each other.
1. they're paid too much! 2. their duties are too complex!
Yeah, buddy, maybe they're paid a bunch because their duties are complex.
But the author's problem isn't that someone would have complex duties and high pay; it's that a new employee would have complex duties and high pay.
Given that ... New employees "normally" have lower salaries and simpler duties.
How could we argue that ... The salaries / complexity of the new employees need not be reduced?
I guess we'd have to argue that these new employees are special. Sure, normally, we wouldn't give pay this high or duties this complex to new employees, but these new employees are rock stars.

label: Evidence
body: No matter how good the teachers, texts, and facilities are, none of these do any good if few students come to school.

label: Goal
body:
Look for a Linking answer like, "if the salaries/complexity is higher then what's normally the case for new employees, then salaries/complexity should be reduced".
Or look for a Defender answer like, "these two new employees are not atypically awesome and thus deserving of high pay / complexity".

label: Information
body:
Drugs companies and health professionals are looking at blood cholesterol.
Volume Dial relationship (more x, more y) The more cholesterol in our blood, the higher the risk that we die of a heart attack.
Strong Quantified Claim (#1 cause of death) Heart disease kills more North Americans every year than any other single cause.
Causal (can influence) Smoking, drinking, and exercise can each influence levels of cholesterol in the blood.

label: Evaluate
body:
We have a couple Overlapping Ideas: blood cholesterol, fatal heart disease
We might be able to derive some synthesis by combining those ideas. For example, combining the first and last sentence, we could say something like, "Drug companies and health professionals are focusing on [something that can be influenced by smoking / drinking / exercise]."
Or maybe we could say something like, "The #1 cause of death is tightly correlated with [something that can be influenced by smoking / drinking / exercise".

label: Goal
body:
Look for the most provable claim. Be wary of answers that seem Too Strong/Specific, Unknown Comparisons, or Unmentioned ideas.
The correct answer will probably pull together two or more ideas by using the overlapping concepts of "blood cholesterol" or "heart disease".

label: Conclusion (concluded)
body: Debbie uses neither sleight of hand, nor a trick deck, nor a planted volunteer to achieve her effect.

label: Evidence
body:
The skeptic was trying to figure out how Debbie achieve the 'magic' effect of cutting the deck to reveal the audience member's secret card.
In trial 1, she was videotaped and no sleight of hand was found.
In trial 2, the skeptic provided the deck of cards.
In trial 3, the skeptic was the audience member who selected the card.
Each time, Debbie was still able to achieve her effect.

label: Evaluate
body:
Given ... what the skeptic was able to discover with those three trials, How could we argue that ... Debbie did use sleight of hand, or a trick deck, or a planted volunteer?
In trial 1, it was videotaped. But could there still have been sleight of hand? Sure, maybe. Maybe the angle of the camera was unable to detect the sleight of hand.
In trial 2, the skeptic provided the deck. But could it still have been a trick deck? Sure, theoretically, the skeptic could have provided Debbie with a trick deck, but that's nonsensical. The skeptic isn't trying to help Debbie succeed in doing the trick. He's trying to figure out how to thwart her.
In trial 3, the skeptic was the audience member who picked the card. But could Debbie still have used a planted volunteer to do the trick? No, that's like what we said with trial 2. That would mean that the skeptic was the planted volunteer. That's nonsensical, too.
So are we really just arguing that Debbie does use sleight of hand, and it's just that the videotape didn't catch it?
Yes, possibly. Otherwise, we're framing the tension like this: Given that ... trial 1 had no sleight of hand, trial 2 had no trick deck, and trial 3 had no planted volunteer, How could we argue that ... Debbie does use sleight of hand, a trick deck, or a planted volunteer?

label: Goal
body: For many of us, we're going to feel pretty stumped by this argument and head to the answers thinking, "let me find an answer that allows me to accept the evidence but still argue that Debbie was using sleight of hand, trick, deck, or planted volunteer.

The "I disagree" is targeted at that last sentence. Tracy and Jean seem to disagree on two points:

label: Evaluate / Goal
body:
We want a normative / prescriptive conclusion, like "you should make X your top priority". And the reason why should sound something like, "Nothing else really matters if you don't have X taken care of."
X is the linchpin of the whole endeavor. The other things have no meaning if X isn't true.
Let's get rid of the four answers that match that.

label: Conclusion
body: There was enough light for Klein to make a reliable identification.

label: Evidence
body: The moon set at 1:45 am. The moon was full enough to provide considerable light before it set. The robbery (and thus the eyewitness identification) occurred between 1:15 and 1:30am.

label: Evaluate
body:
If we're the defense lawyer, tasked with arguing against this prosecutor, how can we respond to this? We know the position we represent (the Anti-Conclusion) is that "there was not enough light for Klein's identification to be reliable".
The prosecution's argument comes down to, "the moon provided considerable light, and the moon hadn't set yet".
But the fact that it hadn't set yet doesn't prove that there was enough light.
What if it was so low in the sky that nearby buildings blocked it from Klein's angle. What if the perpetrator was wearing a brimmed hat that cast a shadow on his face? What if Klein was wearing tinted lenses that make his vision darker?

label: Goal
body: Even though this looks like a Flaw question stem, since all the answers are prefaced by "overlooks the possibility", we'll treat it as a Weaken question. (Whenever we fails to consider / overlooks the possibility starting off an answer choice on Flaw, we think, "if true, would this weaken?") Look for an answer introducing a possible objection about some other factor that could lead to there not being enough light, even though the moon was out.

label: Conclusion
body: Cerebral edema is especially dangerous at high altitudes.

label: Evidence (since)
body:
Cerebral edema has symptoms that are very similar to ordinary mountain sickness, which occurs at high altitudes.
And if you don't correctly treat cerebral edema from the onset, it can quickly become life-threatening.

label: Evaluate
body:
It might take a few reads to understand the argument.
It sounds like cerebral edema is dangerous no matter where it happens, because it can quickly become life-threatening if it's not correctly treated at its onset.
So why does the author think it's especially dangerous at high altitudes? She is apparently worried that at high altitudes, we might confuse it for ordinary mountain sickness, which has the same symptoms and occurs at high altitudes.
If you were at sea level, a doctor would look at your symptoms and think, "Does this person have cerebral edema or ordinary mountain sickness?" and they would probably guess cerebral edema, since it makes no sense to have the high altitude - caused mountain sickness if you're at sea level.
But if you were at high altitudes, someone might diagnose your symptoms as ordinary mountain sickness.

label: Goal
body: So overall, we want to look for an answer that spells out some part of the storyline the author is envisioning: people might be at high altitudes and have cerebral edema, but the medical folks trying to treat that person assume she has ordinary mountain sickness, and so they don't give her the correct treatment for cerebral edema, so the cerebral edema quickly becomes life threatening.

label: Conclusion (Thus)
body: It's likely that the people who spoke Proto-Indo-European lived in a cold climate, isolated from ocean or sea.

label: Evidence (because)
body: Proto-Indo-European lacks a word for "sea", but has words for "winter", "snow" and "wolf".

label: Evaluate
body:
The author seems to be making a pretty direct assumption from "do you have a word for it" to "was it something that was in your life".
He thinks, "if you had words for winter / snow / wolf, then you lived somewhere with winter, snow, and wolves ... i.e. you lived in a cold climate".
And he thinks, "If you didn't have a word for sea, then you didn't live anywhere where there was a sea. You must have been isolated from ocean or sea."
This is definitely a questionable assumption to be making. The German language has a word, "schadenfreude", which means "taking pleasure in the misery of others". Can we say that since American English doesn't have a word for that feeling, that American English speakers don't experience that feeling in their lives?

label: Goal
body:
We want to make it seem like "lacking a word for X doesn't mean X wasn't in your life" or "having a word for Y doesn't mean Y was in your life".
Or we want any other answer that would help us argue that the people who spoke Proto-Indo-European didn't live somewhere cold, or weren't isolated from ocean or sea (i.e. something that helps us make the case that they lived in a warm climate or they had exposure to the ocean/sea).

label: Conclusion
body: It is impossible for there to be real evidence that lax radiation standards once at nuclear reactors actually contributed to the increase in cancer rates near such sites.

label: Evidence
body: You can't say if a particular case of cancer is due to radiation, environmental toxins, smoking, poor diet, or genetic factors.

label: Evaluate
body:
We would assign ourselves the goal of arguing that, "it is possible to have real evidence that overly loose radiation standards contributed to the increase in cancer rates".
How would we respond to the author's idea that you can never say for sure whether a particular case of cancer came from X, Y, or Z?
We might say, "hey, we're talking about EVIDENCE, not PROOF."
Maybe I can't prove that a particular case of cancer was caused by smoking, but I can still provide real evidence for that claim.
I can show how much the person smoked. I can present scientific evidence about how smoking affects lung cells. I can undermine some of these other possible explanations by showing that this smoker had a good diet, lived in a low-toxin environment, and has a family with no genetic history of cancer.
Does that prove that smoking caused the cancer? No, but it's a pretty compelling body of evidence to suspect that smoking probably caused the cancer.
Similarly, couldn't we marshal a lot of evidence to make it very plausible that leaking radiation from the reactors caused the uptick in cancer around those sites?

label: Goal
body: Let's look for an answer getting at this idea that even if we can't prove X caused Y, we can still present a lot of real evidence that X caused Y.

label: Conclusion (is to blame = opinion)
body: The shipping manager is also to blame for the lost business resulting from the facility's delayed opening.

label: Evidence
body: The shipping manager was aware of the contractor's typical delays and should have planned for this contingency.

label: Evaluate
body:
If we want to articulate the classic "If premise, then conclusion" principle, then it would sound something like,
"If you hired a contractor that is typically delayed in their work (and you didn't plan for that contingency), then you are also to blame for the delay".

label: Goal
body:
Let's look for a principle whose right side is helping us to support conclusion language like "you are also to blame".
The trigger just needs to be something that applies to this shipping manager (and should match up with "aware that the person you're hiring is typically late" and/or "should have planned for this contingency but didn't").

label: Conclusion
body: On average, people pay less today (in adjusted dollars) for a Breezeway T->D coach ticket than they did a year ago.

label: Evidence
body:
Today A Year Ago
price of full-fare = price of full-fare coach T->D coach T->D
90% discount vs. 50% discount 10% full-fare 50% full-fare

label: Evaluate
body:
Since we're trying to prove a very mathematical conclusion, we just need all the relevant mathematical data.
We don't need to know anything about raw numbers of tickets, because we're only concerned with averages. We know that a higher proportion of people today buy "discount" rather than full-fare tickets, but that doesn't immediately prove they're spending less money per ticket.
What if the price for a Full-Fare and/or Discount ticket has gone up?
The argument reassures us "full-fare hasn't gone up. It costs the same as last year". But it doesn't tell us whether the price of a discount ticket has stayed the same. If the price of a discount ticket has gone up, then even though a higher proportion of people are buying discount tickets, they might be spending more on average than a year ago.
If you want some math to make sense of it, let's say there were 10 tickets bought each year (so that it's easy to take 90%, 50%, 10% of it).
Last year, 5 full-fare and 5 discount tickets. This year, 1 full-fare and 9 discount tickets.
So in which year did people spend more money? We'd have to know the costs of the tickets. Full-fare stayed the same, but discount could have changed.
Let's pretend that last year,full = $100, discount = $50 5 full + 5 discount = 5(100) + 5(50) = 750 $75 per ticket average.
Let's pretend that this year,full = $100, discount = $90 1 full + 9 discount = 1(100) + 9(90) = 910 $91 per ticket average.

label: Goal
body:
Since our only way to mathematically object to the argument is to say, "What if the price of a discount ticket went up", the way to prove this conclusion true is to shut down that objection.
We either want to hear that the price of a discount coach T->D ticket is the same, or that it's cheaper than before.

label: Statements
body:
Govt: "Our nuclear power plants are entirely safe. The public's fear of a nuclear accident at one of these plants is groundless."
causal difference-maker (did X because Y) Govt: "We recently limited the nuclear industry's financial liability in the event of nuclear accident. It was the right thing to do, because we need to protect the nuclear industry from the threat of bankruptcy."
conditional (only if, must) Govt: "Unlimited liability poses a threat of bankruptcy only if injury claims can be sustained against the industry. Claims can be sustained only if the injury results from a nuclear accident".

label: Evaluate
body:
This is a tall drink of water, but if we ever see conditionals, those become center stage. We want to see if conditionals chain together and whether they can be applied to any of the other facts in the stimulus.
These two conditionals in the 2nd to last sentence have a common ingredient, "claims sustained", so we should chain them together:
Unlimited liability Claims can be injury poses threat → sustained against → from of bankruptcy nuclear industry nuclear accident
Can we apply this chain to any of the provided facts?
Well the 2nd sentence did talk about limiting liability because of threat of bankruptcy. So if the government thinks that unlimited liability poses a threat of bankruptcy to the nuclear industry, then it apparently thinks that injury claims could be sustained against the nuclear industry, so then it apparently thinks that injuries from nuclear accidents might occur. But wait, didn't the first sentence reassure us that there are no grounds to fear about nuclear accidents?
If the government is worried about the nuclear industry's unlimited liability in the event of a nuclear accident, they're worried that people will sustain injury claims from a nuclear accident, which means the government must think there is some reason to worry that there could be a nuclear accident.
So the government is kind of contradicting itself. If they really thought nuclear accidents were never going to occur, then it wouldn't matter whether or not the nuclear industry is protected from exorbitant liabilities in the event of an accident.

label: Goal
body: It's hard to know what the answer will say, but by synthesizing the conditional chain and applying it to the other facts, we seem to be looking at a government that is sort of contradicting itself. Look for a safely worded answer expressing that takeaway, or any other answer we can prove from the passage.

label: Conclusion
body: The public's fear (of nuclear power plants creating some safety concerns) is well founded.

label: Evidence
body:
The government recently acted to limit the nuclear industry's financial liability in the case of a nuclear accident, so that in that even the nuclear industry wouldn't go bankrupt.
They say that unlimited liability would pose a threat only if injury claims can be sustained against the nuclear industry, and injury claims can only be sustained if there's a nuclear accident.

label: Evaluate
body:
This is a tough paragraph to digest, but essentially the author is saying that the government's actions make it look like they think a nuclear accident is a real possibility. Even if it's just a remote possibility, the government is taking actions to limit the nuclear industry's liability so that it wouldn't go bankrupt in the event of a nuclear accident at a power plant.
Since the conclusion is just trying to establish "well founded public fear", we're just trying to strengthen the idea that "there is a meaningful chance that there could be a nuclear accident at a power plant".

label: Goal
body:
We need an answer that sounds something like
the government is doing stuff to protect against → fear of X occurring certain ramifications of is well founded event X occurring

label: Author's Conclusion
body: The environmentalists' proposal — replacing gasoline with methanol — has little merit.

label: Evaluate
body: The author treats both carcinogens as equivalently bad. But carcinogens vary in potency. If formaldehyde is much less potent than benzene, then switching from gasoline to methanol meaningfully reduces cancer risk — making the environmentalists' proposal valuable.

body: Find an answer that establishes formaldehyde is less harmful than benzene — that flips the equivalence the author quietly assumed.
