This could go in a different direction, but the conclusion is really advertising a Net Gain / Loss type claim, so we should probably look for an answer discussing a way in this new type of fridge could be more expensive than our current fridges.
Otherwise, it might point out an overlooked reason why we'd need to still keep our new fridges just as cold, even though bacteria is no longer a risk.

label: Conclusion
body: The existing works of ancient literature, science, and philosophy don't represent the most original work produced in ancient times.

label: Evidence
body: The existing works frequently refer to other works that we no longer have.

label: Evaluate
body:
On most Principle-Strengthen questions, we're just looking to build a linking idea from Evidence to Conclusion.
The Evidence here is that "the works we have cite other works we don't have", and the Conclusion is "the works we have aren't the most original ones". The author must be assuming that these other works, the ones cited, the ones we don't have, are actually the more original works.

label: Goal
body:
Look for an answer saying something like, "If your work cites work X, then work X is more original than your work". We need to connect the ideas of "these works we don't have are frequently cited in the works we do have" with "these works we don't have are the most original ones".
Something like "The more you're cited, the more original you are" would also work.

label: Conclusion (But)
body: This cannot be so. i.e., not all uses of language are metaphorical i.e., some uses of language are not metaphorical

label: Evidence (for)
body: In order for there to be any nonliteral uses of any words, then some uses of words must be literal.

label: Evaluate
body:
Whenever we're doing a Main Conclusion question, we prime our brain before reading the paragraph with the two biggest patterns of where they put the conclusion on Main Conclusion: - first sentence - as some sort of rebuttal
This argument did the second:Some extremists claim X.But.. [I disagree]. Here's why.

label: Conclusion
body: We just want an equivalent rephrasing of "this cannot be so", so we're looking for something like, "not all uses of language are metaphorical" or "some uses of language are not metaphorical".

label: Conclusion
body: The popular belief that "top CEOs behave indifferently to the needs/desires of employees" is unfounded. (i.e. top CEOs behave in ways that are concerned with the needs/desires of employees)

label: Evidence
body: In a recent poll, almost all the top CEOs said that "employee training and welfare" are of the same priority as "customer satisfaction".

label: Evaluate
body:
GIVEN THAT .. most CEOs in this poll ranked "employee training and welfare" as the same priority as "customer satisfaction"
HOW COULD WE SAY THAT .. these CEO's are indifferent to the needs and aspirations of employees?
One objection that might come to mind is that the argument moves from "X just as important a priority as Y" to the idea of "X is an important priority". It's a Relative vs. Absolute move.
When you're picking your law school, you could say that "in selecting a law school to attend, proximity to Santa's Workshop is of the same priority as number of meatballs that come on a plate of dining hall spaghetti."
That doesn't mean that either of those things is a high priority. They could be tied for being "lowest priority". However, in this case, the argument does say "the same high priority as customer satisfaction". So we can't argue that employee training/welfare is tied with customer satisfaction for being a low priority.
So if we're not making that objection, and we're accepting that most top CEOs put a high priority on employee training and welfare, is that the same as "behaving in a way that shows concern to the needs and aspirations of employees"?
Could the CEOs just be telling the pollster what they know is the right thing to say? Could the CEOs consider employee training/welfare a priority for selfish CEO reasons, but still be indifferent to what employees actually need and want?
Goal
We're either looking to fill a gap between "employee training/welfare is a high priority for CEOs" and "CEO's do not behave indifferently to the needs/wants of employees", or we're trying to rule out a possible objection.

label: Conclusion
body: Using the sea lions to film the whales would allow biologists to study the everyday behavior of the whales.

label: Evidence (since)
body:
Introducing novel stimuli, such as divers or submarines, causes whales to behave in unusual ways.
But whales are accustomed to there being sea lions nearby, and we could potentially train the sea lions to carry video cameras on their backs and swim along with the whales.

label: Evaluate
body:
We're trying to solve a problem: we want to study usual, everyday behavior of whales, but we can't introduce novel stimuli into the whale's environment or else they act weird.
This argument recommends a potential solution. So the author assumes that this solution is feasible and would be able to solve the problem.
What does the author need to assume in order to think this this plan is feasible? - sea lions can be trained to, on command, swim along with whales - sea lions would be willing to follow those commands - the extra weight of the camera wouldn't prevent the sea lion from being able to keep up with the whales
What does the author need to assume in order to think that this plan avoids the problem of "novel stimuli"? - a whale wouldn't consider consider a sea lion with a camera on its back, following it around all day, to be "novel stimuli"
This argument is a good example of the Assumes a Difference pattern.
- We can't do X or Y, because it has problem A.can't do divers or submarines, because of 'novel stimuli'
- Thus, we should do Z (which assumes that Z is different in regards to problem A) we should put cameras on sea lions (which assumes that 'cameras on sea lions' would be different from other novel stimuli)

label: Goal
body: Look for an answer saying "the whales won't find it abnormal that sea lions are wearing cameras or tracking them", or for any other answer that, if negated, would allow us to argue that this plan probably won't work.

label: Mall Manager's Conclusion (so)
body: Merchants should do their utmost to discourage teens from congregating near stores.

label: Evidence
body: When teens congregate, it creates an atmosphere in which many adult shoppers feel uncomfortable. As a result adults spend less time shopping. The mall's goal is to prevent a significant loss in overall sales.

label: Merchant's Response
body: The teens who congregate near stores spend money in those stores, which represents a big percentage of their overall sales.

label: Evaluate
body:
Typically, when we're doing Method of Response, the 2nd person does one of these moves: - calls out a dubious assumption - suggests an alternate explanation - highlights bad implications - raises a crucial overlooked consideration
The merchant here is doing both the 3rd and 4th thing. It's a crucial consideration that these congregating teens spend a bunch of money in these stores. After all, the mall manager's stated goal is to prevent a significant loss in overall sales.
(Here's where we get into bad implications ...) If we were to go along with the manager's plan and discourage teens from congregating, that might lead to the teens no longer coming to the mall, and thus no longer spending money at these stores, and thus there would be a significant loss in overall sales.
So the merchant is showing that the manager's plan has implications that would thwart the manager's overall goal of preventing a loss in sales.

label: Goal
body: Look for something like "raises an overlooked consideration" or "shows how the plan recommended by the manager could have implications / repercussions that would undermine the goal of the plan".

label: Conclusion
body: These historians neglect many important repositories of historical knowledge.

label: Evidence
body: These historians believe that written texts are the best source for historical understanding. They don't regard painting, architecture, music, dance, or culinary arts as the best source.

label: Evaluate
body:
It looks like the evidence is talking about whether or not historians consider something "the best source" for historical understanding.
But the conclusion is talking about whether or not historians are neglecting an important source of historical understanding.
Since we're being asked what the author assumes (what she takes for granted), they are probably testing this missing link.

label: Goal
body:
Look for an answer pointing out the move from, "If you don't consider it the best source for historical understanding, then you'll neglect it as a repository of historical knowledge."
Or we could put that as an objection -- "Even if they don't consider it the #1 best, they still might frequently consult it as an important repository of historical knowledge."

label: Principle
body:
To do X, one must do Y is equivalent to saying X requires Y, which is equivalent to writing X → Y.
So we could write this principle like this
Acting responsibly Acting on the basis of in your job's role → info you're reasonably sure is true / complete
But if we're savvy about Apply the Principle questions, we know we want the "judgy" term on the right. Principles are supposed to sound like, "if this description applies to you, then this value judgment applies to you".
Since "You acted responsibly / you acted irresponsibly" is the value judgment half of this answer, we want to contrapose the rule so that it's on the right side, and will thus match the conclusion of the arguments in the answer choices.
If you weren't acting then you weren't on info you tried to → acting responsibly make sure was true in your professional and accurate capacity

label: Goal
body:
Start by checking the conclusion. If it says "thus, X was not acting responsibly", then read the evidence to see it establishes that the person wasn't acting on well-verified information.
If the conclusion says anything other that "X was not acting responsibly" (or something with equivalent meaning), then get rid of it.

label: Statements
body:
conditional (any)
prisoner attempts → must leave station to escape pursue immediately
conditional (unless)
not pursuing → not allowed to leave prisoner station until replacement
facts
May 11, 9pm, C & S just finished a 5-9pm shift, and their replacements arrived.
C had violated the rules. S had not.

label: Evaluate
body:
If C violated the rules then he either 1. failed to pursue a prisoner that attempting to escape or 2. left his station for some reason other than pursuing a prisoner
Since S followed the rules, she 1. pursued any prisoner that tried to escape 2. otherwise did not leave station until replacement showed up.

label: Goal
body:
Since we're looking for a Must Be False, we'll need to flip those.
We need to hear that C "pursued every escapee and never left otherwise", or that S "failed to pursue an escapee or left for some other reason".

label: Faden's Conclusion
body: Your objection (that many customers might lie if a survey asks them , "do you still use your exercise equipment") is absurd.

label: Faden's Evidence
body: You have no way of showing that customers were lying.

label: Why is it that
body: we know of many more lamps associated with the late Upper Paleo period (when the Magdalenian culture was dominant) than with the early / middle Upper Paleo period?

label: Evaluate
body:
Faden seems to be arguing that "if you have no way of proving X is true, then suggesting X as an objection is absurd".
That seems overly harsh. Let's say a man fell to his death from the roof of a building.
Cop 1 says, "Clearly, a suicide." Cop 2 says, "It could be that someone pushed him off the roof".
Could Cop 1 say, "You have no way of showing that he was pushed. Thus your objection is absurd"?
Of course not. First of all, Cop 1 has no way of showing that it was a suicide. So the Cop 1's accusation cuts both ways.
But more importantly, people are allowed to speculate possible Alternate Explanations without needing proof.

label: Goal
body:
Let's look for something saying, "It's not absurd to speculate a possible alternate explanation, even if you don't have proof".
This feels somewhat like one of the 10 Famous Flaws, Unproven vs. Proven False, in the sense that Faden is acting like a lack of evidence for X makes X an absurd/false claim.

label: Sarah's 1st Claim
body:
By deciding which events will get coverage / airtime, reporters are exercising their judgment as to what is newsworthy and what is not. Does Ramon argue that'deciding which stories to cover is not reporters' exercising their judgment'?
No, in fact Ramon seems to agree that reporters exercise their judgment by saying "once [reporters]deem a story to be newsworthy".

label: Sarah's 2nd Claim
body:
Reporters always interpret the news.Does Ramon argue that 'no,sometimes reporters do not interpret the news'?
Yes, kind of. He's saying that they should never interpret the news, which isn't a statement about what reporters do; it's a statement about what they should do.
But it seems to imply that they have a choice whether or not to interpret the news.

label: Evaluate
body:
This is a weird set of statements to digest. Ramon doesn't quite disagree with either of Sarah's claims, but he definitely doesn't vibe with "they always interpret the news".
He's saying, "they should never interpret the news".
How are they ending up at such polar extremes (always vs. never)?
Well,she's saying that they're interpreting the news by deciding which stories 'to platform', which ones get airtime. Interpretation is defined as 'picking which stories get to be told'.
But Ramon is apparently thinking of interpretation of 'deciding how to tell a story' (not deciding to tell a story). We know this because he's saying, "they should tell me the story in untainted facts, not skewed by their interpretation."
He's thinking of interpretation as "the subjective spin you put on a story", while she's thinking of it as "the subjectivity involved in picking a story to report on".

label: Goal
body: It seems like we want an answer that sounds something like, "What does it mean to interpret the news?"

label: Conclusion (thus)
body: At least 50 million people in North America should take lactase supplements.

label: Evidence
body: In an experiment, many subjects who drank a liter of milk on an empty stomach showed signs of lactose intolerance, difficulty digesting dairy because of insufficient lactase.

label: Evaluate
body:
If we're going to be the other lawyer in the room and argue, "No, there aren't 50 million people in North America who should take lactase supplements", the author is gonna say
What do you mean? Many subjects in this experiment had trouble digesting a liter of milk on an empty stomach.
What could we say in response? 1) who are these people in the experiment? How do I know that they are typical North Americans? Maybe this group skewed towards lactose intolerance? 2) who drinks a liter of milk on an empty stomach? That seems like an insane decision. If I ate three steaks before going to bed and had a night of weird sleep, would that show I have a dietary issue with steak or would it just show that I made a stupid decision to eat three steaks before going to bed?

label: Goal
body: Let's look for a way to argue that what happened in the study isn't a fair reflection of North America's tolerance for lactose, either because the people weren't typical, the "liter on an empty stomach" scenario isn't typical, or any other reason an answer could offer us (e.g. they were asked to jog a mile in the hot sun after pounding a liter of milk).

label: Conclusion
body: 50 million in North America should take lactase supplements.

label: Evidence
body: Many subjects showed lactose intolerance after drinking a liter of milk on an empty stomach.

label: Evaluate
body: The test condition may not represent typical dairy consumption.

label: Goal
body: Show that ordinary dairy intake is much smaller than the test dose.

label: The Argument
body: An ad for a lactase supplement points to a study where people who drank a full liter of milk on an empty stomach showed signs of lactose intolerance. From that, the ad jumps to: 50 million people in North America need our supplement.

label: Evaluate
body:
The big assumption: the way people drank milk in the study is how people normally consume dairy. But a liter of milk on an empty stomach is a lot — far more than most people consume at one sitting. If most people only have a splash in their coffee or some cheese on a sandwich, they might never hit the threshold that triggers intolerance. They wouldn't need a supplement for normal eating.
That's like testing how people fare after running 26 miles, finding most are exhausted, and concluding 50 million need recovery drinks. Maybe true for marathoners — but most people don't run marathons.

label: Goal
body: Find an answer that says: typical dairy consumption is much smaller than the study's extreme dose.

label: Jim's Conclusion
body: If my salary isn't raised to match theirs, then it's unfair to raise their salaries.

label: Jim's Evidence (since)
body: I've worked at the company longer than Fred and Dorothy. Their raise would make their salaries higher than mine.

label: Tasha's Position
body: Then by that logic we'd have to give 35 other employees raises, since they've been here as long as you and make what you make.

label: Evaluate
body: It's an odd task, to pick a principle that works for both arguments. It might feel easier to just focus on one person's argument, make a first pass through the answers and eliminate what we can and then compare the remaining options to the other person's argument.

label: Goswami's 3rd Claim
body:
The majority of the striking workers make less than $20k per year. Does Nordecki disagree?
No, cites a different fact about their pay, but the two facts don't contradict each other. They're just different ways of looking at pay. Goswami is talking about majority pay whereas Nordecki is talking about average pay.

label: Goal
body:
Jim's is pretty easy to prephrase, "If someone has worked at the company for less time than I have, then it's unfair for them to make more money than me."
Tasha's is more like, "If people have worked at the company for the same time as you and make the same as you, then it's unfair to only give you a raise."
Both of them relate to tenure and pay disparity, but it's hard to predict the wording of an answer that would help both of them.

label: Jim
body: Longer tenure → at least as much pay.

label: Tasha
body: Equal tenure → equal pay.

label: Goal
body: Find a single principle that justifies both: don't pay one more than another unless the first has worked longer.

label: Jim
body: Jim's claim: "I've been here longer than Fred and Dorothy. So if their pay goes above mine, that's unfair — unless mine matches."

label: Tasha
body: Tasha's claim: "35 of us have been here the same length as Jim, with the same pay. So if Jim's pay goes up without ours going up too, that's unfair."

label: Evaluate
body:
Find the common thread. Jim wants his pay >= the pay of newer employees. Tasha wants Jim's pay = the pay of equal-tenure employees. Both are saying: pay should track tenure. Specifically, you can't pay someone more than someone else unless that person has been there longer.
Tasha's case (equal tenure) means no one should be paid more. Jim's case (longer tenure) means he shouldn't be paid less. Both are sub-cases of the same rule.

label: Goal
body: Find the principle: never pay one employee more than another unless the first has been there longer.

label: Statements
body:
If a constitution provides → must be interpreted framework for nation's law to new situations authors couldn't have predicted
When these modern interpretations happen, the modern people are doing the interpreting but they often make it sound like the authors of the constitution are dictating the interpretation.
If they didn't we'd lose illusion lose make it sound → that laws are → political that (fictional) way part of tradition stability

label: Evaluate
body:
Since we read Most Supported and Must Be True with a special ear for Conditional, Causal, or Pivot wording, we would perk up when we conditional indicator words like must - 1st sentence without it -- last sentence necessary -- last sentence
All three of those code words are Necessary indicators, so we put that idea on the Right side of the arrow.
"Without" can be translated into "This requires That" format or it can be translated via an "If-not" translation.can't have Y without X ... Y requires X Y → X can't have Y without X ...if not X,can't have Y~X → ~Y
If we wanted to contrapose this whole chain, it would read intuitively as a chain of requirements: Pol Stab --> Illus of Long Trad -> This fiction
Political stability requires an illusion that laws are part of long tradition, which requires we pretend when we're interpreting a situation the authors of our constitution couldn't possibly have foreseen that our interp embodies intentions of the authors

label: Goal
body: Look for something rewarding our ability to understand that "the fiction of pretending we're just interpreting new situations through the Founders' eyes is necessary to political stability", but stay receptive to anything we could prove.

label: Evidence
body:
Fiscal → Manage finances security (requires) wisely
Functional → Realistic projections budget (requires) of $ obligations

label: Conclusion (So)
body: Fiscal security manage finance wisely or → or Functional budg realistic $ obligations

label: Evaluate
body: Because we see conditional logic (only if, without, if) and repeating ideas (2 mentions each of functional budget, manage finances, realistic projections, and fiscal security), we would probably want to convert this argument until an algebraic recipe.

label: Goal
body:
Prem 1: X → Y Prem 2: A → B Conc: X or A → Y or B
The quickest thing to scan for at a bird's eye view is probably that we have two conditional premises, and that the conclusion is a conditional, whose trigger is composed of the two triggers from the premises.

label: Conclusion
body: Marmosets learn which hand to use by imitating their parents (if your parent is left handed, then you'll imitate your way into being left handed)

label: Evidence
body: Infant marmosets engage in lots of imitative behavior.

label: Evaluate
body:
Any time we see the word hypothesis in the question stem, we know it will be a Causal conversation, so we can almost always organize it in our usual Curious Fact / Explanation style:
Curious Fact: Why are marmosets the only non-human primates that prefer one hand over the other? How do they develop a preference for one hand?
Author's Story: They engage in a lot of imitative behavior, so if they're imitating a left-handed parent then they'll end up left handed.
The two questions we always ask: - How ELSE could we explain the curious fact? - How plausible is the author's story?
For Strengthen questions, we sometimes rule out a different way to explain the curious fact, but usually we add some plausibility to the author's story.
The most common Strengthener in causal arguments is a No Cause, No Effect strengthener. Since the author thinks that imitative behavior leads to hand preference, any answer structured like "where there isn't imitative behavior, there isn't a hand preference" would strengthen.
It could be that other primates (who don't have hand preference) don't have imitative behavior as much. It could be that marmosets who grow up without a parent to imitate end up having no hand preference.
A "more Cause, more Effect" strengthener would give us other instances of imitative behavior being joined with hand preference (such as establishing that humans ALSO engage in much imitative behavior as kids).

label: Goal
body: Look for something that makes it seem more likely that marmosets learn hand preference through imitative behavior.

label: Juan's Conclusion (hence)
body: Having pro athletes violates the spirit of fairness.

label: Juan's Intermediate Conclusion
body: It's unlikely that amateurs will offer a serious challenge to any pros they face in their events.

label: Juan's Premise (since)
body: Amateurs rarely have the financial resources available to pros.

label: Goal
body: We want to find an answer choice that highlights an overlooked factor which shows the economic advantage of using the new videocassettes, despite the royalties having a significant impact.

label: Evaluating Michiko's Response
body: She says pros should be able to compete. So she seems to disagree with Juan's conclusion. Does she disagree with his premise or intermediate conclusion? Not really. She's just saying that the point of the Olympics is to showcase the best, so if pros have more resources and that makes them dominate amateurs, so be it. They're the best; we wanna showcase the best; so pros should be at the Olympics.

label: Goal
body:
Let's find an answer centered on whether or not pros should be allowed to compete at the Olympics.
Since that disagreement was so obvious and explicit, the answer will probably get at the underlying premises. Juan thinks they shouldn't, because of fairness concerns. Michiko thinks they should, because of concerns about showcasing the world's best.

label: Juan
body: Pros violate the fairness essential to the games — shouldn't compete.

label: Michiko
body: The games showcase the finest — pros should compete.

label: Goal
body: Find the answer about whether mixed participation accords with the games' ideals.

label: Conclusion
body: The current use of plastics actually does less harm to the environment nationwide than that of paper products.

label: Evidence
body: Plastics represent a smaller proportion of all trash than paper, and the damage to the environment done by a given unit of plastic trash is about the same as that of paper trash.

label: Evaluate
body:
At first, this conclusion might seem relatively airtight. If there's less plastic trash than paper trash, and a kg of plastic trash does about the same environmental harm as does a kg of paper trash, then isn't it fair to say that currently plastic is doing less harm than paper?
Yes, it is fair, as long as we say "currently plastic trash is doing less harm than paper trash."
Where the conclusion creates some wiggle room of doubt is by talking about the current use of plastic vs. the current use of paper. That brings in a whole bunch of other considerations: - does it hurt the environment more to make plastic? to transport plastic? to sell plastic? - once in the hands of consumers, do people ever use plastic in a way that hurts the environment?

label: Goal
body:
Given that we know that plastic gets the win when comes to environmental harm of trash, the remaining areas to strengthen this argument would be saying that the environmental impact of plastic beats out (or ties) paper in some other aspect of their life cycle:
Harnessing raw materials -> manufacturing -> distribution -> sale -> consumer use -> trash.
If plastic ties paper in any of these categories, it still strengthens the argument because it rules out a possible objection that "even if plastic is less harmful when it comes to trash, it's more harmful when it comes to ____ . "

label: Given that
body: Most animals don't brave the midday heat of the Sahara,

label: Why is it that
body: The silver ant leaves its nest at midday and scouts for food, typically animals that died from the heat.

label: Evaluate
body: We basically need four answers that give some reason why it's advantageous for the silver ant to scavenge for dead bodies in the scorching midday heat.

label: Conclusion (so)
body: We should not hesitate to use public funds to support works of art that many people find shocking.

label: Evidence (since)
body:
Art is often shocking.
Great works of art have often elicited outrage when first presented.

label: Evaluate
body:
The New Concept in the Conclusion is "using public funds to support" something.
We basically know that art, including great art, is often shocking. And the author concludes from that that we should use public funds to support works of art.
How might we make a counterargument that we should not use public funds to support works of art that many people find shocking?
We might say, "Sure, some great art is shocking, but unfortunately we'll have to let that stuff emerge from private funding. It's asking too much of taxpayers to be happy when their tax dollars go to subsidizing art that they find shocking / disturbing."

label: Goal
body:
We can look for a Linking idea like, "If great art is often shocking, then we should be fine using public funds to support shocking art".
Or we can look for a Defending idea, ruling out a possible objection.
The correct answer, if negated, should weaken, meaning it should help us argue that we shouldn't use public funds to support art that many find shocking.

label: Facts
body:
Caffeine can be as physically addictive as any other psychoactive substance.
Some people have withdrawal symptoms from caffeine (depressed, drowsy, irritable).
As many people consume caffeine as consume any one of the other addictive psychoactive substances.

label: Evaluate
body:
Not sure what to do with these facts. It doesn't seem like any of them chain together or give us conditional rules. It just sounds like caffeine is as addictive as other drugs, has some withdrawal symptoms, and is #1 or tied for #1 in popularity (number of users).
I wouldn't expect the middle sentence to be used in supporting the answer, both because Most Supported is famous for testing inferences that combine the first idea with the last idea, but also because that middle claim is so weakly worded (some = at least one person).

label: Goal
body: Look for something we can basically prove given only those three facts. Beware strong language. Expect that the comparative equalities (as addictive / used by as many people) will somehow come into play.

label: Conclusion
body: If we're gonna add to the school budget, we should spend money on something besides student counseling programs.

label: Evidence
body: A huge poll of students, parents, and teachers show that over 90% of them think an appropriate percentage of the budget is being spent on student counseling.

label: Evaluate
body:
Given that ... Congleton assigned the best people to the project, How could we still say that ... Congleton did want the project to fail?
Hmm, maybe Congleton's actions didn't match her desires. Maybe she assigned the best people in order to not make it apparent that she was hoping the project would fail, but in her heart (and maybe even in her behind-the-scenes actions) she still wanted it to fail.

label: Proponent's Conclusion (so)
body: There is no reason to reject irradiation on the grounds of nutrition or safety.

label: Evaluate
body: When we're picking answer choices that are principles to justify or conform to an argument, we're just prephrasing "If Premise, then Conclusion".

label: Evaluate
body:
Given the poll, wow could we argue that if we add money to the school budget, we should spend more money on student counseling? Our first reaction could just be, "So what if a poll disagrees with us? Who says they're right! Maybe the poll is flawed!" But it is a nationwide poll of students / parents / teachers, so LSAT is giving us no reason to doubt the poll. There must be some other wiggle room.
They're shifting from talking about "an appropriate percentage" in the evidence (in the poll) to the idea of "an increased amount" in the conclusion. So we should think about this% vs. #distinction.
Say the budget is currently $100k, and 1% of it goes to student counseling ($1,000). In the poll, over 90% said "Yup, 1% is an appropriate percentage to allocate toward student counseling".
The poll doesn't comment on whether $1,000 is an appropriate amount to allocate.
If we increased the budget by $50k, and now the budget is currently $150k, then the $1000 we're giving to student counseling will only 0.67% of the budget.
We actually would be failing to comply with the poll if we didn't spend more money on student counseling, because we would have gone from the 1% of budget that they approve of to a lower 0.67% that they might not approve of.

label: Goal
body: Look for an answer that speaks to the percentage vs. amount confusion, or that points out that if we add new money to the budget, then the people in this poll would want X% of that new money (the appropriate percentage they agree on) to go to student counseling.

label: Conclusion
body: Administering placebos is nonetheless ethically questionable.

label: Evidence
body: Even if a placebo benefits a patient, a doctor might have prescribed it just to give the patient the satisfaction that something was being done.

label: Evaluate
body:
If we were just trying to prephrase a Missing Link assumption to connect Premise language to Conclusion language we'd get prescribed a placebo just to give the → ethically questionable patient satisfaction
If we were trying to make an objection that "administering placebos is ethically fine", we might say, "hey, a placebo does not harm. In some cases doctors think it might augment the effectiveness of genuine medicine. In other cases, the doctor may just be giving it to a patient to shut them up and get them out the door, but obviously the doctor doesn't have a better treatment in mind, so a placebo is as good or better than nothing."

label: Goal
body: Look for an answer saying "trying to just give the patient some satisfaction that some treatment was given is ethically questionable", or an answer that, if negated, would allow us to argue that administering placebos is ethically fine.

label: Given that .
body: Most members of parliament in country A supported the UN plan to send international forces into country Z to quell the turmoil there.

label: How can we explain that
body: The parliament of country A passed a resolution condemning their prime minister for committing military assistance to the UN's effort?

label: Evaluate / Goal
body:
We need a way to explain why Parliament seems mad at its Prime Minister for committing to a cause that Parliament largely supports.
If Parliament isn't mad about the cause itself, they must be mad at the Prime Minister for some other reason (the timing? the way she announced it? the amount of assistance she promised is way bigger / smaller than most of Parliament would approve of?)

label: Rules
body:
We're billed every four weeks, in advance, for the next four weeks. If we don't get our paper, we should call right away to request a replacement.
Credit given for → Reported missed w/in 24 hrs missed copy and replacement copy unavailable
Temporary → request must be in at least 3 nondelivery days prior to first stopped day
Subscription → subscriber explicitly requests canceled beforehand in writing

label: Evaluate
body:
There were three different conditional triggers used (only if, must, unless), all of which signify requirements. When we write a conditional statement, we're saying that the LEFT ---requires---> RIGHT so besides using memorized trigger words, we can interpret these rules by saying "Getting credit for a missed copy requires ____ ". "Temporary nondelivery requires ____ ." "Canceling your subscription requires ____ ."
None of these conditionals have overlapping terms, so we don't have to worry about them chaining together. With a set of rules this big and dense, I would normally just take a 2nd read for better comprehension and then head to the answers.

label: Goal
body:
Since we'll be looking to deny giving subscribers what they're requesting, we'll be using the contrapositives to these rules.
Missed copy reported after the 24 hr window? Denied. Replacement copy available? Denied. Requested temporary pause less than 3 days out? Denied. Didn't request cancellation in writing? Denied.

label: Conclusion (I conclude)
body: A single drop of the defendant's blood stains much less than 9.5 cm 2 of the fabric.

label: Evidence
body: Ten times, a single drop of the defendant's blood was allowed to fall onto the fabric, and all ten times the stained area was between 4.5 and 4.8 cm 2

label: Evaluate
body:
This question specifically asks us to weaken the value of the evidence, so we're not necessarily doing our usual thinking of, "Given the evidence, How can we argue the conclusion could be wrong?"
The correct answer might just give us a way to argue that the evidence is sketchy (bad methodology or something like that).
For example, maybe dropping blood straight down out of an eyedropper creates less of a stained area than if you propel blood at the fabric at an angle.
Maybe the cold / hot / humidity conditions of the testing room make the stained area smaller than in would be in other conditions.

label: Goal
body: It's hard to anticipate answers when they go after the evidence. The correct answer should make us feel very differently about the logical force of the evidence, either by making it seem like we can't really trust the evidence we have or making it seem like weaker support for the conclusion than it currently is.

label: Conclusion
body: It is no wonder that environmentalists fail to consider both that spacecraft may damage the ozone layer and that this damage could be serious enough to warrant discontinuing spaceflight.

label: Evidence
body:
The use of this spacecraft is an important development in the conservation movement's history.
It allows us to observe problems long before we'd otherwise notice, allowing us to intervene before we reach crisis stage.

label: Proponent's Evidence
body:
Irradiation kills off Salmonella. And the process of irradiating food leaves no radiation behind.
It kills off some of the vitamin content, but it's comparable to what vitamin losses occur in cooking.

label: Evaluate
body:
When we're shopping for a Principle that conforms to or justifies an argument/reasoning, we're basically looking for something where the trigger idea matches up with something we know from the Evidence and the outcome idea matches up with the language or gist of the Conclusion.
Our conclusion is, "It's no wonder they fail to consider the potentially dealbreaker-level of damage the spacecraft may be causing".
To loosen up our brains for meaning-matches, what's another way we could say the same thing? "It's unsurprising they overlook what could be a fatal flaw with using this device".
There are a couple ideas that could be used for the trigger.
If X is an important unsurprising you're development in your → overlooking X's movement's history potential fatal flaws
If X allows us to see unsurprising you're problems early enough → overlooking X's intervene before crisis potential fatal flaws

label: Goal
body:
Look for an answer that sounds like 1/2 Evidence, 1/2 Conclusion.
It should be talking about whether or not something is important and helpful to you, and it should be talking about whether or not you're likely to fail to consider that something's potential downsides.

label: Conclusion (consequently)
body: Some relatively benign regimes may ironically be toppled by their own "enlightened" move to increase literacy.

label: Intermediate Conclusion (thus)
body: There is an interim period where the populace is vulnerable to clever demagogues calling for change.

label: Evidence
body: Widespread literacy emerges before any comprehensive system of general education is in place.

label: Evaluate
body:
The conclusion lays out a causal / logical path that starts from spread of literacy and ends up with a regime being toppled.
Literacy --------------------------> regime spreads toppled
What does the argument think ultimately topples the regime? Apparently, it's the "clever demagogues calling for change".
demagogues --> regime call 4 change toppled
How does the spread of literacy get us to demagogues calling for change? We just know that it emerges before any comprehensive system of general education is in place.
Literacy ---> no comp spreads edu in place

label: Goal
body:
There seem to be two big missing links:
"When there's no comprehensive education system in place, the population is vulnerable to clever demagogues calling for change".
"When clever demagogues call for change, it can lead to a relatively benign regime being toppled".

label: Conclusion
body:
The predominant theory cannot be right (in the case of these newly discovered island paintings).
rephrase: these paintings were not largely a description of the current diets of the painters.

label: Evidence (because)
body: Painters must have needed to eat the sea animals populating the waters north of Norway in order to make the long journey to and from the islands, but there are no clear paintings of sea animals.

label: Evaluate
body:
If we're trying to argue that the paintings were largely a description of the current diets of the painters, then the author is going to want to know why there aren't any clear pictures of sea animals.
So we're probably going to weaken by making excuses for that fact: - there are paintings of sea animals, but they're ambiguous because ... they've been eroded? the painters don't really understand what sea animals look like, since the animals live underwater until they're caught or speared for food? they're harder to draw?
Or maybe we could say that sea animals weren't part of the current diet of the painters. Maybe while they were painting, they weren't going back and forth to the islands, so they weren't currently eating sea animals.

label: Goal
body:
We want to eliminate four answers that weaken and allow us to defend the predominant theory, to defend the idea that the paintings largely were a description of the current diet of the painters.
Stay flexible. It's very common on EXCEPT for some of those four answers to work in a different style than the other three do.

label: Predominant Theory
body: Cave paintings depict the painters' current diets.

label: Author's Argument
body: Theory is wrong: painters needed to eat sea animals during their journey, but no paintings unambiguously depict sea creatures.

label: Goal
body: Find the answer that does NOT weaken the author's argument against the theory.

label: Setup
body: The popular theory says cave paintings show what the painters ate. The author tries to disprove that for these newly found island paintings: he says the painters had to eat sea animals to make it to the islands and back — but they didn't paint sea animals. So the diet theory must be wrong here.

label: Evaluate
body:
To weaken this argument against the theory, an answer needs to either:
(a) explain why the painters didn't actually need to eat sea creatures (so it's no surprise they didn't paint them), or
(b) explain why sea creatures might have been painted but those paintings aren't around now.
The right answer to "EXCEPT" is the one that does neither— leaves the gap between "needed to eat sea creatures" and "no paintings of sea creatures" intact.

label: Goal
body: Find the answer that doesn't address either side of that gap.

label: Conclusion (should)
body: Attacks on an opponent's character should be avoided in political debates.

label: Evidence
body: Attacks on an opponent's character don't confront the argument, and they cast doub on the opponent's moral right to be in the debate at all.

label: Evaluate
body:
For Strengthen+Principle questions, we have a very predictable pre-phrasing goal of just saying "IF Premise, THEN Conclusion".
If there are multiple premise ideas, as there are here, any one of them can be used as a launching pad that gets us to the landing zone of the Conclusion.

label: Goal
body:
Let's look for either of these,
if something does not then should be not confront the → avoided in opponent's argument political debates
if something casts doubt then should be on opponent's moral → avoided in right to be in debate political debates

label: Conclusion
body: You lied to the court when you said that Congleton wanted the project to fail! i.e. Congleton didn't want the project to fail.

label: Evidence
body: Congleton assigned the best available graphic artist and best writer to the project, and everyone else assigned was also top notch.

label: Evidence
body: If this were the only rule you followed, you'd have fewer and fewer beliefs over time. And we need many beliefs in order to survive.

label: Goal
body:
Since this is Flaw EXCEPT (a very rare task, thankfully), we should probably head to the answers rather quickly, knowing there are going to be four valid responses to this argument. Usually on EXCEPT questions, 3 of the 4 valid responses work one way, whereas the other valid response has a very different style / angle to it.
We aren't likely to anticipate all four of them, so let's just keep the Anti-Conclusion in our heads.
"Yes, she assigned the best people to the project, but she did want the project to fail". Any answer that helps us reconcile those two will work as an objection.

label: Conclusion (therefore)
body: Lhasa requires Xian (anyone who flies from Beijing to Lhasa cannot avoid flying to Xian).

label: Evidence
body:
Lhasa requires Chengdu (cannot fly to Lhasa from Beijing without first flying to Chengdu).
Chengdu requires Xian (must fly to Xian before flying to Chengdu).

label: Evaluate
body:
Parallel questions usually involve conditional logic, and when they do, we lean towards diagramming them symbolically to see their form.
The conditional arrow can be read as "requires", so when we have two premises telling us essentially that L requires C and that C requires X, we get a chain.
P: L → C P: C → X
Those chain together to show L → C → X
The conclusion is just giving us the head to tail connection of that chain: L → X

label: Goal
body:
We want two conditional premises that chain together, and a conclusion that shows the head to tail connection of the chain.
P: A → B P: B → C C: A → C

label: Argument Form
body: Lhasa requires Chengdu; Chengdu requires Xian; therefore Lhasa requires Xian.

label: Goal
body: Find: X requires Y, Y requires Z, therefore X requires Z.

label: Argument Form
body:
Strip the geography away and the argument is a simple chain:
To get to L, you need C. To get to C, you need X. So to get to L, you need X.
That's a valid transitive chain of necessary conditions.

label: Evaluate
body:
The right answer must follow the same shape: A needs B, B needs C, therefore A needs C. Watch out for answers that:
- introduce a sufficient condition where we need a necessary one
- add a conclusion about what could happen rather than what's required
- introduce a different logical structure entirely (existential claims, disjunctions, etc.)

label: Goal
body: Find a clean three-step necessary-condition chain.

label: Conclusion
body: Our next budget proposal will probably be approved.

label: Evidence (because / and)
body: Normally about half of all budget proposals that the VP considers are approved, and our last five budget proposals have all been turned down.

label: Evaluate
body:
Given that ... the VP normally approves about half of these and has turned down the previous five,
How can we argue that ... our next budget proposal won't be approved?
Well, we could maybe say these aren't normal times.
Maybe the VP is in a really weird place with her life / this job right now, and either for strategic or emotional reasons she's going to keep turning stuff down.
Maybe the VP, prior to the last five she turned down, has approved the previous ten (suggesting that if the average rate of approval is 50%, then getting another five proposals rejected could still be in line with that approval rate).
In a sense this is sort of like Gambler's Fallacy -- the idea that "if the last five times we flipped the coin it was heads, then the next flip will probably be tails". That's not how probability or averages work. The next flip of the coin still is a 50/50 chance.

label: Goal
body:
The author is assuming that these are normal times, that prior to this streak of rejecting 5 proposals the VP was not on a long streak of approving proposals, that the next budget proposal does not contain some provision the VP hates, that the next proposal is meaningfully different from the previous five, and so forth. It's hard to predict one specific answer here.
The correct answer, when negated, should sound like a big objection to this argument and allow us to argue that, "even though the VP rejected the last five (and overall approves about 50% of them), this next one is not likely to be approved".

label: Conclusion
body: The new anticollision device is responsible for the sudden disappearance of key information from air traffic controllers' screens.

label: Evidence
body:
The number of airplanes equipped with a new anticollision device has increased steadily during the past two years.
During the same period, it has become increasingly common for key information about an airplane's altitude and speed to disappear suddenly from air traffic controllers' screens.
The new anticollision device operates at the same frequency as air traffic radar.

label: Evaluate
body:
This argument presents a correlation between two events: the increase in airplanes equipped with the new anticollision device, and the increased disappearance of key information from controllers' screens. The author concludes causation; the device is causing the loss of information.
Curious Fact
Why is key information suddenly disappearing from controllers' screens?
Author's Explanation
The new anticollision device is causing the disappearance because it operates at the same frequency as air traffic radar.
We can strengthen the argument by increasing the plausibility that the device is causing the interference or weaken it by offering alternative explanations for the missing information or by disputing the idea that the device operating at the same frequency causes this interference.

label: Goal
body: Let's find an answer that suggests an Alternate Explanation for the disappearing information or disputes the causal link between the anticollision device and disappearing information.

label: Statements
body:
quantified (most, some)
Most stock market don't do research investors of their own
Some non-researching rely totally on investors broker's advice
Some non-researching rely totally on investors their hunches
Some researching still rely sometimes on investors broker or hunches
Few researching always do their own investors research before investing
Most stock market make a profit investors

label: Evaluate
body:
Since this unusual question stem wants something where Grimchester would currently be liable but shouldn't be, we need a situation where an injury occurs because a sidewalk needs repair/maintenance (currently liable) but Grimchester doesn't know about the danger beforehand or isn't negligent in trying to fix it (shouldn't be liable).
It seems like the middle sentence is teasing us with a hint: there are so many sidewalks that it's impossible to hire enough people to locate and eliminate every potential sidewalk danger.

label: Evaluate
body:
That is a mountain of information. It feels wishy-washy: some do this, some don't. Others do something else but also those previous things.
But if we're doing Inference (Must Be True / Most Supported) and we see quantified claims, we can remind ourselves of the two main Trait Overlap inferences that get tested:
Most A's are B Some A's are B+ Most A's are C + All B's are C Some B's are C Some A's are C
To make one of these Trait Overlap inferences, you either need a conditional-strength word like "All", or you need two "Most" claims. None of these claims were all / each / any / every / none.
But we do receive two most claims, and they are about the same group.
Most [investors] do no research Most [investors] make a profit
So they might be testing us on the idea that "do no research" and "make a profit" have to overlap.
If there are 100 investors , at a minimum 51 make a profit and 49 don't make a profit. Meanwhile, at least 51 do no research.
Do some of those "do no research" people have to be in the "make a profit" group?
Yes! Because you can't cram all 51 people who do no research into the 49-person group of people who don't make a profit. At least two of them overlap into the "make profit" group.
None of the other claims have the power to combine with each other to make this sort of Trait Overlap inference, but there are certainly other directions that answer could go.

label: Goal
body: Look for the most provable idea we can find (it might be establishing that there must be some overlap between "people who do no research" and "making a profit").

label: Conclusion (So)
body: General principles of justice are never sufficient to determine the details of social policies fixed within a particular state.

label: Evidence (for example)
body:
Different communities that recognize the dignity and equality of all citizens settle on somewhat different provisions for the elderly.
At some point in a discussion of societal justice, the defense is "That is the way we do things here."

label: Evaluate
body:
The argument suggests that even if societies adhere to similar overarching principles of justice, they will still arrive at different detailed social policies. This suggests that broad principles are not enough to prescribe specific societal policies. If we were being skeptical, we might say, "Never? Even if lots of times the specific policies differ, like for the elderly, maybe there's at least one case where tons of states have a similar social policy based on the same principles of justice."
So an answer can help convince us that "no, never! Even when you might thing the details of social policy would be the same, there are still significant differences from case to case."

label: Goal
body: Let's find an answer that shows societies with similar, general principles of justice implementing different specific policies, reinforcing the idea that these overarching principles don't alone dictate specific policy details.

label: Opposing View
body: Some claim herbs aren't prescribed because their medicinal effectiveness is seriously in doubt.

label: Author's Alternative Explanation
body: Herbs aren't prescribed because of a structural barrier: drugs require regulatory approval ($200M cost), only patent-holders can recover those costs, and herbs and their medicinal uses can't be patented. So the system financially can't support seeking approval for herbs.

label: Conclusion
body: Under the current system, licensed physicians cannot recommend the medicinal use of herbs.

label: Evaluate
body: The author's technique: the opposing view says herbs aren't prescribed because they don't work. The author counters by offering a totally different explanation — herbs aren't prescribed because of a regulatory/economic structure, not because of efficacy. That's a competing explanation for the same phenomenon.

label: Goal
body: Identify the move: questioning a claim about why something is the case by supplying an alternative explanation.

label: Opposing View
body: Herbs aren't prescribed because their effectiveness is doubtful.

label: Author's Counter
body: Actually, herbs aren't prescribed because the regulatory-approval economics don't support it (no patents, no recovery of approval costs).

label: Goal
body: Identify the technique: providing an alternative explanation for the same fact.

label: Conclusion (Implied Rebuttal)
body: Increasing the number of cops isn't the only way to fix crime.

label: Evidence
body: Many major cities have similar ratios of police officers to citizens, yet their crime rates diverged widely.

label: Evaluate
body:
The author isn't claiming police don't matter at all, or that we don't need more police. The author is using the statistics to undercut the strong claim that police count is the only way to fix crime.
Same police levels yielding different crime rates means something else must be influencing crime, alongside police count.
This argument is an implicit variation of the common Faulty Implications style of rebuttal. If they were right (that the only way to fix crime was more cops), then you'd expect cities with similar police presence to have similar crime rates. But statistics show that there are cities with similar police but very different crime rates. So, they're not right.

label: Goal
body: Pick any answer that says something accurate. The author uses statistics to undermine a strong causal claim and to suggest that Alternative influences on crime must exist.

label: Argument
body: Statistics show similar police-to-citizen ratios produced widely different crime rates — suggesting police count isn't the only factor.

label: Goal
body: Find the answer that captures this measured "not the only influence" role.

label: Conclusion (so)
body: The use of a spacecraft to conduct experiments aimed at understanding and eventually reversing damage to the fragile ozone layer is unjustifiable.

label: Evidence (since)
body:
The spacecraft did as much harm to the ozone layer as a year's pollution by the average factory.
The pollution from the factory is unjustifiable.

label: Goal
body: We want a situation where someone gets injured on a Grimchester sidewalk, but they either didn't know about it yet or weren't able to get people there in time to fix it (not because of negligence, but just because they're spread too thin with resources).

label: Conclusion (should = opinion)
body: The best managers in a company should be assigned to development projects.

label: Evaluate
body:
This is an argument by Comparison, so to weaken it, we want to try to think of salient differences between the two things being compared.
The author is arguing, "Same amount of pollution. The pollution was unjustifiable here, so it must be unjustifiable there."
We would have to make an excuse for why it could be wrong in one case but tolerable in another case. We'd probably say, "Yes, the spacecraft caused ozone damage, but if these experiments can bring us the knowledge of how to reverse damage to the ozone layer, it could easily be worth it in the long run. Got to spend money to make money, right?"
The argument is sort of like saying, "The surgeon's scalpel drew as much blood as did the knife from that guy who mugged me in the alley. Since it was wrong for the mugger to stab me, it was wrong for the surgeon to cut me."
The surgeon would be like, "Whoa --- big difference there, buddy. I'm cutting you for the sake of helping you overall. The mugger was not."

label: Goal
body: Look for an answer saying that the ozone damage caused by the spacecraft could be justifiable because it's aimed at helping the ozone layer overall, whereas the factory's pollution is not.

label: Conclusion (so)
body: Governments must help finance the maintenance, advancement, and enrichment of the fine arts today.

label: Evidence
body: Contemporary societies should fulfill their obligation as stewards of cultural heritage without the assistance of aristocracies or religious institutions.

label: Evaluate
body:
This paragraph is pretty dense. Let's dumb it down a bit.
Back in the days of Olde Europe, there weren't legislative bodies of government. There were rich elites and the Church. They ran the show. Part of running the show was commissioning artists to create works. The Church and other rich elites would give artists food and shelter while the artists learned their trades and worked on art.
Without that help, the arts probably wouldn't have survived.
Then the author just pivots into an unsupported opinion of his own. He says, "Clearly", but it's not the typical clearly that signals a conclusion. It's just signaling an opinion the author thinks is a self-justifying truth.
Obviously, modern societies should also give artists the subsidies they need to survive. But obviously, modern societies shouldn't let rich aristocrats or the Church be the ones to give them the money.
Thus,governments need to help finance the maintenance, advancement, and enrichment of the fine arts today.
The author is assuming that the fine arts still need subsidies to survive, and the author is saying "it's not an acceptable option for artists to get that support money from religious groups or aristocrats." By concluding that governments will therefore have to supply the money, she's assuming that governments are the only other possible source of this money.
What about non-rich people all chipping in $20 or so? What about getting sports franchises to sponsor artists?

label: Goal
body: Let's look for a Linking idea like, "If church and aristocracy aren't an option, then government is the only option left", or look for a Defender answer like, "the financial support contemporary artists need to maintain, advance, and enrich the fine arts could not be obtained through many small donations from middle class citizens" .

label: Conclusion
body: A family business is a family's surest road to financial prosperity

label: Evidence
body: In a family business, you can pay the employees (your family members) exceptionally low wages, which lowers your overhead, making profits higher.

label: Evaluate
body:
GIVEN THAT in a family business you can lower your expenses by paying your family members less money, HOW CAN WE STILL ARGUE THAT a family business is not a family's surest road to prosperity?
Well one thing that jumps out is exceptionally low wages. Are we saying that the family is prosperous because the family members make really low hourly wages but somehow share in the dividends of the profits the business makes? It kinda seems like it's taking from the same bank account it's paying. "I'll pay you $5 less per hour, but I'll give you a $40 cut of the family's profits at the end of the day."
Another thing we could say is that "even if a family business has lower overhead than other similar businesses, maybe the family's more sure way to prosperity is to spread out into different business ventures, making it less likely that the entire family would be broke if their one collective venture doesn't pan out. Or maybe the family would be more prosperous if some of the family members went to law school or med school instead of working at the family store for exceptionally low wages."

label: Goal
body: Look for some way to argue that a family business is NOT the surest road to financial prosperity.

label: Raphaelas 1st claim
body:
Forcing people to help others is morally wrong. does Edward argue that forcing people to help others is not morally wrong?
No, not really. Edward never touches on morality.

label: Raphaelas 2nd claim
body:
No government has the right to redistribute resources via taxation. does Edward argue that at least some governments do have the right to redistribute via taxation?
Yes! Edward thinks that "if your government allow you to leave the country if you don't want to live under its authority, then your government has the right to tax you for potential redistribution of resources."

label: Raphaelas 3rd claim
body:
Anyone who wants to help can do so voluntarily. does Edward argue that some people who want to help can't do so voluntarily?
No, he's not talking about that at all.

label: Goal
body:
So, we had an explicit disagreement:
R says no govt has right to tax/redistribute E says at least some govt's do have that right.
Or, if we used E's wording:
E says "if you let your citizens leave, then you have the right to tax/redistribute", and R says "Nope, even if you let them leave, you still don't have that right".

label: Conclusion (these facts support)
body: Galanin causes rats to crave fatty foods.

label: Evidence
body: In an experiment, rats that consistently chose to eat fatty foods when offered a choice between lean and fatty foods were found to have significantly higher concentrations of galanin in their brains than did rats that consistently chose lean over fatty foods.

label: Evidence
body:
Early in a new product's development, the critical resource is talent. New marketing requires managerial skill in disproportionate amounts, relative to short-term revenue prospects.
But talented managers are usually assigned only to established high-revenue product lines, and so most new marketing ventures fail.

label: Evaluate
body: The #1 thing we read for on Most Supported is causal relationships, and this paragraph was stressing different ways that speakers/writers can cause an audience to grasp their intended meaning.

label: Evaluate
body:
This argument fits the Explain Curious Fact pattern because it highlights a correlation between galanin levels and a preference for fatty foods.
Curious Fact Why do rats that choose fatty foods have higher concentrations of galanin?
Author's Explanation Galanin causes rats to crave fatty foods.
To strengthen this argument, we can either increase the plausibility of the author's explanation or rule out alternate explanations. With correlation to causality arguments like this, we know to always consider the alternate explanations of Reverse Causality (maybe eating fatty foods put galanin in their brain) or Third Factor (maybe some other thing, like a DNA mutation, is connected to choosing fatty foods and connected to high galanin)

label: Goal
body: Let's find an answer that makes it more plausible that galanin leads to fat cravings, or one that rules out an alternate explanation for why galanin was correlated with eating fatty foods.

label: Conclusion
body: If nations' economies → must look beyond are to prosper national borders

label: Intermediate Conclusion
body: Economies are always open systems.

label: Evidence
body: International trade significantly affects prices and wages.

label: Evaluate
body:
This is a pretty difficult argument to parse (and a lot of filler to ignore). Consider just the structural clues:
Some economists say _____ . But ______ ; _______ . Just as physicists did ___ , government economists must do ____ .
We can tell from "some ppl say .... But", that the first sentence is background/counterpoint, and the author's argument starts after the "But".
A colon / semicolon can often be a way to show that the 2nd half of a sentence supports the 1st half. We can also use the Support Test to think about whether that makes sense.
Why should we believe that economies are always open systems? Because, international trade affects prices and wages.
The last sentence begins with an analogy (Just as X, Y). Analogies are good fodder for Strengthening / Weakening, but they don't really have any place in the Sufficient Assumption universe, where the logic has to work 100%.
Since the conclusion is conditional we can think about whether we'd rather think about it as, "Prospering national economies require that government economists look beyond their national borders", or as, "if government economists don't look beyond their national borders, their national economies can't prosper".
Either way you slice it, the idea of "what prospering national economies" require or what could make it impossible for a national economy to prosper is a New Idea in the conclusion.
On Sufficient Assumption, new ideas in the conclusion must be in the correct answer.
We did kind of hear about looking beyond national border, when they told us about international trade.

label: Goal
body: We need something like, "If government economists don't look at something that significantly affects prices and wages, then their national economies can't prosper."

label: Conclusion (We Can Conclude)
body: Maria trained hard.

label: Evidence
body: Maria won this year's local sailboat race, beating Sue, the winner in each of the four previous years.

label: Evaluate
body:
We are trying to prove that Maria "trained hard". Did the evidence provide a proving mechanism for that language, i.e. a rule that says "If xyz, then trained hard"?
No, so the correct answer must provide a rule that puts "trained hard" on the right side of the arrow.
What do we know about Maria? - she won this year's local sailboat race - she beat Sue

label: Goal
body:
The correct answer will give us a rule that we know applies to Maria and that outputs the language that she "trained hard".
So it could be "If won this year's local sailboat race, then trained hard" or "If beat Sue, then trained hard"

label: Conclusion
body: If North Americans wants to be healthier without cutting fat intake, they should drink more wine.

label: Intermediate Conclusion
body: French people drink a lot of red wine, which apparently mitigates the bad effects of the fat in their diet.

label: Evidence
body: In France, they have a diet high in fat and yet a low incidence of heart disease. In North America, they have one of the highest rates of heart disease in the world.

label: Evaluate
body:
There seems to be more than one attack point for this argument. We're not sure that the reason French people have low heart disease despite high fat is that they drink lots of red wine. The author is stipulating that as "the most likely explanation" but we don't have to accept that as fact. I listed it as an Intermediate Conclusion to reflect the fact that it's still just an opinion.
But let's say we accept the opinion as fact: drinking lots of red wine helps French people mitigate the harmful effects of the fat in their diet.
Does that prove that North Americans would be healthier by drinking more red wine?
First of all, the argument has to assume a difference. It has to assume that North Americans aren't already drinking as much red wine as the French do.
Secondly, the argument has to assume a similarity. It has to assume that North Americans have this crazy high rate of heart disease (in large part) because of fat in their diet. Otherwise, it makes no sense to prescribe the French 'remedy' for fat, if North Americans don't each much fat to begin with.
Finally, it seems to conflate "lowering your risk of heart disease" with "getting healthier". Maybe red wine would help North Americans with their hearts but harm their health in other ways (liver, blood pressure, etc.)

label: Goal
body: Look for an answer that offers an alternative explanation for why French people have high fat / low heart disease, an answer that makes it seem less plausible that red wine is the causal difference-maker, or an answer that suggests that even if red wine made North Americans less likely to get heart disease, it might make them less healthy in some other way.

label: Conclusion (Therefore / should)
body: Business schools should allow business executives to set curricula for management trainees that could then be taught by academics.

label: Evidence
body:
In business school, we need "action learning" from real experience within business and industry, not theory and academia.
We need to study real cases, not hypothetical ones.
Business schools have been slow to respond to these needs. They seem unable to tear themselves away from the academic, hypothetical stuff.

label: Pat's Evidence
body:
No actions considered bad have favorable consequences. ( bad action → ~favorable consequences )
Some good actions don't have favorable consequences.

label: Evidence
body: Top-down suggestions (from employer to employee) for improved efficiency are unlikely to elicit positive responses.

label: Evaluate
body:
This conversation seems to describe a Problem (we want more actual real world experience taught in business school, but they're teaching academic theory and doing hypothetical case).
The conclusion seems to offer a Solution: business executives will save us! (this is the first time anyone has had that thought unironically)
Whenever a Conclusion on an Assumption question has a New Term that only shows up in the Conclusion, we can nearly count on the fact that the correct answer will discuss this New Term.
What is being assumed about business executives, or about the curricula they would set if they were in charge of business schools?
We're assuming that they would solve the problem -- they would set curricula that involved "action learning" from real experience with real cases.
Whenever we have a Plan / Goal type setup, we have to assume that the Plan is - a feasible solution - going to get the cooperation it needs - doesn't backfire So here we need to assume that business execs would feasibly set curricula we'd be happier with, and that they'd be willing to do so. We need to assume that academics could then teach this curricula that business execs came up with, and that they'd be willing to do so. And we need to assume that having business execs set curricula wouldn't cause some backfire consequence that would make us worse off (or just-as-bad) overall. If the author ends up saying "we should do this Plan", then she's assuming it's the best available plan. If the author ends up saying "we must do this Plan", then she's assuming it's the only available plan.

label: Goal
body: Look for an answer affirming that business executives, if they were setting the curricula, would do it more the way we're wishing for (action learning from real experience with real cases), and that academics would then be able/willing to teach that. Or look for an answer that rules out an objection to putting business execs in charge.

label: Conclusion
body: There is no way that the center can be kept operating for the coming year.

label: Evidence (since)
body:
The center cannot operate on less than $2.5 million.
The budget has been reduced from last year's $4 million to $1.5 million.
The board cannot divert funds from other programs to the computer center.

label: Evaluate
body:
We're trying to prove that the center can't be kept operating for this year. Were we given some proving mechanism that allows us to say "thus, can't operate this year"?
Yes. We were told that the center can't operate on less than $2.5 million.
So in order to prove the conclusion, we have to establish that the center has less than $2.5 million.
The evidence tried to establish that by saying that the budget this year is only $1.5 million, and funds can't be diverted from other programs.
But does that guarantee that the center has less than $2.5 million?
What if they saved $1 million from last year? If they were given $4 million the previous year (and only need $2.5 million to operate), maybe they had a surplus that is still in their account.
What if they have a bake sale and raise $1 million?

label: Goal
body: We need to be convinced that they have less than $2.5 million, so the correct answer should rule out the possibility that they can supplement the $1.5 million they're budgeted with extra money from some other source.

label: Muriel's 1st Claim
body:
I admire Favilla's novels. does John say he doesn't admire them?
No, he makes no reference to Favilla at all.

label: Muriel's 2nd Claim
body:
Favilla does not deserve to be considered a great writer. does John say she should be considered great?
No, he makes no reference to Favilla at all.

label: Muriel's 3rd Claim
body:
Her style is distinctive does John say it isn't distinctive?
No, he makes no reference to Favilla at all.

label: Muriel's 4th Claim
body:
Her subject matter is not varied enough. does John say it is varied enough?
No, he makes no reference to Favilla at all.

label: Evaluate
body:
Since John didn't disagree with any of Muriel's explicit claims (and since John isn't talking about Favilla at all), we can tell that John must be objecting to something more implied or assumed.
In fact, John explicitly says that he's objecting to the "criterion" that Muriel is using.
She is saying, "if you're subject matter is not varied enough, then you shouldn't be considered a great writer".
He says, "a great writer does not need any diversity in subject matter".

label: Goal
body: Let's look for something like,whether or not diversity in subject matter is a necessary criterion for considering someone is a great writer.

label: Statements
body: - A great writer doesn't need any diversity in subject matter - A great writer must have the ability to explore a particular theme deeply

label: Evaluate
body:
My hunch is that since John spelled out two things about what great writers need / don't need, the answer is probably testing the idea that one does not imply the other.
If I say Paul doesn't need A, he needs B then I'm assuming that B doesn't require A.
So if John has said that great art doesn't need diversity, it needs to explore a theme deeply, he would be assuming that "exploring a theme deeply doesn't require any diversity in subject matter".

label: Goal
body: Pick anything derivable from either of John's two statements about great writers or derivable by combining them.

label: Conclusion
body: The moons in solar system S4 all orbit the planet Alpha.

label: Evidence
body: Any moon, by definition, orbits some planet in a solar system.

label: Evaluate
body:
We know that moons always orbit some planet in a solar system, but how would that generic statement prove that all the moons in S4 orbit Alpha?
What would we learn about S4 or Alpha that would guarantee that all the moons in that system orbit Alpha?

label: Goal
body:
Look for an answer choice that, when combined with the idea that all moons orbit some planet in a solar system, guarantees that all moons in S4 orbit Alpha.
Since there is a new term in the conclusion "S4" and "Alpha", we know the correct answer will have to involve those ideas.

label: The Now = (currently)
body: Injury incurred because Grimchester sidewalk needs repair → is liable or maintenance

label: The Should
body: Didn't know about should not danger beforehand → be liable or Didn't negligently fail to fix it

label: Goal
body:
We can anticipate that the correct answer might reward us for assembling the whole chain by testing "If contract negotiator, then practice deception", or its contrapositive.
But the correct answer doesn't have to connect the 1st to the 4th. It might connect 1st to 3rd, or 2nd to 4th.

label: Evaluate
body:
Since this conclusion consists of a Plan / Recommendation, we should think about the Net Gain / Net Loss aspects of comparing our current world to the world the author is suggesting.
In particular, we consider ideas like - feasibility - motives / incentives - the possibility of the plan backfiring
Will companies be better off if they switch their best managers from overseeing established high-revenue product lines to overseeing new product lines that won't make as much revenue in the short term?
If we were objecting to this plan, what might we say?
- Don't worry about new product lines. Most of them fail anyway, regardless of the talent of the manager.
- We need to safeguard the sweet revenue we get from established products. If we take the best managers off those product lines, then we won't make as much money off them as we would have otherwise.
- We make more money by making sure that established lines keep raking in the revenue, than we do by trying to launch new product lines.

label: Goal
body:
Since we're strengthening the argument, our answer might go in the opposite direction from one of our objections:
- The new product lines are not likely to fail, if they are given a great manager.
- You don't need the manager to oversee existing product lines. Even mediocre managers can keep the money rolling in from those.
- There's more money to be made long term by trying to launch as many product lines as we viably can, rather than trying to milk as much revenue out of established product lines.

label: Conclusion (therefore)
