body: Few people ever fully understand current events.

label: Evidence (since)
body:
Few people seek our news sources other than newspapers and TV.
TV provides a sense of direct involvement, but not enough depth to understand significance.
Newspapers provide depth but no direct involvement.
A full understanding of current events requires both enough depth to appreciate significance of events and a sense of direct involvement with them.

label: Evaluate
body:
Since the conclusion is saying that "few people ever fully understand current events", we'd be trying to counter-argue, "nuh-uh ...most people fully understand current events".
"Fully understanding" is defined to require both appreciation of significance and a sense of direct involvement. So if we're arguing that most people fully understand current events, we need to be able to argue that most people have both an appreciation of the significance of current events and a sense of direct involvement.
The author will say, "How could they have both? After all, most people only use newspapers or TV as their news sources. TV fails to provide the significance, and newspapers fail to provide a sense of direct involvement."
We would probably say, "People watch TV and read newspapers. They get their direct involvement by watching TV. And they get the depth they need to appreciate the significance of events by reading the paper."

label: Goal
body:
Look for a specific objection sounding like, "fails to consider that most people consume news about current events by consulting both TV and newspapers".
Or look for an abstract objection sounding like, "the author fails to consider that two things that are each by themselves inadequate to provide a full understanding could still be adequate, in combination, to provide such an understanding."

label: Some Writers
body: 1. Stalin was debatably sane during his last years. 2. His vindictiveness (his cruelty) was due to his paranoia and morbid suspiciousness.

label: Critic
body: Stalin was not especially showing paranoia and morbid suspiciousness in his later years. Stalin was paranoid and morbidly suspicious from the jump (just like any long-lasting tyrant).

label: Evaluate
body:
Where is the critic diverging from the writers? She's saying that it's odd to justify a claim about Stalin's loss of sanity during his waning years, by pointing to the idea that these years were characterized by Stalin being paranoid about people trying to subvert him, and retaliating viciously.
After all, that not only characterizes Stalin's early and middle periods as well, but it characterizes any tyrant who wants to stay in power for a long time.

label: Goal
body:
Let's look for something like, "they're arguing about whether Stalin's vindictiveness in his later years were something new and noteworthy vs. something that had been going on for a while" or "whether his vindictiveness in his later years is compelling vs. weak evidence for a loss in sanity".
p.s. glasnost is a Russian word meaning "openness", that also was a shorthand for describing the end of the Soviet Union / Cold War in the late 1980s, under Mikhail Gorbachev. The other word from that time, perestroika, meant "change". It was sort of a transition period where Gorbachev tried to move Russia out of its Soviet Union, imperial, communist empire into a slightly more democratic, more Western, more worldly entity. So "writers under glasnost" would have had the motivation of being apologists for how scandalously cruel the Stalin regime was. They would be trying to make Russia not seem as crazy as Stalin would make it look on the world stage, and thus "explain away" his atrocities by saying he was just a confused old man losing his sanity, not the logical conclusion of an authoritarian communist system.

label: Conclusion (Therefore)
body: Philosophical thought is unique to humans.

label: Evidence
body: Apes are able to learn human language, but no ape has ever used its human language skills to ask philosophical questions such as, “How am I different from all other creatures?”

label: Evaluate
body: This argument assumes that the way to detect philosophical thought is by the expression of philosophical questions in human language. In other words, the author takes the fact that apes, although capable of learning human language, have not asked philosophical questions as sufficient evidence that such thought is exclusively human.

label: Goal
body: Look for an answer that fills the gap between the evidence and the conclusion by assuming that philosophical thought must be expressed in human language. If philosophical thought could be expressed in some other way, the absence of philosophical questions in apes would not necessarily mean they lack philosophical thought.

label: Proposal
body: Climbers should have to post a "insurance bond" of sorts, so that a large sum of money goes to the government if something calamitous happens to them while climbing.

label: Support
body: 250 rescues cost the government 3 million dollars. 25 people died. More and more people are entering the sport.

label: Conclusion
body: The reform I propose is a good social reform.

label: Evidence (Since)
body: The reform I propose would make my constituents happy.

label: Evaluate
body:
The task force is like, "Damn, y'all. You see all these people dying from this mountain climbing activity, but new people wanna keep trying it? Every time you idiots get stuck somewhere, we have to spend tens of thousands to rescue you. Look, if you wanna keep climbing, then you've got to pre-pay the rescue fee, so that we can afford to put gas in the rescue helicopter".
More or less. That's not a direct quote.

label: Goal
body: We want something like, if your activity is known to be super risky and to potentially cost others a lot of money to save you, then you should be responsible for pre-paying for your own rescue.

label: Conclusion (so)
body: The claim that "the most likely to survive are the most likely to survive" is neither informative nor of scientific interest.

label: Intermediate Conclusion
body: The claim is a tautology (i.e. like "A is A.").

label: Evidence
body:
People use the slogan "survival of the fittest" to express the idea that "the fittest are most likely to survive".
However, biologists use the term "fittest" to mean "most likely to survive".

label: Evaluate
body:
A tautology is a fancy word that means "a self-justifying truth". For example, the sentence "I am speaking English right now" is guaranteed to be true, without recourse to any premises. Similarly, "good things are better than bad things".
The author is saying that "survival of the fittest" is meant to express that "the fittest are most likely to survive". What do we mean by fittest?
Well, you might be thinking, "The strongest / the tallest / the ones with best endurance / the smartest".
But biologists use this term as a synonym for "most likely to survive / the best fit for their environment".
The author is thus explaining that if we use that definition of 'fittest', then saying that "the fittest are more likely to survive" is as silly and empty as saying "the most likely to survive are the most likely to survive".
However, we may ask, when people use the phrase "survival of the fittest", is that what they mean by fittest? Do they mean "most likely to survive" or do they mean "the strongest / biggest / smartest / fastest" type stuff.

label: Goal
body:
The author is assuming that when people use the familiar slogan "survival of the fittest" to express the idea that the fittest are most likely to survive, they are intending to employ the biologists' usage of that word.
(The author is also assuming that "if something is a tautology, then it is neither informative nor of scientific interest)

label: Given That
body: This city council finds preserving individual property rights to be of the utmost importance.

label: Why Is It That
body: People are forbidden by the zoning laws to do any extensive alteration (such as remodeling) to their property?

label: Conclusion
body:
Our team's behavior (enthusiastically celebrating our successes and our opponents' failures) is not unprofessional.
i.e. our team behaves professionally

label: Evidence
body: Some of the professionals in our sport are even more effusive in celebrating their success and taunting their opponents' failures.

label: Evaluate
body:
This argument boils down do this Equivocation: because some Professional athletes do it, if we do it, we're acting Professionally
The argument is using two different senses of the word "professional / unprofessional".
The coach's players are being criticized for acting unprofessionally (immaturely, with poor standards of sportsmanship / decorum).
He defends the players' behavior by saying that it exists as well within the professional league (not amateur, paid to play).
We wouldn't say that Because these pro athletes are paid to play, they're by definition acting maturely, with good standards of sportsmanship and decorum.
Similarly, the author shouldn't be saying Because pro athletes are very effusive / expressive when they win, acting this way is very professional.

label: Goal
body: Find an answer calling out the famous Equivocation flaw, using two different meanings of "professional".

label: Conclusion
body: A business that wishes to retain its power as long as it can must act responsibly.

label: Evidence
body: Avoiding social responsibility leads to the gradual erosion of power. As the famous quote says, if society thinks that power is not being used responsibly, it will act to reduce that power, though it may take decades or centuries.

label: Evaluate
body:
Given that society will eventually act to reduce your power when they deem you're not using it responsibly,
How could we still argue that Businesses that wish to retain their power as long as they can do not need to act responsibly?
Two thoughts come to mind: - given that it may require decades or even centuries for society to ultimately decide to act to reduce our power, maybe we should just not give a crap about acting responsibly, since we don't really believe that our business is going to last many, many decades or even multiple centuries.
In other words, "Don't bother acting responsibly because it'll take 50+ years for society to start trying to reduce your power, and who know if you'll even be able to sustain your business that long (also, you might not be alive any more to see the day of reckoning)."
- given that the trigger for power-reduction is when society thinks power is not being used responsibly, lets just hope that we can fool society into thinking that we're using power responsibly.
In other words, "Don't bother acting responsibly, but try to fool society into thinking that you are, so that we don't trigger the mechanism by which they start trying to reduce our power".

label: Goal
body: We want an answer that would allow us to respond to the evidence with a storyline in which we can evade acting responsibly but still hold on to our power for as long as we can.

label: Conclusion
body: If only evidence of Strep IF only evidence infection is presence of of X is Y Strep in throat, it would be wrong to THEN wrong to conclude Strep infection conclude X

label: Evidence
body: If not physically run down IF not Z then no Strep infection THEN not X then X doesn't occur

label: Evaluate / Goal
body: This argument is essentially saying "Don't conclude X on the basis of Y. After all, some third thing Z needs to be true for X to be true."

label: Terry and Pat's Conclusion
body: Some bad actions are actually good.

label: Terry's Evidence
body:
An action is good only if it has favorable consequences. ( good action → favorable consequences )
Some bad actions have favorable consequences.

label: Evaluate
body:
You gotta love how erudite these two sound ("Well, good sir, I agree with your conclusion, but not with the reasons offered"), while totally botching conditional logic. It's also funny that Terry and Pat are two of the most androgynous names, so I'll randomly assign Terry a male pronoun and Pat a female one.
Whenever we're doing Flaw and see conditional logic trigger words (only if, no), then we should immediately suspect a Necessary vs. Sufficient illegal move, where the author does an illegal reversal or negation to get to their conclusion.
Terry is picturing these two ideas, some actions considered bad have favor conseq.favor conseq. → good and that's how he arrives at some actions considered bad are good
But of course we don't have a conditional that says "if favorable consequences, then good", we have the reverse of that.
Similarly, Pat is picturing these two ideas,
some good actions are not favor conseq.not favor conseq. → considered bad and that's how she arrives at some good actions are considered bad
But of course she didn't say that "if not favorable consequences, then considered bad", she said the reverse of that.

label: Goal
body: Since both authors are doing illegal reversals of the conditionals they provided, they are both confusing a Necessary condition with a Sufficient one.

label: Conclusion
body: The paleo's claim is false. (i.e. Birds are not descendants of dromeosaurs)

label: Evidence
body: The earliest bird fossils that have been discovered date back tens of millions of years before the oldest known dromeosaur fossils.

label: Evaluate
body:
The author is saying, how could species B be a descendant of species D, if we think that B existed millions of years before D did?
Welp --- he's got us there. If birds existed before dromeosaurs, then it's impossible for birds to have descended from dromeosaurs.
How did these "some paleontologists" miss this obvious problem that renders their claim impossible? What could they be thinking that could still allow them to be right and our author to be wrong?
They must be thinking that dromeosaurs existed before birds, so if we point out that "the earliest bird fossils are 10 million years older than the earliest dromeosaur fossils", their only retort would be, "Yeah, but that's just because we haven't found the oldest dromeosaur fossils. In other words, just because we haven't found dromeosaur fossils as old as our oldest bird fossils doesn't prove that birds came before dromeosaurs. Maybe all the dromeosaur fossils that predated birds have been destroyed or just haven't been found yet."

label: Goal
body:
The only possible objection to this argument is to say, "dromeosaurs did exist prior to birds; we just haven't found those older fossils yet (if we ever do)."
Thus, the argument needs to assume - dromeosaurs did not exist prior to birds - there are not older dromeosaur fossils that got destroyed or have so far not been found by us

label: Main Conclusion
body: The proposal to stimulate economic activity by refunding $600 million envisions an illusory benefit.

label: Intermediate Conclusion (So)
body: Either the province's taxpayers or its workers, who are also province residents, will have the $600 million to spend, but there will be no resulting net increase in spending to stimulate the economy.

label: Evidence (since)
body: The budget has to be balanced, so there would either be new taxes needed (defeating the purpose of the refund) or the province would have to lay-off some of its workers (also bad for the economy).

label: Evaluate
body:
If I were trying to describe how the author reached her conclusion, I would probably call this a "Damned if you do, damned if you don't" kind of argument (i.e. "Either way you slice it, it's still bad").
The author tries to show that a plan won't achieve its intended result by introducing considerations that make it seem like whether we go down Road A or Road B, we won't reach our destination.

label: Goal
body: We just want whichever answer choice we can match up to the specifics of this conversation.

label: Conclusion (So)
body: There can be no resulting net increase in spending to stimulate the province's economy.

label: Intermediate Conclusion
body:
Let's say we refund $600 million in taxes to taxpayers --
We would then have to either 1. raise new taxes (defeating the purpose of the refund) or 2. government workers would have to be fired
You're either putting $600 million in the hands of taxpayers or keeping $600 million in the pockets of government workers who would otherwise need to be fired.

label: Evidence (since)
body: The province's budget must be balanced.

label: Evaluate
body:
Given that .. it's $600 million, either in the hands of refunded taxpayers or not-fired government workers.
How could we say that .. there could be a net increase in spending to stimulate the economy?
This is a question where outside knowledge can help. When politicians debate whether to give tax breaks to wealthy people/corporations vs. give money back to lower-earning taxpayers, it's often remarked that the wealthy companies and people are more likely to save that money, whereas the less wealthy people need the money for so many things that they're more likely to spend any refund money they receive.

label: Goal
body: Hard to predict where this is going, so we would just think, we need an answer that plays along with the constraints the author's premises laid out, but gives us a way to say that there could be a net increase in spending / stimulating.

label: Statements
body:
Conditionals
Contract negotiator → Been lied to
Been lied to → Has lied to someone
Has lied to someone → Practicing deception

label: Evaluate
body:
On Must Be True we're primarily looking out for Conditional or Mathematical language. When we see conditional trigger words like "Every", "Whoever", and "Anyone", we think about whether any of these conditional rules would chain together.
In order to chain together, you need an overlapping term, so after turning the first claim into a conditional, we want to find an idea that overlaps with "contract negotiator" or "been lied to".
Hence, we skipped over the 2nd fact so that we could look at the 3rd one, which contains "been lied to". On our paper, we would probably just chain as we go (rather than writing all three out separately as I did above).
Once we've attached the 1st and 3rd claim, we see that the 2nd claim picks up right where our chain left off. So the three fit together like this: Contract Been Has lied to Practice negotiator → Lied to → someone → Deception

label: Intermediate Conclusion (so)
body: Any reform which makes somebody happy is achieving its purpose.

label: Evidence
body: The first purpose of good social reform is to increase the sum total of human happiness.

label: Evaluate
body:
This argument draws two conclusions (the first indicated by the conclusion indicator So, the second indicated by the support indicator Since).
We could potentially weaken the argument by attacking either move.
The "So" conclusion is mangled interpretation of the initial rule stated. She said that the "the first purpose of good social reform is to increase the sum total of human happiness".
Our author then takes that to mean Any reform that makes even one person happy is achieving its purpose.
Hold the phone, there, author. We said "the FIRST purpose, not the only purpose". Maybe a reform could meet the first purpose but fail to meet the second/third/fourth purpose and therefore not qualify as good social reform.
More importantly, the standard was whether the sum total (the net effect) was an increase of happiness. It wasn't whether "at least one person's happiness increased".
After all, if a new reform increases the happiness of the richest 0.1% but lessens the happiness of the remaining 99.9% of the population, it hasn't increased the sum total of human happiness.
The conclusion drawn in the last sentence seems like valid logic, within the logically invalid world of the author. If we accept her flawed Intermediate Conclusion, that "any reform making at least one person happy is meeting the first purpose of good social reform", then we'd accept that this author's reform meets the first purpose of good social reform.
But, naturally, we do not accept the author's Intermediate Conclusion.
Finally, there is a gap between "achieving the first purpose of good social reform" and assuming something therefore "is a good social reform".
Maybe you could meet the first purpose of something but still not be considered that thing.

label: Goal
body: There were several complaints there, so we have to stay flexible. The most likely objection I would be looking for is the wide gap between "as long as someone is happier, we've increased the sum total of human happiness", which fails to consider that as one person's happiness goes up, there might be other people's happiness going down.

label: Conclusion (it is clear that)
body: R's book does not merit attention from serious professionals.

label: Evidence
body:
R has often shown himself to be arrogant, overly ambitious, and sometimes plain nasty.
R frequently accuses other researchers of bad faith inquiries, saying that they basically distort their findings in order to appeal to whatever source it is from which they get their funding.

label: Evaluate
body:
R's book has some pretty damning accusations of scientific research. Scientists are supposed to be concerned only with finding the truth; what does the objective world and empirical data have to say on this issue.
But according to R, the incentives provided by outside funding are distorting the scientific endeavor. He says that scientific investigators are often working backwards from the outcome they know their funding source wants.
Pretty provocative indictment of the current state of science. So why does this author think it doesn't merit attention from serious professionals?
Cuz R's kind of a dork. He's often arrogant / ambitious / nasty.
Okay, so what? We get that those behaviors are bad if you're trying to be friends with R, but we're just curious whether he's right about the corrosive nature of funding on science.

label: Goal
body:
Whenever we're doing Flaw and we see a rebuttal style argument, we immediately think of the two Famous Flaws that relate to rebuttals: - Ad Hominem (dismissing ideas without engaging with them, simply because the source of those ideas is sketchy, has an ulterior motive, or has some conflicting past behavior)
- Unproven vs. Proven False (concluding that X is false by showing that someone's attempt to prove X true was not successful)
This is definitely Ad Hominem. The author is dismissing R's ideas without engaging with them, because of personal aspects of R, which are irrelevant to the truth value of the ideas in his book.

label: Conclusion (clearly, then)
body: Our patrons prefer not to eat potatoes.

label: Evidence
body: We recently introduced three vegetarian entrees: - eggplant and zucchini casserole w/ tomatoes - brown rice with mushrooms - potatoes baked with cheese The first two are frequently ordered, but no one orders the potato dish, even though it costs less than the other two.

label: Evaluate
body:
The evidence introduces an Asymmetric Comparison, also known as a Curious Fact. The author's conclusion is overconfident in assigning a causal explanation for that curious fact.
Curious Fact ... how come people aren't ordering the potatoes and cheese dish?
Author's Explanation ... people don't like potatoes.
Maybe that is the reason, but maybe not. Maybe there's an Alternate Explanation, such as "people don't like cheese / people don't think potato and cheese will be a satisfying entree".

label: Goal
body:
On Flaw, when an author overconfidently concludes or assumes the causal explanation for some funky piece of evidence, the test usually just wants us to acknowledge that the author is too sure of one possible explanation.
And the correct answer is usually worded in a way that sounds like the author is "failing to consider Alternative Explanations".

label: Statements
body:
causal difference-maker
when it comes to newborns 4-6 weeks old that have had Mom as the primary caregiver, Mom's voice - causes them to stop crying temporarily Anyone else's voice - does not cause a temporary halt in crying

label: Evaluate
body:
Usually if Most Supported questions present some causal distinction (a causal difference-maker), the correct answer is a safely worded reinforcement of that. It doesn't speculate why it's occurring; it just reiterates that it's occurring or mentions some spin-off truth that is required for this causal difference-maker to work:
- babies have hearing - the sound of Mom's voice is perceived differently by them - sometimes their crying stops in response to a sound they've heard

label: Goal
body:
Look for a safely worded answer that reinforces the idea that a Mom's voice can effect a temporary pause in crying.
Beware strong wording, unknown comparisons, and out of scope ideas.

label: Conclusion
body:
The notion that "one might be justified in behaving irrationally in the service of a sufficiently worthy end" is incoherent.
i.e. Behaving irrationally is sort of the opposite of serving a sufficiently worthy end.

label: Evidence (for)
body: If any action is justified → you'd be (any end is sufficiently worthy) acting rational

label: Evidence
body: One claim of laissez-faire economics is that raising the minimum wage reduces minimum-wage jobs. But a study found that fast-food restaurants kept roughly the same number of minimum-wage employees after a minimum-wage increase.

label: Conclusion (so)
body: Mullen's proposal does not deserve our consideration. rephrase: We shouldn't even consider raising taxes on the rich.

label: Evaluate
body:
It helps our ability to understand this argument if know that saying two claims are incoherent or inconsistent means that they contradict each other.
If we know the author's conclusion is, "behaving irrationally means you must not be in the service of a sufficiently worthy end", then we go searching the evidence for a discussion of each concept. We have to put in some effort to see the matching symbols of "sufficiently worthy end" and "justified action", but since this is a Parallel question with a conditional rule, we would assume that there are going to be repeating symbols that would allow us to convert this into an algebraic recipe.

label: Goal
body:
We're looking for something like this ...
Prem: If A, then B Conc: The notion that one might be ~B while being A is incoherent.

label: Given That
body: Performing a good action is only praiseworthy if one overcomes a powerful temptation in order to perform it (i.e. if you didn't have to overcome a powerful temptation to perform action A, then you don't deserve praise for performing action A).

label: How Can It Be That
body: Performing good actions out of habit is sometimes praiseworthy?

label: Evaluate
body:
The moral principle in the first sentence is saying that an action is only praiseworthy if you had to overcome a temptation in order to perform it.
The surprise is that an action performed out of habit could ever be praiseworthy, which insinuates that actions performed out of habit wouldn't be expected to overlap with actions that involve overcoming a powerful temptation.
But maybe they do overlap! Maybe I have a habit of calling my mom on Sundays, and because I am strongly tempted to not call her but do anyway, it is a good action.

label: Goal
body: Find an answer that helps us show how actions performed out of habit could also be actions that overcome a powerful temptation.

label: Conclusion
body: The school is currently in violation of its charter.

label: Evidence
body: The charter says that the student body must include some students with special educational needs, but there are no members of the student body with learning disabilities enrolled yet.

label: Evaluate
body:
In order to prove the school is violating its charter, we have to establish that they have no students with special educational needs.
All we've established is that they have no students with learning disabilities.

label: Goal
body:
So we need an answer to let us make this move:
if they have no students → then they have none w/ with learning disabilities special ed. needs

label: Conclusion (thus)
body: These psychologists are wrong. i.e. Deep empathy is not the best way to understand another person.

label: Intermediate Conclusion
body: Suppose they are right -- suppose that deep empathy, whereby you gain direct and complete grasp of someone else's motivations, is the best way to understand another person -- There would be no way at all to achieve understanding.

label: Evidence (since)
body:
It's psychologically impossible to gain a direct and complete grasp of another person's motivations.
But one can understand other people.

label: Evaluate
body:
The author is attempting to refute a position by demonstrating that a logical implication of that position is wrong. It's kind of like arguing by a contrapositive. You say, "If Person X were right, then A would be true. A isn't true, so that shows that Person X is wrong."
That sort of argument isn't flawed if we accept its two premises. Do we accept the two premises here?
"If deep empathy is the best way to understand another person, then that means there would be no way at all to achieve understanding (since it's psychologically impossible to have deep empathy)".
"But it's not true that there is no way at all to understand other people."
The 1st premise seems to contain a shaky move. The author is thinking, "If deep empathy is the best way to do X, but deep empathy is psychologically impossible, then there is no way at all to do X."
That seems to contain a flawed assumption that "if the best way to do X is impossible, then there is no way at all to do X."
I could say, "The best way to heal the political division in America would be for people from red districts and blue districts to switch lives with each other for a year." Clearly that's an impossible plan. Does that then mean that "there is no way at all to heal the political divisions in America?" Of course not.

label: Goal
body:
The move to the final conclusion is logically valid (if we accept all the ingredients of the author's "implications of their logic" rebuttal), so we can really only complain about the move the author made to reach her intermediate conclusion, which is saying that the psychologists' position entails the notion that "there is no way at all to achieve understanding".
Essentially, this author is acting like "if the best way to do X is impossible, then X is impossible."

label: Conclusion (this shows that)
body: Synesthesiacs have senses that don't respect the usual boundaries between the five recognized senses.

label: Evidence
body:
The traditional / usual / typical understanding of the five senses was that they had distinct boundaries, each sense having its own range of stimuli that wouldn't be able to stimulate other senses.
Synesthesiacs report tasting a banana and tasting "blue", or seeing a color and saying they can smell it.

label: Evaluate
body:
Since the author's conclusion is interpreting the findings of an experiment / study, it's a high contender for the Explain Curious Fact mindset.
Curious Fact ... why are synesthesiacs saying they taste blue or can smell a certain color?
Author's Explanation ... most people have well-defined boundaries between their five senses, but in the case of synesthesiacs, a stimulus for one sense is capable of stimulating another sense. (the taste stimulus of a banana is capable of stimulating the visual sense of color / the visual stimuli of color is capable of stimulating the olfactory sense of smell)

label: Goal
body:
We want to weaken these arguments one of two ways:
1. suggest an Alternate Explanation for the curious fact (what could be a different way to explain the research on synesthesiacs? maybe they're just making stuff up? they're messing around with researchers? maybe they have a hard time describing things and so they choose the wrong words?)
2. hurt the plausibility of the Author's Explanation (what could make us doubt that synesthesiacs have atypical brains with senses that can actually impact each other? do brain scans of synesthesiacs look identical to those of average people? are there other experiments we've done with synesthesiacs that make it seem like their five senses DO respect the usual boundaries?)

label: Conclusion
body: Laissez-faire economics is not entirely accurate.

label: Evaluate
body: The argument generalizes from one slice of the labor market — fast-food restaurants in the study — to the broader claim of laissez-faire economics, which is about minimum-wage jobs in general. That step only works if those fast-food restaurants are a fair stand-in for the broader minimum-wage job market. If they aren't representative, the study doesn't actually contradict the laissez-faire claim.

label: Goal
body: The correct answer should fill that gap — the studied fast-food restaurants must be representative of the wider minimum-wage labor market. Negation test: if the studied restaurants are not representative, the argument falls apart.

label: Conclusion
body: Laissez-faire economics is not entirely accurate.

label: Evidence
body: A study found fast-food restaurants kept the same number of minimum-wage employees after a minimum-wage increase, contrary to a laissez-faire prediction.

label: Evaluate
body: To rebut the general claim, the study sample must be representative of minimum-wage jobs overall.

label: Goal
body: The correct answer must establish that the studied fast-food restaurants represent minimum-wage jobs more broadly.

label: Conclusion
body: The essayist is saying: laissez-faire economics is wrong about something — specifically, its claim that raising the minimum wage cuts minimum-wage jobs.

label: Evidence
body: A single study showed fast-food restaurants didn't cut their minimum-wage workers when the minimum wage went up.

label: Evaluate
body:
Watch the leap. The laissez-faire claim is about minimum-wage jobs in general — across the whole economy. The study only looked at fast-food restaurants. To use a fast-food study to attack a general claim, you need fast-food to be a stand-in for the bigger picture.
It's like testing whether "exercise is good for everyone" by surveying just professional athletes. If they're not a fair sample of "everyone," the survey can't actually settle the question.

label: Goal
body: The right answer says: the fast-food restaurants in the study are representative of minimum-wage jobs overall.

label: Conclusion (So)
body:
We are not obliged to take their claim seriously.
rephrase: it's basically a vacuous claim to say that every discovery or invention is an instance of self-expression.

label: Evidence
body:
Some people claim that every human discovery or invention is an instance of self-expression.
These people seem to ignore that trivially, anything we do is self-expressive.

label: Evaluate
body:
The argument suggests that the claim "every human discovery or invention is an instance of self-expression" is trivial because it equates to "anything we do is self-expressive." The argument dismisses the claim until a more interesting interpretation is provided.
To support the overall reasoning, we could strengthen the link between "trivial" claims and the idea that they do not require serious consideration. We could also rule out the idea that discoveries/inventions are a special kind of self-expression that's different from the trivial sense.

label: Goal
body: Let's find an answer choice that connects trivial claims with the notion that such claims don't warrant serious consideration. Ideally, the correct answer will reinforce that something trivial doesn't need to be taken seriously.

label: Conclusion
body: The different resolutions touted in camera advertisements are irrelevant for practical photography.

label: Evidence
body: Resolution is about how much detail the lens is capable of reproducing onto film, but all modern lenses are so good that they have resolution to spare (i.e. they can capture far more detail than any film is even capable of rendering).

label: Evaluate
body:
There are two really big structural clues showing us where to find the conclusion.
Claim 1. Claim 2, however, since Claim 3.
"But / yet / however" tell us that we are leaving Background / Counterpoint territory and entering Author's Argument territory.
"For / after all / because / since" tell us that we're looking at a premise, and that the next-door idea is a Conclusion.
So Claim 2 is apparently our conclusion. It is the author's supported opinion?
Yes, she's saying these resolution differences are irrelevant. Why? Because the extra resolution any given camera would offer is useless. All modern lenses are so good that even the lowest resolution one is still capable of more than film can even use.

label: Conclusion
body: Differences between cameras in terms of what degree of detail the lens is capable of reproducing in the image it projects onto film are irrelevant for practical photography.

label: Evidence
body: All modern lenses are so good that they project far more detail onto the film than any film is capable of reproducing.

label: Evaluate
body:
If all modern lenses are so good that their max resolution far exceeds the max resolution that can be handled by film, then is there way that differences in lens resolution could be relevant to practical photography?
Is there anything else that lens resolution is related to, besides just the degree of detail the lens is capable of reproducing on film? (do some lens resolutions capture color better? do some practical photographers care about resolution because they'll be looking at the images on computer rather than on film?)

label: Goal
body:
The correct answer, if negated, should make it sound like even though all lenses are good enough to max out the detail that film can handle, there is still a relevant difference between different lenses for the sake of practical photography.
Since "practical photography" was a New Term in the conclusion, it will probably be in the correct answer.

label: Conclusion
body: The conclusion that North Americans' life spans can be extended by reduced-calorie diets is not supported.

label: Evidence
body:
Laboratory animals fed reduced-calorie diets lived longer than those not on such diets.
Laboratory animals tend to eat much more than animals in their natural habitats, leading to shorter life expectancies.
Restricting their diets brings their caloric intake back to natural, optimal levels and reinstates their normal life spans.

label: Argument
body: The phrase "people don't reelect inactive politicians" is a premise. Combined with "activity = passing intervening laws," it supports the conclusion that voters reelect politicians whose behavior they resent.

label: Goal
body: Find the answer that calls the phrase a premise.

label: Evaluate
body: The argument proposes that the extended life span observed in laboratory animals on reduced-calorie diets merely reflects a return to their natural life span. The author concludes that this cannot extend North Americans' life spans, because the scenario for humans is different from that of laboratory animals. To weaken the argument, we need to suggest that the reduction in calorie intake could still lead to increased longevity for humans, regardless of the context in which laboratory animals eat more than their natural levels.

label: Goal
body: Let's find an answer that suggests reduced calorie intake in humans could still result in increased longevity, undermining the dietary researcher's argument that this effect is unique to laboratory conditions.

label: Conclusion (Therefore)
body: It is the literature department's responsibility to include the study of advertisements in its undergrad courses.

label: Evidence
body:
The lit dept's courses give students the critical skill to analyze and understand texts.
Advertisements have a powerfully detrimental effect on society, largely because people cannot discern their real messages.

label: Evaluate
body:
The author's conclusion is that "The literature department has a responsibility to study X in its courses". Does the author ever define what the literature department is responsible for covering?
No, there's no rule that says, "If something is A, then the literature department has a responsibility to include it in its courses".
So the author is making some assumption there. What do we know about advertisements?
They have a detrimental effect on society because people can't discern their real messages.
What do we know about the Lit Department?
They give students the critical skills to analyze and understand texts.
The author seems to be thinking that by teaching advertisements, we can give people the critical skills to discern the real messages of ads, and thus ameliorate the detrimental effect that ads have on society.

label: Goal
body:
For a Linking answer, we would want something like, "If the skills that the Lit Department provides could prevent X from having a detrimental effect on society, then it's the Lit Department's responsibility to include X in its undergrad courses".
A possible objection could be that "We don't need the literature department to cover ads. They get studied in some other part of every undergrad's courses." So we could also see a Defender answer that feels like, "Students are not learning to discern the real message behind ads outside of the Literature Department's courses".

label: Conclusion (Implied)
body: The people critiquing the view that "capital punishment for theft was an essential part of the labor discipline of British capitalism" are making an unconvincing rebuttal.

label: Evidence
body: This criticism points out that more people received capital punishment for theft before the industrial Revolution than after, but this overlooks that industrialization and capitalism are two very different things, and that capitalism came several centuries before industrialization.

label: Evaluate
body:
Ouch, this is brutal. When we do Main Conclusion and Role, we know that most of the time we'll be seeing First Sentence Conclusions or Rebuttal Conclusions. Since the first two sentences each begin with an attribution ("some people argue" / "critics of such a view argue"), we'd expect a Rebuttal conclusion.
However, a conclusion never comes. We get the Pivot word "but" and then the author lists her two complaints with "such a criticism", but it's up to us to say what the implied conclusion is. We don't want to go too far and say, "Thus, these critics are wrong. Thus the people from sentence 1 are correct", so we say something more moderate like, "Thus, these critics fail to consider important factors" or "Thus, this criticism has little merit".
In terms of comprehending the conversation itself, the original position is that, "for British capitalism, a crucial component of disciplining the labor force (of keeping them in check as subservient workers) was killing people who stole". Capital punishment means execution.
The critics are like, "What you do mean executing for theft was crucial to capitalism. There were more executions for theft prior to industrialization than after it!"
This objection is hard to understand, unless you equate the beginning of the Industrial Revolution with the beginning of capitalism. If you do, then the critics are saying, "there must be some other explanation for why thieves were executed. It can't be that it was done to discipline labor, since they were executing people for theft (at a higher rate, no less) before industrialization/capitalism even began."
Our author is saying, "Yo, why are you equating industrialization with capitalism? They're two different things. And capitalism existed more than 300 years before industrialization did."
The critics were saying, "how could execution for theft be essentially intertwined with capitalism if execution for theft was happening prior to industrialization?" And the author is saying, "capitalism was happening prior to industrialization too, so your objection doesn't make any sense. You were trying to suggest that there were executions for theft even before capitalism, but you were acting like capitalism and industrialization started at the same time, when it fact capitalism was already on the scene for centuries before industrialization".

label: Goal
body: We're being asked about the 2nd to last claim. We know it's one of the author's two premises. Her voice begins with the word But. She is undermining the critics in the 2nd sentence by presenting the two ideas in the final sentence. (Two ideas joined by "and" are always both playing a Supporting role).

label: Statements
body:
We have three sentences, and each is a conditional. The first sentence uses the structure "to be X, you must be Y". We could rephrase that as "X requires Y" and the word requires is the same as the conditional arrow. The 2nd and 3rd sentences use an "if" on the 2nd half of the sentence, but wherever we see the "if" condition, we put that condition on the left of the conditional arrow.
Horrific monster → Threatening
Physically dangerous → Threatening
Inspires revulsion → Horrific monster

label: Evaluate
body:
Since we were given more than one conditional, we're looking to see whether any of them chain together. (Had we been given any facts, we would look also to see whether we could apply any of these rules to the provided fact)
In order for two rules to chain together, they need the Same idea on Opposite sides of the arrow, or they need Opposite ideas on the Same side of the arrow.
The first two rules have the Same idea (threatening), but it's on the same side of the arrow. So those don't chain.
The first and third rule have the Same idea (horrific monster) on opposite sides of the arrow (the first rule has it on the left, the third rule has it on the right).
So the first and third rule chain together
Inspires revulsion → Horrific → Threatening

label: Goal
body:
It's likely that the correct answer will reward us for putting together this chain. It will probably test the idea that Inspires revulsion → Threatening or it will test the contrapositive~Threatening → ~Inspires Revulsion
The second sentence is probably just there to create trap answers, since people may have been baited into thinking they could chain it to the first statement, since both mention "threatening".

label: Conclusion (we argue that)
body: The defendant maliciously harmed the plaintiff.

label: Evidence (because)
body:
Malice is intention to cause harm.
The plaintiff intended to remove snow from his car and put it on the sidewalk, and unbeknownst to the defendant at the time, that snow would go on to freeze as ice and cause the plaintiff to slip and break her hip.

label: Evaluate
body:
If we're this defendant's lawyer, how would we argue that the defendant did not intend to harm the plaintiff?
We could say, "as you just said, the defendant had no idea that knocking snow off his car and onto the sidewalk would subsequently cause the injury. He only intended to clear snow off his car."
This argument actually combines a Famous Flaw (self-contradiction) and a Semi-Famous Flaw (intent vs. result).
We know the author intended to clear snow off his car onto the sidewalk. As a result, it froze into ice and caused a woman to slip and hurt herself. But just because that action resulted from clearing snow off a car doesn't mean that the plaintiff intended to injure the woman.
That would have been enough, but then this lawyer went and self-contradicted himself. He actually acknowledged that the defendant didn't intend to injure the plaintiff, since it was "unbeknownst to the defendant at the time" that clearing the snow would cause the injury.

label: Goal
body: Let's look for an argument that deals with Intent vs. Result, Self-Contradiction, or both.

label: Main Conclusion
body: Wood burning stoves are more dangerous than open fireplaces.

label: Evidence
body: The smoke from wood burning stoves is cooler than the smoke from an open flame. (causal)-Thus, the smoke from wood burning stoves travels more slowly and deposits more creosote, which can clog a chimney or ignite it.

label: Evaluate
body:
The conclusion is a head to head comparison between wood-burning stoves and open fireplaces, and we're just trying to judge which one is more dangerous.
The author votes for wood-burning being more dangerous because the smoke travels more slowly and deposits more flammable creosote.

label: Goal
body: Let's look for an answer that makes wood-burning sound safer (it's fine when smoke travels slowly / creosote is harmless / cool smoke is so much safer) or an answer that makes open fireplaces sound more dangerous.

label: Statement
body: If a doctor gives a patient only a few options for better living, they're more likely to follow that advice than if the doctor gives many options.

label: Implicit Principle
body: Sounds like, if you give us too many options, we won't do any of them. If you keep it simple, we're more likely to follow the advice.

label: Goal
body: Find an answer choice that sounds like "people did better with a small number of recommendations / choices than they did with a larger number of recommendations / choices".

label: The Practice
body: Some psychologists study the personalities of animals in order to acquire a better understanding of the structure and development of the human personality.

label: Evaluate / Goal
body:
Given that psychologists are trying to acquire a better understanding of the structure and development of human personality,
Why is it that they're studying the personalities of animals?
Presumably there are some transferrable takeaways; I guess the underpinnings of personality are somewhat common to animals and humans?

label: Conclusion (it is obvious then)
body: Widespread reliance on movies and electronic media for entertainment has an inherently corrosive effect on democracy.

label: Evidence
body:
Democracy requires that citizens have strong bonds of mutual trust.
Such bonds require participation in civic organizations, political parties, and other groups outside the family.

label: Evaluate
body:
We have a big New Concept in the Conclusion. It's claiming something about "widespread reliance on movies and electronic media for entertainment", but the argument provides no information about movies, electronic media, or our reliance on the two.
So the correct answer will almost definitely be stating whatever it is the author is assuming about "reliance on movies and electronic media for entertainment".
The first two sentences are both conditionals, and they have a common ingredient (bonds of trust), so we should suspect that these might chain together. Sure enough they do. We get:
Democratic → bonds of → participation in society trust non-family groups
Since the conclusion is talking about something corroding democracy, it would make more sense that the author is intending to use the contrapositive of this.
don't have don't have don't have participation in → bonds of → democratic non-family groups trust society

label: Goal
body: If the author must be assuming that when most of us start relying on movies and electronic media for entertainment, then we are less likely to participate in civic organizations / political parties / other non-family groups.

label: Conclusion (therefore)
body: It is not possible to determine the age of prehistoric paintings on limestone using standard archaeological techniques.

label: Evidence
body:
Prehistoric paintings on limestone were painted with vegetable matter.
Standard techniques for determining the age of vegetable matter require that it is free of minerals containing carbon.
It is impossible to collect samples or prehistoric paint without removing limestone (which has carbon) with the paint.

label: Evaluate
body:
Since the Anti-Conclusion is that "it is possible to determine the age of the paintings using standard techniques", we need to think of a way around this roadblock.
We have to collect samples in order to analyze them for age, and any sample we collect will also contain limestone, which is a mineral containing carbon.
Standard techniques require that an object is free of minerals containing carbon.
Is there any way for this to work?
Maybe every sample will contain some limestone, but not spread the entire sample? In other words, maybe every 4 oz sample of paint will have 1 oz of limestone, but perhaps it's all located on one side of the sample and we can grab a "clean" oz or two of pure paint from the other side.
Maybe we can separate out the limestone from the paint? Is there a centrifuge that could send the limestone to one end and the vegetable matter to the other?

label: Goal
body: Look for an answer that helps us argue, "Even though every sample would contain some minerals that have carbon-containing limestone in it, there's still a way we could use standard techniques to date the age of this paint".

label: Conclusion
body: If these physicists are right, (if non-Euclidean geometry correctly describes our universe), then there are no parallel lines in our universe.

label: Evidence
body: Euclidean geometry thinks that lines can be parallel.

label: Goal
body: It's hard to predict the content of the answer, but the function of the answer should be that it allows us to argue that we still want to be teaching math to these engineers in training.

label: Evaluate
body:
This author is assuming that non-Euclidean geometry rejects every part of Euclidean geometry. The argument would be the same if it said, "Triangles exist in Euclidean geometry. Thus, if non-Euclidean geometry correctly describes our universe, then there are no triangles in our universe."
We could represent this flawed thinking as an illegal negation. The author establishes this:If Euclidean Geo, then parallel lines Then erroneously reasons this:If non-Euclidean Geo, then not parallel lines
That's an illegal negation, a.k.a. confusing Necessary and Sufficient.

label: Goal
body: So what is the author assuming? She thinks that in non-Euclidean geometry, lines can't be parallel. She thinks that, "If X is true in Euclidean geometry, then X is not true in non-Euclidean geometry".

label: Conclusion (therefore)
body: People can find happiness, if at all, only in smaller political units such as villages.

label: Evidence
body: People are not intellectually well suited to live in large bureaucratic societies.

label: Evaluate
body:
There seem to be a few main issues with this argument:
1. the evidence is talking about what types of living arrangements we're intellectually suited to, while the conclusion is talking about what types of living arrangements could allow us to be happy.
The author seems to be assuming that, "If you're not intellectually suited to live somewhere, then you can't be happy there".
2. the author never establishes that we are intellectually suited to smaller political units like a village.
The author seems to be assuming, "people are more intellectually suited to living in villages".
3. the author seems to be offering this False Choice between large bureaucratic societies or villages.
She seems to be assuming, "if you aren't going to be in a large bureaucratic society, then you're gonna be in a village". Maybe there are other possibilities as well?

label: Goal
body:
This question stem is pre-loaded with takes for granted, so we can evaluate every answer choice like we're doing Necessary Assumption.
We can even call this a Necessary Assumption (disguised as Flaw) if we want to.

label: Politician
body: People are saying the squabbling city's leaders should compromise, but the city's charter is based on some definite principles, and if we compromise those principles it would betray the city founders' goals. Thus these people are talking about betraying they goals of the founders.

label: Critic
body:
Are the disagreements between the city's leaders about the principles? i.e., are some leaders saying we should adhere to the principles and others are saying we shouldn't? Or are they instead disagreeing about which actions to take, while agreeing about the underlying principles of the city's charter?
If the differences between the leaders aren't about these principles, then you're argument has a misleading usage of the term ______ .

label: Evaluate
body:
If we assume that the city's leaders all agree about the founding principles and are just fighting over specific details / policies, then what word in the Politician's paragraph sounds misleading?
Honestly, I would probably say "betraying" is the word in the politician's argument that sounds unfair. When she says, "What my opponents are advocating is nothing less than betraying the goals of the city's founders", we would respond, "No they aren't! The opponents aren't asking the city's leaders to betray the principles on which the city is founded. They're just asking the leaders to reach a compromise on their current disagreement."
But "betray" isn't used in a misleading way. It's used consistently, we just object to the validity of saying "asking for compromise is asking city leaders to betray the goals of the founders".
Since the critic is talking about a misleading use of a term, it feels like he's calling out an Equivocation flaw, where the same term is being used in two different ways.
In this spirt, the term "compromise" seems to be the best pick, since it does get used two different ways.
1st sense of "compromise" -- to reach an agreement (compromise) with someone who disagrees with you ... each party making some sort of concession and meeting in the middle
2nd sense of "compromise" -- to compromise your ideals, to compromise your position, to compromise your principles means to abandon / degrade. When I eat a hamburger, I am compromising my ideals to not harm animals. When I'm hiding behind enemy lines and I accidentally shoot off a flare, my position has been compromised.
The politician was using an equivocation to say, "You're asking us to compromise? (i.e. to work with other politicians to strike a deal) Why that's unthinkable. We will never compromise (i.e. abandon) the principles of our founders."

label: Goal
body: Go pick "compromise". :)

label: Information
body:
Quantifiers (many, some, some)
Many insects die soon after reproducing for the first time Some insects live for years after the survival of next gen is safe
Some insects who live work for the for years after benefit of the securing next gen ecosystem

label: Evaluate
body:
We're trying to figure out how we can combine any of these facts to derive something, but Quantified statements only lead to inferences if you have 1. Two Most claims about the same group 2. A conditional (like All / No)
The correct answer might just be trying to combine the 2nd and 3rd claim by testing us on the bridge idea of "among the latter".
That phrase communicates that "among those insects who live for years after having babies, there are insects that work for the benefit of the ecosystem".

label: Goal
body:
Look for a Trait Overlap inference like, "Some things that work for the benefit of the ecosystem live for years after they reproduce".
Or maybe one like, "Bees live for years after the survival of the next generation has been secured".
Or just anything else we can derive with certainty from this paragraph.

label: Conclusion
body: People's political behavior frequently doesn't match their rhetoric.

label: Intermediate Conclusion (thus)
body: Voters often reelect politicians whose behavior they resent.

label: Evidence
body: Many people complain about government intervention in their lives. But people tend not to reelect inactive politicians, and active politicians are passing laws whose enforcement affects voters' lives.

label: Evaluate
body:
The cited phrase, "people tend not to reelect inactive politicians," is one of the supporting premises that helps establish that voters reelect politicians whose behavior they resent.
Voters preferentially reelect active politicians, active politicians tend to pass laws that intervene with people's lives, and people complain about government intervention in their lives.

label: Goal
body: The claim we're asked about is Support. The 2nd and 3rd sentences combine to support the 4th sentence, which provides support for the 1st sentence.

label: Argument
body:
The author is making a point about voter inconsistency: people complain about government intervention, but they reelect the very politicians who do the intervening. How does the author build that case?
Step 1: People complain about intervention.
Step 2: People don't reelect inactive politicians.
Step 3: Politicians' activity = passing intervening laws.
Combine 2 and 3: voters reelect those who pass intervening laws. Combine with 1: voters reelect those whose intervention they resent.

label: Evaluate
body: The phrase in question is Step 2 — a premise. It's one of the supporting facts that, combined with another premise, leads to the conclusion.

label: Goal
body: Find the answer that says it's a premise supporting the conclusion that voters reelect politicians whose behavior they resent.

label: Lea's 1st Claim
body:
Contemporary art has become big business. is Susan saying contemp art hasn't become big business?
Not really. She doesn't talk about contemporary art as a whole.

label: Lea's 2nd Claim
body:
Now, art has less to do with self-expression than with making money. is Susan saying today's art still has at least as much to do with self-expression as it does with making money?
No. She doesn't talk about self-expression or money.

label: Lea's 3rd Claim
body:
The work of contemporary artists is utterly bereft (devoid / lacking) of spontaneity and creativity. is Susan saying that some of the work of contemporary artists does have spontaneity and creativity?
Yes! She said you can find spontaneous / creative, new (i.e. contemporary) art in most small indie galleries.

label: Goal
body: Let's look for something like "whether or not the work of contemporary artists is devoid of spontaneity / creativity", "whether or not you can still find spontaneous and innovate contemporary art".

label: Conclusion
body: It was morally wrong for the company to change its mind and seek restitution from the contractor.

label: Evidence
body: Before the contract, the company had signed a written agreement that the contractor would not be financially liable for inadequate performance. Despite this, a court ordered the contractor to make restitution.

label: Evaluate
body: The ethicist concludes a moral judgment from the fact that the company had previously waived the right to seek financial liability. The argument needs a principle that ties "promised not to seek compensation" to "morally wrong to seek compensation."

label: Goal
body: The correct answer should state a principle that, when applied to these facts, generates the conclusion that seeking restitution after promising not to is morally wrong.

label: Conclusion
body: It was morally wrong for the company to seek restitution from the contractor.

label: Evidence
body: The company had previously signed a written agreement waiving the contractor's financial liability for inadequate performance.

label: Evaluate
body: We need a principle bridging "promised not to seek compensation" to "morally wrong to seek compensation."

label: Goal
body: Find the principle that condemns seeking compensation after agreeing to forgo it.

label: Conclusion
body: The ethicist's point: it was morally wrong for the company to come back later and demand money from the contractor.

label: Evidence
body: Before the contract, the company had signed a written agreement saying it wouldn't hold the contractor financially liable if the work fell short.

label: Evaluate
body:
This is a Principle question: we need a rule that, when applied to these facts, produces the verdict "morally wrong." The relevant facts are (1) the company promised in advance not to seek compensation, and (2) the company then turned around and sought it anyway.
So we're looking for a principle that says: if you promised not to seek compensation, it's morally wrong to seek it. That fits these facts and produces the right conclusion.

label: Goal
body: The principle that says: it's morally wrong to seek compensation for an action when you've already promised to forgo such compensation.

label: Conclusion
body: The fact that animals can signal each other with sounds and gestures does not confirm the thesis that animals possess language.

label: Evidence (for)
body: It fails to prove that animals possess the ability to use sounds or gestures to refer to concrete objects or abstract ideas.

label: Evaluate
body:
It looks like this argument is assuming that "it's does qualify as language unless you're using sounds and gestures to refer to concrete objects or abstract ideas".
After all, if an argument is structured like this ..
The fact that Paul can skate backwards doesn't show he's good at skating, because it doesn't prove he can skate on one leg.
... it would be assuming "you're not good at skating unless you can skate on one leg".

label: Goal
body:
We will probably call out the assumption that "it's not really language unless you're using sounds and gestures to refer to concrete objects or abstract ideas".
But we could also say the author is assuming that in these known instances where animals signal each other with sounds and gestures, they are not referring to concrete objects or abstract ideas.

label: Curious Fact
body:
Given that one is more likely to be disabled as one ages, why is it that 4% of people aged 55-64 receive disability benefit payments, 2% of 65-74 year olds receive it, and only 1% of people 75 and up receive it?
In essence, given that you're more likely to be disabled, the older you are, why is there a smaller % of super old people getting disability benefits than there are of younger old people?

label: Explanation
body: Not as many jobs offered such a disability benefit until recent years.

label: Conclusion (provides evidence that)
body: In the face of television, even some legal professionals are losing their ability to distinguish fiction from reality.

label: Evidence
body: A prestigious attorney said that the death of Raymond Burr (who played a lawyer on TV) makes lawyers feel as if we lost one of our own.

label: Goal
body: Look for the most provable answer. It will probably reflect the fact that we learned of two different ways (gestures/tone vs. stylistic arrangement of words/sentences) to communicate intended meaning.

label: Evaluate
body:
We should sit with this explanation a second if it doesn't immediately seem clear how it's explaining the data.
The author is suggesting that if all jobs offered disability benefits, then the older a segment of the population is, the higher a percent of them would be receiving disability benefits.
But since most jobs weren't offering disability benefits until recently, the people 75 and up (who presumably retired 10 years ago) might be disabled but they wouldn't receive disability benefits from their former employer because back when they were working, employers didn't offer disability benefits.
Ultimately, though, we really don't need to fixate too much on this explanation, since the question stem is seeking some additional explanation. In order for us to show that this explanation is at best incomplete, we can show that something else is also having an effect on why a smaller % of the oldest demographic gets disability benefits.

label: Goal
body:
The correct answer may surprise us and provide a reason to think that the author's explanation cannot plausibly account for all of this 4% / 2% / 1% gradient.
But since the question stem asks us to show that this explanation is incomplete, it seems to be leading us to the idea that "something else is also influencing this 4% / 2% / 1% gradient".
So we need something else, besides the idea that more jobs these days offer disability benefits, that could explain why a smaller % of 75 year olds receive benefits than do 65 year olds, and why a smaller % of 65 year olds do than 55 year olds.
(Maybe something like, "back in the day when the 75 year olds were working, their working conditions were much safer and much less likely to lead to getting disabled on the job")

label: Information
body:
causal chain
Photons hit ⇢ Rhodopsin ⇢ Light is rhodopsin changes shape registered
causal chain
Normal Rhodospin error in molecular ⇢ changes shape ⇢ the visual motion system
causal
Amount of normal directly temp of molecular motion proportional retina

label: Evaluate
body:
We're told about how the retina registers light; it occurs when the rhodopsin changes shape in response to being hit by photons.
But then we're told how something else can also cause it to change shape, which "introduces errors in to the visual system" (i.e. makes us think we're perceiving light, even though we're not actually being struck by photons).
That other thing is "molecular motion".
Finally, we're told that the higher the temperature of the retina, the more molecular motion.
So it feels like we're being set up to comment on some causal chain in which the retina gets hotter, leading to more molecular motion, leading to more shape-shifting of rhodopsin, leading to more errors in the visual system.

label: Goal
body: Look for something safely worded that reinforces the Causal Chain presented.

label: Conclusion (therefore)
body: The society-as-body-governed-by-a-head metaphor promotes greater acceptance of authoritarian repression than do other metaphors (such as society-as-family).

label: Evidence
body: Political utility determines metaphor popularity. The body-with-head metaphor is pervasive in authoritarian societies.

label: Evaluate
body:
The first two sentences give us premises with an overlapping idea of "popularity / prevalence". We can synthesize those two claims to get the idea that
in authoritarian societies, the metaphor of society as a human body has a lot of political utility.
That's what the premises establish: this metaphor has a lot of political utility for authoritarians.
The author takes it from there to the idea that, "This metaphor promotes greater acceptance of authoritarian repression than other metaphors".
We don't know anything about other metaphors. Are they also pervasive in authoritarian societies? Do they also have political utility? The author is Assuming a Difference, thinking that the Body metaphor is more pervasive /useful than the other metaphors.
Even if we grant that the Body metaphor is the most useful metaphor, does its usefulness have to be "promoting acceptance of repression"?
Couldn't there be other things that are politically useful to an authoritarian government? Maybe the Body metaphor encourages different components of society to work more nicely with each other.

label: Goal
body: Let's look for an answer saying that the Body metaphor is useful for some reason unrelated to "getting the people to accept repression", or for an answer making it seem like one of the other metaphors could be just as pervasive / useful.

label: Conclusion
body: The body-with-head metaphor promotes more acceptance of authoritarian repression than other metaphors.

label: Evidence
body: It's pervasive in authoritarian societies.

label: Evaluate
body: If another metaphor (like family) is equally pervasive in authoritarian societies, the body metaphor isn't uniquely promoting authoritarian acceptance.

label: Goal
body: Find the answer showing equal pervasiveness of an alternative metaphor in authoritarian societies.

label: Conclusion
body: The critic claims the body-with-head metaphor specifically promotes more acceptance of authoritarian repression than other metaphors do.

label: Evidence
body: The reason: that metaphor is pervasive in authoritarian societies.

label: Evaluate
body:
The critic's logic: pervasive in authoritarian societies → distinctively pro-authoritarian. But this only works if the body metaphor is more pervasive there than other metaphors — i.e., if it's the metaphor that authoritarian societies prefer.
To weaken the argument, show that the body metaphor doesn't stand out in authoritarian societies. If, say, the family metaphor is just as pervasive there, then the critic can't claim the body metaphor is distinctively authoritarian-promoting. Both metaphors would be equally common in authoritarian contexts.

label: Goal
body: Find the answer showing another metaphor is equally pervasive in authoritarian societies.

label: Conclusion
body: Incomes have risen at a greater rate than the price of food in that period.

label: Evidence
body: Thirty years ago, single people spent twice as big a percentage of their income on food as they do nowadays.

label: Goswami's 2nd Claim
body:
The workers at Ergon Foods are underpaid. Does Nordecki disagree?
Yes, he seems to disagree. He's saying, "If pay is the issue (for striking), I must disagree (with the decision to strike)", which implies "I don't find their pay objectionably low. I don't consider them underpaid." Also, Nordecki's clarification is all about how much they're paid. He's saying, "Hey -- you're quoting this $20k number, but the average salary of the workers who are striking is over $29k."

label: Evaluate
body:
Whenever we see an author interpret the meaning behind a statistical change, we want to think about other possible ways to interpret that statistic.
Curious Fact ... why do single people spend 1/2 as big a percent of their income on food nowadays, compared to 30 years ago?
Author's Explanation .... food is cheaper (in a relative sense). Incomes have risen faster than food prices.
What could be an alternate way to explain this? Let's say that food prices and incomes have both gone up by 20% since 1990. How could it be that single people nowadays are spending a smaller slice of their income on food?
Maybe they're just eating out less. Maybe they're cooking for themselves more. Maybe they're better at using coupons. Maybe they're just eating less food overall.

label: Goal
body: Since we're trying to strengthen the argument, we want to either rule out a different explanation for why single people nowadays spent a lower % of their income on food, or increase the plausibility that incomes have risen faster than food prices.

label: Statements
body:
Viruses can have beneficial effects (such as killing a more-complex microorganism that could be deadly to humans).
Viruses have very simple structures; you could take a beneficial virus, replace a few of its several million atoms, and turn it into a deadly virus.
Random mutations can result is alterations like this (even more complex ones), so any virus could easily become dangerous to humans.

label: Evaluate
body:
Normally on Must Be False, the correct answer either 1. contradicts a conditional 2. contradicts a Must Be True inference we can make by combining claims
There's a conditional in the final sentence, since we hear that all viruses could be come dangerous to humans. So there may be a correct answer that talks about a virus that is purely harmless.
Can we combine claims to derive anything? Is there any Overlapping Concept? The idea "virus" shows up in several claims, so we could say silly things like "at least some things with simple structures can have beneficial effects", combining two things we know about viruses.

label: Goal
body: Let's find an answer we can contradict.

label: Jordan
body: If invest in environmentally sound, market share decreases. If not invest in environmentally sound, pollutes environment and wastes resources.

label: Terry
body: If consumers demand environmentally sound, no particular business gets especially hurt.

label: Evaluate
body:
I would imagine a lot of us don't even fully follow the conversation on first read, because Terry's response involves a lot of outside knowledge / common sense.
Jordan is presumably worried that if a company invests in greener practices, they will add to their costs in a way that their less-green or already-green competitors won't.
Because Company X is spending more on environmental upgrades to their business (and their competitors aren't), X will need to raise prices to cover this rise in costs, and thus customers will start buying X's products less and the competitors' products instead, resulting in X's market share shrinking.
Meanwhile, Terry is responding that if consumers collectively stopped buying products that aren't environmentally friendly, they would switch all businesses to invest in environmental upgrades, so all the companies would have an increase in costs / prices, and thus no company would suddenly stick out in the marketplace as more expensive than the others (thus getting especially hurt).
LSAC is really asking us to fill in a lot of blanks there, and the worst part is it doesn't even make a big difference to getting the right answer.

label: Goal
body: What is the logical relationship between these two people's statements?

label: Jordan
body: If we do X, bad thing happens. If we don't do X, different bad thing happens.

label: Terry
body: If we do Y, then doing X won't lead to first bad thing. X = investing in environmental upgrades Y = consumers demanding environmentally friendly products

label: Conclusion
body: Nowadays vs. ten years ago, the media devote more coverage to crime because the public has become more interested in reading and hearing about crime (not because there is more crime).

label: Evidence (after all)
body: The media crucially relies on the interests of their audiences when making decisions about how much coverage goes to which issues.

label: Evaluate
body:
Whenever we do Main Conclusion and Role, we anticipate that we'll (probably) see the Main Conclusion earlier than the Support. The last claim on over 80% of Role questions is playing some Supporting role (either as a premise or as an intermediate conclusion).
The Support indicator after all (FABS = for,after all, because, since) instructs us that the final claim is supporting the claim before it.
The first fact in this paragraph has the classic asymmetric comparison feel of a Curious Fact:why does the media devote more coverage to crime nowadays?
That provides us with a vocabulary for describing this argument in words other than Premise / Conclusion. We can think of the first sentence as the puzzling background phenomenon. The second sentence rules out one possible explanation (it's not that the crime rate went up) before pivoting into her chosen explanation (it's that people increasingly lust for crime coverage).
Note: the word "because" is being used in the causal sense there, not the reasoning sense of providing a supporting idea.

label: Goal
body:
They're asking us about the Main Conclusion, aka the author's preferred explanation for the curious fact in the first sentence.
This is the author's hypothesis. She supports the plausibility of her hypothesis in the last sentence.

label: Conclusion (consequently / should)
body: In training engineers to work in industry, less emphasis should be placed on mathematical principles, so that space in the engineering curriculum will be available for other important subjects.

label: Evidence
body: It's increasingly unnecessary for practicing engineers to have a thorough understanding of fundamental mathematical principles (since more and more computer programs are being produced that provide solutions to math problems in engineering).

label: Evaluate
body:
Given that... computer programs that can solve math problems are making it increasingly unnecessary for practicing engineers to have a thorough understanding of fundamental math
