body: The right answer says the shipping manager points out the absurd consequence of the sales manager's assumption that necessity earns top priority.

label: Background
body: People who drink 5 or more cups of coffee a day have a risk of heart disease that 2.5 times that of other people their age / with their smoking habits.

label: Plan
body: Limit coffee intake to two cups a day.

label: Goal
body: Decrease risk of heart disease

label: Evaluate
body:
We need a way to argue that these researchers could limit their coffee intake to 2 cups max per day, but **not** decrease their risk of heart disease.
It seems like we'd have two different ways of doing so:
1. Lowering to 2 cups a day isn't enough. Someone drinking 2 cups per day has just as much risk as someone drinking 5+ cups a day.
2. The coffee wasn't the cause for the increased risk of heart disease in the first place.
That 2nd one seems more likely to me as an LSAT type objection, because these researchers are looking at a **Curious Comparison** (ppl who are X are more likely to be Y) and assuming a Causal Explanation.
Curious Fact ... why do people who drink 5+ cups of coffee / day have a 2-3x the risk of heart disease?
Author's Explanation .... the 5+ cups of coffee causes the increased risk of heart disease.

label: Goal
body:
Since we are trying to weaken, we would be looking for an answer that **suggests** an Alternate Explanation for why those heavy coffee drinkers have elevated heart disease risk, or an answer that **undermines** the plausibility of the Author's causal assumption that the coffee drinking is elevating the heart disease risk, or an answer that
**undermines** the notion that cutting back from 5 cups to 2 cups would be enough to reduce risk of heart disease.

label: Conclusion (Therefore)
body: Technical ingenuity usually brings benefits to those who have it, while ethical inventiveness brings only pain to those who have it.

label: Evidence
body: People who have political power tend to see technical ingenuity as a means of extending or protecting their power, while they see ethical inventiveness as a threat to their power.

label: Evaluate
body:
This argument seems to be crying out with missing links since the premise and the conclusion have a parallel structure.
For example, suppose we said, Sharon likes soccer, whereas Paul likes hockey. Therefore, Sharon will fit in well at this party, whereas Paul will not.
This argument would be assuming that "people who like soccer will fit in well at this party, whereas people who like hockey will not fit in well".
In the argument, we're saying, Politically powerful people see tech ingenuity as helping their power, whereas they see ethical ingenuity as threatening it. Therefore, tech ingenuity brings benefits, whereas ethical ingenuity brings pain.

label: Goal
body:
It seems like we need to patch up the big missing language links:
- if people who have political power see your thing as helping their power, it brings benefits.
- if people who have political power see your thing as threatening their power, it brings pain.
Look for an answer helping us out with those missing ideas.

label: Conclusion (surely = opinion)
body: Given a seed eating bird and a nectar eating bird with the same overall energy requirement, the seed-eating bird should spend more time eating than does the nectar-eating bird.

label: Evidence (since)
body: A given amount of nectar provides more energy than does the same amount of seeds.

label: Evaluate
body:
We're trying to judge this Comparison.
Both types of birds need the same overall amount of energy. One gets its energy from eating seeds, the other from eating nectar. A given amount of nectar provides more energy than does the same amount of seeds.
Thus, the author assumes it will take **less time** for the nectar-eater to get to their overall total energy amount.
There is a Missing Link assumption like, "If the type of food the bird eats provides more energy per unit, then that bird will take less time to attain its total required energy."
But this argument seems more ripe for objections that the correct answer will Defend against.
Given that... the nectar eating bird gets more energy per unit from nectar, How could we still argue that... the nectar eating bird needs **more time** (or the same time) to attain its required energy?
Maybe it's harder to find nectar than it is to find seeds. Say that two kids were each trying to collect enough coins that they $10 of money. One kid collects only quarters. The other collects only dimes. Clearly, the quarter-collector gets more value per coin, but what if the dimes are plentiful and easy to grab and the quarters are sparse and hidden? The dime-collector might still get to $10 faster.

label: Goal
body: Let's look for an answer, which will probably have Defender language like "not", that is ruling out some objection that would make nectar-eaters take longer to reach their energy requirement, even though nectar is more energy rich per unit than seeds are.

label: Conclusion (it is obvious, then)
body: There should be a general reduction in the pace of bringing to the marketplace new drugs that are now being tested.

label: Evidence
body: The introduction of a new drug into the marketplace should be contingent upon our having a good understanding of its social impact, but the social impact of the newly marketed antihistamine is far from clear.

label: Evaluate
body:
The first two sentences would allow us to infer that "the newly marketed antihistamine should not yet be introduced into the market". After all, introducing into market requires clear understanding of impact, and we don't have that clear understanding for he new antihistamine yet.
But the actual conclusion calls for **a general** reduction in the pace of brining new drugs to market.
It's kinda like if we said, "One of the students in Patrick's class got a 140 on their real LSAT. Thus, Patrick is **generally** not able to help his students achieve high scores."
When we go from specific evidence to a general conclusion, we worry about Sampling issues. Is it fair to judge Patrick's teaching based on only one student? What if that student is an anomaly? What if there's a good reason for that student getting a lower score, and it doesn't apply to other students? Is that student's experience **representative** of the typical student in Patrick's classes?"
Similarly, what if there's something special behind why this newly marketed antihistamine was brought to market so quickly? What if it's atypical, and the norm is a slow deliberate pace for most new drugs?
In order for the author to think, "based on what happened with this new antihistamine, there should be a **general** reduction in the pace of bringing new drugs to the market", he has to assume that what happened with the new antihistamine is typical (or even slower) than the pace at which most other drugs have recently been brought to market.

label: Goal
body: We want more evidence that other drugs are being brought to the market before their social impact is clearly known, more evidence that we should slow our current pace of bringing drugs to the market, or something that rules out our objection of, "What if the new antihistamine was brought to the market unusually fast, but that isn't generally the case?"

label: Information
body:
Group A had their normal daily caloric intake increased by 25%, entirely in the form of alcohol.
Group B had alcohol replace 25% of their normal daily caloric intake.
All subjects gained body fat, and the amount of body fat gained was the same for both groups.

label: Evaluate
body:
On Inference questions we're trying to figure out whether a given question is testing us on Conditional, Causal, Mathematical, or Comparison based thinking.
This one seems to be testing Causality / Math / Comparisons.
Let's consider some numbers, to help us with the math. We'll say that the average daily caloric intake for all subjects was 1000 calories per day (yes, that's low, but let's keep the math easy).
Group A: 1000 calories of normal diet + 250 calories of alcohol Group B: 750 calories of normal diet + 250 calories of alcohol
They all gained the same amount of body fat. That's pretty surprising since Group A was eating 1250 calories a day and Group B was eating 1000 calories a day.
It looks like the 250 calories of alcohol caused the same gain in body fat, regardless of whether the rest of the diet was 1000 or 750 calories.

label: Goal
body: It's pretty hard to guess how to turn this into a correct answer choice, but let's expect something causal/math-y relating to this idea that the 250 calories of alcohol seemed to cause the same amount of body fat, whether the rest of the diet was 1000 or 750 calories. (naturally, it won't use our made up numbers)

label: Conclusion
body: It is likely that common wisdom (in thinking that chocolate causes acne, based on the fact that people often get an outbreak of acne right after they eat a bunch of chocolate) has mistaken an effect for a cause.

label: Evidence
body: Several recent studies show that hormonal changes associated with stress can cause acne, and there's good evidence that people who are fond of chocolate tend to eat more chocolate when they are under stress.

label: Goal
body: Let's look for some answer that sounds like, "The author is rebutting the CPI / government benefit system by talking about something totally unrelated. The CPI is about measuring **retail** costs for the **consumer**. The author's objection was about production costs for the manufacturer."

label: Evidence
body:
It was once believed that the appropriate psychotherapy for neuroses caused by environmental factors would also work for psychoses.
But now we know that these psychoses are best treated by biochemical (medicinal) means.

label: Evaluate
body:
Whenever we're doing Main Conclusion or Role, we remind ourselves that on these question types, the main conclusion usually isn't the final claim. It's usually the First Sentence or its some Rebuttal sentiment.
Because of that, if we see the first sentence say "it is widely believed", we can tell we're getting the sort of attribution to someone else's point of view that an author would then proceed to rebut.
When we see the Pivot word (but, yet, **however** ), then it starts to definitely look like a rebuttal. The "However" claim does sound like our Author offering her opinion. Does she proceed to support that opinion? Yes, the final sentence is evidence (several recent studies).
This argument is dealing with the frequently recurring Explain Curious Fact pattern that we see a ton in Strengthen / Weaken. There's a before-after correlation happening with chocolate and acne, leading people to believe that chocolate causes the acne.
The author is raising an Alternate Explanation -- both the acne and the chocolate are just symptoms/effects of an underlying Third Factor, stress.

label: Goal
body:
If this question stem were asking for the Main **Conclusion**, then we would just think, "Find something that matches the meaning of the however sentence, which was the conclusion."
But since it asks for Main **Point**, the answer might feel more like a synthesis. There aren't that many question stems that say Main Point, but when it occurs, the answers often feel more implied or holistic.
Look for something like "The fact that chocolate eating is usually followed by an outbreak of acne is probably because both those things are related to stress".

label: Given that
body: Raisins are made from grapes, and nothing is added in the process,

label: Why is it that
body: Raisins contain more iron per calorie than do grapes?

label: Evaluate
body:
There must be something about the process of going from a grape to a raisin that increases the iron per calorie.
A ratio like Iron/Calorie can be increased two ways: increase the numerator (add more iron) or decrease the denominator (subtract calories).
The facts we're provided about the process of going from grape to raisin are these: - some sugar is caramelized - nothing is added - water evaporates (but water contains no calories)

label: Goal
body: Since there's no way to add more iron, we want an answer to talk to us about how going from a grape to a raisin sheds calories.

label: Conclusion (avg quality = opinion)
body: Cotrell can at best write articles of average quality.

label: Intermediate conclusion
body: Cotrell must have plagiarized the few articles submitted by him that are of superior quality.

label: Evidence (since)
body: Cotrell is incapable of writing an article that is better than average.

label: Evaluate
body:
This is certainly a weird argument. The author is trying to prove that Cotrell is a mediocre/poor writer, and the most compelling evidence for that are these articles submitted by Cotrell that are of superior quality?
That makes no sense. How are superior quality articles evidence that Cotrell is an average to poor writer?
The author says, "Because Cotrell plagiarized those articles". To which we should react, "Oh? How do you know Cotrell plagiarized them?"
To which the author says, "Because Cotrell is a mediocre/poor writer. He's not capable of superior writing."
This should make us feel like we're right back at the start, because this is a **Circular** argument. Of the 10 famous flaws, Circular might show up the most in answer choices, although it's almost never correct. So enjoy this rare treasure.:)
It refers to an argument in which a premise restates the conclusion or requires the conclusion to be true. In this argument the premise "Cotrell is incapable of writing an article that is better than average" restates the conclusion, "Cotrell is at best able to write articles of average quality".

label: Goal
body: Look for an answer choice calling out the Circular Reasoning or otherwise making the complaint that the author seems unfairly confident that Cotrell plagiarized these superior articles. Her only premise for thinking he plagiarized the good ones is her pre-conceived notion that he's not capable of writing superior articles.

label: Statements
body:
conditionals ( **any**, **every** - sufficient indicators)
Sale item → returnable for store credit and not refundable
Home appliance → Sale item
Gardening equipement → Sale item
Some selected construction tools are also on sale.

label: Evaluate
body:
They provided us with 3 conditionals and 1 some statement. The only overlapping term is "on sale", so we should focus on that conditional.
If something is on sale, we know it's returnable for store credit but not refundable.
We were told about a bunch of stuff that's on sale, so we can derive inferences that this stuff is returnable for store credit but not refundable.

label: Goal
body:
We'd expect the correct answer to reward one of these available inferences:
- Every home appliance can be returned for store credit but not for a refund.
- Every piece of gardening equipment can be returned for store credit but not for a refund.
- Certain construction tools can be returned for store credit but not for a refund.

label: Conclusion (Therefore)
body: The value of government benefits is sometimes greater than is warranted by the true change in costs.

label: Evidence
body:
The value of some government benefits is based on the consumer price index (which measures the retail prices of goods and services.
The CPI does not consider technological innovations that may drastically reduce the cost of producing some goods.

label: Evaluate
body:
Our author is essentially saying that the CPI is a bit of a flawed metric when it comes deciding on the size of a monthly retirement savings. After all, it's not considering the fact that sometime a factory has a technological innovation that drastically reduces how much it costs to produce a certain good.
We're supposed to be like, "Okaaaaay, what does that have to do with the **consumer** price index?"
Who cares if factories suddenly have their expenses lowered? The consumer price index is just measuring how much it costs Grandpa to buy batteries for his hearing aids. If the battery manufacturer finds some technological innovation that makes it way cheaper to for them to produce batteries, does that matter to Grandpa? If the manufacturer keeps the price of batteries the same, it will now make a bigger profit than before, since its production costs were drastically lowered. But that has nothing to do with the **retail** price of this battery. And if the manufacturer decides to lower the retail price, then the CPI will detect that. That's what it does. It detects monthly changes in retail prices.

label: Evidence
body: Being truly happy requires that we're pursuing personal excellence or willing to undergo personal change.

label: Information
body:
The most significant indicators of an economy's viability are level and rate of growth of aggregate output.
Unemployment and inflation rates are also important.
Pivot (but) Switz, Autria, Israel, Ireland, Denmark, and Finland all have viable economies, **but** none has a very large population.
Switzerland / Austria = 7 million Israel / Ireland / Denmark / Finland = less than 2 million

label: Evaluate
body:
There doesn't seem to be any Conditional Logic or Causality in this paragraph. The last two ideas about population size are a little Math-y, but they pretty much would just mean calculating 1/4 of 7 million, which LSAT wouldn't make us do (too ugly).
We have some Comparative stuff and a one Pivot.
Maybe they'll say something like, "even if country X's population is only 1/4 that of country Y, they can both have viable economies".

label: Goal
body: It's hard to have a prediction here, so we should just be wary of strong wording and pick the most supportable claim.

label: Conclusion
body: Moderate exercise lowers the risk of blocked arteries from blood clots.

label: Evidence (since, and)
body:
Lowers → Lowers risk → lower risk blood chol harden art's blocked art's from blood clots
If the study's data is correct, moderate exercise lowers blood cholesterol levels.

label: Evaluate
body:
On Sufficient Assumption, we ask ourselves what new terms or concepts appear only in the Conclusion (because those must be in the correct answer). Here, there are no new terms. Both "moderate exercise" and "lower risk of blocked arteries from blood clots" get discussed/defined in the evidence. That means that what ever fact or link we're missing is internal to the evidence.
Consider this argument: If Michelle is right, then Tom is a vegan. Vegans never eat meat. Thus, Tom does not eat meat.
Is it airtight? If not, what are we missing?
We're missing confirmation that Michelle is right. The argument, "Tom is a vegan. Vegans never eat meat. Thus, Tom does not eat meat" is logically airtight.
The only reason we can't sign off on the argument yet is that we don't know if Michelle is right or not about Tom being a vegan.
By analogy: If study is right, moderate exercise lowers blood cholesterol. Lower blood cholesterol lowers risk of hardened arteries, which lowers risk of blocked arteries due to blood clots.
The only thing keeping us from concluding that "moderate exercise leads to lower risk of blocked arteries" is knowing whether the study is correct in claiming that "moderate exercise lowers blood cholesterol".

label: Goal
body: Find an answer saying, "The data reported in a recent study are correct".

label: Conclusion
body: The author is saying: Arton's plays look patriotic, but really she was being ironic.

label: Evidence
body: The country was in a glum, non-patriotic mood when she wrote — unemployment, costly food, crime, low morale.

label: Evaluate
body:
Notice the silent leap. Just because the country was glum doesn't mean *Arton* was glum, or that she shared the national outlook. Writers often write against the grain — sometimes their work is uplifting *because* the times are bad. The argument assumes Arton was in tune with the national mood, and so her patriotism must have been a sarcastic mirror of it. But that's not given — it's an unstated assumption.
Imagine a comedian writing jokes during a recession. We wouldn't infer that her jokes are ironic just because the country isn't in a laughing mood. People can write against their times.

label: Goal
body: The right answer says the argument takes for granted that Arton was attuned to the prevailing national mood.

label: Conclusion
body: Your reproduction of K's painting of R will not be a very accurate production of the painting.

label: Evidence
body: K's original painting of R was not a very accurate portrait.

label: Evaluate
body:
This argument is wicked dumb. It's saying, "Because I drew a crappy doodle of Barack Obama, this photocopier is going to make a crappy copy of my doodle of Obama."
Since "not very accurate" is being recycled from the Premise into the Conclusion, it has the feel of the famous **Part vs. Whole** flaw, in which an author thinks that a trait belonging to one must therefore belong to the other.
In this case, though, the relationship isn't Part vs. Whole, it's Original vs. Reproduction.
If the original had a certain quality then the reproduction will have the same quality.

label: Goal
body: Let's look for an answer where it's saying, "Because this rendering had quality X, the act of copying this rendering will also involve quality X".

label: Conclusion (Thus)
body:
No poetry reader's enjoyment depends on attaining a precise understanding of what the poet means.
(i.e. every poetry reader could fail to attain a precise understanding of what the poet means but still enjoy the poem)

label: Evidence
body:
Writer whose purpose → sometimes uses words is personal expression ambiguously
Poet → purpose is personal expression

label: Evaluate
body:
Okay, this is a bit of a mess, since the conclusion kind of has some surprising elements that came out of nowhere.
Let's start with the fact that the first two sentences combine to yield this idea: every poet sometimes uses words ambiguously
We've got to pick an answer that combines with that premise and delivers us proof of this claim: no poetry reader's enjoyment depends on attaining a precise understanding of the poet
Since there is a new idea in the Conclusion (what a poetry **reader** 's enjoyment depends on) and we're doing Sufficient Assumption, that idea must be in the correct answer.
There's definitely some potential similarity between saying that every poet is going to sometimes use words ambiguously and the conclusion's language about "attaining a precise understanding of what the poet means".
We can add our own Dictionary-based assumption that when you use words ambiguously, a reader cannot attain a precise understanding
(that's basically inherent in the meaning of the word 'ambiguous')

label: Goal
body:
So we know that every poet sometimes uses words ambiguously, which means the poem's reader will not be able to attain a precise understanding of the poet means with those words, and yet supposedly (we want to prove that) the reader's enjoyment is not affected at all by this.
I wouldn't know exactly how to phrase what we're looking for, but I know it needs to include "no poetry reader's enjoyment depends on" or some equivalent idea.

label: Given that
body: We know humans during the Upper Paleolithic period used lamps for light in caves

label: and that
body: lamps can be dated to the entire Upper Paleo period

label: Evaluate
body: We need to find four reasons why we find more lamps in the late Upper Paleo period. - maybe there were more of them - maybe it's easy to salvage the later stuff because the earlier stuff got more destroyed / lost - maybe the Magdalenians loved them some lamps, because they were dominant during the late Upper Paleo period

label: Goal
body: The correct answer could be irrelevant to explaining why we've found more late lamps than early/middle lamps. Or it could even go in the wrong direction and make it seem surprising to find so many late lamps.

label: Conclusion
body: 1984 has exercised much influence on a great number of this newspaper's readers.

label: Evidence
body: One thousand readers were surveyed about the one book that had most influenced their lives, and 1984 was the second most chosen book.

label: Evaluate
body:
This argument relies on a survey/sample, so we could ask ourselves **Sampling** concerns, such as.... - is the sample size big enough? yes, 1000 is plenty big for a sample - is the sample representative? probably, since the conclusion is only claiming something about "the newspaper's readers". In order for this sample to be unrepresentative, we'd have to think that 1000 surveyed readers are not similar to the other readers of the same newspaper. That would be a weird concern for us to introduce. LSAT doesn't seem to be offering us a reason to doubt the normalcy of the survey respondents.
Okay, so it doesn't seem like a Sampling problem. Let's try to argue Anti-Conclusion:
given that... 1984 was the book chosen 2nd most often in a survey about "the book that's most influenced your life", how can we still argue that... 1984 has **not** exercised much influence on a great number of this paper's readers?
There's no way to argue there's a language shift between the survey and the conclusion, since both of them are talking about "having the most influence / exercising much influence".
So we could only take issue with "does ranked #2 = a great number of readers?"
Say I surveyed 50 people the same question, and this is how the voting broke down. 1. The Bible (45 votes) 2. 1984 (3 votes) 3. Art of the Deal (1 vote) 4. Everybody Poops (1 vote)
We can see that 1984 could be ranked 2nd, even though it wouldn't be fair to say that "a great number of people" voted for it.

label: Goal
body: Look for an answer addressing the idea that you could be ranked #2 without representing a 'great number of readers', or any other answer that we could answer in a way that would Weaken the argument.

label: Conclusion (Thus)
body: People's voluntary choice not to exercise places a significant burden on society.

label: Evidence
body: If you voluntarily live a sedentary lifestyle, your additional health-care costs are about $1650 higher than someone without a sedentary lifestyle.

label: Evaluate
body:
Given that ... someone living a sedentary lifestyle costs $1650 (on average) more in health care costs than does someone who lives a non-sedentary lifestyle,
How could we still argue that... Choosing not to exercise is **not** placing a significant burden on society?
Maybe the health care costs of being sedentary are higher for society, but some other costs of sedentary lives are cheaper for society? That would help us argue that sedentary people are not significantly more expensive to society.
We could also just acknowledge that sedentary people are more expensive but argue that an extra $1650 over the course of a lifetime fails to qualify as a significant burden.

label: Goal
body: Look for some way to say that even though the health care costs are somewhat higher for a sedentary lifestyle, a sedentary lifestyle overall does not cost society a burdensome extra amount of money, compared to a non-sedentary lifestyle.

label: Conclusion
body: Vermeer was not recycling the same props just because he didn't have enough props.

label: Evidence
body: Many of the props he used were expensive.

label: Evaluate
body:
This argument is pretty thin, and that's very weird for Sufficient Assumption.
We have a **Curious Fact**... why did Vermeer use a lot of similar items in his paintings? Some people pose the potential **Explanation**... maybe he just didn't have that many props.
Our author is saying, "That **Explanation** isn't plausible. After all, the props were often very expensive."
The implication seems to be that "anyone who could afford props that expensive wouldn't have lacked enough money to buy more props if they wanted more props. So it's not plausible that Vermeer reused props because he couldn't afford to buy new ones."

label: Goal
body: Since this is Sufficient Assumption, we're not getting fuzzy with the language. We're pre-phrasing a verbatim idea that connects the pieces we have. Existing evidence: many of the props were expensive Conclusion we're trying to prove: V didn't re-use props because he just didn't have other props he could use. How we get from evidence to conclusion: many props were → recurrent use wasn't expensive from lack of props

label: Conclusion
body: Newspaper sales will decline drastically if these services (where people can subscribe to topics and get continuous updates on their TV) become widely available.

label: Evidence (since)
body: These services will provide people with the information they are looking for more quickly and efficiently than printed newspapers can.

label: Evaluate
body:
Honestly, this is such an old preptest and thus such an outmoded technological premise to think about, that it's hard to put ourselves in a 1999 testwriter's brain and picture the head to head battle they're picturing between what newspapers offer and what these personalized news services would offer.
We know our job is to argue against this prediction. Since the conclusion is Conditional, we know we're supposed to play along with the trigger but dispute the outcome.

label: Goal
body:
Let's look for an answer that helps us argue that "even if these personalized electronic news services become widely available, newspaper sales will **not** decline **drastically** ".
It will probably either feel like, "Even though this new thing is available, people don't want it for some reason" or like "even though this new thing is available and people use it, there's still a compelling reason that newspapers will keep selling."

label: Conclusion
body: The author's headline: to become a champion, an athlete needs superior mastery of athletic techniques.

label: Evidence
body: The reason is a chain: strength is limited, technique stretches it efficiently, and top athletes are roughly equal in strength. So at the very top, what separates champions from also-rans isn't more strength — it's better technique.

label: Evaluate
body:
For Main Conclusion questions, scan for indicator words. "It follows that" introduces the conclusion; everything that precedes it is supporting evidence. The main claim is the requirement — that becoming a champion requires superior technique.
Watch for answers that just restate one of the supporting facts (strength is limited, top athletes have equal strength) or that flip the relationship — those are tempting because they're true, but they're not the conclusion.

label: Goal
body: An answer that says: technique mastery is necessary for championship status.

label: Conclusion (Therefore)
body: We should restructure the workday to allow people flexibility in scheduling their work hours.

label: Evidence
body: Sleep deprivation causes many social ill. Most people today suffer from sleep deprivation to some degree.

label: Evaluate
body:
This conclusion is making a Plan / Recommendation. We want to think about the Goal of this Plan and then skeptically review whether this plan would achieve the goal.
The goal is to lessen the problems caused by sleep deprivation; to make there be less sleep deprivation.
We should ask ourselves about this Plan to allow people more scheduling flexibility with work... - Is is feasible? Can we actually give employees scheduling flexibility or will we end up short-staffed at critical junctures if a bunch of people are choosing not to work at the same time. - Are there incentives for cooperation? Do people want more sleep? Would they be motivated to tinker with their work schedules so that they could get more sleep?
- Could it backfire? Could giving people more scheduling flexibility lead to them figuring out ways to work a 3-day week of 13-hour days, followed by a 4-day weekend in Vegas, thus increasing their sleep deprivation.
- Does it address a significant source of the problem? Is there any evidence that sleep deprivation is related to a lack of scheduling flexibility?

label: Goal
body: Look for an answer that addresses one of those questions above or that otherwise makes us feel better about the idea of giving people more scheduling freedom in the hopes that they'll be able to get more sleep as a result.

label: Definition
body: True belief formed → Knowledge by reliable process

label: Objection
body: If someone was using the process of clairvoyance to reliably come to true beliefs, we wouldn't call that knowledge. (this is trying to show the definition is wrong, by pointing to a counterexample that matches the trigger but not the outcome)

label: Defense
body: You're right, we wouldn't call clairvoyance knowledge under my definition, but not because the definition is wrong. It's because clairvoyance doesn't actually fit the trigger: we don't count it as a reliable process. If we did, then it would fit the definition and we would think of it as knowledge.

label: Evaluate
body:
The author partially agrees with the objection. He agrees to the objection's premise that true beliefs acquired through clairvoyance would not count as knowledge. But disagrees with the objection's conclusion, that this therefore shows the definition is flawed.
He explains that the putative (supposed) counterexample of clairvoyance is not really a counterexample, since it doesn't satisfy the trigger of the definition (since we don't consider it a reliable process).

label: Goal
body: Look for something like "the author explains how this supposed counterexample to the definition isn't really a counterexample since it fails to satisfy the trigger of the definition".

label: Conclusion (But / concur with me)
body: Hogan's actions should not be wholly condemned.

label: Evidence
body: Hogan mistakenly believed Winters to be the robber who had been plaguing this area of town the last few months.

label: Evaluate
body:
This is a chaotic Whenever we do Main Conclusion, we remind ourselves that 90% of the time the conclusion will be the First Sentence or attached to a **but / yet / however** pivot word.
The first three sentences of this paragraph do sound like the author's opinionated voice, but they all sound like concessions, not conclusions.
When authors say things like, "I agree that X..., I don't deny Y..., Indeed, I would not disagree with Z", they conceding certain things are true, before pivoting into their real argument. If I want to argue that Lebron is better than Kobe, I might say, "I agree that Kobe has won more championships, but.." "I don't deny that Kobe's a better shooter, however.."
When we see the magical pivot " **But** ", we lean in thinking, is this the conclusion?
And it is. The first half of the final sentence is the conclusion. It's just that this final sentence has an absurdly difficult-to-understand structure. It takes a simple premise / conclusion combo, like "The kids should bring their heavy jackets because it's going to get cold", and makes it sound really weird:
In asking you to concur with me that the kids should bring their heavy jackets I emphasize again that it's going to get really cold.
The author is acknowledging that Hogan badly and knowingly hurt Winters, which normally would be reprehensible. But Hogan wasn't trying to maim an innocent man. Hogan thought Winters was the robber who had been terrorizing the area recently, and because of that, the author is concluding that we should have some mercy on Hogan.

label: Goal
body:
The author's conclusion is "Let's not wholly condemn Hogan's actions". What could an equivalent rephrasing sound like?
- Hogan's actions weren't totally terrible - Hogan deserves a little leniency in our judgment

label: Conclusion (thus)
body: Under vague laws people cannot feel secure.

label: Evidence
body: Vague laws set vague limits on people's freedom. This makes it impossible for them to know whether their actions are legal.

label: Evaluate
body:
We're trying to prove that if you live under vague laws, you **cannot feel secure**. Did the evidence provide a proving mechanism for that language? In other words, do we have a rule that looks like,
If xyz, then cannot feel secure?
No, not yet. So the correct answer 100% must provide us with such a rule.
What do we know about vague laws? Two things. - set vague limits on personal freedom - impossible to know for certain whether your actions are legal

label: Goal
body:
Since the correct answer is supposed to combine with our premises and allow us to derive the idea that "under vague laws, **cannot feel secure** ", there are two possible correct answers:
if something sets vague → cannot limits on personal freedom feel secure
if imposs to know for sure → cannot whether actions are legal feel secure

label: Conclusion (this is conclusive evidence)
body: Psychoses, unlike neuroses, have nothing to do with environmental factors but rather are caused by some purely organic condition (internal stuff).

label: Evaluate
body:
This is a pretty dense stimulus to parse, but ultimately this argument is going to come down to an assumption that "if best treatment is of type X, then the condition it's treating is of type X".
The evidence and the conclusion are both doing a comparison/contrast between neuroses and psychoses.
We had neuroses that were caused by environmental factors (i.e. your mom used to always lick her finger and fix your bangs, and now you're super neurotic about fixing your hair). The appropriate treatment was psychotherapy (i.e. sitting with a therapist and talking through your problems, trying to get your **mind / psyche** into better shape).
We used to believe that this psychotherapy was also the right treatment for psychoses (such as multiple personality disorder). But now we know that a better treatment is pharmaceutical drugs (i.e. stuff you ingest that changes your body chemistry... and maybe gets your **brain** into better shape).
Because we can better treat psychoses with something (drugs) that changes your **biochemistry** than with something (psychotherapy) that changes your **mind / thoughts**, the author is concluding that psychoses must be more about the body and less about the mind. Thus, they are more caused by body stuff than by environmental factors.

label: Goal
body:
Let's look for an answer that speaks to this weird move from "better treatment" to "the root cause".
The author thinks that a condition that is better treated by changing brain chemistry than by changing mental activity must therefore be caused by something wrong with brain chemistry, rather than something wrong with environmental factors that messed up someone's thoughts.
Since this question stem is putting "ignores the possibility" in front of every answer choice, we're really just going to ask ourselves whether each answer choice Weakens.
Thus, we could call this a Flaw question, or we could call it a Weaken (that's disguised as Flaw).

label: Conclusion
body: In general, attaining technological expertise prepares you no better for tomorrow's job market than does attaining verbal / quantitative skills.

label: Evidence
body: We learn to use most of the machines in our lives through written instructions, not through knowledge of the machines' inner workings, since most machines are specifically designed to be used by nonexperts.

label: Evaluate
body:
The author's argument seems to boil down to this, "Since I don't need to be an A/C technician and understand the inner workings of my air conditioner in order to be able to use it (I can just read the user's manual, written for nonexperts), attaining technological expertise serves me no better in getting a job in the future than would developing more traditional verbal and quantitative skills."
One big objection to this would be, "What if there aren't many jobs that are looking for people with traditional verbal/quant skills, whereas there are many jobs that are looking for people with tech expertise?"
The author has shifted from a premise about whether technological expertise helps us to use the machines in our lives to a conclusion about whether technological expertise helps us to get a job.

label: Goal
body:
It seems unlikely that this question wants us Linking assumption, like, "If you don't need something to use most of the machines in your life, then that something does not prepare you any better for tomorrow's job market", but it could.
I would suspect that we'll see a Defender assumption, saying something like, "It is **not** the case that most of the jobs in tomorrow's job market require some technological expertise".

label: Anticipate
body:
When we're trying to pull out a principle for a parallel argument, we don't think in terms of a formal, algebraic representation of the argument.
Think more holistically, like a slogan or piece of advice.
This argument seems to feel like the old Boy Who Cried Wolf story, in which a boy cries wolf even though there isn't a wolf two different times and the concerned townsfolk fooled by his ruse learn to distrust him. Then, when there really is a wolf, they don't come running to his aide, because he's lost credibility.
Similarly, this argument is saying that environmentalists better be sure there's really a wolf there (with water pollution). If not, people won't listen to them some time in the future when there really is a wolf (dire threat) there.

label: Conclusion
body: Reptiles must be incapable of complex reasoning.

label: Evidence (since)
body: Experiments show that reptiles are incapable of making major alterations in their behavior.

label: Evaluate
body:
The " **but** " signals that our author is rebutting the "some psychologists" in the first sentence. Hence, we don't necessarily need to care about what came before the 'but', other than for context or referential language.
The argument has only one premise (indicated by **since** ). That "since" claim indicates that the other half of that sentence, the latter half, is the conclusion.
"Complex reasoning" is a New Concept in the Conclusion. If there's a new concept in the conclusion of an Assumption question, that concept is almost always in the correct answer.
We use all these indicator words to quickly suppress worrying about the first sentence and focus on the move from the first half of the last sentence to the second half:
**since** reptiles can't make major alterations in behavior **we can conclude** reptiles can't do complex reasoning

label: Goal
body:
We should anticipate a Linking answer here. The author is making this move:
Can't make major → incapable of alterations in behavior complex reas.
We might want to also consider the contrapositive, since Linking answers are so frequently disguised that way:
Capable of → Can make major complex reasoning alterations in behav.

label: Statements
body:
The purpose of a general theory of art is to explain every aesthetic feature found in any arts.
pivot (however) Premodern general theories focused primarily on painting and sculpture.
conditional (every) All premodern general theories fail to to explain some aesthetic feature of music.

label: Evaluate
body:
We read Inference paragraphs looking for ideas that could be combined, usually via some Overlapping idea. In this paragraph, "general theory of art" was mentioned in all three claims. How can we combine them? There's also a pivot word, **however**, which usually signals that we're supposed to Reconcile the Pivot -- figure out how to resolve the tension between what came before and after it.
The purpose of a general theory is to explain **every** feature of **all** the arts. Every premodern general theory fails to explain some feature of music.

label: Goal
body:
It sounds like every premodern general theory of art fails to achieve its purpose.
I would go in anticipating that, but you never know with Inference questions. We just want the most supportable answer.

label: Conclusion
body: If our goal is a society whose citizens are truly happy, then it's bad to say that people should accept themselves as they are rather than being dissatisfied by their abilities.

label: Evaluate
body:
This argument is just a complex way of saying, "if you want X, you shouldn't do Y. After all, X requires Z."
This assumes that "if you do Y, you won't have Z".
Here the author is saying, "if you want genuine happiness, you shouldn't do this principle. After all, genuine happiness requires (pursuing personal excellence / willing to undergo personal change)."
This must be assuming that "if you followed this principle, you won't have pursuing personal excellence / willingness to undergo personal change".

label: Goal
body: Following the principle is accepting yourself rather than being dissatisfied with your abilities. So we're assuming, "If you accept yourself, then you won't pursue personal excellence or be willing to undergo personal change", as well as "if you are satisfied (aren't dissatisfied) with your abilities, then you won't pursue personal excellence or be willing to undergo personal change".

label: Conclusion (so)
body: It is not true that whoever likes potatoes likes turnips. rephrase: Some people like potatoes but don't like turnips.

label: Evidence
body: My father likes turnips but not potatoes.

label: Evaluate
body:
The flaw here, in short, is that the evidence is irrelevant to the conclusion. The argument is trying to prove that some people who like potatoes don't like turnips.
But the evidence is an example of someone who likes turnips but doesn't like potatoes.

label: Goal
body:
Since the error here is that the example presented in the evidence is the reversed version of what the author is trying to prove, we can represent this flaw symbolically:
CONC: It's not true that anything that's X is Y. (i.e. some X's are not Y)
EVID: This example is Y but not X.

label: Conclusion (rebuttal)
body: It is not inconsistent to both support freedom of speech and support legislation that limits the amount of violence on TV shows. rephrase: It is consistent to support both.

label: Evidence
body: We can limit TV content because the damage of violent TV is more harmful than the decrease in freedom of speech this causes.

label: Evaluate
body:
The author is arguing that we're not contradicting ourselves if we say, "I believe in free speech. But I also think it's good that this law limits the amount of violence on TV."
Isn't limiting violence on TV abridging free speech?
Yes, the author agrees. Such laws will decrease freedom of speech somewhat. But the harm of that is outweighed by the harm caused by violent TV.
We have competing values, and in the case of violent TV, it's more important to avert the harm of violent TV than it is to stick up for fully unrestricted free speech.

label: Goal
body:
Since this argument involves competing interests, we're less likely to see a Conditional answer and more likely to see an answer setting Priorities, helping us to Weigh Tradeoffs.
The author is saying, "I'm not contradicting myself by having Principle X and approving of Action A. Sure, Action A goes against Principle X somewhat, but there's more harm if we don't do Action A than if we do."

label: Sandy's Conclusion
body: It's best to play Bigbucks only after there have been a few weeks with no winners.

label: Sandy's Evidence (because)
body: The money pot increases each week that there is no winner.

label: Alex's Conclusion
body: You're more likely to win the lottery when the money pot is small.

label: Alex's Evidence (because)
body: That's when the fewest other people are playing.

label: Evaluate
body:
What a psycho question task: read two different arguments and find a flaw that shows up in one of them?
Okay, let's analyze both reasoning moves: Given that... the money pot increases each week that there is no winner, Are we convinced that... you should only play Bigbucks after a few weeks of no winners?
No, not necessarily. Maybe the tickets become more expensive when the money pot gets bigger. Maybe so many extra people start buying tickets when the jackpot gets high that you're more likely to have multiple winners who have to split the jackpot. (i.e. better to win a smaller jackpot by yourself than have to split a bigger jackpot among multiple winners)
Given that... the fewest people play when the money pot is small Are we convinced that... you're more likely to win when the money pot is small?
No, we don't have to accept that. If you're involved in a raffle, then the fewer people involved (or more precisely the fewer tickets purchased) the better your odds. In a raffle, there's a guaranteed winner because one of the purchased ticket numbers will be randomly drawn.
So if there are 80 tickets, you have a 1 in 80 chance of winning. If there are 800 tickets, you have a 1 in 800 chance of winning.
Meanwhile, Bigbucks is not a raffle. You pick five numbers, and the lottery randomly picks five numbers, and if they all match then you win (at least a share) of the money pot.
The probability of winning is determined here by the odds that the five digit number you chose will match the randomly drawn number they choose.
If each of the five numbers are just one digit (from 0 - 9), then there are 10 possible numbers. You thus have a 1 in 100,000 chance of choosing the winning five digit number. It doesn't matter how many people are playing the lottery. Your odds are still 1 in 100,000 of your number matching the winning number. (the addition of other players only increases the odds that you might have to split the pot if you win, but it doesn't change your odds of winning)

label: Goal
body: Alex's flaw seems like the more egregious, more nameable flaw, so we can probably expect to see an answer saying that "the number of people playing this game doesn't affect your odds of correctly guessing a random five digit number".

label: Conclusion (Therefore)
body: The price difference cannot be accounted for by the greater cost of providing decaffeinated coffee to the consumer.

label: Evidence
body: The process by which the coffee beans are decaffeinated is fairly simple and not very costly.

label: Evaluate
body:
The author's conclusion is Anti-Causal, because it's saying "X cannot be **accounted for** by the greater cost". There's an implied causal mystery: Why is the retail price of decaff way higher than that of regular coffee? The author says, "The process of decaffeinating the beans isn't very costly". So she's making a Part to Whole move. "If one part of the decaff coffee product isn't much more costly, then decaff overall is much more costly."
If we wanted to posit a missing link, we would say something like, "If making the beans decaffeinated isn't very costly, then providing decaff coffee to the consumer isn't very costly."
We could challenge this conclusion by pointing to other potential areas of expense involved in providing decaff to the consumer: maybe the beans that are used are way more expensive to procure, maybe decaff is way more expensive to store or to ship.

label: Goal
body: Look for an answer stating the move from "if the process of removing the caffeine isn't expensive, then the cost of providing decaff to the consumer isn't expensive". But more likely an answer will rule out an objection, so the correct answer might have the signature "ruling-out not" that we see a ton in correct answers for Necessary Assumption.

label: Conclusion (implied)
body: The union's strength was declining.

label: Goal
body: If there's no textual or historical evidence that the author intended an allegorical reading, then just read the book as whatever it superficially seems like.

label: Evidence
body:
People think that the union's strength is declining because of fewer strikes, but strikes are actually a sign that a union's position is too weak in a modern society.
When a union is strong, they don't need to call strikes. They can concentrate on working with others in the labor market to achieve common goals, like more profitable and livable working conditions.

label: Evaluate
body:
If we were looking for an explicit conclusion here, we might torture ourselves, but the question stem indicates that we're talking about an **implied** conclusion.
The argument criticizing the newspaper article is **directed toward establishing** which one of the following as its main conclusion?
The most common place to find an implied conclusion is with a rebuttal argument. When an author starts off with an attribution and then pivots with a **but / yet / however**, then we can pretty safely assume that the conclusion will just sound like it's disagreeing with the original attribution claim.
for example Many people think that Ringo was a very mediocre drummer. However, Ringo's left handedness led to him playing a lot of unusual drum fills that delighted his contemporaries.
The implied conclusion was, "Ringo was **not** a very mediocre drummer".
Similarly, we find our implied conclusion here by noticing the attribution that begins the paragraph: an article **argued that** the strength of unions was declining.
Does our author agree/disagree with that position? Where is the first clue?
When she says, "The article's evidence was fewer strikes, **as if** strikes were the sole reason for unions' existence."
The "as if" is a sarcastic comment, showing us that the author takes issue with the article's logic. From there, we can here that the author is building the opposite case, that a lack of strikes is actually an indication of the opposite conclusion, that the strength of unions is **not** declining.

label: Goal
body: Let's look for something like "the strength of unions is fine / not declining".

label: Curious Fact
body: Why is there less gravitational attraction between bodies than our theories predict?

label: Explanation
body: Maybe there's a 5th universal force, which involves mutual repulsion between particles of matter.

label: Evaluate
body:
Whenever we're trying to Solve a Causal Mystery and we have a potential hypothesis to do so, we're supposed to consider two different questions:
1. is there some **Alternate Way** we could explain / interpret the curious fact? 2. how **plausible** is the Author's Way of explaining it?
How else could we explain why the gravitational attraction between bodies is measured smaller than the predicted amount?
- maybe gravity isn't as strong as we think it is? - maybe the measuring devices were off? - maybe there's some interaction with the other 3 known forces that would explain it?
How plausible is the idea that there is a 5th force that deals with mutual repulsion between particles of matter?
- do any other experiments suggest such a force? - would such a force resolve any other physical mysteries we have? - is there any mathematical modeling of such a force?

label: Goal
body: Since this is Strengthen, we want to either **rule out** an alternate way to explain the curious fact (e.g. "the measurements **aren't** smaller than predicted because gravity is just weaker than we thought / because our measurements were off") or **increase** the plausibility of the presented explanation, that there is fifth force that involves mutual repulsion between particles of matter.

label: Conclusion (so)
body: Advertising time will be no harder to sell next fall than it was last fall.

label: Evidence
body: Advertisers will continue to profit from television advertising, in spite of the 10-15% increase in cost.

label: Evaluate
body:
On Strengthen questions, we often start by thinking of possible objections so that we can think about the vulnerabilities of the argument.
Given that... advertisers will still profit from TV advertising, How could one argue that... advertising time **will** be harder to sell next fall (when it costs 10-15% more)?
The fact that a business still profits from X doesn't mean that X is just as attractive a prospect as it was before. After all, say that I used to make $300 of profit a day making fruit smoothies for people, but then the cost of my supplies goes up and I can only make $200 of profit a day. Yes, I'm still profiting, but the smoothie business might not seem so appealing anymore. I might be tempted to try a different business venture.
Similarly, advertisers might see that their profits from TV advertising have shrunk now that it's more expensive, and thus decide to spend their ad dollars elsewhere. Maybe they think, "Sure, I can still profit from TV advertising... but I could profit **even more** by advertising in magazines or on the internet."

label: Goal
body: Look for an answer that makes alternative options for advertising sound less appealing (thus making TV advertising still an attractive option). Or look for an answer making TV advertising sound more attractive to advertisers than it was before (like, "Sure the commercials will cost a little more to buy, but the audience is bigger / people have more money to spend right now / we can better target customers for each product").

label: Conclusion (thus, clearly)
body: Most people can diagnose swimmer's ear in themselves without ever having to consult a physician.

label: Evidence
body: In a recent study of 1,000 people who suspected they had swimmer's ear, 84 percent made a correct diagnosis, which is slightly better than the accuracy rate of physicians in diagnosing swimmer’s ear.

label: Evaluate
body:
This argument centers around the assumption that because a high percentage of people correctly diagnosed swimmer's ear in the study, most people are generally capable of diagnosing it correctly.
This is a Sampling move. Since **most ppl in the study** can diagnose S.E., most ppl can diagnose S.E.
To weaken this, we need to uncover aspects of the study or broader context that would undermine the conclusion that people can diagnose swimmer’s ear without consulting a physician.
Possible avenues for attack include questioning the representativeness of the study sample, the circumstances under which people achieved high diagnostic accuracy, or whether previous exposure to physician training could have influenced the results.

label: Goal
body: Let's find an answer that suggests a reason why the study’s results don’t apply broadly to most people or reveal a missing factor that questions the generalizability of the self-diagnosis ability reflected in the study.

label: Premises
body: The social critic makes three moves. First: the legal-rights debate is the wrong frame. Second: just because something can legally be said doesn't mean it should be. Third: words have real power to change how people see things and act.

label: Conclusion
body: The town councillor's point: don't ban skateboarding in the park.

label: Evaluate
body:
Put those together. The critic isn't calling for laws — that's why the legal debate is "missing the point." Instead, the implication is that musicians could choose *voluntarily* not to use violent lyrics, and because words shape behavior, that voluntary choice could reduce violence in society.
This is a careful, "if ... may" inference — the critic isn't guaranteeing results, just pointing to the possibility. Most Supported questions reward the safest, most conservative inference, and that's exactly this one.

label: Goal
body: The right answer says: voluntary self-censorship by rock musicians may help reduce violence.

label: Conclusion (clearly / this demonstrates)
body: In general, people are more willing when they are younger than when they are older to reveal personal financial information to strangers over the telephone.

label: Evidence
body:
10,000 people were randomly surveyed over the phone about their income and savings.
The older the person being queried, the more likely it was that they would refuse to answer any questions.

label: Evaluate
body:
Because the conclusion is trying to explain the curious results of a survey, we can use our Explain Curious Fact mindset:
Curious Fact ... why, in this survey, were the younger people more willing to divulge information about their income and savings?
Author's Explanation ... when you're young, you're more willing to divulge that stuff to strangers than when you're old.
We're supposed to now consider 1. Alternate Explanations for the curious fact 2. how plausible is the Author's Explanation
How else could we explain why the younger people were more willing to talk about their financials? Maybe the causal factor isn't really about age, it's about wealth. Wealthier people are less willing to talk about their money and older people are more likely to have wealth.
Or Maybe the causal factor isn't really about age, it's about whether you use Venmo. People who, by using Venmo, get used used to making electronic transactions with witty memo comments that are publicly viewable become less bashful about revealing their financial info. Since younger people are more likely to use Venmo than older people, we get the survey results we got where youth and willingness to divulge are correlated, but it's Venmo not age that is the causal factor.
How would we test the plausibility of the author's hypothesis, that a young version of you was more willing to divulge financial information than an old version of you? We could ask older people whether they were more willing to talk about money when they were young.

label: Goal
body: Look for an answer that suggests an Alternate Explanation for the study (or one that attacks the plausibility of the idea that people get less willing to reveal financial information the older they get).

body:
Since the overlapping ingredient in the Conclusion and the Evidence is "should not have been desired in the first place", we'll be trying to pick an answer that links together the two dangling ideas, "forgone pleasures" and "something that would have been justifiably regretted".
If we're given a rule that, If something is X, then it is Z

They told us a rule that says,

We're trying to prove that Many FP's should not have been desired.
So we just need to hear that Many FP's are JR

label: Goal
body: Let's look for something that gets us Many **F** orgone **P** leasures would have been **J** ustifiably **R** egretted.

label: Some Biologists' Conclusion
body: Capacity for flying first occurred in marine reptiles.

label: Some Biologists' Evidence
body: Feathers are clearly developed from scales.

label: Other Biologists' Conclusion
body: That's not a strong argument that flying first occurred in marine reptiles.

label: Other Biologists' Evidence
body: Bats (which fly) have no scales. Nonmarine reptiles also have scales.

label: Other People's Conclusion
body: Flight first developed in tree-dwelling reptiles.

label: Other People's Evidence
body: It's more likely that tree-dwelling reptiles developed wings to assist their leaps from branch to branch than it is that land-dwelling reptiles just had limbs that developed into wings.

label: Evaluate
body:
This is a pretty unique stimulus for a Role question. It's not an argument. It's more like a summary of three different arguments. Everyone is debating about what type of species was first to develop flight.
We're being asked about what role was played by saying "nonmarine reptiles also have scales". This was uttered as a reason for rejecting the first position, that "capacity for flight first developed in marine reptiles, since feathers developed from scales".
The rebuttal to that point of view was pointing out two things:
1. Bats have no scales/feathers, but bats fly. So should we really assume that the first fliers had feathers, which came from scales?
2. Nonmarine reptiles also have scales. If "scales" are the reason that some people think marine reptiles were the first to develop flight, then why aren't they considering nonmarine reptiles just as much?

label: Goal
body:
The claim "nonmarine reptiles also have scales" is meant to raise doubt about the argument being made by the biologists in the first sentence.
They are arguing, "feathers came from scales" and "marine reptiles had scales", Thus, "marine reptiles were first in flight".
The biologists in the second sentence are saying, "nonmarine reptiles also had scales", so wouldn't they be just as likely a suspect, by the logic of the first biologists?

label: Given that
body: Elderly people are closer to death than are middle-aged people,

label: Why is it that
body: Middle-aged people have more fear of dying than do elderly people?

label: Evidence
body: Some works of art are representational, and what they represent is an aesthetically relevant property of the art. But whether art possesses this property or not depends upon context, and there aren't any clear cut rules for determining if an object does / doesn't have a context-dependent property.

label: Evaluate
body: They were just trying to punish us there. Brutal read. Let's focus on the connection between the final idea and the conclusion:

label: Evaluate
body:
One interesting thing about this stimulus is that it doesn't actually provide the background condition for the Paradox. We would just ask our common sense, "Why is it seemingly surprising that middle-aged people fear death more than elderly people? Why is the popular belief that elderly people fear death more than middle-aged people do?"
On Paradox questions, we don't try hard to anticipate the answer (unless it's a mathematical paradox) because the answer could take so many forms. On EXCEPT questions, we're also less likely to try to anticipate the answer, because there are essentially going to be four valid answers that we need to eliminate.

label: Goal
body: Let's find four answers that give a reason why middle-aged people would be afraid of dying or why elderly people wouldn't be.

label: Conclusion (Thus)
body: Leibniz and Newton each independently discovered calculus.

label: Evidence
body:
Newton had a private notebook which showed he was using calculus ideas for at least a decade before Leibniz published his version of calculus (prior to Newton publishing any version). Newton claims he showed these ideas to Leibniz in a letter shortly before Leibniz's publication.
But close examination of the letter shows that Newton's few cryptic remarks did not reveal anything important about calculus.

label: Evaluate
body:
The story behind this argument is that Newton and Leibniz both published their own version of calculus, and the world kind of wonders, "Who thought of it first? Did one person steal it from the other?"
One could build the case that Newton thought of calculus first and that Leibniz "stole" the idea and published first. After all, Newton has a notebook showing he was working on calculus for at least 10 years before Leibniz published. And Newton even disclosed some of his ideas to Leibniz in a letter shortly before Leibniz's publication.
But the author is saying, "There's no way Leibniz stole Newton's calculus from that letter. After all, the letter didn't reveal anything important about calculus. **Thus, they each independently discovered calculus**."
Is that the only way to Explain the Curious Fact of who invented calculus?
Of course not. There are lots of possibilities: - L invented it, N stole it. - N invented it, L stole it. - L and N each separately invented it. - L stole it from X and N stole it from L. - N stole it from X and L stole it from N. - L and N both stole it from X. - L stole it from X, and N stole it from Y
The author is trying to shut down any story where Leibniz steals calculus from Newton. But that doesn't mean they both invented it.

label: Goal
body:
The fact that this letter from Newton wouldn't have been enough for Leibniz to steal calculus from doesn't prove that Leibniz didn't steal calculus from Newton. Look for an answer ruling out some other way that Leibniz could have stolen the idea of calculus.
And even if we accept that Leibniz didn't steal calculus from Newton, that doesn't prove that they both discovered it independently. So we might see an answer ruling out some other possibility (like Newton **did not** steal it from Leibniz).

label: Statements
body:
Over the course of 10 months,
**Calistan overall** monthly new = constant car sales
**Marvel Auto Company** monthly new = doubled car sales
market share = doubled
After those 10 months,
Emission rules are imposed across the country of Calistan.
**Marvel Auto Company** monthly new = still just as high car sales
market share = declined a lot

label: Evaluate
body:
On Must Be False questions, we expect the answer to contradict a conditional that the paragraph provided, or to contradict some Must Be True inference we can make.
There weren't any conditionals in this paragraph, so we'd shift to Must Be True thinking.
There was a lot of Mathematical information, so there is probably a math-y inference we're supposed to be seeing. The overlapping concepts are "Marvel, Calistan, monthly sales, market share", all of which are mentioned at least twice.
The first two sentences tell us that a country's new car auto market overall was stable for a 10 month period during which Marvel was doubling sales and doubling market share.
Do those two facts yield a mathematical inference?
Sort of. We know that some other new car dealer in Calistan is doing worse than they were doing before, in terms of sales and market share. The extra sales and extra market share that Marvel is earning has to be coming at the expense some other car sellers in Calistan.
The last sentence says that during a 3 month period, Marvel's market share declined while its level of sales remained the same.
Do those two facts yield a math-y inference?
Yes. Suppose a business has been earning x dollars per month and currently has a 20% market share (that means of all the money that gets spent on that type of product, this company is receiving 20% of it). What does it mean if that business continues earning x dollars per month, but now only has a 15% market share?
It means that the market has grown. More money is being spent on that product by consumers than before. Your business is bringing in the same revenue as before, but that pile of revenue is a smaller percentage of the overall market.
Finally, we should address the middle sentence, which tells us that emission standards were imposed in between the 10 month period and the 3 month period. Should we infer that the changes observed during the 3 month period were caused by the emission standards?
No. That is not a **must** be true inference. That's speculating a plausible causal hypothesis, but not a mandatory truth.

label: Goal
body:
Look for an answer contradicting one of the math inferences (probably the 2nd one, since that one was so hard to figure out). Expect trap answers dealing with the causal inferences we can't make regarding the emissions standards.
If we want, as we consider each answer, we can essentially ask ourselves, "Could I infer that the opposite of this must be true?"

label: Conclusion (therefore)
body:
The use of nonaddictive drugs by athletes should not be prohibited.
rephrase: Athletes should be allowed to use nonaddictive drugs.

label: Evidence
body:
People objecting that these drugs are unnatural forget that almost everything in sports is unnatural, such as high-tech running shoes and padded boxing gloves, yet none of these are prohibited for being unnatural.
We should be attending to more serious problems in sports that cause unnecessary deaths and injuries.

label: Evaluate
body:
The final idea of, "What we SHOULD be talking about is X!" is logically trash. We can talk about whatever we want to talk about. Suppose someone says, "People should be allowed to burglarize. After all, we SHOULD be attending to more serious problems like murder." We would say Yes, murder is more serious. But we don't have to choose. Right now we're talking about whether burglary should be okay.
So we should probably ignore that claim and focus on the issue at hand, whether athletes should be allowed to use nonaddictive drugs.
GIVEN THAT we let athletes use other unnatural things (like fancy shoes and gloves and equipment)
HOW CAN WE ARGUE THAT athletes should not be able to use unnatural nonaddictive drugs? Well, the easiest argument would be, "Nonaddictive drugs also harm athletes. Just because they're not addictive doesn't mean they're not harmful. Taking massive doses of aspiring regularly probably has a negative effect on your body!"
The author was Assuming a Difference, that nonaddictive drugs aren't harmful.

label: Goal
body: Let's find an answer that provides a compelling reason to prohibit the use of nonaddictive drugs by athletes.

label: Conclusion (so)
body: There can't be any clear criteria for determining whether an object qualifies as art.

label: Conclusion (Thus)
body: No strictly physical theory can explain consciousness.

label: If... Then...** no clear criteria no clear criteria for determining → for determining context-dependent whether object properties is art **...?
body:
That must be assuming that "in order to determine whether an object qualifies as art, you need to know its context-dependent properties".
We could weaken the argument by attacking that assumption, saying something like, "You can figure out whether an object qualifies as art without needing to know its context-dependent properties".
We could also object to our author thinking that, "If there aren't clear cut criteria for context-dependent properties, then we won't know whether those context-dependent properties are present".
Who said we need clear cut criteria in order to figure out context-dependent properties? I'm pretty sure the Supreme Court famously failed to provide any clear cut criteria for the "it depends" property of obscenity, deeming that "you know it when you see it". They were confident that even if you don't rigorously define it, you may be able to clearly identify sometimes.

label: Goal
body: Look for an answer showing how we could determine whether an object qualifies as art, even though we don't have clear cut criteria for determining context-dependent properties. -- maybe we don't need context-dependent to ascertain whether it's art -- maybe we don't need clear cut criteria to ascertain whether context-dependent stuff is present

label: Conclusion
body: The florist must have made a mistake: either Drew was supposed to get violets, or a card, or the flowers were for someone else.

label: Evidence
body:
If the sender knew Drew well, they would know that Drew likes violets more than roses.
But the flowers Drew received were roses.
If the sender didn't know Drew well, they would have sent a signed card with the flowers.
But there was no card.

label: Evaluate
body:
Given these conditional rules and facts, how could we still argue that the flowers were **not** a mistake, they were violets with no card intended for Drew?
There were two conditionals, and two facts that seemed to trigger their contrapositives.
Sent by someone who doesn't know D → card The fact that there was no card means that the person who sent it was someone who does know Drew well.
But doesn't that contradict the other conditional?
Sent by someone → would know that D who knows D well prefers violets
While it's counterintuitive, there is no contradiction. The conditional is only saying that the sender would know that Drew prefers roses, not that the sender would have definitely sent roses.
Maybe the sender knows that Drew hates roses and sent him roses sarcastically, to troll him.

label: Goal
body: The loose end in this argument is that someone who knows Drew well may have decided to send Drew roses (maybe they were on sale) even though that person knew that Drew prefers violets.

label: Statements
body:
One of historians' biggest problems is when their usual sources have conflicting ideas about when some event occurred.
They should try to have fewer trusted sources, so that there's less likely to be a date mismatch among their group of sources (maybe eliminate the less credible sources from consideration).
Once they winnow it down to just a few sources, the problem still occurs. They still often have conflicting dates.
When this occurs, they may try on their own to figure out what the correct date is, but sometimes they're unsuccessful.

label: Evaluate
body:
This stimulus definitely doesn't seem to have obvious Conditional / Causal / Pivot markers.
The last sentence is vaguely Conditional / Quantified: There's something vaguely Conditional/Quantitative about the once this is achieved, as often happens, though on occasion.
The gist of the paragraph is that when historians are trying to figure out the date of event X, they check their usual sources. When they get conflicting answers, they don't know what's right!
The author advises them to prune away some of their sources, thinking that if you ask too many people the same question, you're gonna always get different answers.
When historians get down to their few, core sources and they still get different answers for the date of event X, then they try to figure out which date is right on their own (sometimes unsuccessfully).

label: Goal
body:
If I had to predict, I would feel like that "though on occasion unsuccessfully" is too weird to be in that sentence if they weren't going to use it for something.
So let's look for the most provable claim, but it might address that idea that "sometimes, historians trim it down to their handful of trusted sources, they get conflicting answers, and they are unable to resolve it on their own".

label: Evidence
body:
conditional (only when = only if = RIGHT side) Credited → made before 3pm **A → B**
fact Alicia knows made before 3pm. **X knows B**

label: Conclusion
body: Alicia knows credited. **X knows A**.

label: Evaluate
body:
The question stem curious asks for **both** logical flaws, which is very atypical (only one or two others like this that have two flaws).
The more obvious flaw is the **Necessary vs. Sufficient** reversal. Famous Flaws are very common on Parallel Flaw questions.
The author provided a conditional relationship, but then misapplied it by thinking "since the right side is true, the left side is true".
If we have no idea what the second flaw is, we can just head to the answers knowing this one and then see what we can rid of. Once you're down to the final couple, seeing the structural similarity that relates to the second flaw would probably be enough to make you pick the right answer.
The second flaw is something that's been used 5-10 times over LSATs history, so recurring but not too common. It's a flaw in which you assume that someone knows an implication of their belief.
You could say "New Orleans was the birthplace of jazz. Tony knows that he's driven through New Orleans, so he knows that he's driven through the birthplace of jazz."
WE know that he's driven through the birthplace of jazz. That is a true implication of the fact that he's driven through New Orleans. But just because Tony believes that he's driven through New Orleans doesn't mean he believes every true implication of that fact. He might have no idea that New Orleans is the birthplace of jazz.
Similarly, Alicia knows she made her deposit before 3pm. WE know that there's a rule saying "credited same day requires before 3pm", so we know that her deposit qualifies for being credited same-day, but we can't say that SHE knows that her deposit qualifies for being credited same-day, because we have no idea if she's aware of this bank's policy. She might have just dropped the deposit off in the morning because it was on her way to yoga, and so she knows it was before 3pm but doesn't have any reason to think 3pm is a special deposit cutoff time for her bank.

label: Goal
