body: Look for a conditional statement that the argument then interprets backwards (if right side is true, left side is true). Then look to see whether those last two moves are about someone's beliefs (since X believes right side, X believes left side).

label: Conclusion
body: We should read Billy Budd as a simple tragedy.

label: Evidence
body: Skateboarding ordinances are supposed to protect children from danger. Banning skateboarding in the park is dangerous on its face, but the alternative — kids skateboarding in the streets — is even more dangerous. So the ordinance, designed to keep kids safer, would actually make them less safe.

label: Evaluate
body: The structural pattern is: an action X has a stated purpose P; but applying X here would push the situation toward an alternative that is *worse* on P; therefore don't apply X. The flaw isn't that the purpose is wrong — the purpose is fine — it's that applying the measure backfires *against its own purpose*.

label: Goal
body: For Parallel Reasoning, find the answer with this exact shape: a measure exists for a purpose, applying it here would worsen that purpose, so don't apply it.

label: Conclusion
body: The councillor's point: don't ban skateboarding in River Park, because the ban would push kids onto something even more dangerous — the streets.

label: Evidence
body: The reasoning is straightforward. Park skateboarding is dangerous, sure. But if the park is closed off, kids will go skateboard in the streets, and that's worse. So the ordinance would produce more danger than it eliminates.

label: Evaluate
body:
The councillor's argument is missing a general principle that says "don't enact a danger-reducing ordinance if it backfires and creates more danger." Plug that principle in, and the argument is airtight: the ordinance would create more danger (streets are worse than park), so by the principle, don't enact it.
Watch for trap principles that say something different — like "only restrict activities that pose danger to *participants* " (too narrow), or "always restrict dangerous activities" (too broad and pulls the wrong way), or principles that defer to parents instead of the council.

label: Goal
body: Pick the principle that says ordinances meant to eliminate danger should not be enacted if they would lead to greater dangers.

label: Conclusion (However)
body: Beginning mediation fairly late in the process, as our human resources department proposes, would be relatively ineffective.

label: Evidence
body: There really isn't any evidence provided for the president's criticism. They open with a pair of concessions: grievence procedures should allow mediation, and mediation can be helpful. Then, they pivot into their criticism.

label: Evaluate / Goal
body: It's unusual for a Strengthen question to ask us to justify a claim that has no evidence to back it up. The pivot (however) away from the concession and into the criticism does give us something to work with, though. The president concedes that mediation is helpful, so why are they concluding that this particular HR proposal for mediation won't be? The only clue we get that might support that this proposal is an exception to the rule is the idea of "beginning mediation fairly late in the process." Predict an answer that connects starting late to being ineffective.

label: Statements
body:
causal difference-maker solidity of depends how deep pilings bridge piers on are driven Prior to 1700, pilings were driven to the point at which they refused to go any deeper.
The Rialto Bridge met the contemporary standard for refusal: "if I hit this 24 more times with my hammer, it would go at most 2 more inches"

label: Evaluate
body:
This feels like a loose assemblage of facts. The Overlapping Concepts are "solidity of piers, how deep pilings are driven, refusal standards".
But it doesn't seem like there is any Conditional logic to use, any Causality to notice, any Math to compute, or any Pivots to create tension.

label: Goal
body: Having no clue what we're looking for, let's just find the most provable answer, while being cautious any time we see stuff that sounds like it's Too Strong/Specific, an Unknown Comparison, or Out of Scope.

label: Conclusion (so it is obvious that)
body: Joan will have to do the class presentation to pass the course.

label: Evidence
body:
If Joan had gotten an A on her term paper, she could pass the course without doing the class presentation.
But she didn't get an A on her term paper.

label: Evaluate
body:
Whenever we're doing Flaw and we see any Conditional Logic, we should immediately be suspicious that the argument is going to commit an illegal negation or reversal (aka, the #1 Famous Flaw, **Necessary vs. Sufficient** ).
The first sentence has a conditional rule, signified by **if**.
If A on term paper, then pass without presentation.
So an illegal reversal would sound like, "Joan passed the course without doing the class presentation. Thus, she must have gotten an A on her term paper."
An illegal negation would sound like, "Joan didn't get an A on her term paper, so she can't pass without first doing the presentation."
And that second thing is exactly what the argument did!

label: Goal
body:
We can describe this flaw formally as confusing Necessary and Sufficient conditions. We were told in the evidence that getting an A on her term paper would have been **sufficient** to get Joan out of having to do the class presentation.
But the author is acting like it's **necessary**. He's acting like if she didn't get the A then she must do the class presentation.
We can describe the flaw conversationally by saying, "Fails to consider that there could be other things Joan potentially could have done to pass the course without doing the class presentation" (a doctor's note / extra credit / a bribe or threat from her parents / etc.)

label: Conclusion (Therefore)
body: People a century ago probably read much more than we do today.

label: Evidence
body: People who lived a century ago had few ways to amuse themselves than we do today.

label: Evaluate
body:
The author is definitely assuming the Linking idea of, "If fewer diversions, then more reading".
If we were trying to argue the Anti-Conclusion we'd be thinking,
Given that ... people 100 years ago had fewer ways to amuse themselves,
How can we still argue that ... people 100 years ago read just as much (or less) than they do today?
We might say most of them weren't literate, so they couldn't read. Or they didn't have access to books. Or they didn't enjoy reading.
We might say that the diversions they did have available to them (like fishing or baseball) were obsessions that ate up all their time.
We might say that nowadays, even though we have a much bigger number of options for how to amuse ourselves, we still gravitate mainly toward reading.

label: Goal
body: Look for a way to argue that people from a century ago didn't read that much, people nowadays read a ton, or "fewer diversions ≠ more reading".

label: Evidence
body: Physical theories can explain only why physical systems have certain physical structures and how these systems perform various physical functions.

label: Evaluate
body:
We are trying to prove that "X can't explain consciousness". So we need a proving mechanism for that, a rule that's like "If such-and-such is true, then it doesn't explain consciousness".
Did the evidence provide any such rule?
Nope. So we know for sure that the correct answer will have that structure: [? ] → can't / doesn't explain consciousness
What were we told about physical theories? How come the author is thinking they can't explain consciousness?
We're told they **only** explain why physical systems have certain structures and how those systems perform functions.
Apparently the author thinks that explaining consciousness goes beyond explaining only that type of stuff.

label: Goal
body:
Let's look for an answer like
if X only explains why physical then X can't systems have certain structures → explain + how systems perform functions consciousness
We could also use an answer that sounds like, "Explaining consciousness requires going beyond [simply explaining why physical systems have certain structures + how systems perform functions]".

label: Conclusion
body: You're assured of a fair price when purchasing a diamond from Gem World.

label: Evidence (because)
body: All diamonds sold at Gem World are certified in writing.

label: Evaluate
body:
How might we object to the conclusion?
Given that... all diamonds sold at Gem World are certified in writing, How could it still be that... you are **not** assured of a fair price when you buy a diamond there?
I guess I would want to know, "Why should I trust this certification in writing? Who certified it? Is there some (inter)national standardization for certifying diamonds? Couldn't the store owner of Gem World have just printed out a certificate that says whatever she wants it to say?
Even if the diamond is certified in writing to have certain qualities, does that mean we're assured of a fair price? Do customers know what a fair price is for a certified diamond of type X? Does Gem World add a "fair" markup to their cost? Are there any other sorts of warranties or cleanings or other add-on fees that they pressure customers into buying, which results in an unfair price?

label: Goal
body:
Since the support for the conclusion is so thin (it's certified in writing), the correct answer will probably try to boost our confidence that "certified in writing" = trustworthy evaluation.
But it could also rule out some other potential concern about ways in which Gem World might get people to pay more than a fair price.
Or it could just offer some independent evidence that makes it more plausible that Gem World sells diamonds at fair prices.

label: Statements
body:
Newtonian physics dominated for over two centuries, being applied successfully consistently and becoming one of the most highly substantiated and accepted theories ever.
Pivot (nevertheless)
Einstein's theories came to show the limits of Newtonian physics and they surpassed his view in the early 1900s, giving rise again to a physics that has so far enjoyed wide success.

label: Evaluate
body:
When we're reading an Inference paragraph and the final claim begins with some Pivot idea (but, yet, however, nevertheless), it usually creates some tension that the correct answer addresses.
Here, the tension is simply that Newtonian physics dominated and was one of the most accepted theories of science ... until it wasn't. Einstein came along and now his theories are accepted and super successful.

label: Goal
body: Let's look for a safely worded takeaway that combines what we know from the Newton / Einstein situation.

label: Given that
body: Conscientiousness is high on most firms' list of traits they want in employees.

label: Why is it that ..
body: A recent study found that when it comes to the unemployed, conscientious individuals are less likely to find jobs within 5 months than are people who when they were employed shirked their workplace responsibilities (i.e., weren't conscientious).

label: Goal
body:
It's always hard to predict answers on Paradox, but even more so when it's an EXCEPT question (because you'd have to predict four separate answers).
So let's just head to the answers, thinking, "How come conscientious people aren't finding jobs as much within 5 months / how come un-conscientious people are finding jobs more?"
What is **different** about these two groups that makes one group have a harder time finding a job and the other an easier time?

label: Setup Ideas
body:
You can't attribute the acquisition of language solely on environmental influences (though such influences do exist).
Innate mechanisms also play a role in the acquisition of language.

label: Conclusion (So)
body: The most reasonable question for us to study then, is ...

label: Evaluate / Goal
body:
We need a logical, safely-worded conclusion that would tie together the two ideas we've heard: 1. language acquisition is influenced by environment 2. language acquisition is influenced by innate mechanisms.
It's hard to predict exactly what question will go in the blank, but it should be something that blends these two influences, like... "Which is a bigger influence: nature (innate) or nurture (environment)?" "Which parts are influenced by environment, which parts are influenced by innate factors"? "How can we improve our assessments of language acquisition to reflect the different contributions of environmental factors and innate factors?"

label: Conclusion (thus)
body: Any interpretation of a literary work tells more about the critic than about the writer.

label: Intermediate Conclusion (so)
body: Interpretations need not consider the writer's intentions.

label: Evidence
body: Interpretations primarily involve imposing meaning on a literary work rather than discovering meaning in it.

label: Intermediate Conclusion (therefore)
body: A number of equally valid interpretations of a literary work may be offered.

label: Evidence
body: The meaning of a literary work is not fixed but fluid.

label: Hypothesis
body: Part of how antarctic seals manage to dive super deep and stay submerged for hours is that they store oxygenated blood in their spleens.

label: Goal
body: Look for some answer that sounds like "the stability of a nation's cultural identity will be more secure in countries without prosperity / latest tech, and less secure in countries with great prosperity / latest tech."

label: Evaluate
body:
There are three conclusions drawn?! We would certainly prioritize the main conclusion in the final sentence, but technically there are Missing Link assumptions being made at each stage of the argument.
The author is assuming all these ideas.
If meaning of work → a bunch of equally valid. is fluid, not fixed interps may be offered
If interps primarily interpretations need involve imposing, not →. not consider the discovering, meaning. writer's intentions
interpretations need. any interp tells us not consider the →. more about the critic. writer's intent than the writer
We could otherwise just ask ourselves, "why does the author think that every interpretation of a literary work tells us more about the critic than the writer", and the author would say, "Because the interpretation doesn't need to consider the writer's intentions. It primarily involves imposing meaning."

label: Goal
body:
Since there are multiple Missing Links, we should probably head to the answers and see if any of those are being tested (rather than try to come up with some potential objections first).
In particular, we should look for answers that involve the New Concept in the Conclusion, "tells us more about critic than writer".

label: Conclusion (So)
body: It is inevitable that the traditional school will not survive in our culture.

label: Intermediate Conclusion
body: Electronic media are bound to end the traditional school in our culture.

label: Evidence (this is because)
body:
The emergence of the traditional school was facilitated by the availability of relatively inexpensive printed books.
But in our current culture, the function of books in communicating information is gradually being taken over by electronic media.

label: Evaluate
body:
This is a weird argument to engage with because the evidence seems very unconvincing for the dramatic conclusion it's supposed to support. We don't really have to worry about the gap between the Intermediate Conclusion in the first sentence and the Main Conclusion in the last sentence, because if the Intermediate Conclusion is correct (if something brings an end to the traditional school) then the Main Conclusion will be correct (traditional school will not survive).
So we need to worry about the move from "electronic media is taking over the function of books" to "electronic media will end the traditional school". Why does the author think that "if something takes over the function of books, it will end the traditional school?"
The only relationship offered between 'books' and 'traditional school' is that the initial emergence of the traditional school, where students gather with a teacher in a classroom, was facilitated by the availability of books.
Couldn't a classroom with electronic media still involve a group of students gathered with a teacher in a classroom?

label: Goal
body:
Let's look for an answer pointing out the author's weird move, "If something (books) that facilitated the emergence of the traditional school is replaced by electronic media, then electronic media will end the traditional school".
Or look for an answer showing how electronic media is compatible with the traditional school continuing: "fails to consider that a group of students gathering with a teacher in a classroom could still happen, now that electronic media has taken over the function of books".

label: Given that .
body: traffic fatalities tend to decline by about 7% in areas where they pass strict laws requiring everyone in a car to wear seat belts.

label: How can it be that
body: In city X, where two years ago they passed seat belt laws, the number of traffic deaths has remained the same?

label: Evaluate / Goal
body:
Since this is Paradox-EXCEPT, we know there will be four answers that find some way to reconcile these two.
Maybe we'll find out this city's law isn't really stringent. Maybe people aren't complying with it. Maybe there are way more people in the city than there were two years ago (so the **percent** of fatalities may have gone down even though the absolute **number** is around the same).
Let's eliminate the four that help explain why the seat belt law doesn't seem like it's having the expected effect, or answers that allow us to see how even if the seat belt law is decreasing fatalities, there's still some counteractive force that is making the raw number of traffic deaths about the same as before.

label: Premises
body: The passage walks through a chain of causes: critics complain about cost; that complaint puts budgetary pressure on the programs; the pressure to be cheaper and faster ends up causing manufacturing flaws — which are a safety problem.

label: Evaluate
body:
So we have two problems on the table: *cost* (the original complaint) and *safety* (the manufacturing flaws). And the passage tells us that the response to the cost problem is making the safety problem worse.
For Most Supported, we want the simplest, most directly supported takeaway. The cleanest one here is: trying to solve one problem (cost) can make another problem (safety) worse.

label: Goal
body: The right answer captures that dynamic — addressing one problem can exacerbate another.

label: Conclusion
body: Hatha yoga is a powerful tool for helping people quit smoking.

label: Evidence
body: In a trial, people who practiced hatha yoga and got individual counseling reduced smoking and cravings as much as did people who went to traditional self-help groups and got individual counseling.

label: Evaluate
body:
Given that yoga + counseling = self-help + counseling (in terms of reducing smoking / craving)
How could we argue that Hatha yoga is **not** a powerful tool?
Well, first of all we need to watch out for the vagueness of "reduced smoking and cravings as much as X".
I can say "throwing eggs at my neighbor's house engendered as much good will as did stealing their mail". That doesn't mean that either action actually engendered good will. (They might be tied for engendering ZERO good will)
Similarly, maybe self-help + counseling doesn't reduce smoking and cravings much at all. In that case, if hatha yoga + counseling reduces a comparable level, then hatha + counseling also don't reduce smoking and cravings much at all. Thus, it would be hard to call hatha yoga a powerful tool.
Finally, maybe self-help + counseling does powerfully reduce smoking and cravings, but it's all because of the counseling. Thus, hatha + counseling would also powerfully reduce smoking and cravings, but not because hatha yoga is a powerful tool, rather because counseling has that effect on its own.

label: Goal
body: Look for an answer saying "self-help + counseling does powerfully reduce smoking and cravings" or an answer saying "the smoking/craving reduction that's occurring is not caused purely / mainly by the individual counseling".

label: Conclusion
body: A newly acted law should be immune from repeal for a while, unless things are dire.

label: Goal
body:
There's nothing to evaluate here. To strengthen a hypothesis, we either need to rule out an Alternate Explanation or increase the plausibility of the Author's Explanation (the latter being way more common).
So let's get rid of four answers that either add plausibility to the idea that part of how antarctic seals can stay underwater for so long is the oxygenated blood stored in their spleens (for example, "When we remove the spleen from one of these seals, it can no longer stay submerged for as long") or that rule out an alternate explanation for how antarctic seals manage to stay submerged for so long.

label: Conclusion (therefore)
body: There is no increased health risk associated with eating fruits and veggies containing pesticide residues.

label: Evidence
body: Studies showing that increased consumption of fruits and veggies can decrease the incidence of cancer used at least some produce that contained pesticide residues.

label: Evaluate
body:
This conclusion is very strong and very counterintuitive -- there's **no** increased risk from pesticide residues? How did the author convince himself of this crazy conclusion?
He saw that in a study where people were eating fruit / veggies that contained some pesticide residues, their risk of cancer when down.
That doesn't prove that pesticides have no health risks attached. First of all, it's possible that the study's subjects would have seen their rate of cancer drop even further if the fruit and veggies were pesticide free.
If I get straight A's while smoking pot every day, that doesn't prove that "there is no downside to smoking pot every day". The fact that a positive outcome is possible while X is true doesn't show that X has no negative implications.
Secondly, the author is only paying attention to the fact that the incidence of some types of cancer went down. What if other things changed for the worse? Maybe the incidence of other types of cancer went up. Maybe the risk of heart disease or stroke went up, due to the pesticide residues.

label: Goal
body: We need a conclusion that is saying, "X is harmless" and evidence that is saying "a good outcome occurred, even while X was present".

label: Conclusion (should)
body: Judges should never mitigate punishment on the basis of motives.

label: Evidence (since)
body: Even though some criminals with admirable motives do deserve mitigated punishments, motives are just a matter of conjecture so even vicious motives can easily be presented as altruistic.

label: Evaluate
body:
The answers on Principle-Justify questions usually come in the form of "If Premise, then Conclusion", so an answer in that form would sound something like,
if motives are inherently speculative and even bad ones can be presented as altruistic, then judges should never mitigate on the basis of motives. Sometimes the answers sound more like a "should-strengthener", so an answer in that form would sound something like,
judges should try to avoid mitigating punishment based on stuff that is essentially conjecture.
The most rare form of an answer only comes into play when the argument involves **Weighing Tradeoffs**, as this one does. When authors mention the pros and cons of doing X, if they conclude "we should do X", then we want an answer saying "the pro is more important than the con". If the author concludes "we shouldn't do X", then we want an answer saying, "the con is a more important consideration than the pro".
In this argument, the advantage of mitigating punishments based on motives is that some people with admirable motives would get the lessened punishment they deserve. The disadvantage is that people who had vicious motives could still present their motives as though they were altruistic, and so they might get a lessened punishment that they don't deserve. Thus, a **Weighing Tradeoffs** answer here might sound like,
It's more important that we don't let vicious people get undeserved lessening of their punishment than it is that admirable people get a deserved lessening of their punishment.

label: Goal
body: We know we need a principle that informs a judge how she should handle punishment / sentencing. Should she or shouldn't she be factoring in motives? We want our answer to help us say, "don't lessen the punishment based on motives".

label: Roxanne's Claims
body:
1. People concerned about protecting endangered elephants from poachers should buy no new ivory.
2. The new and old ivory markets are entirely independent, so purchasing antique ivory is fine (doesn't provide poachers with incentive to obtain more new ivory)
3. If the ivory you're buying isn't at least 75 years old, you can't buy it in good conscience.

label: Salvador's Response (if any)
body:
1. I disagree. People concerned about protecting endangered elephants from poachers should buy no ivory at all.
2. I disagree. They're not entirely independent. If the supply of antique ivory were able to adequately meet the demand for ivory, then the demand for new ivory would go down. There are people who are hoping to buy antique ivory but willing to buy new ivory if they can't find antique ivory.
3. No comment.

label: Goal
body:
Let's look for an answer talking about whether or not people worried about endangered elephants are cool as along as they're buying antique ivory, or whether they should buy no ivory at all.
Or, look for an answer talking about whether the new and old ivory markets are entirely independent.

label: Salvador's Conclusion (therefore / should)
body: People who are worried about protecting endangered species should refrain from buying any ivory at all.

label: Salvador's Evidence
body:
Current demand for antique ivory exceeds the supply, so people who'd prefer to buy antique but are willing to buy new ivory end up buying new ivory instead.
If concerned people refrain from buying any ivory, demand for new ivory will drop.

label: Evaluate
body:
Salvador's conclusion is about people who are worried about endangered species and thus want to buy antique ivory.
He's saying, "Sorry, y'all can't buy any ivory."
Why not? What's wrong with antique ivory? Nothing, directly. But indirectly buying antique ivory reduces the supply of antique ivory which then makes it more likely that someone with less conscience will buy new ivory when they can't get their hands on antique ivory.

label: Goal
body: We need an answer saying something like, "If your harmless action (buying antique) would set off a chain of consequences that would lead to someone else doing a harmful action (buying new, thus keeping demand for new ivory high enough to encourage poachers to kill elephants), then you shouldn't do your harmless action."

label: Conclusion (Thus)
body: Cars with air bags are no safer than cars without air bags.

label: Evidence
body: Stats show that cars without air bags are less likely to be involved in accidents than are cars with air bags.

label: Evaluate
body:
This conclusion is what we might call Anti-Causal. Most of us may think that air bags make a car safer (because they can prevent you from dying in a front-end collision, where your head is thrown towards the steering wheel).
The author is trying to rain on that parade: sorry, cars with air bags aren't safer.
Really? Why not.
Because cars with air bags are more likely to be involved in accidents.
Okay, well whether or not you're involved in an accident isn't really our concern. Air bags aren't designed to prevent us from getting into accidents. They're designed to make any accidents we get into less catastrophic to our bodies.
We could potentially argue that "likelihood of getting into an accident" has nothing to do with how air bags are meant to make you safer.
The author might be thinking that "when an air bag is added to car, it makes the car harder to drive, which is why more accidents involve cars with air bags". We could offer an alternate explanation for the asymmetry and say, "Dude, more accidents involve cars with air bags, not because air bags make a car harder to drive, but just because air bags are now standard in most cars. If 90% of the cars on the road have air bags, then obviously accidents are more likely to involve cars that have air bags. That doesn't mean an air-bagged version of a Civic is less safe than a non air-bagged version of a Civic."

label: Goal
body:
Look for an answer complaining that we don't measure the safety boost of air bags in terms of "avoiding accidents" but rather in terms of "reducing the severity of injuries that come from accidents".
Or look for an answer supplying an alternate explanation (an excuse ) for the statistic that makes air bags look bad, like, "The real reason more accidents involve cars with air bags is because of X, not because of the air bag itself".
Or maybe they will say that this author is guilty of a bit of a Self-Contradiction, since her first claim "air bags greatly reduce the risk of serious injury in an accident" seems to undermine her conclusion that "cars with air bags are no safer".

label: Conclusion (Therefore)
body: Ashley is unlikely ever to collect a stone not originally from Tanzania.

label: Evidence (because)
body: Ashley collects only tanzanite stones, and all known deposits of the mineral tanzanite are in Tanzania.

label: Evaluate
body:
This is a pretty reasonable argument. If you only collect T stones and all known sources of T are from place X, then it's likely that all the stones you collect are originally from place X.
There are several repeating symbols (Tanzania, Ashley, tanzanite are all mentioned twice), so it's probably worth trying to think about how this argument works as an algebraic recipe:
Prem 1: all known X's come from A. Prem 2: This person only collects X's. Conc: This person is unlikely to collect something not from A.

label: Goal
body:
The conclusion should have a probable / likely / unlikely type strength.
The premises should have a clear overlapping term: - all known examples of **X** are from A. - this person/thing uses only **X**.

label: Conclusion (it seems, then)
body: The VNO is a functioning sensory organ in most humans.

label: Evidence
body:
Most humans have a VNO that is detectable microscopically.
When researchers have stimulated VNO cells, research subjects have reported experiencing subtle smell sensations.

label: Evaluate
body:
Given that ... researchers have stimulated VNO cells and subjects have said, "Yup, I feel like I'm smelling something",
How can we argue that... VNO is **not** a functioning sensory organ in most humans?
Hmm, this seems tricky. If stimulating the cells of an organ causes you to have sensory experiences, then doesn't it qualify as a functioning sensory organ?
You don't have to use an organ for it to be considered functioning. I might have a functioning vacuum cleaner in the closet, even though I never plug it in and vacuum my floors.
Technically, the evidence never said that stimulating VNO cells **caused** the subjects to experience smells.
It's just, " **when** those cells were stimulated, the subjects **reported** experiencing smells."

label: Goal
body:
Maybe we could weaken by saying "other cells were stimulated .. like olfactory ones that are also inside noses, so THAT'S why the subjects reported smells", or we could say "even though the subjects reported smells, that doesn't mean they were really smelling something. Subjects often say what they think the researchers want them to say."
Let's find an answer that offers an alternate explanation for why the subjects reported smelling things, as their VNO cells were stimulated. Or look for any answer that undermines the plausibility that the VNO is a functioning organ.

label: Goal
body: Look for an answer reinforcing the idea that they'd prefer soft suede over bare wire if they have that option, but they care way more about the milk than about the suede vs. wire.

label: Background Claims
body:
conditionals (only, will)
Great econ → all the latest prosperity electronic tech
great econ prosperity nation's people and → bombarded w/ how all the latest elec tech ppl elsewhere live
causal chain ( this will increase, leading to)
1. You live in a country with all the latest tech and economic prosperity. 2. You get bombarded with images of how people in other countries live. 3. This increases your tendency to question their own customs and traditions. 4. This leads to a dissolution of those customs and traditions.

label: Setup
body: What do we think will be true about "the stability of a nation's cultural identity"?

label: Evaluate
body:
Inference questions are usually testing our ability to see Overlapping Concepts. We need to see that "a stable cultural identity" is the logical opposite of the concept of "questioning your culture's customs and traditions / a dissolution of your culture's customs and traditions".
That means that "stable cultural identity" is the logical opposite of where our causal chain ends.
Suppose we said, "If you eat that mushroom, you'll get sick. If you get sick, you'll screw up the job interview. If you screw up in the interview, you won't get hired."
Then they say, "Hence, getting hired for this job will likely _____ ", they would be presumably fishing for "... depend on **not** eating that mushroom".
If you don't want the end of the causal chain to happen, then avoid doing the beginning of the causal chain. In this case, we're saying, "If you want to avoid the dissolution of your nation's cultural identity, then... - don't be a nation with great economic prosperity? - don't be a nation with all the latest tech? - don't let your people be bombarded with images of how other countries live?
These don't really sound like preventable things. The first two you wouldn't want to avoid. You want prosperity. You want all the latest tech. The 3rd one is told to us as a non-debatable consequence of the first two. If you have the tech and the prosperity, then you will be bombarded, so you will have your nation's identity destabilized.

label: Conclusion
body: If everybody accepts that we're just natural objects subject to natural forces outside our control, it will inevitably lead to a general moral decline.

label: Evidence (after all)
body:
If people don't think they're responsible for their actions, they'll feel unashamed when they act immorally.
If everybody starts feeling unashamed when they act immorally, it's bound to lead to a general moral decline.

label: Evaluate
body:
The author's conclusion is saying that "X will inevitably lead to a general decline in morality".
The author's evidence gives us a chain of logic that takes us to "general decline in morality". What triggers it?
If people do not believe they are responsible for their actions.
Did the author's conclusion say "people are going to stop believing they were responsible for their actions"?
No it was talking about everybody believing (universal acceptance of theories saying) that humans are just natural objects, subject to natural forces outside our control.
The author must be assuming that, "If we think we're just natural objects subject to forces outside our control, then we will stop believing we're responsible for our actions".
No, so the correct answer will try to establish that. The author just said that
When we find our Conclusion on Sufficient Assumption, we can ask ourselves if anything in the conclusion was never discussed in the Evidence. In this case, "Universal acceptance of scientific theories that regard humans only as natural objects subject to natural forces outside our control" was only discussed in the conclusion.
Thus, that idea will have to be in the correct answer.
If we want to see the Conclusion as the logic path we're trying to build, we can write it with an extended conditional: Univ ------------------------------------> gen mor accept decline
We can think about what pieces of that logic path the evidence has given us: ~believe ---> feel ---------> gen mor resp unashamed decline
The correct answer needs to give us this first piece, in order for us to assemble the logic path the conclusion is taking.
Univ ---> ~believe accept resp
Put more simply, the conclusion is saying A ----------------------------> D and the evidence provided so far has given us B ------> C -------> D so we want the answer to give us A -----> B
When we combine answer + evidence, we get the logic path of the conclusion.

label: Goal
body:
Let's look for "If we all accept that humans are natural objects subject to natural forces, then we will not believe we're responsible for our actions".
The correct answer might be in contrapositive form, and trap answers might combine these ideas but in illegal reversed or negated form.

label: Conclusion
body: Increasing the severity of legal penalties for breaking the law may increase people's tendency to ignore the welfare of others.

label: Evidence
body: Increasing threat of severe penalty for breaking the law decreases tendency to feel guilt or shame when breaking the law, whereas tendency to feel guilt or shame reduces the tendency to break the law.

label: Evaluate
body:
There is essentially a three part causal sequence described: threat of legal guilt / shame tendency to penalty → for breaking → break law goes up law goes down goes up
The author basically establishes that increasing severity of penalties might create a feedback loop that leads to more crimes.
There is a big language shift, though, from "amplify people's tendency to commit transgression" in the premise, to "amplify people's tendency to ignore the welfare of others" in the conclusion.

label: Goal
body:
Look for an answer saying "when you commit a transgression, you ignore the welfare of others"?
Or look for any answer that, when negated, would allow us to argue that we could increase the severity of legal penalties and **not** see an uptick in people ignoring the welfare of others.

label: Curious Fact
body: What caused the disappearance of the dinosaurs?

label: Author's Explanation
body: A large comet collided with Earth, causing a cloud of dust to enshroud the planet, cooling the climate for long enough that it resulted in the dinosaurs' demise.

label: Evaluate
body:
We could have broken this down into a Conclusion (comet theory is plausible) and Evidence (here's what comet theory says), but let's get straight into our real work:
1. Is there an Alternate Explanation for the Curious Fact? 2. How plausible is the Author's Explanation?

label: Goal
body: The correct answer should either give us an alternate explanation for why the dinosaurs disappeared, or it should make it seem implausible that they were killed by a comet that covered the Earth in dust and cooled the climate down for a while.

label: Conclusion
body: Government by referendum (rather than by elected reps) tends to diminish the welfare of society.

label: Evidence
body: The more equally and widely political power is distributed among the citizenry, the less likely [large-scale government projects designed to benefit everyone] are to receive funding. This is because these projects usually benefit some small segments of society, at first at least, more than others.

label: Evaluate
body:
This argument has a sort of **Parallel Claim** conclusion.
for example
Hot dogs are gross. Thus, some delicacies shouldn't be served at a wedding.
This would assume that hot dogs = delicacy gross = shouldn't serve at a wedding
Similarly, this argument is doing this: More widely distrib, less large scale political power govt projects
Thus, govt by diminishes welfare referendum, not reps of a society

label: Goal
body:
So it's assuming that "there's more widely distributed political power in a government by referendum, than in one with elected representatives "
And it's assuming that "having fewer large-scale government projects designed to benefit everyone... diminishes the welfare of a society"

label: Conclusion (it follows that)
body: One who aids other primarily out of a desire for praise does not deserve praise for that aid.

label: Evidence (because)
body: People merit praise only for those actions motivated by a desire to help others.

label: Evaluate
body:
We're trying to prove that a certain group of people do not deserve praise for certain aid.
The evidence kindly provided us with a mechanism for proving that someone doesn't deserve aid:
action is not motivated → don't deserve by a desire to help others praise for it
So all we need to do to prove our conclusion is establish that "people who aid primarily out of a desire for praise" are "not motivated by a desire to help others".

label: Goal
body:
Look for an answer that gets us from
aiding primarily out → not motivated by of a desire for praise desire to help others

label: Evidence
body: In the short-term, a new law is likely to be painful, while the long-term benefits are initially obscure because it takes a while for people to learn how to use the law to their benefit.

label: Evaluate
body:
Normally with Strengthen + Principle question, we anticipate a possible answer by saying, "If evidence, then conclusion". It seems hard to do that here.
We still want to focus a lot of energy on what the Conclusion is trying to prove. It wants a period of immunity for new laws, so that they can't be quickly repealed.
Why? Because at first the law might hurt, but in the long-term it might be for the better, so we need this period of immunity to force us to "stick it out" through the initial rough period.
When a Principle question's evidence contains a good thing and a bad thing, (we call it **Weighing Tradeoffs** in the Question Feature menu), we often are just looking for a strengthener that tells us which of those is more important.

label: Goal
body: Look for something that sounds like, "The possible long-term benefits are worth the short term pain".

label: Conclusion (hence)
body: This stone must be more recent than "very, very old".

label: Evidence
body: The druid stones discovered in Ireland are very, very old. But this druid stone was discovered in Scotland.

label: Evaluate
body:
This argument is so bad that it might be hard to figure out how to object. His argument was, "because this stone was discovered in Scotland, that means it's not an old stone." Why not? Why can't Scotland have old stones?
It's not enough to just find the argument laughable. We have to be able to describe how the author got confused. Why did the author think that "being from Scotland" meant "recent / not old"?
When we're doing Flaw questions, we want to be on the lookout for the 10 famous flaws, since the argument is committing one of them about 40% of the time.
The most famous of the famous flaws is **Necessary vs. Sufficient**, in which the author supplies a conditional premise, but then uses that rule in an illegal backwards or negated way.
This argument feels like an illegal negation. When it comes to druid stones, we know that Discovered in Ireland → very, very old If we made an argument that was an illegal negation of that rule, what would it sound like?This stone was Not-Discovered in Ireland. Therefore, it is Not very, very old.
That's how we're supposed to hear the author's premise to conclusion move.

label: Goal
body: Let's look for something complaining about the Necessary vs. Sufficient move, or something pointing out that "Ireland isn't necessarily **the only** place with very, very old druid stones. Scotland might also have very, very old druid stones."

label: Curious Fact
body: Why was there a decline in wheat production around 2900 B.C. (as barley increased sharply)?

label: Author's Explanation
body: Because of too much irrigation and not enough drainage, there was an accumulation of salt in the soil (and the salt was bad for the wheat, presumably).

label: Evaluate / Goal
body:
We can Strengthen an author's explanation / hypothesis two ways:
**rule out** an Alternate Explanation for the curious fact, or **increase** the plausibility of the Author's Explanation

label: Conclusion
body: ESP is a myth and the public is deluded by these experiments in which ESP is purportedly demonstrated.

label: Evidence (for)
body: A prominent researcher has admitted to falsifying data on psychic phenomena in order to obtain additional grants.

label: Evaluate
body:
The move from premise to conclusion here is so drastic we might get whiplash.
Because one researcher working vaguely in the ESP space has admitted to falsifying data to obtain grants, this author is saying we can therefore conclude that the whole supposed phenomenon of ESP is a myth. Every controlled experiment that has purported to demonstrate its existence has just been a lie that is deluding the public.
This argument would be analogous to saying, "A climate researcher has admitted to falsifying some data in order to obtain additional grants. Therefore, the whole panic over global warming is a myth and the public has been deluded by this fear mongering."

label: Goal
body: Let's find an answer saying that one researcher's dishonest behavior doesn't show that ESP is a myth. We don't even know for sure if this researcher's dishonest behavior related directly to demonstrating ESP's existence. But no matter what it related to, it's not grounds for rejecting ESP.

label: Given that
body: Airport expansion is warranted only by increases in air traffic volume

label: and that
body: Over the past two years passenger volume has dramatically declined (and it'll probably be at least five years before passenger volume returns to the previous level, let alone exceeds it).

label: Why is it that
body: Airports are going ahead with plans to expand their passenger terminal facilities now?

label: Evaluate
body: Since expansion is justified by increases in passenger volume, but we don't expect an increase in passenger volume for at least five years, shouldn't the airport be waiting at least five years before expanding?

label: Goal
body: There must be some positive about doing the expansion now that motivates the airline's decision (cheaper labor? easier to do when the airport is less crowded? extra money in the budget this year? tax incentive?)

label: Conclusion
body: These frequent changes in the classification systems are just a ploy by the publishers to make libraries buy their products.

label: Evidence
body: Because they're expensive, the only way to sell copies of them is to make the potential buyers believe they need to adopt the most recent system.

label: Implied Conclusion
body: Banning cloning because clones would exist to indulge the vanity of their "originals" is not a good reason.

label: Implied Intermediate Conclusion
body: We already tolerate "clones" that exist to indulge the vanity of their "originals": parents and children.

label: Evidence
body: It's not illegal to use a person as a vehicle for your ambitions. Maybe you wanted to be a tennis player or a chemist so you push your child (your 'clone') to achieve in those areas. You don't have to have been born in a test tube to be an extension of someone's ego.

label: Conclusion (therefore)
body: Employers should engage employees in nonthreatening dialogues that emphasize the positive contributions of the employee to the development of ideas that improve efficiency.

label: Evaluate
body:
This feels like a famous **Ad Hominem** at first, since we're dismissing a point of view based on the ulterior motive / vested interest of the source.
So the answer may sound like that. But we should also think about other ways to argue the Anti-Conclusion: these changes are **not** just a ploy to make money.
How could it be that there are legitimate reasons to make frequent changes in the classification systems?
Maybe technology or the publishing industry changes quickly enough that systems need altering or would become much more easy to use by altering?
What about the Premise to Conclusion connection? Can we object to the move from "If the only way to sell your product is to convince buyers that they need it" to "thus your product is just a ploy to make money"?
Sure, aren't all products more or less forced to convince buyers that they need the product? That's how advertising works. Even if a product has value, it might not be obvious to the consumer. When Keurig K-Cups came out, I'm sure people were like, "That looks dumb", until they were convinced they needed that easy and environmentally-reckless a way to make average tasting coffee.

label: Goal
body: Find an answer complaining that the author is concluding there's no legitimacy to the new classification systems just because the publishers make money selling them, or an answer explaining why frequent changes might be legitimately justified, or an answer pointing out that to a certain extent the only way to sell any product is to convince buyers that they need your product.

label: Conclusion (So / it is clear)
body: Experiencing an earthquake can cause people to dream about earthquakes.

label: Evidence
body:
There's a study where students in California and students in Ontario kept records of their dreams for six months.
Almost none of the students in Ontario reported dreaming about quakes. None of them had ever experienced an earthquake.
The California group experienced an earthquake 3 months into the study, and half of that group reported dreaming about earthquakes in the final three months of the study.

label: Evaluate
body:
Since the author is presenting the data from an experiment/study and then concluding something causal, we can use our Explain Curious Fact framework.
Curious Fact ... How come half the Cali students recorded a dream about earthquakes in the latter 3 months of the study?
Author's Explanation ... Those students experienced an earthquake around the 3 month of the study, and that experienced caused the subsequent dreams about quakes.
The two pressure points we care about are, 1. Alternate Explanations for the curious fact 2. the plausibility of the Author's Explanation
Although Weaken / Flaw / Evaluate / Nec Assump are all more likely to test **alternate explanations**, Strengthen is more likely to test **plausibility of author**.
The most common form to a plausibility-strengthener is something that takes the form of No Cause, No Effect.
Since the author thinks that experiencing the earthquake caused the earthquake dreams, we could strengthen with an answer like, "The California students who were traveling out of state during the Cali quake (and thus didn't experience the quake) **didn't** have earthquake dreams."

label: Goal
body: Let's look for something improving the plausibility that the earthquake, not something else, caused these dreams.

label: Statements
body:
Overlapping Idea (wasting resources) It's wrong to waste natural resources. + It's a waste of natural resources to burn huge amounts of trash in incinerators.
**infer:** it's wrong to burn huge amounts of trash in incinerators.
Comparison When trash is recycled, fewer resources are wasted.
**infer:** it's less wrong to recycle trash than it is to burn huge amounts in incinerators
Conditional (if = left side, sufficient) incinerator built → less trash recycled
Reason for Judgment (because X, should not y)
Because building a new incinerator would lead to less trash being recycled, the city shouldn't do it.

label: Evaluate
body:
This feels like too much of a mess to predict. There are five distinct claims. There are several Overlapping Ideas (wasting resources, building incinerators, recycling trash).
There are some opinions and some causal/conditional ideas that don't quite chain together.

label: Goal
body:
Let's stay flexible and lean towards softer more provable language if it's offered. We need something we can derive from any subset of the available facts.
But the gist is that recycling trash is better than burning trash in an incinerator (because it wastes fewer resources), and since building an incinerator would lead to less recycling and more burning, we shouldn't do it.

label: Conclusion (establish that)
body: Most people would want to be informed if they had any serious medical condition.

label: Evidence
body: In a bunch of recent studies, over 80 percent of people surveyed said they would want to be told.

label: Evaluate
body:
Within the survey population, it was true that "most people wanted to be informed if they developed a serious medical condition".
So the only possible way to weaken this argument is to say that the survey population isn't representative: it's too small / it's an atypical group of people / they were biased or pressured into answering a certain way.

label: Goal
body:
Look for answers that either make this survey seem sketchy, like it wouldn't speak for most people in most situations; it's skewed for some reason.
Or just look for any other answer that suggests that people **don't** want to be informed if they end up developing a serious medical condition.

label: Background
body: ASA and TPA are both used for the same purpose, but TPA, which costs more, would save at most two more lives out of every 50 patients.

label: Conclusion
body: But financial saving involved in using ASA over TPA must also be weighed against the extra grieving that using ASA could cause.

label: Evidence
body: The relatives of patients who die just because they were given the less expensive medicine would be particularly upset.

label: Evaluate
body:
We start with a couple background facts before we hit the Author's Pivot with the **However**.
**But / yet / however** usually signals that we're shifting from background and/or counterpoint claims into the Author's Argument.
But the pivot word itself doesn't tell you whether you'll hear, But Conclusion, because Evidence or But since Evidence, Conclusion
In this case, the "since" shows us that the first half of the last sentence is a Premise and the second half is the Conclusion.

label: Goal
body: We need to look for a re-wording of "the money saved by using ASA would have to be weighed against the particular grieving it might cause when people die after having received the cheaper treatment".

label: Evaluate
body: This is a weird argument since the author is rebutting the first sentence but never explicitly issues a rebuttal conclusion. We can just surmise from the context that she's saying, "I don't find your reason for banning cloning compelling: after all, it's similar to what we currently tolerate when it comes to parents and their children."

label: Goal
body: The question is asking us about the second sentence, which was part of the author's **Support** (the 2nd, 3rd, and 4th all helped support the author's implicit rebuttal).

label: Trent's Conclusion (So)
body: The cause of the dinosaur extinctions must have been due not to asteroid impact but some other kind of cause.

label: Evidence
body: Based on the crater, we can tell that the asteroid was not large enough to produce the sort of dust you'd need to block out the Sun. Plus, the extinction took many years, not just one or two.

label: Evaluate
body:
Given that ... the extinction would have taken many years and that the asteroid doesn't seem large enough to create the amount of dust it would take to block out the sun and cool the planet beyond the capacity of the dinosaurs or their plant food to adapt,
How can we argue that... the extinctions **were** due to asteroid impact?
Maybe we could argue that the dust does last in the atmosphere for many years. Maybe there was some other simultaneous thing happening that augmented the ability of dust from the impact to cool the earth. Maybe the asteroid impact caused other stuff to happen (like hurricanes) that killed off the dinosaurs.
But importantly, Trent's conclusion isn't limited to saying, "the extinctions weren't due to the Yucatan impact". He's saying something more broadly, that the extinctions weren't due to any asteroid impact; they were due to some other kind of cause. So even if the Yucatan impact wasn't big enough, maybe there was some other asteroid impact that was big enough.

label: Goal
body: It seems very hard to predict an answer. It's very unlikely to be a Linking answer. We'll probably find an answer that, if negated, allows us to argue that an asteroid impact **was** the cause of the dinosaurs' extinction.

label: Conclusion (Hence)
body: Science is arbitrary.

label: Evidence (since)
body:
The selection of a unit of measurement is always arbitrary.
It is impossible to do science without measuring. It's impossible to measure without having first selected units of measurement.

label: Evaluate
body:
This argument screams to be diagrammed algebraically, because it combines the two telltale signs: conditional logic and repeating symbols.
The concepts "science / measuring / units of measurement / arbitrary " are all used twice, so we'll just assign A / B / C / D to them in order to quickly write an abstract recipe.
P1: It's impossible to A without B. A → B P2: It's impossible to B without C. B → C P3: C is always D. C → D C: A is D. A → D

label: Goal
body:
Let's look for an answer with two premises that give us this A requires B, B requires C chain.
We also want a premise that says that C is D (it might not feel conditional, like the others did). And then we want a conclusion that says A is D.

label: Becksteins Claims
body:
(explicit) 1. ASL is the native language of many N. Americans 2. ASL is not a foreign language 3. No students should be permitted to satisfy the university's foreign language requirement by learning it.
(implicit) 1 → 2. If X is a native language of many North Americans, then it's not a foreign language. 2 → 3. If X isn't a foreign language, then no student should be allowed to satisfy the university's foreign language requirement by learning it. 1 → 3. If X is a native language of many North Americans, then no student should be allowed to satisfy the university's foreign language requirement by learning it.

label: Sedleys responses
body:
1. No comment 2. No comment 3. No comment
1 → 2. Kinda disagrees. Disagreeing would mean that you're saying "something could be the native language of many North Americans but still be considered a foreign language". While it appears that Sedely would consider French and Spanish examples of this, she technically never establishes that she consider them foreign languages.
2 → 3. Kinda disagrees. Sedley thinks that it's okay for a student to satisfy the university's foreign language requirement by learning a language that is the native language of many North Americans. But disagreeing with Beckstein's final move means saying, "sometimes it's okay to satisfy the foreign language requirement by learning a language that isn't a foreign language." Sedley doesn't provide a clear example of "X isn't a foreign language but it **is** okay to satisfy the foreign language requirement.
1 → 3. Definitely disagrees.

label: Evaluate / Goal
body:
Beckstein makes a three part argument: X is native lang → X is not a → Can't satisfy of many NA's foreign lang foreign lang req w/ X
Taken together, Beckstein thinks that if X is a native language of many North Americans, then learning it can't satisfy the university's foreign language requirement.
Sedley disagrees. She gives the examples of French and Spanish, which are the native language of many North Americans, but clearly **can** satisfy the university's foreign language requirement.
So let's look for an answer addressing the connection between those two concepts.

label: Conclusion (Therefore)
body: Consumers have little reason to object to the common practice of modifying existing models without giving the modified versions new names.

label: Evidence
body: Manufacturers' modifications to existing models are invariably improvements that benefit the buyer.

label: Evaluate
body:
Given that ... any modification the manufacturer makes to Product X will be an improvement,
How can we argue that... there **is** a reason for consumers to not like this practice of updating Product X without giving the modified version a new model name?
Maybe someone doesn't want the new and improved model? They liked the older one better for some reason? Maybe they're buying Product X for a friend and they also own an older version of Product X, so it peeves them when they find out that the version of X they just bought for their friend has some dope improvement that theirs doesn't have?
Maybe they think they're getting the newer model, but some store has really old, unsold inventory, so while everyone else is selling the newer model of X, some store is selling the older version.

label: Goal
body: It's hard to predict the specific answer, so we'll just cling tight to our Anti-Conclusion and think, "given that any modification will be an improvement, how could this whole system of not labeling modified versions of the product make a consumer mad or frustrated?"

label: Evidence
body: Selective breeding, as we've done with farm animals for millennia, is a crude form of genetic engineering.

label: Evaluate
body:
This argument is a little hard to organize. We don't necessarily have to call that last idea an Intermediate Conclusion, but it seems like an opinion we could potentially object to or ask about.
In terms of how the plan is supposed to work, the author assumes that "if a plan is unlikely to elicit positive reactions from employees, it'll take longer for the ideas to be implemented" whereas "if a plan is more likely to elicit positive reactions, it'll take less long for the ideas to be implemented".
But in terms of getting from the last sentence to the Main Conclusion, the author assumes that "if a plan would result in ideas getting implemented more quickly and effectively, then an employer should do that idea."

label: Goal
body: We either want to be more convinced that the plan will achieve the goal, or we want to connect the positive idea of "implemented more quickly and effectively" to the conclusion language of "should do it".

label: Conclusion
body: The new health program will lead to an increased risk of heart disease among employees.

label: Evidence
body: A sudden increase in exercise can cause a heart attack. When anyone suddenly increases their amount of exercise, they increase their risk of heart attack.

label: Evaluation
body:
When we see the Conclusion is about "this new health program will lead to X", we would often see a premise that says "after all, this new health program will lead to Y", and then we would know that the author is assuming that "Y leads to X".
In this case, though, we've been given nothing in the evidence about what the new health program will do. Instead we're being given the "Y leads to X", and we'll need to assume that "the new health program will lead to Y".
To say the same thing conditionally, proving the conclusion means creating this logic train: new health ---------------------→ increased program risk of HD
The evidence gives us this part of the train: sudden ----→ increased increase risk of HD
Our answer needs to give us the missing part: new health --→ sudden program increase

label: Goal
body: Look for an answer saying that the new health program will lead to some of the employees of the company suddenly increasing their exercise.

label: Conclusion
body: The similarities between these two computer workstations are too fundamental to be a coincidence.

label: Evidence
body: They look alike, work alike, have the same odd shape, identically placed control panels, same control, and same options for adjustments and enhancements.

label: Evaluate
body:
Whenever we do Main Conclusion and Role questions, remind ourselves that the Conclusion is usually earlier than the Support. 90% of the time, it's the first sentence of the paragraph, or it's some sort of Rebuttal claim.
The first sentence here is not an opinion, so it can't be the author's conclusion. The first and second sentences sound like chronological facts. The third sentence is an attribution: "The two companies **claim...** "
When we hear an attribution, what do we expect?
We expect to hear the author **pivot** (but, yet, however) into a rebuttal. That 4th sentence is our author's opinion. Everything that follows it supports it.

label: Goal
body:
Because this question stem says Main Point rather than Main Conclusion, it may sound like the 4th sentence, our main conclusion.
Or it may sound a little more holistic. Main Point is rare, but the answer tends to involve implied conclusions or broader restatements.

label: Naima's 1st claim
body:
Once implemented, the new comp system would be smoother and more efficient than the current system. Does Nakai argue that the new system would **not** be smoother or **not** be more efficient than the current system?
No, they don't talk at all about its potential smoothness or efficiency.

label: Naima's 2nd claim
body:
We should devote the resources to convert to the new system as soon as possible. Does Nakai argue that we shouldn't devote whatever resources we'd need to switch to the new system as soon as possible?
Yes, they say we should keep the current system for as long as possible.

label: Goal
body: Since person 2 disagreed with one of person 1's explicit claims, we don't really need to go any deeper. We have a good prephrase. Let's look for an answer circling around whether we should convert to the new system as soon as possible or hold onto the current system as soon as possible.

label: Principle
body: Since it's easier for you to see mistakes in other people's work than in your own, it's a good idea to have your work checked by someone else.

label: Evaluate / Goal
body:
This isn't quite a conditional principle, but we still want to look for a scenario that seems to apply to the first half and then deliver the second half.
i.e. we want a situation where it would be easier for you to see what's wrong with someone else's than with yours, and so you ask someone else to check yours out.

label: Scientists' Belief
body: The asteroid that hit 65 million years ago around the Yucatan Peninsula caused the extinction of the dinosaurs.

label: Scientists' Results
body: The debris launched by the asteroid could have blocked sunlight and cooled the atmosphere such that food sources for herbivorous dinosaurs disappeared, and all dinosaurs would have been killed by a prolonged period of low temps. But the debris would have gone away after six months, which is too soon for the dinosaurs to freeze or for the plants to die off.

label: Evaluate / Goal
body:
Given that the debris wouldn't have lasted long enough to freeze all the dinosaurs, how can we say that the asteroid is responsible for causing the extinction of the dinosaurs?
We'll need some causal story that gets us from asteroid impact to dinosaur extinction.

label: Bernard's Rebuttal Conclusion
body: The idea of the original typewriter keyboard layout was **not** to slow down the operator (lest the typebars crash into each other).

label: Bernard's Evidence
body: These technological limitations have vanished, yet the keyboard is still laid out that way.

label: Evaluate
body:
Bernard is assuming that "if X were the original reason for Y, then once X disappears, Y would disappear."
But as many former or non-practicing Christians can tell you, "observing Jesus' birthday was the original reason for Christmas, but even if you stop observing Jesus' birthday, that doesn't mean that Christmas disappears".

label: X's 2nd Idea
body:
The proposed design for a new generating station would allow for the lowest rates. Does Y disagree?
No, Y seems to agree. She acknowledges that such a design would have "the benefit of lower rates".

label: Goal
body:
When we're **logically countering** someone, we're showing them how their rebuttal premise is compatible with our original position (sometimes we even do some logic judo and show that their rebuttal premise is actually a reason for our original position).
But we can basically prep our brain for the answer choices by saying, Slowing down typing speed **was** the reason for the original keyboard layout. Even though we no longer have to worry about typebars running into each other, we've kept that original layout **because...** _______

label: Conclusion (therefore)
body: The incentive of grades serves no essential academic purpose.

label: Evidence
body:
Students with intense interest in the material would learn it without the incentive of grades.
Students lacking all interest in the material are unaffected by such an incentive.

label: Evaluate
body:
This is a semi-famous flaw called **False Choice**, in which the author acts like the options named are the only options to consider.
There's a version of this flaw that simply fails to establish that the options mentioned are the only ones: "We can get to Vegas by limo or by charter bus. But since the charter buses are all booked, in order to go to Vegas we will have to take a limo." (Who said that limo and charter bus are the only options? He's offering us a False Choice)
And then there are versions where the author fails to perceive a middle ground between two options. The author talks about people who **always** jaywalk or who **never** jaywalk, but fails to consider people who sometimes jaywalk.
Here's **an example**, and **another example**.

label: Goal
body: The author established that grades serve no purpose for students with intense interest and for students lacking all interest. But what about all the students in between, with some interest but not intense interest? Maybe for students with a moderate amount of interest, grades still serve an essential academic purpose of incentivizing their learning of curricular content.

label: Conclusion (Hence)
body: Large governmental job retraining programs are no longer a viable option in the effort to retrain workers efficiently.

label: Evidence
body: Periodic retraining can only be efficient if it allows individual companies to meet their own short-term needs.

label: Evaluate
body:
We have a premise and a conclusion that are both talking about whether or not retraining can be efficient.
The premise says, If it doesn't meet individual companies' short-term needs, then retraining won't be efficient.
The conclusion is saying that Large governmental job retraining won't be efficient.
So the author must be assuming that Large governmental job retraining won't meet individual companies' short term needs.
Formally, the conclusion is trying to prove this: Large govt ------------------------> not retraining efficient
The premise provides this part of the chain: doesn't help ---> not companies meet efficient short-term needs
So the linking assumption we're missing is this: Large govt -------> doesn't help retraining companies meet short-term needs

label: Goal
body: Look for the missing link we spotted, 'Large governmental job retraining programs don't allow individual companies to meet their own short-term needs'.

label: Statements
body:
Since we're primarily reading for Causal, Conditional, Comparative, or Pivot wording, we would want the causal verb in each sentence to stick out to us.
Eating more fruits susceptibility to and veggies during **reduces** stroke in later middle-aged years years
This might be **because** fruits and veggies have folic acid.
Low folic acid is associated with high homocysteine (correlation), and homocysteine **contributes** to blocked arteries.
If we were trying to assemble a causal chain, it might look like this:
eat lots of → high folic acid → fruit/vegetables low homocysteine
less blocked → less likely to arteries have a stroke
The one thing that might make us nervous about this is that the middle sentence says "researchers speculate that this may be because", so we don't want to sound overconfident.

label: Goal
body: Look for a safely worded answer that reinforces one (or more) of the causal connections we were told about.

label: Conclusion (Therefore)
body: British people must have, on average, more money to spend on vacations now than they did 30 years ago.

label: Evidence
body:
30 years ago, a much smaller percentage of Brits traveled abroad for vacations than do now.
Foreign travel is, and always has been, expensive from Britain.

label: Evaluate
body:
It doesn't seem like this is testing a Missing Link, but we could say the author is assuming this move: "If a much bigger percentage of the population is taking expensive vacations nowadays, then the population on average has more money to spend on vacations nowadays."
If we switched into our Objection mindset, "given that a higher % is now taking expensive vacations abroad, how can we say that British people on average **don't** have more money to spend on vacations than 30 years ago?"
This argument assumes one possible Explanation for a Curious Fact. The author is wondering why a bigger % of Brits travel abroad for vacations nowadays and assumes the reason must be vacation money.
We want to consider Alternate Explanations (maybe they always had the money to take the trip, but they didn't have the time off from their jobs / they feared going abroad because foreigners were more hostile to Brits / they didn't have a convenient airport close to home / etc.), as well as how Plausible the author's explanation is.

label: Goal
body:
Look for an answer linking "higher % taking expensive vacations abroad" to "higher average vacation budget".
Or look for an answer **ruling out** an Alternate Explanation for why there is now a larger % taking vacations abroad.
Or look for something that would be required for the Author's Explanation to be plausible.

label: Information
body:
Mysteries often have a smart detective and dumb sidekick.
As clues are introduced, the dumb sidekick arrives at incorrect conclusions, whereas the smart detective uses those same clues to arrive at the correct solution.
For the author, having the dumb sidekick in the story is way to give readers a chance to solve the mystery (like the smart detective), as well as a way to throw them off the scent (since the dumb sidekick puts incorrect suggestions in the reader's mind).

label: Background Claims
body:
Causal (X makes Y possible) Technological progress makes economic growth and widespread prosperity possible, and makes a worker's specific skills less crucial to production.
Pivot (yet) / Causal Difference-Maker (depends) Workers' satisfaction in their work depends on believing that their work is difficult and requires uncommon skills.

label: Goal
body: Look for an answer calling out the potential difference between "the only assured way of getting X" and "the most likely way to get X"

label: Evaluate
body:
We're looking for hidden truths we can pull out. Two or more claims with overlapping information that we can combine.
The dull companion is brought up in all three sentences. The **Thus** at the beginning of the last sentence seems to show a causal connection between the 2nd and 3rd sentence.
And there's a Comparison (difference) in the 2nd sentence: companion looks at the clues, wrong solution detective looks at same clues, right solution
Maybe since the last sentence is saying that the story gives the reader enough info to solve the mystery, the answer is going to be combining these ideas to say something like, "some readers can do better at solving the mystery than the dull companion can, using the same clues".

label: Goal
body: With no clear clues, we should just head to the answers and try to find a safely worded claim that is derived by combining 2 or more ideas.

label: Conclusion (Yet ... should)
body: Insurance premiums should increase with frequency with which a person drives.

label: Evidence (after all)
body: The more you drive, the higher your chances of being involved in a mishap.

label: Evaluate
body:
The sentences leading up to the **Yet** pivot seem to just give us the background on how insurance policies determine their premium rates.
The more risk factors, the higher the premium.
So how could we possibly counter this argument.
Given that... driving more frequently increases your chances of getting into an accident, How could we still argue that... premiums **shouldn't** increase with more frequent driving?
We'd probably have to argue that people who drive a lot do have elevated risk because they're on the road more often, but maybe something else is different about them that reduces their risk.
What if the people that drive a lot tend to... - be better drivers - drive safer, better-maintained cars - drive on safe, more-isolated roads etc.

label: Goal
body: Let's look for something that's suggests that people who drive are more have some reason to also be considered a lower risk, thus we shouldn't increase their premiums just because they drive more.

label: Background
body:
The author thinks that happiness is the only thing valuable in and of itself. Other things are valuable if they contribute to happiness.
We don't approve of a bad person's being happy.
Some people think this shows that "if happiness isn't deserved, then we don't value it". And they think this then entails that "there's something besides happiness that we find intrinsically valuable." But, the happiness people deserve is determined by the amount of happiness they bring to others.

label: Evaluate
body:
I'm pretty lost here, but I blame the philosophers, who seem to be making weird leaps of logic. The fact that we don't approve of a bad person's being happy doesn't necessarily show that we value happiness only when it's deserved.
Maybe we just value happiness only when it's ours.
It also doesn't show that we think something besides happiness is valuable. Maybe we just don't want bad people to have things of value. Depriving them of things of value makes us happy.
The author is pivoting against the idea that "we find something besides happiness to be intrinsically valuable", so she presumably wants to conclude as she began: Nope, we only find happiness to be intrinsically valuable.
But she's not going to conclude something she's already said. So given that her motivation is to defend her claim that only happiness is intrinsically valuable, her final Therefore claim should be something that manages to explain away the fact that we don't approve of bad people being happy, without it meaning that we value something besides happiness intrinsically.
But it should also use the principle that "the happiness people deserve is determined by the amount of happiness they bring to others".

label: Fill-in-the Blank
body:
So, "if we don't think that bad people deserve to be happy, it's not because we value something besides happiness; it's because we don't think bad people bring happiness to others."
That's a way to explain why we don't want bad people to be happy **while still** making it seem like it's all about happiness.

label: Statements
body:
Causal Difference-Maker ( **determine** ) Climate and geology have a big causal influence on where human industry can be established.
Causal Chain (always **result** in, **bring about** ) Drastic shifts → migrations → intermingling in climate of ideas
Conditional ( **necessary** ) Rapid advances in civilization → Intermingling of ideas

label: Evaluate / Goal
body:
