Since we were provided with 1 ⇢ 2 ⇢ 3 chain, it's possible the answer will just be 1 ⇢ 3, "Drastic shifts in climate lead to intermingling of ideas (which enables rapid advance of civilization)".
There's an **overlapping idea** - intermingling of ideas. It connects climate instability with rapidly advancing civilization, so the correct answer might softly connect those two concepts.

label: Statements
body:
Some say "only cover basic, but cover it deeply"
they say "if achieve solid grasp of basic stuff, student will explore broader on their own"
Educator says "if they just learn facts w/o significance, students will suck at studying on their own"

label: Evaluate
body:
This is a Most Supported question, but because it's based of an argument structure, it's a fair bet that the Most Supported correct answer will sound a lot like a Necessary Assumption of the reasoning.
We can see our familiar PIVOT friend "But" starting the last sentence. So, since Most Supported loves to make us **Reconcile** what comes after **the Pivot** with what came before, we want to think about how the last sentence interacts with the previous ones.
Since the educators think that "solid grasp of basic" is a path that allows students to be able to study on their own,
whereas "simply learn a lot of factual info" is a path that doesn't set up students to be able to study on their own,
we can tell that the author is **Assuming a Difference**.
She must think that "helping students achieve a solid grasp of basic concepts and investigatory techniques is **not** simply learning a lot of factual information without truly understanding its significance".
In shorter words, she's assuming that "solid grasp of basic concepts" enables students to "truly understand significance of facts".

label: Evaluate
body:
When we see Pivot words in Inference paragraphs, we know we should try to Reconcile the Pivot idea with what came before it. Is there any Overlapping Concept that we see in both the first and second sentences?
Sure, they both talk about "a worker's skills".
Sentence 1 says that technological progress makes a worker's skills less crucial. Sentence 2 says that worker satisfaction depends on believing that their work requires uncommon skills.
If your skills become less crucial, then you won't feel like your job requires uncommon skills, and so your job satisfaction will go down.

label: Conclusion
body: Earth is a living organism, not merely a thing upon which creatures live.

label: Goal
body:
It's hard to predict exactly what the answer will be like, but I would anticipate that it's dealing with the comparison between these two different paths (italicized stuff is assumed) **Plan A** **Plan B** solid grasp of basic just facts on wide array can self-study well can't self-study well truly understanding doesn't truly understanding its significance? its significance (Note: Once I saw the actual answer choices, I realized I had my goal dead wrong. This is really some sort of **Apply the Principle** type question. I decided to leave my original thought process in to honor The Struggle. Once we see that these answers are new situations, to which we'll be applying the educators' advice, we want to see:
solid grasp of basic leading to ability to self-study wider breadth later or just facts without significance leading to inability to self-study later

label: Conclusion (so)
body: Building a dam would yield no overall gain in agricultural productivity in the region as a whole.

label: Evidence
body:
The dam would provide irrigation for the dry land upstream, but would reduce crops in the land downstream by reducing the amount and quality of water available there.
The productivity loss downstream would be greater than the productivity gain upstream.

label: Evaluate
body:
This argument basically said, **if we do this thing,** build the dam **something good happens** more water upstream for crops **but also something bad happens** less water downstream for crops **and bad outweighs good** loss downstream > gain upstream
**so, doing this thing provides no net gain overall.** building the dam doesn't increase crops overall

label: Goal
body: Let's for an argument saying that doing a thing would have good and bad repercussions, but since bad outweighs good, there's no net gain.

label: Principal's Comments
body: Yes, your son wasn't guilty. and Yes, your son suffered from the punishment we issued of "no recess for two days". but Sometimes people who aren't guilty nonetheless have to suffer consequences, like when you aren't involved in an accident but still have to suffer in the traffic jam that builds up because of it.

label: Evaluate / Goal
body:
It feels really hard to predict where we're supposed to go with this. Normally if we're being asked to infer, we look for facts we could combine in order to derive some inference. But the principal just makes a quick analogy.
Let's look for the most safely worded, most derivable answer we can find. It will probably have to do with spelling out how this analogy is meant to apply to the cafeteria situation.

label: Principal's Conclusion (Implicit)
body: It was appropriate that we docked the entire class two days of recess, even though not all of them were culprits.

label: Principal's Evidence
body: It's like being caught in a traffic jam caused by an accident. People who aren't involved in the accident nevertheless have to suffer by sitting in traffic until the road gets cleared.

label: Evaluate
body:
The principal's argument relies on an analogy (this situation is **like** this other situation).
Whenever we're trying to weaken or object to an Analogy, we start by thinking to ourselves, "How are these two situations **unfair** to compare?"
If we were Ms. Smith, what could we say in response to the Principal's analogy?
We might say, "yes, people in a traffic jam behind an accident have to suffer even though they weren't part of the audience. But my kid (and the other kids who didn't throw raisins) didn't **have** to suffer. That was your choice, Principal. You could have decided to just punish the offenders."

label: Goal
body: Let's look for an answer complaining that the two situations are not really fair to compare.

label: Conclusion (for this reason)
body: Computerized "expert systems" cannot be as good as human experts.

label: Evidence
body:
The hallmark of expertise is having an immediate, intuitive response to each new situation.
Computers can store millions of bits of information, but the knowledge of human experts is not stored in the form of rules and facts.

label: Evaluate
body:
This is a Comparative argument. We're comparing computers to humans and **Assuming a Difference**:
Humans do something / have something special that computers don't have.
We know that humans can be experts, but they don't get there by storing rules and facts, they benefit from the experience of thousands of situations.
Are we assuming that computers are **unable** to similarly benefit from the experience of thousands of situations? (computers that model AI often have simulated neural networks that allow them to aggregate experience similar to human brains).
Suppose computers are stuck using rules and facts — are we assuming that rules and facts **do not** enable one to have immediate, intuitive responses to each new situation?

label: Goal
body: Look for an answer establishing a clear difference between humans and computers, that helps to establish the fact that computers will not be able to have an immediate, intuitive response to each new situation.

Returning as much land as possible to an uncultivated state could restore biodiversity without a major decrease in meat production.
Rephrase: The devastation of the North American prairie ecosystem could be largely reversed without significantly decreasing meat production.

label: Evaluate
body:
The conclusion is found at the end of the argument, which is less common for Main Conclusion questions, but it does happen.
The conclusion is indirectly revealed by the premise indicator "since," which introduces the evidence regarding the natural efficiency of the prairie ecosystem. This structure provides support for the claim that reversing prairie devastation could restore biodiversity without significantly impacting meat production. label: Conclusion
body: Reducing speed limits neither saves lives nor protects the environment.

label: Evidence (This is because)
body: The more slowly a car is driven, the more time it pends on the road spewing exhaust into the air and running the risk of colliding with other vehicles.

label: Evaluate
body:
This is one for which we could definitely react with our common sense about the world. We know that driving faster is more dangerous and less eco-friendly.
Why is it more dangerous? The author thinks driving slower is more dangerous because you spend more time on the road (and any second spent on the road is time you could be getting into accidents).
Well, that's silly. If I'm in a traffic jam for an **hour**, trudging along at 2-5mph, I'll be on the highway longer than if there were no traffic and I could just zoom through in **10 mins** at 70mph. But I run zero risk of dying in a car accident if I'm going 2-5mph, whereas I could easily die in an accident going 70 mph.
Risk of dying in a car accident is in part a function of how long you're driving (as the author is thinking) but it's also a function of how fast you're driving / how in control of the vehicle you are.
Why do we know that driving fast is worse for the environment? Well, the faster you go the more gas you're burning. Cars are optimized to go highway speed (55mph) so they get their best gas mileage there. If you go 70 / 80mph, you're burning gas at a less efficient rate.
So even though a slower trip means you're "spewing exhaust" for longer, it's not at the same rate as when you're driving faster. Getting 30 mpg going moderate speeds for 1 hr can spew less exhaust than getting 20 mpg going high speeds for 45 mins.

label: Goal
body:
Ultimately, since this is Flaw, we need to think about how to describe these problems in a more abstract way.
The author focuses on one aspect of risk to life (how long you're on the road) while ignoring others (the higher risk of fatality in a high speed collision).
The author focuses on one aspect of environmental damage (how long you're driving) while ignoring other aspects (the rate of exhaust spewing, based on how efficiently / inefficiently you're running the engine).

label: Conclusion (evidence suggests that)
body: Juvenile Pacific loggerheads that feed near Baja hatch in Japanese waters 10,000 km away.

label: Evidence
body:
Loggerheads live and breed in distinct groups, some in the Pacific and some in the Atlantic.
95% of the DNA samples of the Baja turtles match DNA samples taken from turtles at the Japanese nesting sites.

label: Evaluate
body:
The author is trying to make sense of a Curious Fact: why do 95% of the DNA samples from the Baja population of loggerheads match DNA from the Japanese population of loggerheads?
Her Explanation is that loggerheads are being hatched (i.e. born) in Japan and then end up across the Pacific ocean (Baja peninsula is part of Mexico) by the time they're juveniles.

label: Goal
body:
Since this is Weaken, we either need: 1. to suggest an Alternate Explanation for the curious fact (what could be a different causal storyline that would account for 95% of the DNA samples from Baja/Japan matching?)
or
2. to undermine the plausibility of the Author's Explanation (what could hurt the storyline that these loggerheads were born in Japan and then crossed the pacific ocean to feed in Mexico, by the time they're juveniles?)

label: Conclusion (so)
body: People who tend to trust others think of a hard task as challenging, not threatening.

label: Evidence (since)
body:
People who are confident in their own abilities think of a hard task as challenging, not threatening.
People who do not believe that others distrust them are confident in their own abilities.

label: Evaluate
body:
One great question to ask ourselves once we've found the Conclusion on Sufficient Assumption is, "are there any New Terms in the Conclusion?" (because, if so, they must be in the correct answer).
The conclusion can be divided into a Naming Part and a Telling Part. N A M I N G P A R T | T E L L I N G P A R T People who tend think of hard task as to trust others challenge, not threat
Does the evidence ever talk about "People who tend to trust others"?
Nope. It talks about "People who don't believe that others distrust them". Those are very different things. The first is about whether you trust others. The second is about whether you think that others trust you.
For brevity, we'll call "People who tend to trust others", "Trusting people". We'll call, "People who don't think that others distrust them", "Trustworthy people".
The author must be assuming some link between these, since the closest the evidence ever comes to mentioning the "Trusting people" in the conclusion is the claim we get about "Trustworthy people".
The second half of the conclusion "think of hard task as challenge, not threat" is matched up in the evidence, since the last premise says "this is precisely how Group X regards such tasks".
So formally, here's the logic path we're trying to create with the Conclusion:
tend to think hard task trust -------------------------------> challenge others not threat
Here is what the evidence has given us: think others confident think hard task don't → in own → challenge distrust you abilities not threat
To complete the Conclusion's logic path, what piece needs to be added to our evidence?

label: Evaluate
body:
This is confusing. In general, when we're doing Flaw or Parallel Flaw and we see a Rebuttal style argument, we want to immediately start thinking about the two famous flaws related to rebuttals: - Ad Hominem (dismissing someone's point of view because of their biased interest / conflicting past behavior) - Unproven vs. Proven False (concluding that because someone failed to prove X that X is therefore false)
This argument feels just like Ad Hominem: M's proposal doesn't deserve our consideration, because of [some personal fact about Muller].
The personal fact about Muller seems to be that he might be a rich person (he's enjoyed large profits over the past decade).
If he were proposing to **lower** taxes on the rich, we might be like, "That seems pretty self-serving, Mullen!" But he's actually suggesting that we **raise** taxes on the rich, so it's sort of a selfless suggestion?
So this would fall under that 2nd category of Ad Hominem where we say, "Don't listen to X; they have something in their past that conflicts with what they're currently saying."

label: Goal
body: Either way we're looking for an Ad Hominem flaw, but it will probably be in the style of "something about this person's past situation conflicts with the idea they're currently suggesting, so let's not even consider their suggestion."

label: Main Conclusion (therefore)
body: Researchers would increase their chance of successfully developing a workable thinking machine if they focus on the brain's function and ignore its physical structure.

label: Intermediate Conclusion (So)
body: Thinking machines closely modeled on the brain are likely to fail.

label: Evidence / Intermediate Conclusion
body: The fact that the physical structure of the brain plays an "Important role" does not mean it plays "an essential role".

label: Evidence (after all)
body: No flying machine that's closely modeled on birds has worked. Meanwhile, workable aircraft does not share physical structure with birds.

label: Evaluate
body:
We're being asked about Yang's 3rd claim, which is prefaced by **So**. The word "so" always means you are drawing a conclusion based (at least in part) on the previous claim, or that you are announcing the causal effect of the previous claim.
Here it's a reasoning conclusion (not a report on the causal effect: i.e. "She went to visit her mom at the hospital and so she will miss the morning meeting.")
But we know that it's not the **main** conclusion, because the final sentence uses a **Therefore**. The word "therefore", just like "so", always means that you are deriving a conclusion based at least in part on the previous claim, or that you're saying the causal effect of the previous claim (much more rare).
Since this last claim is a prescriptive recommendation (that's redundant, yes), it's not the effect-half of some cause-effect pair. So we know this final claim is a conclusion that is built upon the 3rd sentence. And we know the 3rd sentence is a conclusion built upon the 2nd sentence.
The 1st sentence is supported ( after all ) by the 2nd sentence. The first two sentences team up to support the 3rd sentence, and the 3rd sentence supports the 4th sentence.
(2nd ⇢ 1st) → 3rd ⇢ 4th
Oh, the magic of keywords.

label: Goal
body:
Let's look for an answer that reflects this hierarchy of who is supporting what. And we'll probably hear this claim described as an Intermediate Conclusion, which both provides support (for the 4th) and receives support (from the 2nd and 1st).
(2nd ⇢ 1st) → 3rd ⇢ 4th

label: Main Conclusion (therefore)
body: Researchers would increase their chances of successfully developing a workable thinking machine if they focus on the brain's function and simply ignore its physical structure.

label: Intermediate Conclusion (So)
body: Thinking machines closely modeled on the brain's structure are likely to fail.

label: Intermediate Conclusion
body: The fact that the brain plays an important role in our thinking doesn't mean it plays an essential role.

label: Evidence (after all)
body: No flying machine based on the structure of birds has worked.

label: Evaluate
body:
On Evaluate questions, we basically want to use the same mindset as on Weaken questions, so we can ask ourselves how we would fight this conclusion: how could ignoring the physical structure of the brain and focusing on the brain's function fail to help us successfully develop thinking machines?
Maybe there's something crucial we can learn from looking at the brain's structure, even if we decide not to copy that structure in the thinking machine we're building. Maybe we can't understand how the brain functions unless we pay attention to its physical structure.
Finally, maybe the analogy to birds / aircraft isn't strong support. Maybe there's some crucial difference when it comes to modeling aircraft after the structure of birds vs. modeling thinking after the structure of the brain, in which the former is a bad idea but the latter is a good one.

label: Goal
body: Look for an answer that gives us some idea we could use to object to Yang's argument, to either argue that the analogy between bird/aircraft and brain/thinking is a weak one, or to argue that researchers shouldn't ignore the physical structure of the brain, because there something important to gain from studying it.

label: Evidence (But)
body: If they lose interest in that hobby, their loneliness may be exacerbated.

label: Evaluate
body:
If we're looking for a linking answer, we'd combine together Premise language and Conclusion language to get something like,
"if potentially losing interest in X would exacerbate a problem, then developing X in the first place is not a successful strategy for overcoming that problem."
How about if we were trying to think of Objections by arguing the Anti-Conclusion?
Given that... losing interest in a hobby may exacerbate loneliness, How could we say that... developing a passionate hobby **is** a successful strategy for overcoming adolescent loneliness?
We might say stuff like - who says we'll lose interest? Maybe the vast majority of people who develop an all-consuming hobby stick with it forever?
- all you're saying is that if we lose interest, our loneliness **may** be exacerbated? If the chance is really low, then is that really enough to tank this strategy? Maybe everything in life carries with it some risk of exacerbating my loneliness.

label: Goal
body:
Let's look for a linking answer like "if risks exacerbating problem, then not a successful strategy for overcoming problem"
or look for a defender answer like "the possibility of losing interest in a hobby is **not** exceedingly small" "at least some successful strategies for overcoming loneliness do not involve a risk of exacerbating that loneliness"

label: Evidence
body: Some democracies in history have resulted in some of the most oppressive societies (i.e. the least political freedom). Likewise, there have been enlightened despotisms and oligarchies that have provided a remarkable level of political freedom to their subjects.

label: Evaluate
body:
This argument feels analogous to saying, "Smoking cigarettes does not promote lung cancer. Some people who smoke cigarettes have incredibly healthy lungs. Likewise, there have been nonsmokers who developed lung cancer".
When we say "X promotes Y", we're not claiming that "X guarantees Y" or that "X is the only thing that is ever associated with Y". It's a much weaker claim than that. It's just saying that X has some causal influence on the likelihood of Y.
The author can't cherry-pick democracies that were not free and non-democracies (despotisms and oligarchies) that were free, and conclude from that that democracies don't tend to help political freedom.

label: Goal
body: Look for something complaining that the author is trying to write off a causal relationship by cherry-picking a few counterexamples that don't fit the causal relationship.

label: Tony's 1st Claim
body:
A short story is little more than a novelist's sketch pad. Does R disagree?
No, no comment on whether that's a fair analogy.

label: Tony's 2nd Claim
body:
Only a novel can depict human lives accurately (because it is long enough to have narrative structures that allow personalities to gradually develop). Does R disagree?
Yes, because he thinks "the short story depicts human lives more faithfully than does the novel".

label: Evaluate / Goal
body:
They seem to be arguing over whether novels or short stories are better at depicting human lives faithfully / accurately.
Since that disconnect is pretty explicit, the correct answer might test the underlying rationale for the disconnect.
In other words, they're arguing over whether "depicting a human life accurately means **narrative structure with gradual character development**, or whether it means **a series of disjointed vignettes allowing glimpses of character**."

label: Conclusion
body: Judges should be well-equipped to answer the question of whether a given administrative decision by a government minister is reasonable or not.

label: Evidence
body:
Given the judges' training and experience, if they were **not** well-equipped to answer this question then that would mean there's something badly wrong with the legal system.
There's no reason to think something is badly wrong with the legal system.

label: Evaluate
body:
Wow! That is a brain full, alright. Dense prose. Distinguished British judges. It's a real stuffy Downton Abbey vibe.
The argument itself breaks down to these pieces.
Background: People are asking whether A is X or not.
Upton's Conclusion: Yes, A is X.
Upton's Evidence: If A were not X, then Z would be true. Z is not true.
It's actually really important to understand that general argument structure, if we're going to make it easier to discern what this argument is trying to say.
We should dumb down that first idea leading up to the quotation: whether some administrative decision by a government minister is reasonable
If people are debating that, they're debating whether the thing some government dude did was unreasonable or not.
Judge Upton is saying judges are well equipped to answer that question. They can tell you whether the thing some government dude did was unreasonable or not.
How does he know this? He provides an argument by contrapositive:
1. If judges **aren't** well-equipped to answer, then there would be something badly wrong with the legal system.
contrapositive: if there **isn't** anything badly wrong with legal system, then judges are well equipped to answer.
2. there is not something badly wrong with the legal system.
One final lifeline we have is that the word **and** almost always joins two premises. So the final **and** before "there is little reason to suppose that there is" can indicate to us that the two claims connected by the **and** are both premises.
Additionally, the word **should**, in the conclusion, is an Opinion Indicator, which can help us identify that claim as the conclusion.

label: Goal
body: We want something like, judges should be well-equipped to answer the question of whether some administrative decision by a government minister is reasonable

label: Conclusion (therefore)
body: Any student, whatever their major, will be served well later in life by taking any philosophy course.

label: Evidence (since)
body:
Any course that teaches students how to write is one that will serve them well in later life.
And some philosophy courses teach students how to write.

label: Evidence (this is supported by the fact that)
body:
Earth, like all organisms, can be said to have a metabolism and to regulate its temperature, humidity, and other characteristics, divorced from the influences of its surroundings.
Naturally, Earth does not literally breathe, but neither do insects (which have no lungs), and they still respire successfully.

label: Evaluate
body:
Whenever we're doing Flaw and we see conditional logic premises, we want to assume we're probably being tested on an illegal reversal or negation (aka the famous "Necessary vs. Sufficient" flaw).
The first sentence has the sufficient indicator "any". All words or phrases that indicate a **universal** provide an idea for the left side of a conditional.
That first sentence is saying
**if** course teaches → **then** serves them students how to write well later in life
An illegal reversal would sound like, "The course Pam just took will serve her well later in life. Thus it must be a course that teaches students how to write."
But this argument doesn't do anything like that.
It's saying, "Some Philosophy courses teach you how to write", from which we can fairly derive the idea that "some Philosophy courses would serve you well later in life".
The problem is the conclusion makes a leap from that correct conclusion to an exaggerated conclusion: " **any** philosophy course will serve a student well in later life".

label: Goal
body:
Let's look for an answer saying the author is going from evidence that says "some philosophy courses will serve students well later in life" to a conclusion that too-strongly asserts that "every philosophy course will serve students well later in life".
The author is failing to consider that some philosophy courses might not teach you how to write, and thus might not serve you well later in life.

label: Setup Claims
body:
Poor writers often try to make up for their boring ideas with complicated sentence structure and vocabulary.
Inattentive readers might be fooled and impressed, while not really understanding the writing.
Alert readers will easily see through the charade and realize the bad writer is covering up for lack of substance with fancy language.

label: Conclusion (Thus)
body: A good principle for writers would be ....

label: Evaluate / Goal
body:
We need a safely worded takeaway that synthesizes these two sentences.
We've been warned about a certain style of writing, in which we're not saying anything interesting, we're just trying to write in a complicated way so that we sound smart.
We might be able to fool some people with this style, but alert readers will see we're being a chump.
So a good principle for writers could be... "if alert readers are going to be reading your stuff, don't write in that fake-smart style"?

label: Background of Hypothesis
body: The kind of thoughts that keep a person from falling asleep can arise in either half of the brain.

label: Hypothesis (Therefore)
body: If that's the only thing preventing sleep, then "closing eyes and counting sheep" should allow someone to fall asleep.

label: Evidence (because)
body: This activity fully occupies the left half of the brain with counting and the right half of the brain with imagining sheep, thereby excluding the sleep-preventing thoughts.

label: Evaluate
body:
Is this method guaranteed to allow someone to fall asleep, assuming that the only thing that was preventing the person from falling asleep was thoughts arising in the brain?
We know that both the left half and the right half of the brain are fully occupied, excluding sleep-preventing thoughts.
But what if what the brain is fully occupied with (counting from 1 to infinity / picturing sheep) qualifies as sleep-preventing thoughts?

label: Goal
body:
In order for this method to work, we'd have to assume that neither counting nor picturing sheep is a type of thinking that can prevent sleep.
There might be other necessary ideas as well, in order for this technique to work, such as "someone is capable of both counting and imagining sheep at the same time".
We could potentially use the negation test on these answers. The correct answer will be something required for this technique to work, so it should be that if we negated the correct answer it would sound like a serious objection to the notion that this technique will work.

label: Claude's Conclusion (should)
body: France should hold referenda on major foreign-policy issues, in order to introduce greater public accountability into French foreign policy decisions.

label: Claude's Evidence
body: Elections are decided on multiple issues, so they're too imprecise to count as a mandate (they don't clearly send a message about what people think the foreign policy should be).

label: Lorraine's Conclusion
body: Introducing foreign policy referenda would lead to foreign-policy disaster.

label: Lorraine's Evidence
body: The general public, unlike the government, is unwilling or unable to become informed about foreign-policy issues.

label: Evaluate
body:
When we're doing a Logical Counter, we want to specifically respond to the objection while defending the original position.
Given that ... we want to defend the idea of holding referenda (letting people vote on individual issues) on major foreign-policy decisions,
How can we respond to the objection that ... the general public, unlike the government, is unwilling or unable to become informed about foreign-policy issues?
We could try to argue that, "It doesn't matter if the general public is un-informed. If France is considering a war with Australia, members of the French general public are going to have to go fight that war, so the French people should get to vote on whether or not they want that war in the first place."
But it's pretty bad, from a common sense point of view, to try to argue that "it doesn't matter if the general public is uninformed about foreign-policy issues; they should still vote to determine the foreign policy."
Is there a way to say we could help the general public make more informed decisions? Maybe if we switch over to this referenda system, we could start mailing out informative brochures or creating informative websites, so that the public would be better able to get informed and thus make a wise foreign policy decision with their referendum vote.

label: Goal
body: Defend the idea of having referenda on major foreign policy issues, while responding to the objection that the general public is too uninformed to be qualified to vote on these issues.

label: Conclusion (therefore)
body: The introduction of referenda on major foreign-policy issues would lead to foreign-policy disaster.

label: Evidence
body: The general public, unlike people in government, is unwilling or unable to become informed about foreign-policy issues.

label: Goal
body:
They're asking us about the "since" claim, so from our four main buckets (Main Conclusion, Support, Opposing, Neutral), we know to choose **Support**.
Any claim attached to FABS (for, after all, because, since) will be playing a Support role.
But if we wanted to get more technical with our prediction, this "since" claim is supporting the Intermediate Conclusion (the final claim of the paragraph), which supports the Main Conclusion in the first sentence.

label: Evaluate
body:
Our author is assuming a Linking idea like,, "If you let people who are unwilling or unable to become informed about foreign-policy issues have decision making power over major foreign policy issues, then it will lead to foreign-policy disaster.
An opponent might resist that move by saying that "even informed decisions in foreign-policy often lead to disaster. It's ultimately just a guess that someone is making, so that someone might as well be the general public."
Or an opponent might resist the idea that the public would continue to be uninformed / unwilling to become informed about foreign-policy issues, in this hypothetical new world.
In a world where we the people got to vote on whether or not to send troops to the Ukraine to resist Russian advances, maybe we would take more initiative to learn up on the situation.

label: Goal
body:
Look for an answer that shuts down one of our objections, - when people make informed decisions about foreign policy, it **much less frequently** leads to disaster
- giving people the power to vote on foreign policy would **not** inspire them to become more informed about foreign policy issues
... or just look for any answer that adds more credence to the idea that letting the public vote on major foreign policy issues would lead to foreign-policy disaster.
Note: the question stem does say to support Lorraine's **conclusion** (usually we're told to strengthen someone's argument / reasoning) Often that distinction doesn't matter, but sometimes it suggests that the answer will affect the plausibility of the conclusion, without really dealing with what the evidence was talking about.

label: Principle 1
body: not intended to benefit recipient gift not or → generous not worth more than what is expected or typical in the situation

label: Principle 2
body: given to benefit giver or → gift is selfish less valuable than customary

label: Evaluate
body:
The first rule is triggered by **unless**, which means the same thing as " **if** it is **not** the case that".
When we see, "It is not X unless it's Y", then we could rephrase that as, " **if it is not the case** that it's Y, then it is not X". ~Y → ~X
There's a tricky aspect here, though because we're applying the "if-not" to a complex idea. If we're given, "It is not X unless it's Y and Z", then we're saying, "If it's not the case [that it's both Y and Z], then it's not X".
Negating (Y and Z) turns it into ~Y or ~Z.
That makes sense, since we know that if Y is not true, then it's certainly "not the case that both Y and Z are true". Similarly, as soon as we know Z is not true, then it's not the case that Y and Z are true.
Thus, "it is not X unless it's Y and Z" becomes ~Y **or** ~Z → ~X
The second conditional is easier to deal with because the word " **if** " indicates the idea that goes on the trigger. So "it is X **if** it is Y or Z" becomes, Y or Z → X

label: Goal
body:
When we're provided with two conditional principles, the correct answer (almost?) never uses both of them. So the first thing we do when we read each answer is check to see what it's conclusion is.
If it's concluding "not generous", then we'll use rule 1 and see whether the answer choice establishes the trigger.
If it's concluding "selfish", then we'll use rule 2 and see whether the answer choice establishes that rule's trigger.
If it's concluding "it is generous" or "it isn't selfish", we'll just throw it out without reading it. These rules have no power to prove something is generous or isn't selfish.
