If failure to restrict wrong for govt wouldn't cause → to restrict the liberty harm of individuals
Publishing something is a liberty.
Being offensive doesn't cause harm.

label: Evaluate
body:
"To offend doesn't cause harm"? Wow, test 39. What an old fashioned notion.
When we're looking to make inferences, we're looking for overlapping information. The 2nd and 3rd facts contain the ideas "liberty" and "harm" from the principle in the first sentence.
We heard something like "if there's no harm, don't restrict liberty".
And we were told that "offending is not harm". So maybe, if publishing is offensive, don't restrict it?

label: Jenkins' first claim
body:
Research at North Pole should be conducted in January and February. does Lurano disagree?
Yes. She's implicitly saying that research at North Pole should be in April or May.

label: Jenkins's second claim
body:
The weather is cold enough in January/February that snow will definitely not melt.
does Lurano disagree?
No. She seems to agree it's super cold then, and still pretty cold a couple months later.

label: Jenkins's third claim
body:
It's important that research money not be wasted. does Lurano disagree?
No, she probably agrees that research money shouldn't be wasted.

label: Jenkins's fourth claim
body:
If we wait until later than February, we risk sending researchers when they will be unable to carry out research successfully. does Lurano disagree?
No, not quite. She isn't ready to say that if we send people in April/May there is **no risk.** In fact, she even acknowledges the risk by saying, "it will **likely** still be quite cold then".

label: Evaluate
body: It looks like, of the explicit claims, the only one Lurano is specifically arguing the opposite of is the first one. Jenkins would say "we should do the research in January/February, so that we don't risk melted snow" and Lurano is saying, "we should do the research in April/May, so that we have less risk of the researchers being harmed by the cold.

label: Conclusion
body: The author argues that citation analysis pushes scientists away from good research.

label: Evidence
body: If you're trying to rack up citations, you'll pick short-term faddish projects over multiyear ones.

label: Evaluate
body:
For this to make sense, multiyear projects need to be at a citation disadvantage. If multiyear research actually gets cited the whole way through (interim papers, midpoint findings), then choosing it wouldn't hurt the citation count, and the alleged incentive to avoid it would disappear.
So the strongest support for the argument would be a fact that confirms multiyear projects don't generate citations until they're finished. That cements the incentive structure the argument relies on.

label: Goal
body: The right answer says: research isn't referred to in journals until it's completed.

label: Conclusion (Thus)
body: Anyone who can distinguish the significant from the insignificant is a historian.

label: Evidence
body:
All historians are able to spot trends.
Anyone able to spot trends is able to distinguish the significant from the insignificant.

label: Conclusion
body: The ad's underlying claim is simple: trust Barr Motor — they'll make more winning cars than their competitors.

label: Evaluate
body:
When the arguments we read on Parallel or Parallel Flaw have conditional logic and repeating symbols (able to spot trends and historian and distinguishing significance all show up twice), then it lends itself well to writing an algebraic recipe for how the argument works.
All H's can spot trends. X → Y All trend-spotters can distinguish. Y → Z So, all distinguishers are H's. Z → X
It looks like the conclusion is flawed by trying to reverse the chain of logic created by the two premises.
The two premises link up, X → Y → Z able to able to Historian → spot trends → distinguish sig vs. insig
So a valid conclusion would be saying,
able to Historian → distinguish sig vs. insig
But this conclusion is doing the reverse, saying that if you're the right side then you're the left side.

label: Goal
body:
Let's look for this pattern. There should be two conditional premises that chain together. And then the conclusion should be concluding a conditional that is an illegal reversal of the endpoints of the chain.
prem 1: X → Y (X → Y → Z) prem 2: Y → Z conc: Z → X

label: Conclusion (Hence)
body: This proposal (to prohibit experimentation on those species that humans empathize with" should be extended to all experimentation on all mammals.

label: Evidence
body: Extensive neurological research on mammals shows that they are all capable of feeling pain.

label: Evaluate / Goal
body:
We're trying to extend a prohibition to all mammals, so we need a rule whose trigger applies to these other mammals, and whose outcome sounds like or supports the language of "you can't do scientific experimentation on them".
So let's look for something like,
If they're capable → then can't of feeling pain experiment on them

label: Conclusion (So)
body: High productivity does not depend on having high-tech equipment.

label: Evidence
body: High productivity cannot be achieved without adequate training of workers.

label: Evaluate
body:
The author gives us a premise about "high productivity" and then concludes a claim about "high productivity", so the author is assuming a link between the ideas attached to "high productivity".
X can't be achieved w/o → X doesn't depend adeq. training of workers on high tech equip
This is one of those arguments that's so incoherent it's hard to judge what they were even going for. What if we looked at it from an abstract level?
X can't be achieved without Y. Thus, X doesn't depend on Z
The author seems to be thinking that if X requires Y then it can't **also** require Z. Either the author is thinking that X can only require **one thing**, or the author is thinking that Y is sufficient to bring about X.
It would be totally valid to argue: Y is sufficient to guarantee X. Thus, X doesn't depend on Z.

label: Goal
body:
Conversationally, we're saying, " Even Though... high productivity depends on adequately training workers, It Could Still Be True That... high productivity **does** depend on having high-tech equipment. After All... high productivity might depend on more than one thing."
In more formal, abstract terms, we could say, "the author treats a condition required for a phenomenon to obtain as though it's the only condition required".

label: Conclusion
body: Some people who are good at abstract reasoning are famous.

label: Evidence
body: Most skilled artists are very creative people, and all people who are very create are also good at abstract reasoning.

label: Evaluate
body:
Whenever we do Sufficient Assumption, we can ask ourselves, "Is there any **New Term** in the Conclusion?" If there is, then that term/idea has to appear in the correct answer, or else we'll have no way to derive that conclusion.
In this case, the evidence does talk about people being good abstract reasoning, but it never talks about anyone who is famous.
Confusingly, it does talk about people who are not famous.
Not all skilled artists are famous = some skilled artists are not famous.
Whenever we see any negative formulations, we want to perform a **Negative to Positive** translation: No A's are B = All A's are ~B Few A's are B = Most A's are ~B Not all A's are B = Some A's are ~B
When we say that "Not all A's are B", it does **not** imply that Some A's are B.
For example, it's false to say "All NFL players are female", thus it's true to say "Not all NFL players are female".
All that statement means is "there is at least one NFL player who is **not** female".
So since the evidence only told us "some skilled artists are **not-famous** ", we don't yet have any information about any famous people.
Thus, the correct answer has to be a fact about famous people, in order for it to allow us to derive a conclusion about famous people.
What do we know about "good at abstract reasoning" (the other half of the conclusion)? We know that if you're very creative, you're good at abstract reasoning.

label: Goal
body:
So one possible answer could say, "Some famous people are very creative", and that would then allow us to prove that "Some famous people are good at abstract reasoning".
But we'll consider any answer that talks about famous people and allows to prove that at least one of them is good at abstract reasoning.

label: Conclusion (should)
body: As we relax the regulations on making/selling new meds (to increase their availability), we should not simultaneously deregulate all industrial activity, in general.

label: Intermediate Conclusion
body: Deregulating in general could actually undermine the original intent of relaxing regulations on making/selling new meds (increasing their availability).

label: Evidence (since)
body: A large majority of new meds are derived from plants and animals, and if we got rid of our strict environmental regulations, endangered plants and animals would become extinct.

label: Evaluate
body:
Whenever we're reading Main Conclusion or Role, we're priming our brain with the reminder that the Main Conclusion is usually **earlier** in the paragraph than are its Supporting Ideas.
We want to always read the first sentence of Main Conclusion/Role with the suspicion that it may be the Main Conclusion. If it sounds like an opinion belonging to our author, and our author goes on to try supporting it, then we correctly "hear" the conclusion from the start.
In this case, the "should" told us that yes, indeed, the first sentence was the author's opinion and therefore most likely the Main Conclusion.
The "since" in the final sentence tells us that the first half of that sentence is supporting a Conclusion in the second half. But the second half of that last sentence is still Support for our first sentence.

label: X's 1st Idea
body:
We're obliged to ensure that electricity rates are the lowest possible. Does Y disagree?
No, Y seems to agree. She is saying "that's not our only job", but this implies that "yes, this is one of our jobs".

label: X's 3rd Idea
body:
This proposed design must be the design we endorse, if we agree that we're making a new plant. Does Y disagree?
Yes, Y seems to agree. She is saying, assuming we had decided to approve construction of a new plant, we do **not** necessarily have to or want to pick that design.
Even though we're obliged to ensure low rates, we're also obliged not to lower the quality of life in our community, and this new design would damage air quality.

label: Evaluate / Goal
body:
This proposed design pits two competing obligations against each other, says Y. The design's ability to satisfy one goal is outweighed by its potential to violate our other goal.
In X's mind, since the proposed design would best achieve our obliged goal of lowest rates, it's our obliged choice if we're choosing a new plant.
We should keep in mind that no one ever said they **are** approving construction of a new plant. This disagreement is happening in a hypothetical world, where we are deciding on a design for a new plant.
X would say, in that case, "we must choose this new proposed design" and Y would say "no way."

label: Statements
body:
good students (universal - left side)
learn more than Good student → what parents/teachers compel them to learn
requires (necessary - right side)
learn more than students derive pleasure what parents & → from satisfaction teachers compel of their curiosity
cannot / unless (required / if-not)
deriving pleasure capable of concentrating from satisfaction → so deeply you lose track of curiosity of identity

label: Evaluate
body:
Because **Must Be False** questions love to test conditional logic (the correct answer usually contradicts a conditional relationship we're given), we want to read these with a listening ear for conditional logic trigger words.
All three sentences here were conditional, the first sentence being a universal about good students and the second and third sentences giving us requirements (the **R** equired thing goes on the **R** ight side).
When we have multiple conditionals, we want think about whether they chain together, which requires that they have some overlapping ingredients. The first and the second sentences are connected by the pronoun "this", and the second and third are connected by the pronoun "such pleasure".
We can chain all four of these ideas together to get this chain:
Good learns derives concentrating student → more than → pleasure → so much compelled from curiosity lose self

label: Goal
body:
When we have conditionals on Must Be False, the correct answer just usually contradicts them.
Remember that contradicting a conditional is not the same as making an illegal move.
Given: A → B, If we see an answer doing B → A or doing ~A → ~B, we're not picking those.
Those are illegal inferences but they're not contradictions. A contradiction provides the trigger but denies the outcome. So we'd be looking for an answer that says "something is A but not B."
Given a chain: A → B → C, we'd probably see something contradicting the chain, like "Something is A but not C".

label: Conclusion
body: Parents would be wise to reduce the amount of stimulation their babies receive.

label: Evidence
body: A study shows that babies with a less stimulating daytime routine slept an average of two hours more per day than those with a more stimulating routine. Since sleep plays a very important role in a child's development, it is suggested that reducing stimulation would be beneficial.

label: Evaluate
body: This is a "Weaken" question where we want to find an answer choice that challenges the conclusion that reducing stimulation is wise. We should look for reasoning or evidence that highlights the potential benefits of maintaining or even increasing stimulation, which might outweigh the benefits of additional sleep.

label: Goal
body: Identify an answer choice that illuminates a reason why stimulation might still be important, despite its impact on sleep, thus challenging the conclusion that reducing stimulation is beneficial.

label: Conclusion
body: Choice E effectively weakens the argument by highlighting that stimulation contributes to intellectual development. It introduces important developmental benefits that could balance or outweigh the advantage of increased sleep, directly challenging the advice to reduce stimulation. The other options either do not directly impact the argument or indirectly support it.

label: Statements
body:
conditional (if = Left side, sufficient)
**if... then...** politician is known not reelected to be involved in → and any serious scandals will be censured
specific facts
These prominent politicians are involved in a serious scandal. These politicians will not be reelected.

label: Evaluate
body:
Our reading / thinking goal on Must Be True and Most Supported (i.e. Inference questions) is to see whether we can combine or synthesize any of the claims they've provided in order to derive some other true claim. To do this, we pay attention to whether we're given any Conditional rules, Causal relationships, or Math-y facts. And we pay attention to whether we see any Overlapping Ideas that show up in multiple claims.
The first sentence was conditional, signified by the sufficient indicator "If", so we put the "If" idea on the left of the arrow. When we see "neither Y nor Z", we need to translate this into "not this **and** not that". People often write "or" because it rhymes with "nor". But the expression neither / nor is banning both things, not one or the other.
"At this hotel swimming pool, you can neither set off fireworks nor swim naked."
That is banning both things, not one or the other.
So "if X, then neither Y nor Z" looks like this: X → ~Y and ~Z
The contrapositive of that rule (reversing the order and the positive/negative value of everything) looks like this (remember that and/or switches when we contrapose): Z or Y → ~X
The first sentence, contraposed, would be saying, If you've been reelected **or** you never got censured, then you were never known to be involved in any serious scandals.
(you've got to get nostalgic for Test 39's worldview, when being involved in serious scandals had political or electoral consequences)
Since we have a conditional rule, we're looking to see whether any other claims (rules or facts) mention the ideas on the left side or the right side of that rule. The second sentence tells us about politicians who have been involved in a serious scandal.
The rule applies to them! What does the right side tell us about those politicians?
It says, "these politicians can neither be reelected nor avoid censure". (Censure = harsh criticism. In the American political system, and others I believe, **Impeachment** is the most severe rebuke that the political system can give towards its leader. **Censure** is a non-binding official condemnation. It's like "let's get it in writing that we don't approve of what you did".)
The last sentence tells they will not be reelected. Yeah, last sentence, we know! We're following the rule. We **also** know that they can't avoid censure.

label: Goal
body:
Since combining the second sentence with the rule in the first sentence provides us with inferences (these politicians can't be reelected or avoid censure), we have good reason to think the correct answer will just be testing us on these available inferences.
However, because the last sentence stole one of them from us, we'd expect the answer to deal with the other one: these prominent politicians cannot avoid censure (harsh criticism )
But on Must Be True there's no such thing as what the answer should be. We pick whatever answer we can prove from the provided information.

label: Local Citizens' Conclusion
body: These actions are inconsistent. rephrase: Pleading with the public to help find the victim contradicts not allowing the public to attend the trial.

label: Jorge's 1st claim
body:
You won't be able to write well about the rock music of the 1960s, since you were an infant then. Does Ruth disagree? Does she argue she would be able to write well about rock in the 60s, even though she was an infant then?
Yes! First of all she says, "Your **reasoning** is absurd", so we know that she objects to the conclusion drawn on the basis of the evidence ( **since** you were an infant, can't write well).
Secondly, her final sentence is clearly pushing back against this notion? "Why should my youth be enough to prevent me from writing well about 60s music?"

label: Jorge's 2nd claim
body:
60s rock was created by and for people who were in their teens and early 20s then. Does Ruth disagree? Does she argue that 60's rock was not created by and for people who were in their teens and early 20s at the time?
No. She doesn't speak at all to who created 60s rock or for whom 60s rock was created.

label: Goal
body: They are arguing over whether someone who wasn't in their teens / early 20s at the time can write well about 60s rock music.

label: Conclusion
body: This opinion is wrong. rephrase: We should **not** be required to carry ID cards and show them on demand.

label: Evidence (after all)
body: The writers of the article should not have asserted that the right to remain anonymous was trivial, unless they were prepared to put their names to that assertion.

label: Evaluate
body:
This author's evidence doesn't seem to have anything to do with her conclusion. She's trying to convince her audience that we shouldn't be required to carry ID cards and show them on demand.
Why shouldn't we? Would it be too hard to disseminate ID cards to everyone? Would people too frequently forget to have their ID card on their person and get in trouble as a result? Would authorities employ their power to stop people and demand to see their ID cards in some way that would target or terrorize subsets of the population?
She doesn't say anything like that. In fact, she doesn't say anything about this Plan at all. There's no discussion of what positive or negative ramifications would result of installing a policy of mandatory ID cards.
Instead, she just says something about the people who wrote the article.
Attacking the **source** of ideas rather than the **content** of the ideas is one of the 10 famous flaws, called Ad Hominem. In almost all examples of Ad Hominem, the author tries to dismiss some idea because the source of the idea either (1) has a biased interest in the matter, or (2) has conflicting past behavior.
This is a case of #2. The author is saying the person who wrote this article behaved in a way that's inconsistent with their claims (they wrote an article anonymously while agitating for a policy of everyone being required to show their identification).

label: Goal
body: Look for an answer saying that this author failed to respond substantively to the article's position, and that it instead tried to disqualify the position based merely on the fact that the writer behaved in a way that seems at odds with their position.

label: Hypothesis
body: Misidentification by eyewitnesses is a common reason for mistaken convictions in criminal trials.

label: Evaluate / Goal
body: There's no argument here, so there's nothing to think about. We just have to find four answers that make it seem like eyewitnesses commonly identify the wrong person as the culprit of a crime, leading to an eventual mistaken conviction.

label: Conclusion
body: There is good evidence that complexity is correct.

label: Evidence
body: The computerized models based on complexity evolve much like the real-world phenomena actually evolve.

label: Evaluate
body: We're trying to prove that there is "good evidence" that a theory is correct, based on the premise that mathematical models based on the theory evolve much like real-world phenomena do.

label: Goal
body: Let's look for something like, "If computer models based on a theory do a good job matching reality, then that's good evidence that the theory is correct".

label: Ruth
body: Politicians should be required to have a diversity of experience, since diversity of experience goes along with understanding the need to compromise.

label: Steph
body: Simply having diverse experience does not make you worthy of public trust, as you suggest. One might have diverse experience but still not be worthy of public trust.

label: Evaluate
body:
Steph's argument is a bit circular, honestly, since she's saying "Diverse experience doesn't guarantee worthy of public trust. It's possible to have diverse experience but not necessarily be worthy of public trust."
That conclusion is a restatement of the premise.
However the first thing that's supposed to catch our ear, before we even read the circular premise, is that Stephanie is unfairly accusing Ruth of having said something wacky: "As long as you have diverse experience, you're guaranteed to be worthy of public trust".
Ruth didn't say anything like that. She just listed diversity of experience as being among the (possibly many) qualities one should have to be a politician.

label: Goal
body: Find an answer saying that Stephanie is attacking a Straw Man, a claim that Ruth never actually said or implied.

label: Information
body:
Causal (X inspired Y)
Cezanne's art inspired the following generation (20th century modernist creators of abstract art)
Quantifiers (most / small few)
Most experts say Cezanne's is an early modernist.
Small few say he's not an early modernist (we just see his work from a modern point of view).

label: Evaluate
body:
Okay ... our goal on Inference questions is to find facts that can be combined in order to derive some other truth. But 2/3 of the claims in this paragraph are opinions.
The first sentence makes it sound like there's reason to believe the "most experts". Since Cezanne inspired modernist creators of abstract art, it seems pretty reasonable to call him an early modernist.
But we certainly couldn't say that in any Must Be True sense.

label: Goal
body: This stimulus isn't lending itself to predicting an answer, so we'll just see what's offered and look for mild, provable language we can support with the small amount we know.

label: Conclusion (should)
body: Forest fires should be left alone and allowed to burn themselves out naturally.

label: Evidence
body: Forest fires are a natural phenomenon that is required for many forests to flourish (they facilitate seed pods, limit insects, and promote diversity).

label: Evaluate
body:
The final sentence is the Conclusion, indicated by "In view of this (evidence)". It's technically two claims joined by a semicolon. We might wonder whether LSAC wants us to prove "preventing / controlling forest fires is **ill-advised / shortsighted** ", or whether they want us to prove "we **should leave them alone** and let them burn out naturally".
In either case, we know that the evidence launchpad we have includes supporting buzz phrases such as: - required for forests to flourish - facilitate seeds dispersal - limit insects - promote diversity I see the last three in that list as sub-components of the first one. The bottom three seem like reasons why forest fires are required for many forests to flourish.

label: Goal
body: We want an answer to give us a rule that takes us from one of the Evidence launchpads and gets us to one of the Conclusion landing zones. **If.... Then....** req'd for forests to flourish ill-advised and or shortsighted to helps w/ seed dispersal prevent/control or or limits insects should be left or alone to burn out promotes diversity

label: Conclusion
body: The extinctions of super large North American mammals during the last ice age was caused by the dramatic shift to a harsher climate.

label: Evidence
body: The climate changed so rapidly that the species could not adapt.

label: Evaluate
body:
Since Foster and Fisch are trying to Solve the Causal Mystery of what caused the extinction of the large NA mammals at the end of the last ice age, we can use our Explain Curious Fact mindset.
Curious Fact Why did super large mammals go extinct at the end of the last ice age?
Fisch's Explanation The dramatic shift to a harsher climate did it. The climate changed more rapidly than these large species could adapt to it, so they eventually died off from challenges dealing with this new climate.

label: Goal
body:
We either want an answer to **rule out** an alternate explanation for the extinctions (such as ruling out that the idea that the presence of humans caused the extinctions), or more likely we want an idea that bolsters the plausibility of the author's explanation.
The most common way to Strengthen an Explain Curious Fact argument is to provide an answer that shows "where the Cause was absent or less present, the Effect was absent or less present". So we might see something like, "in the areas where the climate change the least or the most gradually, we saw the fewest or slowest extinctions."

label: Conclusion (it is obvious)
body: One ought to have a will stating how one wishes one's estate to be distributed.

label: Evidence
body: If you don't have a will, then distant relatives you've never even met have a greater legal right to one's estate than one's beloved friends do.

label: Evaluate
body:
Suppose we say this, "One ought to say bless you after someone sneezes. After all, if you don't say bless you after someone sneezes, they will think you're rude."
What does this assume? It assumes "you shouldn't do something that will make people think you're rude".
If we say, "You should never break up with someone via text. After all, if you do it will hurt the person you're breaking up with more than needed."
What does this assume? It assumes "you shouldn't do something that will hurt the person you're breaking up with more than needed".

label: Goal
body:
So since this argument is saying, "You ought to have a will. After all, if you don't, your distant relatives will have a greater legal right to your estate than your beloved friends will",
it must be assuming that "You ought to avoid letting your estate go to your distant relatives rather than to your beloved friends", or something similar to that meaning.

label: Conclusion (Thus)
body: Good health is largely the result of making informed lifestyle choices.

label: Evidence
body: Studies from many countries indicate a strong correlation between good health and high educational levels.

label: Evaluate
body:
We know that one of LSAT's favorite argument patterns is presenting a correlation in the evidence and then assuming some causal relationship in the conclusion. In this argument, it literally says "correlation" in the evidence. The causal wording in the conclusion is "result".
We can use our Explain Curious Fact mindset when the conclusion seems to be assuming some sort of causal explanation for the evidence.
Curious Fact ... why is there a strong correlation in many countries between good health and high educational levels?
Author's Explanation ... Education leads to informed lifestyle choices, and informed lifestyle choices lead to good health.
We always think about these types of arguments by asking two questions: 1. Could there be some Alternate Explanation for the curious fact? 2. How plausible is the Author's Explanation?

label: Goal
body:
When it comes to Flaw questions, we're either going to complain that the author is overconfidently assuming a causal connection from a mere correlation, or complain that the author is failing to consider alternate explanations, or call out an assumption the author is making in thinking that her explanation is plausible.
So look for anything like this - infers cause from correlation - fails to consider correlation between health and ed levels could be from X - takes for granted that high educational levels lead to more informed lifestyle choices

label: Conclusion
body: A country with a controlled economy that isn't trying to bring about a pure free market economy is not doing what is most likely to bring about maximum total utility.

label: Evidence
body: Only pure free market economy assures maximum total utility.

label: Evaluate
body: This is a tricky flaw to pin down. Both the Premise and the Conclusion are saying or implying something about "If you're not doing free market economy, then ...", so it's useful to consider them in parallel so that we can see the gap.

label: Premise:
body: not doing free market → not assured max utility

label: Conclusion:
body:
not doing free market → not doing most likely way to get max utility
The author is apparently assuming "if you're not doing the thing that assures max utility, then you're not acting in the way most likely to attain max utility".
That sounds pretty reasonable, but we could probably think of cases where the most assured way isn't the most likely way.
There's 5 seconds left in the basketball game. Your team is down by 1. Let's say "making the winning basket is assured only if you dunk the ball". But that doesn't mean that trying to run down the court and dunk the ball is the most likely way to make the winning basket. It's too hard to get all the way to the other hoop and dunk it in 5 seconds with the other team's whole defense trying to stop you.

label: Evaluate
body:
Whenever we do Role and Main Conclusion, we remind ourselves that the conclusion will be the First Sentence or a Rebuttal about 90% of the time.
Here, the conclusion is the first sentence, signified by the transition into the 2nd sentence which cues us that "this hypothesis [in the first sentence] is **supported by** " what follows.
We're being asked about the claim that "insects do not literally breathe". That doesn't seem like a Premise supporting the idea that "Earth is a living organism", but it's not an Opposing idea either. Superficially, it seems irrelevant. Why was it talked about?
In the final sentence the author makes a concession, signified by concession wording: " **Of course** / Naturally / Granted / Although / While". Concessions are when the author acknowledges a potential objection someone might make to their reasoning.
Someone who doesn't think that Earth is a living organism might say, "Whoa there, author. Earth is a living organism? What are you talking about? Earth can't breathe!"
The author would respond by saying, "Do you think insects are living organisms? Of course you do. Can insects breathe? No, they don't have lungs. You can respire successfully without breathing. So the fact that Earth doesn't breathe doesn't show it isn't a living organism."

label: Goal
body: Look for something in the realm of "we talk about insects not being able to breathe as part of some sidebar where the author is trying to shoot down a potential objection to her conclusion".

label: Facts
body: Average temp for each of the last five years has yet a new record. Some claim the average temp has permanently increased, However, in the past there have been periods of up to ten consecutive years of then-record highs that were part of the random fluctuations that are always occuring.

label: Evaluate
body:
This paragraph creates some tension by starting with a Claim and then pivoting with a However to some counterevidence.
Normally, when a Most Supported paragraph has a **But / Yet / However** style pivot before the last sentence, the correct answer **Straddles the Pivot**, meaning it somehow reconciles what came before with what came after.

label: Goal
body:
We probably want to find a safely worded synthesis of the claim and the counterevidence. We can't say that the claim was right or wrong for sure. It's possible that this recent temp increase is permanent, but there's at least historical precedent suggesting it might just be a random fluctuation.
We could say something like "5 years of record temps do not necessarily mean that global temps have permanently increased".

label: Conclusion
body: The justifications employers offer for increasing surveillance of employees do not justify the increased surveillance.

label: Evidence
body: The justifications are obviously self-serving.

label: Evaluation
body:
I don't know, those seemed like potentially substantive reasons the employers offered. Employees would be more honest if they knew a video tape were documenting everything that happened. They might be more efficient because there would be tape of them slacking, otherwise. They might be more polite because there would be recordings of them being rude, otherwise.
Yes, having more efficient, honest, and polite employees would benefit the employers, so those explanations are self-serving, but they might also be valid. If we want to fight the move to increase surveillance, we should be acknowledging the positives it could bring but then arguing that those are outweighed by some negative repercussions.
We can't just say, "Since the employers want to believe that, let's ignore those ideas."

label: Goal
body: This is committing the famous flaw **Ad Hominem**, but answer choices describing Ad Hominem normally sound like "attacks the source of the argument rather than the content", or "dismisses the legitimacy of ideas because they would benefit the person holding them"

label: Conclusion
body: Students are more likely to learn from criticism by humans than from criticism by computers.

label: Evidence (since)
body:
Accepting criticism requires that one respond positively to it.
Students are less likely to respond positively to computer criticism than to human criticism.

label: Evaluate
body:
The two premises have an overlapping concept, "responding positively". When we're doing Inference questions (e.g. Must Be True, Most Supported), we look for these overlapping concepts as a way to synthesize two claims.
If we say, "Responding positively is required for accepting criticism" and we say, "students are more likely to respond positively to human criticism than to computer criticism", then what can we infer by combining?
We can infer "students are more likely to **accept** human criticism than to accept computer criticism".
Any time the premises can be synthesized, they should be. LSAC is testing our ability to connect related thoughts and understand the implication of combining them.
So, from our two premises, it's been established that: students are more likely to accept human criticism than to accept computer criticism.
Now the conclusion comes, and it has a **New Concept** in it: students are **more likely to learn** from human criticism than from computer criticism.
What is being assumed in going from the Premise to the Conclusion?

label: Goal
body: "If you're more likely to accept criticism, then you're more likely to learn from it", or maybe something more conditional like, "Learning from criticism requires accepting it".

label: Conclusion
body: Earth and its inhabitants are not important

label: Evidence
body: People used to think we were important because they thought Earth was at the center of the universe, but now we realize that Earth is just a random planet in a random solar system in a random galaxy.

label: Evaluation
body:
Given this evidence, how would we still argue that Earth and its peeps are important?
Well ... maybe we're in a random spot of the universe, but we're one of the only intelligent, self-aware species? Maybe we're important because we're the only planet with coal? Who knows.

label: Goal
body: Conversationally, we're thinking, "Maybe we're important for some other reason, besides being at the center of the universe." Formally, this author committed the **Unproven vs. Proven False** flaw, because she's thinking "Since that old center-of-the-universe argument for Earth's importance failed, the claim that Earth is important must be false."

label: Davis's claim
body: Davis says: only the value of damaged or stolen property matters for compensation. Nothing else affects the harm.

label: Higuchi's claim
body: Higuchi disagrees and gives a counterexample: a victim deprived of property for two years is owed more than one deprived for only one year. So duration of deprivation matters.

label: Evaluate
body: For Point at Issue questions, find the claim where one speaker says yes and the other says no. Davis denies that anything besides property value matters — including duration. Higuchi affirms that duration matters. So they directly disagree about whether duration of deprivation entitles a victim to more compensation.

label: Goal
body: The right answer says that some victims are owed more because they were deprived of property for longer. Davis denies this; Higuchi affirms it.

label: Conclusion (should = opinion)
body: Residents of the area should not consider the loss of farming to be a tragedy.

label: Evidence
body: The area now supports over 20 times the number of jobs it used to, with high tech / high wage jobs.

label: Evaluate
body: To support the conclusion that losing farming isn't tragic, we should look for evidence showing that the new economic opportunities outweigh any sentimental or economic loss associated with farming. We'd also wanna make sure that the residents of the area who used to be employed by farming are included among the ones now benefiting from the high tech / high wage jobs.

label: Goal
body: Find an answer that helps us say, "Don't be sad that farming is gone. This area is even more economically healthy now!"

label: Given that
body: Kendrick thinks that governments are justified in trying to prevent cigarettes from being advertised,

label: How can it also be that
body: Kendrick thinks that cigarette ads should remain legal?

label: Evaluate
body:
Of all the Paradox questions I've done, this one ranks 2nd for me I think in terms of difficulty in sorting out what the intended paradox is to begin with.
Kendrick is talking about cigs and about fatty foods, and so a lot of people think the paradox has to do with cigs vs. fatty foods, but there's no conflict there.
Kendrick thinks that advertisements for both encourage people to engage in unhealthy practices. Ads for fatty foods are legal, so Kendrick's recommendation that ads for cigs be legal as well is entirely consistent.
Like almost all Paradox paragraphs, a **pivot** word (But) indicates where the surprising idea is coming from.
**But**... ads for cigs should remain legal.
Okay, what does that conflict with? The only thing before that pivot that sounded like ads for cigs should not remain legal was when Kendrick claimed that governments are justified (i.e. correct) in trying to prevent cigarettes from being advertised.

label: Goal
body: We need an answer that helps reconcile "governments should try to prevent these cigarette ads from airing" with "they should not make the ads illegal".

label: Conclusion (Thus)
body: Governmentally mandated environmental protection in regions of natural beauty can help those regions' economies overall, even if such protection harms some older local industries.

label: Evidence
body: Many people want to live in regions with natural beauty. Such regions often get an influx of new residents, and as the population grows it encourages businesses to relocate to those regions.

label: Evaluate
body:
There is a New Term in the conclusion: governmentally mandated environmental protection. We're drawing a conclusion about this thing, even though the author's argument didn't tell us anything about this thing, other than that it might harm some older local industries (which would weaken the author's conclusion).
So it's a very high percentage bet that the correct answer will refer to this. The author seems to be assuming that without the mandated environmental protection, the natural beauty would be spoiled in some way that would fail to encourage as many new residents and businesses to move in.
And it's assuming that with the mandated protection in place, the natural beauty is better preserved, and thus that new residents and businesses move in, which overall is a net gain for the region's economy.

label: Goal
body:
Look for an answer affirming the author's internal logic (the mandated protection helps to preserve the natural beauty, which then acts as a magnet for more residents and businesses, which then helps the local economy overall).
Or look for an answer ruling out an objection (like mandated protection does **not** raise local taxes and prohibit activities in ways that have a net negative effect on the economy).

label: Statements
body:
There are a lot of conditionals here (no, no, each) and then one Some statement. We should get those conditionals ready (possibly diagram them) and then see if any of the chain together. Then we can check to see if the Some statement triggers any of the conditionals.
Small country → ~perm seat on UNSC
In southern → ~perm seat on UNSC hemisphere
perm seat → favor more peace efforts AND on UNSC favor greater role for UN in moderating regional disputes
Do these chain together? No. But if we contrapose the first two, they will **also** have the trigger of "perm seat on UNSC".
There are basically four things we know if you have a permanent seat on the UNSC: not small, not southern, favor increased peacekeeping efforts, and favor greater role for UN in moderating regional disputes.
The last statement says Some who favor greater are firmly against role in moderating more spending regional disputes on refugees
Are either one of these ideas the trigger for a conditinoal? Nope. The 2nd idea (firmly against refugee spending) is brand new. The other idea (increased peacekeeping efforts) is an outcome, not a trigger, so there's no inference we can make combining the Some fact with the All facts.
(If I said "Each person on the Dallas Cowboys is a man. Some men live in France", you would probably realize there's no forced overlap where Some member of the Dallas Cowboys lives in France. Same thing here. "All A's are B" + "Some B's are C" doesn't lead to any inference).

label: Goal
body: So since the last fact was useless, the correct answer will probably make a Trait Overlap answer out of the four things we know are true about permanent seats on the UNSC: not small not southern favor increased peacekeeping favor greater role moderating regional disputes

label: Conclusion (It is clear that)
body: "Health education" is usually propaganda rather than education.

label: Evidence
body:
Propaganda and education are never the same thing.
Propaganda is nothing but an attempt to influence behavior through the repetition of simplistic slogans.

label: Local Citizens' Evidence
body: Pleading with the public to help find the victim aroused the public interest. But they're saying that allowing us to attend the trial would not serve the public interest.

label: Evidence
body: The Survey Group — a neutral polling company — has tracked tea sales at numerous stores for the last 20 years and has found no change in the amount of tea sold.

label: Evaluate
body:
Since we were given a definition of propaganda (nothing but an attempt to influence behavior through repetition of simplistic slogans), if we're trying to prove that,
Health education is usually propaganda
then we need to know that
Health education is usually [nothing but an attempt to influence behavior through repetition of simplistic slogans].
We don't have to worry about education, since we are told that it is never the same thing as propaganda. We also don't have to worry about the fact that propaganda is much more successful than education, because our only job here is to prove that "health education" is usually propaganda (whether it's successful or not).

label: Goal
body: Since the question stem already cues up the first few words of what we're looking for, we just need the backend. Health education is usually **nothing but an attempt to influence behavior through the repetition of simplistic slogans**.

label: Conclusion
body: The magazine story was very misleading in its story on "the reaction of local residents to our controversial art exhibit".

label: Evidence
body: All three of the quoted residents were morally outraged, and this was meant to suggest that most local residents oppose the exhibit. But these three residents were close friends.

label: Evaluate
body:
When we're trying to pick a Principle to conform to or justify an argument, we can generally just start with an "If Premise, then Conclusion" linking idea. This author is trying to prove that story was misleading.
Why is it misleading? The reactions of the three local residents quoted are supposed to suggest the reactions of most local residents, but the three quoted people were close friends.
So, the author must be assuming a principle like,
If three people then it's misleading to act are close friends → like their opinions represent those of most locals

label: Goal
body: The author is essentially mad that the magazine acted like 3 close friends are a "representative sample" of the majority of local opinion. So the author is also implicitly assuming that "close friends usually don't represent a representative sample of local opinion".

label: Conclusion (should = opinion)
body: The use of dioxin should be completely banned.

label: Evidence
body: Recent research has shown that dioxin causes cancer in rats.

label: Evaluate
body:
This is one of those rare cases on Main Conclusion / Role where the conclusion is actually the final claim.
They tried to hide it by starting the final sentence with some concessions, but the Opinion Indicator "should" helps us find it.
We're being asked about the first sentence, which was the supporting premise. Since dioxin causes cancer in rats, the author thinks dioxin should be banned.

label: Goal
body: Let's look for "premise / support / evidence" for the conclusion that the use of dioxin should be banned.

label: Conclusion
body: If we stopped granting patent rights, no one would engage in original development and no new inventions would happen.

label: Intermediate Conclusion
body: If we stopped granting patent rights, inventors wouldn't have any financial incentive to invent.

label: Evidence
body: If we stopped granting patent rights, anyone could just copy someone else's invention.

label: Evaluation
body:
The author seems to be assuming that if other people can copy your invention, then that will greatly reduce or eliminate your financial incentive for inventing. So he must be assuming that, "at least some people who copy your invention would do so for the sake of selling it" and that "other people selling your invention would significantly cut into the potential profit you would make by selling your own invention."
In addition, even if we grant that other people would saturate the market with copies of your invention and you'd barely be able to make any money yourself, we still have to assume that people won't invent without a financial incentive.
But don't a lot of inventors just like the problem-solving process? Or maybe they're inventing for the fame that comes from inventing something useful. Maybe they're inventing for the sake of saving someone's life?

label: Goal
body: Look for an answer relating to the intermediate conclusion (assuming that people who copy would also try to sell your invention and that doing so would significantly cut into your own ability to achieve financial gain from your invention), or one relating to the main conclusion (that if you don't have a financial incentive, you won't bother inventing / people don't invent for non-financial ends)

label: Curious Fact
body: What caused those two broken bottles on the kitchen floor?

label: Hypothesis
body: Kids broke into the open back door, attempted to raid the kitchen, knocked over the bottles, and then left.

label: Evaluate
body:
Whenever we see "hypothesis" in the question stem, we know we can apply the Explain Curious Fact template.
The two ways to strengthen such arguments are two make the author's hypothesis more plausible (most common) or to rule out an alternate explanation for the curious fact.

label: Goal
body: Get rid of the four answer choices that either make the "kid" hypothesis more plausible or that rule out an alternate explanation for the broken bottles.

label: Conclusion
body: Your conclusion (any disciplinary structure in schools is bound to create resentment) is incorrect.

label: Evidence
body: Educational research shows that when parents list the things that they most want their children’s schools to provide, good discipline is always high on the list.

label: Evaluate
body: Sometimes there's just so much wrong with an argument that it's hard to know where to start. Stephanie's evidence provides very little support for her rebuttal of Sydonie because it fails to address the concepts in Sydonie's evidence or her conclusion. There's no mention of resentment, and no mention of what Sydonie believes will guarantee resentment: parental beliefs about which rules their children should be subject to.

label: Goal
body: Look for an answer that says something along the lines of "Stephanie doesn't rebut Sydonie's actual argument."

label: Statements
body:
Quantifiers (most, some)
people who are **Most** lecturers and are eccentric effect. teachers
**Some** noneccentric are very lecturers effective
Conditional (every)
Effective → Good teacher Communicator

label: Evidence (since)
body: Immoral actions harm other people but also eventually harm those who perform them.

label: Evaluate
body:
Whenever we see quantifiers like most / some / all, we want to see if there are two Most facts about the same group. If we know "Most **A** 's are B and Most **A** 's are C", we can infer "Some B's are C".
But there's only one most fact here.
Whenever we see conditionals, we ask ourselves 1. does this chain up to any other conditional? 2. can I apply this rule (or its contrapositive) to any of the other facts provided?
There's only one conditional, so there won't be a conditional chain. Can we apply this rule to any facts? Were we told about any **effective teachers**?
Yes, we heard about lecturers who are also effective teachers. Most of them are eccentric. And since all of them by definition are effective teachers, we know that all of them are good communicators.
That would allow us to derive a Trait Overlap inference: there are people who are both **eccentric** and **good communicators**.
We're also told that some noneccentric lecturers are very effective teachers, so according to this conditional rule they are also good communicators.
Thus we can also derive the Trait Overlap that some people are both **noneccentric** and **good communicators**.

label: Goal
body: It seems like the Trait Overlap inferences are the most likely options for the correct answers, so look for a safely worded answer that acknowledges that "eccentric/noneccentric" and "good communicator" overlap.

label: Conclusion
body: The author argues that the simultaneous arrival of photons and neutrinos from a supernova is evidence for Einstein's claim that gravity bends space.

label: Evidence
body: The two particles arrived at virtually the same time.

label: Evaluate
body:
For this observation to support Einstein's theory, simultaneous arrival has to be something that *only* Einstein's theory predicts (or at least something the alternative theory would deny). Otherwise, the observation is consistent with both views and doesn't favor either.
The cleanest way to strengthen is to show that without Einstein's curved-space gravity, the photons and neutrinos *wouldn't* have arrived together. That makes simultaneous arrival a real signature of curved space — not something we'd see anyway.

label: Goal
body: The right answer says: if Einstein's theory were wrong, simultaneous emission would lead to different arrival times.

label: Conclusion (thus)
body: Funding for human gene research should be reduced while funding for other genetic research should be increased.

label: Evidence
body:
Human gene research has few practical consequences (but billions are spent on it).
Other genetic research are more mundane and practical, and grossly underfunded.

label: Evaluate
body:
While most Strengthen + Principle questions want us to pick an answer that supplies a good Linking idea ("If Premise, then Conclusion"), there is a sizable minority that deal more with Weighing Tradeoffs.
This seems like a ripe contender for that sort of answer, since the conversation is about weighing the tradeoffs between where we invest our funding dollars.

label: Goal
body:
If the answer is in a Linking style, it should stress the advantage that "other genetic research" has over "human gene research":
**if** research X has more **then** more funding practical consequences → should go to X than research Y than to Y
If the answer is a Weighing Tradeoffs style, then it should say the upside of "other genetic research" is more important than the upside of "human gene research":
In terms of how we spend our limited funding dollars, practical consequences is more important than a new understanding of human nature.
But we'll consider any answer that strengthens.

label: Conclusion (so)
body: There are things that fail to catch our attention but that are miracles of nature.

label: Evidence
body: Everything that is commonplace and ordinary fails to catch our attention.

label: Evaluate
body:
If it weren't for that magic Conclusion Indicator " **so** ", we'd have no easy way of figuring out which claim is the premise and which is the conclusion.
This argument isn't easy to intuitively understand, because it's mathematical sounding and involves a big language-shift leap from one concept to another.
But since this is Sufficient Assumption, we can usually get by with a mathematical understanding. Our job is to prove the conclusion. To prove that "there are things that are X but that are also Y", we just need one example of something that is both X and Y.
"See? Look at this thing: it's X, it's Y! So there are things that are X but that are also Y."
We need an example of something that - fails to catch our attention and also - is a miracle of nature
Does the premise give us anything like that?
Not really, but it talks about "fails to catch our attention". From a purely structural standpoint, this idea of "fails to catch our attention" is the overlapping part of the argument:
PREM: everything that's A is B. CONC: so there are B's that are C. Without understanding anything else, we can predict that the correct answer needs to somehow spell out a connection between A and C. (On this question, that would get us down to only two answers)
The correct answer will be connecting "commonplace and ordinary" to "miracles of nature".

label: Goal
body:
We're trying to prove that - there's at least one thing that both **fails to catch our attention** and is a miracle of nature.
All we know so far is that - commonplace and ordinary things always **fail to catch our attention**.
So we're predicting the correct answer will link "commonplace and ordinary things" to "miracle of nature"

label: Statements
body:
bi-conditional (then and only then)
if, then, effect of mutation favored in natural makes substantial selection contribution
if, then, effect of mutation **not** favored in **doesn't** make a natural selection substantial contribution
The second sentence is giving a potential exception to the first statement, saying that a mutation that leads to some good stuff (favored) and some bad stuff (not favored) can't be so negative that it cancels out the positive.
So if we were trying to amend the original rule to capture that proviso, I would just qualify the wording of the rule so that we capture this idea of "the mutation has to be a net gain (the negatives can't annul the benefits of the positive)".

label: Goal
body:
Since this is a Must Be False question, we're anticipating that it will contradict the conditional we were provided. Contradicting a conditional usually means saying the Left side is true but the Right side is false.
But contradicting a bi-conditional works either way.
We know: if a mutation offers a net gain, it's favored. if it doesn't offer a net gain, it's not favored.
So a must be false would be either of these: - this mutation is favored / doesn't offer a net gain - this mutation is favored / does offer a net gain

label: Conclusion
body: Either you have the satisfaction of having influenced the results, or you have no right to complain.

label: Evaluate
body:
The citizen is finding a contradiction based on the concept of "public interest". Engaging the local citizens in the manhunt for the victim got them very interested in this kidnapping. So naturally, the citizen, is thinking, they are now very **interested** in attending / watching the trial.
How could the judge declare that the public interest would not be served by viewing the trial, if the public is so interested in viewing the trial?
There isn't any contradiction here. It's just two different senses of the term "public interest".
When we say that they pleaded with the public for help in finding the victim, thereby arousing the public's interest, we mean... arousing the public's **curiosity / intrigue**.
When the judge says that allowing the public to attend this trial would not serve the public interest, she means... it would not be good for the integrity of the judicial proceedings / it would not **uphold the court's mission to deliver equal justice under the law**.

label: Goal
body: Using the same term / concept in two very different ways is one of the ten famous flaws. The fancy word for it is **Equivocation**. But we often see answer choices alluding to this flaw (almost always incorrect answer choices, by the way), that simply say that the author used the term "X" in two different ways.

label: Conclusion (Hence)
body: A disease that strikes only a few strains of crops, which would have had only minor impact in the past, would devastate the food supply nowadays.

label: Evidence
body: Today's farmers only plant a handful of different strains of a given crop, whereas in the past they had more diversity.

label: Evaluate
body:
Given that ... today's crops lack the diversity that they had a few generations ago,
How could we argue that... a disease that strikes only a few strains of crops would **not** devastate the food supply today?
Since this argument is basically a Comparison between the past and now, we would want to offset the bad thing about today's era (less crop diversity) with some other consideration that makes us sound less vulnerable to the threat of crop disease threatening our food supply.

label: Goal
body: Look for an answer that either makes us feel like less diversity is not really a bad thing that increases the threat of crop disease, or find an answer that makes it sound like something else nowadays is better than before, so that even though diversity would make us more vulnerable, this improved other thing could offset that and make us less vulnerable.

label: Conclusion
body: There's no chance of future microprocessor design flaws.

label: Evidence
body: All microprocessors are now entirely-computer designed.

label: Evaluation
body:
Pretty straightforward argument core to analyze: given that all these microprocessors are now entirely computer designed, how would we argue that there might be some microprocessor design flaw in the future?
We could just say — what, is the computer design process **perfect**? Why should we believe that? Can't computers make mistakes? In fact, didn't we get into this conversation by talking about a computer that was making a mistake?

label: Goal
body: Look for an answer that points out the possibility that a computer-designed microprocessor could still be flawed since the computer designing it could mess it up.

label: Statements
body:
conditional (each), quantifier (at least some)
Participated in town's → Received comm spring cleanup recog. certificate
Some spring cleanup are not active in town's participants artistic circles
embedded assumption (because X, Y)
Not being part of ⇢ not active in town's downtown arts fair artistic circles

label: Evaluate
body:
Of the three claims, the **conditional** is the one that should be our first priority. Whenever we get a conditional claim in Must Be True or Most Supported, we ask ourselves: 1. could I chain this up with other conditionals? 2. could I apply this rule to any specific facts?
We don't get any other conditionals here, but do we have any facts that apply to the conditional's trigger, or contrapositive trigger?
i.e., were we told about anyone who participated in the spring cleanup? Were we told about anyone who didn't receive a community recognition certificate?
Yes, we were told about some spring cleanup participants. We're told that some of them aren't active in the town's artistic circles. According to the conditional, we know they also received a community recognition certificate.
They aren't active in the town's artistic circles, but they received a community recognition certificate. That is probably what the correct answer will be saying. When we see Must Be True question bust our quantifiers (some, most, each, all, none), the inference we are most often being tested on is our ability to derive some Trait Overlap.
Some B's are A + All A's are C -------------------------- Some B's are C
Here they gave us these two claims
Some NAAC are SCP + All SCP are RCRC ---------------------------------------- Some NAAC are RCRC
(NAAC = not active artistic circles, SCP = spring cleanup participant, RCRC = received community recognition certificate)

label: Goal
body: Look for the Trait Overlap inference that "not active in artistic circles" and "received community recognition certificate" overlap at least once, or look for any other answer we can derive from the available facts.

label: Conclusion
body: Taking advanced math should raise your GPA.

label: Evidence
body: Numerous studies have shown that students who take at least one advanced math class are more likely than those who don't to have high GPA's.

label: Evaluation
body:
This is a classic move from **Correlation to Causality**. Whenever we see a correlation formulated like, "people who are X are more likely than those who aren't to be Y", we can expect the author to overconfidently assume/conclude that X causes Y, or that Y causes X.
We are supposed to think about alternate explanations for this correlation (such as **Reverse Causality** or **Third Factor** ). It's possible that high GPA is a prerequisite to get into advanced math classes (reverse causality). It's possible that being really smart, or having a tutor, or having involved parents is the third causal factor that accounts for both high GPA and taking advanced math.

label: Goal
body: We need an argument that presents a correlation and then concludes that one thing causes the other, but seems vulnerable to objections of reverse causality or third factor.

label: Conclusion (probably)
body: The reason that every human hormones has the power to raise glucose in the blood is probably a metabolic quirk of the brain.

label: Evidence (to see this, consider)
body: Brain cells can use only glucose. So if blood glucose falls too low, brain cells will starve, resulting in unconsciousness and death.

label: Evaluate
body:
This is a famously hard Main Conclusion question. Whenever we read Main Conclusion we prime our brain to listen for a Conclusion that comes **earlier** than its Supporting ideas, because 85% or more of the time that's where we find the Conclusion on Main Conclusion questions.
In particular, we usually see the conclusion be - the first sentence, or - some sort of rebuttal
The first sentence does kind of seem like it could be the Conclusion, because if we were to ask, "Why is it that every hormone has the power to raise glucose levels", then the rest of the paragraph would seem like a response.
But the first sentence is a science fact, not an opinion. Science facts can't be our Conclusion.
The word "probably" in the second sentence indicates that it's an Opinion. The **support indicator** "to see this, consider" shows us that the final two sentences are trying to support this 2nd sentence.
The "thus" in the final sentence also indicates either a Conclusion or a Cause/Effect relationship.
Conclusion "thus" Sam likes my dog. Thus, Sam must be a dog lover.
Causal "thus" Sam fell off his roof and thus broke his leg.
Because the last two sentences are telling us biological facts, the final claim about "if no glucose, then death" seems more like a Cause/Effect statement than a reasoning conclusion.
But whichever we would call it, it would still just be an Intermediate Conclusion, because the final two sentences stand in support of the 2nd sentence.

label: Goal
body: Since we've identified the 2nd sentence as the foremost Opinion the author is Supporting, we're just looking for an answer choice that matches the 2nd sentence in meaning.

label: Statements
body:
Countries that were allies during the Cold War found it more difficult to have international relations after the Cold War.
There were tensions between these former allies that had previously been overlooked, so now leaders of these nations had to conduct tactful economic negotiations.

label: Evaluate / Goal
body:
These **proposition / generalization** versions of Most Supported like to express a "moral to the story", but we want to be cautious about picking something too strongly worded.
Since the story tells of two timeframes with some differences, the correct answer may try to "explain one Difference using another Difference".

label: During Cold War After Cold War
body:
X, Y, and Z were allies Not technically allies
tensions overlooked tensions not overlooked
int'l relations between int'l relations between XYZ less difficult XYZ more difficult (tactful negotiations)
Let's look for an answer that safely reinforces that being Cold War allies was a causal difference-maker that allowed these countries to overlook tensions and have easier international relations.

label: Conclusion
body: The magnitudes of tidal ranges must be explained entirely by gravitational forces.

label: Evidence
body: The only forces involved in inducing the tides are the sun's and moon's gravity.

label: Evaluate
body:
Given that... only gravitational forces (from the sun and moon) are involved in inducing tidal ranges,
How could we argue that ... there are non-gravitational forces that affect the magnitude of tidal ranges?
To induce something means to trigger it, to start it. In maternity wards around the world, doctors and nurses will induce labor with a drug if it's not happening on its own.
The magnitude of something is its scale. In this case, it's the difference between high tide and low tide.
Is it possible that only X is involved in starting something, but other factors besides X affect the scale of how that thing plays out?
Sure. The catalyst of something doesn't have to be the only thing determining its shape / scale. Maybe without the sun and moon, there'd be no such thing as a tidal range. But maybe other things affect how big that tidal range is (such as weather / strong winds / local underwater topography ... i.e. does the beach slowly ramp down to the ocean floor or reach a cliff's edge where it suddenly drops a ton).
If Max went around town shoving people down to the ground, we could say that he's the only force involved in inducing people falling to the ground, but is the magnitude of people's fall entirely determined by Max?
No, it might matter how heavy they are. Whether they're standing near a stairwell. Whether they're standing on soft ground vs. concrete.

label: Goal
body: Look for an answer addressing the fact that even though one thing (gravity) is responsible for starting some action/event, other factors could still contribute to the size of that action/event.

label: Conclusion (therefore)
body: Musical training, particularly when it begins at a young age, causes certain anatomic brain changes.

label: Evidence
body: The corpus callosum of musicians, particularly those of adults who began training around age 7, are larger on average than those of adult nonmusicians.

label: Evaluate
body: This is a classic Causation Flaw: we have evidence of a correlation between two things and conclude that one of them must have caused the other.

label: Anticipate
body: This sort of Causation Flaw typically overlooks the reverse causality objection: what if the larger corpus callosum isn't the effect of early musical training but something that causes someone to want, or respond well to, that training? The correct answer might neutralize that objection by saying that a big ol' corpus callosum doesn't help you become a musician. But it also might do any number of other things because Necessary Assumption questions aren't consistently predictable, so read every answer with an open mind.

label: Conclusion
body: Adopting the recommendation (that headphone manufacturers offer a style of headphones that automatically turns off when a dangerous level of loudness is reached) would not significantly reduce the occurrence of hearing loss in teenagers.

label: Evidence
body: Almost all teenagers buy their own headphones.

label: Evaluate
body:
The author seems to think, "It's pointless to offer these Hearing-Protection headphones, because only parents would buy them out of concern for their children. Children would buy them for themselves, because they want to be able to rock out at max volume, hearing be damned."
How do we know? Why should we believe that teenagers aren't smart enough and responsible enough to care about their long-term hearing? Maybe they would embrace the chance to have their max volume be a safe volume.
Additionally, maybe we could make these Hearing-Protection headphones "cool", so that even if teenagers don't want to buy them for the hearing protection, they want to buy them for some other reason and we still then end up saving the teens' hearing.

label: Conclusion
body: This is a Resolve the Paradox question, so there's no argument — just a puzzle. Captive leatherbacks are exposed to fatal diseases they'd never get in the wild, yet they live about as long (in terms of reaching their max life expectancy) as wild ones do.

label: Goal
body:
Since this is Strengthen, we either want to rule out one of these objections - "teenagers would not buy these headphones, thinking that they're cool" - "teenagers are not super concerned about preserving their long term hearing"
or to affirm an assumption - "teenagers wouldn't buy these headphones"
or to add more evidence to the conclusion - "headphone manufacturers start offering this style of headphones, but it does not lead to a significant reduction in hearing loss among teens, because.... [answer choice]"

label: Conclusion (Therefore)
body: The additional threat posed by synthetic pesticides sprayed on crop plants by humans is minimal.

label: Evidence
body:
The average plant contains about 40 natural pesticides, that it has evolved as chemical defenses against parasites.
Humans ingest these natural pesticides without harm every day.

label: Evaluate
body:
Given that... humans ingest **natural** pesticides without harm every day,
How could we still argue that... there is a significant additional threat posed by the **synthetic** pesticides that are sprayed on crop plants?
We would probably need some way to argue that what's true of natural pesticides isn't true of synthetic pesticides. Even though the natural ones are harmless, maybe the synthetic ones are harmful because they have different ingredients / potency / concentration? We could also potentially argue that even though synthetic pesticides are relatively harmless as well, when you add synthetic pesticides atop natural pesticides the cumulative amount of poison is harmful (or maybe there's a harmful chemical reaction that occurs by adding synthetic pesticides on top of natural ones).

label: Goal
body: Look for four ways to argue that, "even though we're safely eating natural pesticides, synthetic pesticides could still pose some threat to humans".

label: Conclusion (therefore)
body: An expensive wine is not always a good wine.

label: Evidence
body: The reputation of the vineyard where the grapes originate plays a role in determining the price of a finished wine.

label: Evaluate
body:
To prove that "X is not always Y", we have to establish that sometimes X occurs even though Y doesn't.
So in this case, the author is trying to prove that sometimes you have an expensive wine, but it's not a good wine.
Does he supply an example of an expensive wine that isn't a good wine? No, his evidence is really bad and loose.
He just talks about three things that could make a wine more expensive: - the labor used to make the wine - the materials used to make the wine - the reputation of the vineyard
He must be assuming that it's possible to have an expensive wine (through some combo of how much labor went into it, the quality of materials used, and the reputation of the vineyard) that is not a good wine.

label: Goal
body: It's hard to pinpoint what language this answer will say. But it should reinforce the idea that you could have an expensive wine (because of the reputation, labor, materials or some combo of the three) that is still not a good wine.

label: Statements
body:
For a long time people thought only classical Euclidean geometry could correctly mathematically represent the universe.
Pivot (nevertheless)
Scientists now believe that non-Euclidean geometry is more useful for some areas of scientific theory.
A non-Euclidean representation underlies the cosmological theory that now most widely accepted as accurate.

label: Evaluate
body:
We aim to find Overlapping Language in Inference paragraphs, and the both the 2nd and 3rd claims are about "non-Euclidean representations". The 3rd sentence refers to it with a pronoun, though, so it's subtle (" **such** a representation").
This pronoun callback means that we should really read the 3rd sentence as "a non-Euclidean representation underlies the model most accepted as accurate".
We get a big Pivot tension in the paragraph between the Old belief and New belief.
We used to think that only Euclidean could provide a correct way of representing the universe.
But now the model of the universe most widely accepted by scientists is a non-Euclidean representation.

label: Goal
body:
When there's a big Pivot creating tension between the before and after, we expect the correct answer to safely reconcile those two.
If we read something like, "Tony thought that Maria hated pasta. **But**, Maria is eating rigatoni tonight", then an overreaction might be something like "Tony was wrong" or "Maria loves pasta" or "the only pasta Maria likes is rigatoni".
None of those are provable. Maybe Maria had to eat rigatoni as part of a business dinner, even though she hates pasta.
A safely worded version of reconciling those two would be more like (A) Either Tony is wrong about Maria or people are sometimes willing to eat things they hate.
So we should watch out for answers that go too far in the new direction and trash classic Euclidean as worthless or dumb.

label: Facts
body:
Expert witnesses need to make convincing presentations, because juries evaluate them mainly by their ability to present their reasoning steps clearly and confidently.
Because of this, lawyers will sometimes hire an expert witness who is **less** of an expert than others in their field but **better** than average at producing skilled testimony.
Principle Illustrated
This passage seems to be stressing a **Causal Difference-Maker** and its counterintuitive result. Because what matters most in hiring an expert witness is their ability to present well to a jury, we see that people get hired who are superficially a worse pick (they're less of an expert) but meaningfully a better pick (they're more likely to produce convincing testimony).

label: Goal
body:
If we're subtracting out the topic to make this more general and portable, we probably want something like this:
1. ostensibly, you'd think that in picking an X you're looking to max out quality A 2. but really quality B is what matters more 3. so sometimes people pick X's that aren't as good at A but are better at B

body: Solutions not made → most serious ecological economically enticing problems not solved

label: Evidence
body:
Solving any problem → major changes not the result of consumer habits government mismanagement
Major changes → solutions economically consumer habits enticing
