body:
Look for an answer vulnerable to a similar objection of, "Couldn't they both be wrong?"
Structurally, it'll probably resemble: - X and Y have incompatible predictions when it comes to Matter A. - Matter A will soon be resolved. - Thus, we'll soon know that either X or Y is correct and the other is wrong.

label: Conclusion (clearly, then)
body: In addition to undermining life's charm, much modern technology diminishes the overall well-being of its users.

label: Evaluate
body:
The "as a result" tells us which claim is the Conclusion. All three claims are conditional. We need to know how to deal with these common trigger words: - only / only if (put it on the right) - unless (put the opposite on the left -- "if not")
In Sufficient Assumption, we know that any New Idea that appears in the conclusion **must** appear in the correct answer. The concept of "few/most serious ecological problems" only appears in the conclusion, so it will have to be in the correct answer.
"Few" is one of the three main negative words that we see on LSAT. When we see these negative words, we want to perform a Negative to Positive translation.
No A's are B = All A's are ~B Few A's are B = Most A's are ~B Not all A's are B = Some A's are ~B
We can see that "economically enticing solutions" and "major changes in consumer habits" are each mentioned twice. On Assumption questions, generally if a term is mentioned twice, it won't show up in the correct answer. Being mentioned twice usually means that you've already served a role in linking two things.
So if we were lost and trying to fake a fuzzy guess, we'd expect the correct answer to talk about "few/most serious ecological problems" and relate it to the only other idea that is mentioned only once: the solution to any problem that is not the result of government mismanagement.
If we're being more savvy than that, we're taking the conditional conclusion and stretching out the trigger and the outcome, so that we can see what internal pieces of that Logic Chain have been provided in the Evidence.

The evidence gave us a three idea chain, starting from "solutions not econ enticing".
EVIDENCE

This illustrates the gap we have: "If the environmental problems that aren't the result of government mismanagement aren't solved, then most serious ecological problems aren't solved."

Look for an answer saying

label: Information
body:
The economy is doing badly: We have a real estate slump that's been going on for a while. Car sales are at their lowest in years.
If real estate was looking goor or if car sales were looking good, then it would still be possible to say "the economy is healthy".
causal (X makes it quite probable that Y) pivot (But)
When real estate is bad and car sales are bad, it's quite probable that the economy is doing badly.

label: Evaluate
body:
This gives us a couple facts about the current economy and then a couple considerations about whether we should conclude the economy is doing badly or not.
There aren't any obvious wording clues to go off, but the last sentence seems tempting. It has a Pivot, and we know that when Inference paragraphs use a Pivot word (like "but, yet, however, nonetheless) to introduce the final claim, that final claim almost always plays a .... [wait for it] .... pivotal role in the correct answer.
There is also some causal language in the final sentence, that having bad real estate and car sales at the same time is a strong indicator of bad economy.

label: Goal
body: It's hard to make any prediction here, so we'll just look for the most provable answer we can find, but our suspicions are that the final sentence will be important.

label: Conclusion (Therefore)
body: It is likely that the melting of the ice at the end of the Ice Age contributed to earthquakes that racked Sweden during that time period.

label: Evidence
body: The melting of ice at the end of the Ice Age reduces the weight pressing on the earth's crust in certain spots, which leads to lasting cracks in the crust at these spots.

label: Evaluate
body:
The conclusion is saying that melting contributed to earthquakes.
The evidence lays out a mini-Causal Chain that gets us from melting to cracks.
Melting → reduced weight → cracks of ice or parts of crust in crust
In order to get from melting to earthquakes, there's still a missing link in the causal chain:
cracks → earthquakes? in crust

label: Goal
body:
If this is testing a Missing Link, then we want an answer that's saying something like "cracks in the earth's crust contribute to severe earthquakes". Or we could pick anything else that increases the plausibility that the melting of ice contributed to these earthquakes (for example, "In Sweden, during that time, there was a lot of melting of ice").
Usually, with causal conclusions, we could also consider strengthening by ruling out an Alternate Explanation (for the severe earthquakes, in this case).
But the author didn't say the quakes were **caused by** melting ice, rather that melting ice is **one of the causes**. So Alternate Explanations technically don't matter here.

label: Counterpoint
body: If you're aiming for democracy, you should have free markets, because that way people can vote with their money.

label: Conclusion
body: People who want democracy can still want regulated (un-free) markets.

label: Evidence
body: Voting with money is a question of "What do I want", whereas voting in an election is a question of "What do we want". The private consumer and the public citizen are different entities ( so supporting regulation and supporting democracy are not contradictory positions)

label: Goal
body:
This is an unusual feeling... we're doing Main Conclusion, and the conclusion is the last claim? With a clear conclusion indicator like Hence?
Since this argument is still a rebuttal argument, we might want to prime our brain with the sound of negating the opponent's position.
Opposing position Unregulated markets should accompany democratic sovereignty.
Author's rebuttal position Regulated markets can accompany democratic sovereignty.
Ultimately, that rebuttal position does sound like the final claim, so let's look for a meaning match for the final sentence.

label: Statements
body:
We're usually scanning Statements for Conditional / Causal / Math-y / Pivot language as a clue to what claims they want us to synthesize.
Here we see a bunch of comparative relationships that are Math-y.
Vol / Weight Egg % of weight H-bird: tiny / little 15% Goose: much bigger 4% Ostrich: even bigger 1.6%
We can definitely see a certain relationship her — as the volume and weight of the adult gets bigger, the egg as a percentage of weight gets smaller.

label: Goal
body: Look for some safely worded answer that reinforces this inverse correlation between the volume/weight of the bird and the % of the bird's weight that its egg is.

label: Conclusion
body: This assumption is false. rephrase: A vampire's being able to turn into a bat is **not** an essential part of vampire myths. rephrase of the rephrase: it's possible to have a vampire myth where the vampire isn't able to turn into a bat.

label: Evidence (for)
body: Vampire myths existed in Europe long before Bram Stoker's book.

label: Evidence
body: Modern technology provides relief from the drudgery of physical labor, but it makes its users more dependent on this technology and on the elaborate energy systems required to run it.

label: Evidence
body: Two facts collide: (1) captive leatherbacks face an extra threat (diseases unique to captivity), but (2) the survival rates between captive and wild leatherbacks are about the same.

label: Evaluate
body:
The most challenging technical part of this is undressing the conclusion. " **This** assumption is false" contains a pronoun, so we need to search back for what assumption was just said, and then invert the truth value.
If they were assuming "Coke is tasty" then this author is concluding "Coke is not tasty".
They were assuming "X is an essential part of Y", so this author is concluding that "X is **not** an essential part of Y". It's very easy to prove that: you only need one example in which Y was true but X was not.
So all this author needs to present as evidence in order to win her case that "being able to turn into a bat is not an essential part of vampire myths" is one example in which there's a vampire myth but the vampire was not able to turn into a bat.
Does she present an example of that?
No, she just says that vampire myths existed before Stoker's book.

label: Goal
body: She must be assuming that "at least one of the vampire myths that existed before Stoker's book **didn't** involve vampires having the ability to turn themselves into bats".

label: Conclusion (unlikely = opinion)
body: It's unlikely the world will ever be free of disease.

label: Evidence
body: Most diseases are caused by prolific microorganisms whose response to the pressure of medicine is predictable: they evolve immunities to those medicines while maintaining their power to infect or kill humans.

label: Evaluate
body:
Whenever we do Main Conclusion or Role, we remind ourselves that the vast majority of the time the main conclusion will be found in the First Sentence or as some Pivot / Rebuttal in the middle.
That helps us to hear the first sentence as the main conclusion, in realtime. We're listening for whether it sounds like an opinion from the author. When we see that it's a prediction about the future (not attributed to anyone else), we know it's an opinion from our author.
If she goes on to defend / support this claim, then we know it was the conclusion.
She does. The final two claims explain how our action of treating disease with medicine just spawns newly-evolved forms of the disease that elude our medicines. Thus, we'll unlikely ever be free of disease.

label: Goal
body: We're being asked about the first sentence, which is our Main Conclusion, so let's look for something that means Main Conclusion.

label: Conclusion (I conclude that)
body: There is a causal relationship between this gene variant and an inclination toward thrill-seeking behavior.

label: Evidence
body: Children who engage in impulsive behavior (similar to adult thrill-seeking behavior) are twice as likely as other children to have a gene variant that increases sensitivity to dopamine.

label: Evaluate
body:
The author presents a Correlation, "people who are X are twice as likely to be Y", and then assumes a specific causal relationship. This looks like the ol' Explain a Curious Fact template.
Curious Fact... why are impulsive children twice as likely to have variant X? Author's Explanation.... variant X causes the inclination toward thrill-seeking behavior.
The author actually just says "there is a causal relationship between the two", so technically she might think that being inclined toward thrill-seeking behavior causes this gene variant, but it's so beyond the realm of common sense to think that behavior would cause genetics that it feels natural to interpret this as "genetics causes the behavioral inclination".
The author's causal story also suggests that the variant makes someone more sensitive to dopamine, and that because these people feel so much from a release in dopamine, they get more out of thrill-seeking impulsivity (which presumably triggers a dopamine release).

label: Goal
body: Since this is Weaken, we'd be thinking we want either of these things: 1. to suggest an **Alternate Explanation** for the correlation between impulsive behavior and variant X 2. to undermine the plausibility of the author's explanation, which is that having this gene variant causes a bigger inclination to impulsive / thrill-seeking behavior.

label: Conclusion
body: It is highly likely that Claudette is a classical pianist.

label: Evidence
body:
Claudette recognizes many of Clara Schumann's works.
Most classical pianists recognize many of Clara Schumann's works.
Most people who aren't classical pianists do not recognize many of Clara Schumann's works (many of them have never even heard of Clara Schumann).

label: Evaluate
body:
It's very hard to diagnose what's going wrong in this argument if we don't have some familiarity with how to use Most claims to derive a Likely conclusion. If we do, this argument will seem like almost like the illegal reversal we're used to seeing on Necessary vs. Sufficient flaws.
Suppose we know that Most X's are Y, X --m--> Y and we learn that Danny is an X, Danny is X. then we can conclude that Danny is likely Y. Danny is probably Y
Most Senators are men. A Senator is visiting our class today. Thus, today's visitor will probably be a man.
But if we know Most X's are Y, and then we're told Danny is Y, we are not allowed to read that backwards and conclude that Danny is probably X.
- paragraph
Most Senators are men. A man is visiting our class today. Thus, today's visitor will probably be a Senator.
- paragraph
The argument is trying to read that Most claim backwards. That's how it's concluding that Claudette is probably classical pianist.

label: Goal
body:
If we had these two claims, 1. Claudette recognizes Clara Schumann 2. Most who recognize Clara Schumann are classical pianists We could conclude Claudette is probably classical pianist
But the premise they gave us is a reversal of that 2nd claim: - Most classical pianists recognize Clara Schumann
It's hard to predict how the correct answer will describe this flaw, since it's not technically a Necessary vs. Sufficient move (and there's no fancy term for "reading a Most statement backwards"). When in doubt, it's good to remember the Anti-Conclusion. We want an answer to help us argue that "even though Claudette recognizes many of Clara Schumann's works, she is not likely to be a classical pianist".

label: Conclusion (therefore)
body: The result of this experiment will confirm one of these theories at the expense of the other.

label: Evidence
body: The predictions that Dr. Grippen's theory and Prof. Heissmann's theory make about the result of the planned experiment cannot both be true.

label: Evaluate
body:
Given that both predictions can't be right, why is it flawed to say that the experiment will show that one of them is right and one of them is wrong?
Because, they could both be wrong!
If you think Oprah is 65 and I think she's 70, we can't both be right. But when we ask the internet what her age is, that doesn't guarantee that one of us is right. We might both have predicted the wrong number

label: Evaluate
body: Need a wild-only mortality factor to offset captivity's disease problem.

label: Evaluate
body:
There are two new terms in the conclusion, "undermining life's charm", and "diminishing the overall well-being of its users".
The author must be assuming stuff in relation to both phrases. Did the evidence talk about anything like "undermining life's charm"?
Not really. We know that modern technology relieves us from the drudgery of physical labor. Was the author assuming that "doing the drudgery of physical labor was part of life's charm"? Maybe.
But we should also consider the possibility that the phrase "in addition to undermining life's charm" is a random aside. It's not part of the main clause of the conclusion, and it's the main clause that the author is concluding.
Did the evidence talk about "diminishing the overall well-being of its users"? The closest match would be the one negative thing we heard, which was that modern technology makes its users more dependent on technology and the energy systems that run it.
So the author seems to have a Linking assumption that "becoming more dependent on technology and the energy systems that run it diminishes your overall well-being".
We've covered Links. What about Objections? How could we accept the evidence but argue that almost all modern technology **improves / maintains** the well-being of its users?
We could argue in a Net Gain / Loss style that even though modern technology has the negative of making us more dependent on tech / energy systems, it has positives that offset or outweigh that negative.

label: Goal
body:
Look for a Linking assumption connecting "more dependence on tech / energy systems" with "diminishes overall well-being".
Or look for a Defender assumption saying, "modern technology does **not** have a lot of advantages to our well-being that outweigh the disadvantage of making us more dependent on it."

label: Main Conclusion (mistakenly - opinion)
body:
Psychologists mistakenly argue that dreams must be understood purely in terms of their physiological content (because they result from electrical discharges).
i.e., dreams **can be** understood in non-physiological terms as well

label: Intermediate Conclusion
body: Electrical discharges cannot completely explain the phenomenon of dreaming.

label: Evidence (since)
body: Dream content varies enormously.

label: Evaluate
body: We're being asked about a claim that is prefaced by **since**, so it's a guarantee that it's performing the role of **supporting** the other half of its sentence. (FABS = for, after all, because, since = Support Indicators)

label: Goal
body:
Let's look for something like **Premise / Support / Evidence** for the claim that "electrical discharges cannot completely explain the phenomenon of dreaming".
If they're getting mean, we may need to worry about whether that final claim is the main conclusion or just an intermediate one, but we won't worry about that until we see it.

label: Conclusion
body: Some change in values must have occurred between 1817 and 1860.

label: Evidence
body: Bike was invented in 1817. There was a brief fad, but bikes basically disappeared until the 1860s, when they finally "caught on". New technology accepted → Coheres with values

label: Evaluation
body:
Any time we're doing Flaw and see conditional logic language (like "only when") we should examine whether the author is illegally using that rule in backwards or opposite fashion (aka, **Necessary vs. Sufficient** flaw).
Our author is looking at the **Curious Fact** of why wasn't the bike accepted in 1817? and looking at the rule he presents that says, doesn't cohere w/ values → new not accepted
He thinks, "Ah! Here's an explanation for why the bike wasn't accepted: it didn't cohere w/ values. I guess if it was finally accepted in 1860, that must mean that at that point the bike now cohered with values, so the values must have changed from 1817 to 1860."

label: Goal
body:
We could describe this flaw as a Necessary vs. Sufficient error. The author has this conditional: doesn't cohere → new tech not accepted
and he is reasoning in this style: bike wasn't accepted → bike didn't cohere
We could also describe this flaw as a **Causal Flaw**, in which the author has overconfidently settled on one possible explanation for why bikes weren't initially accepted.

label: Conclusion (Therefore)
body: Long breaks should be removed from the school calendar.

label: Evidence
body:
Long breaks were originally put in the school calendar so that children could have long breaks during which they could stay home and help with the harvest.
But most of the citizens are no longer engaged in agricultural lives, so we can make changes that better serve the children.

label: Evaluate
body:
From a Missing Link perspective, the author is assuming that "removing long breaks from the school calendar" would be a change that "serves the interests of children".
We could also try to think of possible Objections. How could we accept the evidence but still argue that, "We shouldn't get rid of the long breaks / we should keep them"?
- the teachers really need these breaks; they're exhausted - even though only a minority of kids are on farms, we still have to build a schedule that can accommodate all of them - getting rid of the long breaks would be destructive to many industries, like summer camps, that depend on students being out of school
The argument would be assuming - teachers **don't** need a long break - we **don't** have to accommodate the farm kids - this **wouldn't** destroy lots of summer-themed industries

label: Goal
body: Look for an answer linking premise language to conclusion language, or look for an answer that, if negated, would turn into an objection and help us argue that we shouldn't get rid of these long breaks.

label: Given that
body: Captive leatherbacks are exposed to fatal diseases they'd never encounter in the wild.

label: How can it be that
body: The likelihood of reaching maximum life expectancy is about the same in captivity and in the wild?

label: Evaluate
body:
We're told there's something worse / life-shortening about living in captivity.
So if max life expectancy is the same for captive vs. wild, then we either need to hear: - something good / life-elongating about captivity - something bad / life-shortening about the wild - these fatal diseases that become a risk on captivity are not actually shortening the lives of any leatherbacks

label: Goal
body: I'd be looking for a distinction between captivity and the wild, something GOOD about captivity or BAD about the wild, when it comes to life span.

label: Conclusion
body: Paradox; no conclusion.

label: Evidence
body: Captive leatherbacks face fatal diseases the wild ones avoid, yet life-expectancy odds are similar in both environments.

label: Evaluate
body:
For survival to come out even despite captives facing extra disease risk, there must be some other threat the *wild* ones face that captives don't. That extra wild-side threat is what would cancel out captivity's disease threat.
Think of it as a balance scale: captivity's extra weight on the "dies young" side has to be matched by something on the "wild" side. The most natural candidate is predators — something wild leatherbacks face all the time and captive ones never do.

label: Goal
body: Pick the answer that names a deadly wild-only threat. Predators are the obvious one.

label: Conclusion
body: Countries with tight control over economic information are more likely to experience economic crises than are countries with free flowing economic information.

label: Evidence
body: In countries with tight control over economic information, the vast majority of the population is denied information vital to their welfare.

label: Evaluate
body:
Since we have an argument structured like this: Countries with tight control have **this** trait Thus, Countries with tight control have **that** trait
We just need a rule that says " **this** leads to **that** ".
Countries with tight control have **[** a majority of the population denied vital information about factors determining their welfare **]** Thus, Countries with tight control have **[** more likely to experience frequent economic crises **]**

label: Goal
body: We need an answer that allows us to get from "when a majority of the population is denied vital info about their welfare" to "more likely to experience frequent economic crises"

label: Conclusion
body: At least some of Hana's brothers must have been among the guests at Hana's birthday party after all.

label: Evidence (since)
body: Even though Hana said she wasn't going to invite her brothers, one of the gifts Hana received at her party was a recording she had been saying she wanted. Her brothers planned to give her that recording.

label: Evaluate
body:
Since Hana got a recording that her brothers were planning to give her, does that prove that some of the brothers were at the party?
No that doesn't prove that. Couldn't we think of alternate explanations for how Hana would get that gift, even though her brothers weren't at the party?
- it's possible her brothers just left that gift at the party location ahead of time, but didn't attend the party
- it's possible her brothers sent the gift with someone else who they knew was invited to the party
- it's possible someone else got her the recording, too, since Hana had apparently expressed an interest in it.

label: Goal
body: The author is too sure of one possible causal explanation for how Hana got that recording as a gift. Let's look for an answer calling out that overconfidence or suggesting an alternative explanation.

label: Rossi's argument structure
body: Rossi states a general principle ("It is undemocratic for people to live under a government in which their interests are not represented") and applies it to children: since children's interests are sometimes different from their parents', children should have the right to vote.

label: Smith's response (background)
body: Smith concedes Rossi's point about different interests but raises a separate practical objection: children's conceptions and time horizons are too immature for voting responsibility.

label: Evaluate
body: The question asks how Rossi's argument is structured. Rossi opens with a general principle (about democracy and representation) and then applies it to a specific case (children). That's an appeal to a general principle.

label: Goal
body: Find the answer that describes Rossi as appealing to a general principle.

label: Rossi's argument
body: States a general principle about representation and applies it to children to argue for child suffrage.

label: Goal
body: Pick the answer describing Rossi as appealing to a general principle.

label: Rossi's argument
body: Rossi opens with a sweeping rule: it's undemocratic for people to be governed without representation. Then Rossi applies that rule to children, arguing they should have the right to vote because their interests sometimes differ from their parents'.

label: Evaluate
body: This is a Method-of-argument question: how does Rossi's argument work? The structure is "general principle, then application." Rossi doesn't evaluate consequences, doesn't attack Smith's motives, doesn't shift definitions of a term — Rossi just appeals to a general democratic principle and shows it applies to children.

label: Goal
body: The answer that says: Rossi appeals to a general principle.

label: Conclusion (hence)
body: If people hadn't generally been using personal automobiles, the geography of modern cities would be quite different from the one we have now.

label: Evidence
body: Houses are built on widely scattered lots, far from places of work / shopping malls have huge parking lots that leave little room for wooded areas, all to accommodate the personal automobile.

label: Evaluate
body:
The author establishes that some of the geography of modern cities got the way it did because of trying to accommodate cars.
Her argument is essentially saying, In order to accommodate X, we made something that looked like Y. Thus, if we weren't trying to accommodate X, we would have made something that looks quite different from Y.
It's a variation on the Flip the Causal Difference-Maker inference that we see as a correct answer on Most Supported tasks. It is supportable to say, "if we hadn't been trying to accommodate the car, the geography of cities would probably be different".
The author is only going too far by thinking it definitely would be quite different. How could we potentially argue that even if we hadn't been concerned with cars, we still would have had fairly similar geography to modern cities?
We'd probably just have to say that there could have been other factors that would have similarly inclined us towards having spaced apart houses and big parking lots eating up the forest space.

label: Goal
body: Look for a way to argue that "even though our use of cars affected the layout of cities, the layout of cities may have ended up being fairly similar even without the impact of cars".

label: Premises
body: Per-band musicians decreased; total professional musicians increased.

label: Evaluate

label: Statements
body:
quantified (many) Many of the leaders with the most successful foreign policies had no prior experience in foreign affairs when they became leader.
conditional (anyone) if you have acute political sense, cool temperament, and can quickly absorb/retain info, then you can quickly learn to have successful foreign policy.
anti-causal (little value) If you lacked all three of these traits, then prior experience alone wouldn't be of much value in terms of your foreign policy abilities.

label: Evaluate
body:
We had a curious mix of claims. I left out the snarky "although scholars would have us think otherwise", just because it seemed too little like a fact for me to think LSAC would use that.
Is there any overlapping idea?
Foreign policy is mentioned in all three claims. Foreign policy experience is explicitly mentioned in two of them (implicitly it's in all three). Three traits are mentioned in two of them.
It's hard to see an obvious synthesis. If you have the three traits you can be successful, even if you don't have experience. If you don't have the three traits, you might not be successful even if you do have experience.

label: Goal
body: Not really sure what we're looking for, so just find the most provable answer choice.

label: Conclusion
body: Polar bears can navigate over considerable distances.

label: Evidence
body: Navigation in animals is defined as the animal's ability to find its way from unfamiliar territory to points familiar to the animal but beyond the immediate range of the animal's senses.

label: Evaluate
body:
The argument is structured around presenting a single piece of evidence — a specific instance of a polar bear returning home from a long distance — to support the broader claim that polar bears possess substantial navigational abilities. This is a classic case of using anecdotal evidence to make a general claim.
To cast doubt on this evidence, we should look for an alternative explanation for how the bear managed to find its way home, which doesn't rely on a specialized navigational ability. Additionally, we should check for factors that might question the reliability of this evidence as a representative example of polar bear navigation.

label: Goal
body: Let's find an answer that suggests an alternative explanation for the bear's return or that undermines the reliability of using this one instance as evidence of polar bears' navigational ability.

label: Conclusion (It Is Clear That)
body: In blocking bills that would impose fees on real estate development, the mayor is sacrificing the city's interests to personal interests.

label: Intermediate Conclusion (Thus)
body: The mayor's family has a strong financial interest in these bills.

label: Evidence
body: The mayor's family is heavily involved in real estate development.

label: Evaluate
body:
This towering paragraph is a tough read. When we do Main Conclusion or Role questions, we need to remind ourselves of their pattern, so that we can make it easier to understand when we're hearing the Main Conclusion.
In 90% of Main Conclusion questions, the Main Conclusion is **earlier** than (at least some of) the Supporting ideas. It's usually the very First Claim, if that first claim sounds like the author's opinion, or it's some Rebuttal / Pivot moment.
This first claim sounds part opinionated / part factual: The city badly needs money / the mayor has blocked a bill to impose real estate fees.
Does the 2nd sentence try to support the opinion that "the city has a desperate need to exploit any available source of revenue"?
No, instead it begins with Opinion Indicator language like " **It is clear that** ". Our author thinks the mayor is looking out for himself, not the city. Does she defend that claim?
Yes, but she starts by citing the mayor's defense of his actions. She's saying that even if you can make a statistical argument that the fees the bill would impose would be a net loss for the city, the real reason the mayor is tanking these bills is because his family is involved in real estate and thus would be financially harmed by these new fees.

label: Goal
body:
Once we've found the conclusion, we just need to pick the answer that best matches it.
Let's look for "In blocking bills that would impose real estate fees, the mayor is sacrificing city interests to personal interests".

label: Conclusion (it is clear that = opinion)
body: By blocking council's attempts to pass legislation that would impose real estate development fees, the mayor is sacrificing the city's interests to personal interests.

label: Intermediate Conclusion (thus)
body: The mayor has a strong financial interest in the matter of real estate development fees.

label: Evidence
body: The mayor's family is heavily involved in real estate development.

label: Evaluate
body:
Since two reasoning moves are made, we can potentially scrutinize each of them.
Given that ... the mayor's family is involved in real estate development,
Should we accept that ... the mayor has a strong financial interest in the matter of real estate development fees?
No, not necessarily. It sounds like members of the mayor's family have a strong financial interest in these fees, but we have no idea whether the mayor benefits from her family members' real estate financials. Do they share money with her? Are they even in touch with her? If she's estranged from the family, the fact that they are involved in real estate doesn't really affect her.
Given that ... the mayor has a strong financial interest in the matter of real estate development fees,
Should we accept that ... by blocking this bill the mayor is sacrificing city interests to financial interests?
No, blocking the bill might still be in the city's financial interests. After all the mayor cites figures that show these fees would cause a **net loss** of revenue for the city.
So isn't blocking the bill in the city's financial interests?

label: Goal
body:
Let's look for an answer saying, "Just because someone's family might financially benefit from X doesn't mean that this someone will also benefit."
Or look for an answer saying, "Didn't the mayor cite figures showing that this bill would not be in the city's financial interests?"

label: Conclusion
body: Seemingly inconsequential changes in sea temperature due to global warming eventually result in declines in fish and seabird populations.

label: Evidence
body: Even just a seemingly inconsequential two degree increase in sea temperature prevents vertical mixing of seawater, which limits how many nutrients flow up to phytoplankton (which imperils the population of phytoplankton), which imperils the population of zooplankton which feed upon it, which imperils the rest of the food chain, which feed upon zooplankton.

label: Evaluate
body:
Whenever we do Main Conclusion and Role, we prime our brain to listen for a First Sentence Conclusion or a Rebuttal Conclusion, since those are the two dominant strains for those question types.
Without that tendency-awareness on Main Conclusion and Role, our work can be much harder. If we listen to this first sentence knowing there's a high probability it's the conclusion, then it's easier to hear the rest of the paragraph as fleshing out the causal chain that gets us from a change in sea temperature to a decline in fish and seabird populations.
They don't give us any keywords to go off of, other than the Support Indicator "since" in the final sentence. "Since X, Y" always indicates that Y is a conclusion supported by X (or, in causal contexts, that Y is an effect of X).
In this paragraph, we could call "the declines are inevitable" an intermediate conclusion, but it seems more appropriate to just see that last sentence as we do the 2nd and 3rd sentences: presenting cause/effect relationships.
Words like since / because / thus / so can be used in causal ways, where we don't attach our normal Support Indicator or Conclusion Indicator thoughts to them.
for example: Kevin broke his leg because he fell off the roof. Kevin fell off the roof, thus breaking his leg.

label: Goal
body: They're asking us about the second to last claim, which was part of the Support (everything after the first sentence was part of the support).

label: Conclusion
body: The embezzler is probably one of the actuaries.

label: Evidence
body: The embezzler must have had specialized knowledge / access to financial records, so

label: Intermediate Conclusion
body: The embezzler must have been an accountant or an actuary.

label: More Evidence
body: But an accountant probably wouldn't make the mistakes in ledger entries that gave away the crime.

label: Evaluate
body:
The author is trying to solve the causal mystery of who embezzled, so we could use a Curious Fact / Explanation template:
Curious Fact: who is the embezzler? Author's Story: it's probably an actuary.
We can weaken either of two ways: 1. suggest a **different explanation** for who the embezzler is 2. hurt the plausibility of the **author's explanation**

label: Goal
body:
Look for an answer saying that people other than accountants and actuaries had specialized knowledge and access to records (which introduces an **alternative explanation** for who the embezzler might be).
Look for an answer talking about the ledger entries and either making it seem like an accountant might easily have made those mistakes, or make it seem like an actuary likely wouldn't make those mistakes.

label: Information
body:
Pre-1985: replenished air once every 30 min Post-1985: replenish air once every 60 min
The less frequently cabin air is replenished, the higher the level of CO2 in the plane and the easier it is for airborne illnesses to be spread.

label: Evaluate
body:
Jeez, I hope airline went back to the pre-1985 standard during the era of COVID.
Here, the information establishes a difference between pre/post 1985, and then we get a rule we can apply to that difference.

label: Goal
body: It sounds like pre-1985: less CO2, less chance of airborne illness spreading post-1985: more CO2, more chance of airborne illness spreading

label: Conclusion
body: There is no genuinely altruistic behavior.

label: Evidence
body: Behavior that appears to be altruistic can be understood as being motivated by the desire to reinforce the belief that we are useful and needed, a belief we need in order to maintain a minimum of self-esteem.

label: Evaluate
body:
How can we accept the Evidence, but argue the Anti-Conclusion, that there is such a thing as genuinely altruistic behavior?
I guess we could say, "sure, you could understand helpful behavior as secretly selfish behavior from someone craving a sense of being useful. But maybe it's not that. Maybe it's genuine altruism."
We wouldn't accept an argument like, "Cashiers never flirt with their customers. Cashiers are supposed to be friendly to their customers. Behavior that appears to be flirtatious can be understood as an employee trying to be friendly with their customers."
Sure you can understand it that way, but we still think sometimes cashiers be flirtin'.

label: Goal
body: Look for an answer saying something like, "Just because you can understand seemingly altruistic behavior as non-altruistic doesn't mean you should understand it that way."

label: Claim
body: These new maps (compiled using computerized data from several thousand modern weather stations and input from home gardeners across NA) will be far more useful than the old maps (gathered 60 years ago from a few hundred primitive weather stations).

label: Evaluate
body:
The question stem doesn't say we're supporting an argument, just that we're supporting a Claim, so we don't necessarily have to think of this as "Conclusion, supported by Evidence".
We just need four reasons why these new maps would be better.
We can focus on the current differences we know about them

label: OLD MAPS NEW MAPS
body: weather data gathered computerized data 60 yrs ago from a few from several thousand a few hundred primitive modern weather stations weather stations + input from gardeners

label: Goal
body: Find four ways that support that these new ones are more useful when it comes to showing where different types of garden plants will flourish.

label: Conclusion
body: Individuals cannot easily adopt a strategy in which the danger of some habit they want to break is greatly exaggerated, unless a doctor or some other third party provides the warning.

label: Evidence (since)
body: These strategies involve deception.

label: Goal
body: Pick the answer that says the total number of professional bands has increased.

label: Premises
body: The stimulus gives us two trends. First, the average band has gotten smaller (fewer musicians per band). Second, the total number of professional musicians has gone up.

label: Evaluate
body: Do the math. If the total pool of musicians is bigger and they're spread across smaller average bands, the only way that fits is more bands. Imagine 100 musicians at 5 per band = 20 bands. Now grow the pool to 150 musicians at 3 per band = 50 bands. Same logic here: bigger pool divided into smaller bands means more bands.

label: Goal
body: The right answer says: the total number of professional bands has increased.

label: Evaluate
body:
Since the conclusion is Conditional, two things are true: 1. If we want to make any objections to this argument, they have to be to the **outcome** of the conditional, not to the the trigger. (We can essentially treat the trigger of a conditional conclusion as though it's another premise. It's baked-in to the reasoning as something we need to accept.)
2. The author is probably making a conditional assumption.
The author's move from premise to conclusion is essentially, "Since these strategies involved deception, you can't easily adopt them without a third party providing the warning".
So the Linking assumption the author is making is,
"If a strategy involves deception, then it can't easily be adopted without a third party".
In terms of Objections, we would try to think of a way to argue that one could easily adopt this strategy **without** some third party providing the warning.
Let's say we want to quit drinking alcohol. We want to the danger of continuing to drink alcohol greatly exaggerated, so that it will motivate us to kick the habit. Can we carry out this plan without a third party providing the warning? (our friends / family / a doctor / the internet ... all of those are third parties)
Sure, couldn't we just warn ourselves? We could be brushing our teeth in the mirror and say, "I hear that if you don't quit drinking by age 30, your liver can only last until age 60."

label: Goal
body: Look for an answer proving the missing link of, "If it involves deception, then it's hard to do without a third party", or look for a Defender answer ruling out our objection, saying something like, "We can **not** just greatly exaggerate the danger of our habit to ourselves."

label: Conclusion (Therefore)
body: In Hallstown, most people buy prepared frozen dinners regularly.

label: Evidence
body:
In Hallstown, most people shop for groceries no more than three times a month.
Most people who shop for groceries no more than three times a month buy prepared frozen dinners regularly.

label: Evaluate
body:
When we're doing Parallel / Parallel Flaw, and the argument contains conditionals, quantifiers, or pairs of repeating ideas, it's usually a good idea to convert the argument into an algebraic recipe. If possible, we go straight to generic variables like A/B/C or X/Y/Z, but below we'll go in steps.
(Prem 1) In Hallstown, most people shop for groceries no more than three times a month. **Most H's are 3max.**
(Prem 2) Most people who shop for groceries no more than three times a month buy prepared frozen dinners regularly. **Most 3max are FDR.**
(Conc) In Hallstown, most people buy prepared frozen dinners regularly. **Most H's are FDR.**
We can see that all three claims are most claims, and they're trying to form this sort of chain: Most A's are B + Most B's are C --------------------------- Most A's are C
That is illegal. The only legal inferences we make with two Most claims are these: Most A's are B Most A's are B + Most A's are C Most B's are ~A ------------------- ------------------ Some B's are C More B's than A's
We can demonstrate how chaining most statements doesn't work with an analogy: Most Senators are men Most men make < $100k ----------------------------------------- Most Senators make < $100k?

label: Goal
body: Look for an argument with two Most premises and a Most conclusion. The two premises should be trying to "chain together". The overlapping concept they share should be the beginning of one of the claims and the ending of the other claim.

label: Conclusion (So)
body: This party's policy is clearly inconsistent (i.e. they are contradicting themselves).

label: Evidence
body:
On some occasions they've expressed the view that increasing spending on education is a worthy goal.
On other occasions, they've claimed that the government should not increase spending on education.

label: Evaluate
body:
Is it really a contradiction to sometimes support increased spending on education and other times not to?
No, because the two situations might not be fair to compare.
Perhaps in the year 2010, schools were badly underfunded and so Party X supported increased funding for education.
And then in the year 2020, schools were operating with a huge budget surplus, so Party X opposed increased funding ("they already have enough funding, clearly!").
Or perhaps in the year 2010 there was a bill to increase spending on S.T.E.M. education, and Party X supported that, but in the year 2020 there was a bill to increase spending on racial sensitivity education and Party X opposed that.

label: Goal
body: In order for these two different occasions to be contradictory, the author has to assume that they're fair to compare. She has to assume that there wasn't a good reason why the Party switched from supporting increased spending in one case and opposed it in another.

label: Conclusion
body: It is immoral to threaten to use force, even in self-defense.

label: Evidence (since)
body:
It is immoral to do anything that causes harm to another person.
Using force causes harm to another person

label: Evaluate
body:
The two premises have a common concept, causes harm to another person. Our Inference-brain should read these first two ideas and synthesize them. It's a conditional rule and a specific case to which we can apply that rule.
RULE: if causes harm, immoral SPECIFIC: using-force causes harm INFER: using-force is immoral
Once we've merged the two premises into one, it's easier to hear the gap:
Using force is immoral. Thus, threatening to use force (even in self-defense) is immoral.

label: Goal
body: Look for something like, "If X is immoral, then threatening to do X , even in self-defense, is also immoral".

label: Facts
body:
causal (by, which has enabled, because, increased)
electrical >> play w/ >> avg # of musicians instruments more volume per band decreased
pivot (nevertheless)
electrical >> greater # of professional instruments musicians

label: Evaluate
body:
The #1 thing we read for on Most Supported is Cause / Effect relationships, and we got four of them here.
There's a causal chain, and then a pivot that creates a **mathy tension** between two different things caused by electrification: 1. fewer musicians per band 2. more musicians overall When we see a Pivot creating a mathy tension, the correct answer usually addresses / resolves that tension.
If we have fewer musicians in each band nowadays, how can also have more musicians total?
We would need there to be more bands than before.
Maybe there used to be 10 ppl / band, and there were 80 bands, giving us 800 musicians.
If we only have 5 ppl / band now and want to end up with 1000 musicians (some larger number), then we'd need 200 bands.

label: Goal
body: The correct answer will probably reward us for understanding the causal chain between electrified instruments and fewer people per band, or it'll test this mathy inference that there are more bands.

label: Evaluate
body:
We're trying to argue that tea **is** more popular than before.
The author will say, "Then how come there's no change in the amount of tea sold at these numerous stores over the past 20 years?" We could either try to make an excuse for that survey data (they measured wrong, etc.), or we could try to bring up other data that makes it sound like tea IS more popular.
Maybe the stores that are selling the most tea weren't even open 20 years ago, so they're not involved in this comparison.

label: Goal
body: We either want an answer that helps us argue that tea is more popular than before or an answer that makes an excuse for the author's evidence (i.e. if tea is more popular than before, then why is this survey showing no change in the amount of tea sold at these stores?)

label: Conclusion
body: Tea is no more popular now than it ever was.

label: Evidence
body: A neutral polling company tracked tea sales at numerous stores for 20 years and found no change.

label: Opposing Point
body: The Tea Association says tea's visibility in ads and articles shows it is becoming more popular.

label: Evaluate
body: Barr assumes the surveyed stores represent tea sales generally.

label: Goal
body: Find an answer that gives us a reason to doubt the Survey Group's data really tracks overall tea popularity.

label: Conclusion
body: Barr is pushing back on the Tea Association. The Association says tea is getting more popular (look at all the ads and magazine pieces). Barr says no — actual sales numbers from a neutral source have not budged in 20 years, so popularity has not budged either.

label: Evaluate
body:
Barr is leaning entirely on the Survey Group's sales numbers. The whole argument rises or falls on whether those numbers really tell us about tea drinking nationwide.
Think of it like this: if you wanted to know whether running shoes are getting more popular in the country, and you only checked sales at stores in one snowy mountain town, you would miss the trend. The data is real, but it is not painting the whole picture.

label: Goal
body: Find an answer that gives us a reason to suspect the Survey Group's sample is not actually capturing the national picture — or some other reason their flat-sales finding does not prove tea is no more popular.

label: Conclusion
body: One may need to make more than moderate dietary changes, such as veggie diet.

label: Evidence
body: Moderate dietary changes often don't lower your cholesterol levels, and doctors urge people to reduce their cholesterol levels.

label: Evaluate
body:
The last sentence has a **therefore**. The word "therefore" always signals a conclusion, but not necessarily the Main Conclusion (and on Role and Main Conclusion questions, they often mess with us and put a "Therefore, [Intermediate Conclusion]." at the end of the paragraph.
What is the support for the conclusion in the last sentence? Why do we need to make more dramatic changes than just a moderate diet?
Because moderate diets don't help with your cholesterol, and doctors urge you to reduce your cholesterol.
Since the other two sentences are support for the third, it looks like the third sentence really is the Main Conclusion.

label: Goal
body: They're asking us about the 2nd sentence, which was one of the two **Premises,** supporting the Conclusion in the 3rd sentence.

label: Conclusion
body: Civilized society could not exist without empathy. ~Empathy → ~Civilized society

label: Evidence (since)
body:
Moral codes sometimes require people to ignore their own welfare to help others, and empathy is required to follow those moral codes.
~Empathy → ~Follow moral codes that say sometimes ignore own welfare

label: Evaluate
body:
If a conclusion is making this logic path ~Empathy -------------------> ~CS And our evidence has provided us this much ~E -----> ~FMC Then the argument is assuming this missing link: ~FMC -------------> ~CS
What does that diagram mean? It's saying "without following moral codes that sometimes require us to ignore our welfare in order to help others, there would be no civilized society".
We would have also conceived of this whole thing in **requirement** language.
The conclusion is saying "civilized society requires empathy", but the evidence never mentions civilized society at all (so we know the correct answer will).
The evidence says that "following these moral codes requires empathy", so that would tell us that the author is assuming that "civilized society requires following these moral codes".

label: Goal
body: Look for an answer that sounds like, "Civilized society requires that we follow moral codes that sometimes ask us to ignore our own welfare for the sake of others" or that sounds like "If people weren't willing to sometimes ignore their own welfare for the sake of others, we couldn't have civilized society"

label: Setup Ideas
body:
When an insurgent party forms that is angry at the dominant party and its ideology, that insurgent party always produces factions whose goals and views are as different from each other's as they are from the dominant party's.
They ignore these disagreements for the sake of toppling the dominant party, but then their disagreements inevitably come forward upon victory.

label: Evaluate
body:
Since this is prefaced by a Conclusion indicator like "Therefore", we're drawing a conclusion from these claims. In other words, we're making a supportable inference (like on Most Supported).
The first and second sentence both had causal/conditional words. Insurgent parties **always produce** factions Victory over dominant party **inevitably** leads to disagreements among factions coming to surface.
They don't quite chain together, but they do both mention these factions within the insurgent (and eventually victorious) political party.

label: Fill-in-the-Blank Goal
body:
It sounds like we're being led up to a moment of, "Therefore, once they win, they'll start fighting with each other, just like they were fighting with the dominant party before".
When they had that common enemy, they ignored their disagreements with each other (even though those disagreements were just as vast as those with the dominant party).
So once that common enemy is gone, they'll start bickering with each other.

label: P's Claims
body:
1. If you see an instance of pollution and inflate that into a criticism of our society, you're an alarmist.
2. These alarmists fail to distinguish between the [this specific pollution event and what caused it] and [the fact that people, overall, are inclined not to pollute].

label: Q's Responses
body:
1. Disagrees. Q is making it seem like it's reasonable, not alarmist, to make that leap. Q spells out how a common sense principle of "follow the path of least resistance" allows us to think, "If this specific company dumped pollution in the creek behind the factory, because that was the easiest way to deal with its waste, then many other companies probably also would do it."
2. Disagrees partially. P is acting like alarmists fail to consider that people are predisposed not to pollute. Q seems to be challenging that supposition. Q is like, "people **are** predisposed to pollute. after all, polluting is easier than not polluting, and people are predisposed to follow the path of least resistance".

label: Evaluate
body:
Wow, it took a lot of effort to see that Q kind of was disagreeing with at least part of each of P's claims. By directly interrogating yourself ... "Does Q disagree with P's 1st claim?!" you help your brain to see whether there's support for disagreement.
Since the disagreement isn't usually a match for the explicit wording, you want to look for the meaning of the disagree position. So take the original position, "If you see one instance and freak out about society, you're an alarmist", and say the rebuttal position to yourself: No ... seeing one instance and freaking out about society doesn't make you an alarmist.
Then ask your brain whether you can support that Rebuttal position.
I initially thought that Q had **no** comment on either of P's claims until I started asking myself some more questions: e.g., "Does Q think that people are predisposed not to pollute?"

label: Goal
body:
Let's look for either of the two sentiments we think they disagree about: - is it alarmist or not to look at a single instance of pollution and then worry about society?
- are people predisposed to pollute or not pollute?

label: Conclusion
body: The board of directors is full of corruption and should be replaced.

label: Evidence
body: Wagston is on the board of directors, and there are various persons on on his staff that committed well documented bribes that unduly influenced the awarding of government contracts.

label: Evaluation
body:
Given the illicit acts of various persons on Wagston's staff, how could we argue that the board of directors is **not** full of corruption or **shouldn't** be replaced?
Well, we could just say, "Maybe it's just Wagston, not the rest of the board. In fact, maybe it's not even Wagston, his staff members. Or maybe it's not even all of Wagston's staff, just a few bad apples among them?"
This author seems to commit the famous **Part vs. Whole** flaw. Since Wagston's staff members are a Part of the board of directors (debatably), and they are corrupt, the author assumes the entire board is corrupt.
We could also think of this as **Sampling**. The author assumes that the corruption of some of Wagston's staff members is representative of the rest of the board's members and staff.

label: Goal
body: Look for an answer calling out the Part vs. Whole or Sampling flaw, or one that makes the objection that "Maybe it's just those few bad apples that are corrupt and should be replaced. Why are you trying to get rid of the whole board?"

label: Information
body:
causal (cause / causes)
drinking coffee ⇢ more vasopressin produced or tea (b/c of methylxanthines)
vasopressin ⇢ clumping of blood cells (esp. in women)
causal (X is probably the explanation of y)
women's blood cells ⇢ women have ~10x clump more than men's risk after angioplasty (clearing of arteries)

label: Evaluate
body:
All three sentences involve some causal relationships. Do any of them chain together?
We could say that, 1. you drink coffee / tea 2. you get more methylxanthines in you 3. increased production of vasopressin 4. clumping of blood cells (esp. for women)
So when women drink coffee or tea they are more likely to get clumping of blood cells.
The causal connector between sentence 2 and sentence 3 is implying that after an angioplasty, there is (possibly more vasopressin produced but definitely) more clumping of blood cells, and this clumping of blood cells increases the risk of complications.

label: Goal
body:
An answer that would tie all this together could be something like, "If a woman is having an angioplasty, she should lay off the coffee and tea for a while".
But they could also test any of subset of these causal connections discussed. Look for a safely worded answer that rewards us for understanding these cause/effect relationships.

label: Conclusion
body:
P-fat is required for the development of eyesight.
- paragraph

label: Evidence
body:
Babies fed low-P-fat formula have worse eyesight than babies fed with mother's milk, which is high in P-fat. Babies that are 5-6 weeks premature have worse eyesight than those carried to term.
- paragraph

label: Evaluate
body:
The first piece of evidence seems like pretty good support that P-fat contributes to eyesight development. But does it really prove that P-fat is necessary? That seems like a stretch. We might object that other differences between formula and mother's milk are to blame for the worse eyesight.
The second piece of evidence is even less helpful. What does being premature have to do with P-fat?
- paragraph

label: Anticipate
body:
The right answer might strengthen this argument by connecting premature birth to P-fat in some way. If we knew that babies get more P-fat in utero than they do from milk after they're born, that would make this a better argument. But, because Strengthen questions aren't the most predictable, we'll still read every answer with an open mind.
- paragraph

label: Statements
body:
Distinction Artists differ in terms of their ways of producing contours and hatching.
Causal Analyzing contours/hatching **can help to** distinguish a famous work from a forgery or from a similar artist.
Causal Analyzing contours/hatching **has shown** many of the drawings we used to think were Michelangelo's are really by Giulio Clovio, an artist from the same period as Michelangelo.

label: Evaluate
body:
When we're presented with causal connectors, the usual Must Be True inferences are: - A has some effect on B - anything that would need to be true for that causal connection to be plausible
For example, if we say "hearing the words of that song made Timmy cry, thinking about his mom."
We can infer stuff like - the lyrical content of music can have an emotional impact on the listener - Timmy was able to discern or remember the lyrics over the background noise of the room.

label: Goal
body:
We probably want something like:
- distinctive techniques used by artists can help when categorizing pieces of art with unknown authorship or - Michelangelo and Giulio Clovio had different ways of producing contours / hatching.

label: Conclusion
body: Those who act immorally do so only through ignorance of some of their actions' consequences rather than through a character defect.

label: Evaluate
body:
If we were just pre-phrasing a Linking idea, we'd go with a simple "If Premise, then Conclusion" form:
if an immoral action is then the actor going to eventually → does that action harm the actor due to ignorance not character defect
If we want to try to think of a possible objection, we can switch to our Debating Mindset:
Given that... an immoral action will eventually harm the person who does it,
How could we say that... people who act immorally are **not** ignorant of their actions consequences?
In other words, is it possible that someone performs immoral action X, even while being clear-eyed about the fact that this action will ultimately harm them?
Sure! I'm known to smoke a lot and drink a bit, even though I know those actions are ultimately harming me. People are self-destructive sometimes. Or maybe we're just convinced that the harm the action causes is outweighed by some gain we get out of it. Or maybe we're not ignorant about the eventual consequences, we're just such stupid shortsighted creatures that we do the bad action anyway (like doing things that exacerbate climate change).

label: Goal
body:
Look for a Linking answer saying, "If an action would eventually harm you, then you would only do it if you're ignorant of the consequences".
Or look for a Defender answer ruling out an objection. Something like, "People do **not** do immoral actions even while knowing it will harm them".

label: Conclusion / Hypothesis
body: The reason Earth has undergone a regular sequence of ice ages starting around 800,000 years ago is that Earth passes through dense clouds of cosmic dust, which dim the Sun, resulting in an ice age.

label: Evidence
body: The Earth's orbit around the Sun has fluctuations that coincide with the ice-age cycles.

label: Evaluate
body:
As soon as we see the word hypothesis, we know we can use our Curious Fact / Explanation mindset.
Curious Fact Why has the Earth gone through a regular sequence of ice ages, starting around 800k years ago.
Author's Explanation During these periodic weird orbits around the Sun, the Earth passes through dense clouds of cosmic dust, which dim the Sun and result in an Ice Age.
As always, we're considering two pressure points: 1. **Alternate Explanations** for the curious fact 2. The **plausibility** of the Author's Explanation
On Strengthen questions, the correct answer more often adds plausibility than rules out an alternative explanation. (This is even more common when we're strengthening a hypothesis, as opposed to strengthening an argument, if you can handle that extra nerdiness)

label: Goal
body: Look for four answers that add some plausibility to the author's story that ice ages are caused by Earth having a funky orbit that takes it through dense of clouds of cosmic dust (or an answer ruling out an alternate explanation for the ice ages).

label: Statements
body:
Rational pursuit ≠ Always doing what you of happiness most strongly desire to do
causal connector (this is because / moreover) Rational must involves long term and desires are usually short term.
contrast (ordinary desire vs. compulsion) ordinary = offer at least momentary happiness desires when goal is attained
compulsive = drive us to pursue goals that, desires if attained, offer no happiness

label: Evaluate
body:
It looks like it will be hard to guess this one. Most **Must Be False** questions follow one of two patterns: 1. the correct answer contradicts a conditional There weren't any obvious conditionals here other than **must** in the second sentence. We could maybe turn the last two statements into conditionals, like, "If ordinary desires, then achieving goal provides some happiness". So we might see a correct answer offer one of these contradictions - This situation involved rational pursuit of happiness, but consideration of long-term consequences didn't happen. - This situation involved an ordinary desire being satisfied, but there was no happiness at all attained. - This situation involved a compulsion, and there **was** happiness when the goal was attained.
2. The correct answer contradicts a Must Be True inference we can make by combining claims.
It's not super obvious which claims we could combine here to derive something.

label: Goal
body: So, let's stay flexible and look for any answer that contradicts the passage. We can ask ourselves, "Using this paragraph, can I prove that the opposite is true?"

label: Argument Structure
body: Any government worthy of WR → PC respect permits criticism No govt worthy of respect protects minorities WR → PM ⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯ ⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯ Any government that PM → PC protects minorities permits criticism

label: Evaluation / Goal
body:
Both premises and the conclusion are conditionals. Thus, we would lean towards diagramming this argument, which is why the argument breakdown did whatever finessing was needed to find the repeating symbols (permits criticism, worthy of respect, protects minorities) so we could look at the conditional logic.
In even more generic form, the argument goes Premise 1: A → B Premise 2: A → C Conclusion: C → B
It wouldn't matter whether the conclusion is B → C or C → B, just that the conclusion creates a conditional between the right sides (outcomes) of the two conditionals in the premises.
Prioritizing answers? Get rid of anything that doesn't have three conditionals. Make sure the two premise conditionals have the same trigger.

label: Conclusion
body: The Acme plan is probably a good retirement plan for anyone with retirement needs similar to the last 25 yrs worth of Economic Merit Prize winners.

label: Intermediate Conclusion (thus clearly)
body: The Economic Merit Prize winners recognize that the Acme plan offers them a financially secure future.

label: Premise
body: Each of the Economic Merit Prize winners from the last 25 years is covered by the Acme plan.

label: Evaluate
body:
The first three sentences give us three conditionals. Must = right side ( **R** equired = **R** ight) Only if = right side Unless = rephrase into 'X requires Y' form, or do an "If-not" (put the negated version of one of the ideas on the left side of an arrow, the regular version of the other idea on the right side of the arrow)
The easiest way to mentally or conditionally chain them is to take advantage of the "X requires Y" way of reading "X → Y".
For all members to have strong foreign policy it requires responding aggressively to problems which requires perceiving the problems as grave which requires all agreeing it threatens their economy
So the evidence gives us a conditional chain. Str FP → Rsp Agg → Per Grave → Agree Threat And the conclusion is stating factually, Str FP.
It looks like we need to use the contrapositive of this chain. ~Agree → ~Per Grave → ~Resp Agg → ~Str FP

label: Goal
body: To prove that Str FP, we just need to know that - they won't all agree it threatens economy - they won't all perceive as grave or - they won't respond aggressively

label: Evaluate
body:
This argument has a 3-part structure.
Claim 1. **Since** [Claim 2], Claim 3.
The "since" guarantees that Claim 3 is a conclusion based on Claim 2. However, there are also some keywords within Claim 2.
Claim 1. **Thus clearly** Claim 2.
The "thus clearly" indicates that Claim 2 is a conclusion built on Claim 1. So we can potentially call out a flaw in how we get from Claim 1 to Claim 2, or in how we get from Claim 2 to Claim 3.
Given That all the Economic Merit Prize winners are covered by Acme, How Could We Say That they do not clearly recognize its a plan that offers them a financially secure future?
Maybe they're on the Acme plan for some other reason (the free airline points? they can't afford better? it's their idol Alan Greenspan's favorite plan?).
What about the move from claim 2 to claim 3.
Given That all the Economic Merit Prize winners recognize that Acme offers them a secure future, How Could We Say That it probably would not be a good plan for people with similar retirement needs?
It's pretty hard to think of a good counterargument here. We would usually try to argue that the winners of the Economic Merit Prize are atypical people, so what's good for them wouldn't be good for others.
But this conclusion is very qualified and nuanced -- it would probably be a good plan for people with similar needs.
There's still room for these Economic Merit Prize nerds to be different from people with similar retirement needs, but I can't think of any storyline offhand for what would make a plan good for **their** future but not for someone with similar needs.

label: Goal
body:
I would not know exactly what I'm looking for here.
We need an answer resisting the move from "since all the Economic Merit Prize winners are covered by Acme, they clearly recognize that it's a plan that offers them a financially secure future", or an answer resisting the move from "since they recognize it offers them a financially secure future, it's probably a good plan for anyone with retirement needs similar to theirs".

label: Conclusion (better = opinion)
body: It's better to drive a small car.

label: Evidence (since / because)
body: Even though a small car offers less protection in an accident than a large car does, you're less likely to get into an accident because smaller cars are more maneuverable.

label: Evaluate
body:
This is a Comparative argument. We're saying one thing is better than another. And we're weighing positive and negative tradeoffs.
The negative about small cars is that **if** you get into an accident, you'll get crunched and more likely hurt.
The positive about small cars is that since they're more maneuverable, it's easier to steer clear of accidents.
Since the author concludes that it's better to drive small cars, she thinks there's a net gain. The positive outweighs the negative. Why?
Well, the negative about small cars only comes into play **if** you get into an accident. But the positive about small cars helps you avoid getting into an accident. The positive beats the negative because the positive makes the negative less likely to happen in the first place.

label: Goal
body:
Let's look for an argument where the author chooses one thing over another, mentioning a positive and a negative, and thinking that the positive outweighs the negative.
(In this case, the positive outweighed the negative by making the negative thing less likely to occur. But it's hard to know whether to get that granular with our pre-phrase.)

label: Conclusion
body: If you want to protect your dog from arthritis, don't neuter it until it's full grown.

label: Evidence
body: If you neuter a dog in early puppyhood, its legs bones usually don't develop properly. Improper bones lead to arthritis when the dog is older.

label: Evaluation
body:
The author is laying out a causal chain and then trying to conclude, "If you don't want the last thing, don't do the first thing".
Neuter early puppy → bad bones → arthritis
Her conclusion, though, should read "If you want to protect your dog from arthritis, don't neuter them in early puppyhood"
So the flaw in the argument is the gap between the correctly drawn advice, "don't neuter them in early puppyhood" and the erroneously drawn conclusion, "don't neuter them until it is full-grown"

label: Goal
body: The author seems to present a **False Choice**: you'd either have to neuter you dog in early puppyhood or wait until it's full-grown. What if there's some middle ground there, like adolescence?

label: Conclusion (implied)
body: Private ownership of the means of production is not going to ultimately destroy a technological society, if it sanctions it.

label: Intermediate Conclusion
body: If the means of production become public property, that will actually endanger the survival of a technologically advanced society.

label: Evidence (Since)
body: Only private ownership of the means of production permits individuals to test new technologies without the majority's consent.

label: Evaluate
body:
Whenever we read Role or Main Conclusion arguments, we prime our brains with a reminder that the conclusion will usually be the First Sentence or a Rebuttal.
This paragraph begins with an attribution: "Some people have maintained". We would anticipate that the author will disagree, starting with some pivot word like But, Yet, However. Instead, the author initially concedes a point: "This may be true [in some cases]". And then she hits us with the Rebuttal Pivot: "But... **since** [premise], [conclusion]."
We could say that the final claim is the main conclusion, but because of the rebuttal structure it feels fair to say that there is an implied conclusion that is disputing the accuracy of the attributed claim in the first sentence.

label: Goal
body: We're being asked about the first claim, which plays an Opposing role, as the entire argument exists to partially rebut this claim. The author concedes that the claim may be partially true when it comes to less advanced societies, but she's implicitly arguing that it's not true when it comes to technologically advanced societies.

label: Conclusion (Thus)
body: Not all members of the EU will be strong in foreign policy. rephrase: At least one member of the EU will not be strong in foreign policy.

label: Evidence
body:
All members → Respond strong in FP aggressively
Respond → all see as aggressively grave
all see as → all agree grave threat to $

label: Conclusion
body: Economists' obsession with consumption as a measure of economic well-being has prevented us from understanding the true nature of economic well-being.

label: Evidence
body: We don't get much satisfaction out of our clothing wearing out, our cars depreciating, and the gas in our gas tanks needing to be replaced.

label: Evaluate
body:
Whenever we're doing Main Conclusion or Role, we first remind ourselves before reading the paragraph that the Conclusion will usually be earlier than the Evidence (that's the trick they play on those two question types).
Since there are only two claims in this paragraph, we could proactively ask ourselves, "Is the first claim the conclusion? Does it sound like the author's opinion? Is it supported by some other claim?"
The first sentence **does** sound like the author's opinion, because she's saying, "The obsession economists have has prevented us from understanding the true nature of economic well-being."
How is this supported? Why should be believe that by obsessing over consumption we're missing the true nature of well-being?
The author's premise is super aloof. We have to work to understand it, but she's saying when we fill up our gas tanks, when we buy a new car, or when we have to buy new clothes, we are consuming. From the economists' point of view, this is helping economic well-being. More consumption = more well-being.
But the author is citing these examples as the opposite of "more well-being". The author thinks we are sad that are clothes now look worn and our car now looks old and our gas tank is thirsty. Even though it's good for the economy that we have to buy more stuff, it doesn't feel like it's good for our well-being.

label: Goal
body:
This question stem is not the traditional "Find the Main Conclusion" version of a Main Conclusion question. It's more like the occasional variation we see where instead of asking for the Main Conclusion, it asks for the Main Point. These are functionally similar to Main Conclusion in terms of how we read the paragraph, but the answer choices might be somewhat different. Rather than just regurgitating the actual claim that was the Main Conclusion, the answer to Main Point may speak to an implied conclusion or synthesize the conclusion and the evidence.
Thus, we want to look mainly for a paraphrase of the first sentence, but if the answer also seems to bring in the second one or an implied idea, we can live with it.
But the answer needs to express that "economists' obsessions with consumption prevents us from understanding the true nature of economic well-being", or "the true nature of economic well-being is not consumption".

label: Conclusion
body: The chlorofluorocarbons in the ozone layer of the atmosphere don't harm humans by letting increased ultraviolet radiation reach Earth.

label: Evidence
body: 300,000 years ago there was a supernova that damaged the ozone layer, and it had no significant effect on our earliest ancestors. And the supernova had more of an effect than the chlorofluorocarbons are estimated to have.

label: Evaluate
body:
I'm sorry, author, how do you know it had no significant effect on our earliest ancestors. Did the cavemen keep meticulous longitudinal statistics on cancer rates?
Since this is an argument based on Comparison (because ozone damage was harmless in Situation X, it will be harmless in Situation Y), we weaken this argument by pointing out meaningful differences.
Maybe the damage to the ozone layer before was in an area where humans didn't live, so they weren't affected by the influx of ultraviolet, but the damage today is in areas of the atmosphere where humans do live.
Maybe humans didn't live long enough 300,000 years ago to suffer the long term effects of ultraviolet radiation.
Maybe there are other chemicals in our atmosphere nowadays that interact with chlorofluorocarbons to create a more damaging effect.

label: Goal
body: We can predict the specific storyline, but we go to the answers thinking, "Gimme a meaningful difference between the two Situations, so that I can argue that the chlorofluorocarbons damage to the ozone layer could be harmful, in terms of ultraviolet radiation."

label: Conclusion
body: Analysts are being overly optimistic (in thinking that baby boomers will flow money into the stock market, as they switch from consuming to planning for retirement).

label: Intermediate Conclusion (thus)
body: Boomers' retirement money will more likely flow into investments other than stocks.

label: Evidence
body: As boomers stop consuming, corporate earnings will be lower, and thus they wouldn't be able to make as much retirement money by investing in stocks.

label: Evaluate
body:
For **Method** questions, we're just trying to characterize what kind of evidence the author used or what sort of reasoning move she made.
