These are the basic options they cycle through. - analogy - example / counterexample to general claim - undesirable implications of logic or plan - rule out alternatives - suggest an alternate explanation - raise an overlooked consideration - make a distinction / definition - call out a dubious assumption
Here, our author seemed to raise an overlooked consideration ... "I agree with your premise, analysts ... baby boomers will be looking to invest money rather than spend it via consumption. But what you overlook is that baby boomers are a big reason why corporations make so much money and thus why their stock prices can get so high (raising money for their stockholders)."
The author is saying, "Once boomers turn their spending faucet off, this hurts corporations, their stock prices won't get as high, and that makes investing in stocks seem like a less lucrative pathway for investing your money."

label: Goal
body: Look for any answer that we can match up with the argument. It will probably sound something like, "the author opposes a prediction by bringing up some overlooked consideration that works against that prediction".

label: Conclusion (should = opinion)
body: The proposal to require milk labels to detail what artificial substances were used to make the milk should not be implemented.

label: Evidence (colon)
body: Just imagine trying to list every synthetic fertilizer used to grow the grass and grain the cows ate, or every fungicide used to keep the grain from spoiling.

label: Evaluate
body:
On Method, we ultimately just need to pick an answer with a true description, but we can benefit by being aware of the 8 options these questions usually come down to:
- analogies - (counter)example to general claim - ruling out other options - suggesting alternative explanations - troublesome implications - definitions / distinctions - raising an overlooked consideration - calling out a dubious assumption
Here, it seems like the author was doing the "troublesome implications" move. This either takes the form of arguing, "If X were true, then Y and Z would follow as well. But they don't follow (thus X is wrong)" or it takes the form we're seeing here, where someone talks through the implications of a plan / recommendation.
Our author is saying that if milk producers were required to talk about **all** artificial substances used in milk production, that would have absurd / untenable / unacceptable consequences, such as having to list the fertilizer used to grow the grass the cows ate or the fungicide used to keep the grain from spoiling.

label: Statements
body:
Long-lasting → trust → mutual relationship respect (personal or professional) Long-lasting → natural affinity relationship (personal)
The last sentence is just a restatement of what we already have here (long-lasting personal relationship requires trust, mutual respect, and affinity), so we don't need to notate it separately.

label: Evaluate
body:
Since this is **Must Be True**, we're primarily reading for Conditional or Quantitative ideas (keeping an eye out for Causality, otherwise).
We see conditional words galore: "can't be sustained in the absence of" (introduces right side) "essential" (the essential thing goes on right side) "require" (introduces right side) "if" (introduces left side) "must" (introduces right side)
Are there repeated ideas? If so, it's probably worth diagramming, to see if stuff chains together. If not, it's probably worth just re-reading the paragraph and then looking back at the paragraph as needed as we survey answer choices.
Yes, there are repeated ideas: mutual respect, affinity, personal relationship. So let's get diagramming.

label: All of these expressions...** X can't be sustained in the absence of Y Y is essential to X X's additionally require Y X must be supported by Y **... mean the same thing: "X requires Y"
body: if you don't have Y, can't have X **~Y → ~X** X requires Y **X → Y**

label: Goal
body: Look for something derivable from these conditionals. Beware illegal reversals or negations, and get rid of out of scope ideas.

label: Principle (when)
body: an apparent counterex → inappropriate to use has just been given saying like "as they say"

label: Evaluate
body: The right answer must contain a story whose events run *against* the saying that follows — i.e., the saying does not actually fit what just happened, so the introductory phrase ("as the saying goes") is being used inappropriately.

label: Goal
body: Find the choice where the situation described is the opposite (or at least not an example) of the saying that follows it.

label: Principle
body: "As the saying goes" is misused when the story just told is a counterexample to — not an illustration of — the saying that follows.

label: Goal
body: Pick the choice where the story does not actually illustrate the quoted saying.

label: Principle
body: The principle is simple: "as the saying goes" should follow a story that *illustrates* the saying. If the story is actually a counterexample — the opposite of what the saying claims — then using "as the saying goes" is inappropriate.

label: Goal
body:
So we are looking for the answer where the story and the saying do not match. Either the story is the reverse of what the saying claims, or it just does not illustrate the saying at all.
Read each example, ask: "Does this story actually fit the proverb?" The one where the answer is no is correct.

label: Conclusion
body: Butter and eggs will cost more next month

label: Evidence
body: The average cost of groceries will be higher next month

label: Evaluate
body:
Pretty straightforward — the author thinks that if the average price of groceries is going up, then these two specific groceries (butter and eggs) will also see their price go up.
This is a failure to understand the concept of "average". We don't expect every data point in a set to behave in the exact way the average behaved. This is a **Part vs. Whole** flaw.

label: Goal
body: Look for an argument that abuses the concept of "average" in the same way, or look for an argument that similarly commits a **Whole to Part** move.

label: Conclusion
body: Dioxin is probably not the cause of the fish's reproductive abnormalities.

label: Evidence
body: Even though the fish recover quickly when the mill shuts down, dioxin decomposes very slowly in the environment (so it would still be in the fish's habitat).

label: Evaluate
body:
The author's support is extremely weird. In general, if we said "When the mill shuts down, the fish recover", that would make it seem like the mill is responsible for the fish's abnormalities. And this is the opposite of what the author is concluding. So how is that support for the idea that "dioxin from the mill is not the cause"?
Well, it's because when the mill shuts down, that doesn't necessarily mean there's no dioxin in the water any more. The author is suggesting that even though the mill is shut down, there's still dioxin in the water near the mill, since dioxin decomposes very slowly in the environment.

label: Goal
body:
Most of us would have no idea where to go with this thing (this problem is legendarily tough). But with Weaken we can always take a mindset of "Given the evidence, How can I argue the anti-conclusion?"
So we can think, "Given that fish recover normal hormones during mill shutdowns even though dioxin decomposes very slowly in the environment, how can we argue that dioxin from the mill is the cause of their hormonal problems?"

label: Conclusion
body: The play won't become a movie nor will it be revived at the Decade Festival.

label: Evidence
body: If the play were successful, it would become a movie or get revived at the Festival. But, it is not successful.

label: Evaluation
body:
Whenever we see any conditional logic ("If") on a Flaw question, we should immediately be on the lookout for whether the author commits a **Necessary vs. Sufficient** flaw by reasoning in a backwards or opposite fashion.
The author provided this conditional, successful → adapted or revived Then proceeded to argue that SINCE successful, adapted and revived
If we're given A → B or C we can't infer ~A → ~B and ~C

label: Goal
body: Look for an answer calling out the Necessary vs. Sufficient flaw or one that conversationally explains that there might be more than one possible route to getting adapted or revived (yes, being a successful play is one way, but maybe being a play that is beloved by a famous actor is another way)

label: Conclusion
body: The proposed study (giving HGH to children whose bodies don't make enough of it) should be prohibited.

label: Evidence
body: If a medical research is not likely to reveal important information study about a medical → should be condition prohibited OR if the medical research isn't known to pose only a minimal risk to subjects

label: Conclusion
body: This suggests that if night-lights cause nearsightedness, the effect disappears with age.

label: Evaluate
body:
Because this paragraph already gave us the Principle, this question feels more like Strengthen + Apply the Principle.
We're given a principle that allows us to say "this medical research **should not** be permitted", and the author's conclusion is saying "this researcher's proposed study **should not** be permitted (should be prohibited)".
So we can tell she's trying to say that this Principle is relevant to this proposed study.
Since the principle was in this form Permitted → Likely helpful AND known safe
the contrapositive version that allows us to prove "not permitted" looks like this: Likely helpful OR Known Safe → Permitted
So to justify this conclusion, we don't need both ideas in the trigger. Either would do.

label: Goal
body: Look for an answer either saying, "Giving HGH to these children is not **likely** to reveal important info about a medical condition" or saying, "We're not sure whether giving HGH to these children poses only a minimal risk."

label: Conclusion
body: It's unfair that they built speed bumps in Grove Park.

label: Evidence
body: It's a public community, its streets were built with public funds, and so all drivers have a right to use those streets whenever they want.

label: Evaluation
body: Okay .... author, I'm wondering if you realize what "speed bumps" are. They are preventing anyone from using the street. They just encourage people to slow down, because otherwise your car jostles pretty severely if it drives too fast over the bump.

label: Goal
body: This seems like an **Irrelevant Response**, and so LSAT presumably just wants us to react by saying, 'What does having the right to use those streets whenever they want have to do with speed bumps?'

label: Conclusion (Hence)
body: A successful writer who decides not to publish a recently completed manuscript should destroy it immediately.

label: Evidence
body: Often the heirs of a successful writer will decide to publish any manuscripts they can find, even though many writers have manuscripts they would not like to be publicly associated with even after they die.

label: Evaluate
body:
The problem the author identifies is that if you're a famous writer, then when you die, your family might be tempted by the "money grab" of selling off any of your unreleased material. But what if you hate this unreleased material and would be mad to know that your relatives let the world see this crap with your name attached to it?
The author then moves to a pretty drastic solution -- if you're a successful writer and you recently finished a manuscript that you decide not to publish, then you should **destroy it immediately** so that your greedy heirs can't posthumously embarrass you with it.
Isn't there a more moderate prescription that would work? Couldn't you label it with a Sharpie that says, "Don't publish this. I hate it and don't want the world to see it"? Couldn't you modify your will to say, "I do not give permission for anyone connected to my estate to publish my unreleased manuscript Revenge of the War Turtles. I wrote that book purely for my nieces and nephews. It is not meant for the world to see."?

label: Goal
body: Let's look for an answer that would make this sound like bad advice, a reason that a successful writer **should not** immediately destroy a manuscript they just finished but don't plan to publish.

label: Conclusion
body: But that does not mean that the government’s view is necessarily the correct view. Rephrase: The government's view of individual rights may not be correct.

label: Evidence
body: In practice, the government will have the last word on what an individual’s rights are because its police will do what its officials and courts say.

label: Evaluate
body:
Like most Main Conclusion questions, there is an important pivot (But / Yet / However) that comes before the conclusion, and then the conclusion is followed by support. The argument presents an initial statement about the government's practical authority over defining individual rights, which might lead someone to assume this view is correct. However, the author immediately pivots with "But that does not mean," signaling that the statement following this pivot is the beginning of the author's argument. We aren't given a keyword to distinguish whether it's saying, "But [conclusion]. After all [evidence]" or saying "But [evidence]. Therefore [conclusion]." However the sentiment "the government isn't necessarily correct" is the same as "the government may be wrong", which sounds opinionated, and thus like our conclusion.
And the semicolon " ; " after that claim is signaling that we will now hear support for that claim.

label: Goal
body: Find the best available meaning match for "The government's view of individual rights may not be correct."

label: Conclusion (therefore)
body: It seems that early humans possessed an aesthetic sense.

label: Evidence
body: Our cave-dwelling ancestors polished many of their flints to a degree far surpassing what was necessary for hunting purposes.

label: Evaluate
body:
Most of the time that arguments deal with archaeological discoveries (found artifacts / bones / etc), the author tries to interpret the significance of the discovery, so we end up with an Explain the Curious Fact type argument. A flint, in case you don't know, is a type of rock that cavemen would use to make weapons or tools. It's basically a chunk of rock that has a pointy spot that humans could sharpen and affix to a spear.
Curious Fact ... Why were these flints polished beyond what was necessary for hunting purposes?
Author's Explanation ... They polished them like that simply because they found them beautiful that way.
This conclusion is one of those implied causal conclusions --- the author doesn't explicitly say, "1) Humans have an aesthetic sense. 2) Part of that aesthetic sense is liking shiny things. 3) Cave-dwellers polished their flints to a shine because they liked how pretty it looked when it was shiny."
We have to put all that together in our brains, simply by thinking about the connection between the premise and the conclusion and filling in the blanks.
When an author concludes a causal explanation for a curious fact, we always evaluate it two ways: 1. Could there be some Alternate Explanation for the curious fact? 2. How plausible is the Author's Explanation?

label: Goal
body:
Since this is a Weaken question, we either want 1. to suggest an Alternate Explanation for why these flints were polished so much.
or
2. to undermine the plausibility of the story that cave-dwellers possessed an aesthetic sense that favored shiny things and that's why they polished their flints.

label: Goal
body:
In order to get from that premise to that conclusion, we would need something like
only know some of don't know if the consequences → action has the best of an action consequences

label: Conclusion
body: Maybe those people saying, we're not in imminent ecological doom, and if we're too stringent with environmental regulations, we might lose the revenue that pays for these preservation programs are correct.

label: Evidence
body: Much of North America and western Europe is better forested and has less acid rain now, compared to five decades ago.

label: Evaluate
body:
This has a very loose argument structure, so I would assume we can treat it pretty conversationally. Just picture the age old debate about the environment.
the Left: by 2050 Earth will be unlivable if we don't immediately take drastic measures!
the Right: c'mon, you've been prophesying imminent doom forever and things aren't as bad as you thought. plus, if we take drastic measures, we'll mess up the economy, and the economy is what's currently able to pay for the environmental initiatives
The author is saying that the recent successes we're seeing (two continents have more forest and less acid rain than before) is support for the people on the Right.

label: Goal
body: Look for something that helps the Right — the environment is not on the brink of doom / the environmental victories we've achieved over the last five decades were paid for with natural resource wealth (i.e. oil money) / were we to restrict use of natural resources, it could lead to less funding for future environmental initiatives.

label: Conclusion (clearly)
body: We cannot accept these proclamations of objectivity. rephrase: These historians who are claiming that in their own treatment of subject matter they are unaffected by any moral or aesthetic preconceptions are wrong; their treatment of subject matter is affected by moral / aesthetic preconceptions.

label: Evidence (for)
body: It's easy to find instances of false historical explanations embodying the ideological or other prejudices of their authors.

label: Evaluate
body:
This is a tough argument to understand, but it boils down to this. "Many historians claim to be unbiased in their work. But they're wrong. After all, it's easy to find instances where historians have been biased in their work."
This would be like if we argued, "Many NBA players claim to be faithful to their wives. But we cannot accept these proclamations of faithfulness, for it is easy to find examples of NBA players who cheated on their wives."
Just because some NBA players cheat on their spouses doesn't mean we should reject the claims of other NBA players who claim that they don't.
Similarly, just because some historians let their biases affect their work doesn't mean we should dismiss the claims of other historians who claim that they don't less bias affect their work.

label: Goal
body: Look for an answer saying, "Just because some historians have been biased doesn't mean we should reject the notion that these historians claiming to be unbiased are also biased."

label: Conclusion (Thus / this suggests that)
body: There is no consistent causal link between major meteor impacts and mass extinctions.

label: Evidence
body: Many mass extinctions did not follow any known major meteor impact. Many major impacts were not followed by mass extinctions.

label: Evaluate
body:
The author is trying to establish that "there's no consistent causal link between X and Y". How do we prove that "there is no consistent causal link" between two things? Did the evidence provide that sort of proving mechanism?
No. So, since we have this New Wording in the conclusion, "no consistent causal link", we know that the correct answer will have to give us some rule that outputs "no consistent causal link" on the right side of the conditional arrow.
Our evidence is that the association between X and Y is splotchy. Many Y's didn't come after some X had occurred. And many X's occurred without a Y happening afterwards.

label: Goal
body:
We primarily want to look for a rule that proves the wording "no consistent causal link". When we find an answer offering such a rule, we'll check out its trigger and see if our evidence clearly applies to the trigger. Maybe an answer will sound something like
**If** major meteor impacts **Then** there is no and mass extinctions → consistent causal occur many times w/o link between them the other occurring

label: Statements
body:
On Must Be True we primarily read for wording clues of a Conditional, Causal, or Quantitative variety.
This paragraph has a Conditional "when", which is a sufficient indicator (put it on the left of the arrow).
And there is definitely causal language, such as "causes" and the implied repercussions of that first effect.
We can kind of combine our Conditional and Causal thinking then, and just articulate to ourselves the chain of causality.
1. Some uncontrollable factor such as a lack of rain causes wheat crops to fail.
2. The seed and fertilizer industry gets hurt.
3. Truckers and mechanics get hurt.
4. Fuel suppliers struggle.
The paragraph essentially describes an ecosystem of the economy that is intertwined with the wheat farmers.

label: Goal
body:
It's hard to make a specific guess here, but one would think it would reinforce connecting that first cause from the final effect (or some subset of the causal chain).
Since a lack of rain could lead to fuel suppliers being unable to make a profit, you can say something like "failing to make a profit as a fuel supplier is not always due to personal ineptitude".
We don't know what to expect, but we'll be on guard for stuff that's Too Strong, Out of Scope, or Illegal Logic (reversals / opposites).

label: Conclusion
body: If "morally right" = "action has best consequences", then we can never no what action is morally right.

label: Evidence
body: For each action we perform, we can know only some of its consequences.

label: Evaluate
body:
The conclusion is a conditional claim, "if X, then Y". When we evaluate conditional conclusions, we're essentially granting to the author the hypothetical truth of the "if" part. If you wanted to, you could add the "if" part to the premises.
But in this case, I think it's nice to just sit with the conclusion for a second to hear what it's really saying. Since "morally right" appears in the "if" and the "then" part of the conditional, it's allowing us to synthesize this into an easier to digest conclusion.
Consider this analogy: "If your friend Tommy is my old coworker Tommy, then your friend is a jerk."
Assumption? "My old coworker Tommy is a jerk".
Now try it on the conclusion: "If morally right = best consequences, then we'll never know what action is morally right".
Assumption? "We'll never know what action has the best consequences".
So the author is really trying to conclude that "in no situation can we know which action has the best consequences".
Why? Because in all situations, we only know some of the consequences of an action.

label: Conclusion (Hence)
body: It's a mistake to exonerate a suspect simply because that person's DNA didn't match the DNA samples takes from the scene of the crime.

label: Evidence
body: DNA tests often fail to distinguish among DNA samples taken from distinct individuals.

label: Evaluate
body:
The author's conclusion is saying, 'We shouldn't just let a suspect go and presume them innocent (exonerate them) simply because the DNA sample we have of them doesn't match the DNA sample taken from the scene of the crime.'
Let's think about that. Why shouldn't the cops let me go, if my DNA doesn't match the DNA taken from the scene of the crime?
The author thinks that even though my sample didn't match the crime scene sample, I might still be the killer. So she apparently thinks it's possible that the sample of blood they got from me at the crime scene doesn't match the sample of blood they got from me in custody. The DNA test yielded a false negative. It said, "Nope Patrick's DNA doesn't match the crime scene DNA", even though they are both blood samples from the same person, me.
Meanwhile, the evidence is talking about false positives.
It's saying that DNA tests would often say, "Yup, Patrick's DNA matches the crime scene DNA", even though I wasn't the killer. Let's say Eddie is the killer but he and I have similar enough DNA, that a DNA test fails to distinguish his DNA (from the crime scene sample) from my DNA.

label: Goal
body:
Based on their evidence, the author's conclusion should be saying, "it's a mistake to **convict** someone simply because that person's DNA **does** match the DNA samples taken from the crime scene. (After all, DNA tests yield false positives. They think that person 1's DNA is a match for the crime-scene sample of person 2's DNA )."
Instead it's saying that "it's a mistake to **exonerate** just because DNA **didn't** match." That would require evidence about false negatives.
Let's look for an answer that's complaining that the evidence is dealing with false positives, while the conclusion is dealing with false negatives.

label: Evidence
body:
Some visitors engage in Some people do thing practices that seriously that causes X. harm the animals.
No one who knew that knew X → wouldn't these practices seriously do thing harm the animals would engage in them.

label: Conclusion
body: Some visitors don't know Some people these practices seriously don't know X harm the animals.

label: Evaluate
body:
At its bare bones, this argument is just a contrapositive argument.
P1: If knew harm → wouldn't engage P2: Some people do engage. C: Some people do not know harm.
The correct answer may or may not maintain the "no one who knows X would do Y" type vibe to the conversation. Sometimes they drop the extra colors to the conversation and just mimic the contrapositive aspect.

label: Goal
body:
Initially just make sure that an argument has a conditional premise, a premise that establishes the outcome isn't happening, and a conclusion that says the trigger isn't happening.
If more than one contender remains, get more nuanced with similarities.

label: Conclusion
body: When a city experiences a sudden influx of people, it can be disastrous.

label: Evidence
body:
The rapid population growth overwhelms city services, such as getting utilities set up or obtaining permits, and city budgets typically don't allow for the immediate hiring of new staff.
Additionally, there is a standard of having at least one municipal employee for every hundred residents, which may be disrupted by the influx.

label: Evaluate
body: This is a "Strengthen" question aiming to reinforce the conclusion that rapid population growth can be disastrous for cities. Possible strengthening points could involve underscoring the difficulties in managing growth, like budget constraints, resource demands, or delays in receiving new revenue from residents.

label: Goal
body: Identify an answer that amplifies the negative consequences of rapid population growth on city services or reinforces the notion that such growth is hard to manage within existing city budgets.

label: Principle
body: someone knows action X risks consequence Y person is and → responsible for action X was consequences of X undertaken voluntarily

label: Evaluate / Goal
body:
The question stem is only asking about Michiko's principle, which is her second sentence.
We just need an answer choice to establish that someone voluntarily undertook an action, and knew that their action risked a certain result. The conclusion should then say that this person is responsible for that result.
(this rule does **not** have the power to prove that someone is **not** responsible, so if we see any conclusions like that, we can immediately get rid of that answer)

label: Conclusion (So)
body: There are always situations in which it is healthy to try to express one's anger.

label: Evidence
body: There are always situations in which it is healthy to try to express [any visceral emotion you care to consider].

label: Evaluate / Goal
body:
Given the parallel structure of the evidence and the conclusion, we're just trying to match up where they diverge.
If the argument is saying, "It's always healthy to chug something delicious. Thus, it's always healthy to chug a Coke", then the missing assumption is "Coke is delicious".
Since the argument is saying, "It's always healthy to try to express a visceral emotion. So, it's always healthy to try to express anger", then the missing assumption is "Anger is a visceral emotion".
The correct answer **definitely** has to have "anger" in it, since we're trying to prove a conclusion about "anger" but received no facts (i.e. premises) so far about "anger".

label: Given that
body: Some smokers are having a pack of low-nicotine cigarettes, and others are having a pack of high-nicotine cigarettes.

label: How can it be that
body: All of these people had the same level of nicotine in their blood at the end of the day.

label: Evaluate
body:
If I smoke a pack of low-nicotine cigs and you smoke a pack of high-nicotine cigs, how can it be that we have the same nicotine in our blood at the end of the day?
There are three possibilities that might come to mind:
1. Low and high nicotine cigarettes actually have the same amount of nicotine in them
2. I am more sensitive to nicotine than you, so when I smoke low-nicotine, my blood ends up having as much nicotine in it as when you smoke high-nicotine.
3. The body can only absorb so much nicotine in the blood before the rest is just excreted. Maybe a pack of low-nicotine cigarettes already maxes out the body's capacity to retain nicotine, and so anything extra that high-nicotine cigarettes provides would be excreted. (This is true with Vitamin C ... once you've consumed a certain amount, your body doesn't absorb any more)

label: Goal
body: Find a way to explain how someone smoking a pack of low-nicotine cigs has as much nicotine in their blood as someone smoking a pack of high-nicotine cigs.

label: Conclusion (Thus)
body: Development would cause no net reduction of wetlands and pose no threat to the species that inhabit them.

label: Evidence
body: Future wetland development must be offset by the construction of replacement wetland habitats.

label: Evaluate
body:
This author is concerned that we might endanger species when we allow development on wetlands.
She's got a Plan / Recommendation: if a developer wants to build on 10 acres of wetlands in area A, then they have to build 10 acres of wetlands in some other area to offset that.
This is supposed to result in **no net reduction** in wetlands and pose **no threat** to the species that inhabit them.
Can we think of any way that if we enacted this regulation there would be a net reduction in wetlands or there could be a threat to the species inhabiting them?

label: Goal
body: The correct answer, when negated, should weaken. So let's look for an answer whose negation makes it sound like even though construction companies will have to construct replacement wetland habitats, there still will be a net reduction in wetlands or a threat to wetland species.

label: Wildlife Commission Conclusion
body: Future wetland development in Figoria must be regulated and offset by replacement habitats so that there is no net reduction of wetlands and no threat to species.

label: Wildlife Commission Evidence
body: Wetland development in industrialized nations has endangered many species.

label: Development Commission Conclusion
body: Figoria should be allowed to develop its wetlands.

label: Development Commission Evidence
body: Figoria has already conserved (unlike other nations that flagrantly developed wetlands), the development might not affect wildlife, and it is necessary for growth. Figoria has the same right to govern its own resources as nations that already used theirs commercially.

label: Evaluate
body:
We're trying to support the second speaker, whose agenda is "let us develop wetlands at the expense of wildlife".
They're kind of saying, "Why do WE have to be the responsible nation that protects these wetland species. It's costing us economically. Other nations have derived commercial benefit from their natural resources. We should be allowed to do the same. We need this for growth and it might not even affect wildlife."

label: Goal
body: We have a lot of premises to work with, and the correct answer doesn't have to use all of them. We just want an answer that takes us FROM something we know is applicable to the FDC's argument helps us take us TO the idea that it's okay to develop wetlands at the expense of wildlife.

label: Wildlife Commission
body: Regulate development now, with mandatory replacement habitats, so species are not threatened.

label: Development Commission
body: Figoria has conserved and the development might not affect wildlife, so allow development; we have the same right to govern our resources as nations that already used theirs.

label: Goal
body: Find a principle that supports allowing development unless damage to species has actually been shown.

label: The Two Sides
body: The Wildlife Commission wants to regulate up front: any new wetland development must come with a replacement habitat. The Development Commission says Figoria has already played nice while other nations have not, the development "might not" affect wildlife, and growth requires it — so let development happen.

label: Evaluate
body: The Development Commission is essentially saying: do not regulate until you actually see harm. Figoria has not yet caused harm; the proposed development might cause none either. So regulation is not yet warranted.

label: Goal
body: The principle we want is one that says: regulation kicks in only after observed harm — not before. That fits the Development Commission's "wait and see" stance and supports their position over the precautionary one the Wildlife Commission is taking.

label: Conclusion
body: Shellfish is not necessarily bad for the heart.

label: Evidence
body:
High blood cholesterol is bad for the heart.
Shellfish is very low in saturated fat, which affects blood cholesterol levels much more than dietary cholesterol does.

label: Evaluate
body: The argument is trying to say that shellfish is okay for the heart. After all, X is bad for the heart. Y has a big effect on X, and shellfish is very low in Y. Even if saturated fat is bad for the heart, and shellfish is low on saturated fat, there might be other things that are bad for the heart, and shellfish might be high on those things.

label: Goal
body: Let's find an answer that helps us argue that shellfish is fine for the heart, or that rules out potential objections that would make it sound bad for the heart.

label: Statements
body:
conditional ( **every** = suff. indicator, put on LEFT)
Moral theory developed → Purports to tell us in Western tradition what a good life is
pivot (but, yet, **however**, nevertheless)
Most people would judge someone perfectly embodying what these theories explain to be a good life as not living a good life (not want they would want for themselves or their kids).

label: Evaluate
body:
This paragraph gives us two claims, joined by a Pivot word, so normally that means the correct answer will **Reconcile the Pivot**; it will find some safely worded way of combining what came before pivot with what came after.
The **overlapping** idea in both claims is "good life". Every moral theory from the West tries to tell us what a good life is. But most people would disagree (for themselves / for their kids) that any of these definitions qualify as "good life".
So we could synthesize into something like, Most people do not agree with Western moral theories, when it comes to what makes a good life.

label: Goal
body: Let's look for something safely worded, probably that reinforces the disconnect between what Western moral theories consider a good life and what most people consider a good life.

label: Conclusion
body: If we humans had descended from six-phalanged fish and thus has six fingers, we'd be just as content with a six-fingered hand as we are with a five-fingered one.

label: Conclusion (Therefore)
body: Wooly mammoths that lived on the island were smaller on average than those who lived elsewhere.

label: Evidence
body:
We have five-fingers through an accident of evolution (our ancestor had five phalanges).
Our five-fingered configuration is no more or less useful than several other configurations, such as six-fingers per hand.

label: Evaluate
body:
Since the author is making a comparison between our Actual World and the 6-Fingered World, we should look at what comparison is happening in the Evidence and think about comparison we're measuring in the Conclusion.
The evidence establishes that in the 6-fingered world, our configuration of fingers would be just as **useful** as our current 5-fingered configuration is.
The conclusion is saying that we would be just as **content**.

label: Goal
body:
It looks like this argument is relying on the assumption that, "if two configurations are equally useful, then we'd be equally content with them", but maybe there's more to our contentment than just usefulness?
Maybe we would aesthetically prefer the look of the 5-fingered hand to that of the 6-fingered hand, for example.
Since objections to this argument spring from this source, even though 6-fingers would be just as useful, we wouldn't necessarily be just as content, because.... we can strengthen this argument by making "usefulness" seem like the main / only game in town.
Look for an answer saying "all we care about is usefulness" or ruling out the idea that we care about something else.

label: Conclusion
body: Models need not be taken only from outside the psyche. (i.e. it's okay to take some models from inside the psyche)

label: Evidence
body: If we only used the power of art to preserve and reinforce objects that would exist even without artists (i.e. outside the psyche), that would be an ironic waste.

label: Evaluate
body:
When we're doing **Main Conclusion** questions, we read the paragraph expecting that most of the time the Conclusion will appear earlier than the Evidence.
In particular, we look out for the two most common patterns: - the Conclusion appears after a **pivot** word like "but, yet, however" - the Conclusion is the first sentence
We can tell that the first sentence of this paragraph is the conclusion because it's the Author's Opinion (and the conclusion on Main Conclusion is rebutting someone else's idea about half the time).
Our author is implicitly saying, "Many artists think that models can only be taken from outside the psyche" and then she is disagreeing with that by throwing in the mistakenly adverb.
When an author is disagreeing with "X is Y", we should say to ourselves that the author's conclusion is really "X is not Y".
So here, since our author is disagreeing with "models need to be taken only from outside the psyche", the author's conclusion is "models should also be taken from inside the psyche".
Why should we believe that it's a mistake to take models **only** from outside the psyche?
Because... if artists used the power of art **solely** to deal with stuff that would exist even without artists (outside the psyche), that would be an ironic waste.
Note: we're not addressing the "Although" claim, since that word indicates the first half of the sentence is a counterpoint, not the author's actual emphasis.

label: Goal
body: Once we've found the conclusion, choosing an answer is just looking for the best meaning match. So we want an answer that means: - it is a mistake to take models only from outside the psyche or - it would be appropriate sometimes to take models from within the psyche

label: Conclusion
body: Harrold dominates the market now and need only maintain its current market share in order to continue to do so.

label: Evidence (since)
body:
Any product with more than 50% of the sales in a market dominates that market.
Survey results show that 72% of consumers think that Harrold's soda "Hero" already dominates the market.

label: Evaluate
body:
The conclusion makes two claims, so we can decide how we might object to each of them.
Has the author convinced us that "Harrold Foods dominates the market now"?
Not quite. He defined "dominates" as "more than 50% of sales", but he never established that Harrold has more than 50% of sales. He just said more than 50% (72%) of consumers think that Harrold dominates.
That's their opinion, not necessarily a fact. A semi-famous flaw we see now and then is this distinction between Opinion vs. Fact.
Has the author convinced us that "Harrold Foods need only maintain its current market share in order to continue to dominate"?
No, but that's because we're not convinced that Harrold Foods currently has a market share above 50%. If they really do currently have more than 50% of sales, and they were to maintain that market share, then they would continue to dominate (since dominate is defined as "more than 50%").

label: Goal
body:
So it seems like we should be objecting to the first prong of the two-pronged conclusion. The author hasn't established that Harrold currently has more than 50% of sales in the market.
If he thinks that a survey showing 72% of consumers believe that Harrold's soda already dominates the market, then he's acting like we should just blindly trust that this survey opinion is factually correct.

label: Conclusion
body: If their goal is to make medicine more cost-effective, medical schools spend insufficient time teaching preventative medicine.

label: Evidence
body: Using preventative techniques cuts down medical costs greatly, but the ratio of preventative time to curative time in med school is 1:10.

label: Evaluate
body:
Whenever we have a conditional conclusion, it is never our responsibility to judge the "If" part (the trigger). We're never trying to strengthen the idea that the trigger is true or will happen. We can never weaken the argument by making it seem like the trigger won't happen. It's just an accepted background condition of the argument.
So suppose that med schools do have the goal of making medicine more cost-effective.
The LINKING assumption the author is making is that, time spent on preventative is insufficient time 1/10 time spent on curative → spent on preventative
What if we were trying to think of Objections?
How could we argue that, even though only 1/10 as much time is spent on preventative as curative it's still the case that med schools **are** spending sufficient time on preventative?
Maybe it's way easier to teach preventative than curative? Maybe preventative doesn't vary that much from person to person, so teaching a doctor to do preventative medicine is basically rehearsing the advice of, "Eat less red meat / drink a lot of water / eat more veggies and fruits / get regular exercise / get good sleep / try to avoid prolonged stress".
Meanwhile, curative medicine is an insanely complicated endeavor, because there's a whole encyclopedia of conditions a doctor might be trying to cure, and each one has its own treatment protocol.

label: Goal
body: Look for the linking assumption of, "if spending 1/10 the time, then insufficient time", or look for some sort of defending assumption like, "teaching preventative medicine well does **not** take way less time than teaching curative medicine".

label: Dana's 1st Claim
body:
The same educational methods should not be used with all children. does Pat say the same **should** be used?
No, he's not saying the same methods should be used with all children. That's an extreme position, and he doesn't sound extreme.

label: Dana's 2nd Claim
body:
Many kids have been raised in more communal environments than others and would therefore learn better through group than individual learning. does Pat deny that many kids have raised in more communal settings, or deny that those kids would learn better through group learning?
No. He seems to implicitly agree that such kids exist and might prefer group activities, but thinks that because the real world will require proficiency at group and individual activities, those kids should learn in both modes.

label: Dana's 3rd Claim
body:
A kid's accustomed style of learning should always dictate by what method you them. does Pat think you shouldn't always pick the teaching method that best matches the kid's style of learning?
Yes! He thinks it would be bad for kids to only learn one style of learning. Since there is much real world value at being comfortable with group and individual skills, children should be exposed to both (even if that means sometimes they're learning through their less-preferred method).

label: Goal
body: The debate is in regards to the decision to use group vs. individual educational methods on a given child. One person thinks pick the method that best matches that kid. The other person thinks expose all kids to both methods.

label: Statements
body:
In order to count how many people were employed, Country X would count the number of paychecks per pay period (probably every two weeks) by employers.
When the government had gotten through the first quarter (3 months) of using this new method, it said that there was a large increase in the number of people employed, compared to the previous quarter when they weren't using that method.

label: Stem
body: During this 1st quarter, employers issued separate paychecks for base pay, overtime pay, and bonuses/commissions.

label: Evaluate
body:
It's a little confusing for me to understand how the government is even capable of comparing 1st quarter of 1988 to the last quarter of 1987, since the job-counting thing started in 1988.
But I guess we're meant to assume that the government has some other way of estimating employment, prior to beginning this computer program method in 1988.
The question stem seems to be baiting us into thinking that "the reason the government thinks there's a big increase in the number of people employed is because the computer method would see a single employee getting 3 paychecks (one for base pay, one for overtime, and one for bonuses/commission) and think to itself, '3 paychecks = 3 people employed'."
But it's hard to say this is a must be true inference. We don't know anything about the old method of how they estimated jobs.
Also, it's possible that the computer program is in fact over-counting jobs (because it thinks that each paycheck is a separate person employed), but still possible that in addition to that there was an increase in people employed during the 1st quarter.

label: Goal
body: We just have to be careful that we pick some safe wording. It feels like we're being baited into using the crumbs they've provided us with to make a Most Supported inference, but this is "properly concluded", so we need to feel rock solid on what we're picking.

label: Conclusion (implicit)
body: It's possible that one of the reasons vegetarians cite as sufficient for avoiding meat (we shouldn't live at the expense of other conscious creatures) is not clearly sufficient of a reason to avoid meat.

label: Evidence
body:
The other reasons they cite as being sufficient for avoiding meat is health considerations.
But if we found out that eating meat was essential to good health, then one of their sufficient reasons would eat the other sufficient reason.

label: Evaluate
body:
This is a weird "argument". I wouldn't really call it that. Our author can't really be said to be rebutting the vegetarians, because his rebuttal is based on a hypothetical idea.
So I wouldn't be expecting the answer to use classic Premise / Conclusion language.
They're asking us about the "Suppose" sentence. We would probably just say the role is plays is, "It's a hypothetical idea that allows the author to derive the last sentence, which pushes back at the original claim the some vegetarians have made".

label: Goal
body: I have no idea what to call this weird ingredient, so I would just plan to be flexible and consider every answer's language to see if we can match it up.

label: Statements
body:
Causal (led to)
increasingly complex ⇢ lots of mult-author scientific inquiry technical articles
Quantified-Most (usually / generally)
Most **reports of trials** are co-authored **involving patients** by docs from **from several hospitals** each hospital
Most **physics papers** are co-authored **relying on systems** by ppl from **from several labs** each lab

label: Evaluate
body:
Was there any Overlapping Idea amongst these claims, that might allow us to synthesize them?
Maybe -- all three claims dealt with "multi-authored technical articles". But I'm not sure how we could synthesize any of those claims. It feels like the passage is insinuating that "increasing complexity" is explaining sentence 2 and sentence 3.
Those last two sentences feel like examples of "increasing complexity leading to more multi-authored stuff".

label: Goal
body:
Maybe the answer will have something to do with the idea of "increasing complexity" meaning that we want to get docs from several hospitals in on the same report, or that we want to use subsystems developed at various labs.
Mostly, though, I would feel pretty helpless to guess where this is headed and would just err on the side of avoiding Strong/Specific language, unknown comparisons, or unmentioned concepts.

label: Helena's Conclusion
body: Social extroversion is not biologically determined.

label: Helena's Evidence
body: Kids whose biological parents are introverts but who are adopted by introverts tend to end up more socially extroverted than do children who live with their biological introverted parents.

label: Jay's Conclusion
body: That evidence does not show that social extroversion isn't biologically determined.

label: Jay's Evidence
body: Some of these children adopted by extroverts remain introverted forever, even when they basically lived with the extroverts their whole childhood.

label: Goal
body: Look for something like, "supports the idea that we should be skeptical of anonymous sources in news stories by presenting an analogy about unsigned letters".

label: Evaluate
body:
This is an unusual question stem, of which there might be 10 total ever. When they ask how the 2nd person "interpreted" the 1st person, they always are implying that the 2nd person mis-interpreted the 1st person.
So we want to identify a moment where the 2nd person seems to have not listened to something the 1st person said or seems to be distorting the meaning of something the 1st person said.
We can also just consider, "What would person 1 say in response to this?"
Helena would probably say, "Jay, I realize that **some** children of extroverts remain introverted indefinitely. I never said that **all** children of extroverts end up being extroverted. I said that children (of introverted biological parents) adopted by extroverts **tend to** be **more** extroverted than are the biological children of introverts who are raised by those introverts."

label: Goal
body:
In other words, Helena's wording left plenty of room for some exceptions. By saying that "extroversion is not biologically determined", she's saying "your biology does not determine your extroversion / the parents who raise you (an environmental influence) seems to make some difference because kids whose biology would suggest introversion can end up more extroverted if they're adopted by extroverted parents."
Jay seems to think Helena is arguing that "biology has **no influence** on extroversion" or that she's saying, " **all** children adopted by extroverts end up being extroverted".

label: Ariel's 1st Claim
body:
Government art subsidies never benefit art. Does Sasha argue government art subsidies sometimes **do** benefit art?
Yes! It sounds like Sasha is saying that those subsidies benefit art in a democratic society by ensuring that artists can be fully committed to their work while expressing themselves freely.

label: Ariel's 2nd Claim
body:
Art's role is to challenge society's values. Does Sasha argue art's role is **not** to challenge society's values?
No. Sasha actually explicitly agrees with this claim of Ariel's.

label: Ariel's 3rd Claim
body:
A society's values are expressed by its government. Does Sasha argue that society's values are **not** expressed by its government?
No. In fact, it seems like Sasha is agreeing that government expresses values, because he's pointing out that democratic governments are okay with people challenging the values it expresses.

label: Ariel's 4th Claim
body:
Artists cannot challenge the very institution upon which they depend. Does Sasha argue that artists **can** challenge the very institution upon which they depend?
Kind of. Sasha seems to be saying that in a democratic society, since the government respects dissent and encourages challenges, a subsidized artist **can** challenge the very institution upon which they depend.

label: Goal
body:
Since we found a couple explicit claims that Sasha would disagree with, we probably don't need to dive deeper into Ariel's assumptions.
Let's look for Sasha's objection that, in a democratic society, - artists **can** challenge the source of their monetary support and thus - government art subsidies **can** benefits art

label: Conclusion (therefore)
body: The most rational public health strategy would more emphasize the goal of fully informing people about the transmission of diseases caused by microorganisms.

label: Evidence
body: Current medical research shows that these microorganisms reproduce so quickly that medicines designed to kill one leads to an evolved mutant version that is immune to that medicine.

label: Evaluate
body:
When we read Main Conclusion and Role, we know that the main conclusion is the final claim only about 10-15% of the time. Usually, the conclusion is found in the First Sentence or attached to some Pivot/Rebuttal moment in the middle.
This first sentence is ineligible to be the conclusion because it's definitely not an opinion coming from the author. It's just a past tense fact about what people have believed until recently.
The magical **Pivot** happens to introduce the 2nd sentence, but it too is not an opinion coming from the author. It's factually reporting what current medical research has discovered.
So we're left with the final claim, which happens to be adorned with a Conclusion indicator, "therefore". We might worry that this is just an Intermediate Conclusion, because we're used to trickery on Main Conclusion questions, but this is the only opinion from the author in the paragraph.
She is making a **recommendation** about what the most rational public health strategy would be. And it's supported by the 2nd sentence.

label: Goal
body: Let's find a meaning-match for the final sentence.

label: Conclusion
body: Medieval societies were much less concerned with money than contemporary Western cultures.

label: Evidence
body: Surviving writing from monks who lived in medieval societies show that these monks enthusiastically accepted an ascetic lifestyle of minimal subsistence.

label: Evaluation
body:
Whoa, LSAC, when did this become a vocab / outside knowledge test? This is a pretty clear **Sampling** flaw, but it'll be hard to see it if you don't know what monastic and ascetic mean.
Monastic = monastery = where priests / monks / bishops lived Ascetic = forsaking money and material goods for a bare, minimal, austere, spartan existence.
This is an extremely biased sample. Monks are known to live an ascetic lifestyle. But they're the weirdos of society (no offense, monks). They're not representative of society.
This would be like a human anthropologist a thousand years from now saying, "Surviving writings from NASCAR and Formula-1 drivers from the year 2020 indicate that they had little fear of driving over 150mph. Apparently, 21st century societies weren't too fearful of driving over 150mph."

label: Goal
body: Look for an answer suggesting that the devotional religious types at a monastery aren't necessarily the most representative members of society, from which to base a generalization about that society.

label: Conclusion
body: It makes sense to be skeptical of anonymous sources in news stories.

label: Evidence (for)
body:
If you received an unsigned letter, you would likely have some doubts about the truth of its contents.
Similarly, the anonymity of an unnamed source makes it possible for them to plant inaccurate or slanted statements without ever having to answer for them.

label: Evaluate
body:
Method questions want us to characterize the reasoning move or type of evidence used, and the correct answers usually pull from this list: 1. make/ break an analogy 2. show faulty implications of logic / plan 3. eliminate / suggest an alternative
This argument definitely makes an analogy (two specific cases with some similar general principle).
In both the case of the unsigned letter and the anonymous source, it makes sense to be skeptical about the accuracy of what you hear.

label: Evidence
body: The recent food crisis involved faltering crops and rising agricultural prices. + Insufficient rain can cause faltering crops and rising agricultural prices.

label: Evaluation
body:
This argument is essentially the same as saying: Billy apparently jumped off a building. After all, Billy recently died, and jumping off a building can cause death.
Insufficient rain is one possible cause of bad crops / rising prices, but there may be other possible causes of bad crops / rising prices, so we can't just assume that weather (i.e. insufficient rain) was the cause of this recent food crisis.

label: Goal
body: Find an answer describing the **Necessary vs. Sufficient** flaw of assuming that one possible cause is the cause. Or find an answer making the objection that something else could have caused the bad crops / rising prices in this instance.

label: Conclusion
body: The issue of whether the value of an artwork is intrinsic to the work is related to the issue of whether judgments about a work's quality are objective or matters of taste.

label: Evidence (for) / + Intermediate Conclusion (thus)
body: If an artwork's value is not intrinsic, then it must be extrinsic (in which case judgments about the quality of the work can only be a matter of taste.)

label: Evaluate
body:
This is a pretty brutal argument to understand on a first read. The main conclusion is only claiming that "whether value is intrinsic vs. extrinsic" is related to whether "judgments about quality are objective vs. matters of taste".
She establishes a binary we probably already assumed: If it's not intrinsic, then it must be extrinsic
But then she goes from "extrinsic" via the Conclusion indicator **thus** to the idea that "judgments about quality would be based on taste".
This seems to be the reasoning move where the author is making a big assumption. The question stem asks what the argument "takes for granted", so we're being asked for a Necessary Assumption.

label: Goal
body:
The author thinks that this chain exists:
not intrinsic → extrinsic → judgments about quality are just a matter of taste
The link between 1 and 2 is provided to us by the conditional "if an artwork's value is not intrinsic, then it's extrinsic".
But the link between 2 and 3 is just assumed as the author moves from "extrinsic" to "quality judgments are only a matter of taste" via a conclusion indicator. Let's look for that missing link.

label: Statements
body:
causal / conditional Decentralization **enables** divisions to function autonomously.
causal / conditional This **always permits** more realistic planning and encourages innovation.
causal This better planning / more innovation is because the people responsible for decision making are directly involved in implementing the policies they design.
causal Decentralization lets the central admin focus on big picture issues without being overwhelmed by details of daily operations.

label: Evaluate
body:
It sounds like decentralizing large institutions has a lot of upsides: 1. more realistic planning 2. big emphasis on innovation 3. allows central admin to focus on big picture, not drowning in daily details
There are several causal verbs, **enables / permits / permits**, and there is one true conditional word, **always**.
It's not really clear how we would chain together or synthesize these. We could probably make a causal chain.
1. Decentralization lets divisions of a big institution function autonomously. 2. thus, the people who have to make decisions are directly involved in implementing the policies they design. 3. thus, there is more realistic planning and a strong incentive for innovation, and the central admin is not overwhelmed with daily details.

label: Goal
body: I wouldn't have any strong prediction here. Let's just find the most provable claim based on what we were told.

label: Conclusion (this warrants)
body: We should spend some money to determine whether there's a way to protect our planet from meteorite strikes.

label: Intermediate Conclusion (so)
body: We can expect Earth will be struck by an ice-age-causing meteorite in the near future.

label: Evidence
body:
Earth gets hit by an ice-age-causing meteorite an average of once every 100 million years.
The last one came about 100 million years ago.

label: Evaluate
body:
There are a couple complaints that come to mind. One is the sense in which the author is interpreting average / probability too literally.
If we know that "the probability of rolling a 3 on an individual die is 1/6", and the last five times we've rolled we haven't gotten a 3, it's not correct to say "we're likely to get a 3 on the next roll". It's still just a 1/6 probability.
if we say "on average, there is a Presidential scandal about once every 18 months, and since there hasn't been a scandal for the last 17 months we can expect one next month". That's interpreting average too literally.
Similarly, just because Earth has averaged one huge meteorite every 100 million years doesn't mean that we can expect the gaps between each meteorite to be literally 100 million years.
That's just an average. If it's 101 million years this time between meteorite strikes, then we're still 1 million years away from the next meteorite strike.
Thus, it wouldn't be true to say "we can expect we'll be struck in the near future" nor do we need to scramble into meteorite-defense planning. We have 1 million years to work on that, more than the entire species history of homo sapiens up to this point.

label: Goal
body: Find an answer complaining about interpreting average too literally, or failing to consider that if we're even slightly off from 100 million years, we're talking about a million year difference!

label: Conclusion
body: There is little or no connection between recognition of cigarette brand logos and smoking.

label: Evidence
body: An overwhelming majority of 9 year old's can identify the logos of major cigarette brands. However, less than 1% of those 9 year old's smoke.

label: Evaluate
body:
How could we argue that, despite this evidence, there **is** a connection between recognition of cigarette logos and smoking?
We could say, "Sure, they don't smoke **yet...** they're 9. But when these guys are 12 or 13 and they start to have friends who smoke, maybe they will be much more likely to start smoking, having already become accustomed to cigarette brands."
We could also say, "Sure, maybe there's no connection **for 9 year old's**, but what about for older age groups? When it comes to 16 year old's, for example, are the people who can correctly identify logos more likely to smoke?"

label: Pivot
body: We can finally warn people well in advance that they will probably develop a fatal genetic disease. However, we can't prevent them from getting most of those diseases.

label: Goal
body:
Our objections were of two different forms: 1. just because there isn't a visible connection **yet**, doesn't mean there won't be one eventually (i.e. the author is judging something using too narrow a snapshot of time)
2. just because there isn't a visible connection for **9 year old's** doesn't mean there isn't one for other age groups. (i.e. the author is judging something using too narrow a sample of age group)
One way or the other, they're both **Sampling** flaws. So we should look for an argument that is judging something broad in the conclusion, but relying on a sample that only represents a narrow slice of people / narrow slice of time.

label: Principles
body:
obscene or → firmly opposed malicious talk
offensive, disturbing, or controversial should be expressed and → and discussed in a appropriate situation civil manner for dealing w/ such ideas

label: Evaluate / Goal
body:
We definitely don't need to necessarily convert these to conditionals (and there are alternative ways of writing the conditionals that would also be valid).
Let's look for an answer that is scolding someone for being obscene/malicious in any context, scolding someone for being offensive/disturbing/controversial in an inappropriate context or for discussing such stuff in an un-civil manner.
Or we could have an answer condoning the opposite of those behaviors.

label: Conclusion
body: Most classic jazz recordings will not be transferred onto CD.

label: Evidence
body: Most classic jazz recordings are not played on the radio, and if record companies don't believe something will sell enough on CD to be profitable, then they won't transfer those recordings onto CD.

label: Evaluate
body:
When we see our conclusion is "most classic jazz recordings will not be transferred", we want to ask ourselves two questions: - have they told me anything that is true of most classic jazz recordings? (if not, that must be in the correct answer) - have they given me a rule / law / mechanism that lets me derive the idea of won't be transferred to CD (if not, that idea must be in the correct answer)
In this argument, they gave us information about the Naming Part of the conclusion (most classic jazz recordings) and they gave us a rule that lets us derive the Telling Part (won't be transferred onto CD).
But we need a little skill to manipulate those two premises.
When we see negative quantifiers like "no / few / not all", we want to make a habit of always switching them over to their positive restatements: No A's are B = All A's are ~B Few A's are B = Most A's are ~B Not all A's are B = Some A's are ~B
That's how we turned "few classic jazz recordings are played on the radio" into "most classic jazz recordings are **not** played on the radio".
The first sentence uses the conditional indicator "the only", which indicates a sufficient condition (put the attached idea on the LEFT of the arrow).
This can be confusing, since "only" and "only if", which appear much more frequently, are always indicating necessary (put it on the RIGHT) ideas.
But "the only" is "the only time that only means Left".
So that conditional looks like preexisting recording → record companies transferred to CD think will be profitable
Since the conclusion is trying to create this path Most classic --------------> not jazz recordings transferred
and we currently have these two pieces: Most classic → not played jazz recordings on radio
RC's don't → not think will be transferred profitable
All we're missing is that internal link.

label: Goal
body:
We need to get from "not played on radio" to "record companies don't believe it will sell enough on CD to be profitable".
Most classic → **not played** jazz recordings **on radio →**

label: Conclusion (hence / conclude)
body: Violent TV imagery does not cause violence.

label: Evidence
body:
Although TV ads affect buying habits, that could be a result of those ads being specifically designed to alter buying habits.
Meanwhile, TV violence is not designed to cause violent behavior.

label: Evaluate
body:
If we wanted to counter-argue that "violent TV imagery **does** sometimes cause violence", how could we respond to this author's evidence?
She said "the effectiveness of TV ads in changing audience behavior **could be** a result of the fact that the ads were designed to do that".
We might say, "Sure it could be that. But it also could be that seeing something on TV, whether it was designed to influence you or not, has the power to influence you."
She said, "TV violence is not designed to cause violent behavior."
We might say, "Sure, but it might cause violent behavior anyway. The caps on ballpoint pens weren't designed to pick U-shaped bike locks, but bike thieves ended up using them for that anyway. A soda can or apple isn't designed to be a pipe, but resourceful potheads might use it in that capacity anyway. When a woman wears a sun dress, it's not an action designed to get obnoxious men to catcall her, but that might happen anyway."

label: Goal
body:
Let's look for something like either of our objections - the author assumes that "because the influential nature of TV ads could be due to their intentionally manipulative design, that they are influential due to that reason."
- the author assumes that "because TV violence isn't designed to cause violence, that it therefore won't cause violence".

label: Conclusion (Thus)
body: Some staff may be dismissed merely because their personal views conflict with those of their supervisors.

label: Evidence
body:
According to regulations, if performing unsatisfactorily → then dismissal
But there's no definition of "unsatisfactory".

label: Evaluate
body:
On Strengthen + Principle questions, we're expecting the correct answer to feel like a conditional rule: **If** [this thing that matches the Evidence] is true, **then** [the conclusion] is true. Usually the conclusion is an action we should take or a value judgment we should have. However, this conclusion is causal. We're trying to strengthen the idea that one thing will causally lead to another.
Let's think about the Causal Chain the author is envisioning:
1. If your supervisor deems your performance unsatisfactory, it's grounds for dismissal. But there's no definition of what "unsatisfactory" behavior means.
2. So supervisors will stretch "unsatisfactory" to mean whatever suits their purposes, when they want to fire someone.
3. So if a supervisor gets into a fight with an employee because their personal views conflict, the supervisor will employ her prerogative to say, "Guess what, sport --- I find your performance unsatisfactory. Stop by HR on the way out the door."

label: Goal
body: We need to strengthen this causal story the author is envisioning where we get from lacking a definition for "unsatisfactory performance" to employers actually abusing that ambiguity in order to make up grounds for firing employees whose personal views they don't like.

label: Causal
body: Knowing you'll get a fatal / incurable disease can be quite harmful.

label: Evaluate / Anticipate
body: It sounds like we need a safely worded statement that reconciles the coolness of the new test with the crappy factor that it just tells people bad news that we can't help them with.

label: Conclusion
body: These successes (by extremist parties) pose no threat to democracy in those countries.

label: Evidence (X. Furthermore, Y.)
body: The extremists won pluralities, not majorities, and won only when the moderate parties were fighting amongst themselves.

label: Evaluate
body: The language we need to prove is "Pose no threat to democracy". The argument didn't provide any proving mechanism like, "If X is true, then poses no threat to democracy", so the correct answer will have to provide that proving mechanism.

label: Goal
body:
We know two facts, so either one of them could be the Launchpad that takes us to the Landing Zone of "poses no threat to democracy". Let's look for one of these:
won plurality, not majority → poses no threat to democracy
won only when moderates → poses no threat were in-fighting to democracy

label: Facts
body:
conditionals (must, no, universal noun)
Flexible —requires→ large # of neurons behavior
Insect brain → doesn't have large # of neurons Instinctual → No reasoning and behavior fewer nerve cells than flex behavior

label: Evaluate
body:
The #1 thing we read for on MBT is conditionals. We found three of them. Do they chain together? Do they have any overlapping concepts?
Yes, two of them mention flexible behavior. Two of them mention a large # of neurons. The last two claims chain together to give us this,
Insect → not large # → not flexible brain of neurons behavior
That idea of "not flexible" behavior is the same as instinctual behavior, so we could also chain on the first claim.
Insect → not large # → not flexible → no reasoning brain of neurons behavior fewer nerve cells

label: Goal
body: Let's look for anything we can prove. It'll probably reward us for having assembled this chain, though not necessarily with a Head → Tail inference.

label: Conclusion
body: Fact-set, no conclusion offered.

label: Evidence
body: Flexible behavior needs many neurons. Insect brains don't have enough.

label: Evaluate
body: Insects can't produce flexible behavior, so all their behavior is instinctual.

label: Goal
body: Find the answer about insect behavior being exclusively instinctual.

label: Conclusion
body: This is a fact-set, not an argument. Your job is to chain the facts and find what they force.

label: Evidence
body: The setup is a clean conditional chain. Flexible behavior requires a brain with many neurons. Insect brains do not have many neurons (at least not enough). Behavior is split into two types — instinctual or flexible.

label: Evaluate
body:
Walk the chain. Insects don't have enough neurons → insects can't produce flexible behavior → if insect behavior exists, it must be the other kind, instinctual.
So everything insects do, behavior-wise, is instinctual. That's the modest, direct conclusion the facts force.
Watch out for trap answers that try to extend the inference to all organisms, to non-insects, to brain-elaborate organisms in general — the passage only gives us facts about insects specifically.

label: Goal
body: Pick the answer that says insect behavior is exclusively instinctual.

label: Conclusion (should)
body: The trend in which the laboratory experiment disappears from most secondary school curricula (as students just simulate experiments with computers) should be stopped.

label: Evidence
body: The lab experiment is the most effective method for teaching science. When secondary schools don't have lab experiments, many students complete secondary school and go to university without knowing how to work with laboratory equipment.

label: Evaluate
body:
Given that ... not teaching lab means not using the most effective method for teaching science, and that ... students head off to university w/o knowing how to work with lab equipment,
How could we argue that... the trend of getting rid of lab experiments (and replacing them with simulated experiments on computers) should **continue**?
Ultimately, this is a Comparative conversation about the **net gain / loss** of getting rid of lab experiments and and simulating them on computer as well.
We can argue that the negatives the author mentioned aren't that negative:
- university students don't need to know how to work with lab equipment (maybe universities don't make their students work with lab equipment / maybe they do simulated experiments on computers also)
- even though the lab experiment was the most effective method for teaching science, doing it computer is 95% as good
We can also argue that there are positives that the author has failed to consider:
- fewer accidents with simulated experiments than with real lab experiments? - give students more familiarity doing science on computers (which might be relevant to future careers)? - we save money by simulating experiments on computers and we use that money on something else that benefits students even more than lab experiments?

label: Goal
body: We want an answer to help us say, "It's okay that we're phasing out lab experiments and doing them on computer instead. It's okay that students go to university without knowing how to work with lab equipment. This current trend is better than what we were doing before."

label: Alice's 1st Statement
body: In democracies, politicians emphasize the differences between them and their opponents in order to win support.

label: Elwell's Response?
body: He seems to accept that this is true. In saying, "Despite election rhetoric", he seems to acknowledge that while campaigning, politicians will SAY lots of stuff about how different they are from their opponents.

label: Alice's 2nd Statement
body: In democracies, politicians must rule in accord with their rhetoric.

label: Elwell's Response?
body: He seems to resist this idea. He thinks that there's a difference between what they say in their election rhetoric and how they actually act once elected. He thinks that politicians usually soften their stands once they are actually ruling.

label: Alice's 3rd Statement
body: In democracies, policies fluctuate wildly as one party succeeds another.

label: Goal
body: The right answer should call out that increased theta waves do not always come with creativity — so producing them by playing music will not necessarily produce creativity.

label: Elwell's Response?
body:
He would probably disagree with this claim too, since he thinks politicians soften their stance once elected. In other words, they may seem to be a more extreme liberal or more extreme conservative while trying to get elected (emphasizing differences), but once in office politicians need to put together majority coalitions (which is code for "working with your opponents"). So he thinks that politicians soften, compromise, and "move towards the center" in order to get people with different views to form a coalition with them.
Thus, he wouldn't think that policies would fluctuate wildly because he thinks the actual policies enacted are probably moderate.

label: Evaluate
body: There is technically a fourth idea implied by Alice (that "ruling in accord with rhetoric that emphasizes differences will lead to wildly fluctuating policies". Elwell doesn't seem to disagree with that implicit connection. Plus, we already have him disagreeing with Alice's 2nd and 3rd claims, so we don't need to look at deeper issues.

label: Goal
body:
Let's look for Alice's 2nd or 3rd claims: - whether or not democratic politicians actually rule in accord with their polarizing election rhetoric
- whether or not policies fluctuate wildly from one party to the next

label: Conclusion (should)
body: Resident physicians should also be restricted from working exceptionally long hours (like 80 hour weeks).

label: Evidence (since)
body:
Air traffic controllers and nuclear power plant operators are restricted from exceptionally long hours, because working exceptionally long hours would jeopardize lives.
Resident physicians, just like the air traffic controllers and nuclear plant operators, are engaged in work of a life-or-death nature.

label: Evaluate
body:
Since this argument is based on a Comparison, we want to think about what similarities are being assumed or about what potential differences could be currently overlooked.
The author is **Assuming a Similarity** when it comes to the effect of long hours in residency training. We ban long hours for air traffic control and nuclear plants because to do so would jeopardize lives.
Did the author ever establish that long hours in resident training would also jeopardize lives? Not quite. They just said that physicians in residency are also engaged in work of a life-or-death nature.
The one big difference that might matter here is that physicians in residency are training, whereas air traffic controllers and nuclear plant operators presumably are not. Maybe we need to ban long hours for people who are "in charge" of doing the work, but we don't need to ban long hours for people who are just "in training"?
