body: Let's look for an answer making the anti-causal objection that, "Sure these neighborhoods are #1 for crime, but if we didn't have all those cops there, there would be even more crime than there currently is", or for an answer making the reverse causality objection that the whole reason we have so many cops in this area is because it was already #1 for crime.

label: Conclusion (it is clear that)
body: Efforts to protect the natural habitats of endangered species are wasted.

label: Evidence
body: The rate at which endangered species are becoming extinct continues to rise.

label: Evaluate
body: **Given that** the rate of extinctions is increasing, **how could we argue that** conservation efforts are not wasted? We would need to show that these efforts have had successful outcomes, such as preventing certain extinctions or providing other positive impacts, which the argument has not accounted for.

label: Goal
body: Let's find an answer that provides an example of how conservation efforts have positively impacted the survival of species or contributed to other benefits, thus demonstrating that they aren't a waste.

label: Principle
body: People believe that they can be genuinely moved **only** by those things and events that they believe to be actual, yet they have genuine emotional responses to what they know to be fictional.

label: Evaluate / Goal
body:
Usually principles are conditional rules, and so we could latch onto the "only" part and write half of the 'apparent paradox' as a conditional rule:
**If** X is not something → ppl don't believe that X ppl believe to be actual can genuinely move them
But it seems like this principle is intended to stress both halves of the paradox. We think we can only be genuinely emotionally triggered by real stuff, but in reality we have genuine emotional responses to fictional stuff.

label: Background
body: In all earthquakes there is a seismic shock known as a displacement pulse, and high-rise buildings are especially vulnerable to them (according to computer models).

label: Surprise
body: When we examine high-rise buildings in cities damaged by recent powerful earthquakes, there doesn't seem to be much significant damage to the buildings.

label: Evaluate / Goal
body:
Given that.... high rise buildings are especially vulnerable to displacement pulses How come... the high rise buildings in cities damaged by powerful earthquakes aren't showing much damage?
Since we already know a "negative distinction" when it comes to high-rise buildings (they're more likely to get rocked by a displacement pulse), if it turns out they're not getting damaged in earthquakes, then high-rise buildings must have some type of "positive distinction" that is protecting them.

label: Conclusion (conclude that)
body: The company is deliberately avoiding paying up.

label: Evidence
body: Submitted a claim to insurance company months ago. Heard nothing for weeks. Called them. They had never seen the claim. Resubmitted the claim twice. Called repeatedly. Still haven't gotten the settlement.

label: Evaluate
body:
This question stem is highly unusual, so let's understand our task. The correct answer is a principle that is violated by Terry's reasoning.
What does it mean to **violate a principle**?
This is synonymous with the question, "how do you **refute a conditional?** ", since almost all principles are phrased in conditional form.
If a principle said, "Look before you leap", then violating it would mean that you leapt without looking.
Conditionally, "look before you leap" means "leaping requires looking first" leap → look first
Violating a principle / refuting a conditional, means that we're providing an example in which the LEFT side happens but the RIGHT side doesn't.
So if these answers are conditionals, we'll ask ourselves, "is the LEFT side of this true in Terry's argument? If so, is the RIGHT side not the case in Terry's argument"?
If we don't need to get this nitty gritty we won't, but that is the technical sense of violating a principle.

label: Goal
body: We can kind of treat this like a Must Be False or Weaken question, since we want a principle that Terry is going against. It should feel like Terry's reasoning breaks the rule or goes against its advice.

label: Conclusion (So)
body: Human life has the same origin as all other known life.

label: Evidence
body: All life is made of the same basic kinds of matter; it's all carbon based; and it's all equipped with genetic codes.

label: Goal
body:
We know three ways in which human life is similar to all other life, so let's look for any of these as possible answers:
both made same kind of matter → same origin both carbon cased → same origin both equipped w/ genetic codes → same origin

label: Evaluate
body:
The phrase "this shows that" tells us that we're trying to draw a conclusion. This is typically what we're doing on Logical Completion, and we want to use our Inference brain to think about what a safely worded conclusion would sound like.
We also want to use our Inference brain in the sense that the correct answer will feel like it's synthesizing two or more claims. This argument only has two claims. Is there any overlapping information?
Yes, "duty" is talked about in each claim.
All societies have duties. Duties are so important to a properly functioning society that you have to do them even if they're harmful to your self interest.
So we could fuse those together and say something like, "All societies have things that are so important you have to do them even they're harmful to your self interest".

label: Goal
body: It's hard to get a great feel for where this would be headed, but we want to think like we do on Most Supported questions: pick whichever answer feels most provable based on what we read. Beware strong language or out of scope ideas.

label: Conclusion (so)
body: Even if we were to unify the world economy and be forced into adopting a universal language for trade, this language will inevitably develop many regional dialects.

label: Evidence
body: Regional dialects are responses by local populations to their own particular communicative needs.

label: Evaluate
body:
The conclusion has two noteworthy features: 1. it's a conditional (when) 2. there's a new concept (a unified global economy forces the development of a universal language)
Each of these features is suggestive that this will be testing a Missing Link. Generally, when there's a new concept in the conclusion, the correct answer is telling us what the author is assuming about that concept.
Why does the author think this universal language of the global trade economy would inevitably develop many regional dialects?
We have to use the premise, which defines "regional dialects".
The fact that we have an overlapping term that's defined in the evidence also suggests Missing Link.
If I argued... "A blipsy is anything that can do X. Therefore, anyone who can do Y is a real blipsy"
... you would know that I'm assuming that "anyone who can do Y can do X".
The new concept in the conclusion 'anyone who can do Y' gets connected to the definition 'can do X", via the overlapping term "blipsy".
In this argument it said, "A regional dialect is a response by local populations to their own particular communicative needs. Therefore, the universal trade language of the future will have regional dialects".
So we know that it's assuming "the universal trade language of the future will have responses by local populations to their own particular communicative needs".
The new concept in the conclusion "universal trade language of the future" gets connected to the definition "responses by local populations to their own particular communicative needs", via the overlapping term "regional dialects".

label: Goal
body: Let's look for an answer reinforcing the idea that the author assumes that in this future world where we have a global economy and a universal language used in trade, it will cause there to be local populations who have their own particular communicative needs (leading to new regional dialects).

label: Conclusion
body: It's fine to pay for status if that's what you want, but you should know when you're paying for a more expensive product that you're paying for prestige, not more quality.

label: Evidence
body: It's often the case that a product most people believe is the best of its type is actually no better than competing products; it's just that the reputation provides the owner with status.

label: Evaluate
body:
This argument didn't contain any conditional logic or quantifiers, so it's probably not worth trying to turn it into an algebraic recipe.
Instead, we can ask ourselves what general principle is operating under the surface, or what the "moral to the story is".
The author seems to more or less be saying, "sometimes you're just paying extra for reputation/prestige, which is fine as long as you're clear eyed about what you're paying for".

label: Goal
body: I'm a little tentative about how this answer is going to look, but I'm anticipating a comparison between two things, which are basically equally good other than some tangential difference, even though one is more "expensive"? Then the conclusion should probably say, "you should know that if you're going for the harder option, you're doing it purely for this tangential difference".

label: Conclusion
body: Designating land as a wilderness area does not necessarily violate the multiple-use philosophy (i.e. designating land as wilderness could mean that we're utilizing that land in the way that best meets the present and future needs of the public).

label: Evidence (for)
body: Even if we don't get the most money from designating land wilderness, we can still get the greatest overall benefit from that site.

label: Evaluate
body:
The soft language of "does not necessarily violate" in the conclusion means that the author is only claiming that there is at least one case in which designating land as a wilderness area would "best meet the present and future needs of the public".
She is saying that designating the site as wilderness "can provide the greatest overall benefit from that site".
So if we were predicting a Linking assumption, it would sound like: provides greatest best meets present overall benefit → and future needs from site of the public
There is little bit of **Weighing Tradeoffs** happening as well within the evidence. Pro - greatest overall benefit Con - doesn't provide greatest dollar return
So the author is also assuming that "providing greatest overall benefit" is better than "providing greatest dollar return", when it comes to best meeting the present and future needs of the public.

label: Goal
body: Look for something essentially saying that if we're getting the most benefit from the site, then we're best meeting the present / future needs of the public.

label: Statements
body:
mathematical comparisons
In the **troposphere** (lowest level of atmosphere), higher you rise, colder it gets Top of Troposphere = -50° poles to -85° equator
Then **stratosphere** starts (next level of atmosphere), higher you rise, warmer it gets
Stratosphere is warmed by ozone, which generates heat when it absorbs UV.

label: Evaluate
body:
There's a lot to chew on here. We essentially have two different Inference patterns:
1. the mathematical comparison
temp decreasing Bottom ----> Top Troposphere Troposphere
temp increasing Bottom ----> Top Stratosphere Stratosphere
2. the causal relationship
Sun sends ---> ozone ----> heat is out UV rays absorbs generated

label: Goal
body: It's hard to predict where they're going, but it will probably test the mathematical comparison or the causal relationship.

label: Evaluate
body:
Given That... using IPV would probably result in half as many vaccination-caused polio cases as OPV, How Can We Still Argue That... we should **not** make IPV the more common vaccine?
When arguments are comparative in nature, we're usually being shown an Incomplete Comparison, and we need to judge what other similarities or differences two things may have.
Sure, IPV has an advantage when it comes to how many cause of vaccine-caused polio it's likely to lead to. But what are IPV's disadvantages? - does it lead to more naturally occurring cases of polio (I'm assuming that inactivated polio vaccines might not trigger the desired immune response as reliably as live polio vaccines)?
- does it cost way more?
- is it way harder to administer to kids?
Obviously 12 cases of pediatric polio is a big concern, but it's not a huge number. If the IPV has significant downsides, it might be something we choose to live with.

label: Goal
body: Find an answer that says something comparative negative about IPV.

label: Conclusion
body: Governments should help finance high-quality care.

label: Evidence
body: Such day care will be available to families of all income if and only if it's subsidized, and governments should do all that they can to do to improve the well-being of all the children in its society.

label: Evaluate
body:
We have a conclusion about what governments should do and we were provided a principle/rule about what governments should do.
Rule: governments should do all they can to **improve the well-being of the children.**
Conclusion: governments should **help finance high-quality daycare.**
So there's definitely a missing language link: "enabling children to attend high-quality daycare would improve their well being".
We could have potentially objected, "why should the governments subsidize it? Maybe there's some non-governmental way to get everyone high-quality daycare."
But the bi-conditional "if and only if" rules out that. If the government doesn't subsidize, then at least some families will not have high-quality daycare available to them.

label: Goal
body: So it seems like they're just testing the missing gap between "high-quality daycare" and "improve the well-being of children".

label: Conclusion
body: Our highest court is the least fair of any court on the continent and ought not to be emulated.

label: Evidence
body: Our country has the least fair court system of any country on the continent and ought not to be emulated.

label: Evaluate
body:
The evidence and conclusion both deal with the idea of "least fair of any / shouldn't be emulated". They are only different because the evidence is saying this idea is true about the court system, while the conclusion is saying this idea is true about the highest court.
If something is true about the court system, does that mean it's true of the highest court?
Not necessarily. This is a famous flaw called **Part vs. Whole**. Maybe the average turnaround time for a case in the court system is 1 month, but the average turnaround time for a case in the highest court is 3 months. The Whole and its Parts do not necessarily have identical traits. Maybe this country's court system overall is the worst, but their highest court is actually pretty decent. It would be like a basketball team who is one of the worst in the league and ought not to be emulated, but their best player might still be good and worthy of emulation.

label: Goal
body: Look for an answer that also makes this illegal move: "Because The Whole has trait X, Some Part of the whole must have trait X"

label: Conclusion
body: This practice of making and exporting pesticides that are banned for use in the US greatly increases the health risk to US consumers.

label: Evidence (for)
body: These pesticides are often used on agricultural products imported into the US.

label: Evaluate
body:
Given that... the US is sending pesticides out into the world (that it has banned domestic farmers from using) and that... these pesticides are often used on food products that then get imported back into the US,
How could we argue that... sending these pesticides out into the world is **not** greatly increasing the health risk to US consumers?
Maybe we could say the amounts of these pesticides that are on products we import back into the US is negligible.
Maybe we could say that the pesticides weren't banned because of health risks but for some other reason.
Maybe we could say that the vast majority of Americans don't consume enough of these imported products for the pesticide consumption to be significant.

label: Goal
body: We need some way of arguing that this practice of exporting banned pesticides (which come back to us on some of the food we import) is **not** greatly increasing the health risk to US consumers).

label: Conclusion
body: One can attain a state of profound creativity merely by listening to a tape of recorded music.

label: Evidence
body: Profound creativity is accompanied by an increase of theta brain waves. Listening to music dramatically increases theta waves.

label: Evaluate
body: The argument observes that theta waves accompany creativity (creativity → theta waves) and that music produces theta waves (music → theta waves). It then leaps to "music produces creativity." But theta waves coming with creativity does not mean theta waves *cause* creativity. Music could raise theta waves without producing creativity at all.

label: Goal
body: Find an answer that points out theta waves can rise without creativity following — i.e., the argument confuses an accompaniment of creativity with something that produces creativity.

label: Conclusion
body: Listening to recorded music can produce profound creativity.

label: Evidence
body: Theta waves accompany creativity, and music increases theta waves.

label: Goal
body: Find an answer that points out theta waves can rise without creativity following.

label: The Argument
body: Creativity comes with high theta waves. Music makes theta waves spike. Conclusion: music makes you creative.

label: Evaluate
body:
Watch the leap. Theta waves *accompanying* creativity is not the same as theta waves *causing* creativity. Maybe creativity causes the waves, or maybe both come from a third thing. So even if music boosts theta waves, that does not guarantee creativity follows.
Think of it like this: tall people often own bigger shoes. If I make my shoes bigger, that does not make me taller. The two things go together, but making one of them happen does not produce the other.

label: Principle
body:
The instructions should make it easier to for most people to put together the product than it would have been if they didn't have the instructions.
We could turn this into a conditional:
not much easier for people shouldn't write to assemble product with → instructions this these instructions than way w/o these instructions

label: Evaluate / Goal
body:
This is a weird question stem. It almost feels like an Apply the Principle task, except it's asking "where would this principle **not** be applicable".
If we're looking for a situation in which the advice "can't always be followed", then we would want a situation where it's not possible to write instructions that make assembly easier (for most users) than it would be without any instructions.

label: Conclusion (this suggests that)
body: Producing characters more automatically frees up mental resources for other activities.

label: Evidence
body: Among first-graders who got handwriting lessons, those whose composition skills improved most were those who had learned to write letters most automatically.

label: Evaluate
body:
The most common argument pattern on Str / Wkn is Explain Curious Fact, and when we see we're dealing with an Experiment / Study, we're almost always going to hear about some data from the study which creates the causal mystery that our author wants to solve.
CURIOUS FACT How come the kids whose composition skills had improved the most were the same as the kids who had learned to write letters most automatically? (you'd never guess this, but the LSAT author is about to assume that this correlation proves causation)
EXPLANATION We gave them handwriting lessons; they learned to write letters automatically. Once their handwriting became automatic muscle memory, that freed up mental resources for them to focus on what they were writing about / how they were communicating their ideas. So their composition skills improved. Notice how much I fleshed out the causal story being implied by the conclusion. Causal conclusions often suggest a longer story than they explicitly say, so we need to take a few secs to play out the author's causal chain in our brain.

label: Goal
body:
For Explain Curious Fact arguments, Strengthen questions usually **increase the plausibility** of the Author's Explanation, but sometimes they **rule out** an Alternate Explanation. So we want more evidence that becoming more automatic with your writing frees up cognitive bandwidth for you to focus on the quality of your composition.
Or we want to rule out some alternate explanation for why the kids with the biggest uptick in automaticity also had the biggest uptick in composition skills (f.e. the kids with the most automatic handwriting were **not** more likely to have English tutors they worked with outside of school).

label: Conclusion
body: Automatic handwriting frees mental resources for other activities (like composition).

label: Evidence
body: The students whose composition improved most also learned to write letters most automatically.

label: Goal
body: Strengthen by tightening the link — show that gains in automatic handwriting track with gains in composition.

label: The Argument
body: Researchers found that the kids whose composition improved the most were the ones whose handwriting became most automatic. From this they conclude: automatic handwriting frees up mental resources for other things (like composing).

label: Evaluate
body: The story is plausible but not airtight. The argument depends on a causal chain: more automatic handwriting → freed-up mental capacity → better composition. To strengthen this, we want evidence that the two improvements move together — that students who got more automatic at writing letters also got more improved at composition.

label: Goal
body: Look for an answer that tightens the relationship between gains in automatic handwriting and gains in composition skill.

label: Conclusion
body: Being near woodlands (i.e. near bees) promotes the health of crops that depend on pollination.

label: Evidence
body: Bees visit flowers far from woodlands less often than they visit flowers close to woodlands.

label: Evaluate
body:
Without any keywords to guide us, it's a little tricky to figure out which claim is the Conclusion. They both sound more like facts than opinions, but we can ask ourselves which idea is Supported?
Why should we believe that ... being near woodlands (i.e. being near bees) promotes the health of crops that depend on pollination? Because ... bees are the #1 pollinator and they visit crops closer to woodlands more than they visit crops far from woodlands.
If we flipped that, it wouldn't make as much sense.
Why should we believe that ... bees visit flowers far from woodlands less than flowers close to woodlands? Because ... bees live in the woodlands. (it wouldn't make any sense to say, "because, [1st sentence].")
Once we have the argument pieces sorted out, we can think that this argument is making a **Missing Link** assumption, "If visited more often by bees, then promotes health of crops".
Or we could consider possible **objections** (so that we could think about answers going the opposite way). How could we argue that even though bees would visit it more, putting a crop near the woodlands wouldn't promote the crop's health?
Maybe other conditions near the woodlands are worse for the crop -- more pests, less sunshine, less water.

label: Goal
body: Look for an answer connecting "visited more" to "promotes health", or look for an answer ruling out an objection (or even going in the opposite direction) ... there is at least as much sun / water near the woodlands; there are same or fewer pests near the woodlands.

label: Conclusion
body: If you're in favor of developing good character in children, then you should vote against allowing the first race track to be built here.

label: Evidence
body: Gambling is wrong, and children raised in an atmosphere where the goal is to get something for nothing will not develop good character.

label: Evidence
body: Abstract paintings are nonrepresentational, but a painting must represent social injustice in a clearly comprehensible way in order to spur the viewer into political action.

label: Evaluate
body:
Maybe there just aren't that many big-budget movies. Even if each one profits $20 million, if there are only 20 of those but 2000 low-budget movies, you could still see most of the industry's total revenue come from smaller-budget films.
Maybe the profit margin on low-budget films is four or five times the cost to make and promote them.

label: Goal
body: Find the answer that mirrors that exact branching dichotomy.

label: Evaluate
body:
The fight with a conditional conclusion (If X, then Y), we have to argue that it's possible that X is true but Y is not. So in this case that means arguing that it's possible that we favor developing good character in children but still want to vote for this racetrack to be built here.
The author is going to say: but children raised in an atmosphere where the goal is to get something for nothing will not develop good character.
We'd have to argue that building a racetrack in our area will not suddenly turn it into "an atmosphere where the goal is to get something for nothing".
We could say that even though there will be gambling, the kids won't see it. Or even if they see it, we'll talk to them about why we don't think it's a high character move to gamble. Or the kids will see all the hard work of the people who build the racetrack and work at the racetrack: those people certainly aren't trying to get something for nothing; they're doing hard work.

label: Goal
body: In the simplest sense, we should try to defend the idea of building the racetrack, while addressing L.E.'s concerns about how it would potentially corrupt our children.

label: Commentator's Conclusion (thus)
body: We should set a max allowable level for each carcinogenic food additive, a nonzero amount that's somewhat below the threshold where it becomes problematic.

label: Commentator's Intermediate Conclusion
body: An absolute prohibition on these additives is excessive.

label: Commentator's Evidence
body: A test can detect a single molecule, but you can eat way more than that and it still doesn't increase your risk of getting cancer.

label: Evaluate
body:
We're being asked to represent the Legislator, whose main vibe is, "We should **prohibit** these additives."
When we logically counter an argument, we address their ideas (we don't just independently offer new reasons for our idea). So we want to think about how someone who wants to ban these additives altogether would respond to the commentator's argument / suggestion.
She's worried that we'll be overly aggressive in policing these bans, flagging foods that have even a single molecule in them. We could maybe say, "It's very easy to avoid having a single molecule in your food. Just don't use the prohibited additive!" She's saying humans can safely tolerate much higher levels. We could maybe say, "Sure, in one sitting, a small amount wouldn't hurt you. But maybe over time the cumulative effect of eating those molecules would hit something harmful."

label: Goal
body: Let's look for an answer that helps us go, "What you say is true, but we still should reject your plan and just ban these carcinogenic additives entirely."

label: Conclusion (ample evidence that)
body: The model of car one drives greatly affects the chances that one's car will be stolen.

label: Evidence
body: The model of car stolen most often in our country last year, for example, was also the model stolen most often in the preceding year.

label: Evaluation
body:
Since the author's evidence is a statistic and her conclusion is assuming a causal explanation for that statistic ("affects" = causal), we can use our Explain Curious Fact framework.
Curious Fact ... why is the car that was stolen the most two years ago the same model as the car that was stolen the most last year?
Author's Explanation ... it must be that this model is super desirable. Thieves apparently really want this model and seek it out. So when people choose to drive this model of car they're making it more likely that their car will be stolen.
We want always consider 2 things: - could there be some Alternate Explanation for the curious fact? - how plausible is the Author's Explanation?
However, on Flaw questions, more than 90% of the time the correct answer cares about the author's failure to consider Alternate Explanations (we call this the **Causal** flaw, and it's one of the 10 famous flaws).
So what could be a different way to explain why the same model of car has won the title of "stolen most often" two years in a row? Is it really that thieves desire that specific model?
Maybe it's just that this model happens to be really easy to break into; maybe it's an economy model and the people who can only afford to buy this modest car cannot afford to invest in other anti-theft devices. Thus it's not the model of car affecting their chance of the car being stolen, it's the fact that the people who buy this model don't put any anti-theft devices onto the car.
Or maybe it's just the most common car, period. In America, there was a long stretch of years where the Honda Civic was the #1 most frequently bought car. All other things being equal, that would lead to the Honda Civic being the model of car most often stolen. It's not because thieves are seeking out that model. It's because they find Civics everywhere they look.

label: Goal
body: Look for an answer saying that the author is overconfidently assuming one potential explanation for the Curious Fact, failing to consider alternative explanations for why the same model of car has been "most stolen" two years running.

label: Laird's claim 1
body:
Pure research provides us with new technologies that contribute to saving lives. Does Kim disagree?
No, she never denies that pure research sometimes provides us with life-saving technology.

label: Laird's claim 2
body:
The role pure research plays in expanding our knowledge and providing new ideas is more worthwhile than the role it plays in providing us with new live-saving technologies. Does Kim disagree?
Yes. She does **not** think that Laird is currently ranking priorities. She thinks that live-saving technology is more worthwhile than expanding our knowledge and providing new ideas.

label: Evaluate / Goal
body:
"Even more worthwhile than X is Y" vs. "Your priorities are mistaken. X is what counts most of all" is our disagreement.
Since the question stem cues up the first couple words of the sentence, we need to express the disagreement beginning with "pure research".
whether **pure research**.. is more valuable / useful / worthwhile when it is saving lives or when it is giving us new knowledge and ideas

label: Statements
body:
Conditional (to be X, must Y)
Dependable take into account all accounting → of our nation's assets framework
Fact
The current framework assigns no value to government-owned natural resources, which are clearly assets.

label: Evaluate / Goal
body:
Since our task is to pick a principle that blames the 1st but not the 2nd magazine, we should focus on the difference between the two.
The 1st one tried to catch offensive ads and filter them out. The 2nd one had a policy to just publish everything.
So let's look for something like, "If you tried to eliminate offensive stuff but let something offensive slip through the cracks, then you're morally delinquent."
That would apply to the 1st magazine but not to the 2nd one.

label: Given that
body: Big-budget movies often gross two or three times the cost of making and promoting them.

label: Evaluate
body:
Whenever we see a conditional rule presented on an Inference question, we know to look for two things: 1. does this rule get chained up with any other conditional rules?
2. is there a fact we can apply this rule to (usually via contrapositive)
Also, when we see that the final idea in the paragraph is set up with a Pivot ( **but**, yet, however), it usually means that the correct answer tries to integrate that final idea with what came before it.
There's only one conditional here, so we don't have to worry about chains. If we did the contrapositive of that rule, we would get:
framework doesn't take not dependable into account all of a → accounting nation's assets framework
Does the "current accounting framework" take into account **all** of this nation's assets?
No, it assigns no value to government-owned natural resources, which is one of this nation's assets.

label: Goal
body: By applying the contrapositive of the rule to what we're told about the current framework, we can derive that the current framework is not "dependable". Let's look for an answer like that.

label: Attribution (critics argued)
body: Freudianism is incompatible with rationalistic Western thought, because it holds that people's unconscious desires can defeat their rational life plans.

label: Author's Pivot (But)
body: Freudianism also says that you can become conscious of these unconscious desires and avoid being defeated by them.

label: Evaluate
body:
Since the blank is prefaced by **Therefore**, we know that we're trying to pick whichever answer feels like the Most Supported conclusion.
if we read this paragraph as a regular Most Supported stimulus (where we read mostly for Causal, Conditional, or Pivot wording), the **But** introducing the final claim would get our attention.
Most of the time that an Inference paragraph Ends with a Pivot, it means that the correct answer will be the takeaway you get from combining this final claim with what came before it.
When we see an Attribution followed by a Pivot, then the takeaway is usually, "The original attribution was wrong" (a rebuttal).
The critics' conclusion was that Freudianism is not compatible with Western rationalism, based on the premise that Freudianism talks about unconscious desires defeating our rational plan. The author is saying, 'Yeah, but you can learn to **avoid** being defeated by those unconscious desires."
This suggests that rationality **can** still win. You can still follow your rational life plan, so long as you learn to be conscious of these unconscious desires.

label: Goal
body: Thus, we'd logically arrive at a Rebuttal conclusion: these critics are wrong to think that Freudianism can't co-exist with Rationalism. Freudianism **is** compatible with the rationalistic spirit of Western thought.

label: Recommendation
body: Everyone should put adequate sunblock on skin exposed to strong sunlight.

label: Evidence
body:
Overexposure to certain wavelengths of strong sun is the main cause of melanoma (bad skin cancer).
Adequate sunblock = any preparation that prevents sunburn over a prolonged period of exposure.

label: Evaluate
body:
This argument seems to have a big missing link as it tries to connect "adequate sunblock" to the concern about skin cancer:
adequate → prevents — **?** **→** prevents sunblock sunburn overexposure to melanoma wavelengths?

label: Goal
body: Look for something suggesting that adequate sunblock may prevent sunburn, but won't help protect against melanoma, or look for something bringing up a potential bad thing about putting adequate sunblock on exposed skin (maybe it has some chemical in it that's bad for us).

label: Given that
body: Parents rated the violence of each TV show their kids watched on a 1 - 5 scale.

label: and that ..
body: The number of times kids were disciplined in school was also recorded.

label: How can we explain that ..
body: Kids who watched programs ranked 3-5 were 50% more likely to have been disciplined than other children.

label: Evaluate / Goal
body:
We need ways to explain why there's a correlation between more violent shows and being disciplined in school (the causality could flow in either direction, or they could both be symptoms of a third factor).
Those explanations assume that shows ranked 3-5 really were more violent. But it's possible that they weren't; it's just that the parents were more sensitive to violence and ranked them higher. So we could also explain these facts by some relationship between "parents who are more likely to rank a show as violent" and "kids getting disciplined in school."

label: Conclusion (reveals that)
body: Reporters allowed the personal biases reflected in this voting pattern (89% of reporters voted for the incumbent) to affect their news coverage.

label: Evidence
body: 54% of coverage of the challenger was negative, whereas only 30% of the incumbent was negative.

label: Evaluate
body:
Since this author is interpreting the causal meaning behind a statistical change / disparity, we can use our Explain Curious Fact mindset.
Curious Fact ... How come 54% of the coverage of the challenger was negative whereas only 30% of the incumbent was negative?
Author's Explanation ... it must be that the reporters favored the incumbent (after all, 89% of them voted for the incumbent) and so their bias caused them to skew more negative coverage towards the challenger.
Whenever we use this framework, we consider the same two questions: 1. can we think of Alternate Explanations for the Curious Fact? 2. how **plausible** is the Author's Explanation?
On Flaw questions, though, 90% of the correct answers are about #1, the failure to consider alternate explanations.
So what else could be an explanation for why 54% of the coverage of the challenger was negative whereas only 30% of the incumbent was negative.
Maybe the challenger was embroiled in a big scandal during the campaign, and so coverage of that scandal felt inherently negative. Meanwhile the incumbent wasn't in a scandal, so their 30% negative coverage was the "normal" amount.
Maybe in general challengers get more negative coverage than incumbents. Maybe when you're first running for office, they dig up everything bad about you and so you have a lot of negative coverage. But if you are elected and then you run again as an incumbent, they're not going to bother re-running all the negative stories they ran on you when you first got elected.

label: Goal
body: Look for an answer pointing out that the author is overconfidently arriving at one possible way to explain the 54% / 30% disparity, when other possible explanations exist.

label: Conclusion (Therefore)
body: Abstract painting can never be a politically significant art form.

label: How is it that
body: Most of movie industry's total revenue comes from low-budget movies?

label: Evaluate
body:
Because there are repeating ideas here (abstract paintings / represent vs. non represent / political action vs. politically significant), we could potentially approach this with a Conditional Logic mindset.
If we wanted to represent the Conclusion’s logic path with a long conditional, it would look like this:
Abstract -------------------> not politically Paintings significant art
We would then scan the evidence to see whether we were told any facts about Abstract Paintings, and whether we were provided with a rule that proves “not politically significant art”.
We were given the fact that Abstract Paintings are “nonrepresentational / only measured by color, texture, and form”. We were told that “if something isn’t clearly representing social injustice, it doesn’t spur into political action.
Abstract → non (→) can’t → can’t spur Paintings represent represent into social injustice political action
We are basically adding our own common sense link that “If something is nonrepresentational, then it can’t represent instances of social injustice in a clearly comprehensible way”.
That seems pretty definitional, so we don’t need to worry about adding that move. If something is non-representational, then it represents nothing, including social injustice.
Our chain is getting us from abstract paintings to something political, but the evidence only gets us to “won’t spur political action”, not to the conclusion's, “can never be a politically significant art form”.
Do you have to spur someone into political action to be considered a politically significant art form?

label: Goal
body: It looks like the missing link here is “if you’re not spurring people into political action, then you’re not a politically significant art form” (or its contrapositive — all politically significant art forms spur people into political action)

label: Conclusion (should = opinion)
body: If a North American is going to Europe for the first time, they should plan to spend significant time in Italy.

label: Evidence
body:
To develop an appreciation of a continent that goes beyond merely accumulating impressions, you should get thorough knowledge of at least one country.
And Italy seems to be easier to get to know than other European countries.

label: Evaluate
body:
We need to move this into a more abstract realm, so let's try to remove all the specific nouns.
C: If you're going to do X for the first time, spend a good chunk of time on Y.
P1: Rather than just skimming the surface of several things, you should get deep knowledge of at least one thing.
P2: Y is very conducive to getting deep knowledge.

label: Goal
body: Let's find the answer we can best match up with that implicit principle.

label: Conclusion
body: There is no reason for anyone to make dietary changes for the sake of preventing heart disease.

label: Evidence
body: Dietary changes that affect cholesterol levels have no effect on lipoprotein(a) levels (and lipoprotein-a seems to sometimes be a cause of heart disease).

label: Evaluate
body:
This is a weird argument, to say the least. The first sentence doesn't seem involved in the author's reasoning at all. She makes an **incredibly over-strong** conclusion by saying NO reason for ANYONE to make dietary changes for the sake of heart disease.
That should strike us terrible advice. Could I cut down on my alcohol intake and possible lower my risk of heart disease? What about all the fat I'm eating clogging my arteries?
She singles out one possible way you might lower your heart disease risk (lowering your lipoprotein-a levels), tells us that dietary changes have no affect on that, and then concludes that dietary changes are useless for the sake of preventing heart disease.

label: Goal
body:
It seems like this author is thinking that lipoprotein(a) is the only way that dietary changes could have helped lower your risk of heart disease.
But what if there are other dietary changes you could make that would lower your heart disease risk some other way?

label: Conclusion
body: It's absurd to say that people are morally obligated to act in way X, because acting in way not-X would be unnatural.

label: Evidence
body:
An unnatural action is either a violation of the laws of nature, or a statistical anomaly.
You can't act in a way that violates the laws of nature, and the fact that something isn't usually done isn't a good reason not to do it.

label: Evaluate
body:
There aren't any keywords indicating the conclusion, so we need to mainly identify it from the fact that the first sentence has the opinion of a Rebuttal. Since our author is saying, "people claiming X are being absurd", she will need to defend that position, and the rest of the paragraph tries to defend that position.
Since this argument is pretty hard to understand, it might help to come up with an example of something where "acting that way would be unnatural".
Maybe we could say "giving your Dad flowers on Mother's Day would be unnatural". According to this position the philosopher is fighting, we are morally obligated to avoid giving our Dad flowers on Mother's Day because doing so would be unnatural.
That does sound absurd!
The philosopher digs in to this concept of "unnatural". She's like, which sense of "unnatural" do we mean:
1. unnatural, like transcending natural law? outside the realm of physics? or 2. unnatural, like 'weird, not customary'?
Her final sentence is exploring both of those options and saying, if we mean #1, then the original position is saying, "you're morally obligated to follow the physical laws of the universe". The author is like, "That's absurd. We don't need to be morally warned against doing something impossible."
if we mean #2, then the original position is saying, "you're morally obligated to only do normal, customary things. Don't be weird or different." And the author is like, "That's absurd, the fact that something is weird or uncustomary doesn't provide a good reason to avoid doing it."

label: Goal
body:
How would we describe the argument in general terms?
The author sort of creates an either / or (does "unnatural" mean impossible or unusual) and then follows both roads to say, "either way you slice it, this original claim is absurd".
We might seen language like the author considers two options and **rules them out**. Or we might see something like, "the author considers different implications of a claim to show that they all lead to absurdity".

label: Conclusion (clearly)
body: Fitness consultants who smoke can't help their clients become healthier.

label: Evidence
body: If they don't care about their health, they can't care about their clients' health. If they don't care about their client's health, they can't help their clients become healthier.

label: Goal
body: We basically want an answer to point out something that makes big-budget movies not that lucrative for the movie industry overall, or something that makes low-budget movies good money makers.

label: Evaluate
body:
On Sufficient Assumption, it's very useful to ask ourselves whether there are any "New Ideas" in the Conclusion (something never mentioned in the Evidence).
"Can't help clients become healthier" is definitely in the evidence (it ends the paragraph).
But we aren't given any facts about "fitness consultants who smoke cigarettes". So "smoke cigarettes" is destined to be in the correct answer. We won't be able to prove the conclusion until we have info about people who smoke.
On Sufficient Assumption, it's also very useful (in most cases) to think of the conclusion as a logic path from the Naming part of the sentence to the Telling part.
Fitness can't consult --------------------------------> help who clients' smokes healthier
This allows us to visualize what parts of that logic path the Evidence has supplied, so we can go shopping in the answers for the missing part of the path. The evidence gave us a conditional chain (if A then B, and if B, then C).
don't don't can't care -----> care -----> help own clients' clients' health health healthier
So the missing part of the logic path is the first link, from the Naming part of the conclusion to the start of this conditional chain that takes us all the way to the Telling part.
Fitness don't consult ------> care who own smokes health

label: Goal
body:
Naturally, if we're averse to all things conditional, then we just need to hear that switchover from sentence 1 to sentence 2. When sentence 2 starts off like, "After all, if they don't care about their health ... "
We need to be like, "Whoa, whoa, whoa! Who said they don't care about their health?"
The author is assuming
smokes → don't care about own health
Sufficient Assumption loves to test the contrapositive of our prediction, which would be
do care about ⇢ don't smoke own health

label: Conclusion
body: The popular ghost TV shows are not going to encourage superstition and thereby impede the public's scientific understanding.

label: Evidence
body: Throughout history there have been ghost stories, and yet scientific understanding has steadily progressed.

label: Evaluate
body:
Part of our analysis of this argument should be it's Past = Present **Comparison** form. Are those really fair to compare? Are ghost stories told my dramatists throughout recorded history really fair to compare with ghost TV shows that have spooky sound effects and special computer generated ghosts?
Even though past ghost stories allowed scientific understanding to steadily advance, maybe present ghost TV shows are meaningfully different in a way where they will actually impede the public's scientific understanding.
If we wanted to try arguing the Anti-Conclusion, then we would probably be thinking: "given that ghost stories have always happened, and the scientific understanding of the populace has steadily advanced, **how could we argue that** these ghost tv shows **are** impeding the public's scientific understanding?"
Maybe we could say that, "Yes, our understanding has steadily advanced, but it would have advanced even faster without ghost stories".
For example, can you prove that the bathroom tile spray i use on my moldy tiles does nothing, simply by saying "the mold has steadily advanced"?
No, because I could say, "Look at that area of the shower where I don't spray -- the mold has advanced much faster there. So, yes, the mold is steadily advancing in the areas where I spray my bathroom cleaner, but it's advancing more slowly, so the cleaning spray is still doing something to impede / inhibit the mold's growth."

label: Goal
body: Look for an answer dealing with the Past ≠ Present objection, or one dealing with the "steadily advancing ≠ having no effect" objection.

label: Conclusion
body: The new mandatory sentencing law caused the drop in the crime rate.

label: Evidence
body: The new law was enacted at the beginning of the year. No other major policy changes were made last year. Last year's crime rate was 15% lower than the previous year's.

label: Evaluate
body:
Since the author is looking at a statistical change (-15% on crime rate) and then concluding what caused it, we can use our Curious Fact / Explanation mindset.
Curious Fact... why did the crime rate go down by 15%? Author's Explanation... the new mandatory sentencing law caused there to be less crime (presumably because mandatory jail time was enough of a deterrent that it scared off 15% of violent criminals from committing a crime)
We always ask the same two questions of these: - could there be some **other way** to explain the curious fact? - how **plausible** is the Author's Way?
Could the 15% drop be from a population decline? From a boosting economy? From a pandemic?
Is it plausible that some potential violent criminals knew about the enactment of the mandatory sentencing law and considered it enough of a deterrent that they refrained from committing a violent crime?

label: Goal
body: Since this is Weaken, our #1 prediction is that we'll see an answer suggest an Alternate Explanation for why the crime rate went down 15% last year, but we'll keep our minds open for an answer that undermines the plausibility that would-be criminals were deterred by this new sentencing law.

label: Conclusion (Thus)
body: The new division must have been among the most effective, efficient, and creative divisions the corporation had ever created.

label: Evidence
body: The applicants selected to staff it were among the most effective, efficient, and creative workers that the corporation had ever hired.

label: Evaluate
body:
Just because the people in this division were among the most effective, efficient, and creative workers doesn't mean this new division will be among the most effective, efficient, and creative divisions.
After all, maybe these people don't work well together, which drags down their effectiveness and efficiency.
Unfortunately, this kind of specific objection isn't super useful on Parallel Flaw, since we need a more abstract sense of the problem, so that we can match up the same abstract essence to the correct answer. One helpful thing is to know that Parallel Flaw loves to test us on the five most famous flaws: Necessary vs. Sufficient, Part vs. Whole, Causal, Unproven vs. Untrue, and Ad Hominem.
This argument is an example of Part vs. Whole: Since every ingredient in a group has quality X, the group itself must have quality X.

label: Goal
body: Let's look for another Part to Whole flaw. The premise should be saying that all the parts of something collective have a certain trait. And then the conclusion should be saying that the collective itself must have that trait.

label: Background Facts
body:
First magazine: tried to screen all classified advertisements and if they found any offensive, they would reject it for publication.
Second magazine: publish any advertisement received from subscribers.
Both magazines published an ad that was highly offensive to some people.

label: Conclusion
body: First magazine was morally delinquent. Second magazine was not.

label: Conclusion
body:
Even successful predictions of human behavior do not provide an understanding of it.
Rephrase: Successful predictions of human behavior do not constitute an understanding of that behavior.

label: Evidence (for)
body: Understanding a human action requires knowing its goal. Such knowledge of goals either cannot or need not be obtained in the case of nonhuman behavior.

label: Evaluate
body: Like most Main Conclusion questions, there is a Pivot (but/yet/however) that signals the beginning of the author's argument. We know that we're getting "However, conclusion. After all, evidence" rather than "However, evidence. Therefore, conclusion" because the claim after the "However" is prefaced by a support indicator "for", which is part of FABS (for, after all, because, since). The concluding claim sounds like the author's opinion and is directly supported by the subsequent evidence about understanding human actions requiring knowledge of goals. This matches the typical pattern where the main conclusion is a rebuttal introduced by a pivot word.

label: Goal
body: Find the best available meaning match for "successful predictions of human behavior do not constitute an understanding of that behavior".

label: Curious Fact (Evidence)
body: How come the sickles found at site 1 had scratched blades, while the sickles at site 2 had unscratched blades?

label: Premise (Since)
body: If you use a sickle to harvest grain, it gets scratched.

label: Explanation (Conclusion)
body: So the the sickles at site 1 were used to harvest grain, but the sickles at site 2 weren't.

label: Evaluate
body:
We can't fight the second half of this two-pronged conclusion. The author is correct to conclude that the sickles at the 2nd site weren't used to harvest grain.
After all, we were told that if a sickle was used to harvest grain, it always gets scratched, and the sickles at site 2 weren't scratched.
But we can fight the first half of the conclusion: we don't have to believe that the sickles at Site 1 were used to harvest grain.
We can say they got scratched some other way.

label: Goal
body:
On all Explain Curious Fact arguments, the correct answer deals with 1. an Alternate Explanation for the curious fact or 2. the Plausibility of the Author's Explanation
Let's look for an **Alternate Reason** for why the sickles at site 1 were scratched, or let's look for an answer that lowers the **Plausibility** of the idea that sickles were being used to harvest grain at site 1.

label: Given that
body: If cold fusion worked, it would provide almost limitless power from very inexpensive raw materials, materials far cheaper than coal or oil.

label: How can it be that
body: Replacing all traditional electric generators that use coal/oil with cold-fusion power plants would result in a reduction of no more than 25% in the average residential electric bill.

label: Evaluate
body:
If cold fusion provides almost limitless power from very inexpensive raw materials, then how come using all cold fusion generators would only reduce electric bills by 25?
Is there some other part of cold fusion electricity delivery that adds a big expense? (Maybe buying a suitable site for the power plant is way more expensive / maybe transporting the energy is more expensive)
Is there some other part of the electric bill that isn't "cost of electricity"? (maybe most of it is fees and taxes that don't change, even when the electricity gets cheaper).

label: Goal
body: Get rid of the four answers that give us a way to explain why the electric bill would still be close to as expensive as ever (even though the cold fusion plants would provide almost limitless power from cheap raw materials).

label: Statements
body:
In the 1800's, people would make children who misbehaved sit alone outside.
Passersby would be thinking, "Look at that kid who misbehaved."
Nowadays, many child psychologists would say that this was a dumb punishment, since it hurts the kid's self-esteem, which makes them less confident as adults.
pivot (however)
Adults who were raised with the "sit outside" tradition grew up just as confident as adults who weren't raised with that tradition.

label: Evaluate
body:
This is a pretty loose paragraph of historical facts and opinions. It doesn't suggest any conditional logic / mathematical thinking.
But we do have a **Pivot** word before the final sentence. Usually, when an Inference question prefaces that final claim with a pivot word, the correct answer represents a safely worded way of Reconciling the Pivot idea with what came before it.
What came directly before the pivot was, "Many psychologists think that making kids sit outside when they misbehave messes up their self-esteem, which makes them less confident as adults". But, after the pivot, it seems like we're hearing that this idea is wrong!
After all, whether you were forced to sit outside or not, you grew up to have the same level of confidence as adults.
Does that mean the psychologists were wrong to think that "sit outside" doesn't really damage self-esteem, or wrong to think that damage to self-esteem makes kids less confident as adults? Or were they right about all that, and the kids who weren't told to sit outside grow up to be just as confident because their upbringing had some other tradition that chipped away at their self-esteem and confidence?

label: Goal
body: It's really too hard to know how reconcile the pivot idea with what came before it, so we just want to look for the most supportable answer we can find.

label: Conclusion
body: Grammar books are useless as reference sources for authors

label: Evidence
body: thinks ungrammatical → write → consult sure grammatical → consult

label: Evaluation
body:
"Useless" is so strong. All we need to push back is to argue that "at least sometimes a reference source would have some value to an author".
However, these two conditionals try to convince us it will always be useless. In both cases, the author won't consult the grammar book. Is there a way to argue that a grammar book is useful, even though you won't consult it? Maybe it's a paperweight or a weapon? Oh, wait. We have to be arguing that it's useful as a reference source.

label: Evaluate
body:
This is "affirming the consequent" — a classic logic mistake. The premise gives one cause of underperformance (never being pushed). The argument then sees underperformance and assumes that one cause must be at work. But underperformance can come from many sources: laziness, illness, lack of resources. Just because everyone never-pushed underperforms does not mean every underperformer was never pushed.
It is like saying: "Everyone who has the flu has a cough. Bob has a cough. So Bob has the flu." Bob could have a cold or allergies. Coughing does not narrow it down.

label: Goal
body:
If we weren't able to crack the riddle, then we would just go to the answers now thinking, "I need some answer to think of a scenario in which these books would be useful to an author as a reference source.
If we're hip to the feel of **False Choice**, then we might see what's happening. Sometimes authors lay out two cases, which are supposed to be exhaustive, but fail to consider some middle ground. (i.e. "If most people want it, we won't have enough. If too few people want it, we'll lose money. Thus, we're screwed" would leave out the in-between possibility of "what if the # of people who want it is less than most but more than too few?")

label: Conclusion
body: Britain's strict quarantine of imported domesticated animals cannot succeed in indefinitely preventing widespread outbreaks of rabies.

label: Intermediate Conclusion
body: This policy cannot control rabies spread by wild bats.

label: Evidence (since)
body: Bats fly into Britain from continental Europe. Wild bats cannot be quarantined.

label: Evaluate
body:
In the vernacular of Method questions, we usually think about whether the argument ever did one of these things: - analogy - bad implications - (counter)example to general - calls out dubious assumption - raises overlooked consideration - makes a definition / distinction - suggests alternate explanation - rules out other options
This felt like the author was rebutting a plan by raising an overlooked consideration. The plan might solve part of the problem (rabies from domesticated animals) but not other parts of the problem (rabies from wild bats who fly in).

label: Goal
body: Let's find an answer whose language descriptively matches the argument.

label: Conclusion (So)
body: The joker is apparently someone besides Miller.

label: Evidence
body:
The only clue we have to far as to the identify of the practical joker is the handwriting on the note.
I was assuming it was Miller, who hates me, but the handwriting on the note isn't hers.

label: Evaluate
body:
This author is trying to **Solve a Causal Mystery**. If we're doing Flaw and we see any sort of Explain a Curious Fact argument, we want to be on the lookout for bad **Causal** reasoning.
Bad causal reasoning is essentially just being too sure about one possible explanation for a curious fact, when other possible explanations potentially exist.
Here, the Curious Fact would be, "Who's the practical joker?", and the author's Explanation is "someone besides Miller", since the handwriting doesn't match hers.
But alternate explanations abound -- it could have still been Miller if she disguised her handwriting or asked someone else to supply the handwriting, so that her friend Franklin didn't get wise.

label: Goal
body: Look for some answer saying the author was too quick to disqualify Miller's involvement based on the mismatching handwriting, when there are possible ways to reconcile Miller being the joker with the handwriting on the note not matching hers.

label: Conclusion (as a result)
body: Companies rarely hire people who have doctorates in liberal arts.

label: Evidence
body:
Companies rarely hire people who are not concerned with the financial gain you can achieve by hard work in business.
People with doctorates in the liberal arts are interested in improving their intellects.

label: Evaluate
body:
On Sufficient Assumption, we have to mathematically prove the words/ideas in the conclusion, so we always start by asking ourselves, "is there a New Idea in the conclusion?"
In this conclusion, there was nothing new, because both "companies rarely hire" and "people with doctorates in liberal arts" were both defined in the evidence.
That means that we're missing an internal link in the evidence.
Sentences have naming parts and telling parts:
NAMING PART TELLING PART Joe is a real jerk. The color of money resembles that of peas. People who like flan talk about flan constantly. People with doctorates are rarely hired in liberal arts by companies
We can think about the conclusion as a big conveyor belt of logic we're trying to build, to get from the naming part to the telling part.
We scan the evidence to see what ideas we have. People with interested in doctorates in → improve liberal arts intellects People not want rarely financial gain of → hired by hard business work companies
We're just missing an internal link
Interested in People not want improve → financial gain intellects of hard biz work
to build our conclusion's logic conveyor belt:
People with rarely doctorates in ---------------> hired by liberal Arts companies

label: Goal
body:
So we're looking for that missing internal link:
"if you're interested in improving their intellects, then you're not concerned with financial gain from hard work in business"
No matter what, we know that in order to prove "Companies rarely hire Dr. Libs", we need to know that "Dr. Libs are not concerned with the financial gain that can be obtained by hard work in business".

label: Original Argument
body:
Premise: People who have never been pushed beyond their comfort zone never do all they can. (Never pushed → never doing all they can.)
Premise: Alex has not done all he is capable of doing.
Conclusion: Alex has never been pushed beyond his comfort zone.

label: Evaluate
body: The flaw is affirming the consequent / mistaking necessary for sufficient. The first premise gives: never pushed → not doing all you can. The argument observes that Alex is not doing all he can and concludes he was never pushed. But "not doing all you can" can have causes other than "never pushed" — laziness, illness, bad luck. The condition (never pushed) is sufficient for "not doing all you can," but the argument treats it as if it were necessary.

label: Goal
body: Find an answer with the same flaw: a conditional ("X → Y"), then observation that Y holds, then conclusion that X holds — affirming the consequent.

label: Argument Form
body: Never pushed → not doing all you can. Alex is not doing all he can. Therefore Alex was never pushed.

label: Goal
body: Find an answer that takes a conditional, observes the consequent (Y) holds, and concludes the antecedent (X) holds — the same affirming-the-consequent flaw.

label: The Original
body: The argument says: "People never pushed always fail to do all they can. Alex is failing to do all he can, so Alex must never have been pushed."

label: Goal
body: Find the answer with this exact form: a conditional, an observation that the conclusion side of the conditional holds, then a conclusion that the original cause holds.

label: Conclusion
body: Benton is the best bait for anyone who is fishing for trout

label: Evidence
body: In a study, 12 top anglers tried out the five top selling baits, and Benton gave them most success fishing for speckled trout in a northern stream.

label: Evaluation
body:
The conclusion speaks for a wide range of people, "anyone who is fishing for trout". Will Benton always be the best? We have to think of ways in which Benton could be #1 in this study but not be #1 for someone else who is fishing for trout?
This is essentially a **Sampling** flaw, because we're assuming that the experience top anglers had in using Benton bait to fish for speckled trout in a northern stream would generalize to anyone doing trout fishing.

label: Goal
body: Look for ways in which the results of this experiment wouldn't carry over. - maybe it works for top anglers but not amateurs - maybe it works for speckled trout but not other kinds - maybe it works in northern streams but not other streams - maybe there's a bait beyond the top 5 sellers that would work better for someone

label: Conclusion (Thus)
body: People who bemoan the seemingly anticapitalistic measures certain governments are currently taking are being hasty.

label: Evidence
body: History shows that repressive measures against certain capitalistic developments are required during the transition from a totalitarian regime to a democracy.

label: Evaluate
body:
This is a lot to process. The conclusion is a Rebuttal, so we might want to first hear the position with whom the author is fighting:
People: Oh, no. Certain governments are currently taking anticapitalistic measures. That sucks! Democracies need free-market capitalist economies.
Author: Hey, easy there. You're being too hasty with this concern. Give it time and you'll see it's alright. History shows that when you're transitioning from a totalitarian regime to a democracy, you have to take repressive measures against some capitalistic developments.
Do we hear anything the author is assuming? If not, can we think of how we would argue with her? How could we defend the concern of the original people?
We could say, "Sure, author --- when you're transitioning from totalitarian to democracy, you do have to take repressive measures against **certain** capitalistic developments. But the governments who are currently taking anticapitalistic measures aren't targeting **those** kinds of capitalistic developments."
Or we could say, "Sure, author --- when you're transitioning from totalitarian to democracy, you do have to take repressive measures against certain capitalistic developments. But the governments who are currently taking anticapitalistic measures aren't transitioning from totalitarian to democracy. They're going from democracy to totalitarian, by way of shutting down capitalism!"

label: Goal
body:
Necessary Assumptions provide missing links / missing ideas, or they rule out a potential objection. Since we only came up with objections, let's look for an answer ruling one of those out:
- the capitalistic measures being repressed by certain governments **are** among the group of certain capitalistic developments that you need to repress when transitioning.
- the governments doing the anticapitalistic stuff **are** transitioning from totalitarianism to democracy.

label: Conclusion
body: We must reduce faculty salaries.

label: Evidence
body: We need to reduce next year's budget. We could do that be eliminating faculty positions. We could also do it by reducing salaries. And we're not going to eliminate faculty positions.

label: Evaluation
body:
This almost seems like airtight logic, where you lay out the available options, eliminate all but one of them, and then conclude that the final option must be the case.
So where's the wiggle room? They never actually said that these are all the available options. They are just assuming we only have the two options mentioned. We call that **False Choice**, when you present two options and assume that they represent an exhaustive set of possibilities.

label: Goal
body: We need an answer that says, "Are we sure these are our only two choices? Maybe there's some other action besides cutting jobs or salaries that could also reduce next year's budget?"

label: Conclusion
body: The act of inhibiting displays of emotion (consciously or unconsciously) causes a sharp rise in heart rate.

label: Evidence
body:
People who unconsciously inhibit emotion (repressors) have a sharp rise in heart rate when they encounter emotion-provoking situations.
People who consciously inhibit emotion (nonrepressors) also have a sharp rise in heart rate when they encounter emotion-provoking situations.

label: Evaluate
body:
This argument seems pretty logically sound on first read, so I would shift into Debate mode to figure out where the wiggle room is.
Given that ... both conscious and unconscious inhibitors have a sharp rise in heart rate when they encounter emotion-provoking situations,
How could we argue that... the act of inhibiting emotion **does not** cause a sharp rise in heart rate?
I guess we would have to explain the rise in heart rate some other way. Maybe the emotion-provoking situation is something that causes fear or anger, and fear / anger cause your heart rate to rise. Whether or not you show emotion or repress emotion doesn't actually make a difference.
If your boss is chewing you out, your heart rate will spike. The fact that some people are consciously or unconsciously hiding their emotional reaction is just part of how they're reacting to the situation, but the heart rate spike is caused by the situation, not by their conscious/unconscious decision to repress their emotions.

label: Conclusion (Thus)
body: It is reasonable to assume that the plant could fire 10 workers without any loss in production.

label: Evidence
body: The plant has 1,000 workers, though an average of 10 are absent on any given day. On days when exactly 10 workers are out, the plant experiences no loss in production.

label: Evaluate
body:
Since the author is interpreting the results of a study, we can use the Explain Curious Fact framework.
CURIOUS FACT - how were these people correctly guessing that they were being watched at a better than random rate?
EXPLANATION - people possess a sixth sense of "whether they're being watched".
Since this is related to a study suggesting a causal conclusion (people have a sixth sense), we should look for answers that either rule out alternate explanations for the study's findings (e.g., use of the five senses to detect being watched) or make the causal claim more plausible.

label: Goal
body: Identify an answer choice that helps rule out alternative explanations such as noises, smells, or shadows influencing participants, or provides additional evidence supporting the idea of a sixth sense.

label: Evaluate
body:
Given that... the plant experiences no loss when they're at 990 workers vs. 1000, How can we still argue... the plant **would** experience a loss in production if they fired 10 of their 1000 workers?
This is inherently a **Comparison** -based argument, as we're comparing our current world (1000 employees, average of 10 absent per day) to a hypothetical Plan World in which we have 990 employees.
What could be different in that world that could possibly affect production? - what if some of the 10 employees we fire are the really, really useful productive employees, whereas the ones that were typically out on those days when exactly 10 were absent were really expendable, useless employees. That would allow us to say, "Sure when exactly 10 were absent, production was the same, but only because the 10 who were missing were useless. If we fire a different 10, our production would go down".
Whenever LSAT authors talk about **average** they tend to interpret it way too literally. It sounds like this author is doing the same.
If the average is 10, and days with **exactly** 10 people missing are fine, the author thinks we can ditch 10 employees. But the average being 10 might mean that on some days 30 employees are out, on other days 1 is out.
If we used to range from 970-1000 employees there, then if we fire ten people, our new range will be 960-990 (because we'll still presumably be averaging about the same number of daily absences).

label: Goal
body:
The author is thinking, "if we can tolerate our average shortfall without a loss in production, then let's just reduce our total to meet that average shortfall."
But of course, now the average shortfall would just be applied to the reduced total, so you'd still have an average of 10 fewer employees per day.

label: Evidence
body:
Inflation rates → economic growth stabilize decreases
economic growth → full cooperation decreases of world leaders

label: Conclusion
body: Unlikely that inflation rates stabilize.

label: Evaluate
body:
Since we see repeating ideas (inflation rates stable / economic growth is slowed) and conditional logic (unless / required), it makes sense to try to write the "algebraic recipe" to this argument.
P1: A requires B. A → B P2: B requires C. B → C C: A probably won't happen soon.
This argument is assuming that "it would be overly optimistic to expect the full cooperation of world leaders in the near future", so it's not airtight, but it's pretty reasonable.

label: Goal
body: We want two conditional premises that chain together. The conclusion should be saying that the head of the chain, A, is unlikely (based on an assumption that the tail of the chain, C, is a pretty unlikely concept).

label: Conclusion
body: Interest in a career in art history as a career has declined in the last four years, among recent NA college grads.

label: Evidence
body: The number of applications for art history Ph.D. programs has declined over the last four years.

label: Evaluate
body:
If we're trying to weaken, we can ask ourselves, "GIVEN the evidence, HOW CAN I FIGHT the conclusion?"
GIVEN THAT the number of Ph.D. apps for art history has declined, HOW CAN WE SAY there's still just as much interest in art history as a career?
Maybe you don't need a Ph.D. as much any more to get a job in art history. Maybe these programs have jacked up their tuition or gotten a bad reputation.
This argument has the classic Curious Fact / Explanation structure. The author is asking himself, "Why are there fewer Ph.D. applications for art history?" and then coming up with the explanation, "It must be that there's less interest in getting an art career."
We always evaluate two different pressure points to these arguments: 1. How ELSE could we explain that Curious Fact? 2. How plausible is the Author's Explanation?

label: Goal
body: We want to eliminate four answers that either **pose an alternate explanation** for why the number of Ph.D. applications has declined, or one that make it seem like interest in art history careers is just as strong as ever.

label: Conclusion
body: Lie-detector tests that can detect these reactions are a sure way of determining when someone is lying.

label: Evidence (since)
body: The effort involved in lying is accompanied by physiological reactions such as a sped up heartbeat.

label: Evaluate
body:
Given that ... lying is accompanied by physiological reactions like a sped up heart beat.
How could we argue that... lie-detectors tests that can detect these reactions are **not** a sure way of determining when someone is lying?
Maybe other things also speed up our heart beats. What if you feel intense romantic chemistry with the person who's administering the lie detector test?
You might start sweating and pulse-pounding like humans do when they have a crush, and the lie-detector test would indicate that you're lying about whatever you're saying, since you're having similar physiological reactions.

label: Goal
body:
We need an answer that helps us argue that lie-detector tests are **not** perfect. They are not a sure indication of someone lying.
(and let's hope that this person who's administering our lie-detector test doesn't ask us, "Are you falling in love with me?")

label: Conclusion
body: It is unlikely that we will sell at least 100,000 books.

label: Evidence (since)
body: Of the twelve titles we sell, the one likely to be our #1 seller is unlikely to sell as many as 100,000 copies.

label: Evaluate
body:
Given that... our top prospect is unlikely to sell 100,000 copies How could we argue that... it **is** likely that our company will sell at least 100,000 books?
We could say, "Sure the #1 book isn't going to sell 100,000 copies all on its own, but if it sells 50,000 copies and the #2 book sells 30,000 and the #3 book sells 20,000, we're already there at 100,000 copies!" The author is thinking "if our best chance won't get us to 100k all by itself, then we won't get to 100k."
In a sense, it feels like the famous **Part vs. Whole** flaw. That #1 prospect book is part of this year's suite of books. Since this Part won't sell 100,000 copies, the Whole year's worth of books won't sell 100,000 copies?

label: Goal
body: Look for an answer saying that cumulatively the sales of all the books together could still get us over 100,000 copies.

label: Conclusion (proves)
body: Some people possess a sixth sense that allows them to know when someone is watching them.

label: Evidence
body: A study showed that individuals correctly guessed they were being watched 60% of the time (more than 50% of the time, which would be the rate expected by random chance alone).

label: Conclusion
body: Thus, such colonies will almost certainly be built and severe overcrowding on Earth relieved.

label: Principle
