body: The argument assumes that if T → ~ASwe are going to teach pre-university students calculus, then we must make sure that they will not abandon the study of it.

label: Evidence
body:
In 1955, legislation in a certain country gave the government increased control over industrial safety conditions.
Among the high-risk industries in that country, the likelihood that a worker will suffer a serious injury has decreased since 1955.

label: Conclusion
body: The legislation, therefore, has increased overall worker safety within high-risk industries.

label: Evaluate
body: This argument mistakes correlation for causation. An answer that provides a possible alternative cause of the decreased likelihood that a worker will suffer a serious injury would weaken the argument.

label: Given
body:
Historically, sunflower seed was one of the largest production crops in Kalotopia.
It continues to be a major source of income for several countries.
The renewed growing of sunflowers would provide relief to Kalotopia's farming industry, which is quite unstable.
Sunflower oil can provide a variety of products, both industrial and consumer, at little cost to Kalotopia's already fragile environment.

label: Given
body:
Several major earthquakes have occurred in a certain region over the last ten years.
Detected before each of these major quakes were certain changes in the electric current in the earth's crust.

label: Conclusion
body: A new earthquake prediction method promises to aid local civil defense officials in deciding exactly when to evacuate various towns.

label: Evaluate
body: In order for the earthquake prediction method to aid officials in deciding when to evacuate towns, it needs to be consistent from one earthquake event to the next. While the detected changes in the electric current occurred before each earthquake, were those detected changes consistent enough to base predictions on?

label: Information
body:
contrastFax machines must work with other fax machines,whereas many machines work in isolation from others.
causal chain
Fax machines must work with other fax machines. Thus, having lots of incompatible formats limited usefulness.Hence, fax machines weren't as commercially viable.
causal diff-maker
Fax machines weren't as commercially viable until they agreed to adopt a common format.
(adopting a common format led to more commercial viability)

label: Evaluate
body: It's hard to know what sort of correct answer to predict, but it will most likely reward our understanding of how incompatible formats limited usefulness/profitability or how a compatible common format helped profitability.

label: Principle
body: If critique of teacher performance OF → EEO is accompanied by the information that teacher performance is merely one of several factors that, in concert with other factors, determines the educational outcomes, then critique of teacher performance leads to enhanced educational outcomes.

label: Goal
body: We would want an answer where someone realizes that their performance is only one of several factors being judged, and thus that person performs better than if they thought that only their performance was being judged.

label: Evidence
body:
A novel cannot be of the highest HQ → EEquality unless most readers become Emotionally engaged with the imaginary world it describes.
Shifts of narrative point of view SN → FAwithin a novel tend to make most readers Focus on the author.

label: Conclusion
body: Thus shifts of narrative point of SN → ~HQview within a novel, either between first and third personor of some other sort, detract from the merit of the work (not high quality).

label: Evaluate
body: The argument assumes that FA → ~EEreaders who focus on the author do not become emotionally engaged with the imaginary world the author describes.

label: Apparent Paradox
body:
People aged 46 to 55 spend more money per capita than people of any other age group.
So it is puzzling that when companies advertise consumer products on television, they focus almost exclusively on people aged 25 and under.
Indeed, those who make decisions about television advertising think that the value of a television advertising slot depends entirely on the number of people aged 25 and under who can be expected to be watching at that time.

label: Evaluate
body: The first two statements set up the apparent paradox. People aged 25 and under spend less than people aged 46 to 55 and yet companies think that the value of television advertising depends entirely on those aged 25 and under. The final statement rules out one possible explanation. It’s not that only those aged 25 and under watch television.

label: Premises
body:
Expensive new tastes are a drain on your purse and in the course of acquiring them you may expose yourself to sensations that are obnoxious to you.
Furthermore, the very effort that must be expanded in their acquisition attests their superfluity.

label: Conclusion
body: You should never make an effort to acquire expensive new tastes.

label: Evaluate
body: The moralist argues against acquiring expensive new tastes by pointing out some of the drawbacks connected with achieving that goal. However, it fails to consider any of the advantages connected with acquiring expensive new tastes that may outweigh those drawbacks.

label: Given
body:
Zack’s Coffeehouse schedules W -most⇾ PR free poetry readings almost every Wednesday.
Zack’s offers half-priced PR → HPCcoffee all day on every daythat a poetry reading is scheduled.

label: Evaluate
body:
By combining the two sentences, we know that "almost every Wednesday, Zach's offers half-priced coffee".
We'd guess that the correct answer will reward us seeing that inference.

label: Given
body:
An event is intentional if it is HA + SM → Ia human action performed on the basis of a specific motivation.
An event is random if it is ~SM + ~NPP → Rnot performed on the basis of a specific motivation and it is not explainable by normal physical processes.

label: Goal
body:
If an answer choice is concluding that something was "intentional" we'll check to see whether it was a human action with a specific motivation.
If an answer choice is concluding that something was "random", we'll check to see whether had no specific motivation and isn't explainable by normal physical processes.
If it's concluding anything else, we'll just automatically eliminate the answer.

label: Conclusion
body: Just because ancient languages didn’t have any expression for “moral right” doesn’t mean those ancient people didn’t know what moral rights were.

label: Evidence
body: That’d be like saying someone who keeps going back to harvest fruit from an apple tree but doesn’t have an expression for it doesn’t know what it is.

label: Evaluation
body: When LSAT unfurls an analogy, we often have to match up piece for piece. We have two different situations here (ancient people not having a word for moral rights / person not having a word for a fruit tree) that are being connected to a similar question: does the ancient person know what moral rights are? Does the fruitpicker know what the fruit tree is?

label: Goal
body: It’s hard for a lot of us to hear the missing idea here, so we’d probably just look for something that reinforces the idea that, “The author is assuming that these two cases are fair to compare”.

label: Intermediate Conclusion
body:
There is little plausibility to the claim that it is absurd to criticize anyone for being critical.
rephrase: It's coherent for someone to criticize someone else for being critical.

label: Premise

label: Main Conclusion
body: The superiority [some painters have relative to others in the execution of their artistic visions] must be measured in light of the artist's purposes.

label: Conclusion (thus)
body: There must be something about mammalian chromosomes that precluded parthenogenesis.

label: Goal
body: Look for an answer addressing the assumption that "corporations promote communal ties".

label: Evidence
body: Parthenogenesis occurs in a wide variety of nonmammalian vertebrates, no studies have yet demonstrated parthenogenesis in mammals, and the one study that supposedly did was shown to have flawed methods.

label: Evaluation
body: This is an (unusually hard) example of a famous flaw called Absence of Evidence (or Unproven vs. Untrue). The idea here is that it’s flawed to think that just because no one has ever successfully proven X that X is therefore false. We could otherwise argue, “Since no one has ever proven that God exists, apparently there is no God”, and the faithful could equally respond, “Since no one has ever proven that God does not exist, clearly there is a God”. When we hear the author saying that someone’s attempt to prove an idea failed (whether it’s because of shaky methodology, failure of others to replicate, reliance on a dubious assumption, etc.), then we should be left in a state of doubt about that idea. Maybe it’s true, maybe it’s not. That’s how the author should feel about mammalian parthenogenesis. Instead, the author accepts the pessimistic notion that parthenogenesis doesn’t occur in mammals, and her conclusion goes on to speculate why there isn’t.

label: Goal
body: We either want an answer that says, “Whoa, just because no one’s proven parthenogenesis in mammals yet, doesn’t mean you can just assume it doesn’t exist”, or we could look for an answer that targets the conclusion and says, “Hey, why’s it gotta be chromosomes? Couldn’t there be some other reason why mammals don’t have parthenogenesis?”

label: Conclusion (thus)
body: If you feel like a TV show is worth preserving, then you should buy the stuff advertised during that show.

label: Intermediate Conclusion (so)
body: If most people fail to buy the stuff advertised during their favorite shows, the show will be canceled.

label: Evidence
body: If many people don't buy the stuff advertised during a show, then advertisers won't pay for those commercials anymore, which would lead to most shows being canceled.

label: Goal
body:
We want a principle that will tell us to buy stuff advertised during the show. The trigger should have something to do with the idea that, "if most people don't buy the stuff, then the show will go off the air".
So we want something like, "If most people not doing X would cause something you want preserved to disappear, then you should do X".

label: Evidence
body:
It is well known that becoming angry often induces temporary incidents of high blood pressure.
A recent study further showed, however, that people who are easily angered are significantly more likely to have permanently high blood pressure than are people who have more tranquil personalities.
Those with permanently high blood pressure are especially likely to have heart disease.

label: Conclusion
body: The recent findings indicate that heart disease can result from psychological factors.

label: Evaluate
body:
The argument opens with a causal claim: getting mad often causes your blood pressure to get high, but it's temporary. The next two claims express correlations. People who get mad easily are way more likely to always have high blood pressure than more mellow folks. Permanently high blood pressure is correlated with a special likelihood of heard disease. From this, the author drew a causal conclusion: psychological factors can cause heart disease.
Because this is a Weaken question, it's useful to think about what's already wrong with this argument, because the right answer is likely to exploit an existing weakness. Broadly speaking, any time an argument takes correlary evidence and draws a causal conclusion, we should consider two things: could the author have it backwards? Could the thing they think is the effect actually be the cause? Or, could both of the correlated things be effects of some third thing?
So, could heart disease be the cause and psychological factors (being quick to anger) the effect? Sure. Maybe having heart disease causes you to have permanently high blood pressure and having high blood pressure all the time makes it easier to get mad.
Could heart disease and psychological factors (being quick to anger) both be effects of the same cause? Sure. Maybe high blood pressure is the root cause of both heart disease and getting mad easily. Or maybe all 3 of those things are effects of some 4th cause: maybe people are genetically predisposed to all 3 conditions, for example.

label: Goal
body: Look for an answer that exploits a classic causal weakness. But, because this is the guantlet (the hardest stretch of LR questions from 15-23), if you don't find your prediction, try each answer on for size with an open mind.

label: Evidence
body:
A professor of business placed a case-study assignment for her class on her university’s computer network.
She later found out that instead of reading the assignment on the computer screen, 50 out of the 70 students printed it out on paper.

label: Conclusion
body: Thus, it is not the case that books delivered via computer will make printed books obsolete.

label: Evaluate
body: The conclusion generalizes from the anecdotal evidence observed by the professor. To support this argument it would be helpful to know that what is true of the students in the professor’s class is true of people more generally.

label: Conclusion
body: Anyone who follows our diet is sure to lose weight

label: Evidence
body: Our diet provides more calories from protein than anything else and requires breakfast to be the biggest meal of the day. In a study, researchers found that the people who lost the most weight got more calories from protein and made their biggest meal early in the day.

label: Evaluation
body:
This is the famous flaw of Correlation -> Causality. The author presents a study in which there was a correlation between “losing the most weight” and “protein #1 source of calories / biggest meal early”. She then assumes that making protein #1 and eating biggest meal early are the causal reasons why these people lost the most weight. What if they are just coincidental things that are correlated with the weight loss group, but something else was the real causal factor? (Maybe they ate fewer calories overall / exercised more / etc)
There is another famous flaw at work here: Sampling. Even if we accepted that “high protein / early big meal” caused the people in the study to lose weight, we don’t have to accept that this strategy would work for all people. The conclusion is boldly proclaiming “Anyone who follows this diet is sure to lose weight.”

label: Goal
body: We either want a different explanation for why the “high protein / early big meal” group lost weight, or we want a reason to think that even though this diet worked for them it might not be sure to work for anyone who tries this diet.

label: Apparent Paradox
body:
Aristophanes’ portrayal of Socrates (written when Socrates was in his mid-forties) presents an atheistic philosopher primarily concerned with issues in natural science.
Other surviving portrayals of Socrates, written after his death at age 70, portray Socrates as having a religious dimension and a strong focus on ethical issues.

label: Evaluate
body: How could the portrayals of Socrates be so different. There are many ways to explain this difference. First, it could be that Socrates shifted over time from someone who matched Aristophanes’s portrayal to someone who matched the other surviving portrayals. Second, it could be that one of the portrayals is inaccurate.

label: Given
body:
Several cases that exhibit the following pattern:

2. At this point the child, having obtained the desired goal, stops the problematic behavior, to the parent’s relief.

label: Evaluate

label: Conclusion
body: We can’t conclude from this study that R is safe for humans.

label: Evidence
body: In the study R didn’t cause cancer in rats, but many substances known to cause cancer in humans don’t cause cancer in rats (probably because a rat’s life span isn’t long enough for the carcinogenic effect to materialize).

label: Evaluation
body: Our conclusion is the 2nd sentence. Since we pivot into that conclusion with a “But”, we know that the previous idea was some sort of counterpoint. The first sentence is potentially evidence for the idea that “R is safe for humans”. The author makes an argument to resist making this hasty leap in logic.

label: Goal
body: We want something like counterpoint, or a fact that the author says is not grounds for making some other inference.

label: Evidence
body:
If most customers take the offer (free gift wrapping), it will be expensive and time-consuming for us.
On the other hand, if only a few customers want it, there is no advantage in offering it.

label: Conclusion
body: There is absolutely no reason to offer our customers free gift wrapping again this holiday season.

label: Evaluate
body: The argument points out two extreme cases where there is no advantage in offering free gift wrapping this season. But there are other possible cases. If the number of customers is more than a few and less than most, there may be good reason to offer free gift wrapping this season.

label: Evidence
body:
Among people who have a history of chronic trouble falling asleep, some rely only on sleeping pills to help them fall asleep, and others practice behavior modification techniques and do not take sleeping pills.
Those who rely only on behavior modification fall asleep more quickly than do those who rely only on sleeping pills.

label: Conclusion
body: So behavior modification is more effective than are sleeping pills in helping people to fall asleep.

label: Evaluate
body: First, there could be different degrees to which people have a difficult time falling asleep and those who have milder forms of difficulty may not seek pills to help them fall asleep; they may be comfortable with less aggressive measures. Second, there could be other factors influencing how difficult it is to fall asleep and perhaps those other factors do not permit the effectiveness of pills and behavior modification techniques to be compared.

label: Conclusion
body: The difficulty of adapting to ice ages was not a causal factor in the evolution of the human brain.

label: Evidence
body: Most other animals adapted to ice ages with no evolutionary changes to their brains.

label: Evaluation
body:
In simple terms, the author seems to be thinking, “If it wasn’t true for most animal species, then it wasn’t true for humans”. This is a sketchy move; naturally, some things could be unique to a given species. We could call it a sampling problem: the author assumes that humans are a representative sample, so that what is true for most animals would be true for them. What if humans are an atypical sample?
We could also maybe call it a soft version of Necessary vs. Sufficient. We have paleontologists saying, “In the case of humans, the challenges of ice ages were sufficient to produce brain evolution”, and the author is arguing, “How could X explain Y, if I see cases of X in which Y did not occur?” We would respond, “We’re only saying that ice age challenges could be sufficient to change brains, not that it’s necessary in all cases that ice age challenges would change brains.”

label: Goal
body: Look for something like, “takes for granted that if it wasn’t true for most species then it wasn’t true for humans” or something that speaks more formally to the Sampling or Necessary vs. Sufficient issues.

label: Given

Retail sales of new titles, as measured in copies, increased rapidly in the early days of television, though the rate of increase has slowed in recent years.

label: Opposing Evidence
body: Child-rearing books commonly list poinsettias as poisonous and therefore dangerous.

label: Opposing Conclusion
body: People with children or pets should keep poinsettia plants out of their homes.

label: Conclusion
body: The building we’re looking at was probably not a dwelling.

label: Evidence
body: The building we’re looking at was made of quartz, granite, and limestone. Most of the buildings at this settlement were dwellings, but most of the building at this site are made only of limestone.

label: Evaluation
body: This is a weirdly terrible argument. It’s almost hard to sympathize with the argument the author thinks that she’s making. When you have two Most facts about the same group, you can always infer that there is Some overlap between the traits you learn. So if we know “most buildings at site were dwellings” and “most buildings at site were only limestone”, then you can infer “at least one building was a dwelling made only of limestone”. But our author is making it seem like “most dwellings were made only of limestone”. Essentially, the author thinks that if most buildings were dwellings and most were only limestone, then a building with a mix of lime/quartz/granite was probably not a dwelling. But it’s possible that most of the mixed-stone buildings were dwellings, in which case her conclusion would be wrong.

label: Goal
body: We need to help out her terrible argument by making it more likely that dwellings would not be a mix of stones.

label: Evidence
body:
Theodore will be able to file his OT → APR + ~AADtax return on time only in theevent that he has an accountantprepare his tax return and theaccountant does not askTheordore for any additionaldocumentation of his businessexpenses.
If he does have an accountant APR → AADprepare his return, theaccountant will necessarily askTheodore to provide thisadditional documentation.

label: Conclusion
body: Therefore, Theodore will not be ~OTable to file on time.

label: Evaluate
body: To file his taxes on time Theodore must do two things that cannot both occur, since the second premise states that those two things are incompatible. Therefore, Theodore cannot file his taxes on time.

label: Conclusion
body: Rigorously structuring playtime for your kid will not enhance the kid’s cognitive development.

label: Evidence
body: Expecting rigorous playtime to produce a creative and resourceful kid is like thinking that imposing a rigorous plot/character structure on a writer will result in the writer making a good novel.

label: Evaluation
body:
This argument relies on a comparison/analogy, so we object to these sorts of arguments by pointing out meaningful differences.
Is there some reason why imposing a plot/characters on a writer wouldn’t have good results, but imposing a rigorous schedule on a child could help his/her cognitive development?
Novelists are usually full-grown adults, whereas kids have developing brains, so maybe we could say that rigorous structure is good for a developing brain, even if it isn’t great for creative adult tasks like novel writing.
The author has also not spelled out the missing part of his analogy: he’s assuming that if you told someone what plot/characters they had to use, they would not be likely to produce a good novel. The author is also drifting from the idea of “enhancing cognitive development” to the idea of “creative and resourceful child”.

label: Goal
body: Look for an answer spelling out the author’s missing assumption, the author’s language drift, or, more likely, pointing out a salient difference between the effect of structure on a child’s brain vs. the effect of imposing structure on a novelist.

label: Conclusion
body: An ideal bureaucracy will have an ever-expanding system of regulations.

label: Evidence
body: The #1 constant goal of an ideal bureaucracy is to find all problems and write regulations to address each of them. It also provides an appeal process to handle complaints. If a complaint reveals a new problem, then regulations are expanded to cover this new problem.

label: Goal
body: Let’s look for any answer that can help us argue that, “even though modern culture brings with it a dizzying array of subcultures / fringe movements, it’s still not threatening national identities.”

label: Evaluation
body:
The author has given us a really strong conclusion: in an ideal bureaucracy, regulations will be forever expanding. What is the reason that we have to keep writing more and more regulations forever? We're hoping to write a regulation for every problem we find, and the author leaves us (before her conclusion) with the idea that complaints can help us find new problems, for which we need to expand our regulations.
If we were playing Devil's Advocate, we'd have to accept the evidence but come up with a storyline where an ideal bureaucracies regulations do NOT forever expand. They eventually stop where they are. That line of objection would sound something like, "What if you eventually find all possible problems and thus you're done writing regulations?" The author seems to be assuming we'll never be done finding new problems.

label: Goal
body: The argument needs to defend its idea that in an ideal bureaucracy, we will forever be finding new problems (hence, we will forever be writing new regulations).

label: Opposing Evidence
body: Scientists studying a common type of bacteria have discovered that most bacteria of that type are in hibernation at any given time.

label: Opposing Conclusion
body: Bacteria in general are usually in hibernation.

label: Evidence
body:
The conclusion that bacteria in general are usually in hibernation would be reasonable if all types of bacteria were rather similar.
Bacteria are extremely diverse.

label: Conclusion
body: It is unlikely that most types of bacteria hibernate regularly.

label: Evidence
body: Any student who is not required to ~WH → ~RHhand in written homework based onthe reading assignments in a coursewill not complete all of the readingassignments.

label: Conclusion
body: If the students in a course are given ~WH → ~HGseveral reading assignments and nowritten assignments, no student inthat course will receive a high gradefor the course.

label: Evaluate

label: Evidence
body:
In a study, one group of volunteers was fed a high-protein, low-carbohydrate diet; another group was fed a low-protein, high carbohydrate diet.
Both diets contained the same number of calories, and each volunteer’s diet prior to the experiment had contained moderate levels of proteins and carbohydrates.
After ten days, those on the low-carbohydrate diet had lost more weight than those on the high-carbohydrate diet.

label: Conclusion (thus)
body: The most effective way to lose body fat is to eat much protein and shun carbohydrates.

label: Evaluate
body: This conclusion is very strong. To know for certain the most effective way to do anything is nearly impossible—the unknown is typically too vast. Furthermore this argument conflates correlation with causation. Finally, there’s a term shift—losing weight is not the same as losing body fat.

label: Conclusion
body: The human mind is a type of computer.

label: Evidence
body: Computers have the capacity to represent info and do logical transformations on it. So does the human mind.

label: Evaluation
body: Hmm, not sure what to call this flaw. We could say, “A shovel has the capacity to scoop up sand and dump it out. A shoe also has this capacity. Thus, a shoe is a type of shovel.” That would sound pretty dumb. Just because Thing X has the capacity to do Action A, that doesn’t mean that everything that is capable of doing Action A is type of Thing X.

label: Goal
body: It’s hard to say whether the overlapping sameness will still be “capacity to do something”. So we could start out looking for a more general sense of “these two things have something in common. So the second thing is a type of the first thing.”Thing X has trait A.Thing Y also has trait A.Thus, Thing Y is a type of Thing X.

label: Opposing Point
body: It is popularly believed that a poem has MRwhatever meaning is assigned to it bythe reader.

label: Evidence
body: The aesthetic value of a poem cannot DAV → ~MRbe discussed unless it is possible for atleast two readers to agree on the correctinterpretation of the poem [meaning isnot from the reader].

label: Conclusion
body: But objective evaluation of poetry is OE → ~MR possible only if this popular belief is false [meaning is not from the reader].

label: Evaluate
body: The argument assumes that objective OE → DAVevaluation of poetry is possible only ifthe aesthetic value can be discussed.

label: Conclusion
body: We shouldn’t give the math department sole responsibility for teaching Stats for Social Sciences.

label: Evidence
body: This course has no more math than a high school algebra class. And the fact that it has math in it doesn’t mean it needs a math professor, any more than a course that has some history in it means it needs a history professor.

label: Evaluation
body: We might not see any obvious flaw here. If so, we should just think of how we would accept the evidence but argue that this class should be taught solely by the math department. Maybe we would say, “A course with history does need a history professor!” in the author’s analogy, he is assuming that a class with history in it doesn’t need a history professor. But why not? We’re free to disagree with that assumption.Another reaction we might have is, “If a class has math that’s as complicated as high school algebra, then it should probably be taught by a math teacher. After all, aren’t high school algebra classes taught by math teachers?”

label: Goal
body: Keep a flexible mind. The answer might call out one of the author’s assumptions or make a possible objection that would allow us to argue that it should be a math teacher who teaches this class.

label: Conclusion (clearly)
body: Carl is an incompetent detective.

label: Evidence
body: Carl has solved the smallest percentage of his assigned cases over the last 3 years (1 out of 25) — lower than any other detective on the force.

label: Evaluate
body:
The evidence is comparative and the conclusion is suggesting a causal explanation for that evidence, so we have the ol' Explain Curious Fact template.
CURIOUS FACT - why is Carl's success rate of solving cases so much worse than all the other detectives?
AUTHOR'S EXPLANATION - he's incompetent at his job, so he's unable to solve cases.

label: Goal
body:
We most commonly weaken this style of argument by pointing to an Alternate Explanation for the curious fact. Maybe Carl isn't incompetent; he just fails to solve as many cases because he's given the toughest cases, or he's given less time to solve them, or he's given fewer resources with which to solve them. We'd love any type of answer that "makes an excuse" for his low solve rate, so that we don't have to blame it on incompetence.
Otherwise, we'd love an answer attacking the plausibility of the author's story and making it seem like Carl is competent!

label: Conclusion
body: Carl is an incompetent detective.

label: Evidence
body: His case-solving rate is the worst on the force.

label: Evaluate
body: Solve rate only reflects competence if cases are comparable in difficulty. If Carl gets the hardest cases, his low rate could be due to difficulty, not skill.

label: Goal
body: Find an answer giving an alternative explanation for the low solve rate.

label: Conclusion
body: The author looks at Carl's low solve rate and concludes Carl must be bad at his job.

label: Evidence
body: 1 out of 25 — the worst rate on the force.

label: Evaluate
body:
Here's the unspoken assumption: that all detectives get equally tough cases. If they do, comparing solve rates is fair. But if Carl gets handed the cases nobody else could crack, his low rate could mean the opposite of incompetence — it could mean he's the one trusted with the impossible ones.
Think of it like a hospital ER. If one surgeon has the worst patient survival rate, that sounds bad — until you find out she only operates on the most desperate cases everyone else turned down. Now her low survival rate looks completely different.

label: Goal
body: The right answer will give us a reason Carl's low solve rate isn't about Carl's skill.

label: Conclusion
body: Hypertensive personality likely causes high blood pressure

label: Evidence
body: People with high blood pressure are more nervous and anxious than those who don't have high blood pressure

label: Evaluation
body:
The formulation of "People who are X are more likely than those who are not to be Y" is correlation language. Author's usually are too quick to conclude that one of those causes the other. Here, our author concludes that being nervous and anxious came first and led to the high blood pressure.
We're supposed to consider alternative explanations for that correlation, such as maybe having high blood pressure came first and that led to these people becoming nervous and anxious. Or perhaps there's an underlying cause (like a high stress job) that is causing the higher blood pressure and the nerves/anxiety.

label: Goal
body: We need an answer that calls out the famous Correlation to Causality flaw or one that otherwise deals with a different possible way to interpret this same correlation.

label: Conclusion (Therefore)
body: It's very likely that Grey read Jordan's book.

label: Evidence
body: Both books contain the same weirdly specific metaphor, suggesting a connection between them. Jordan's book was published 7 years before Grey's.

label: Evaluate
body:
The author is identifying a Curious Fact and offering a causal interpretation, so we can use our Explain Curious Fact template.
CURIOUS FACT: how is it that the same weird metaphor shows up in both of these books?
EXPLANATION: Jordan put it in his 1885 book. Grey read the book and "stole" it for his own 1892 book.
We can weaken this style of argument by either suggesting an Alternate Explanation for the curious fact (most common) or by undermining the plausibility of the author's explanation.

label: Goal
body: Find an answer that offers a different explanation for how the metaphor shows up in both books, or that debunks the storyline that Grey read the metaphor in Jordan's book and learned of it that way.

label: Background
body: Patients with back injuries who receive a combo of drugs and physical therapy do only as well as those who just receive physical therapy.

label: Surprising Claim
body: Medical specialists say that the drugs are a necessary part of the treatment for all patients who receive them for back injuries.

label: Evaluate
body:
Given That ... the people who get (physical therapy + drugs) do only as well as the people go get (physical therapy + no drugs)
How Can We Say That .... the drugs are a necessary part of the treatment for the people who got it?
It looks like the drugs are doing nothing, since people who only had physical therapy are doing just as well, but our correct answer will give us some way to say that the people who got [physical therapy + drugs] wouldn't have done as well if they had only gotten physical therapy (or maybe it will say that the people who didn't get drugs would have done worse if they had been given drugs).

label: Goal
body:
Even though we don't usually try to predict answers for Paradox, those of us who know the Anti-Causal arguments we see in the Assumption family may recognize a pattern here.
If I say, "the students who got tutoring scored just as high on the math quiz as the students who didn't get tutoring. Therefore, the tutoring did nothing", how could we object to that argument?
We can say, "The students who got tutoring were the ones who were most struggling with math; had they not gotten tutoring, there's no way they would have scored as high as the other students".
In other words, when two groups are measured as being the same, if we want to argue that some special property one of them had was meaningful, we have to say that "without it, they wouldn't have been measured the same".

label: Conclusion (hence)
body: Modern culture threatens the national identities that now exist in the world.

label: Evidence
body: Modern culture reflects the increasing influence of fringe movements, giving us new fashions, ideologies, religions, artistic movements, economic theories, cults, and dogmas at a rapid rate.

label: Evaluate
body:
Given that … modern culture contains an increasing plurality of points of view, each with its own aesthetics / ideas / rules / beliefs.
How can we still argue that … modern culture does not threaten the national identities that exist in the world?
Maybe we could argue that the more your country seems to fragment into a thousand difference sub communities, the more you need a national identity to tie everyone together.

label: Conclusion (should = Opinion)
body: Funding for children's athletic programs should not be eliminated.

label: Information
body:
causal (X is vital to Y)Packaging is vital to a product's commercial success.
example illustrating this causalityNew improved version of drink X succeeded in blind taste tests.
pivot (however) / causal (mainly because)However, customers didn't buy it, mainly because the can looked basically the same, making consumers expect that the new product would share features of the old product that it no longer had.

label: Evaluate
body:
We know that people like the taste of this new drink when they have no expectations about what they're about to drink.
Let's say it's a new lemon flavored soda from Dr. Pepper.
"Oh, what a refreshing lemon soda. Love it!"
But when consumers drank it from a can that looked too much like the old Dr. Pepper can, they were not expecting that lemon taste at all. They were expecting whatever plum flavor normal Dr. Pepper normally has, and so it was off-putting when they tried new Dr. Pepper Lemon.We're already told the explicit causal relationship that packaging can have an impact on commercial success. We're more likely being tested on the mainly because Causal Difference-Maker language in the middle.
Since the packaging created expectations that mismatched with reality, customers didn't buy the soda.

label: Goal
body: Let's look for the most provable claim, but it will probably touch on this idea that "when product packaging creates a gap between expectation and reality, it can turn off customers".

label: Principle
body: Paying attention to gain insights importanthow we emotionally ⇢ into our own ⇢ sourceand physically react weaknesses of self to a challenge knowledge

label: Evaluate
body:
Usually when we're given a principle and asked to apply it, the principle is phrased like a conditional rule.
But this one doesn't seem like that. It's actually written more like an argument. We're representing it above as a chain of causality / reasoning.

label: Goal
body: Let's look for something where people are challenged, they pay attention to how they react, emotionally and physically, to the challenge, and learn something about their own weaknesses / broaden their self knowledge.

label: Assertion
body: National leaders could solve the problems resulting from migration from rural to urban areas by trading goods or services produced by their urban populations in order to obtain agricultural products that used to be produced domestically (in rural areas).

label: Evaluate
body:
This isn't called an argument or reasoning, so we don't need to be looking for a Conclusion and Premise.
The assertion seems to make a few assumptions:- one of the problems (if not the only one) with people migrating from rural to urban is that we're worried that once they leave the rural area, we'll no longer have the agricultural products that used to be made there- these soon-to-be-missing agricultural products are available on world markets- our urban places produce enough desirable goods that other countries would want that it would feasible to entice other countries into trading with us

label: Goal
body: Let's look for an answer affirming something this plan is assuming, ruling out a potential objection to the plan (alternate plans aren't objections ... it only weakens to argue that this play couldn't do it), or just providing a new fact that makes it seem like this plan could work.

label: Conclusion (this can seen from fact)
body: Technological innovation rarely serves the interests of society as a whole.

label: Evidence
body: People responsible for technological advances are striving to develop commercially viable technology, so they're almost always motivated by considerations of personal gain, rather than societal benefit.

label: Evaluate
body:
There's a bit of an intermediate conclusion happening when the author says "tech innovators are almost always motivated by personal gain, in that they strive to develop commercially viable technology".
I don't have to accept that striving to develop commercially viable technology means you're motivated by personal gain. Perhaps you're motivated to have a company that is solvent (it can pay its bills), but you could be developing something commercially viable as a service to manking.
But the bigger gap here seems to be between the idea that, "If you're motivated by personal gain / commercial viability, then your innovation won't serve the interests of society as a whole." Doesn't something usually have commercial viability because people see value in it? It's useful or desirable to them?
So isn't producing a commercially viable item creating something useful / valuable to those who buy it, and thus potentially benefiting society as a whole?
This argument is committing the semi-famous flaw Intent vs. Consequences
The author is saying, "Since the tech innovator's intent is not societal benefit, then the consequence of their invention will not be societal benefit".
The giveaway for this flaw is that the evidence is talking about someone's motivation, but the conclusion is talking about actual results.

label: Goal
body: Look for an answer complaining about the Motivation vs. Result move, or an answer pointing our that commercial viability usually means that a wide swath of people think they would benefit by having your product.

label: Statements
body:
Comparison (2 kinds of horror stories)
Type 1: mad scientist | Type 2: monstrous beast
most of these some of theseexpress author's monster symbolizesskepticism about "inner monster" of science protagonist
all of these i. describe violations of laws of nature ii. intended to produce dread in reader

label: Evaluate
body:
What a mess! There are too many facts to know where they want to go with this one. When we see quantifiers being bandied about, such as Some / Most / All, the biggest priority is the All / None statements, because those are Conditionals.
The final sentence gives us this conditional: describe violations of laws of natureHorror Story → and intended to produce dread
A lot of Inference questions that use quantifiers have correct answers that just establish that Two Traits Overlap.
Given a conditional like A → B and C,if we hear a fact like Some A's are Xwe can infer that X overlaps with B X overlaps with C

label: Goal
body: Stay flexible. Look for a possible Two Traits Overlap inference, but who knows what they'll try to connect.

label: Conclusion
body: It's unwarranted to reduce social expenditure

label: Evidence
body: Some said that we should reduce social expenditure, on theoretical grounds that we spend too much on social programs. But they should have been highlighting the bigger problem with our excessive spending: the government is just too big because of self-aggrandizing bureaucracies and politicians.

label: Conclusion (we must = opinion)
body: We must do whatever it takes to ship books in that category on time.

label: Evaluation
body:
I'm confused -- doesn't the author want to reduce social spending? He's saying it's unwarranted to do so because some people want to do so for the not-#1 reason?
If you wanted to see a movie because of the lead actress, would it make any sense if I said, "You should be focusing on the innovative directing this movie is known for. It is unwarranted, therefore, for us to go see this movie."

label: Goal
body: This sort of has an Unproven vs. Proven False vibe, since the author is saying, "Since the argument you're making for claim X is unsatisfactory, claim X is unwarranted". But we might just see an answer saying, "There can be more than one good reason to do something".

label: Statement
body: It's more likely that flowers developed colors in response to the type of vision that bees have, rather than that bees evolved their vision in response to the type of colors that flowers have.

label: Evaluate
body:
This wasn't an argument, as the question stem indicated by telling us to support the statement.
It's basically a Natural Selection riddle of the chicken and the egg. We know that bees have vision suited for flower color and flowers have colors that attract bees vision, but which came first?

label: Goal
body: We need an answer that makes it seem more likely that bees had their vision first, and then flowers developed their colors in order to take advantage

label: Conclusion
body: This argument for freedom of thought fails:We can't say that because freedom of thought lets people pursue their ideas wherever that takes them, "intellectual progress requires freedom of thought".

label: Evidence
body: Intellectual progress requires "mining the full implications of interrelated ideas", and that requires intellectual discipline.

label: Evaluate
body:
Are we sure we want to go back to school, if this is how professors talk?
It's a little unspecific what our conclusion means. An argument can fail because a premise is false, the conclusion is false, or simply because the conclusion doesn't follow from the premises.
But since the author's evidence talks about "intellectual progress", let's focus on the intellectual progress part of the conclusion and assume our author wants to argue that,
intellectual progress does not require freedom of thought.
"Freedom of thought" doesn't show up in the evidence, so it needs to show up in the correct answer.
What do we know about intellectual progress from the evidence?
Intellectual Mining full Intellectual progress → implications of → discipline interrelated ideas
Let's just think about how this argument would work on a basic level.Conclusion: X doesn't require A. Premise: X requires B which requires C.
It looks like we're missing "if it requires C, then it doesn't require A".We'd also accept "if it requires B, then it doesn't require A".

label: Goal
body:
We need an answer that helps us make either of these moves:
If we need intellectual discipline, then we don't need freedom of thought.If we need to mine full implications of ideas, then we don't need freedom of thought.

label: Conclusion (Thus)
body: A jury trial is not a fair means of settling disputes involving scientific or technical issues.

label: Evidence
body: People with specialized knowledge about the issues are excluded from juries, if that issue is relevant.

label: Evaluate
body:
We can apply our generic Weaken template to this argument:
GIVEN THAT people with specialized knowledge are excluded from juries if the case involves that specialty,
HOW CAN WE ARGUE THAT jury trials are still fair, when they deal with specialized subjects/
To weaken the argument, we can counter the negative perception of excluding specialists or argue that fairness is achieved through other means.

label: Goal
body: Identify an answer choice that supports the idea of fairness in jury trials by highlighting the benefits of excluding specialists or reinforcing the ability of jurors to reach fair decisions.

label: Proposition
body: have evidence that action X will benefit they will other people → usually and benefitdo X to benefit them

label: Goal
body:
We want an answer that seems to establish both ideas in the trigger and then leads to the idea in the outcome.
1. have evidence X will benefit others2. do X to benefit others3. X helps others
It could be like, "Gabe has heard from massage therapists that rubbing someone's shoulders can help them relieve neck tension. He rubbed his friend's shoulders to help her relieve her neck tension, so she will probably feel better as a result".

label: Conclusion
body: Our cereal makes true claims about its health benefits

label: Evidence (since)
body: If the claims weren't true, health-conscious people wouldn't be buying it.

label: Intermediate Conclusion (implied)
body: The people buying it are health-conscious.

label: Evidence for Intermediate Conclusion
body: If the claims weren't true, then no health-conscious consumer would be buying it.

label: Evaluation
body:
Yikes, this is a train that wrecked into a dumpster fire. It seems to be doing something Circular.
It's trying to prove that its printed label is accurate by pointing to evidence that health conscious people by the product. But how do we know health conscious people by the product? Because the label is accurate.
Let's look at our two provided rules:
Health conscious consumers → health claims buying this cereal on label true
Health conscious consumers → health claims buying a food on package true
The author is trying to establish that the health claims on the package are true, so he needs to establish that health conscious consumers buy this food.
But he's never established that the people who buy the food are health conscious. He tries to prove that by citing a rule in the last sentence that is essentially the same as the rule stated in the second sentence.

label: Goal
body: We would probably anticipate that these answers could be a slog, so I might gamble on the first one I see I like. We seem to need a circular-feeling argument where the author is trying to use a rule to prove his conclusion, but we can't tell that rule is being triggered without some other rule that seems to hinge on itself.

label: Conclusion (clearly)
body: Support group meetings do not help patients with disease T live longer.

label: Evidence
body:
In a study of 86 patients with disease T, who all received the same standard medical treatment, one group attended weekly support group meetings, but no one from the other group did.
After 10 years, 41 patients from each group had died.

label: Evaluate
body:
When we see causal arguments in Strengthen / Weaken (as we so commonly do), they usually start by presenting an Asymmetric Comparison, which we nickname "a curious fact". The author's conclusion states or assumes the causal story behind that difference.
But anti-causal arguments usually start with a Symmetric Comparison, which allows the author to claim, "See? This thing didn't make any difference". With anti-causal arguments, if we're going to defend the idea that thing X did make a difference, then we usually need to "make an excuse" for why two things appeared to be the same.
For example, if we wanted to defend the idea that Laura's LSAT book is better than Matt's LSAT book, but students who used Laura's book scored the same on their eventual test as did students who used Matt's book, we would need to "make an excuse" for why Laura's students (supposedly using the better book) ended up scoring similarly.
We can say, "Her students started a lower score. Her students had more learning disabilities. Her students achieved their score in less study time." We show that Laura's students and Matt's students didn't start on an even playing field, so that we can argue that "it's actually a WIN for Laura's students to end up tied with Matt's students".

label: Goal
body: Here, we'd be thinking,Given that .... 41 patients in each group died,How can we argue that ... the support group meetings did help patients with disease T live longer than they would have without the support group meetings?

label: Conclusion
body: My opponents should admit that I'm correct (that our solar system doesn't have enough random debris to cause the extensive cratering on the far side of the Moon).

label: Evidence
body: My opponents have failed to refute me. Their evidence is inconclusive.

label: Evaluation
body:
Okay, just because they failed to refute you doesn't mean you're right. Maybe you think that Trump conspired with Putin over the 2016 election. I can't conclusively prove that you're wrong. But that doesn't prove that you're right.
This type of reasoning is a famous flaw called Unproven vs. Proven False.

label: Goal
body: Look for an answer saying, "Just because their attempt to refute you didn't succeed doesn't mean that you've been proven right."

label: Evidence
body: This region’s swimmers generally swim during the day because they are too afraid of sharks to swim after dark. The swimmers feel safe swimming during daylight hours. All recent shark attacks on swimmers in the area have occurred during the day.

label: Conclusion (indicating that)
body: It is not more dangerous to swim here at night than during the day.

label: Evaluate
body: Why are the shark attacks only during the day? It could be that sharks are more aggressive during the day than during the night. But it also could be that no shark attacks occur at night because no swimmers swim during the night.

label: Denise
body: The only way to reduce crime is to make punishment strong and certain, so that people will be deterred from committing a crime.

label: Reshmi
body: The best way to reduce crime is to make educational opportunities more widespread, so people see that they can choose a non-crime lifestyle and still secure comfort.

label: Evaluation
body: Denise only makes one claim. Does Reshmi agree with that claim? No, he disagrees. Given that he thinks some other way to deal with crime is more effective than Denise's strategy, he definitely doesn't think that Denise's strategy is the only way to reduce crime. When there are no explicit statements upon which the two people agree (or disagree, if we're doing a Disagree question), then we should start asking ourselves about any assumptions the people might be making. Is there anything they're both assuming?

label: Goal
body: It seems like the overlap is something like, "Crime should be reduced? There are ways to reduce crime?"

label: Conclusion
body: Acme Corporation offers unskilled workers excellent opportunities for advancement.

label: Evidence (as evidence)
body: The president of the Acme Corporation, Ms. Garon, worked as an assembly line worker, an entry level position requiring no special skills, when she first started at Acme.

label: Evaluate
body: We would probably react to this by thinking, "That's great for Ms. G, but is that a common thing? Or is she an unrepresentative sample of someone who started at the bottom and made it all the way to the top?" Could there be an alternate explanation (her Dad owns the company) that she was able to go from entry-level to president? Maybe her story wouldn't apply to most employees.

label: Goal
body: The author wants Ms. Garon's story to seem indicative of a company that gives employees the opportunity to come in, unskilled, and ultimately climb the ranks to upper management. We need to pick an answer suggesting that the company doesn't have a lot of upward mobility, or an answer that makes an excuse for Ms. G's upward mobility.

label: Evidence
body: However, a warbler sings a special M → S song when it molts (sheds its feathers). Other yellow warblers will not enter S → ~OWE the smaller core territory of a yellow warbler singing its molting song.

label: Conclusion
body: Therefore yellow warblers, have no M → ~CF competition for the food supply within the range of their restricted flying.

label: Evaluate
body: The argument assumes that if a ~OWE → ~CF molting warbler has no other warblers enter its core territory, then it has no competition for food.

label: Evidence
body: But television is expressly for the viewing public. Just as a company would be foolhardy not to consider consumers’ tastes when developing products, the TV producer must consider viewers‘ preferences.

label: Main Conclusion
body: So a producer is more like a CEO than like an artist.

label: Evaluate
body: Lana attacks Chinh’s comparison of television producers to great painters and argues instead that television producers are more like company CEOs. This suggests that the analogy made by Chinh is faulty.

label: Evidence
body: High consumption of sodium increases some people’s chances of developing heart disease. The potassium in plant foods helps to prevent sodium’s malign effects.

label: Conclusion
body: To maintain cardiac health without lowering sodium consumption, therefore, these people should eat fresh, rather than canned or frozen, fruit and vegetables.

label: Evaluate
body: The argument assumes that canned or frozen fruit and vegetables have less potassium than fresh fruit and vegetables.

label: Conclusion (therefore)
body: Dana intentionally killed the plant.

label: Evidence (since)
body: Dana intentionally watered the plant every other day, which was too much for a succulent that needs dry soil. The overwatering killed the plant.

label: Evaluation
body: Do we really know that Dana was trying to kill the plant? Maybe she just didn't know the rules for how often to water a succulent (I just learned them while reading this LSAT question). The fact that she was intentionally doing the thing that led to the plant's death doesn't mean that she was intentionally trying to be bring about the plant's death.

label: Goal
body: We'll need an example where someone deliberately does X, which happens to cause Y, and then the author concludes that the person was deliberately trying to cause Y (when it's possible they didn't realize that X would cause Y).

label: Evidence
body: This boulder is volcanic in origin and yet the rest of the rock in this area is sedimentary. This area was covered by southward-moving glaciers during the last ice age.

label: Conclusion
body: This boulder was probably deposited here, hundreds of miles from its geological birthplace, by a glacier.

label: Evaluate
body: Since glaciers once covered the area it is plausible that the bolder was deposited here by a glacier. For that to be the case there would need to be a source of volcanic rock north of the boulder.

label: Evaluation
body: If they're asking us to describe the 2nd person's response, they usually want us to assess whether the 2nd person took issue with 1st person's conclusion, one of her premises, or one of her assumptions. It seems here like Craig definitely disagrees with Rifka's conclusion. She says "we don't need to stop and ask for directions", he says "we do". (And I'd be willing to be that LSAC was proud of themselves for avoiding the male/female trope of the female who wants directions and the male who is too proud to admit that they're lost). It also kind of sounds like Craig disagrees with Rifka's assessment of whether or not they're lost too.

label: Goal
body: Craig is saying "we are lost, so we should stop and ask for directions". So the function of his comment is to pretty much disagree with everything Rifka said.

label: Evidence
body: Comedy and tragedy require that CT → MQC the moral qualities of major characters change during the course of the action.

label: Conclusion
body: Neither tragedy nor comedy can CT → ~SRL be classified as satirical literature or romance literature.

label: Evaluate
body: The argument assumes that SRL → ~MQC moral qualities of major MQC → ~SRL characters in romance literature and satirical literature do not change during the course of the action.

label: Evaluation
body: Wow. Frank just blew my mind. He took Lance's rule and redirected it back onto itself, making it blow up. It's almost like if I said, "There's only one rule you should live by: don't follow any rules." It would be a self-contradiction, since I'm telling you to follow a rule that says don't follow rules. Frank is pointing out that the statement "all universals have an exception" is itself a universal. So, according to that rule, it should have an exception (i.e. a counterexample). A counterexample to "all universals have an exception" is a universal that doesn't have an exception. I think I just made it more confusing by explaining it, but essentially Lance's rule contradicts itself.

label: Goal
body: Look for something saying that Frank pointed out how if you follow the logic of Lance's rule, it will invalidate that rule.

label: Evidence
body: Throughout a certain nation, electricity has actually become increasingly available to people in urban areas while energy production has been subsidized to help residents of rural areas gain access to electricity. Even with the subsidy, many of the most ~EA isolated rural populations still have no access to electricity (not everyone has access).

label: Conclusion
body: Thus, the energy subsidy has failed to ~AP achieve its intended purpose.

label: Evaluate
body: The argument assumes that the energy AP → EA policy achieved its intended purpose only if everyone has access to electricity.

label: Apparent Paradox
body: Heart attacks are most likely to occur on Mondays. The accepted explanation is that because Monday is the first day of the workweek, people feel more stress on Mondays than on other days. However, research shows that even unemployed retired people are more likely to have heart attacks on Mondays than on other days.

label: Evaluate
body: How can Monday being the first day of the workweek explain the greater incidence of heart attacks when unemployed retired people experience the same thing? Could be a legacy factor? If somehow people were influenced in certain ways because they had undergone the stress of those Mondays that might work. Or if the stress of family and friends who continued to work somehow influenced unemployed retired people that might work as well.

label: Evidence
body: We asked 100 entrepreneurs and 100 business managers to answer various questions and rate how confident they were that their responses were correct. While members of each group were overconfident, in general the entrepreneurs were much more so than the business managers.

label: Conclusion
body: This indicates that people who are especially overconfident are more likely to attempt to start a business in spite of the enormous odds against success than people who are less confident.

label: Evaluate
body: Notice the shift in subject between the evidence and the conclusion. The evidence compares the average amount of overconfidence of two groups, while the conclusion is about people who are especially overconfident. To strengthen the conclusion, the correct answer should discuss people who are especially overconfident.

label: Conclusion
body: The 4th floor lab must be cleaned out. If Agnes's proposal is approved, the 4th floor lab must be cleaned out. Only the proposals the director supports will be approved, and the director will support Agnes's proposal.

label: Evidence (since
body: In a study, smokers given the main ingredient in NoSmoke reported no decrease in cravings. There's only one other ingredient in NoSmoke.

label: Evaluation
body: This might seem pretty valid at first, but whenever we're doing Flaw and we see conditional language, we should examine the directionality to make sure the author is thinking through it properly. The conditional trigger word here is "only", which always indicates the Necessary condition (right-side of the arrow). Approved → Director Supports The author is reasoning, "Since Agnes's proposal is supported by the director, her proposal will be approved, hence the 4th floor lab will get cleaned out." His reasoning looks like "Director Supports → Approved", so he is doing an Illegal Reversal of the conditional logic.

label: Goal
body: When authors mess up conditional logic, the fancy name for it is confusing Necessary with Sufficient (or vice versa). The informal way to object to it is to say, "Hey, author, the right side doesn't guarantee the left side. i.e., It's possible that a proposal is supported by the director but never approved."

label: Evidence
body: Offering financial incentives to customers RDIR if they provide the e-mail addresses of their friends risks damaging the integrity of those relationships.

label: Conclusion
body: Offering such financial incentives to ~E customers is an unethical business practice.

label: Evaluate
body: The argument assumes that if a business RDIR → ~E practice encourages people to act in a way that risks damaging the integrity of their relationships, that business practice is unethical.

label: Glen
body: The primary role of law should be to create virtuous citizens, but when we emphasize law's purely procedural side, it makes people more concerned with personal rights and less concerned with society's welfare.

label: Sara
body: If the role of law were to create virtuous citizens, it would mean that the government was deciding which types of life were virtuous. That would be a worse situation than having a government that's overprotective of individual's rights.

label: Evaluation
body: Does Sara argue against either of Glen's explicit claims? Does she argue that emphasizing procedural law does not emphasize personal rights over societal well being? No, she seems to accept that part. She alludes to the idea that the government in this scenario might be overprotective of personal rights, which sounds like emphasis. Does she argue that law's primary role should not be to create virtuous citizens? Yes, it seems like she's arguing in that direction, because she thinks it's dangerous for the government to be trying to decide with types of lives are truly virtuous.

label: Goal
body: They seem to be fighting over whether law's primary role should be to create virtuous citizens, or whether it's better for a government to be overprotective of personal rights or better for a government to be deciding on what would make a virtuous citizen.

label: Evidence
body: Some credit card companies allow cardholders to skip payments for up to six months under certain circumstances. Finance charges accumulate during the skipped-payment period. The cost to the cardholder is much greater in the long-run.

label: Conclusion
body: It is almost never in a cardholder’s interest to skip payments.

label: Evaluate
body: The argument provides a long-term disadvantage that outweighs the short-term advantage of skipping payments.

label: Given
body: None of the students taking literature L → ~P are taking physics. Several of the students taking physics P ↢some↣ A are taking art. None of the students taking rhetoric R → ~P are taking physics.

label: Conclusion
body: Psychotherapists should never provide psychotherapy on talk shows.

label: Evidence
body: On a talk show, you're expected to entertain a broad audience, which is nearly always incompatible with providing high quality help.

label: Evaluation
body: We know our conclusion is that psychotherapists should never do something, so we need a rule about what psychotherapists should never do. Why should they never go on talk shows? It's almost always incompatible with providing high-quality help. So the rule could sound like, "you should never do something if you'll almost never be able to provide high-quality help." The question stem asks what must be assumed, so there are other necessary assumptions we could say: - psychotherapists appearing on talk shows sometimes provide therapy in the way they're expected to - medium-quality psychological help is not significantly helpful to broad audiences - when a psychotherapist appears on a talk show, the purpose involves at least some high-quality help

label: Goal
body: We want a conditional bridge like If it's almost always incompatible with high-quality help, then psychotherapists should never do it or anything else that would qualify as a Necessary Assumption.

label: Tania
body: A good art critic isn't fair/unbiased/disinterested. Art is a passion, so good criticism is always intertwined with the critic's emotion.

label: Monique
body: Art is not only a passion. The best art critics do approach their subjects passionately, but not from a personal bias type of passion, rather one based on general principles of aesthetics.

label: Evaluation
body: Does Monique disagree with any of Tania's four claims? Monique disagrees with the first and second claim: she's arguing that a good critic (the best ones) are fair/objective. They shed their own biases before rendering criticism. They're interested and passionate, but they're unbiased. Monique agrees that art is a passion, and potentially agrees that good art criticism is always infused with emotion (or at least passion).

label: Goal
body: It mainly came down to whether good art critics are objective or subjective, with Tania thinking that good critics are subjectively infused with emotion, while Monique argues that the best critics have shed their subjectively and are infused with passion for general (objective) aesthetics.

label: Apparent Paradox
body: The writing styles in works of high literary quality are not well suited to the avoidance of misinterpretation. For this reason, the writing in judicial decisions, which are primarily intended as determinations of law, is rarely of high literary quality. However, it is not uncommon to find writing of high literary quality in dissenting opinions, which are sometimes included in written decisions in cases heard by a panel of judges.

label: Intermediate Conclusion (Thus)
body: The important social function of positively reinforcing helpful behaviors can be served only if the helping person knows the source of the gratitude.

label: Evaluate
body: The reason why the writing in judicial decisions is rarely of high literary quality is that judicial decisions are intended as determinations of law. So to explain why dissenting opinions are sometimes of high literary quality, it would make sense to anticipate that dissenting opinions are not determinations of law.

label: Given
body: Without the intervention of ~I → E conservationists, squirrel monkeys will become extinct. But they will survive [not go FP → ~E extinct] if large tracts of second-growth forest habitat are preserved for them. Squirrel monkeys flourish in PSIF >> F second-growth forest because of the plentiful supply of their favorite insects and fruit.

label: Evaluate
body: The only common term are the logical opposites of "surviving vs. going extinct". If we realize we can represent that with the same term, ~E vs. E, then we'll see that the two conditionals chain together to give us this: ~I → E → ~FP FP → ~E → I The last claim is causal, and "flourishing" is more than just not-going-extinct. It's a particular type of surviving, so we don't want to equate with "survive vs. go extinct". So we'll just leave that last claim alone. The correct answer will probably reward us for recognizing the conditional chain.

label: Conclusion (thus)
body: The number of documents sealed with a lead seal was many times the number of remaining lead seals.

label: Evidence
body: There are about 40,000 lead seals that remain. Most lead seals would serve their purpose when the document was opened, and once they had served their purpose, most lead lead seals would be recast (i.e. recycled so that they could be used again).

label: Evaluate
body: This is a tough conclusion to disagree with. It's just saying that, "If we've found 40,000 lead seals that still remain, then there must have been many times that number of documents that were sealed with lead seals". Let's just say "3 times as many" to make this more concrete. That means that the author is claiming that if we've found 40,000 remaining lead seals, then there must have been at least 120,000 documents sealed with lead seals. Why? Because the author is assuming that lead seals got reused, because it cost money to make each one. She is thinking that they would make a lead seal, attach it to a document, that document would be opened (and thus the seal had served its purpose), and then the seal would be recast to be used again. If we were trying to fight the conclusion, we'd either have to say that a ton of these 40,000 lead seals that remain were never attached to a document, or we'd have to say that they were attached to a document but weren't recycled multiple times and used on several documents.

label: Goal
body: Since we want to strengthen, we want to counter those possible objections. We want to be more convinced that the remaining seals WERE attached to documents; the seals attached to documents WERE recycled multiple times.

label: Conclusion
body: In the long run, it is counterproductive for farmers to use insecticides.

label: Evidence
body: Farmers have to use greater and greater amounts of costly insecticides to control insect pests, since insects' resistance to insecticides increases with insecticide use.

label: Evaluate
body: Whenever we do Role or Main Conclusion, we prime our brains for the possibility of First Sentence Conclusions and Pivot/Rebuttal conclusions. This first sentence sounds like advice, so it seems like an author opinion, and thus could be our conclusion. Does the paragraph go on to support this first claim? Yes the second sentence gives a reason why it's bad in the long run to use insecticide: you have to use more and more, in the long run, and it's very costly.

label: Goal
body: Since they're asking us about the final claim, we'd say it's part of the Support / Evidence. (Since the first half of the final sentence starts with the word Because, we might be thinking the second half has to be a conclusion. But the words "since / because" can also be used in a causal context. When we say, "Because I have the flu, I have chills", that isn't a Premise/Conclusion relationship; it's a Cause/Effect relationship. That's what is happening in this final sentence as well).

label: Conclusion
body: Pliny can't be right about claiming that rainbows always occur opposite the sun.

label: Evidence
body: Pliny said a lot of crazy stuff (dog-headed people, shoulder-eyes, curing headaches with snails)

label: Evaluation
body: Hey, William, a broken clock is still right twice a day. Just because Pliny has said some patently false stuff before, that doesn't mean we get to assume that every time he claims something it's false. You'd be within reason to conclude that "His claim should be viewed with some initial suspicion", based on that previous rap sheet. But you can't assume that just because someone has lied / been wrong before, that they must be lying / incorrect in this case.

label: Goal
body: This is a form of Ad Hominem, attacking the source of the argument rather than the legitimacy of the ideas. When authors invalidate a point of view based on the source, it's almost always because the source has some ulterior motive / vested interest, or, as it is with this question, because the source's previous claims/behavior somehow undermine their present claim/behavior.

label: Statements
body: Causal Moving into food services may siphon off funds for existing operations Contrast Existing operations are time-proven successes. Food services is risky, volatile, higher inherent risk. Pharmaceuticals is less risky than food services.

label: Evaluate
body: The gist of this paragraph seems to be a rebuttal directed again a Plan. The company is considering a Plan to move into food services, and the author is being negative about that. It might steal money we need for our existing, successful operations. Meanwhile it's volatile and riskier than other options we have for expanding (such as pharmaceuticals).

label: Goal
body: We might anticipate a safely-worded rebuttal like, "We shouldn't move into food services."

label: Evidence
body: Adam has no experience in critiquing ~E essays.

label: Conclusion
body: Adam should not judge the contest. ~J

label: Evaluate
body: The argument assumes that if one J → E should judge an essay contest, then one should have experience critiquing essays.

label: Conclusion (thus)
body: If testing shows the 2nd ingredient doesn't decrease cravings, then NoSmoke does not reduce smokers' cravings.

label: Evidence
body: Human psychology is driven primarily by personal interaction.

label: Evaluation
body: This is a Famous Flaw called Part vs. Whole. Even if each part doesn't reduce cravings, the whole of NoSmoke (the combined chemistry of those two ingredients) might still reduce cravings. Analogy: A water manufacturer claimed that his product was wet. However, we tested all the hydrogen atoms and found they were not wet. Since the only other ingredient in water is oxygen atoms, if similar results are found for oxygen atoms, then we can conclude that water is not wet.

label: Goal
body: Look for Part vs. Whole language or something that expresses the potential objection of, "What if the combination of the two ingredients is critical for the cravings to be reduced?"

label: Opposing Evidence
body: Certain kinds of weeds can repel caterpillars from the garden.

label: Opposing Point
body: It is wise to allow certain kinds of weeds to grow among garden vegetables.

label: Evidence
body: It is wise to avoid unnecessary use of insecticides. For all we know, those kinds of weeds can deplete the soil of nutrients and moisture that garden crops depend on. Those kinds of weeds might even attract other kinds of damaging pests.

label: Conclusion
body: It is premature to accept the advice of researchers to allow certain kinds of weeds to grow among garden vegetables.

label: Conclusion
body: Consumer response to the print ads was probably worse than average, like the response for the website ads.

label: Evidence
body: We don't have any direct info about the print ads, but we ran a set of ads in print and on our website, and the response to the website ads was way worse than what's typical for website ads.

label: Evaluation
body: This seems to present a classic Comparison. The author assumes that "what was true for website will probably be true for print as well", without considering possible important differences that would lead the print ad to perform better than the website ad. Our job here is just to describe, though, so we just need to say the author got to her conclusion via a comparison.

label: Goal
body: The author concludes that something was likely true of X, since it was true for Y (which similar, but not identical, to X)

label: Apparent Paradox
body: Conservation officers justified their decision to remove a pack of ten coyotes from a small island by claiming that the coyotes, which preyed on wild cats and plover, were decimating the plover population and would soon wipe it out. After the coyotes were removed, however, the plover population plummeted dramatically, and within two years plover could no longer be found on the island.

label: Evaluate
body: In their attempt to make things better, the conservation officers made it worse. The question is, what did they forget to consider? If removing the coyotes was bad for the plover population, then coyotes must have been good for the population. Since coyotes preyed on plover, there must be something else that coyotes did that benefited plover.

label: Evidence
body: During a recession, a company can cut personnel costs either by laying off some employees without reducing the wages of remaining employees or by reducing the wages of all employees without laying off anyone. Both damage morale, but layoffs damage it less, since the aggrieved have, after all, left.

label: Conclusion (thus)
body: When companies must reduce personnel costs during recessions, they are likely to lay off employees.

label: Evaluate
body: Morale may only be one of many factors that companies consider when deciding whether to reduce wages for all employees or lay some employees off. They may also consider like the expected duration of the recession as well as the difficulty recruiting new employees once the recession ends.

label: Evidence
