body: There are far fewer independent ↑CB -cause→ ↓IB bookstores than there were 20 years ago, largely because chain bookstores prospered and multiplied during that time. The shortage of independent ↓IB -cause→ ↓VB bookstores has prevented the variety of readily available books from growing as much as it otherwise would have.

label: Conclusion
body: Chain bookstores’ success has ↓CB -cause→ ↓BC been to the detriment of book consumers.

label: Evaluate
body: The argument assumes that a ↓VB -cause→ ↓BC reduction in the variety of books available to consumers is to their [book consumers] detriment.

label: Conclusion
body: Critics are wrong; our concert series does have popular appeal

label: Evidence
body: Income from T-shirts and other memorabilia at our concerts is at least as much as that type of income for comparable concert series.

label: Evaluation
body: Given that the memorabilia income at this concert series is at least as much as the memorabilia income for similar concert series, how would we argue that this concert series does not have popular appeal? - We could say those other concert series aren't that popular either - We could say that you don't measure popular appeal by memorabilia sales - We could come up with some weird alternate explanation for why memorabilia sales are as high (maybe in our case it's not indicative of tons of people buying stuff, but rather a few people buying tons of stuff or really expensive stuff)

label: Goal
body: Tough to say where this is going. There are missing link assumptions that could be called out, and there are questions surrounding how fair a comparison this is. Look for stuff calling out a missing linking idea or raising an objection that would make the comparison feel like an apples and oranges one.

label: Given
body: The sun emits two types of ultraviolet radiation that damage skin: UV-A, which causes premature wrinkles, and UV-B, which causes sunburn. Until about ten years ago, sunscreens protected against UV-B radiation but not against UV-A radiation.

label: Evidence
body: Several scientific studies have CS → RI shown that, when participating in competitive sports, those people who have recently been experiencing major stress in their lives are several times more likely to suffer injuries [risks injury] than are other participants in competitive sports. Risking serious injury is RI → ~W unwise.

label: Conclusion
body: No sports activity should be S → ~W used [is wise to use] as a method for coping with stress.

label: Goal
body: Let's look for something like, "a potential objection to the conclusion that the author argues, by analogy, is a surmountable problem".

label: Evaluate
body: The argument assumes that no (CS → ~W) → (S → ~W) sports activity should be used [is wise to use] as a method for coping with stress if competitive sports should not be used [is not wise to use] as a method for coping with stress.

label: Evidence
body: Tent caterpillars' routes between their nests and potential food sources are marked with chemical traces called pheromones that the caterpillars leave behind. Routes from food sources back to the nest are marked more heavily than are merely exploratory routes that have failed to turn up a food source.

label: Conclusion (thus)
body: Tent caterpillars are apparently among the insect species that engage in communal foraging, which consists in the conveying of information concerning the location of food to other members of the colony, nest, or hive.

label: Evaluate
body: The argument assumes that the marking of routes by pheromones is intended to communicate a message to other caterpillars.

label: Conclusion (therefore)
body: Movies starring unknown actors are unlikely to do well.

label: Evidence
body: Many movies starring top actors will do well at the box office, since the actors are well known and loved.

label: Evaluation
body: The author appears to be committing an Illegal Negation. We can't argue, "Many short children love their moms. Children that are very tall therefore are unlikely to love their moms."

label: Goal
body: We need an argument that performs an illegal negation: Things that are type X have trait A. Thus, things that are not type X are unlikely to have trait A.

label: Given
body: As part of a new trend in the writing of history, an emphasis on the details of historical events and motivations has replaced the previous emphasis on overarching historical trends and movements, with the result that the latter are often overlooked. In consequence, the ominous parallels that may exist between historical trends and current trends are also overlooked, which lessens our ability to learn from history.

label: Evidence
body: Without trust there can be no EC → T meaningful emotional connection to another human being. Without meaningful emotional ~FI → EC connections to others we feel isolated.

label: Conclusion
body: The ability to trust other people H → T is essential to happiness.

label: Evaluate
body: The argument assumes that H → ~FI happiness requires that one not feel isolated.

label: Evidence
body: Of all the Arabic epic poems that have been popular at various times, only Sirat Bani Hilal is still publicly performed. Furthermore, while most other epics were only recited, Sirat Bani Hilal has usually been sung.

label: Conclusion
body: The musical character, therefore, is the main reason for its longevity.

label: Evaluate
body: The argument establishes a correlation a play still being performed publicly and being sung. But to assert that the relationship is causal goes too far.

label: Evidence
body: A charitable organization rarely gives its donors the right to vote on its policies. The inability to directly influence RV –causes→ EC [vote] how charities spend contributions makes potential donors feel less of an emotional connection to the charity.

label: Conclusion
body: Thus, most charities could RV –causes→ RM probably increase the amount of money they raise through donations by giving donors the right to vote.

label: Evaluate
body: The argument assumes that the EC –causes→ RM emotional connection a donor feels to a charity can influence how much money that charity will raise.

label: Evidence
body: You would not sacrifice one of your hands in order to possess the world. Your hands are more important than possessing the world. Your entire body is necessarily more important to you than your hands. You are ruining your health and harming your body in your quest for a treasure that is much less valuable than the whole world.

label: Conclusion
body: Your quest for the treasure is irrational.

label: Conclusion
body: People who take vitamin C supplements tend to be healthier than average.

label: Evidence
body: A study investigating the relationship between high doses of vitamin C and heart disease showed that people who regularly consume high doses of vitamin C supplements have a significantly lower than average risk of heart disease.

label: Evaluate
body: We're given a curious fact — why is there a correlation between high doses of vit C || lower risk of heart disease ? Does the author offer a causal explanation for the correlation? Not really. The conclusion isn't causal. It's just saying that ppl who take vit C supplements tend to be healthier than average. "Tend to be" is just a statistical claim, not a causal one. So we probably shouldn't be trying to attack this question like we would a causal argument (trying to think of Alternate Explanations for the curious fact or trying to hurt the plausibility of the causal storyline the author is selling us). So we can just think, in typical weaken fashion, "how can I accept the evidence but reject the conclusion?"

label: Goal
body: Given that ppl who take high doses of vit C have lower risk of heart disease, how can we say that ppl who take vitamin C do not tend to be healthier than average? Maybe most ppl who take vitamin C don't take high doses of it, so the evidence is irrelevant to the conclusion. Maybe most ppl who take vit C are good when it comes to heart disease, but have lots of other health problems (thus they wouldn't be healthier than average, overall).

label: George
body: Given that ballroom dancing was super unpopular in the 80's and early 90s, why is it exploding now?

label: Boris
body: It's because people started learning ballroom dances like the merengue and a few similar ones in 1995. Those dances are super popular, so other ballroom dances are also gaining popularity.

label: Evaluate
body: The first sentence isn't part of the argument (it's ascribed to some sociologists). Our author ends up disagreeing with this position. The "Although ..." part of the 2nd sentence is a concession to this opponent, so only the second half of the 2nd sentence is her premise. Thus, we have very little to look at or think about here. The author makes a move from, Because capitalism requires corporations, we know capitalism promotes communal ties.

label: Evaluation
body: Boris is trying to answer George's question of "Why did ballroom dancing become popular after a major lull in the 80s and early 90s?" What's wrong with Boris's explanation? He might be wrong, of course. Like most LSAT authors conjecturing some hypothesis, he sounds overly confident. Maybe he's failing to account for some other factor that is more responsible. Do we think George would be satisfied by Boris's answer? What could George possibly say in response to Boris to shoot down that explanation? He might ask, "why did people start learning the merengue and several related ballroom dances in 1995?" From that language, you can't quite tell if merengue is a ballroom dance, but the several related ballroom dances certainly are ballroom dances. Why did people start learning those in 1995?

label: Goal
body: Stay flexible. Look for something that sounds like a reasonable way George could push back against Boris's explanation.

label: Facts
body: Some scientists say that Neanderthals and Cro-Magnons are two different species. They lived in different environments but used the same tools. If you use similar tools → then you face same daily challenges. This suggests they were actually the same species, and their minor differences were due to different environments.

label: Evaluation
body: Correct answers to Must Be False almost always do one of two things: - contradict a conditional statement provided - contradict an inference we could make by combining 2 or more claims Is there a conditional statement? Yes. use similar tools → face same daily challenges A correct answer could say, "these two groups used similar tools but did not face same daily challenges" Are there any available inferences? Yes. Since we know Neanderthal's and Cro-Magnon's used the same tools, we can apply the conditional rule and infer that Neanderthal's and Cro-Magnon's faced the same daily challenges Since facing the same daily challenges suggests that the two species were members of the same species, we can infer that members of a given species tend to face similar daily challenges.

label: Goal
body: Look for an answer that says, "same tools, but NOT same daily challenges" or one saying "Neanderthal's and Cro-Magnon's did NOT face same daily challenges" or one saying "members of the same species do NOT tend to face same daily challenges" or anything else that contradicts something we were told

label: Given
body: A summer day is "pleasant" W + T<84°F → P if there are intermittent periods of wind and the temperature stays below 84°F (29°C) all afternoon. A summer day with high HH + (T>84°F or ~W) → O humidity levels is "oppressive" either if the temperature stays above 84°F (29°C) all afternoon or if there is no wind.

label: Evidence
body: In the past ten years the station has never finished better than fifth place in the ratings. The station’s manager has not responded to its dismal ratings by changing its musical format or any key personnel. The competition has often sought to respond to changing tastes in music and has aggressively recruited the region’s top radio personalities.

label: Conclusion
body: The local radio station will not win the regional ratings race this year.

label: Evaluate
body: The conclusion predicts that the local radio station will not win the regional ratings race. This is based on the fact that the radio station has never finished better than fifth place in the ratings in the past ten years and other evidence about what has happened in the past. However, the present is not doomed to forever repeat the past.

label: Conclusion
body: I can skip the step of sprinkling the live mussels with cornmeal.

label: Intermediate Conclusion (therefore)
body: The mussels available at seafood markets don't contain sand.

label: Premise (because)
body: The mussels available at seafood markets are farm raised.

label: Evaluate
body: This is a three part argument, so we have to look at both reasoning moves. There's definitely a missing link going from the premise to the intermediate conclusion, because both claims are about mussels available at seafood markets. If farm raised, then don't contain sand. The next reasoning move is "If mussels available at seafood markets don't contain sand, then I can skip the step of sprinkling the live mussels with cornmeal. That sounds like a pretty awkward missing link, so it's unlikely that we'll see an answer that looks like this. We could go into Objection mode (to prepare ourselves for a Defender answer): GIVEN THAT mussels available at seafood markets don't contain sand, HOW COULD WE ARGUE THAT the chef still needs to go through the first step of sprinkling the live mussels with cornmeal? The only thought that would come to my mind would be, "even if you don't need to sprinkle the cornmeal to eject the sand, maybe it serves some other purpose as well, like maybe it contributes to the flavor at the end or it helps the mussels cook properly?"

label: Goal
body: Look for an answer supplying a missing link or one ruling out a potential objection.

label: Conclusion
body: Allow bilirubin levels in newborn babies to remain high.

label: Evidence (since)
body: If bilirubin enters the brain, it might cause the tetanus that sometimes occurs in newborns. But the brain's own natural defenses normally prevent bilirubin from entering.

label: Evaluate
body: If we were playing the skeptic to the position of these 2nd doctors and trying to defend the idea of reducing high levels of bilirubin, what might we say in response to their argument? We could say, "I'm glad that the brain's natural defenses normally prevent bilirubin from entering the brain, but what about all the other cases in which the brain doesn't prevent the bilirubin from entering? Wouldn't it make sense to reduce high levels of bilirubin, just in case the brain doesn't do a good job of keeping it out?" We could say, "What's the harm in taking the bilirubin out, just to be on the safe side?"

label: Goal
body: The correct answer should make us feel better about the tradeoffs involved in deciding whether or not to reduce high bilirubin. It can tell us something bad about the decision to reduce the bilirubin (it's expensive / it has its own hazards / it's a risky procedure). Or it can tell us something good about the decision to let the child remain with bilirubin (it's actually good for your body to have high bilirubin, as long as it's not going into your brain / kids aren't really harmed by tetanus so if a kid ends up getting that from the bilirubin it's no big deal).

label: Conclusion
body: Modern capitalism promotes communal ties.

label: Evidence
body: Modern capitalism requires that there by large corporations.

label: Evidence (since)
body: Research has shown that adults with feelings of inferiority become more successful than those free of such anxieties. Participating in organized competitive athletics may increase a child's strength and coordination.

label: Evaluate
body: Whenever we read Role or Main Conclusion, we expect that the Conclusion will usually be the First Sentence or some sort of Rebuttal. This is the latter. In the second sentence, we get an attributed opinion, "as critics point out". The author then pivots away from that (but, yet, however), showing that she will go in a different direction. The word since always indicates a claim is supporting the other half of the sentence (top 4 support indicators are FABS = for, after all, because, since), and so we know the final claim is being supported by the 1st half of the final sentence. Also, the final sentence expresses the author's opinion using the word "should", making it a promising contender for the author's main conclusion.

label: Goal
body: We're being asked about the very first sentence. While not the major premise of the argument, it still is a potential good thing about children's athletic programs, so we can still count it as support for the conclusion. So let's look for something like "partial support for the conclusion that funding for children's athletic programs shouldn't be eliminated".

label: Given that ...
body: It's only hours after birth

label: How can it be that ...
body: Infants can already distinguish faces from other images (f.e. infants stare at face drawings longer than at blank ovals or scrambled-feature drawings)

label: Goal
body: Let's look for an answer that explains how infants seem to already know what a "face" is, despite the fact that they've only been alive a few hours (seemingly too soon to have learned anything). It's likely going to have to say that we have some knowledge of faces already "baked-in" to our mental software.

label: Phenomenon
body: Newborns distinguish faces from non-faces only hours after birth.

label: Goal
body: Find an answer that explains how this is possible despite no time to learn it.

label: The Puzzle
body: Babies distinguish face drawings from non-face drawings hours after they are born. They have not had time to learn this — they have barely been alive. So how can they tell?

label: Evaluate
body: The natural explanation: the ability is built in. Babies are born with the equipment to recognize faces; it does not have to be learned.

label: Goal
body: The right answer should make the observation sensible. Look for innate ability — that explains why even hours after birth, faces are recognized. Be careful of answers that just describe the data again (like "longer staring means more interest") without explaining the underlying ability.

label: Statements
body: When did the last ice age end in North America? We got one date by figuring out when warmth-adapted open-ground beetles replaced cold-adapted arctic beetles. We got a different date (500 years later), by figuring out when ice masses yielded to spruce forests.

label: Evaluate
body: Since Inference questions are all about us combining ideas that have Overlapping Concepts, we should be thinking about what we can derive by combining the two different dates for the end of the last ice age. The final sentence compares the two dates in terms of the 1st being 500 years earlier than the 2nd. So we could potentially say that the beetle stuff happened 500 years earlier than the spruce forest stuff?

label: Goal
body: If we assume that the sediment test and pollen grain tests yielded accurate results, it seems like we can derive that warmth-adapted open-ground beetles came back on the scene more than 500 years before ice masses receded and allowed spruce forests to come back.

label: Conclusion (So)
body: Once humans begin to tap into this tremendous source of creativity and innovation, many problems that today seem insurmountable will be within our ability to solve.

label: Intermediate Conclusion
body: Over 90% of the human brain currently serves no purpose.

label: Evidence (as is evident from the fact)
body: Many people with significant brain damage show no discernible adverse effects.

label: Evaluate
body: We have a three part argument structure: Premise → Intermediate Conc → Main Conc So we need to consider flaws occurring with each of those reasoning moves. Given that … many people with lots of brain damage show no discernible adverse effects, Should we accept that … over 90% of the brain currently serves no purpose? It seems like a really big leap to go from “people can act totally normally even though they have significant brain damage” to “90% of the brain is useless”. How do we know it’s 90%, exactly? Given that … 90% of the brain currently serves to purpose, Should we accept that … once we tap into this unused part of the brain, many currently-unsolvable problems will be solved? The author must be assuming that this unused portion of the brain can be used and that using it would somehow expand our problem-solving capabilities.

label: Goal
body: Look for an answer complaining that the 90% figure seems to come out of nowhere, or look for an answer sounding skeptical that this “unused” part of our brain would provide us with more insight / value / brain power were we to tap into it.

label: Conclusion (warrant)
body: We should accept quantum theory.

label: Evidence
body: There have been rigorous attempts to show that quantum theory's predictions are inaccurate, but in all cases quantum theory's predictions were shown to be accurate within the generally accepted statistical margin of error. Meanwhile, none of quantum theory's competitors can boast that level of predictive success.

label: Evaluate
body: We generally want to prephrase "IF premise, THEN conclusion" linking ideas on Principle-Strengthen questions. If ... Then ... a theory's predictions have we should been very accurate, more so accept that than those of its competitors theory

label: Goal
body: Let's look for a conditional whose trigger matches stuff we know about Quantum Theory, and whose outcome helps us to argue that "we should accept Quantum Theory".

label: Conclusion
body: The obligation to express gratitude cannot be fulfilled anonymously.

label: Conclusion (therefore)
body: Some people who have a sense of social justice do not engage in political action.

label: Evaluate
body: Whenever we do Main Conclusion or Role (but only for these two question types), we prime our brain before reading the paragraph with the reminder that LSAC usually puts the Main Conclusion earlier than at least some of the Supporting ideas. We listen specifically for "1st Sentence Conclusions" and "Rebuttal Conclusions". Does this first sentence sound like the author expressing an opinion? Yeah, sure. She's saying "when you're obligated to thank someone, you can't do it anonymously. They need to know it's you who's thanking them." That sounds like an opinion. Does she go on to try to convince us that we should let people know that it's us who are thanking them? She does. She says that human psychology is still driven by personal interaction (the opposite of anonymous interaction). The social value of expressing thanks can be served only if the thankee knows who the thanker is. Since the first sentence was an opinion and then the rest of the paragraph supports that opinion, we know we (once again) have a First Sentence Conclusion on Main Conclusion / Role.

label: Goal
body: Now we look at which claim the question stem is asking about and see they're asking about the first sentence. So let's look for an answer that says or means Main Conclusion.

label: Statements
body: conditional (only) Museum → 20th century work displays it Museum → On loan from private collector displays it or in museum's perm collection conditional (all) Museum's → Prints available in perm collection museum store quantifier (some) Some ~Museum's prints available in Perm Collection museum store Hopper's Nighthawks: not part of museum's permanent collection, but a print of it is sold in the museum store.

label: Evaluate
body: We have three-ish conditional ideas, followed by some specific facts, so we have a couple jobs: 1. Do any of these conditionals chain together? 2. Can we apply any of these conditional rules (or their contrapositives) to the specific facts? We seem to have a bit of a chain, because "museum's permanent collection" is an overlapping idea in the 1st and 2nd sentence. We know there are some 20th century works on display that are from the museum's permanent collection and thus whose prints can be purchased in the museum store. Can we infer anything about Nighthawks? The fact that it's not in the permanent connection doesn't really tell us anything. We don't have any rule triggered by "not in permanent connection". And the fact that its print is available in the museum store tells us nothing, because that's just the right side of one of our conditional rules.

label: Goal
body: It doesn't look like we can infer anything additional about Nighthawks. Maybe the correct answer will test the connection between the 1st and 2nd sentence, made possible by the overlap of "in the museum's permanent collection". But ultimately we're just looking for the most provable answer we can find.

label: Conclusion
body: Drinking three glasses of wine daily would not benefit health overall.

label: Evidence (since)
body: The decrease in the risk of stroke associated with that level of consumption is negated by its associated increased risk of sudden heart attack. A recent study said that consuming three glasses of wine daily substantially decreases risk of stroke. But ... the people who are most likely to drink three glasses in one day are binge drinkers, who are more likely to die from sudden heart attacks than are other drinkers.

label: Evaluate
body: Given that ... the people who are most likely to drink three glasses of wine in a day are binge drinkers, who are more likely to die from sudden heart attacks, How could we still argue that ... drinking three glasses of wine daily would benefit health overall? This is a weird argument, because it's shooting down a plan by saying that the people who are most likely to currently be abiding by the plan have some risk factor associated with them. But would the plan be good for people who don't have that risk factor? Suppose I said, "Exercising at least 2 hours every day would benefit health overall" and someone said, "No it wouldn't, because the people who are most likely to exercise 2 hours each day are people who serve in the military, and the average life span of people in the military is lower than that of people not in the military". We'd be like ... okay, but the lifespan of military people isn't lower because of the exercise. It's because of the hazards of being in the military. If Jane Doe were to adopt the exercise plan without enlisting in the military, wouldn't it benefit her health? Similarly, the reason binge drinkers are more likely to die of sudden heart attacks isn't because they drink 3 glasses of wine in one day. It's because they go on all out benders and drink themselves to within an inch of alcohol poisoning, slowly corroding their livers. If Jane Doe were to adopt the 3 glasses of wine a day plan, without becoming a binge drinker, wouldn't it still benefit her health?

label: Goal
body: Look for an answer objecting that the critics are shooting down the claim that "X benefits health" by saying "the people who are currently most likely to do X have some health risk attached to them (even though the health risk isn't caused by X)".

label: Conclusion (Thus)
body: Recent scientific research may also become part of everyone's intellectual heritage.

label: Counterpoint
body: Even though recent scientific research requires language that seems esoteric (hard to understand) to most modern readers,

label: Intermediate Conc (this shows that)
body: Barriers to communication between scientists and the public are not impermeable.

label: Evidence
body: Netwon's Principia was not understandable to most of its contemporaneous audience, but a basic understanding of Newton's ideas eventually spread globally and it served as the cornerstone of physics for over two centuries.

label: Evaluate
body: They're asking us about the grammatically inessential modifier in the final sentence, which contains our Main Conclusion. When a Main Conclusion packages in a noun modifier, we treat that modifier as a fact. For example, given this conclusion ... Thus, Dan's attorney, who went to Harvard, is clearly capable of solving this tax problem. .... we would think that it's being factually presented to us that Dan's attorney went to Harvard, whereas the Conclusion is presenting the speculative opinion that she would clearly be capable of solving this tax problem. The claim from the last sentence that they're asking us about is technically an Opposing idea, since the conclusion is that "recent science may one day be part of everyone's intellectual heritage" whereas the claim we're being asked about is saying "recent science is inscrutably confusing to most modern readers". That undermines the idea that this modern science will ultimately be absorbed into our common wisdom. However, the author's argument is trying to show by analogy that science that is initially too confusing for the masses (like Newton's was) can still eventually be accepted.

label: Evidence
body: Only a minority of those who engage in political action do so out of a sense of social justice. (rephrased: most people who engage in political action do not do so out of a sense of social justice)

label: Evaluate
body: The conclusion is just claiming that there is at least one person who has a sense of social justice, but doesn't engage in political action. The evidence tells us about people who engage in political action, and have a sense of social justice (that's the minority) and it tells us about people who engage in political action and don't have a sense of social justice (the majority). But the evidence never talks about people who don't engage in political action.

label: Goal
body: Since the premise and the conclusion are repeating the same symbols (engaging in political action / sense of social justice), it makes sense to write this algebraic recipe: CONC: Some A's are not B some [social justice] are not [political action] EVID: Only a minority of B's are A only a small number of [political action] are [social justice] We may have to recognize the evidence turned from negative to positive. Saying "only a minority of B's are A" is equivalent to saying "most B's are not A".

label: Conclusion (should = opinion)
body: University education should emphasize the liberal arts rather than the more narrow kind of technical training that prepares one for a particular sort of job.

label: Evidence (this is because)
body: The reasoning skills one acquires from a liberal arts education allow one to adapt to new intellectual challenges and thus to perform jobs for which one has received no specialized training.

label: Evaluate
body: How would an opponent push back at this argument and argue that we shouldn't emphasize liberal arts? Maybe he would say that the primary purpose of university education is to make students employable, and they're much more employable if they have a narrow kind of technical training. He could argue that most jobs don't need people who can adapt to new intellectual challenges; they need people with narrow technical expertise.

label: Goal
body: To strengthen the argument we could try to rule out one of these objections (saying that there are lots of jobs that value an employee who can adapt to new intellectual challenges). However, there is also a broader Net Gain / Loss issue at play in this argument. Whenever an author's conclusion is making a recommendation, they're implicitly saying "the world where you follow my advice is on the whole better than the world where you don't." So we could also strengthen the argument by hearing of any other benefit we would get by emphasizing liberal arts over technical training (or at least by ruling out a negative).

label: Hypothesis
body: The mysterious Maltese limestone tracks were made by animal-drawn carts around 1000 B.C.

label: Evidence
body: They wander around, sometimes disappearing under modern structures. It's thought that they may have connected settlements or water sources.

label: Evaluate
body: It's the #1 pattern on Strengthen / Weaken: explain curious fact. CURIOUS FACT: What are these ancient tracks all about? AUTHOR'S HYPOTHESIS: They were made around 1000 B.C. by animal-drawn carts. We can strengthen by Ruling Out an Alternate Hypothesis or by making the Author's Hypothesis More Plausible. Strengthen questions more often do the latter.

label: Goal
body: Find an answer that makes it more plausible that these tracks came from animal-drawn carts around the year 1000 B.C. (or one that rules out an alternate explanation for the tracks).

label: Hypothesis
body: The Maltese tracks were made by animal-drawn carts around 1000 B.C.

label: Goal
body: Find an answer that places animals in the area at that time.

label: The Argument
body: An archaeologist hypothesizes that the mysterious tracks on Malta were made by animal-drawn carts around 1000 B.C. The argument is built on physical appearance — the kind of wear pattern, surroundings, and so on.

label: Evaluate
body: The hypothesis makes two specific claims: (1) animals (not humans alone) drew the carts, and (2) the tracks date to about 1000 B.C. To strengthen, we want evidence that ties animals to the right place at the right time.

label: Goal
body: Look for an answer that puts animals near the tracks at around 1000 B.C. Ideally something direct — like physical evidence of animals in the area at that period.

label: Statements
body: The demand for out-of-print books is increasing. causal (spurred) The rise of the Internet, specifically the search capabilities that make it easier to locate out-of-print books caused the increasing demand for out-of-print books.

label: Evaluate
body: We have three claims: a change that has occurred, the catalyst for the change, and the specific aspect of the catalyst that is the causal difference-maker. We could potentially assemble these three ideas into a Causal Chain rise of ⇢ easier to locate ⇢ demand internet out-of-print books increasing

label: Goal
body: Usually when an Inference paragraph involves causal relationships, the correct answer is a safely worded restatement of that causal connection. Maybe we'll see something like, "making it easier to find something can influence how much that thing is in demand". Ultimately, though, our job is just to find the most provable answer. We want to be wary of language that's too strong, unknown comparisons, and out of scope ideas.

label: Conclusion
body: Farmers would be better off using the mix of paper and manure than using paper or manure alone.

label: Evidence
body: Paper is ineffective as a mulch to guard against soil erosion, but paper and manure is very effective. In test plots, the mixture significantly decreased the amount of soil erosion. And paper costs roughly the same as manure.

label: Evaluate
body: In order to argue against this conclusion, we have to try to argue that farmers would be better off "just using paper" or "just using manure". The argument does a decent job of talking us out of "just using paper'". After all, paper is super ineffective at guarding against soil erosion. But we never hear anything about the "just use manure" option. We know that the paper/manure mix is very effective, but maybe "just manure" is even more effective. We're not saving any money by adding paper to manure (since they cost roughly the same), so what's the benefit of adding paper? Why not just use manure.

label: Goal
body: Find the assumption that imagists' poems do not represent sequences of events — so they become a counterexample to Lessing.

label: Goal
body: To complete this question stem with something like our objection, we'd say that the author provides no evidence that "using manure alone wouldn't be at least as good as, if not better than, using a manure/paper mix". provides no evidence that X is the same as takes for granted that X presumes, without providing justification that X fails to establish X The top one is very uncommon, but those bottom three all mean "the argument had to assume X", so we can read these answer choices as though we're doing Necessary Assumption.

label: Statements
body: causal (the effects are profound / complex) Technology ⇢ language ⇢ culture causal (X changed Y, in turn made Z) telegraph, changed the way telephone, ⇢ people speak to television one another loosening of relationships Email ⇢ language usage ⇢ between people rules more casual

label: Evaluate / Goal
body: The correct answer on Proposition / Generalization questions is usually a very safely worded takeaway that summarize or reinforces the Causal relationship identified in the passage. In this case, the statements emphasized the impact of technology (such as email) on language (loosening of the rules), and the effect of language on culture (relationships are more casual). There is a causal chain from Technology to Culture / Interpersonal Relationships, so the answer may reward us for seeing that A ⇢ B ⇢ C connection.

label: Conclusion
body: Raising the minimum wage to the level recently proposed will actually hurt, rather than help, workers with low incomes.

label: Evidence
body: As the minimum wage increases, businesses must compensate for higher wage costs by increasing prices for the goods and services that low-income workers must buy but can already barely afford.

label: Evaluate
body: There are no new ideas in this conclusion that might help us identify a Missing Link. Instead, consider the Anti-conclusion: Given that prices of goods will go up and it's hard enough to buy them already, how could we still argue that a minimum wage increase would help? What if their wages go up more than the cost of goods? In that case, the wage hike could still be a net positive for workers.

label: Goal
body: Look for an answer that neutralizes this objection by saying that the wages won't increase more than the cost of goods.

label: Conclusion
body: Exercise can actually increase one's life span.

label: Evidence
body: In a study of several hundred similar aged people, people who exercised regularly during the study were much less likely to die.

label: Evaluate
body: Because the evidence involves a Curious Comparison (people who were X were much less likely to be Y) and the evidence uses a Causal verb (X can actually increase Y), we can use our Curious Fact / Explanation mindset. Curious Fact ... why was there a correlation between exercising regularly and living longer? Author's Explanation ... exercising is causing them to live longer We want to consider Alternate Explanations and how plausible the Author's Explanation is. Whenever there's a correlation between two factors (in this case, regular exercise and living longer), authors will conclude one thing caused the other. We need to consider Reverse Causality and Third Factor alternate explanations. In this instance, Reverse Causality doesn't make any sense. We couldn't argue that not dying caused them to exercise regularly. But it makes sense to argue there could be a Third Factor, such as lack of illness, that is creating the correlation. People who are sick / enfeebled are both less likely to exercise regularly and more likely to die.

label: Goal
body: Since this is Strengthen, we need an answer choice to rule out an alternate explanation for the correlation, or increase the plausibility that exercise can increase life span.

label: Levin's Implied Conclusion
body: We shouldn't set regulatory limits based on long-term average (we should set them based on peak emission levels).

label: Levin's Evidence
body: Short periods of high pollution emissions pose dangers to the environment. Your proposal would be like dealing with the speed limit by thinking about a driver's average speed (including traffic slowdowns and stoplights), rather than thinking about their peak speed.

label: Evaluate
body: We don't need to breakdown Levin's argument at all. We just need to understand the analogy that is being made between speed limits and regulatory limits, so that we can match part to part. Limits on Emission | Speed Limits calculate emissions calculate speed by by long-term average avg speed (including traffic / stoplights) calculate emissions calculate speed by by peak levels peak speed short periods of short periods of high pollution high driving speeds emissions are are dangerous dangerous

label: Goal
body: The question stem wants to know what we would match up with "time spend at a stoplight". Well, at a stoplight, a vehicle's speed is zero miles/km per hour. So, by analogy, we'd be talking about a power plants emissions being zero. Let's look for something like, "a period during which power plants pollution emissions are zero", which would presumably be when the plant is closed or non-operational for whatever reason.

label: Conclusion
body: The ice ages were caused by the usually rich growth of vegetation worldwide.

label: Evidence
body: Vegetation converts CO2 into O2, so a rich growth of vegetation would deplete the CO2 in the atmosphere. CO2 helps to retain the sun's heat, so if the CO2 is depleted, then the earth cools significantly, thereby causing an ice age.

label: Information
body: Cultural anthropological theory falls into two camps: 1. focus on everyday behavior, which is a response to human needs in a given environment. 2. focus on systems of meanings that give way to thoughts, rituals, and mythology. It should employ both of these and do a third, often neglected one: 3. see community as a set of individuals whose actions are the essence of everyday life.

label: Evaluate
body: That's a tough paragraph to grasp. There aren't any apparent Conditional, Causal, or Mathematical keywords to make us think in those directions. There is a Pivot (however), and there is an implicit Comparative dynamic to it. So the answer will probably have something to do with comparing these three approaches to each other. Atypically, there is also a normative opinion! The paragraph says cultural anthropologists should employ both and also use this third neglected dimension.

label: Goal
body: We could probably say something like the author thinks that "cultural anthropologists should be using at least three approaches", or that "the 3rd approach isn't being adequately captured by the 1st or 2nd approach". But this one seems hard to anticipate. We'll just look for the most provable answer.

label: Evaluate
body: Whenever we do a Main Conclusion or Role question, we prime our brains before reading the paragraph with the crucial reminder that the conclusion is usually earlier than the evidence! That's the opposite of arguments in all the other question types, where the conclusion is usually the final claim (or at least in the final sentence). They are trying to hide the conclusion from us on Main Conclusion and Role, so we remind ourselves of the two big patterns: - conclusion is the 1st sentence - conclusion is some sort of "I disagree" rebuttal When we read the first sentence, if it sounds like the author's opinion, and then the rest of the paragraph goes on to support that opinion, then we know the first claim was the Main Conclusion. In this case, the first sentence doesn't sound quite like an opinion, because "there is little doubt" sounds like the author is reporting an established fact. But "there is little doubt" still means "we're pretty darn sure", not "we're sure". Also, the rest of the paragraph is just as scientific and factual, so we still need to pick whichever claim sits at the top of the hierarchy of ideas. The first sentence gives us the causal chain that all the other ideas fit into. CONCLUSION rich growth -—--—--—--—--—--—--—--—--> ice of vegetation ages EVIDENCE rich growth --> CO2 to --> less CO2 -—-> ice of vegetation O2 retaining heat age

label: Goal
body: Let's look for an answer that matches the meaning of the first sentence.

label: Conclusion
body: This classification is inappropriate. i.e. The Time Machine should not be classified as science fiction.

label: Evidence (because)
body: The Time Machine has a quality that science fiction generally lacks (compelling characters worth caring about).

label: Evaluate
body: The argument core here is very simple: If a book has a then inappropriate quality that genre X → to classify the book generally lacks as part of genre X The hard part is finding those elements. The word But is a pivot indicator that means we're starting to hear the Author's Argument. However, we might hear Conclusion then Support. We might hear Support then Conclusion. The first claim after But is "this classification is inappropriate". The word "inappropriate" is an opinion indicator and this claim feels like an "I disagree" rebuttal, both of which suggest that this is the Conclusion. The next word is "because", which is a support indicator (f.a.b.s). This confirms that the first claim after But was indeed the Conclusion. When conclusions have pronouns in them ("this classification is inappropriate"), we need to import the referenced language. "Classifying Time Machine as sci-fi is inappropriate". We can interchangeably switch in other normative language like 'should not' for 'inappropriate'. "We shouldn't classify Time Machine as sci-fi." What's the support for this conclusion? What is it about Time Machine that doesn't match sci-fi? It has compelling characters, which sci-fi generally lacks.

label: Goal
body: Let's find an answer that allows us to prove that Time Machine shouldn't be classified as sci-fi. Most likely it will be based on possessing a trait that sci-fi generally lacks.

label: Conclusion
body: The contemporary novel is incapable of making important new contributions.

label: Evidence (the evidence is clear)
body: Contemporary psychological novels have been failures. Contemporary action novels lack social significance. Contemporary romance novels are stale and formulaic.

label: Evaluate
body: There are missing link assumptions being made here: "if failure, can't make important new contribution" "if lacks social significance, can't make important new contribution" "if stale and formulaic, can't make important new contribution" But those missing link assumptions would be pretty impossible to replicate on an analogous parallel flaw. So we should probably think instead about the fact that this argument's conclusion is about all contemporary novels, whereas the evidence only deals with psychological, action, and romance. Are those the only three types of contemporary novels?

label: Goal
body: Let's look for a broad conclusion: All X's are Y Then let's look for premises that deal with subtypes of X, but not necessarily all subtypes. And they should be saying things that aren't necessarily revealing in terms of whether or not that qualifies as Y. The evidence is clear. Blue X's are A. Red X's are B. Green X's are C.

label: Background
body: The reported crime rate (crimes per 100,000 people) has gone up a bunch over the last 20 years, countrywide.

label: Surprising Claim
body: A bunch of different surveys of randomly selected citizens finds that people think that the total number of crimes has been lower recently than it was 20 years ago.

label: Evaluate
body: Given That the crime rate has been rising Why is it That people think fewer crimes have been committed? I don't try to do too much predicting on Paradox questions, but a couple things stick out to me: - the first fact was about Reported crimes, whereas the survey is about actual crimes. Maybe there's a difference between how many crimes get reported and how many crimes people perceive existing. - the first fact is a crime rate, the second fact is about total number, so it's possible there are fewer crimes but divided by a shrinking population, you'd still get a higher crime rate. - the second fact is surveys of randomly selected citizens, whereas the first is a countrywide tabulation. It's possible that the mismatch is a geographic accident of where these random surveys were taken (maybe they were taken in lower-crime areas).

label: Goal
body: Find a way to reconcile a higher reported crime rate with a survey that shows people feel like there are fewer total crimes.

label: Conclusion (Thus)
body: The new method is unlikely to be useful.

label: Evidence (since)
body: The new method can predict an earthquake is coming, but it can only estimate the strength within a range of 2.5 points on the Richter scale. That size of a difference can be the difference between a barely noticeable quake and hugely damaging one.

label: Evaluate
body: We're trying to prove that the new method is unlikely to be useful. Did we ever define that term? Did the evidence provide a proving mechanism that lets us say, "If X applies, then it's unlikely to be useful?" No, so we know the correct answer will need to be structured that way. What do we know about the new method that sounds not-useful? It can't predict whether we're going to have a barely noticeable quake or a hugely damaging quake.

label: Goal
body: So, we should look for a linking idea like "If method can't differentiate between marginally perceptible and considerably damaging, then unlikely to be useful". We can be flexible on the trigger idea, but we need this answer to help us prove "unlikely to be useful".

label: Evidence (since)
body: If changing to online then we would increase the → shouldn't change cost of publication to online A benefactor will cover the costs of conversion, and once the conversion is made, the cost of publication per issue is much lower.

label: Evaluate
body: Any time we're doing Flaw and see conditional logic (only if), we should start thinking there's a 90% or better chance they're going to mess up the conditional logic and test us on the #1 famous flaw, Necessary vs. Sufficient. When we see the "only if" in the first sentence, we can mentally or physically diagram what this conditional relationship is saying. We know that "if" indicates an idea that goes on the left of the arrow but that "only if" indicates an idea that goes on the right of the arrow, so we'd get Should change to online → doesn't increase cost At this point, we would expect the author to apply this conditional rule in a backwards or opposite fashion. OPPOSITE Bob says we shouldn't change to online. Thus, he must think that it would increase cost. REVERSAL Bob says It doesn't increase our cost to switch. Thus, we should change to online. The argument we read did the illegal reversal. It establishes that the cost of publication will not go up (since a donor will cover the cost of converting to online and the per issue costs will be lower with online). And then it thinks we can therefore conclude that we should switch to online.

label: Goal
body: We can look for an answer saying, "not-increasing costs" was Necessary in order for us to make the switch, but it wasn't identified as being Sufficient to guarantee we should make the switch. After all, there may be other things to consider (some of them may also be necessary). There might be other considerations, like If it would cause us → shouldn't switch to lose any readers to online If it would cause us → shouldn't switch to lose any sponsors to online

label: Clarissa's 1st Claim
body: The natural sciences wouldn't have made such progress without the power of math. Does Myungsook disagree? Is he saying that natural sciences would have made this progress even without math? Not really. It doesn't seem like M's directly addressing how much progress natural science would / wouldn't have made.

label: Clarissa's 2nd Claim
body: No observation is worth serious attention unless it is stated precisely in quantitative terms. Does Myungsook disagree? Is he saying that even if something isn't yet stated precisely in quantitative terms, an observation could still be worthy of serious attention? Yes, M does seem to be saying that. M's saying 1st you "explore" the observations themselves (you give them serious attention). Stating them precisely in quantitative terms is the last task. So M thinks that observations can be worthy of serious attention, even before they're converted precisely to numbers.

label: Goal
body: Let's look for something like Clarissa's 2nd claim: whether or not you have to wait until something is stated precisely in quantitative terms in order to find it worthy of serious attention, or if it's worth exploring before it's been converted to numbers.

label: Conclusion
body: Assuming that the most populous fish species in the pond is the bullhead catfish (BC) then it must be that the local fishing guide believes that the BC has adapted best to living in polluted water.

label: Evidence
body: That pond has been polluted for years, and the fishing guide says that "the most populous fish species in the pond is also the one that has adapted best to living in polluted water".

label: Evaluate
body: At first it's pretty hard to disagree with this logic. You have a rule that says "Most populous → best adapted", and so it's appropriate to say that if BC is most populous, then BC is best adapted. I think the problem is that the conclusion specifically accuses the local fishing guide of believing something. Even if that something would be a true inference, we can't prove that some entity believes it. The author is taking the fishing guide's belief that "most populous → best adapted", applying it to the finding of some recent studies to derive a possible inference, but then accusing the fishing guide of believing that inference. How do we know the fishing guide is aware of these recent studies, or that the fishing guide trusts them enough to form beliefs off of them? This type of flaw is assuming that someone believes an Implication of a Belief. For example, it's flawed to say, "Lois Lane knows she went skiing with Clark Kent. Clark Kent is Superman. So, Lois Lane knows she went skiing with Superman." Even though we know that she went skiing with Superman, she might not know that missing link, that CK = Superman.

label: Goal
body: Look for an answer saying that local fishing guide might not know about these studies, might not trust them, might know of other studies that are more compelling, etc .... any possibility in which the recent studies say that BC is the most populous fish, but the local fishing guide have not formed a belief that BC has adapted the best to pollution.

label: Conclusion (conclude, therefore)
body: The work done in Department F subjects workers to higher stress levels than does the work in the other departments in the company.j

label: Evidence
body: Department F has a higher percentage of workers with syndrome X than does any other department, and syndrome X is often attributed to stress.

label: Evaluate
body: This argument follows a common pattern: - it presents a Curious Fact (almost always an asymmetric comparison) in the evidence - the conclusion assumes or states a causal explanation for that curious fact. Curious Fact ... why do workers in Dept F have a higher rate of getting this syndrome that's associated with stress? Author's Explanation ... it must be that workers in Dept F undergo more stress than do workers in other departments. We always approach Explain Curious Fact arguments looking at the same two pressure points: - Alternate Explanations for the curious fact - the plausibility of the Author's Explanation What could be an alternate reason for why people in Dept F have higher rates of this syndrome? - maybe the syndrome isn't really caused by stress; it's caused by something else like lack of sleep, and people in Dept F get less sleep. - maybe it is caused by stress, but the stress isn't coming from Dept F; it's just that the workers who work in Dept F have more stressful lives for other reasons (maybe Dept F is full of parents of young children, whereas the other departments more often have people without children or with low-maintenance children).

label: Evidence
body: (True, the tapes were only released after the poet had died and only released to the poet's official biographer) But it was still divulging patient information. It doesn't matter that the poet wrote in a confessional manner (the poet still has a right to privacy). It makes no difference that the poet told the psychiatrist he could do whatever he wants with the tapes (the Hippocratic oath still constrains the psychiatrist from divulging patient information).

label: Goal
body: Since this is Strengthen, we would want an answer to rule out an Alternate Explanation. Or, more commonly on Strengthen, we would want it to increase the plausibility of the Author's Explanation. The most common way to increase plausibility of a Cause / Effect connection on LSAT is to hear about data points that show No Cause / No Effect (i.e. when the cause was absent, the effect was absent). So if we heard something like "once people leave Department F, the syndrome goes away", that would heavily suggest that Department F was the causal difference-maker responsible for the syndrome.

label: Conclusion: As a result
body: Metallic mirrors cannot be used in applications in which minimizing energy loss is important.

label: Evidence: Because
body: Metallic mirrors absorb some light. When light strikes a metallic mirror, electrons in the mirror move, using energy and dimming the reflected image.

label: Intermediate Conclusion
body: They (metallic mirrors) waste energy.

label: Evaluate
body: In most Main Conclusion questions, the main conclusion is somewhere in the first few lines of the argument, typically with no conclusion indicator words to draw you in. That trend makes it easy to mistake the Intermediate conclusion in this argument for the Main Conclusion. But if you look at the structure language that connects the second sentence to the third (As a result), you can see that claim three follows from claim two. It also seems to follow from claim one, but if you're unsure about that, you can try the Support test. Metallic mirrors waste energy. Why? Because metallic mirrors cannot be used in applications in which minimizing energy loss is important. That doesn't make a lot of sense. Metallic mirrors cannot be used in applications in which minimizing energy loss is important. Why? Because metallic mirrors waste energy. Much better.

label: Goal
body: Find an answer that paraphrases the final claim. It may or may not include the example of high-powered lasers, since that's essentially a clarifying example given to show the reader what types of applications require minimizing energy loss.

label: Conclusion (so)
body: Confronting your fears probably increases your self-confidence.

label: Evidence
body: People who participate in risky sports often do so to confront their fears. Rock climbers are more likely than others to have once suffered from a fear of heights. People who participate in risky sports also have more self-confidence than others.

label: Evaluate
body: The author is concluding a causal connection (X increases Y) between two things (confronting fear / higher self-confidence) based on the fact that both of those things are correlated with people who do risky sports. The author's conclusion is trying to offer an explanation a curious comparison between risk-takers and the rest of the population, when it comes to self-confidence. Curious Fact ... Why is it that people who do risky sports tend to have higher than average self-confidence? Author's Explanation ... It's because they participate in risky sports to confront their fears, and confronting your fears increases your self-confidence.

label: Goal
body: As always, we can weaken an Explain Curious Fact argument two different ways: (more common) 1. Suggest an Alternate Explanation for why people who do risky sports have higher than average self-confidence. 2. Hurt the plausibility of the Author's Explanation that people engage in a risky sport, in doing so confront their fears, and in doing so increase their self-confidence. We know that the two classic Alternate Explanations are Reverse Causality "having higher self-confidence is causing people to take part in risky sports" and 3rd Factor, "risky sports usually cost a lot of money, so participants are often from wealthy families, which increases self-confidence".

label: Conclusion
body: Parents should feed cow's milk formula to their infants.

label: Evidence
body: (Even though there are studies linking cow's milk formula to eventual diabetes) cow's milk has a lot of ingredients in it that are excellent for infants' development.

label: Evaluate
body: Given That formula has a lot of valuable ingredients in it How Could We Still Say That Parents should not feed formula to their infants? Well, one direction would be to say that the risks of eventual diabetes are high enough that the nutritional benefits of formula aren't worth it. Since we've acknowledged a downside and an upside, we can still argue about which one is more important. Secondarily, the author seems to be assuming a difference between formula and other available infant beverages. Maybe breastmilk also has those valuable ingredients but doesn't have the same risk of eventual diabetes? Maybe there's a formula that isn't from cow's milk, but goat's milk or sheep's milk, and it has the good ingredients without the diabetes risk.

label: Goal
body: Look for an answer complaining that the author failed to establish that the potential benefit of formula (nutritional ingredients) outweighs the potential downside of formula (eventual diabetes), or for an answer that asks whether we could get those same desirable nutritional ingredients that formula has in some other beverage or some other way that didn't carry with it a similar risk of diabetes.

label: Conclusion
body: One should use the product advertised.

label: Evidence
body: product provides → always preferable faster relief This advertised product has higher concentrations of the active ingredients than do competing products (and higher concentrations are perfectly safe).

label: Evaluate
body: Since the argument presents a principle, "provides faster relief → preferable" we know the argument is trying to use this rule. Does the argument ever establish that this advertised product (Product X) provides faster relief? No. But it establishes that it has higher concentrations of active ingredients, so the author is probably assuming that "if a product has higher concentrations of the active ingredients, then it provides faster relief, thus it's preferable".

label: Goal
body: Look for an answer calling out the missing link assumption of "if higher concentrations of active ingredients, then faster relief", or pointing out the objection that higher concentrations might not provide faster relief, or some other way to argue that we shouldn't necessarily use Product X.

label: Conclusion (So)
body: Archway must use shoddy, substandard components in its clothes dryers.

label: Evidence
body: Their dryers are of poor quality. Crucial bolts are missing. Some sections are assembled in the wrong order, creating a shock and fire hazard. Concern for safety and quality is very lacking.

label: Evaluate
body: We should be curious about this brand new term in the conclusion, shoddy, substandard components. Where does the evidence ever talk about cheap parts? - crucial bolts are missing (okay, but maybe the bolts that are there are high quality bolts) - sections are assembled in the wrong order (okay, but maybe the sections are constructed from high quality components) - concern for safety and quality is very lacking (okay, but maybe we just mean the overall safety and quality of the product, not the quality of its component parts) Wait a sec ... is this Part vs. Whole? The argument is establishing that the dryer as a whole is shoddy and substandard, and then it's concluding that the parts used in the dryer must therefore be shoddy and substandard.

label: Goal
body: If this were a regular Flaw question stem ("how is this argument vulnerable to criticism"), then we would look for an answer calling out the famous Part vs. Whole flaw. But since the question stem has baked in the "fails to consider" prefix, we'll really just be interpreting all these answer choices as though we're doing a Weaken question. So we want a way to argue that you could potentially build a terrible dryer out of high quality parts (if some parts were missing and sections were assembled in the wrong order). "EVEN THOUGH the overall dryer sucks, IT'S STILL POSSIBLE THAT the components used are high quality, BECAUSE ... [correct answer]"

label: Statements
body: Making a new baby involves the gamete of the male parent and the gamete of the female parent equally linking up to make the genetic material in the nucleus. Outside the nucleus, in the cytoplasm, it's just the female's genetic material. GM62 is found only in cytoplasm.

label: Evaluate
body: It sounds like we could say that "GM62 is genetic material that comes exclusively from the female", since we know GM62 is in the cyto, and the cyto is 100% from the female.

label: Goal
body: Look for something reinforcing the idea that "GM62 comes only from the female", or maybe a weirder extension of that, like, "Any GM62 that the male parent has will not be passed on to the baby".

label: Conclusion (thus)
body: Reducing academic plagiarism will lead to a reduction of professional misconduct.

label: Evidence
body: Students who plagiarize are more likely to engage in subsequent professional misconduct than are those who don't.

label: Evaluate
body: This is trying to disguise an age old problem, but it's just presenting a correlation between X and Y in the evidence and then concluding something that implies that the author thinks that X causes Y. Our best chance of catching these Causal flaws is making sure we're sensitized to more likely / less likely type correlation language. The most common way to hear a correlation expressed is something like, "People who are A are more likely than those who aren't to be B". From there, it's almost a guarantee that the author will end up assuming that A causes B or B causes A. Since plagiarizing in school is correlated with professional misconduct later, the author assumes that plagiarizing in school has some causal influence on whether or not someone will engage in professional misconduct later. Whenever we're evaluating these moves from "X and Y are correlated" to "X causes Y", we want to consider Alternate Explanations such as Reverse Cause (maybe Y causes X) or Third Factor (maybe both parts of the correlation are connected to Z). In this conversation, Reverse Causality is off the table. We can't say that their professional conduct later in life is what caused them to plagiarize back when they were in school. But, we could definitely try to explain the correlation in relation to a Third Factor. Maybe people who have low moral integrity, or people who had criminal parents, or people who have Impostor Syndrome and don't think they're as qualified as their peers are more likely both to plagiarize in school and to engage in professional misconduct during their career years. Preventing them from plagiarizing in school won't change the root cause of their professional misconduct later.

label: Goal
body: Look for an answer formally complaining that the author has inferred a Causal relationship from a mere Correlation. Or look for something saying the author assumes that "eliminating earlier illicit behavior somehow impacts the likelihood of later illicit behavior", or an answer that poses an alternate explanation for the correlation, like "maybe both things are connected to some root cause that wouldn't disappear just because you cracked down on plagiarism".

label: Background
body: Since the 1960s ... Hunters kill at least as many deer. Natural predators of deer are on the rise. Suburbs are increasingly encroaching on deer habitats.

label: Surprise
body: Since the 1960s ... The number of deer has increased dramatically.

label: Evaluate / Goal
body: Given all these factors that are working against deer, we need an answer to tell us something positive for deer that would help explain why their numbers have increased dramatically.

label: Conclusion (clearly = opinion)
body: The contention that "the use of calculators in math will undermine students' knowledge of the rationale underlying calculational procedures" is clearly false. rephrase: Using calculators in math isn't going to undermine students' knowledge of the rationale underlying calculational procedures.

label: Evidence
body: Every new information-handling technology has produced virtually the same accusation.

label: Evaluate
body: This doesn't seem like any of the ten famous flaws, so let's switch into "Find an Objection" mode: Given that ... every time there's been a new information-handing technology, there's been accusations that it will somehow corrupt the way we think, How can we argue that ... using calculators in math will undermine students' knowledge of the rationale underlying calculation processes? We could say a couple different things: 1. These accusations have been correct! Each new information-handling technology has corrupted our thinking. 2. Sure, those previous accusations turned out to be false. But this one's different! In the case of calculators, it really will mess up how people think.

label: Goal
body: The author is assuming that the previous times when people freaked out about a new technology, it just a bunch of overblown fear. It didn't turn out to be any sort of problem. And the author is also failing to consider that even if a pattern were true in the past (concerns about a new technology have always turned out to be overblown), it might not be true in the present.

label: Conclusion (Hence)
body: The psychiatrist who released tapes of a poet's therapy sessions after the poet died violated his Hippocratic oath, i.e. The psychiatrist "divulged information about his patient", when he released tapes of the poet's sessions)

label: Evaluate
body: Scott is evaluating the psychiatrist's actions to be a violation of the Hippocratic oath's rule against divulging patient information. After all the psychiatrist released tapes of the poet's sessions. He disseminated private patient information. Were we to try defending the psychiatrist, we'd say - the poet was dead - the psychiatrist only gave the tapes to the poet's official biographer, clearly someone the poet trusted with all kinds of personal information - the poet actually gave the psychiatrist her blessing that he could do anything with the tapes that he saw fit

label: Goal
body: Look for any answer that helps us be stringent and say, "Look, you divulged information. That breaks the Hippocratic oath. It doesn't matter that the patient said you could do what you want with the tapes or that you only divulged it to the biographer."

label: Conclusion
body: Professor G's principle must be false. i.e. At least some political systems that aim at preventing conflict are not legitimate

label: Evidence (since)
body: Totalitarian political systems are not legitimate, and

label: Intermediate Conclusion
body: Totalitarian systems are usually good at preventing conflict.

label: Evidence (since)
body: Those not in power are subject to the will of the powerful.

label: Evaluate
body: In order for this author to refute Professor G's conditional, she must supply at least one example of something that matches the trigger but doesn't match the outcome. His principle was Pol sys aims to prevent conflict → legitimate So she is trying to provide at least one example in which 1. a political system aims to prevent conflict 2. it is not legitimate Her example is totalitarian political systems. Does she establish both 1 and 2? Not quite. She establishes that totalitarian political systems are not legitimate, but she never establishes that they aim to prevent conflict. She only establishes that they are usually good at preventing conflict. This is actually an example of the 11th or 12th most common famous flaw: Intent vs. Result (or Motive vs. Consequence)

label: Goal
body: So she is assuming, "if they're usually good at preventing conflict, then they are aiming to prevent conflict". (We could also potentially see an answer linking the Intermediate Conclusion to its Premise, something like, "If the powerless are subject to the will of the powerful, conflict will usually be prevented")

label: Claims
body: Beethoven started losing his hearing when he was 30. He gradually lost more and more until he was finally totally deaf late in life. causal (it gave his later music) Hearing loss gave Beethoven's later music a wonderfully introspective quality that his earlier music lacked.

label: Evaluate
body: We generally mine the text of Inference questions for clues about whether they're going to be using Conditional, Causal, Math-y, or Pivot wording to derive the correct answer. In this paragraph, the biggest clue would be the causal claim that "hearing loss led to the music having a wonderful introspective quality it didn't have before".

label: Goal
body: Who knows how the correct answer will reinforce this, but look for something safely worded like, "Not all losses of sensory information result in only bad things", or "What seems to be a deficit can sometimes lead to a benefit".

label: Conclusion (Thus)
body: Histories reveal more about the presuppositions underlying different historians' attempts to understand what happened than about what actually happened.

label: Evidence
body: By choosing what to include or exclude in their narratives, historians impose patterns rather than discover inherent ones.

label: Evaluate
body: We only have one premise. We know what historians do, and the conclusion is about what histories reveal. So it seems like they're setting up a Missing Link type of assumption: "If historians do X, then history reveals Y". What do historians do? They choose what to include/exclude from history, thereby imposing patterns. What does history supposedly reveal? The presuppositions (i.e. assumptions) that historians have in their heads as they attempt to understand what happened in the past.

label: Goal
body: It seems like the answer will connect "imposing patterns" or "choosing what to include/exclude" to "the historian's presuppositions".

label: Conclusion
body: CC's proposal to increase school funding by raising property taxes will be opposed by CM and supported by CP.

label: Evaluate
body: I'm not exactly sure what they want us to identify as the flaw here. Miller will oppose this proposal, because he opposes all proposals that raise taxes. The looseness would probably have to do more with not knowing whether Philopoulos will definitely support CC's proposal. It seems like someone could be broadly in favor of increased funding for schools but still opposed to one specific proposal that involves increased funding for schools.

label: Goal
body: I'd be looking for something like this: - Entity 1 always rejects X. - Entity 2 likes Y. - Thus, Entity 3's proposal to do Y via doing X will be rejected by Entity 1 and accepted by Entity 2.

label: Conclusion (So)
body: It is clear that the revolutionary party was not overambitious and caused no suffering.

label: Evidence
body: Most of the revolutionary party's goals were quickly achieved and the party didn't have enough power to cause the suffering the critics claim it caused.

label: Evaluate
body: The conclusion actually makes two claims, so we should separately analyze each's validity. Given that ... the party quickly achieved most of its goals, Do we have to accept that ... the party was not overambitious? No, we could say they were still overambitious. Maybe the remaining un-achieved goals are hopeless, pie-in-the-sky fantasies that are overambitious. Given that ... the party didn't have enough power to cause the suffering the critics claim it caused, Do we have to accept that ... the party caused no suffering? Heck no. Maybe the critics claimed that the party caused 10 megatons of suffering, whereas the party in really only caused 3 megatons of suffering. There's a wide range between "less than critics accuse them of" and "nothing".

label: Goal
body: Look for an answer choice saying, "Even though most goals were achieved, many huge ones weren't, so we could still say the party was overambitious". Or look for one saying, "Even though the party did less suffering than the critics accuse them of doing, they still may have caused some suffering, so we can't say they caused no suffering."

label: Evidence
body: While it may be painful for Jason to learn his supervisor is displeased, having this information would allow him to improve his supervisor's opinion. Withholding information is unjustified if the person would benefit from having it.

label: Evaluate
body: The argument essentially states that while it might hurt Jason to find out about his supervisor's displeasure, causing him pain is justified because he would benefit from the knowledge by being able to improve his work. We're looking to bridge the gap between "knowing the information allows improvement" and "improvement is beneficial." Why should Jason be informed if it's going to hurt him? Because he can improve his supervisor's opinion, which is assumed to be advantageous for Jason.

label: Goal
body: Look for an assumption indicating that the benefit of knowing outweighs the pain or establishing that improving his supervisor's opinion would indeed benefit Jason.

label: Evidence
body: The tenant need not pay for PD + R → ~TP preexisting damage recorded on the preexisting damage list. The tenant must pay for damage ~R → TP that was not recorded on the preexisting damage list, except BTC → ~TP for any damage caused by a circumstance beyond the tenant’s control.

label: Conclusion
body: The tenant is not required to pay ~TP for the damage.

label: Evaluate
body: There are two reasons that PD + R establish that the tenant is not required to pay. First, if the damage is preexisting and was recorded on the preexisting damage list. And second, if the damage BTC was caused by circumstances beyond the tenant’s control.

label: Evidence
body: After Mega Cable Television Company refused to carry the competing Azco News Service alongside its own news channels, the mayor used her influence to get Azco time on a community channel.

label: Conclusion
body: The mayor's action is rewarding Azco's owner, a political supporter of hers.

label: Evaluate
body: Marion speculates a reason (rewarding a political supporter) for the mayor’s action (using influence to get Azco News Service time on a community channel). To weaken this argument an answer could provide an alternative reason, identify a supporter who was not provided some benefit, or identify someone who received a similar benefit who was not a political supporter.

label: Evidence
body: On the first day of trout season a team of biologists went with local trout anglers to the Macawber River. Each angler who caught at least 2 trout chose exactly 2 of these trout for the biologists to weigh. A total of 90 fish were weighed.

label: Conclusion
body: The measurements show that at the beginning of this season the average trout in the Macawber River weighed approximately 1.6 kilograms.

label: Evaluate
body: The biologists did not find the most scientific method of measuring the weight of the average trout. Leave it up to the anglers and they’ll pick they’re biggest fish and the average weight of the selected fish won’t be representative of the average fish in the river.

label: Conclusion (thus)
