body: Knowing what people value can help one predict their actions.

label: Intermediate Conclusion
body: A strong correlation exists between what people value and the way they act.

label: Premise (for example)
body: Those who value wealth tend to choose higher-paying jobs in undesirable locations over lower-paying jobs in desirable locations.

label: Evaluate
body: The opening claim is supported by the 2nd sentence, so it's fair to call the opening sentence a conclusion. But the opening sentence is also the support for the final claim, so the final claim is the main conclusion. While we're usually suspicious of picking the last claim as the conclusion on Main Conclusion, it does happen 10-15% of the time, especially on lower difficulty questions. Since this is just a Q4, we can tell ourselves, "It's ok." :)

label: Apparent Paradox
body: How come elderly people who are long-time residents are worse off, health-wise, than elderly people who are new residents?

label: Evaluate
body: We need a distinction between long-time residents and new residents, that is common sensically related to health.

label: Evidence
body: Classical Roman architecture is beautiful, primarily because of its use of rounded arches and its symmetry. Postmodern architecture is dramatic, primarily because of its creative use both of materials and of the surrounding environment.

label: Conclusion (therefore)
body: An architectural style that combines elements of both classical Roman and postmodern architecture would be both beautiful and dramatic.

label: Evaluate
body: The argument assumes that what is true of the individual parts to be true of the whole. Combining architectural styles will not necessarily produce a new style with each of the characteristics of the original two.

label: Evidence
body: After being subjected to clinical tests like those used to evaluate the effectiveness of prescription drugs, a popular nonprescription herbal remedy was found to be as effective in treating painful joints as is a certain prescription drug that has been used successfully to treat this condition.

label: Conclusion
body: The manufacturer of the herbal remedy cited the test results as proof that chemical agents are unnecessary for the successful treatment of painful joints.

label: Evaluate
body: The manufacturer assumes that chemical agents are not part of the herbal remedy’s successful treatment of painful joints.

label: Apparent Paradox
body: When companies’ profits would otherwise be reduced by an increase in the minimum wage, the companies often reduce the number of workers they employ. Yet a recent increase in the minimum wage did not result in job cutbacks in the fast-food industry, where most workers are paid the minimum wage.

label: Evaluate
body: The recent case appears to be a counterexample. But to what? It’s a counterexample to the notion that when there’s an increase in the minimum wage, companies often reduce the number of workers they employ. Spot the difference between that and the first sentence? The latter includes something else in the trigger about reduced profits.

label: Given that
body: These ten loans all had graduated payment plans, i.e., the scheduled monthly loan payment increased slightly each month over the five-year term of the loan.

label: Facts
body: conditionals (always, never) Main word of title → should capitalize First or Last word of title → should capitalize Article / prep / conj < 5 LTRS and → shouldn't capitalize Occurs in middle of title

label: Evaluate
body: The #1 thing we read for on MBT is conditionals. We have two of them here. Do they chain together? No, they sort of outline different rules for different words in a title. We end up feeling like we know which words we should / shouldn't capitalize, other than for prepositions / conjunctions 5 letters or longer. They don't qualify under the rule that says can't capitalize. And (unless we'd call them a "main word"), they don't qualify under the rule that says must capitalize. So it seems like we have some freedom there to capitalize or not capitalize.

label: Goal
body: No way to know where this is going, so just find the most provable answer.

label: Rules
body: Always capitalize main words and first/last words. Never capitalize middle-of-title articles or short prepositions/conjunctions (under 5 letters).

label: Goal
body: Find the inference that follows from these rules — likely a contrapositive about middle-of-title capitalization.

label: The Rules
body: Two rules in the stimulus. Rule 1 says some words always get capitalized (main words, first/last words). Rule 2 says some words never get capitalized in the middle of a title — articles, and prepositions or conjunctions with fewer than five letters.

label: Evaluate
body: The trick on Must-Be-True questions is to combine the rules to draw a tight inference. If a middle-of-title word should be capitalized, then it cannot be in the never-capitalize category. That is, it cannot be an article, and it cannot be a short conjunction or preposition.

label: Goal
body: Find the answer that exactly captures this contrapositive. Watch for answers that switch directions, overstate, or stray from the rules.

label: Evidence
body: Recently, the city council passed an ordinance that prohibits loitering at the local shopping mall. The council's declared goal was to eliminate overcrowding and alleviate pedestrian congestion, thereby improving the mall's business and restoring its family-oriented image. Even when fully implemented, the ordinance would not accomplish them.

label: Conclusion
body: Despite these claims, reducing overcrowding and congestion cannot be the actual goals of this measure.

label: Evaluate
body: The argument mistakes an outcome for intent. Just because the ordinance would not accomplish the city’s declared goals, does not mean that the those goals were not what the city intended to achieve.

label: Statements
body: Cynthia: Marketable technologies get plenty of funding from corporations, but science is actually trying to solve the mysteries of the universe, so the govt. should help fund that purely theoretical stuff. Luis: The point of using govt money for science is to fund discoveries that would benefit society as a whole. So it should only fund research that’s expected to yield practical applications.

label: Evaluation
body: Does Luis try to argue against any of Cynthia's explicit claims? Does Luis argue that corps do not amply fund research that generates sellable new tech? No. Does Luis argue that the fundamental goal of science is not to achieve a comprehensive knowledge of the universe? No. Does Luis argue that the govt should not be helping to fund basic science that is just about advancing our knowledge of nature? Yes, that seems to be fair, since Luis is saying that the govt should only fund stuff that is expected to yield practical applications.

label: Goal
body: So, essentially, they disagree over whether the govt should only fund science stuff expected to yield practical benefits, or whether the govt should also fund science stuff aimed merely at advancing our theoretical knowledge of nature.

label: Conclusion
body: Evaluate the consequences of an action, not its morality ...

label: Subsidiary Conclusion
body: .. because it’s impossible to tell whether an action is moral ...

label: Premise
body: ... since you can’t tell whether an action came from an ulterior motive.

label: Evaluation
body: Principle questions are about defining a bridge idea that gets you from the Premise to the Conclusion. Since this argument contains two different conclusions, signified by ‘therefore’ and ‘so’, we can prepare two bridge ideas. One of them gets us from Prem to Subsid Conc, the other from Subsid to Main Conc. Don’t know motive -> can’t judge moral -> should eval conseq

label: Goal
body: We can look for an answer that gets at this move: “If you don’t know the motive for an action, you can’t judge its morality” Or there could be an answer that gets at this move: “If it’s impossible to know whether an action is moral, then we should evaluate its consequences instead.”

label: Conclusion
body: It’s probably possible for fossil-fuel producers to reduce emissions of CO2 from fossil fuels enough to halt global warming, without it being prohibitively expensive.

label: Evidence
body: Fossil fuel producers say it would be too expensive, but they said the same thing years ago about fixing the CFC problem. When they were forced to fix the CFC problem, they managed to do so in a timely and profitable fashion.

label: Evaluation
body: This argument relies on an analogy, so you strengthen it by making the two cases seem more fair to compare. You weaken it by making the two situations seem Importantly different.

label: Goal
body: It’s hard to predict what detail the correct answer will focus on, but need something that makes us more likely to believe “If chemical industry was wrong about it being too expensive to fix the CFC problem, then fossil fuel industry is probably wrong about it being too expensive to fix the CO2 problem”.

label: Conclusion
body: Contemporary legislatures fail to enact beneficial laws.

label: Evidence
body: Legislators have to consider the consequences of a potential law, or else that law won’t benefit constituents. Contemporary legislatures present legislation in polemical terms, arousing polemical reactions of strong support or strong rejection.

label: Goal
body: Sounds like a long distance runner would rather do dissociative strategies the day before the race, since it won't leave them feeling mentally depleted on race day the way associative strategies would.

label: Evaluation
body: This argument is murderously tough to parse. First, ‘polemical’ is a vocab word many might not know. It means “divisive, extreme, polarizing” language. Mainly, though, it’s hard to know what they want us to consider the Conclusion, since the connection between Evidence and Conclusion is so thin or non-existent. Ultimately, they want us to see the 2nd sentence as the conclusion, but there really aren't strong clues. I thought the 1st sentence, which is prescriptive in nature, was the conclusion, until I saw the correct answer choice. If we treat the 2nd sentence as the conclusion, then the argument wants to prove this path: Contemp -—--—--—--—--—--—--—--—--—---> laws don't legislature benefit The 1st sentence is a proving mechanism that would allow us to say "laws don't benefit". don't -—> laws don't consider benefit conseq. So the argument must be assuming that in Contemporary Legislatures, they aren't considering the consequences of proposed laws. We are never told that, but we are told that they are presenting legislation in polemical terms, arousing repugnance or enthusiasm. Contemp --> present -> arouse legislature polem hate/love

label: Goal
body: So the author must be assuming that, “As legislators present legislation in polemical terms, arousing extreme reactions, they are not considering the consequences of the potential law.” Maybe there could be a conditional that says, “When you feel repugnance or enthusiasm for a potential law, you don’t consider the consequences of enacting it.”

label: Conclusion
body: Anderson is too harsh on today’s travel writers.

label: Evidence
body: It’s way more challenging nowadays to be a travel writer, since your audience is so much more well-traveled. The fact that there still even is travel writing is a testament to the talent of modern writers.

label: Goal
body: The claim we’re asked about is part of the Evidence, the Support. If they wanted to use easy language, we’d see something like “it provides partial support for the author’s conclusion that today’s travel writers are still producing quality work”. If they wanted to describe it more subtly, “it points to a salient difference between travel writing audiences of the past and those of today”.

label: Conclusion
body: The multi-party democracies with the fewest number of parties have the most-productive legislatures.

label: Evidence
body: The fewer the parties, the more issues they have to take a stand on, so the more they have to prioritize those issues, leading to more compromise.

label: Evaluation
body: The conclusion is trying to make this voyage: “Fewest parties → most productive legislature” The evidence takes us this far: “Fewest parties → more issues -> prioritize -> compromise That final missing link in the chain of reasoning would have to get us from 'compromise' —to→ 'most productive legislature'. When we see a new term in the conclusion, like “most-productive legislatures”, that never gets discussed in the evidence, we know our job is almost always to figure out what part of the evidence was intended to match up with that new guy in the conclusion.

label: Goal
body: Look for something connecting "more compromise" with "more productive legislature"

label: Conclusion
body: Air temperature is increasing.

label: Evidence
body: Over past five years, rainfall totals for most continents have increased. As humidity of air increases, rainfall increases, and warm air tends to be humid.

label: Evaluation
body: The first sentence has a syllogistic feel (i.e. A is B, and B is C). We always want to pause and synthesize that "A is C" inference we get. Given: Warm air → Humid air → More Rain Infer: Warm air → More Rain We are being fuzzy here by representing these as conditional, as the first claim is definitely not conditional. But it’s important that we hear the intended link: “When you have warm air, the amount of rain will tend to increase”. That’s what allows us to spot the famous Illegal Reversal flaw. The author is saying, “Since there’s increased rain, we probably have warm air.”

label: Goal
body: We want a causal chain of A → B → C, and then for the author to say, “Since C is happening, it’s strong evidence that A is happening”.

label: Facts
body: Toddlers can follow a rule like sort by shape, but then have trouble following a new rule like sort by color (they keep following the first rule). Researchers think a still-developing prefrontal cortex is to blame, because the cortex is essential for adapting to new rules and toddlers don’t have a fully developed cortex.

label: Evaluation
body: A ton of Most Supported questions have correct answers that pinpoint the Causal Difference-Maker in a situation, something that explains the curious fact or observed difference. What explains why the toddlers couldn’t follow the new rule? The researchers say it was an undeveloped cortex, which is often a cause of a failure to adapt to a new rule.

label: Goal
body: Find a safely worded claim that reinforces the story about why the toddlers weren’t able to follow the new rule.

label: Main Conclusion
body: Eating raw carrots (which are rich in beta carotene) by themselves is nonetheless not an effective means of obtaining vitamin A.

label: Premise
body: The body cannot transform beta carotene into vitamin A unless it is consumed with at least some fat.

label: Concessions
body: It is true that nutrients are most effective when provided by natural foods rather than artificial supplements. It is also true that fat in one's diet is generally unhealthy.

label: Conclusion
body: The worry that dumping fossil fuel’s CO2 into the ocean would trade one pollution for another equally bad one is unfounded.

label: Evidence
body: Tons of the CO2 that comes from fossil fuels already ends up in the ocean, and it’s not causing any environmental problems as bad as global warming.

label: Evaluation
body: This follows a classic template for Main Conclusion questions in which you hear a Counterpoint, hear the author’s disagreeing Conclusion, and then hear the author’s support for that disagreement.

label: Goal
body: We just need a paraphrase of “Environmentalists don’t have good reason to worry that dumping CO2 in the ocean would trade one pollution for an equally bad one.”

label: How can it be that
body: The average payment received by MetroBank for these loans had decreased by the end of the five-year term.

label: Paradox
body: Health officials believe that all the people who got food poisoning from a bacteria in seafood got it from the same restaurant on the same date, via contaminated seafood. YET Most people who ate seafood at that restaurant on that date did not come into contact with this bacteria.

label: Evaluation
body: There could be lots of ways to resolve this paradox, but it seems like a pretty easy one to offer a solution for. If there was only one contaminated flank of salmon at the restaurant that day, then all the people who ate it would have gotten the illness, whereas most of the people who ate seafood at the restaurant that day would not have come into contact with the bacteria, since they weren’t served any of that one contaminated piece of fish. Somehow, the answer will probably make use of the fact that seafood is a broad category, so the people who got sick may have all eaten the same type of seafood or even same specimen of animal, whereas the people who didn’t get exposed to the bacteria probably just ate a different type of seafood or a different specimen of the contaminated type.

label: Goal
body: How can it be simultaneously true that all the sick people got it from bacteria-contaminated seafood at this restaurant on a given day, while most people who ate seafood there that day did not get exposed to the bacteria?

label: Evidence
body: Real wages in this country will increase significantly only if productivity increases notably. This country's businesses are currently investing very little in new technology and this pattern is likely to continue for at least several more years.

label: Conclusion
body: Thus, it is unlikely that real wages will increase significantly in the near future Evaluate The argument assumes that if there is little investment in new technology, then productivity does not increase.

label: Conclusion (so / should)
body: There should be full public disclosure of scientific author’s financial holdings.

label: Evidence
body: Sometimes author and reviewers in sci journals will praise companies that they’ve invested in, raising fears of conflict of interest and calling into question the integrity of scientific inquiry.

label: Evaluation
body: For almost all Principle questions, we’re prephrasing an If/Then or “Should rule-of-thumb” that gets us from premise to conclusion. Here it could sound something like, “If a certain practice would undermine the integrity of scientific inquiry, then we should be transparent about that practice”.

label: Goal
body: Since the answers will venture to new topics, we’re mainly looking for something that reiterates the idea of, “If it looks sketchy or self-serving, then you should be transparent about it”.

label: Conclusion (then)
body: We can expect a decrease in the bad environmental effects of acid rain.

label: Evidence
body: Acid rain is caused by acidic pollutants, and the amount of those released into the air has decreased over the last few decades.

label: Evaluation
body: If we’re releasing less acidic pollutants into the air, how could we argue that the environmental damage caused by acid rain will not go down? Well one way would be to say that even though we’re releasing a smaller amount, perhaps it’s of a worse type. A small amount of something really bad could do more damage than a larger amount of something milder. Maybe there are thresholds of acid rain that we’ll hit that trigger worse events (the straw that finally broke the camel’s back).

label: Goal
body: Look for four answers that give us a way to argue that there will still be as much, or more, environmental damage coming, despite the fact that a smaller amount of acidic pollutants is being released.

label: Conclusion
body: How we morally judge an action goes beyond the intentions of the person who performed it (and includes the consequences of the action).

label: Evidence
body: If a cook put the wrong ingredient in something, it wouldn’t usually be thought of as immoral, but if that wrong ingredient accidentally killed someone, then it would be judged by many as morally negligent.

label: Evaluation
body: Even though the stem describes the paragraph as “statements”, this reads as an argument, and so we should probably use our typical thinking of “what bridge idea gets us from premise to conclusion”. The author is thinking that if “whether or not the eater dies” affects how we think about the morality of “a cook adding the wrong ingredient”, then our moral judgment includes external circumstances.

label: Goal
body: We probably want a safely worded claim that reinforces this notion that the consequences of an action are part of how we morally judge the action.

label: Conclusion (so / should)
body: Doctors should never prescribe antibiotics to treat colds.

label: Intermediate Conclusion (so)
body: Antibiotics have no effect on colds.

label: Premise
body: Colds are caused by viruses. Antibiotics have no effect on viruses.

label: Premise
body: Prescribing antibiotics for a cold can have dangerous side effects.

label: Evaluate
body: The argument offers two reasons why doctors should not prescribe antibiotics to treat colds. The first points out that antibiotics are ineffective against colds. And second, antibiotics can have dangerous side effects. So the operative principles seems like, "If a treatment would have no effect on the underlying condition and could create dangerous side effects, we shouldn't prescribe it".

label: Facts
body: Long distance runners either use associative strategies (attend to your senses ... this requires so much concentration that it results in mental exhaustion for more than a day) or dissociative strategies (ignore your senses ... this does not require so much concentration that it exhausts you for more than a day). + It's really important for long distance runners to be mentally refreshed when they race.

label: Evaluation
body: We were given a comparison between associative and dissociative, and then we were given a fact about long-distance runners: they need to be mentally refreshed. Is there overlap between the two threads of discussion? Yes - in the comparison we talked about mental exhaustion. And we're learning that a runner wants the opposite of that (mental refreshment) on race day.

label: Conclusion
body: Lessing's claim about literature should be rejected.

label: Evaluate
body: Something must have changed along the way. If all ten loans were all making escalated payments month over month, then the average payment would have to go up. Maybe some people made "extra" payments early on, which could reduce the principal on the loan and make the residual payments lower?

label: Conclusion (this shows)
body: Universities these days do not foster fair-minded and tolerant intellectual debate.

label: Evidence
body: At one talk in a single Political Ideologies class at one university, two students taunted the speaker and several others applauded.

label: Evaluate
body: The conclusion is sweeping, about "universities these days" in general, but the evidence is one incident in one class at one university. Even within that one talk, only "two students" did the taunting and only "several others" applauded; the rest of the audience is unaccounted for. This sample size is way too small to establish a generalization about all universities. It couldn't even establish a generalization about this university, or even about the students who attended this talk (98% of them might have been fair-minded and tolerated intellectual debate).

label: Goal
body: This seems like a classic Sampling flaw, so let's see if we find an answer like that.

label: Conclusion
body: Universities don't foster fair-minded debate.

label: Evidence
body: One incident — two students taunted a speaker and a few others cheered — at one talk in one class.

label: Evaluate
body: One incident can't support a sweeping conclusion about universities in general.

label: Goal
body: Find the answer that names the leap from one incident to a broad generalization.

label: Conclusion
body: The professor concludes something huge — that universities, in general, no longer support fair, tolerant debate.

label: Evidence
body: One talk. One class. Two rude students. A few who applauded them.

label: Evaluate
body: This is the classic small-sample problem. It's like watching one customer be rude in one cafe and concluding that all the cafes in the country have an etiquette problem. Even within that single talk, the rude students were a small minority — most of the audience just sat there. So the leap is enormous: from "a couple of students at one event" to "universities don't foster fair-minded debate." A correct Flaw answer should name that leap.

label: Goal
body: Find the answer that says the conclusion is way too broad for the evidence.

label: Evidence
body: Studies reveal that most people select the foods they eat primarily on the basis of flavor. Nutrition is usually a secondary concern at best.

label: Conclusion
body: Health experts would have more success in encouraging people to eat wholesome foods if they emphasized how flavorful those foods truly are rather than how nutritious they are.

label: Evaluate
body: The argument assumes that people would be more willing to try a particular food based on the way it is emphasized. It could turn out that emphasizing flavor does not influence a person’s perception of flavor.

label: Evidence
body: Studies show that individuals with a high propensity for taking risks tend to have fewer ethical principles to which they consciously adhere in their business interactions than do most people. On the other hand, individuals with a strong desire to be accepted socially tend to have more such principles than do most people. In general, the more ethical principles to which someone adheres, the more ethical is that person’s behavior.

label: Conclusion
body: Therefore, business schools can promote more ethical behavior among future business people by promoting among their students the desire to be accepted socially and discouraging the propensity for taking risks.

label: Evaluate
body: The evidence establishes a negative correlation between a propensity to take risks and ethical behavior and a positive correlation between a desire to be accepted socially and ethical behavior. But the conclusion asserts that the relationship is causal and goes too far.

label: Conclusion
body: Lessing's claim about literature must be rejected. rephrase: Literature does not have to represent events or actions occurring in sequence to be legitimate.

label: Evidence
body: The imagist poems are legitimate. The imagist poems consist solely of amalgams of disparate images.

label: Evaluate
body: When we have a Conditional Conclusion, we play along with the IF half. We can add it to our evidence as a background constraint of the conversation. We're always debating / trying to prove the outcome. The conclusion is saying, "if we accept imagist as legit poetry, L's claim about literature must be rejected". So play along with imagist poetry as legitimate. And we try to prove L's claim must be rejected. We're trying to refute someone's strong claim. In fact, it's so strong ("must represent"), that we're Refuting a Conditional. This is a specific style of argument which lends itself to a specific plan of attack. To refute the conditional "If X, then Y", you need a counterexample with these two qualities - X is true - Y isn't true For example, to refute, "If you're a boy, you like sports", you need a counterexample example with these two qualities - this person is a boy - this person doesn't like sports We're trying to refute, "if it's legitimate literature, then it must represent events or actions occurring in sequence." So we need a counterexample with these two qualities - it's legitimate literature - it doesn't represent events / actions occurring in sequence The evidence will always establish one of these must-have's, but we won't know the other one; we'll usually just have some proxy idea. (Some say all boys like sports. But this must be rejected, because Bob is a boy and he doesn't play outside. This counterexample establishes that we're dealing with a boy, but doesn't establish "doesn't like sports". Instead it uses a proxy idea, "doesn't play outside". So the missing link would be "if don't play outside, then don't like sports".

label: Goal
body: Our evidence has established that we're dealing with "legitimate literature". (We're allowed to think that poetry is a subset of literature, without them having to spell that out). But we've never established "doesn't represent events / actions occurring in sequence." We just have a proxy idea "consists solely of amalgams of disparate images". So the missing link is, "if it consists solely of amalgams of disparate images, then it doesn't represent events/actions occurring in sequence."

label: The Argument
body: Lessing said literature must represent events in sequence. The essayist wants to reject that claim by pointing to imagist poetry — poems that are just amalgams of disparate images and are still considered legitimate.

label: Evaluate
body: For imagist poetry to actually disprove Lessing, it has to be (a) legitimate literature and (b) not representing events in sequence. We are told it is legitimate. But the essay does not say whether amalgams of disparate images can represent sequences. If they can, then imagist poetry would still be following Lessing's rule, and the rejection would not work.

label: Goal
body: The right answer should plug that hole — say that an amalgam of disparate images cannot represent a sequence of events. With that, imagist poetry becomes the genuine counterexample the essayist needs.

label: Conclusion
body: There is no such thing as multiple personality disorder

label: Evidence
body: In all my years of clinical practice, I've never seen one case of it.

label: Evaluation
body: This is a little bit circular, in that maybe the psychiatrist has never seen a case of multiple personality disorder simply because she assumes it doesn't exist. But the safer angle on this is probably just that she's relying on her own personal sample, arguing that "If I ain't never seen it, then it don't exist!"

label: Goal
body: Look for something that has the feel of, "If it wasn't true in all the cases I observed, then it's never true"

label: Claim
body: Even if many more people in the world excluded meat from their diet, world hunger would not thereby be significantly reduced.

label: Evaluate
body: To weaken this claim, the correct answer should imply that if many more people excluded meat from their diet, world hunger would be significantly reduced.

label: Given
body: On our farm, we have great concern for our cows’ environmental conditions. We have recently made improvements that increase their comfort, such as providing them with special sleeping mattresses. These changes are intended to increase blood flow to the udder. This increased blood flow would boost milk output and thus increase profits.

label: Pat
body: Because email is anonymous, people are more inclined to reveal themselves, which gets to a level of intimacy that otherwise would take years of personal contact to achieve.

label: Amar
body: Being bluntly honest (in an anonymous email) is not the same thing as intimacy. Actual intimacy requires a social bond that can only be made with direct personal contact.

label: Evaluation
body: It sounds like they're disagreeing about intimacy. Pat thinks that intimacy is achieved when we are being self-revelatory. Amar doesn't think that this alone qualifies as intimacy. He thinks social bonds are required.

label: Goal
body: Look for something surrounding whether or not something qualifies as intimacy: - whether being self-revealing is / isn't sufficient to be intimacy - whether direct personal contact is / isn't required to have intimacy

label: Conclusion (therefore)
body: Criminal orgs will try to get more involved in biotech and IT.

label: Evidence
body: Criminal orgs' main purpose is to generate profits. Biotech and IT promise to generate enormous profits.

label: Evaluate
body: We often scan the conclusion of Sufficient Assumption for a New Concept, because we know that this new concept must show up in the correct answer. In this conclusion, we have "criminal orgs", which were discussed in the evidence and "biotech and IT" which was discussed in the evidence. The new concept would be "try to become increasingly involved in". Why is the author saying that criminal orgs will try to be increasingly involved in biotech and IT? Biotech and IT are going to generate profits, and that's the main purpose of criminal orgs.

label: Goal
body: If we're going to roll that into one conditional prephrase, it sounds like the author is assuming that, "If X is gonna do something that matches your main purpose, then you will try to become increasingly involved in X".

label: Main Conclusion
body: But this reason is mistaken.

label: Intermediate Conclusion
body: Any reduction in the number of teachers would require an accompanying reduction in courses offered.

label: Premises
body: Computerized instruction requires more, not less, time of instructors.

label: Opposing Point
body: Administrators of educational institutions are enthusiastic about the educational use of computers.

label: Opposing Support
body: Administrators of educational institutions are enthusiastic about the educational use of computers. Many teachers fear computers for the same reason.

label: Evidence
body: Scientists have shown that older bees, which usually forage outside the hive for food, tend to have larger brains than do younger bees, which usually do not forage but instead remain in the hive to tend the newly hatched bees. Foraging requires greater cognitive ability than does tending to newly hatched bees.

label: Conclusion
body: It appears that foraging leads to the increased brain size of older bees.

label: Evaluate
body: The argument mistakes correlation for causation. A possible alternative cause for the increased brain size would undermine the argument. The other way to weaken this argument is to find foraging bees that do not have increased brain size or to find bees with increased brain size that do not forage.

label: Conclusion
body: (implied) Professors should not receive paid leaves of absence to allow them to engage in research

label: Evidence
body: Even if research does advance human knowledge and improves professors' teaching, why should we devote any of our limited resources to fund professors taking time off from teaching?

label: Evaluation
body: Calling it "taking time off from teaching" makes it sound like they're on vacation. If they're doing research that improves their teaching by keeping them up to date with developments in their field, then how is that even time off? When a teacher is prepping a lesson, is that "taking time off from teaching"? No, that's part of being a good teacher: training / preparation.

label: Goal
body: Look for answer that says that David is failing to consider that this research time isn't time off from teaching; it's basically a form of teacher training/prep so that they can be better teachers.

label: Main Conclusion
body: [Dictation software] fails to live up to its billing.

label: Premises
body: The laborious part of writing is the thinking and the editing, not the typing. And proofreading the software's error-filled output generally squanders any time saved in typing.

label: Opposing Point
body: Dictation software has been promoted as a labor-saving invention.

label: No Role
body: Dictation software allows a computer to produce a written version of sentences that are spoken to it.

label: Evidence
body: The Brick Wall Review makes enough money from sales of its anthologies to cover most operating expenses. Most poems published in your magazine are very similar to those published in The Brick Wall Review.

label: Conclusion
body: So, if your magazine also published an anthology of poems first printed in your magazine, you could depend less on donations.

label: Evaluate
body: Given that ... The BWR makes enough from its anthology to cover operating expenses, How could we argue that ... if our magazine copied BWR's idea and published an anthology of poems first printed in our magazine, it wouldn't help us raise money (which would make us less dependent on donations? The argument assumes that what is true for the Brick Wall Review will also be true for the magazine under discussion. We need a way to argue that even though this anthology has been a successful revenue raising plan for Brick Wall Review, it wouldn't be for our magazine. The only similarity the argument has established is that our poems are similar to their poems. But maybe their marketing team is better. Maybe their readership is more interested in anthologies. Maybe buying a copy of the anthology is required to see one of the poets give a live reading. If there's something that makes this plan a success for BWR that we wouldn't necessarily be able to do if we were doing an anthology, then that weakens the assumption that we will see similar success from this plan.

label: Goal
body: Look for answer that would help us to argue that "if we tried to do an anthology, it wouldn't do as well as BWR's has done, because ...".

label: Facts
body: No one with a bad medical issue would trust the average person to prescribe treatment. And since a good public servant has the interest of the public at heart ...

label: Evaluation
body: Huh? Whenever we see "similarly", we will usually be dealing with an analogy, and LSAT likes to make us Complete the Analogy. But here I think we need to do a little mental effort to figure out how these things will line up. In the first case, the author is saying, "if you have a medical problem, you wouldn't go to some random average person, you'd go to a doctor (presumably because they have better knowledge of how to treat you). So how is "good public servant" meant to match up — is it the person with the medical problem, the doctor, or the average person being asked for a treatment suggestion? A good public servant has the interest of the public at heart, just as a doctor has the interest of the patient at heart? I would think this should line up with doctor, so a fitting conclusion could be, "if we have a serious public interest problem, we should rely on a good public servant rather than the average person".

label: Goal
body: Hard to guess this one, but look for something safely worded that seems to complete an analogy between the medical problem case and the good public servant case.

label: Evidence
body: Winning requires the W → WC willingness to cooperate. Which [willingness to cooperate] WC → M in turn requires motivation.

label: Conclusion
body: So you will not win if you are not ~M → ~W motivated.

label: Evaluate
body: This argument combines two if/then relationships to conclude another if/then relationship. This argument is valid since the conclusion follows as an inference of the two premises.

label: Conclusion
body: Setting speed limit at 55 mph has reduced accident rate by at least 15%

label: Evidence
body: Every year since the 55 mph speed limit was introduced has had an accident rate at least 15% lower than the peak rate of a decade ago (when there no speed limit)

label: Evaluation
body: This is a Correlation to Causality type argument: the introduction of the 55 mph speed limit coincided with ten years in which the accident rate was at least 15% lower than the peak year right before we had the speed limit. The author then becomes firmly sure that speed limit is the causal reason for that. We are supposed to consider the plausibility of the author's story line (does anyone care about the speed limit? do they see the signs? does it affect their behavior), but more importantly we're supposed to consider whether there is some other way to explain the curious fact. How else could we explain why the ten years since the speed limit have had a 15% lower accident rate? Maybe there are fewer drivers .. safer cars ... we can't argue that this is just a "regression towards the mean", meaning that ten years ago when we had that peak year it was just anomalously high, because they told us that the accident rate was steadily climbing each year prior to that speed limit.

label: Goal
body: We would primarily look for some other way to interpret that 15% lower (so that it doesn't seem like the speed limit has caused the reduction), but we can also like any answer that makes it seem less plausible that the speed limit is having an effect. There will probably be some other change that occurred around the same time as the speed limit was instituted.

label: Main Conclusion
body: The criticism is misplaced.

label: Premises
body: Rocket technology is much simpler than the human psyche. Until we adequately understand the human psyche we cannot solve the great social problems.

label: Opposing Point
body: It is a travesty of justice that we can launch rockets into outer space but cannot solve social problems that have plagued humanity.

label: Opposing Support
body: The assumption underlying this assertion is that there are greater difficulties involved in a space launch than are involved in ending long-standing social problems, which in turn suggests that a government's failure to achieve the latter is simply a case of misplaced priorities.

label: Evidence
body: After the last ice age, groups of paleohumans left Siberia and crossed the Bering land bridge, which no longer exists, into North America. Archaeologists have discovered in Siberia a cache of Clovis points—the distinctive stone spear points made by paleohumans.

label: Conclusion
body: This shows that, contrary to previous belief, the Clovis point was not invented in North America.

label: Evaluate
body: The archaeologist’s conclusion is about where the first Clovis point was made. Since it is possible that the cache of Clovis points discovered in Siberia were made by people who had traveled back to Siberia from North America, it could be that the Clovis point was invented in North America even though Clovis points were found in Siberia.

label: Facts
body: Taxi drivers decide on a certain total amount of money they want to work in a day (say, $150), and then as soon as they hit that amount, they stop working. Because of this, they typically work fewer hours on a busy day than a slow day.

label: Evaluation
body: When we see causal connector language — due to, because of, this means that, this makes possible, this allows for, etc — we usually see correct answers reinforcing the causal relationship. And when we're presented with two mathematical ideas, the correct answer usually involves what can be inferred by combining those two math ideas. So, if we know that on busy days they take fewer hours to reach amount X, and on slow days they take more hours to reach amount X, then on busy days they are earning more money per hour.

label: Goal
body: Since we want to go against the passage, look for an answer saying that busy days have better hourly revenue than do slow days.

label: Evidence
body: No one who is writing a great GP → ~ICI poem intends it to communicate contradictory ideas. Sometimes one reads a poem GP + BCI and believes that the poem expresses contradictory ideas, even if it is a great poem.

label: Conclusion
body: So it is wrong to think that the meaning of a poem is whatever he author intends to communicate to the reader by means of the poem.

label: Evaluate
body: The argument assumes that if BCI → CI the reader believes that a poem expresses contradictory ideas then contradictory ideas are part of the meaning of a poem.

label: Given
body: All contributions $100+ to these campaigns + in excess of $100 ~Residents → Registered made by + nonresidents of ~Former Residents Weston who are not former residents of ~$100 Weston must be or registered with Residents → ~Registered the city council. or Former Residents Brimley’s mayoral Residents campaign clearly Contributions → or complied with this Former Residents law since it accepted contributions only from residents and former residents of Weston.

label: Evidence
body: Flavius, an ancient Roman governor who believed deeply in the virtues of manual labor and moral temperance, actively sought to discourage the arts by removing state financial support for them. There are a large number of satirical plays that were written about him during his administration.

label: Conclusion
body: Flavius was widely unpopular among his subjects.

label: Evaluate
body: That there were a large number of satirical plays written about Flavius does not prove that he was widely unpopular among his subjects. It only shows that he was widely unpopular among playwrights—for whom Flavius removed state financial support.

label: Apparent Paradox
body: Educators studied the performance of 200 students in a university’s history classes. They found that those students who performed the best had either part-time jobs of full-time jobs, had their history classes early in the morning, and had a very limited social life. Whereas, the those students who performed the worst had no jobs, had their history classes early in the morning, and had a very active social life.

label: Evaluate
body: Both the best and worst performers had their classes in the morning. The differences between the groups are the extent of their social life and whether they had a job. Both activities consume time making it harder to study. So why does one group perform better than the other. It must be that lost time to work does not impede study time to the extent that an active social life does.

label: Conclusion
body: We shouldn't be persuaded by Kuyler's argument.

label: Evidence
body: Kuyler implied it would be wrong to enter into a contract with the government, yet his company has had contracts with the government.

label: Evaluation
body: This argument has the reasoning of a kid yelling at this parent, "What do you mean it would be wrong for me to smoke? You used to smoke!" What would the parent say? "Yes, but I learned it was wrong." or "Yes, but I was an adult and you are a kid". When we try to invalidate someone's advice based on the fact that they previously took an opposite course of action, we ignore that they may now realize they were mistaken to take that course of action. Or, it's possible that the two situations are just not fair to compare for some reason.

label: Goal
body: Perhaps Kuyler regrets the decisions to enter into contracts with the government and is passing on his wisdom. Perhaps the situation with Kuyler's company was very different, so in their case government contracts were not improper. Or maybe the answer will just call out the Ad Hominem argument: "Don't listen to their advice. They previously behaved / believed contrary to their advice."

label: Opposing Point
body: Free international trade allows countries to specialize, which in turn increases productivity.

label: Evidence
body: Small Countries often rely on one or two products for the bulk of their exports. If those products are raw materials, the supply is finite and can be used up. If they are foodstuffs, a natural disaster can wipe out a season’s production overnight.

label: Conclusion
body: Specialization within international trade carries risks.

label: Apparent Paradox
body: Two randomly selected groups of 30 adults each were asked to write short stories on a particular topic. One group was told that the best stories would be awarded cash prizes, while the other group was not told of any prizes. Each story was evaluated by a team of judges who were given no indication of the group from which the story came. The stories submitted by those who thought they were competing for prizes were ranked on average significantly lower than the stories from the other group.

label: Evaluate
body: It would seem that believing one’s story would be evaluated actually reduced the average quality of one’s short story. Maybe the pressure to perform was just too much. Or maybe those who write short stories to win prizes take less risk and produce bland writing. Or maybe it’s the opposite and they take too much risk, writing outlandish and unbelievable stories.

label: Evaluation
body: How would we describe Hernandez's response? It sounds like he understands Green's concern --- some cars get extra use because they have big territories and they wear out sooner. He's re-framing his suggestion to Green, "Yes, those need to be replaced sooner, but how about we replace the other cars every four years." When we carve out exceptions or narrow the scope of what we're talking about, we are qualifying a claim / a suggestion / a definition.

label: Goal
body: Look for something like narrowing the parameters of his suggestion, acknowledging that Green has brought up exceptional cases that indeed should not apply.

label: Evidence
body: As should be obvious, raising the minimum wage significantly would make it more expensive for businesses to pay workers for minimum-wage jobs.

label: Intermediate Conclusion
body: Therefore, businesses could not afford to continue to employ as many workers for such jobs.

label: Main Conclusion
body: So raising the minimum wage significantly will cause an increase in unemployment.

label: Evaluate
body: There are two arguments here. The correct answer could attack the argument containing the premise and the intermediate conclusion or could attack the argument containing the intermediate conclusion and the main conclusion.

label: Apparent Paradox
body: Scientists removed all viruses from a seawater sample and then measured the growth of the plankton population in the water. They expected the rate to increase dramatically, but the population actually got smaller.

label: Evaluate
body: To explain this result the answer should indicate why the plankton declined when viruses were removed from a sample of seawater.

label: Conclusion
body: We must deny the Senior Guild's request.

label: Evidence
body: Got to prevent anarchy! How would granting the Senior Guild's request lead to anarchy? Well if we grant this exception, even though it is deserved, we'll be granting other exceptions which won't be merited. Soon thereafter, we'll be granting exceptions to every Tom, Dick, and Harry that come wandering off the street.

label: Evaluation
body: Couldn't they just not grant exceptions to undeserved parties? We could certainly call out their assumption that "excessively granting exceptions to city ordinances" qualifies as "anarchy". But the most objectionable line of attack just seems to be this dubious move from, "If I give you a cookie, since you cleaned your room, then I have to give everyone a cookie, regardless of whether they deserve one." To which we might reply: no you don't. Just give cookies to the people who deserve them. Similarly, we want to tell this council member, "Just only give exceptions to those who deserve them, and anarchy will not result."

label: Goal
body: Look for something reflecting the internal contradiction of "they deserve this exception, but let's not give it to them" or something challenging the slippery slope argument he's making.

label: Evidence
body: In comparing our country with two other countries of roughly the same population size, I found that even though we face the same dietary, bacterial, and stress-related causes of ulcers as they do, prescriptions for ulcer medicines in all socioeconomic strata are much rarer here than in those two countries.

label: Conclusion
body: It's clear that we suffer significantly fewer ulcers, per capita, than they do.

label: Evaluate
body: This explanation is only one of several possible. An alternative explanation could be that although people in the physician’s country suffer from ulcers at the same rate as the other two countries, they are less likely to be prescribed ulcer medications. Maybe their access to physicians is more limited or maybe physicians in that country are more concerned about long-term side effects of ulcer medications.

label: Conclusion
body: Bicyclists are least partially responsible for over half of accidents involving bikes.

label: Evidence
body: More than 1/4 of accidents involving bikes involve a biker failing to obey a traffic rule. More than 1/4 of accidents involving bikes involve a biker with inadequate safety equipment.

label: Evaluation
body: The intended logic is that if more than 25% of accidents come from breaking rules and more than 25% come from inadequate equipment, then more than 50% of accidents come from "breaking rules or inadequate equipment" (i.e. bikers who are at least partially responsible). Quick analogy: 50% of Americans follow the NBA. 50% of Americans follow the NFL. Thus every American is either an NBA fan or an NFL fan. The problem there is that those 50% groups can be highly overlapping. Let's go overboard with stereotyping to make the math easy to see. Suppose that all males like sports, so they follow the NBA and the NFL. Suppose that all females don't like sports so they don't follow the NBA or the NFL. In this case, it would be true to say that 50% of the US follows the NBA, and 50% follows the NFL, but it would only be 50% of Americans that are an NBA fan or NFL fan. Similarly, in this argument with the bicyclists, there could be responsible bikers who always follow traffic rules and have adequate safety equipment. They aren't involved in either type of accident we heard about. Then there are irresponsible bikers (like me), who break traffic rules and have inadequate safety equipment. When we get into accidents, it's possible that our rule-breaking and our shoddy safety equipment are both causal factors. So even if we're only involved in 27% of all accidents involving bikes, the premises would still be true (more than 25% of accidents involved rule breaking ... more than 25% involved bad equipment) but the conclusion would not.

label: Goal
body: Look for something like, "fails to consider the possible overlap between two causal factors".

label: Claim
body: We can make a vaccine that will produce permanent immunity to hepatitis E.

label: Evidence
body: A suitable portion of hepatitis E has been isolated, that will stimulate antibody production. People who take the vaccine will produce antibodies that would recognize hepatitis E and and kill it if the person ever encountered the actual hepatitis E virus.

label: Evaluation
body: It seems like a pretty reasonable claim, given what we're told about how vaccines work. However, the claim is strongly worded. A "permanent" immunity? Nothing in the evidence talked about permanent immunity. In order to fight this conclusion, we need an idea that prevents the next part of the plan from being carried out (maybe we've isolated the part of hepatitis E, but we don't have a good way to introduce it into a person's body), or an idea that shows why even if we achieved immunity for a while, it wouldn't be permanent (maybe hepatitis E mutates and a newer version wouldn't be killed by the old hepatitis E antibodies).

label: Goal
body: They're NOT gonna be able to produce a permanent-immunity vaccine because ... [answer choice]

label: Evidence
body: To qualify as an effective law, as opposed to merely an impressive declaration, a command must be backed up by an effective enforcement mechanism. That is why societies have police. The power of the police to EF → EN enforce a society’s laws makes those laws effective. But there is currently no ~IP international police force.

label: Conclusion
body: Hence, what is called ~EF “international law” is not effective law.

label: Evaluate
body: The argument assumes ~IP → ~EN that if there is no international police force, then international law will not be enforced.

label: Statements
body: causal (this is because) In still-life painting, the artist invariably chooses, modifies, and arranges the objects to be painted. This results in still-life painting being conducive to the goal of the artist's self-expression. causal (thus) The fact that still-life painters can manipulate the objects to be painted means that still-life painters have more control than landscape or portrait painters.

label: Evaluate
body: Since the most common pattern on Most Supported is causal inferences, we would be most attracted to the Causal Connector Language like "this is because" and "thus". The correct answer will probably reward us for understanding those causal relationships. Being able to choose and modify the objects to be painted leads to better self-expression and leads to more control over composition/subject. We can tease out hidden truths there such as - choosing, modifying, and arranging the objects to be painted is an act of self-expression (implied difference) - in a lanscape or portrait painting, the painter doesn't have much control when it comes to choosing, arranging, and modifying the things being painted.

label: Given
body: Food of a type that does not ~OCF + ~MBF → ~LN ordinarily contain fat cannot be labeled “nonfat” unless most people mistakenly believe the food ordinarily contains fat. If most people mistakenly MBF and LFO → may LN believe that a food ordinarily contains fat, the food may be labeled “nonfat” if the label also states that the food ordinarily contains no fat.

label: Evaluate
body: The labeling regulation presents two conditional relationships. The right answer will violate one of them. Since the second rule is wishy-washy (it's just saying you MAY do something), it would be hard to contradict. To contradict it, we'd need to hear that someone CAN'T label their food nonfat. Simply saying they AREN'T labeling their food nonfat wouldn't contradict it. So we can anticipate that the correct answer will break the first rule. It'll give us something that - doesn't ordinarily contain fat and - isn't something ppl wrongly think does contain fat and this food will be getting labeled nonfat, thereby breaking the rule.

label: Conclusion
body: It's never acceptable to offer an experimental treatment to patients who don't have any extreme symptoms of that disease.

label: Evidence
body: If a patient is showing extreme symptoms from a disease, then it's acceptable to offer an experimental treatment. Those patients are best able to weigh the tradeoffs of doing an experimental treatment.

label: Evaluation
body: The second premise is there to potentially hide the Necessary vs. Sufficient flaw. The author is performing an illegal negation: If a patient has extreme symptoms, then it's acceptable to offer experimental. thus, if a patient does not have extreme symptoms, then it's not acceptable to offer experimental.

label: Goal
body: Look for an argument that says, If you're of type X, then thing Y applies. Thus, if you're not of type X, then thing Y doesn't apply

label: Given
body: As modern methods of CTI -causes→ FPL communication and transportation have continued to improve, the pace of life today has become faster than ever before. This speed [faster pace of life] has FPL -causes→ FNT created feelings of impermanence and instability, making us feel as if we never have enough time to achieve what we want—or at least what we think we want.

label: Conclusion
body: According to the department store's standard, B's Store should give me a refund for my watch.

label: Evidence
body: If you buy a watch at a department store and use it only as intended, but it stops working the next day, the department store will refund your money. I bought a watch from B's Store and it stopped working the next day. B's Store isn't a department store, but let's assume it's adopting this very reasonable standard.

label: Evaluation
body: Whenever we see conditional logic show up, we should think about what the trigger and consequence are (diagramming it if desired): Buy Watch and Use Only as Intended and Stops Next Day → Refund The author has established that he bought the watch and it stopped working the next day, but he never established that he used it only as intended.

label: Goal
body: The most likely answer would be one that spells out the missing fact from the trigger of that conditional rule. Look for something like, "he used the watch only as intended".

label: Evidence
body: A study found that patients referred by their doctors to psychotherapists practicing a new experimental form of therapy made more progress with respect to their problems than those referred to psychotherapists practicing traditional forms of therapy.

label: Conclusion
body: Therapists practicing the new form of therapy, therefore, are more effective than therapists practicing traditional forms.

label: Evaluate
body: The argument establishes a correlation between a new form of psychotherapy and better outcomes for the patients. The argument concludes that it is the therapists who practice the new form of therapy who are responsible for the better outcome. But something else could be behind the patients’ improvement.

label: Conclusion
body: One should not support systems that allow extreme freedom.

label: Evidence
body: People often make unwise decisions with extreme freedom, and once they see the destructive consequences, they may prefer to go for a totalitarian regime with almost no freedom.

label: Evaluation
body: Any time you have an argument that's structured like, "Don't do X, or else Y will happen", it's missing the assumption that "We don't want Y to happen". In more formal prose, "Actions that would result in Y should not be done." This argument is saying, "Don't do extreme freedom, or else people will see the downsides and consider totalitarian regimes instead."

label: Goal
body: So we should be looking for something like, "Don't choose any political system that might lead people into being tempted by totalitarian regimes".

label: Evidence
body: Every moral action is the MA → KA keeping of an agreement. Keeping an agreement is KA → MB nothing more than an act of securing mutual benefit. Clearly, however, not all KA ↢some↣ ~MA instances of agreement- keeping are moral actions.

label: Conclusion
body: Therefore, some acts of MB ↢some↣ ~MA securing mutual benefit are not moral actions.

label: Evaluate
body: The conclusion follows logically from the second and third premises.

label: Main Conclusion
body: The more technologically advanced a society is, the more marked its members' resistance to technological innovations.

label: Premise
body: The more technologically advanced a society is, the more aware its members are of technology's drawbacks. People realize that sophisticated technologies deeply affect the quality of human relations.

label: Conclusion
body: Candidates won't compromise their views in order to win the support of wealthy patrons.

label: Evidence
body: Even though you need money to win elections and a non-wealthy candidate will need some money from wealthy patrons, the wealthy are dispersed proportionately among the various political parties.

label: Evaluation
body: A healthy dose of real world common sense will help us here. In America, let's pretend that rich people are pretty evenly divided among Republicans and Democrats. Does that mean that candidates who need money won't compromise their views in order to get the support of wealthy patrons? The author is thinking, "Why would they need to pander if rich people don't represent any particular political constituency more than others?" We might say, well the Democratic candidates will pander to the rich liberals to get their money. The Republican candidates will pander to the rich conservatives to get their money.

label: Goal
body: We need an answer that helps us make an objection that sounds like, "Even though rich people can be found throughout the political spectrum, candidates still end up compromising their beliefs in order to appeal to the specific rich people they have the best chance of eliciting donations from".

label: Given
body: In modern "brushless" car washes, cloth strips called mitters have replaced brushes. Mitters are easier on most cars' finishes than brushes are. This is especially important with the new clear-coat finishes found on many cars today, which are more easily scratched than older finishes are.

label: Evidence
body: It strongly resembles the RSH structure of the heart of certain other sea animals. The muscular contractions RCH in the lancelet's vessel closely resemble the muscular contractions of other animals' hearts.

label: Conclusion
body: This vessel is indeed a H heart.

label: Evaluate
body: The argument assumes RSH + RCH → H that if a vessel has the structure of a heart and has contractions that resemble a those of a heart, then that vessel is a heart.

label: Evaluate
body: We don't see any of the normal Causal / Conditional stuff to grab on to. There's a little bit of an Important Pivot in the last sentence, setting up some tension. GIVEN THAT employees can all use the new software, WHY IS IT THAT many of them continue to use the old software? There could be a lot of potential reasons for that, but we wouldn't want to speculate, since we're looking for the most provable answer.

label: Goal
body: Overall, we know the manager thinks we shouldn't get rid of the old and go for the new, because when employees are given the option of both, many still opt for the old. Let's find the most provable answer.

label: Facts
body: Two groups read the same article but with different headlines. When quizzed on the articles, the answers in each group were consistent, but they were different from those of the other group.

label: Evaluation
body: Most Supported correct answers frequently point to the Causal Difference-Maker. How come the two groups had different answers, given that they read the same article? We’d probably assume that it was because of the different headlines.

label: Goal
body: Find a safely worded answer that reinforces the idea that having a different headline led these groups to have different responses to the questions they were asked.

label: Conclusion
body: The natural world is a work of art.

label: Evidence
body: Works of art are beautiful and instructive, as is the natural world.

label: Evaluation
body: Just because you share a trait with something doesn’t mean that you are thing. If we said that “mammals are living organisms that live on Earth, as are roses”, that wouldn’t allow us to conclude, “Thus, roses are mammals.” More formally, the author has provided us with a conditional claim, signified by the universal all. “If work of art, then beautiful and instructive”. Next, the author provides the necessary condition, “X is beautiful and instructive”, and infers the sufficient condition, “Thus, X is a work of art”. We aren’t allowed to do that Illegal Reversal. When we mess up the direction of conditional logic, we can call it confusing the sufficient and the necessary conditions.

label: Goal
body: Find an answer that describes the Necessary vs. Sufficient flaw, or find an answer that makes the objection that “something can share properties with works of art without itself being a work of art.”

label: Example 1
body: Copernicus made a breakthrough by looking different at info already available.

label: Example 2
body: Jenner made a breakthrough by shifting his focus from the common emphasis to something different.

label: Evaluation
body: As we usually do when we read Inference paragraphs, we pay attention to overlapping ideas. In both examples, the idea of “looking differently” or “shifting focus” came up in association with an important discovery.

label: Goal
body: The correct answer will likely be some safely worded claim that associates breakthroughs and discoveries with “looking at things differently”.

label: Evidence
body: Suppose censorship is wrong in itself, as modern liberals tend to believe. Then an actor's refusing a part in a film because the film glamorizes a point of view abhorrent to the actor would be morally wrong. But this conclusion is absurd.

label: Conclusion
body: It follows that censorship is not, after all, wrong in itself.

label: Evaluate
body: There are two reasoning structures at play in this argument. The conditional reasoning takes the form of a contrapositive, which is used properly. The second is the comparison made between an actor refusing a part and censorship. On this second issue, the argument assumes the two issues are comparable.

label: Conclusion
body: Cheaper brands of oil are the best buys

label: Evidence
body: (It doesn’t seem like there’s any benefit to buying the more expensive stuff), since in this study of taxis that drove 6000 miles all brands of oil did equally well at their goal of retarding engine wear.

label: Evaluation
body: Given that all the brands did equally well at their job, how could we still argue that more expensive brands of oil do give you some extra value? We might think about other good things motor oil can provide, like “Sure, all brands are the same in regards to X. But pricier oils are better at Y.” However, it seems like the argument restricted us to caring only about X (retarding engine wear). Could we say that the sample tested is misleading? Maybe there’s an important difference between taxis and regular consumer vehicles. Maybe there’s an important difference to how these oils would perform if we judged them at longer intervals, of 15,000 miles, 30,000 miles, etc.

label: Goal
body: Find an answer that would allow you argue that even though all the oils did equally well in this study, there is still a compelling reason to buy a higher priced motor oil.

label: Elena’s Conclusion
body: Democracy is the best form of government.

label: Elena’s Evidence
body: The best form is when the citizens believe that they have a say in how the government is run.

label: Marsha’s Response
body: In many forms of government, you can trick citizens into thinking they have a say even when they don’t.

label: Evaluation
body: If Elena is picking democracy based on this rule, Marsha is asking, “don’t other governments, some of which are non-democracies, also qualify for the same rule: their citizens believe, perhaps falsely, that they have a say”? She’s saying that based on Elena’s evidence, we wouldn’t be able to draw Elena’s conclusion, because you could equally draw the same conclusion about non-democracies.

label: Goal
body: Something like, “it is used to show that the criterion Elena used for selecting the best form of government would actually apply to several different forms of government”.

label: Evidence
body: The treatment usually wreaks havoc with the normal functioning of the human body, causing severe side effects such as total loss of hair, debilitating nausea, and intense pain in the joints.

label: Conclusion
body: The use of the newest drug in treating this disease should be discontinued.

label: Evaluate
body: There may negative consequences to using the newest drug in treating this disease. And the listed side effects sound terrible. But the consequence of not using the drug could be even worse. When deciding whether or not a drug should be used, the outcomes of both using it and not using it should be compared.

label: Otis's 1st Claim:
body: Aristotle's principle of justice says that we should treat relevantly similar cases similarly. Does Tyra dispute this? No. She explicitly accepts it.

label: Otis's 2nd Claim:
body: Therefore, it is wrong for a dentist to schedule an after-hours appointment to suit a family friend but refuse to do it for anyone else. Does Tyra dispute this? Yes. She explicitly says "it's not unjust for dentists to do that."

label: Evaluate
body: In addition to accepting Aristotle's principle and disputing Otis's conclusion about dentists, Tyra offers a particular type of pushback: she defines / distinguishes something Otis has said. This is a common Rebuttal archetype and it shows up frequently on 2-Speaker Method questions. When Otis applies Aristotle's principle to the Dentist situation, he's assuming the situation triggers the principle: that the situation of a friend and a non-friend are relevantly similar, and should therefore be treated similarly. Tyra distinguishes friends from non-friends, showing them to be meaninfully different. It is on these grounds that she disputs Otis's conclusion: she implies that Aristotle's principle isn't applicable to this case.

label: Goal
body: Look for an answer that says they disagree about Otis's conclusion, or his assumption that Aristotle's principle should apply in this case.

label: Evidence
body: Typically, people who have diets high in saturated fat have an increased risk of heart disease. Those who replace saturated fat in their diets with unsaturated fat decrease their risk of heart disease.

label: Conclusion
body: Therefore, people who eat a lot of saturated fat can lower their risk of heart disease by increasing their intake of unsaturated fat.

label: Evaluate
body: The trigger in the conclusion (increasing the intake of unsaturated fat) is only half of the trigger in the evidence (replace saturated fat with unsaturated fat). The argument assumes that those who increase their consumption of unsaturated fat also reduce their consumption of saturated fat.

label: Conclusion
body: Omega-3’s from fish tend to lower cholesterol, and a diet with a good amount of fish would have a lot of health benefits.

label: Evidence
body: A study found that middle-aged people who ate fish twice a week were less likely to get heart disease than those who didn’t eat fish.

label: Evaluation
body: The evidence is a correlation, the most famous of all LSAT’s Curious Facts. Why is there a correlation in this study between eating fish and having lower risk of heart disease? The author believes the Causal Explanation for it is that fish contain Omega-3’s, which lower cholesterol, thereby lowering risk of heart disease. LSAT usually wants us to object to this line of reasoning by considering alternative explanations. Necessary Assumption provides missing links or defends against objections. So the author is assuming that something else is not the real reason the fish group had lower risk of heart disease. There are also some language shifts that could create bridge assumptions: “eating fish twice a week” = “a diet with a modest amount of fish”? “lowering blood cholesterol” = “lowering risk of heart disease”?

label: Goal
body: Correct answer will probably rule out an alternate causal explanation, but it may provide a missing link for either term shift.

label: Conclusion
body: Any improvement clients get out of short-term psychotherapy must be some common denominator to all psychotherapy (like maybe just having someone listen to you)

label: Evidence
body: In a few studies, clients had similar levels of improvement regardless of what type of psychotherapy they got.

label: Evaluation
body: If clients show similar improvement regardless of type of therapy, does that mean that something common to all those types is what’s providing the improvement? Is it possible that different therapies are helping in different ways, but it’s still resulting in similar levels of improvement? It is possible, but that doesn’t seem like a great objection. What if the level of improvement all these clients have in common is “almost none”? That would be a more plausible way in which the different types of therapy are trying to help in different ways, and yet they all show similar levels of improvement. There are lots of ways to be un-helpful. :)

label: Goal
body: Pretty murky. It seems like we need a different way to explain why people are ending up with similar levels of improvement, despite going to different types of therapy, or we need to weaken the plausibility of the author's notion that there is some common ingredient to all these therapies that is the real causal help.

label: Evidence
body: Journalists sometimes use historical photographs to illustrate articles about current events. But this recycling of old photographs overstates the similarities between past and present, and thereby denies the individual significance of those current events.

label: Conclusion
body: Hence, the [recycling of old] photographs in this manner by journalists distorts public understanding of the present by presenting current events as mere repetitions of historical incidents.

label: Evaluate
body: The argument assumes that overstating the similarities between past and present distorts public understanding of the present. It also assumes that denying the individual significance of the current events distorts public understanding of the present.

label: Evidence
body: If Juan went to the party, it is JW → ~ME highly unlikely that Maria would have enjoyed the party. But in fact it turned out that Maria ME did enjoy the party.

label: Conclusion
body: It is highly likely that Juan was at ~JW [went] the party.

label: Evaluate
body: This argument contraposes the first premise and is a valid argument.

label: Facts
body: If you’re not constantly aware of how precious life is, your mind is clouded with illusion. If you are constantly aware of how precious life is, you have a tainted emotional outlook.

label: Evaluation
body: To figure out where an Inference synthesis is going to come from, we look for Overlap. We may need a thesaurus here, but both claims talk about whether or not we’re constantly/perpetually aware/cognizant of how fragile and precarious life is. We learn that if we’re not aware, we’re clouded with illusion. If we are aware, we have a tainted emotional outlook. Since it’s a binary (you are or aren’t aware), there’s no way out.

label: Goal
body: Look for something reinforcing the idea that either way you slice it, there’s some bad news: you’re either clouded with illusion or have a tainted emotional outlook.

label: Paradox
body: Shoppers didn’t have a list but only bought stuff that was at least 50% off, YET they spent far more money (on similar number of items) than did shoppers who did have a list and bought all regularly priced items

label: Evaluation
body: How are the people only buying stuff 50% off spending more money on their items than the people who are only buying full-price stuff? Could it be because of the other difference – the sale-buying group didn’t have a shopping list, whereas the full-price buying group did have a list? Our real world thinking tells us that people with a list tend to stick to their plan and buy fewer items than people who don’t have a list and meander around the store possibly buying too much. But that causal difference-maker wouldn’t work here to explain one group’s bigger bill, because we’re comparing a similar number of items. The items on sale must have been way more expensive to start out with than were the items bought for full-price.

label: Goal
body: We need a way to explain how buying x items at 50% off was more expensive than buying x items (not same type of items) at full-price.

label: Evidence
body: A group of mountain climbers was studied to determine how they were affected by diminished oxygen in the air at high altitudes. As they climbed past 6,100 meters above sea level, the climbers slurred words, took longer to understand simple sentences, and demonstrated poor judgment.

label: Conclusion
body: This combination of worsened performances disproves the theory that the area of the brain controlling speech is distinct from that controlling other functions.

label: Evaluate
