body: This could be a reasonable explanation of the study's results. However, alternative explanations also exist and represent potential criticisms of the argument. One possible alternative is that many areas of the brain were affected by the diminished oxygen in the air and so the various things controlled by these areas of the brain would all perform worse—as was witnessed in the study.

label: Conclusion
body: If the studies are accurate, either E and Z should be banned or TSX should be legal.

label: Evaluate
body: The argument assumes that if the C → A figures are consistent, then they are accurate.

label: Evidence
body: We banned TSX, thinking that it was terrible while E and Z were okay. But these new studies say that E and Z are worse than TSX.

label: Evaluation
body: This is similar to the real world debate about whether or not cannabis should be legal. Alcohol and tobacco are legal, and they have more harmful effects than cannabis does. So consistent policy would either say all three should be illegal, or that cannabis should join the ranks of the legal. It wouldn’t make any sense for the mildest of the three (in this case TSX) to be the only one that is illegal.

label: Goal
body: We need a principle that argues in favor of consistency. We shouldn’t have the least harmful thing be illegal while the more harmful things are legal. Either make them all legal or make them all illegal.

label: Conclusion
body: There’s a positive correlation between drinking caffeinated beverages and developing heart disease (i.e. people who drink caff beverages are more likely than those who don’t to develop heart disease)

label: Evidence
body: People who smoke are more likely than those who don’t to develop heart disease. People who smoke are more likely than those who don’t to drink caff beverages.

label: Evaluation
body: This is a weird argument, because it’s not going from correlation to causality. It’s just trying to chain together correlations. If is A is correlated with B, and A is correlated with C, is it fair to say that B is correlated with C? It seems reasonable, but it doesn’t have to be true. Consider this example: People who are friends with Jenny are more likely than those who aren’t to like Taylor Swift. (Maybe 80% of her friends like T-Swift, while only 40% of her non-friends do) People who are friends with Jenny are more likely than those who aren't to go to Palomar High School. (Maybe 80% of her friends go to Palomar, whereas an insanely tiny fraction of the 8 billion strangers who aren't her friends go to Palomar). Does this mean that People who like Taylor Swift are more likely than those who don’t to go to Palomar High School? No, we couldn’t possibly get that sort of data from the first two facts. Just because A is correlated with B and with C doesn’t mean that B is correlated with C.

label: Goal
body: Look for an answer that says you can’t assume a correlation between two traits that are each separately correlated with a given trait, or something that allows us to argue that people who drink caff beverages are not more likely than those who don’t to develop heart disease.

label: Facts
body: causal wanting customers >> layout of markets to go to back of store (bread in back) pivot + causal popular items >> alienate customers in the rear the inconvenience >> shoppers dislike of supermarkets supermarkets

label: Evaluate
body: Normally, when Most Supported comes in this substyle of Proposition / Generalization, we hear some sort of Causal Difference-Maker or Pivot-Tension story. In this case we sort of get both. We're hearing that the same cause, "having an inconvenient layout, with popular items at the back" leads to mixed outcomes for the supermarket. The Good: customers have to pass tempting displays en route to the popular items. The Bad: customers dislike this / can get alienated by this

label: Goal
body: Look for the most provable claim. It'll probably reward us for understanding this tension between two effects of the same cause.

label: Conclusion
body: Fact-set illustrating a principle.

label: Evidence
body: Supermarket layouts manipulate shoppers by forcing them past displays; this alienates customers.

label: Evaluate
body: The structure is: manipulation → unwelcome consequence (alienation).

label: Goal
body: Find the principle: manipulation can have unwelcome consequences.

label: Conclusion
body: This is asking what general principle the supermarket story illustrates. The story is about a plan that backfires.

label: Evidence
body: Supermarkets are deliberately laid out to make you walk past tempting displays on your way to grab basics. That's a manipulation of customer behavior. But surveys say inconvenience is the #1 reason shoppers dislike supermarkets — so the layout that's supposed to drive impulse purchases is also driving customers crazy.

label: Evaluate
body: For a "principle illustrated" question, abstract away from the topic and ask: what general lesson does this scenario teach? The shape of the story: someone manipulates other people for their own benefit, and the manipulation produces a side effect they don't want (alienation). That's a story about manipulation backfiring. Watch for trap answers that capture only one piece of the picture (e.g., "alienation is bad for business" — true, but doesn't mention the manipulation; "even good plans fail" — not specific enough; "distracting customers is bad" — supermarkets aren't exactly distracting customers, they're routing them).

label: Goal
body: Pick the principle: manipulation of people can have unwelcome consequences.

label: Conclusion
body: It’s healthier to rely on lifestyle changes than on medication to reduce blood pressure.

label: Evidence
body: Medication has unhealthy side effects. Lifestyle changes, meanwhile, reduce blood pressure just as much as meds do.

label: Evaluation
body: Which is healthier, meds or diet/exercise, when it comes to reducing blood pressure? Here’s what we know: - Both of them reduce blood pressure by the same amount. - Meds often have unhealthy side effects. So they tied on the 1st thing, and meds lost out to diet/exercise on the 2nd thing? Doesn't that mean that diet/exercise wins, in this comparison? Not quite. We were never told that diet/exercise is different or better when it comes to unhealthy side effects.

label: Goal
body: While the argument could be assuming there isn’t some other component of meds or diet/exercise that would make meds healthier, the correct answer will likely just be the missing part of the comparison: the side effects of diet/exercise aren’t that bad.

label: Evidence
body: Several recent studies show, and insurance statistics confirm, that more pedestrians are killed every year in North American cities when crossing with the light than when crossing against it.

label: Conclusion
body: Crossing against the light in North American cities is therefore less dangerous than crossing with the light.

label: Evaluate
body: The argument equates 105 visits with 105 different patients — but one patient could have visited multiple times.

label: Evaluate
body: The argument's conclusion compares the riskiness of crossing with the light at a crosswalk to the riskiness of crossing against the light at a crosswalk. However the evidence compares the number of people killed crossing with the light at a crosswalk to the number of people killed crossing against the light at a crosswalk. But "riskiness" should be measured as a likelihood of being killed while crossing the street in both cases.

label: Conclusion
body: Studies showing melatonin can induce sleep doesn’t mean it’s useful for treating insomnia.

label: Evidence
body: These studies mostly didn’t include insomniacs, and only a few people even seemed significantly affected by the melatonin.

label: Evaluation
body: Do we hear any assumptions? Not really, other than “if only a few are significantly affected by melatonin, then it wouldn’t be helpful in treating insomnia”. It’s probably better to think through the lens of how we might object to this argument. If you wanted to defend the idea that these studies do help make the case that melatonin could be helpful for insomniacs what could we say or ask? I would want to know about the studies that DID examine people with insomnia. Was the melatonin useful for them? What about those few subjects who appeared significantly affected by melatonin – were they insomniacs? We basically want reassurances that within these studies, we don’t have any compelling data that makes it look like melatonin could help insomniacs. The author has left a few blank spots in his re-telling of the studies, so a correct answer might fill in those blanks.

label: Goal
body: Look for something like, “the insomniacs who were among the study were not seemingly affected by the melatonin”, or look for a brand new detail that corroborates the author’s notion that melatonin wouldn’t be useful for insomniacs.

label: Conclusion (hence)
body: We can’t say that the asteroid impact caused the T’s extinction.

label: Evidence
body: The asteroid impact caused a huge fire, and it caused climate change. We can’t prove that the fire caused T’s extinction, nor can we prove that climate change caused T’s extinction.

label: Evaluation
body: This is probably one where many students aren’t sure exactly what to call the flaw, but they could still think about the structure of the argument and make eliminations based on mismatches in the answers. This argument is flawed because you can sometimes be sure that something had a certain effect, even if you’re unclear on the exact specifics of how. Say that someone dies in a helicopter crash. You might not know whether they died on impact or died from the resulting fire, but you still know that the helicopter crash killed them. Similarly, we might know that the asteroid impact killed off the T’s, even if we don’t know whether it was the fire or the climate change that ultimately did them in (maybe it was a combination of both). This is a subtle variation of part vs. whole. We can’t say that either part of the asteroid’s impact killed the T’s, but maybe we can still say that asteroid impact as a whole killed the T’s.

label: Goal
body: X did thing A and thing B. We can’t prove that Z happened because of thing A. We can’t prove that Z happened because of thing B. Thus, we can’t prove that X made Z happen.

label: Conclusion
body: Across the board tax cuts for all brackets tends to favor the wealthy.

label: Evidence
body: When you cut taxes across the board, you have to raise that missing revenue either through nonprogressive tax increases (which favor the wealthy) or by deficit spending, which leads to govt borrowing and higher interest rates, which favors the wealthy lending class.

label: Evaluation
body: It’s always good to remind yourself when you go into a Main Conclusion question that the Conclusion will usually be the first sentence, or it will be some form of rebuttal. Priming your brain for the possibility of a First Sentence Conclusion makes it easier to hear that first claim as the umbrella idea that gets unpacked/supported by all the subsequent claims. Our author spells out a “damned if you do, damned if you don’t” (A or ~A) type argument. When you do across the board cuts, then you either raise nonprogressive taxes or you don’t, but each of those roads still leads back to the same finish line of favoring the wealthy.

label: Goal
body: We just need something that sounds like “across the board cuts for all brackets tend to have a disproportionate benefit for the wealthy”.

label: Evidence
body: The human population will increase substantially over the next few decades, drastically increasing the need for freshwater.

label: Conclusion
body: Hence, restrictions on water use will be necessary to meet the freshwater needs of humankind in the not-too-distant future.

label: Evaluate
body: The argument concludes that restricting water use will be necessary, but an alternative approach also exists. If additional freshwater could be sourced, then there would be sufficient freshwater and no need for water restrictions.

label: Conclusion
body: The best way to remember something you can't quite remember is to focus on something else.

label: Evidence
body: Often, the more we try to remember the thing that's eluding us, the less likely we'll actually succeed at remembering it.

label: Evaluation
body: We need a generic principle, not related to recall/memory, that could apply to an argument on a different topic. The general moral to this story is that we have a problem, and we're being advised to distract ourselves with something else, because the more we focus on the problem, the less likely it is we'll find our solution.

label: Goal
body: Look for an answer recommending that we temporarily distract ourselves from the thing we're trying to accomplish, because the more we focus on it, the less likely it is we'll succeed.

label: Given that ...
body: The Planning Department budget increased from $100,000 in 2001 to $524,000 for this year.

label: How can argue ..
body: The department does not spend five times as much money as it did in 2001 to perform the same duties?

label: Evaluate
body: Since the money is definitely fives times as much, I guess the answer would have to say the duties aren't the same?

label: Evaluation
body: We need to draw a safely-worded moral to the story. Maybe something like "simplifying isn't always the best way to tackle problems", or "the problem solving skills of industrialists aren't best suited to every type of problem".

label: Given
body: At mock trials in which jury instructions were given in technical legal jargon, jury verdicts tended to mirror the judge’s own opinions. Jurors had become aware of the judges nonverbal behavior: facial expressions, body movements, tone of voice. Jurors who viewed the same case but were given instruction in clear, nontechnical language, however, were comparatively more likely to return verdicts at odds with the judge’s opinion.

label: Evaluate
body: The example compares mock trials where the jury instructions are presented in technical language and those where it is not. Where it is, the jury verdicts more frequently mirror the judges own opinions than where it was not. The explanation that this because jurors had become aware of the judges nonverbal behavior when the instructions were presented in technical language.

label: Opposing Point
body: A few alternative medicines have dangerous side effects.

label: Premise
body: Some [alternative medicines], such as many herbs, have been proven safe to consume.

label: Intermediate Conclusion
body: Their patients will not be harmed, and might be helped, by the use of these products.

label: Main Conclusion
body: Advocates of these herbs as remedies for serious illnesses should always be allowed to prescribe them.

label: Evaluate
body: This argument considers some of the impacts of allowing some alternative medicines to be prescribed to patients for serious illnesses. But the argument fails to consider all possible negative consequences. The right answer should provide a negative consequence of allowing such remedies to be prescribed.

label: Conclusion
body: It's not a violation of free-market principles if a government on the verge of a economic collapse needs to limit the extent to which foreign investors and lenders can pull out their money.

label: Evidence
body: It's not a violation of free-speech principles to say that you can't yell "Fire!" in a crowded movie theater, because that could lead to a harmful stampede. Similarly, letting foreign investors and lenders stampede to get their money out of an imperiled economy could do harm.

label: Evaluation
body: Our job is just to characterize the type of evidence or type of move the author made to support her conclusion. The most common type of correct answer on Method is questions is that the author used an analogy to support her argument, and that seems to be what's happening here. To make a point about governments limiting free-market activities, the author used an analogy about a case we already accept in which governments limit free-speech activities. In both cases, the point of doing so is the avoidance of harm.

label: Goal
body: Look for something saying that the author used an analogy to show that placing some limits on an activity in order to avoid harm can be a reasonable position and not a violation of the underlying principle of freedom.

label: Conclusion
body: Being the target of attack ads actually helps a candidate

label: Evidence
body: Most elections have been won by candidates who were the targets of attack ads.

label: Evaluation
body: How could an attack ad help you? It portrays you in a negative light. The conclusion seems fishy, but then how do we explain why most elections are won by people who were the targets of attack ads? - maybe everybody is the target of attack ads! It could be true that the losing candidates in most elections are also the targets of attack ads - maybe the winner won the election in spite of the attack ads, not because of them. We would probably say that "most marathons have been won by runners who experienced cramps at some point during the race", but that wouldn't make us say "having cramps actually benefited these runners". We just think the runners were powerful enough to overcome the cramps. - maybe there's an element of reverse causality: who is most likely to be the target of attack ads in any election? The front-runner. So it's not that being the subject of attack ads is causing them to be the front-runner / winner. Being the front-runner is causing them to be the subject of attack ads.

label: Goal
body: We need something to replicate this Correlation vs. Causation move: Since most people who were X were also Y, it must be that Y helps them to be X. The correct answer will probably be vulnerable to the same objection of Reverse Causality.

label: Apparent Paradox
body: Working residents of Springfield live, on average, farther from their workplaces than do working residents of Rorchester. Thus, one would expect that the demand for public transportation would be greater in Springfield than in Rorchester. However, Springfield has only half as many bus routes as Rorchester.

label: Evaluate
body: Buses are only one form of public transportation. Anything that would provide an alternative form of public transportation in Springfield would explain the unexpectedly low number of bus routes in Springfield. In fact, anything that reduces the need for transportation in Springfield would help explain the low number of bus routes.

label: Conclusion
body: N5 (a fat substitute) is of no use to people who need to eat less fat and fewer calories.

label: Evidence
body: In studies, people who ate foods prepared with N5 almost always felt hungrier after that than they would have had they eaten a meal with real fat. Because they were hungrier, they ate more food, which made the total calories about the same as if they had just eaten the real fat meal.

label: Evaluation
body: When authors make such extreme conclusions as "N5 is of no use to these people", all we have to do to strike back is point out some usefulness. Is there a way that N5 was in any way useful to people trying to reduce their fat intake and consume fewer calories? Sure, it helped them reduce their fat intake! That was useful. It would be better if it accomplished both goals, but if you compare a meal with 500 calories and 10g of fat to a meal with 500 calories and 2g of fat, isn't the second one usefully better to you?

label: Goal
body: We need a way to argue that N5 could be useful to people who are trying to eat less fat and fewer calories. One potential answer might point out that in the study, even though the people ended up consuming the same calories as before, making meals with N5 was at least allowing them to eat less fat.

label: Evidence
body: In order to survive, we must make our products more competitively priced. And if we refurbish the factory, our products would be more competitively priced, since one reason that our products are expensive is that our equipment is old and inefficient.

label: Given
body: Some critics lament the fact that impoverished postwar recording studios forced early bebop musicians to record extremely short solos, thus leaving a misleading record of their music. But these musicians’ beautifully concise playing makes the recordings superb artistic works instead of mere representations of their live solos. Furthermore, the conciseness characteristic of early bebop musicians’ recordings fostered a compactness in their subsequent live playing, which the playing of the next generation lacks.

label: Conclusion (So)
body: There is no causal connection between damage to chromosome number six and adult schizophrenia.

label: Evidence
body: There are people who have adult schizophrenia, but don't have damage to chromosome number six, and there are people who have damage to chromosome number six, but don't have adult schizophrenia.

label: Evaluation
body: We probably all know someone (or are someone) with an allergy to cats. When they're around a cat, they start having noticeable symptoms. We would accept that there is a causal connection between the cat and the symptoms. This author is saying, aren't there people with cats, who don't have allergy symptoms? Aren't there people who have allergy symptoms, but not cats? Yes, author. There isn't a causal connection between cats and allergy symptoms for everyone, but there still is a connection for some.

label: Goal
body: Look for an answer addressing the idea that there can be an occasional causal connection between two things, even if there are times when the two things don't have a causal connection.

label: Opposing Evidence
body: Art critics are divided over whether the edifice really qualifies as art.

label: Opposing Conclusion
body: Many city residents oppose the city art commission’s proposed purchase of an unusual stone edifice.

label: Evidence
body: The purpose of art is to CED → FPA cause experts to debate ideas, including ideas about what constitutes art itself. The edifice has caused CED experts to debate what constitutes art itself.

label: Conclusion
body: The edifice does qualify QA as art.

label: Evaluate
body: The argument assumes FPA → QA that if the edifice fulfills the purpose of art, it qualifies as art.

label: Problem
body: It is a given that to be IP → IC an intriguing person, one must be able to inspire the perpetual curiosity of others.

label: Conclusion
body: Constantly broadening PE → IC one's abilities and extending one's intellectual reach [perpetually expanding one’s mind] will enable one to inspire that curiosity.

label: Premise
body: For such a perpetual PE → ~FC → CM expansion of one's mind makes it impossible to be fully comprehended, making one a constant mystery to others.

label: Evidence
body: Theater managers will not ~BGP → ~RF rent a film if they do not believe it will generate enough total revenue— including food-and- beverage concession revenue—to yield a profit. Film producers want their RF films to be shown as widely as possible (rent the film).

label: Conclusion
body: Film producers tend to AYA make films that theater managers consider attractive to younger audiences.

label: Evaluate
body: The argument assumes BGP → AYA that theater managers believe that films that generate profits are likely to be those that are attractive to younger audiences.

label: Facts
body: Causal Almost all advances in genetic research give rise to ethical dilemmas. Binary Funding for genetic research comes either entirely from the government or entirely by corporations (most from the govt). Conditional Genetic Research → Govt Funding or Corp Funding

label: Evaluate
body: There's no obvious direction this is heading. We have overlapping ideas like "genetic research" / "govt funding" / "corp funding". The only difference between the second sentence and third sentence seems to be that 2nd sentence is saying "All genetic research is funded by G or C", while the 3rd sentence is saying, "All genetic research must be funded by G or C". So there's not much we can do to combine those. We have the causal idea in the first sentence that genetic research usually leads to ethical dilemmas, so maybe we could combine that with the 2nd/3rd sentence in order to say, "ethical dilemmas can arise from stuff that was funded by the government or corporations"?

label: Goal
body: Find an answer that is provable based on the provided facts.

label: Evidence
body: Corporate businesses, S → A like species, must adapt to survive. Businesses that are no ~EF → EX longer efficient will become extinct. Sometimes a business A → CCP cannot adapt without changing its core corporate philosophy.

label: Conclusion
body: Hence, sometimes a S → DC business can survive only by becoming a different company.

label: Evaluate
body: The argument assumes CCP → DC that a business can change its core corporate philosophy only if it becomes a different company.

label: Apparent Paradox
body: A survey taken ten years ago of residents of area L showed that although living conditions were slightly below their country’s average, most residents of L reported general satisfaction with their living conditions. However, this year the same survey found that while living conditions are now about the same as the national average, most residents of L report general dissatisfaction with their living conditions.

label: Evaluate
body: The question is, “how could the living conditions in area L improve relative to the country’s average while declining in absolute terms?” It’s possible if the average living conditions in the country experienced a dramatic decline.

label: Conclusion
body: Passengers are safer on a major airline than the new low-fare ones.

label: Evidence
body: Major airlines have long-standing records reliably indicating their level of safety. New low-fare airlines have had few, if any, accidents, but they haven't been around long enough to have a reliable record of their safety.

label: Given
body: Beginners typically decide each chess move by considering the consequences. Expert players, in contrast, primarily use pattern-recognition techniques. That is, such a player recognizes having been in a similar position before and makes a decision based on information recalled about the consequences of moves chosen on that prior occasion.

label: Evaluation
body: Is there a way for us to argue that the low-fare airlines are at least as safe as the major airlines? There's no way to reliably know that a new airline is safe (since they don't have long-standing records), but maybe there are some major airlines that have a long record of being unsafe, and so taking a chance on a low-fare airline could actually be safer than buying a ticket from a major airline with a history of accidents. All the author said is that the major airlines have records that reliably indicate their degree of safety, but these records may indicate that a major airline has a low degree of safety. The other direction we could take, since this argument is based on a comparison, is to think about what meaningful differences might exist between low-fare and major airlines that could impact safety. For example, if new low-fare airlines have state of the art collision-avoidance technology that major airlines don't have, then we have some reason to suspect that low-fare airlines might be at least as safe, even if we don't have the records to back it up.

label: Goal
body: Look for something saying, "An unknown new airline could still be safer than a known-to-be-dangerous major airline." or something saying "low-fare airlines have some safety feature that major airlines don't".

label: Evidence
body: Our economy’s weakness is the direct result of consumers’ continued reluctance to spend, which in turn is caused by factors such as high-priced goods and services. This reluctance is exacerbated by the fact that the average income is significantly lower than it was five years ago.

label: Conclusion
body: Thus, even though it is not a perfect solution, if the government were to lower income taxes, the economy would improve.

label: Evaluate
body: Lower income taxes is a new term. The argument assumes that lowering income taxes will reduce consumers’ reluctance to spend.

label: Given
body: A person with a type B lipid profile is at much greater risk of heart disease than a person with a type A lipid profile. In an experiment, both type A volunteers and type B volunteers were put on a low fat diet. The cholesterol levels of the type B volunteers soon dropped substantially, although their lipid profiles were unchanged. The type A volunteers, however, showed no benefit from the diet, and 40 percent of them actually shifted to type B profiles.

label: Principle
body: There should be complete freedom of thought and expression, as there is. But it's still wrong to exploit depraved popular tastes for the sake of financial gain.

label: Evaluation
body: Usually, principles are conditional statements. This one, though, seems more like balancing ideas that are somewhat in tension. Yes, we should allow free expression, but we can still condemn when people try to make money off other people's depraved tastes. I think this is saying something like, "A lot of people like violent movies, but this is an unhealthy depraved taste. People who want to make a lot of money off making violent movies should be free to do so, but we can still judge them negatively for doing so."

label: Goal
body: Look for a situation where we're scorning someone for doing X, but not forbidding them to do X, where X is meant to make money off of people's unhealthy tastes.

label: Conclusion (thus)
body: We can measure the rate at which a society is changing by measuring how much deference its younger members show to elders.

label: Evidence
body: In times of slow change, young people find great value in the advice of older people. In times of rapid change, young people do not value the advice of elders.

label: Evaluation
body: Part of how this argument is laid out feels like a False Choice: the author considers two extremes without thinking about the middle ground. What happens in terms of medium change? The author only covered what happens in terms of slow vs. rapid change. Another potential issue is the language shift between "how much young people do / don't value the advice of older people" vs. "how much deference young people do / don't show towards elders". Are those equivalent concepts? Not really. I could show deference to my elders whether or not I valued their advice. Deference means "respect". I can outwardly nod and look respectful while inside thinking, "What do you know, you old coot?" Goal Look for something connecting "how much you value advice" to "how much deference you show", or something dealing with what happens during periods of intermediate change.

label: Conclusion
body: We should impose a tariff on imported fruit, so that the price consumers pay for it is more than that for domestic fruit.

label: Evidence
body: If we don't impose the tariff, then foreign growers will be able to sell their better fruit at a lower price, resulting in our farmland being converted into more profitable industrial uses. We'll end up losing the unique farming way of life.

label: Evaluation
body: The consequences of not imposing the tariff sound pretty good: - better fruit at lower prices (from foreign sources) - our farmland is converted into more lucrative uses What was the downside? We would lose the farming way of life. When we're asked to find a supporting principle and the argument has competing concerns, we usually see a correct answer tell us that one concern is more important than the other.

label: Goal
body: Look for something saying, "we shouldn't let a unique way of life vanish", or "it's more important to protect unique ways of life than to have cheaper/better produce and more lucrative uses of land".

label: Conclusion
body: If the road through the preserve is kept close, the Valley's bear population will increase.

label: Evidence
body: During the eight years that the road has been closed, the population of bears inside the Kiffer Preserve has nearly doubled. Most of the bears in the Valley live in this Preserve.

label: Apparent Paradox
body: Because water content is what makes popcorn pop, the kernels must dry at just the right speed to trap the correct amount of water. The best way to achieve this effect is to have the sun dry the corn while the corn is still in the field, but I always dry the ears on a screen in a warm, dry room.

label: Evaluate
body: To resolve the apparent discrepancy between the farmer’s theory and practice, the right answer should provide some reason to believe that the farmer’s situation is not typical and warrants deviation from the standard best practice.

label: Conclusion
body: In order to survive, we must refurbish the factory

label: Goal
body: Beware strongly-worded answers. Look for something that safely reinforces the story we were told.

label: Evaluation
body: The author is making a causal assumption. She she's that the preserve's population of bears has nearly doubled while the road has been closed and then assumes that "the road being closed is causing there to be more bears there". Maybe, but there could be other ways to explain the uptick in bear population, so we could weaken the argument by coming up with a different way to explain why the bear population has gone up. The author is also shifting from talking about a population increase in the preserve to talking about a population increase in the valley. We might want to think about the difference there. Maybe the population goes up in the preserve (which is in the valley) but goes down in other parts of the valley. Finally, the author is making a prediction. Even if we granted that the road closure was the causal reason for the uptick in bears, there could be factors now that are different from 8 years ago. Maybe something meaningful has changed where further road closures would not have continuing effect on increasing the bear population (maybe they have a max population limited by the size of that habitat).

label: Goal
body: There are lots of attack points. Let's focus on the anti-conclusion and look for a way to argue that "we could keep the road closed, but it wouldn't lead to an increase in the valley's bear population."

label: Evidence
body: If a wig has any handmade HMC → ME components, it is more expensive than one with none. A made-to-measure wig MM → M-E ranges from medium- priced to expensive. Handmade foundations ~HH → ~HMF are never found on wigs that do not use human hair. Any wig that contains HH → DC human hair should be dry cleaned.

label: Conclusion
body: All made-to-measure wigs MM → DC should be dry cleaned.

label: Evaluate
body: The argument assumes that M-E → HMF if a wig is medium-priced to expensive, then it has a handmade foundation. MM → M-E -assumption→ HMF → HH → DC

label: Conclusion
body: You can't say that "animals don't have rights" based on the notion that "only humans can obey moral rules".

label: Evidence
body: Foxes, dogs, and wolves all follow a rule that "thou shalt not attack another, if they are being submissive and baring their throat".

label: Evaluation
body: We just need to describe the type of evidence or type of move the author made. The author supplied a specific example of a non-human animal that appears to follow some sort of moral rule, in order to make a very general conclusion. The author's conclusion isn't saying that animals do or don't have rights; it's saying you can't argue that animals don't have right based on the notion that animals can't follow moral rules ... because I just showed you an example of animals following moral rules.

label: Goal
body: Look for an answer that describes the conclusion as rejecting an argument or rejecting the basis for a certain general conclusion, and that describes the evidence as a specific example that seems to contradict that basis.

label: Apparent Paradox
body: Automated flight technology can guide an aircraft very reliably, from navigation to landing. Yet this technology, even when functioning correctly, is not a perfect safeguard against human error.

label: Evaluate
body: Why can’t automated flight technology perfectly safeguard against human error? Accidents often involve more than party. It’s possible that a plane flying with automated flight technology could be struck by another that was under human control. Alternatively, automation simply executes commands that programmed by humans. If the programmer makes a mistake, the machine can perfectly execute the prompted commands and still run into trouble.

label: Premise (after all)
body: Keeping one’s vital organs warm can keep one’s hands warm as well.

label: Intermediate Conclusion
body: One can always keep one’s hands warm simply by putting on an extra layer of clothing, such as a thermal undershirt or a sweater.

label: Main Conclusion
body: To keep one’s hands warm during the winter, one never needs gloves or mittens.

label: Evaluate
body: There are two arguments here. While the main conclusion seems reasonable given the intermediate conclusion, the intermediate conclusion does not seem to follow from the premise. Because keeping one’s vitals warm can keep one’s hands warm does not mean one will always be able to do so. The intermediate conclusion is much stronger than the premise.

label: Premise
body: The first sound heard within the womb is the comforting sound of the mother’s regular heartbeat.

label: Intermediate Conclusion (so)
body: In taking away from us the warmth and security of the womb, birth also takes away a primal and constant source of comfort.

label: Intermediate Conclusion (thus)
body: It is extremely natural that in seeking sensations of warmth and security throughout life, people would be strongly drawn toward simple recurring rhythmic sounds.

label: Main Conclusion
body: The reason music with a simple recurring rhythm exerts a strong primordial appeal is that it reminds us of the womb environment.

label: Given
body: Most people can tell whether a sequence of words in their own dialect is grammatical. Yet few people who can do so are able to specify the relevant grammatical rules.

label: Evaluate
body: The linguist’s statements illustrate that some people cannot specify how they know something that is true.

label: Conclusion
body: We will eventually select one of the best consultants available.

label: Evidence
body: We plan to interview only applicants who have worked for the top 1% of consulting firms.

label: Evaluation
body: If you only interview people who work for the top 1% of consulting firms, are you guaranteed to get someone who is a top 1% consultant? Not necessarily. Are we assuming that only the best consultants work at the best firms? Couldn't a firm be really good but still have some employees that are pretty mediocre? This author is committing a Whole vs. Part flaw, thinking that since the the company these employees work for are the best at consulting, each employee from those firms will be the best at consulting.

label: Goal
body: Look for something naming the Whole vs. Part flaw, or something pointing out the possible objection that there could the best firms in the world could still have some mediocre employees.

label: Goal
body: An answer pointing out the multiple-visit possibility.

label: Evaluation
body: Here's an analogous argument: In order to buy a house, I would need a lot more money. If I win the lottery, I will have a lot more money. Thus, in order to buy a house, I must win the lottery. Sure refurbishing the factory is one way to make our products more competitively priced, but is it the only way? Do we have to go that route, or are there any other ways to lower our prices? The argument even specifies "one reason our products are expensive", not "the reason our products are expensive".

label: Goal
body: Look for an answer describing the "takes one possible way to be the only way" move (aka Necessary vs. Sufficient), or something raising the objection that maybe there is another way for us to make our products more competitively priced.

label: Given
body: Many pythons hatched in HA ↢some↣ LD Africa are afflicted with a deadly liver disease. A few pythons recently HNA ↢some↣ LD hatched in North America have this disease. All pythons die within six LD → DSM months of contracting the disease.

label: Conclusion (thus)
body: Most people need to take vitamin pills.

label: Evidence
body: Most people eat far less than the five servings of fruits/veggies per day that nutritionists say would get them to their daily requirement for vitamins.

label: Evaluation
body: Anytime we have a problem to solve (getting our daily requirement of vitamins) and an author says "You need to do X", he's assuming two things: 1. X would actually be an effective solution 2. There aren't any other possible ways to solve the problem

label: Goal
body: We could attack the argument by saying that vitamin pills wouldn't be a viable solution for getting our daily requirement, or we could attack it by coming up with some other way for people to get their daily vitamins.

label: Premises
body: This fall I returned to a research site to recover the armadillos I had tagged there the previous spring. A large majority of the armadillos I recaptured were found within a few hundred yards of the location of their tagging last spring.

label: Conclusion
body: Armadillos do not move rapidly into new territories.

label: Evaluate
body: The author assumes that since the armadillos were in the same place during the spring of two different years, that they remained there the entire time. If armadillos were like birds, they might be in the same place each spring, and yet travel great distances during other parts of the year.

label: Sahira's Conclusion (that is why)
body: Government subsidies for artists are justified.

label: Sahira's Evidence
body: Without subsidies, artists who want to make a living would have to produce work for popular acclaim instead of their best work.

label: Rahima's Response
body: Rahima just says that one of Sahira's underlying ideas is wrong. Is it a premise? An assumption? Sahira says that artists "would have to produce work that would gain widespread popular acclaim, instead of their best work". She's assuming that an artist's best work wouldn't gain popular acclaim. Rahima seems to disagree.

label: Goal
body: A lot of correct answers on Method talk about the 2nd person challenging an assumption the 1st person made. In this case, it would seem fair to say that Rahima challenges a premise, as well as an assumption.

label: Sahira's Argument
body: Government subsidies for artists are justified because otherwise artists would have to compromise their best work for popular acclaim.

label: Rahima's Move
body: Rahima points out that Sahira's argument depends on assuming an artist's best work can't also be popular — and rejects that assumption.

label: Goal
body: An answer describing this as disputing an implicit assumption.

label: Sahira's Argument
body: Sahira says: without subsidies, talented artists would have to make popular work instead of their best work — so we should subsidize them.

label: Rahima's Move
body: Rahima isn't arguing about subsidies directly. She's pointing at a hidden premise of Sahira's argument: that an artist's "best work" and "widely popular work" must be different things. Think of it like this. Sahira is saying, "to keep up with rent, you have to take a boring job — so we should subsidize artists." Rahima responds, "wait — your whole argument assumes the only way to keep up with rent is a boring job. What if artists can make a living from their best work too?" That's an attack on an unstated assumption — not the conclusion directly, but the hidden premise the argument depends on.

label: Goal
body: An answer that describes Rahima's move as challenging an implicit assumption.

label: Given
body: Adult frogs are vulnerable to dehydration because of their highly permeable skins. Unlike large adult frogs, small adult frogs have such a low ratio of body weight to skin surface area that they cannot survive in arid climates. The animals' moisture requirements constitute the most important factor determining where frogs can live in the Yucatan peninsula, which has an arid climate in the north and a wet climate in the south.

label: Evidence
body: A recent survey shows that 77 percent of people feel that crime is increasing. The survey also showed that 87 percent feel the judicial system should be handing out tougher sentences.

label: Conclusion
body: Therefore, the government must firmly address the rising crime rate.

label: Evaluate
body: The argument assumes that because people believe the crime rate has increased, that it has actually increased.

label: Given
body: Proofs relying crucially on computers provide less certainty than do proofs not requiring computers. Human cognition alone cannot verify computer-dependent proofs. Such proofs [those that RCC → ~CC rely crucially on computers] can never provide the degree of certainty [not completely certain] that attends our judgments concerning, for instance, simple arithmetical facts, which can be verified by human calculation. Of course, in these cases one often uses electronic calculators, but here the computer is a convenience.

label: Facts
body: Industrialists try to solve problems by simplifying, but in farming that can lead to oversimplification. For example, they would use separate things to accomplish draining and water retention, whereas farmers would presumably use good topsoil to do both. You get more farming problems when industrialists, not farmers, are doing the farming.

label: Evidence
body: Works of modern literature T → PN cannot be tragedies as those of ancient playwrights and storytellers were unless their protagonists are seen as possessing nobility, which endures through the calamities that befall one. In an age that no longer ~GF takes seriously the belief that human endeavors are governed by fate.

label: Conclusion
body: It is therefore impossible ~T for a contemporary work of literature to be a tragedy.

label: Evaluate
body: The argument assumes that ~GF → ~PN if the protagonists’ endeavors are not perceived to be governed by fate, then the protagonists will not be seen as possessing nobility.

label: Conclusion (thus / should not)
body: The grad students should not unionize

label: Intermediate Conclusion (since / obviously)
body: The majority of them disapprove of the attempt to unionize

label: Evidence (Premises)
body: Of the small minority of students who have even heard of the attempt to unionize, most of them are pessimistic that a union would succeed or even try to effectively represent them.

label: Evaluation
body: The numbers in this argument don't add up. Let's say there are 100 grad students. The first sentence says that only a small minority of them (let's say 15 of them) have tried to unionize, while most of the 100 are unaware of the attempt (at least 51 of the 100 students have no idea that anyone is trying to unionize). Then the author zooms in on the 49 or fewer grad students who are aware of the attempt to unionize, and says that most of them disapprove. Since the author has established that most of 49 or fewer grad students disapprove, she's established that at least 25 of the 100 students disapprove. But her conclusion is saying that a majority (at least 51 of the 100 students) disapprove. So the flaw is either calling out her mathematical shadiness, or calling out her apparent assumption that "if most of the aware students disapprove, then most of the unaware students would also disapprove, were they to learn of the attempt to unionize."

label: Goal
body: Look for an answer talking about the author's bad math or about the author's sampling assumption (that the unaware students would also tend to disapprove of the attempt to unionize).

label: Conclusion (thus)
body: Griley does not believe in democracy.

label: Premise
body: Anyone who believes in democracy has a high regard for the wisdom of the masses. Griley is an elitist who believes that any popular artwork is unlikely to be good.

label: Evaluate
body: We're trying to prove that someone "doesn't believe in democracy", and the evidence did provide a way to prove that. don't have high regard → don't believe in for wisdom of masses democracy When the evidence provides a rule that proves the Telling Part of our conclusion, then our whole job becomes proving the trigger of that rule. We need to prove that Griley doesn't have high regard for wisdom of the masses.

label: Goal
body: We have to get from something we know about Griley (he's an elitist / he thinks popular art is unlikely to be good) to what we need to know about him, that he doesn't have high a high regard for the wisdom of the masses.

label: Argument
body: Believing in democracy requires high regard for the masses. Griley thinks popular artwork is unlikely to be good. So Griley doesn't believe in democracy.

label: Evaluate
body: To finish the chain, we need: Griley's belief about popular art implies not having a high regard for the masses.

label: Goal
body: An answer linking "thinks popular art is unlikely to be good" to "doesn't have high regard for the wisdom of the masses."

label: Argument
body: The author wants to get from "Griley thinks popular art is bad" to "Griley doesn't believe in democracy." The bridge: believing in democracy = high regard for the masses. Contrapositive: not having high regard for the masses = not believing in democracy.

label: Evaluate
body: So if we can establish that Griley's art belief means he doesn't have high regard for the masses, the conclusion follows. Think of it as a chain: Griley's belief -> ?? -> no high regard -> doesn't believe in democracy. We need to fill in the missing middle link: anyone who believes popular art is bad doesn't have high regard for the masses.

label: Goal
body: An answer that says: thinking popular art is unlikely to be good means not having a high regard for the wisdom of the masses.

label: Apparent Paradox
body: A recent study confirmed that salt intake tends to increase blood pressure and found that, as a result, people with high blood pressure who significantly cut their salt intake during the study had lower blood pressure by the end of the study. However, it was also found that some people who had very high salt intake both before and throughout the study maintained very low blood pressure.

label: Evaluate
body: Why would some people who had a very high salt intake have very low blood pressure? Maybe the people with very low pressure can eat a very high salt intake without it increasing their blood pressure.

label: Evidence
body: The odds of winning any major lottery jackpot are extremely slight. However, the very few people who do win major jackpots receive a great deal of attention from the media. Most people come to have at least some awareness of events that receive extensive media coverage.

label: Conclusion
body: It is likely that many people greatly overestimate the odds of their winning a major jackpot.

label: Evaluate
body: The evidence establishes that most people come to have some awareness of the very few people who do win major jackpots. The argument assumes that one’s awareness of someone else winning the jackpot increases one’s estimate of the likelihood of winning the jackpot themselves.

label: Conclusion
body: Julia's book tour must have been well publicized

label: Evidence
body: If a book tour is well publicized and involves an established writer, it will be successful. Julia is an established writer. The book tour was successful.

label: Main Conclusion:
body: It is a mistake to think, as ecologists once did, that natural selection will eventually result in organisms that will be perfectly adapted to their environments.

label: Evidence
body: Lead poisoning has steadily declined since the 1970s, but 25% of this area's homes still contain lead paint that poses a health hazard.

label: Evaluation
body: Since this involves conditional logic, it is probably advisable to diagram its structure, so that finding mismatches will be easier. Premise 1: A and B → C (a conditional with two things on the left) Premise 2: B is true. Premise 3: C is true. Conclusion: Thus, A must be true. Conversationally, we would say that the flaw is failing to consider that a book tour doesn't NEED those two components to be successful. The combo of famous writer / well publicized is guaranteed to be successful, but there's still room for tours that are famous writer / poorly promoted, unknown writer / well promoted, and unknown writer / poorly promoted to succeed.

label: Goal
body: Scan initially for a conditional premise, with an "and" in the trigger. Look for premises that factually assert half of the trigger and the consequence. Then look for a conclusion that factually asserts the other half of the trigger.

label: Opposing Point
body: Some of the craters contain rocks that have undergone high-pressure shocks characteristic of meteorites slamming into Earth.

label: Evidence
body: Eight large craters run in a long straight line across a geographical region. These shocks could have been caused by extreme volcanic events. Because of the linearity of the craters, it is very unlikely that some of them were caused by volcanoes and others were caused by meteorites. The craters are all different ages.

label: Conclusion
body: The craters were probably caused by volcanic events rather than meteorites.

label: Evaluate
body: While the argument compares two possible causes of the eight large craters, the evidence is not conclusive that the cause is more likely to be one or the other of the two possible causes.

label: Evidence
body: The genuine creative genius is someone who CG → ~HA is dissatisfied with merely habitual assent to widely held beliefs. Those who are ~HA → SC dissatisfied with merely habitual assent to widely held beliefs tend to seek out controversy. Controversy seekers SC → DF enjoy demonstrating the falsehood of popular viewpoints.

label: Conclusion
body: These rare innovators CG → AM tend to anger the majority.

label: Evaluate
body: The argument assumes DF → AM that those who enjoy demonstrating the falsehood of popular viewpoints tend to anger the majority.

label: Conclusion
body: It's silly to knock a job candidate's judgment because they're salting their food before tasting it (acting without sufficient information). i.e. It's perfectly reasonable to salt your food at a restaurant before tasting it.

label: Evidence
body: It's reasonable to wear a sweater to the grocery, before you've felt the temperature inside the store that day. It's reasonable to throw away credit card mail without finding out exactly what's being offered.

label: Evaluation
body: The analogies are meant to defend someone acting without having all the relevant information. Larissa is saying, "if you have a well established stereotype, like groceries = freezing / credit card offers = undesirable / restaurant food = not salty enough, then it's reasonable to expect your previous experience will be repeated."

label: Goal
body: Claude is negatively judging candidates who preemptively salt their food. Larissa thinks that's silly, and that preemptively salting your meal is totally reasonable. What principle is she invoking in criticizing Claude? If it's perfectly reasonable in these other cases to act preemptively based on expectations about what will likely be the case, then it shouldn't reflect poorly on your job candidates if they're preemptively salting.

label: Opposing Support
body: Almost every year the Smithfield River floods the coastal fishing community of Redhook, which annually spends $3 million on the cleanup Damming the river would cost $5 million. Damming the river would prevent the flooding.

label: Opposing Point
body: Some residents have proposed damming the river.

label: Evidence
body: A dam would prevent nutrients in the river from flowing into the ocean. Fish that now feed on those nutrients would start feed elsewhere. The loss of these fish would cost Redhook $10 million annually.

label: Conclusion
body: However, their position is misguided.

label: Conclusion (so)
body: 2nd driver wasn’t liable for the accident.

label: Evidence
body: Accident was caused by 1st driver changing lanes without signaling or by 2nd driver speeding. Either action would make a driver liable. We now know that 1st driver changed lanes without signaling.

label: Evaluation
body: How could we accept the evidence but still fight that conclusion and say that the 2nd driver is liable? We could just say that he was speeding. In life, sometimes we hear an either/or and assume it’s one or the other, but not both. In LSAT, we need to be told explicitly that it can’t be both. Otherwise, our default understanding of “Either X or Y is true” is that “X is true, Y is true, or both”. The author is getting caught up in a False Choice, that either driver 1 or driver 2 is liable, but not both. However, it’s possible that both drivers are liable, so we need to know whether the 2nd driver was speeding.

label: Goal
body: Was the 2nd driver speeding?

label: Apparent Paradox
body: Grizzly bears foraging for iceberg lilies annually destroy a large percentage of the lilies. Scientists have determined that the bears’ feeding habits actually promote the survival of iceberg lilies.

label: Evaluate
body: One explanation for how it could be that grizzly bears’ feeding habits actually promote the survival of iceberg lilies is that they provide population control for iceberg lilies that benefits that particular plant. Another possible explanation is that they serve a vital role in the reproduction of iceberg lilies—possibly helping with pollination or with spreading fertilized seeds.

label: Evidence
body: Seventy-five percent of dermatologists surveyed prefer Dermactin to all other brands of skin cream. We consulted dermatologists during the development of Dermactin to ensure that you have the best skin cream on the market.

label: Conclusion (so)
body: If you need a skin cream, use Dermactin.

label: Conclusion (opinion = not surprising)
body: It would not be surprising if the trade routes between China and the West were open way earlier than is currently thought (~2200 years ago).

label: Evaluate
body: It's pretty compelling to hear that 3/4 of dermatologists prefer Dermactin to all other brands of skin cream. So if we're hoping to argue that skin-cream users should NOT use Dermactin, we'd either need to argue - even though most dermatologists pick it as the best, it's not realistic for lots of people (too expensive? interacts poorly with other commonly used body products?) or - this survey was biased / self-selecting / too small, or something else that would cheapen its value as evidence

label: Evidence
body: If the screen between these Hedge → Hemlock or Leyland two areas is to be a hedge, that hedge must be of either hemlocks or Leyland cypress trees. Leyland cypress trees ~Leyland cannot be grown this far north.

label: Conclusion
body: If the screen is to be a Hedge → Hemlock hedge, it will be a hemlock hedge.

label: Evaluate
body: This is a valid argument. The conclusion restates an if/then relationship taking into account that one of the two options in the “or” statement has been ruled out.

label: Evidence
body: Many philosophers have argued that the goal of every individual is to achieve happiness—that is, the satisfaction derived from fully living up to one's potential. They have also claimed that happiness is elusive and can be achieved only after years of sustained effort. Simply walking along the seashore on a sunny afternoon causes many people to experience feelings of happiness.

label: Conclusion
body: They have clearly exaggerated the difficulty of being happy.

label: Evaluate
body: Deirdre confuses two very different forms of happiness. While the philosophers discuss the happiness derived from fully living up to one's potential, Deirdre discusses a momentary form of happiness.

label: Evidence
body: Global ecological problems reduce to the problem of balancing supply and demand. Supply is strictly confined by the earth's limitations. Demand, however, is essentially unlimited, as there are no limits on the potential demands made by humans. The natural tendency for there to be an imbalance between demand and sustainable supply is the source of these global problems.

label: Conclusion
body: Any solutions require reducing current human demand.

label: Evaluate
body: When an author is concluding that we MUST take a certain course of action (to solve a problem / achieve a goal), the most likely direction the correct answer is headed is considering whether there are Alternative Options. When an author says, "in order to get X, you must do Y", they are automatically assuming: 1. Y is a way to get X 2. there are no other ways to get X But correct answers almost always deal with #2, the possibility of Alternative options. If we're trying to balance demand and sustainable supply, we could potentially raise/lower demand to meet supply, or we could raise/lower supply to meet demand (or both). The author thinks our only option is lowering demand, so she's assuming - we can't correct an imbalance by increasing demand - we can't correct an imbalance by increasing / decreasing supply

label: Evidence
body: A scientific study of the effects of three common sugars—sucrose, fructose, and glucose—on children who have attention deficit disorder, with experimental groups each receiving a type of sugar in their diets and a control group receiving a sugar substitute instead of sugar, showed no statistically significant difference between the groups in thinking or behavior.

label: Conclusion
body: We can now dismiss the widely held suspicion that sugar consumption often exacerbates hyperactivity in children with attention deficit disorder.

label: Evaluate
body: The argument refutes a causal relationship by providing a study that supposedly demonstrated a counterexample. The argument concludes that sugar does not exacerbate hyperactivity in children with attention deficit disorder, because children who consumed sugar did not exhibit more hyperactivity than those who consumed a sugar substitute. The argument assumes that sugar substitutes do not exacerbate hyperactivity in children with attention deficit disorder.

label: Given
body: An action is morally good if it both AIG + BSO → MG achieves the agent’s intended goal and benefits someone other than the agent.

label: Evidence
body: A recent research report suggests that by exercising vigorously, one significantly lowers one’s chances of developing certain cardio-respiratory illnesses. But exercise has this effect, the report concludes, only if the exercise is vigorous.

label: Conclusion
body: Thus, one should not heed older studies purporting to show that nonstrenuous walking yields the same benefits.

label: Evaluate
body: The columnist has two studies. One says that exercise needs to be vigorous to significantly reduce one’s risk of developing cardio-respiratory illnesses. Another says that it doesn’t. So how does the author know which is correct? The flaw in this argument is the author assumes that one of them is correct.

label: Given
body: The curves generated by traditional statistical methods to analyze empirical data on human longevity predict that some humans would live beyond 130 years. According to the curves EVT generates, however, the limit on human life spans is probably between 113 and 124 years. To date, no one has lived beyond the upper limits indicated by EVT analysis.

label: Evidence
body: The number of different synthetic chemical compounds that are known to be carcinogenic but are nonetheless used as pesticides, preservatives, or food additives is tiny compared to the number of nonsynthetic carcinogenic compounds widely found in plants and animals.

label: Conclusion
body: It is therefore absurd to suppose that the rise in the cancer rate in recent decades is due to synthetic carcinogens.

label: Evaluate
body: The number of synthetic and nonsynthetic carcinogenic compounds is only part of the equation when determining the cause of the rise in the rate of cancer in recent decades. Other factors are also relevant, such as the level of exposure to each carcinogen and how carcinogenic each compound is.

label: Opposing Point:
body: Natural selection will eventually result in organisms that will be perfectly adapted to their environments.

label: Premises:
body: An individual’s environment can vary tremendously. No single set of attributes could possibly prepare an organism to cope with all the conditions that it could face.

label: Intermediate Conclusion:
body: Perfect adaptation of an individual to its environment is impossible.

label: Evidence (after all, and)
body: These trade routes were attractive because of their easily traversable terrain. This trait would have likely made it an attractive option for migrations that began one million years ago.

label: Evaluation
body: The conclusion is the first sentence, as is very common on Role and Main Conclusion questions. The "after all" tells us that what follows will be Support for that first sentence. The final sentence makes two claims, joined by an "and". 99% of the time "and" is connecting to supporting ideas.

label: Goal
body: The claim they're asking about is one of our two premises, for the conclusion that is found in the first sentence.

label: Opposing Point
body: The typological theory of species classification, which has few adherents today, distinguishes species solely on the basis of observable physical characteristics, such as plumage color, adult size, or dental structure.

label: Premises (since)
body: However, there are many so-called “sibling species,” which are indistinguishable on the basis of their appearance but cannot interbreed and thus, according to the mainstream biological theory of species classification, are separate species. The typological theory does not count sibling species as separate species.

label: Conclusion
body: The typological theory is unacceptable.

label: Evaluate
body: The argument assumes that sibling species should be counted as separate species. That the mainstream biological theory views sibling species to be separate species does not establish that they are.

label: Evidence
body: Individuals are responsible for only R → UC what is under their control. Whether one feels such an FE ↢some↣ ~UC emotion is not always under one's control.

label: Conclusion
body: The belief that a person is always FE ↢some↣ ~MB morally blameworthy for feeling certain emotions, such as unjustifiable anger, jealousy, or resentment, is misguided.

label: Evaluate
body: The argument assumes that if ~R → ~MB someone is not responsible for something, then that person is not morally blameworthy for it.

label: Given:
body: If two new processes NP + ~SDC → LED under consideration are not substantially different in cost, then the less environmentally damaging process should be chosen. If, however, a company EP + RSC + CR → LR or LTS already employs an environmentally damaging process and retooling for a less damaging process would involve substantial cost, then that company should retool only if retooling is either legally required or likely to bring long-term savings substantially greater than the cost.

label: Evidence
body: In a poll of a representative sample of a province's residents, the provincial capital was the city most often selected as the best place to live in that province. The capital is also the largest of that province's many cities.

label: Conclusion
body: Most residents of the province generally prefer life in large cities to life in small cities.

label: Evaluate
body: There is a difference between a city being most often selected as the best place to live and being the place that most people prefer to live. The argument mistakes a plurality with a majority.

label: Evidence
body: Genes, like viruses, have a strong G → SR tendency to self-replicate. Creating replicas of oneself is not SR → ~S selfish.

label: Conclusion
body: The label "selfish" as applied to G → ~S genes is a misnomer.

label: Evaluate
body: This argument is valid. But there is an intermediate argument inside the main argument. The claim that creating replicas of oneself is not selfish is an intermediate conclusion supported by a premise. And it is within this intermediate argument that there is an assumption.

label: Premise
body: Selfishness only concerns bringing S → BC about the best conditions for oneself.

label: Intermediate Conclusion
body: Creating replicas of oneself is not SR → ~S selfish.

label: Evaluate
body: The argument assumes that creating SR → ~BC replicas of oneself does not bring about the best conditions for oneself.

label: Conclusion
body: I am not an experienced salesperson.

label: Evidence
body: Only experienced salespeople will meet quota. I will only meet about half the quota.

label: Evaluation
body: When we’re doing flaw questions and see conditional wording (“only”), we should become very suspicious that the author will mess up the directionality of the conditional logic (known as the Necessary vs. Sufficient flaw). The author provides this rule: Meet quota → Experienced ~Experienced → ~Meet quota. His move from Premise to Conclusion is saying, “Since I don’t meet quota, I am not experienced”. That would look like this: ~Meet quota → ~Experienced We can see that she’s reading that rule backwards. Meeting the quota is sufficient to tell us that someone is Experienced, but it’s not necessary in order to be considered Experienced.

label: Goal
body: Something with this structure: A → B. X is not A. Thus, X is not B.

label: Given
body: Any garden and adjoining living SGD → CVM room that are separated from one another by sliding glass doors can visually merge into a single space. If the sliding doors are open, as DO → VM may happen in summer, this effect will be created [visually merge] if it does not already exist and intensified if it does. The effect remains quite strong WC + SVI → VM [visually merge] during colder months if the garden is well coordinated with the room and contributes strong visual interest of its own.

label: Apparent Paradox
body: Last summer, after a number of people got sick from eating locally caught anchovies, the coastal city of San Martin advised against eating such anchovies. The anchovies were apparently tainted with domoic acid, a harmful neurotoxin. However, a dramatic drop in the population of P. australis plankton to numbers more normal for local coastal waters indicates that it is once again safe to eat locally caught anchovies.

label: Evaluate
body: What changed? The answer should connect the drop in P. australis plankton to the assertion that it is now safe to eat anchovies.

body: Claim 1: It has been noted that Background Claim 2: Some say Counterpoint Claim 3: However, Conclusion Claim 4: for Premise

The traditional definition When people are juggling of full employment as a 5 several part-time jobs percent unemployment with no benefits, or rate is correct. working in a series of temporary assignments, as is now the case, 5 percent unemployment is not full employment. At levels below 5 percent, inflation rises.

label: Evaluate
body: Constance and Brigita disagree with each other about whether the definition of full employment as a 5 percent unemployment rate is correct.

label: Evidence
body: The supernova event of 1987 is interesting in that there is still no evidence of the neutron star that current theory says should have remained after a supernova of that size. This is in spite of the fact that many of the most sensitive instruments ever developed have searched for the tell-tale pulse of radiation that neutron stars emit.

label: Conclusion
body: Thus, current theory is wrong in claiming that supernovas of a certain size always produce neutron stars.

label: Evaluate
body: To strengthen this argument it is helpful to think of reasons why a neutron star, if it existed, would not have been detected. Couldn’t it also be the case that the most sensitive instruments are not sensitive enough to detect the neutron star because it’s too far away? Just because the instruments are the strongest, doesn’t mean they’re strong enough.

label: Evidence
body: On average, corporations that encourage frequent social events in the workplace show higher profits than those that rarely do.

label: Conclusion
body: This suggests that the EZ Corporation could boost its profits by having more staff parties during business hours.

label: Evaluate
body: It could be the case that more social events in the workplace could lead to higher profits. But the reverse could be true as well. It’s possible that companies with higher profits reward their teams for good work.

label: Evidence
body: On the Caribbean island of Guadeloupe, a researcher examined 35 patients with atypical Parkinson’s disease and compared their eating habits to those of 65 healthy adults. She found that all of the AP → EF patients with atypical Parkinson’s regularly ate the tropical fruits soursop, custard apple, and pomme cannelle. Whereas only 10 of the AP -most→ EF healthy adults [did not have atypical Parkinson’s] regularly ate these fruits.

label: Conclusion
body: From this, she EF -causes→ AP concluded that eating these fruits causes atypical Parkinson’s.

label: Evaluate
body: The researcher establishes a correlation between eating the tropical fruit and atypical Parkinson’s disease and then concludes a causal relationship between the two.

label: Price Albrecht
body: A corporation’s primary The corporation’s responsibility is to its primary responsibility shareholders. should be to [employees]. [Shareholders] take the Shareholders typically greatest risks. have diversified investment portfolios. For employees, however, the well-being of the corporation for which they have chosen to work represents their very livelihood.

label: Evaluate
body: Price and Albrecht disagree about where the primary responsibility of the corporation should be and whether shareholders or employees take the greatest risk

label: Claim
body: Despite the enormous number of transactions processed daily by banks nowadays, if a customer's bank account is accidentally credited with a large sum of money, it is extremely unlikely that the error will not be detected by the bank's internal audit procedures.

label: Evaluate
body: This is not an argument, so there is no reasoning to evaluate. The right answer will simply make the claim more likely to be true and should keep in mind that there is an opposing point. One could imagine that the large number of transactions every day might make it less likely that the error would be detected.

label: Conclusion
body: In this case, atmospheric pollution did cause global temps to rise

label: Evidence
body: In the 1500s, several years of high atmospheric pollution coincided with a period of higher than average global temps.

label: Evaluation
body: Just because pollution coincided with higher temps doesn't mean that pollution caused the higher temps. This is a classic Correlation vs. Causality argument.

label: Goal
body: Look for an answer naming the illicit move from "X coincided with Y" to "X caused Y", or look for an answer saying that the author has failed to consider other possible causes for why global temps were higher in the 1500s.

label: Evidence
body: Alphahydroxy acids also ON are found occurring naturally in sugarcane.

label: Conclusion
body: This food label is not AN mistaken (the alphahydroxy acids are natural).

label: Evaluate
body: The argument assumes ON → AN that chemically synthensized alphahyrdoxy acids are natural if alphahydroxy acids occur naturally in sugarcane.

label: Conclusion
body: Yancey's new book accurately portrays the lives of fishery workers

label: Evidence
body: Yancey used the same research methods in this book as in her other history books, which have all been very popular. This new book is also popular locally.

label: Evaluation
body: I'm not convinced that Yancey's book is accurate. I know her research methods are consistent, but that doesn't mean they're accurate. I might consistently call the security guard Arthur, even though his name is really Albert. Furthermore, the fact that these books are popular doesn't speak to their accuracy. It's certainly possible for an inaccurate book to still be popular.

label: Goal
body: Look for an answer that calls out one or both of our objections: "just because it's popular doesn't mean it's accurate" or "just because she's using her same ol' methods doesn't mean they're accurate".

label: Conclusion
body: The reason we feel like live concerts are better than recorded music can't just be that with recorded music we don't see the performers.

label: Evidence
body: It's not like there's a big difference between hearing a story read in-person vs. hearing a story read over the radio (in which you wouldn't see the performer).

label: Goal
body: Since they're asking about the first claim, we want an answer that sounds like "an accepted background fact that some people would explain one way, but that the author concludes we would need to explain a different way"

label: Conclusion
body: More and more people are choosing get calcium from cheddar cheese rather than ice cream.

label: Evidence
body: Over the last ten years, sales of ice cream have gone way down, sales of cheddar cheese have doubled.

label: Evaluation
body: From a correlation between ice cream going down and cheddar cheese going up, the author is convinced that they are causally related phenomenon. People switched away from ice cream to cheddar cheese, as a means of switching where they get their calcium boost. These two phenomena might be completely coincidental. Perhaps the sales of bacon went up over the last ten years as well. Should we conclude that "people are choosing to treat themselves with bacon instead of ice cream"?

label: Goal
body: Look for an answer that calls out the bad correlation to causality move, or one that raises a possible alternate explanation for why ice cream lost steam while cheddar got better. (sorry, couldn't resist)

label: Conclusion
body: Leon and Marta are both performers of the Richardson Theater Group.

label: Evidence
body: Leon and Marta are both members of the Richardson Theater Group. No member of the Richardson Theater Group is both a performer and an administrator. Leon and Marta are not administrators.

label: Evaluation
body: This seems like a False Choice: is every member of the Richardson Theater Group either a performer or an administrator? Maybe some of them are promoters or janitors. The author is getting boxed in for no reason, thinking that "if you can be both P and A, then you must be exactly one of them". But it's possible that you could be neither of them.

label: Goal
body: Premise 1: Nothing in this category is both X and Y. Premise 2: Thing A is in this category. Premise 3: Thing A is not X. Conclusion: Thing A must be Y.

label: Premise
body: The castings earthworms leave behind are much richer than the soil they ingest.

label: Intermediate Conclusion
