body: A garden rich in earthworms is more fertile than a garden without them.

label: Intermediate Conclusion
body: Earthworms are highly beneficial to soil.

label: Premise
body: Chemical fertilizers destroy earthworms.

label: Main Conclusion
body: For this reason alone the use of chemical fertilizers should be avoided.

label: Background
body: It's known that Beta Diet is healthier than an average diet.

label: Surprising Claim
body: People who have been on the Beta Diet are on average more likely to be in poor health than people on an average diet.

label: Goal
body: Given that it's a healthy diet, why are people on Beta in poorer health than the average eater?

label: Setup
body: A theoretical framework helps organize and expand research, and many historians think historical analysis is best done within a theoretical framework. Sadly, you can't use a theoretical framework for historical analysis (the past is too complex). So, ....

label: Logical Completion
body: So, ... we'll have to hope there's a different way to organize and expand research? So, ... we won't be able to use the method that many historians think is the best?

label: Goal
body: Find a safely worded answer that ties together the consequence of us not being able to use theoretical frameworks when it comes to studying history.

label: Conclusion
body: Psychologists should direct efforts to finding kids who have lots of nightmares, so that they can teach them this technique and hopefully prevent them from growing up as adults who have lots of nightmares.

label: Evidence
body: They've successfully taught this technique to nightmare-prone adults, and kids who are nightmare-prone are more likely to grow up to be such adults.

label: Evaluation
body: What "if Premise, then Conclusion" bridge idea would get us from Evidence to the Conclusion? Maybe something like ... If there's a technique that works on adults, then psychologists should direct efforts at finding the kids who are most likely to need this as adults.

label: Goal
body: Somehow strengthen the idea that because kids with nightmares grow up to be adults with nightmares, we should direct our efforts towards those kids.

label: Evidence
body: At one sitting, a typical doughnut eater consumes 4 doughnuts containing a total of 680 calories and 40 grams of fat. The typical bagel eater consumes exactly one bagel, at 500 calories and one or two grams of fat per sitting, though the addition of spreads can raise calorie and fat content to the four doughnut range.

label: Conclusion
body: Thus, as far as total calorie content is concerned, there is very little difference between what a typical doughnut eater and a typical bagel eater each consumes at one sitting.

label: Evaluate
body: According to the statements the typical bagel eater consumes the same number of calories between bagel and spreads as the doughnut eater consumes with just the doughnuts. The argument assumes that doughnut eaters do not also put spreads on their doughnuts.

label: Conclusion
body: Pay no attention to these theorists saying that society could flourish in a state of anarchy, with no government (essentially so "hands-off" that there are not any laws or regulations).

label: Evidence
body: If a social philosophy isn't promoting peace and order, it's unacceptable. And these theorists clearly aren't promoting peace and order, if they're talking about anarchy, i.e. chaos.

label: Evaluate
body: Like the vast majority of arguments involving Studies / Experiments, the data from the study/experiment involves some curious asymmetry or difference. Curious Fact: why did the productivity of Plant A's workers increase, while B's didn't? Author's Explanation: because A's workers were eating nutritious breakfasts, which made them more productive.

label: Goal
body: An answer prohibiting acquiring money in ways that make happiness unobtainable.

label: Evaluation
body: This argument is murderously hard to parse / understand. We're giving you the easiest to digest version, but don't think this one is easy to digest. The word anarchy has multiple usages. It can be used in a formal political science way to talk about a society that lacks government structures. Humanists and Libertarians essentially want something approaching anarchy, because they think that humans and free markets will be willing and able to solve the same problems that governments attempt to. Anarchy is also used in a colloquial way to talk about a scene of great pandemonium. "Whoa, it was anarchy at the grocery store, when all the quarantined people were desperately trying to buy some toilet paper". This argument goes from using 'anarchy' in the theoretical way, to talk about an absence of government, to using 'anarchy' in the colloquial way, to talk about a scene of chaotic pandemonium.

label: Goal
body: Look for an answer calling out the Famous Flaw Equivocation, or something to the effect of, "This author is not seriously grappling with the theorists' views; he's just saying ignore them, they're proposing a world of utter chaos."

label: Evidence
body: All poets, aside from those who write only epigrams, have wit. All lyrical composers are poets. Azriel does not write epigrams, though he is a lyrical composer.

label: Conclusion
body: So Azriel has wit.

label: Evaluate
body: This argument is valid because the conclusion follows from the evidence. Since Azriel is a lyrical composer, he is poet (second and third premise). Since he is a poet (previous inference) and he does not write epigrams (third premise) it follows that he has wit (first premise).

label: Evidence
body: Teachers should not ~SLR do anything to cause their students to lose respect for them. And students can sense when someone is trying to hide his or her ignorance.

label: Conclusion
body: A teacher who does ~KA → ~PTK not know the answer to a question a student has asked should not pretend to know the answer.

label: Evaluate
body: The argument PTK + ~KA → SLR assumes that students lose respect for teachers if they try to hide their ignorance.

label: Conclusion
body: Malthus's prediction will come true: insufficient food will doom humanity to war, pestilence, and famine at some point in the future.

label: Evidence
body: Even though our capacity to produce food has outpaced the growth in human population, at some point a lack of biodiversity will erode our capacity to produce food, because these advances in agricultural often compromise biodiversity.

label: Evaluation
body: Claim 1: Contrary to Malthus [counterpoint to Malthus] Claim 2: Yet, [support for author's argument] Claim 3: Therefore, [author's conclusion] Claim 4: Because, [support for author's argument] We're being asked about the first claim, which we know is on the other side of the Author's Pivot (but / yet / however). It's a counterpoint, going against both Malthus and the author, who ultimately thinks Malthus's prediction will come true, even if this first fact goes against Malthus's arguments.

label: Goal
body: Look for something like "an idea that goes against Malthus's arguments", but it has a repercussion that actually goes with Malthus's prediction / with the author's conclusion.

label: Given
body: All of the bankers are B → A athletes. None of the lawyers are L → ~B bankers. Some bankers are present (they are also athletes). Some athletes are present. Some lawyers are present (they aren't bankers).

label: Conclusion
body: The manufacturer has violated its contract, i.e. the rate of defects is at least 5%

label: Evidence
body: Our field inspectors went out to various sites and sent samples back to our lab, where found that 20% of the samples were defective.

label: Evaluation
body: Given that 20% of the samples were defective, how would we argue that the rate of defects is still under 5%? We'd have to somehow make an excuse for that elevated 20% number. Maybe the lab messed up. Maybe you just happened to grab a disproportionately high batch of defective items (f.e. most of the items in box 1 were defective, while all the items in the other 20 boxes were perfect, and the inspectors just happened to grab their samples from box 1)

label: Goal
body: We need their sample to be unrepresentative. If 20% of the samples being defective means that 20% of the total items are defective, then we've violated the contract. So in order for us to argue that in total we're still under 5% defective, then we need to make an excuse for why the samples have a higher defection rate.

label: Conclusion
body: Microorganisms on the new humans and their new animals is probably what led to a bunch of animal extinctions that occurred about 2000 years after these humans arrived in North America.

label: Evidence
body: It's implausible that hunting from these small bands of humans could have caused so many extinctions. Also, the new arrivals and their animals definitely had foreign disease-causing microorganisms on them.

label: Evaluation
body: If we want to weaken a causal hypothesis, we have to either have a different way to explain the Curious Fact or think of a way to render the author's hypothesis less plausible. What else could have caused the extinction of many North American species, 2000 years after the arrival of humans? Maybe climatic stuff. Maybe some change in the local predator / prey dynamics. Maybe humans still caused the extinctions, but not via causing diseases or overhunting. What would make the author's hypothesis that microorganisms from Asia led to the extinctions less plausible? Maybe the new microorganisms didn't cause any diseases virulent enough to cause extinctions. Maybe the diseases were just one of a few things, not "the crucial factor".

label: Goal
body: We need an answer that offers a different explanation for the extinctions, or an answer that undercuts the plausibility that disease-causing microorganisms were the crucial factor in the extinctions.

label: Conclusion
body: A recent study confirms that nutritious breakfasts make workers more productive.

label: Evidence
body: For one month, workers at Plant A received free nutritious breakfasts every day before work, while workers in Plant B did not. The productivity of Plant A’s workers increased, while that of Plant B’s workers did not.

label: Mayor's Response
body: See? Even my challenger admits that jobs are up 8%, which is more job growth than that of my predecessors. Good news for the unemployed voters of this city!

label: Goal
body: We can strengthen by ruling out an Alternate Explanation for the curious fact (f.e. "A's workers didn't increase their productivity because Plant A, unlike Plant B, was holding some sort of competition where the most productive employee would get a lucrative prize"), or we can strengthen by helping the plausibility of the Author's Explanation (f.e. "nutritious breakfasts are high in fiber, and fiber is known to make people work more productively.")

label: Background Facts
body: A few years ago - there was a highly publicized earthquake elsewhere, and Hollyville sent a small amount of aid to victims. Last year - there was a deadly tornado in Hollyville, and a large amount of aid was sent to Hollyville. This year - there was a terrible flood elsewhere, and Hollyville sent a large amount of aid to victims.

label: Evaluation
body: From the timeline, it looks like Hollyville became more generous about giving out aid once they had gone through their own disaster and been the recipient of aid. It's also possible that Hollyville gave more aid to the flood victims because those victims, like Hollyville citizens, live in a river town. But in order to think that Hollyville didn't give as much to earthquake victims because citizens couldn't relate as well to that tragedy, we'd have to assume that Hollyville doesn't get earthquakes, which we don't know.

label: Goal
body: Look for a safely worded answer that sounds like, "A town might become more generous about giving aid, once it has gone through its own tragedy and received aid."

label: Setup
body: Most credit card users don't plan to carry a balance forward on their credit cards. They plan to pay them off each month so that they don't have to pay any interest charges. Credit card companies try to improve the services their customers are most interested in.

label: Logical Competition
body: What would tie those two ideas together? What are credit card customers most interested in? Apparently, they're most interested in paying off cards in full each month, and using them as a replacement for carrying cash and writing checks.

label: Goal
body: Look for a safely worded answer that sounds like credit card companies should focus on improving customers' ability to pay off their cards before interest rates kick in, or improving customers' ability to use the cards as a replacement for cash/checks.

label: Conclusion
body: There was probably way more CO2 in Earth's atmosphere 3 billion years ago.

label: Evidence
body: The sun was only 80% as bright, which in today's atmosphere would mean frozen oceans. Since we know the oceans were liquid, the atmosphere must have had more greenhouse gases, like CO2 and methane.

label: Evaluation
body: This seems like a bit of an arbitrary choice. We know we need there to have been a higher level of greenhouse gases in the atmosphere 3 billion years ago, but why does it specifically have to be more CO2? Maybe it was more methane? Maybe it was more of some other greenhouse gas?

label: Goal
body: Look for an answer that addresses the possibility that the atmosphere had higher greenhouse gases, via some alternative to CO2 like methane or some other greenhouse gas.

label: Evidence
body: For a free market to FP → all buyers can contact function properly, each sellers / comp prices prospective buyer of to what item is worth an item must be able to contact a large number of independent prospective sellers and compare the prices charged for the item to what the item is worth.

label: Conclusion
body: The auto repair ~FP industry does not constitute a properly functioning free market.

label: Evaluate
body: Since the conclusion is saying the trigger is not true, we must be trying to use this rule in its contrapositive form: At least one buyer can't → ~FP contact sellers / comp prices So we need the answer to give us this trigger idea.

label: Background
body: Investing in new life-saving and life-extending tech is pretty risky: You have to put up a ton of money (capital) to pay for the research, and there's only a small chance you'll get the kind of breakthrough that would make money.

label: Surprising Claim
body: Some people are willing to invest in this stuff.

label: Goal
body: Given that investing in life saving/extending technology requires lots of up front money with a low probability of making money back, why do people invest in it?

label: Opposing Point
body: A university psychology department received a large donation from a textbook company after agreeing to use one of the company’s books for a large introductory course. The department chair admitted that the department would not have received the donation if it used another company’s textbook.

label: Evidence
body: The department’s textbook committee had given that textbook its highest rating.

label: Conclusion
body: The book was chosen solely for academic reasons.

label: Evaluate
body: Fortunately for the department chair, motivation is a tricky thing to prove. It’s possible that the book is amazing and the donation was a nice bonus, but did not influence the decision. Of course, it’s also possible that the textbook committee was motivated to give the textbook the highest rating by the impending donation.

label: Given
body: Hemoglobin, a substance in human blood, transports oxygen from the lungs to the rest of the body. With each oxygen molecule it picks up, a hemoglobin molecule becomes more effective at picking up additional oxygen molecules until its maximum capacity of four oxygen molecules is reached. Grabbing an oxygen molecule changes the shape of the hemoglobin molecule, each time causing it literally to open itself to receive more oxygen.

label: Background
body: On short trips, people with passengers are more likely to get into an accident (probably because passengers distract drivers).

label: Surprising Claim
body: On long trips, people with passengers are less likely to get into an accident.

label: Goal
body: What's the crucial difference between short trips and long trips that would make having passengers a safety asset? (Maybe they keep you awake, or read maps and signs for you)

label: Challenger
body: The mayor claims she delivered on her promise to boost jobs in our city, citing an 8% increase since she took office, but that 8% increase is wholly attributable to a national government office that relocated to the city, bringing all of its employees with it.

label: Evaluation
body: The point the challenger was making was that even though the total number of jobs has risen by 8%, there hasn't been an increase in "employment opportunities in our city", since those new jobs that came to the city were already staffed by employees from outside the city. So, yes, the city has more jobs than before, but city residents didn't get any of those jobs. The mayor's response fails to acknowledge the challenger's point, and just reiterates the misleading statistic that jobs have gone up by 8%.

label: Goal
body: Look for an answer saying that the mayor fails to address the point the challenger was making, or something pointing to the distinction between "jobs going up" and "whether anyone in the city who was unemployed got any of these new jobs".

label: Evidence
body: There is currently no technology that can detect the order of activation of brain areas.

label: Conclusion
body: Criticizing psychologists for not attempting to establish the order in which different areas of the brain are activated during a cognitive task such as imagining the face of a friend.

label: Evaluate
body: The argument assumes that it is unfair to criticize someone for not doing something that is not possible to do.

label: Given
body: Although most people know what their bad habits are and want to rid themselves of them, a majority of these people find it very difficult to do so. This is because cessation of habitual behavior is immediately and vividly painful, while whatever benefit is to be gained by the absence of the habit is perceived only dimly because it is remote.

label: Conclusion
body: The Mayan people in general seem to have had a strong grasp of advanced math.

label: Evidence
body: The writings of Mayan religious scribes exhibit a high degree of math competence.

label: Evaluation
body: Can we trust that what was true of the religious scribes (strong grasp of math) was true of the Mayan people in general? This seems like a potential Sampling issue. What if the scribes tended to be educated elites, and the mathematical training / prowess that they had was not at all common among the regular Mayan people?

label: Goal
body: Look for an answer calling out this potentially unrepresentative sample, or an objection about whether the scribes knew way more about math than Mayan people in general.

label: Evidence
body: Many jobs require little or no creativity and, in those positions, using creativity is more likely to be disruptive than innovative. Furthermore, even if creativity were in demand, there is no evidence that it can be taught.

label: Conclusion
body: There is no good reason to suppose that promoting creativity is a proper goal of an employee training program.

label: Evidence
body: If the public boycotted PB → CA the advertisers, then they would cancel their advertisements. Causing some shows to CA -causes→ GOA go off the air. The result would be a GOA -causes→ R restriction of the shows that the public can watch.

label: Conclusion
body: A public boycott of the PB → C advertisers of shows that promote violence and erode our country’s values would be censorship.

label: Evaluate
body: The argument assumes R → C that whatever restricts the number of shows that can be watched is censorship.

label: Opposing Point
body: Research libraries may find an electronic format more convenient for scholars and scientists.

label: Evidence
body: Bookstores and public libraries will stock books in the format desired by the general public, which will be something other than an electronic format.

label: Conclusion
body: Predictions that printed books will soon be replaced by books in electronic formats such as CD-ROM are exaggerated.

label: Evaluate
body: There is a difference between the books that will be stocked at libraries and bookstores and the books that will be printed. Libraries and bookstores may seek to stock books in the printed format, but may not be able to if printed books are not available.

label: Evidence
body: To cut costs, a high school modified its air conditioning system to increase its efficiency. The modified system, however, caused the humidity in the school air to decrease by 18 percent. Twenty-four hours after the decrease in air humidity, a 25 percent increase in the number of visits to the school nurse was reported.

label: Conclusion
body: This shows that a decrease in humidity can make people ill.

label: Evaluate
body: The argument notes a correlation between decreased air humidity and a 25 percent increase in the number of visits to the school nurse. It’s possible that decreased air humidity can make people ill. It’s also possible that the two issues were completely unrelated. Furthermore, the argument does not establish the reason for the trips to the nurse’s office. It’s possible that the trips that day to the nurse’s office were to administer vaccinations to students who were not ill.

label: Conclusion
body: One is less likely to be injured in a car accident if driving a larger car.

label: Evidence
body: A study of 10,000 people who were in an accident found that a much lower percentage of large-car drivers were injured than small-car drivers.

label: Evaluation
body: Does this statistic show that drivers of larger cars are less likely to be injured in a car accident? Not quite. As always, with statistics, we have to be cautious about what it slice of the story it's giving us. To support the claim the conclusion is making, we would want to look at 10,000 drivers and then find out what percentage of large-car drivers have ever been injured in an accident, and what percentage of small-car drivers have ever been injured in an accident. This stat, meanwhile, looks at 10,000 people who were in an accident, and then finds out what percentage of large/small was injured. To put it another way, the conclusion is about all drivers of large/small cars, regardless of whether they've been in an accident. The evidence is only about drivers who have been in an accident. The correct conclusion we could draw would be, "Therefore, this study suggests that if you're in an accident, you're less likely to be injured in a large car than in a small car."

label: Conclusion
body: Saying "you have a legal obligation" to do something is the same as saying that "you're required to fulfill your agreement" do perform that action.

label: Goal
body: Find an answer pointing out the statistical flaw that we're only looking at a subset of drivers (those who have been in an accident) but concluding something about all drivers. Or find an objection that would help us argue the anti-conclusion, that small car drivers are less likely to be injured in an accident.

label: Conclusion
body: Restricting imports to reduce a trade deficit would be like putting a thermometer in cold water in the hope of bringing down someone's fever.

label: Evidence
body: A trade deficit measures a weakness in an economy, but a trade deficit doesn't itself hurt the economy.

label: Evaluation
body: How would we characterize the technique of reasoning? The author definitely uses an analogy in the conclusion (which is atypical; usually there's an analogy in the evidence).

label: Goal
body: Look for something that matches the argument, probably in the realm of "explains the function of something and then concludes a relevant analogy".

label: Conclusion
body: There are times when it isn't immoral to ask for money/favor while making a threat.

label: Evidence
body: There are times when it isn't immoral to make a threat, and there are times when it isn't immoral to ask for money/favor.

label: Evaluation
body: This author has apparently never read Test 63's comparative passage about blackmail. It's all about the paradox of how these two actions which can separately be legal all of a sudden become illegal when you combine them. Threatening someone for money/favors is extortion / blackmail, which we could potentially argue is always immoral. How did we get to this flawed conclusion? Premise 1: Sometimes action A is X. Premise 2: Sometimes action B is X. Conclusion: So, sometimes doing action A and B together is X.

label: Goal
body: Let's find an argument that uses the same trait (e.g. "not immoral") three times, once with one thing, once with a second thing, and then a conclusion that combines those two things with that same trait.

label: Conclusion
body: Once we can restore the cathepsin C enzyme to normal levels, we will eliminate periodontitis.

label: Evidence
body: When a mutation lower levels of cathepsin C enzyme, it severely increases a person's chances of developing periodontitis (the enzyme would usually assist in the immune response to this gum disease).

label: Evaluation
body: The conclusion is so harshly worded ("eliminate periodontitis") that to beat this argument all you need is a line of objection that says, "even if we could restore these people's cathepsin C enzyme level, periodontitis would still happen at least sometimes". The author is not only assuming that restoring normal levels of cathepsin C would successfully prevent this form of periodontitis, he's also assuming that there aren't other sources of periodontitis that would still exist.

label: Goal
body: Look for an answer assuming that this solution works, or an answer ruling out the possibility of developing periodontitis through some other means.

label: Apparent Paradox
body: A recent study of major motion pictures revealed that the vast majority of their plots were simply variations on plots that had been used many times before. Despite this fact, many people enjoy seeing several new movies each year.

label: Evaluate
body: The wrong answers will all make it more clear why many people enjoy seeing several new movies each year, when the plots of these movies are for the most part ones that have been used before. For example, if people prefer plot lines that they are familiar with, it could explain why people enjoy such movies.

label: Conclusion
body: Governments should continue to devote resources to space exploration

label: Evidence
body: If governments hadn't devoted resources to space exploration, then society might have missed the benefits of modern technologies that were unexpected consequences of space exploration.

label: Evaluation
body: The author wants to keep funding space exploration on the grounds that it accidentally leads to cool, useful technologies.

label: Goal
body: As a conditional, something like "If an investment has been known to yield useful things as an unintended byproduct, governments should continue to invest in it." As a "should rule-of-thumb", something like "We should invest in things that have previously yielded unexpected but widely impactful technologies."

label: Given
body: If understanding a (UW → KD) → (UW → UWD) word always involves knowing its dictionary definition, then understanding a word requires understanding the words that occur in that definition. But clearly there are B → ~KD people—for example, all babies—who do not know the dictionary definitions of some of the words they utter.

label: Conclusion
body: The darkest peppered moths were the least likely to be seen and eaten.

label: Evidence
body: Peppered moths avoid predators by blending into backgrounds, typically tree bark. In the late 19th century, the lightest moths had the most contrast with their backgrounds, so they were the most likely to be seen and eaten.

label: Evaluation
body: If the lightest ones were the most likely to be seen, do we have to make the author's assumption, that the darkest ones were the least likely to be seen? Not necessarily, we would only accept the idea that "the darker you are, the more camouflaged you are" if we knew that they were trying to blend into something at least as dark as the darkest moth. Picture a tree bark that is sort of a medium gray. A moth that is too light will show up against that background, but a moth that it is too dark will also show up against that background. The hardest moths to see would be medium dark, so that they best match the medium-dark of the tree bark.

label: Goal
body: Look for an answer saying that "too dark could also be a problem for camouflage" or saying "what if the tree barks they're hiding against were medium dark".

label: Given
body: The standard "QWERTY" configuration of the keys on typewriters and computer keyboards was originally designed to be awkward and limit typing speed. This was because early typewriters would jam frequently if adjacent keys were struck in quick succession. Experiments have shown that keyboard configurations more efficient than QWERTY can double typing speed while tremendously reducing typing effort. However, the expense and inconvenience of switching to a new keyboard configuration prevent any configuration other than QWERTY from attaining widespread use.

label: Evaluation
body: The question stem oddly asks about the arguments flaws. The argument makes two moves, so maybe we need to critique each one. Here's the structure: Since [ claim 1 ], it follows that [ claim 2 ]. Hence, [ claim 3 ]. Going from 1 to 2, the author performs an illegal reversal: Since "make agreement → obligated to do it", it follows that "obligated → made agreement". Going from 2 to 3, the author adds the idea of "legal", a specific type of obligation. Claim 2: "obligated → made agreement" Hence, "legal obligation → made agreement"

label: Goal
body: We need an answer that calls out the illegal reversal (Necessary vs. Sufficient) and that calls out the weird conflation of "being obligated" vs. "being legally obligated".

label: Conclusion
body: The notion of preventing an invention is self-contradictory

label: Evidence
body: Predicting a device requires that you have a somewhat detailed conception of how the device will function / what its users will experience. Inventing something means coming up with a detailed conception. You can't predict what has already taken place.

label: Evaluation
body: The author is saying that I can't predict there will one day be a device invented called a "ketchup-gun", which would shoot ketchup onto burgers and hot-dogs using water gun technology, because when I came up with the detailed conception I just provided above, I basically just became the inventor of the "ketchup-gun". And of course I can't predict that someone will one day invent the ketchup-gun, when I just invented it a second ago.

label: Goal
body: The author's conclusion is to show that a contradiction has occurred. He fleshes out the definitions of inventing and predicting to show that their definitions would contradict each other. Hard to predict answer wording, but we just need anything that matches the argument.

label: Conclusion
body: There can be no complete theory of aesthetics.

label: Evidence
body: We thought we had a pretty successful theory that seemed complete, until the 1960s when rebellious artists managed to make beautiful stuff that didn't fit within earlier notions of art.

label: Evaluation
body: The author thinks that since these 1960s rebels made art that should be encompassed by a complete theory of aesthetics, but isn't encompassed by the 18th century aesthetic theory, then we'll just never have a complete theory. We should probably be responding with something like, "Couldn't we try to come up with a new theory of aesthetics that would be able to accommodate all the previous styles of art, including the rebellious 1960s stuff?"

label: Goal
body: Look for an answer naming the assumption that "if our last theory couldn't cover the rebellious 1960s art, then no theory will ever be able to expand in order to also cover that art", or an answer raising the objection that there might one day be a theory that covers what the 18th century theory covered as well as the weird 60s stuff.

label: Conclusion
body: Biased interpretations of data will generally be removed before publication.

label: Evidence
body: Before publication, scientific analyses of data will be carefully reviewed by many other scientists. These scientists are likely to notice and object to any biases they don't share with the scientist(s) who wrote the analysis

label: Evaluation
body: Given that a bunch of scientists are going to call out whatever biases they see in the pre-publication papers they review, how could we still argue that some biased interpretations will make it through to the publication stage? What if the panel of scientists reviewing a paper have the same biases as the scientist who wrote the paper? The reviewers are going to notice and object to biases that they do not share. But if they share the same bias, then that bias might make it through to publication. We can think of this as an untriggered conditional: If Reviewers notice a → object to and bias they don't share remove that bias

label: Goal
body: Look for an answer that rules out the aforementioned objection, something like "the reviewers will not generally share the same biases as the scientist who wrote the paper".

label: Given
body: In a recent study, a group of young children were taught the word “stairs” while walking up and down a flight of stairs. Later that day, when the children were shown a video of a person climbing a ladder, they all called the ladder stairs.

label: Evidence
body: Among people who live to the age of 100 or more, a large proportion have led “unhealthy” lives: smoking, consuming alcohol, eating fatty foods, and getting little exercise. Such behavior often leads to shortened life spans.

label: Conclusion
body: It is likely that exceptionally long-lived people are genetically disposed to having long lives.

label: Evaluate
body: The argument offers an explanation for longevity after undermining an alternative. The argument suggests that it is not healthy living that causes long life spans, but rather genetic predisposition. To strengthen this, rule out an alternative cause or strengthen the correlation between genetic predisposition and a long life span.

label: Evidence
body: Medications with an unpleasant PT (T or C or SG) taste are generally produced only in tablet, capsule, or soft-gel form. The active ingredient in T medication M is a waxy substance that cannot tolerate the heat used to manufacture tablets because it has a low melting point. The company developing M S does not have soft-gel manufacturing technology and manufactures all its medications itself.

label: Conclusion
body: M will most likely be produced C in capsule form.

label: Evaluate
body: The argument assumes that PT medication M has an unpleasant taste.

label: Given
body: Carol Morris wants to own a majority of the shares of the city’s largest newspaper, The Daily. The only obstacle to Morris’s amassing a majority of these shares is that Azedcorp, which currently owns a majority, has steadfastly refused to sell.

label: Prediction
body: Morris will soon be the majority owner of The Daily.

label: Evaluate
body: The prediction is need of an explanation since there is no evidence yet that supports the view that Azedcorp will sell any of its shares to Morris.

label: Conclusion
body: If we get rid of lead paint in these homes, then childhood lead poisoning in the area will be eradicated.

label: Evaluate
body: The author is assuming that, "If we get rid of lead paint in these homes, then there will be no more lead poisoning in the area". She must be thinking that lead paint in homes is the only way to get lead poisoning. If we were trying to think of a way to fight her conclusion, we need to a way argue that "No, even if we eliminate lead paint in homes, childhood lead poisoning in the area will not be eradicated". We could argue that there are other possible sources of lead poisoning ... maybe there's lead paint in schools? Maybe there's lead in the water?

label: Goal
body: The conclusion is way too strong. Why would getting rid of lead paint in homes totally eradicate lead poisoning from the area? Look for an objection pointing out other possible sources of lead poisoning or naming the author's assumption that "lead paint in homes" is only possible source of lead poisoning in the area.

label: Given
body: Although some nutritional facts about soft drinks are listed on their labels, exact caffeine content is not. Listing exact caffeine LCC → ELC content would make it easier to limit, but not eliminate, one's caffeine intake. If it became easier for ELC → IH people to limit, but not eliminate, their caffeine intake, many people would do so, which would improve their health.

label: Conclusion
body: I can't afford any of these works

label: Evidence
body: This collection is among the most valuable collections ever assembled by a single person

label: Evaluate
body: Given that the collection is among the most valuable (costly) ever, How could we still say we can afford at least one of these works? Maybe there are some really cheap items. If we go to an Estate Sale, for some crazy rich person, will we be able to afford anything? Possibly, there might be small-ticket items, like doilies and coasters and hangers. Similarly, at this art auction, there might be Picasso's and Rembrandt's and such that make the collection worth $50 million, but there might also be a watercolor by Vidmar's barber, Lou, that is only going for $20.

label: Goal
body: This argument is making a Whole to Part assumption: since the collection is super expensive, each item in the collection must be super expensive.

label: Conclusion
body: Explorers would be likely to survive the trip to Mars.

label: Evidence
body: There would be a robust backup system in place at every stage of the journey. And with that backup system in place, a fatal accident is unlikely at any given stage.

label: Evaluation
body: This one is a tough nut to crack: if the astronauts are likely to survive every stage, given the backup system, how could we fight the conclusion and argue that they are unlikely to survive the trip? A conversational example would be something like shoplifting. It's not that hard to run into a 7/11, grab a drink, and run. You'll usually get away with it. But even though each individual act of shoplifting is likely to be successful, a chronic shoplifter is still likely to get caught. That's because the more you engage in a behavior that carries risk (even a small risk), the more likely it is that at some point something bad happens. The actual math behind it is more complex than anything we have to usually face on LSAT. If you wanted to know the probability of getting heads three times in a row, you take the probability of getting heads each time (50%, or 1/2) and multiply it three times: 1/2 * 1/2 *1/2 = 1/8 = 12.5% probability of getting heads three times in a row. If each stage in this journey had a 70% likelihood of survival, then surviving three such stages in a row would be 7/10 * 7/10 * 7/10 = 343/1000 = 34.3% chance of surviving all three stages. So even though surviving each stage is likely, one would be unlikely (lower than 50%) to survive all three stages.

label: Goal
body: We need an answer that gets at this idea that even if each stage is most likely not going to result in death, it might still be unlikely for astronauts to make it through all the stages safely.

label: Evidence
body: Retrospective studies of human RS → SR subjects must use the subjects’ reports about their own pasts.

label: Conclusion
body: Retrospective studies cannot RS → ~R reliably determine the causes of human subjects’ present characteristics.

label: Evaluate
body: The argument assumes that SR → ~R studies that rely on the subjects’ reports are not reliable.

label: Evidence
body: Gigantic passenger planes currently being developed will have enough space to hold shops and lounges in addition to passenger seating. The number of passengers flying the air-traffic system is expected to triple within 20 years. It will be impossible for airports to accommodate enough normal-sized jet planes to carry that many passengers.

label: Conclusion
body: The additional space will more likely be used for more passenger seating.

label: Scientist
body: To study a new med for athlete's foot, we split up a representative sample of people suffering from that condition into group 1 and 2. Group 1 received only M. Group 2 received only N. The only people whose athlete's foot was cured were those were were given M.

label: Reporter
body: So you're saying, "If you didn't have your athlete's foot cured, then you didn't receive M (i.e. you did receive N).

label: Evaluate
body: Since the scientist's final claim and the reporter's claim are both conditionals (the only / if), we should be highly suspicious that we're being tested on some Necessary vs. Sufficient error, i.e. a conditional logic mistake, an illegal reversal or negation. The trigger "the only" is a sufficient / Left side indicator (by contrast, the much more common triggers "only" and "only if" are necessary / Right side indicators). So the scientist's final claim looks like this: Your AF was cured → You took M You didn't take M → Your AF wasn't cured The trigger "If" is a sufficient / Left side indicator. So the reporter's claim looks like this: Your AF wasn't cured → You didn't take M We can see that the reporter's interpretation is an illegal reversal of what the scientist said. In conversational terms, the scientist is telling us that if you were in group N, you definitely didn't get your athlete's foot cured. If you were in group M, maybe you did. At least some people in group M had their athlete's foot cured. But it doesn't have to be all. Consider this example data: 100 ppl with athlete's foot, divided into M and N M: 10 cured, 40 not cured N: 50 not cured It's true to say, "the only people whose AF was cured were given M". But it's not true to say (as the reporter does), "If your AF wasn't cured, then you didn't get M". After all, there were 40 people whose AF wasn't cured but were given M.

label: Conclusion
body: The author concludes: don't trade away your health to get money.

label: Goal
body: We can describe the reporter's reasoning error in formal terms, by saying she confused necessary and sufficient conditions. Or we can describe it in conversational terms, saying that she fails to consider that some of the people who were given M might have not had their athlete's foot cured.

label: Opposing Point
body: Most experts believe that plesiosauromorphs lurked and quickly ambushed their prey.

label: Evidence
body: Plesiosauromorphs were gigantic, long-necked marine reptiles that ruled the oceans during the age of the dinosaurs. Plesiosauromorph fins were quite long and thin, like the wings of birds specialized for long-distance flight.

label: Conclusion
body: However, Plesiosauromorphs probably hunted by chasing their prey over long distances.

label: Evaluate
body: The argument assumes that the comparison between plesiosauromorph fins and the wings of birds specialized for long-distance flight applies to their function as well as their form.

label: Conclusion
body: Buying elaborate screensavers can cost a company far more in employee time than it saves in electricity and monitor protection.

label: Evidence
body: Employees can't resist spending time playing with screensavers that flash interesting graphics across their screens.

label: Evaluate
body: We need to extrapolate a Principle from this situation/argument. A company buys a screensaver as a way to save money in the long run (because screensavers help protect their equipment from getting damaged), but the purchase sort of backfires when it turns out that employees start wasting time zoning out, watching the cool screensaver. So the abstract elements here seem to be, "it's not a good Net Gain decision to do X, because even though it would help you with Y, it ends up having this backfire effect with Z".

label: Goal
body: Let's look for something that sounds like cautionary advice: "You'd think that X would help you, but it has this unexpected downside that can make it a net loss overall".

label: Evidence
body: It's individualistic, because rappers work alone in a studio so they're not beholden to the wishes of any bandmates. It's nontraditional because learning to rap isn't as formal as learning an instrument.

label: Critic's Implicit Conclusion
body: You're overstating how individualistic and nontraditional rap is.

label: Evidence
body: It is not purely the rapper's individual whims; it's also the preferences of the public. And there is very much a tradition, when it comes to samples, themes, and styles.

label: Evaluation
body: How does the critic respond? She brings up some additional considerations / information that impact the sort of assumptions the professor was making. He was thinking: - if you don't have bandmates, then you're just trying to please yourself - if you aren't learning an instrument, then you're not partaking in traditional music form

label: Goal
body: Look for an answer that says the critic brought up some other considerations that argue against the two things that the professor was concluding.

label: Evidence
body: The true meaning of an author’s TM → IASC statements can be understood only through insight into the author’s social circumstances.

label: Conclusion
body: Smith herself is not aware of ~TM the true meaning of her own words.

label: Evaluate
body: The speaker assumes that ~IASC Smith herself lacks insight into the her own social circumstances.

label: Conclusion
body: Snoring can damage the snorer's throat

label: Evidence
body: Patients who snored frequently were more likely to have serious throat muscle abnormalities than those who didn't snore as much.

label: Evaluation
body: This argument highlights the classic Correlation to Causality move. The author takes a Curious Fact: why is there a correlation between snoring and throat abnormalities? and assumes a Causal Explanation that one side of the correlation causes the other: snoring causes the throat abnormalities. We always deal with causal arguments by asking ourselves: - How else could we explain this curious fact? - How could we better assess the plausibility of the author's hypothesis?

label: Goal
body: Since we're strengthening, we either need to Rule Out a different way to explain the Curious Fact (e.g. "it's not the throat abnormalities that cause the snoring" / "it's not some cigarette smoking that causes both the snoring and the throat abnormalities") or to boost the plausibility of the author's hypothesis (e.g. "snoring is an unhealthy throat process that over time messes up some part of your throat" / "when people used techniques to stop snoring, their throat abnormalities got better")

label: Conclusion
body: One should never sacrifice one's health in order to acquire money.

label: Evidence (for)
body: Without health, happiness is not obtainable.

label: Evaluate
body: One of the hardest missing links for students to hear is the "missing Should-rule". example: Washing your clothes with yogurt will make them smell funny. Thus, you shouldn't wash your clothes with yogurt. What is the assumption / the missing link? You shouldn't do something that will make your clothes smell funny. Any time an author says, "You shouldn't do X, because X would lead to Y", we're missing the idea of "you shouldn't do something that leads to Y". Here the author was saying, "You shouldn't sacrifice your health to acquire money, because sacrificing your health means you can't obtain happiness." So we're missing the should-rule that "You shouldn't do something that means you can't obtain happiness".

label: Goal
body: Look for something like "You shouldn't do something that makes happiness unobtainable." We can think of the idea "should" in the conclusion as a New Concept that must be in the correct answer. We can't derive a should-claim without a should-rule, and the premise doesn't provide a should-rule. It just descriptively tells us that without health you can't have happiness.

label: Conclusion
body: Don't sacrifice health for money.

label: Evidence
body: Without health, happiness is unobtainable.

label: Evaluate
body: The argument needs a bridge: money shouldn't be acquired if doing so makes happiness unobtainable.

label: Evaluate
body: Notice the gap. The premise is about health and happiness. The conclusion is about money — but happiness isn't mentioned in the conclusion at all. We need a rule that ties them together. Think of it like this. The author is implicitly saying: happiness matters more than money. Specifically, we shouldn't pursue money in ways that destroy happiness. Add that rule, and the chain closes: sacrificing health makes happiness unobtainable -> shouldn't acquire money that way.

label: Goal
body: An answer establishing that money should only be acquired in ways that don't make happiness unobtainable.

label: Principle 1
body: Because we want to All code should be prevent one person → written by a pair of writing code that only programmers at a they would understand single workstation

label: Principle 2
body: Because most of the best programmers are 100x we should let better than others and → these best ones carry the projects they're work alone working on and work better alone

label: Evaluation
body: It sounds impossible at first to satisfy both principles, since one says "everybody should pair up" and the other one says "the best ones should work alone". So where is the wiggle room? The first one says that "all code has to be written by a team", not that "all programmers" have to work in teams. So we could have a scenario where the non-best programmers are always writing code in pairs, but the best programmers are allowed to do other stuff by themselves.

label: Goal
body: A correct answer has to violate at least one of the principles, so it either has to allow for someone to write code by themselves or it has to force one of the best programmers to work on a team.

label: Given
body: In West Calverton, most pet PS -most→ SEB stores sell exotic birds. Most of those [pet stores] PS + SEB -most→ STF that sell exotic birds also sell tropical fish. Any pet store there that sells PS + STF + ~SEB → SG tropical fish but not exotic birds does sell gerbils. No independently owned IO + PS → ~SG pet stores in West Calverton sell gerbils.

label: Apparent Paradox
body: Earlier estimates of the distances of certain stars from Earth would mean that these stars are about 1 billion years older than the universe itself, an impossible scenario. My estimates of the distances indicate that these stars are much farther away than previously thought. And the farther away the stars are, the greater their intrinsic brightness must be, given their appearance to us on Earth. So the new estimates of these stars' distances from Earth help resolve the earlier conflict between the ages of these stars and the age of the universe.

label: Evaluate
body: Since the stars are much further away than previously estimated, they must burn more brightly than was thought before. Why would increasing the brightness of these stars resolve the conflict between the ages of the starts and the age of the universe. If brighter stars were younger stars, then the age of these stars would be reduced.

label: Given
body: Most large nurseries sell raspberry LN -most→ CRG plants primarily to commercial raspberry growers. Most large nurseries sell only LN -most→ GDF plants that are guaranteed to be disease-free. However, the shipment of raspberry WP → ~DF plants that Johnson received from Wally's Plants carried a virus that commonly afflicts raspberries [not disease free].

label: Conclusion
body: We should try a new marketing campaign.

label: Evidence
body: Our new product isn't selling and a new marketing campaign would have a chance of saving it.

label: Evaluation
body: Given that the new marketing campaign has a chance of saving the new product, how could we argue that we shouldn't try the new marketing campaign? Maybe there are other options that are much better than the marketing campaign? Maybe, even though the marketing campaign has a chance, it's a very small chance and not worth the time / money / effort? Maybe the possible good we would get out of the marketing campaign saving the new product is outweighed by whatever possible bad stuff it could trigger.

label: Goal
body: Find a reason not to do the new marketing campaign.

label: Conclusion
body: TMD has not been shown to be an acceptable practice.

label: Evidence
body: Although TMD seems to have no effect on human health when an average amount is ingested, there is a small minority that eats tons more peaches than average and thereby ingests much more than an average amount of TMD.

label: Evaluation
body: Because of the wording of the conclusion, we know we'll want a Principle that feels like, _______ → not shown to be acceptable practice What is the author's rationale for thinking it hasn't been shown to be acceptable? For the 20% of the population that eats more peaches than average, they would consume much more than the amount of TMD that has been shown to be safe.

label: Goal
body: We want something like, a practice could lead to some portion of people → not acceptable being exposed to unsafe levels

label: Facts
body: This smoking ban was meant to protect employees from secondhand smoke. This smoking ban does not prohibit people from smoking in their own homes.

label: Evaluation
body: In general, with Inference Must Be False, we're either contradicting a conditional or contradicting an available inference. Can we infer anything by combining these ideas? Not quite, but when we look for where there is potential overlap, we can think about one case in which the ban wouldn't accomplish its goal: what if you have employees that work in your house? The ban wouldn't prohibit you from smoking in your house, and thus it wouldn't protect the employees in your house from your secondhand smoke.

label: Goal
body: Maybe the correct answer will deal with this weird scenario where the two facts about the ban could overlap in a weird way, but we just need any answer that goes again either or both of our facts.

label: Conclusion
body: If we want to increase the size of our applicant pool, we need to raise out tuition and fees.

label: Evidence
body: It's possible that the reason we've seen our pool shrink over the past few years is that we charge too little for tuition and fees, giving off the impression that we're not as high quality an institution.

label: Evidence
body: Over the past 25 years, more and more people are using sunscreen, but the incidence of skin cancer caused by harmful sun rays has continued to go up.

label: Evaluation
body: Any time an author says "In order to get X, we'll have to do Y", she's assuming - Y is actually a viable way of getting X - There aren't other ways of also getting X So this author is assuming that "raising tuition and fees could lead to a bigger pool of applicants" (assuming it wouldn't turn even more people away). Our author is assuming that "there isn't some other way we could increase the size of our applicant pool". And then there seems to be a Possible vs. Certain move in her argument, where she goes from "It's possible that X is the explanation" to "We'll have to do something about X".

label: Goal
body: Look for any of the three assumptions we've noted, or any other answer that, if negated, would make it sound like we don't need to raise tuition in order to increase our applicant pool.

label: Evidence
body: Clean water is essential for E human health. The purpose of a private PC → PP + ~PH company is to produce profit, not to promote health.

label: Conclusion
body: Water should not be ~PC supplied by private companies.

label: Evaluate
body: The argument assumes that if something is essential for human health then it should be provided by an organization whose purpose is to promote health.

label: Phenomenon
body: Scientists have long wondered why the fish that live around coral reefs exhibit such brilliant colors.

label: Opposing Point
body: One suggestion is that coral reefs are colorful and, therefore, that colorful fish are camouflaged by them.

label: Opposing Premise
body: Many animal species, after all, use camouflage to avoid predators.

label: Premise
body: Most corals, it turns out, are relatively dull browns and greens.

label: Intermediate Conclusion
body: A reef stripped of its fish is quite monochromatic.

label: Main Conclusion
body: The explanation that reefs are colorful and that’s why the fish that live around them are colorful is mistaken. rephrase: The reason that reef fish are colorful is NOT because the reefs themselves are colorful and thus provide camouflage.

label: Conclusion
body: The survey's responses are also ambiguous.

label: Evidence (because)
body: The statement the survey asked about was ambiguous.

label: Evaluate
body: This argument is recycling the same trait in its premise and its conclusion. Because the statement the survey asked about was ambiguous, the responses to the survey will be ambiguous.

label: Goal
body: It seems like the author's thinking is guided by some assumption like, "If you're asking people about something with quality X, their responses will have quality X"

label: Conclusion (this shows that)
body: Having perfect pitch is a consequence of genetic factors.

label: Evidence
body: In a study, the people with perfect pitch were much more likely to have relatives who had perfect pitch than were people who didn't have perfect pitch.

label: Evaluate
body: Usually, when there's a study, the data yields some sort of correlation or Asymmetric Comparison we call a Curious Fact. Curious Fact ... how come people who have perfect pitch (PP) have relatives with PP, whereas people who don't have PP don't have relatives with PP? Author's Explanation ... PP must be something genetic. It seems to "run in the family", so it must be innate, not learned. The two pressure points for Explain Curious Fact style arguments are always: 1. Alternate Explanations for the curious fact 2. the plausibility of the Author's Explanation What could be a different reason why perfect pitch seems to be associated within a family? Maybe if you're a parent that possesses the skill of perfect pitch, you naturally teach it to your kids, who then teach it to their kids. We could probably say that "a high percentage of people who are good at repairing cars have family members that are good with cars, whereas people who are not handy with cars usually don't have family members that are good with cars". We certainly wouldn't conclude that being good with cars is an innate trait. It's more likely that if your grandparents or parents knew how to fix a car, you got to watch them do it and you learned, and then you taught your kids. What could increase the plausibility that perfect pitch is genetic, not learned? The most common way to Strengthen a cause-effect conclusion is to present an answer with a "No Cause, No Effect" form. If we found out that the adopted children of parents who had perfect pitch did not have perfect pitch, that would be strong evidence that perfect pitch is genetic. The adopted children don't have the same genes (No Cause), so they don't have perfect pitch (No Effect).

label: Goal
body: Let's look for something that rules out an Alternate Explanation for the study's correlation or something that increases the plausibility that perfect pitch is innate, not learned.

label: Conclusion (this suggests that)
body: The predatory dinosaur was chasing the grazing dinosaur and attacked immediately afterwards.

label: Evidence
body: There were two sets of tracks, one from a grazing dino and one from a predatory dino, that seemed to make abrupt turns in tandem, suggesting that the predator was following the grazing dino and matching its stride. Modern predatory mammals match stride of prey right before they strike those prey.

label: Evaluate
body: The keywords of "this suggests that" always indicate a conclusion. We can feel good calling that last sentence the Main Conclusion, since all the previous ideas are support for it. (Usually, the conclusion does not show up in the last claim when we're doing Main Conclusion or Role questions, but because this is earlier in the section, they're not going to great lengths to be sneaky about hiding the conclusion). They're asking about the second half of the second sentence, which followed the modifier "suggesting that". So this second half of the second sentence is also a Conclusion. Why should we believe that "the predator was following the grazing dinosaur and had matched its stride"? Because, the two sets of tracks make abrupt turns repeatedly in tandem.

label: Goal
body: Since everything leading up to the last sentence is Support for the Main Conclusion in that last sentence, we could call the claim they're asking us about things like Support, Evidence, Premise. But we could also call it an Intermediate Conclusion, also known as Subsidiary Conclusion / Supported Premise

label: Conclusion
body: Using sunscreen is unlikely to reduce your risk of skin cancer.

label: Evaluation
body: Anti-causal arguments such as these can be weakened by showing an important difference between the two groups / cases being compared. The group 25 years ago used less sunscreen, but had a lower incidence of skin cancer than the group nowadays. But maybe something else is different about them that preserves our ability to think that sunscreen is actually effective. Maybe the sun's rays are more harmful now (bigger holes in the ozone layer?), so we'd expect 50% more skin cancer, but because of sunscreen's effectiveness it's only 20% more skin cancer. Maybe people are spending way more time in the sun, so we'd expect 50% more skin cancer, but sunscreen is keeping it down to only 20% more. Maybe people don't put on sunscreen as frequently / effectively as they used to.

label: Goal
body: In order for us to argue that sunscreen does reduce your risk of skin cancer, we need a way to make an excuse for the fact that the incidence of skin cancer is rising. So we need something that makes today's sunscreen wearers more likely to be getting skin cancer than their counterparts from 25 years ago.

label: Given
body: Any proposal for a new >50 + 25% → F department will not be funded if there are fewer than 50 people per year available for hire in that field and the proposed department would duplicate more than 25 percent of the material covered in one of our existing departments. The proposed Area 25% Studies Department will duplicate more than 25 percent of the material covered in our existing Anthropology Department. However, we will fund F the new department.

label: Given
body: Storytelling appears to be a universal aspect of both past and present cultures. Comparative study of traditional narratives from widely separated epochs and diverse cultures reveals common themes such as creation, tribal origin, mystical beings and quasi-historical figures, and common story types such as fables and tales in which animals assume human personalities.

label: Conclusion (so)
body: It is likely that J's first child was not born before its due date.

label: Evidence
body: If a mom's first child is born before its due date, it's likely that her second child will be also be born before the date. J's second child was not born before its due date.

label: Evaluate
body: There is enough symbol repetition here that we could probably beat this question just by diagramming the argument, even if we didn't understand the flaw. This argument feels like it's almost doing a contrapositive, but because it's working with probability, not conditional logic, that move doesn't work. Here's the structure: Prem 1: If 1st born was early, then 2nd was probably early X → probably Y Prem 2: J's 2nd was not born early. this thing was not Y. Conc: J's 1st was probably not born early. this thing was probably not X.

label: Goal
body: Let's look for something with this structure: P1: X → probably Y P2: this thing was not Y. C: so, this thing was probably not X -—--—--—--—--—-- If you're curious why this is a flaw, consider this argument: If you live on Earth, it's likely that you've heard of Taylor Swift. Paul has never heard of Taylor Swift. Thus, it is likely that Paul doesn't live on Earth.

label: Conclusion
body: It's likely that at least primitive life has evolved on Europa.

label: Evidence
body: Life can evolve only in the presence of liquid water, and there seems to be liquid water on Europa.

label: Evaluate
body: This argument essentially works like this: Prem 1: In order to have X, you must have Y. Prem 2: Bob has Y. Conc: Bob likely has X. We can see how silly this argument is by using a real world example: P1: In order to have an AMEX Black card, you must have a bank account. P2: Bob has a bank account. Conc: Bob probably has an AMEX Black card. Just because you meet one requirement for an AMEX Black card doesn't mean you're suddenly likely to have one. Your bank account might need to have a minimum balance of $100,000. You might need to have a credit score of at least 750. Similarly, just because Europa has water doesn't mean it's more than half of the way to having life. Maybe you also need proteins, amino acids, an ozone layer to filter out destructive layers of UV radiation, etc.

label: Goal
body: Look for an answer saying, "Just because Europa meets one of the requirements for life doesn't mean we get to immediately assume there's probably life there. There might be other requirements for life that we know Europa doesn't possess.

label: Given
body: A bacterial species will BDGR → BEC inevitably develop greater resistance within a few years to any antibiotics used against it, unless those antibiotics eliminate that species completely. However, no single NOM → BEC antibiotic now on the market is powerful enough to eliminate bacterial species X completely.

label: Premise
body: As every politician knows, political mobilization requires commonality of purpose.

label: Intermediate Conclusion
body: Political agendas promoted in a manner that cannot be understood by large numbers of people will not be realized.

label: Conclusion
body: Politicians who criticize their political opponents by claiming that their exposition of their ideas is muddled and incomprehensible are being insincere.

label: Conclusion
body: Organic factors that affect symptoms of mental illness are not evenly distributed around the globe.

label: Evidence
body: Many symptoms of mental illnesses are affected by organic factors, but there's tons of variation among different countries in the incidence of these symptoms.

label: Evaluation
body: Given that there's lots of variation around the globe when it comes to these symptoms, How could we still argue that the organic factors underlying these symptoms are evenly distributed around the globe? That's a tough riddle to crack. If we want to argue that these organic factors are evenly distributed, then how would we explain why the symptoms vary so much around the world? Maybe there's some combo of organic factors and other factors that combine, and it's the other causal factors that are unevely distributed? Since the language here is that symptoms are affected by organic factors, it's possible that there is more than one thing affecting the symptoms.

label: Goal
body: Look for a way to explain why symptoms vary across the globe, even if organic factors are evenly distributed.

label: Conclusion
body: Privatizing national parks would probably benefit park visitors.

label: Evidence
body: Privatizing the telecom industry benefited consumers (it allowed competition between telecom companies, which improved service and brought down prices).

label: Evaluation
body: Whenever authors make arguments by Comparison, we can weaken them by making the two things being compared seem meaningfully different. What could be different between privatizing national parks and doing so with telecom problems? - Would privatizing national parks lead to more competition, improved service, or lower prices? - Is there some way that privatizing national parks would have a bad outcome for customers?

label: Goal
body: Look for an important difference between privatizing telecom and national parks, or just something that sounds like a negative repercussion of privatizing national parks.

label: Conclusion (should)
body: Both jewels should be deemed of equal value.

label: Evidence
body: A counterfeit diamond would seem to give just as much aesthetic pleasure as a real diamond, if the naked eye can't distinguish one from the other.

label: Evaluate / Goal
body: Since we normally pre-phrase a possible answer on Principle-Justify questions by thinking, "IF premise, THEN conclusion", it seems like we want something like this: if it gives an equal then should deem amount of aesthetic → it of equal value pleasure We're only interested in principles that can help us argue that "two things should be deemed equal in value", so if any answer wouldn't help us get to that language, we're not interested.

label: Opposing Point
body: Some bladed etching tools B + ET ↢some↣ EN are used for engraving.

label: Evidence
body: All etching tools are either ET → PT or B pin-tipped or bladed. Some bladed etching tools B + ET ↢some↣ EN are not used for engraving. On the other hand, all pin- PT → EN tipped etching tools are used for engraving.

label: Conclusion
body: Thus, there are more ET + EN > ET + EN etching tools that are used for engraving than there are etching tools that are not used for engraving.

label: Evaluate
body: According to the argument all pin-tipped etching tools and some bladed etching tools are used for engraving. Furthermore it’s established that some bladed etching tools are not used for engraving. Could be it be that there are more etching tools not used for engraving than are used for engraving? It’s possible. If the majority of etching tools are bladed and the majority of those are not used for engraving, then it could be that more etching tools are not used for engraving than are used for engraving. A possible set of numbers that would undermine the reasoning: 100 Etching Tools Pin-tipped Bladed Used for Engraving 10 10 Not Used for Engraving 0 80

label: Apparent Paradox
body: A 24-year study of 1,500 adults showed that those subjects with a high intake of foods rich in beta-carotene were much less likely to die from cancer or heart disease than were those with a low intake of such foods. On the other hand, taking beta-carotene supplements for 12 years had no positive or negative effect on the health of subjects in a separate study of 20,000 adults.

label: Evaluate
body: Why would the two studies have different implications about the impact of beta-carotene on one’s likelihood of dying from cancer or heart disease? For one the beta-carotene in the former study was food, while in the latter study it was a supplement.

label: Conclusion
body: If there are sentient beings on planets outside our solar system, we won't be able to determine this anytime soon unless some of them are at least as intelligent as humans.

label: Evidence (X and Y)
body: We won't be able to send spacecrafts outside our solar system anytime soon. and Any sentient being on another planet capable of communicating with us in the near future would have to be as intelligent as we are.

label: Evaluate
body: There's a lot of symbol matching and conditional logic here, so we might go down the road of diagramming (watch the class recording, via the ▶︎ button on the highlighter toolbar, if you'd like to see a diagramming discussion). But essentially the argument boils down to this missing link: if we can't send spacecraft there, then we'll need these aliens to be capable of communicating with us. If we translate the "unless" in the conclusion into "if-not" form, the conclusion is saying, "If none of the aliens are as smart as us, then we won't be able to discover them anytime soon". Why? Because, "If none of the aliens are as smart as us, then they won't be capable of communicating with us". We're trying to line up the Conclusion's verbiage with that of the Evidence so that it's clearer what's being assumed. If I say, "If Sheila doesn't come, we won't have beer. Thus, If Shelia doesn't come, this party will suck.", then I'm assuming "If we don't have beer, this party will suck". This argument is saying, "If they aren't as smart, they won't be able to communicate with us. Thus, if they aren't as smart, we won't be able to determine their existence." So it's assuming, "If they can't communicate with us, then we won't be able to determine their existence". We might skeptically attack that assumption by thinking, "Wait — that's the only way for us to determine their existence? They have to communicate with us? Couldn't there be some other way to determine their existence?" The author would say, "No, sadly. I thought of that too, but there's no way for us to send spacecraft there." We would then reply, "the only way for us to determine their existence is to send spacecraft there or have them communicate with us? Why are those the only two ways? Couldn't we detect their presence through some sort of bio-marker we can observe via spectral analysis? If they're communicating with each other via radio waves, couldn't we potentially pick up on their signal with a radio telescope? They might not be smart enough to send a signal to us, but we might be smart enough to detect signals they're sending to each other."

label: Goal
body: The author needs to rule out alternative modes of discovering sentient beings. In his head there are only two ways: 1. send a spacecraft 2. the aliens are capable of communicating with us The author has established we can't do #1 anytime soon and thus is thinking that #2 is the only hope, but maybe there are other ways he's failing to consider. To lock in his conclusion, we need an answer to convince us that these are the only two ways.

label: Conclusion
body: Bulging or slipped disks cannot lead to serious back pain in people who experience back pain.

label: Evidence
body: In a study of people who had never experienced serious back pain, half of them had bulging or slipped disks.

label: Evaluation
body: This argument is essentially saying, "if all these people in the study who had slipped / bulging disks didn't have back pain, then slipped / bulging disks never cause back pain". In most Anti-Causal arguments such as this, we need to Weaken by making some excuse for the evidence. Given that we want to still believe that slipped / bulging disks can cause back pain, why is that the people with slipped / bulging disks in this study didn't have back pain? - maybe they don't know what back pain is, so they're experiencing it but not reporting having experienced it? (stupid idea, I know) - maybe more than one thing has to combine to give you back pain, so the slipped / bulging disk is part of it but not sufficient (maybe you also need weak abdominal muscles) - maybe the people with the slipped / bulging disk who didn't feel the back pain have a lifestyle or a job that makes them sit / stand / move in ways that somehow hide the pain that others would feel

label: Evaluate
body: The argument assumes that when companies can hire freely in response to changing conditions, wage levels will not be static or slow changing.

label: Goal
body: Find an answer that points out the illegal move, "just because SOME PEOPLE don't experience Y as a result of X, that doesn't mean that X can never be the cause of Y" or one that makes an excuse for why the people in the study w/ the bulging / slipped disks somehow weren't feeling the pain we'd expect

label: Conclusion / Hypothesis:
body: Being exposed to more germs during infancy (such as via your gross older siblings) makes you less likely to develop allergies

label: Evidence
body: Children in large families, particularly the younger ones, tend to have fewer allergies than do children in smaller families.

label: Evaluation
body: The researchers have observed a curious fact: why do the kids in larger families grow up with fewer allergies? Their explanation - exposure to germs during infancy helps to prevent allergies later in life. With all curious fact / explanation arguments, we consider the same two pressure points: - how else could we explain the curious fact? - how plausible is the author's story On a strengthen, question, we would either want to Rule Out a different way to explain the Curious Fact, or we would (more commonly) try to add some plausibility to the author's hypothesis.

label: Goal
body: The most common way to add plausibility to a hypothesis are to show an example of No Cause, No Effect (i.e. "large families who over-sanitize their homes are just as likely as people from small families to have allergies), or to give an example of More Cause, More Effect (i.e. "these other people who had germs during infancy ended up with no allergies")

label: Conclusion
body: Some films from the earliest years of Hollywood will be lost.

label: Evidence
body: There is no way to transfer all currently deteriorating nitrate films to acetate before they disintegrate.

label: Evaluation
body: The "new guy" in the conclusion is films from the earliest years of Hollywood. What is the author assuming about these? He must be thinking that there are so many of them in deteriorating nitrate form that we can't complete the preservation in time. However, his evidence only said that we can't transfer all currently deteriorating nitrate films in time. What if the majority of those are from Hollywood's "middle years"? What if only 10% of the currently deteriorating nitrate films are from Hollywood's early years? In that case, we could prioritize saving ALL of them and thwart the author's conclusion.

label: Goal
body: Look for an answer ruling out the idea that Hollywood's early films comprise a very small proportion of currently deteriorating nitrate films, or look for an answer that, when negated, gives us some other way of showing how all of Hollywood's early films could be saved.

label: Given
body: In a recent study of arthritis, researchers tried but failed to find any correlation between pain intensity and any of those features of the weather—humidity, temperature swings, barometric pressure—usually cited by arthritis sufferers as the cause of their increased pain. Those arthritis sufferers in the study who were convinced of the existence of such a correlation gave widely varying accounts of the time delay between the occurrence of what they believed to be the relevant feature of the weather and the increased intensity of the pain. Thus, this study _______ .

label: Conclusion
body: People seeking jobs should move to high tech cities.

label: Evidence
