body: Most high tech cities have healthy economies. Most healthy economies have lots of job openings.

label: Evaluation
body: We have two "most" premises (typically, generally, usually, likely, tends to). They have an overlapping term. And the conclusion makes a connection between the other two terms.

label: Goal
body: Premise 1: Most A's are B. Premise 2: Most B's are C. Conclusion: If you want a C, get an A.

label: Apparent Paradox
body: A recent study of 5,000 individuals found, on the basis of a physical exam, that more than 25 percent of people older than 65 were malnourished, though only 12 percent of the people in this age group fell below government poverty standards. In contrast, a greater percentage of the people 65 or younger fell below poverty standards than were found in the study to be malnourished.

label: Evaluate
body: The wrong answers will all make it more clear why a difference between those 65 and older and those under 65 exists.

label: Evidence
body: Jocko, a chimpanzee, was once given a large bunch of bananas by a zookeeper after the more dominant members of the chimpanzee’s troop had wandered off. In his excitement, Jocko uttered some loud “food barks.” The other chimpanzees returned and took the bananas away. The next day, Jocko was again found alone and was given a single banana. This time, however, he kept silent.

label: Conclusion
body: The zookeeper concluded that Jocko’s silence was a stratagem to keep the other chimpanzees from his food.

label: Evaluate
body: It’s possible that Jocko had learned from his mistake and had decided to keep quiet the second time as a way to keep his banana. It’s also possible that a single banana did not excite Jocko as much as a large bunch of bananas. And because Jocko didn’t get so excited, he didn’t accidentally alert the other chimpanzees of the banana’s arrival.

label: Conclusion (this indicates that)
body: Today's trends in publishing are based on false assumptions about the interests of the public. rephrase: the public is not that interested in stories covering lifestyle trends and celebrity gossip

label: Evidence
body: In a survey of journalism students, a significant majority said they wanted to see stories dealing with serious governmental and political issues and had little tolerance for the present popularity of stories covering lifestyle trends and celebrity gossip.

label: Premise
body: A large company has been convicted of engaging in monopolistic practices. The information provided by the trial has emboldened the company’s direct competitors, alerted potential rivals, and forced the company to restrain its unfair behavior toward customers and competitors.

label: Intermediate Conclusion
body: The trial provided useful information about the company’s practices.

label: Main Conclusion
body: The trial was worthwhile.

label: Evidence (and)
body: The new year is approaching, and with it the seasonal demand for books on exercise and fitness. Our competitors have demonstrated a high level of organization. We cannot afford to be outsold.

label: Evaluate
body: The author's conclusion is saying that the public isn't really interested in stories covering lifestyle trends and celebrity gossip (those types of stories are presently popular, but the author thinks that this is based on false assumptions about what the public wants). How does the author know what the public is really interested in? She cites a survey of journalism students. Are the interests of journalism students a good reflection of what the interests of the public are? Probably not. First of all, journalism students are just a specific subcategory of people, so they're not a good proxy for the general public regardless of the issue. But in particular with this issue, it seems like journalism students are way more likely than an average person to want to see stories dealing with serious governmental and political issues. The whole reason these students are majoring in journalism is because they want to write stories dealing with serious governmental and political issues (people don't major in journalism to write articles about lifestyle trends or celebrity gossip).

label: Goal
body: So it seems like we're dealing with the Famous Flaw, Sampling. This argument relies on a sample group that likely has a biased, self-selecting interest in serious news stories over easy-to-read crap about trends and celebrities.

label: Given that ...
body: Electric bug zappers are a very effective means of ridding an area of flying insects.

label: How can it be that ...
body: Most pest control experts say not to use them, and to use insect-eating birds or insecticide sprays instead?

label: Goal
body: In order to explain why pest control experts would tell people not to use this effective pest-removal device, we need to hear something BAD that electric bug zappers do (or something that birds or sprays can do that's BETTER than what bug zappers can do).

label: Evidence
body: The design of Japanese gardens should display harmony with nature. Rocks found in nature vary widely in appearance.

label: Conclusion
body: Hence, rocks chosen for placement in such gardens should vary widely in appearance.

label: Evaluate
body: The recommendation in the conclusion comes from an assumption that choosing rocks that vary widely in appearance will help display harmony.

label: Given
body: Small experimental vacuum VT → OH tubes can operate in heat that makes semiconductor components fail. Any component whose OH + P → CS resistance to heat is greater than that of semiconductors would be preferable for use in digital circuits, but only if that component were also comparable to semiconductors in all other significant respects, such as maximum current capacity. However, vacuum tubes' VT → ~CS maximum current capacity is presently not comparable to that of semiconductors.

label: Conclusion
body: It was Ebola that devastated Athens in 430 B.C.

label: Evidence
body: We know they experienced hiccups (which is only known to be a symptom of Ebola) and that other symptoms they had are also symptoms of Ebola.

label: Evaluation
body: This is a Curious Fact / Explanation type argument. curious fact: What was the epidemic that devastated Athens in 430 B.C. author's explanation: Ebola

label: Goal
body: We can Weaken it in two different ways: - supply a different explanations for the curious fact (why else did so many people die? / why else did so many people have hiccups?) - undermine the plausibility of the author's explanation (what sort of evidence makes it seem less likely that 430 B.C. Athens had a case of Ebola)

label: Conclusion
body: Your article was unjustified in criticizing environmentalists for claiming that more wolves on Vancouver Island are killed by hunters than are born each year. rephrase: It may be true that more wolves are killed by hunters than are born, so you shouldn't criticize them for saying it.

label: Opposing Point
body: You stated that this claim was disproven by recent studies that indicate that the total number of wolves on Vancouver Island has remained roughly constant for 20 years.

label: Premise
body: But you failed to account for the fact that, fearing the extinction of this wolf population, environmentalists have been introducing new wolves into the Vancouver Island wolf population for 20 years.

label: Given
body: For several decades, the number of transistors on new computer microchips, and hence the microchips’ computing speed, has doubled about every 18 months. However, from the mid-1990s into the next decade, each such doubling in a microchip’s computing speed was accompanied by a doubling in the cost of producing that microchip.

label: Evidence
body: Ms. Sandstrom’s newspaper CD column describing a strange natural phenomenon on the Mendels’ farm led to many people to trespass on and extensively damage their property.

label: Conclusion
body: Ms. Sandstrom should pay RED → PD for this damage if, as the Mendels claim, she could have reasonably expected that the column would lead people to damage the Mendels’ farm.

label: Evaluate
body: The argument assumes RED → PD that if Ms. Sandstrom could have reasonably expected her column to lead people to damage the Mendels’ farm, then she should pay for damage caused by her column.

label: Decision
body: Let's go ahead and revoke Meyer's PhD

label: Evidence
body: Even though we looked into it and found out that he didn't falsify any scientific data for his doctoral thesis here, he was recently discovered by his employer to have done so there.

label: Evaluate
body: If you did nothing wrong while you were in college, but then your college decided to disown you once you did something bad later in life, then what is the principle guiding their behavior?

label: Goal
body: Let's look for something like, "even though this person was supposedly fine when we knew them, we have since found out that they've now done a shady thing, so we want to disavow our endorsement of them."

label: Given
body: Compared to many forms of exercise, kickboxing aerobics is highly risky. Overextending when O -causes→ kicking often leads to hip, knee, or lower-back injuries. Such overextension is BMK → O very likely to occur when beginners try to match the high kicks of more skilled practitioners.

label: Opposing Evidence
body: The penalty imposed on the company will probably have little if any effect on its behavior.

label: Waller's Claim 1
body: If there were ESP, public would generally accept does Chin argue that "No, even if there were ESP, it's possible that most of the public would not accept?" Yes, it seems like Chin does argue that. He lays out a scenario in which the influence of the elite would lead the media and thereby the general public to remain skeptical and not accept ESP.

label: Waller's Claim 2
body: Anyone with ESP could convince the general public of ESP by clearly demonstrating their powers. does Chin argue that, "No, someone with ESP wouldn't be able to convince the general public by demonstrating their powers?" Yeah, kind of. Our author thinks that the influence of the elite would bias the media which would bias the general public against accepting ESP.

label: Waller's Claim 3
body: Anyone who was recognized to have ESP would get rich and famous as a result. does Chin argue that, "No, someone who was recognized to have ESP wouldn't get rich and famous?" No. Chin doesn't get into this hypothetical of what would happen with someone who was recognized to have ESP, mainly because Chin is pessimistic that the general public would ever accept that someone has ESP.

label: Goal
body: They seem to disagree about whether the public would generally accept ESP, if it actually existed, and whether someone who possessed ESP could convince the general public by clearly demonstrating those powers.

label: Conclusion
body: Hagerle owe me a sincere apology too.

label: Evidence
body: Hagerle told the same lie to me and to the physician, and Hagerle gave the physician a sincere apology.

label: Evaluate
body: This makes use of the famous principle every kid uses when their sibling is getting something they're not getting: "No fair! If she gets one, then I get one too!" In this case, the principle should probably sound something like, "It's not fair if you lied to both of us but only apologized to one of us. If she (the physician) gets an apology, I should get one too."

label: Goal
body: We want to find a principle whose trigger applies to this situation and whose outcome would strengthen or prove the idea that this counselor should also get a sincere apology from Hagerle.

label: Evidence
body: A survey of address changes filed with post offices and driver’s license bureaus over the last ten years has established that households moving out of the city of Weston outnumbered households moving into the city two to one.

label: Conclusion
body: Therefore, we can expect that next year’s census, which counts all residents regardless of age, will show that the population of Weston has declined since the last census ten years ago.

label: Evaluate
body: The fact that households moving out of Weston outnumber households moving into the city two to one does not guarantee that more people are moving out of Weston than are moving into Weston. If the households moving out do not have many children while the households moving into Weston do, the conclusion would not necessarily follow from the premise.

label: Conclusion (should = opinion)
body: People should not necessarily try to rid themselves of the tendency to erroneously think about how a given event would affect future happiness.

label: Evidence (after all)
body: People often erroneously see parallel lines as converging. But people should not try to rid themselves of that habit, if a surgeon offered to restructure their eyes and brain to remove that tendency.

label: Evaluate
body: The author seems to be arguing, "The human machine has foibles, but it's still a worthwhile machine. If we have a glitch that makes us see parallel lines as converging, or a glitch that makes us mis-estimate how a given event would affect future happiness, we shouldn't try to change it. We might accidentally mess up what makes us otherwise so wonderful." We're obviously filling in some blanks there, but that's how one would charitably interpret this argument. It's sort of like when you tell someone, "I know you wish you could go back in time to fix that mistake you made, but your mistakes made you who you are today, and so we have to accept the bad with the good." In terms of our job on Method, we're just supposed to try to characterize the type of evidence or reasoning employed. Almost all Method questions pull from this list of eight options: - present analogy - (counter)example to general claim - rule out alternatives - show bad implications of logic/plan - call out a dubious assumption - raise an overlooked consideration - suggest an alternate explanation - introduce a definition / distinction

label: Goal
body: This argument seems to make the most common move on Method questions: present an analogy. The conclusion is about cognitive errors related to happiness. The evidence is about cognitive errors related to parallel lines. The author is implying that the two situations are analogous (the deeper principle they share being, "Yes, you're glitchy, but don't try to fix it")

label: Principle
body: If a description (cited as opinion or not) → misrepresentation deliberately tries to mislead bidders

label: Application
body: Healy's committed misrepresentation when it described a vase as dating from the mid 18th (when it's really a modern reproduction).

label: Evaluation
body: Did we trigger the criteria that "the description deliberately tries to mislead bidders"? No, not yet. We know the description is misleading (i.e. wrong), but we haven't yet established intent.

label: Goal
body: We need to know that Healy's intentionally wrote that description to mislead.

label: Conclusion
body: Neanderthals and early-humans did not interbreed.

label: Evidence
body: The DNA of a Neanderthal from from back in the day is very different from the DNA of a contemporary human.

label: Evaluation
body: This seems like a shady comparison. Neanderthals lived more than 100,000 years ago. We're comparing that DNA to contemporary human DNA? Is a contemporary human's DNA even that similar to an early-human's DNA? Maybe DNA changes enough over 100,000 years that of course it's very different now, whether they were interbreeding or not.

label: Goal
body: The author seems to be assuming that "if they were interbreeding, then our modern DNA would look more similar to that of Neanderthals"

label: Evidence
body: If you choose to associate with people who share many of your personal beliefs, it's possible see your lifestyle choices accepted by others. And if you see your lifestyle choices are accepted by others, it's much less difficult to live an enjoyable life.

label: Given
body: The profits of downtown ↑C → ↑P businesses will increase if more consumers live in the downtown area. A decrease in the cost ↓CL → ↑C of living in the downtown area will guarantee that the number of consumers living there will increase. However, the profits of ↑P → ↓TC downtown businesses will not increase unless downtown traffic congestion decreases.

label: Conclusion
body: Domestic + long distance → costs 15 cents + doesn't cost 10 cents

label: Evidence
body: Domestic + long distance → costs 15 cents + 9am - 5pm Domestic + long distance → costs 10 cents + 5pm - 9am

label: Evaluation
body: This argument is valid, since we basically know that domestic long distance calls in two rates: 10 cents and 15 cents. So the conclusion makes sense — if it ain't 10 cents, it must be 15 cents. If we were trying to diagram this original argument, we basically need to be convinced that a certain thing (domestic long distance calls) is always going to either be X or Y. Then we can conclude that if it's not X, it's Y.

label: Goal
body: Premise 1: If X is A, then it's Y. Premise 2: If X is ~A, then it's Z. Conclusion: If X is ~Y, then it's Z.

label: Conclusion
body: If 1st child intended harm → wrong to push

label: Evidence
body: 1st child understands the difference between right and wrong.

label: Evaluation
body: This is weirdly simple. We might argue that even if the first kid didn't intend harm, it was still wrong to push the second kid. But this author seems to care about whether the first kid knows right from wrong.

label: Goal
body: We just need a rule that we know applies to the 1st kid and outputs the judgment that pushing the 2nd kid was wrong.

label: Conclusion
body: Certain makes of car must be more common in some areas than others.

label: Evidence
body: If that were so, then many people would overestimate how common their type of car is. + In a study, many people overestimated how common their type of car is.

label: Evaluation
body: This is committing a Necessary vs. Sufficient flaw by doing backwards logic on a conditional. If my hypothesis were true, we would see X. We see X, thus my hypothesis is true. Here's a parallel argument: I hypothesize that people think their own lives are typical of other people's lives. If this were so, then many people would overestimate how typical their car is. Since people in this study overestimated how typical their car is, it must be that people think there own lives are typical of others'.

label: Goal
body: Look for an answer pointing out that there are other possible ways to interpret the fact that people overestimate how common their car is, or an answer calling out the backwards logic (Nec vs. Suff) move the author made.

label: Conclusion
body: Most parking citations in college towns are issued to students.

label: Evidence
body: In college towns, police issue more parking citations during the school year than not during the school year.

label: Evaluation
body: This is a Curious Fact / Author's Interpretation type argument. curious fact: Why are more parking tickets issued when school is in session? author's story: When school is in session, there are more students around, and the students are the ones getting most of the tickets. What's the flaw with that type of argument? The flaw with almost all Causal arguments is that the author is too sure of one potential explanation. Maybe there is some other way to explain that data: - maybe there are more parking enforcement officers during the school year - maybe there are just more people in general (not just students) during the school year

label: Goal
body: The form of this argument is a loose sense of Correlation → Causation. If we assume that more students are around when school is in session, the author sees a correlation: Students In Town || More Tickets and then she draws a causal inference that the students being there are the cause of more tickets. Look for a similar "A is happening more when B is present, so B must be the reason for A."

label: Conclusion
body: Only harsh criticism will cause the person critiqued to change.

label: Evidence
body: Changing requires a motive, and harsh criticism provides a motive.

label: Evaluation
body: Okay, but couldn't something else also provide a motive? What if a reward for good behavior provided a motive? Maybe that could also cause a person to change. This author is using conditional logic words like "only, requires", so we should be on the lookout for a Necessary vs. Sufficient flaw. Here's what the author's argument looks like in conditional logic. Change requires a motive. C → M Harsh criticism provides a motive. HC → M ⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯ ⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯ Only harsh criticism causes change C → HC The author is picturing this chain: C → M → HC But that second link is the fraudulent one. Harsh criticism is sufficient to produce a motive, but it's not necessary to have a motive.

label: Goal
body: Look for an answer describing the Necessary vs. Sufficient flaw, or one making the conversational objection that there might be other ways to provide a motive besides harsh criticism.

label: Conclusion
body: Almost everyone in this country really wants to be an artist.

label: Evidence (after all)
body: Just about everyone I know hopes to one day make a living as a painter, musician, or poet.

label: Evaluate
body: Why would blackouts continue if residents were heed the request for residents to cut back on air conditioner use in their homes. This would be more likely the smaller the percentage of electricity that is used by residential homes. If most of the power is consumed by companies, then reducing residential consumption would have little impact on reducing the frequent power blackouts.

label: Evidence
body: Long-term and short-term relaxation training are two common forms of treatment for individuals experiencing problematic levels of anxiety. Yet studies show that on average, regardless of which form of treatment one receives, symptoms of anxiety decrease to a normal level within the short-term-training time period.

label: Conclusion
body: Thus, for most people the generally more expensive long-term training is unwarranted.

label: Evaluate
body: The conclusion and evidence are making very similar claims, but about two different groups. EVID: almost everyone I know wants to be an artist, even if they're working a day job. CONC: almost everyone in the country wants to be an artist, even if they're working a day job. When we see that copycat language repeating on Flaw questions, it's often a Sampling flaw or Part vs. Whole flaw. In this case, the author is using a sample of "almost everyone I know" to extrapolate a true statement about "almost everyone in the country". To make such a generalization, the author needs to assume that the sample of people she knows is representative of people in the country. We would already be concerned about the small sample size of "everyone I know", but we can also worry that this sample is potentially unrepresentative given that artists tend to live and associate with other artists. Artists tend to know other artists — friends, collaborators, people in the same scene. They're all living in lofts together and still on their parents' phone plans / health plans. (I say this with love. I was an artist living in my van before I became an LSAT teacher.)

label: Goal
body: Find an answer that calls out the famous Sampling flaw.

label: Conclusion
body: Almost everyone in the country wants to be an artist.

label: Evidence
body: Almost everyone the artist personally knows wants to be an artist.

label: Evaluate
body: An artist's personal acquaintances are not representative of the country.

label: Goal
body: Find the answer that points out the unrepresentative sample.

label: Conclusion
body: The artist concludes that almost everyone in the entire country wants to be an artist.

label: Evidence
body: The artist looks at the people they personally know — and yep, almost all of them want to be artists.

label: Evaluate
body: Here's the obvious problem. Artists tend to hang out with other artists. The people in the artist's circle are almost certainly not a fair cross-section of the country. They're a self-selected group of like-minded folks. It's like a doctor concluding that "almost everyone wants to go to medical school" because almost everyone the doctor knows is a doctor or pre-med student. The sample isn't representative of the country — it's representative of the doctor's social circle.

label: Goal
body: The right answer will name the sampling problem — generalizing from a non-representative group of acquaintances.

label: Sam Meli
body: Mountain lions, a protected species, are preying on bighorn sheep, another protected species. Nonsense. We We must let must do what nature take its we can to ensure course and hope the survival of the bighorns the bighorn, even survive. if that means limiting the mountain lion population.

label: Evaluate
body: We can go by process of elimination through Sam's claims and verify that there's only one there that Meli seems to be arguing the opposite of. She's not saying - Mountain lions aren't protected - Bighorns aren't protected - Mountain lions aren't preying on bighorns But she does seem to be saying - We shouldn't let nature take its course and hope the bighorns survive Because she's arguing that we should intervene and do whatever it takes to protect the bighorns. Intervening is the opposite of "letting nature take its course". So let's look for an answer about "whether or not we should intervene and try to protect the bighorns", or "whether or not we should let nature take its course and just hope the bighorns survive".

label: Causation Comparison
body: Pro Con Primary School Rigorous Work Secondary School Rigorous Work

label: Opposing Point
body: Bus drivers complain that evaluating drivers by having supervisors ride with each driver affects their performance.

label: Evidence
body: A transit company’s bus drivers are evaluated by supervisors riding with each driver. The supervisor’s presence affects every driver’s performance.

label: Conclusion
body: Those drivers performing best with a supervisor aboard will likely also be the best drivers under normal conditions.

label: Evaluate
body: This author is assuming, "Since they're all affected (Absolute), there's no difference in the way that they're affected (Relative)." But as taking a real LSAT will remind us, everyone is affected by the stress of the real test, but those effects manifest in different ways for different people. Some people perform way worse than usual because of the anxiety caused by the stress. Other people perform way better than usual because of the adrenaline of the pressure. The argument assumes that the influence of supervisors riding on the bus with each driver is approximately the same for each driver.

label: Information
body: causal (X accelerates Y) Econ growth → more demand for new tech comparison (few vs. many) Lots of companies want to buy the new tech. Only a few businesses can supply the new tech. pivot (Yet) causal (X can cause Y) Accelerated tech change can cause suppliers and buyers of new tech to fail.

label: Evaluate
body: When we see multiple causal claims (just like with conditionals), we want to ask ourselves whether they chain together. It's possible here to construe a sort of causal chain: 1st, econ growth accelerates demand for new tech 2nd, an acceleration of new tech leads to supplies / buyers of new tech failing We could pull out of that the "1 to 3" connection, that "Accelerating economic growth can lead to the failures of some businesses." (i.e. the buyers / suppliers of new tech) Does the middle sentence have any value? Does it tell us anything that there will be a few businesses who have the new tech, and many who want it? We can use our common sense about supply and demand to think that if demand outpaces supply, then the price of new tech will likely be high.

label: Goal
body: It's hard to predict what the answer will be, but if they were rewarding us for finding a causal chain, then maybe something like "when economic growth accelerates, some businesses may fail as a result". Ultimately, we'll pick the most provable answer we can find.

label: Apparent Paradox
body: During this record-breaking heat wave, air conditioner use has overloaded the region's electrical power grid, resulting in frequent power blackouts throughout the region. For this reason, residents have been asked to cut back voluntarily on air conditioner use in their homes. But even if this request is heeded, blackouts will probably occur unless the heat wave abates.

label: Evidence
body: The average salary for teachers in our society is lower than the average salary for athletes.

label: Evaluate
body: It’s fantastic that the symptoms of anxiety decrease to a normal level so quickly. However, what happens after the treatment ends? It seems likely that for some people, their symptoms are likely to return once the treatment has ended and for them it makes sense that they may need treatment even after their symptoms of anxiety have abated.

label: Opposing Point
body: Many critics of consumerism insist that advertising persuades people that they need certain consumer goods when they merely desire them.

label: Evidence
body: In life, it is often impossible to determine whether something is merely desirable or whether it is essential to one’s happiness.

label: Conclusion
body: This accusation rests on a fuzzy distinction, that between wants and needs.

label: Conclusion
body: People who rely on the web when attempting to diagnose their medical conditions are likely to do themselves more harm than good.

label: Evidence
body: People who browse the web for medical information often cannot differentiate between scientifically valid info and quackery (and the quackery may be even more appealing than the valid info).

label: Evaluation
body: There's a small difference between the trigger in the conclusion and trigger in the premise: conclusion - people who rely on the web when attempting to self-diagnose vs. premise - people who browse the web for medical info Since the author is equating those, we can say that she's assuming that "at least some people who rely on the web when attempting to self-diagnose will browse the web for medical info". However, that's a very fair assumption, so it might not be very likely that LSAT would test that one. The author is arguing this chain of ideas: rely on browse can't tell do more web to → web for → between → harm self med science & than good diagnose info quackery The middle arrow has been established, but the first and third have not.

label: Goal
body: Look for an answer attaching "rely on web to self-diagnose" to "browse web for medical info", or one attaching "can't tell different between science and quackery" to "do more harm than good".

label: Given
body: Like a genetic profile, a functional magnetic-resonance image (fMRI) of the brain can contain information that a patient wishes to keep private. An fMRI of a brain also contains enough information about a patient’s skull to create a recognizable image of that patient’s face. A genetic profile can be linked to a patient only by referring to labels or records.

label: Conclusion
body: The shoe factory would be a better site for the municipal emergency shelter than the courthouse would be.

label: Evidence
body: The people who prefer the courthouse have provided no evidence of this.

label: Evaluate
body: This is a He Said / She Said type situation, where we have two conflicting opinions and no way to choose between them. Just because the courthouse crew has no evidence their site is better doesn't mean that the shoe factory crew is immediately right. What's their evidence? This is also a Unproven vs. Proven False situation, where the author goes from saying "Person X hasn't successfully proven claim Y, thus claim Y must be wrong / untrue / false."

label: Goal
body: Let's look for something sounding like Unproven vs. Proven False or something making the objection that no evidence has been offered in favor of using the shoe factory.

label: Conclusion
body: James was misleading when he told the Core Curriculum Committee that the Anthropology chair had endorsed his proposal. rephrase: What he said was technically true, but it gives off the wrong impression.

label: Evidence
body: The chair's endorsement was conditional: it applied only if what she was looking at was the same set of recommendations as what James was showing the committee.

label: Evaluate
body: The idea of "misleading" is that it's technically true but giving off the wrong impression. In a sense, James DID have the chair's endorsement. She was like, "Sure, if THIS is the version going before committee, then I endorse it". The author is saying this gives off the wrong impression. It makes people think that the chair endorsed James's proposal even though she really didn't. That seems to imply that the version James is submitting to the committee is NOT the same as the one he got conditionally approved by the chair.

label: Goal
body: This argument has one clear missing idea, so it's very likely that our prediction will be similar to the answer. If the proposal James is presenting to the committee is the same as what he showed to the chair, then he genuinely DID get her endorsement. It's only misleading to say he got her endorsement if the proposal James is offering the committee is different in some way from what he showed the chair.

label: Conclusion
body: James was misleading when he claimed the Anthropology chair endorsed his proposal.

label: Evidence
body: The chair's endorsement was conditional on her seeing all of James's recommendations.

label: Evaluate
body: For James to have been misleading, that condition must have failed — the draft the chair saw must not have included all his final recommendations.

label: Goal
body: An answer saying the draft the chair saw didn't include all the recommendations James proposed.

label: Conclusion
body: The author says James's claim that the chair endorsed his proposal was misleading.

label: Evidence
body: Why? Because the chair's endorsement came with a string attached: it only applied if the draft she saw matched what James actually ended up proposing.

label: Evaluate
body: For the conclusion to make sense, that condition must have failed. If the draft she saw did include everything James later proposed, then the endorsement was real and James wasn't misleading. Think of it like this. A friend says, "Sure, I'll vouch for you for the loan, but only if you're putting up the same collateral I saw." If you tell the bank "my friend vouched for me" but secretly changed the collateral, that's misleading. If you used the same collateral, it's not.

label: Goal
body: The answer should establish that James's final proposal contained recommendations the chair never saw.

label: Conclusion
body: Travaillier Corporation must be attempting to enlarge its consumer base by attracting new customers.

label: Evidence
body: Travaillier Corporation has traditionally catered to air travelers, and those travelers are still taking similar vacations. Meanwhile, Travaillier Corporation recently hired employees who have experience in the tour bus industry, and its execs have been in talks with companies that subcontract charter buses.

label: Ealuation
body: This is a classic Curious Fact / Author's Interpretation type argument. Curious Fact: Why is Travaillier Corporation hiring employees w/ tour bus industry experience and talking to companies that rent out charter buses? Author's Interpretation: They must be trying to enlarge their base (which is mostly air travelers) by trying to attract bus travelers as well. The correct answers to these arguments deal with one of two things: - a different way to explain the curious fact - the plausibility of the author's way

label: Goal
body: Most Weaken answers on causal arguments deal with a different way to explain the curious fact, so we'll primarily look for a different reason (besides trying to attract new bus customers) that Travaillier Corporation is hiring people with bus experience and talking to a charter bus companies. But we'll stay receptive to answers that lower the plausibility that Travaillier Corporation is trying to enlarge their base, or that they are seeking new, bus-traveling customers.

label: Evidence
body: Education in [a traditional TC → ~SP classroom] is not truly a social process. Only social processes can DSI → SP develop students’ insights. In the traditional classroom, TC → R + A the teacher acts from outside the group and interaction between teachers and students is rigid and artificial.

label: Conclusion
body: Traditional classroom TC → ~E education is ineffective.

label: Evaluate
body: The argument assumes E → DSI that developing student insights is a requirement of effective education.

label: Conclusion
body: If you avoid dairy foods, avoid >> prob GH probability of maintaining dairy increased good health is increased.

label: Evidence
body: If you avoid dairy foods, avoid >> eat less you're less likely to eat fat dairy fat If you avoid eating fat, avoid prob of probability of avoiding fat >> avoiding heart disease goes up HD goes up

label: Evaluation
body: The author is arguing this causal chain: avoid >> eat less >> prob of >> prob GH dairy fat avoiding increased HD goes up We go from talking about "being less likely to eat fat" to "avoiding fat in one's diet". There's a little different there, so an answer could call out that gap. But more likely to be addressed in the answer is the last gap, where we go from saying "you've increased the probability of avoiding heart disease" to "you've increased the probability of maintaining good health".

label: Goal
body: Look for an answer that addresses the difference between avoiding heart disease and maintaining good health.

label: Conclusion
body: Any history book gives only a distorted view of the past.

label: Evidence
body: Just as a single momentary perception wouldn't give you an accurate sense of your physical environment (because it's only from one perspective), a single history book will only show you one perspective (the biases and prejudices of its author).

label: Evaluation
body: The most common correct answer on Method is an author presenting an Analogy. That seems to be happening here, since the conclusion is about history books only offering one perspective on history, and the author supports this with an analogy about seeing your physical environment.

label: Goal
body: Look for an answer saying that the author supports her conclusion about history books with an analogy about having more than one perspective on your physical environment.

label: Conclusion
body: Any future proposal endorsed by CL will probably be passed.

label: Evidence
body: So far, most proposals endorsed by CL have been passed.

label: Evaluation
body: This is essentially arguing, "because a certain thing (proposals endorsed by CL) has usually gone a certain way (passed) most of the previous times, any future instance like this will probably go that same way".

label: Goal
body: Look for an argument that says "because Most X's have been Y, any future X will probably be Y".

label: Conclusion
body: Much of the data on the effects of this weed-killer are probably misleading.

label: Evidence
body: Because the weed-killer has two different forms of molecule (one that kills weeds, one that does nothing), the weed-killer can be very effective or not at all effective depending on local soil conditions, since those determine whether the killer form or the non-killer form of the molecule ends up being more concentrated in the soil.

label: Evaluation
body: The new guy in the conclusion is "much of the data on the effects of this weed-killer". What is the author assuming about much of the data, that would make it misleading? It sounds like he's saying, "Maybe they only looked at the type of soil where the killer molecule is higher concentrated, and thus the data makes the weed-killer look more effective than it would be in many circumstances" / vice versa where the data is based on soil where the non-killer molecule would be predominant, in which case the weed-killer would look weaker than it should.

label: Goal
body: If the weed-killer has been tested on a wide variety of local soil conditions, then we should have a pretty accurate sense of how it performs on average. But if it's only been tested on a narrow variety of local soil conditions, then the data might mislead by making it seem more widely effective or ineffective (depending on which narrow type of soil we studied) than it really is.

label: Principle
body: exemplary record ←→ eligible for Mayor's Commendation eligible for MC + should receive did something → Mayor's beyond expectations Commendation to save someone's life

label: Application
body: Franklin should get a Mayor's Commendation, but Penn should not.

label: Evaluation / Goal
body: To establish that Franklin should get the Mayor's Commendation, we need to know - exemplary record (thus eligible) - did more than expected to save a life To establish that Penn should not get the Mayor's Commendation, we could hear either of these disqualifiers: - doesn't have exemplary record - didn't do more than expected to save a life

label: Conclusion
body: No one should be denied the freedom to choose who they associate with.

label: Evaluation
body: There's a little causal / conditional chain in the evidence: choose to (possible to) much less associate see your difficult to w/ people → lifestyle choices → live an who share accepted by enjoyable your beliefs others life If we're told that A leads to B, which leads to C, and the conclusion is "no one should be denied the freedom to do A", then we're assuming that "no should be denied the freedom to obtain C".

label: Goal
body: In this case, A possibly leads to B, which leads to C, so we're assuming "no should be denied the freedom to do something that possibly leads to C".

label: Conclusion
body: Some older people can lower their blood pressure by drinking milk.

label: Evidence
body: When people get older, it's common for them to get a calcium deficiency, which is caused by a lack of the active form of vitamin D that the body needs and which leads to a rise in blood pressure. One glass of milk per day can make up for a calcium deficiency.

label: Evaluate
body: This is a causal mouthful. The overall causal chain that ends in higher blood pressure goes like this: 1. not enough active form of vitamin D 2. body isn't absorbing calcium 3. calcium deficiency causes rise in blood pressure How does our hero milk enter the story? Milk makes up for any underlying calcium deficiency. I have two questions, as I try to remain skeptical of the idea that milk can help older people lower their blood pressure... 1. Does milk provide the "active form of vitamin D" needed for body to absorb calcium? 2. Even if we say milk is making up for the underlying calcium deficiency, that would prevent a rise in blood pressure from calcium deficiency, but would it trigger a lowering of blood pressure?

label: Goal
body: Since this is sufficient assumption, one of my two worries is apparently wrong (in LSAT's mind). There's only one missing vulnerability here, but I can't figure out which one they want to address. It isn't clearly established that milk provides "the active form of vitamin D needed in order for the body to absorb calcium", and it seems like we're prescribing milk as a solution for that specific ailment. But it also isn't clear to me that we take this causality backwards the way the conclusion is doing. I can understand how not enough milk could lead to a rise in blood pressure, but am I allowed to say that more milk would lead to a lowering of blood pressure?

label: Conclusion
body: Each person should be taxed solely in proportion to their income.

label: Evidence
body: A just system of taxation would require each person to be taxed in proportion how much society serves that person's interests. The most objective way to determine how well society has served someone is wealth.

label: Evaluation
body: What is the reasoning flaw here? The author tries to establish that figuring out taxation by wealth is the most objective way of figuring out how much society as benefited each person, and then concludes that we should be taxed solely according to income. 2 thoughts: - is "wealth" the same as "income"? (wealth includes your assets, like houses and cars, whereas income just refers to how much money you receive each month or year) - is the "most objective" way automatically the best way? Should we "solely" go off the most objective way? Could we combine 'wealth/income' with other metrics?

label: Goal
body: We need an argument that lays out a way to measure something (tax should be based on how much society gives you). Then we should hear about the most ____ way of measuring that (maybe "objective", maybe something similar but different). Then we should get a conclusion that says that we should solely rely on that ____ way, although there will probably be a concept shift (like we had with wealth vs. income) Premise 1: To determine X, we should consider Y. Premise 2: The best / most objective way to determine Y is Z. Conclusion: Determining X should be solely based on *Z*.

label: Apparent Paradox
body: A recent poll showed that almost half of the city's residents believe that Mayor Walker is guilty of ethics violations. Surprisingly, however, 52 percent of those surveyed judged Walker's performance as mayor to be good or excellent, which is no lower than it was before anyone accused him of ethics violations.

label: Evaluate
body: How could 52 percent of those surveyed judge Walker’s performance to be good or excellent, when nearly half of the city’s residents believe that Mayor Walker is guilty of ethics violations? Nearly half of the city’s residents believe the mayor is not doing a good or excellent job, it could be these residents who believe that the mayor is guilty of ethics violations. In a hotly contested, partisan atmosphere such a divide is imaginable.

label: Evidence
body: Studies have shown that treating certain illnesses with treatment X produces the same beneficial changes in patients' conditions as treating the same illnesses with treatment Y. Treatment X is quicker and less expensive than treatment Y.

label: Conclusion
body: In treating these illnesses, treatment X should be preferred to treatment Y.

label: Evaluate
body: There are several advantages to treating these illnesses with treatment X rather than treatment Y. But are there are disadvantages? Perhaps there are some disadvantages that are simply unacceptable that would change which treatment is recommended.

label: Evidence
body: Any government must be defined and controlled by laws that determine its powers and limits. It is inevitable that some individuals EPP will learn how to interpret these laws to gain a greater share of political power than others have.

label: Conclusion
body: A form of government in which every ERR citizen's rights are respected is impossible.

label: Evaluate
body: The argument assumes that a system EPP → ERR where political power is not distributed equally is one in which not everyone's right's will be respected.

label: Opposing Point
body: The cost of fuel for nuclear plants is significantly lower than the cost of conventional fuels, such as coal and oil.

label: Evidence
body: Nuclear plants are far more expensive to build than are conventional power plants.

label: Conclusion
body: Safety considerations aside, nuclear power plants are not economically feasible.

label: Evaluate
body: The argument has accounted for several factors that determine the economic feasibility of nuclear power, but not all of them. Other factors could include the costs of complying with regulations, labor to operate the plants, and the length of time a plant is expected to operate.

label: Evaluate
body: Anytime the argument presents the average value of something, it’s a good idea to consider other ways of looking at that value, such as the median or total values. In this case, the total amount earned by each profession might be a better indicator of how much society values each.

label: Given:
body: Gauge field theory was investigated in the nineteenth century, but only recently has been applied to problems in quantum mechanics. Differential geometry was investigated in the early nineteenth century, but only recently has been applied to the exploration of general relativity.

label: Evaluate:
body: The common relationship between these two examples is that some applications of a theory may not be initially apparent.

label: Evidence
body: Recently discovered bird fossils are about 20 million years older than the fossils of the birdlike dinosaurs from which the birds are generally claimed to have descended.

label: Conclusion
body: So these newly discovered fossils show, contrary to the account espoused by most paleontologists, that no bird descended from any dinosaur.

label: Evaluate
body: The conclusion goes too far. It might be fair to say that the bird fossils that predate the birdlike dinosaurs by 20 million years are from birds who did not descend from the suspected birdlike dinosaur. But these birds could have descended from another birdlike dinosaur.

label: Evidence
body: A classic suit may stay in style for as long as five years. A trendy hat will go out of style in a year or two.

label: Conclusion
body: It is worthwhile to pay more to get a well-constructed hat, while the trendy hat should be purchased as cheaply as possible.

label: Evaluate
body: The argument assumes that the amount of money one should spend on a piece of clothing depends on how long one expects to wear it.

label: Apparent Paradox
body: One report claims that the region suffers relatively little erosion, while another claims that regional erosion is heavy and a cause for concern. Both reports are accurate.

label: Evaluate
body: A way to explain the accuracy of the different conclusions in these reports is to have them report on different things. If one report is about wind erosion and another is about water erosion, both reports could be accurate while still reaching different conclusions.

label: Evidence
body: Vehicle-related fatality rates are rising in the areas with lower speed limits.

label: Conclusion
body: Areas with lower speed limits will not have lower vehicle-related fatality rates than other areas.

label: Evaluate
body: An increasing fatality rate in one area does not prove a relative comparison about fatality rates with other areas, unless we know whether the fatality rates in those other areas are changing. The argument fails to consider that vehicle-related fatality rates could be rising in other areas as well.

label: Apparent Paradox
body: Human settlement of previously uninhabited areas tends to endanger species of wildlife. The Mississippi kite flourishes in areas that people have settled. In fact, during the five years since 1985 its population has risen far more rapidly in towns than in rural areas.

label: Evaluate
body: So why has the Mississippi kite done so well in towns compared with rural areas? The right answer should provide a benefit to kites living in towns compared with rural areas.

label: Main Conclusion
body: It is only fair for a major label to take a large portion of the profits from the record sales of any band signed with it.

label: Intermediate Conclusion
body: The band does not need to assume nearly as much risk as it would if it produced its own records independently.

label: Premises
body: When a major record label signs a contract with a band, the label assumes considerable financial risk. It pays for videos, album art, management, and promotions.

label: Given
body: Recently, articles criticizing the environmental movement have been appearing regularly in newspapers. According to Winslow, this is due not so much to an antienvironmental bias among the media as to a preference on the part of newspaper editors for articles that seem “daring” in that they seem to challenge prevailing political positions. It is true that editors like to run antienvironmental pieces mainly because they seem to challenge the political orthodoxy. But serious environmentalism is by no means politically orthodox, and antienvironmentalists can hardly claim to be dissidents, however much they may have succeeded in selling themselves as renegades.

label: Conclusion (thus)
body: Democracy is a better choice than rule by a few.

label: Evidence (since)
body: The inherently best and the inherently worst forms of government are those that concentrate political power in the hands of a few. Democracy is consistently a mediocre form of government.

label: Evaluate
body: The argument chooses one form of rule (democracy) over another (rule by a few) and it provides one detail about each. The argument assumes that a form of rule that is consistently mediocre is preferable to one that could be either the best or the worst. When the argument involves a positive thing (you won't get the worst) and a negative thing (but you also won't get the best), we generally see a comparative answer that is Weighing Tradeoffs.

label: Given
body: Some have suggested that any substance that at least some habitual users can cease to use is nonaddictive. However, if this is taken to be the sole criterion of nonaddictiveness, some substances that most medical experts classify as prime examples of addictive substances would be properly deemed nonaddictive. A substance is addictive only if withdrawal from its habitual use causes most users extreme psychological and physiological difficulty.

label: Evidence
body: [The large difference between wages] means that companies will be able to hire freely in response to changing conditions. Social friction arises not from large wage differences, but from wage levels that are static or slow changing.

label: Conclusion
body: A contention of many of my colleagues—that the large difference between the wages of the highest-and lowest-paid workers will inevitably become a source of social friction—is unfounded. Indeed, the high differential should have an opposite effect.

label: Evaluate
body: The argument makes a recommendation. Recommendations are a common way to identify the conclusion on Main Point questions. (Hint: Decisions, predictions, hypotheses, and explanations also tend to be conclusions.)

label: Evidence
body: The VersaTool can perform more functions than any other tool.

label: Conclusion
body: If you use the VersaTool, therefore, you will need additional tools less often than you would using any other multiple-function tool.

label: Evaluate
body: This argument completely ignores which functions the VersaTool can accomplish and which functions are most frequently needed. The VersaTool could possibly perform functions only infrequently needed, even though it performs more functions than any other tool.

label: Evidence
body: The flagellum, which bacteria use to SW → MP swim, requires many parts before it (~MP → ~SW) can propel a bacterium at all.

label: Conclusion
body: Therefore, an evolutionary ancestor of ~MP → ~SA bacteria that had only a few of these parts would gain no survival advantage from them.

label: Evaluate
body: The argument assumes that if the ~SW → ~SA flagellum would not have been able to help the bacteria swim, the flagellum would not have conferred a survival advantage.

label: Given
body: Archaic spellings and styles of punctuation in direct quotations from older works are to be preserved if they occur infrequently and do not interfere with a reader’s comprehension. However, if they occur frequently, the editor may modernize them, inserting a note with an explanation to this effect in the text, or if similar modernizing has been done in more than one quotation, inserting a general statement in the preface. On the other hand, obvious typographical errors in quotations from modern works may be corrected without explanation.

label: Evidence
body: Whoever murdered Jansen was M → O undoubtedly in Jansen's office on the day of the murder. Both Samantha and Herbert were H → O in Jansen's office on that day. S → O Herbert is not the murderer. M → ~H

label: Conclusion
body: Samantha must be the killer. M → S

label: Evaluate
body: The argument assumes that O → H or S Samantha and Herbert were the only ones in Jansen’s office on the day of the murder. NOTE: There is a distracting H → FI or FO intermediate argument that ~FI + ~FO. establishes that Herbert is not ჻ ~H the murderer by way of fingerprints and footprints. This intermediate argument is valid.

label: Given
body: Most opera singers who add demanding roles to their repertoires at a young age lose their voices early. It has been said that this is because their voices have not yet matured and hence lack the power for such roles. But young singers with great vocal power are the most likely to ruin their voices. The real problem is that most young singers lack the technical training necessary to avoid straining their vocal cords—especially when using their full vocal strength. Such misuse of the cords inevitably leads to a truncated singing career.

label: Conclusion
body: The fat-free brownies are healthier than the cookies.

label: Evidence
body: The brownies have no fat, while the cookies are high in fat. And food that is very high in fat tends to be unhealthy.

label: Evaluation
body: How could we possibly say that the fat-free brownies are not healthier than the cookies? We’d have to point out some other ingredients in the brownies that make them less healthy: lots of sugar, lots of sodium, too much arsenic? J The author is thinking that because the brownies are healthier when it comes to fat, they’re healthier overall. This fallacious move is called the Part vs. Whole flaw.

label: Goal
body: We need a situation in which because X beats Y on one specific level, the author thinks that X wins out overall.

label: Conclusion
body: It’s dumb to say that people don’t deserve praise for an action unless they were tempted to do otherwise.

label: Evidence
body: Obviously it’s commendable when people transcend a temptation to act badly in order to act rightly, but it’s still commendable when people do something right, even if they weren’t tempted to act badly or have managed to eliminate that temptation from their lives.

label: Evaluation
body: The conclusion is the first idea, and the support is what comes after for (the common premise trigger words are F.A.B.S. = for, after all, because, since). That premise says, “Although _______ “. Structurally, we know that the first half of that idea is a counterpoint, while the main clause is what the author really wants us to hear. The claim we’re asked about is the although half of the premise. So we would call this idea a disclaimer, a counterpoint, a concession that the author makes before giving us her actual premise.

label: Goal
body: Something like a concession/counterpoint/disclaimer to people who want to only praise those who’ve overcome temptations.

label: Evidence
body: Ecologists predict that the GWC or P↑ → M↑ incidence of malaria will increase if global warming continues or if the use of pesticides is not expanded. The use of pesticides is P↑ → GWC known to contribute to global warming.

label: Conclusion
body: So it is inevitable that we M↑ will see an increase in malaria in the years to come.

label: Evaluate
body: The structure contains two if/then relationships that together prove the necessary condition of the first relationship. Two good quick checks for structure include 1) a conclusion that is a statement of fact; 2) an “or” statement in the trigger of one of the premises.

label: Evidence
body: It was extremely important for litigants to make a good impression on the jurors.

label: Conclusion
body: Courtroom oratory by litigants is a good source of data on the common conceptions of morality held by the citizens of ancient Greece.

label: Evaluate
body: The argument assumes that impressing the jurors was best accomplished by reflecting the common conceptions of morality held by the citizenry.

label: Intermediate Conclusion (should = opinion)
body: The same should be true for silencing groups with certain views on human nutrition.

label: Conclusion
body: The author concludes lots of residents forgot they consulted a doctor for headaches.

label: Evidence
body: The patient often worries that the first physician will be alienated. In addition, for the first physician there is the issue of pride: a second opinion tacitly highlights a physician’s fallibility. And the second physician is in the position of evaluating not only a patient’s health, but also, inevitably and uncomfortably, a colleague’s work.

label: Conclusion
body: This process can be awkward for both the patient and the physicians.

label: Conditional Logic
body: Their population must Sustain → 250+ reach at least 250 if it is to be self-sustaining. Their current habitat is Current not large enough to → ~250+ support any more [than Habitat 70-100] of these animals, however.

label: Evidence
body: In an experiment, 50 patients with chronic back pain were divided into two groups. Small magnets were applied to the backs of one group; the other group received no treatment. Most of the patients in the first group, but very few in the second group, reported a significant reduction in pain.

label: Conclusion
body: Magnetic fields are probably effective at relieving some back pain.

label: Evaluate
body: The argument identifies a correlation between magnetic treatments and then goes on to assert a causal relationship. To weaken this the correct answer could provide an alternative cause or undermine the correlation.

label: Conclusion (it is clear that)
body: If you wait long enough, almost any food will be reported to be healthful.

label: Evidence
body: Chocolate was formerly considered a health scourge, but now it's touted as an effective antioxidant with health benefits. Oily foods were thought to clog arteries and contribute to heart disease, but now reports say that olive oil has a positive influence on the circulatory system.

label: Evaluate
body: The author provides two examples of foods that had an unhealthy reputation and that are now being recognized for their health benefits. Do those two examples persuade us that "almost any food" will one day be reported to be healthful? Certainly not. The conclusion seems overdramatic and too extreme.

label: Goal
body: Let's look for something like, "The author over-generalizes from a small sample, that may not be typical".

label: Evidence
body: The availability of edible plants in an ecosystem is what determines how many herbivores the ecosystem can support. The number of herbivores determines how many predators an ecosystem can support.

label: Intermediate Conclusion
body: The availability of edible plants is what primarily determines an ecosystem’s characteristics.

label: Main Conclusion
body: A reduction in the number of predators will have little impact on the rest of the ecosystem.

label: Evaluate
body: The theory’s assertion that the number of predators will have little impact on the rest of the ecosystem does not follow from the intermediate conclusion that the number of edible plants primarily determines an ecosystem’s characteristics. It could be that the primary influence is the number of edible plants, while the number of predators also has a significant influence on the rest of the ecosystem.

label: Conclusion
body: The diets of children who don't develop healthy bones must not include enough calcium.

label: Evidence
body: If a child is to develop healthy bones, the diet must include enough calcium.

label: Evaluation
body: We have one conditional premise: healthy → diet has HB → SC bones sufficient calcium And we have a conditional conclusion that performs an illegal opposite move. not healthy → diet not have ~HB → ~SC bones sufficient calcium Conversationally, the flaw is that healthy bones may require more than one thing. Perhaps healthy bones require sufficient calcium as well as sufficient exercise. Thus, seeing a kid without healthy bones doesn't immediately mean they don't get sufficient calcium. Maybe they get plenty of calcium but not sufficient exercise.

label: Goal
body: So, we're looking for an argument that presents a conditional premise, "if A, then B", and then gives us an illegal opposite conclusion that says, "things that aren't A apparently aren't B"

label: Conclusion
body: Social inertia is a more powerful than a desire for comfort/safety, as a determinant of human behavior.

label: Evidence
body: History provides lots of examples of technological innovations being resisted by people whose working conditions were miserable without those innovations.

label: Evaluation
body: This premise is saying, "I work at a factory in miserable working conditions, and I'm resisting a technological innovation that would make working conditions less miserable." The author thinks that I'm resisting it because I'm used to how things are (inertia), and I care more about keeping things as is than I do about improving the comfort / safety of my workplace. Are we convinced that these employees resisted technological innovations because they didn't want to switch up their routine? They wanted to keep things going as is, even if status quo is less comfortable or safe? What's the most common sense reason why an employee would resist a technological innovation? Probably because they're afraid that the technology will replace them, and they'll be out of a job (#YangGang).

label: Goal
body: Look for an answer that suggests a different reason why the employees are resisting technological change (besides the author's idea that they just want things to stay the way they are). Or look for an answer that suggests that people care more about comfort / safety than they do about keeping things the way they are.

label: Evidence

label: Evaluation
body: Okay, this was terrible. The most important thing to notice would be that what we're trying to prove in the conclusion is a conditional statement about someone's beliefs. Valid inference: Mark is a 3-time pig racing champion. Samika had dinner with Mark. So Samika had dinner with a 3-time pig racing champion. Invalid inference: Mark is a 3-time pig racing champion. Samika knows she had dinner with Mark. So Samika knows she had dinner with a 3-time pig racing champion. Why is the 2nd one invalid? Because we don't know if Samika actually knows that Mark is a 3-time pig racing champion. We know it, but she might not. (He might not bring it up on a first date) Similarly, we know, from having read these premises, that if you believe "People only care about themselves", then you have logically committed yourself to the idea that government by consent is impossible, which would make democracy impossible. But you might not realize those implications/consequences of your "people only care about themselves" belief. So it's not right to say that if you believe the first thing, you also believe that "democracy is impossible'. You might not realize that the latter is an inference that can be derived from the former.

label: Goal
body: Look for an answer explaining that the author is presenting a logical chain of beliefs, and then illicitly assuming that someone else is aware of this logic chain of beliefs.

body: An overabundance of algae must be harmful to the smaller fish in this pond.

body: During the 15 or so years I've lived here, the few times that I've seen large numbers of dead small fish wash ashore in late summer coincide exactly with the times that I have noticed abnormally large amounts of algae in the water.

label: Evaluate
body: There aren't obvious keywords here indicating Conclusion vs. Evidence, but the 2nd sentence is clearly evidence, because it's a historical fact, not an opinion or inference the author is deriving. The first sentence's keyword is "must". That word often shows up in conditional statements (such as "In order to do X, you must do Y"). But it's also used to convey that tone when we're trying to solve a causal mystery (my wife said goodbye, but then I heard the door open and close again a second later: she must have forgotten something and come back inside to grab it.) Whenever we see an argument where the author's conclusion is saying or assuming a causal explanation for some curious fact in the evidence, we use our Explain Curious Fact mindset: Curious Fact ... how come the times I've seen large numbers of dead small fish wash ashore, it's coincided with lots of algae in the water? Explanation ... the algae is killing the small fish. The two pressure points for such an argument are 1. Alternate Explanations for the curious fact 2. the plausibility of the Author's Explanation However, when we're doing Flaw and see Explain Curious Fact, the correct answer almost always deals with #1. One of the 10 Famous Flaws is this idea of Causal Overconfidence. Authors are too sure of one possible explanation, while failing to consider other possible explanations.

body: Let's look for an answer that simply calls out the illegal move from Correlation to Causation (i.e. just because high algae and dead small fish are correlated doesn't allow the author to be this sure that there's a causal relationship between those two things). body: It's easy to get sucked into the content of this conversation and start thinking, "Can the government be trusted? Could the government be changed in a way that would eliminate our biggest social problems?" But all LSAT wants us to notice is that the author has concluded that a claim is false because the argument made for it contained a dubious (potentially untrue) assumption. I could argue "President Trump won't be reelected, because his supporters skew towards more elderly voters, and elderly people are more vulnerable to the pandemic." body: Because of the "only if", it's worth thinking of this conditionally if you want to write an algebraic recipe. But the gist of the argument can also be conversational: Something's about to happen. A potential solution hinges on some requirement, and if the past repeats itself, we won't hit that requirement. So that thing is likely to happen.

label: Evidence
body: Acquiring complete detailed ACDI → D + E information about all the pros and cons of a product one might purchase would clearly be difficult and expensive. It is rational not to acquire ~R → BOC such information unless one expects that the benefits of doing so will outweigh the cost and difficulty of doing so.

label: Conclusion
body: Therefore, consumers who ~ACDI → R do not bother to acquire such information are thereby behaving rationally.

label: Evaluate
body: The argument assumes that ~ACDI → ~BOC people who do not bother to acquire complete detailed information about all the pros and cons of a product do not believe the benefits of doing so will outweigh the cost and difficulty of doing so.

label: Evidence
body: Certain companies require their managers to rank workers in the groups they supervise from best to worst, giving each worker a unique ranking based on job performance. The top 10 percent of the workers in each group are rewarded and the bottom 10 percent are penalized or fired. Good workers could receive low ranking merely because they belong to groups of exceptionally good workers. Furthermore, managers often give the highest rankings to workers who share the manager's interest outside of work.

label: Conclusion
body: A system that rewards the top 10 percent and punishes the bottom 10 percent of workers within each group is unfair.

label: Evidence
body: A study of 436 university students found that those who took short naps throughout the day suffered from insomnia more frequently than those who did not. Moreover, people who work on commercial fishing vessels often have irregular sleep patterns that include frequent napping, and they also suffer from insomnia.

label: Conclusion
body: So it is very likely that napping tends to cause insomnia.

label: Evaluate
body: The two premises provide a correlation between daytime napping and insomnia, while the conclusion asserts causation.

label: Evidence
body: Whenever Joe's car is JVC → K&L V vacuumed, the employees of K & L Auto vacuum it; they are the only people who ever vacuum Joe's car If the employees of K & L K&L V → K&L F Auto vacuumed Joe's car, then Joe took his car to K & L Auto to be fixed. Joe's car was recently JVC. vacuumed.

label: Conclusion
body: Joe took his car to K & L K&L F. Auto to be fixed.

label: Evaluate
body: This argument triggers the sufficient condition in the first of two if/then relationships that link together. The conclusion is the necessary condition of the second if/then statement.

label: Evidence
body: In a large corporation, one of the KIS → PD functions of the corporation's president is to promote the key interests of the shareholders.

label: Conclusion
body: The president has a duty to keep P → PD the corporation's profits high.

label: Evaluate
body: The argument assumes that P → KIS keeping the corporation’s profits high is a key interest of the shareholders.

label: Given
body: Everyone in Biba's neighborhood is permitted to swim at Barton Pool at some time during each day that it is open. No children under the age of 6 are permitted to swim at Barton Pool between noon and 5 P.M. From 5 P.M. until closing, Barton Pool is reserved for adults only.

label: Evaluate
body: There was a little bit of cognitive dissonance when we go from reading that everyone is permitted to swim at the pool at some time each day, into reading "Except ... kids under 6 can't swim from noon - 5pm, and people under 18 can't swim from 5pm - close." When do the little kiddos get to swim? Everything from noon to close is shut off from them: no children adults under 6 only I I ● noon 5 P.M. close

label: Given
body: Inertia affects the flow of water pumped through a closed system of pipes. When the pump is first switched on, the water, which has mass, takes time to reach full speed. When the pump is switched off, inertia causes the decrease in the water flow to be gradual. The effects of inductance in electrical circuits are similar to the effects of inertia in water pipes.

label: Evidence
body: A nation with a low average income may still have a substantial middle class better able to pay for new drugs than are many of the poorer citizens of an overall wealthier nation.

label: Conclusion
body: The practice of selling a drug in rich nations at one price and in poor nations at a much lower price is unjustified.

label: Evaluate
body: The argument assumes that it is more important to consider the ability of an individual to pay for a drug than the ability of the average citizen within a country to pay.

label: Conclusion
body: Getting rid of summer break and teaching year round won’t lead to teachers covering more new material.

label: Evidence
body: Under this plan, the 3 month break is replaced by six 2-week breaks, which adds up to about 3 months. So the it’s basically the same number school days either way.

label: Evaluation
body: Frame it like a paradox – “Given [this evidence], How can I argue [the anti-conclusion]?” Given that it’s the same number of school days with either plan, ;How can Robert argue that teachers would get to cover more new material with the new plan?

label: Goal
body: Find an answer that explains how they can cover more new material if the 12 weeks are spread out into six fortnights than if the 12 weeks are a 3 month summer vacation.

label: Evidence
body: In order to reduce traffic congestion and raise revenue for the city, the mayor plans to implement a charge of $10 per day for driving in the downtown area. Payment of this charge will be enforced using a highly sophisticated system that employs digital cameras and computerized automobile registration. This system will not be ready until the BENY → ~S end of the next year. Without this system, however, mass ~S → E evasion of the charge will result.

label: Conclusion
body: When the mayor's plan is first PI → E implemented, payment of the charge will not be effectively enforced

label: Evaluate
body: The argument assumes that the plan PI → BENY will be implemented before the end of next year.

label: Apparent Paradox
body: A recent study revealed that the percentage of people treated at large, urban hospitals who recover from their illnesses is lower than the percentage for people treated at smaller, rural hospitals.

label: Evaluate
body: Any answer that provides an advantage to smaller, rural hospitals or a disadvantage to large, urban hospitals would help explain the discrepancy.

label: Evidence
body: Worker-owned businesses require workers to spend time on management decision-making and investment strategy, tasks that are not directly productive. Worker-owned businesses have less extensive divisions of labor than do investor-owned businesses. Such inefficiencies can lead to low profitability, and thus increase the risk for lenders.

label: Conclusion
body: Lenders seeking to reduce their risk should not make loans to worker-owned businesses.

label: Evaluate
body: This list of drawbacks associated with worker-owned businesses does present a gloomy outlook for such businesses. But it fails consider any possible advantages associated with worker-owned businesses.

label: Facts
body: Some paleontologists are saying Some dinosaurs apparently guarded their babies in the nest for a while after they’re born since they found some fossils of baby dinosaurs and older kid dinosaurs in a really elaborately designed nest. MEANWHILE ... Modern crocs have similarly deluxe looking nests, but they don’t guard their babies very long after they’re born.

label: Evaluate
body: This paragraph has a rebuttal structure. Recognizing that makes it easier to anticipate a rebuttal-type conclusion. Some paleontologists believe .... As evidence, they cite .... But ..... Hence, _____ . What would be a safely worded way that the author could tell those paleontologists that they’re wrong about something?

label: Goal
body: Since our author is pushing back against the paleontologists’ argument, it should be something like, “Can you really be sure that dinos watched their young for a long time?”

label: Apparent Paradox
body: The students who spent the most time studying did not earn grades as high as did many students who studied less. Nonetheless, the researchers concluded that the results of the observation supported the initial hypothesis that studying more increased a student’s chances of earning a higher grade.

label: Evaluate
body: While the observation compares students with other students, the hypothesis compares one student’s grades at different amounts of study time.

label: Given
body: Researchers had three groups of professional cyclists cycle for one hour at different levels of intensity. Members of groups A, B, and C cycled at rates that sustained, for an hour, pulses of about 60 percent, 70 percent, and 85 percent, respectively, of the recommended maximum pulse rate for recreational cyclists. Most members of Group A reported being less depressed and angry afterward. Most members of Group B did not report these benefits. Most members of Group C reported feeling worse in these respects than before the exercise.

label: Evaluate
