body: We have this set of contrasts. This seems like the type of stimulus that could set up a "One Difference Explains Another" type of inference. Maybe difference in pulse rates explains the difference in psychological benefits. We'd want a very safely worded answer though, since this is speculative causality, not explicit causality.

label: Conclusion
body: It’s false to believe in extraterrestrials (extraterrestrials don’t exist)

label: Evidence
body: Everyone who believes in extraterrestrials believes in UFOs. But it is a fact that UFO’s do not exist.

label: Evidence
body: The assumptions that appear to guide AGL → WA legislators will often become widely accepted. Widespread acceptance of the idea WA → ID that individuals are incapable of looking after their own welfare is injurious to a democracy.

label: Evaluation
body: This feels like a valid argument by contrapositive. If we were given extraterrestrials → UFO, and then we learn ~UFO, then we can conclude ~extraterrestrials. But this argument is shifting between belief and fact. If you tell me Tanya doesn’t believe in UFO’s, I can infer that Tanya doesn’t believe in extraterrestrials. If you tell me that UFO’s don’t exist, that doesn’t tell me anything about whether or not extraterrestrials exist.

label: Goal
body: We need an argument that introduces a contrapositive, tries to factually trigger the contrapositive, but shifts from beliefs to facts. Premise 1: if you believe X, you believe Y Premise 2: Y is not true. Conclusion: X is not true.

label: Evidence
body: Those persons who are AP → R perceived as forming opinions of others only after cautiously gathering and weighing the evidence are generally resented.

label: Conclusion
body: It is imprudent to appear AP → ~P prudent.

label: Evaluate
body: The argument assumes R → ~P that it is not prudent to be resented.

label: Facts
body: Most of the time, smokers have better short-term memories than nonsmokers, after they’ve smoked a cigarette. And the advantage for the smokers usually lasts at least 8 hours.

label: Evaluation
body: Correct answers to must be false usually contradict a conditional rule or contradict an available inference. There’s no conditional here, so is there an available inference we can get by combining the two facts? It sound like for most regular smokers, if they smoke a cigarette every eight hours or less, they’ll indefinitely have better short term memory than nonsmokers.

label: Goal
body: Find an answer that contradicts the idea that smokers have a short-term memory advantage in most cases, after they’ve smoked a cig, and the advantage lasts for at least 8 hours.

label: Evidence
body: The vote of any given individual is much more likely to determine organizational policy by influencing the election of an officer than by influencing the result of a direct vote on a single issue.

label: Conclusion
body: To have members vote for officers who in turn make the decisions is a better way to go than to have a direct vote of all members on a single issue.

label: Evaluate
body: The argument assumes that the right process is the process that maximizes the voters likely influence.

label: Conclusion
body: Thus, the amygdala exerts a greater influence on the cortex than vice versa.

label: Evidence
body: Neural connections carrying signals from the cortex (the brain Cortex region responsible for neural ⇑ ↓ thought) down to the connections Amygdala amygdala (a brain region crucial for emotions) are less well developed than connections carrying signals from the amygdala up to the cortex.

label: Evaluate
body: The argument assumes that the amount of influence one part of the part exerts on another part of the brain is positively correlated with the development of neural connections transmitting signals in that direction.

label: Evidence
body: The Iliad and the Odyssey DTV differ greatly in tone and vocabulary and in certain details of the fictional world they depict.

label: Conclusion
body: The Iliad and the Odyssey SP are almost certainly not the work of the same poet.

label: Evaluate
body: The argument assumes that DTV → SP two works that differ greatly in tone and vocabulary and in certain details of the fictional world they depict are not the work of the same poet.

label: Given
body: A statement is wholly WT → T + ~ID truthful only if it is ID or ~T → ~WT and made without intended deception. A statement is a lie if ID or (LM + ~C) → L it is intended to deceive or if its speaker, upon learning that the statement was misinterpreted, refrains from clarifying it.

label: Principle
body: If ... then ... engaging in an activity not healthy that promotes for children intellectual development to engage would detract from their social development

label: Application
body: Since .... Therefore ... engaging in frequent not healthy reading (stimulates for Megan to Megan intellectually engage in this but) reduces the amount much reading of time Megan spends interacting with other people.

label: Evaluate
body: The flow of these Application questions is that we're given a conditional rule. Then we're given an attempted Application of it. Someone tries to use this principle to get from their Evidence to their Conclusion. The Conclusion of the Application always (or almost always) matches the right side of the principle. But the Evidence fails to clearly establish all the ideas the left side (trigger) of the principle needs to know. The conditional indicator words "only if" mean that the idea that follows belongs on the right side. So when we see "only if engaging does not detract", we'd put that idea on the right side of the arrow. → doesn't detract from social development The other half of the sentence, "healthy to engage", would thus go on the left. healthy → doesn't detract from social development Since the conclusion of the Application is saying "not healthy", we want the contrapositive version of this rule, so that our right side will match our Conclusion: does detract from social development ⇢ not healthy Okay, so we're concluding "not healthy to read this much". So did the evidence establish that "reading this much is detracting from social development?" No, the closest it came to talking like that was when it said, "it reduces the amount of time she spends interacting with other people". Apparently the author is assuming that "if you reduce the amount of time you spend interacting with other people, then you're detracting from social development". Do we have to believe that? Not necessarily. We don't know if every extra hour you spend interacting with people contributes meaningfully to your social development.

label: Goal
body: Look for something discussing the gap between "reduces the amount of time spent interacting with other people" and "detracts from her social development". (technically, we also need to say that Megan is a child, for the principle to apply to her)

label: Given
body: In response to several bacterial infections traced to its apple juice, McElligott now flash pasteurizes its apple juice by quickly heating and immediately rechilling it. Intensive pasteurization, in which juice is heated for an hour, eliminates bacteria more effectively than does any other method, but is likely to destroy the original flavor. However, because McElligott’s citrus juices have not been linked to any bacterial infections, they remain unpasteurized.

label: Evaluate
body: The argument assumes that a legislator PBNH → AGL who proposes prohibiting behavior that is not harmful to anyone besides the person engaging in it will seem to be guided by the assumption that individuals are incapable of looking after their own welfare.

label: Conclusion (so)
body: A diet can protect the heart even though it is not low in fat.

label: Evidence
body: Mediterranean diet has a good bit of fat, but meanwhile a study showed that people on a Mediterranean diet were less likely to have a second heart attack compared to those on a Western diet limiting fat.

label: Evaluate
body: This is the Explain Curious Fact template, because the author presents a non-causal comparison in the evidence and interprets a causal relationship from it. CURIOUS FACT - why were the people following the Med Diet significantly less likely to have a second heart attack than those on a diff diet? EXPLANATION - the Med Diet was protecting their heart

label: Goal
body: To strengthen the argument, we can either rule out alternate explanations for why people on the Med Diet were less likely to have a 2nd heart attack, or increase the plausibility of the causal relationship between the Med Diet and the lower heart attack risk.

label: Premise
body: Flowers that are naturally green are extremely rare.

label: Intermediate Conclusion
body: It is very difficult for plant breeders to produce green carnations.

label: Premises
body: Some people like to have green carnations on St. Patrick’s Day. White carnations are fairly inexpensive and quite easy to dye green.

label: Main Conclusion
body: Before St. Patrick’s Day, then, it is wise for florists to stock up on white carnations.

label: Background
body: Pools should have fences to protect kids from drowning, but even more important is that we teach children to swim. This principle applies even more generally to childrearing. (what principle? Protecting them from X is good, but teaching them to handle X safely is even better) While it's good to restrict access to soda / candy,

label: Setup
body: it's even more important to teach them ...

label: Evaluate / Goal
body: ... "how to swim" with soda and candy? We need to Complete the Analogy, figuring out what the equivalent of "teaching children to swim" would be when it comes to soda / candy. Restricting access to soda / candy matched up with building a fence to restrict access to a pool. So we're looking for whatever the "teach them how to swim" equivalent would be with "teach them how to be safe with soda and candy".

label: Conclusion (therefore)
body: The TV program is biased against the proposed freeway.

label: Evidence
body: Of the interviews shown on the program, those conducted with people against the new freeway outnumbered those conducted with people in favor of the freeway by a 2 to 1 ratio.

label: Evaluate
body: We have a Curious Comparison: - why were there twice as many interviews with people who oppose the new freeway as there were with people who favor the new freeway? The conclusion reveals the Author's Explanation: - The TV program is biased against the proposed freeway (so they chose to try to influence public opinion by presenting more interviews with people opposed, hoping it would sway opinion) As always, when an author's argument is trying to Explain a Curious Fact, we think through two different issues: 1. could there be some Alternate Explanation for the Curious Fact? 2. how plausible is the Author's Explanation?

label: Goal
body: Since this is weaken, we would either want an answer choice that suggests an Alternate Explanation for why twice as many opposing interviews as endorsing interviews were shown (like maybe there were just twice as many people in the sample they interviewed who opposed it), or one that undermines the plausibility that this TV station is biased against this proposed freeway and purposefully put on a skewed ratio of interviews, thinking that might help shape public opinion against the freeway.

label: Evan's Criticism
body: My pescatarian friends (vegetarians who otherwise eat fish) should not be eating fish.

label: Evan's Premise
body: Even though we're not sure that sea creatures experience pleasure or pain, if we're trying to avoid inflicting pain, we should give them the benefit of the doubt (and act as though they DO feel pain, so we shouldn't murder them for our food).

label: Evaluate
body: This is like a Parallel question, but it uses the language of "illustrated Principle". Some Parallel questions are testing formal logical structures (like "All X's are Y. All Y's are Z. Since this thing is not Z, it is not X"). Other Parallel questions are just testing slogan / principle type ideas: - if it was true before, it'll be true again - if the extra effort yield little in return, don't bother - if you behaved that way in this situation, you should behave the same way in a similar situation We need to think about what Principle Evan is implicitly using (but we can't name it using words like vegetarian / pain / seafood). He seems to think: if you aren't sure whether or not you're hurting something, err on the side of not hurting them by not risking it.

label: Goal
body: Let's try to find an argument in which someone is saying, "You're usually worried about X. You know it's possible that X would happen with action Y. Even though you can't be sure, you should play it safe and not do action Y."

label: Conclusion (This shows that)
body: Reading labels on food products promotes healthful dietary behavior.

label: Evidence
body: People who read the labels have a lower proportion of fat calories in their diets than do people who don't read labels.

label: Conclusion
body: Last year's mild winter is responsible for this year's larger-than-usual bird population.

label: Evidence
body: The mild winter allowed many species to stay in their summer range all winter, rather than migrating (and a bunch of them never make it home when they migrate). The mild winter allowed them forage naturally, rather than visit bird feeders.

label: Given
body: All coffeehouses CH or R → P and restaurants are public places. Most well-designed WD + P -most↣ FA public places feature artwork. If a public place is P + ~C → ~WD uncomfortable it is not well designed. All comfortable C + P → SI public places have spacious interiors.

label: Evaluate
body: As we read the first sentence and see it takes the form, People who are X are more likely to be Y than those who aren't we know we're getting a Correlation. What do LSAT authors do 99% of the time after they present a correlation? They assume that one of those factors is causing the other factor. Here the author presents a correlation between reading labels on food products and having a lower proportion of fat in their diet. Does he think that "eating less fat causes them to read the labels", that "reading the labels causes them to eat less fat", or does he not conclude anything causal? Oh, he steps in it, just like we thought he would. His conclusion uses a Causal Verb (x promotes y). So we know he's being too hasty in assuming that one half of this correlation causes the other. After all, people who own vacation homes are more likely than those who don't to drive a luxury car, but it's not like vacation homes cause you to drive luxury cars or vice versa. Those things are correlated because of an underlying condition: dollar-dollar bills, y'all (i.e. wealth). Similarly, maybe "Low fat in your diet" and "reading labels on food products" are both symptoms of the same underlying cause: trying to eat healthy. Maybe if you're put on a diet that is supposed to restrict your fat intake, then you suddenly have reason to start reading food labels carefully to inspect the fat content.

label: Goal
body: We want to call out the author's Causal Overconfidence (this is one of the 10 famous flaws). Correlations support the notion that two things might be causally connected, but the author isn't allowed to be so confident that one things causes the other. We otherwise expect an answer to raise the possibility of an Alternate Explanation for the correlation (such as we just did with someone who is health-conscious or trying to remove fat from their diet).

label: Main Conclusion
body: Apatosaurus was probably not able to gallop.

label: Intermediate Conclusion
body: Galloping would probably have broken Apatosaurus’s legs.

label: Evidence
body: Experiments with modern bones show how much strain they can withstand before breaking. By taking into account the diameter and density of Apatosaurus leg bones, it is possible to calculate that those bones could not have withstood the strains of galloping.

label: Evaluate
body: Whenever we do Main Conclusion / Role, we remind ourselves that 85% of the time it's an upside down argument (the conclusion appears earlier than the support). Specifically about 65% of them are pivot/rebuttal conclusions and about 25% are first-sentence conclusions. Since this paragraph begins with an Attribution (some P's have suggested that), we'd anticipate a pivot-pushback from the author. We get that at the start of the 2nd sentence with "This however is unlikely". As soon as we can tell the author is supporting that idea, we know that this was our conclusion. The next clause begins with the Support Indicator "because galloping ...".

label: Goal
body: We want the best meaning match for "This is unlikely". Since it is a rebuttal, we need to articulate the rebuttal conclusion. THIS = Apatosaurus was able to gallop. So we want, "Apatosaurus was likely not able to gallop".

label: Conclusion
body: The new process of fortifying table salt with iron could help reduce the high incidence of anemia in the world's population due to iron deficiency.

label: Evidence (and)
body: Salt is used all over the globe to preserve and flavor food, and people eat enough salt that this fortified kind would provide significant iron amounts.

label: Evaluate
body: Whenever we do Main Conclusion and Role, we prime our brain with a reminder, before reading the argument: the Conclusion will usually be earlier than the Support. Since those two questions types are primarily testing our ability to find the Main Conclusion, LSAC wants to make it harder to find. Putting it as the last claim is too easy. So they often make it one of the first couple claims, or make it part of a rebuttal, or use some pronouns or referential language (or any combo of the three) to increase the challenge. When we read Main Conclusion and Role, listen for an early claim that sounds like an Opinion. If it belongs to the author and the paragraph goes on to support that Opinion, then you know you've found the Main Conclusion. The first sentence is definitely a fact — a new process has been invented. The second sentence is an opinion, because it's a prediction. Anything about the future is pretty much automatically an opinion. And we can tell it's the author's opinion because it's not being attributed to anyone else. Finally, the keyword "and" is always joining together two Supporting ideas, so seeing the last two claims attached by "and" lets us know that those two claims work in tandem to support what came before.

label: Goal
body: Since they're asking us about the final claim, we want something like - Premise - Support - Evidence - Partial Support (since there is more than one premise)

label: Conclusion
body: Whoever has the diamonds belonging to Mr. Tannisch's guest must have worn gloves.

label: Evidence
body: Mr. Tannischs fingerprints are the only ones at his house.

label: Evaluation
body: The flaw here is overconfidently deciding on one causal possibility. Who says they used gloves? Maybe they fished for the diamonds with a long candy cane! More plausibly, why are we letting Mr. Tannisch off the hook? Shouldn't he be the primary suspect?

label: Goal
body: Look for an answer with a curious fact, and a conclusion in which the author reaches some specific causal hypothesis while failing to consider a possibly more obvious possibility.

label: Apparent Paradox
body: Populations of a shrimp species at eleven different Indonesian coral reefs show substantial genetic differences from one reef to another. This is surprising because the area’s strong ocean currents probably carry baby shrimp between the different reefs, which would allow the populations to interbreed and become genetically indistinguishable.

label: Evaluate
body: The apparent paradox is that shrimp species show substantial genetic differences when the ocean currents probably carry baby shrimp between the eleven different Indonesian coral reefs.

label: Conclusion
body: Seawater agriculture near sea level should be cost-effective in desert regions.

label: Evidence
body: There are some salt-tolerant plant species, halophytes, that require more water than normal crops but can be irrigated with seawater. It's cheaper to pump seawater into farms near sea level, than to pump freshwater from deep wells.

label: Given that ...
body: Sugar maples, spruce, and fir all need calcium to survive, and given that acid rain causes calcium levels in the soil to decline.

label: Evaluate
body: We're trying to analyze whether this agricultural plan will be cost-effective, which really means will it be profitable — will the expected revenue at least exceed the expected costs. All we know is that one cost (watering the plant) will be more expensive in one sense (higher quantity needed) but less expensive in another sense (the type of pumping is cheaper). The author seems to be assuming that what we'd spend in having to give these plants more water would be matched or exceeded by what we'd save in terms of getting to use a seawater pump rather than a deep freshwater pump. If we wanted to argue that this wouldn't be cost-effective, we could bring up all the unmentioned factors that go into an agricultural enterprise: will the other expenses, such as seed / manual labor / equipment / energy for the equipment, be paid for by eventual revenue? is there a market for halophytes? do animals like eating them? would farmers buy halophytes for their animals?

label: Goal
body: I'd be going to the answers with almost no specific goal in mind. We just need some more reason to think that raising halophytes by the seaside, using a pump to irrigate with seawater, would be a cost-effective (i.e. profitable) enterprise.

label: Principle
body: If a insurance policy the reasonable too complicated for expectations of the reasonable person → policy holder to read it thoroughly outrank the actual before signing policy language.

label: Application
body: Celia got hail damage on her car. The insurance policy specifically says hail isn't covered. But according to this principle, the insurance company should have to cover the hail damage.

label: Evaluate / Goal
body: Our answer has to establish that Celia's case is an accurate application of this principle, so we need to ask ourselves about all the "boxes we need to check" to trigger this rule. - the insurance policy had to be written in a way that no reasonable person would have read it thoroughly before signing it. - it must be the reasonable expectations of a policyholder concerning the policy's coverage that, "hail damage is covered by this policy"

label: Evidence
body: Every year approximately the same number of people die of iatrogenic “disease”—that is, as a direct result of medical treatments or hospitalization—as die of all other causes combined.

label: Conclusion
body: Therefore, if all medicine could find ways of preventing all iatrogenic disease, the number of deaths per year would decrease by half.

label: Evaluate
body: The argument assumes that 100 percent of the people who did not die of iatrogenic disease would survive for the remainder of the year or longer. If someone were to die that same year, then the number of deaths per year would be reduced by less than half. Also, keep in mind that iatrogenic disease is the result of medical treatments or hospitalization. Such people are bound to include at least a few who die as a result of the complication for which they were seeking medical care.

label: Evidence
body: Any member of the city CC → VA or AB council ought either to vote against the proposal or to abstain. But if all the members AB → MDV abstain, the matter will be decided by the city's voters.

label: Conclusion
body: So at least one member CC ↢some↣ VA of the city council should vote against the proposal.

label: Evaluate
body: There is a should in the conclusion. Is that a New Concept, or do we have a should in the evidence? We have the idea that We know that each city council member should/ought vote against the proposal or abstain from voting (those two ideas are mutually exclusive; if you abstain from voting, then you can't vote against it, and vice versa). So we know that every city council member should take action 1 or action 2, from the evidence. The conclusion is saying that at least one of them should take action 1. Why? What happens if they all take action 2? Well, if they all take action 2 ... if they all abstain ... then the matter is decided by voters. If the author is saying that "at least one member should vote against", that's equivalent to saying "we shouldn't have everyone abstain". And we know that everyone abstaining leads to the matter being decided by voters. The author must be assuming that we should avoid that outcome. If I say, "Eating this cupcake will make you hallucinate. Thus, you shouldn't eat this cupcake", then I'm assuming that "you shouldn't do something that will lead to you hallucinating."

label: Goal
body: Our author seems to be assuming, "We shouldn't do something that would lead to this matter being decided by the city's voters".

label: Opposing Support
body: Such reports [negative news reports on the state of the economy] damage people’s confidence in it [the economy]. This lack of confidence in turn adversely affects people’s willingness to spend money.

label: Opposing Point
body: Some critics of the media have contended that negative news reports on the state of the economy can actually harm the economy.

label: Evidence
body: Studies show that spending trends correlate very closely with people’s confidence in their own immediate economic situations.

label: Conclusion
body: Thus these media critics are mistaken.

label: Evaluate
body: The argument assumes that one’s confidence in one’s own economic situation is not affected by reports about the overall state of the economy.

label: Conclusion
body: Most wild large mammals today would either be difficult to domesticate or not worth domesticating.

label: Evidence
body: Every domesticated large mammal today was domesticated thousands of years ago. Since that time, people have tried tons of times to domesticate any of the wild large mammals that seemed worth domesticating.

label: Evaluate
body: It's pretty hard to disagree with this conclusion. Since people have looked at all the wild large mammals, filtered out the ones that are worth domesticating, and then tried tons of times to domesticate to domesticate each of those, it seems like whichever wild large mammals are left wild were either initially given up on because they didn't seem worth domesticating or were eventually given up on because they weren't able to domesticate them. In order to fight this conclusion, we'd need a way to argue that most wild large mammals nowadays would be worth domesticating and not-difficult to domesticate. (Seems hard to think of an objection that would allow us to argue that)

label: Goal
body: Because the premise is about thousands of years ago but the conclusion is about "now", we're probably looking for an answer that says the author is assuming that what was true in the past is still true today.

label: Evaluation
body: There is causality in the evidence and the conclusion. We know that mild winter caused two things, from the evidence: forage naturally rather than visit birdfeeders, and stay local instead of migrating. In order to say that the mild winter caused a bigger than average bird population, we want to argue that either / both of the effects we are told about in the evidence would result in a bigger than average bird population. We know that when birds migrate over the winter, there's a typical rate of attrition (attrition normally means people dropping out or dropping dead). So if 1000 birds head south, maybe only 800 come back. But how does that compare to when birds say local over the winter? Does that lead to more of them surviving / dying? We know that because local birds were able to forage, they didn't have to use birdfeeders. But what does that have to do with a larger than average bird population? Do more / fewer birds survive when they're foraging naturally vs. using birdfeeders?

label: Goal
body: We either want to hear that not migrating results in a net gain for bird population, or that foraging naturally rather than using birdfeeders results in a net gain for bird population.

label: Conclusion
body: A small observational study must be more likely than a large randomized trial to have dramatic findings.

label: Evidence
body: Newspapers, which generally only report on dramatic scientific findings, more often feature stories about small observational studies than about large randomized trials.

label: Evaluate
body: Since the author is interpreting a statistical correlation, we can use our typical Curious Fact / Author's Interpretation schema. Curious Fact - Why are there more newspaper stories about small observational studies than about large randomized trials? Author's Interpretation - Small observational studies are more likely to have dramatic findings, which are the only kind of findings a newspaper will do a story about. We always ask ourselves - How else could we explain the Curious Fact? - How plausible is the Author's Interpretation?

label: Goal
body: On a Flaw question, the correct answer is almost always that "the author has failed to consider some other way to explain the Curious Fact" and only very rarely "the author has proposed an implausible explanation". So we should primarily be looking for an answer that says "the author is overly convinced of one possible interpretation when others may exist", or the an answer that actually supplies a possible alternative reason for why there are more newspaper stories about small observational studies than about large randomized trials.

label: Conclusion
body: Government incentives to plant trees are helping to hasten (speed up) global warming.

label: Evidence
body: The incentives are to plant trees, but trees don't absorb and store CO2 as well as native grasses do.

label: Evaluate
body: This sounds like a crazy conclusion: planting trees is speeding up global warming? It sounds like native grasses would be a better plan, but it doesn't sound like planting trees makes the problem worse. Isn't planting trees better than nothing? They still absorb and store some CO2, so they slow down global warming?

label: Goal
body: The author isn't comparing "plant trees" to "not plant trees", because "planting trees is better for global warming than not planting trees". Instead, the author is apparently comparing "plant trees" to "plant native grasses", since "planting trees is worse for global warming than planting native grasses". So we want an answer that reflects the author's thinking, that this is a choice between "planting trees vs. planting native grasses", as opposed to a choice between "planting trees vs. planting nothing".

label: Main Conclusion
body: [The position of a car driver’s seat] probably does [have a significant impact on driving safety].

label: Premises
body: Driving position affects both comfort and the ability to see the road clearly. A driver who is uncomfortable eventually becomes fatigued, which makes it difficult to concentrate on the road. Likewise, the better the visibility from the driver’s seat, the more aware the driver can be of road conditions and other vehicles.

label: Physician's 1st Claim
body: There were 83,000+ trampoline injuries last year. Does Trampoline enthusiast claim or imply that there weren't 83,000+ trampoline injuries last year? No.

label: Physician's 2nd Claim
body: 83000+ injuries suggests that trampolines are quite dangerous. Does Trampoline enthusiast claim or imply that 83,000+ trampoline injuries doesn't mean that trampolines are dangerous? Hmmm. A little bit. Trampoline enthusiast stresses that the absolute number doesn't tell the story. They're actually getting safer over the past 10 years, because even though trampolines have gone up 260% injuries have only gone up 154%.

label: Physician's 3rd Claim
body: Trampolines should only be used under professional supervision. Does Trampoline enthusiast claim or imply that trampolines don't need to be used under professional supervision, that it's okay sometimes to use them without professional supervision? Yes, basically. Trampoline enthusiast downplays the concern over the 83,000 injuries and reminds us that trampolines are inherently risking, with or without supervision.

label: Evaluation / Goal
body: Physician is saying trampolines are dangerous and should only be used under professional supervision. Trampoline enthusiast is saying trampolines are not that dangerous and they can be used without professional supervision.

label: Conclusion
body: The recent coverage of the personal problems of a local politician's nephew was good journalism.

label: Evidence
body: The information was accurate. The newscast had higher than average viewership on that story, since many people were very curious about the nephew's problems.

label: Evaluate
body: Strengthen + Principle questions aren't really about trying to come up with objections or new ideas. They're just about picking an answer that helps to connect the evidence to the conclusion. If we say, "That milk smells funny. Thus, you shouldn't drink it", then we would want an answer to say, "If something smells funny, then you shouldn't drink it."

label: Goal
body: In this case, our Premise to Conclusion connector would sound something like this: "If a story was accurate and many people were curious about it, then covering it was good journalism."

label: How can it be that ...
body: Acid rain seems to result in more calcium deficiency for sugar maples than for spruces or firs?

label: Evaluate / Goal
body: We're going to need a distinction between sugar maples and spruces/firs. Why is the former more susceptible to acid rain decreasing the calcium in the soil? Why is the latter showing less damage from acid rain?

label: Evidence
body: Syndicated political columnists often use their newspaper columns to try to persuade readers to vote a certain way. By the time such a column appears, nearly all who will vote in the election will have already made a decision about which candidate to vote for.

label: Conclusion
body: However, their efforts to persuade voters rarely succeed.

label: Evaluate
body: The argument assumes that anyone who has made a decision about which candidate to vote for cannot be persuaded to vote a different way.

label: Conclusion (should)
body: Airlines are too worried about business class passengers and should instead focus on the comfort of leisure travelers.

label: Evidence (because)
body: Leisure travelers purchase 80% of all airline tickets.

label: Evaluate
body: This argument seems reasonable ... shouldn't airlines focus on 80% of their customer base, rather than a share that is 20% or less? There is a famous rule called the 80/20 rule in which you find out that "80% of the business comes from 20% of your customers". On Twitter and Facebook, "80% of the views come from 20% of the accounts". Given that ... leisure travelers are 80% of customers and business travelers are 20% or less, How could we still argue that ... the airlines are smart to focus on business travelers rather than leisure travelers? Maybe even though the business travelers buy fewer tickets, they're the bulk of the airlines' Yelp reviews? Or maybe disgruntled business travelers have enough influence to get people fired at the airline? Maybe they buy more last second airfare, which is usually more expensive?

label: Goal
body: Find some way to justify focusing on business travelers, rather than leisure travelers, even though the business travelers buy less than 1/5 of all airline tickets.

label: Gaby's Claims
body: 1. In school, kids should be allowed to fully follow their own interests while being supported by experienced teachers offering minimal guidance. 2. Fully following their own interests (with hands-off support) enables them to be the most successful in their adult lives.

label: Logan's Responses
body: 1. Is he arguing, "No, we shouldn't allow kids to fully follow their own interests with minimal guidance from experienced teachers"? Yes, it seems like he arguing that, since he's saying we should instead of disciplined, systematic instruction. That's the logical opposite of students following their own path with minimal guidance. 2. Is he arguing, "following their own interests w/ minimal guidance doesn't enable them to be most successful as adults"? Not really; he never gets into whether his suggested method yields most successful adults. He thinks certain fundamental knowledge is necessary for success, but he's not ranking what method enables most success.

label: Evaluate
body: It looks like the disagreement comes down to the "should" statements about how we teach children. Gaby thinks we should let the kids decide their own path with minimal guidance from teachers, while Logan thinks we should have teachers heavily guiding kids with disciplined, systematic instruction.

label: Conclusion
body: We cannot grant the request that the plaintiff be able to question each defendant one at a time (their counsel is allowed, but the other defendants and the other defendants' lawyers would have to leave the room).

label: Evidence
body: Two of the codefendants share the same lawyers, and we're not going to make any of these defendants find a new lawyer.

label: Evaluate
body: If all the defendants had their own lawyers, then granting this request would just mean that each defendant would have their lawyer present for some solo questioning, while all the other defendants and lawyers left the room. But since Eddie and Bob have the same lawyer, Teresa, we're in a conundrum: If we're questioning Eddie, does Teresa get to stay or go? Because Teresa is Eddie's lawyer, she should be able to stay. But because Teresa is one of the other defendants' lawyers (Bob's), she should go. How can we resolve this? One possible way would be to tell Eddie and Bob that they can't share a lawyer. But the judge says that we're not going to do that. The only other possible way would be to tell Eddie that he can't have his lawyer present.

label: Goal
body: Since the only way to grant this request (given that we can't make anyone get a new lawyer) is to make those two codefendants have their questioning without their lawyer present, in order to solidify the judge's ruling that we can't grant the request, we have to establish that we can't tolerate the idea of having the codefendants questioned without their lawyer present.

label: Given
body: The calm, shallow S -causes→ ON waters of coastal estuaries are easily polluted by nutrient-rich sewage. When estuary waters ON -causes→ A become over- nitrified as a result, algae proliferate. The abundant algae, A -causes→ FD in turn, sometimes provide a rich food source for microorganisms that are toxic to fish, thereby killing most of the fish in the estuary.

label: Hypothesis
body: These huge 40 ton stones were transported from Copacabana to Tiwanaku, 90 km away and across a lake, on reed boats.

label: Evidence
body: We transported some 9-ton stones from C to T using a reed boat built with locally available materials and techniques traditional to the area.

label: Evaluate
body: Since we're dealing with the word 'hypothesis', we can use our Curious Fact / Explanation mindset. CURIOUS FACT - how did these prehistoric people get 40 ton stones from C to T?! AUTHOR'S EXPLANATION - they used reed boats There are two different ways to affect this sort of argument: - Alternate Explanations for the curious fact. - the Plausibility of the Author's Explanation What could be a different way that they got the 40 ton stones that far? Maybe the stones float? Maybe they broke them apart into smaller chunks and glued them back together? How plausible is the hypothesis that they used reed boats? Well, I wouldn't usually think of reeds as being strong enough to hold 40 tons. We can see from the experiment that the reed boats the experimenters made can carry 9 ton stones, but that's only 20% as heavy. Could the reed boats really handle 40 tons? In general, we have to wonder if the "proof of concept" voyage that the experimenters took with their 9 ton stones was relevantly similar to the reed boat voyage that the prehistoric people would have taken. If there are significant differences about terrain / weather / locally available materials, that might break down the comparability of the analogy.

label: Goal
body: Look for an answer that could be answered in a way that would sound like an Alternate Explanation for how the prehistoric people moved 40 ton stones 90km from C to T, or for an answer that could be answered in a way that would damage the plausibility of the Author's Explanation.

label: Conclusion
body: We must not strike now.

label: Evidence
body: A strike would cut into our strike fund and would lead to a steep fine, which would be a major financial loss.

label: Evaluate
body: Okay, no famous flaws stick out. Let's just try to debate this guy: GIVEN THAT the strike fund would cut into our strike fund / lead to a steep fine, HOW CAN WE STILL ARGUE that we should strike now? We could say, "The strike fund is for strikes! If I created a Savings account specifically for my wedding, I would sound crazy if I didn't want to buy a wedding dress because it would cut into my wedding fund. That's what it's there for!" We might also say, "Yes, the fine would be steep, but that would be a short term loss. By going on strike, we could leverage getting higher wages and better benefits, which might more than make up for the initial fine."

label: Goal
body: Basically, it seems like we need some answer that allows us to argue that the strike could still be worth it, because a negative isn't really a negative (cutting into the strike fund is fine — it's for strikes), or because a negative could be outweighed by a positive (what we would gain from a strike might be more than what the fine costs).

label: Given
body: Birds and mammals can be infected with West Nile virus only through mosquito bites. Mosquitoes, in turn, become infected with the virus when they bite certain infected bird or mammals. The virus was originally detected in northern Africa and spread to North America in the 1990s. Humans sometimes catch West Nile virus, but the virus never becomes abundant enough in human blood to infect a mosquito.

label: Given that ...
body: Over the last two decades, people trying to reduce the amount of fat in their diet have decreased their red meat consumption by 50%.

label: How can it be that ...
body: Those people who reduced their consumption of red meat are actually consuming more fat than those who didn't.

label: Evaluate / Goal
body: The people who wanted to reduce fat in their diet are eating less red meat. (I guess red meat has fat in it, or so they think.) But in reducing the amount of red meat they eat, they are somehow ending up with more fat in their diet. So something else must have changed that is putting more fat in their diet. We need to know what's different about the reduced-meat crowd vs. the regular-meat crowd that is putting more fat into the former group's diet.

label: Rolanda's Conclusion
body: The house on Oak Ave is the best one to rent.

label: Rolanda's Evidence
body: It had a bigger yard than any other house we've seen in Prairieview.

label: Tom's Conclusion
body: That Oak Ave house wasn't the best.

label: Tom's Evidence
body: The yard's not as big as it looks, because in Prairieview the first 20 feet of yard from the street belong to the city.

label: Rolanda's Response
body: So what? How is does that make any other property we've seen better than this one? They've all been in Prairieview, so that objection you made applies to all of them.

label: Evaluate
body: How would we describe Tom's reasoning error? Well he tried to object to Rolanda's pick for which was the best house, but the negative thing he had to say about the house on Oak Ave would apply identically to all the other houses they've seen, since he's citing a city-wide Prairieview ordinance about property lines. Is there a name for "objecting that one thing is better than a bunch of similar things, by citing something that they all have in common"? If there is, I don't know it.

label: Goal
body: Look for an answer saying, "Tom tried to reject something as being the best option, based on an objection that applies equally to all the other options."

label: Main Conclusion
body: Jazz consists largely of voice-like horns and horn like voices.

label: Intermediate Conclusion
body: The best jazz singers use their voices much as horn players use their instruments.

label: Premises
body: The great Billie Holiday thought of her singing voice as a horn, reshaping melody and words to increase their impact. Conversely, jazz horn players achieve their distinctive sounds by emulating the spontaneous twists and turns of an impassioned voice.

label: Conclusion
body: Reducing class sizes in our district probably wouldn't improve overall student achievement.

label: Evidence
body: Even though smaller classes can help students get more individualized instruction, reducing class sizes would require hiring more teachers, and there is already a shortage of qualified teachers. Education suffers when teachers are underqualified.

label: Evaluation
body: The author is thinking that since this move would result in us needing more teachers, and since we already have a shortage of qualified teachers, we'd end up hiring underqualified teachers, and education suffers when teachers are underqualified. To argue that this move would result in overall improvement of student achievement, we could take a couple different angles: - maybe we could argue that it's still a net gain (the improvement to education caused by more individualized instruction might outweigh the degradation to education caused by having less qualified teachers). - maybe we could argue that there are ways to solve the potential problem of "underqualified" teachers. Maybe teachers could rotate to different classes, so that all classes had a qualified teacher at least part of the time. maybe it doesn't take very long for an underqualified teacher to become qualified (maybe on the job training very quickly turns them into qualified teachers)

label: Goal
body: Find an answer that, if negated, would weaken (i.e. would help us argue that reducing class sizes could still lead to improved student achievement). Or look for an answer spelling out the author's assumption that "if we reduce class sizes, we'll have more underqualified teachers in schools than we previously did".

label: Opposing Evidence
body: Because tropical storms require heat and moisture, they form especially over ocean surfaces of at least 26 degrees Celsius, ocean temperatures that global warming would encourage.

label: Opposing Point
body: Many early discussions of global warming predicted that it would cause more frequent and intense tropical storms.

label: Evidence
body: Other factors, such as instabilities in wind flow, are likely to counteract global warming’s effects on tropical storm development.

label: Conclusion
body: Recent research shows that global warming is unlikely to cause more frequent and intense tropical storms.

label: Evidence
body: Copyright was originally the grant of a temporary government-supported monopoly on copying a work. Its sole purpose was to encourage the circulation of ideas by giving authors the opportunity to derive a reasonable financial reward from their works.

label: Conclusion
body: Copyright sometimes goes beyond its original purpose.

label: Evaluate
body: The argument concludes that the purpose of copyright was more limited than is sometimes the case. This assumes that the holders of a copyright sometimes receive greater financial rewards than was originally intended.

label: Critic
body: You messed up again. You said that if the government didn't change its policies, we'd go into recession. But we didn't go into recession. The economy is even stronger this year.

label: Economist
body: Right, we're not in a recession because the government did change. So I was actually right.

label: Evaluation
body: The critic presented a conditional claim the economist had made (if no changes, then recession) and argued that it wasn't true, because the outcome (the recession) didn't happen. And the economist is saying, "right, but the trigger didn't happen. I convinced the government to make changes." A conditional claim is only being broken if a situation conforms to the trigger but not to the outcome.

label: Goal
body: It seems like we want an answer that sounds like, "the critic responded by saying that the trigger of my conditional didn't apply, so of course the outcome didn't come true".

label: Conclusion
body: It would be wrong to conclude from 1970s music videos that the music of that era was dominated by synth pop and punk (i.e. the music of that era was not dominated by synth pop and punk)

label: Evidence
body: Music videos were such a new art form, that the types of musicians most likely to be in music videos were a skewed sample of "cutting-edge" musicians.

label: Evaluate
body: The author is saying that we shouldn't extrapolate a generalization about 1970s music from 1970s music videos, because the music that appeared in 1970s music videos is not a representative sample.

label: Goal
body: Conclusion: It would be misleading to look at the X's involved in Y and conclude something broadly about X's. Premise: The X's involved in Y are a skewed sample of X's.

label: Facts
body: Even though individual staff members at hospitals, universities, and other institutions are doing what they do for selfish reasons, they end up successfully achieving public purposes.

label: Evaluate
body: This is an Inference task (the paragraph is supposed to support the answer). When we're doing Most Supported and we see a Pivot word, such as but / yet / however / even though, the correct answer is usually a safely worded claim that Straddles the Pivot.

label: Goal
body: Look for a safely worded claim that reconciles "acting for selfish reasons" with "successfully achieves public purposes".

label: Conclusion
body: There are some good reasons to avoid irradiated foods.

label: Evidence
body: Those foods have been exposed to the radioactive substances that produce the gamma rays. Irradiation can reduce vitamin content. Irradiation can leave behind harmful chemical residues. Irradiation spawns unique radiolytic products that can cause serious health problems such as cancer.

label: Evaluate
body: To fight this author's conclusion, we're arguing "there aren't good reasons to avoid irradiated foods", so we would have to debunk all these concerns she is raising. And since we will be getting rid of four answers that weaken (and she presented four reasons), it's probably pretty likely that we'll see answers that pick apart these objections.

label: Goal
body: Look for stuff saying "the radioactive exposure isn't bad / there's usually a good bit of vitamin content still there / you don't have to worry about those chemical residues or unique radiolytic products"

label: Conclusion
body: When teaching students about color, teachers should use colored paper rather than paint.

label: Evidence
body: Colored paper permits an exact replica of the same color, used in different contexts. Meanwhile, it's hard to mix paint so that you get the exact same color twice, and it's more liable to looking different based on the texture of surfaces you're applying it to.

label: Evaluation
body: If we're giving advice about how teachers should teach about color, we must have some assumptions about what should be taught in a color lesson. If we argued, "If you're teaching about A, you should use X rather than Y, because X is better at achieving Z", I would be assuming that "when you're teaching about A, it's important to achieve Z". What is the comparative advantage that colored paper has over colored paint? The former makes it way easier to exactly reproduce the same color, so that students can see the pure effect of that color in different contexts.

label: Goal
body: So the author must be assuming that when you're teaching about color, it's important to use the exact same version of a color / it's important to let students make a precise comparison of that color's impact in varying contexts. She's also assuming that "colored paint does not have significant teaching advantages over colored paper that would outweigh the one teaching advantage we know that colored paper has".

label: Conclusion
body: In order to determine the causes of cultural phenomena, you need to have data from multiple societies.

label: Evidence
body: If you didn't have data from lots of societies, you wouldn't be able to look at how strongly correlated certain ecological / climatic factors are with certain structural features of society. (The more data points you have, the more you can see whether certain structures co-varied with certain climatic/ecological factors)

label: Evaluate
body: They're asking us about the first sentence, which is the main conclusion. Both the colon that proceeds it and the "for example" show us that it's being supported. The support is just a complicated way of saying, "In order to figure out whether X causes Y, we want to see if X shows up when Y is absent, and if Y shows up when X is absent."

label: Goal
body: Look for something that sounds like Main Conclusion.

label: Conclusion
body: It would be good for progress in physics if they enhanced their safeguards against scientific fraud.

label: Evidence
body: Even though physicists claim their fraud-protection system is good because of peer review, we heard that same thing from biologists 20 years ago who turned out to be wrong. Since biology started strengthening it's fraud-protection guardrails, it's had fewer major incidents of fraud.

label: Evaluation
body: This is an argument by Comparison, since the author is leaning on Premises about biologists to make an argument about what physicists should do. To weaken an argument by comparison, we'd look for important differences: - maybe biologists were wrong 20 years ago when they said "we have good fraud-prevention systems" but physicists are correct now when they claim they do - maybe biologists didn't use peer review until recently, but peer review is the secret to fraud prevention. To strengthen the comparison, we would want to know that physicists now and biologists-20 years ago are fair to compare in terms of their rate of fraud, their protection against fraud, and the sort of measures that would help prevent fraud. However, we could also dig into the "New Term" in the conclusion: progress. It's not really clear where that enters the discussion. We were just talking about whether or not fraud was being effectively prevented, until the author said, "Physicists should get better at preventing fraud, for the sake of progress."

label: Goal
body: The main thrust seems to be an argument by comparison, so we would look for a correct answer that makes biology and physics more fair to compare, when it comes to this fraud prevention discussion. But it's possible LSAT will test us on that "new guy" in the conclusion: progress. Is progress related to fraud prevention? A correct answer could help us believe that it is.

label: Conclusion
body: All dogs descended from domesticated wolves, but some dogs descended from more recently domesticated wolves.

label: Evidence
body: Some breeds of dog are more closely related genetically to wolves than to most other breeds of dog.

label: Evaluate
body: Since we know that all dogs broke off the evolutionary tree from some domesticated wolf, the author is saying these more recently domesticated wolves must have broken off from the tree more recently. Presumably she thinks that the longer it's been since you branched off the evolutionary tree and became your own species, the more genetically you would drift away from wolves and towards other breeds of dogs. We could think of alternate explanations for how these more recently domesticated wolves have DNA that's more like wolves than dogs, but since this is a Principle question, we're probably not ruling out new objections. Principle answers are usually just connecting bridge ideas that get us from Premise language to Conclusion language.

label: Goal
body: The premise is that "these more recently domesticated wolves have DNA that's closer to wolves than dogs", and the conclusion is "they more recently branched off from a domesticated wolf". So a principle could sound like "the closer your DNA is to wolves, the more recently your branched off from wolves".

label: Evidence
body: Paleomycologists always know P → know SP's the scholarly publications of of other P's all other paleomycologists. Professor M knows the M knows SP of D. scholarly publication of D is a P. Professor D, who is a paleomycologist.

label: Conclusion
body: Professor M must be M is a P. a paleomycologist.

label: Evaluation
body: Like a lot of Parallel Flaw arguments, this one commits a Necessary vs. Sufficient flaw, reading a conditional backwards. If Professor M is a paleo, then he would definitely know the SP of Professor D. We know that Professor M knows the SP of Professor D, but that doesn't prove Professor M is a paleo. We can't read that rule backwards and think "if the right is true, then the left is true".

label: Goal
body: The flaw was presenting a conditional "X --> Y" and then reasoning that if someone is Y, then they must be X. The other details are extraneous.

label: Lutsina Priscilla
body: Because futuristic science fiction does not need to represent current social realities, its writers can envisage radically new social arrangements. That futuristic science fiction writers more skillfully envisage radically new technologies than new social arrangements shows how writers’ imaginations are constrained by current realities. Thus it has the Because of this potential to be limitation, the most a richer source effective social of social criticism results criticism than from faithfully is conventional presenting the fiction. current social realities for critical examination, as happens in conventional fiction.

label: Evaluate
body: Lutsina and Priscilla disagree about whether futuristic science fiction or conventional fiction is more effective at providing social criticism.

label: Conclusion
body: Our club will almost certainly be city champions this year.

label: Evidence
body: The best team in the city will be the team most likely to win the championship this year, and ...

label: Intermediate Conclusion
body: We will have the best team in the city.

label: Evidence
body: We recruited the best players in the city.

label: Evidence
body: Infants lack the motor ability required PS → MC to voluntarily produce particular sounds, but produce various babbling sounds randomly. Most children are several years old before they can voluntarily produce most of the vowel and consonant sounds of their language.

label: Conclusion
body: We can conclude that speech SA → MC acquisition is entirely a motor control process rather than a process that is abstract or mental.

label: Evaluate
body: The argument assumes that speech SA → PS acquisition is entirely a function of one’s ability to produce particular sounds.

label: Evaluate
body: The argument assumes that in CG → ~C countries where collective goals are put before individuals’ goals people do not have confidence in the economic policies of their country.

label: Evaluate
body: The "Because [claim 1], [claim 2]" structure of the first sentence gives us a mini-argument that says "if you recruited the best players, you'll be the best team". That would be a Part vs. Whole fallacy. You could add 3 new recruits who are the best, to a team of otherwise terrible players, and not necessarily end up with the best team. Or these new recruits could have terrible chemistry. They could get injured. But if we play along with that first mini-conclusion and pretend they'll have the best team in the city, then do we know that they are almost certain to win the championship? There's a premise rule that says the best team will be the team that's most likely to win. Does "most likely to win" = "almost certain to win"? No. Sports fans may have an easier time understanding the gap here, because we know the #1 seed is always the team that's most likely to win, but they're far from almost certain to win. "The team most likely to win" means "more likely than anyone else", but "almost certain" means like 90% or better odds. There might be 3 teams, the Bears, the Lions, the Sharks. The team most likely to win is the Bears, with a 40% chance. The Lions have a 25% chance, and the Sharks have a 15% chance. Are the Bears, who are the team most likely to win, almost certain to win? No, there's only a 40% they win, but a 60% chance they lose.

label: Goal
body: Look for an answer that calls out the Part vs. Whole distinction or one that calls out the difference between "higher probability than any other team" vs. "almost certain probability".

label: Evidence
body: If the stamp is displayed, it will Displayed → Damaged be damaged.

label: Conclusion
body: The stamp should not be ~Displayed displayed

label: Evaluate
body: The argument assumes that if (Displayed → Damaged) → ~Displayed displaying an item in a museum would damage it, then it should not be displayed.

label: Opposing Point
body: Many diet-conscious consumers are excited about new “fake fat” products designed to give food the flavor and consistency of fatty foods, yet without fat’s harmful effects.

label: Evidence
body: Research has shown that when people knowingly or unknowingly eat foods containing “fake fat” they tend to take in at least as many additional calories as are saved by eating “fake fat.”

label: Conclusion
body: Consumers who expect the new fat substitute to help them lose weight are likely to be disappointed.

label: Conclusion
body: Offering free services to new customers is not an ideal practice.

label: Evidence
body: Regular, long-term customers who comprise the bulk of a bank’s business are excluded from these offers.

label: Evaluation
body: We might strengthen this argument by supporting the missing bridge idea: “If you’re excluding the bulk of your customers from a special offer, it’s not an ideal practice”. But we could also strengthen by ruling out objections. How might someone defend giving freebies to new customers? They could say, “Oh, don’t worry the regular customers don’t even know about the special offers”, so we could strengthen by saying something like “the regular customers are aware of these special offers and disappointed that they can’t take advantage of them”. A defender of this plan might say, “We need these free special offers in order to convert a potential new customer into a regular”, so we could strengthen by saying “There are other effective ways to entice new customers into opening an account that don’t exclude the regular customers”.

label: Goal
body: We want an answer that makes it sound like a bad idea to offer freebies to new customers while denying them to the majority of your customers, the regulars.

label: Evidence
body: Medical articles cited in popular newspapers or magazines are more likely than other medical research articles to be cited in subsequent medical research.

label: Conclusion
body: It appears that medical researchers’ judgments of the importance of prior research are strongly influenced by the publicity received by that research and do not strongly correspond to the research’s true importance.

label: Evaluate
body: The conclusion offers an explanation of why being cited in popular newspapers or magazines and being cited in subsequent medical research is positively associated. But it’s only one of many possible explanations of the correlation.

label: Conclusion
body: We should have a majority vote on meeting agendas.

label: Evidence
body: Our options are unanimous vote, majority vote, or assigning to a committee. It’s unlikely we’d get unanimous consensus, and using committees has usually led to bad stuff.

label: Evaluation
body: We want to characterize the evidence or reasoning, to offer some general description of how the author arrived at her conclusion. She mentioned three options and then said bad things about two of them, settling ultimately on the remaining option.

label: Goal
body: Something to the effect of presented multiple options but then shot down all but one of them.

label: Evidence
body: Surveys show that cigarette sales drop substantially in cities that impose stiff tax increases on cigarettes.

label: Conclusion
body: There is strong evidence that the taxes themselves would produce the sought after reduction in smoking.

label: Evaluate
body: The surveys establish a correlation between higher taxes on cigarettes and a drop in cigarette sales. CURIOUS FACT Why are cig sales dropping in cities that have imposed stiff tax increases on cigs? AUTHOR'S CAUSAL INTERPRETATION The taxes are discouraging people from smoking, so people are smoking less, so cig sales are dropping. We know that on Weaken the most common way to attack the Explain Curious Fact argument archetype is to suggest an alternate explanation for the curious fact. The other way is to undermine the plausibility of the author's causal story. Finally, even if we granted that taxes in these other places did lead to a drop in smoking, we could weaken this argument by providing some reason why in OUR CITY things would be different.

label: Goal
body: Look for an alternate way to explain lower cig sales, an answer that makes it seem like the higher cigarette tax did not cause the drop in smoking in other cities, or an answer that makes it seem like a cig tax in our city wouldn't lead to a drop in smoking.

label: Conclusion
body: Countries that put collective goals CG → ~RE before individuals' goals cannot emerge quickly from an economic recession.

label: Evidence
body: The government recently demolished a former naval base. Among the complex's facilities were a gymnasium, a swimming pool, office buildings, gardens, and housing for hundreds of people. Of course the government was legally permitted to use these facilities as it wished. But clearly, using them for the good GCBE of the community would have benefited everyone.

label: Conclusion
body: The government's actions were not ~E + ~M only inefficient but immoral.

label: Evaluate
body: There is difference between what is GCBE → ~E+ ~M moral and what benefits the community. Simply acting in a way that does not benefit a community does not suggest that an action was immoral. Or put another way the argument assumes that if an alternative course of action would have benefited everyone, then the chosen course of action was inefficient and immoral.

label: Evidence
body: Researchers played extended audiotapes to patients before they underwent surgery and afterward while they were recovering. One tape consisted of conversation; the other consisted of music. Those who listened only to the latter tape required less anesthesia during surgery and fewer painkillers afterward than those who listened only to the former tape.

label: Conclusion
body: Reducing stress lessens a person's sensitivity to pain.

label: Evaluate
body: There are a couple issues we could look at. There's a study with a difference between two groups, i.e. a Curious Fact CURIOUS FACT: why did the ppl who listened to music need less anesthesia / painkillers than the ppl who listened to conversation? AUTHOR'S EXPLANATION: the music lessened their sensitivity to pain, so they didn't need as much pain relief. The argument is assuming that there are NOT alternate ways to explain why the music group needed less pain relief. Additionally, there's a New Concept in the Conclusion: reducing stress? What did any of the rest of this conversation have to do with "stress"? It was never mentioned in the evidence, so the author must be assuming something about it. Given that she thinks that listening to music lessened sensitivity to pain, if she's concluding from that that reducing stress lessens sensitivity to pain, she must be thinking that listening to music reduces your stress.

label: Samuel's Claims
body: 1. Communication via computer is usually private and anonymous, between people who would otherwise interact in person 2. Communication via computer contributes to the dissolution, not the creation of lasting communal bonds. 3. Due to the word "Because" connecting Sam's two claims, we also know Sam assumes a causal relationship between the two claims: when two people who would otherwise meet in person meet instead privately and anonymously on computer, that helps to dissolve lasting communal bonds.

label: Tova's Responses to Those Claims
body: 1. She doesn't speak about which form computer communication usually takes, but she does seem to push back against Samuel's assumption that people talking via computer would be interacting in person otherwise. Tova suggests, "computer communication is not replacing the more intimate face-to-face meetup." 2. Tova does speak to its net effect on helping / hurting social bonds. She says it usually replaces "asocial or even antisocial behavior". So she thinks that computer communication is at worst harmless, but probably a net positive. She would disagree that computer communication is helping to dissolve communal bonds.

label: Goal
body: There seemed to be two potential disagreements: Claim 1-- are people talking on the computer sacrificing what would otherwise be a more intimate in-person meetup? Claim 2 — is computer communication really dissolving communal bonds?

label: Evidence
body: The side-effects of an iron-seeding ~SSE strategy have not yet been studied.

label: Conclusion
body: We should not respond immediately ~SI to the greenhouse effect by spreading iron particles over the surface of the Earth’s oceans.

label: Evaluate
body: The argument assumes that we SI → SSE should be responding ~SSE → ~SI to the greenhouse effect only if we understand the possible side-effects of that strategy.

label: Evidence
body: No matter how conscientious they are, historians always have biases that affect their work.

label: Conclusion
body: Rather than trying to interpret historical events, historians should instead interpret what the people who participated in historical events thought about those events.

label: Evaluate
body: The problem with this argument is that the historians are interpreting in both cases. So if they’re likely to bias is likely to affect their interpretation of historical events, it’s also likely to affect their interpretation of what the people who participated in historical events thought about those events as well.

label: Premise
body: Timely access to the kind of medical care that only specialized centers can provide could save the lives of many people.

label: Intermediate Conclusion
body: The earnings of these people would result in a substantial increase in country X’s gross national product, and the taxes paid on those earnings would substantially augment government revenues.

label: Main Conclusion
body: Humanitarian considerations aside, sheer economics dictates that country X should institute, as country Y has done, a nationwide system of air and ground transportation for conveying seriously injured persons to specialized trauma centers.

label: Evaluate
body: There are two arguments made. First, it may not follow from saving the lives of these people that the gross national product would be substantially increased. And second, even if it did result in a substantial increase in gross national product, it doesn’t necessarily follow that it is economically advantageous to institute a nationwide system of air and ground transportation for conveying seriously injured persons. The costs of instituting such a system could outweigh any increase in the gross national product.

body: Early urban societies could not have US → LSF been maintained without large-scale farming nearby. Which remained unfeasible in areas ~RL → ~IR far from rivers or lakes until more recent times.

label: Evidence
body: The average length of stay for patients at Edgewater Hospital is four days, compared to six days at University Hospital. Studies show that recovery rates at the two hospitals are similar for patients with similar illnesses.

label: Conclusion
body: University Hospital could decrease its average length of stay without affecting quality of care.

label: Evaluate
body: It could be that University Hospital is keeping their patients for too long. Of course, it also could be that the kinds of illnesses each hospital tends to treat are different. If the University Hospital tends to treat more elderly patients with more serious illnesses, it may not be able to decrease the average length of stay without affecting quality of care.

label: Main Conclusion
body: We should not be persuaded by Graham's argument

body: People sleep, and at least sometimes when sleeping they are truly happy, even though they are not doing anything.

label: Facts
body: Some say West didn’t really influence Stuart, since West’s work is only mentioned once in Stuart’s diaries. However, Stuart’s diaries mention meeting with West several times, and Stuart’s close friend studied under West. Also, Stuart’s work uses West’s terminology which nobody else at that time was using.

label: Evaluation
body: The author is definitely defending her idea that West influenced Stuart. While we can’t prove it, it seems pretty supportable based on the three ideas she presented.

label: Goal
body: Some safely worded claim that sounds like maybe West did have an influence on Stuart.

label: Evidence
body: Angiosperms, a certain class of plants, first appeared at the time that dinosaurs became extinct. These plants produce amino-acid-based alkaloids that are psychoactive agents. Most plant-eating mammals avoid these potentially lethal poisons because they taste bitter. Mammals have livers that help detoxify such drugs. Dinosaurs could neither taste the bitterness nor detoxify the substance once it was ingested. This theory helps explain why so many dinosaur fossils are found in unusual and contorted positions.

label: Conclusion
body: The sudden extinction of all dinosaurs points to "drug overdoses" as the cause.

label: Evaluate
body: To weaken this argument the correct answer could provide an alternative cause, an example of animals eating certain angiosperms but not finding their fossils in unusual or contorted positions, or an example of animal fossils found in unusual or contorted positions but from animals known not to eat angiosperms.

label: Apparent Paradox
body: There are two ways to manage an existing transportation infrastructure. Continuous maintenance is far less expensive than radical reconstruction. Continuous maintenance almost never happens.

label: Evaluate
body: The challenge is to explain human behavior that prioritizes that prioritizes the short term over the long term.

label: Evidence
body: Over half of people who have parachuted only once report being extremely frightened by the experience. Less than 1 percent of those who have parachuted ten times or more report being frightened by it.

label: Conclusion
body: A good way to get over one’s fear of an activity one finds terrifying is to do it repeatedly.

label: Evaluate
body: The problem with this argument is that it suggests that engaging in an activity can reduce one’s fear of that activity, but the evidence is only a snapshot and so cannot prove a change in one’s attitude over time.

label: Apparent Paradox
body: Most economists believe that reducing the price of any product generally stimulates demand for it. However, most wine merchants have found that reducing the price of domestic wines to make them more competitive with imported wines with which they were previously comparably priced is frequently followed by an increase in sales of those imported wines.

label: Evaluate
body: Why would stimulating demand for domestic wines be followed by an increase in sales of imported wines? It’s not clear, but it’s possible that consuming more domestic wine somehow further encourages more consumption which to some extent increases demand for imported wines as well.

label: Given
body: Certain bacteria that produce hydrogen sulfide as a waste product would die if directly exposed to oxygen. The hydrogen sulfide reacts with oxygen, removing it and so preventing it from harming the bacteria. Furthermore, the hydrogen sulfide tends to kill other organisms in the area, thereby providing the bacteria with a source of food. As a result, a dense colony of these bacteria produces for itself an environment in which it can continue to thrive indefinitely.

label: Conclusion
body: Gloomy books predicting end times are unlikely to be popular.

label: Evidence
body: Books that present a vision of a happy future are always popular, and gloomy books predicting end times are not in that genre.

label: Evaluation
body: Lots of Parallel Flaw questions test famous flaws, and this one is giving us the Necessary vs. Sufficient flaw. It helps us to spot that if we notice the conditional certainty of “will always”. The author’s logic is basically, “Things of type X will always achieve Y. Gloomy books are not type X, so they will not achieve Y.”

label: Goal
body: If A, then B. Since this thing is not-A, it will be not-B.

label: Given
body: Contemporary historians and archaeologists find current g geography, geology, and climate to be rich in clues about a given region’s distant history. However, the more distant the period we are studying is, the less useful the study of the present becomes.

label: Evaluate
body: The relationship illustrated in the passage is that one can learn about the past by studying the present, but the further back in time one wants to look the less useful the study of the present becomes.

label: Conclusion (we conclude that)
body: This hippo was not a toy; it was a religious object.

label: Conclusion
body: Computers cannot currently be made significantly faster.

label: Evidence
body: It was discovered in a tomb with the legs broken off. Breaking the legs off a representation of an animal was thought to help a deceased person in the eternal war the dead are fighting with beasts (fun afterlife, ancient Egyptians!).

label: Evaluate
body: When it comes to Linking assumptions, we know we have New Terms in the Conclusion. We're trying to derive a conclusion about whether something was or wasn't a toy or a religious object, but we never defined those nouns. So the author is assuming if legs are broken and → religious object they might be broken to (not toy) help the dead in eternal war But since this is more of a real world argument, we should probably be approaching this thinking about possible Objections that a Defender answer could ward off. Given that ... these legs were broken off and that broken off an animal effigy's legs was an act that was thought to help dead people fight beasts in the afterlife, How could we argue that ... This was a toy or it wasn't a religious object? If we say it's a toy, we know the author is going to say, "Oh, yeah?! Then how come it's legs were broken off?"
