What could we say? - I don't know, maybe they just broke but the kid kept playing with the toy? - maybe a dog ate the legs off The author is also assuming that this object could not have doubled as both a toy and a religious object.

label: Goal
body: Find an answer that links "toy" or "religious object" to wording in the premise, or find an answer that rules out an objection. When we negate the correct answer, it should sound like an objection (potentially like an Alternate Explanation for why the legs are broken off).

label: Conclusion
body: Physicians will eventually be able to treat psychological disorders as effectively with drugs (pharmacological intervention) as we currently can with "talk" methods.

label: Evidence
body: "Talk" methods produce chemical changes in the brain. These changes seem to correspond with (and the author assumes account for) the patient's behavior changing.

label: Evaluate
body: The author is thinking that since Talk therapy -> changes chemicals -?> changes behavior it makes sense that Drug therapy -> changes chemicals --> changes behavior This argument is triggering our normal Causal and Comparison questions. When it comes to causal, the author is assuming from a correlation between chemical changes / behavioral changes, the chemical changes caused the behavioral changes. That's why the author assumes that drugs could work just as way. She's thinking, "if we can find a way via drugs to attain the same chemical changes, we'll achieve the same behavior changes". Besides assuming that correlation is causation, the author is also assuming that drugs have the ability to change the same chemical changes that talk therapy causes, and she's assuming that the drug way of causing those chemical changes doesn't come with enough compelling negative side effects that it wouldn't be acceptable as a treatment method.

label: Goal
body: Look for an answer calling our the "correlation to causality" shift, or an answer calling out the assumption that "drugs could achieve similar chemical changes that talk therapy does, and without significant side effects".

label: Opposing Evidence
body: Bacteria that benefit human beings when they are present in the body are called commensals. Stomach ulcers occur in less than 10 percent of those harboring H. pylori. H. pylori allegedly strengthens immune response.

label: Opposing Point
body: Many scientists now consider H. pylori a commensal.

label: Evidence
body: Only about 10 percent of the people who harbor Mycobacter tuberculosis—a bacterium that can cause tuberculosis—get sick from it. No one would call M. tuberculosis a commensal.

label: Conclusion
body: The view that H. pylori is a commensal is misguided.

label: Evaluate
body: The argument assumes that if M. tuberculosis is not a commensal, that H. pylori is also not a commensal. However, if H. pylori provides more benefit to human beings when present in the body than M. tuberculosis, then the comparison may not be valid.

label: Evidence
body: Most apartments on the UF -most↣ SV upper floors of The Vista Arms apartment building have scenic views.

label: Conclusion
body: So there is in the SA ↢some↣ SV building at least one studio apartment with scenic views.

label: Evaluate
body: The argument assumes UF -most↣ SA that most apartments on the upper floors of The Vista Arms apartment building are studio apartments.

label: Conclusion
body: Even though Tom didn't tell me I could use his computer, it would be not wrong for me to do so.

label: Evidence
body: Last week Tom used Mary's bike even though she never told him he could use it.

label: Evaluate
body: Why are we allowed to take Tom's computer without asking? Because we've seen Tom take somebody else's stuff without asking before. If we've ever seen someone toilet-paper someone else's house, then it's not wrong to toilet paper their house. What is the abstract principle we're using here?

label: Goal
body: Look for something like, "If someone has previously done X, then it's not wrong to do X to them."

label: Situation
body: Eddie leaves the room. He thinks that Marsha is going to tell everyone about a dream she recently had. When he's allowed to return to the room, he tries to figure out what her dream was all about by asking everyone in the room Yes / No questions. But Marsha never actually told them any dream. They just created some rule for when they'll say Yes / When they'll say no. (e.g. Every 3rd question, say "yes" / If your name starts with a vowel, say "yes") By piecing together the Yes and No answers that he gets, Eddie actually ends up thinking he has figured out the story, and the story he thinks he's figured out is coherent and ingenious.

label: Evaluate
body: When we're asked to listen to a situation / story and then figure out which generalization / proposition it best illustrates or matches, we're hoping to extract from the stimulus some safely worded takeaway. Most of the wrong answers are too strongly worded. We use our Inference brain and look primarily for Causal or Comparison/Contrast language to figure out what sort of synthesis we could say. Here, there's a contrast (dramatic irony) between Eddie and the rest of the partygoers. They know there is no actual story, and are just giving random Yes/No answers. He thinks there is an actual story, and the one he is guessing is surprisingly coherent.

label: Goal
body: Look for an answer that Straddles the Pivot, that synthesizes what's going on with the partygoers with the surprising effect it's having on Eddie.

label: Evidence
body: Manufacturers have tried to make CPU chips smaller, because if you can make a CPU chip smaller without decreasing its sophistication, it makes the computer faster. But currently CPU chips can't be made significantly smaller without decreasing their sophistication.

label: Evaluate
body: This would seem like a fairly airtight argument — making CPU chips smaller makes computers faster, but we can't make them any smaller right now, so we can't make computers faster right now. The only thing missing is restrictive wording like, "the ONLY way to make computers faster is by making CPU chips smaller". Maybe there's something else that could be done to CPU chips to make them faster (keep them same size but make them out of a different substance? put several of them operating in parallel?) or something else that could be done to computers to make them faster.

label: Goal
body: Look for an answer saying that making CPU chips smaller is the only way to make computers faster, or an answer ruling out some other way of making computers faster.

label: Conclusion
body: It looks like pollution is not eliminating many amphibian species each year.

label: Evidence
body: In the past year, we've learned that there are many more species of amphibians in existence than we previously thought.

label: Evaluation
body: Given that last yr we realized there are more A species than we previously thought, How could we still say that pollution is eliminating many A species each year? Maybe we can see amphibian species disappearing from the Gulf of Mexico, but we discovered a bunch of new amphibians on the Galapagos Islands. It certainly seems possible that scientists could simultaneously discover new amphibian species while witnessing known amphibian species in decline elsewhere.

label: Goal
body: Since the question stem is predicated on "the author has confused ____ with ____ " language, how would we express the author's flaw in terms of confusion? She seems to think that "# of amphibian species is not going down" because "# of species we now realize exist went up". The confusion is that just because we now realize a species exists doesn't mean it adds to the total species of amphibians on Earth. Those species existed on Earth even before we discovered them. To assess whether the environmentalists' claim is true, we would need to know "how many amphibian species existed last year? how many this year?" If we just discovered 100 new species, we would retroactively add that to the total of last year as well, because they also existed then (we just didn't realize it). So, there's a confusion between "the total # of amphibian species on Earth" vs "the total # of amphibian species we know about on Earth".

label: Conclusion
body: (They are mistaken) Using sphagnum moss as a soil conditioner is not environmentally sound.

label: Evidence
body: Sphagnum moss is maybe the biggest single contributor of oxygen to the atmosphere, and the garden soil industry is depleting is.

label: Evaluate
body: We know we want the conclusion to let us prove that using SM as a soil conditioner isn't an environmentally sound practice, so that's the right side of our principle: practice → environmentally is not sound What should go on the right side? Why is this practice environmentally unsound? Because it depletes one of the biggest oxygen providers in the world.

label: Goal
body: So we want something like depletes one of practice is not the biggest sources → environmentally sound of oxygen globally

label: Conclusion
body: You might as well just quit your job.

label: Evidence
body: The only risk in quitting a job is that of not finding another job. And if you don't find another job, you'll be unhappy. But you already are unhappy.

label: Evaluation
body: Given that Brooks is already unhappy in his job, and the only risk in quitting is not being able to find a new job (which would make him unhappy), how could we argue that Brooks should not quit his job? Well, Brooks only said he's unhappy in his job. If he quit and then were unemployed because he couldn't find a job, he would be unhappy with having no job. Maybe those are two different types of unhappiness and the latter is worse than the former. Additionally, we were given a conditional that says "if you don't find a new job, you'll be unhappy", and then Morgenstern thought that was a moot point since Brooks is already happy. But maybe there are other downsides as well to not finding a new job. Morgenstern didn't establish that being unhappy is the only result of not finding a job. Maybe other results would include needing to sell your car, losing your partner, and having to move back in with your parents. Even if we assumed unhappiness is equivalent in this world vs. world where he quits, there might be other ramifications of quitting that make that world worse than this world.

label: Goal
body: Find an answer pointing out a meaningful difference between his current unhappiness and the unhappiness he'd get from not being able to find a job, or find an answer discussing other possible negative ramifications of quitting his job.

label: Given
body: Only Canadian films LNFF → CF are shown at the Lac Nichoutec Film Festival. This year, most of the LNFF + WP -most↣ IFF + WP films that won prizes at that festival also won prizes at international film festivals.

label: Conclusion
body: It's absurd to say that "the tendency of cynical journalists to point out the selfish motives of philanthropists is undermining society's well-being by convincing them rich people are greedy / mendacious".

label: Evidence
body: Cynical journalists can't be a contributing factor to undermining society's well being, since journalists have always been cynics and today's cynics are more restrained than previous eras'.

label: Evaluate
body: This argument boils down to saying "the fact that J's have trait X can't be a contributing factor to Y, since J's have always had trait X." We could just object by saying — "Yup. And J's have always been causing Y." This argument is similar to saying "the smoke from cigarettes cannot be a contributing factor to lung cancer, since cigarettes have always had smoke, and today's cigarettes, if anything, offer more smoke filtration than their predecessors."

label: Goal
body: Look for an answer saying, "Just because cynicism has always been there, doesn't mean it isn't undermining well-being. Maybe it has always been undermining our well-being, or maybe something else in society has changed that now allows this cynicism to undermine our well-being."

label: Annie's Position
body: Annie wants students to pay a new fee to fix the libraries fast. She blames the admin but accepts students paying anyway.

label: Opposing Support
body: They [the owners of Uptown Apartments] do not believe that the increased rents they could charge for improved apartments would not cover the costs of the improvements.

label: Opposing Point
body: The owners of Uptown Apartments are leaning toward not improving the apartment complex.

label: Evidence
body: The improvements would make the surrounding housing, which they also own, more valuable and rentable for higher rents.

label: Conclusion
body: So the owners should make the improvements.

label: Evaluate
body: This argument boils down to whether a certain action (improving the apartments) is a Net Gain. The author is arguing that the owners should make the apartments, so she thinks this action will yield a net positive. And she is rebutting the owners, who think it will be a Net Loss (the cost of the improvements > the increase in rent that they could charge). The author ends up changing the math on their calculation by bringing in another factor that would be affected by improving the apartments: they would also raise the property values and revenue ceiling on other assets owned by the owners of the apartments.

label: Goal
body: We would potentially want an argument that has something resembling this structure. Opposing idea: Don't do action A, because upside X doesn't offset downside Y. Author's Conclusion: You should do action A. Author's Evidence: Action A would also have upside Z The argument may even care that upside Z (raising the values / rental potential of the surrounding housing) isn't directly affected by action A, but seems to be indirectly affected by action A.

label: Evidence
body: Ditalgame Corporation’s computer video games are subject to widespread illegal copying. To combat this piracy, Ditalgame will begin using a new copy protection feature on its games.

label: Conclusion
body: Ditalgame’s president predicts a substantial increase in sales of the company’s games once the new copy protection feature is implemented.

label: Evaluate
body: Ditalgame’s president assumes that the copy protection feature will be effective at restricting access. The president further assumes that people will pay for games if they are not available for free.

label: Opposing Evidence
body: The government would electronically record all transactions.

label: Opposing Point
body: It may soon be possible for an economy to function without paper money.

label: Evidence
body: If the government recorded all transactions, it would give the government too much power. People are rightly distrustful of governments with too much power.

label: Conclusion
body: While recording all transactions would be feasible it would never be willingly accepted by a society.

label: Premise
body: The body of thought known M → DHM as Marxism claims to describe rigorously an inexorable historical movement toward the socialization of the means of production.

label: Intermediate Conclusion
body: [Marxism] should be M → ST regarded as a scientific theory.

label: Main Conclusion
body: Thus, certain interpreters, M → ~PP in taking Marxism as a political program aimed at radically transforming society, have misconstrued it.

label: Evaluate
body: The argument assumes ST → ~PP that scientific theories are not political programs.

label: Daniel's 1st Claim
body: Sometimes, moral duty obliges us to perform certain actions regardless of their consequences. Does Carrie imply that there are never times when moral duty requires us to do something, regardless of consequence? No.

label: Daniel's 2nd Claim
body: Just because an action fulfills a moral obligation doesn't establish that an action is morally good. Does Carrie imply that fulfilling a moral obligation does establish that an action is morally good? Yes! She says the only thing that can be required for a morally good action is that it fulfills a moral obligation. If that's the only criterion to satisfy, then satisfying that criterion is sufficient to to establish that an action is morally good.

label: Daniel's 3rd Claim
body: If an action isn't performed with the right motivations, it can't be morally good. Does Carrie imply that an action performed without the right motivations can be morally good? Yes! She stresses that motivations aren't even under our conscious control, and thus the only thing that can be required for a morally good action is that it fulfills a moral obligation. If that's the only criterion to satisfy, then satisfying that criterion is sufficient to to establish that an action is morally good. Hence, someone who fulfilled a moral obligation, even with not-right motivations, would still have committed a morally good action.

label: Goal
body: Carrie pushed back against both of Daniel's last two claims, so we have two possibilities for the correct answer - whether or not fulfilling a moral obligation is enough to call an action morally good - whether you ALSO need the right motivations for an action to be morally good

label: Conclusion
body: The bridge renovation did waste taxpayers' money. (the mayor was lying when he said otherwise)

label: Evidence
body: He set up a commission to look into government waste, and it found out that the Southern Tier Project was super wasteful. The bridge renovation was part of that Project.

label: Evaluate
body: Given that the bridge renovation was part of the STP, and the STP was super wasteful, how could we still argue that the bridge renovation was not wasteful? We'd have to say that the bridge renovation was one of the rare parts of the STP that wasn't wasteful. Maybe the bridge renovation was performed efficiently well within budget at a competitive rate, unlike other parts of the STP. If we know our famous flaws, we'll see the giveaway language of Part vs. Whole: the bridge renovation was a part.

label: Goal
body: Look for an answer calling out the author's move from Whole (the Project was wasteful) to Part (the bridge renovation was wasteful).

label: Given
body: The airport's runways are too close to each other to allow simultaneous use of adjacent runways when visibility is poor. The airport allows only 30 planes an hour to land in poor weather; In good weather 60 planes an hour are allowed to land. Because airline schedules assume good weather, bad weather creates serious delays.

label: Apparent Paradox
body: As a general rule, the larger a social group of primates, the more time its members spend grooming one another. The main purpose of this social grooming is the maintenance of social cohesion. Furthermore, group size among primates tends to increase proportionally with the size of the neocortex, the seat of higher thought in the brain. Extrapolating upon the relationship between group size and neocortex size, we can infer that early human groups were quite large. But unexpectedly, there is strong evidence that, apart from parents grooming their children, these humans spent virtually no time grooming one another.

label: Evaluate
body: If the main purpose of social grooming is social cohesion why didn’t these humans spend more time grooming one another? Maybe the large neocortex of these humans somehow reduced their need for maintaining social cohesion.

label: Evidence
body: Theories Succeeded Inflation been and implementing → lessened sound program considerably Inflation didn't lessen considerably.

label: Conclusion
body: Theories weren't sound.

label: Evaluate
body: We're given a conditional premise, with an "and" in the trigger. A and B → C Then we're given a factual premise, that the outcome didn't occur. ~C. Finally, the author concludes that one of trigger ideas didn't happen. ~A. The flaw here is that when you contrapose the original conditional, you would have ~C --> ~A or ~B We can't be sure that "theories weren't sound" because it's possible that the reason C wasn't achieved was because the other half of the trigger didn't obtain, i.e. it's possible that "theories were sound" but "program wasn't implemented".

label: Goal
body: Premise 1: A and B → C Premise 2: ~C. Conclusion: ~A It doesn't matter whether the conclusion rules out A or rules out B; as long as it only rules out one of them it's the same flaw.

label: Conclusion
body: If you're mad at a fellow group member because the group can't agree on something, and you want to call them some label that will stick, you should use "unyielding".

label: Evidence
body: It'll be pretty undeniable that this person has not yielded on this issue, so it will be undeniable that they are "unyielding" on this issue.

label: Evaluate
body: What weird advice for an LSAT argument to offer: "The most enduring and provable insult is unyielding!" On Method questions, we're trying to characterize the type of evidence or type of journey we took to get to the conclusion, and the correct answer almost always involves one of these concepts: Analogy Implications of Logic Rule Out Alternatives Call Out Dubious Assumption Raise Overlooked Information (Counter)example to Principle Make a Distinction Define a Term Alternate Explanation This argument seems to involve some "ruling out alternatives", since the author is suggesting that we do not go with "stubborn or bull-headed".

label: Goal
body: Look for an answer possibly saying that the author endorsed one option over a couple others by distinguishing it from the other two in terms of its undeniable truth.

label: Conclusion
body: Information on the Internet should somehow be regulated.

label: Evidence
body: Usually it's good to have unregulated information, but the Internet is a messy mix of truth and fiction. If you can't differentiate the accurate from the inaccurate information, then the accurate information is useless.

label: Evaluate
body: When authors weigh tradeoffs on a strengthen question, we often want an answer to tell us "the good thing outweighs the bad thing" (or vice versa). The bad thing with regulating the Internet would be that it would spoil the pure unregulated info the Internet currently provides. Access to unregulated info is usually desirable. The good thing about regulating the Internet would be .... Did they say why we should regulate? Their concern with unregulated internet was that it rendered the accurate information useless, because people couldn't separate truth from fiction. How is regulating the internet going to help with people being able to separate truth from fiction? They must be talking about attempting to remove misinformation via regulation. Because we see a conditional word — unless — in the final premise, we should think about how this rule works: if we can't easily distinguish → accurate info real info from fake info is useless When there's a conditional rule in a Strengthen question (not that common), we need to make sure it's actually triggered. So we could strengthen the argument by affirming the trigger, "it's difficult to tell which info is accurate".

label: Goal
body: Look for something saying that we can't easily distinguish accurate info from misinformation, or for an answer weighing tradeoffs, like, "making it more likely that accurate info will be useful is a more important goal than keeping the internet a pure source of unregulated. information".

label: Evidence
body: Some members have criticized the club’s president for inviting Dr. Hines to speak at the annual awards banquet without consulting other club members beforehand. But a few years ago the previous club president hired a tax accountant even though he had not discussed it with club members beforehand.

label: Conclusion
body: So the current president acted appropriately in the way in which she invited Dr. Hines.

label: Evaluate
body: The argument assumes that the examples are similar. Furthermore it assumes that previous club president acted appropriately in hiring the tax consultant.

label: Conclusion (implied rebuttal conclusion)
body: Filterer X water filter effectively removes chemical contaminants in significant amounts.

label: Evidence
body: Millions of Filterer X owners are satisfied with the product's performance.

label: Evaluate
body: We need to challenge the spokesperson's claim that the water filter effectively removes chemical contaminants based on owner satisfaction. We can do this by highlighting that consumer satisfaction isn't necessarily linked to the filter's actual ability to remove contaminants.

label: Goal
body: Find an answer choice that demonstrates why consumer satisfaction does not reliably indicate actual contaminant removal, thus weakening the argument made by the spokesperson.

label: Opposing Point
body: A famous artist once claimed that all great art imitates nature.

label: Premises
body: If this claim is correct, then any music that is great art would imitate nature. But while some music may imitate ocean waves or the galloping of horses, for example, most great music imitates nothing at all.

label: Conclusion
body: The conclusion is implicit and it challenges the famous artist. Either the famous artist is wrong, or the principle is not applicable; if for example, great music is not necessarily great art. While this is not explicitly stated, it is implied by the pivot term “but.”

label: Tamara's Conclusion
body: Most Japanese did fear ninjas.

label: Tamara's Evidence
body: Many wealthy Japanese had their houses constructed with extra-squeaky floors so that they had a better chance of hearing a ninja.

label: Evaluate / Goal
body: If P wants to defend her claim that "most Japanese didn't fear ninjas", what could she say in response? The first thought that comes to my mind is, "cool, so wealthy people feared ninjas. But I said most people. Most people weren't wealthy."

label: Conclusion
body: Moral agency requires free will

label: Evidence
body: Moral agency requires a desire to conform to a principle

label: Evaluate
body: The nonetheless that starts the 2nd sentence shows us that the first sentence is not part of the argument core. The because tells us that the 2nd half of the 2nd sentence is our premise, which makes the 1st half of the 2nd sentence our conclusion. For those of us not acquainted with the nerdy philosophical vernacular of "moral agent / moral agency", it basically means "a capacity for making moral decisions". We would hold a 12 year old accountable for hitting the dog in the face, because she has moral agency, whereas we wouldn't hold her 1 year old brother accountable for hitting the dog in the face, because he doesn't yet have moral agency. The good news is that we could solve this argument formally, even if we didn't understand the constituent ideas. If we're concluding "moral agent must have free will", we either use our knowledge that must = Right Side and write down Moral agent → free will Or we use our knowledge that Required things go on Right to write Moral Agent → Free will (requires) For the premise, we either use our knowledge that Without = If-Not and write down ~Desire to Conform To a Principle → Can't be Moral Agent Or we think through Required things go on Right and write down Moral Agent → Desire to Conform To a Principle

label: Goal
body: Since the conclusion wants to build this logic connection: Moral Agent -—--—--—--—--—--—---> Free Will and the premise has provided us with this: Moral Agent -—-> Desire to Conform to Principle our missing link would be this: Desire to -—--—-> Free Will Conform to Principle Or more conversationally, "Desiring to conform to a principle requires free will"

label: Conclusion
body: In most cases, publishing a scholarly journal must be more profitable now than several years ago.

label: Evidence
body: Over the last several years, the average subscription rate libraries pay for these journals has gone up a bunch, while the costs of publishing the journals have remained constant.

label: Evaluation
body: Given that the average revenue per subscription is higher than before, but the costs per subscription are the same, how could we resist thinking that they're more profitable? We should be very careful with Relative concepts like average / percent / ratio / fraction, and always ask ourselves, "What about the real numbers? If the journals used to be $50 / subscription but now they're $60 / subscription, are we definitely making more money? Only if we're still selling as many subscriptions (technically, as long as we're selling more than 5/6 as many subscriptions in my example but LSAT would never get that mathy).

label: Goal
body: Look for an answer saying that they're not selling as many subscriptions as before.

label: Opposing Evidence
body: Gurney’s books tell interesting stories.

label: Opposing Point
body: Terrence Gurney suggests that because his books appeal to a wide audience, he is not given due credit for his literary achievements.

label: Premise
body: Gurney’s writing is flat, leaving no lasting impression on the reader.

label: Intermediate Conclusion
body: This is likely the reason that Gurney has not received praise for literary achievement.

label: Main Conclusion
body: Surely he is mistaken. rephrase: People aren't refraining from giving TG credit for his literary accomplishments because TG's books are too mainstream.

label: The Paradox
body: Given That Earth's atmosphere had high oxygen, low nitrogen And That lightning only produces amino acids in reducing atmosphere (high hydrogen / low oxy environment) How Could It Be That Lightning produced amino acids?

label: Goal
body: Try to find a way in a high oxy / low nitro atmosphere for there to be a way that lightning could still produce amino acids.

label: Conclusion
body: It was wrong to give the criticism award to Paulsen for auto review.

label: Evidence
body: The award should be given for criticism; Paulsen's auto review was not that. It was about cars, which are utilitarian things, not art. And only art reveals important truths about the producing culture.

label: Evaluate
body: We can think about this conversationally and try to link the author's last two sentences to her goal of establishing that Paulsen's review doesn't count as criticism. Why doesn't it count as criticism? The final idea in her train of thought is that this review of cars is not going to reveal important truths about our culture. So she must be assuming that "criticism needs to try to reveal important truths about the culture that made a given object". Formally, her last two sentences kind of looked like this: Paulsen's → about → not about → won't reveal review cars art objects important culture truths Since her conclusion is trying to establish Paulsen's -—--—--—--—--—--—--—--> ~criticism review we need a principle that provides that final link on the Evidence chain: won't reveal → ~criticism important culture truths

label: Goal
body: "if it doesn't reveal important truths, it's not criticism" or "criticism should reveal important truths"

label: Conclusion
body: Our change in policy to offer free shipping on all times (not just those over $50) caused the recent increase in mail-order sales.

label: Evidence
body: The increase started right around the time we changed our shipping policy.

label: Matilda's Position
body: Matilda agrees the admin is at fault — but draws the opposite conclusion. Since the students didn't cause the problem, they shouldn't pay to fix it.

label: Evaluate
body: This is a Causal Argument, in which the author presents a Curious Fact (why did mail-order sales go up 25% recently) and posits a Causal Explanation (changing our shipping policy led to the more sales). We evaluate all causal arguments by thinking: - how else would we explain the Curious Fact? - how plausible is the Author's Story? What are other ways to explain why sales went up? Better website design? New products? Christmas season? How would we assess the plausibility of the Author's Story? Did customers not like the old shipping policy? Are they aware of the new policy? Were most of the orders before under $50 (thus, they would be affected by the shipping change)?

label: Goal
body: - Rule Out some other way to explain why the sales went up or - Boost the plausibility of the story that the new shipping policy is the causal difference-maker

label: Opposing Point
body: Proponents of nuclear power point out that new nuclear plants are so technologically sophisticated that the chances of a meltdown are extremely small.

label: Evidence
body: The consequences of a meltdown are absolutely catastrophic.

label: Conclusion
body: It would still be unwise to build nuclear power plants.

label: Evaluate
body: The argument reasons by comparing the small chance of a meltdown with the catastrophic consequences of a meltdown and argues that the small chance of the meltdown make the it unwise to take such a risk.

label: Principle
body: research shows some research institutions promise of yielding have an obligation to insights into causes → promote research in of practical problems any field of theoretical affecting quality of life justification

label: Evaluate / Goal
body: This principle only allows us to say that an institution does have an obligation, so if there are any answers saying that an institution doesn't have an obligation, we can immediately discard it. Principles can only be used to support the ideas on their Right sides. We want to hear about research that might yield insights with practical benefit, and then we want to see a conclusion saying "institutions are obliged to (should) promote that research".

label: Apparent Paradox
body: Carpal tunnel syndrome, a nerve disorder that affects the hands and wrists, is often caused by repetitive motions such as typing on a keyboard. A recent study of office workers found that, among those who do similar amounts of typing, workers reporting the least control over their own work had almost three times the risk of developing carpal tunnel syndrome as did those who reported the most control.

label: Evaluate
body: Why would workers with similar amounts of typing experience different likelihoods of developing carpal tunnel syndrome? That carpal tunnel syndrome is often caused by repetitive motions such as typing does not mean that such tasks are the only cause of carpal tunnel syndrome. It’s possible that workers with the least control over their own work are more likely to have one of these other factors that contribute to carpal tunnel syndrome.

label: Principle
body: predisposes people to → telemarketing employee dislike agencies' clients should never do it

label: Application
body: Telemarketing employees should never try to talk a person into buying a client's product, if the person has already told them they don't want the product.

label: Evaluate
body: In (almost) all of these Strengthen-Application questions, the application is concluding the outcome of the Principle. What's missing is clearly establishing the trigger. The application is attempting to conclude that a telemarketing employee should not do something (keep pushing someone to buy someone, after they've already said they don't want it). In order to trigger this principle, we need to establish that an action would "Predispose someone to dislike one of the agency's clients".

label: Goal
body: So we need to hear that "pushing someone to buy a client's product even after they've already said they don't want it" is an action that would "predispose someone to dislike that client".

label: Opposing Point
body: Although Pluto has A + LA an atmosphere and is much larger than any asteroid.

label: Evidence
body: Pluto formed in FAP orbit around the planet Neptune and was then ejected from orbit around Neptune when Triton, Neptune's largest moon, was captured by Neptune's gravity.

label: Conclusion
body: Pluto is not a true ~TP planet.

label: Evaluate
body: The argument TP → ~FAP assumes that true planets do not form around other planets.

label: Apparent Paradox
body: A high-calorie diet providing adequate fats was a crucial requirement for the evolution of the anatomically modern human brain, a process that began among our early human ancestors. Food resources that could support such a diet were most abundant and reliable in the shore environments that were available to early humans. Nevertheless, the human brain's evolution took place almost exclusively in savanna and woodland areas.

label: Evaluate
body: Why would it be that the human brain’s evolution would take place in an area that is not the most abundant and reliable.

label: Editor Y Editor Z
body: This is a good It’s very pretty. photograph: the But it’s a bad composition is photograph. attractive, especially in the way the image is blurred by smoke in one corner. It doesn’t make a statement; there’s no obvious reason for the smoke to be there.

label: Evaluate
body: The editors disagree about whether a photograph is a good one solely because it is attractive.

label: Evidence
body: We will be forced to ~↑E → ↓S reduce spending next year if we do not increase our enrollment. Without [more aggressive] marketing ~↑M → ~↑E we will be unable to increase our enrollment.

label: Conclusion
body: If we are to maintain MQ → ↑M the quality of the education we provide, we must market our programs more aggressively.

label: Evaluate
body: The argument assumes MQ → ~↓S that to maintain the quality of the education the university provides it must not reduce spending next year.

label: Evaluate
body: The argument provides two points on which peach trees have an advantage over apricot trees. If nothing else is considered, peach trees seem like the logical choice. However, if other points are considered and they favor apricots over peaches, the argument could be called into question.

label: Given
body: If the city starts requiring RSM → RWG residents to sort the materials that they put out for recycling, then many residents will put more recyclables in with their regular garbage. This [more recyclables in ↑RG → ↑RL with the garbage] will result in more recyclables being buried in the city's landfill. However, because of the SWB → RSM cost of having city workers do the sorting, the sanitation department will not stay within its budget unless the sorting requirement for residents [sort materials] is implemented.

label: Conclusion
body: The sentinel's behavior is not entirely self-interested / it's at least somewhat altruistic.

label: Evidence
body: Even though the sentinel gets killed by predators less often than the foragers do, the sentinel's loud bark alerts the foraging meerkats to the presence of danger.

label: Evaluate
body: The author is concluding that the sentinel is acting at least somewhat altruistically because its bark warns the other meerkats of danger. If we were trying to argue the anti-conclusion (that the sentinel's behavior is entirely self-interested, not altruistic), then how would we explain the barking? Well, maybe the sentinel just starts barking because he's freaked-out by seeing a predator. The stimulus says the loud bark is emitted as the sentinel dashes for cover. So it's not like the sentinel runs back to the others and says, "I just wanted to warn you, there's a predator coming". It's more like the sentinel gets freaked out, yells "Aaaaaaahhhh!", and dives for cover. Meanwhile, the foraging meerkats hear the yelp of terror and think, "Eddie's scared — there must be a predator."

label: Goal
body: This seems to test a distinction LSAT goes back to a lot (in the top 15, but not top 10 of famous flaws) between Intent vs. Result The barking Results in a beneficial warning to the other meerkats, but the author is acting like we know that the Intent of the barking was to benefit others; it's possible the barking was just an expression of sheer terror. Accordingly, an answer might describe this with Causal flaw language, since the author is concluding one causal interpretation for the barking (trying to warn others) when other possible interpretations are available (involuntary sounds of terror).

label: Alex's 1st Claim
body: Shrimp farming results in damage to the environment. Does Jolene imply that shrimp farming doesn't result in damage to the environment? No. If anything "unsustainable" may be a reference to damaging the environment, so if anything Jolene possibly agrees with Alex here.

label: Alex's 2nd Claim
body: Investors make quick profits on shrimp farms and then abandon the farms. Does Jolene imply that investors don't make quick profits and then abandon the farms? Yes, pretty much. She says that these farms take "a long time to construct and are costly to operate", both of which don't like "not-quick profits". She also says that most owners try to make sure the farms are productive for many years, which sounds like "not-quickly abandoned"

label: Goal
body: Look for an answer that talks about - whether or not shrimp farmers make quick profits and then quickly abandon the farms

label: Evidence
body: No one at LE has gotten ~bad evaluation both a bad performance work at LE → or evaluation and a raise. ~raise Lester hasn't gotten a raise. L = ~raise.

label: Conclusion
body: Lester's had a bad L = bad evaluation performance evaluation

label: Evaluate
body: The flaw in this argument, in technical terms, is that "or" is inclusive. When we say, X → Y or Z, that means that if X is true, then at least one of Y and Z is true (could be both). Our author is interpreting "or" in exclusive terms, that you either are Y or Z, but not both. In conversational terms, the flaw in this argument is that our author fails to consider that when we say "no one has both Y and Z", that means "people only have Y, people only have Z, or people have neither one of them". She is forgetting that last option, that you might lack both. Since Lester lacks "raise" she thinks he must have "bad evaluation", but it's possible he's had neither a raise nor a bad evaluation. Consider how silly this would sound with a more familiar context: Nobody orders a large soda and a large milkshake. Since Denise didn't order a large soda, she must have ordered a large milkshake. (Why? couldn't she have ordered neither of those things?)

label: Goal
body: Look for a flaw that is vulnerable to the objection of "couldn't both things not be the case?", or look to match this structure: X → ~Y or ~Z X is ~Y. Thus, X is Z.

label: Conclusion
body: Insufficient fiber consumption causes colon cancer, and sufficient consumption prevents it.

label: Evidence
body: Several studies show a negative correlation: high-fiber diet || lower incidence of colon cancer Scandinavia: higher colon cancer || less cereal eating (cereal is high fiber)

label: Evaluate
body: Well the conclusion is way too strongly worded. Correlations between X and Y strengthen the plausibility that X causes Y, but they don't prove it (maybe Y causes X / maybe some third factor explains the correlation). The first correlation could be vulnerable to reverse causality (maybe people who have colon cancer are put on low fiber diets). The Scandinavian finding could be easily weakened if we were to learn that even though they don't eat as much cereal, they eat way more fruits and veggies than usual (so they actually do have plenty of fiber in their diets).

label: Goal
body: It's hard to predict which angle the correct answer will take, but it will be some form of Causal-weakener that either - provides a different way to explain the correlation or - undermines the plausibility that eating fiber is good for preventing colon cancer.

label: Opposing Evidence
body: Both humans and chimpanzees evolved from a common ancestor.

label: Opposing Point
body: Chimpanzees are indeed closely related to humans.

label: Evidence
body: Humans did not evolve from chimpanzees.

label: Conclusion
body: It simply does not follow that chimpanzees have anything like human language.

label: Opposing Point
body: Fresh, locally grown apricots are very popular in this area.

label: Evidence
body: Peaches are also very popular in this area. Individual peach trees cost much less to purchase and plant than do apricot trees. Peach trees also begin bearing fruit at a much younger age.

label: Conclusion
body: Planting peach trees on their farm makes more sense for the Johnsons than planting apricot trees.

label: Apparent Paradox
body: For years, a rare variety of camel was endangered because much of its habitat was used as a weapons testing range. After the testing range closed, however, the population of these camels began falling even more quickly.

label: Evaluate
body: After the testing range was closed, the population of these camels began falling even more quickly than when the camel was protected. Things went from bad to worse. How could this be? Anything that would increase the challenges facing this species of camel would help to explain the turn for the worse experienced by this species of camel.

label: Conclusion (thus)
body: It is better to read fewer books and spend more time on each than to read as many books as you can.

label: Evidence
body: The author draws an analogy between reading new books and traveling to new places, suggesting that both activities aim to enlarge understanding.

label: Evaluate
body: This is a "Strengthen" question focusing on an analogy between reading books and traveling. To bolster this analogy, seek additional evidence that supports the strategy of focusing on fewer books or places for deeper comprehension. We are particularly interested in highlighting cases where spending more time on fewer subjects leads to a better understanding.

label: Goal
body: Look for an answer that supports the analogy by showing that focusing deeply on a few subjects (in reading or traveling) is more effective for understanding, compared to quickly skimming through many.

label: The Paradox
body: Given That they're of the same size and same quality Why Is It That the modular (multi-piece) version of a sofa costs almost twice as much as the standard (one-piece) version of a sofa?

label: Goal
body: We need to eliminate four answers that explain why modular furniture costs so much more than standard furniture (can't use bigger or better materials).

label: Given
body: Antibiotics are standard A -causes↣ ↑M ingredients in animal feed because they keep animals healthy and increase meat yields. Scientists have recommended phasing out this practice, believing it may make antibiotics less effective in humans. If meat yields are ↓M → FLB reduced, however, some farmers will go out of [lose their] business.

label: Guideline
body: If influencing the award of a official contract, or performing other → shouldn’t job-related acts, would appear do it to benefit a public official

label: Application’s Conclusion
body: The mayor shouldn’t have influenced the awarding of the street maintenance contract to a company owned and operated by one of the mayor’s relatives.

label: Application’s Evidence
body: That relative’s business would have been in serious financial trouble had it not been awarded the contract.

label: Evaluate
body: On all the Strengthen-Application questions (there aren’t that many of them), the Application concludes the right side of the Principle / Guideline. What’s missing, what we’re meant to evaluate, is how the Application fell short of triggering the left side of the Principle. Did the application establish that the mayor influenced the awarding of a contract in a way that benefits or appears to benefit herself? No, it just hinted at that by saying that contract was a lifesaver for the business of one of the mayor’s relatives.

label: Goal
body: We just need to get from the application language of “awarding this contract helped save a relative from serious financial trouble” to the trigger language of “this benefits, or appears to benefit, the mayor”.

label: Conclusion
body: Sarah must use the pool at City Gym at least sometimes.

label: Evidence
body: To use that pool you have to have a membership to City Gym, and Sarah has a membership to City Gym.

label: Evaluate
body: Those of us who have been members of fitness clubs probably know that just because you pay for a membership doesn't mean you use all the stuff at the fitness club. Maybe Sarah just goes for free weights and yoga and never uses the pool. So conversationally, our objection might sound like, "Just because she has the option of using the pool doesn't mean she uses it. Maybe she has a membership there for the sake of using other stuff." But since we have conditional logic (to do X, you must Y) and this is Flaw, we should consider whether this is the famous Necessary vs. Sufficient flaw, in which an author presents a conditional relationship and then applies it using illegal backwards or opposite logic. The author presents a conditional: Use Pool at CG → Membership Then he illicitly argues, Since Sarah has Membership, Sarah Use Pool That's applying the conditional rule in an illegal backwards fashion, in other words, confusing the Sufficient and Necessary conditions.

label: Goal
body: Look for a Necessary vs. Sufficient answer or one pointing out that Sarah might a membership but not use the pool.

label: Annie's Conclusion
body: The univ admin should admit their policies were messed up and fix it the fastest way possible, which is charging students a library fee.

label: Annie's Evidence
body: The univ libraries have been neglected, with few new books purchased and most of the older books damaged.

label: Evaluating Matilda's Response
body: Does she disagree with any Annie's explicit claims? Is she arguing: - the libraries haven't been neglected? - lots of new books have been bought? - most of the older books are in fine condition? - the admin shouldn't admit their policies were bad? - they shouldn't remedy the situation the fastest way possible, by charging students a library fee? It seems like Matilda is arguing that last position. She doesn't think the student fee is fair, because the problem isn't the fault of the students.

label: Goal
body: Let's look for an answer addressing whether or not we should charge the students a library fee, in order to fix the libraries.

label: Annie
body: Charge students a fee — fastest way to fix the libraries.

label: Matilda
body: It's not the students' fault, so they shouldn't pay.

label: Anticipate
body: Disagreement: should those not responsible (students) pay to fix the problem?

label: Goal
body: An answer Annie supports and Matilda denies — about non-responsible parties bearing the cost.

label: Conclusion
body: Many residents must have forgotten consulting their physician for headaches.

label: Anticipate
body: So they actually agree on who caused the problem. Where they disagree is on who should pay for fixing it. Annie says: students should pay (it's the fastest fix). Matilda says: students shouldn't pay (they didn't cause the problem).

label: Goal
body: Find an answer that Annie endorses and Matilda denies — about whether the non-responsible party should bear the cost of fixing the problem.

label: Information
body: Diamonds, formed on Earth, about 2.9 billion years ago had a higher than normal concentration of sulfur-33. causal (X can be explained only by Y) chemical reactions ⇢ higher than normal stimulated by UV concent of sulfur-33 conditional (if = left side) more than a trace not enough UV of oxygen in Earth's ⇢ to reach Earth's atmosphere 2.9 billion surface to stim chem reactions

label: Evaluate
body: Whenever we see a conditional on an Inference question, we ask ourselves two questions: 1. are there other conditionals here that could be chained up with this? 2. is there any fact that triggers this conditional (or more frequently, its contrapositive)? Of the first three sentences, only the 3rd could seemingly be translated into a conditional. We would say, higher than normal → chem reactions concentration of S-33 stim by UV Whether we think of that 3rd sentence as a conditional chain or think of it as a causal fact, it definitely interacts with the last sentence, if we contrapose it: enough UV light reached less than a Earth's surface to stim → trace of oxy chemical reactions in Earth's atmos We know that sulfur-33's concentration was higher, which was caused by chemical reactions stimulated by UV. According to the contrapositive of this last sentence, this means that "there was less than a trace of oxygen in Earth's atmosphere 2.9 billion years ago".

label: Goal
body: By applying the contrapositive of that last sentence to the facts presented before it, we derived that "there was less than a trace of oxygen in Earth's atmosphere 2.9 billion years ago", so that's likely to be what the correct answer is testing. But as always, we'll stay flexible and pick whichever answer we can best support.

label: Doctor's Initial Hypothesis
body: First dosage was insufficient.

label: Support
body: When patient took the initial dosage, their symptoms remained. Even when they stopped drinking their herbal beverage, their symptoms remained at the initial dosage. While doubling the dosage didn't work on its own, doubling the dosage in tandem with quitting the herbal beverage made the symptoms disappear.

label: Evaluate
body: What was the second set of recommendations? She first advised doubling the dosage. She then advised "resuming initial dosage but stopping herbal beverage". What was the point of that? It was to rule out the possibility that dosage wasn't the problem, herbal interference was. The results showed that even after the patient quit the herbal drink, the initial dosage still wasn't producing any effect. Ultimately, the doctor came to realize that both the herbal drink and the initial dosage were to blame. First dosage / Yes herbal: didn't work First dosage / No herbal: didn't work Double dosage / Yes herbal: didn't work Double dosage / No herbal: did work Neither doubling the dosage nor quitting the herbal drink were sufficient on their own to made the meds work, but doing both together did make the meds work, so they both had an influence.

label: Goal
body: Look for something like, "Ruled out the idea that the first dosage's failure to work could be blamed (exclusively) on the herbal drink".

label: Conclusion
body: Papercrete is probably a great option for large-scale construction.

label: Evidence
body: Even though most builders would disagree, builders who regularly work with papercrete (mostly on small-scale stuff) think it is a good option, and people who regularly use papercrete are familiar with its properties.

label: Evaluate
body: This is a He Said / She Said type argument, in that the author presents two opposing points of view, which sets up a "Well — who should we trust?" type feeling. Sometimes author's 'pick a winner' without justifying their choice. Here, the author is like, "I believe the people who think papercrete is promising for large-scale, because they regularly work with it and people who regularly work with it are familiar with its properties." This argument could potentially be described as a self-selecting sample. The papercrete enthusiasts primarily use it on small-scale stuff, but that implicitly means they sometimes use it on large-scale stuff. If they use it on large-scale stuff sometimes, then by definition they think it's promising for large-scale stuff. So why should the author trust their biased assessment over that of most builders?

label: Goal
body: Look for an answer that helps us stick up for "most builders" side of the He Said / She Said battle, or make the author's reason for choosing the Enthusiast side of the battle seem like a poor justification for picking.

label: Conclusion
body: None of last year's plays will be popular several centuries from now.

label: Evidence
body: The only plays that continue to be performed regularly over many decades and centuries are those that skillfully explore human nature, and none of last year's plays skillfully explore human nature.

label: Evaluate
body: It's pretty tough to even diagnose what's intended to be the Conclusion vs. the Evidence. We know the first sentence is a fact. The second sentence makes three predictions (predictions are always opinions), so any of those claims could have been a conclusion, but the author didn't offer any support for why "some will gain popularity" or why "some will receive high critical acclaim". She pivots with a "but", and usually in arguments, pivots like "but, yet, however" indicate that everything before the pivot was NOT the argument, and everything following it IS the argument. Her last prediction in that sentence is that "none of last year's plays will be popular several centuries from now". Why should we believe that? She supports this prediction with the last two claims, which combine a conditional rule about "what will be regularly performed centuries from now" and then a fact about last year's plays that triggers that conditional. Whenever we read two consecutive claims that chain together or that synthesize into one takeaway, we should pause and perform that step. The 2nd to last claim is a conditional: continue to be regularly → skillfully examine performed for centuries human nature ~skillfully examine → ~continue to be regularly human nature performed for centuries And the last claim is a fact (or a conditional, if you want to think of it that way) that triggers that contrapositive: Last year's plays → ~skillfully examine We can chain those two together, or if you prefer, we can apply that rule we were given to the fact we were told about last year's plays. Either way you slice it, the synthesis is this: Last year's plays are not going to be performed regularly over many decades and centuries. How does that compare to the conclusion the author derives? Last year's plays are not going to be popular several centuries from now. Comparing the inference we get from the final sentence to the inference the author thinks we get, in her conclusion, allows us to see a gap.

label: Goal
body: The author is going from If it's not performed regularly over many decades and centuries, then it's not going to be popular several centuries from now.

label: Conclusion
body: It's wrong for medical researchers to keep their research confidential.

label: Evidence
body: If they don't share their research, it might take longer to develop effective treatments, and thus in the meantime humans may suffer unnecessarily.

label: Evaluation
body: Any time we're saying, "You shouldn't do X, because X ultimately leads to Y", we're assuming that "you shouldn't do something that results in Y." Here we're saying "You shouldn't withhold your research, or else it'll delay treatments and people will suffer."

label: Goal
body: So we're looking for something like, "You shouldn't do something that will delay treatments or cause people to suffer."

label: Marife's 1st Claim
body: That was a bad movie Does N argue it wasn't bad (it was good)? Not quite. We can't really derive N's opinion about whether or not this movie was good overall.

label: Marife's 2nd Claim
body: It didn't provide viewers with all the information necessary to solve the murder. Does N argue that it did provide enough info? No, it almost seems more like N is agreeing to this idea.

label: Marife's 3rd Claim
body: Not providing viewers with enough info to solve the murder is a violation of a requirement of murder mysteries. Does N argue that it isn't a requirement of murder mysteries to provide enough info to solve the murder? No, N doesn't say anything like that.

label: Evaluate
body: Since we got through all of Marife's explicit claims and didn't find any disagreement from Nguyen, we turn to ask ourselves, "Okay, well what assumptions was Marife making? Maybe Nguyen disagreed with one of those." M's argument says, because that movie violated a requirement of murder mysteries, we can conclude that was a bad movie. What is M assuming there? - this movie was a murder mystery - if you violate a requirement of the genre you're in, then you're automatically a bad movie Does N object to either of these ideas? Is N arguing either of these claims? - this movie was not a murder mystery - you can violate a requirement of the genre, but still be a not-bad movie Yes! It seems like N is arguing that the move was not a murder mystery, since he says that the murder just provided context and should not be taken as a defining characteristic of the film.

label: Goal
body: Let's look for an answer saying something like, "they disagree over whether this movie should be analyzed as though it is a murder mystery".

label: Evidence
body: Experimental educational programs, based on the principle that children’s first education should take place at home, instruct parents in how to be their child’s “first teacher.” The school performance of the children in these programs is better than average.

label: Conclusion
body: Experimental educational programs, based on the principle that children’s first education should take place at home, are successful and should be expanded.

label: Evaluate
body: The argument establishes a correlation between experimental educational programs better than average school performance. This argument fails to consider alternative causes of the better than average performance or whether expanding programs to more children would yield similar results.

label: Conclusion
body: It's permissible to ban an anarchist novel that would do more harm than good.

label: Evidence
body: All anarchist novels have a subversive outlook and depict wholesale violence.

label: Evaluate
body: There are two traits we know about anarchist novels, so the principle would need to take either or both of those traits and get us to the idea of, "permissible to ban". The weird thing is that the conclusion is not about all anarchist novels; it's about the subset of them that would do more harm than good.

label: Goal
body: "If it would do more harm than good, and if it has a subversive outlook or depicts wholesale violence, or both, then it's permissible to ban it"

label: Evidence
body: In '96, all RT projects were during time X, funded by govt or private All A's were contractors B or C The GS, was an RT project this thing was an in '96, and was not funded A during time X, by govt and was not B.

label: Conclusion
body: Thus GS was funded by this thing was A private contractors

label: Evaluate / Goal
body: We need a premise that sets out a conditional with an either / or outcome. If you fit a certain set of criteria, then you're X or Y. Then we need to hear that something fits that criteria, but isn't X. Then we conclude that this thing must be Y.

label: Conclusion
body: Life may have come to Earth from Mars.

label: Evidence
body: There was this period where Earth was getting pummeled by comets and asteroids and couldn't possibly support life. Meanwhile, Mars was in the clear. It could have had microbial life. Sometimes chunks of Mars fall off and fly over to Earth, so they could have served as the transport mechanism for these microbes.

label: Evaluate
body: The author is just pitching a theory here. Since there was a period way back when, during which Earth was inhospitable for life but Mars was good to go ... , simple microbial life may have actually started on Mars and then gotten randomly carried to Earth on top of a meteorite. The claim they're asking us about is part of the author's Support. The hypothesis is that "Life originated on Earth, because a meteorite with microbial life from Mars landed on Earth." The claim that "Mars could have had microbial life" is a necessary assumption of this hypothesis. The author says it to establish the plausibility of her causal story.

label: Goal
body: Look for something sounding like "supports the hypothesis that life came to Earth via a meteorite from Mars, by establishing the plausibility that life could have come from Mars."

label: Conclusion
body: Gardeners with no use for honey will not have excellent pollination

label: Intermediate Conclusion
body: Gardeners with no use for honey will tend not to have beehives

label: Evidence
body: Keeping bees is economical keep use only if use for bees → for homegrown honey. econ honey Establishing beehive beehive → bees ensures presence of bees. present Presence of bees is excellent bees necessary for excellent pollination → present pollination. Excellent pollination usually results in abundant fruits and veggies

label: Evidence
body: 35 residents self-reported, but physician records show 105 consultations.

label: Evaluate
body: Good God, what a train wreck. So many premises! And two conclusions. Let's try to focus on what each conclusion is trying to prove. The intermediate conclusion is saying, "if you don't have use for honey, you probably won't have a beehive". What did the evidence tells us? "If you don't have use for honey, keeping bees is not economical." So the author is definitely assuming that "if keeping bees is not economical, you probably won't have a beehive". Maybe people have such passion for bees that they want to keep beehives even though it's not economical to do so. The main conclusion is saying "if you don't have a beehive, you won't have excellent pollination". What did the evidence tell us about excellent pollination? It said "if you don't have bees present, you won't have excellent pollination". So the author is assuming that "if you don't have a beehive, you won't have bees present". Wait a sec — was this a rule we were told? Close. We were told "if you do have a beehive, you will have bees present". So this author is doing an illegal negation, or what LSAT calls a Necessary vs. Sufficient flaw. We were told that beehives are sufficient to ensure the presence bees. We were never told that they are necessary to have bees. Maybe a lovely flower garden would be enough to attract bees.

label: Goal
body: Look for an answer testing the move from Premise to Intermediate Conclusion (just because having no use for honey would make beekeeping uneconomical, can we really say most of those people wouldn't have a beehive?), or for an answer testing the move from Intermediate Conclusion to Main Conclusion (just because they wouldn't have a beehive, does that mean they wouldn't have bees around, and thus wouldn't have excellent pollination?)

label: Conclusion
body: It's wrong to say that "expressing something true contributes to the aesthetic merit of a poem". (i.e. expressing something true does not contribute to the aesthetic merit of a poem)

label: Evidence
body: Most commonplace beliefs are true, and the basis of poetic excellence must be rare, not common.

label: Evaluate / Goal
body: We're being asked about the last sentence, which is a Premise, so we'll look for an answer that sounds like "Support for the conclusion that saying something true doesn't contribute to aesthetic merit" (in Role questions, the Conclusion is only the last claim about 10% of the time. 90% of the time the last claim is part of the Support)

label: Evidence
body: Three million dollars was recently stolen from the City Treasurer’s Office. The suspects are all S → ECT former employees of the City Treasurer’s Office. The mayor’s staff MS ↢some↣ ECT includes former employees of that office [the City Treasury].

label: Conclusion
body: Some members of the MS ↢some↣ S mayor’s staff are suspects.

label: Evaluate
body: The argument reverses the second premise. If it were the case that all former employees of the City Treasurer’s Office are suspects, then the conclusion would be valid.

label: Background
body: People wonder why Stradivarius violins from the early 1700s are superior to most other violins. Some say secret varnishes, but there's no evidence. Pivot (however) Climatologists have found that in the 1600s and 1700s, there were weather patterns in the area where Stradivarius worked that affected tree growth to produce wood with special acoustic properties.

label: Evaluate
body: What could we reasonably infer by combining the ideas? In particular, when the last claim of an Inference paragraph has a Pivot word attached, the tested inference is almost always what you get by Reconciling the Pivot idea with what came before it. People are trying to solve the mystery of why Stradivarius violins are so superior. Is the causal difference-maker a secret varnish? There no evidence to suggest it is. But there is evidence that the wood near Stradivarius's workshop had special acoustic properties.

label: Goal
body: So, it seems like this is heading towards the idea that, "Stradivarius violins are superior to most others probably because they're made from wood with special acoustic properties"? We want the most safely worded version of that.

label: Conclusion
body: Prof S doesn't need to make an official determination about whether Walters committed plagiarism.

label: Evidence
body: As incomes rise, more people spend money on energy-consuming devices such as cars, thereby producing more carbon dioxide. Also, in countries that experienced deep economic recessions, there were steep drops in carbon dioxide emissions.

label: Conclusion
body: Prosperity is a driving force behind increases in the release of carbon dioxide, the main cause of global warming.

label: Evaluate
body: The argument is designed to support a causal relationship between economic prosperity and increases in the release of carbon dioxide. The word “also” implies that the second and third statements both support the first statement.

label: Conclusion
body: Our group's "Clean City" campaign has been a rousing success.

label: Evidence (after all)
body: The amount of trash on the city's streets today is significantly lower than when the campaign began.

label: Evaluate
body: If we wanted to articulate the Linking assumption going down, it would sound like, If today's street trash then campaign level is much lower → was a rousing than before campaign success But it's more likely that this type of causal interpretation is testing our ability to think through the lens of causality, not conditional logic. The evidence presents a Curious Fact (an asymmetric comparison): Why is there way less trash on the streets nowadays than there was when the "Clean City" campaign first started? And then the author's conclusion implies a causal assumption. His explanation for why there's less trash is that the campaign successfully caused people to behave differently, in such a way that there's less trash on the streets. We always evaluate Explain Curious Fact arguments along their two pressure points: 1. could there be some Alternate Explanation for the curious fact? 2. how plausible is the Author's Explanation? Goal Look for an answer ruling out an Alternate Explanation for why there's less trash on the street nowadays. (e.g. "there are not way fewer people living in the city now than when the campaign began") Or look for an answer dealing with some idea that is necessary for the author's explanation to seem plausible (e.g. the Clean City campaign had at least some messaging that related to getting trash off the streets).

label: Given that ...
body: Consuming sugar causes the level of unmetabolized sugar in the blood to rise.

label: How can it be that ...
body: People who consume large amounts of sugar tend to have below-average levels of unmetabolized sugar in their blood.

label: Evaluate
body: This is sort of a Relative vs. Absolute paradox. Consuming sugar makes the level of unmetabolized sugar in the blood higher than it was before eating sugar. But people who consume a lot of sugar have low average unmetabolized sugar in their blood. Maybe there are certain people whose bodies naturally have very low unmetabolized sugar in the blood. And because they're bodies start off with such low blood sugar, they consume more sugar than the rest of us. Consuming that sugar raises their blood sugar from very low to below-average. We could use a similar analogy with LSAT studying. "Practicing logic games helps you to increase your score at logic games. Yet people who do large amounts of practicing logic games tend to have below-average scores on the LG section." We could resolve the paradox similarly by saying, "People who are already crushing LG don't need to practice as much. People who are super-struggling with LG are the ones more likely to practice LG. So even though their practice is improving their LG scoring ability, their LG scoring ability is still lower than average".

label: Goal
body: Let's look for an answer that gives us a way to describe a person who eats a lot of sugar but still has below-average levels of blood sugar.

label: Evidence
body: Without competition, a corporation can raise prices without spending nearly as much on advertising. The corporation can then invest the extra money in expensive research or industrial infrastructure that it could not otherwise afford, passing the fruits of these investments on to consumers.

label: Conclusion
body: Consumers often benefit when government permits a corporation to obtain a monopoly.

label: Evaluate
body: The economist is quick to point out a potential benefit of letting a corporation obtain a monopoly. But there are likely to be drawbacks as well. The economist mentioned that the corporation would raise its prices. Do consumers believe the fruits of expensive research outweigh the higher prices? The economist assumes that they do.

label: Statements
body: Causal (by) Drying and mounting → displays of wild animal skins animals Causal (because) low humidity and → skins are deteriorating heat of lights Comparison (older vs. newer) Older Newer lit by tungsten lit by compact fluorescent same light given off more heat less heat

label: Evaluate
body: We read Inference statements primarily looking for overlapping ideas, usually relating to Conditional / Causal / Comparative type language. We talked about displays of animals skins and we talked about the different lamps used, and in both cases (haha, no pun intended), we talked about the heat given off by the lights. When we were hearing about a Causal Difference-Maker, we learned that the heat given off by the lights was starting to cause the animals' skins to deteriorate. In this Comparison, the old tungsten give off more heat than the new compact fluorescent. So by applying what we learned from the Causal Difference-Maker, the old tungsten leads to more deterioration of the skins than does the new compact fluorescent.

label: Goal
body: It's tough to know exactly where this will go, but it seems like they would want us to prove we see the connection between different lamps giving off different amounts of heat and how heat from the light affects the deterioration of the animal skins.

label: Conclusion
body: The number of species on Earth is probably not dwindling (i.e. the number of species is probably holding steady or going up)

label: Evidence
body: About as many species will go extinct this year as went extinct in 1970. And the number of new species will emerge this year will be about the same as the per/year average of the last few hundred centuries.

label: Evaluate
body: The truth value of this conclusion is purely mathematical. Every year we gain species and lose species. We just need to know if right now we're at "net gain" or "net loss". So how do we evaluate if we're gaining more species than we're losing or vice versa. We're gaining whatever the average # of new species / year has been for the past few centuries. We're losing whatever number of species went extinct in 1970.

label: Goal
body: Since the author is assuming we're gaining more than we're losing, she must be assuming this comparison: Average number of number of new species per year → species lost in (over the last few 1970 centuries) We could weaken the argument by making it seem like 1970 was a year with a "net loss", where the number of species lost outweighed the number of species gained. No matter what, our answer needs to help us argue that the number of species on Earth is dwindling.

label: Principle
body: Burden of proposed policy change policy change would → shouldn't fall disproportionately on be made people with low incomes

label: Application's Conclusion
body: The policy change of reintroducing rock salt as a road de-icing agent should not be made (should be halted).

label: Evaluate
body: In order to use this principle in order to conclude that the plan to reintroduce rock salt as a road de-icing agent should not happen, we have to establish the trigger. Have we established that reintroducing rock salt as a de-icing agent is a policy change whose burden would fall disproportionately on people with low incomes? Not at all. That's what we need our answer to do.

label: Goal
body: Pick whichever answer best convinces us that reintroducing rock salt as a de-icing agent will have a burden that falls disproportionately on people with lower incomes. All we know about this policy change is - we used to do it a while ago - we stopped doing it because it accelerated corrosion of automobiles - cars are now better protected from salt's corrosive properties

label: Conclusion
body: Many residents who consulted physicians for severe headaches did not remember doing so.

label: Evidence
body: 35 residents reported consulting their physician for severe headaches last year, but physicians' records show 105 consultations for severe headaches.

label: Evaluate
body: The argument equates "105 consultations" with "105 different residents." But one resident could have visited multiple times for the same condition. If the average resident with severe headaches went three times, only 35 distinct residents account for the 105 consultations — exactly matching the self-reported count, with nobody forgetting anything.

label: Goal
body: An answer pointing out that the same resident might have had multiple visits — i.e., the argument confuses number of consultations with number of patients.

label: Evidence
body: The math: 35 people said yes, but the records show 105 consultations. So 70 of those visits must have been forgotten.

label: Evaluate
body: Wait — that math has a problem. The author treats "105 consultations" as if it means "105 different patients." But one patient with chronic headaches might visit the doctor three times in a year. If you have 35 patients each visiting three times on average, you get 105 consultations and 35 distinct patients. Nobody forgot anything. It's like counting ten coffees sold and concluding ten different customers came in. Maybe one customer came back three times.

label: Goal
body: An answer that points out the same residents could have had multiple consultations.

label: Conclusion (thus)
body: Business executives have become public officials.

label: Evidence
body: In a free market, corporate executives make significant decisions about industrial technology, work organization, location of industries, and resource allocation. Despite being subject to consumer control, they decide on what to produce and in what quantities.

label: Evaluate
body: GIVEN THAT, business execs are making a bunch of decisions that affect the country at large, HOW CAN WE ARGUE they have not become public officials? One way to weaken this argument is to challenge the notion that the duties performed by executives align with what defines a public official.

label: Goal
body: Identify an answer that shows a key difference between the roles or responsibilities of business executives and public officials, thereby breaking the assumed equivalency in the argument.

label: Conclusion ("no doubt" = clearly)
