body: One effect of science fiction has been to create an unproductive dissatisfaction with the way the world actually is.

label: Evidence (since)
body: Gaps between expectations and reality spur discontent. Science fiction creates an appetite for interstellar space exploration, but that's not going to happen with any technology humanity will soon possess.

label: Evaluate
body: On Assumption questions, it's a very powerful habit to ask ourselves, "Is there a New Concept in the Conclusion"? Because, if so, the correct answer will usually deal with that concept. By "New", we mean, "it was never talked about in the evidence". This conclusion talks about "sci-fi" and talks about "an unproductive dissatisfaction with the way the world actually is". Did the evidence talk about "sci-fi"? Yes, we have a premise saying that sci-fi creates an appetite for interstellar space exploration (which won't be satisfied anytime soon). Did the evidence talk about "an unproductive dissatisfaction with the way the world actually is"? Certainly not in those words. But the final premise before the conclusion is talking about discontent, which is an equivalent synonym for dissatisfaction. Is the "discontent" being talked about a discontent "with the way the world actually is"? Sure, the premise is talking about a gap between expectation and reality. So to be discontent about that gap is to be dissatisfied with how reality measures up to our expectations. Since there isn't a New Concept in the Conclusion, since both of them are actually talked about in the evidence, that tells us that this argument is missing a Link Between Premises. While we don't have to formally diagram the argument, the visual might help. The conclusion represents this logic path: Sci-fi -—--—--—--—--—--—--—---> Discontent The premises have established these two parts of that path: appetite gap between Sci-fi --> for space expectation --> Discontent travel & reality What we're missing is a connection from idea 2 to idea 3. appetite gap between for space → expectation travel & reality If you hate all that formal logic, then play Opposing Counsel and argue that, "Sci-fi has not created some discontent with the world." This lawyer is arguing that it has, because gaps between expectations and reality spur discontent. So you need to argue that, "Sci-fi has not created a gap between expectation and reality". This lawyer will say, "Of course it has! Sci-fi has created an appetite for space exploration, and we know in reality we won't have that capacity any time soon." So you need to argue that, "Having an appetite for space travel isn't the same as having an expectation of space travel. I have an appetite for ripe watermelon three meals a day, 365 days a year, but I have no expectation of having constant ripe watermelon in reality."

label: Goal
body: Look for an answer saying that the author assumes "the people who have this appetite for space travel now have an expectation of space travel that has created a gap between expectation and reality".

label: Conclusion
body: You can't explain the recent trend among medical professionals toward being susceptible to fraudulent marketing claims by saying that they don't have the medical knowledge necessary to see through the seller's fraudulent claims.

label: Evidence
body: The medical professionals have no lack of medical knowledge.

label: Evaluate
body: The argument itself is pretty short and sweet. You can't explain X's behavior by citing Y. After all, Y wouldn't apply to X. In more generic Method language, we could say that Tamika "rules out one possible explanation for a phenomenon by showing that this explanation would be inapplicable to this phenomenon".

label: Goal
body: Look for any answer whose wording we can match up with the argument.

label: Evidence
body: Managers of corporations SW have an obligation to serve shareholders as the shareholders would want to be served.

label: Conclusion
body: Therefore, corporate SBI managers have an obligation to act in the shareholders’ best interest.

label: Evaluate
body: The argument assumes SW → SBI that the way shareholders want to be served is in their best interest.

label: Conclusion
body: Tagar's view cannot be right (it's wrong to say that the mysterious structures on this meteorite are not fossilized bacteria just because they're 0.1% the volume of Earth's smallest bacteria)

label: Evidence
body: According to Widerski and Tagar, Martian bacteria would shrink to 0.1% of their normal volume, if water or other nutrients were in short supply.

label: Evaluate
body: Since the author is trying to make these two positions seem mutually exclusive, I would probably be tempted to figure out how they could both simultaneously be true. How do we know that what W and T claim about Martian bacteria is even relevant to the stuff we're looking at on the meteorite? Is that stuff thought to be Martian bacteria? Is Martian bacteria's smallest size comparable to Earth bacteria's smallest size? Would the stuff on meteorite, if it were bacteria, have been in short supply of water or other nutrients?

label: Goal
body: I would honestly be confused about what we're looking for here and go to the answer choices for help. I know that our correct answer should help us fight the author's conclusion, so in this case it should help us argue that Tagar could be right.

label: Given
body: Any good garden compost GGC → SDF may appropriately be used for soil drainage and fertility. The best compost is 40 to BC → 40-60% + DB 60 percent organic matter and is dark brown in color. However, compost that SA → ~SDF emits a strong ammonia SA → ~D smell should not be used for drainage and fertility, for that smell means that the organic matter has not sufficiently decomposed.

label: Conclusion
body: The test pilot flying the plane tomorrow probably won't find it difficult to operate the plane.

label: Conclusion
body: If we don't get more funding from non-profit institutions, then the chemistry department is unlikely to gain the prestige that only basic science achievements can bring (i.e. the chemistry department is unlikely to make any significant advances in basic science).

label: Evidence
body: If we at this chemistry department don't get more funding for basic research, this chemistry department is unlikely to make significant advances in basic science. Currently, nearly all our funding comes from for-profit institutions.

label: Evaluate
body: There is a New Term in the Conclusion ("prestige"). New terms in the Conclusion on Assumption questions are a big deal. The correct answer almost always involves that new idea. But that's only if the new idea is central to what the author is trying to prove in her conclusion, only if the truth value of the conclusion hinges on that new idea. In this case, 'prestige' is a meaningless toss-on. The argument is just trying to reiterate the same concept as before "unlikely that any significant advances in basic research will come out of the department". It's just adding some dramatic flourish by talking about what this lack of achievements will cost us. We don't have to call out the idea that the author is assuming "if we don't have basic science achievements, we won't have prestige", because his language explicitly says that: only achievements in basic science can confer the type of prestige he's talking about. So we should get prestige of our docket and worry mainly about the case of, "If we don't get more funding from nonprofit institutions, are we really screwed? Are they our only hope of getting more funding?" The author seems to be making a move from "if we can't get more funding from Big Pharm and for-profit institutions, then we have to get it from nonprofit institutions." Is that a False Choice? For-profit vs. nonprofit is an all encompassing binary when it comes to institutions, but what about individual donors? Could the chemistry department get more funding for basic research by rich, individual philanthropists making donations? The argument is assuming "no, not enough". The argument is also assuming that "we can't get more funding from Big Pharm and for-profit institutions." Did it ever say we can't? No, it just conversationally implied that asking them was a dead end, but arguments need to establish assumptions like that.

label: Goal
body: Look for an answer ruling out the objection of "could we get more funding from the for-profit institutions?" or an answer ruling out the objection of "could we get more funding from donations from wealthy individuals?"

label: Given
body: In order to save money, many consumers redeem coupons that are distributed by retail stores. However, in general, retail stores that distribute and accept store coupons as a way of discounting the prices on certain products charge more for their products, on average, than other retail stores charge for the same products even after lower prices available on coupon-discounted products are factored in. This is because producing and distributing coupons usually costs a great deal. To compensate for this expense without reducing profits, retail stores must pass it on to consumers.

label: Conclusion
body: Birth-order has no lasting effect on personality; it just affects how a sibling's behavior is perceived.

label: Evidence
body: If you test adults using standard personality tests, then birth-order does not seem to have any effect on personality. But if you test adults by asking for responses from parents and siblings, you'll notice differences based on birth order.

label: Evaluate
body: This is a He Said / She Said type argument. The author presents two different things that have different views on a subject. She then arbitrarily acts like one of them is the correct view, without justifying why that view has more credibility than the conflicting view. We usually see this in Flaw: "Although older studies say eggs are unhealthy, newer studies say eggs are healthy. Therefore, we should all start eating more eggs." How do we know the newer studies are correct and old ones are wrong? Does "newer = more likely correct"? In this argument, does "standard personality test = probably the correct data", whereas "asking parents / siblings = less trustworthy data"?

label: Goal
body: Look for an answer saying that the author assumes the standard personality test provides more accurate data than the interviews with siblings and parents do.

label: Evidence
body: If the jury did not ~RV → MT return a verdict, there would still be media trucks outside the courthouse. There are no media ~MT trucks outside the courthouse.

label: Conclusion
body: The jury must have RV returned a verdict.

label: Evaluate
body: This argument reasons by way of contrapositive and is a valid argument.

label: Given
body: A salesperson who makes a sale does not change the desires of the customer. Rather, the salesperson finds out what these desires are and then convinces the customer that a particular product will satisfy them. Persuading people to vote for a politician to whom they are initially indifferent is not significantly different.

label: Most Supported
body: After discovering what policies the prospective voter would like to see in place, one tries to _______

label: Conclusion
body: She is wrong. rephrase: My pesticides are not spreading to her farm in runoff water

label: Evidence
body: I use only organic pesticides, which are seemingly harmless to people or domestic animals. Also, I am careful to avoid spraying on my neighbor's land.

label: Evidence
body: Unless the building permit LC → OP or OALT is obtained by February 1 of this year or some of the other activities necessary for construction of the new library can be completed in less time than originally planned, the new library will not be completed on schedule. It is now clear that the ~OP building permit cannot be obtained by February 1.

label: Conclusion
body: So the new library will ~LC not be completed on schedule.

label: Evaluate
body: The argument assumes ~OALT that the other activities necessary for construction of the new library cannot be completed in less time.

label: Evidence
body: In a study of patients who enrolled at a sleep clinic because of insomnia, those who inhaled the scent of peppermint before going to bed were more likely to have difficulty falling asleep than were patients who inhaled the scent of bitter orange. It is known that inhaling bitter orange does not help people fall asleep more easily.

label: Conclusion
body: This study shows that inhaling the scent of peppermint makes insomnia worse.

label: Evaluate
body: When we're doing Flaw and we see that an author is rebutting some position or person, there are three main tendencies: 1. Ad Hominem - the author rejects someone's position because that person has some vested interest / ulterior motive, or because they have conflicting past behavior. 2. Unproven vs. Proven False - the author points out that someone has failed to prove X or made an unsuccessful argument for X, and then concludes that X is therefore false. 3. Irrelevant Response - the author responds to a different position (Straw Man) or just fails to address what the first person was talking about. Here, we've got ourselves a #3. The issue being debated is whether or not pesticides are spreading to a neighboring farm, via runoff water. The fact that this farmer uses organic pesticides has absolutely no bearing on whether or not pesticides are spreading. And the fact that the farmer avoids spraying pesticides (like from a hose) onto the neighbor's land has no bearing. The neighbor was never saying, "Hey, you sprayed your pesticides on my land." She was saying, "Hey, when you water your plants, the runoff water, which contains your pesticides, is running off into my farm". Some students aren't familiar with the concept of run-off, but picture washing a car on a hilly driveway. You're only spraying your car, but the soapy water runs down the driveway, into the gutter, and then usually is continues to trickle down the gutter until it hits a sewer drain.

label: Goal
body: Find an answer saying that neither of the author's responses were at all relevant to the question of whether or not runoff water from Farmer X's farm is trickling over to his neighbor's farm.

label: Main Conclusion
body: Their disagreement is not over the meaning of the word “art.”

label: Intermediate Conclusion
body: [There are paintings that] should be ignored in the manner suggested by the first group

label: Premise
body: The second group grants that there are paintings that are not works of art.

label: No Role
body: One group of art critics claims that postimpressionist paintings are not really art and so should be neither studied nor displayed. Another group of critics disagrees, insisting that these paintings are works of art

label: Apparent Paradox
body: Biologists found that off the northeast coast of a certain country the P-plankton population has recently dropped 10 percent. Additionally, fish species X, Y, and Z are beginning to show extraordinarily high death rates in the region. Since these species of fish are known to sometimes eat P-plankton, biologists believe the two phenomena are connected, but the exact nature of the connection is unknown. No other species in the ecosystem appear to be affected.

label: Evaluate
body: Perhaps fish species X, Y, and Z are dependent on P-plankton for their food supplies. Or perhaps both P-plankton and fish species X, Y, and Z are all being attacked by the same virus. There are many possible ways the drop in P-plankton could be impacting the fish species X, Y, and Z. Of course it could also be that P-plankton are dependent on the fish species, and the death of those fish could be reducing the P-plankton population.

label: Conclusion (therefore)
body: The unsigned painting was painted by one of Laroque's students.

label: Evidence
body: Experts agree that the painting was done by either Laroque or one of his students, and the painting contains a pigment (orpiment) that has never been found in Laroque's attributed works.

label: Evaluate
body: We could interpret this as an Explain Curious Fact argument: CURIOUS FACT: who painted Nightbird? EXPLANATION: one of Laroque's students We would either want an alternate explanation for who painted it (maybe it was Laroque, maybe someone else that isn't his student), or we would want to undermine the plausibility that it was painted by one of L's students. Or we could just use our classic Weaken framework, and think, "GIVEN THAT this painting has orpiment, which has never been found in a work attributed to Laroque, HOW COULD WE ARGUE this painting wasn't done by one of his students?"

label: Goal
body: Identify an answer that provides a reason to doubt that the painting was done by Laroque's students, or an answer that suggests it was done by someone else.

label: Background
body: Highways near urban areas are widened and lengthened in an attempt to reduce traffic congestion / delays.

label: Surprising Idea
body: The traffic congestion / delays get even worse!

label: Evaluation
body: Given that the highways are now wider (i.e. more lanes), we would think the same volume of cars would be less congested. We probably need a story where the volume of cars using the highway has also changed, or maybe their style of driving has changed (leading to more accidents, which cause congestion). Or maybe the newly built lanes were shoddily constructed and have potholes and using them leads to more accidents than before.

label: Conclusion (apparently = opinion)
body: These ads are effective.

label: Evidence
body: In a study, consumers reaching checkout lines within 40 mins after the airing of an ad for a given product were significantly more likely to purchase the product than were consumers who checked out prior to the airing.

label: Evaluate
body: We have a study; we have an Asymmetric Comparison (people who checked out in the 40 mins after the ad were more likely to buy the advertised product than were people who checked out prior to the ad). And the author's conclusion is definitely assuming a causal explanation for that curious comparison. So we can use our Explain Curious Fact framework. Curious Fact ... why were people who checked out after the ad more likely to buy the product advertised than were people who checked out before the ad? Author's Explanation ... people who checked out after the ad heard the ad at the store and the ad convinced them to buy that product.

label: Goal
body: We can strengthen this by 1. ruling out an Alternate Explanation or by 2. increasing the Plausibility of the author's explanation Strengthen questions most commonly increase plausibility, using some answer with a "No Cause, No Effect" form. In this case that would mean something like, "People who checked out after the ad, but were listening to their own headphones as they shopped did not buy the advertised product". This would show that "if you weren't exposed to the ad because you couldn't hear it, then you weren't affected by the ad".

label: Evaluate
body: Finding an alternative cause is a safe way to undermine a conclusion that asserts causation after merely establishing a correlation. Since the correlation is a relative comparison, an answer that explains even a portion of the difference in the two groups would weaken the argument.

label: Evidence
body: The many test pilots who have flown this plane before didn't find it difficult to operate.

label: Evaluate
body: This argument has a pretty straightforward structure of, "Because all the cheerleaders I've met before have been energetic, the cheerleader I'm meeting tomorrow will probably be energetic". If it was true in the past, it'll probably be true in the future. Is this airtight logic? No. There are sampling concerns — what if the pilot testing tomorrow is meaningfully different from all the pilots who have tested before? However, the author isn't being certain about her conclusion. She's just saying it's "likely" that things will go down the way they've always gone down before. So that's a pretty reasonable conclusion.

label: Goal
body: Find an argument that says, "Since in past situations X was true, it's likely that in this present/future situation, X will be true again."

label: Conclusion
body: Just because a theory affects our perception of the world does not show that we should take it seriously.

label: Evidence (to see this)
body: Look at astrology. (apparently, the author thinks that astrology affects our perception of the world but shouldn't be taken seriously)

label: Evaluate
body: The first sentence gives us a conditional rule, signified by the sufficient indicator any. taken seriously → affects our perception The author then pivots by saying, even though [affects perception] is necessary, it's not sufficient. The author's actual words are: "Of course, A is not, in itself, enough to mean B." If we thought that A was, in itself, enough to establish B, we'd be saying that A is sufficient to prove B. So our author is saying, this condition of [affects our perception] is not sufficient to establish that [theory taken seriously]. To demonstrate this, he then cites the example of astrology, using Support Language: To see X, one need only consider Y.

label: Goal
body: The point of mentioning astrology was to provide evidence that [affects our perception] is not in itself enough for [theory to be taken seriously]. If we're trying to prove that X does not guarantee Y then we want an example where X is true but Y isn't. So, astrology was an example of a theory that affects our perception but shouldn't be taken seriously.

label: Conclusion (So)
body: Michaela must be a critically acclaimed playwright.

label: Evidence (since)
body: Michaela's new play will be performed by the local theater this season. They often produce plays by critically acclaimed playwrights, and the director says that "critical acclaim is one of the main factors considered in the selection of plays to perform".

label: Evaluate
body: Given all the evidence, how could we argue that it's possible that Michaela is not a critically acclaimed playwright? It seems pretty doable to argue that she might not be critically acclaimed (which is all we need to argue in order to defeat a conclusion that says she must be critically acclaimed). The first premise says that the local theater often produces plays by critically acclaimed playwrights, but that doesn't mean they always do. So maybe Michaela's play is just one of the non-critically acclaimed plays that the theater puts on. The second premise says that the "critical acclaim is one of the main factors considered in selecting which play", but that doesn't mean "they will refuse to select a play unless it's critically acclaimed". Harvard Law's admissions board will say that "having a 170+ LSAT score is one of the main factors considered in selecting which students to admit". But can we assume that anyone admitted to Harvard had a 170+ score? Of course not. Maybe they had a great GPA, a compelling personal statement, and a famous Mom.

label: Goal
body: Look for an objection saying, "Just because the theater often puts on critically acclaimed plays doesn't prove that Michaela's play must be critically acclaimed." Or look for an objection saying, "Just because critical acclaim is one of the main factors doesn't mean that every single play they produce must be critically acclaimed."

label: Conclusion
body: Governments should not be allowed to use the personal diaries of someone as evidence against themselves in a criminal prosecution.

label: Evidence
body: A diary is a silent conversation with oneself, equivalent to speaking to yourself or keeping your thoughts to yourself.

label: Evaluate
body: By analogy, it sounds like author is assuming that "governments should not be allowed to use one's private thoughts against them as evidence in a criminal prosecution". She's saying, whether it's a diary, muttering to oneself, or just saying your thoughts "out loud" in the privacy of your mental theater, it's all the same --- these are your thoughts, a private conversation between you and you. She apparently thinks this type of conversation is inadmissible.

label: Goal
body: Since our focus on Strengthen + Principle questions is the Conclusion, we want to remind ourselves what kind of idea we're trying to prove. We're hoping to support that "Governments shouldn't be allowed to X as evidence against someone in a criminal prosecution". So whatever principle we pick to support this claim should sound like a principle about what governments should / shouldn't be allowed to use as evidence in a trial.

label: Premise
body: A ring of gas flickering 450 times per second has been observed in stable orbit around a black hole.

label: Premise
body: That flickering rate is best explained, given accepted physics, if the ring has a 49-km radius.

label: Premise
body: A gas ring couldn't maintain such a close orbit (49-km radius) unless the black hole was spinning.

label: Anticipate
body: Chain: observed 450/sec flickering -> ring has 49-km radius -> black hole must be spinning. So the most supported claim is that this particular black hole is spinning.

label: Goal
body: Find the answer that says this black hole is spinning.

label: Premises
body: The flickering rate implies a 49-km ring radius. A ring that close requires the black hole to be spinning.

label: Anticipate
body: Chain: 450/sec flicker -> 49 km radius -> black hole spinning.

label: Goal
body: An answer saying this black hole is spinning.

label: Premises
body: The argument hands us a chain of physics. We see a gas ring flickering 450 times per second. Physics says that flickering rate fits best with a 49-km-radius ring. And a ring that close to a black hole can only stay in stable orbit if the black hole is spinning.

label: Anticipate
body: Walk it down: flickering at 450/sec -> ring is 49 km out -> black hole is spinning. The conclusion most strongly supported is that this particular black hole is spinning.

label: Goal
body: Look for the answer that picks up the bottom of that chain — this black hole is spinning.

label: Conclusion
body: At no point in the past two centuries, has black water been intense as it was last year.

label: Evidence
body: The black water wiped out five species of coral, including some that were more than two centuries old.

label: Evaluation
body: If this round of black water killed 200+ year old coral, does that mean that it was the strongest round of black water in the last 200 years? The author is thinking, "Well, if any previous round of black water had been this strong or stronger, than that black water would have destroyed this coral." To find the wiggle room, we would need to solve this riddle: if a previous wave of black water was stronger than last year's wave, how could it be that the previous wave didn't wipe out this old coral, but last year's wave did? Maybe that (hypothetical) stronger previous wave just entered at a different angle, so it didn't impact the coral the same way. Maybe it "loosened the lid on the jar" and the second wave finished off the job. Maybe weather differences contributed to how the black water interacted with that coral (strong winds kept previous masses of black water from doing as much damage?)

label: Goal
body: The correct answer should either name the author's connective bridge, "If you destroyed something over 200 years old, then nothing in the last 200 years attacked that thing with as much intensity as you did", or the correct answer will rule out an objection that allows one to argue that a previous, stronger wave might have occurred but just not wiped out the coral for some reason.

label: Conclusion
body: Many of our inclinations are genetically caused and not affected by environmental influence.

label: Evidence
body: Identical twins, who have the same genes, tends to be similarly inclined when it comes to ethics, fashion, and career choice, even when they've been brought up in vastly different environments.

label: Evaluation
body: The author looks at these cases of different upbringings (environment) but similar ethics/fashion/career ambitions and attributes that sameness to the similar genes. If we were trying to argue the Anti-Conclusion, we'd have to think, "Even though some identical twins that are brought up in different environments end up with similar inclinations, how could I argue that these inclinations are either not genetic in origin or are affected by environmental factors."

label: Goal
body: We could look for an alternate explanation (non-genetic) for why these identical twins raised in different environments ended up with similar inclinations, or we can look for an answer that suggests that these inclinations aren't genetic, or are affected by environment.

label: Background
body: conditional (only) Live happily → Love/friendship are primary motives for actions Love/friendship are not → can't live happily primary motives for actions Pivot (Yet) Economic needs can be satisfied even when love / friendship are not the primary motives for actions.

label: Setup
body: So, human beings ....

label: Evaluate
body: Usually with Logical Completion (i.e. fill in the blank) questions, it's pretty doable to predict where the fill in the blank is going, because we'll have two different strands of thought that we are going to try to safely bring together. In this case, it's a little weird. The Pivot word suggests that we should be trying to figure out how to reconcile the 1st and 2nd sentence. It sounds like Happiness and Economic Needs are two different things. Happiness requires love and friendship being the primary motives for action whereas economic needs can be satisfied even if economic utility is all that motivates action.

label: Goal
body: Most wrong answers on Logical Completion are too strongly worded. So, given that we don't have much of a prediction, let's just look for something safely worded that balances the differing needs of "living happily" and "satisfying economic needs".

label: Conclusion
body: This infrastructure is likely to appear and grow rapidly. (i.e. The national system of fuel stations for hydrogen fuel is likely to appear and grow rapidly)

label: Evidence
body: It's already possible to produce nonpolluting hydrogen cars. And, a century ago there was no fuel infrastructure for gas powered vehicles, but it quickly developed in response to consumer demand.

label: Evaluation
body: When we're doing Conclusion questions, we're primarily expecting the conclusion to be the very first claim, or to appear after some sort of But / Yet / However pivot. Here we get the latter form. There is a pivot with "but" that introduces a fact: this system of stations does not yet exist. Then there is a pivot with "however" that introduces an opinion: this infrastructure is likely to appear soon. The author then supports that opinion with the historical comparison premise in her last sentence.

label: Goal
body: Just look for an answer that says "this system of hydrogen fuel stations is likely to appear and grow rapidly".

label: Conclusion
body: Wildlife management experts shouldn't interfere with natural habitats of creatures in the wild.

label: Evidence
body: Trying to interfere with a natural habitat for the sake of making it easier for an endangered species to survive will make it harder for the other, non-endangered species to survive in that habitat.

label: Evaluation
body: If we wanted to object to the conclusion, we have to argue that "EVEN THOUGH tinkering with a habitat will make it harder for the nonendangered species to survive, we should still do it for the sake of the endangered." This is kind of like someone arguing, "Peanut bans shouldn't be enforced at elementary schools, because banning peanut butter for the sake of protecting kids with peanut allergies makes it harder for parents of kids who don't have peanut allergies to think of what to make them for lunch". We might say ... "Suck it up? The inconvenience it causes everyone else is worth it, compared to the importance of doing it for the sake of the kids with the peanut allergies."

label: Goal
body: Look for an answer objecting that "even if interfering comes with a negative, it is outweighed by the positive it does". The author is failing to consider that the nonendangered species might be thriving enough that making things "harder" for them is still not any significant threat or hardship.

label: Facts
body: conditionals (any, once/no, each) ~Sterilized or ~Sealed → could have bad bacteria Sterilized + Properly Sealed → no bacteria Acceptable food → Sterilize-and-Seal preserve tech or Slow Bad Bacteria

label: Quantified Facts
body: Some Acceptable food-preservation techniques may destroy enzymes that cause food to spoil or discolor quickly.

label: Evaluate
body: In two of these claims, "sterilize and seal" are acting as one compound idea. The first sentence is saying, "If you haven't done that combo, it might have bacteria." So we can write the conditional as saying, if you're failed to Sterilize, Seal, or both, then it could have bacteria. Formally, it looks like ~ (Sterilized and Sealed) which distributes into ~Sterilized or ~Sealed. The last sentence talks about two different methods of acceptable food preservation. One method is the combo of Sterilize & Seal, the other is to Slow Growth of Bad Bacteria. We check to see whether our conditionals chain together (they don't), and we check to see whether any facts talk about the trigger of these conditionals (the last sentence talks about the trigger of the 3rd conditional. We could make an Overlap Inference with the last two ideas: at least one technique that involves either sterilizing and sealing or Slowing Bad Bacteria also has the potential to make food spoil or discolor less quickly.

label: Goal
body: With so many facts on our plate, we should just check out the answers, wary of overly strong answers and backwards/opposite answers, And we'll research the contenders to see if they seem provable.

label: Principle
body: Life-threatening risk ⇿ gains special benefit acceptable or bears risk voluntarily

label: Evaluation
body: Because of the "if and only if", we get a bi-conditional, which is an either/or idea. If you gain a special benefit you couldn't get otherwise or bear the risk voluntarily, then it's okay to do something that is potentially life-threatening. But if you're not getting a special benefit and you're not bearing that risk voluntarily, then it's not acceptable to do something that risky.

label: Goal
body: As we read each answer, we can first peek at whether we're trying to hear that the risks are unacceptable, in which case we need to establish two things (not a special benefit and not bearing that risk voluntarily), or whether the risks are acceptable, in which case we only need to establish one of two things (it's for a special benefit or the risk is borne voluntarily).

label: Conclusion
body: The compounds the sea butterflies make aren't the reason they are able to avoid predation.

label: Evidence
body: In a study, they added one compound per pellet to see if predators would eat it. For each of the compounds, the predator still ate the pellet with the added compound.

label: Evaluation
body: Given that the predators ate each pellet with the added compound, how could we still say that the compounds really are the reason predators avoid these butterflies? The loophole seems to be that maybe the compounds have to all be present at the same time. After all, if we just felt hydrogen atoms and just felt oxygen atoms, neither one of them would feel "wet". It's only once you put the 2 hydrogen atoms and the oxygen atom together that you get water and its properties. So maybe we can argue that the compounds only work to fend off predators when they are all consumed together (the recipe that predators hate is not triggered by just one compound at a time).

label: Goal
body: We could actually call this the famous flaw, Part vs. Whole, since the author is saying, 'Since each compound does not deter predators, the group of compounds together does not deter predators".

label: Principle
body: Criticism will seriously harm the critiqued or → Don't criticize Not hoping to benefit other people

label: Application
body: Jarrett shouldn't have criticized O, because the defects in O's essay were so obvious that pointing them out benefited no one.

label: Evaluation
body: Since the application is trying to conclude that J shouldn't have criticized, we want to look at rule (contrapose if needed) so that "shouldn't have criticized" is on the right side, where conclusions go. To justify that conclusion, we just need to establish one (or both) of the criteria on the left of the arrow, since it's an "or" rule. the critique seriously harmed Ostertag or Jarrett had no hope or expectation that the critique would benefit someone else

label: Goal
body: We know that the critique benefited no one, but we would need to know that Jarrett had no hope or expectation of benefiting others. Or we need to know the critique seriously harmed Ostertag.

label: Conclusion
body: Minivans have a better safety record because they're driven mainly by low-risk drivers.

label: Evidence
body: Minivans have the lowest number of injuries per vehicle, but in crash tests they do no better at protecting occupants than do other vehicles of the same size.

label: Evaluation
body: We have a Curious Fact: why are minivans lowest number of injuries per vehicle? One might think it's because they're big and boxy and can take a punch, but crash tests show they're no better than similar sized vehicles. So the author assumes that it must be safer drivers that explain why minivans have this injury advantage. With all Curious Fact → Causal Interpretation arguments, we ask ourselves: 1. What else could explain the Curious Fact? 2. How plausible is the Author's Hypothesis?

label: Goal
body: Since this is strengthen, we need an answer that rules out a different reason why minivans incur fewer injuries (f.e. "Drivers do not usually drive more cautiously around minivans than around other vehicles, out of fear that babies are on board"), or an answer that increases the plausibility of the hypothesis. The most common way to Strengthen causal arguments is "no cause, no effect", so you could see an answer like "When a random sampling of people was given minivans, the rate of injuries per vehicle was no longer lower than average".

label: Conclusion
body: The government is responsible for the higher cost of gas

label: Evidence
body: The government's policies have increased consumer demand for fuel, and as a result of that, the price of gas has gone up.

label: Evaluate
body: The argument assumes that the rental market performance is an indicator of the future sales market market.

label: Conclusion
body: If an animal control office finds a stray cocker spaniel anywhere near Flynn Heights, it is likely that the dog belongs to someone in Flynn Heights.

label: Evaluation
body: At first blush, this just sounds like a valid argument. The government caused A, and A caused B, so the government is responsible for B. If we were trying to argue the Anti-Conclusion, what would we say? Given the evidence, how could we argue that the government wasn't responsible for the increased cost of gas? Maybe we could say, "Look, we can't hold the government responsible for every ramification of every policy. Aren't the oil companies more directly responsible for raising the price? Do oil companies have raise the price when consumer demand goes up? If not, then why is the government responsible for that?"

label: Goal
body: Tough to know what we're looking for other than something like, "The government is responsible for the ripple effects of its policies".

label: Conclusion
body: A species in which mutations frequently occur will survive dramatic environmental changes.

label: Evidence
body: A species in which mutations frequently occur will develop new adaptions every generation. + Only species that develop new adaptions every generation can survive dramatic environmental changes

label: Evaluation
body: Because we see conditional logic triggers (will, only if, will) and repeating ideas ("survive dramatic" / "frequent mutations" / "adaptations each generation" are all mentioned twice), we should try to diagram this. Frequent Mutations → New A's each gen A → B Survive Dramatic → New A's each gen C → B ⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯ Freq Mutations → Survive Dramatic A → C

label: Goal
body: This is making a Necessary vs. Sufficient error with the second premise, thinking that it goes B → C. How can we make some quick eliminations? We can look for 2 conditional premises and 1 conditional conclusion. We can verify that both conditional premises have the same outcome (right side).

label: Conclusion
body: How well an underground rock group's recordings sell is no mark of that group's success as an underground group.

label: Evidence (after all)
body: You could have strong sales, but not for a cool reason, rather because your music is too trendy to be authentically undergroun. You could have weak sales, but not for a cool reason, rather because you're just incompetent.

label: Evaluate
body: This argument can be hard to understand. It helps to start by thinking of how you prove a claim like "X is no mark of Y", for example, "How attractive you are is no mark of how good a person you are". Maybe some people think "beautiful people are good people". But we could show them that beautiful people are sometimes bad. Maybe people think the opposite: "beautiful people are bad people". But we could show them that beautiful people are sometimes good. Ultimately, we're trying to show that beauty doesn't go hand in hand with good or bad. An attractive person might be good or bad, just as an unattractive person might be good or bad. Some people might think that if a band's recording sells really well, then they are a success! No, our author says, because sometimes a band sells well but their music is too trendy to be authentically underground. The author is assuming that they're not a success, if they're music isn't authentic / it's just trendy. Some people might actually think to be a successful underground group, you should be so weird and provocative that you aren't popular, that your recordings don't sell well. But, no, our author says, because you might sell poorly just because you're incompetent. The author is assuming that if you're incompetent, then you're not successful.

label: Goal
body: Essentially this author is thinking that SUCCESS as an underground group requires being authentic and competent. She thinks that if you're too trendy to be authentic, or if you're incompetent, then you're not really a success. Let's look for an answer that strengthens any of these missing links.

label: Conclusion
body: Sales numbers are not a mark of an underground group's success.

label: Evidence
body: Strong sales may mean trendy/inauthentic music; weak sales may mean incompetence.

label: Evaluate
body: Need a principle that disqualifies both — incompetence and trendy music — from being marks of success.

label: Goal
body: Find a principle treating either incompetence or trendy music as enough to make a group unsuccessful.

label: Conclusion
body: The critic argues that you can't tell whether an underground rock group is successful from how well their records sell.

label: Evidence
body: The critic gives two reasons: 1. Selling well might mean their music is too trendy — so they're not really underground anymore. 2. Selling poorly might just mean they're bad at their craft.

label: Evaluate
body: For this argument to land, we need a rule that says: if a group is incompetent, they're unsuccessful, AND if their music is too trendy, they're unsuccessful. With both of those covered, sales numbers really do tell us nothing — high sales might mean trendy (= unsuccessful), low sales might mean incompetent (= unsuccessful).

label: Goal
body: Pick the principle that disqualifies both incompetent groups and trendy-music groups from being considered successful as underground groups.

label: Conclusion
body: Country F's producers are dumping shrimp.

label: Evidence
body: Dumping = selling a product in another country for less than production cost. Shrimp producers from Country F are selling shrimp in Country G for less than it costs to produce shrimp in Country G.

label: Evaluate
body: At first glance, this argument might feel airtight. They provide a definition of dumping and then they seem to provide a fitting example of dumping. Where's the wiggle room? Well, the definition of "dumping" is that you're selling something in another country for less than it cost to produce. Doesn't that mean how much it cost to produce in YOUR country, not the country where you sell it? It makes more intuitive sense to interpret "selling for less than production cost" as "the cost someone paid to produce it", which implies we're talking about the production cost in country where it's produced, not where it's sold. So if we're saying that Country F is dumping shrimp, we would be saying that Country F is selling its shrimp in another country for less than it cost to produce the shrimp in Country F. But we only know that they're selling it for less than it cost to produce the shrimp in Country G.

label: Goal
body: Look for an answer saying "are they selling it for less than it costs to produce shrimp in country F" or an answer relating the cost of producing shrimp in G to that in country F.

label: Conclusion
body: It's not justified or admirable for managers to donate company profits to charity.

label: Evidence
body: Profits belong to the owners, not the managers. Analogy: Robin Hood gave to the poor from the rich, but he was still stealing.

label: Evaluate
body: Since our task is to weaken an analogy, we know that we need to make these two cases NOT fair to compare. What could be an important difference between Robin Hood stealing money from rich people and giving it poor people, and managers donating a certain percentage of company profits to charity?

label: Goal
body: Find an answer that makes these two cases unfair to compare, or that helps us to legitimize the practice of managers' donating some % of profits to charity.

label: Conclusion
body: Manager-driven corporate donations are not actually justified.

label: Evidence
body: Profits belong to the owners. Robin Hood stole even when giving to the poor.

label: Evaluate
body: The analogy assumes managers donate without the owners' consent — like Robin Hood did. If owners actually consent, the analogy fails.

label: Goal
body: An answer establishing owner consent (explicit or tacit).

label: Conclusion
body: The columnist says: managers donating company profits to charity isn't actually justified — it might look noble, but it's wrong.

label: Evidence (the analogy)
body: Profits belong to the owners. So a manager giving them away is like Robin Hood — giving to the poor with someone else's money. Robin Hood was still a thief.

label: Evaluate
body: The whole argument hangs on the Robin Hood analogy. What made Robin Hood a thief was that he took the rich people's money without their permission. If the owners actually agree with what the managers are doing — even quietly, by allowing it to keep happening — then the manager isn't taking anything against the owner's will. The Robin Hood comparison falls apart.

label: Goal
body: An answer that says the owners do, in fact, consent.

label: Application (should = opinion)
body: Snake charmers who violate the law against capturing wild snakes should not be prosecuted.

label: Principle
body: If a law's purpose is to protect wild animal law should populations → not be and person X's actions enforced do not threaten wild against animal populations person X

label: Evaluate / Goal
body: Whenever we're using a Principle to support a conclusion, we want the right side of the principle to match the conclusion. We could have alternatively written this rule as, "If law's purpose is to protect wild animal pops, then the law shouldn't be enforced against people whose actions don't threaten animals pops". But since the idea we're trying to prove is "This law should not be enforced against snake charmers", we want to be clear on what facts we need to know about the law and about snake charmers in order to know this principle applies to them. We need to know that the law's purpose is to protect wild animal populations. Did they establish that? Yes, they said there is a law against capturing wild snakes "which was enacted to protect wild snake populations". Did they establish that snake charmers' actions "do not threaten wild animal populations"? No, they didn't. That's what we're missing.

label: Goal
body: Let's look for, "Snake charmers' actions do not threaten wild animal populations".

body: If the number of people who see a movie generates enough ticket sales revenue to more than offset the money spent on making the movie, then the film makes a profit. (thanks, LSAT ... we know what "profit" means) Accordingly, the primary goal of movie execs is to max out how many people will see a film.

body: The primary goal TV execs is not to max out how many people will see their shows.

label: Evaluate
body: Given That Movie execs' #1 goal is to maximize the number of people who see films (since that potentially increases profitability) Why is it That TV execs aren't making it their #1 goal to maximize the number of people who see their shows?

label: Goal
body: We know that the correct answer will need to provide a salient difference between Movies vs. TV, that would explain why the primary goal of execs in each field are different. We don't need to predict answers in Paradox, but presumably our real world knowledge tells us one big difference between films and TV .... films get their money from box office sales / TV shows get their money from advertisers that run commercials during the show (unless it's subscription TV like HBO, but that's not the usual) We can assume that since the first sentence connected profit to "number of viewers" for a movie, the correct answer will probably say "when it comes to TV, profit is not as directly connected to number of viewers".

body: More cocker spaniels are registered to addresses in Flynn Heights than to addresses in all other neighborhoods combined.

label: Intermediate Conclusion
body: Scientific studies cannot be used to disprove a correlation between personality type and any other phenomenon.

label: Evaluation
body: The author's argument is saying, "Since no definitive study has claimed X, then it is false to claim X." But just because a study hasn't proven X is true doesn't mean that X is false. Maybe the right study hasn't yet been conducted that could prove X is true. LSAT wants us to recognize the distinction between an idea that has not been sufficiently proven and an idea we know to be untrue. This is one of the 10 Famous Flaws, and it goes by the name Unproven vs. Untrue.

label: Goal
body: Look for an answer saying, "Just because no study has proven that ginseng relieves stress, that doesn't mean that ginseng doesn't relieve stress", or for a more abstract answer like, "the author treats an absence of evidence for a claim as proof that the claim is false".

label: Given
body: Scientists conjecture that certain microbes consume organic molecules in exposed shale and similar sediments. In so doing, the microbes remove oxygen from the atmosphere and generate carbon dioxide, a gas that, evidence indicates, promotes global warming. They also conjecture that these microbes reproduce more quickly at higher temperatures.

label: Opposing Point
body: A diet whose protein comes from fish is much healthier than one whose protein comes from red meat.

label: Evidence

label: Given
body: Sentence 1 before the semi colon tell us that people with cat allergies aren't allergic to cats, per se, but to specific proteins found in their skin secretions (gross) and their saliva. After the semi colon, we're told that the specific protein responsible for the allergy varies from one person to another. Sentence 2 starts with the evidence indicator word "since" which is unusual, though not unheard of, for a Most Supported question. Typically, these are non-argument stimuli but occasionally they are arguments. When they are, the right answer tends to feel a lot like a Necessary Assumption answer, so we'll keep that in mind when we try to make a prediction. The evidence claim is that ALL cats shed skin and spread saliva (also gross), from which an equally strong conclusion is drawn: there's NO such thing as a cat that can't provoke an allergy. Sentence two ends with a concession following the concession indicator word "although" - it's common for a cat to cause a reaction for some people who suffer from cat allergies but not for others.

label: Evaluate
body: There are a lot of overlapping ideas in these two long, multi-clause sentences: cats, proteins, allergies, allergy sufferers. A correct answer could deal with any of these ideas. Circling back to that idea of the Necessary Assumption style of prediction, we might also consider the relationship between the claim "all cats shed and spread" and the conclusion that "there's no such thing as a cat that can't cause allergies." That argument seems to assume that all cats have proteins in their skin secretions and saliva that are capable of causing an allergic reaction. Sentence 1 before the colon establishes that "certain proteins" are the source of these reactions, but it didn't go so far as to say "all proteins" of these types are capable of doing so, so that would be a Necessary Assumption style prediction. All that being said, Most Supported questions are not the most predictable, so read the answers with an open mind. Beware of claims that are stronger than the stimulus, and get rid of answers that introduce a new idea. For this question type, new ideas are Out of Scope.

label: Main Conclusion
body: [We] should not think that most people are not susceptible to being misled by maps.

label: Premises
body: Most people are taught to be cautious interpreters of language, but education in the sophisticated use of maps is almost nonexistent. Maps are like language: they can be manipulated in order to mislead.

label: Conclusion
body: The physician's critique is not legitimate grounds for rejecting what the book said about the new drug's side effects. (translation: we shouldn't reject the warnings this book made about the new drug's side effects, just because of this physician's critique)

label: Intermediate Conclusion
body: The physician probably has personal reasons to deny that the drug is dangerous.

label: Evidence
body: The physician is employed by the manufacturer of the new pill.

label: Evaluate
body: One of the ten famous flaws is Ad Hominem, where an author dismisses a point of view because the Source of the ideas is someone who has a biased interest, or who has conflicting past behavior. If we're doing a Flaw question and the author seems to be doing a Rebuttal, then we're usually looking at one of these two flaws: Ad Hominem Unproven vs. Proven False We could argue with the first move, from Premise to Intermediate Conclusion, that working for a drug company automatically makes you likely to have personal reasons to protect the company's reputation when it comes to its drugs having dangerous side effects. But even if we grant that the physician does have some personal reasons for wanting the drug company to do financially well, that doesn't allow us to invalidate what the physician has said without evaluating the merits of her claims. Sometimes what we're saying is both true and serves our vested interests. So we can complain that the author has not told us what the physician's criticisms are and why they are unwarranted.

label: Goal
body: Look for an answer that sounds like, "just because someone has a biased interest in something being true doesn't mean we shouldn't listen to them, that we should just disqualify their testimony"

label: Evidence

The game can be purchased from retail outlets or rented for two-day intervals. The publisher offers a rebate equal to the cost of one rental for renters who go on to purchase the game, saving them a significant portion of the purchase price. The rate of sales now meets expectations and rentals are exceeding expectations, the publisher predicts that soon sales of the game will also exceed expectations.

body: The publisher predicts that soon sales of the game will also exceed expectations.

label: Evaluate
body: Okay, I know this isn't officially part of our job on this problem, but wtf is going on is Flynn Heights that they are this obsessed with cocker spaniels? The author's conclusion is a probabilistic one. When someone is saying, "If I see an X, then it's probably Y", the evidence we need for that is that "Most X's are Y". for example, if we knew Most of Lenny's socks have holes in them. we could fairly conclude If we are randomly given one of Lenny's socks, it is likely to have holes in it. Since this argument is concluding that a stray cocker spaniel near Flynn Heights likely belongs to someone in Flynn Heights, it requires evidence that most strays near Flynn Heights belong to someone in Flynn Heights. Instead, what we know is most registered cocker spaniels belong to someone in Flynn Heights. If we wanted to object to this argument, we could say that most strays do not belong to anyone near Flynn Heights. Maybe they belong to no one. Maybe they belong to people in the neighboring city. We know that Flynn Heights has most of the registered cocker spaniels, but maybe other neighborhoods love cocker spaniels but hate registering their dogs (i.e. maybe there are a ton of unregistered cocker spaniels, and maybe more of them are likely to be stray).

label: Goal
body: Evaluate answer choices are written as questions or toss-ups, but we want to find an answer choice where one of the possible answers to that answer choice's question could be an Objection. Since these are all phrased as "whether or not", we're looking for an answer choice where one of those two answers would weaken; it would allow us to argue that if an animal control officer finds a stray spaniel, it's actually likely that it's doesn't belong to a Flynn Heights resident.

label: Evidence
body: Psychologists recently WDC conducted a study in which people from widely disparate cultures were asked to examine five photographs. Each photograph depicted the face of a person expressing one offive basic human emotions—fear, happiness, disgust, anger, and sadness. The people in the study were asked to identify the emotion being expressed in each photograph. For each photograph, SE everyone identified the same emotion.

label: Conclusion
body: This shows that people GP are genetically predisposed to associate certain facial expressions with certain basic emotions.

label: Evaluate

A mechanism exists that would make national building codes applicable regardless of whether the defendant thought local or national codes applied to the area, while making it sometimes possible that local codes would not apply. If local codes required any behavior required by national codes, then violation of national codes could not be an excuse.

label: Conclusion
body: If ed. psychologists' views are correct, then parents should doubt their own ratings of the educational value of kids TV shows.

label: Evidence
body: When parents rate the educational value of kids TV shows, they usually don't take into account the view of how educational an educational psychologists would say this show is.

label: Evaluate
body: This argument is concluding, "If Group A is usually right, then Group B is usually wrong". The logic of that statement implies that Group A and Group B believe different things. Did the author ever establish that psychologists and parents believe different things about the educational value of these shows? No, she only established that when parents decide on their own rating, they don't take into account the rating given by psychologists. That would be like if I asked you to grade a movie on a 1-100 scale, and you didn't take into account what score from 1-100 this movie got on Rotten Tomatoes. Would I be able to conclude that, "If the Rotten Tomatoes score is correct, then you should doubt your own ability to rank the quality of a movie"? No, because maybe your ranking was really close to what the Rotten Tomatoes ranking was.

label: Goal
body: Look for an answer saying that the author is assuming that parents end up rating these TV shows differently than the psychological experts rate them, or something presenting that Illegal Move, "assumes that if you don't take into account view X while deciding on issue A, then you will have a different conclusion about issue A than view X had."

label: Justine's 1st Claim
body: Pellman, Inc. settled the lawsuit out of court by paying $1 million. does Simon disagree? No he seems to implicitly accept this.

label: Justine's 2nd claim
body: Since Pellman settled instead of going to trial, it indicates that their corporate leaders expected to lose in court. does Simon disagree? Yes! He's saying, "Settling instead of going to trial doesn't indicate that the corporate leaders expected to lose in court. It's unclear whether they expected to lose. I think they probably thought that they would just end up getting more money if they settled than if they paid their lawyers to go through trial."

label: Evidence
body: Only when we know J → KE a lot about the events that led to an action are we justified in praising or blaming a person for that action.

label: Conclusion
body: We must therefore ~(KE → ~RFP) reject Tolstoy’s rash claim that if we knew a lot about the events leading up to any action, we would cease to regard that action as freely performed. This can also be KE ↢some↣ RFP expressed as, there are some actions for which we know a lot about the events that led to that action that we would regard as freely performed.

label: Evaluate
body: The argument assumes J → RFP that to be justified in praising or blaming a person for an action we must regard that action as freely performed.

label: Conclusion
body: Crying must have the effect of reducing stress.

label: Intermediate Conclusion
body: Shedding tears removes significant quantities of hormones that body produces in times of emotional stress.

label: Evidence
body: Human tears contain many of the same hormones that the body produces in times of emotional stress.

label: Evaluate
body: So, let me try to understand this argument: - when we're emotionally stressed, we produce X-hormones. - human tears contain X-hormones. - So when we cry, we're shedding significant quantities of X-hormones. - So when we cry, we're reducing emotional stress? The "hence" shows us that the author drew an Intermediate Conclusion en route to the "therefore" of the Main Conclusion. Can we object to that first Conclusion? Just because tears have X-hormones, do we have to accept that shedding tears removes significant quantities of X-hormones? Not necessarily. When I eat a can of tuna, it contains the element mercury, but that doesn't mean that eating a can of tuna involves putting significant quantities of mercury into my body. Similarly, maybe trace amounts of X-hormones are found in tears, but given that we don't cry more than a couple ounces of tears at the most, perhaps we aren't shedding that much of those hormones (maybe the amount produced by emotional stress is 10x what we shed in an average cry). Can we object to the main Conclusion? Given that these hormones are produced in times of stress, does that mean that getting rid of the hormones will reduce stress? Not necessarily. My body produces beads of sweat in times of being overheated. Does that mean that removing the beads of sweat will reduce my feeling of hotness? Of course not.

label: Goal
body: Look for an answer saying that "just because tears contain X, shedding tears doesn't necessary shed a significant quantity of X", or that "just because X is produced in times of Y, getting rid of X doesn't mean you'll be getting less of Y".

label: Conclusion (so)
body: If a bird feeder doesn't have protective cover, a bird feeder will not attract many birds.

label: Evidence
body: If a bird feeder has a protective cover, then squirrels won't eat from the feeder. If squirrels eat from the feeder, it won't attract many birds.

label: Evaluate
body: Since this has three conditional logic claims (if / only if / if) and has ideas that show up multiple times (squirrels eat / attract birds / protective cover), we would probably be wise to diagram this symbolically. And since we're doing Flaw / Parallel Flaw and we're seeing conditional logic, we can already be 90% sure that the flaw in the argument is an illegal negation or reversal (i.e. the Necessary vs. Sufficient flaw). The author is trying to put together two conditionals to arrive at her conclusion. Since "squirrels eating" is the common term in the two conditional premises, it's supposed to be the middle link in the chain. The author thinks she's combining these two premises: No cover → Squirrels eat Squirrels eat → Not many birds If those were actually the two premises, then she would correctly be deriving her conclusion: No cover -—--—--—--—> Not many birds The problem is the second premise says, Squirrels eat → No cover The word "only if" is the opposite of "if". When we see "if", the idea that goes with that word ends up on the left side of the arrow (the sufficient condition). When we see "only if", the idea that goes with that ends up on the right side (sufficient condition).

label: Goal
body: The author is trying to make this sort of argument P1: A → B P2: B → C C: A -—--> C But one of the premises is reversed. So let's look for something like this: P1: B → A P2: B → C C: A -—--> C In the original argument, both premises started with the same trigger "squirrels eat", just as in this algebraic recipe both premises start with the trigger B. So we can have a couple things to look for quickly: - 2 premises, 1 conclusion, all conditional - the two conditional premises should have the same trigger

label: Conclusion (should)
body: The restoration should continue.

label: Evidence (for)
body: The frescoes in their present condition cannot be seen as they appeared when painted by Michelangelo.

label: Evaluate
body: We start by anticipating answers on Strengthen + Principle by simply saying some version of "If Premise, then Conclusion": If frescoes can't be seen we should as they appeared when → do / continue the painted by Michelangelo restoration But since the answers on Principle questions are more generic and universal, we might try to be a little less specific in our trigger: If an artwork presently we should can't be seen as it appeared → try to restore to the artist who made it its orig form Some answers are phrased conditionally, but still reference the Conclusion and the Evidence, so we might see an answer like, "the decision over whether or not to restore a piece of art should be based on whether it can presently be seen as it appeared when it was first created" or like "the most important factor in considering whether to restore a painting is trying to make it look the way it appeared when first painted". However, this argument has a counterpremise as well, a reason we shouldn't do the restoration. When a Strengthen + Principle question mentions an upside as well as a downside, we sometimes refer to it as Weighing Tradeoffs. The upside of doing the restoration is that we remove the grime and get the frescoes back to appearing like they did when painted by Michelangelo. The downside of doing the restoration is that we'll expose them to air and breath that will potentially erode the original paint more quickly. If the author is saying we should not do the restoration, then they have a principle in their minds like, "It's more important that we protect these paintings from exposure to erosive substances than that we make them appear like they originally did".

label: Goal
body: Since the author is saying we should do the restoration, then they have a principle in mind like, "It's more important that we make these look like they did when Michelangelo created them than it is for us to shield them from acidic degradation." Let's look for that Weighing Tradeoffs sentiment or something more like our original Linking ideas, "if you can't presently see art the way it appeared to the artist who made it, then you should try to restore the art".

label: Paradox
body: Generally, doctors recommend vitamin C to maintain health (it's an antioxidant that protects from disease). They especially recommend it to people who already have ailments and want to avoid more health problems. But for some cancer patients — even those whose treatments are physically harmful — doctors discourage vitamin C.

label: Evaluate
body: Why would the recommendation flip for cancer patients specifically? The general logic of "antioxidants are protective" should make vitamin C more appealing to people facing harsh therapy, not less. The explanation must give cancer patients a unique reason vitamin C becomes harmful in their case — most likely because it interferes with the cancer therapy itself.

label: Goal
body: Find the answer that explains why vitamin C is bad specifically for cancer patients undergoing therapy — a reason unique to them that overrides the general benefit.

label: Paradox
body: Vitamin C is generally recommended for health, but discouraged for some cancer patients even during harsh therapy.

label: Evaluate
body: We need a reason vitamin C becomes specifically harmful for cancer patients in treatment.

label: Goal
body: Find the answer giving a unique downside of vitamin C for cancer patients undergoing therapy.

label: Paradox
body: The puzzle: vitamin C is normally recommended — it's an antioxidant, it protects against disease. People who are already sick are especially told to take it. But cancer patients in treatment? Doctors say no, even though the treatment itself is wrecking their health.

label: Evaluate
body: So what's special about cancer patients? They're sick, undergoing harsh therapy — by the general logic, they should be the most in need of vitamin C's protective effects. Something must be unique about their situation that flips the recommendation. The likely candidate: vitamin C interacts badly with cancer therapy. If it interferes with how the therapy works, taking vitamin C would actually undermine the treatment itself — which would be much worse than missing out on its general benefits.

label: Goal
body: Find the answer that gives a specific reason vitamin C is bad for someone in cancer treatment.

label: Premises
body: Birds may simply navigate using landmarks, just as humans do. We do not say that humans have an innate sense of direction simply because they find their way home time after time.

label: Intermediate Conclusion
body: The studies testing whether the accuracy of birds’ migratory patterns is due to such an innate ability are inconclusive.

label: Conclusion
body: There is little evidence to support the belief that migratory birds have an innate homing sense.

label: Conclusion (Therefore)
body: There's no reason to suppose that "eco-friendly" laundry detergents are less damaging to the environment than other laundry detergents are.

label: Evidence
body: All detergents have surfactants, which can harm aquatic life. And the environmental effects of most other ingredients in eco-friendly detergents are unknown.

label: Evaluate
body: Given that ... the environmental effects of most ingredients in eco-friendly detergents are unknown, How could we argue that ... There is some reason to think that eco-friendly detergents are less damaging to the environment than other detergents? Maybe the environmental effects of these eco-friendly detergents haven't been tested yet, but we know from the list of the ingredients that none of the ingredients involved are known to have bad environmental effects. Maybe there is an ingredient in normal detergents that we know is very damaging, so knowing that ingredient is absent in eco-friendly detergents would itself be "a reason to suppose" that the latter is less damaging to the environment.

label: Goal
body: We wouldn't be able to convince anyone for certain that eco-friendly detergents are less damaging, since the data isn't in. It's unknown. But the author is going one step further by saying, "We have zero reason to even speculate that they're less damaging". We might not know for sure whether the mRNA vaccines for COVID are going to have bad long-term effects, but we can still have reason to suppose that they will not (such as the fact that mRNA technology has been used in cancer therapies for years with no ill effects). Let's look for an answer that allows us way to say, "We have some grounds for hoping that eco-friendly detergents are less damaging".

label: Problem
body: If the razor-toothed pike slips out of Lake Davis and into the adjoining river, it could threaten local salmon and trout population.

label: Possible Solutions
body: Can't inject a disease that only kills pike. Can't drain the lake. Adding poison hasn't been ruled out, but it outraged local residents when they did it recently, so not a popular or likely solution.

label: Causal Relationship
body: Poison —c→ tainted water —c→ hurt tourism

label: Evaluate
body: There didn't seem to be any particular tension between ideas or overlap. I organized my understanding with the Problem / Solution framework, but I would head to these answers with a very fuzzy sense of what I want.

label: Goal
body: It's probably most likely that the correct answer restates a truism that you can get from the causal ideas at the end. I'm guessing trap answers might try to bait me into saying something too strong about the possible solutions.

label: Conclusion
body: Everyone who knows Ellsworth will be unsurprised to hear he is offended by allegations that he's engaged in unethical business practices.

label: Evidence
body: Everyone who knows Ellsworth knows he's bursting with self-righteousness, proclaiming that his generation is idealistic whereas previous ones were greedy.

body: Given the structure, "Everyone who knows E knows that X. So, everyone who knows E will be unsurprised to hear that Y," we're looking for a logical connector that says if you know X, you'll be unsurprised to hear Y

label: Goal
body: Thus, we could take either of two things we know about E and try to get to the language of the conclusion: "If you know someone's self-righteous, you'll be unsurprised that they're offended of being alleged of unethical business practice" or "if you know someone's been saying that their generation is less greedy than were previous generations, then you'll be unsurprised that they're offended of being alleged of unethical business practice.

label: Evidence
body: If people believe that important problems can then people be addressed only by → become large numbers of ppl unenthusiastic drastically changing about voting their attitudes and that Big attitudinal changes usually don't result from government action.

label: Evaluate
body: Well, this feels like a mess. When we're doing Flaw and we see conditional logic, we want to immediately consider the #1 famous Necessary vs. Sufficient flaw. Does the author use her conditional premise in an illegal backwards or negated fashion? Does she seem to be thinking, "People don't believe that important problems can only be addressed with big changes in attitude, or they don't believe that politicians are incapable of solving them. Therefore, people are enthusiastic about voting"? No. So she's not doing an illegal negation. How about an illegal reversal? Is she arguing, "People are unenthusiastic about voting. Therefore, they must believe that big problems can only be addressed by big attitude shifts?" Maybe in a diffuse way, but not in any obvious way. The author's conclusion discreetly establishes that there has been decreasing voter turnout recently. This would be a Curious Fact that would prompt an author to try to Solve the Causal Mystery, and the author's conclusion is doing just that. It's saying, "Thus the guilty party responsible for X is entirely Y." Curious Fact ... what's causing decreasing voter turnout? Author's Explanation ... it's exclusively being caused by people's belief that big problems require big attitude shifts combined with people's understanding of the fact that big attitude shifts rarely come from government action.

label: Goal
body: We can object to / weaken this argument by pointing out some Alternate Explanation (even if it's in addition to the one the author supplied) for decreasing voter turnout. Or we can object to / weaken this argument by attacking the plausibility of the author's causal story that people believe big problems requires big attitude shifts and don't believe that politicians or government action can trigger those attitude shifts.

label: Geophysicists' Claim
body: Asteroids have struck the earth through a highly organized process.

label: Evidence
body: Check out that weird pattern of impact craters that form a halo across the Northern Hemisphere. (They preceded some mass extinctions)

label: Evaluate
body: Since the geophysicist is looking at an unusual pattern and then assigning it a causal explanation, we can use a Curious Fact / Explanation mindset. Curious Fact ... Why is there a halo-like swath of impact craters? Geo's Explanation ... Because asteroids don't hit the earth at random locations; they strike the earth through a highly organized natural process.

label: Goal
body: Since this is Strengthen, we either want to rule out a different explanation for the halo-swath of craters or increase the plausibility that they were caused by a "highly organized natural process" that determines how asteroids strike the earth.

label: Conclusion (So)
body: Once the company has moved, most Acme employees will have a commute of more than 30 minutes.

label: Evidence
body: Most Acme employees cannot afford housing within a 30-minute commute of Ocean view, the location where the company is moving.

label: Evaluate
body: We can name the Missing Link here by saying the author is assuming that, "If you can't afford living within a 30-minute commute of where your job is moving, then you will have a commute of more than 30 minutes". But since this conclusion involves a Prediction it's probably more likely that the test wants us to mentally fight that prediction by thinking of some Objection (setting us up for a Defender answer that says the author is assuming that Objection isn't true). Given that ... most of the employees won't be able to afford housing within a 30-minute commute of Ocean View, How could we still argue that .... in the world where the company has moved to Ocean View, most employees will not have a commute of more than 30 minutes? Maybe the current employees who can't afford housing within 30 minutes of Ocean View will hit up their friends that live closer to Ocean View and ask if they can crash on the couch every night, so that when they wake up they're already close to work.
