Maybe the current employees who can't afford housing within 30 mins of Ocean View will just quit their job when the company moves, not willing to tolerate such a long commute. Maybe there's a workforce of 100 currently, but once the company moves to Ocean View, they're going to hire another 200 local workers. Thus, even if those original 100 employees now have a commute of more than 30 minutes, most ACME employees (200 out of 300) will have a commute of less than 30 minutes.

label: Goal
body: Look for an answer linking "can't afford housing within 30 mins" to "will have a commute of more than 30 minutes". Or look for an answer ruling out an objection: - many employees will not crash at the house of their Ocean View friends on work nights - the current employees won't just quit their job and find another job closer to Milltown. - once moved, ACME won't hire so many new local workers that the majority of workers ends up being local Ocean View residents

label: Setup Claims
body: conditional (only if) Each layer of paint → underlying layer adheres satisfactorily properly applied analogy (X is, in this respect, like Y) Education is like painting, in this sense that each new layer only sticks if the previous layers were properly applied. The most important steps in painting are preparation of the surface and application of the primer coat.

label: Fill-in-the-Blank
body: It makes sense to suppose that ....

label: Evaluate
body: The language setting up the blank is signaling that we should be inserting a conclusion. The answer should be making a safely-worded inference that synthesizes the discussion so far. The author just set up an Analogy between painting and education, so the blank should probably have the feel of Complete the Analogy.

label: Evidence
body: Cancer-patient support groups reduce stress for their participants. And a weakened immune system increases vulnerability to cancer.

label: Goal
body: Let's look for an answer like, "The most important steps in education are preparation of "the student's surface" and application of "the primer coat" to the student. Since preparing the surface and then adding the primer coat are the first two steps of painting, we could surmise that the answer might say that the most important steps in education are the initial, foundational ones.

label: Conclusion
body: The odds are slim that colonization of the galaxy by trillions of humans will ever happen.

label: Evidence
body: If trillions of humans were to colonize the galaxy, then the vast majority of humans who ever lived would be alive during that phase. Since we have no reason to think that we are unrepresentative humans, the odds would therefore be overwhelming that we would be alive during the period of galactic colonization. But we're not alive during that period (there are not currently trillions of humans colonizing the galaxy).

label: Evaluate
body: This is a real crappy argument, but our job on Method isn't to evaluate the argument. In real life, smart tech people like Elon Musk make arguments similar to this to argue that we probably live in a simulation: if there were simulated universes, there would be way more simulated universes than real universes, so the probability would be much higher that you live in a simulated universe than in the real universe. Thus, you probably live in a simulated universe. On Method, our job is just to characterize the type of evidence used or the type of move the author made, and the correct answer usually sounds like one of these options: analogy, rule out alternatives, implications of logic, example / counterexample, definition / distinction, overlooked consideration, dubious assumption, alternative explanation The key moment that would stick out to me in this argument is the moment of "Suppose they're right ...." / "If that were really so ... " This is what we mean when we say "implications of logic". The second half of an If/Then statement is called its outcome, its consequence, its necessary implication. So authors will either say, "Let's follow the logic of your plan or your rule ... it ultimately ends at this undesirable place, so it looks like the plan / rule is no good". Or, like we're doing in this argument, authors will say, "If you were right, then X would follow. But X isn't true. So you must be wrong." This 2nd style is arguing via contrapositive logic. If you were right → implication X But implication X is not the case. Thus, you are not right.

label: Goal
body: We will probably see an answer saying the author discussed the implications of a certain belief, and then established that an implication is not true, thus that the belief is not true. (on in this case, "the odds are slim" that the belief is true)

label: Conclusion
body: If there aren't other ways to tell if the speech was inflammatory, then the speech was appropriate.

label: Evidence
body: Riley said the president's speech was inflammatory, and therefore inappropriate, but Riley's testimony has to be taken with a grain of salt, since he's had a long standing feud with the president.

label: Evaluate
body: This has two conclusions. There is an intermediate conclusion signified by "so", that "if Riley has had a long feud with the president, then Riley's testimony isn't sufficient proof that the speech was inflammatory." Do we have to accept that move? Not really. Someone could have a feud with X, but be scrupulously honest and not easily offended, in which case we might still trust their testimony that a certain speech was inflammatory. But the main conclusion is signified by "Therefore". Since the author is saying "it's not true that the speech was inappropriate", she's concluding that "the speech was appropriate". What is her evidence it was appropriate? Oh, wait. She doesn't have any positive evidence it was appropriate. She only has negative evidence rejecting Riley's argument that it was inappropriate. This is a famous flaw called Unproven vs. Proven False. Shooting down an argument for Claim X doesn't mean that you've proven Claim X is false.

label: Goal
body: Look for an answer complaining about the the author's inability to trust Riley's testimony, given his feud with the president, or for an answer pointing out that the author went from saying "Riley's argument that the speech was inappropriate fails to persuade; therefore, the speech WAS appropriate."

label: Premise
body: Our failure to attract new listeners over the past several years has forced us to choose between devoting some airtime to other, more popular genres of music, and sticking with classical music that appeals only to our small but loyal audience.

label: Premise
body: This audience, however loyal, did not generate enough advertising revenue for us to pay our bills.

label: Intermediate Conclusion
body: So if we appeal to them alone, our station risks going out of business.

label: Premise
body: We should not take that risk.

label: Main Conclusion
body: We should, therefore, devote some airtime to other, more popular genres of music.

label: Evaluate
body: This argument limits the options to two, presents evidence that one option possesses an unacceptable risk, and then advocates for the other option. The problem with this being that the argument never addressed whether the other option is just as likely to possess the unacceptable risk.

label: Conclusion (Hence)
body: This painting is definitely not a genuine Cassatt.

label: Evidence
body: The brush style of this painting is not found in any work known to be Cassatt's.

label: Evaluate
body: This is a pretty thin argument. The historian concedes that the painting does resemble a lot of what we see in Cassatt's canvas, materials, and subject matter. But the brush style?! Nay.

label: Goal
body: Let's look for a Linking answer like, "If the brush style doesn't match any known painting by Cassatt, then the painting is not a genuine Cassatt". Or let's look for a Defender answer saying something like, "This painting is not just an atypical work by Cassatt, in which she experimented with a brush style she doesn't normally use." "There is not an entire collection of Cassatt paintings using this brush style in a storage room somewhere, unbeknownst to the world of art".

label: Evidence
body: For all apartments at Riverview, If an apartment has a balcony, A → B it also has a fireplace. None of the ones with A → ~C balconies are 1-bed.

label: Conclusion
body: None of the 1-beds C → ~B have a fireplace (B → ~C)

label: Government's Conclusion
body: This company's collectibles shall not be classified as toys.

label: Evaluation
body: Since both conditionals have the same trigger (A), there's no way to conclude any conditional connection between their outcomes (B and ~C). If a 1-bedroom had a fireplace, that wouldn't contradict any premises (unless that 1-bedroom also had a balcony, but it's possible that there's a 1-bedroom, with no balcony, but with a fireplace). Since this argument is highly conditional / quantified logic, we can probably match our way to the correct answer whether or not we understand why the structure is flawed.

label: Goal
body: Two conditional premises with the same trigger. A conclusion that makes a conditional relationship between the two outcomes.

label: Alissa's 1st Claim
body: If the city can no longer fund both the kids museum and kids TV programming, it should stop funding the TV programming. Does Greta disagree? Is she arguing that if the city needs to make a choice, they should choose to keep TV programming and stop funding the kids museum? Yes! She explicitly says that.

label: Alissa's 2nd Claim
body: The interactive character of the exhibits makes for a richer (more active) educational experience than watching TV, which is largely passive. Does Greta disagree? Is she arguing that the exhibits at the museum are not more rich and active than passively watching TV? No, she doesn't talk about that comparison at all.

label: Evaluate
body: We know that Greta disagrees with Alissa's 1st claim and is silent on Alissa's 2nd claim. In fact, the disagreement is so apparent and explicit, that I would suspect the answers will go one layer deeper. When there is a very obvious and explicit disagreement, then the correct answer usually compares the reasons each person had for reaching their position. Person 1: I think Harvard is the best law school because its grads are most likely to be President or appointed to SCOTUS. Person 2: I think Stanford is the best law school because its grads make the highest average salary in their first job. Rather than giving us an easy, superficial answer like, They disagree over which law school is the best the correct answer will compare reasons, like Average first job salary is a better determinant of a law school's quality than is likelihood of holding prestigious government positions

label: Goal
body: So in this case, we know the superficial debate is "Keep the museum vs. No, keep the TV shows". But the underlying debate is, "Keep (the more engaging, active educational experience) vs. No, keep (the educational asset that reaches more people)"

label: Conclusion
body: The substance has iron.

label: Evidence
body: A magnet was attracted to the substance, and magnets attract iron.

label: Evaluate
body: Consider this analogy — "Jim's teacher asked him to determine whether Tanika is an NBA player. Jim knew that NBA players are rich, so he asked Tanika if she is rich. She said yes, so he concluded that she is an NBA player." We would object by saying "couldn't she be rich for some other reason? It's not like NBA players are the only rich people. Jim is failing to consider the possibility that some rich people don't play in the NBA." This is the famous Necessary vs. Sufficient flaw. We were given a conditional rule: Iron in it → Magnet is attracted. From that rule Jim thought, "since the magnet is attracted to this substance, this substance must have iron in it." He's reasoning backwards through that conditional statement, a.k.a. confusing the sufficient condition with the necessary condition.

label: Goal
body: Similarly, Jim is failing to consider that magnets might be attracted to other things besides iron. Maybe they're also attracted to nickel and copper. The fact that the magnet was attracted to the substance doesn't prove it's iron, because there might be other things besides iron that magnets are attracted to.

label: Conclusion
body: The book Horatio wants was either misplaced or stolen.

label: Evidence
body: Horatio wants a book but can't find it in its proper place on the shelves. No one in the library is using it. It's not checked out to anyone nor is it waiting to be shelved or in an unusual place because it's part of a special display.

label: Evaluate
body: Method questions tend to pull from a pretty consistent list of moves In this argument, the author rules out a lot of competing alternatives to arrive at the two remaining possibilities: misplaced or stolen.

label: Goal
body: Look for something like "considers and rejects other explanations" or "rules out competing alternatives".

label: Facts
body: comparison Sulfur dioxide now > sulfur dioxide 10 yrs ago causal connector (this is troubling because) we imposed stricter it's troubling that regulations on coal >> sulfur dioxide levels plants 10 yrs ago are higher conditional regulations followed → level of sulfur diox lower

label: Evaluate
body: On Most Supported, the #1 thing we look for is Causality, so that causal connector of "this is troubling because" would seem real enticing. On Must Be True, the #1 thing we look for is Conditionals, so that last sentence should be our priority. When we see conditionals, they're usually testing us on some combination of these skills: 1) can we contrapose the rule? 2) can we chain together connected rules? 3) do any facts trigger the rule? (usually it triggers the contrapostive) There aren't any other conditional rules, so we're not making a chain. But the first sentence does trigger the contrapositive of rule. The contrapositive: levels of sulfur diox not lower → regulations not followed We know the levels aren't lower. The first sentence tells us that they're actually slightly higher. So we know that the regulations were not followed.

label: Goal
body: Let's look for an answer like, "The stricter regulations on emission from coal-burning power plants imposed ten years ago were not followed."

label: Opposing Support
body: Landfills are generally designed to hold ten years’ worth of waste.

label: Opposing Point
body: Some people maintain that as the number of active landfills consequently dwindles over the coming decade, there will inevitably be a crisis in landfill availability.

label: Premise
body: However, their prediction obviously relies on the unlikely assumption that no new landfills will open as currently active ones close.

label: Main Conclusion
body: [Their prediction] is therefore unsound.

label: Evaluate
body: That there will be a crisis in landfill availability is the opposing point in the ecologist’s argument.

label: Conclusion
body: Cancer-patient support groups might have genuine therapeutic value

label: Evaluate
body: Sorry, what? What is the argument? Sometimes LSAC throws us these convoluted messes where it's hard to process what the author is even trying to argue, let alone argue with him. The good news is that when the logic is this hard to put together, it normally means that once you figure out the author's thought process, the correct answer is just testing the connective tissue you assembled. Since our author's conclusion is saying cancer support groups —c→ therapeutic value we need to figure out how the author got from cancer support group to therapeutic value. The evidence definitely talks about support groups (it says they reduce stress), but where does the therapeutic value come in? Here we have to exert some will power / outside knowledge. The first sentence is talking about immune system and vulnerability to cancer. And the following sentence begins "So". That means the author thinks the first sentence is a reason we should believe that cancer-support groups have a therapeutic value (i.e. they help you with your cancer). The author must be assuming that cancer-support groups have something to do with how strong or weak your immune system is, if the first sentence supposedly supports the conclusion. Obviously, a weaker immune system wouldn't help your cancer, so the author must be thinking that cancer support groups lead to a strengthened immune system, which leads to decreased vulnerability to cancer. How do cancer support groups lead to a strengthened immune system? We'll take the one thing the author told us about them (reduce stress) and assume the author is drawing some connection from stress to immune system. It seems like this is the intended causal story the author is making. Cancer Reduced Stronger Less vulnerable support → stress → Immune → to cancer groups

label: Goal
body: The link we invented there for the author was the middle one, so we should look for an answer saying that "reduced stress" can lead to "stronger immune system" or some other way of stating that those two are connected.

label: Evidence
body: [Adobe] conducts heat very slowly. As a result, a house built of adobe retains the warmth of the desert sun during the cool evenings and then remains cool during the heat of the day, thereby helping to maintain a pleasant temperature. In contrast, houses built of other commonly used building materials, which conduct heat more rapidly, grow hot during the day and cold at night.

label: Conclusion
body: Adobe is an ideal material for building in desert environments.

label: Evaluate
body: The argument compares adobe with other building materials with regard to their ability to conduct heat and argues that adobe is an ideal material for building in the desert.

label: Background
body: One study of a plant species says 70% of them have patterned stems.

label: Surprising Fact
body: The second study, which covered the same basic area, showed only 40% had patterned stems.

label: Evaluation
body: We need some way to explain the different measurement, so the answer will have to give us a difference between the two studies that would account for 70% vs. 40%. - time of day / lighting? - how well trained the researchers were? - how picky their criteria were? - how long they worked? etc.

label: Conclusion
body: The approach you suggest for disposing of nasty dredge spoils would damage commercial fishing operations.

label: Evidence
body: Over 20,000 people have signed petitions opposing your approach and preferring using sand-capped pits in another area.

label: Evaluation
body: Is this petition good evidence that commercial fishing operations would be damaged? Tough to say. Did the petition even mention commercial fishing operations? Were most of the 20,000 signatories aware of what effect this approach might have on commercial fishing operations? All we know from the petition is that these people opposed this approach and favored another. But we don't know anything about why they opposed this approach, so this could be an Irrelevant Response to whether the approach hurts commercial fishing, and we have no idea whether these people knew anything about commercial fishing, so this could be an Inappropriate Appeal to people who might lack the knowledge or expertise to evaluate this situation.

label: Goal
body: Find an answer complaining about, "We don't know who these people are, whether they were qualified to judge, or why they oppose this approach".

label: Conclusion
body: Most universities today offer a more in-depth and cosmopolitan education than ever before.

label: Evidence
body: Most history courses used to only require reading that barely covered African or Asian history other than ancient stuff and barely covered Native American cultures. But now the history courses at most schools do cover that stuff more.

label: Evaluate
body: If we were analyzing this argument for missing Idea Math, we could say that the author is assuming, "if you're now studying African / Asian / Native American cultures, then you're getting a more in-depth and cosmopolitan education than ever before". If we were thinking of objections (that could be ruled out by a correct answer), we might think, "Where did you steal curriculum time from to start including more coverage of A/A/NA cultures? If you use to cover European, South African, Scandinavian, and Australian cultures more but now you barely cover them, then are you really more in-depth or more cosmopolitan, or did you just swap one set of deficiencies for another? There's also a bit of a Part vs. Whole feel to this argument. The conclusion is about "your education" at most universities, but the premises are exclusively about "history courses" at most universities. Are history courses a good indicator of the overall depth and cosmopolitanism of the education at that university?

label: Goal
body: Look for an answer saying, "yes, history is a representative sample", or "in order to cover these topics we were barely covering before, we didn't have to give up covering other topics sufficiently", or "if you now cover A/A/NA cultures, then you're more in-depth and cosmopolitan than before".

label: Conclusion
body: Having the government publish airline stats about near collisions and fines for safety violations will undermine the goal of making the public more informed about airline safety.

label: Evidence
body: Airlines will be much less likely to give complete reports if this info is going to be public.

label: Evaluate
body: The author is reasoning in this way: Publish → incomplete → public not safety info → reports → more informed That first link is established in the premise. The second link is something the author is assuming.

label: Government's Evidence
body: The collectibles are marketed as collector's items, not toys.

label: Goal
body: If we're arguing the Anti-Conclusion, we need to think, "GIVEN THAT the airlines will give incomplete reports, HOW CAN WE ARGUE THAT this is helping make the public more informed about airline safety".

label: Conclusion
body: Financial rewards do not provide the strongest incentive for people to choose one job over another.

label: Evidence
body: In many surveys, most people don't name salary as the most desirable feature of a job.

label: Evaluation
body: How would we defend the economists original claim in light of this evidence? Given that most people don't list salary as their #1 desirable feature, how could we argue that financial rewards do provide the strongest incentive for people? One possible line of attack is to say that, "even though most people don't name salary as their #1 feature, it could still be that more people picked salary #1 than anything else." To steal an old LSAT argument, if you asked everyone what their #1 book was, there would be so many different answers, that no answer would be said by more than 50% of people. Say 13% of people said The Bible, then 9% said "Atlas Shrugged", and 7% said "Catcher in the Rye", etc. With those results, we could say "Most people do not list The Bible as their favorite book", but it would nonetheless be true that The Bible was the #1 vote getter. In reality, what this question is testing is "financial rewards" vs. "salary". Salary is part of financial rewards, but not identical. But since most of us don't see that Term Shift, we don't want to pretend like it was obvious to us.

label: Goal
body: We need a way to argue that financial rewards ARE the biggest incentive for people in selecting their job, but we have to accept that in these surveys salary is not #1.

label: Conclusion
body: We don't think that making classes smaller allows teachers to devote more time to each student, with the result being that students become more engaged in the learning process. (Specifically, we disagree with that last part about students becoming more engaged)

label: Evidence
body: We studied schools who underwent reductions in class size, and the teachers did devote more time to each student, but the grades were unchanged.

label: Evaluate
body: It takes some (very important) mental effort to figure out what the conclusion is specifically saying. It's objecting to a 2-part claim, but it acknowledges in the premise that the first part of the claim is valid. So by process of elimination, we know the conclusion is arguing that "students didn't become more engaged". The evidence doesn't talk about whether or not they were more engaged at all. It only talks about whether or not their grades went up.

label: Goal
body: Apparently this argument is assuming that "grades = engagement in the learning process". Specifically the author is thinking, if their grades → their engagement in the didn't go up learning process didn't go up or by contrapositive, more engaged → grades change in learning process

label: Conclusion
body: The manufacturers' claims are not exaggerated. (Water-saving faucets do save you as much money as they claim)

label: Evidence
body: I have had lower water bills since I installed a water-saving faucet.

label: Evaluation
body: If we are trying to argue the Anti-Conclusion, then we're thinking GIVEN THAT ... she's had lower water bills since she installed her water-saving faucet, HOW WOULD WE STILL ARGUE ... that she's not saving as much as the manufacturers' claimed? Well ... how much did they claim she would save? How much is she saving? If they claimed she'd save 30% and she's saving 10%, then it seems like the manufacturers did exaggerate how much money she would save.

label: Goal
body: Find an answer asking questions about how much they claimed she'd save vs. how much she is actually saving, or an answer that points out "even if you're saving money, you might not be saving as much money as you were promised".

label: Conclusion
body: We'll reduce air pollution more by buying old cars than by redesigning our plants.

label: Evidence
body: Our plants account for only 4% of local air pollution, while automobiles that predate 1980 account for 30%.

label: Evaluation
body: The conclusion is only about comparing these two possible actions, so we can only disagree with the author by saying that the plan to redesign plants would actually reduce air pollution more. But how can we argue that? If they succeeded in getting all the pre-1980 cars off the road, they'd reduce 30% of the current pollution. If their plant redesign went as well as possible, it would only reduce 4% of the current air pollution.

label: Goal
body: We need a way to argue our attempt to buy up the old pre-1980 cars and get them off the road, would only amount to 4% or less. Either we have to be unable to buy up all the cars (so that the pollution savings is way less than 30%), or the people whose old cars we buy would have to THEN create more air pollution as a result (so that the net savings of air pollution is way less than 30%).

label: Evidence
body: Humankind survived. Survived Survival required Survived → Sac sacrifice. Sacrifice is Sacrifice → Altruism Altruism.

label: Conclusion
body: Ancestors were altruistic. Altruism

label: Evaluation
body: This is a tough argument to see in conditional logic, but because of the repeating symbols (sacrifice shows up twice, so does altruism) and because of the "if" in the first sentence, we probably should try to see the math in the argument. It ends up being a straightforward type of argument, with two conditional premises that chain together, a fact that triggers the chain, and a conclusion that states the outcome of the chain.

label: Goal
body: We need something resembling this. A → B B → C A. ⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯ C.

label: Conclusion
body: The bus company should not reprimand me for the accident.

label: Evidence
body: Even though I might have been able to avoid the collision if I had reacted more quickly, the garbage truck that hit me was over the speed limit, and this speeding directly led to the accident. Meanwhile, I was abiding by all traffic regulations.

label: Evaluate / Goal
body: If we need a rule to get us from their Evidence to their Conclusion, it should sound something like, "If it's marketed as X, then it should be classified as X". Or the negative version, "If it's not marketed as a toy, then it shouldn't be classified as a toy."

label: Evaluation
body: We know we need the right side of → should not the arrow on this reprimand me rule to be saying What were his reasons why? - the other driver was breaking the law by speeding, and the speeding was a causal factor in the accident. - he was not breaking any law He also acknowledged a counterpoint, that he probably could have still avoided the accident, but that's not a reason why he shouldn't be reprimanded. It's potentially a reason why he should be reprimanded.

label: Goal
body: Something like, If I was following the rules and the other driver broke a rule which led to the accident, then I shouldn't be reprimanded (even if I could've reacted quicker)

label: Evidence
body: Radio drama requires its listeners to think about what they hear, picturing for themselves such dramatic elements as characters physical appearances and spatial relationships. Earlier generations, for whom radio drama was the dominant form of popular entertainment, regularly exercised their imaginations.

label: Conclusion
body: Today's generation of television viewers do so [regularly exercise their imaginations] less frequently.

label: Evaluate
body: The argument's conclusion is too strong. Without knowing everything else that has changed for today's generation, it's not possible to say how much more or less today's generation exercises their imaginations While it may be true that television provides less opportunity to exercise one's imagination, it could also be true that other activities more than compensate for any loss that resulted from the switch from radio to television.

label: Conclusion (so)
body: Most candidates in this year's election have the skills necessary to be a good mayor.

label: Evidence
body: Each candidate in this year's election is a small-business owner (SBO). Most SBO's are competent managers. No competent manager lacks the skill necessary to be a good mayor.

label: Evaluation
body: With all those overlapping terms mentioned twice (SBO, competent manager, skills necessary), it makes sense to try to diagram the formal recipe of this argument. Each candidate is a SBO. All X's are A. Most SBO's are comp mgrs Most A's are B. All comp managers have nec. skills All B's are C. ⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯ Most candid's have necessary skills Most X's are C. Because of how many structural signposts there are here, I wouldn't bother to even think about why this is flawed. But the flaw is that there are no overlap inferences to be made by combining "All X's are A" with "Most A's are B". There doesn't have to be any overlap between X and B. I can say "All NBA players are men" and "Most men make less than $100k". There doesn't mean there's any NBA player that makes less than $100k.

label: Goal
body: - We should be able to get rid of any answer whose Conclusion isn't a Most statement. - We can get rid of anything that doesn't have three premises: 2 All/None and 1 Most. - And to orient ourselves to a correct answer, we want to see an "All X's are A" premise as well as a "Most A's ..." premise.

label: Evidence
body: One of the most useful social conventions is money, whose universality across societies is matched only by language. Unlike language, which is rooted in an innate ability, money is an artificial, human invention.

label: Conclusion
body: Hence, it seems probable that the invention of money occurred independently in more than one society.

label: Evaluate
body: This argument overlooks the possibility that money was invented in one society and then shared from one society to the next until every society adopted its use. To ensure that money was invented independently in more than one society, the right answer should rule out the possibility that some societies adopted the use of money after observing its use in another society.

label: Evidence
body: The result of strong libel SLL → ~BR laws is that, for fear of lawsuits, no one will say anything bad about public figures.

label: Conclusion
body: Strong laws against SLL → ~GR label can make it impossible for anyone in the public eye to have a good reputation.

label: Evaluate
body: The argument assumes ~BR → ~GR that if no one has a bad reputation, then no one can have a good reputation.

label: Evaluation
body: Too much stuff here to diagram. We'd be better served trying to get a rough sense of all the facts and then coming back to the paragraph as needed once we see what type of idea each answer is floating us. Humans can't eat wood, turning its cellulose in to glucose, but mushrooms can. Mushrooms use that to make polymers called B-G's, which can be used to fight cancer (the more branches, the better B-G's fight cancer) by increasing immune-cell activity, not by killing cancer cells.

label: Goal
body: I wouldn't expect an answer to tie all this stuff together, but if we were trying it might sound like, "Mushrooms can do something mammals can't do, and in doing so, they make something that can help mammals fight cancer". Overall, though, we should just be wary of extreme wording in the answers and research the promising ones.

label: Evaluate
body: Since this question stem is asking what sort of Comparison the argument makes, we should primarily read with that goal. The structure of "Just as X , so Y" implies a comparison between X and Y. "Just as Lucky Charms put marshmallows in their cereal as 'treats', so Ben & Jerry's puts chunks of cookie dough into their ice cream as 'treats'." We're comparing Lucky Charms cereal to Ben & Jerry's ice cream. In this argument we just read, it said, "Just as manners are ____ .... , so societal laws are ____ ." We know we're comparing manners and societal laws. What is similar about them? They both get their authority mainly through our habit of obeying them. Contrary behavior becomes unthinkable because abiding behavior becomes customary, not because people are afraid of the penalties that await were they to violate a rule of manners or law.

label: Given that ...
body: Cops are usually prohibited from drinking on the job.

label: Why is it that ...
body: Cops are allowed to drink in moderation during work if they're working undercover in nightclubs?

label: Evaluate / Goal
body: This one seems to play off common sense, so we can probably predict the answer. Why are cops allowed to drink if they're working undercover in a nightclub? Because they're supposed to be blending in with all the normal people there, most of whom are drinking. Let's look for that, or any other reason why cops working undercover in a nightclub are allowed to have a couple drinks.

label: Jake Karolinka
body: I Companies have recently introduced antibacterial household cleaning products that kill common bacteria on surfaces like counter-tops and floors. But studies also suggest that the use of these antibacterial cleaning products can be harmful, since common bacteria that survive the use of these products will eventually produce strains of bacteria that are resistant to It’s clear that That’s why people who want antibacterial agents to minimize the should not be used amount of bacteria in household in their homes cleaning products. should use cleaning products that contain antibacterial agents.

label: Evaluate
body: Jake and Karolinka agree that household cleaning agents kill some common bacteria.

label: Conclusion
body: If you have more galactose in your body than what the body can process, it is carcinogenic (cancer-causing).

label: Evidence
body: In a study, the group of people with cancer had such a low level of a certain enzyme that they couldn't process the galactose in the yogurt they were consuming.

label: Evaluate
body: The author is taking one fact she knows that is distinct to the cancer group and then concluding that that factor caused the cancer! What if we had said, "In the people with cancer, the level of hair loss was much higher than in the non-cancer group. Therefore, losing hair is carcinogenic"? That would be a silly conclusion to reach. Maybe the hair loss is unconnected to the cancer. Maybe it's actually an effect of the cancer (or the chemotherapy treatment received by people who have cancer). When an author presents a correlation, f.e. "the people who were X were also Y", she is likely to conclude that X causes Y. But we always evaluate causal arguments with the same two-pronged mindset: - Is there any other way to explain this correlation? (maybe Y causes X. Maybe some third factor, Z, is causing both of them) - How plausible is the author's causal storyline? (is there any explanation of how X would cause Y? are there any data points that show when someone stopped having X, they stopped having Y?) We are trained to react to correlations primarily by thinking, "What if it's Reverse Causality? What if there's some Third Factor that's the real cause that we haven't identified with?"

label: Goal
body: Find an answer simply describing the author's illegal move of thinking, "Since all the cancer people had low enzyme, the low enzyme is causing the cancer", or find an answer bringing up one of the alternative explanations the author has failed to consider: "Maybe the cancer led to the low enzyme. Maybe there's some other factor, like a certain gene, that both leads to cancer and leads to low levels of this enzyme."

label: Conclusion (Clearly)
body: Our company releases more pollutants than most chemical companies similar to us in size.

label: Evidence
body: According to a study of 30 small chemical companies, our company and four other companies together account for 60% of the total pollutants.

label: Evaluate
body: There are two separate issues we should think through: 1. Does the evidence show that this company releases more pollutants than do most chemical companies in the study? 2. If so, it is fair to extrapolate from this study to "most chemical companies of a similar size"? When it comes to #1, Given that ... our company and four others together account for 60% of the pollutants released by the 30 companies in the study (the other 25 companies combine to account for 40% of the pollutants), How could we still argue that ... our company does not release more pollutants than do most chemical companies in the study? Let's say that 100 tons of pollutants were released. And here's the list of who did what: Company A — 25 tons Company B — 20 tons Company C — 15 tons Company D — 8.9 tons Company E — 1.1 tons Company F — 1 ton Company G — 1 ton Company H — 1 ton etc. Suppose that our company is Company E. If we add up our company with companies A thru D, then we'll get 60 out of the 100 tons of pollutants, or 60%. But does that mean that Company E releases more pollutants than most companies our size? No, it might be that the Top 4 are polluting juggernauts and we are very ordinary. It's like if you were thrown on an NBA All-Star Team. You and the other four players on your team would collectively score 150 points, but that doesn't mean that you contributed your 30 point share. Maybe the rest of your teammates all had around 40 points and you had 1 or 2 points. This argument is saying that "collectively these five companies account for most (60%) of the pollutants". Thus, each of those five companies accounts for more pollutants than most companies. It's almost like a Whole to Part flaw, where the author fails to consider that the five companies might contribute very unevenly to that total.

label: Goal
body: We either want an answer that rules out the possibility that the other four companies are responsible for like 59% of that 60% and we're just contributing around 1%. Or we want an answer relating to the sampling move from "if it's true of the 30 companies in this study, then it's true of most chemical companies this size".

label: Conclusion (clearly)
body: Decaffeinated coffee must contain something that isn't present in regular coffee that damages connective tissue.

label: Evidence
body: In a study, people who drink 3 cups of decaf every day were twice as likely to develop arthritis as people who drink 3 cups of regular coffee per day.

label: Evaluate
body: Any time the author's conclusion is stating or assuming a causal explanation for the results of a study, we go into Explain Curious Fact mode. Curious Fact ... How come people who drink 3 cups of decaf are twice as likely to get arthritis, compared to people who drink 3 cups of regular? Author's Explanation ... There is a special ingredient in decaf, not in regular, that damages connective tissue, which leads to the arthritic inflammation of joints. We're always supposed to consider 1. Alternate Explanations for the curious fact 2. the plausibility of the Author's Explanation Any time we're given a correlation between x and y (in this case between decaf and arthritis), there are two automatic alternate explanations we want to consider: - could it be Reverse Causality? is it possible that the arthritis came first, and since the arthritis made it harder to grasp the coffee mug securely, those people switched to decaf so they wouldn't have the shaky hands a caffeinated person might have? The problem with that storyline here is that the correlation seems to have a built in before/after. It says that the people drinking decaf are more likely to develop arthritis (in the future). If it said they were more likely to have arthritis, then we could definitely consider this reverse causality angle. - could there be a Third Factor that is the real causal agent, and the two parts of the correlation are just symptoms of that third factor? is it possible that "old age" is the common ingredient? If older people are more likely to drink decaf and more likely to develop arthritis, then that would explain why decaf and arthritis are correlated, but it wouldn't be decaf causing the arthritis. When it comes to the plausibility of the author's story, she has to assume that the process of decaffeinated coffee involves adding some new ingredient. If it's only removing caffeine, then decaf and regular coffee are chemically the same, other than caffeine, and so her story would make no sense.

label: Goal
body: Let's look for answer that either allows us to argue that there's an Alternate Explanation for why decaf is correlated with higher rates of arthritis, or one that deals with the plausibility of the author's storyline that decaf has a special ingredient that damages connective tissue.

label: Evidence
body: If the store doesn't process pictures properly, then the store owes a refund. The pictures are unsatisfactory. The film wasn't defective. The camera wasn't defective.

label: Evaluate
body: The author us trying to combine the store's refund policy ("if they process the pictures wrong, then the customer is owed a refund") with a Solve the Causal Mystery type argument in which he rules out other possible causes of the unsatisfactory pictures: - film defective - camera defective - handled improperly - not processed properly Are we sure those are all the possible causes for unsatisfactory photographs?

label: Goal
body: The author is assuming that there are only these four possible causes of unsatisfactory photos. She thinks that if she rules out the other three, she is establishing that the store didn't process the photos properly, which means a refund is owed.

label: Conclusion (should)
body: When weeding a garden, one should not try to remove all the weeds.

label: Evidence
body: Even though, fewer weeds would make a garden more productive, the slight productivity loss you get from leaving those last few weeds in pales in comparison to how annoying it is to find and remove every single one.

label: Evaluate
body: We need to ask ourselves what principle underlies this argument. The author seems to be Weighing Tradeoffs. One the one hand, the more weeds you remove, the more productive a garden you have. On the other hand, leaving a few of them doesn't hurt productivity much, and it allows you to avoid the painstaking effort of finding and pulling every single one. The author seems to be citing a general principle of Diminishing Returns. When you compare the effort invested to the return on investment, you're getting diminishing returns by the time you hit those last few weeks, so just leave them.

label: Goal
body: Let's look for something like: Even though an A+ job is better than an A, the extra effort to get from A to A+ isn't worth it, so one should not try to get the A+.

label: Evidence
body: Not only in this country but in many other countries as well, the excessive proportion of junk food in people's diets contributes to many common and serious health problems. If junk food were much more expensive than healthful food, people would be encouraged to make dietary changes that would reduce these problems.

label: Conclusion
body: It would benefit public health if junk food were taxed.

label: Evaluate
body: The argument is designed to support the view that taxing junk food would benefit public health.

label: Premise
body: When asked to name a poet contemporaneous with Shakespeare, 60 percent of high school students picked a twentieth-century poet.

label: Intermediate Conclusions
body: It might show that most high school students do not know any poets of Shakespeare’s era. It might show that most high school students do not know what “contemporaneous” means.

label: Conclusion
body: However, either way, there is clearly something deeply wrong with the educational system.

label: Evaluate
body: The statement that the majority of students picked a twentieth-century poet is a premise in the argument.

label: Statements
body: Conditionals (only = right side) to person wronged should apologize → and apologizing for wronging (to X is to Y = X→Y) acknowledge you've sincere apology → acted wrongfully (unless = Required goes on Right) intend not to repeat sincere apology → wrongful act (unless = Required goes on Right) acknowledge a wrong sincere accept → and apology vow not to hold a grudge

label: Conclusion (therefore)
body: The copper-alloy implements were dropped into the well no earlier than 375 A.D.

label: Evidence
body: They were found in a well, and beneath them was a cache of coins, some of which dated to 375 A.D.

label: Evaluate
body: How does the author think that the date of these coins tells us anything about the date of the kitchen implements? She's thinking, "if you drop something in a well, it lands on top of whatever is already in there. So the stuff farther down is older; the stuff farther up is newer." The coins were from as recently as 375 A.D., so, she reasons, anything on higher up in the well than the coins would have been dropped in after the coins, and thus after 375 A.D. How can we fight this logic? How could we argue "even if I accept your premise, you conclusion could be wrong"? Given that ... the coins below the copper implements were deposited as recently as 375 A.D, How could we still argue that ... the copper implements themselves were deposited earlier than 375 A.D.? We could say that, "unlike bulkier objects, coins can drop through to the bottom. So maybe those copper implements were dropped in the well around 100 A.D., and then 275 years later (in the year 375 A.D.) someone comes along, makes a wish on one of these coins, and tosses it in the well. Couldn't that coin drop beneath the copper implements, even though it was dropped in later?"

label: Goal
body: Let's look for something that rules out our objection of "couldn't the coins have been deposited later and just fallen down beneath the copper implements" or look for an answer that finds some other way to increase the plausibility that these implements were no older than 375 A.D.

label: Therefore (So)
body: The investigators have not proved that the blaze was caused by campers or lightning.

label: Evidence
body: The investigators haven't proved that the forest fire was started by campers, nor have they proved it was started by lightning.

label: Evaluate
body: At first it seems like this conclusion is pretty reasonable, right? Given that ... they haven't proved the fire was from campers and haven't proved the fire was from lightning, How could we say that ... they have proved that fire was caused by campers or lightning? Can you prove that "X or Y" is true even though you haven't proven that X or Y separately are true? I guess so. There might be only two suspects at the scene of the crime. If you know someone committed an act of graffiti on the night of March 10, and you can prove that the only people who were there the night of March 10 were Sam and Pam, then you've proven that "Sam or Pam (or both) is responsible for the graffiti", even though you can't prove that it was Sam and can't prove that it was Pam.

label: Evidence
body: In a survey, most respondents who had recently listened to a taped reading of a certain best-selling novel said they enjoyed the novel, while most who read the novel said they didn't enjoy it.

label: Goal
body: In a sense this is a Part vs. Whole flaw. Since each part of "campers or lightning" has the trait "haven't been proven to be responsible for fire", the author assumes that the collective "campers or lightning" also shares that trait. But it's a weird manifestation of Part vs. Whole, so it might be easier to just look for a similar conversational objection: Even though we can't prove it's thing X vs. thing Y, it still might be possible that we're sure it had to be one of those two.

label: Given that ...
body: Hundreds of fruiting trees were planted in the hopes that birds would be attracted to the area.

label: and that ...
body: As the trees matured, the summer bird population in the area greatly increased, and the birds ate many mosquitoes.

label: How can it be that ...
body: Since the trees were planted, the mosquito population has gotten bigger?

label: Evaluate
body: There might be something unrelated to the trees that has caused the mosquito population to grow over the same time period since the trees were planted. For example, maybe the trees were planted 10 years ago, and during the last 10 years there have been more tropical storms than usual, and tropical storms leave lots of standing water where mosquitoes breed. Maybe people who live in that area have started installing more bird baths in their yard, and the standing water of a bird bath help mosquitoes breed. Or the uptick in mosquitoes could be related to the trees or the birds themselves (the two variables that have changed).

label: Goal
body: Look for an answer that helps us do any of these things: - these trees do something that boosts the mosquito population - this influx of birds does something that boosts the mosquito population - something that boosts the mosquito population changed, around the same time as when the fruit trees were planted

label: Setup Claims
body: If you promised a friend that you would meet them for lunch but just before lunch you felt ill, it wouldn't be wrong for you to miss lunch. Your friend wouldn't expect you to be there. Roxanne promised Luke that she would finish the report while he was on vacation but the deadline got pushed back.

label: The Blank
body: Similarly, _______ . Because of that comparison keyword 'similarly', We know our job is to complete the analogy.

label: Evaluate
body: The story about Roxanne / Luke provides the initial ingredients of that if/then principle we were given: - a promise was made - the situation changed We need think through what the other two parts of the principle would sound like, as applied to the Roxanne and Luke story.

label: Goal
body: It should sound like - it would not be wrong to fail to deliver on the promise [of having the report done by vacation's end]. - Luke wouldn't expect Roxanne to finish it by the promised deadline, if the deadline has now been pushed back.

label: Conclusion
body: Watching violent films is at least partly responsible for children hurting other children.

label: Evidence
body: In a study, the kids who watched a video of children hitting Bobo were more likely to subsequently hit Bobo than were the kids who didn't see that video.

label: Evaluate
body: Since the author is interpreting the results of a study, we can use our Curious Fact / Explanation template. Curious Fact Why are the kids who watched the Bobo video more likely to hit Bobo than the kids who didn't see the video? Author's Story Watching violence on TV makes kids more aggressive. We always then consider two different pressure points: - How ELSE could we explain the curious fact? - how plausible is the author's explanation? Maybe the video-watching kids are hitting Bobo not because they learned violence from TV but because they just have cooped up energy, from having to sit still while watching the video. Maybe after any video, a kid has so much pent up energy that they're liable to act more aggressively. Maybe all kids feel the aggressive urge to hit the Bobo doll, but only the kids who watched the video realize that they're allowed to.

label: Goal
body: Find an answer offering an alternate explanation for why the video-watchers were more likely to hit Bobo, an answer lowering the plausibility that watching "violent" TV causes more aggressive behavior, or an answer that allows us to accept the evidence but argue the anti-conclusion that "watching violent films is not a reason why children are hurting other children".

label: Principle
body: wouldn't be preventing society shouldn't negative effects on others → restrict actions of adults

label: Evaluate / Goal
body: Since we're looking to be inconsistent with a principle, we're basically trying to contradict it. Whenever we're contradicting a conditional / refuting a conditional, we're looking for a case where the Trigger happens but the Outcome doesn't happen. In the case of this rule, we want a situation where "society isn't preventing negative effects on others (a victimless crime), and they ARE restricting the actions of adults.

label: Conclusion
body: L. Rubellus is probably responsible for the goblin fern's disappearance.

label: Evidence
body: The goblin fern requires a thick layer of leaf litter. In spots where the fern has vanished, the litter is unusually thin and teeming with L. Rubellus, which eats leaf litter. L. Rubellus is not found in areas where the fern still thrives.

label: Evaluate
body: The author is trying to Solve the Causal Mystery of the disappearing goblin fern, so we can use our usual Curious Fact / Explanation template. Curious Fact: Why is the goblin fern disappearing? Author's Story: L. Rubellus is eating the leaf litter until it's unusually thin, which they kills of the goblin fern, which needs thick leaf litter to survive. We're supposed to now ask - how else could we explain the curious fact? - how plausible is the author's story? Why else could the goblin fern be disappearing? The argument doesn't leave any breadcrumbs for possible alternate explanations, but changing climate / changing animal populations in the fern's habitat could be possible causes. This author is assuming "the goblin fern isn't being killed off by climate change" or "isn't being killed off by some invasive caterpillar species that likes to eat goblin ferns". The author did a pretty good job of establishing plausibility, since she showed covariation: in areas in which the fern is gone, the suspected culprit (L. Rubellus) is present. In areas where the fern still thrives, the suspected culprit is absent.

label: Goal
body: Hard to know exactly what we're looking for, but functionally the correct answer has to either - rule out a different explanation for the goblin fern's disappearance or - establish some idea that's essential for the plausibility of the causal story the author is telling.

label: Given
body: Winners of a Nobel prize for science, who are typically professional scientists, have all made significant contributions to science. But amateur scientists AS ↢some↣ SC have also provided many significant contributions. And unlike professional AS → LD scientists, who are often motivated by economic necessity or a desire for fame, amateur scientists are motivated by the love of discovery alone.

label: Conclusion
body: When we hire sales reps, we should favor applicants who have engineering degrees but little sales experience over applicants with lots of sales experience but no engineering degree.

label: Evidence
body: Most of our best sales reps came to the job with engineering degrees but little sales experience.

label: Evaluate
body: The author is taking a trait possessed by most of her best sales reps and assuming that this trait is causally important to their superlative performance at this job. She could have just as easily argued, "Most of our best sales reps were born in Pennsylvania, so when we're hiring sales reps, we should favor applicants who were born in Pennsylvania". This is a Correlation → Causality type move. Curious Fact: Why is it that most of our best sales reps had engineering backgrounds, but no sales experience? Author's Story: Apparently this type of background makes you a great salesperson at this company. We can weaken this by appealing to one of two pressure points: 1. what is some OTHER WAY to explain why most of the best sales reps have this engineering + no sales background? 2. how could we make the AUTHOR's WAY seem less plausible, i.e. how can we make it seem like this engineering / no sales background is not one of the main reasons for their success as sales reps?

label: Goal
body: Whenever we're weakening a Causal interpretation, we either want an Alternate Explanation for the curious fact or to hurt the Author's Explanation.

label: Conclusion
body: The conclusion that food taboos originated for practical reasons (certain animals are worth more alive than dead) is unwarranted.

label: Evidence
body: Food taboos might have originated for symbolic, ritualistic reasons, and then since people weren't allowed to eat these animals, they then figured out practical uses for them.

label: Evaluate
body: This feels like how we often analyze the Curious Fact / Explanation arguments we see in Strengthen and Weaken. There was a curious phenomenon: why does every human culture have some taboos against eating certain animals? One possible explanation (posed by some researchers) is that humans invent taboos for the animals they want to keep alive for practical reasons. Our author says, "Hey you can't be so sure of that explanation. After all, you could seemingly explain that a different way (humans invent taboos for religious reasons, and then since no one can kill these animals they invent practical uses for them)."

label: Goal
body: Look for something like, argues that one possible explanation for a phenomenon is unwarranted on the grounds that an alternate explanation for that phenomenon exists.

label: Conclusion (this seems = opinion)
body: This effort by the Dept of Health to reduce underage drinking seems to be successful. rephrase: The pledge that they're having adolescents take, "I won't drink alcohol until I'm 21", seems to be causing a reduction in underage drinking.

label: Evidence (survey found = data)
body: Many 17 year olds who don't drink took a pledge like this. Almost all the 17 year olds who do drink never took such a pledge.

label: Evaluate
body: The author is looking at experimental / survey data and then assuming something causal in his conclusion, so we can use our Explain Curious Fact framework. Curious Fact ... why is it that the 17 year olds who don't drink signed a pledge to not drink while the 17 year olds who do drink didn't sign such a pledge? Author's Explanation ... a 17 year old, by nature, is going to drink alcohol underage. But, if they sign one of these pledges, then they won't. The pledge causes them to not drink. Notice we have to fill in the blanks of the causal story being assumed. Our next job is to ask the two questions that go with this framework: 1. Could there be an Alternate Explanation for the curious fact? 2. How plausible is the Author's Explanation? Maybe a different way to explain this survey would be that by the time a kid is 17, they've figured out for themselves whether they want to drink underage. Some do, some don't. When someone from the Dept of Health comes a-knockin' at the door and says, "How would you like to sign this pledge that says you won't drink until you're 21?" A non-drinking 17 year old will be like, "Sure, I'll sign the pledge." A 17 year old who's already drinking or assumes they will be as soon as they get to college will be more like, "No, I'm not making that promise". We could call the people who sign the pledge a potentially self-selecting sample of 17 year olds who don't drink and don't plan to.

label: Goal
body: While an answer could potentially attack the plausibility that the pledge was a causal difference-maker for the 17 year olds who signed it (the 2nd question), Flaw is much more likely to test Alternate Explanations (the 1st question). So let's look for an answer suggesting an alternate way to explain the data, such as our Reverse Causality scenario in which the teens had already decided on whether or not they were drinkers, and only signed the pledge if they already were planning to not drink. Or look for the Famous Flaw answer calling out the "correlation to causation" move the author is doing here.

label: Opposing Evidence
body: A folktale is a traditional story told in an entertaining way.

label: Opposing Conclusion
body: Folktales lack deeper meaning.

label: Evidence
body: A folktale is passed along IWC by a culture for generations, and each storyteller adds something of his or her own to the story, and in this way folktales provide great insight into the wisdom of the culture.

label: Conclusion
body: But this [folktales lack DM deeper meaning] is not the case.

label: Evaluate
body: The argument assumes that IWC → DM stories that provide great insight into the wisdom of the culture possess deeper meaning.

label: Conclusion
body: They need to reassess that view. rephrase: Some deep-sea creatures can detect red light.

label: Evidence
body: Researchers recently discovered a sea creature with bioluminescent red lights on its tentacles, which probably function as lures to attract prey (since they're shaped like prey fish's food).

label: Goal
body: We're being asked about the role of the 2nd claim, which is our main conclusion. So let's go looking for Main Conclusion.

label: Evaluate
body: Whenever we do a Main Conclusion question, we remind ourselves of a few things: 1. the conclusion is only going to be the final claim like 10% of the time (it's too obvious a place to put it, so on a Main Conclusion question they usually avoid it) 2. there might be Intermediate Conclusions, to trick us. 3. the conclusion is usually going to be the First Sentence or connected with some Rebuttal / Pivot. In this case, it's both of those patterns. The first sentence opens with an Attribution to another point of view: "Scientists generally believe X". That cues us to expect a Rebuttal, which is usually signified by Pivot language (but, yet, however). Sure enough, the 2nd half of the 1st sentence is that rebuttal. The rest of the paragraph tries to support the idea that some deep-sea creatures can detect red light (the prey species of Erenna).

label: Goal
body: Many, if not most, conclusions on Main Conclusion questions use pronouns or other referential language. We want to take the time to substitute Specific language in for any Referential language, like "they need to reassess that view". We want the closest meaning match for, "Scientists need to reassess the view that there are no deep-sea creatures that can detect red light". Or a cleaned up version, "There are some deep-sea creatures that can detect red light".

label: Conclusion
body: Philanthropists do not want to make the nonprofit sector as efficient as private business in this country.

label: Evidence
body: Why would we (or anyone) want to make nonprofits as inefficient as Byworks Corporation, which has posted huge losses for years?

label: Evaluate
body: Early questions reward common sense about the real world more than later questions. Would common sense tell us that private business or nonprofits are more likely to be efficient? Kind of a hard question to answer, right? In one sense, the profit-motive incentivizes cost-cutting efficiencies and productivity maximization (i.e. maxing out profit is related to maxing out efficiency). Meanwhile, nonprofits are not going to ever be getting rich from their nonprofit, so they don't have that same incentive. Still, one may think, "Yes, but aren't most nonprofits very strapped for cash, so they need to use their limited funds as efficiently as possible? Sure." Ultimately, we can probably agree that it's going to vary a lot from company to company. Some private businesses will be be wasteful, even though their business model incentivizes efficiency. Some nonprofits will be motivated to be efficient with their limited funding, even though their business model doesn't incentivize efficiency the same way. So since there's going to be a lot of variation among private and nonprofit businesses in terms of their efficiency, the fact that this author uses one example of a for-profit corporation as a way to make it seem like "THIS is what private business is like — so inefficient, posting huge losses for years. "

label: Goal
body: We want to complain about the small, potentially unrepresentative sample of Byworks, one measly company, as a way to impugn the efficiency of all private for-profit businesses.

label: Conclusion
body: Statistical records of crime rates probably often reflect as much about the motives and methods of those who compile or cite them as they do about the actual incidence of crime.

label: Evidence
body: The police may underreport crime in order to convey the impression that they're are successfully preventing crime, or they may overreport crime in order to plausibly request a bigger operating budget. Politicians might over-hype crime to get elected ("Only I can fix this!") or under-sell crime to remain in office ("Look at the peace and stability I've presided over"). Newspapers often sensationalize crime to increase readership ("if it bleeds, it leads").

label: Evaluate / Goal
body: Wow. Five different examples of how someone's motives could bias the way they compile or cite crime stats. Let's look for an answer saying that the author supports her general conclusion in the first sentence with several examples.

label: Given that ...
body: Calcium deficiencies greatly increase the risk of osteoporosis,

label: and that ...
body: Dairy products usually have more calcium per serving than do fruits and veggies.

label: How can it be that ...
body: In countries were dairy is rare and fruits and veggies are common, the incidence of osteoporosis is much lower than in countries where they consume a lot of calcium from dairy?

label: Goal
body: We need a way to explain how people who are eating little dairy have a lower incidence of osteoporosis than are people eating a great deal of dairy (given that dairy has lots of calcium and calcium helps protect again the risk of osteoporosis).

label: Principle
body: Most principles are conditional, and this one has an unless. When we see that trigger word, how do we turn it into a conditional? f.e. "A shouldn't happen, unless B happens" One method people use for 'unless' is to replace it with 'if-not'. "A shouldn't happen, if B not happens", which looks like ~B → ~A Another method people use is to translate the sentence into 'X requires Y' wording. When we hear "A shouldn't happen unless B happens", we can re-write that as "A requires B" which looks like A → B. Naturally, we'll get the same conditional either way. These two methods just yielded a contrapositive version of the other: ~B → ~A A → B The conditional principle here is more complex: X shouldn't happen unless Y or Z. If we do the 'if-not' method, then we're saying X shouldn't happen if not (Y or Z) If we're saying "it's not the case that Y or Z is true", that's akin to saying "both Y and Z are false". Negating (Y or Z) means we get ~Y and ~Z. Whenever we're negating an idea, Or turns to And and vice versa. ~Y and ~Z → X If we used the "turn it into A requires B" method, then "X shouldn't happen unless Y or Z is true" would become "X requires Y or Z", which looks like X → Y or Z So the two ways to write this rule would be this: X → Y or Z ~Y and ~Z → X Do we know / care which way we write it? Yes! We want to get the "judgy" (the normative / evaluative) term on the right. What do we mean by judgy? - good / bad - justified / unjustified - should / shouldn't - permissible / impermissible Stuff like that. In this principle the words "should not be" are the judgment words. So the right side looks like this. should not be → on finance committee We need to put all the qualifying criteria on the left side: 1st-term board member and should not be not an accountant → on finance and committee membership not supported by all

label: Goal
body: Okay, the hard part is over. When we read answer choices, we know that the only legal conclusion is "should not be on committee". If any answers are saying "should be", they're automatically wrong.

label: Conclusion (these results support)
body: A person who listens to a taped reading of a novel is more likely to enjoy the novel than a person who reads it is.

label: Evaluate
body: Since the conclusion is offering an explanation for the curious asymmetric comparison in the survey results, we can use our Explain Curious Fact mindset. Curious Fact ... why is it that most who listened to the novel said they enjoyed it while most who read the novel said they didn't enjoy it? Author's Explanation ... people are more likely to enjoy hearing a taped version of a novel than reading the novel itself. We want to consider Alternate Explanations as well as the plausibility of the Author's Explanation. Maybe a different explanation for the survey results is simply that the particular person who did the voiceover really added a lot to the experience (in a way that isn't typical for novels). Maybe most novels are read by their authors, but this one was read by someone with an iconic voice or great speaking/acting talents. Maybe the sort of person who listens to a novel is different from the sort who reads one. Perhaps people who listen to novels are less discerning about the quality of what they're hearing so they are more likely to rank it favorably, whereas people who read novels are literature snobs that insist on high quality. To test the plausibility of the author's theory, we'd want to test the same reader with both the taped / written version of the novel and see if they prefer the taped version to the written version. Or we'd want to try another 10 novels with the same respondents and see if we keep getting results where the listeners had more favorable reactions than the readers.

label: Goal
body: Since we're trying to Weaken, we want to either offer an Alternate Explanation for why the listeners liked the novel better than the readers did, or to hurt the plausibility of the conclusion by making this novel seem atypical (since the conclusion is making a generalization about all taped vs. written versions of novels).

label: Conclusion (therefore)
body: Anyone who has qualified as a recognized medical specialist is competent to practice in his or her specialty.

label: Evidence
body: Medical specialists have usually graduated from a university, then done 4 years of med school, then 2-6 years of residency. And then a recognized specialist must complete an evaluation program directed by a medical specialty board.

label: Evaluate
body: The conclusion is a conditional claim (anyone), so we might want to analyze this one's internal logic: Qualified as competent recognized -—--—--—--—--> to practice med specialist in specialty This concept of "competent to practice in their specialty" was never defined in the evidence, so the author must be assuming something that establishes definitively "they're competent". What were we told is involved in qualifying as a recognized medical specialist? Well, it's weird because the first sentence is about qualifying as a medical specialist, and the second sentence is about qualifying as a recognized specialist. Are those the same? No. We can safely assume that the recognized specialist term in the second sentence means the same thing as the recognized medical specialist in the conclusion. After all, the second sentence is talking about a physician going before a medical specialty board. If that person is a recognized specialist, they're a recognized medical specialist. So if we're trying to find the piece of Evidence that matches part of the Conclusion's logic path, we would go to the 2nd sentence, which is also about recognized specialist. It tells us that qualifying as a recognized specialist requires completing an evaluation by a medical specialty board. Qualified as completed recognized -—> eval by medical med specialist specialty board Does that logic go any further? Were we told an implication of completing an evaluation program by a specialty board? No. The first sentence wouldn't hook onto this conditional, because there isn't any overlapping concept.

label: Goal
body: If this answer is testing the internal logic, then the link we need to add onto the Evidence in order to derive the Conclusion's logic path is this: completed competent eval by medical → to practice specialty board their specialty If the answer is ruling out an Objection, then when we negate it, it will help us argue that someone might be qualified as a recognized medical specialist, but not competent to practice their speciality. for example (A) Medical specialty boards do not sometimes let unqualified physicians complete the evaluation program as a personal favor to the physician.

label: Statements
body: They're studying plant remains form a site that hasn't been occupied in the last 10,000 years. conditionals (if) plants were people who lived at that site cultivated → discovered agriculture 1000's of years before 1st known ppl plants were people who lived at that site not cultivated → ate a wider variety of wild plants than did their peers

label: Evaluate
body: Whenever we see conditional logic claims in an Inference question, we have two thoughts: 1. Am I supposed to chain this conditional to some other conditional? 2. Am I supposed to apply this conditional (usually via contrapositive) to some fact they gave me? The two conditionals do chain. We could contrapose one and chain it to the other: ppl there didn't plants ppl there ate discover agriculture → were not → wider variety 1000's of years cultivated than peers earlier than 1st known However, the other thing that sticks out is that we're basically getting a prediction either way. If they were cultivated, we'd know X. If they were not cultivated, we'd know Y. So that means at least one of X and Y will be true. Suppose we say: "If it rains, we'll play Scrabble. If it doesn't rain, we'll play baseball." We know that we will play at least Scrabble or baseball (it's possible for both to be true as well). And if there's a common denominator to both outcomes, then we know that for sure. For this example we could say, In Either Case we're "going to play some game".

label: Goal
body: Is there a common denominator between the two outcomes here? "discovered agriculture 1000s of years before the first known occurrence" vs. "ate a wider variety of wild plants than did any other people at the time" It sounds like in either case, these people will be blowing our minds a little bit. They're either "setting a record" for 1st known use of agriculture or setting a record for widest variety of wild plants consumed.

label: Conclusion
body: This was not mere frivolousness. rephrase: It wasn't frivolous for early Egyptian pharaohs to spend as much on ceremonial/impressive architecture as they did on roads and irrigation.

label: Evidence (for)
body: If people could be made to realize the pharaoh's mastery of the physical world, their loyalty could be maintained without military coercion.

label: Evaluate
body: Whenever we do Role or Main Conclusion, we remind ourselves that 90% of the time the conclusion is the First Sentence or it's some Rebutal/Pivot claim. This one is the latter, signified by however, and then confirmed by the fact that the following claim is prefaced by the Support Indicator ''for'. (F.A.B.S. = for, after all, because, since).

label: Evidence
body: Under current rules, PC → DC researchers have one full year after the initial publication of a new discovery to patent the discovery. This allows research results to be shared widely prior to the patent application. The proposed change would have the application precede initial publication, which would delay the communication of discoveries.

label: Conclusion
body: The proposed change DC → CESR to the patent system is bound to have a chilling effect on scientific research.

label: Evaluate
body: The argument assumes DC → CESR that if communication of discoveries is delayed, it would have a chilling effect on scientific research.

label: Conclusion (we can conclude)
body: No one fundamentally desires anything except pleasure.

label: Evidence
body: Every time people get what they want they feel pleasure, which is the natural result of getting what one wants.

label: Evaluate
body: The author is arguing that the only fundamental desire we have is pleasure, since pleasure occurs whenever we achieve something we desire. This logic seems weird. Let's say that Sally desires a spicy meal for dinner. And every time Sally eats spicy foods she gets a runny nose. A runny nose is a natural result of eating spicy foods. Would we conclude from that "Sally fundamentally desires nothing other than to get a runny nose"? Of course not.

label: Goal
body: This argument is basically saying, "Since pleasure accompanies every satisfied desire, it must be that pleasure is the goal of every desire." Let's look for an argument that is saying something like "Thing X accompanies every example of Y. Thus, thing X is the goal of Y."

label: Linguist's Original Claim:
body: You've provided no evidence that we linguists lack a deep understanding of language.

label: Philosopher's Conclusion
body: This cannot be the case ("J and I are siblings" is not identical in meaning to "I and J are siblings")

label: Philosopher's Evidence (for)
body: For two things to identical, they must have all the same attributes, and these two sentences are physically different.

label: Evaluate
body: If we were the linguist, how would we defend ourselves? According to us, "J and I are siblings" is identical in meaning to "I and J are siblings". (That does seem accurate, to say they have identical meaning) The philosopher is saying "being identical requires having all the same attributes, and these are physically different". Okay, sure, but we never said they were identical in physical appearance. We said they were identical in meaning. Two things can look physically different but mean the same thing. This philosopher is proving that the these two sentences are not identical, which we agree with. We only said they were identical in meaning.
