Does the philosopher think that these two sentences have different meanings?

label: Goal
body: Look for an answer addressing the disconnect between the more limited claim made by the linguists, "X an Y are identical in meaning", and the broader claim being attacked by the philosopher, "X and Y are identical."

label: Conclusion (hence)
body: When you buy vitamin supplements in a major health store, you can be sure that the claims the salespeople make about the quality of the products are inaccurate.

label: Evidence
body: In a major health store, salespeople always work on commission and always steer customers toward products from which they make their highest commissions.

label: Evaluate
body: The conclusion is very strongly worded. You can be sure that all the claims the salespeople make about the quality of the products is inaccurate? Where does the author come off, acting this skeptical? Her evidence is that the salespeople are motivated by commission. She's thinking, "they're gonna steer you toward the products where they stand to earn the most commission and then tell you that those products are of the highest quality so that you'll buy the products and thus provide them with that commission." But how do we know these claims are inaccurate? Isn't it possible that the highest quality products also have the highest commission?

label: Goal
body: One of the ten famous flaws is Ad Hominem, where we dismiss the merit of someone's ideas because they have a vested interest / ulterior motive in the conversation, or because they have conflicting past behavior. This definitely seems like a case of the former. The author thinks that "if they're motivated by commission, then all their remarks about quality are inaccurate". We can call out the Ad Hominem flaw or point out the possibility that their interests and the truth may converge --- it might be that their quality claims are sometimes true, even while they're steering you toward the products that provide them with the highest commission.

label: Opposing Support
body: Because no other theory has been able to predict it so simply and accurately, the advance of the perihelion of Mercury is sometimes cited as evidence in support of Einstein’s theory of general relativity.

label: Evidence
body: This phenomenon was already well known when Einstein developed his theory. He quite probably adjusted his equations to generate the correct numbers for the perihelion advance.

label: Conclusion
body: Therefore, accounting for this advance should not be counted as evidence in support of Einstein’s theory.

label: Evaluate
body: The argument assumes that if a theory is adjusted to account for a phenomenon, then the fact that the theory predicts that phenomenon should not be counted as evidence in support of that theory.

label: Conclusion (should = opinion)
body: We should sell only low-end models.

label: Intermediate Conclusion
body: This would maximize our profits.

label: Evidence (since)
body: We have a 25% profit margin on low-end models, but only a 13% profit margin on high-end computer models. There's a limit to how many models we can display and sell. And if we only sold low-end, we'd probably sell as many computers as we would if sold both kinds.

label: Argument
body: The accountant is doing two things back-to-back. First, she pushes back on the industry's claim that rising newsprint costs are the problem — she points out that, after adjusting for inflation, newsprint hasn't actually gotten more expensive. Then she replaces that explanation with her own: the real problem is that fewer people are subscribing and fewer companies are advertising.

label: Evaluate
body: How can argue against this plan and say, "it's not a good idea to sell only low-end models / it wouldn't maximize our profits"? Arguing it wouldn't maximize profits will take some mathematical thinking. The author is thinking, "Since there's a limit to how many models we can make (let's say we can only make 100 computers per year), we should make all 100 of them the low-end kind and 0 of them the high-end. We'll sell all 100 either way, but the low-end ones get 25% profit whereas the high-end ones only get 13% profit." Does that actually get us more profit? Not necessarily. The low-end models have a higher profit margin, but they don't necessarily make more profit in total dollars (this is a Relative vs. Absolute flaw). Let's say the low-end computers cost $400. A 25% profit is 1/4, or $100. Let's say the high-end computers cost $1000. A 13% profit is $130. So every high-end computer we sell gets us $130 in profit, while selling each low-end computer only gets us $100 in profit. Therefore, the author's math is wrong. We wouldn't maximize profits by selling all low-end. We'd actually make more (100 units) x ($130 profit / unit) if we sold all high-end computers.

label: Goal
body: Look for an answer pointing out the Relative vs. Absolute mathematical flaw. The item with the higher profit margin might still make less profit in absolute terms. Or, the answer might fight the link from Intermediate Conclusion to Main Conclusion and argue that, "even though selling only low-end models would maximize profits, that doesn't mean we should do it".

label: Conclusion
body: It's faulty to reason that lotto tickets are a poor use of money, just because the average payout for a ticket in a lottery is much lower than the cost of a ticket.

label: Evidence
body: Nobody would say that individual insurance policies are a poor use of money, and they also have an average payout that's less than the amount paid by the policy.

label: Evaluate
body: The easy part of this argument is that it's making a Comparison between lotto tickets and insurance policies, so if we're going to Weaken this Comparison, we're probably going to want an answer that points out an important difference between the two things. The hard part of this argument is understanding the whole "average payout" concept. We can remind ourselves that running a lotto and running an insurance company are both profitable ventures. They take in more money than they give out. Lotto's might collect 10 million in revenue and then pay out 1 million as the grand prize. Insurance companies might collect 10 million in premiums and then pay out 1 million to people who file claims when their property is damaged. Since the average payout of the lotto or an insurance policy would be calculated by thinking of how much money is paid in vs. how much money ever goes back to the customers, any profitable lotto or insurance company will have a smaller amount going back to customers than is being taken in. Put another way, it might cost $5 to buy a lotto card, but the average return on buying one is $2. An insurance policy might cost $500 and the average payout to policy holders is $75.

label: Goal
body: In both cases, we know that we're putting money into a system that in the long run is meant to collect more money than will be distributed. (gamblers in Vegas know that "the House always wins", meaning, in the long run the casinos must take in more money than they give away) So how can we fight this conclusion and argue that "Even though both lotto tickets and insurance policies usually involve losing money, insurance policies are a wise use of resources and lotto tickets are an unwise use of resources?"

label: Facts
body: There are some CAUSAL claims here: A is susceptible to B because of the C caused by D That causal chain says D caused C, which led to A being susceptible to B. Big El Niño → Drought → Susceptible to fire Many scientists believe there's a causal precedent to D (I just made up that term). They think that Air Poll. → Glob Warm → Big Niño → Drought → Fire risk ↑

label: Evaluate / Goal
body: Since they've tantalized us with a Causal chain, they're likely to reward us for having seen it, in the correct answer. We'd probably either anticipate "Big El N. caused greater susceptibility to fire", or "according to many, Air Pollution led to greater susceptibility".

label: Conclusion
body: The book is as important and as well → Skiff will be promoted written as Skiff claims

label: Evidence
body: N recommends Skiff's book → dean will promote Skiff Skiff's book is published → Nguyen recommends S's book

label: Evaluate
body: We can chain together the two conditionals: Skiff's book is → Nguyen will → Dean will published recommend promote Skiff to dean Since our goal is to prove that Skiff will be promoted, and this chain ends with Skiff being promoted, we know our job is to trigger this chain. So, we need an answer to convince us that S's book will be published. Once we establish that, these rules take us on a logic conveyor belt ride to "the book getting promoted". Do we have any reason to think that Skiff's book will be published? No, so that has to be in our correct answer. The conclusion is teasing this new idea of "If Skiff's book is as important and as well written as Skiff claims". If S claimed that the book was "very important" or "very well written", then we could use a rule like, "If a book is very important or very well written, then it will be published". However, we don't know how important or well written Skiff claimed the book was.

label: Goal
body: Primarily, we're looking for an answer that establishes that Skiff's book will be published, because that idea will guarantee our conclusion. Based on how the conclusion is written, we might guess it will say "If the book is as important / well written as Skiff claims, then the book will be published".

label: Conclusion (this suggests that)
body: Resistance to pesticides could probably be passed from domesticated crop plants to their weedy relatives.

label: Evidence
body: Resistance to pesticides is often a genetically engineered trait, and in an experiment with radishes, scientists raised domesticated radishes with some weedy wild radishes and after a while the trait of flower color passed from domesticated to wild ones.

label: Method
body: So the move is: knock down the existing explanation, then put forward a new one. That's a classic two-step in argumentative writing.

label: Goal
body: Look for an answer that captures both halves — challenging an explanation and offering a different one.

label: Conclusion
body: Alcohol consumption is, on balance, beneficial.

label: Evidence
body: According to recent evidence, moderate alcohol consumption has certain beneficial effects on health (such as killing off some bacteria that can cause illness).

label: Evaluate
body: Okay, that was a lot to process. We put some "custom" radishes in a field with wild, weedy radishes, and within a few generations the wild ones had turned the color of the "custom" ones. The author looks at this phenomenon and thinks, "Wow, flower color passed from the customized radishes to the wild ones? Well, then we can probably generalize this: we could take a trait such as resistance to pesticides, which we genetically engineer in the "customized" version of a crop, put that customized crop in a field with wild, weedy relatives, and then the trait of pesticide-resistance would pass from the customized crop to the weedy wild version of the crop. The author is extrapolating from a small sample to a broader one. She's going from "because it worked with flower color, in the case of domesticated vs. wild radishes, it should work with pesticide-resistance, in the case of any genetically engineered crop plant vs. the wild version of that crop plant." There are three big differences to consider: radishes vs. other plants flower color vs. pesticide resistance domesticated vs. genetically engineered We could hurt this argument by saying, "Sure it'll work with radishes, but not with corn / wheat / carrots / etc." Or by saying, "Sure flower color is a trait that can pass just by co-habitatting in the same field, but pesticide resistance can't pass in the same way." Or by saying, "Sure it works with domesticated radishes — we've selected for red radishes through horticulture, but we haven't tried to play Mother Nature and manipulate the DNA of radishes. This same thing won't work if we're talking about a trait that we hand-coded into DNA through genetic engineering."

label: Goal
body: Since we're trying to strengthen the argument, we'd like to push back against any of those objections. We want to believe that "if it worked with flower color in radishes, it can work with pesticide resistance on other types of crops."

label: Conclusion
body: Parents who consistently praise their children for every attempt to accomplish something, whether the kids were successful or not in their attempt, actually erode the youngsters' sense of self-esteem.

label: Evidence
body: If children are uniformly praised for both what they attempt and successfully accomplish as well a what they attempt and fail, they will eventually discount all words of praise and, in effect, stop hearing any praise at all.

label: Evaluate
body: Whenever we do Main Conclusion (and Role) we read the paragraph differently, knowing that 90% of the time the conclusion is the very first sentence, or it's some rebuttal signified with a pivot word (like "but, yet, however"). As we read this first sentence, we immediately ask ourselves whether it's eligible to be a conclusion (does it sound like an opinion coming from the author?) This first sentence makes a causal claim, so it's not clear whether to hear it as opinion or accept it as fact. But it is definitely the author talking. If next claim or two feel like the author is trying to support / defend that opening claim, then we can confirm our suspicion that the first claim was the conclusion. Indeed, the 2nd and 3rd sentences combine to explain how constantly praising your kids would erode their self-esteem.

label: Goal
body: We know the first sentence is the main conclusion, so we're just looking for whatever answer best matches the meaning of the first sentence.

label: Pauline's first claim
body: Some environmentalists claim that saving salmon requires us to breach the hydroelectric dams on the river. Does Roger agree that some environmentalists claim this? He doesn't have any comment.

label: Pauline's second claim
body: Given the region's growing population and booming industry, breaching the dams would cause electrical costs to skyrocket. Does Roger agree with any of this? He seems to agree with Pauline's general background concern that a growing population and booming industry create a big demand for electricity, one we will struggle to meet. She thinks that breaching the dams (denying ourselves the hydroelectric energy they were providing) would reduce the supply of electricity, causing the price of electricity to skyrocket (because there is high demand). Roger thinks that even with the supply of hydroelectric power that we currently enjoy, we will need to find new supply of energy. So he also thinks there is high demand for electricity.

label: Goal
body: Let's look for something like, "They both acknowledge that we currently barely have enough energy supply to meet energy demand / the growing demand caused by population and industry will outpace our energy supply".

label: Conclusion
body: The agency is unlikely to achieve its goal (i.e. the banking system will not be strengthened).

label: Evidence
body: If the former owners of these banks buy them back, the banking system will not be strengthened. If an argument gives us a conditional premise X → Y and then concludes So, Y. then what is the missing idea? We're missing this: X. We know if the former owners buy back, the banking system will not be strengthened. Our author concludes the banking system will not be strengthened.

label: Goal
body: So, we want to hear that the former owners will buy these banks back.

label: Implied Conclusion (rebuttal)
body: The rising cost of newsprint isn't why newspapers have falling profits.

label: Intermediate Conclusion
body: The real threats to profitability are falling circulation and falling advertising, not newsprint costs.

label: Premise
body: Adjusted for inflation, newsprint isn't any more expensive than it was a decade ago.

label: Evaluate
body: The three most common things we see on Method are 1. Analogies 2. Faulty Implications of Logic / Plan 3. Alternatives The context of this conversation is Explain Curious Fact ("why are profits falling for newspapers?"). Our author is disputing one hypothesis ("rising cost of newsprint") by showing that it's implausible ("the cost of newsprint hasn't risen") as well by proposing an Alternative explanation ("profits are falling because of falling circulation and fallen advertising").

label: Goal
body: Let's look for any answer that matches. The author derailed one explanation for a phenomenon by showing it wasn't plausible and proposed an Alternate explanation for it.

label: Argument
body: The accountant rejects the industry's explanation (rising newsprint costs) by showing it's false, then offers an alternative explanation (falling circulation and advertising).

label: Goal
body: An answer describing this method: challenge an explanation, introduce a different one.

label: Intermediate Conclusion
body: Oil reserves are unlikely to remain unchanged from one year to the next.

label: Evaluate
body: Given That ... moderate alcohol consumption seems to have some beneficial effects How Could We Argue That ... alcohol consumption is not beneficial overall? We'd probably have to say that the author is failing to talk about the downsides of alcohol consumption (empty sugars? raises blood pressure? hurts liver?), and that the downsides might outweigh the "certain beneficial effects" such as killing off some harmful bacteria that would be living in your mouth / throat.

label: Goal
body: Look for an answer that says the author is only presenting part of the story. If we're trying to conclude that something is "on balance / overall" beneficial, then we should have laid out all the pros, all the cons, and established that the pros outweigh the cons.

label: Conclusion (So)
body: Grodex should probably conduct its employee-training seminars using these innovative methods.

label: Evidence
body: Most jobs at Grodex require thinking creatively but don't require being great at memorizing. Children taught using these innovative new educational methods learn to think more creatively than children taught using rote methods, but they are less adept at memorizing.

label: Evaluate
body: The blank is prefaced by a Support Indicator, because, so we know that we're supposed to pick an answer that would strengthen the claim before it. Our correct answer should make it more plausible that Grodex should use these new methods in employee-training. We already know that what the methods are good at (teaching creativity) is more important to most jobs at Grodex than what the methods are bad at (teaching memorization). So it makes sense that this author would see these methods as a good fit for most Grodex jobs. But let's be skeptical. What could be a reason not to implement these methods? - maybe they're cost prohibitive - maybe the people who conduct employee-training seminars don't have the ability to employ these innovative methods well - maybe these methods work to promote creativity in whatever context the children are using them in, but that wouldn't transfer over to the type of creativity needed for a Grodex job - maybe even though most jobs at Grodex value creativity more than memorization, the employee-training seminars are more about memorizing policies than about thinking creatively.

label: Goal
body: This correct answer could really come from any number of directions. We want it to add another reason for Grodex to adopt these methods in its employee-training, or to rule out an objection to Grodex adopting these methods for employee-training.

label: Conclusion
body: This would be a temporary solution at best. (i.e. colonizing other planets would only temporarily solve the problem of overpopulation on Earth)

label: Evidence
body: Suppose the population is doubling every 30 years — in the year 2500, half of Earth's population could emigrate to Mars, and you'd be right back to being just as crowded as you were on Earth by 2530.

label: Evaluate
body: When we're doing Main Conclusion questions, we read the paragraph expecting that most of the time the Conclusion will appear earlier than the Evidence. In particular, we look out for the two most common patterns: - the Conclusion appears after a pivot word like "but, yet, however" - the Conclusion is the first sentence The first sentence of this paragraph is a mathematical fact. Facts aren't conclusions. Opinions are (supported Opinions, to be specific). When the second sentence begins "some people have claimed ... ", we anticipate the classic form of a rebuttal argument: Some people say X. But / yet / however, they're wrong. Here's why. The third sentence begins with the "however" pivot we were anticipating. The author says that the solution these 'some people' are peddling is a temporary one, because if we're doubling ever 30 years, then losing half the population only solves the problem for 30 years.

label: Goal
body: Look for an answer that sounds like the first clause of the final sentence: "colonizing other planets would be a temporary solution (to overcrowding) at best".

label: Conclusion
body: The complexity of chocolate probably masks any difference in taste due to the lack of fat.

label: Evidence
body: In a taste test, most people liked low-fat chocolate ice cream as much as full fat chocolate ice cream, whereas previous tests found that people tended to dislike low-fat vanilla ice cream, saying it tasted harsh. Chocolate is a very complex flavor, requiring around 500 distinct chemical compounds.

label: Evaluate
body: Since we're trying to explain the meaning behind a Curious Comparison from two study results, we can use our Curious Fact / Explanation mindset. Curious Fact ... how come people like low-fat chocolate ice cream, but think low-fat vanilla ice cream has a harsh taste? Author's Explanation ... the complexity of chocolate masks the different taste of low-fat chocolate ice cream. The two pressure points with these types of arguments are - Alternate Explanations for the curious fact - the plausibility of the Author's Explanation How else could we explain the difference in reactions to the low-fat chocolate vs. the low-fat vanilla? - Maybe the low-fat chocolate was done by a very boutique ice cream maker (Ben & Jerry's) while the low-fat vanilla was done by Rite-Aid. - Maybe the vanilla taste test warned them in advance that they were going to taste something low-fat, whereas the chocolate test just let them try the samples first without warning them to expect something "worse". How plausible is the Author's Explanation? - well, we need to know that vanilla is not as complex a flavor (complexity can't be the Causal Difference-Maker here if it's not actually a difference) - we could appeal to other examples in which people preferred the healthier version of a complex flavor to the healthier version of a simpler flavor

label: Goal
body: Find an answer that rules out an alternate explanation for the difference reactions to low-fat chocolate vs. vanilla, or an answer that increases the plausibility of the causal explanation the author is selling, that "complexity is the causal difference-maker".

label: Conclusion (however)
body: Gillette's argument is not persuasive. (it's not clear that a thorough knowledge of genetics would certainly benefit humanity, just because it could cure diseases)

label: Evidence (because)
body: He fails to consider that such thorough knowledge of genetics might harm human beings more than it would benefit them.

label: Argument
body: The author opens with the claim that urbanization might cut nationwide pollution. Then everything that follows is evidence — city people use mass transit, live in smaller dwellings — and the final "Thus..." restates that opening claim in different words. So that opening line is the conclusion.

label: Evaluate
body: Whenever we're doing a Main Conclusion question, we prime our brains before reading the paragraph with the prevailing tendencies on Main Conclusion questions: Rather than put the Conclusion as the final claim, the conclusion on Main Conclusion questions is usually found earlier than the evidence. Typically, it's ... - the very first claim of the paragraph - it's rebutting some previous or external point of view that isn't the author's In this paragraph we start with an external point of view, Gillette's. Most of the time in LR and RC, after an author attributes a point of view to someone, she pivots away with a but / yet / however. That pivot doesn't necessarily mean we're hearing a conclusion. It could go: However, Conclusion. After all, Support. But it could also go: However, Support. Thus, Conclusion In this paragraph, the word because clearly indicates that the last idea is Support, so that makes "G's argument is not persuasive" our Conclusion. F.A.B.S. = for, after all, because, since (the four Support indicators you should memorize)

label: Goal
body: Since this conclusion is using referential language, "Gillette's argument is not persuasive" we need to substitute-in the specific language being referred to. "The idea that deeply knowing genes will benefit humanity is not persuasive"

label: Information
body: In a study, subjects listened to a long, unfamiliar piece of instrumental music. Once hypnotized, half the people were asked to remember parts of the musical piece and half were asked to describe scenes from the movie they had just seen (they hadn't seen a movie). Both groups were equally confident and detailed in their recollections.

label: Evaluate
body: It feels like the correct answer will want to synthesize these research results. What does it mean that both groups are equally confident and detailed, even though one group is seemingly pulling from true memories (they did hear a piece of music, so when they're asked about it, they're answers might be legit) while the other group is seemingly pulling from 'false' memories (they didn't see a movie, so they're answers about the movie seem like confident, detailed lies). Maybe we could say something like, when you're hypnotized you're equally confident and detailed whether you're accessing 'true' memories or 'false' memories.

label: Goal
body: Hard to say what to expect. Let's just pick the most provable answer we can find.

label: Conclusion
body: The health of a newborn depends to a large extent on the amount of food available to the mother during pregnancy.

label: Evidence
body: From 1850 to 1900, babies' birth weights varied with the success of the previous year's crops: more successful crops were associated with higher birth weights.

label: Evaluate
body: Our job on Method questions isn't to evaluate the soundness of the argument, so if you're thinking, "Whoa, dude ... health of a newborn isn't the same as birth weight", you're correct, but call off your dogs. We're not here to fight the logic, just to describe it. Hopefully, though, our familiarity with causal arguments provides us with some mental vocabulary for describing the move from evidence to conclusion. The evidence provides a correlation (X varies with Y ... the more X, the more Y). And the conclusion posits some causal relationship (X depends to a large extent on Y).

label: Goal
body: We just want an answer that descriptively matches what we saw. We can anticipate that the answer might sound something like "the author concludes a causal relationship between two things based on some study data that shows a correlation between two things".

label: Vincent's Statements
body: 1. can't be measured → sci discipline can't study 2. happiness is an entirely subjective experience 3. happiness can't be measured 4. (assumes: subjective experiences can't be measured)

label: Yolanda's Statements
body: 1. Optometry and happiness research rely on subjects' reports of how they feel. 2. Optometry is a scientific discipline

label: Evaluate
body: Does Yolanda disagree with any of Vincent's explicit claims? Does Yolanda suggest ... 1. some scientific disciplines do study something that can't be measured? 2. happiness isn't entirely subjective? 3. happiness can be measured? Yolanda definitely isn't arguing #2. It's a little unclear whether "relying on subjects' reports" qualifies as "can be measured" for Yolanda. I would lean towards thinking we're allowed to make that equivalence. If we're researching happiness, and we try playing Mozart for you over while you eat breakfast, and then we ask to self-report your happiness on a 1 to 10 scale, the number you give us is a measurement. It's a data point. If Yolanda doesn't think that self-reporting counts as measuring, but she thinks optometry is a scientific discipline, then she thinks that scientific disciplines can study something that can't be measured. If Yolanda does think that self-reporting counts as measuring, then she thinks that happiness can be measured and thus that subjective experiences can be measured.

label: Goal
body: I'd be hoping for the answers to give me more clarity on how to interpret Yolanda's statements. She's either disagreeing with Vincent's first claim, or she's disagreement with his last claim (and the assumption that got him from claim 2 to claim 3).

label: Main Conclusion
body: Increasing urbanization may actually reduce the total amount of pollution generated nationwide.

label: Intermediate Conclusion (thus)
body: A given number of people will produce less pollution concentrated in a city than spread among many small towns.

label: Premise
body: City residents rely more on mass transit and live in smaller, more energy-efficient dwellings.

label: Anticipate
body: Whenever we do Main Conclusion and Role, we remind our brain that the conclusion is only the last claim like 20% of the time. The vast majority of the time the main conclusion is some Pivot/Rebuttal claim or it's in the first sentence. When we listen actively for whether this first sentence is an Attribution the author might rebut or an opinion she might support, we see that it sounds like an opinion, "increasing urbanization may reduce pollution". And the rest of the paragraph supports that claim. The "thus" on the final sentence signals another conclusion, but that conclusion is there to support the first sentence.

label: Goal
body: They're asking us about the main clause of the first sentence, which is our main conclusion.

label: Argument
body: The claim "increasing urbanization may reduce nationwide pollution" is what the argument tries to prove. Mass transit and energy-efficient dwellings are the supporting evidence.

label: Goal
body: An answer identifying this claim as the main conclusion.

label: Method
body: It's a classic LSAT trick: putting the conclusion early in the stimulus and burying the supporting evidence after it. Indicator words like "Thus" at the end signal that the closing line is the conclusion or a restatement of it.

label: Goal
body: An answer that identifies the urbanization-reduces-pollution claim as the main conclusion.

label: Conclusion
body: The mountain snowpack will probably melt more quickly and earlier, leading to greater spring flooding and less storable water for summer.

label: Evidence
body: The winter temperatures are likely to increase, causing more precipitation to fall as rain instead of snow.

label: Evaluate
body: Tall mountains usually receive a lot of snowfall over a winter, and the "snowpack" is basically the accumulated height of that snow. In the spring, that snow starts to thaw, sending pristine fresh water tricking down all the mountain streams. The author is thinking that warmer winters will bring less snow (it won't be cold enough for snow, so the precipitation will fall as rain). Hence, the snowpack will be smaller. Maybe in previous years, the snowpack was 10 ft deep, and now it'll be like 6 feet deep. Why will it melt earlier? Well, if the winter temperatures are warmer then it's probably the case that we reach the thawing / melting temperatures of spring earlier, too. Why will it melt more rapidly? This is probably just referring to 6 ft vs. 10 ft, the idea that once temperatures rise enough to start the thawing / melting process, it will take less time to melt 6 ft than it will 10 ft. (We might also plug in outside knowledge that the thicker the snowpack is, the more it self insulates, kind of like the way the deeper water in a swimming pool will stay colder than the shallow water) Why will there be more spring flooding? Well, floods come from a rapid increase of water, so the author must be thinking that because the snow will melt more rapidly, there will be more floods. Why will there be less storable water? If there's only 6 ft of snow vs. 10 ft., then that's less water. I guess I'm confused though why the extra rain doesn't make up for it. I don't really understand where storable water comes from (is it gathered more easily from melting snow than from rain?) Yeesh, what an exhausting argument to try to unpack and understand. If we were trying to think of potential objections, we'd pull out our Comparison + Prediction toolbox and think, "What else might change in this future world that could actually compensate and either add more snow than the author is thinking or slow down the melting process?"

label: Goal
body: Look for an answer strengthening the causal story the author is selling us or one that rules out an objection that would keep her prediction from coming true.

label: Conclusion
body: Animal feed shouldn't include any GMO plants.

label: Evidence
body: In a study, rats that were fed GMO potatoes for 30 days tended to develop intestinal deformities and a weakened immune system, whereas rats fed a normal diet of non-GMO food didn't have these problem.

label: Evaluate
body: Since the author is making a cause/effect assumption about something that went down with a study, we can use our Curious Fact / Explanation mindset. Curious Fact How come the rats fed GMO potatoes ended up with intestinal deformities and a bad immune system, whereas rats fet a non-GMO diet didn't have those problems? Author's Explanation The GMO potatoes caused the gut and immune system problems. We always affect these arguments in one of two ways: - Alternate Explanations for the curious fact or - Plausibility of the Author's Explanation What else could explain why the GMO potato group ended up with gut / immune problems? Well ... potentially anything. Were we ever told that the two groups were otherwise fair to compare? Were they kept in the same environment? Were they allowed to sleep the same amount? Were they given similar exercise? Were there any other potentially funky parts of the GMO potato rats' diet? Since the argument failed to establish that the only difference between these two groups was GMO potatoes vs. non-GMO potatoes, there is a whole world of potential alternate causes for why those rats got gut / immune problems (that would have nothing to do with the GMO-aspect of the potatoes they ate).

label: Goal
body: Since this is Weaken, we would want a correct answer to suggests a different explanation for why the rats in the GMO potato group ended up with gut / immune problems, or we would want a correct answer to say something that undermines the plausibility that GMO potatoes were really to blame. Or, we would like any answer that goes against the conclusion and gives us a way to argue that animal feed should have GMO plants in it.

label: Conclusion
body: It can't be the case that visual perception consists of a mental image that forms in our mind.

label: Evidence
body: If that were so, it would require something inside us that can see that mental image, and so would its visual perception consist of a mental image inside it, which would then require another viewer and another mental image, and so on and so on. This goes on infinitely, and hence is absurd.

label: Evaluate
body: The most basic formal structures in this argument are these: CONC = rebuttal "X must be wrong" EVID = the author attempts to show that the implications of a certain claim result in absurdity (there's some fancy Latin term like reductio ad absurdum for this type of argument, "it reduces to absurdity")

label: Goal
body: Look for a Conclusion saying "X can't be true / correct", and then Evidence that sounds like like "After all, if X were true, A would be true, and then B would be true, and then C would be true, etc. which would be crazy."

label: Information
body: Causal Greatly exceeding dangerously recommended daily ⇢ toxic intake of vitamins A Pivot for some foods, one "serving" has 100% of the recommended daily intake but many people overestimate what counts as a "serving", thereby consuming two to three times that much. Evaluate There are definitely overlapping ideas: recommended daily intake comes up multiple times, and so does standard servings. The standard serving is 100% of the recommended daily intake, but many people are having 2x or 3x a standard serving, so they'd be getting 200-300% of the recommended daily intake. This feels like it matches up with the Causal idea from the first sentence. If they're getting 200-300% of the recommended daily intake, are they "greatly exceeding the recommended daily intake"? Yeah, that seems fair. So are they eating toxic levels of these vitamins? Yeah, maybe!

label: Goal
body: The correct answer will probably reinforce putting together the ideas that people, by overestimating what counts as a standard serving, are probably consuming vitamins A and D in somewhat toxic levels.

label: Conclusion
body: Most of the nations claiming their oil reserves are unchanged are wrong (their oil reserves have changed).

label: Evidence
body: Oil reserves drop, when old fields are drained, and rise, when new fields are discovered.

label: Evaluate
body: We can use the keywords to interpret the structure. Claim 1. (counterpoint) But Claim 2. (author's arg starting) Therefore Claim 3. (intermed conc) So Claim 4. (main conc) But here the intermediate conclusion and the main conclusion are pretty similar, so thinking about them will not require two separate thought processes. If the author thinks is unlikely that any country's oil reserves would stay the same from one year to the next, she must be thinking that most of the time, you have a oil field drained or a new one discovered. "Oil reserves" are kind of like a country's oil bank account. They can see how much oil they have. Draining oil is like spending money. Discovering a new field is like adding money to the account. It's theoretically possible that a country drains 100 barrels of oil from an old field and then discovers a new field with 100 barrels of oil in it. That would end up leaving the oil reserves unchanged by the end of the year. So the author is also assuming that it's unlikely that the oil a country drains would cancel out with the oil a country discovers, within a given year. In terms of the move from Intermediate to Final conclusion, the author is thinking, "If it's unlikely for X to be true about a country, then the countries saying that X is true for them are probably wrong." This ignores the possibility that the countries saying that X is true are in the minority of all countries but still telling the truth. After all, we could say "It's unlikely that anyone would get fired from two different jobs in the same year", but I wouldn't necessarily conclude that "thus, most of the people saying they got fired from two different jobs in the same year are probably incorrect". Maybe they did get fired twice! "Unlikely" doesn't mean never, so there is some minority of people to whom this might happen. Similarly, the nations saying that their oil reserves are unchanged might be telling the truth; they might just be the exceptional cases.

label: Goal
body: Look for an answer saying "usually, countries are going to drain an oil field or discover one in any given year", "those effects usually don't cancel out", or "there isn't some good reason to think that the countries claiming their reserves are unchanged are the exceptional cases".

label: Statements
body: When we read Must Be True paragraphs, we're primarily looking for Conditional, Quantified, or Causal wording. All three claims here are Conditional / Quantified (if, if, none) If.... Then.... Motor is sound quiet enough to use insulated in home appliances If.... Then.... quiet enough to use can be used in in home appliances institutional settings If.... Then.... manufactured not quiet enough to use by EM industries in institutional settings Whenever we get more than one conditional, we check to see if any chain together. The 2nd sentence begins right where the the 1st one one leaves off, so they chain to give us this, sound → quiet enough → can be used in insulated for home apps instit. settings Then what about the last conditional? made by EM → not quiet enough for home apps The overlapping term is whether or not it's quiet enough for home appliances. In the chain, we say "it is quiet enough", but this last conditional is saying "it is not quiet enough". So let's contrapose the chain. can't be used → not quiet enough → not sound in instit. settings for home apps insulated According to this contrapositive chain, if something is "no quiet enough for home apps" then it is "not sound insulated". We wouldn't be able to judge whether or not it can be used in institutional settings, since the chain doesn't flow to the left.

label: Goal
body: Most likely, the answer will reward our ability to chain together sentence 1 and sentence 2 if sound insulated, then can be used in institutional settings or it will reward our ability to chain together sentence 1 and sentence 3, if manufactured by EM, then not sound insulated

label: Conclusion
body: This worry can be dismissed. rephrase: We can ignore the concern that the chemical plant could cause health problems.

label: Evidence
body: Most of the people who showed up to protest this plant were only there because they were paid to show up by people who don't want the factory to be built for property-value reasons.

label: Evaluate
body: Whenever we're doing a Flaw question and we see the author rebutting someone's claim, we want to immediately become suspicious that we might be seeing Ad Hominem or Unproven vs. Proven False (two of the ten famous flaws). With Ad Hominem, we dismiss someone's point of view because they are a biased source ( they have some vested interest in matter) or because they have conflicting past behavior. With Unproven vs. Proven False, we describe how someone's effort to prove X failed (through lack of evidence or flawed argument) and then we illicitly conclude that X is therefore false. So what about this argument? If some people at a protest say "Stop eating Snickers bars. They have a chemical dye that has been traced to cancer!", are we allowed to dismiss it simply by saying, "Ahhh, don't listen to them. They were paid to be there by Butterfinger, who wants to cut into their market share." No. We're not allowed to conclude that what the protesters are saying is factually wrong just because they have a biased reason for saying it. We have to investigate the merits of the position itself — is there any evidence that Snickers does have a chemical that is linked to cancer? Do we have any evidence for arguing that Snickers does not have any carcinogen in it?

label: Goal
body: Let's look for an answer that is objecting that the author is too harsh is dismissing the concerns of the protesters. Even if they were paid to be there, there may be some legitimacy to their claims. We should address the content of their argument rather than dismiss it because of the source of who's saying it. Or we should responsibly conclude that these protesters are not strong evidence that the factory could cause health problems, but we should otherwise stay agnostic about whether the factory really could cause health problems, unless we're producing evidence of our own.

label: Principle
body: Unless = "if it's not the case that" If you're not acting then you shouldn't in the interest of → purposefully misrepresent person X person X's beliefs

label: Evaluate
body: To violate a principle = to refute a conditional To rebut / contradict / refute a conditional or principle, you just need to provide at least one example in which the trigger is true but the outcome is false. (LEFT side = happening, RIGHT side = not happening) If the principle were "If X applies → then you should do Y", then violating that principle would feel like, X applies, but we didn't do Y. Since we had a principle that was "If you're not acting in Person X's interest, you shouldn't misrepresent X's beliefs" then violating that principle would feel like, We weren't acting in Person X's interest, but we did misrepresent X's beliefs.

label: Goal
body: Look for an answer that establishes 1. not acting in Person X's interest 2. misrepresented Person X's beliefs

label: Background
body: 1840-1860 - the price for wool on the world market was higher than the price paid in domestic markets - this family sold more wool on the world market - this family made a lot more money from wool sales

label: Surprising Claim
body: During this period, the family didn't see much, if any, increase in prosperity.

label: Evaluate
body: Sharita and Chad agree that there are too many stray cats and that so many stray cats is a problem.

label: Evaluate
body: Hmm, tricky one. A lot of background details to carefully absorb. Given That The family made much more money from wool sales How Can We Explain The family didn't see much of any increase in prosperity? We don't try to predict specific answers on Paradox, since the correct answer often takes a very surprising angle. However, we can think through some general types of ways that a family could make much more money on wool but not see an increase in prosperity: - maybe money isn't worth as much as it used to be? Inflation could mean that even though you make more money, your spending power (and thus prosperity) hasn't gone up. Wait a sec, the first sentence says "Adjusted for inflation", so we can't actually explain it that way. - maybe they faced financial difficulties of some sort? We could make more money from our business but have to spend more money on parking tickets / medical bills / funerals for family members, etc.

label: Goal
body: Look for an answer that gives us a way to explain their lack of prosperity.

label: Conclusion
body: It wasn't wrong for Meyers to take the compost in the public garden.

label: Evidence
body: If you take something you had good reason to think was someone else's property, that's stealing, that's wrong. But Meyers had no good reason to think that the compost in the public garden was anyone else's property.

label: Evaluate
body: First of all, this is pretty hilarious for once. Someone stole compost from a public garden? That's hilarious. They just double-parked, put on their hazard lights, and popped the trunk. Started shoveling compost into their trunk? So, the author provides us with a conditional rule: Take something w/ good reason to think it belongs → Stealing → Wrong to someone else Then the author says "Since Meyers didn't do the thing on the left, what he did wasn't wrong." That's an illegal Opposite move. Given a conditional relationship like "if you lie, then you did something wrong", we can't think to ourselves "if you didn't lie, then you didn't do something wrong". Even if you didn't lie, you still might have done something wrong. Similarly, even though Meyers had no good reason to think he was taking someone else's property, he still might have done something wrong.

label: Goal
body: The fancy name for presenting a conditional logic premise and then reasoning illegally in a Backwards or Opposite fashion is confusing Necessary vs. Sufficient. Taking something you had good reason to think was someone else's is one Sufficient reason that guarantees you did something wrong, but no one said it's the only way to have done something wrong.

label: Conclusion
body: The practice of predatory pricing (i.e. where WalMart comes into town, prices themselves less than all the local mom-and-pops, until the latter go out of business), should be acceptable.

label: Evidence
body: Sure, predatory pricing may allow a company to establish a monopoly, but the mere threat of renewed competition will keep them from getting too cocky with the prices.

label: Evaluate
body: As you can see, I'm trying to make this argument more relatable to myself so that I can better engage with it. Many of us will not hear the buried missing language link in here, and instead will have only a vague sense of what we're looking for. At this point, we should try to argue the anti-conclusion, to sharpen our thinking about where one could make potential objections to this argument. Given that the threat of renewed competition will be enough to keep Company X from raising its prices, How can we still argue that it would not be acceptable for Company X to use predatory pricing to drive all the other local stores out of business? Are prices all we care about, when assessing whether or not this is acceptable? Maybe we think our city thrives more when the aggregate business done by Company X is spread out among lots of local mom-and-pops.

label: Goal
body: Since we could make objections by saying, "there's something besides prices you should consider, before you give the green light to Company X to run the other businesses out of town", we can say that the author is assuming "All you have to worry about is prices".

label: Conclusion
body: Frank is not an embezzler

label: Evidence
body: If the prosecutor wanted to charge Frank with embezzlement, then Frank would have been indicted. But Frank has not been indicted.

label: Evaluate
body: The proper conclusion we can infer from pairing that conditional with the fact that prosecutor didn't indict Frank is that the prosecutor didn't want to indict Frank. The author's argument is making an illicit leap from "the prosecutor didn't want to indict him" to "he isn't guilty of embezzlement". Maybe Frank is an old friend of that prosecutor, or Frank works for a mafia kingpin who owns the prosecutor.

label: Goal
body: We want to see some sort of conditional premise: If A wanted to do X, then Y. Then we want a factual premise that triggers the contrapositive. But not Y. Then we want a conclusion that goes too far. Instead of saying "A doesn't want to do X", it makes a speculative leap about what that means, even though there could be other possible explanations / interpretations.

label: Conclusion
body: Removing tonsils before swelling will ensure that children don't experience any breathing problems during sleep.

label: Evidence
body: Swollen tonsils give rise to breathing problems, and surgically removing swollen tonsils can alleviate sleep disturbances.

label: Evaluate
body: This conclusion is comin' in hot! It's promising us that if we remove a kid's tonsils before they start to swell, it guarantees that kids will not experience any breathing problems during sleep. Really? They'll never have any breathing problems? - what if they have asthma? - what if they have sleep apnea? - what if they have COVID / flu / cold / congestion? - what if they cry themselves to sleep headfirst in a pillow (just me?)

label: Goal
body: If we were trying to describe this in formal terms, we might say that the author thinks "addressing one potential source of a problem will therefore eradicate the problem". Conversationally, we can object as we just did by saying, "Even if a kid isn't going to have breathing problems from swollen tonsils, there are myriad other ways that they might still have breathing problems sometimes".

label: Principle
body: Knowledge isn't available to the general public and → Unethical Government official uses it to financially benefit self

label: Conclusion (therefore)
body: It is likely that most people who commit embezzlement or bribery will eventually be caught.

label: Evidence
body: The people who originally adopted and enforced these taboos didn't have access to this type of data.

label: Evaluate
body: When we're given a Principle and asked to apply it, it will usually be a conditional rule. We want to set it up as in If / Then format, making sure the "judgy" idea is on the right. "Judgy" = normative, expressing value or judgment In this principle, the idea of whether or not something is ethical or unethical is the judgy term. When something is phrased, "It is X to Y", that is saying that "if you are or do Y, then you are X". So the first part of this sentence, "It is unethical to use your knowledge of impending policies to your benefit" would be a conditional itself. If a govt official is using knowledge of impending → unethical policy to benefit themselves The if clause at the end adds another qualifier to the trigger ... "assuming this knowledge is not already public domain".

label: Goal
body: When we're using a rule set up like X and Y → Z then we can only prove "Z". We can't prove "not Z". In this case, we don't have to worry about any answers trying to prove that something "was ethical", because the question stem has already pre-loaded the outcome of "unethical". So we're just looking to make sure all the criteria is established: 1. govt official 2. info about an impending policy 4. info not available to general public 3. official uses info to benefit themselves

label: Conclusion
body: If we don't get stronger evidence of wrongdoing or a confession from someone, we can't be certain enough who polluted river to impose a penalty on the suspected repair shop.

label: Evidence
body: The penalty for this pollution is very severe.

label: Evaluate
body: The author acknowledges that the repair shop is a likely suspect, but then pivots to say, "still, since we'd be issuing a VERY severe penalty, we need to be closer to 100% sure." The author seems to have some principle in mind like, "If you're not really confident that X did the crime, and the crime carries with it a very severe penalty, then you shouldn't impose the penalty on X."

label: Goal
body: Look for something like , "It's only okay to impose a really harsh penalty if you're pretty darn sure of who the culprit is."

label: Information
body: Depression is a big problem for nursing home residents. Pivot (however) In a recent study, residents who had bonds with pets had significantly lower rates of depression than did residents who didn't develop a bond with a pet.

label: Evaluate
body: When an Inference stimulus Ends with a Pivot, it's a strong clue that the inference the correct answer is testing is whatever idea we can safely derive by combining that Pivot idea with what came before it. What do you get by combining: residents of nursing homes struggle with depression + in a study, residents who had pet-love had way less depression than did residents without pet-love?

label: Goal
body: Let's look for a safely worded takeaway that sounds something like, "Let's try to get more residents of nursing homes to have bonds with pets, in order to help with the problem of depression". Or the answer could give a trickier version of that, like, "At least one potential method of alleviating depression in nursing homes does not involve giving the residents anti-depressant drugs".

label: Conclusion
body: Humorous television advertisements are the only effective ones.

label: Evidence (for)
body: If something is humorous it will not only attract people's attention, it will hold their attention long enough for a message to be conveyed. For an advertisement to be effective, it must convey its message.

label: Evaluate
body: Whenever we're doing Flaw and we see conditional logic ("the only", "if", "must"), we should be immediately suspicious that they're testing the #1 famous flaw, Necessary vs. Sufficient, in which an author presents a conditional rule but applies it illegally in a backwards or negated fashion. The conclusion looks like this: Effective -—--—--—--—--—--—> Humorous ~Humorous -—--—--—--—--—--> ~Effective What do the two conditionals in the evidence look like? Humorous -—> holds attention long enough to convey message Effective → conveys message When two conditionals are being used, only one is being broken, so we have to figure out which one that is. We can tell here that the 1st one must be the one that's broken, since the Conclusion involves "Effective" on the left of the arrow, but it does not involve "Humorous" on the left of the arrow. The author is apparently thinking that the two premises fit together like this: Effective → conveys → Humorous message That's how she's deriving her conclusion, Effective -—--—--—--—> Humorous But the 1st conditional premise doesn't say, conveys message → Humorous it says Humorous → conveys message

label: Goal
body: Look for an answer calling out a Necessary vs. Sufficient flaw with the conditional connecting "Humorous" and "holds attention long enough to convey message". Humor is sufficient to do that, but the author is acting like it's necessary. Or look for a conversational answer saying, "Hey, there might be other styles of ads, besides humorous ones, that are also able to attract and hold people's attention long enough for a message to be conveyed."

label: Conclusion
body: Even if the stories of health problems shortly after vaccinations are true, they're no need for concern.

label: Evidence
body: With millions of vaccinations, you're bound to have some coincidental cases where people got their vaccine, happened to develop some serious health problem right after by coincidence, and then blamed the health problem on the vaccine.

label: Evaluate
body: This author wants to explain away the stories of people getting vaxxed and then experiencing health problems right after as mere coincidence. Someone attacking this argument would say, "Whoa - whoa ... these were healthy people before they got the vaccine. And all these people reporting these health problems are reporting similar things: 3 days later, there was numbness and dizziness."

label: Goal
body: In order to strengthen the idea that these health problems occurring after the vaccinations are just random coincidences, not side effects of the vaccine, it would help the author to show us that there's too much variety in terms of when people feel "side effects" and what side effects they feel for these to truly be symptoms of the vaccine's aftermath. Let's look for an answer like that or any other answer that increases the plausibility that people are blaming a health problem on a vaccine just because the health problem developed coincidentally after they got vaccinated.

label: Evidence
body: People who repeatedly commit crimes like embezzlement or bribery without getting caught tend to become more confident and believe that getting caught is less likely. The more crimes a person commits, the greater the chance that one of those crimes will be solved.

label: Evaluate
body: Given that … not getting caught makes you more confident you won’t get caught, and given that the more crimes you commit, the greater the chance that one of those crimes will be solved by law enforcement, How could we still argue that … Most people who commit embezzlement or bribery will not eventually be caught? One way to object could be to say that even though the risk of getting caught increases with each additional crime committed, it still never gets to the point of being likely (i.e. above 50% that you’ll get caught). In other words, maybe there was a 0.5% chance your first crime would be solved, then 0.7% for your 2nd crime, 0.9% for your 3rd crime, etc. That might mean by the time you commit your 20th crime you’re at a 4.5% chance of getting caught. That still means you have a 95.5% chance of not getting caught. Just because a certain number (probability of getting caught) is always increasing doesn’t mean it will ever hit a certain threshold (over 50% = likely). We would also try to prevent the author’s move from “you become more confident that you won’t get caught” to “you’ll commit more crimes”. Just because you become more confident that you can get away with a crime doesn’t mean you’ll necessarily commit more crimes. Maybe you had a really good reason to commit bribery or embezzlement, but it was a one-time thing. You committed your crime and you think, “Wow, it’s pretty easy to get away with that crime”, but you have no further reason to keep committing crimes.

label: Goal
body: Let’s look for an answer speaking to the move from “if the chance is always increasing, then the chance of getting caught is likely” or one speaking to the move from “you don’t get caught and you become more confident that you wouldn’t get caught were you to try it again” to “you will try it again”.

label: Given that ...
body: A doubling in the price of grain will only cause the average price of break to rise 10-15%

label: Why is it that ...
body: A doubling in the price of grain will cause the price of grain-fed beef to double?

label: Evaluate
body: We really could have framed this paradox either way, switching these two ingredients. We're really just trying to explain why a doubling in the price of grain would have a smaller effect on the price of bread than it would on the price of grain-fed beef. Generally speaking, if you make a certain product, you have a lot of different expenses that go into setting your price. If one of those expenses (such as grain) were to rise by 30%, it wouldn't necessarily make the price of your product go up by 30%, because grain might be a very part of the expense to make your product. For example, if strawberries rose in price, it might only modestly affect the price of a mixed berry yogurt, because there are other fruits in there as well, whereas it might more drastically affect the price of strawberry yogurt.

label: Goal
body: Look for an answer saying that grain is a more important ingredient / bigger category of expense when it comes to grain-fed beef than when it comes to a loaf of bread.

label: Mark's Conclusion (So)
body: Qualzan probably increases the risk of heart attack.

label: Mark's Evidence
body: Zokaz increased the risk of heart attack, and Qualzan is also a decongestant and works by essentially the same physiological mechanism as does Zokaz.

label: Kathy's Response
body: Yes, but they're different chemically, so they probably have different side effects.

label: Evaluate
body: Kathy acknowledges that Mark's premise is true (they do operate by the same physiological mechanism), calls into question his conclusion (Q probably doesn't have the same side effect of increasing heart attack risk), and bases this on a premise that offers a distinction (Q and Z are putting different chemicals into our bodies).

label: Goal
body: Let's look for something like, "Offers a distinction to call into question Mark's conclusion".

label: Conclusion
body: We have been falsely criticized as being a "not environmentally responsible" corporation. rephrase: We are an environmentally responsible corporation.

label: Evidence
body: Do all you can → environmentally to pollute less responsible No methods come with zero pollution. Our newer methods pollute less than our older methods did.

label: Evaluate
body: Given that ... their new methods pollute less than their older ones, and that no method is pollution free How can we still argue that ... they are not an environmentally responsible corporation? Well, the author supplied us with a conditional rule that would prove that a corporation is environmentally responsible. And the author is acting like she triggered that rule. But the trigger is "do all you can to pollute less" and all we know is that "new methods > old methods". We could argue that, "even though your newer methods are definitely an improvement over your older methods, that doesn't mean you're doing as much as you can. Maybe there's some other method you haven't tried yet (or combination of methods) that would yield less pollution." It's like the author was saying, "I'm an environmentally friendly driver doing as much as I can to reduce CO2 emissions. After all, no car is totally emission free, and I traded in my Hummer for a Civic." We would similarly be saying, "Sure, the Civic is an improvement over the Hummer, but that's not doing as much as you can. What about getting a Prius / Leaf / Tesla? What about riding a bike?"

label: Goal
body: Look for an answer that speaks to the gap between "new methods are less polluting than older methods" and "doing all we can to pollute as little as possible".

label: Conclusion (clearly indicate that)
body: Some forms of gum disease are caused or aggravated by suppression of the immune system.

label: Evidence (since)
body: Stress can have a negative effect on the immune system + People who address problems quickly/directly are way less likely to get gum disease than are people who refuse to think about problems.

label: Evaluate
body: On Strengthen+Principle, we usually just predict an "If Premise, Then Conclusion" linking idea. For this argument it would sound like, If you're "stealing" wages in then this order to fund an account to → "stealing" is compensate burglary victims justified In other words, the argument seems to be that "since we're taking their money for a good cause, it's okay to take their money".

label: Conclusion
body: Magno-Blanket is probably able to relieve arthritic pain in older dogs.

label: Evaluate
body: This argument is almost incomprehensible to understand on a first read because of the assumptions being made. We have to figure out how gum disease / immune system are related, and we need to figure out how stress and people's rate of addressing problems are related (our common sense tells us to pair up these somewhat related ideas). The author's conclusion is making a causal claim: suppressed → some gum immune system disease When we look at the premises we have to ask ourselves how the author thinks each idea connects to this causal path. The premise that "stress can have a negative effect on the immune system" would be saying that Stress is causing "suppressed immune system". stress → suppressed → gum immune disease So what about the premise that "people who address problems quickly/directly are less likely to have gum disease than are people who refuse to think about problems"? This is a Curious Comparison, so our author will probably be trying to come up with some causal explanation for, "Why are people who address problems quickly/directly less likely to have gum disease?" Like with almost all correlations, our author will assume that one side causes the other. Since the author's conclusion is saying that something is causing gum disease, we know that our author is interpreting this direction of causality: addressing problems lowers your risk of quickly / directly gum disease What does stress, in the 2nd premise, have to do with this? Apparently the causal story the author is envisioning is that 1. you refuse to think about problems 2. that causes stress 3. that causes worse immune 4. that causes gum disease

label: Goal
body: Because this is Necessary Assumption and we're dealing with a Curious Fact / Explanation argument, we would expect a correct answer to either rule out an alternate explanation for why "address problems quickly" is correlated with "less gum disease" or establish something that needs to be true for the author's explanation to be plausible Since her story currently involves a really big missing link, refusing to think of problems → stress the answer will probably address that.

label: Conclusion
body: The cooler the temperature we store the fruit at, the longer it'll stay fresh.

label: Evidence
body: One group of various fruits was stored at 30 degrees, one at 20, one at 10. In the end, the freshest to least fresh were 10 degrees, 20 degrees, 30 degrees

label: Evaluate
body: Since there were similar fruits in each selection, we can't really fight this by saying, "What if the 10 degree fruit group was freshest not because of the colder temperature but because of [different fruits]?" But we could potentially object by saying there was some other difference between the 10 / 20 / 30 degree groups that is the real explanation for why the cooler the temp, the fresher the fruit. However, what LSAC really wants us to take issue with is the crazy strength of the conclusion: the more X, the more Y That's one of the strongest formulations on LSAT, since it means that X and Y covary infinitely in both directions. So this conclusion is committed to the idea that 0 degrees would be fresher than 10 degrees, and that -100 degrees would be fresher than 0 degrees. That seems corny. If your just flat-out freeze fruit, then you're not quite keeping it "fresh" longer.

label: Goal
body: Look for an answer complaining that the conclusion is so strongly worded that it commits the author to believing that frozen fruit would be fresher than cool fruit, or an answer saying the author has failed to consider some other possible explanation for the freshness/temperature gradient observed in the experiment.

label: Conclusion (Thus)
body: Claims that water shortages will plague humankind in the near future unless population growth trends change are simply mistaken. rephrase: Even if population growth trends continue, water shortages aren't necessarily going to plague humankind.

label: Evidence
body: Even though human population is increasing, it currently uses only a relatively small fraction of Earth's supply of fresh water.

label: Evaluate
body: Given that ... we only currently use a small fraction of Earth's supply of fresh water How can we say that ... as population continues to increase, water shortages will plague humankind? When we're dealing with Predictions, we usually want to consider what other sort of stuff could change in the future. Maybe currently we're only using a small fraction of Earth's fresh water supply, but we haven't yet faced the ravages of climate change. Perhaps we will soon face climatic feedback loops from climate change that will evaporate tons of our water or taint our water or make a lot of it inaccessible. Maybe the (natural or man-made) distribution networks that move water from one place to another will get impaired.

label: Goal
body: It's hard to know what the correct answer will be addressing, but it will probably deal with something other than Earth's water supply, as a potential factor in how water shortages will soon plague us. Let's just keep the Anti-Conclusion in mind, "We want an answer that helps us to argue that if population trends continue, we will potentially see water shortages plaguing humankind."

label: Given that ...
body: During the Industrial Revolution, businesses found ways to dramatically improve productivity, by solving assembly line processes and central planning.

label: How can it be that ...
body: In recent years, productive companies have found ways to improve their productivity by doing less central planning (i.e. giving individual employees more influence in decision making and in how they do their work).

label: Evaluate / Goal
body: We either need a distinction relating to timeframes, so that we can explain why during Industrial Revolution era it helped productivity to be more centrally planned whereas during Current era it helps productivity more to decentralize and empower employees to make their own decisions. Or we need a distinction relating to "already-productive companies", so that we can explain how for many companies (such as those in the Industrial Revolution), more central planning boosted productivity, whereas for these already-productive companies, decentralizing helps productivity.

label: Conclusion (So)
body: Even if we call confiscating a portion of burglars' wages a form of stealing, it would still be justified.

label: Evidence
body: We'd be confiscating wages in order to fund an account to compensate burglary victims.

label: Goal

label: Conclusion
body: Unrelieved heartburn is not likely to cause esophageal cancer. (The author signals this by saying "This is simply false" in response to the advertisers' implication.)

label: Evidence
body: Only about 5 percent of people with severe heartburn have Barrett's esophagus, and only those people have an increased risk of developing cancer because of heartburn.

label: Evaluate
body: The first sentence reports what some heartburn-medication ads imply (the opposing position). The second sentence ("This is simply false") is the author's rebuttal — the main conclusion. The remainder of the stimulus supports that rebuttal: only a small subset of heartburn sufferers face elevated cancer risk, so heartburn-as-cancer-cause is rare, not the norm.

label: Goal
body: Find an answer that paraphrases the rebuttal: it is not the case that unrelieved heartburn is likely to cause esophageal cancer. Avoid answers that paraphrase the supporting evidence (Barrett's esophagus details) or the opposing claim being rebutted.

label: Conclusion
body: Unrelieved heartburn is not likely to cause esophageal cancer. ("This is simply false" is the author's rebuttal of the ads.)

label: Evidence
body: Only ~5% of heartburn sufferers (those with Barrett's esophagus) have increased cancer risk from heartburn.

label: Evaluate
body: The structure is opposing claim → rebuttal → supporting facts. The rebuttal is the main conclusion.

label: Goal
body: Pick the answer that paraphrases the rebuttal of the ads, not the supporting Barrett's detail or the opposing claim itself.

label: Conclusion
body: The author's point is straightforward: those heartburn-medication ads are wrong — heartburn doesn't typically cause esophageal cancer.

label: Evidence
body: The reason is statistical: only about 5% of severe heartburn sufferers have Barrett's esophagus, and those are the only people whose heartburn raises their cancer risk. So the cancer-from-heartburn link applies to a small subset, not to heartburn sufferers in general.

label: Evaluate
body: The trick on Main Conclusion questions is to identify the author's own claim — what they are arguing for — and not confuse it with (a) the position they are rebutting or (b) the evidence they are using to make their case. Here, the opposing position comes from the ads: heartburn is likely to cause cancer. The author rebuts that with a flat "This is simply false." The Barrett's esophagus statistic is the support, not the conclusion. The main point is: the ads are wrong, heartburn does not typically lead to cancer.

label: Goal
body: Pick the answer that says, in some form, "unrelieved heartburn is not likely to cause esophageal cancer."

label: Evidence
body: On display at → well X → Y Furniture Labyrinth crafted Most major lamp manufacturers Most A's have have halogen lamps on display B's that are X. at Furniture Labyrinth.

label: Conclusion
body: Some halogen lamps are Some B's are Y. well crafted.

label: Evaluate
body: The reason this argument is valid comes from the conditional rule. As soon as you establish that anything is on display at Furniture Labyrinth, then you've established that it's well crafted. So, structurally, I wouldn't be surprised to see them tinker with the details of the "Most major manufacturers", since the Most has nothing to do with why the conclusion can be validly drawn. It could have said Some and the conclusion would be just as valid.

label: Goal
body: Look for two premises: 1 of them gives a conditional rule. The other is a fact about something that triggers the conditional rule. The conclusion then says that the outcome of the rule applies to that same something.

label: Information
body: causal + contrast (do /don't increase) Implementing more flexible scheduling doesn't usually increase managers' happiness or efficiency, but it does increase happiness / productivity / attendance by nonmanagerial employees. limits on causality Over time the benefits dissipate, and if the schedules are too flexible, the benefits basically disappear.

label: Evaluate
body: Our goal is to think about how we can combine at least two of the facts we were given, but it's hard to see any obvious way we should be combining these. There seems to be a tenuous benefit to flexible schedules, but it primarily applies to nonmanagerial employees in the short term, with schedules that are less than totally flexible.

label: Goal
body: Let's just look for the most supportable answer we can find.

label: Conclusion
body: The viewers surveyed who thought Lopez did better in the debate may have been biased in favor of Lopez.

label: Evidence
body: Lopez did go on to win the election.

label: Evaluate
body: Since the author is interpreting the cause behind a piece of data (they favored Lopez's arguments because they were biased in favor of Lopez), we can use our Curious Fact / Explanation mindset. Curious Fact ... why did most viewers surveyed immediately after the debate think that Lopez had made the better arguments? Author's Explanation ... those viewers had already decided they were voting for Lopez and so they watched the debate through that biased prism and thus rationalized that their preferred pick had made the better arguments. We can weaken this type of argument, either of two ways: 1. Suggests an alternate explanation for why people said that Loped made the better arguments (such as .. because Lopez actually made the better arguments, or Lopez holds policy positions more similar to theirs) 2. Undermined the plausibility of the author's story, which is that people watching the debate were already planning to vote for Lopez and that bias made them think that Lopez had made the better arguments.

label: Goal
body: The correct answer should provide a different way to explain the survey's results (not because people were biased in favor of Lopez, but because _____ ), or it should undermine the author's causal storyline.

label: Conclusion
body: The recent data showing that food taboos served important societal and medical functions in ancient cultures can't explain the origin of these food taboos.

label: Evaluate
body: At a basic Missing Link level, this argument is assuming if X didn't have access to data set Y, then data set Y can't explain X's behavior. On a more conversational level, given that these ancient societies didn't have the medical data we have to show how, for example, a taboo against eating shellfish actually served a valuable socioeconomic and medical function for these societies, could this data still explain the origins of the taboo? i.e., given that ancient cultures wouldn't have had the ability to scientifically prove that refraining from eating shellfish was good for them, can data showing that eating shellfish would have been bad for them help convince us that the reason they avoided shellfish was for health reasons? Sure. Before there was data showing that smoking cigarettes led to lung cancer, there were probably families who prohibited their kids from smoking cigarettes because they were worried that the cigarettes would do harm to the kids' lungs. Even though they didn't have access to the data, the origin of the smoking prohibition might still have been fear of the medical dangers that we now can demonstrate with actual data.

label: Goal
