body: Look for an answer linking "if you didn't have access to certain data, then that data can't explain the reasons for your behavior", or an answer ruling out an objection that would allow us to say that "even though they didn't have the data, the data is explaining the origin of these prohibitions."

label: Facts
body: Most [published fiction] was submitted by agents. The remainder of [published fiction] was from a requested submission. Nonfiction manuscript and Not given serious attention ~Renowned Figure → and not published and ~Requested after review

label: Evaluate
body: On MBT, we care most about conditionals. The final sentence is a conditional. Do either of the first two facts trigger the rule? No, because the first sentence is about fiction and the rule is about nonfiction.

label: Goal
body: It's hard to know what to predict since the facts didn't interact with each other.

label: Evidence
body: If the budget does not allow ~↑DI → ~DMS for more dairy inspectors to be hired, most of the large dairies in the central valley will not meet federal standards governing the disposal of natural wastes, which can seep into streams and groundwater. The new district budget, ~↑DI however, does not allow for the hiring of more dairy inspectors.

label: Conclusion
body: Consequently, most of the DWP district's drinking water is likely to become polluted.

label: Evaluate
body: The argument assumes ~DMS → DWP that if most large dairies in the central valley do not meet federal standards, then most of the district’s drinking water is likely to become polluted.

label: Evidence
body: Almost every really successful Almost all X's product in last 10 yrs was in past time launched by massive TV period used Y ad campaign. We're using a massive We're using Y TV ad campaign for for Thing A. Vegetaste Burger.

label: Conclusion
body: Vegetaste Burger will Thing A will probably be very successful. prob be X

label: Evaluate
body: We could call this argument a few different things. Past = Future Since massive ads have gone with successful products in the past, the massive ad we're doing now will probably go with a successful product. Correlation = Causation Since almost every successful product was preceded by a major TV ad launch, we can conclude that massive ad launch for Vegetaste will cause it to be successful. Necessary vs. Sufficient (with Most claims) Most successful products had a massive ad launch. VB has a massive ad launch. So, VS will probably be a successful product. The flaw, conversationally, could be "just because Y has usually been preceded by X, that doesn't mean that this X will probably be followed by a Y. There might be tons of times that ~Y is also preceded by X. Maybe most of the time X occurs, Y doesn't. But most of the time Y occurs, X does."

label: Goal
body: My guess is they probably care most about the 3rd thing, but we'll have to stay flexible as we look at the choices. Let's look for this structure: Premise 1: Most X's are Y. Premise 2: Thing A is Y. Conclusion: Thing A is probably X. All the answers are starting with the conclusion, so we'll get rid of them if they're not matching the strength of probably (typically, generally, usually, likely, most, tends to). If the strength of language is correct, and the conclusion is saying 'probably X', then we'll look for a premise that talks about 'Almost every X' or 'Most X'.

label: Conclusion (this suggests that)
body: Life may be able to arise under many difficult conditions throughout the universe.

label: Intermediate Conclusion (so)
body: The first life on Earth must have appeared soon after the planet's formation, when conditions were harsh.

label: Evidence
body: Earth is only 4.6 billion years old, and we've found fossils 3.5 billion years old, and ...

label: Intermediate Conclusion (so)
body: Those fossilized organisms had already had a long evolutionary history.

label: Evidence
body: These bacterial organisms were quite complex.

label: Evaluate
body: We have multiple so's, which always indicate a conclusion. And we have a this suggests that, which also indicates a conclusion. In order to figure out which one is the Main conclusion, we can think about which ideas support the other, or we can just think about how these indicator words show us which claim is supporting which. Scientists have discovered.... background fact The fossils indicate that ... conclusion based on claim 1 and so must have ... conclusion based on claim 2 However, Earth is 4.6 old ... pivoting into main argument with a fact so, the first life ... conclusion based on claim 4 This suggests that that life ... conclusion based on claim 5 The claim they're asking us about claim 3.

label: Goal
body: We would say that this 3rd claim is a conclusion (it's prefaced by "so") based on the fact that the bacteria are quite complex. But it's an intermediate conclusion, because it is a stepping stone along the path to the eventual main conclusion, that life apparently can arise despite harsh conditions.

label: Conclusion
body: The stars aren't more than a few million miles from Earth .

label: Evidence
body: The Earth stays in one place, while the stars orbit around it. If the Earth were more than a few million miles from Earth, the distance of that orbit would be so big, that they'd have to be traveling at CRAZY speeds, in order to make a circle around Earth every day.

label: Evidence
body: This season's sales figures show sales are down for LRG, with their new products selling especially poorly.

label: Evaluate
body: This question is testing a relatively simple assumption, but in pretty complicated clothing. Suppose we said this: Target must not be more than a mile from here. If it were farther than that, then Tina would have taken her skateboard. What obvious but unstated thought are we assuming? Tina didn't take her skateboard. The assumption is triggering the contrapositive of the rule. If farther than a mile, then skateboard. Tina no skateboard. Thus, Not farther than a mile. Or in the original argument: If farther a few million miles, stars would have to move crazy fast. [ assumption? ] Thus, not farther than a few million miles

label: Goal
body: The astronomers were assuming that "stars wouldn't go that fast, right?"

label: Implied Rebuttal Conclusion
body: People are wrong to dismiss the work of abstract expressionists as artistically worthless.

label: Intermediate Conclusion
body: Obviously exact replication is not the only thing that people prize in a painting.

label: Evidence
body: If realism were the only thing that people wanted out of a painting, then photography would have entirely displaced painting as an art from.

label: Evaluate
body: The author proves her intermediate conclusion by showing that the negation of her conclusion would entail a falsity. Fun language, right? A lot of Method questions involve "Implications of Logic" type argument. An author might try to shoot down a claim by arguing like this: Some say X is true. But if X were true, then Y would be true, which would require Z. Since Z is untrue/absurd, this means that we shouldn't believe X. Other times (like here), an author will argue for the truth of a claim by talking about the implications of rejecting it. X is true. After all, if it weren't, then Y would be true (which we know it isn't).

label: Goal
body: It will be hard to predict the language here, but it will probably be something like "argues for a claim by showing that if the claim were not true then something would have happened that hasn't happened".

label: Conclusion (So, clearly)
body: It costs more to bank at TekBank than at GreenBank.

label: Evidence
body: GreenBank gives all customers unlimited free ATM usage. TekBank charges 25 cents for each ATM transaction.

label: Evaluate
body: Given that ... a GreenBank customer pays nothing to use the ATM, whereas a TekBank customer pays 25 cents each time they use the ATM, How could we argue that ... it actually costs more (or the same) to bank at GreenBank? Well, when it comes to ATM transactions, clearly GreenBank is cheaper, but is that the only potential source of cost when it comes to evaluating "how much it costs to bank" somewhere? Maybe there's a fee to open your account. Maybe there's a fee for buying checks or placing money orders. Maybe there's an online banking fee. It's possible that TekBank is costlier when it comes to ATM usage, but cheaper when it comes to setting up the account, getting checks, paying insufficient fund fees, wiring money, etc.

label: Goal
body: Look for an answer saying that even though ATM fees are cheaper at GreenBank, there might be other costs involved with banking at GreenBank that make it more costly overall than TekBank. Technically, we could call this a Part vs. Whole or Sampling flaw (two of the 10 famous flaws), because the evidence is looking at a part/sample of the cost of banking at each bank and then assuming the same thing would be true about the overall cost of banking at each bank.

label: Klein's Claims
body: 1. The amount of matter we've found in our galaxy is only 1/10 of what Einstein's theory predicts. 2. Because what we've found is only 1/10, that's good reason for abandoning his view.

label: Brown's Responses
body: 1. Implicitly agrees. Brown doesn't directly comment on this, but her response seems to be acting as though she accepts that there is "missing matter". 2. Disagrees. Brown does not think that finding only 1/10 is a good reason for abandoning Einstein's view. Brown is saying, "given how successful Einstein's theory has been, we should probably assume that he is right in his prediction and we are wrong in terms of how we're currently searching for matter."

label: Goal
body: They're disagreeing over whether the "missing matter" problem is / isn't a sign that we should abandon Einstein's view.

label: Given that ...
body: Chimpanzees sometimes gesture a threat, and sometimes attack.

label: Why is it that ...
body: Attacks are almost never preceded by threats, and threats are rarely followed by attacks?

label: Anticipate
body: Why would two behaviors that both express anger almost never co-occur? We often think about Threats being stage 1 of anger and Attack being stage 2. So how come they either stop at stage 1 or go straight to stage 2? Maybe they are just very aware of whether they're likely to get their ass kicked, to put it elegantly. If they think they'd lose to an opponent, they just Threat because they don't want that smoke. But if they think they'd win, they don't bother threatening; they get straight to winning.

label: Goal
body: Find a storyline for why a chimp almost never threatens prior to attacking / almost never attacks after a threat?

label: Paradox
body: Threat gestures and attacks both come from anger, but the two almost never co-occur.

label: Anticipate
body: The natural explanation: gestures and attacks are substitutes — gesturing burns off aggression that would otherwise lead to attack.

label: Goal
body: An answer establishing the substitution relationship.

label: Paradox
body: Here's the puzzle. Both threat gestures and physical attacks happen when chimps get angry. So you'd expect them to go together — angry chimp makes a threat, then attacks. But they almost never overlap. A chimp that gestures rarely attacks, and a chimp that attacks rarely gestures first.

label: Anticipate
body: The natural way to resolve this: the two behaviors are substitutes, not stages. If the chimp gets the anger out by gesturing, it doesn't need to attack. If the chimp goes straight to attack mode, the gesturing isn't needed. Think of it like venting. Some people yell to let off steam — and once they've yelled, they don't throw a punch. Other people skip the yelling and just throw the punch. Yelling and punching can both express anger, but they're alternatives, not stages of the same response.

label: Goal
body: An answer that explains the gestures as a release valve for aggression that would otherwise become physical.

label: Evidence
body: In a hospital study, humans suffering from severe joint pain found that 76% of the them who were treated with magnets reported less pain after 3 weeks. Dogs and humans have similar physiologies, and using a Magno-Blanket on a dog would bring the magnets into similar proximity to the bad joints.

label: Evaluate
body: Since the author is interpreting a study and making a causal assumption about it, we can use our Curious Fact / Explanation mindset. Curious Fact .. why did people report less pain 3 weeks after being treated with magnets? Author's Explanation ... the magnet caused the pain reduction. We always address this type of template by asking two question: - how else could we explain why they reported less pain? - how plausible is the author's story that the magnets caused the pain reduction? There is also a Comparison dimension to this argument, in addition to that Causal one just discussed. Even if we granted that the Magno Blanket did cause pain relief in humans, we still would have to wonder whether that would hold true for old dogs with arthritic pain. Maybe old dogs aren't fair to compare to these hospital patients. Maybe arthritic pain isn't fair to compare to severe joint pain.

label: Goal
body: We have three possibilities - rule out an alternate explanation for why the humans felt better 3 weeks after magnets - increase the plausibility that the magnets caused pain relief - make it more likely that it's fair to compare old dogs w/ arthritic pain to these hospitalized humans with severe joint pain.

label: Setup Ideas
body: Some people think that advertising is messed up, because it brainwashes people into wanting things they wouldn't otherwise want. But, isn't that what music art classes do to? They kind of "brainwash" you into now liking new things about art and music. And nothing's wrong with them.

label: Evaluate
body: Claim 1 — Some people believe X Claim 2 — However, idea 1 and idea 2. Claim 3 — Therefore, _______ . Because of this structure, we know that this paragraph is a rebuttal argument, and the blank we're filling in is its conclusion. What does the conclusion sound like on a rebuttal argument? It sounds like, "Thus, they are wrong." In this case, that would mean "They're wrong — advertising is not socially pernicious."

label: Goal
body: The #1 thing to consider with Logical Completion is look for more provable language. So we want something safely worded like, "We shouldn't conclude that advertising is socially pernicious just because it manipulates preferences".

label: Conclusion (thus)
body: High school career counselors should tell students who are interested in journalism what life is like for a typical reporter, that is a reporter for a local newspaper.

label: Evidence
body: Many high school students thinking of a career in journalism picture glamorous international news gathering, but most journalists cover primarily local news and work for local newspapers.

label: Evaluate
body: There's seems to be a mismatch between the career that prospective journalists envision and the career that eventual journalists end up with. High schoolers picture themselves being Anderson Cooper or some gritty war correspondent in Ukraine. Meanwhile, the vast majority of people who graduate with these journalism degrees are going to just be covering the installation of new speed bumps near the mall for their local paper. The conclusion introduces a brand new concept of what "career counselors should do", so we want the correct answer to be a principle that would guide the behavior of career counselors. Since the conclusion is instructing the counselors to tell students what life is like for a typical reporter, we want this principle to tell the counselor it's their job to set the student straight.

label: Goal
body: Let's look for something like, "If there's a mismatch between what a student thinks a career is all about vs. what it's really likely to be about, the a career counselor should tell them about what it's really likely to be about."

label: Conclusion (obviously)
body: These so-called safety features (striping and flashing lights at crosswalks) are a waste of taxpayer money.

label: Evidence
body: This is an Anti-Causal conclusion, because the author is saying that these safety features are a waste of money (implying "they don't do anything / they might even make the situation worse"). Since our job here is to object to the author's conclusion, we have to try to argue that "These safety features are not a waste. They are improving safety." The author will retaliate by saying, "Then how come we see more pedestrian injuries occur at crosswalks with these features than they do at crosswalks without these features"? We would have to Make an Excuse for that evidence, as we often do on Anti-Causal arguments. Given our view that ... the stripes and flashing lights do increase safety at crosswalks, How can we explain why ... more pedestrian injuries occur at crosswalks marked in such a way? Maybe those crosswalks were already terrible before the stripes and flashing lights arrived. Perhaps the flashing lights and stripes are an attempt to deal with a terrible intersection. They make the situation better, but those crosswalks are still the worst. It would be like if China or the U.S. took some steps to curb greenhouse emissions. Their measures might reduce greenhouse emissions but China and the U.S. would still be the worst polluters in the world, because they're so much worse than everyone else. LSAT has used this type of argument a bunch (click on the bold if you'd like to see other examples): "The areas with the most cops have the most crime. Clearly, cops don't help stop crime". "The roads with bike lanes have the most incidents of bikes getting hit by cars. Clearly, bike lanes don't help increase safety". Our objections: - We sent the cops there because the area was so bad in terms of crime. - We added the bike lanes because there were so many bikes getting hit by cars.

label: Goal
body: Look for an answer saying we added these stripes and flashing lights because these crosswalks were already a travesty. These safety features are taking an awful situation and making it somewhat less awful, even if these intersections are still the worst overall.

label: Conclusion
body: The Korean sighting helps to confirm John of Worcester's sighting.

label: Evidence
body: John recorded two unusually large sunspots on Dec 8th, 1128. Five days later there was an aurora borealis observed in southern Korea, and sunspot activity is typically followed about five days later by an aurora borealis.

label: Goal
body: Since we know the first claim is supported by the rest of the paragraph, we know the first claim is the Main Conclusion. So, let's go find an answer that looks like the first sentence. We want "the heavier can might not contain more food", or anything similar in meaning.

label: Evaluate
body: The author already provides some plausibility for the connection between sunspots and aurora borealis, but it's like this ... If .... there is sunspot Then ... aurora borealis activity, five days later. This argument is kind of going backwards. It establishes that an aurora borealis was sighted five days later and then tries to reason backwards to, "I guess there was sunspot activity". We would potentially object to this argument by saying something like, "Maybe it was really common for aurora borealis to occur in Korea, so there's no reason to think that this one was necessarily from sunspots". Goal If we make it seem like aurora borealis is a rare thing, that strengthens the likelihood that the one observed in 1128 was linked to sunspots. We could also strengthen by establishing the plausibility of the causal story --- would a sunspot seen from England actually materialize as aurora borealis in Korea? Those two places are so geographically removed from each other that maybe we would doubt the events are connected because of that. Look for something to rule out an alternate explanation for the Korean aurora borealis, or an answer that increases the plausibility that the Korean aurora borealis was the five-day follow-up from the sunspots that John observed.

label: Conclusion (Thus)
body: Anyone who wants to improve society should reject the belief that its future will be determined entirely by vast historical forces that individuals are powerless to change. rephrase: if you believe that the future will be controlled by things you're powerless to change, this will not improve society.

label: Evidence
body: If you believe that future is beyond your control, you will feel to helpless to act to change society for the better.

label: Evaluate
body: Consider this similar argument: Anyone who compliments Obama gets approval from Lisa's Dad. Thus, if you want Lisa to like you, you should not compliment Obama. This is missing the idea "if you want Lisa to like you, you don't want approval from Lisa's Dad." The argument we read had the same form. Anyone who believes "the future is out of our control" will feel too helpless to act. Thus, if you want to improve society, don't believe that "the future is out of our control". So we'd be missing the idea, "if you want to improve society, you don't want to feel too helpless to act."

label: Goal
body: Look for some answer stressing that "we don't want people to feel too helpless to act to change society for the better / that will made it harder to improve society".

label: Statements
body: conditional (whenever = Left side, sufficient) Subcontract the Lose some control manufacturing of → over quality of a product that product We subcontract some manufacturing (i.e. we lose some control over the quality of some of our products) conditional (only = Right side, necessary) We subcontract They have complete with a company → control over quality of their products

label: Evaluate
body: We see two conditional claims, signified by "whenever" and "only". Do they chain together? Is there any Overlapping Idea? They're both talking about subcontracting, and they're both talking about control over the quality of products. Hmm. Sometimes we need to contrapose a conditional to see how it would fit. If we contrapose the first sentence is saying, not lose some control not subcontract over quality of product → manufacturing Here, we hope that it clicks that "not losing some control over quality" is a match for "maintain complete control over quality". If you've maintained complete control, then you haven't lost any control, and thus you haven't subcontracted.

label: Goal
body: Since this company subcontracts, they are losing some control over the quality of their product. Since the companies they subcontract with maintain complete control over quality, those companies do not subcontract. Maybe the answer will say "the companies this company subcontracts with maintain a greater degree of control over quality than this company does (since this one subcontracts and they don't)"?

label: Conclusion
body: If broad mastery isn't achieved by students in a certain secondary school, then we know they weren't taught with method appropriate to their learning styles.

label: Evidence
body: If secondary school students are taught with methods appropriate to their learning styles and devote significant effort to their studies, then they will achieve broad mastery.

label: Evaluate
body: The premise is a conditional with an AND in the trigger. Taught with approp meth and → Broad mastery Devote signif effort The contrapositive: ~Taught w/ appropr meths ~Broad Mastery -> or ~Devote signif effort Our author's conclusion resembles this contrapositive, only it is saying ~Broad Mastery -> ~Taught w/ appropr meths That's cheating! Given a rule like, A → B or C I can't just go around concluding that A → B It would be like saying this: "Everyone who goes to Harvard Law has a great LSAT score or has an influential parent. Thus, If you meet someone who goes to Harvard Law, you can be sure that they have a great LSAT score." Our one possible objection to this argument is, "Hey, author, if broad mastery isn't achieved, it might be that they weren't taught with appropriate methods or it might be that they didn't devote significant effort (or both). How can you so confidently conclude that if they don't have broad mastery, they definitely didn't have appropriate methods?

label: Goal
body: We need an answer to eliminate the other idea in the Or outcome. The author established that if broad mastery isn't achieved, it's either because of inappropriate methods or lack of sufficient effort. To prove her conclusion that it always shows a lack of appropriate methods, we need to rule out the possibility that it's because of a lack of sufficient effort. If we know these secondary students DID devote significant effort and they still didn't achieve broad mastery, then we would have to blame inappropriate methods, as the author's conclusion is doing.

label: Conclusion
body: Even if one can of fruit/veggies is heavier than another, the heavier one doesn't necessarily contain more food.

label: Evidence
body: Canned fruit/veggies are typically packed in water, and some companies include more water than others.

label: Evaluate
body: Whenever we do Main Conclusion questions, we prime our brains before reading the paragraph, "Remember — on Main Conclusion, the conclusion is most likely going to be the First Sentence or a Rebuttal". That way as we're reading that first sentence, we're specifically listening for whether it sounds like the Author's Opinion. This first sentence doesn't have any obvious opinion giveaway, but we confirm that it is indeed the conclusion when we continue reading the paragraph and feel the following ideas supporting that first one. why should we believe that the heavier can might not have more fruit? - because, they put water in cans, so the heavier can might just have more water.

label: Situation
body: Some 3 year olds, who knew the digits 0 thru 9, were trying to learn their phone number, but none of them could remember it. Then, the teacher taught them their phone number embedded in a song. By the end of the day the children could remember their phone numbers.

label: Evaluate
body: It sounds like putting their phone number into a song was a real Causal Difference-Maker. The kids weren't able to remember the number without the song, and they were able to remember the number with a song.

label: Goal
body: Look for a safely worded answer that reflects the idea that "putting the phone number into a song made it easier for a 3 year old to memorize their phone number".

label: Conclusion
body: Some theorists are mistaken about what is an appropriate goal for literary criticism. (i.e. theorists should not strive to be value-neutral in their literary criticism)

label: Evidence
body: Literary criticism cannot be completely value-neutral.

label: Evaluate / Goal
body: This argument is pretty sparse ... the author is just saying "If critics cannot be completely value-neutral, then striving to be value-neutral is an inappropriate goal for literary criticism". So that's what we're looking for. The most important skills here are making sure when we hear a conclusion like "they're mistaken / they're wrong", we don't leave it like that. We actually say the specific counter-claim that the author is making by saying that they're wrong. The other big skill is seeing the "But" as the author's pivot that introduces her Premise / Conclusion combo.

label: Conclusion (thus)
body: All microscopic organisms must also be capable of feeling pain.

label: Evidence
body: Amoebas, like human beings, generally withdraw from stimuli that cause them physical damage. Humans do this because such stimuli cause them pain.

label: Evaluate
body: We could choose to take advantage of the repeating symbols (humans, pain, withdrawing from damaging stimuli) and turn this into algebra. Premise 1: X's, like Y's, generally do A in response to B. Premise 2: Y's do it because of reason Z. Conclusion: All things like X must have some sensitivity to reason Z. We can also focus on the type and strength of claims used. The premises should involve a comparison between two categories of things. There should be a second premise about one of those categories of things. The conclusion should be an all claim. But we can also choose to respond conversationally. Why does this argument fail to convince us that "all microscopic organisms are capable of feeling pain"? 1. Microscopic organisms don't have a nervous system or a brain or, probably, any consciousness at all. How could they feel pain? 2. Why is the conclusion talking about all microscopic organisms? The evidence only talked about amoebas. This seems to be a Sampling flaw, because the author seems to be thinking that "what's true of amoebas is true of all microscopic organisms", of which amoebas are just one type.

label: Goal
body: The easiest thing to look for at a glance would be the relationship between the conclusion "All things in category X" and a premise, which needs to be about one specific type of X. If an answer has that, we'll try to confirm that the argument uses a comparison structure, and argues, "A and B both have X in common. Since B has Y, then the A must also have Y."

label: Curious Fact / Evidence
body: Why do we observe snowshoe hares everywhere following this same cycle? more hares -> more predators -> hares retreat to less food -> hare population drops -> predators decline -> hares rebound

label: Explanation / Conclusion
body: Sunspot activity is probably also a causal factor in the hare cycle.

label: Evidence
body: Hare population cycles are well correlated with the regular cycle of sunspot activity, AND the local predator-prey dynamic alone can't explain why hare populations everywhere cycle simultaneously.

label: Evaluate
body: When we're trying to strengthen an Explain Curious Fact style argument, we primarily expect answers to 1) increase the plausibility of the author's causal storyline but we also see answers 2) rule out an alternate causal storyline for the curious fact

label: Goal
body: Get rid of four answers that either 1) make it more plausible that sunspot activity from the sun influences this population cycle of the snowshoe hare 2) undermines some alternate explanation for the snowshoe hare's population cycle.

label: Argument
body: The zoologist concludes sunspots are a causal factor in hare population cycles, based on correlation and the inability of local predator-prey dynamics alone to explain synchronized cycles.

label: Evaluate
body: To strengthen, give a mechanism, tighten the correlation, or rule out alternatives.

label: Goal
body: The EXCEPT — find the answer that doesn't strengthen.

label: Argument
body: The zoologist sees that hare populations cycle in sync everywhere — and notes that the predator-prey explanation alone doesn't explain why they cycle at the same time across the country. So she points to sunspots: the cycles match up with sunspot activity, so sunspots are probably part of the cause.

label: Evaluate
body: This is a "correlation -> causation" argument. Strengtheners come in three flavors: (1) a plausible mechanism for how sunspots could affect hares or predators, (2) tighter, deeper correlation, or (3) ruling out alternative explanations. The trick on this question: we're looking for the answer that doesn't do any of those. Maybe it's neutral. Maybe it points to an alternative explanation that competes with sunspots.

label: Goal
body: Look for the answer that's either neutral or weakens the sunspot link.

label: Statements
body: conditional (essential = necessary, Right side) Successful → Flourishing nat'l economy sci community conditional (requires = necessary, Right side) Flourishing nat'l many young sci community → ppl excited to be pro scientists conditional (necessary = necessary, Right side) many young good communication ppl excited to → between scientists be pro scientists and public

label: Conclusion (So)
body: If concrete settles evenly, either it as poured while the ground was dry or it will crack.

label: Evidence
body: If the concrete is poured while the ground is wet, it will not form a solid foundation. If the concrete doesn't form a solid foundation, it will settle unevenly or crack.

label: Evaluate
body: We were given three conditionals, each of them saying "one thing is required for another thing". We know that Required things go on the Right of the arrow (the necessary condition). Any time we read a conditional, X → Y, we can choose to read it as "If X, then Y" or as "X requires Y". A successful economy requires a flourishing science community, which requires many young people excited to be pro scientists one day, which requires good communication between scientists and the public. We can conversationally list out the chain of requirements, as I just did, or we can try to diagram them, knowing that any LSAT question that tests conditional logic will be trying to bait us into picking illegal Reversals or Negations once we get to the answers: Succ Flourishing excited Good econ → sci comm → young ppl → comm. sci/pub We could contrapose that whole thing and say, "if you don't have good communication, you won't have excited young people, so you won't have a flourishing science community, so you won't have a successful economy."

label: Goal
body: Expect an answer to reward us for putting this chain of four ideas together. It might not test the connection from 1 to 4, but it will test some remote connection, like 1 to 3, or 2 to 4. Expect wrong answers to do illegal negations and reversals.

label: Conclusion
body: This is clearly not true. (i.e. most companies would not be wasting their money if they purchased videoconferencing equipment)

label: Evidence
body: In a recent survey of businesses that have purchased videoconferencing equipment, most respondents stated that the equipment was well worth the cost.

label: Evaluate
body: Given that most of the people who bought videoconferencing equipment said it was worth the cost, the author is concluding that most companies would find it worth their money. So the author is assuming that the businesses that have bought videoconferencing equipment are representative of most companies. If we were trying to accept the evidence but fight the conclusion, we might say stuff like this: - the people who bought videoconferencing equipment did so a long time ago, before there was stuff like Zoom / Google Meet / etc. It was "well worth the cost" to them, because they didn't have a great, free alternative when they bought it. However, nowadays, it wouldn't be worth it to most companies, because nowadays there are better cheaper options than buying your own videoconferencing equipment - maybe the people who bought the equipment are the businesses for whom it would make the most sense. For example, do most businesses need to buy a greenscreen and professional lighting, so that they can shoot really slick corporate videos? No, but some do. If you're part of the 10% of businesses that need to produce really slick corporate videos then you'll probably invest in the greenscreen and pro lighting. If someone surveys you about whether the cost was worth it, you'll say "Sure!" But that doesn't mean that it would be worth it to most companies, because most companies don't need to make slick corporate videos.

label: Goal
body: Look for an answer pointing out the Sampling flaw (we're assuming that the people who bought this equipment already are representative of most companies, when maybe they're an atypical subset of businesses for whom videoconferencing is worth the cost). Or look for an answer pointing out the Temporal comparison (maybe videoconferencing equipment was well worth the cost back when these companies bought it, but it would no longer be true that it's worth buying such equipment).

label: Conclusion (thus conclude)
body: None of the 20 trucks purchased 3 years ago were diesel powered.

label: Evidence
body: None of the 20 trucks purchased 3 years ago were sold last year. All of the company's diesel trucks were sold last year.

label: Evaluate
body: Because this argument seems to have more to do with numbers and a timeline (rather than conditional logic rules and term shifts), we'd probably anticipate a Defender type answer, rather than a Linking one. In order to figure out what sort of Objection the correct answer may defend against, let's try to make an Objection. Given that ... all the company's diesel trucks were sold last year and that ... none of the 20 that were bought 3 years ago were sold last year, How could we still argue that ... some of the 20 that were bought 3 years ago were diesel? At first we feel trapped by the logic, because if they were diesel, then they would have been sold last year, but we were told that none of these 20 were sold last year. What does this timeline look like? 3yrs ago 2yrs 1yr (last year) Now bought sold all diesel these 20 trucks sold none of the 20 The wiggle room lies in the 2yrs ago gap. It's possible that some of the 20 trucks we bought were diesel, and that those got sold 2 years ago (or any time in between when we bought them and last year). 2018: bought 20 trucks (only 1 was diesel) 2019: sold that 1 diesel 2020: sold all other diesels we owned 2021: still have those other 19 trucks from 2018

label: Goal
body: The one way to beat this argument is for the company to have bought a diesel truck 3 years ago but sold it prior to last year. That avoids the intended conflict between "last year we sold all our diesels" and "last year we didn't sell any of the trucks from 3 years ago". Since this is Necessary Assumption, we would look for an answer that rules out that objection: "the company did not buy a diesel 3 years ago that they then sold off prior to last year". If we never "solved this riddle", we would just go to the answers thinking, "Which of these, if I negate it, will give me a way to say that the company did purchase at least one diesel 3 years ago?"

label: Conclusion
body: Telepathy (sending invisible thought messages into someone else's brain) is possible between people with close psychic ties.

label: Evidence
body: I observe my close friends and relatives, and there is an amazing frequency with which a good friend or family member knows what someone else is thinking. This can't just be a coincidence!

label: Evaluate
body: Since both premises and the conclusion are all conditionals (and since we see repeating symbols like "ground is wet" / "solid foundation" / "settle evenly"), we should convert this into some algebra. If the concrete is poured Gw → ~Sf while the ground is wet, won't form a solid foundation. If not form solid foundation, ~Sf → ~Se or C settle unevenly or crack If concrete settles evenly, Se → ~Gw or C ground was dry or crack We have to make sure we're seeing "ground is wet / ground is dry" as the same symbol, just with two different truth value, and we have to see "settle evenly / settle unevenly" as well as logical opposites (two sides of the same coin). Ideally, our abstract algebra is in generic variables, not ones that match the subject matter of the stimulus argument.

label: Evidence
body:
For a play to succeed, audiences must care what happens to at least some of the characters.
In BB's plays, audiences always find it difficult to discern any of the characters' personalities.

label: Evaluate
body: The author is interpreting a Curious Fact and offering an Explanation, so let's use our trusty template: Curious Fact: How is it that so often a friend or family member knows what another friend or family member is thinking? Author's Story: They are telepathically sending each other thoughts. Our two-pronged evaluation for these arguments is always: 1. is there some OTHER WAY to explain the curious fact? 2. how plausible is the AUTHOR's WAY of explaining it? With Flaw questions, they will almost always have a #1 way of describing the problem — the author's failure to consider other possible explanations. How else can you explain why close friends or family members know what you're thinking? Do you ever correctly guess what a close friend or family member is thinking? How do you do it? That other person telepathically sends you their realtime thoughts? Of course not. We're just experts on the behavior and thinking patterns of the people we spend a lot of time with (or have spent a lot of time with). If my wife sees me heading towards the fridge at 11:30pm, she knows I'm thinking about getting some ice cream. That's not because I telepathically sent her that thought — it's because she's observed me get ice cream in the 11pm - midnight hour for the last 3000 consecutive nights of our marriage. If I hear an old Whitney Houston song and know that my brother is thinking about my Mom, it's not because he telepathically sent me his thoughts, it's because we both grew up in the same household and were heavily imprinted by our mom's love of the golden voice of Miss Whit.

label: Goal
body: Look for an answer chastising the author for being too confident about one possible causal interpretation when other causal interpretations still exist.

label: Conclusion
body: Prolonged exposure to sulfur fumes permanently damage's one's sense of smell. why should we believe that?

label: Evidence
body: In a study, they asked 100 workers from a sulfur factory and 100 workers from other occupations to identify a variety of chemically reproduced scents. On average, the factory workers only identified 10% of the scents correctly, whereas the control group had a 50% accuracy rate.

label: Evaluate
body: Since the argument is interpreting the results of a study, we can use our Curious Fact / Explanation mindset. Curious Fact ... why are the workers from the sulfur factory scoring so much worse on this smell test than the workers from other occupations? Author's Explanation ... the prolonged exposure to sulfur fumes has permanently damaged the sulfur workers' sense of smell (making them unable to detect as many smells in the smell test). We always evaluate these arguments two different ways: 1. Are there any Alternative Explanations for the Curious Fact? 2. How plausible is the Author's Explanation? As a (silly) example of #1, maybe the sulfur factory workers are bunch of tough guys/gals who don't want to admit to some fancy smell-test scientist that they know the scent of lavender, so they fudge an incorrect response to save their image. As a (legit) example of #2, have the 100 workers from the sulfur factory actually been working there long enough to have the "prolonged" exposure that the author thinks is the causal factor here?

label: Goal
body: Since this is EXCEPT we might see a variety of ways to weaken the argument, but each one will do one of two things: - give us an Alternate Explanation for why the sulfur workers are scoring lower on the smell test than the other occupational workers are. or - undermine the plausibility of the Author's Explanation that prolonged exposure to sulfur has damaged their sense of smell and made it hard for them to do well on a smell test.

label: Principle
body: Let's make sure we get all the qualifiers here on the left side. more than 1 overdue book + at least one overdue is → must be fined not-children's book + been previously fined for overdue books

label: Application Conclusion
body: Kessler must be fined

label: Application Evidence
body: Kessler has 3 overdue books.

label: Evaluate / Goal
body: There were three criteria we had to establish 1. more than 1 overdue book 2. at least one of those is non-children's 3. fined in the past for overdue Have we established any of these yet for Kessler? Just #1. He has more than 1 overdue book. Thus, our correct answer needs to establish two things: - at least one of Kessler's overdue books is non-children's - Kessler has been fined in the past for overdue books

label: Reading Goal
body: We're primarily reading for Causal, Comparative, Quantified, or Conditional wording, with an overall desire to combine 2 or more claims to derive some idea.

label: Statements
body: quantified (most) / causal (arise out of) Most malpractice suits are caused by patients' thinking that the doctor acted carelessly or negligently. quantified (many) / causal (as a result) Many docs think of medicine as science, not art. This mentality makes one less compassionate. quantified (sometimes) Busy/stressed (harried) doctors sometimes treat patients rudely or dismissively. conditional (if) Docs learned to → avoid lawsuits listen better causal (encourage) Economic incentives create reasons for doctors to treat patients rudely.

label: Evaluate
body: There are sort of too many disconnected blips here. We have a "most, many, and sometimes", from which you can't make any Trait Overlap quantity inference. We have causal claims, but do any of them chain together? Kind of. Economic incentives lead to doctors treat patients rudely (at least sometimes). Most malpractice suits start because the patient feels like the doctor is being negligent or careless. That's not quite the same as being rude, though, so I don't think we can say anything as strong as, Econ Incentives → Rude → Malpract lawsuits We're told that if doctors learned to listen better to patients, there would fewer malpractice lawsuits. Does that mean, by No Cause, No Effect causal difference-maker logic, that when doctors aren't listening well to patients, the patients do perceive the doctor is being negligent/careless, and thus malpractice lawsuits arise? It's not a crazy idea, but it's not that well supported. We know MOST malpractice suits come from perception of negligence/carelessness, and we know that if docs listened better, SOME lawsuits could be avoided, but we don't actually know that the lawsuits we would be avoiding are coming from that group of lawsuits caused by perception of negligence/carelessness.

label: Goal
body: So, this is a case where we don't push too hard to diagram; we take that overwhelming feeling of, "There are like 5 or 6 facts? Which ones should I care about and how?" and decide - let's read the paragraph one more time, thoughtfully, for conversational understanding of what's going on - we'll look back at the details as needed as we survey the answers Since the correct answer is the most provable claim there, we are on guard against language that's Too Strong/Specific, Unknown Comparisons, or Out of Scope ideas.

label: Conclusion
body: BB's plays are not genuinely successful dramas.

label: Goal
body: So, we need two conditional premises, which should chain together, the second of which should have an "or" outcome. Premise 1: A → B Premise 2: B → C or D Our conclusion should start with the opposite of one of the "or" ideas (C or D). And then it should also have an "or" outcome, combining the opposite of the trigger from the first conditional (A) and the other half of the "or" outcome (whichever one of C/D we didn't use). Conc: ~C → ~A or D

label: Conclusion
body: The recent property development bordering the national park has not adversely affected the park's wildlife.

label: Evidence
body: The amount of wildlife has increased in the decade since the new property development opened. And the park has enough resources to comfortably support its current wildlife populations.

label: Evaluate
body: I would try to figure out how to attack this argument by using a Weaken mindset: GIVEN THAT there is more wildlife now then before, and that the park has plenty of resources, HOW COULD WE ARGUE THAT the property development has adversely affected wildlife? Maybe there's more life than before, but the quality of life has gotten worse. They're sick more often? They die younger? They are born with abnormalities? The evidence is narrowly looking at amount of wildlife in terms of whether or not they've been adversely affected, but is amount of wildlife a good measurement? There might be many ways for amount to go up even though the animals are being adversely affected.

label: Goal
body: Look for an answer that rules out a way that wildlife might be affected (they're not hiding more, they're not getting sick more, they're not dying at a younger age, etc.), or for an answer that just gives more evidence that the park's wildlife is doing well.

label: Given that ...
body: Life spans have increased and overall health has improved (due to improved ability to diagnose and treat a wide variety of illnesses and injuries)

label: Why is it that ...
body: Over the past few decades there has been a steady and significant increase in the rate of serious infections?

label: Evaluate / Goal
body: We just need something that has changed that could explain why there are more serious infections nowadays. It could relate to the change we've already heard about (improved ability to treat / diagnose diseases, or life span increasing, or health improving), or it could come from something we haven't heard about that also changed over the past few decades. Stuff we know has changed that could explain the change - some of the new ways we treat or diagnose diseases lead to serious infections - as people's life spans get longer, that invites more serious infections - as people's health improves, that somehow (probably indirectly) leads to more serious infections Stuff we haven't talked about that could explain the change - Over the past few decades, air pollution has worsened, which can lead to serious infections

label: Given that ...
body: We say "you're welcome" when a friend says "thank you for doing me that favor".

label: Why is it that ...
body: We say "thank you" when a cashier says "thank you for your purchase"?

label: Evaluate / Goal
body:
We need a way to differentiate these two situations so that it makes sense why in a store we reciprocate a "thank you" with our own "thank you", whereas with friends we reciprocate a "thank you" with a "you're welcome".
While it's usually dangerous to predict answers to Paradox, this one seems fairly normal to understand from normal life.
With a friend for whom we've done a favor, they've gotten benefit but we haven't (other than the fuzzy feeling of doing something nice for a friend).
But when you make a purchase at a store, the cashier has benefited by getting your money and you have benefited by getting the product you just purchased. So maybe we say "thank you" because we appreciate the product we're receiving, or maybe the salesperson helped us find the right product or did something else to benefit us.

label: Conclusion
body: Selling movie rights is rarely good business for video game makers.

label: Evidence
body: StarQuanta sold the rights to Nostroma, the film flopped, and subsequent Nostroma game sequels (despite being better than the original) sold poorly.

label: Evaluate
body: The conclusion is a general claim about all (or most) video game makers selling movie rights. The evidence is one company's experience with one game. A single case can't establish what's "rarely good" across the industry. The argument leaps from one example to a broad rule.

label: Goal
body: Find an answer that names the move from a single case to a general conclusion — i.e., the small-sample/anecdote-to-rule flaw.

label: Conclusion
body: Selling movie rights is rarely good business.

label: Evidence
body: One company (StarQuanta) had a bad experience with one game.

label: Evaluate
body: One case can't support a general claim about how the industry usually fares.

label: Goal
body: Find the answer that names generalizing from a single instance.

label: Conclusion
body: The author argues that video game makers selling movie rights is rarely a good idea.

label: Evidence
body: The entire case is built on one company — StarQuanta — and its experience with one game, Nostroma. The film bombed, the sequels sold poorly.

label: Evaluate
body:
That's a single data point. To argue that something is "rarely good," you'd want to look at a bunch of cases and see how they generally turn out — not just point to one bad outcome.
It's like saying "Restaurant chains rarely succeed when they expand internationally" and then citing only one chain's failed expansion. Maybe that one chain blew it. Or maybe the next ten chains all succeeded. We can't tell from one case.

label: Goal
body: The right answer will say the argument is built on too small a sample — one case generalizing to a rule.

label: Conclusion
body: Lemaitre's theory (that the universe began with the explosion of a singular point of infinite gravity in space and time) must be considered inadequate.

label: Evidence (because)
body: Even though his theory predicts galaxies accelerating away from one another, which matches our observations, there is another theory (oscillating universe) that makes exactly this same prediction.

label: Conclusion
body: LRG's latest ad campaign was poorly conceived.

label: Evaluate
body:
When your theory predicts X, and we observe X, that counts as evidence for your theory (definitely not proof of your theory).
If someone else's theory also predicts X, and we observe X, then where does that leave your theory?
In the same exact spot! Both your theory and this other person's theory both have some support. At this point, we wouldn't have any reason for believing more in yours or in theirs.
Yet our author here thinks that if someone else's theory also predicts X, then that shows your theory must be inadequate. This doesn't make any sense. Their theory making the same correct prediction as our theory shows us that the two theories are currently tied, in terms of how accurate they seem.

label: Goal
body: Look for an answer complaining that "Just because another theory also makes the same prediction Lematire's theory makes doesn't mean that reflects poorly on Lemaitre's theory. His theory is currently just as likely to be correct as is the other theory."

label: Conclusion
body:
The criticism of the comedy Quirks, that it's not realistic, is misguided.
(i.e., it's dumb to criticize Quirks for not being realistic)

label: Evidence
body: The film is funny. That's the important thing for a comedy.

label: Evaluate
body: The argument is essentially saying, "Sure, it's not realistic, but we're talking about a comedy! We don't care about realism as long as it's funny, and this one was funny."

label: Goal
body:
So we're probably looking for something like,
"If a comedy manages to funny, we don't care if it's realistic",
or something like
"As long as it did the important thing for its genre, we shouldn't criticize it for being unrealistic."

label: Conclusion
body: The accusations that Party X illegally accepted international campaign contributes is ill founded.

label: Evidence
body: Party X is being accused by Party Y, who three years ago were involved in a scandal in which they violated campaign laws.

label: Evaluate
body:
Whenever we do Parallel Flaw, we know to listen extra carefully for the Top 5 famous flaws (not the argument always commits one of those, but a high percentage of the time it does): *Necessary vs. Sufficient, Part vs. Whole, Unproven vs. Proven False, Ad Hominem,* and *Correlation vs. Causation.*
This seems to be an example of Ad Hominem, in which the author disqualifies the legitimacy of a claim because of its source, rather than its content. Specifically, the author argues "Don't listen to A. After all, A has a biased interest in the matter / After all, A has conflicting past behavior".
This is an example of the latter. "Don't listen to Y when it says that X violated a campaign law. After all, three years ago, Y violated a campaign law."
According to this logic, an arsonist can't tell you who started the fire. Someone who has cheated on their taxes can't tell you whether someone else is committing tax fraud. Someone who has made a grammatical error in the past can't correct your grammar.

label: Goal
body: Look for an argument in which the author disqualifies a point of view because their past behavior includes some offense similar to the one they're alleging against someone.

label: Conclusion (this shows that)
body: Eyes are adapted only to an animal's needs rather than to some abstract sense of how a good eye would be designed.

label: Evidence
body: Despite the fact that box jellyfish have eyes with well-formed lenses capable of fine detail, their retinas are too far forward to receive a clear image, so the jellyfish get only a blurry image that reveals prominent features but no fine detail.

label: Evaluate
body:
This argument is presenting the somewhat curious fact that these jellyfish have lenses that could handle fine detail, but the positioning of their retinas only gives them a blurry image without fine detail.
The author might have been asking herself, "Why don't these jellyfish have the fine detail vision that their lenses make possible?"
And her answer is, "I guess eyes are adapted only to what an animal needs, rather than to some abstract sense of how a good eye would be designed".
There are multiple New Concepts in the Conclusion, so we should take a sec and think about how they're intended to match up with the conversation.
"adapted only to its needs" is supposed to match up with the jellyfish's actual vision. So the author must be assuming that "the jellyfish only needs a blurry image that reveals prominent features. It doesn't need fine detail."
"an abstract sense of how a good eye would be designed" is supposed to match up with the best case scenario for what this jellyfish's vision could be. So the author must be assuming that "a good eye would be designed in a way that produces sharp images with fine detail".

label: Goal
body:
We have some clear Missing Links being assumed, based on these New Concepts in the conclusion.
Let's look for an answer defining what the author thinks "adapted only to an animal's needs" means, or what "how a good eye would be designed" means.

label: Conclusion (this provides grounds for)
body:
Tobacco companies are wrong to claim that advertising has no significant causal impact on the tendency to smoke.
*rephrase:* Advertising **does** have a significant causal impact on the tendency to smoke.

label: Evidence
body: Research shows significant reductions in the number of people smoking, especially the number of first-time smokers, in those countries that have imposed stringent restrictions on tobacco advertising.

label: Evaluate
body:
This argument is presenting a *Correlation* in its evidence:
"in countries where X is true, Y is true"
And the argument is assuming *Causation* in its conclusion:
"X has a significant causal impact on Y"
Hence, we could use our *Explain Curious Fact* mindset.
*Curious Fact ...* How come countries that impose stringent restrictions on tobacco advertising see significant reductions in the number of people smoking?
*Author's Explanation ...* the restrictions on advertising cause the reduction in smoking, because advertising has a significant causal impact on the tendency to smoke.
These types of Explain Curious Fact arguments always have the same two pressure points:
- Alternate Explanations for the curious fact
- the plausibility of the Author's Explanation

label: Goal
body:
On Weaken questions, it's more common for them to weaken a causal conclusion by suggesting an Alternate Explanation for the curious fact.
So let's look for an answer that gives us a different way to explain why the countries that imposed restrictions on tobacco advertising saw significant reductions in smoking (maybe there's some 3rd factor that explains both the laws against tobacco advertising and the reduction in smoking).
But we'll keep our mind open to any answer that undermines the plausibility of the idea that "ads for cigarettes have a significant causal impact on the tendency to smoke".

label: Evaluate
body:
There's no new term in the Conclusion. BB's plays are described in the evidence, and there's a logical rule provided that allows us to conclude that a drama is unsuccessful.
The latter is more important, since that's our job on this problem:
```
audiences don't care what        not successful
what happens to any of      →    drama
the characters
```
Our #1 job in the answer choices, then, is to establish that when it comes to BB's plays, audiences don't care about what happens to the characters.
The one detail we currently have, that an answer choice could build onto, is that when it comes to BB's plays, audiences find it difficult or impossible to discern any of the character's personalities.

label: Goal
body:
The most likely answer would connect what we know about the audience reaction to BB's plays (can't discern personality), to the audience reaction that proves unsuccessful drama (don't care what happens to the characters).
So we'll look for
```
can't discern personality   →   don't care what
of characters                   happens
```
But we'll take any answer that would allow us to establish that when it comes to BB's plays, audiences don't care about what happens to the characters.

label: Conclusion (surely = *opinion*)
body: There would be no problem in accepting the lighting company's gift of several high-tech streetlights.

label: Evidence
body:
Sure, some people fear that the company is trying to influence the city's decision regarding park lighting contracts.
But favoritism in city contracts is prevented by our competitive bidding procedure.
The only ulterior motive I can find is the company's desire to have its products seen by mayors who will visit the city for an upcoming convention.

label: Evaluate
body:
We know that when we're doing Main Conclusion (or Role) questions, 90% of the time the conclusion will be **earlier** than the supporting ideas.
Specifically, the conclusion is usually
- the first sentence
- some pivot/rebuttal idea
The first sentence here is an attribution, telling us something someone else has said. That's typically the warm-up for a "but / yet / however, I disagree".
Here, though, the author is actually going along with the mayor and rebutting people who are against the mayor (despite SOME people's fear).
The author supports the idea that there's nothing wrong with taking this gift because the fear some people have is moot (there's no way to influence the decision regarding awarding contracts, given the competitive bidding procedure) and the only ulterior motive the author can think of wouldn't be harmful to the city in any way.

label: Goal
body: Let's find a meaning-match for the 2nd sentence.

label: Conclusion
body: The chairperson should not have released the EC's report to the public.

label: Evidence
body: The chairperson didn't consult any other members of the EC before releasing the report.

label: Evaluate
body: This is a pretty easy missing link to prephrase, because there's just one premise, so we only need to say "IF premise, THEN conclusion".

label: Goal
body:
```
didn't consult              shouldn't have
any other members    →      released EC
```
We want to be receptive to contrapositives, alert for illegal opposite/reversed answers, and ready to quickly get rid of any answers that are unrelated to our goal:

label: Conclusion
body: Putting more people in prison can't help to reduce crime.

label: Evidence
body: In a recent survey of the last 20 years, the crime rate has held steady, while the % of the population in prison has gone up a ton and spending on prisons has gone up a ton.

label: Evaluate
body:
When we're dealing with anti-causal conclusions like this one, we're trying to figure out how we can accept the evidence but argue that there IS a causal influence.
*Given That*
spending on prison went up, % of people in prison went up, but crime rate stayed same,
*How Can We Argue That*
putting more people in prison **can** help to reduce crime?
I don't have any great ideas with this one. We might say that the crime reduction effects of the past 20 years of hyper-jailing can't be seen *yet*, but they'll be seen in the next 20 years (maybe we got a bunch of criminals off the street that would have been adding to the crime rate had they still been out).
Or maybe we could do the typical Anti-Causal objection which is that it would have been even worse without our actions of putting people in jail.
i.e., maybe there were economic factors over the past 20 years that should have made the crime rate increase, so the fact that it didn't shows that putting people in jail may have reduced crime.

label: Goal
body: Look for some sort of objection that allows for the possibility that even if this evidence is true, putting more people in prison might be able to help reduce crime.

label: Inez's Argument
body: We must invest in space exploration because it produces useful technological advances.

label: Winona's Move
body: Winona doesn't deny the technological advances. She points out that if those advances are the actual goal, the goal could be achieved more directly — by funding technology development directly, without space exploration.

label: Method
body: Winona attacks Inez's justification by showing the goal Inez cites can be pursued without the program Inez wants to fund.

label: Goal
body: An answer describing this method: claiming that the goal Inez mentions could be pursued through alternative means.

label: Argument
body: Inez argues for space exploration because it produces practical tech advances. Winona responds that if tech advances are the goal, fund them directly — no need for space exploration.

label: Goal
body: An answer saying Winona shows the goal could be achieved without the program.

label: Argument
body: Inez says we should fund space exploration because it gives us useful technology. Winona replies: if the goal is technology, just fund technology directly.

label: Method
body:
Winona's move is clever — she doesn't dispute that space exploration produces tech. She just points out that the link is unnecessary. You can get to the goal (useful tech) without the route (space exploration).
Think of it like this. If someone said "we should buy a yacht because it has great air conditioning," you'd respond: "If you want air conditioning, just buy an air conditioner." You're not denying the yacht has AC — you're saying that's a roundabout way to get it.

label: Goal
body: An answer that describes Winona showing the goal can be reached without Inez's preferred program.

label: Evaluate
body:
Because this author is looking at a statistical change (sales are down) and inferring a cause (the ad campaign sucked), we can use our Curious Fact / Explanation mindset.
*Curious Fact ...* Why are sales down (especially of new products)?
*Author's Explanation ...* The new ad campaign sucked.
We can describe the flaw for any Curious Fact / Explanation type problem a few ways:
1. the author is overconfidently picking one possible explanation as though it's definitely the explanation.
2. the author is failing to consider other possible explanations for the curious fact.
3. the author is failing to consider that her explanation is implausible for some reason.
We could also just think about this argument through our Debate mindset:
*given that ...* sales are down, particularly for new products
*how could we still argue that ...* the ad campaign was well conceived?
Maybe the ad campaign's intended effect wasn't to boost sales, especially with new products. Maybe it was more about shaping / shifting brand awareness. Like maybe LRG had an ad campaign that signaled it supported gun control, and the company knew it would cost them some business (from gun lovers) but that it was worth it for the long term brand identity.
Or maybe the ad campaign was intended to boost sales and was well conceived (focus groups loved it), but the implementation of the ads bungled their effect (the company that printed the billboards and subway posters promoting the new campaign made a mistake).

label: Goal
body: Look for an answer allowing us to argue that the ad campaign wasn't ill conceived; sales were down for some other reason.

label: Background
body: The Pritzker Prize is given to individual architects (like Nobel Prizes for science).

label: Premise
body: Architects are judged by their buildings, and buildings are made by teams.

label: Premise (analogy)
body: Buildings are not like scientific discoveries — they're like movies, which compete for "best picture" awards (given to the work, not the individual).

label: Conclusion
body: The architecture prize would be better awarded to the best building, not the best architect.

label: Method
body: The argument compares architecture to two other fields (science, film), notes that buildings are like movies and unlike scientific discoveries, and uses the movie comparison to argue architecture should follow film's practice (award the work, not the individual).

label: Goal
body: An answer describing this method: reaching a conclusion about how something should be done in one field by comparing it to corresponding practices in other fields.

label: Argument
body: Compares architecture to film (similar — team-based) and science (different — individual). Concludes architecture should follow film's practice of awarding the best work, not the best individual.

label: Goal
body: An answer describing this as drawing a conclusion about one field based on comparisons with practices in other fields.

label: Argument
body: The author lines up three fields: science, film, and architecture. Each has a top prize. The author notes that architecture awards individuals (like science does), but buildings are made by teams (like movies). And in film, the prize goes to the work — best picture. So architecture should follow film's practice and award the best building, not the best architect.

label: Method
body: The whole move is comparison-based. The author looks at how prizes work in other fields and uses those comparisons to argue for what architecture should do.

label: Goal
body: An answer that describes this comparison-driven method.

label: Conclusion (thus)
body: If the most qualified candidate is elected and Suarez is not elected, then Anderson will be.

label: Evidence
body: If Suarez is not the most qualified candidate for sheriff, then Anderson is.

label: Evaluate
body:
There is conditional logic and repeating symbols within this argument, so it's a prime contender for diagramming with an algebraic recipe.
*Premise:* If X is not most Q, then Y is most Q.
*Conclusion:* If most Q is selected and it's not X, then it must be Y.
But we could also get through this one conversationally. The premise is telling us that either S or A is the most qualified candidate.
Thus, if the most qualified candidate is selected, it will have to be S or A. Thus, if the most qualified candidate is selected and it's not S, then it must be A.
We could have alternatively concluded that "if the most qualified candidate is selected and it's not A, then it must be S."

label: Goal
body: Look for a premise that gives you only two options for a certain thing. Then look for a conclusion that's saying, "If you're selecting this certain thing and you don't get option 1, then you must get option 2".

label: Conclusion
body:
(This art historian's conclusion is wrong)
15th century painters did not have greater mastery of painting than 16th century painters.

label: Evidence
body: The historian believes this because 15th century were more planimetric, but "how planimetric a painting is" has nothing to do with whether you have greater mastery.

label: Evaluate
body:
This is one of the top 5 famous flaws, but it's always so subtle when it happens. You have to distinguish between two types of rebuttal conclusions:
- their conclusion is **unwarranted**
- their conclusion is **false**
This author is allowed to conclude the first, but not allowed to conclude the second.
John thinks that Megan likes him because she kissed him on the cheek when he arrived at her apartment. But Megan kisses all her friends and acquaintances on the cheek (because she spent a semester in Europe and came home insufferable).
The valid conclusion here is, "So John's assumption that Megan likes him is unwarranted on the basis of her cheek kissing."
A going-too-far flawed conclusion here is, "So John's assumption that Megan likes him is wrong." (i.e. Megan doesn't like John)
We can't conclude she doesn't like him. Maybe she does. Where's our evidence she doesn't?
We call this famous flaw Unproven vs. Proven False (you may also have heard it called Absence of Evidence or Failure to Prove).
This author showed that the art historian's premise was irrelevant. But that doesn't mean the art historian's conclusion is wrong.

label: Goal
body: Look for an answer pointing out the Unproven vs. Proven False move, or raising the objection that there might be some other reason to consider 15th century painters' having more mastery.

label: Conclusion
body: The carved flint object (depicting a human head w/ an open mouth) was probably the head of a speaking staff.

label: Evidence
body:
Some people think it was a weapon -- the head of a warrior's mace -- but it's too small for that purpose.
Also, the open mouth symbolizes speaking.

label: Evaluate
body:
Because the author is interpreting the meaning of a found object, we can use our Curious Fact / Explanation mindset.
*Curious Fact ....* What is this carved flint object, a human head with an open mouth?
*Author's Explanation ...* It was probably the head of a speaking staff (since open mouth symbolizes speaking)

label: Goal
body:
If we're weakening this type of argument, we primarily look for
- an Alternate Explanation for the curious fact
(this carved flint object isn't the head of a speaking staff, it's ______ . )
or we look for
- something that hurts the plausibility of the Author's Explanation.
(it's unlikely that this carved flint object was the head of a speaking staff, because _____ .)

label: Conclusion
body: To improve the soil structure, farmers will have to abandon chemical fertilizers.

label: Evidence
body: As chemical fertilizers came to the region, farmers stopped growing "green-manure" crops to rejuvenate the soil. As a result, the soil structure is now poor.

label: Evaluate
body:
We're thinking, "How can we argue that they can keep chemical fertilizers but still improve soil structure?" Did they tell us that chemical fertilizers ruin the soil structure?
No, not at all. The thing that killed the soil structure was when farmers stopped growing "green manure". Did they tell us that chemical fertilizers cause farmers to stop growing "green manure"?
Kinda. That did happen in the past: the advent of chemical fertilizers *led* them to abandon "green manure".
The author must be assuming that "as long as we still have chemical fertilizers around, they aren't going to bring back green-manure crops."
If we look at this formally, the conclusion is saying
```
Don't abandon   ------------------->   poor soil
chem fertilizers                       structure
```
The evidence provided
```
not growing    ----->   poor soil
green-manure            structure
```
So what the flow of logic is missing is that first piece,
```
Don't abandon   --->   not growing
chem fertilizers       green-manure
```

label: Goal
body: Look for an answer connecting "if we don't abandon chem fert, we won't bring back green-manure", or an answer ruling out some way that we could improve soil structure while still using chemical fertilizers.

label: Statements
body:
*Most* Spanish 101 students attended every class.
*Each* student with a grade lower than B- missed at least one class.

label: Evaluate
body:
We have a conditional ("each/all/any/every" are all sufficient LEFT side triggers) and a Most statement. Is there any overlapping idea?
Yes, they're both talking about whether or not someone attended every class. Our priority is always the conditional, so let's get that diagrammed with its contrapositive so that we can see if the Most fact triggers either version.
```
Grade lower than B-      →   missed at least 1 class
~Miss at least 1 class   →   ~Grade lower than B-
```
Let's flip these negatives to positives:
*didn't miss at least 1 class* = attended all
*didn't get lower than B-* = B- or higher
So, it's really
```
Attended all   →   B- or higher
```
Most Span 101 students attend all,
so Most Span 101 got B- or higher.

label: Goal
body: Since they are likely rewarding us for synthesizing the two claims, we should expect something like "Most students who took Spanish 101 last semester got a B minus or higher".

label: Hypothesis
body: The two populations of sockeye salmon differ genetically because they have each adapted genetically to their distinct habitat.

label: Evidence
body: In 1940 a genetically uniform group of sockeyes was introduced into the lake. Now there's a group in the deep part of the lake and a group in shallow part, who don't interbreed and now differ genetically.

label: Evaluate
body:
As soon as we see the word *hypothesis* (a causal explanation for a phenomenon) in the question stem, we know we can use a Curious Fact / Explanation template.
*Curious Fact:* Why are the deep water sockeye now genetically different from the shallow sockeye?
*Author's Story:* They have each adapted genetically to their distinct habitat
We then evaluate this via two lenses:
1. is there some OTHER WAY to explain the curious fact?
2. how plausible is the AUTHOR'S WAY of explaining it?
Usually Strengthen questions deal with plausibility of the author's way. Is it plausible that each sockeye population has adapted genetically to its distinct habitat?
Can evolution actually work that quickly? Normally the genetic drift of a species takes thousands or millions of years, not the 80 years since 1940. The only time that evolution works super quickly is with a very isolated population and a very distinct selection pressure (like, all of a sudden, there's sulfur in the water and only the fish that mutate a gene that tolerates sulfur will survive and pass on their genes, so within a few generations, the sulfur-tolerant fish dominate and effectively the "genes" of that species have been changed).
To strengthens the AUTHOR'S STORY, we would want to know that the deep lake and the shallow lake have very different and very important selection pressures, in order for us to think that over the course of 80 years we would have had a mutation so strongly selected for that the populations of sockeye are now genetically different.
Is there some OTHER WAY to explain how these once genetically identical populations of sockeye are now different? Hmmm, how can you change genetic makeup, other than by mutation / natural selection? The only other way that genes get affected is through mating. When two animals have sex, their offspring is a genetic blend of each of the component animals. So maybe the deep lake sockeye and shallow lake sockeye now differ from each other because at least one of them is mating with some other animals, thereby changing the gene pool.

label: Goal
body:
We either need something that strengthens the idea that the two different parts of the lake have such different survival needs that it's plausible that evolutionary selection pressure could have changed the genetic makeup of the two populations over just 80 years,
or we need something that rules out an alternate explanation for why the two populations now have different genetic makeup.

label: Statements
body:
*weak conditional (if X, Y can occur)*
```
Businesspeople willing        developing country
to invest in 'new'       →    can increase econ
modern industries              growth a lot
```
*pivot (But)*
