Being the first to invest in a 'new' industry is very risky, and there's not a lot of incentive to take this risk.
*causal / conditional (Since / if)*
```
'New' business     →   many others will invest in
succeeds                similar, diluting profits
```

label: Evaluate
body:
Usually when we see a big Pivot word in an Inference paragraph, we want to Reconcile the Pivot, meaning figure out what the net effect is of combining what came before it with what came after.
The first sentence is saying that a country could economically benefit a lot if businesspeople were willing to invest in 'new' modern industries. But, businesspeople won't want to invest in such industries because it's a big risk without the promise of big rewards (success in that industry would result in other people diluting the profits of the risk-taker).

label: Evidence
body: A financial planner would be guilty of gross malpractice if they said to a 30 year old client, "Don't worry about saving for retirement now ... you won't have to deal with that problem for 35 years".

label: Goal
body:
If we were trying to synthesize that, we might say something like, "An action that could potentially benefit developing countries will probably not be frequently taken by businesspeople".
It's hard to predict any specific wording, but the correct answer will likely connect "boosting the economy of a developing country" to "carrying unpalatable risk to investors", since the Overlapping Idea connecting those two things is "investing in modern industries".

label: Given That ...
body: Almost all the concertgoers surveyed were dissatisfied with the local concert all (most of them wished for wider seats and better acoustics).

label: And that ...
body: They know that current concert hall can't be feasibly modified to provide these features.

label: Why is it that ...
body: Most of them oppose the idea of tearing down the existing structure and replacing it with a new concert hall with wider seats and better acoustics?

label: Evaluate / Goal
body:
Given that this new concert hall would potentially solve their gripes with the existing one (and given that fixing the existing one isn't an option), why are they opposed to this plan?
Is it going to raise their taxes too much? Is it going to need to raze a nearby shopping center for the sake of an expanded parking lot?
It seems like they would only object to this new hall that gives them what they're wishing for if it was outweighed by some negative.

label: Background
body:
I need to find a book that I quoted in my paper.
```
without   →   no accurate   →   can't include
book          citation           quotation
```
The paper will be much better with the quotation than without, so ....

label: Evaluate / Goal
body:
We basically can extend that final conditional
```
without   →   no accurate   →   can't include   →   paper will be
book          citation           quotation           much worse
```
If we don't find the book we can't include the quote and thus the paper will be much worse than it would otherwise.
Let's find a safely worded answer that sounds like, "I have to find that book, or else my paper will be much worse".

label: Conclusion (Clearly then)
body: Chocolate interferes with one's ability to taste coffee.

label: Evidence
body:
Five of the ten people in the experiment were given chocolate with their coffee, and this group reported that all the coffee samples tasted pretty much the same as one another.
The other five tasted coffee only, and they were able to detect differences.

label: Evaluate
body:
Since this author is looking at a Curious Comparison from a study and then arriving at a causal conclusion (X *interferes* with Y), we can use our Explain Curious Fact mindset.
*Curious Fact ...* how come the people who had chocolate didn't taste differences, whereas the people who didn't have chocolate did taste differences?
*Author's Explanation ...* eating the chocolate interfered with people's taste buds so that all the different coffee samples they tasted seemed pretty much the same to them.

label: Goal
body:
Since we're doing a Weaken question, our answer could come in two flavors:
1. suggest an Alternate Explanation for the curious fact (what could be a different reason the coffee groups didn't find the coffee samples to taste different? Maybe they already had messed up taste buds. Maybe they were all stuffed up or had long covid, so their sense of taste was impaired. Maybe they never drink coffee, so all the coffee just tasted like awful dark liquid to them.
2. undermine the plausibility of the author's explanation (try to make it seem unrealistic to think that chocolate interferes with ability to taste coffee)

label: Conclusion (implied)
body: That family shouldn't build a large house on the iconic land depicted in that famous painting from the recently deceased local artist.

label: Intermediate Conclusion (hence)
body: Building a house there would damage the artistic and historic heritage of the community.

label: Evidence
body: The house would alter the pristine landscape.

label: Evaluate
body:
On Strengthen + Principle, we primarily pre-phrase a linking idea that feels like "If Premise, Then Conclusion".
There are two moves in this argument we could prep a linking idea for:
1. If it alters the pristine landscape, then it damages the community's artistic and historic heritage.
2. If it damages the artistic and historic heritage, then (even though it's within the families legal rights to do it), they shouldn't do it.

label: Goal
body: Look for an answer that strengthens the idea that building this large house would be tainting our local artistic heritage and thus we shouldn't do it.

label: Conclusion
body: Sunscreen lotions do not effectively block skin-cancer-causing UV radiation.

label: Evidence
body: Many studies show that people who have consistently used these lotions develop, on average, as many skin cancers as those who have rarely, if ever, used them.

label: Evaluate
body:
This is an *Anti-Causal* argument, because the conclusion is saying "X does **not** cause Y". The evidence is that people who use sunscreen tend to get as much skin cancer as do people who don't. The classic *Anti-Causal* objection is to say, "yes but those two groups aren't fair to compare".
Consider this *Anti-Causal* analogy:
Contact lenses, which are designed to improve people's vision, do not do so effectively. Studies show that people who wear contact lenses are able, on average, to see as far down the road as are people who don't wear contact lenses.
We would shout, "That's because the first group of people is wearing their contact lenses! Compare these two groups with no one wearing contact lenses and you'll see that the first group can barely focus 10 feet in front of them, while the group of people who doesn't wear contacts can see 200 feet in front of them. Since wearing contact lenses allows this first group to *also* see 200 feet in front of them, clearly these contact lenses *are* effectively improving their vision."
Similarly, maybe the people who wear sunscreen are people who really need it (they are super fair-skinned or they spend tons of time out in the open sun) whereas people who don't wear it are darker-skinned, indoor types.
If the first group weren't wearing sunscreen, then their skin cancer levels would be through the roof. The fact that wearing sunscreen brings their skin cancer numbers down to the same level as those of darker-skinned, indoor types makes it seem like the sunscreen is effectively blocking some cancer-causing radiation.

label: Facts
body: (1) Stress is a common cause of high blood pressure. (2) Calming the mind reduces stress, and for some people this lowers their blood pressure. (3) Most people can calm their minds by exercising.

label: Goal
body: We need to defend the idea that sunscreen DOES help block our cancerous UV radiation, so we need to "make an excuse" for the evidence. We need a way to explain why sunscreen users have similar skin cancer rates to non-sunscreen people, such that we can still argue that the sunscreen IS helping the sunscreen users to block out cancerous UV rays.

label: Conclusion (should = *opinion*)
body: Patients with immune system disorders should take this new drug (that enhances growth of new bone cells) in addition to the drug that helps to preserve existing bone.

label: Evidence (since)
body:
Patients with immune system disorders usually get treated with drugs that increase the risk of osteoporosis, a bone-loss disease.
They take a drug that helps to preserve existing bone, and this new drug enhances the growth of new bone cells.

label: Evaluate
body:
How could we potentially argue that these patients should not take this new drug that enhances the growth of new bone cells?
We'd probably have to either argue that it won't help them or that it will harm them.
Maybe enhancing new bone cells doesn't really do anything to lower the risk of developing osteoporosis (or lessen the severity of the disease once it's present).
Or, maybe this new drug has side effects that outweigh the positives. In particular, maybe it has side effects that are bad for people with immune system disorders, or maybe this new drug would have a harmful interaction with one of the existing drugs they're taking.

label: Goal
body:
Look for an answer posing a question that could be answered in a way that would weaken the argument.
In other words, "which of these questions could be answered in a way that would help us argue that these patients with immune system disorders should not take this new drug in addition to the bone-preserving drug they currently take?"

label: Conclusion
body: The new concert hall cannot fulfill the purpose of a civic building.

label: Evidence (because)
body:
The new concert hall is far from the center of the city.
A successful civic building is the art museum, which is in a densely populated area and thus encourages social cohesion and makes the city more alive.

label: Evaluate
body:
The author seems to be assuming that "the purpose of a civic building is to encourage social cohesion and make the city more alive".
He also seems to assume that if something is far from the center of the city it will not do those things.

label: Goal
body: Let's look for an answer attaching the New Concept in the Conclusion, "the purpose of a civic building" to language from the evidence, like being close to the city, encouraging social cohesion, and making the city more alive.

label: Findings
body:
*causal/conditional (when)*
```
Rain dissolves         fluoride enters
minerals w/       →    groundwater
fluoride in soil
```
*correlation*
```
higher fluoride    ||    higher sodium
concentrations           in soil
in soil
```

label: Evaluate
body:
There are only two claims -- how can we synthesize them? Is there any Overlapping Ingredient?
They both talk about rainfall, fluoride-bearing minerals, and fluoride in the groundwater.
We know that rain + FL minerals = fluoride in the groundwater, but this final sentence seems to be telling us that how much fluoride makes it to the groundwater is heavily contingent on sodium.
For a given amount of rain onto a given amount of fluoride-bearing minerals, there ends up being more fluoride in the groundwater where there's more sodium.
Is the sodium somehow helping the rain dissolve the fluoride so that it gets in the groundwater. Or is the sodium a byproduct of the fluoride running into the groundwater (or neither)?

label: Goal
body: It seems hard to predict a definitive inference from that correlation (because correlations, famously, can be explained different ways). Let's just look for the most supportable answer.

label: Conclusion (rebuttal)
body:
F's assertion that HB belonged to the Brethren of the Free Spirit is unlikely to be correct.
*Rephrase:* HB probably didn't belong to the Brethren of the Free Spirit.

label: Evidence
body: There's evidence that HB was a member of a mainstream church and no evidence he was a member of the Brethren.

label: Evaluate
body:
Whenever we do Main Conclusion or Role, we remind ourselves that the Conclusion is typically
- the first sentence
and/or
- some rebuttal or pivot idea
Here the first sentence was a rebuttal. The author then makes a concession towards her opponent in the 2nd sentence before introducing her supporting idea in the 3rd sentence.

label: Goal
body:
We're being asked about the role of the final sentence, which is the author's evidence.
It has two claims, connected by "and" (claims connected by "and" are almost always supporting ideas).
So we're being asked about one of the two premises.

label: Conclusion (proving that)
body: The Super Xl is better than your old vacuum cleaner.

label: Evidence
body: I ran your old vacuum once over this dirty carpet. Then I ran the Super XL over the same area. It was able to pick up all the dirt that the old vacuum left behind.

label: Evaluate
body:
This doesn't seem like a fair way to compare two vacuums.
What if you wanted to see which pink paint will better hide that brown wall:
You paint a coat of Paint 1. You can still see some brown spots poking through; the color seems thin in other places.
You paint a coast of Paint 2. Now the brown spots are covered up. The color seems nice and saturated everywhere.
Do you conclude that Paint 2 did the better job of covering up the wall? No, because it wasn't a fair fight. A better head-to-head experiment would be dividing up the original brown wall into two halves, and painting a coat of Paint 1 on one half and a coat of Paint 2 on the other half. That would allow us to judge how well each paint covers up a dark brown wall.
Similarly, to measure the suckitude of these vacuums, we should let the old vacuum do this half of the room, let the Super XL do that half of the room (assuming both halves are equally dirty), and compare which carpet has the most residual dirt.

label: Goal
body: Look for an answer complaining about the unfair head-to-head comparison. Judging one vacuum's 2nd lap around a dirty carpet against another vacuum's 1st lap around that carpet isn't an apples to apples comparison we can really evaluate.

label: Conclusion (irresponsible = *Opinion*)
body:
That is an irresponsible approach.
*rephrase:* It's irresponsible to put off making changes to our vendor contracts in order to shore up our supply chain, because the problem will not materialize for quite a while.

label: Evaluate
body:
Whenever we do Main Conclusion or Role, we prime our brains before reading the paragraph with the reminder that the Conclusion (on these questions) will almost always be
- First Sentence, or
- Rebuttal
This first sentence sounds a bit like it could be the Main Conclusion. It's a claim about the future so it's inherently opinionated. If we read on and feel like the author is giving us supporting reasons why failing to make changes to our vendor contracts could imperil our supply chain, then we'd know the first sentence was the conclusion.
Instead, the second sentence gives us an attribution, "Some will argue". This feels like a setup for a Rebuttal, and then sure enough the following claim starts with a classic rebuttal Pivot word (but, yet, however). The final two sentences are supporting that rebuttal with an analogy.

label: Goal
body:
We want an answer that matches "That is an irresponsible approach". Since our conclusion has a pronoun, "That", we need to import the referential text:
"Kicking the can down the road / not worrying about changing vendor contracts now because we won't see problems in our supply chain until far into the future" is an irresponsible approach.
An equivalent way of saying "X is an irresponsible approach" could be to say "we shouldn't do X".

label: Statements
body:
*Math-y Comparison*
Last year > any previous year

label: # of books sold
body: Last year > any previous year

label: # of cookbooks sold
body:
Last year, 1st time ever, cookbooks sold
intended for beginners < 50%
intended for non-beginners > 50%
Last year > any previous years

label: # of cookbooks bought by pros
body:
*Distinction (one of the few)*
*Problem-Free Cooking* is a cookbook, written for beginners, and, unlike almost all other books, it's available on every continent.

label: Evaluate
body:
Is there any way to combine any of these ideas?
Typically, if we're handed a few general statements/rules and then given a specific fact (like Problem-Free Cooking), we want to see if any of those rules/statements apply to that specific fact.
We know that it's a cookbook, but there's no rule "if cookbook, then ___ ", so the fact that it's a cookbook doesn't tell us anything.
We know it's written for beginners. Does that mean purchased by beginners? Not necessarily. Professional cooks might buy cookbooks intended for beginners for their friends as gifts. We can't clearly connect this with our factoid that for the first time ever, most of the cookbooks purchased were bought by professional cooks.
And we know it's available on every continent, but that doesn't combine with any of the earlier facts.
The other place we'd look for combining ideas is with the multiple Mathematical Comparisons. Is there something we can mathematically derive by combining those?

label: Goal
body: Look for the most provable answer we can find, probably having to do with combining 2 or more of those first four math-y ideas.

label: Conclusion
body: Any methane in the Martian atmosphere must have been released relatively recently.

label: Evidence
body: Methane falls apart when it's hit by UV radiation from sunlight.

label: Evaluate
body:
This argument makes sense, as long as UV radiation is constantly hitting the methane on Mars. Since UV breaks it apart into its constituent atoms, a methane compound's lifespan is only as long as it takes to get hit by UV radiation.
Missing Link:
*if Martian atmosphere → continually hit by UV*
The whole argument is thinking
**1.** when you're in Martian atmosphere, you're continually hit by UV.
**2.** methane dies whenever its hit by UV.
**infer:** methane in the Martian atmosphere is constantly dying.
**conc:** any methane you find is near the beginning of its very short life span (cuz all this methane's gonna get zapped by UV in no time).
If a linking answer doesn't occur to us, we should be looking for an Objection.
GIVEN THAT methane falls apart whenever it's hit by the Sun's UV,
HOW COULD WE ARGUE it's possible to find methane in Mars' atmosphere that was released a really long time ago?
We would just say, that old-ass Martian methane never got hit by the Sun's UV. Maybe this methane was released into some ridged crater that provided permanent shade from the sunlight.
Or maybe there's a "Dark Side of the Mars" that never faces the Sun.

label: Goal
body: Since our main way to object is to say, "What if there's some methane that just hasn't been hit by UV yet?", we can say the author must assume "There is not methane that has been on Mars for a long time but has never been hit by UV."

label: Statements
body:
*causal (X contributes to Y)*
Pollution from gas burned by cars contributes to big environmental problems.
*pivots (But, however)*
The cost of these problems isn't reflected in prices of gas.
*causal (X, hence Y / as a result)*
The fact that problems aren't reflected in prices leads to lots of consumers not taking that into account when deciding how much to drive.
Heavier taxes on gas would reflect the cost and lead to consumers polluting less.

label: Evaluate
body:
In normal life, if someone were to ask us, "What should we conclude from all this?", we would probably just say "We should raise taxes on gas! That way it'll reflect the true cost of burning fossil fuels to the environment, and so people will drive less and pollute less."
But in LSAT life, who knows what angle they might take. It could be something boring but technically true like, "at least one form of tax increase would reduce pollution".

label: Goal
body: Let's just look for the most provable answer, something safely-worded that can be supported by combining two or more claims.

label: Given that ...
body: Hine's emerald dragonflies (HED) are endangered, live in wetlands, and have larvae that can survive only in the water, where they might be preyed upon by red devil crayfish (among others).

label: Why is it that ...
body: HED populations are more likely to remain healthy in areas where red devil crayfish are present than in areas w/o red devil crayfish.

label: Evaluate / Goal
body:
Given that red devil crayfish are one of the species that eat dragonflies' babies, why is it a **good** thing for dragonfly populations when red devil crayfish are present?
Maybe the red devil crayfish, despite eating the dragonflies' babies, do other stuff that outweighs that downside (maybe they kill off other dragonfly predators or maybe they help dragonflies obtain food somehow).
Or, maybe red devil crayfish in general are bad for dragonflies, but they are a "marker" of a good habitat for dragonflies for some other reason (like the dragonfly needs bamboo to mate, and red devil crayfish are only found where bamboo is found).

label: Executive
body: Pay is based on seniority, and many writers have been here longer than many programmers — so the gap is justified.

label: Evaluate
body: This is a chain: exercise → calmer mind → less stress → lower blood pressure for some. The logical move is "for at least some people." The strongest direct chain is exercise → calmer mind → reduced stress, since "most people can calm their minds by exercising" applies broadly enough that at least some of those people are covered. The blood-pressure end of the chain only works for "some people," which is a weaker bridge.

label: Goal
body: Find an answer that is directly supported by the chain of facts — most likely a "for at least some" claim that links exercise to one of the closer steps in the chain (calming, stress reduction).

label: Facts
body: Stress causes high blood pressure; calming reduces stress (and for some, blood pressure); most people calm their minds by exercising.

label: Evaluate
body: The chain supports: at least some people have their stress reduced by exercise.

label: Goal
body: Find a "for at least some" claim that follows from the chain.

label: Facts
body:
Three pieces of information:
1. Stress causes high blood pressure (often).
2. Calming the mind reduces stress; for some people this lowers their blood pressure.
3. Most people calm their minds by exercising.

label: Evaluate
body:
Most Supported questions reward small, careful inferences. The safest move chains the closest links. Most people can calm their minds by exercising. Calming reduces stress. So at least some people — those covered by "most" — get their stress reduced by exercising.
Watch out for answers that go too far: claiming exercise directly lowers blood pressure (skips the chain), or claiming most people can lower their blood pressure this way (the stimulus only says "some" can).

label: Goal
body: Pick the answer that's a small, conservative inference: at least some people get stress reduction from exercise.

label: Conclusion (probably)
body: The soot itself probably doesn't cause this ailment.

label: Evidence (since)
body: Even though there's a positive correlation between amount of soot and frequency of the ailment, in cities where there are large amounts of soot, there are also usually high concentrations of many other air pollutants.

label: Evaluate
body:
This argument is an Anti-Causal spin on the normal Explain the Curious Fact template.
*Curious Fact ...* why is there a correlation between atmospheric soot and ailment X?
*Potential Explanation ...* the soot causes ailment X.
*Author's Anti-Causal Alternate Explanation ...* No, the soot probably isn't causing ailment X. The ailment is probably being caused by other air pollutants, because the cities that have lots of atmospheric soot also have these other air pollutants.

label: Goal
body:
If we're trying to weaken this argument, we'd like to either find an answre that helps us argue:
1. It is the soot that's causing the ailment
2. It's not these other pollutants that are causing the ailment
(or both)

label: Conclusion (probably)
body: It will probably rain in the valley within the next week.

label: Evidence (since)
body:
There are usually a few inches of rain each summer.
Only one week of summer is left, and so far there's been no rain.

label: Evaluate
body:
There isn't any conditional logic here, but there are some repeating ideas:
"rain / summer / last week" are mentioned a couple times, so we could potentially assign them symbols.
The author is predicting rain in the coming week because we normally have rain each summer, we haven't so far, and there's only one week of summer left. This is a *Math-y* flaw where an author interprets the concept of average or probability too literally.
The conclusion has a "probably" strength, so we can start reading each answer by verifying it has the same type of conclusion.

label: Goal
body:
Let's look for something like
- We usually see X happen by marker Y.
- X hasn't happened yet and we're almost at marker Y.
- Thus, X will probably happen in the remaining time before we get to marker Y.
Or more conversationally, "since a thing we'd usually see by now hasn't happened, it will probably happen soon".

label: Conclusion
body: We must enable our children to believe that better futures are possible.

label: Evidence
body: Young people are pessimistic about reducing pollution, poverty, and war. This pessimism is harmful because people lose motivation to work for goals they think are unrealizable. We must prevent this loss of motivation.

label: Evaluate
body: The argument moves from "we must prevent the loss of motivation" to "we must enable children to believe better futures are possible." That step only works if enabling that belief actually does prevent the loss of motivation. Negation: if enabling the belief does not prevent the motivation loss, the recommendation doesn't serve the goal — and the conclusion fails.

label: Goal
body: Find the assumption linking "enable belief in better futures" to "preventing loss of motivation." Most directly: enabling that belief actually does prevent the loss of motivation that pessimism causes.

label: Conclusion
body: We must enable children to believe better futures are possible.

label: Evidence
body: Pessimism causes loss of motivation; we must prevent that loss.

label: Evaluate
body: The argument leaps from "prevent loss of motivation" to a specific recommendation; that link requires the recommendation to actually prevent the loss.

label: Goal
body: Find the assumption that enabling belief in better futures will prevent the motivation loss caused by pessimism.

label: Conclusion
body: The author concludes: we must enable our kids to believe better futures are possible.

label: Evidence
body: The reasoning chain: young people are pessimistic → pessimism makes people lose motivation → we must prevent that loss → so we should make kids believe better futures are possible.

label: Evaluate
body: The last step is the gap. The author wants to prevent loss of motivation, and proposes a specific solution: enable belief in better futures. But for that solution to actually serve the goal, enabling the belief has to actually prevent the motivation loss. If it doesn't — say, if loss of motivation comes from other sources, or this belief doesn't restore it — then the recommended action doesn't solve the problem.

label: Goal
body: The assumption is the bridge from the proposed action to the goal it's supposed to serve. Negation test: if enabling the belief does NOT help prevent motivation loss, the conclusion doesn't follow.

label: Conclusion
body: Glutamate leaking from damaged or oxygen-starved nerve cells is a cause of long-term brain damage resulting from strokes.

label: Evidence
body:
If glutamate leaks from damaged or oxygen-starved nerve cells, glutamate can kill surrounding nerve cells.
In a study of stroke patients, there was a correlation between those with long-term brain damage and those with highest levels of glutamate in their blood.

label: Evaluate
body:
Since the evidence involves a study with a correlation (people who were X had the highest levels of Y) and the conclusion involves causality (Y is a cause of X), we can use our Curious Fact / Explanation template.
*Curious Fact*
Why did the stroke patients with the long term damage to their brain's nerve cells have the highest levels of glutamate in their blood?
*Author's Explanation*
Glutamate leaked from damaged or oxygen-starved nerve cells and killed surrounding nerve cells.
We now start asking questions like
- can we think of some Alternate Explanation for why the patients with brain damage had high levels of glutamate in their blood?
- how plausible is the Author's Explanation?
With correlations, we usually consider Alternate Explanations like reverse causality or third factor.
Is it possible the brain damage came first, and the high glutamate level came second? Seems hard to argue in that fashion, but maybe something else caused the deteriorating nerve cells, and once the damage had been done, the glutamate leaked out into the brain.
Could there be some third factor that is separately causing both? Sure, maybe, there's some underlying genetic trait that makes these patients more likely to suffer from brain damage and high glutamate levels.
In terms of the plausibility of the author's explanation, it would help the author's story if we established that these patients with brain damage could have had damaged or oxygen-starved nerve cells. It would also help to know that the high glutamate level came before the brain damage.
The most common way to strengthen causality is No Cause, No Effect, so we might see an answer that says "Stroke patients with the least amount of glutamate did not have continuing deterioration."

label: Goal
body: Find an answer that rules out a different explanation for the correlation between "continuing deterioration and high glutamate" or that adds some plausibility to the author's explanation.

label: Conclusion (So)
body: If the next song Amanda writes is not a blues song, it probably will not involve more than three chords.

label: Evidence
body: The only songs Amanda has ever written are blues songs and punk rock songs. Most punk rock songs involve no more than three chords.

label: Evaluate
body:
This argument combines several different reasoning patterns.
At the heart of this argument is a "**Past = Present**" type assumption. In the past, Amanda has only written B or P (blues or punk). And so the author is assuming that in the future, Amanda will only write B or P.
The argument also has the structure of a "**ruling out competing alternatives**". It's basically arguing, "Every song is B or P. So if the next song is not B, it will be P."
The argument is also using a "**most = probably**" type move. The author is thinking, "<u>Most</u> P songs involve no more than three chords. Thus, if this next song is P, then it will <u>probably</u> involve no more than three chords."
Since there lots of repeating concepts and there are also conditionals / quantifiers, it probably makes sense to try diagramming this argument.

label: Goal
body:
Let's look for something with this structure.
Premise 1: The only X's in the past have been A or B.
Premise 2: Most B's have trait Z.
Conclusion: If the next X is not A, it will probably have trait Z.
We'd expect the conclusion to be a conditional, with a probable outcome, so that might be an easy way to get rid of some answers.

label: Background
body: Advertising tends to have more influence on customers when it comes to brands of yogurt than brands of milk.

label: Surprising Claim
body: LargeCo supermarket chain started advertising its store-brand of products, and sales of its milk increased more than sales of its yogurt.

label: Evaluate / Goal
body:
GIVEN THAT advertisements are supposed to have more effect on yougurt-buying than on milk-buying,
WHY IS IT THAT since these ads started, sales of LargeCo milk has gone up more than sales of LargeCo yogurt?

label: Principle
body:
```
don't believe person          should never be
you're speaking to      →     insincere (should
prefers kindness               always be sincere)
to honesty
```

label: Problem
body:
```
S congratulates       →   she'll be insincere
S not congratulate    →   hurt D's feelings
```

label: Evaluate
body:
Since the question stem wants us to justify a conclusion using the principle, we'd have to be justifying the conclusion that "Shayna shouldn't be insincere". You can only prove/conclude what's on the right side of the Principle, so we can only use this principle to justify a conclusion that sounds like, "Thus, Shayna shouldn't be insincere" / "Shayna should be sincere" / "Shayna shouldn't congratulate Daniel" (since congratulating would be insincere)
"Except possibly" works like Unless / Without / Until. It's an "if-not" trigger.
When we say "Todd ... Melanie will never go out with you, except possibly if you invite her to a Cardi B concert", we're definitely not guaranteeing Todd that Melanie would agree to a date even if it were a Cardi B show. We're saying he has a chance (possibly) in that scenario, whereas he has no chance in any other scenario. This is the only possible exceptional case. Thus the way to get certainty with "except possibly / unless / without / until" is to say, "If we're not in that exceptional case, then you definitely won't get a date".

label: Goal
body:
Since we want to apply this principle to this problem, we want to
1. establish that Shayna doesn't believe that Daniel prefers kindness to honesty
and then
2. conclude that Shayna shouldn't be insincere (i.e. that she shouldn't congratulate him on his award)

label: Conclusion (Clearly)
body: A democracy cannot thrive without effective news media.

label: Evidence (after all)
body:
A democracy cannot thrive without an electorate that is knowledgeable about important political issues.
An electorate can be knowledgeable only if it has access to unbiased information about the government.

label: Evidence
body:
Thermophotovoltaic generators are devices that convert heat into electricity.
The process of manufacturing steel produces huge amounts of heat that currently go to waste.

label: Evaluate
body:
On Sufficient Assumption it's always a great idea to ask ourselves whether there's a New Concept in the Conclusion (because it basically **must** be in the correct answer).
This conclusion talks about "effective news media", but none of the evidence says anything about effective news media, so *effective news media* must be in the correct answer.
That alone actually gets rid of 3 of the 5 answers.
Since we see conditional logic and repeating symbols here, this argument is a good contender for diagramming. The two premises chain together, via the overlapping ingredient of "an electorate being knowledgeable".
The conclusion is trying to prove that:
```
no effective    ------------------------->   dem can't
news media                                    thrive
```
The evidence has provided us with this subset of that logic path:
```
no acc to   -->   elect not   -->   dem can't
unbiased          knowledg          thrive
```
So the correct answer has to give us that missing piece:
```
no effective   -->   no acc to
news media            unbiased
```
If we don't like diagramming, then we can use our principle of Mentioned Twice? That'll Suffice.
The concepts of "democracy cannot thrive" and "knowledgeable electorate" each appear twice, so they are not missing links. That tells us that the missing link is between "effective news media" and "access to unbiased information".

label: Goal
body: Let's look for, "If no effective news media, then the electorate doesn't have access to unbiased information", or its contrapositive, "access to unbiased information requires an effective news media".

label: Conclusion
body: Roberta is almost certainly irritable.

label: Evidence (since)
body:
Roberta has been yawning all day and has lost her keys.
She is irritable only when she is tired, and loses things only when she is tired.

label: Evaluate
body:
Whenever we're doing Flaw and see any conditional logic in the premises, we immediately suspect that we're headed into the #1 most famous flaw, **Necessary vs. Sufficient**.
Here, the conditional logic is signified by "only when", which is the same as "only if", a *necessary* indicator (right side of the arrow). So here are the two rules:
```
Irritable       →   Tired
Loses Things    →   Tired
```
Since Roberta has lost her keys, we know from the 2nd rule that she is definitely tired. The author mentions that she's been yawning all day, but we don't actually need that idea at all as a "premise" (we don't have to worry whether all-day yawning = tired, because the 2nd rule tells us that if she lost her keys, then she's tired).
The author is then moving from proving that Roberta is tired to concluding that she must be irritable. That, however, is an illegal reversal. The author is arguing like this:
if she's Tired, then she must be Irritable
But the conditional goes the other way:
Irritable → Tired

label: Goal
body: Look for an answer complaining about the illegal reversal (aka 'confusing necessary with sufficient'). The author does soften the conclusion by saying almost-certainly, so the answer may reflect that. But the argument is failing to consider that Roberta might frequently be tired but not irritable.

label: Evidence (Since)
body:
Too much insecticide has harmed the wildlife that live near the crops.
But ... we have new GMO crops that you don't need to spray with insecticide.

label: Conclusion
body: Using GMO crops more would be good for wildlife near crops.

label: Evaluate
body:
This makes sense, superficially. If insecticides were harming wildlife, then GMO crops with no insecticides should be better, right?
This is an **Incomplete Comparison**.
When an author is pitching a Plan, she's implicitly making a comparison between the Current World and the hypothetical Plan World.
When we go from normal crops to GMO crops, **one difference** is that with the GMO crops won't need insecticide.
But there could potentially be other differences. How could the Plan fail to achieve its Goal?
*We grow more GMO crops (w/o insecticide),*
*but it doesn't help the local wildlife to recover.*
What if people don't want to buy the GMO crops? Would the farms go out of business? Maybe, but the conclusion is only making a claim about the effects of GMO crops on helping wildlife to recover.
If farms went out of business would that negatively impact local wildlife? Would something else about GMO negatively impact local wildlife?

label: Goal
body: Find an answer that, when negated, sounds like a way to argue that this plan, if enacted (doing more GMO crops), wouldn't help wildlife to recover (maybe would even be harmful to them).

label: Curious Fact
body: How did the Parthenon's builders manage to carve columns that all bulged outward in the center in the exactly the same way?

label: Hypothesis
body: They relied on a scale drawing like the one at Didyma (it's a profile view of a column surrounded by a grid, which makes it possible to determine the correct width at every height of the column).

label: Evaluate
body:
Whenever the question stem uses the noun hypothesis (rather than argument / reasoning), we know going into the paragraph that the author will be trying to Explain a Curious Fact (i.e. trying to solve a causal mystery).
We find the curious fact and ask it as a question, although in this case it actually was presented as a question!
We find the author's explanation / hypothesis and make sure we understand the causal story they're telling.
Then we think along two different dimensions:
1. Could there be some Alternate Explanation for the Curious Fact?
2. How plausible is the Author's Explanation?
How else could they have carved columns that bulged outward in precisely the same way?
Hmm. Maybe someone stood back 100 yds to get a good view of all the columns and yelled through a bullhorn, "Take a little more off column 3!" Maybe they created a giant mold for the columns, so every column came out the same because it was mixed and hardened in the same mold.
Honestly, for a question as technical as "how did they get columns to bulge identically in the center", LSAT doesn't expect us to have any common sense imagination for Alternate Explanations. If they haven't given us any crumbs of a hint or if it's not the sort of situation that has a common sense hypothesis attached to it, then they probably aren't testing Alternate Explanations.
How plausible is the notion that they used a scale drawing like the one at Didyma?
Are the two construction projects similar enough that the same tactic could have worked for both, or are there important differences where you could use a scale drawing for Didyma but not for the Parthenon?
Did the stonemasons who worked on the Parthenon have the same knowledge and training that those who worked on Didyma did? Were they familiar with this scale drawing technique?

label: Paradox
body: The puzzle is this. Treated chicks have less Salmonella (good!) but a week later have higher concentrations of all kinds of bacteria. How can a treatment that reduces a specific bad bacterium also lead to overall higher bacterial loads?

label: Goal
body:
Like most Explain the Curious Fact arguments, we don't have a specific prediction.
Since this is Strengthen, we will justify our answer by saying it either
1. rules out an Alternate Explanation (for how they got the columns to bulge similarly)
or
2. adds plausibility to the Author's Explanation (that they used a scale drawing like the one at Didyma)
Strengthen questions are more likely to add plausibility than to rule out an alternate explanation, so on a first pass, we primarily look for answers that seem to do #2.

label: Conclusion
body: The best medical approach would be to take lower doses of these medicines with prescribed amounts of grapefruit juice.

label: Evidence
body: It's always desirable to take the lowest effective dose of any medicine, and there is a chemical in grapefruit juice that affects how certain medicines are absorbed, such that it turns a normal dose into a "higher" dose.

label: Evaluate
body:
Since grapefruit has a chemical that essentially augments the effects of certain medications, the author is thinking, "Let's use this to our advantage! If we want people to experience a medium dose but we want them to consume as little medication as possible, then we can give them a low dose + grapefruit juice and it will act like we gave them a medium does of the medicine."
Whenever we're arguing with Plans / Recommendations, we try to think of how this Plan could fail to achieve its goal:
- maybe it's not feasible
- maybe people aren't incentivized to cooperate
- maybe it will backfire in some way

label: Goal
body:
Let's look for an answer that makes it sound like it's not feasible to do lower dose + grapefruit juice (i.e. some people have other conditions that won't let them take grapefruit juice / grapefruit juice isn't available year round), that makes it sound like the incentives are off (maybe people hate the taste of grapefruit juice so they would take their pill but then toss the grapefruit juice down the sink), or that makes it sound like the plan could backfire (people start experimenting with grapefruit juice to see if it can augment other medicines or give them amped-up symptom relief, and they accidentally harm themselves).
We can preface our reading of each answer choice with, "This plan to do low dose + grapefruit juice probably won't work, because ...."

label: Conclusion
body: Buy the FreezAll.

label: Evidence
body: Even though the Sno-Queen is the most powerful unit for the price, the FreezAll is powerful enough for your needs.

label: Evaluate
body:
Well we know what principle this salesperson wasn't using: "Live your best life, Landlord. You know you want that Sno-Queen".
Given that these two models are the same price, it's a little weird to say "buy the model that has less performance capacity", but that's what the salesperson did.
He must be thinking something like "it's pointless to buy a machine that's more powerful than what you need".

label: Goal
body: We want something like, "if two things are the same price but one has functionality you don't need, don't buy that one".

label: Conclusion (Thus)
body: To focus our attention on the flaws of our leaders is to indulge in a pointless distraction.

label: Evidence
body: These flawed leaders were chosen democratically. The real question that needs answering is how our nation's institutions and procedures enable such people to attain positions of power.

label: Evaluate
body:
Our author thinks that focusing on the flaws of our leaders is a pointless distraction, because we should be trying to answer the question of how our institutions allow such flawed people to attain positions of power.
In terms of a Linking assumption, we'd be looking for, "If it isn't directly addressing the real question that needs answering, then it's indulging in a pointless distraction".
What about objections? How could we argue that "even though the real question we need to answer is how our institutions and procedures allow flawed people to attain positions of power, it could still be true that focusing our political discussions largely on the flaws of our nation's leaders is not a pointless distraction"?
We could try to argue that by focusing our attention on the flaws of our leaders we are somehow helping ourselves answer the question about how our institutions and procedures allow such flawed people to attain positions of power.

label: Goal
body: Look for the aforementioned Linking idea or for a Defender answer saying, "Focusing on flaws of leaders does not help us to answer the question about how our institutions/procedures allow flawed people to attain positions of power."

label: Principle
body:
only if = necessary (put it on the right)
so we could write
```
                    Confident of its Authenticity
Should buy   →      and
                    Desirable for its intrinsic qualities
```
However, you always want to contrapose principles, if necessary, so that you have the judge-y, normative term on the right side (should, ought, right, wrong, permissible, impermissible, justified, unjustified)
```
~Confident Authenticity
or                          →   shouldn't buy
Only value as investment        antique
(not cuz it's pretty)
```

label: Application Conclusion
body: M shouldn't buy this antique vase offered for sale on the Internet.

label: Evaluate
body:
In order to trigger the outcome of "shouldn't buy" we have to establish that this vase Matilda found for sale on the Internet fits either of the criterion in the trigger of the Principe:
1. can't be confident of authenticity
or
2. only like it as an investment property, not inherently attracted to it

label: Goal
body: Look for an answer convincing us that we can't be confident of the authenticity of this vase, or one convincing us that Matilda only wants this as an investment property.

label: Statements
body:
Waverly claims: "I've presented only objective accounts. I'm not trying to praise or critique the stuff I've included."
Attempts to be objective never succeed, as evidenced by the fact that Waverly writes better about art she likes than about art she is indifferent to.

label: Evaluate
body: This set of statements is very opinion-heavy. Waverly is trying to be objective. This critic thinks she is not succeeding in being objective. Since the question stem tells us to accept the critics' statements as true, we have to take the critic's side.

label: Evidence
body:
If the number of visitors increases, the tax revenues will increase.
If several large conventions are held in the city, then the total number of visitors will increase.
And if we build the convention center, then several national professional organizations will hold conventions there.

label: Goal
body:
It's very hard to know where this is headed. The critic was essentially saying "by writing better about art she likes than about art to which she is indifferent, Waverly failed in her attempt to write about art objectively."
I guess we could synthesize that and say that "writing better about something you like is not objective writing".
Mainly, let's be wary of strong or unmentioned ideas and find the most provable answer available.

label: Conclusion (Thus)
body: The Sals did not smelt iron.

label: Evidence
body: The Sals did not have a word for iron (even though they had some for copper and bronze, which we know they did smelt).

label: Evaluate
body:
The #1 reason the author offers for why we should think the Sals did not smelt iron is that they didn't have a word for iron.
If we picture the conclusion as a logic path we're trying to build, it would look like this:
```
Sals -------------------------------------->  didn't
                                               smelt iron
```
What part of that path does the evidence provide?
```
Sals -------->  didn't have
                distinct word for iron
```
So what part of the path is missing?
```
didn't have --------------->  didn't
distinct word for iron        smelt iron
```

label: Goal
body:
The correct answer will need to take us from that launching pad "didn't have a distinct word for iron" and get us to the landing zone of "didn't smelt iron".
Any answer choice that isn't providing a rule in the form of,
if xyz, then didn't smelt iron
or its contrapositive
if smelted iron, then not xyz
is functionally useless to us.

label: Conclusion
body: Community organizations wanting to enhance support for higher education programs need to convince the public that such programs benefit society as a whole.

label: Intermediate Conclusion
body: Taking the approach of "this'll benefit society as a whole" makes the public more receptive.

label: Evidence
body: It's easier to get people to support road building (which is seen as benefiting all) than to get support for programs seen as benefiting only a small segment of society.

label: Evaluate
body:
Whenever we do Main Conclusion or Role questions, we prime our brains before reading the paragraph with the reminder that the conclusion on these questions will be earlier than the support, the vast majority of the time.
In particular, we read the argument listening for
- 1st sentence conclusion
- Attribution followed by rebuttal conclusion
When we read the first sentence here, we're actively asking ourselves, "Does this sound like the author expressing an opinion or announcing the claim she plans to defend?"
Yes! It's saying "community organizations need to do X", which in this context is the same as saying "they should do X". So it's expressing the author's opinion. Do we feel like the following ideas try to lend support to this opinion?
Yes. The 2nd sentence is already a reason why we should believe the advice offered in the first sentence: "if you follow my advice, the public will be more receptive to what you're selling".

label: Goal
body: Once we've correctly identified the conclusion, the hard work is done. Now we just need to find an answer that matches the meaning of the first sentence.

label: Premise
body: Currently, no satellite is at significant risk of colliding with other satellites or fragments.

label: Conclusion (the claim in question)
body: The risk of such collision is likely to increase dramatically in the future.

label: Premise
body: Once a collision occurs, it will produce thousands of fragments, each capable of shattering other satellites.

label: Premise (intermediate)
body: Those resulting collisions produce more fragments, and the cascade leaves space heavily cluttered with debris.

label: Anticipate
body: The "After all" indicator tells us what follows are reasons supporting the previous claim. So the claim that risk will increase dramatically is supported by the cascading-debris argument. That makes it the conclusion.

label: Goal
body: An answer identifying the claim as the conclusion of the argument.

label: Argument
body: The claim "risk will increase dramatically" is what the argument is trying to establish, supported by the cascading-debris reasoning that follows.

label: Goal
body: An answer identifying it as the main conclusion.

label: Argument
body: The claim in question — that the risk will increase dramatically — is followed by "After all," which signals supporting evidence is coming. So everything after that ("once a collision occurs, fragments shatter more satellites...") is the support, and the claim itself is the conclusion.

label: Method
body: This is a textbook conclusion-then-support structure. "After all" is one of the cleanest signals on the LSAT — what follows it supports what came before it.

label: Goal
body: An answer that identifies the claim as the main conclusion of the argument.

label: Given that ..
body: The chicks who underwent the Salmonella treatment had a lower rate of the Salmonella bacterial infection.

label: Why is it that ...
body: One week after treatment, treated chicks had higher concentrations of a variety of bacteria than the untreated chicks did?

label: Anticipate
body:
This one might not read as obviously paradoxical at first, but the tension seems to be that Salmonella is a bacteria, so presumably the treatment the young chicks got was some sort of anti-bacterial treatment.
If the treatment is successfully keeping Salmonella bacteria at bay (preventing infection), how are other types of bacteria flourishing more than usual?

label: Goal
body: We need an answer that provides a distinction about the chicks who got the Salmonella treatment. It will probably relate to the treatment itself and show how suppressing the Salmonella bacteria indirectly leads to the flourishing of other types of bacteria (maybe they're in competition with each other, so limiting one allows the other to multiply).

label: Paradox
body: Treated chicks have less Salmonella but more bacteria overall.

label: Anticipate
body: Resolution: the increased bacteria are harmless competitors that crowd out Salmonella.

label: Goal
body: An answer establishing the competitor-bacteria explanation.

label: Anticipate
body:
The classic answer: the treatment populates the chicks with helpful or harmless bacteria that compete with Salmonella for resources — so the harmless bacteria thrive (driving up the total bacterial count) while Salmonella struggles to get a foothold.
Think of it like seeding a garden with grass to crowd out weeds. The total plant cover goes up, but the weed cover goes down. Same principle here.

label: Goal
body: Find an answer that says the bacteria found in the treated chicks are harmless and outcompete Salmonella.

label: Debater's Conclusion (thus)
body: Hierarchy in lecturing is a great weakness.

label: Debater's Intermediate Conclusion
body: Lecturing involves hierarchy.

label: Debater's Evidence (since)
body: The lecturer is more expert than student in the subject; but people learn best from peer interaction.

label: Respondent's Conclusion (thus)
body: The hierarchy in lecturing is a strength.

label: Respondent's Evidence
body: All teaching and learning are hierarchical because content must proceed from simple to complex (e.g., arithmetic before calculus).

label: Evaluate
body:
When we're being tested on what's flawed with a rebuttal there are some usual suspects:
- ad hominem (denying their right to make an argument)
- unproven vs. proven false (going too far in opposite direction)
- straw man / equivocation (distorting their argument)
- irrelevant response (not seeming to listen to their argument)
The debater was saying that students would learn better from a peer than from an "expert" who stands above them with superior mastery and, in some sense, must talk down to them.
The respondent doesn't discuss this at all! They act like they're responding to the same conversation because they use the word hierarchy, but they're not addressing whether students are better served by learning from a peer rather than an expert.
Instead, the respondent talks about the sequence in which we teach topics. That's tangential to the conversation we were having. We can agree on a sequence of topics, but we still need to discuss whether it should be taught by an expert or by a peer.
The sense in which the respondent is discussing hierarchy has nothing to do with the sense in which the debater was discussing hierarchy.

label: Goal
body: The respondent failed to address what the Debater was talking about. Instead, they're equivocating (distorting the meaning of 'hierarchy') by talking about what order we sequence topics, rather than by talking about whether the teacher is domineering or at the same level as the students.

label: Debater
body: Lecturing has person-to-person hierarchy (expert vs. student), and that's bad for learning.

label: Respondent
body: All teaching has hierarchy because content goes from simple to complex, so hierarchy is good.

label: Evaluate
body: The respondent's "hierarchy" is between concepts; the debater's is between people. Different aspects.

label: Goal
body: Find the answer naming the shift in what "hierarchy" applies to.

label: The two arguments
body:
The debater says: lectures are hierarchical because the lecturer knows more than the student, and that person-to-person hierarchy makes for worse learning.
The respondent says: all teaching is hierarchical because the subject matter has to proceed from simple to complex (arithmetic before calculus), so hierarchy is a strength.

label: Evaluate
body:
Watch how "hierarchy" shifts. The debater is talking about a hierarchy between people. The respondent is talking about a hierarchy among ideas. They're both calling it "hierarchy," but they mean different things.
Even granting that subject matter has internal order (arithmetic before calculus), that doesn't address whether the lecturer-student hierarchy is good or bad for learning. The respondent's reply applies "hierarchy" to a different aspect of education than the debater was discussing.

label: Goal
body: Find the answer that says the respondent applies the key concept to a different aspect than the debater did.

label: Conclusion
body: Han purple was probably discovered by accident during glass production.

label: Evidence
body: The chemical ingredients of Han purple match those of white glass. Both are produced in processes that involve high heat and mixing in lead.

label: Evaluate
body:
Since the conclusion is proposing a causal story, we can use our Curious Fact / Explanation mindset.
Curious Fact
Where did Han purple come from?
Author's Story
It came from people who were making white glass. They accidentally created Han purple, since it has the same chemical ingredients and similar mixing process that white glass has.
We can impact these arguments two ways:
- Alternate Explanations for the Curious Fact
- The plausibility of the Author's Explanation

label: Goal
body:
Since this is Strengthen, we either want our correct answer to
rule out an Alternate Explanation for where Han purple came from
or
add plausibility to the Author's Explanation that Han purple came by accident from people who were making white glass.

label: Conclusion
body: Mild sleep deprivation isn't unhealthy, and it probably even helps, by helping us to avoid illness.

label: Evidence
body:
(correlation: greater frequency of X among people who are Y)
In a huge survey, there was a correlation between
```
sleeping 8+ hours  ||  higher rate of illness
```
Like almost all LSAT authors, they went on to overconfidently state their presumed version of the causal story that's goin' on here.
"I get it. You know why these two things are correlated?
```
sleeping 8+ hours  ||  higher rate of illness
```
It's because this is happening:
```
sleeping 8+ hours  ⇢  higher rate of illness"
```
When an author presents a Curious Fact and then concludes her presumed Explanation, we're supposed to ask two different questions:
- is there some Alternate Explanation for the Curious Fact?
- how plausible is the Author's Explanation?
With a correlation, the two Alternate Explanations that should come immediately to mind are
REVERSE CAUSALITY
```
sleeping 8+ hours  ←  higher rate of illness
```
THIRD FACTOR
```
sleeping 8+ hours          higher rate of illness
      ↑                            ↑
genetic condition?      exhausted school teachers?
```

label: Goal
body:
For an answer doing one of these things:
- calling out the illegal correlation proves causation move
- suggesting it could be reverse causation
- suggesting the correlation could be tied to some third factor

label: Conclusion
body: Building the convention center will increase the city's tax revenues.

label: Evaluate
body:
We see a lot of conditional logic and overlapping terms in the Evidence and Conclusion, so this could be a good contender for diagramming the logic in order to find the missing link.
Since our conclusion is trying to get from building the convention center to increased tax revenue, we can represent that with a big arrow.
```
Build
convention  →  tax
center          rev
```
That's the logic connection we're trying to create. The premises give us a series of three ideas that get us to that endpoint:
```
several large    number of      more
conventions   →  visitors    →  tax
held in city      increase       rev
```
And there's a conditional that almost connects "build convention center" on to this:
```
Build              several national
convention   →     professional organizations
center             conventions held in city
```

label: Goal
body:
The only thing missing here is that "several national professional organizations will hold conventions in the city" is not identical to "several large conventions are held in the city".
We need to know that these "national professional organization conventions" would be "LARGE conventions".

label: Conclusion
body: Dogs have an aversion to being treated unfairly.

label: Evidence
body: In a study, a pair of dogs were given a command. After both obeyed, only one dog was given a treat. Over time, the unrewarded dogs began to disobey the command.

label: Evaluate
body:
Since the author is interpreting the results of a study, we can use our Curious Fact / Explanation mindset.
Curious Fact ... Why did the unrewarded dogs begin to disobey the commands?
Author's Explanation ... The dogs saw that the other dog in the pair was getting a treat, thought to themselves "well that isn't fair!", and then started disobeying the commands resentfully.
We ask,
1. Is there some other way to explain the curious fact?
maybe the dogs just stopped because they weren't getting treats. They may not have thought, "This is unfair, so I'll stop listening" and instead just thought "I'm not getting any treats, so I'll stop listening".
2. How plausible is the author's explanation?
Is there any other evidence that dogs can perceive fairness? Have they tried this experiment without the other dog present? Have they tried this experiment where they withhold treats from both dogs? Those types of variations would help us figure out whether the dog is ceasing to obey commands because of no-treat or because of perceived unfairness.

label: Goal
body: We want to pick a question from the answer choices that could be answered in a way that would Weaken the argument, and it would either do so by suggesting an Alternate Explanation for why the unrewarded dogs stopped obeying, or it would do so by undermining the plausibility

label: Statements
body:
contrast / causal difference-maker:
people's satisfaction with their incomes is not seemingly caused by the absolute amount of money they make.
rather,
people's satisfaction with their incomes is seemingly caused by the relative amount of money they make to other people in their neighborhood (usually from a similar economic class)

label: Goal
body: Look for an answer that safely reinforces or explains the fact that people mainly evaluate their income in relative terms to their neighbors, not absolute terms.

label: Conclusion
body:
(Their theory is refuted)
Petroleum didn't form from deep carbon deposits dating from the formation of the earth.

label: Evidence
body: Within petroleum are biomarkers, molecules indicating the past/present existence of a living organism.

label: Evaluate
body:
Since this is rebuttal conclusion, and we're trying to Weaken, we'll basically be playing the role of the people being rebutted. We need to defend the theory that petroleum came from deep carbon deposits from back when Earth formed.
Given That (evidence)
Petroleum has biomarkers in it (marks left by living organisms),
How Can We Argue (anti-conclusion)
Petroleum came from deep carbon deposits from when Earth was formed?
There was no life when Earth was formed. That came way later. So if we think petroleum came from Earth formed, we need to explain how it got biomarkers in it.

label: Goal
body: Look for an answer that can explain-away the presence of biomarkers and allow us to defend the idea that petroleum came from carbon deposits that formed when Earth first started.

label: Statements
body:
Conditional: any (left side), unless (if-not)
```
Driver involved in accident
and
personal injury or          Driver must
prop damage > $500      →   report
and                          accident
capable of reporting
```

label: Fact
body: Ted was the driver in an accident, but is not required to report it.

label: Evaluate
body:
When we see conditionals in Must Be True, they will usually either be chained to other conditionals or applied to some fact that triggers the rule (or more often the contrapositive).
This fact about Ted triggers the contrapositive, because Ted is not required to report.
With a conditional that says
```
A and B and C  →  D
```
Then knowing ~D triggers this contrapositive:
```
~D  →  ~A or ~B or ~C
```
So since Ted is not required to report, he either
- wasn't a driver involved in an accident
- the accident didn't injure anyone or do
more than $500 in property damage
- he is incapable of reporting it
He can be more than one of those things, but we do already know he's a driver in the accident.
So either he's incapable or reporting it, it didn't injure anyone or do more than $500 of damage, or both.

label: Goal
body: Find an answer rewarding our understanding that either Ted is incapable or he didn't trigger the injury/damage part of the rule.

label: Conclusion (it follows that)
body: Many people have an immunity to infection by staphylococcus.

label: Evidence (since)
body:
```
If you have immunity   →   then don't develop
to infection by X          harmful symptoms
```
Many people don't develop harmful symptoms from staphylococcus.

label: Evaluate
body:
Whenever we're doing Flaw or Parallel Flaw and we see Conditional Logic, we suspect that we're about to see the #1 famous flaw of them all -- Necessary vs. Sufficient, which just means that the author presents a conditional rule in the evidence and then applies that rule in an illegal backwards or opposite fashion.
EXAMPLE
If you go to Harvard Law, you'll be a good lawyer. Tanya is a good lawyer. Thus, Tanya attended Harvard Law.
This argument gave us a conditional in the first sentence, then gave us a premise saying that many people are the Right Side of that conditional rule. Then it concluded that many people are the Left Side of that rule.

label: Merton's Conclusion (I conclude)
body: Air pollution from auto exhaust causes an elevated rate of heart disease.

label: Goal
body:
So we need two premises, one a conditional logic rule and one a factual claim about the outcome of the rule. The conclusion then should be a factual claim about the trigger of the rule.
Premise 1: A → B
Premise 2: Thing X is B.
Conclusion: Thing X is A.

label: Ming's Conclusion
body: It's fortunate for the consumer that so many cookie manufacturers have completely eliminated trans fat from their products.

label: Ming's Evidence (since)
body: Trans fat is particularly unhealthy.

label: Carol's Implied Conclusion
body: It's not fortunate for consumers.

label: Carols' Evidence
body: Even without trans fat, desserts do not make for healthy eating.

label: Evaluate
body:
Whenever a question stem asks us about how the 2nd person is interpreting the 1st person, they really mean misinterpreting.
The 2nd person is implicitly hearing the 1st person say something they really didn't say.
One way to articulate where the disconnect is would be to think about how the 1st person would respond. What would Ming say in response to, "even without trans fat, desserts do not make for healthy eating"?
He'd probably say,
"Well, obviously. I never said that desserts were healthy. What am I, a crazy person? I was just saying that trans fat is particularly unhealthy. So a dessert without trans fat is still healthier (less unhealthy) than a dessert with trans fat. Thus it's a win for the consumer."

label: Goal
body: Since Carol is responding, "Nuh-uh ... desserts are still unhealthy!", she must be thinking that Ming was saying, "Now that the trans fat is gone, desserts are healthy!"

label: Conclusion (So)
body: No one should accept the economist's explanation until historical evidence demonstrates that a change in values occurred prior to the Industrial Revolution.

label: Evidence
body: The economist theorizes that growth was made possible by the spread of values such as hard work and thrift. Successful explanations need to be based on facts.

label: Evaluate
body: This is a classic example of a rebuttal conclusion found after a pivot (here, the word "But"). The historian starts by mentioning a theorized explanation from an economist and then provides a rebuttal by saying no one should accept that explanation without evidence. This claim is our historian's opinion and is supported by the claim that successful explanations need to be based on facts.

label: Goal
body: Find the best available meaning match for no one should accept the economist's explanation until historical evidence demonstrates that a change in values occurred prior to the Industrial Revolution.

label: Conclusion (thus)
body: The donated trees are probably consistent with the master plan.

label: Evidence
body:
The master plan wants trees native to this area, but don't grow very large.
The donated trees come from the Three Rivers Nursery, which sells mostly native trees and shrubs.

label: Evaluate
body:
Are we convinced that the donated trees are "trees native to this area, but don't grow very large"?
No. All we know is that the donated trees are from a nursery that sells mostly native trees and shrubs. So there could be two possible ways these would fail to conform to the master plan:
1. Even though Three Rivers sells mostly native trees, they do sell some non-native trees. So, maybe the donated trees are non-native.
2. Even if we get a native tree from Three Rivers, it might be a type that grows to be very large.

label: Goal
body:
We want an answer to convince us that #1 or #2 (or both) aren't happening.
We want reassurance that the trees we got from Three Rivers are, in fact, native, and aren't a species that grows to be very large.

label: Conclusion (Thus)
body: Diplodocus must have fed on plants on or near the ground, or underwater.

label: Evidence
body:
Diplodocus had neck bones that would prevent it from raising its very long neck to browse for high growing vegetation.
But the neck could bend downward and even extend below ground level, letting Diplodocus dip its head underwater and reach underwater vegetation, while still standing on land.

label: Evaluate
body:
This doesn't feel like an Internal Math / Missing Link type of argument, so we should probably switch into Debate mode.
Given that ... Diplodocus couldn't reach high leaves by raising its long neck,
How can we argue that ... it didn't feed on ground level or underwater plants?
It seems like we may be dealing with a False Choice here, because the argument went from "If they couldn't grab the high leaves, then they must have eaten low or super-low leaves". Is it possible they ate medium height leaves?
We have to assume that raising their neck was the only way for them to eat the high leaves. Maybe they could have just kicked the bark of a tall tree and waited for the leaves to fall off into their mouths.
We have to assume it's feasible that they fed on ground level or underwater plants: were there plants near the ground or underwater that were available and part of this dino's diet?
Was there anything dangerous or physically hard about the act of eating food that low?

label: Goal
body:
We should probably go looking for an answer that, if negated, would weaken.
The correct answer, when negated, should help us say, "See, author --- Diplodocus didn't need to feed on ground level or underwater plants."

label: Conclusion (should not = opinion)
body: The government should not assist in rebuilding trails that have been washed out by landslides.

label: Evidence
body: There is a strong likelihood that future landslides could cause serious injury if the trails are rebuilt, thereby posing a risk to users.

label: Evaluate
body:
We can predict an "If Evidence, then Conclusion" answer on Principle-Strengthen.
"If an action would lead to a strong likelihood of injury or worse, then the government shouldn't assist that action".

label: Goal
body: Look for an answer that aligns with both the conclusion's normative stance about what the government "should not assist" and the evidence concerning risk.

label: Conclusion (should = opinion)
body: The fact that human behavior may be responsible for large-scale climate change should be seen more as an opportunity than as a problem.

label: Evidence
body: If human behavior is responsible for climate change, then we can control future climate change to make it less extreme than previous climate shifts.

label: Evaluate
body:
We could spell out a missing Link, such as "If humans can control future climate change to make it less extreme, then we should view climate change as an opportunity not a problem".
But because this argument is very real-world, it's more likely to have an answer that is dealing with Objections than with Links.
How could we object to this argument and say, "No ... we should for sure see it as a problem"?
- first of all, we are responsible for climate change but that doesn't mean we know how to reverse it. Sally might be responsible for spilling that milk; that doesn't mean that the can control future spills.
- even if we do have the power to make climate change less extreme than previous climate shifts, couldn't it still be problematic? (Some previous climate shifts have led to mass extinctions in which Earth loses 75% or more of its species --- if we make future climate change less extreme and only lose 40% of Earth's species, isn't that still a problem?)

label: Goal
body:
Let's look for an answer that sounds like something the author would need to believe in order to be optimistic about our ability to steer future climate change into a non-problematic direction.
Or look for an answer that, when negated, weakens. The negation should allow us to argue that climate change should be seen as a problem.

label: Setup Claims
body:
We've got some heart patients suffering from reduced blood flow to the heart.
Some of them already know what treatment they'll need to address this. Other patients are waiting to find out whether they'll need surgery.
The patients still waiting to find out experienced less pain overall from their blood flow condition than did the people who already knew what kind of treatment they were going to receive.

label: Fill-in-the-Blank
body: If we were to assume that the uncertainty o fnot knowing whether you were going to need surgery is more stressful than knowing what your treatment would be, then we can conclude ⎽⎽⎽⎽⎽ .

label: Evaluate
body:
The blank we're filling in (like the vast majority of Logical Completion questions) is prefaced by Conclusion language, so the answer choice should sound like a reasonable inference we can conclude by synthesizing the claims we were given.
This final sentence starts with "Assuming X is true". We should just pretend that's one more fact we have to go off. What can we infer by combining these ideas?
Are there any overlapping ideas?
Yes, both the first sentence and the second sentence are talking about "uncertainty/knowledge about the future". Let's line up the two things we know about those.
```
        Uncertain about future        Know future
        (might need surgery?!)        (type of treatment)
1st:    less likely to                more likely to
        experience pain               experience pain
2nd:    more stressful                less stressful
```

label: Goal
body:
The conclusion will likely connect "more stress, thus less likely to experience pain". The author will probably be thinking there's some causal chain like, "Not knowing if you have surgery makes you more stressed, and being more stressed makes you not experience as much pain from your heart condition."
(It's kind of like the old folk remedy for toothaches, which is to hold an ice cube. It's not that the toothache goes away, but you're distracted by the ice cube.)
Let's look for a safely worded answer that synthesizes the two things we know about people who do / don't know their upcoming treatment for a heart problem.

label: Conclusion (Thus)
body: Walking on hind legs is instinctive and not a learned behavior of the Kodiak.

label: Evidence
body: Given their hip shape and foot bones, standing and walking upright is completely natural behavior for these bears.

label: Evaluate
body:
The link here seems to be "if a certain behavior is a 'natural' one given your anatomy, then it's instinctive not learned."
Do we accept that move? Is it possible that a learned behavior just happens to conform 'naturally' to certain anatomical traits you have?
Do all Kodiak bears walk? Or is it only the ones you have seen humans traipsing around upright on their legs? There may be counterevidence to the idea that walking on hind legs is instinctive. There may be evidence that walking on hind legs is learned (for exmaple, none of the Kodiak bears in a certain group walked on hind legs until they saw a human doing it).

label: Goal
body: This argument doesn't seem to be any of the famous flaws, so we can anticipate that the correct answer will call out its central assumption (if walking upright is a completely natural behavior, then it's an instinctive, not learned, behavior) or it will bring up potential objections that one could use to argue that walking upright is a learned behavior for the Kodiak.

label: Given that ...
body:
People are interested in anecdotes but not interested in statistical information.
and that ...
Anecdotes are generally misleading.

label: Why is it that ...
body: People still seem to have fairly accurate beliefs about society?

label: Goal
body:
We need an answer to help us understand where people are getting their accurate beliefs about society.
They don't seem to get them from statistical information, because they rarely pay attention to it.
And they don't get their accurate beliefs from the anecdotes they love, because anecdotes are usually misleading atypical cases.

label: Statements
body:
Correlation (when X happened, Y happened)
