The professor reports that when she pulled an all-nighter, she found it harder to lecture for a number of reasons, (tired, no enthusiasm, poor focus).
Pivot (interestingly)
Her students, when asked, were generally not able to guess which lectures were the ones when she was feeling so crappy.

label: Evaluate
body:
When we get a surprising idea as our final fact (usually introduced with "But, Yet However"), the correct answer usually Reconciles the Pivot idea with what came before it, but it does so in very safe, measured language.
EXAMPLE: Jennifer always assumed Tom was from New York, because she thought of him as a big Yankees fan. However, Tom isn't a Yankees fan. In fact, Tom doesn't even like baseball.
The temptation is to go overconfidently in any direction:
- Tom isn't actually from New York
- Jennifer has Tom confused with some other person
- Tom doesn't like any sports
- all New Yorkers like baseball
The supportable (i.e. provable / defendable) truth is something weak and watered down like,
(A) Not all reasons people have for believing Tom is from New York are legitimate ones.
Decoded, that just means, "At least one reason for believing Tom is from New York is not a legitimate one". That would Reconcile the Pivot idea (Tom isn't a Yankees fan) with what came before the pivot (Jennifer thought Tom was a Yankees fan and thus thought Tom was from New York).

label: Conclusion (probably)
body: Loss of nesting habitat is probably the reason for the decrease in the mourning-dove population in this area.

label: Goal
body:
Without going too far, what can we derive from the fact that the teacher felt like lecturing was harder than normal. She probably perceived that she was doing a worse-than-average job, given her perception that she was less good-humored and less focused with her speaking.
The students clearly didn't perceive a marked difference. That could be because she was hiding it well. That could be because they aren't paying enough attention to her, or are paying too much attention to themselves or their phones.
It's less safe to speculate on why this mismatch occurred. It's safer to just find an answer that reiterates that there was a mismatch that occurred. But some correct answers are speculative in a Solve the Causal Mystery kind of way, if everything else is less supportable.

label: Given that ...
body:
the people of our country are equal in worth to the people of other nations
and that ...
therefore it's no more objectively important to satisfy our people's needs than any other people's needs

label: How can we still say that ...
body: Our nation's government should give priority to satisfying our nation's people over satisfying the needs of others?

label: Evaluate / Goal
body:
We need a way of justifying why our government should focus on satisfying the needs of this country, even though all people have equal value and importance.
The answer will probably say that each government is better positioned to know the specific problems and appropriate solutions for its local people's needs. In other words, we care about taking care of all humans on the planet, but we think we can best achieve that by having lots of smaller units that managing themselves.

label: Statements
body:
Every street in town will be swept at least once a month.
If a neighborhood needs to be swept more than once a month, that neighborhood will be qualified for interim sweepings.
All requests from interim sweepings from qualified neighborhoods will be satisfied immediately.

label: Evaluate
body:
All three sentences are conditional in nature ("every / if / all"), so we should be checking to see whether any of these conditionals chain together.
In this case, only the 2nd and 3rd would seem to be connectable.
If your neighborhood needs more than one sweeping in a month, it will qualify for interim sweeping, and thus it will get swept immediately..

label: Goal
body: Look for anything provable. It might deal with combining the 2nd and 3rd statements, since they have an overlapping concept (qualify for interim sweepings)..

label: Implicit Conclusion
body: It isn't unethical for a journalist to withhold relevant information in interviews, in order to elicit new info.

label: Evidence
body:
The argument that "it's unethical for a journalist to withhold relevant info, because it's intentional deception" fails to recognize the distinction between failing to prevent a false belief and actively encouraging one.
Lying is unethical because it actively encourages a false belief.

label: Evaluate
body:
We get an attribution, "Some argue that X", and then a pivot (but, yet, however), so we know our author is rebutting a point of view. Thus, even if she doesn't spell out her conclusion, we can assume it to be "this view is wrong".
Our job is to characterize the type of evidence or reasoning pattern. The author calls out a distinction that's being overlooked. The argument she's rebutting tries to argue by analogy. "Withholding info, like lying, is intentional deception. And if lying is unethical than shouldn't withholding info also be unethical?"
Our author is pointing out a meaningful difference between the two cases that makes them disanalogous.

label: Goal
body: Look for any answer whose language we can match up with the stimulus. It will probably talk about making a distinction in order to show that two things aren't fair to compare.

label: Conclusion (So)
body: Currently there is no reason lower interest rates further.

label: Intermediate Conclusion
body: Some say we should lower interest rates to stimulate economic growth, but no stimulation is needed.

label: Evidence
body: The economy is already growing at a sustainable rate.

label: Evaluate
body:
Whenever we're doing Flaw and see a Rebuttal argument, we should immediately look out for the 2 famous flaws that relate to rebuttals:
1. Ad Hominem: dismissing an idea because of its source, rather than its content (saying that "because X has a biased interest / conflicting past behavior, we should ignore X.")
2. Unproven vs. Proven False: arguing that because people have no evidence for X or have made an unsuccessful argument in favor of X, that X is therefore false.
We got ourselves a #2, here. Some people say "we should lower interest rates further", and our author concludes that claim is false, because those people made an unsuccessful argument in favor of that claim.
They argued that we should lower interest rates for reason Y (stimulate growth) and our author said reason Y isn't applicable.
The correct conclusion, then, is "So, we shouldn't lower interest rates further for the sake of stimulating economic growth."
But the author concludes "So there is no reason to lower them."

label: Goal
body:
Technically there could be an answer objecting to the subsidiary conclusion, saying "Even though the economy is growing at a sustainable rate, it still might be desirable to stimulate economic growth".
But it's much more likely that they want us to complain that "even though stimulating economic growth doesn't seem to be a good reason to lower interest rates, that doesn't mean that there is no reason, unless you assume that the only possible reason we'd lower interest rates is to stimulate economic growth".

label: Conclusion (therefore)
body: One must abandon the opinion of this majority of commentators or reject Mather's definition that says Baroque paintings must display opulence, heroic sweep, and extravagance.

label: Evidence
body: Most commentators consider Caravaggio an early Baroque artist.

label: Evaluate
body:
The conclusion is saying, "You must make a choice here; both things cannot be true".
Either the commentators' opinion is wrong, or Mather's definition of Baroque is wrong. They're mutually exclusive.
Once we insert the specific ideas into those placeholders, the conclusion becomes, "Either it's wrong to say that Caravaggio was making Baroque paintings, or it's wrong to say that Baroque paintings must have opulence, heroic sweep, and extravagance."
Apparently, our author doesn't think that Caravaggio's paintings fit Mather's definition of Baroque.

label: Evidence
body: Many mourning doves used to nest in the nearby orchards, but after they installed overhead sprinklers last year, the doves stopped building nests there.

label: Goal
body:
We need to prove that Caravaggio's paintings don't fit Mather's definition. So we need to know at least one of these things about Caravaggio's paintings:
- they don't display opulence
- they don't have heroic sweep
- they don't have extravagance

label: Conclusion (implied)
body: The doctrine of jury nullification is questionable.

label: Evidence
body: The doctrine of jury nullification relies too much on jurors' objectivity. When you entrust juries with the power to decide what's fair, they too often make serious mistakes.

label: Evaluate
body:
We're being asked what technique the author used to respond to the proponents.
She pointed out a downside of jury nullification -- we're entrusting the jury with the power to decide on which laws are unjust, and they're prone to serious mistakes.
How would we describe that rebuttal in more general terms?

label: Goal
body: Look for something like, "The author raises overlooked considerations about negative outcomes of a certain practice"?

label: Conclusion
body: The recent claims made by manufacturers of melatonin supplements are correct: the pineal gland produces less melatonin as it ages.

label: Evidence
body:
A large study of people aged 65-81 who suffer from insomnia showed that insomnia's symptoms were greatly alleviated by ingesting melatonin.
Melatonin is a hormone produced by the pineal gland and plays a role in regulating the body's biological clock.

label: Evaluate
body:
The study seems to show that taking melatonin helps with lessening the symptoms of insomnia. Does that prove that the insomniacs had less melatonin to begin with?
Not really. Ibuprofen might lessen the symptoms of my headache, but that doesn't mean that my headache was caused by having too little ibuprofen in my system.
So one possible answer could be, "it assumes that if X treats a condition's symptoms, then the condition is caused by having a shortage of X."
Let's say we granted that the insomniacs did have a shortage of melatonin. Does that mean that the pineal gland is producing less melatonin? Not necessarily. We could try to argue that the pineal gland makes just as much as before, but the melatonin goes to the wrong part of the body or gets flushed out of the body more than it used to.
What about the time dimension of the conclusion: "as the pineal gland ages, it produces less melatonin". Do we have evidence that the 81 year olds had worse melatonin production than the 65 year olds? How do these compare to younger age groups?

label: Goal
body: Look for an answer complaining that "just because melatonin helps doesn't mean a shortage of melatonin was the problem", or an answer complaining that "just because melatonin helped these people doesn't mean that the pineal gland makes less melatonin as it ages".

label: Evidence
body:
Wells (a knowledgeable person on this subject) says,
"the concern would sell out unless it was poorly promoted".
The concert did not sell out.

label: Conclusion
body: The concert was probably poorly promoted.

label: Evaluate
body:
Since we see conditional logic (unless) and repeating symbols (sell out / poorly promoted each mentioned twice), we would probably try to turn this into an abstract recipe.
```
Premise 1: Sell out unless poorly promoted.
           ~PP → SO
           ~SO → PP
Premise 2: Concert didn't sell out.
           concert was ~SO.
Conclusion: Concert was probably poorly promoted.
           concert was probably PP.
```
This seems like valid logic; in fact, it's weird that the conclusion is hedging its certainly by saying "probably poorly promoted". We have a conditional rule that says, "If it didn't sell out, then poorly promoted". We know this concert didn't sell out. So shouldn't we be sure of concluding, "Thus, is was poorly promoted"?
The reason the author is softening her certainty is because we don't "know" this conditional rule of "if didn't sell out, then poorly promoted". It's not presented as a fact. It's presented as a certain opinion of Wells.
The author does trust Wells, who is quite knowledgeable on this topic, but she is also probably thinking people are sometimes wrong. Wells is probably right about this, since he is knowledgeable, and if he is right, then the concert was definitely poorly promoted. So the concert was probably poorly promoted.

label: Goal
body:
If we're really on top of our game, we want to include this appeal to expert opinion as part of the way we understand the structure of this argument.
If we don't notice that layer, we'll go looking for something like this.
```
Premise 1: A → B
Premise 2: X was B.
Conclusion: X was probably A.
```
If we do notice that layer, we should be looking for something like this,
```
Premise 1: Trusted source says, "A → B"
Premise 2: X was B.
Conclusion: X was probably A.
```

label: Conclusion
body: Global recessions can never be prevented.

label: Evidence (for)
body:
Recessions could be prevented only if they were predictable.
But economists, using their best tools, consistently fail to accurately predict global recessions.

label: Evaluate
body:
The author is trying to prove "can never be prevented" and provides a proving mechanism, a conditional rule using the necessary indicator "only if":
```
Global recessions   →   global recessions can
are not predictable      not be prevented
```
So the author proves her conclusion as soon as she establishes that trigger idea, that global recessions are not predictable.
However, her premise doesn't fully establish that. It only establishes that global recessions have not been predictable for economists using their best techniques.

label: Goal
body:
Look for an answer saying, "Just because global recessions have not been predictable for these economists, that doesn't convince us that global recessions are not predictable."
Maybe future economists or people from some other discipline will innovate better techniques or theories and then one day be able to predict global recessions.

label: Conclusion
body: Your newspaper exhibits an unjustified bias.

label: Evidence
body:
The tone of your coverage of Mr. Hanlon's claim that he saw a spaceship was very skeptical, even though Hanlon has proven to be a trusted member of the community and even though you wouldn't have had a skeptical tone had he claimed to have observed a large meteor.
(A large meteor is a a rare natural phenomenon / an alien spaceship sighting would be extraordinary)

label: Theodora's Conclusion
body: You're wrong to say vegetarianism can't lead to nutritional deficiencies (i.e. vegetarianism can lead to nutritional deficiencies)

label: Merton's Evidence
body: A study showed that people who live on very busy streets have higher rates of heart disease than average.

label: Evaluate
body:
To conflict with a principle means that the Trigger of the principle applies, but the Outcome does not.
Our author is arguing that,
```
since Mr. H is trusted        there was unjustified
and                       →   bias in being skeptical
since paper would have        about Mr. H's claim
not been skeptical had he     saw a spaceship
Mr. H seen large meteor
```
A conflicting principle would be saying, "given the facts of the case, there WAS not bias being exhibited by the newspaper".

label: Goal
body: If we were trying to defend the paper and say they were being correct, not biased, in showing skepticism of Mr. H's spaceship claim, we might want a principle like "No matter who the source is, if they're claiming something extraordinary, it makes sense to report it with a skeptical tone".

label: Conclusion (thus)
body: The algae-scraping specialization evolved more than once.

label: Evidence
body:
There are fish with an algae-scraping specialization in both Flower Lake and Blue Lake.
If they are closely related, then the algae-scraping specialization evolved only once.
But genetic tests show that they're not closely related.

label: Evaluate
body:
Whenever we're doing Flaw and we come across a Conditional premise (in this case, signified by If), we know to be on red alert for the #1 Famous Flaw, confusing Necessary with Sufficient.
This flaw is when the author presents a conditional premise, like "If X, then Y" and then either argues via an illegal reversal (Pam is Y. Thus Pam is X) or via an illegal negation (Pam is not X. Thus Pam is not Y).
This was our conditional premise:
```
the two fish are   →   , algae-scraping
closely related          evolved only once
```
An illegal reversal would sound like, "We know that algae-scraping evolved only once. Thus, we can conclude that these two fish are closely related."
An illegal negation would sound like, "We know these two fish are not closely related. Thus algae-scraping evolved did not evolve only once (i.e. it evolved more tan once)".
That second argument, the illegal negation, is exactly what this author did. She established the two fish are not closely related (the trigger isn't true) and then concluded from that that algae-scraping evolved more than once (the outcome isn't true).

label: Goal
body:
Since this is such a famous flaw, we'd head to the answers hoping to find the classic Necessary vs. Sufficient answer choice.
Sometimes they give us a more conversational objection to these arguments, rather than naming their formal error, which would sound like "Fails to consider that two fish could be distantly related, and a trait they both share may have only evolved once."
But we only worry about that if we have to.

label: Rules
body:
```
                          sell for highest price
govt sells a              it can get on open market
state-owned          →    and
entity                     citizens have majority
                           ownership of new
                           company for 1+ year
```

label: Goal
body:
We need a situation where we'd be violating at least one of the requirements, so let's think about what it would sound like if they were at odds with each other:
What if there were only 2 buyers: one would offer highest open market price, but wouldn't allow for citizens to have ownership for at least a year. The other would allow for citizen ownership but wouldn't offer highest open market price.

label: Conclusion
body: Activite must be effective.

label: Evidence
body: If Activite weren't effective at promoting energy and mental alertness, it wouldn't be in the company's interest to offer a free month's supply to new customers.

label: Evaluate
body:
This feels like a rare argument where we will want to object to the evidence, rather than the reasoning move.
In terms of the reasoning move, the author is providing a conditional premise,
```
If it's in the company's interest        Activite
to offer a free month's supply     →     effective
of Activite
```
And then he's concluding the outcome:
Thus, Activite is effective.
So he must be assuming the trigger:
The company benefits by offering
a free month's supply of Activite.
We could weaken the argument by countering the assumption, saying something like, "Actually, the makers of Activite have been losing money ever since they started offering a free month's supply."
But my suspicion is that they want us to attack the author's opinionated premise --- if we were to suppose that Activite were not effective, is there any way that giving a free month's supply could still be in the company's interest?
Sure. Maybe it's not effective but the placebo effect is strong enough that people who try out the free supply convince themselves that their energy and alertness has improved.
Maybe it's not effective, but it's delicious or addictive, so people who try out the free supply choose to keep ordering it just because they want to consume more of it.
Maybe it's not effective, but sending out the free supply creates some goodwill with customers who then buy other products that do make the company some money.

label: Goal
body: Look for an answer that helps us to solve this riddle, "Given that the company is offering a free month's supply of their energy/alertness elixir, how could it still be that Activite is not actually effective at what it claims to do?"

label: Conclusion (So)
body: Theresa probably approves of the prime minister's overall job performance.

label: Evidence
body:
Most people who disapprove of the PM's performance do so because of the PM's support for increasing the income tax.
But, Theresa believes that the income tax should be increased.

label: Evaluate
body:
Because of the symbol repetition in this argument (theresa / income tax / prime minister are all mentioned twice) and because of the quantifier most, this argument seems like a good contender for turning into an algebraic recipe.
```
Prem 1: Most people who are X are Y
        (X = disapprove of PM, Y = don't want income tax increased)
Prem 2: Person A is not Y.
        (A = Theresa)
Conc:   Person A is probably not X.
```
Conversationally, we could say that "even though Theresa supports the increased tax, that doesn't mean she probably supports the PM". We don't know whether most people who support the tax support the PM .
There could be 100 people, 98 of whom oppose the PM.
Most of those 98 oppose the PM because of the increased tax.
So let's say 60 of the 98 oppose the PM because of the increased tax.
That leaves 38 people who oppose the PM, but not because of the tax.
And 2 people who support the PM.
If we know that Theresa is not opposed to the tax, does that mean she's more likely to be one of the 2 people who support the PM or the 38 people who oppose the PM for some reason other than the tax?
Numerically, the latter is more probable.

label: Goal
body:
The conversational objection is harder to deal with, so we should probably look for our algebraic structure:
```
P1: Most people who are X are Y.
P2: Person A is not Y.
C: Person A is probably not X.
```

label: Evaluate
body:
Since the author is speculating the reason for a Curious Change (fewer mourning-doves), we can use our Curious Fact / Explanation mindset on this.
Curious Fact
Why has the mourning dove population in this area decreased?
Author's Explanation
The orchards installed overhead sprinklers last year, and the mourning doves stopped building nests in the orchard, and that's why we don't see as many in this area.
We can Strengthen this argument by ruling out an Alternate Explanation for the Curious Fact, or by boosting the Plausibility of the Author's Explanation.
What could be a different reason why there are fewer mourning-doves in the area? Maybe there are more predators than before. Maybe there is less food than before. Maybe the mourning-doves migrated away and many of them didn't make it back for some reason (if the mourning-dove is a non-migratory bird, then any ornithologist reading this is thinking, "Patrick, you're an idiot.)
How plausible is the author's explanation? Well I can see how overhead sprinklers would be a poor match for raising babies in a nest. But does this one change in the orchards really explain their decrease in the area? Couldn't they just make their nests somewhere besides the orchard, but still in this city?

label: Goal
body: We want an answer that rules out a different cause of fewer mourning-doves in the area, or we want an answer that adds some plausibility to the storyline that losing their nesting habitat in the orchards is the catalyst for seeing fewer of them in the area.

label: Conclusion
body: Your statements taken together are absurd.

label: Evidence
body:
You're simultaneously saying
- I have the legal right to sell this business
- I have no right to sell this business, since loyal employees will suffer

label: Evaluate
body:
Mary is trying to catch Jamal in a contradiction, claiming that he's simultaneously saying "She does have the right and doesn't have the right to sell the business".
How would we defend Jamal? How could he say, "I'm not contradicting myself!"
He would just make a distinction between the two different senses of "have the right" we're using. He'd say, "I acknowledge that you have the legal prerogative to sell your asset (the business) but you have a moral obligation to the welfare of your loyal employees."

label: Goal
body:
When the same term / concept gets used in two different ways, that's the famous flaw of Equivocation.
The answer might use that word or just otherwise say that Mary is conflating two different senses of "the right".

label: Evidence
body: There is no survival value in an animal's having an organ that is able to function when all its other organs have broken down to such a degree that the animal dies.

label: Conclusion
body: It is a result of the efficiency of natural selection that no organ is likely to evolve in such a way that it greatly outlasts the body's other organs.

label: Evaluate
body: The principle illustrated is that if there is no advantage to a whole for any of its parts to outlive the others, then the whole will evolve in such a way that no part will outlive the whole.

label: Conclusion (should)

The bill should be enacted
(i.e. fishing should be prohibited in Eagle Bay)

label: Evidence
body: The bay has one of the highest water pollution levels in the nation, and a recent study found that 80% of the bay's fish contained excessive toxins.

label: Evaluate
body:
Our job on method is just to characterize what type of evidence was used or describe the process by which the author reached her conclusion.
None of the evidence here sticks out as a frequently-tested pattern (like analogy, implications of logic, etc.).
The author is arguing in favor of a proposal to ban fishing, because the bay is super polluted and a recent study found tons of the fish have toxins, so if people are allowed to fish there it could have bad effects on human health.

label: Goal
body:
Not sure what to look for. The conclusion is prescriptive. The evidence is mix of statistics, a recent study, and a speculative worry.
Since the spirit of Method is just "if the answer choice is descriptively accurate, then it's correct", I wouldn't try to predict the wording.
Let's just find something that matches.

label: Evidence
body: Its contemporary art collection is small because its curators believe that there is little high-quality contemporary art [the amount is appropriate].

label: Conclusion
body: The relatively small size of the museum's contemporary collection is appropriate.

label: Evaluate

label: Evidence
body:
Over the last five years, every new major alternative-energy initiative that initially was promised government funding has since seen that funding severely curtailed.
In no such case has the government come even close to providing the level of funds initially earmarked for these projects.
Large corporation have made it a point to discourage alternative-energy projects.

label: Conclusion
body: It is likely that the corporations' actions influenced the government's funding decisions.

label: Evaluate
body: The argument establishes a difference between what was promised and what was given to alternative-energy projects and then suggests an explanation—it's because large corporations have influenced the government's funding decisions. The right answer will likely eliminate an alternative explanation or somehow strengthen the connection between corporations and the decision to curtail funding of alternative-energy projections.

label: Marcia's Conclusion
body: Some vegetarian diets don't lead to nutritional deficiencies.

label: Marcia's Evidence
body: Research shows that vegetarians can get all the proteins/minerals they need from nonanimal foods.

label: Goal
body: Something safely worded that sounds like "that's why we end up with a lot of the same body parts / organs"

label: Theodora's Evidence
body: If most people went veggie, some people in the meat industry would lose their jobs, fall into poverty, and hence not be able to afford a nutritionally adequate diet.

label: Evaluation
body:
Where to begin, Theodora? First and foremost, out of the gate you accused Marcia of something she never said. Marcia said that some veggie diets aren't nutritionally deficient. She never said that if you're on a vegetarian diet, it's impossible have a nutritional deficiency.
This type of inappropriate response is a somewhat recurring flaw we might call Irrelevant Response or Straw Man, in which an author is responding in a way that feels totally inappropriate to the original position.
We might also critique Theodora's use of indirect causation to prove direct causation. She is trying to argue that vegetarian diets can lead to nutritional deficiencies. We would commonly understand that conversation to be about whether the ingredients of a vegetarian diet lead to nutritional deficiencies for the person on that diet, whereas Theodora is stretching that conversation to include the eventual economic consequences that could affect people who might not be vegetarian.
This is an Equivocation based on the idea of "lead to". In Marcia's sense of it, she meant "would eating vegetarian directly lead to that eater having nutritional deficiencies. In Theodora's sense of it, she meant "would the consequences of a world in which more people ate vegetarian result in anyone having a nutritional deficiency"?

label: Goal
body: Either look for an answer describing Theodora's false charge against what Marcia supposedly claimed, or an answer calling out Theodora's abuse of stretching the concept of "this diet leads to nutritional deficiencies".

label: Evidence
body:
Classification of a musical instrument depends on the mechanical action through which it produces music.
The strings of the piano are caused to vibrate by the impact of hammers.

label: Conclusion
body: The piano is properly called a percussion instrument, not a stringed instrument.

label: Conclusion
body: Drivers feel possessive of their parking spaces even when pulling out, and the more a driver wants their space, the more posscoressive they feel.

label: Evaluation
body:
We have a Curious Fact - why are drivers taking longer to back out when someone is waiting and even longer to back out when someone is impatiently waiting?
The author's hypothesis is that people are really protective of their parking spaces, even more so if the person waiting is being a jerk about it. Like all Causal Interpretation arguments, we ask ourselves the same 2 questions:
- How else can we explain the Curious Fact?
- How plausible is the Author's hypothesis?

label: Goal
body: Since we're trying to Weaken, we either need a different way to explain why drivers are taking longer to back out, or we need some idea that undermines the hypothesis that drivers feel possessive of the parking spot they're leaving.

label: Conclusion
body: The mystery marks are probably the traces of a geological processes, not worms.

label: Evidence
body: The marks were made more than 500 million years ago, which is earlier than the earliest known traces of multicellular animal life (i.e. before we think worms could have possibly existed)

label: Evaluation
body:
This is a classic Curious Fact / Explanation argument.
(Curious Fact) What's up with these weird marks in this sandstone?
(Author's Explanation) They're probably traces from geological processes, since they predate when worms existed
We can weaken the argument by
- providing a different way to explain the marks
- undermining the plausibility that the marks are from geological processes
This argument also has an Anti-Causal element to it, because it's saying that traces are not from worms. So we could also weaken this argument by somehow making the worm possibility seem more plausible.

label: Goal
body:
Three possibilities:
- different way to explain marks
- make geological process less plausible
- make worm hypothesis more plausible

label: Background
body: A lot of organs or body parts are the only feasible physical way to do what that thing does, so it's not shocking that lots of completely unrelated species will evolve similar organs or body parts at different times.

label: Setup
body: No matter their lineage or habitat, animals have fundamentally similar needs. So, ...

label: Evaluation
body:
We need to connect these two threads. It's unsurprising that lots of different animals have evolved the same organs or body parts, since there's only one way to accomplish certain tasks and lots of animals have similar needs.
A logical completion might sound like, they have similar needs and so "they evolve similar parts", or "the mutations that help one organism succeed are similar to the mutations that help other organisms succeed" (since successful mutations become "selected" by evolution)

label: Conclusion
body: So if steel-manufacturing plants could feed the heat they produce into thermophotovoltaic generators, they would greatly reduce their electric bills, thereby saving money.

label: Evaluate
body: The argument assumes that value of the energy produced would exceed the cost to implement the program. The savings must be greater than the costs for the company to save money.

body:
This is a really weird one-off question. There are lots of Logical Completion questions that ask us to complete the analogy, but I've never seen a question stem structured this way.

label: Conclusion
body: Once a barn owl has developed an auditory scheme for estimating the point from which sounds originate, it ceases to use vision to locate sounds.

label: Evidence
body:
In an experiment, scientists put distorting lenses over the eyes of young barn owls before the owls first opened their eyes. The lenses made them behave as if objects making sounds were farther to the right than they actually were.
Once the owls matured, the lenses were removed, yet the owls continued to act as if they misjudged the location of the source of sounds.

label: Evaluate
body:
Since we're dealing with a study/experiment, we're probably being set up for a causal conclusion. As soon as we see "the scientists consequently hypothesized", then we know we're dealing with a causal conclusion. "Hypothesis" on LSAT almost always means "a causal explanation for a phenomenon".
So we can use the Explain Curious Fact framework we often use for causality.
Curious Fact .... how come these adult owls are still misjudging the whereabouts of objects making sounds, even after we've removed the distorting lenses from their eyes?
Author's Explanation .... While the owls were wearing these distorting lenses, they developed an auditory scheme based on that distorted vision, and then they stopped using vision at all to locate sounds. So even though the lenses are removed and they would be able to see the correct whereabouts of the sounds, they're relying on an auditory scheme that is still "distorted".

label: Goal
body:
When we see an author conclude/assume a causal explanation for a phenomenon on Flaw, the issue is almost always that the author is too sure of one possibility, and is failing to consider other possible explanations.
So let's look for an answer saying that these scientists are failing to consider some alternative explanation for why the owls continue to misjudge the location of the sounds, even though the distorting lenses have been removed from their eyes.
(Or we'd love an answer suggesting that the owls still ARE using their vision at least in part to locate sounds)

label: Apparent Paradox
body:
As often now as in the past, newspaper journalists use direct or indirect quotation to report unsupported or false claims made by newsmakers.
However, journalists are becoming less likely to openly challenge the veracity of such claims within their articles.

label: Evaluate
body: Each of the wrong answers will help explain why reporters continue to use direct or indirect quotation to report unsupported or false claims made by newsmakers, while not challenging the veracity of those claims directly. There are many things that could explain this, such as pressure from management to appeal to the tastes of the readership or a growing sense that the role of the journalist does not include the views of the journalist.

label: Conclusion
body: Interpreting EKG data should be left to computer programs.

label: Evidence
body: In a study, a computer program went up against a skilled cardiologist, and of the cases that were later confirmed to be heart attacks, the computer guessed "heart attack" more than the the cardiologist did.

label: Evaluation
body:
There are two very different attack lines to consider here:
A) I do not accept that the EKG won this study
B) I accept that the EKG won, but we still shouldn't leave interpreting EKG to computers
A) When it comes to diagnosing an EKG for whether someone had a heart attack, you can be wrong in two different ways: false positives (you said "heart attack" but it wasn't) or false negatives (you said "no heart attack" but it was). We only know that the computer won the false negative battle. The doctor was more often guilty of a false negative, where she said it wasn't a heart attack but later it was confirmed that it was. But it could be that the computer was way worse at false positives. Maybe the computer almost always said "heart attack", so of course it nailed all the cases of genuine heart attacks but made tons of mistakes when the case was not actually a heart attack.
LSAT has rolled out this type of argument multiple times -- (45-1-24 about DNA tests and 54-4-20 about forecasting rain)
B) Even if the computer were more accurate in diagnosing EKG's, there could be other factors that would argue against making computers the exclusive diagnostic device for EKG data (cost, availability, bedside manner, patient perception, etc.)

label: Goal
body: Look for an answer that suggests that the EKG didn't necessarily win the study's contest (because it may have generated tons of false negatives), or look for a consideration beyond accuracy that would make it seem like we should use humans, not exclusively computers, to diagnose EKG.

label: Conclusion
body: We should make 75 mph (120km /hr) the standard speed limit for all level, straight high-speed roadways.

label: Evidence
body:
75mph is the actual average speed cars travel on level, straight high-speed roadways
+
a study shows that if speed limits matched the actual average speed of cars, it would reduce the accident rate.

label: Evaluation
body: So 75 mph, according to this study, would reduce the accident rate. And the conclusion is saying we should set that as our uniform speed limit. Correct answers on Principle-Strengthen questions usually just have a conditional form that sounds like "If premise, the conclusion".

label: Goal
body: "If a speed limit would reduce the accident rate on a certain type of road, then we should set it as the uniform standard for that type of road".

label: Conclusion
body: 1st yr students who spend a lot of $$ on recreation could reduce that spending without increasing their anxiety or depression.

label: Evidence
body: the 1st yr students who spend a lot of $$ on recreation score at about the same level for anxiety / depression as do those who spend the lowest on recreation.

label: Evaluation
body:
In an Anti-Causal argument such as this, it's usually two groups of people being compared. Since they achieve the same result (score the same on anxiety / depression), the author assumes that some difference (spending lots of $ on recreation vs. spending little) makes no causal difference.
We weaken these arguments by making the groups unfair to compare to begin with. Maybe the students who spend lots of money on recreation would be WAY WORSE if they didn't spend that money. (e.g. "I can't believe Paul goes to therapy. He seems so well adjusted", "He's well adjusted because he goes to therapy.")

label: Goal
body:
Since we would weaken this argument by pointing out differences that make the spend more group seem more prone to anxiety / depression, we can expect strengthen answers that equalize out these factors (or make the spend less group seem more prone).
There also might be an answer that just corroborates the anti-causal conclusion, i.e. it provides more reason to believe that spending $ on rec is not likely to decrease your anxiety / depression.

label: Conclusion (so)
body: Most of the BH's on R St. have two stories.

label: Evidence
body:
Every BH on R St. has a front yard.
Most of the H's on R St. w/ front yards also have two stories.

label: Evaluation
body:
Since this argument has symbol matches ("brick house" / "river street" / "front yard" / "two stories" all appear twice) and quantifiers ("every / most / most"), this argument is ripe for being turned into an algebraic recipe.
In doing so, we don't really need to worry about the flaw. As long as we re-create this recipe, it'll re-create the flaw.
```
Every [BH, R] has FY.               A and B → Y
Most [H, R, FY] have 2S.            Most *A, B, Y = Z
⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯
Most [BH, R] have 2S.               Most A, B = Z
```
The *A is because the first sentence is about "brick houses" and the second sentence is about "houses".
That switch from a narrower category "brick houses" to a broader one "houses" is why we can't infer the conclusion.

label: Goal
body:
We have our recipe, but we can hopefully make quick eliminations by just scanning for things such as
- 1 All Premise, 1 Most Premise, 1 Most Conclusion
- The All Premise should be a subset of the group mentioned in the Most Premise

label: Conclusion
body:
```
more --------------------------------> less you see
you                                    history as
know                                    W.O.M.T.
history
```

label: Evidence
body:
```
more --->  less you're
you        inclined to
know       morally
history    judge H.B.
don't hold ->  won't see
C&U moral      history as
beliefs        W.O.M.T.
```

label: Goal
body:
To derive the logical connection in the conclusion (going from the 1st idea to the 4th idea), we need to get from that 2nd idea to that 3rd idea.
We want something like this:
```
less inclined      don't hold
to morally    →     C&U moral
judge H.B.          beliefs
```

label: Given that ...
body: The poll showed that most students prefer that the university hire a new president who has extensive experience as a university president.

label: How can it be that ...
body: The same poll showed that most students said their favorite candidate on the list of candidates was someone who has never served as a university president?

label: Evaluate
body:
In essence, given that the students are saying they value experience as a university president, why is their favorite candidate on the list a person with no experience?
- maybe the students have no idea that favorite candidate is inexperienced
- maybe the students prefer picking someone experienced, but it's not such a overwhelming preference that it outweighs other considerations (in other words, maybe their favorite candidate from the list kicks butt in every other category, so she's their favorite candidate despite the fact that she has no experience)
- maybe the list of leading candidates doesn't include anyone experienced

label: Goal
body: Find a way to explain why students most like Candidate X, despite the fact that X has no experience and students would prefer someone with experience.

label: Conclusion
body: Rock music has nothing going for it.

label: Evidence
body:
Rock music [has always been] musically bankrupt and socially destructive, but at least the album covers of rock LPs in the 60s and 70s were great art.
Now, digital music has basically ended the production of LPs.

label: Evaluate
body:
We could anticipate a Missing Link assumption by connecting premise and conclusion language like, "if a genre of music doesn't have musical value, social value, or artistic value, then it's got nothing going for it".
But since the conclusion is so strongly worded, it's also tempting to spitball some objections.
Given that ... rock is musically bankrupt, socially destructive, and no longer has the cool art-on-LP cover thing,
How can we argue that .... rock music does have at least something going for it?
Well, besides the music, the socializing, and the album art ... how about the fact that it gives a political voice to some people? It's a good way to do drugs together, off the streets? It helps plants to grow?
I don't expect any of these to be answers, but we would weaken the argument with any potential use or virtue of rock music, so the author is assuming all kinds of Defending assumptions like, "Rock music is not extremely useful for accelerating the growth of crops".

label: Goal
body:
We anticipated a linking idea, but I don't really think that's what's being tested. I would go to the answers a little fuzzy, thinking:
- if I see what looks like a conditional / linking idea, I'll ask myself "Did the author really go from this idea to that idea?"
- if I see any answer (especially ones with "not"), I'll use the Negation Test. If negating an answer turns it into a weakening objection, then it's correct.

label: Conclusion
body: Babbling turns out to be a linguistic task.

label: Conclusion (So)
body: Some of the planets in oval orbits around distant stars were probably thrown into those orbits by close encounters with other planets orbiting the same stars.

label: Evidence
body:
To test whether babbling was linguistic or random, they filmed the mouth of babbling babies.
Babbling babies open their mouths wider on the right.
Past studies show that nonlinguistic vocal sounds involve opening mouths wider on the left.

label: Evaluate
body:
Our job is to describe the argument in general terms: what type of evidence / how did the parts relate to each other / how did the path to the conclusion work?
This argument relies on a study. In the study they were considering two hypotheses. They got a piece of data that went against one of the hypotheses (based on what had been learned from previous studies). So the author concludes the remaining hypothesis must be the correct one.

label: Goal
body:
If it matches, it's right. So we need to look for mismatching language to eliminate stuff.
Most answers on Method involve two parts:
[doing] the Conclusion [by] presenting Evidence
[inferring] the Conclusion [on the basis of] Evidence
So we need to match the Evidence half to the premises and the Conclusion half to the conclusion.

label: Conclusion
body: Planting large numbers of trees will help us to significantly reduce CO2 emissions over the next 10 years.

label: Evidence (since)
body: Trees absorb carbon dioxide.

label: Evaluate
body:
This argument could otherwise be fed into our Plan / Goal framework. The Goal is to reduce CO2 emissions. The Plan is to plant trees.
We skeptically engage with this by thinking, "How could we go along with the Plan to cut trees, but fail to achieve the Goal of reduced CO2 emissions?"
Maybe the planting of trees involves clearing land or using a lot of machines that themselves emit CO2, so the process of enacting the Plan might increase CO2 emissions.
Maybe trees take like thirty years of growing before they start sucking up any appreciable amount of CO2.

label: Goal
body: Our goal is to find an answer choice that demonstrates why planting trees might not significantly contribute to lowering CO2 emissions within the next decade.

label: Given that ...
body: SUV's are heavy, so in an accident they are safer for their occupants than those of smaller vehicles.

label: How can it be that ...
body: Auto safety experts look at traffic fatality stats and say the increasing popularity of SUVs is an alarming trend?

label: Evaluate / Goal
body:
We need a way of saying that even though the occupants of SUV's are safer than if they were in a smaller car, it's still a bad thing for safety that SUVs are getting more popular.
Maybe there are safety risks from SUV's that apply to people who aren't occupants of the SUV.
Maybe there are safety risks from SUV's that apply to occupants of the SUV, but not when they're in an accident (like maybe SUV's are more likely to let carbon monoxide into the cabin, which can cause lung cancer over time).
We need to find something relating to increased use of SUVs that would connect to a safety risk.

label: Conclusion (implicit)
body:
In anybody really fooled by Sherwood's attempt to campaign as an opponent of higher taxes?
rephrase: Sherwood doesn't oppose higher taxes

label: Evidence
body: For the last 10 years, Sherwood served on the city council, and the city council consistently increased taxes year after year.

label: Evaluate
body:
Given that ... Sherwood served on the city council for 10 years, during which the city council repeatedly increased taxes,
How could we still argue that ... Sherwood sincerely opposes higher taxes?
There are several rebuttals we might make:
- Maybe Sherwood approved of the past tax increases, but now something has changed that makes Sherwood oppose higher taxes (perhaps taxes have been raised high enough that Sherwood is happy with the current tax rate and opposes further increases / or maybe the economic climate has changed so Sherwood doesn't think that raising taxes would be a good choice in this economy)
- Maybe Sherwood always opposed tax increases, but she was outvoted on the city council, so the city council kept raising taxes despite her protests.
Since the argument is essentially arguing, "The city council didn't oppose taxes. Sherwood was a part of that city council. Thus, Sherwood didn't oppose taxes", we could also call this an example of the famous Part vs. Whole flaw.

label: Goal
body: Look for an answer describing the Whole to Part move the author committed, or an answer reconciling the ideas that Sherwood could sincerely oppose higher taxes despite having been on a city council that increased taxes.

label: Curious Fact
body: Why do red admiral butterflies fly in a highly irregular fashion, constantly varying speed and flight path in a way that is clearly not energy efficient?

label: Author's Hypothesis
body: It's because the red admiral, unlike other butterflies, is not poisonous, and so it uses this funky flying style to elude predators.

label: Evaluate
body:
The two pressure points of any Explain Curious Fact conversation are ....
1. Could there be some Alternate Explanation for the curious fact?
2. How plausible is the Author's Explanation?

label: Goal
body:
Since this is Strengthen, we would either rule out an alternate explanation for the red admirals weird flying style (f.e. "they do not fly in weird ways as part of a courtship ritual), or we will add plausibility to the Author's Explanation.
The most common way that LSAT strengthens plausibility of a causal hypothesis is using the "No Cause, No Effect" form. It's essentially the Control Group.
If I wanted to convince you that X causes Y, it would help to hear that "when X is present, Y is present .... and when X goes away, Y goes away".
So we might see an answer like, "The red admiral doesn't start its funky flying until a predator is nearby" or "once the predator leaves, the red admiral stops doing its funky flying."

label: Conclusion 1 (so)
body: Some kind of copyright statute is justified.

label: Evidence
body: Copyright statutes benefit society by providing incentive to produce original works.

label: Conclusion 2
body: Granting copyright protection for the life of the author plus several decades is too long.

label: Evidence (since)
body: The societal benefit from additional years of copyright is more than offset by the society cost.

label: Evidence
body: Many comets orbiting our sun have been thrown into oval orbits by close encounters with planets orbiting our sun.

label: Goal
body: Look for a way to argue that even though this study is true, Neanderthals still would have needed language to create their sophisticated tools the way they did.

label: Evaluate
body:
This is a weird argument because there are two conclusions here, but we would probably assume that the first one was background and that our job is really to support the one in the final sentence.
If we were just spelling out the missing link, it would sound like this:
```
Societal benefit of              Too long a
several decades after   →        period to
death is more than               grant protection
offset by societal cost
```

label: Goal
body: Look for an answer that talks about societal cost outweighing societal benefit as a way to argue that giving copyright protection for decades after an author dies is too long / too much.

label: Curious Fact
body: Why has crime in this city fallen by 20% during my tenure as chief?

label: Chief's Explanation
body: It's because of my policing strategy of using real-time crime data and focusing police resources on the areas with the most crime.

label: Evaluate
body:
Whenever we want to Weaken an Explain the Curious Fact type setup, we either want
1. an Alternate Explanation for the curious fact
or
2. to hurt the plausibility of the Author's Explanation

label: Goal
body:
Let's look for something that provides a different reason why crime has fallen by 20% (e.g. population has decreased / economic opportunities have improved / mandatory minimum sentencing has deterrent effect, etc.)
Or let's look for something that makes it seem implausible that the chief's strategy of using real-time data to focus on where to send police resources wouldn't be doing it (e.g. we were already doing that sort of stuff before the chief arrived / real-time crime data can't be interpreted quickly enough to mobilize police resources in time to stop any more crimes from occurring).

label: Conclusion (then)
body: Concern for the welfare of the people is necessary for the successful governance of Acredia.

label: Evidence
body: When Acredians governments have fallen, their falls have always been during the rule of one who viciously disregards the people's needs.

label: Evaluate
body:
The conclusion is making a bold claim, using wording like "necessary". It's saying that "if you don't have concern for the welfare of the people, then you cannot possibly successfully govern Acredia".
All we would need to beat this conclusion is one example of a Acredian leader who wasn't concerned about the welfare of the people but was still able to successfully govern.
The author's evidence never addresses leaders that were successfully able to govern (maybe one or more of them didn't have concern about the welfare of the people).
Instead, the author tells us that all the people who were unsuccessful leaders of Acredia did not have concern for the people's welfare.
We can't just take a quality that's has been associated with unsuccessful leaders and then suddenly assume that the opposite is necessary for successful leaders.
If I said, "every failed CEO at American Airlines has been right handed", could I conclude, "Thus being left handed is necessary for the successful governance of American Airlines"? Of course not.

label: Goal
body: Let's look for something like "just because quality X has always accompanied outcome Y doesn't mean that the opposite of quality X is necessary for the opposite of outcome Y", whether it's said in abstract or specific terms.

label: Statements
body:
Recent observations fail to confirm earlier ones that apparently showed a comet reservoir far out in our solar system (i.e. recent observations did not provide evidence of a comet reservoir far out in the solar system).
Professor B recognizes this and claims that this nonconfirmation is enough to show that earlier observations were incorrect.
pivot (But)
The recent observations occurred under poor conditions.

label: Evaluate
body:
We have to distinguish between factual claims and attributed opinions sometimes on Inference questions, but the first sentence is both.
Saying that "Professor Bums recognizes X" means both that X is true (according to the speaker, whose statements we are accepting as true) and that Professor Bums believes it.
There isn't any Conditional, Causal, or Mathematical wording in this paragraph but there is a Pivot. Typically, if a Most Supported paragraph ends with a Pivot sentence, the correct answer represents a safely worded way of resolving the tension created by the pivot word. We call that sort of pattern Reconcile the Pivot.
The tension here is that Professor Bums thinks that new observations refute old observations, but the speaker is pointing out that these new observations occurred under poor conditions.
This seems to suggest that the new data points aren't super trustworthy. Would we be a little hasty to toss out the old observations as invalid, based off some sketchy new observations?

label: Goal
body:
The wrong answers will probably go overboard and say, "Thus, the recent observations are worthless. Thus, we should still believe the earlier observations. Thus, there is a comet reservoir far out in the solar system."
But we want something much more moderate, like, "Thus, it may be hasty to deem to old observations as incorrect based on this somewhat questionable new data" or "Thus, we don't have a good grasp right now on whether or not evidence of a comet reservoir exists".

label: Conclusion
body: Society would not be better off if the government enacted laws requiring people to be polite to each other.

label: Evidence
body: Enforcing such laws would create even more problems than does impoliteness.

label: Evaluate
body:
Whenever we read the argument in Role or Main Conclusion, we remind ourselves that in 85% of more of these, the conclusion is earlier than the evidence. Specifically, it's either
- the very first claim
- some sort of rebuttal / pivot
Could this first sentence be the conclusion?
Sure, it sounds like an opinion. "Society would be greatly improved if people stopped being impolite to each other". Does the author support that opinion. It's not a conclusion until it gets supported. Does she tell us why society would be better if people were polite?
No. If there were support for why society would be better if people were more polite, it would sound like, "Being polite to people builds public trust, and society would be greatly improved if the public trusted each other more."
The second sentence has a pivot word, "But", so this is also a ripe contender for being the conclusion. Is this an opinion from our author?
Sure. The opinion is that "enacting laws to make people be polite would not make society better off". Does the author support / defend that claim?
Yes, the final sentence supports it. We wouldn't be better off because enforcing politeness laws would create even more problems than our normal impoliteness does.

label: Goal
body: We're being asked about the second sentence, which was the Main Conclusion. So let's look for "Main Conclusion".

label: Evaluate
body:
Since the author's conclusion is speculating a causal explanation for something, we can use a Curious Fact / Explanation mindset.
Curious Fact ... why do these planets we see have oval orbits?
Author's Explanation ... the planets had some close encounter with another planet orbiting the same star, which threw it into an oval orbit.
We always react to think with the same two questions:
1. Could there be some Alternate Explanation for the curious fact?
2. How plausible is the Author's Explanation?

label: Goal
body:
Since this is Strengthen, we want to either
- rule out some Alternate Explanation for how these distant planets got their oval orbits (e.g. It is very unlikely that these planets just originated with oval orbits / very unlikely that they had a close encounter with a planet orbiting a different star)
or
- increase the plausibility of the Author's Explanation, so any detail that helps us to believe that these planets with oval orbits got that orbit by having a close encounter with a planet orbiting the same star.

label: Conclusion
body: Farming in which crops are irrigated with seawater, if done near oceans, would actually be cheaper than most other irrigated agriculture.

label: Evidence (since)
body: The greatest expense in irrigated agriculture is in pumping water, the pumping costs increase with the distance water is pumped, and the water wouldn't have to be pumped far (if done near oceans).

label: Evaluate
body:
Whenever we read the argument on Role or Main Conclusion, we prime our brain with the expectation that first we'll see the Main Conclusion and then we'll hear the supporting ideas ("upside-down arguments").
In this argument, the first sentence sounds like it might be an opinion, but the author doesn't try to convince us that it's possible to grow crops irrigated with seawater.
Meanwhile, the 2nd claim, that such farming would be cheaper is immediately followed by the Support Indicator 'since' (FABS = for, after all, because, since), which shows us that this 2nd claim is probably the conclusion.
Our theory is confirmed when we see that the final sentence also is supporting that idea that irrigating with ocean water, if done near the ocean, would be cheaper.
The last sentence has two claims, joined by "and". The word 'and' (99% of the time) joins together two supporting claims.

label: Goal
body:
We're being asked about the 2nd to last claim, which is one of our 3 premises.
So look for an answer like, "Partial support for the idea that farming irrigated by seawater, if done near the oceans, would be cheaper than most other irrigated agriculture".

label: Statements
body:
Causal Opinion (critics)
pessimistic news reports about the economy harm the economy by causing people to lose confidence in it.
Causal Opinion (journalists)
In order to do their job well, they can't worry about the effects.
Conditional Fact
```
If it's not a matter of        people don't defer
which people have         →    to journalists
no direct experience
```
We would want to clean up that double-negative in the trigger:
```
it is a matter of              not deferring
which people have         →    to
direct experience               journalist
```
"Except" is like unless, without, until = "if-not"
Jerry hates musicals, except the ones Lin-Manuel makes.
TRANSLATION
```
musical and ~Lin-Manuel   →    Jerry hates
```

label: Evaluate
body:
We have two opinions and one fact. The fact is the most trustworthy thing, and it's Conditional, so we should start there.
Can we apply this conditional to either of the first two sentences? Is there any overlapping information?
Yes, the first sentence and the conditional talk about whether or not someone has "direct experience" of something.
According to the first sentence, everyone has direct experience of the economy every day.
Thus, according to the rule in the third sentence, people would not defer to journalists when it comes to the economy.
Does that inference then take us any further with the Critics' or the Journalists' opinion?
It sounds like the journalists don't have to worry about the effect they're having on people when they write articles about the economy, since people don't defer to journalists on the economy.
And it seems like the critics have little to worry about when it comes to news reports harming the economy by causing people to lose confidence in it. Since people don't defer to journalists on matters of the economy, the news report has no power to change the confidence level that any given person has in the economy.

label: Goal
body:
Look for an answer rewarding us for figuring out that "people don't defer to journalists when it comes to the economy" or an answer that applies that to the critics to say "so I guess the critics have nothing to worry about".
But, as always, beware of strong language and unknown comparisons. And stay flexible.

label: Conclusion
body: The recent accusation of graft in my precinct are unfounded (i.e. there's no good reason to think that there's been any graft in my precinct).

label: Evidence
body:
Gifts of cash
```
or   →   graft
objects > $100
```
No officer in my precinct has ever taken a gift of cash or an object worth more than $100.

label: Evaluate
body:
At first this argument seems pretty compelling. The captain knows with certainty that none of her officers have ever taken the graft-y gifts described in the first sentence.
So we mobilize into Anti-Conclusion mode:
How can we accept that [no officer in this precinct has ever taken such gifts],
but still argue that [there has been graft in this precinct]?
The first loophole I thought of was, "Okay, maybe no officer has ever been guilty of graft, but what about the captain or any other non-officer person working at the precinct?"
But then we might notice that the definition of graft in the first sentence is not exhaustive. The chief has indicated that X or Y count as graft. But no one ever said those are the only two things that count as graft.
Maybe accepting an invitation to sit courtside at a Lakers game is also graft. That's not cash, and that's not an object. But it's definitely a bribe-y type of favor.
The argument has made a Necessary vs. Sufficient move.
We go from thinking in a Sufficient way,
if you do X or Y, you've committed graft
to thinking in a Necessary way,
as long as you avoid X and Y, no graft

label: Goal
body: Look for an answer either making the "what if other things also count as graft" objection or the "what if some non-officer in the precinct has committed graft" objection.

label: Given that ...
body: In every region of the country, the average hourly wage for full-time jobs increased last year.

label: How is it that ...
body: In the country as a whole, the average hourly wage for full-time jobs decreased last year?

label: Evidence
body:
When TV is unavailable, reading goes up among parents and children.
When TV comes back, reading goes back down for both parents and children.

label: Evaluate
body:
This is a tricky mathematical paradox. If the average wage went up in each region, then how could the average wage go down nationally?
Normally, we don't spend too much time up front on Paradox questions trying to guess the answer because there could potentially be a lot of ways to resolve the Paradox. But when it's mathematical, there is often only one way.
In this case, in order for every region's average to go up while the national average went down, we need there to be a net effect of people moving out of regions whose average is higher than the national average into areas whose average is lower than the national average.
Say that the average wage nationally is $25 / hr. Some regions, like San Francisco, will have regional average wage of $30 / hr. Some regions like, like Oklahoma City, will have a regional average wage of $20 / hr.
Let's say, last year, OKC's average rose to $21 / hr and SF's average rose to $31 / hr.
We'd expect the national average to start creeping towards $26 / hr. But now consider the effect if tons of people move from SF to OKC.
Someone who used to be making $30 / hr in SF now lives in Austin and makes $21 / hr.
When it comes to the national average hourly wage, people who made $30 / hr last year but make $21 / hr this year are going to bring that average down.
Or in case this makes more sense, suppose that SF is a region with a $30 / hr average wage. OKC is a region with a $20 / hr average wage. Bob lives in SF and makes $28 / hr.
Now he moves to OKC and makes $25 / hr. What has he done to the average wage in SF, OKC, and nationally?
He raised the average wage in SF, because if the average is 30 and you get rid of a data point that is 28, then that will boost the average. (If you kick a teenager off your team, then the average age of your team will go up).
He raised the average wage in OKC, because the average there was $20, but he makes $25. And he lowered the national average, because he went from making $28 to $25.

label: Goal
body: We need to hear that people moved out of higher paying areas into lower paying areas.

label: Information
body:
math-y / contrast
35% of the recently dead people who had schizophrenia had damage to subplate (a structure of nerve cells).
0% of the recently dead people who didn't have schizophrenia had damage to subplate.
causal
The damage must have occurred prior to the 2nd fetal trimester.
During that period, the development of the connections between different parts of the brain are controlled by the subplate.

label: Evaluate
body:
The fact that the paragraph starts by establishing a weird difference that is only found in the brains of the schizophrenics should pique our curiosity: what does it mean that 35% of schizophrenics had damage to this subplate but none of the brains without schizophrenia had it?
The last two ideas make it seem like if you had a damaged subplate prior to the 2nd fetal trimester, it could mess up the development of connections between the different parts of the brain.
Since outside knowledge of schizophrenia tells us that such patients often seem to have "multiple personalities", you wonder whether this paragraph is trying to make us speculate that schizophrenia is caused (in some cases) by damage to the subplate, resulting in a disconnected brain.

label: Goal
body: It seems hard to guess exactly where this one is going, so let's look for the most supportable answer, being wary of answers that are Too Strong, make an Unsupported Comparison, or bring up something Out of Scope.

label: Given that ...
body: Putting a GPS chip on all the cattle in a herd is far more expensive than other means of keeping cattle in their pastures (such as fences).

label: How can it be that ...
body: Ranchers will purchase the device at its current price.

label: Evaluate / Goal
body:
In order for ranchers to be motivated to buy this device, the steep price tag has to be worth it to them.
Maybe you spend more money up front, but you save money trying to round up stray cattle later (since the GPS device basically steers the cow back towards home).
Or maybe there's some other additional value ranchers get out of having the GPS chip in their cattle that will incentivize this purchase.

label: Conclusion (therefore)
body: It's more economical to shop at a food co-op than at a supermarket.

label: Evidence
body: Food co-ops are a type of consumer cooperative. Consumer cooperatives offer the same products as other stores, usually more cheaply.

label: Evaluate
body:
Given that ... food co-ops are a type of CC, and CC's usually offer the same products as other stores but more cheaply.
How could we still argue that ... it is not more economical to shop at a food co-op than a supermarket?
Well, it seems possible that food co-ops could be an exception to the general rule that CC's are usually more cheap than their alternative.
(It helps me that any time I've gone to a food co-op, I've felt like the prices were a little higher than my local grocery store).

label: Goal
body:
We seem to want something like like
P1: X is a type of A.
P2: A's are usually more B than ~A's.
C: X will be more B than [example of ~A].
In a more conversational sense, we're objecting that, "Just because things of that type are usually a certain way doesn't mean that everything of that type is automatically that way".

label: Conclusion (rebuttal)
body:
This is a mistake.
rephrase: The fact that people can drive their cars around the railroad crossing arms and get into an accident does not make these accidents partly the fault of the railroad company.

label: Evidence
body:
A licensed driver is a capable adult who should know better.
The gates give clear warning of oncoming trains.

label: Evaluate / Goal
body:
The key wording we're trying to prove is that the railroad company is not partly at fault, so we just need a rule that says, "If such-and-such is true, then you're not at fault".
We have two possible things we could say:
"If the gates give clear warning, then the railroad company isn't at fault".
or
"If a licensed driver is a capable adult who should know better (than to try to circumvent the crossing gates when an oncoming train is coming), then the railroad company isn't at fault".

label: Conclusion (So)
body: If a survey is well constructed, survey respondents' desire to meet surveyors' expectations has no effect on the survey's results.

label: Evidence
body: Even though people often try to give answers that the surveyor expects to hear, in well-constructed surveys the questions are worded so as to provide respondents with no indication of which answers the surveyor might expect.

label: Evaluate
body:
This is a pretty plausible argument so we might not have any organic reactions to it. Hence, we switch into Anti-Conclusion debate mode:
Given that ... the questions are worded so as to provide respondents with no indication of which answers the surveyor might expect,
How could it still be that ... respondents' desire to please the surveyor's expectations could still have some effect?
Maybe the respondents just come to their own conclusions about what answer they think would please the surveyor, and thus answer that way.
So even though the questions weren't designed to indicate a preferred answer, just like a Rorschach test, we can all see in it what we want to.

label: Goal
body: Look for an answer that addresses the possibility that even though the questions don't signal some preferred answer, the respondents desire to meet surveyors' expectations could still tilt the data somehow.

label: Conclusion
body: The availability of TV reduces the amount of reading that kids do.

label: Evaluate
body:
This conclusion is Causal (reduces).
X's presence reduces Y's presence
There are two premises, and they play off the idea of Covariation.
when X is absent, the level of Y goes up
when X returns, the level of Y goes back down

label: Goal
body: Let's look for a causal conclusion, and then two premises that say "when the supposed cause is absent, the effect is absent / when the supposed cause returns, the effect returns".

label: Setup Claims
body:
causal-conditional (when X happens, so do Y and Z)
```
If an industry rapidly  →   ppl with needed skills
applies new tech             and brains prosper
                              while others lose jobs
```
pivot (but)
conditional (those who are X will eventually be Y)
```
Resist new tech    →   superceded by those
                        that don't (and all your
                        employees lose jobs)
```

label: The Blank (obviously, then = conclusion)
body: Resisting the application of new tech ....

label: Evaluate
body:
We know with Logical Completion that when we're picking something to be the Conclusion of the paragraph (as we usually are), then we want a safely worded way of pulling together the ideas that have been mentioned.
And on all Inference questions, when the final idea begins with a pivot word (But, Yet, However), that's a strong clue that the test wants us to reconcile that pivot fact with the thing that came before it.
So we have two ideas we need to reconcile / synthesize:
- if a business rapidly adopts new tech, many lose their jobs
but
- if a business resists new tech, then all the employees lose their jobs.
Notice, that we're focusing on the Overlapping Concept (people losing jobs).

label: Goal
body:
It looks like it's better to adopt new tech (and only have some workers lose jobs) than to resist new tech (and have all your workers lose jobs).
However, since the blank is prefaced by the idea of "resisting new tech", we'd probably complete that sentence like,
"resisting new tech is worse than rapidly applying new tech, when it comes to jobs lost"
or "resisting new tech causes a higher proportion of jobs to be lost than does rapidly applying new tech".

label: Given that ...
body: Home ownership is a sign of economic prosperity.

label: How can it be that ...
body: Across various regions of Europe and North America, high levels of home ownership correspond with high levels of unemployment.

label: Evaluate
body:
The paradox here seems to be, "If you're unemployed, you don't have money. You need money to buy a house (that's why it's a sign of economic prosperity). So if you're unemployed and don't have money, then how could you buy a house?"
And yet, in areas where lots of people own homes, lots of people are unemployed.
Maybe the homeowners are not the same as the unemployed. In other words, maybe in these areas 80% of people own homes (which is higher than average) and 15% of people are unemployed (which is also higher than average). But those two categories don't necessarily have to overlap. We would just need a story that allows us to explain how 80% of the residents are making enough money to buy homes but 15% of them can't even find a job.

label: Goal
body: We need a way to understand how cities with high unemployment could also have high rates of people who own homes.

label: Conclusion (causal hypothesis)
body: When a hornworm's first meal is nightshade, its taste receptors become habituated to a chemical unique to nightshade, making other foods unappealing.

label: Evidence
body:
If a hornworm starts with nightshade, it won't eat anything else forever.
But if it starts with a different plant, it will eat other sorts of plants.

label: Evaluate
body:
The second we see "hypothesis" in the question stem, we know this argument will have the Explain Curious Fact structure.
CURIOUS FACT - why do hornworms get hooked on nightshade if it's their first meal?
EXPLANATION - nightshade has a unique chemical, indioside D, which changes the taste receptors of the hornworm, making other food taste nasty.
We can strengthen this type of argument by
1) ruling out an alternate explanation for the curious fact
or
2) helping the plausibility of the author's explanation
While alternate explanation answers are more common on Weaken / Flaw / NA / Evaluate, plausibility answers are more common on Strengthen. In particular, they love to strengthen with a "no cause, no effect" scenario. Like, "if you remove the indioside D, then a hornworm no longer gets hooked on nightshade".

label: Goal
body: Find an answer that reinforces the plausibility of the author's explanation (or maybe that rules out an alternate reason for getting hooked on nightshade).

label: Conclusion (so / clearly)
body:
My boss is incorrect.
rephrase: My presentation to the accounting team should not have included more detail about profit projections.

label: Evidence
body: People's attention tends to wander when they are presented with too much detail.

label: Evaluate
body:
Given that ... people's attention tends to wander when they're presented with too much detail,
How could we still argue that .... the presentation should have included more detail about profit projections?
Maybe the presentation included no details! We're only worried about people's attention wandering when we present too much detail, but there might be a happy middle ground. Maybe the employee provided too little detail, and providing "more detail" wouldn't immediately take the presentation into the realm of having "too much" detail. It would just move it into the realm of having "the right amount of detail / the sweet spot between having too much and too little".

label: Goal
body: Look for an answer saying, "Even though too much detail is a problem, it's possible that this presentation was so low on details that it could have benefited from more detail without it suddenly becoming too much."

label: Conclusion (this demonstrates)
body: The local media show too much deference toward public figures.

label: Evidence
body:
