They long heralded Clemens as an honest politician, but were proven wrong when Clemens was caught up in a corruption scandal.
And even the editor of the local paper admitted that her reporters neglected to follow leads that might have exposed the scandal earlier.

label: Evidence
body: Even though TA's teach classes (and get paid for it), the sole purpose of having them do stuff for the university is to give them money that will fund their education. If they could afford their education without the TA income or if they weren't pursuing their education, they wouldn't hold their teaching posts at all.

label: Evaluate
body:
Whenever we do Main Conclusion (or Role) we remind ourselves that the Conclusion is usually earlier than the Support. The conclusion, on these two question types, is most often found in these two places:
- First sentence
- Pivot / Rebuttal idea
This argument begins with a fact, so we know the first sentence isn't the conclusion. The 3rd sentence has a rebuttal tinge to it, since we're saying that the local media have been bad.
We can also lean on the conclusion indicator wording we're getting. The obvious conclusion indicators (so, thus, therefore, hence) are usually not going to show us where the conclusion is on a Main Conclusion question (that would be too easy, unless it's a really easy problem).
But we might see more obscure conclusion indicator wording like,
this shows that
this demonstrates that
this suggests that
this reveals that

label: Goal
body:
Once we've found the conclusion, we've done the hard part. Now we just have to find a meaning match for the 3rd sentence.
It is sometimes useful to limber up our language faculties by trying to think of our own equivalent paraphrase:
- "the local media's deference toward public figures is excessive"
- "when it comes to public figures, the local media is too trusting"

label: Conclusion
body: There must be good reason to think that the defendant isn't completely innocent.

label: Evidence
body: If the defendant were completely innocent, then the prosecutor wouldn't have brought charges.

label: Evaluate
body:
By contrapositive, since we can tell that the prosecutor did bring charges (there was a jury trial), that would mean that the defendant was not completely innocent.
So, wait — did we just concede the conclusion to the author? That's the opposite of our goal.
The problem is, if we accept the conditional in the last sentence, we have no way to argue around the logic. It's the same problem we face in a Circular argument.
for example:
Since no flavor of candy is as good as toffee,
toffee is the best flavor of candy.
If we accept the premise of this Circular argument (no flavor of candy is as good as toffee), then we have no way to avoid drawing the conclusion that toffee is the best flavor.
That's why Circular arguments are cheating.
So the author's move in that final sentence feels like a Circular one in which the author is seemingly assuming the truth of the conclusion. Although technically it's not really circular since it's not repeating the conclusion; it's just inventing a ridiculous rule that prosecutors always have good reasons.
In real life, we would find the last sentence of this paragraph the most objectionable, because we don't have to accept that in 100% of cases where the prosecutor brings charges there is good reason to believe that the defendant is somewhat guilty.
Maybe there are dirty prosecutors who sometimes bring charges in order to exact revenge on the guy sleeping with their husband. Maybe there are complicit prosecutors who bring charges against a powerful person's political enemies, as a way to make those people look less trustworthy.

label: Goal
body: We can either look for an answer calling out the unfair premise in the final sentence, or complain that the author is undermining his own conclusion with acknowledgements like "strong alibi / considerable exculpatory evidence / quick acquittal", or we can point out the possibility that the author's extreme premise could be wrong ... i.e., it's possible that sometimes prosecutors bring charges even though there isn't any good reason to think the defendant is somewhat guilty.

label: Conclusion
body: The critics argument should be rejected (it's not legit to say that Sauk lacks aesthetic merit just because he stole his hero's style and used it for a political purpose his hero would reject).

label: Evidence
body: Sure, Sauk stole the style from his mentor and the mentor wouldn't approve of Sauk's politics, but no one has shown that his writings are any less subtle or powerfully crafted than those of his mentor.

label: Evaluate
body:
The author is rebutting a position by conceding the points made in support of that position (yes, stole style and had potentially objectionable political views) but arguing that they're not sufficient to prove the conclusion because something crucial is missing.
In this case, the something-crucial is that the people claiming Sauk's writings don't have aesthetic merit haven't really delved into analysis of the writings themselves. They seem caught up in tangential concerns, whereas this author thinks we should evaluate the material itself.

label: Goal
body:
This question stem already has the Conclusion part baked into the question stem. It's cueing us up with "on the grounds that", which always indicates we're referring to the evidence.
So we need the best match we can find for, "it has yet to be shown that these facts make his writing any less subtly or powerfully crafted than those of his esteemed mentor".

label: Principle (unless = if not)
body:
```
if a new manufacturing
process hasn't been used
safely for more than a year          safety
at another factory            →      inspector
and                                   should not
it won't demonstrably                approve it
increase safety here
```

label: Application's Conclusion
body: The new proposed welding process should be not be approved by the safety inspector.

label: Application's Evidence (for)
body: The process cannot be shown to increase safety at the factory.

label: Evaluate
body:
The policy, in stripped down form, is saying "You shouldn't do X unless Y or Z is true". We could rephrase that as, "In order to do X, it must be that Y or Z is true", which would look like this:
X → Y or Z
Or in the language of the argument:
```
should      →   used safely elsewhere
approve         or will demonstrably help
```
We are motivated to contrapose this rule for two reasons:
1. We always put the "judgy, normative, evaluative" label on the right side of the arrow, so we want the concept of should/shouldn't on the right.
2. We want the right side of our principle to line up with the conclusion it's designed to support, and the conclusion is that "the safety inspector should not approve the new welding process".
So when contrapose, the "or" turns to "and".
```
not safely used elsewhere            should
and                            →     not
not demonstrably help                approve
```
The application has established the 2nd idea from the trigger. If "it cannot be shown to increase safety at the factory", then we know "it does not demonstrably increase safety".
But the application failed to establish the 1st idea from the trigger.

label: Goal
body: We just need to know that the new welding process "has not been used safely for more than a year at another factory".

label: Conclusion
body: TA's should not be considered university employees and thus be entitled to the usual employee benefits.

label: Evaluate
body:
Given That TA's wouldn't have their jobs if they didn't need money to go to school where they teach,
How Can We Still Argue That TA's should be considered university employees and thus be entitled to usual employee benefits?
Maybe there's a law that requires it. Maybe common decency argues in favor of it?
Does it really matter why the TA's have the job they have? If they're teaching like other teachers, shouldn't they be considered employees and receive benefits?
The administrator must be arguing, "we have enough money to pay them for teaching so that they can afford to go to school here, but we don't have enough money to pay them for teaching and pay for their healthcare benefits."
So I guess we could even weaken by showing that the school is not on a tight budget.

label: Goal
body: Look for something that would help us argue that TA's should be considered university employees and thus be entitled to usual employee benefits.

label: Conclusion (So)
body: If many people in our largest cities were to move to rural areas, air pollution in the country as a whole would be reduced.

label: Evidence
body: Most of the air pollution in this country comes from our largest cities. These large cities would pollute less if they were less populated.

label: Evaluate
body:
Wouldn't the small cities pollute more if these people from large cities move there?
The author seems to think that by reducing the problem of pollution in the largest cities, we will have decreased air pollution in the country as a whole. But if we send a bunch of people to small cities, then those smaller cities will start to have more air pollution than they used to.
It's almost like if I said, "Most of my debt comes from student loans. If I paid off this student loan, I would have less debt overall. So if I took out a second mortgage on my home so that I could pay off my student loans then I would have less debt overall."
That's crazy talk! If I borrowed another $200k from my mortgage to pay off $200k of student loan, I've just moved my debt from a student loan account to a mortgage account.
Similarly, if people move from the biggest cities to smaller cities, then they will move their pollution with them. The pollution in the large city account will go down, but the pollution in the small city account will go up, and the country's overall pollution will probably be the same.

label: Goal
body: Let's look for something where an author is moving a problem from one place to another, and concluding that the overall incidence of the problem is therefore reduced.

label: Conclusion (Thus)
body:
These other buyers were mistaken in saying that safety was important to them.
rephrase: safety was not important to these buyers

label: Evidence
body: They relied on advertisements and promotional materials, rather than consulting objective sources of vehicle safety information.

label: Evaluate / Goal
body:
We know we need to prove that "safety was not important" to a group of buyers who didn't consult objective sources of vehicle safety info; they relied on ads and promo materials.
So there are two Missing Link style answers we could anticipate:
"If you didn't consult objective sources of vehicle safety info, then safety was not important to you"
or
"If you relied on ads and promo materials, then safety was not important to you".

label: Conclusion (Thus)
body: An organism incapable of planned locomotion does not have a central nervous system.

label: Evidence
body: An organism capable of planned locomotion must be able to form an internal representation of its environment and to send messages to muscles, both of which requires a central nervous system.

label: Evaluate
body:
Whenever we're doing Flaw and we come across Conditional Logic, we immediately start suspecting that the argument will commit the #1 famous flaw, Necessary vs. Sufficient, in which the author presents some conditional logic premise that he then applies in an illegal reversed or negated fashion.
Both premises stated requirements, using the necessary indicator "must".
We read conditionals like A → B two main ways:
1. if A, then B
2. A requires B
There are other ways too ("all A's are B" / "A implies B"), but these two are the most common and useful.
So if we're reading that "planned locomotion requires internal representation and message-sending to muscles", it would look like this:
```
Planned         →   internal rep
locomotion           + msg-sending
```
When the 2nd sentence adds on another requirement, we can keep the chain going.
```
Planned      →   internal rep    →   central
locomotion        + msg-sending       nerv sys.
```
The two premises combine to show us that "Planned locomotion requires a central nervous system".
```
capable of planned   →   central
locomotion                nerv sys.
```
The conclusion is an illegal negation of this:
```
incapable of planned   →   no central
locomotion                   nerv sys.
```

label: Goal
body:
Look for an answer calling out the illegal negation, which LSAT describes as confusing a Necessary and a Sufficient condition.
Or look for an answer pointing out the possibility that an organism could have a central nervous system and still be incapable of planned locomotion (a central nervous system is required for locomotion but it doesn't guarantee an organism would have it.)

label: Conclusion (Thus)
body: To work most effectively throughout their ascents, all rockets must have both short nozzles and long nozzles on their engines.

label: Evidence
body:
To work most effectively, rocket engines need their exhaust gases to be the same pressure as the surrounding atmosphere.
A short nozzle matches the pressure of low altitudes, whereas a long nozzle matches the pressure in the thin upper atmosphere.

label: Evaluate
body:
Because the conclusion is conditional "to do X, it must be that Y", we might be wise to guess that LSAT is testing a missing link. Is there any new term in the conclusion?
Throughout their ascents / all rockets is new. The evidence talked about short/long nozzles and defined what it means for a rocket to work most effectively.
You need a short nozzle for low altitudes and a long nozzle for the thin upper atmosphere. So I guess the author is assuming that "throughout their ascents, all rockets will have exhaust gases escaping at low altitudes and at the altitude of the thin upper atmosphere."
If we were trying to use an Objection mindset, we'd be thinking, "How can I argue that some rockets can work most effectively throughout their ascent, without needing both short and long nozzles?"
Maybe some rockets only ascend to low altitudes, so they could get away with just having short nozzles. Maybe some rockets only "turn on" once they reach the thin upper atmosphere, so they could get by with just long nozzles.

label: Evaluate
body: "Many writers more senior than many programmers" doesn't establish that average writer seniority is higher; we need the average comparison.

label: Goal
body: Look for an answer dealing with the new Conclusion language (throughout their ascents, all rockets) establishing that we will be dealing with both low altitudes and the thin upper atmosphere, or look for an answer ruling out an objection like the ones we made.

label: Conclusion
body: Manufacturers of kids' toys shouldn't overstate the dangers of their products.

label: Evidence
body:
```
if overstating dangers          product-warning
doesn't reduce injuries   →     labels shouldn't
                                 overstate
```
Manufacturers don't overstate dangers for the sake of injuries; they do it for the sake of lawsuits.

label: Evaluate
body:
The author provided us with a conditional rule (only if = right side, Necessary, indicator), and her conclusion matches the outcome of that rule.
So did her evidence establish the trigger of that rule? Did she establish that overstating dangers on labels doesn't reduce injuries?
Nope. She just said that manufacturers overstate dangers for a different reason. But their overstating may still be having the effect of reducing injuries!
This is probably the 11th or 12th most common famous flaw:
Intent vs. Consequence (i.e. motive vs. result)
Even though the manufacturers aren't intending to reduce injuries, that may still be the result/consequence of their action.

label: Goal
body: Look for an answer raising the possibility that the overstated warning are reducing injuries, calling out the author's assumption that the warnings aren't reducing injuries, or pointing our how the author is assuming that "if the manufacturer's intent in doing Action X wasn't to bring about injury-reduction, then the result of Action X won't bring about injury-reduction."

label: Conclusion (Thus)
body: Drinking tea boosted the participants' immune system defenses.

label: Evidence
body: In a study, the people who drank tea but no coffee had immune systems that took half as long to respond to germs as did the blood cells of people who drank coffee but no tea.

label: Evaluate
body:
This has all the making of an Explain Curious Fact type argument, since we're citing a study's correlation in the evidence and then concluding something causal (X boosted Y).
Curious Fact ... why was tea w/o coffee correlated with faster immune response times than was coffee w/o tea?
Author's Explanation ... the tea is doing something good to the immune system.
We always react to this type of argument by asking two questions:
1. could there be some Alternate Explanation for the curious fact?
2. how plausible is the Author's Explanation?

label: Goal
body:
The correct answer will either rule out a different explanation for why the tea drinkers had faster immune responses (they were not taking more multivitamins than the coffee drinkers / they were not getting more sleep and exercise / etc.).
Or it will provide something that needs to be true for the author's explanation to be plausible (certain chemicals in tea can have an affect on the immune system / the tea drinkers didn't already have this superior immune response before they started drinking the tea).

label: Conclusion (thus)
body: Semiplaning monohull's will probably be profitable.

label: Evidence
body:
Semiplaning monohull's are faster than conventional ships.
And even though it will be more expensive to travel on Semiplaning monohull's than on conventional ships, it was like that when jet airplanes first came out (they were more expensive than conventional planes), but jets were still able to be profitable (because they were faster and more reliable).

label: Evaluate
body:
We're being asked about the 2nd sentence. Is it Main Conclusion, Support, Opposing, or Neutral?
The main conclusion is the last sentence, "Semiplaning monohull's will probably be profitable".
Is it support for that?
Why will they be profitable? Because ...
"traveling on Semiplaning monohull's will be much more expensive than on conventional ships"?
No that doesn't make sense. When something costs more, all other things being equal, it will be less desirable in the marketplace.
So this is an Opposing idea.
The author is conceding a downside to Semiplaning monohull's, but then saying, "if it follows the same pattern as with jet airplanes, even though it's more expensive it can still be profitable."

label: Goal
body: Let's look for something like, "The author acknowledges an opposing point to his conclusion that semiplaning monohulls will probably be profitable".

label: Conclusion (therefore)
body: Paraguay is likely the place where mate originated.

label: Evidence
body: There are more varieties of it found in Paraguay than anywhere else, and it is used more widely there than anywhere else.

label: Evaluate
body:
On a basic Linking level, this argument seems to think,
"If the most varieties of X and most usage of X is found in place Y, then place Y is where X originated."
That, of course, doesn't have to be true. Something could originate in one place / one culture but then REALLY take off in popularity somewhere else.
We could potentially construe this as an Explain the Curious Fact type argument as well.
Curious Fact .. Why do we find more varieties / more usage of mate in Paraguay than anywhere else?
Author's Explanation ... Because that's where mate originated (and so there has been more time for spin-off varieties to develop? more time for it to become a stable of their culture?)

label: Goal
body: We want to either rule out an alternate explanation for where mate originated, rule out an alternate explanation for why Paraguay has the most varieties / usage of mate, or boost the plausibility that mate originated in Paraguay.

label: Curious Fact
body: From 1996 to 2004, the average family income in a certain country decreased by 10% (adjusted for inflation).

label: Opponents' Explanation
body: This is because the ruling party during that time mismanaged the economy.

label: Goal
body: We're supposed to find and eliminate four answers that either point to an Alternate Explanation for why average family income decreased by 10% during that 8 year span, or that make it seem less plausible that the ruling party mismanaged the economy during that time span.

label: Conclusion (So)
body: Amateur gardeners who use the phases of the moon are less likely to lose plants to a frost.

label: Evidence
body: Amateur gardeners who plant during the first warm spell of spring can lose plants when a frost follows.

label: Goal
body: Find the question whose answer would tell us how average programmer seniority compares to average writer seniority.

label: Evaluate
body:
The conclusion is comparative. Those who use "phases of the moon" are less likely to lose plants to a frost. Less likely than whom?
It has to be the people from the previous sentence, the ones who plant during the first warm spell of spring.
Why are "moon phase" gardeners less likely to lose plants to a frost than "first warm spell" gardeners?
The argument doesn't identify anything that "moon phase" gardeners are doing that's better. We just know that they plant based on the phases of the moon.

label: Goal
body: Look for something like, "when you plant based on phases of the moon, you're less likely to lose plants to frost than when you plant during the first warm spell of spring".

label: Statements
body:
Math-y
70% of tourism profit in developing countries goes to foreign owners of tourist businesses.
The more establish a country becomes as a tourist destination, the higher a proportion of tourism bucks get exported to the foreign owners.
Causal (counteract this effect)
Pivot (However)
Tourists can counteract this effect by obtaining accommodations and other services directly from local people.

label: Evaluate
body:
When an Inference stimulus Ends with a Pivot, it's usually a strong clue that the correct answer will be some same synthesis of the Pivot idea with some idea(s) that came before it.
It would be tempting here to slide into should territory here with our prediction. When we hear about foreign owners getting increasing richer off developing countries, it rankles our woke consumerism instinct and makes us think, "Tourists should only buy stuff or pay money to businesses that are locally owned."
But Inference is asking what we can derive and there's no should on the page.

label: Goal
body: Look for something safely worded reflects the synthesis of "most tourism profit flows out of the country where the money is spent / consumers could limit that to some extent by choosing to spend their money on locally owned businesses".

label: Conclusion (therefore)
body: It's impossible to be sure that the recent decline in those amphibian populations is due to industrial pollution.

label: Evidence
body: Most amphibian species' populations vary greatly from year to year because of natural variations in the weather.

label: Evaluate
body:
The Linking assumption for this argument would just be "If Premise, Then Conclusion":
If most populations of a group of species vary greatly from year to year due to weather, then it's impossible to be sure that any decline is due to pollution.
Since that seems like an unlikely answer, we should probably shift into Objection mode, trying to think of a weakening idea that the correct answer might rule out (a Defender style answer).
Given that ... most amphibian populations vary greatly from year to year because of natural variations in the weather,
How could we say that ... it is possible to be sure that this recent decline in certain amphibian populations is due to industrial pollution?
Maybe we could say that the recent declines don't resemble the sort of declines that are caused by natural variations in the weather -- they're way steeper / they happen at the wrong time of the year / they accelerate at a much faster pace / etc.
Maybe we could say that these declines happened right after the industrial pollution started. They stop happening whenever pollution is lighter. They basically ebb and flow in perfect tandem with industrial pollution.

label: Goal
body:
We might see an answer linking "natural variations from year to year" with "impossible to be sure that declines are due to pollution".
But more likely we'll see an answer that, if negated, turns into an objection. Whenever we're anticipating a Defender type answer, we're especially tantalized by answers that are ruling out an idea with wording like "not / no".

label: Premise
body: Among Trinidadian guppies, large-spotted males attract more mates (good for procreation) but small-spotted males avoid predators better.

label: Premise
body: In waters with abundant predators, only small-spotted guppies live to maturity.

label: Anticipate
body: Large spots help with mating but, in dangerous waters, get the guppy killed before he can mate. So a trait that aids procreation (large spots) actually hinders procreation in some environments. The same trait helps and hurts depending on context.

label: Goal
body: An answer expressing this generalization: a trait helpful for procreation can hinder it in certain environments.

label: Argument
body: Large spots aid mating but get guppies eaten in predator-heavy waters. So large spots help procreation in safe waters and hurt it in dangerous ones.

label: Goal
body: An answer saying a procreation-helping trait can hurt procreation in some environments.

label: Argument
body: Here's the situation. Big spots are great for guppy mating — they attract females. But in waters full of predators, big spots get the male killed before he can mate. The small-spotted guppies survive and pass on their genes; the big-spotted ones get eaten.

label: Anticipate
body:
So big spots help procreation in some environments (safe ones) but actually hurt it in others (dangerous ones). The same trait works for or against the same goal depending on context.
Think of being tall in a crowd. Helps you see over people, but bad if there's a low ceiling. Same trait, different effect by environment.

label: Goal
body: An answer that captures this idea: a trait that aids procreation in one environment can undermine it in another.

label: Programmer's argument
body: The 20% pay difference (writers earn more) is unfair and intolerable.

label: Executive's argument
body: Salary is tied to seniority, and many writers have more seniority than many programmers, so the difference is acceptable.

label: Evaluate
body: The executive's defense relies on writers being more senior on average than programmers. But "many writers have more seniority than many programmers" is weaker than it sounds — it's consistent with writers and programmers having similar average seniority, or even programmers being more senior on average. To know whether the seniority-based pay system actually justifies a 20% gap, we need to know how the average seniority of the two groups compares.

label: Goal
body: Find the answer that targets this comparison: the average seniority of programmers versus the average seniority of technical writers.

label: Programmer
body: 20% pay gap is unfair.

label: Executive
body: Pay tracks seniority, and many writers are more senior, so the gap is fine.

label: Evaluate
body:
The executive's response is shaky. "Many writers have more seniority than many programmers" sounds reasonable, but it's not actually a strong claim. You could have a few super-senior writers and a few brand-new programmers, but the averages for the two groups could be roughly the same — in which case the seniority story doesn't justify a 20% gap at all.
To evaluate the executive's defense, we'd need to know how the average seniority of writers compares to the average seniority of programmers. If the averages are similar, the seniority story breaks down.

label: Goal
body: Find the question that gets at the average seniority comparison between the two groups.

label: Premise
body: In polluted industrial English cities during the Industrial Revolution, two plant diseases—black spot, which infects roses, and tar spot, which infects sycamore trees—disappeared.

label: Conclusion
body: It is likely that air pollution eradicated these diseases.

label: Evaluate
body: The argument mistakes correlation for causation. To strengthen this argument the correct answer should rule out an alternative cause, find another example where the cause is present and so is the effect, or find another example where the cause is absent and the effect is absent.

label: Given
body:
Many scholars are puzzled about who created the seventeenth-century abridgment of Shakespeare's Hamlet contained in the First Quarto.
Two facts about the work shed light on this question.
First, the person who undertook the abridgment clearly did not possess a copy of Hamlet.
Second, the abridgment contains a very accurate rendering of the speeches of one of the characters, but a slipshod handling of all the other parts.

label: Conclusion
body:
The criticism that there's too little text, given the amount of music, in Handel's da capo arias is wrong (refuted).
rephrase: Even given the amount of music in this piece, it's okay for there to be so little text.

label: Evidence
body: Yes, the text repeats a ton, but that repetition serves a vital function, allowing the audience to focus on the music itself, which can speak to audiences of any language.

label: Evaluate
body:
On Main Conclusion questions, the conclusion is almost always found in one of two places:
- the very first sentence
- after some "but / yet / however" rebuttal
Knowing that tendency helps to locate the conclusion here. The argument starts with "many critics", which potentially foreshadows a rebuttal. And then the "Yet" is one of the typical pivots.
The other indicator is the colon: <--- see? Colons introduce support.
Kathleen's desk is a mess: she has pens and paperclips and coffee stains everywhere.
So even if we don't count the "I refute this criticism" as the conclusion, we would use the "repetition serves a vital function". Why should we believe that? Because, [all the stuff after the colon].

label: Goal
body: Find an answer that either sounds like "this criticism is wrong" or one that sounds like "the repetition serves a vital function".

label: Statements
body:
conditionals (only = right side)
When it comes to corporate managers
```
Solicit design   →   believe unlikely
proposal              to go bankrupt
believe unlikely  →   very large
to go bankrupt         companies
```
facts
Boxe has a near monopoly in the corporate market.
Boxe has never won a prestigious award for its corporate work, whereas several small design companies have.

label: Evaluate
body:
We're given two conditionals that chain together, so it's likely that the correct answer will reward our ability to connect those. Can we apply them to any of the facts we learned?
We know that if corporate managers are soliciting all this design work from Baxe (which we can tell from the fact that they have a near monopoly in the corporate market), then corporate managers apparently believe that Baxe is unlikely to go bankrupt, which means that Baxe is a very large company.
Since we also know that Baxe hasn't won any awards for their corporate work, we could infer some Trait Overlap type inference like, "some very large companies haven't won any awards for their corporate work".
The fact that some small design companies have won awards for their corporate work is interesting, because if a company is small (not very large), then corporate managers aren't confident the company won't go bankrupt, and so they won't contract with such companies.
It's kind of confusing that small companies won't get contracts with corporate managers but are still wining awards for their corporate work.

label: Goal
body:
Find the most provable claim. Be wary of language that's Too Strong, Unknown Comparisons, or Unmentioned ideas.
Perhaps the correct answer will be applying the conditional chain to either Baxe or to the small companies that have won awards.

label: Conclusion
body: The big asteroid that hit Chicxulub was probably not responsible for most of the final dinosaur extinctions.

label: Evidence
body: Major asteroid impacts kill a lot of stuff near the impact site, but there's not much evidence they'd have a worldwide effect. In fact, there have even been bigger asteroids hitting Earth, when there weren't any contemporaneous extinctions.

label: Evaluate
body:
Given That asteroid strikes aren't known to have worldwide effect (just to kill animals locally)
How Could We Argue That the big asteroid that hit Chicx was responsible for most of the final dinosaur extinctions?
Hmmm, maybe the remaining dinosaurs were all having some sort of Burning Man in that area of Mexico? They got together for a party and so the asteroid was able to wipe them all out at once?
Maybe even though there's little evidence for a worldwide effect, there's enough of a local or regional effect to kill off the dinosaurs?
Maybe it does something to their food supply?

label: Goal
body: Look for an answer that allows to make a causal story in which this asteroid strike leads to the extinction of most of the remaining dinosaurs.

label: Evidence
body:
In a sample containing 1,000 peanuts from lot A and 1,000 peanuts from lot B, 50 of the peanuts from lot A were found to be infected with *Aspergillus*.
Two hundred of the peanuts from lot B were found to be infected with *Aspergillus*.

label: Conclusion
body: Therefore, infection with *Aspergillus* is more widespread in lot B than in lot A.

label: Evaluate
body: So long as the samples from lot A and lot B were representative of the lots themselves, this argument is valid. It reasons by comparing samples from two different groups and argues that what is true of the samples is true of the groups.

label: Goal
body: Look for something that contradicts something we were told or something we can derive from what we were told.

label: Facts
body:
conditional:
```
Everyone believed that            growth in societal
losing job wasn't your      →     demand for govt.
fault, but society's              to fix this
```
conditional:
```
govt tried to fix this   →   economic disaster
job loss situation
```

label: Evaluation
body:
We have multiple conditionals. Do they chain together? Kind of. There is some overlap between the two ideas, since both involve "the government controlling the economy".
The first conditional deals with people wanting that, the second conditional deals with that actually happening.

label: Goal
body:
We can still see the gist is that people thought society was to blame for job losses, they'd turn to the government to intervene. And if the government intervened, then we'd get an economic disaster.
The contrapositive of that whole chain of events would feel something like, "If you don't want an economic disaster, then keep on believing that job losses are the fired person's fault, not society's."
Since it's not a perfect chain, we should be careful with the wording of the answer choices if they're too strong or too sure of themselves.

label: Conclusion
body: It's unlikely that the airport will be built.

label: Evidence
body:
If a majority of residents favor the proposed airport, it'll be built
+
It's unlikely that a majority will favor the proposal, since most of them think the airport would create noise problems.

label: Evaluation
body:
If we're doing Flaw and we see conditional logic, we should be on guard for the Necessary vs. Sufficient flaw, where an author presents a conditional rule but then applies it in a backwards or opposite fashion.
This argument tried to illegally argue the opposite of the conditional. We know:
majority favors → airport will be built A → B
and this is arguing
majority favors → airport will be built ~A → ~B

label: Goal
body: Look for an answer describing the Necessary vs. Sufficient flaw. Or look for a conversational objection, that even if a majority doesn't favor the airport, there might be some other possibility that would also trigger the airport being built (a rich donor, for example).

label: Evidence
body:
```
An art critic, by ridiculing an   R -causes→ ↓P
artwork, can undermine the
pleasure one takes in it.
Conversely, by lavishing          P -causes→ ↑P
praise upon an artwork, an
art critic can render the
experience of viewing the
artwork more pleasurable.
```

label: Conclusion
body:
```
So an artwork's artistic merit   R or P -causes→ ↓M or ↑M
can depend not only on the
person who creates it but
also on those who critically
evaluate it.
```

label: Evaluate
body:
The argument assumes that
```
                                  ↓P or ↑P -causes→ ↓M or ↑M
the amount of pleasure one
experiences when viewing an
artwork contributes to the
artistic merit of the artwork.
```

label: Facts
body:
Over the last 5 years,
- Number of car thefts has steadily declined
- Likelihood of being convicted for car theft (if you steal a car) has gone up

label: Evaluation
body:
What could explain both of these? It sounds like the 2nd could explain the 1st. If you a car thief and you see that more and more car thieves are being convicted of crimes, that could serve as a deterrent, leading to fewer cars being stolen.
But we would still need a causal reason for why the % of car thefts that lead to convictions has gone up. Better policework? Better evidence collected? More traceable cars? Better prosecution? Sloppier criminals?

label: Conclusion
body: My constituents would support this bill that reduces the corporate income tax.

label: Evidence
body: In a poll, more than 97% of my constituents said they do not favor high taxes.

label: Evaluation
body:
Given that 97% said they don't favor high taxes, how could we argue that the constituents largely would not support a bill that lowers corporate income tax?
The poll question was phrased generically (and was a leading question ... "Do you favor high taxes?" Of course not. That's like asking, "Do you like too much dressing on your salad?")
So the overwhelming "No" doesn't tell us much about the constituents feelings on taxes.
However, another crucial question is how the constituents feel specifically about the corporate income tax. Maybe on the whole people don't like high taxes, but they're okay with high taxes on corporations.
We also don't know if the corporate income tax is currently something the people would consider "high". What if corporate income tax is like 8% while personal income tax is 28%. Would people likely support a reduction in that 8% rate? Of course not.

label: Goal
body:
- is the corporate income tax actually "high"?
- do people make an exception to their general antipathy towards high taxes and actually tolerate higher taxes for corporate income?
- can we really take anything away from the survey, given how loaded a question the people were asked?

label: Evidence
body:
The presence of an animal companion can yield health benefits by reducing a person's stress.
A pet can also make one's time at a home more rewarding, which will be important to more people as the average life span of our population increases.

label: Conclusion
body: Many nursing homes have prohibitions against having pets, and these should be lifted.

label: Evaluate
body: The argument provides several reasons why having a pet can enhance the welfare of those who live in a nursing home and argues that bans on pets in nursing homes should be lifted.

label: Conclusion (Thus)
body: Water itself is among the biggest water polluters.

label: Evidence
body:
Contamination of lakes and rivers from pollutants in rainwater runoff exceeds that from industrial discharge.
As runoff washes over building and pavements, it picks up oil and other pollutants.

label: Evaluate
body:
It's very unusual to see the main conclusion as the final claim, when we're doing Role or Main Conclusion (but it still happens 10% of the time).
The first two sentences both help support the last sentence. The 2nd sentence explains how it is that water pollutes at all. The 1st sentence supports the comparison that water is one of the biggest polluters by telling us that water outranks industrial discharge when it comes to contaminating lakes and rivers.

label: Goal
body:
They're asking us about the first sentence. We would call it part of the Support. Is it just an unsupported premise or is it a supported intermediate conclusion?
Let's wait to worry about that if an answer choice makes us.

label: Conclusion
body: Arvue should not hire Krall for the new position

label: Evidence
body:
Delacruz is a candidate and is fully qualified.
```
no fully qualified candidates   →   hire candidate
currently work for company           who'd be most
                                      productive
```

label: Evaluation
body:
This looks like a rule that can't prove what we want. This rule only tells us a condition under which we should hire someone. It doesn't actually look like a rule that instructs us not to hire someone.
However, because it says that we should hire the most productive, that outcome implies that anyone who isn't the most productive shouldn't be hired (assuming we're only hiring one person to fill the position).

label: Goal
body: So we would want to know that there are no fully qualified candidates that work at the company, so that we trigger the rule, and then we would want to know that Krall isn't the most productive.

label: Conclusion (thus)
body: If the rain forests are not preserved, important types of medicine will never be developed.

label: Evidence
body:
If the rain forests are not preserved, then thousands of plant species that have yet to be studied by scientists will be lost.
Many important types of medicine have been developed from substances in tropical rain forest plants, and it's very likely that many of the plants our scientists have yet to study also contain substances of medicinal value.

label: Evaluate
body:
The conclusion is ambiguously phrased --- is the author saying that "if the tropical rain forests aren't preserved, then we will never again develop an important type of medicine", or is she just saying, "we'll miss out some important medicines that we would have been able to develop had we preserved the rainforest"?
I'm more inclined to hear it the 2nd way. It seems like she's saying a world in which the rain forests aren't preserved is a world with fewer important types of medicine than a world in which the rain forests are preserved.
So,
GIVEN THAT .. there are thousands of species we haven't yet studied, and that it's very likely that many of those species have substances of medicinal value,
HOW COULD WE ARGUE that getting rid of the rain forest will not lead ot us being deprived of some important new meds we'd otherwise have developed?
It's tricky to find the wiggle room here. Let's say we keep the rain forest ... what assumptions are being made that go into the idea that important medicines will be developed from the plants that contain substances of medicinal value?
- we're assuming that scientists will be able to locate plants that have medicinal value (if it's just "many" out of thousands, that could be a tiny, tiny percentage -- many has no precise definition but "at least 5 or 10" is a good functional definition. If there are like 10 to 15 plants with medicinal value out of thousands of unstudied plants, there's no guarantee scientists would ever find them)
- if scientists do locate plants with medicinal value, then we're assuming that they're able and willing to remove these plants for the sake of drug development. We're assuming that drug companies would be able to extract the medicinally useful substances. We're assuming the drug companies would be able / willing to develop new drugs based on these substances. And we're assuming some of these new drugs would be important types of medicine.
- finally , we're assuming that whatever special substances the thousands of unstudied plants may contain are found only in the tropical rain forest. We were told that many important existing drugs came from substances growing only in the tropical rain forest. But we were never told that "it's very likely that many such plants also contain substances of medicinal value that are only found in the tropical rain forest".

label: Goal
body: We might see a missing link objection, like, "If we don't investigate those thousands of unstudied plants, then some important types of medicine will never be developed", or we might see an answer ruling out one of our many objections.

label: Conclusion
body: Ichthyosaurs were deep divers

label: Evidence
body:
Ichthyosaurs had porous outer bones.
+
Modern deep diving mammals have porous outer bones.

label: Evaluation
body:
This is an argument by Analogy / Comparison. Since deep-diving mammals and ichthyosaurs have one thing in common (porous outer bones), they probably have another thing in common (deep diving).
We strengthen these types of arguments by adding more similarity between the two cases. We weaken them by pointing out important differences.
Maybe porous bones are different when it comes to modern vs. prehistoric, or mammal vs. reptile. Maybe we'll learn of a different functionality for the porous bones in ichthyosaurs.

label: Goal
body: Find an answer that makes it less fair to compare Ichthyosaurs to modern deep-diving mammals, or find an answer that makes it seem like ichthyosaurs had porous bones for a different adaptive reason than deep-diving.

label: Main Conclusion
body: The money would be better spent preserving documents that have significant scholarly value.

label: Premises
body:
We are a research library and not a museum.
[This document] has no scholarly value

label: Opposing Point
body: The preservation grant we received should be used to restore our original copy of our town's charter

label: Opposing Support
body:
If the charter is not restored, it will soon deteriorate beyond repair.
This document [is] sentimentally important.

label: Conclusion
body: If we're gonna try to preserve any species, we should try to preserve the maximum number

label: Evidence
body: The world is super connected in ways we don't fully understand, so if we let some species die (because we don't perceive their value), we may find out that they were necessary to the preservation of species we do value.

label: Evaluation / Goal
body:
We need a Principle that sort of sounds like, "If you don't know or can't know which things are most worth saving, then try to save as many as possible."
Or maybe something that sounds like, "If there's a chance that saving X might be important to saving Y, which we care about, then try to save X too."

label: Conclusion
body: Long-term friends are probably of the same approximate age as each other

label: Evidence
body:
Most long-term friendships begin because someone feels comfortable approaching a stranger
+
If a stranger is of the same approx. age, one is likely to feel comfortable approaching them.

label: Ortiz's Rebuttal
body: Are you use the heart disease is from auto exhaust? Could it be that people who live on busy streets have other lifestyle factors that would lead to more heart disease?

label: Evaluation
body:
If we're doing flaw and we see conditional logic wording (here indicated by the sufficient trigger "if"), we should get deeply suspicious that we're being tested on Necessary vs. Sufficient and look our for backwards or opposite moves.
Here the author provided a rule,
A -> B,
said that most X's are B,
and then concluded that X's are probably A.
This is an illegal backwards move. We know that most of these deep friendships started with someone comfortably approaching a stranger.
If someone is the same age, you'll comfortably approach them as a stranger. But there might be a million other conditions under which you'd feel comfortable approaching a stranger:
```
Stranger at your church        →   comfortably approaching
You attended private school    →   comfortably app stranger
You can win any fight          →   comfortably app stranger
etc.
```

label: Goal
body: Look for an answer that names this illegal Necessary vs. Sufficient move or one that points out that there might be other situations in which you're also comfortable approaching a stranger.

label: Evidence
body:
```
There is no individual   IF → SI
freedom without social
integrity.
Pursuing the good life is   GL → SI
not possible without social
integrity.
```

label: Conclusion
body:
```
There can be no individual   IF → RL
freedom without the rule of
law.
```

label: Evaluate
body:
The argument assumes that
```
SI → RL
```
social integrity requires the rule of law.

label: Conclusion
body: Any nation whose govt committed serious $$ to public education will avoid economic and political weakness

label: Evidence
body:
Countries with uneducated citizens are destined to be economically and politically weak.
+
Countries with an educated population have govt who committed serious $$ to public education.

label: Evaluation
body:
Since there is conditional logic and repeating symbols throughout, we should diagram what's going on here.
```
Uneducated → E + P weak         A → B
Educated → serious $$ to PE     ~A → C
⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯⎯
Serious $$ to PE → ~(E + P weak)   C → ~B
```
Since we have a solid diagram, we don't really need to think about why this is flawed, but conversationally we could say a couple things:
1. committing money to public ed doesn't guarantee an educated population. It's just a trait that is true of all the population that HAVE managed to get an educated population.
2. we have a rule that says uneducated countries will end up weak, but that doesn't allow us to infer that educated companies will avoid being weak.

label: Goal
body: I would look for two conditional premises. The trigger of one of them should be the opposite of the trigger of the other one. The conclusion should bring the remaining two ideas together, but one of them will be the opposite of how it appeared in the premise.

label: Doris's 1st Claim
body:
Everyone in student government is outspoken.
  - *Does Zach say some members of student government aren't outspoken?*
  - No he explicitly agrees with this claim.

label: Doris's 2nd Claim
body:
If we want students to be more outspoken, we should encourage them to become involved in student government.
  - *Does Zach object to the idea of encouraging people to get involved in student government, as a way to get students to be more outspoken?*
  - Yes, kind of! This conditional form that Doris used, "If you want A, you should do B" implies a causal relationship: B is a way to cause more A to happen.
  - Doris was thinking that getting a student to be involved in student government is a way to get students to be more outspoken. She's assuming that the reason she's noticing that everyone in student government is outspoken is because being involved in student government makes you more outspoken.
  - Zack is countering this assumption by offering an alternate explanation for that correlation: the outspoken nature comes first, and that's what gets them into student government.
  - Since he sees the causality going the other way (outspoken ⇢ involved in govt), he says that Doris's plan to get people to be more outspoken by having them join student government is not gonna work.

label: Goal
body:
They disagree explicitly about this plan. Doris thinks that getting people involved in student government could make them more outspoken. Zack doesn't think that will work.
  - But they also disagree implicitly in terms of their causal assumptions about why there's such a strong correlation between being in student government and being outspoken.
  - Doris thinks it's because being in student government makes you more outspoken. Zack thinks it's because being outspoken makes you want to get into student government.

label: Conclusion
body: The government does not support freedom of popular expression.

label: Evidence
body:
Supporting freedom of popular expression means accepting the expression of ideas that the government opposes as well as those it supports.
  - The message of the protest rally was one that the government entirely supports.

label: Evaluate
body:
To prove you support freedom of expression, you have to show that you can tolerate views you oppose.
  - The government tolerated the recent protest rally, but it wasn't a view they oppose. They support the view.
  - The conclusion would be correct to say, "This rally does not prove that the government supports freedom of expression". It goes to far by saying, "the government doesn't support freedom of expression". (This is an Unproven vs. Proven False flaw, not that it really helps us here)
  - GIVEN THAT this rally doesn't show the government tolerating a view they oppose,
  - HOW CAN WE ARGUE THAT the government does support freedom of expression?
  - We'd probably need to say, "If you look at protest rallies with view the government opposes, you'll see that they also support those rallies".

label: Goal
body: The author is Assuming a Difference. They're assuming that if the rally hadn't been a message the government supported, then the government wouldn't have tolerated it.

label: Given that ...
body: Since 1945, our country has increasingly become a service economy, decreasingly become a manufacturing economy.

label: Why is it that ...
body: We have engaged in less and less international trade?

label: Evaluate / Goal
body: We need to know something about manufacturing jobs that goes along with our country doing more international trade, something about service jobs that goes along with our country doing less international trade, or just something else that's been happening in the country since 1945 that has led to less international trade.

label: Evaluate
body:
As soon as an LSAT student reads that first sentence, she should be thinking, "This is a study presenting a correlation. The author will probably assume or state some causal explanation for this correlation in just a sec. I should organize this with my Explain Curious Fact mindset."
  - Curious Fact ... why is there a correlation between living on busy streets and having higher rates of heart disease?
  - Author's Explanation ... living near busy streets is causing the higher rate of heart disease (via air pollution from auto exhaust).
  - In the Assumption Family, we're supposed to react to this by thinking
    1. Could there be some Alternate Explanation for the curious fact?
    2. How plausible is the author's explanation?
  - Whenever we deal with a correlation between X and Y, which our author interprets to mean X causes Y, we're supposed to always think of these same two alternate explanations:
    - Y causes X (reverse causality)
    - Z explains X and Y (3rd factor)
  - Ortiz responds with a 3rd factor style objection. He's saying what if there is some other trait that correlates with living on busy streets, and that trait is the causal factor that's leading to higher risk of heart disease. For example, maybe people who live on busy streets are much more likely to be cigarette smokers, or heavy drinkers, or heavy eaters. That would explain why busy streets and heart disease are correlated, even though it's not the busy street's fault.

label: Goal
body: Look for something like, "Ortiz is suggesting an alternate explanation for the correlation Merton cites between busy streets and heart disease".

label: Conclusion
body: The ban on fishing probably caused the fish population at Quapaw to rebound.

label: Evidence
body: Ever since the ban on fishing started, the fish population at Quapaw has recovered, whereas the fish population at the nearby lake, Highwater, has not recovered.

label: Evaluate
body:
We've got a Curious Comparison, since the author is looking at an asymmetry between Quapaw / Highwater (Q's fish population has been growing, H's hasn't). And the conclusion makes a causal claim because it says "X is probably responsible for Y". So we can use our Curious Fact / Explanation mindset.
  - Curious Fact ... How come the fishing population has recovered at Quapaw but not at Highwater?
  - Author's Explanation ... The ban on fishing at Quapaw lake is what allowed the fish population to recover.
  - We should ask ourselves two questions:
    1. could there be an Alternate Explanation for the curious fact?
    why else might the fish be returning to Quapaw lake? Maybe some invasive predator has disappeared. Maybe an algal bloom that messed up the oxygen levels of the water is gone. Maybe someone dumped fish food and live fish into the lake.
    2. how plausible is the Author's Explanation?
    was fishing ever contributing to the decline of fish at Quapaw? Do people like to go fishing there? Since the ban, has there been less fishing?

label: Conclusion
body: Since we're Weakening, the correct answer is most likely going to provide some alternate explanation for why fish are recovering at Quapaw but not at Highwater, but it may undermine the plausibility of the Author's notion that "the ban on fishing is why the fish population is recovering at Quapaw, but not at Highwater".

label: Argument
body: The author says: the Asian elephant always has at least two feet on the ground, so it doesn't actually run.

label: Evaluate
body:
The argument is treating "having feet on the ground" as the disqualifier from running. For that to work, we need a definition of running that requires the opposite — having all feet off the ground at some moment.
  - Think of it this way. The author is implicitly using a definition: "to run, an animal must have a moment of being airborne." That's a real biological definition (it's how scientists distinguish running from fast walking). Add that, and the argument closes: elephant always has feet down -> elephant is never airborne -> elephant doesn't run.

label: Goal
body: The answer should give us this definition of running.

label: Given That ...
body: This store usually sells about an equal number of Maxlast and Styron hammers, and given that last all the Maxlast were put on sale and in a display case just inside the store entrance.

label: How Can it Be That ...
body: The Styron hammers (at their usual price and location) sold slightly better.

label: Evaluate / Goal
body:
We're essentially wondering,
  - Why was it bad for sales of Maxlast, to put it on sale and put it near the front?
  - or
  - Why was it good for sales of Styron, to remain in their usual location (with all the Maxlast hammers moved elsewhere)?
  - Maybe the sale price seemed to good to be true so people didn't trust buying a Maxlast (they paid more for Styron thinking the higher price indicated better quality).
  - Maybe the display case was ugly, or people were turned off that they couldn't touch the Maxlast's and see how they felt in their hands.

label: Conclusion (however)
body: The superior ability of the ginkgo mice to navigate the maze on day 2 might not be directly attributable to a memory boost from the ginkgo.

label: Evidence (studies have found .. and .. )
body: Ginkgo reduces stress in mice, and lowering very high stress levels is known to improve recall.

label: Evaluate
body:
This question ends up testing a really small language shift that I did not catch the first time I tried the problem, so I'm writing this explanation as though I am that person, since we can still put ourselves in a position to understand the correct answer without noticing it.
  - Because we're interpreting the results of an experiment, which featured a Curious Comparison, we can use our causal mindset.
  - Curious Fact ... why were the ginkgo mice more likely to remember how to navigate the maze on day 2 than were the normal mice?
  - One Explanation ... ginkgo extract directly boosts memory
  - Author's Explanation ... ginkgo, as we know, reduces stress, and lowering stress is known to improve memory.

label: Goal
body:
Since this is Weaken, we'd either want to
  - suggest an Alternate Explanation for why the ginkgo mice were better able to remember the maze (we could return to the notion that ginkgo directly boosted memory, but some 3rd explanation could also weaken)
  - or
  - lower the plausibility of the Author's Explanation that the ginkgo mice were better able to remember the maze because the ginkgo had lowered their stress.

label: Statement
body: Some politicians who supported free trade among Canada, the United States, and Mexico are now refusing to publicly support the idea that free trade should be extended to other Latin American countries.

label: Evidence
body: GIAPS is a just a tool, so it can't be responsible for bad presentations. The responsibility lies with the users, who are apparently using this tool poorly.

label: Evaluate
body:
This is weird. A Must Be True question that only gives us one fact? How are we supposed to do our normal job and combine facts?
  - This almost gives us two facts in an embedded way, because we know 2 things about these politicians:
    - supported North American free trade
    - refuse to publicly support extending that to other Latin American countries.

label: Goal
body:
When we're given a Pivot like "Patrick is a mean teacher, but he gives his students candy", it must be true that "some mean teachers give their students candy" or "not all candy-giving people are nice".
  - Maybe the answer will just find a way to safely get "supported free trade with Mexico/US/Canada" and "refuse to publicly support extending free trade to other Latin American countries" in the same sentence.

label: Principle
body: If you knowingly aid someone's infringement on copyright → then you are also guilty of copyright infringement.

label: Conclusion
body: Grandview is guilty of copyright infringement

label: Evidence
body: A customer used the kiosk to infringe on the copyright of a wedding photographer.

label: Evaluate
body:
On Strengthen Application-of-Principle, the conclusion of the application always matches the right side of the principle. But the evidence always fails to fully establish the left side of the principle.
  - In order to trigger this principle and use it to derive that GDS is guilty of copyright infringement, we need to know that GDS was knowingly aiding someone's infringement on a copyright.
  - All we know is that some customer used a (self-service) kiosk to infringe on a copyright.

label: Goal
body:
Let's look for an answer that establishes that GDS was knowingly aiding someone's infringement on a copyright. Maybe they helped the customer use that kiosk and saw that they were infringing on a wedding photographer's copyright.
  - Maybe they know that people use that machine all the time to copy copyrighted material without permission.
  - However the answer does it, it needs to establish that GDS "knowingly aided someone's infringement".

label: Setup
body: The purpose of journalism is to inform people about stuff relevant to the choices they have to make.

label: Pivot (yet)
body: People consume journalism precisely because it contains sensationalistic gossip about people who no relevance to their lives.

label: Evaluate
body:
Logical Completion is a subtype of Most Supported, so our thinking task is still to combine claims together. Since there is a big Pivot word, we surmise that we're probably supposed to Reconcile the Pivot, i.e. think of a safely worded takeaway that combines the before-pivot with the after-pivot idea.
  - The purpose of journalism is to inform us about stuff relevant to our lives, but the reason people often consume journalism is to hear gossip about people who aren't relevant to their lives.
  - Can we combine those to say that "journalism isn't living up to its purpose"?
  - That's probably a little too strong. After all, you might buy a newspaper for the sake of a gossip column but then read the rest of it and end up getting informed about relevant stuff.
  - So a safer synthesis would be something like "The reason people often consume journalism is unrelated to its purpose".

label: Goal
body:
The final sentence begins with "the gossip in journalism", so we would need to rejigger our synthesis to match that subject noun.
  - "The gossip in journalism ... does not embody the purpose of journalism, even if it succeeds in getting people to consume journalism"?

label: Conclusion
body: Assuming the survey is reliable, most citizens want the legislature to be about 40% Conservative, 20% Moderate, and 40% Liberal.

label: Evidence
body: In the survey, 40% said they'd like to see the conservative party in the legislature, 20% said the moderate party, 40% said the liberal party.

label: Evaluate
body:
The author seems to be totally misunderstanding the survey results.
  - 40% of people surveyed were saying, "I would like to see the Conservative party in the legislature". In other words, I wish the legislature were 100% conservative (or at least, I wish it was mainly conservative).
  - There was probably no one in this survey who actually said, "I'd like to see a 40/20/40 split", so how could the author possibly think that most citizens want a 40/20/40 split?

label: Goal
body:
Look for an answer objecting to the author's total misread of this survey was measuring.
  - 40% of people want it 100% conservative.
  - 20% of people want it 100% moderate.
  - 40% of people want it 100% liberal.
  - 0% are asking for it to be 40/20/40%.

label: Conditional (If)
body: adopt new tourism plan → tourists would spend an extra $2 billion annually

label: Causal (-ing)
body: The extra $2 billion being spent by tourists would create as many jobs as a new car plant.

label: Comparison / Pivot (but)
body: Adopting the tourism plan would cost less than convincing an auto manufacturer to build a car plant here.

label: Judgment
body: It would be reasonable for the city to spend what it would take to convince an auto manufacturer to build a plant here.

label: Evaluate
body:
This is a weird variety of facts. We have a couple facts about the tourism plan a couple facts about building a car plant, so maybe the synthesis they want us to do has to do with comparing the two.
  - Whenever the last claim of the paragraph begins with a Pivot word (but, yet, however), that typically means that LSAT intends for us to reconcile that last idea with what came before it.
  - What should we make out of the fact that the tourism plan would cost less (than it would to entice an auto manufacturer to our city)?
  - Well we know that the tourism plan would create as many jobs as the new car plant would. So I guess we could say something like, "We could spend less money to get the same number of jobs we'd get from a new auto plant".

label: Goal
body: Pick the most provable answer we can find. It might relate to the idea that the tourism plan would get us at least as many jobs but for less money than would getting an auto manufacturer to build a plant here.

label: Conclusion
body: We shouldn't trust the idea that many medical patients have an instinctual ability to predict sudden changes in their medical status.

label: Evidence
body:
Each person in the study tasted Sparkle Cola and one of five competing colas (each group a different cola).
  - Most of the volunteers said they preferred Sparkle Cola to the competing cola tasted.

label: Evidence
body:
The evidence is anecdotal and analogous to empirically disproven reports that babies are more likely to be born on nights with full moons.
  - Once the rumor got out that "full moons bring out da babies", maternity room staff became more likely to remember busy nights with full moons than busy nights without full moons.

label: Evaluate
body:
This is a tough argument to grasp. It's about whether medical patients have an instinctual ability to predict sudden changes in their medical status, but the evidence is all about babies and full moons.
  - Since this argument relies on an analogy, the author has to assume that the two cases are relevantly similar.
  - What parts of analogy are important?
  - The full moon thing is an example of a false claim (more babies are born on full moons) that was believed because of selective memory.
  - Once maternity room staff had the thought of "more babies are born on full moons", there was a confirmation bias happening -- they would be extra likely to remember full moon nights with lots of babies.
  - Since our author's argument is saying, "We should not trust this potentially-false claim (patients have an instinctual ability to predict sudden changes in their medical status", the author must be assuming that people got this idea in their heads and then confirmation bias led to selective memory where they're more likely to remember times when patients did predict sudden changes than they are to remember times when patients didn't.

label: Goal
body: Hard to predict the right wording, but look for an assumption connecting a relevant similarity between the evidence about "full moon babies" and the conclusion about "clairvoyant patients".

label: Conclusion
body: Legislators should reject this argument. (i.e. legislators should reject the pleas for strong worker protections that oppose increases in multinational control)

label: Evidence
body: The union leaders making the argument have a vested interest in seeing workers' wages remain high, so naturally they don't want multinational corporations to ship manufacturing jobs to nations w/o strong worker protections.

label: Evaluate
body:
As soon as we see Flaw + Rebuttal + Vested Interest we might recognize one of the top 6 most common famous flaws, Ad Hominem, when an author rejects an argument because of its source, not its ideas.
  - Just because the union leaders have a vested interest in warning against multinational corporations outsourcing labor to countries where workers are paid less doesn't mean that union leaders are wrong to worry about this.
  - Shouldn't legislators be trying to keep as many manufacturing jobs as they can within the borders of their country?
  - The fact that someone has a vested interest (ulterior motive) doesn't mean their perspective is flawed or wrong. We need to engage with their reasoning and see if their logic makes sense.

label: Goal
body:
Look for an answer calling out the Ad Hominem move, or an answer otherwise objecting that the legislators should be taking seriously the concern that multinationals are outsourcing manufacturing jobs to other countries.
  - Union leaders argue that there should be legislative resistance to multinational control over manufacturing, since multinational corporations are shifting labor to nations without strong worker protections.

label: Given that ...
body: The same number of new university students enter as chemistry majors.

label: and that ...
body: Job prospects for graduates with chemistry degrees are better than ever.

label: How can it be that ...
body: Over the past ten years, there's been a significant decline in the number of people earning chemistry degrees.

label: Evaluate / Goal
body:
We're trying to explain why fewer people are earning chemistry degrees, and the sensitive time period is over the past decade.
  - So we need something that has changed in the past ten years that would be a force working against people earning a chemistry degree.
  - And since the number of students entering college as chemistry majors is the same, this change has to be effecting students while they're at college (but it probably can't be related to job prospects, since they have every reason to think if they finish their chemistry studies and get a degree, they have a good shot at a job).

label: Evidence
body: More than 55 different species went extinct 10,000 years ago, and no single disease could be fatal to animals across that many different species.

label: Conclusion
body: Human-borne diseases probably did not cause the mass extinction of large land animals and birds 10,000 years ago.

label: Evaluate
body:
There's no conditional logic or quantifiers in there, so this probably isn't a great contender for symbolizing / turning into algebra.
  - Instead, we should probably just figure out how we would object to this argument.
  - Given That no single disease could take out 55 completely different species,
  - How Could We Still Say That human diseases did probably cause those extinctions?
  - What if there were more than one disease? What if a dozen or so different human-borne diseases collectively took out those 55 species?
  - What is the abstract form of that objection? We can help ourselves here by reminding ourselves whenever we're doing Parallel Flaw that they love to test some of the Famous Flaws:
    - Necessary vs. Sufficient
    - Part vs. Whole
    - Unproven vs. Proven False
    - Correlation vs. Causality
    - Ad Hominem
    - Sampling
  - This is Part vs. Whole, since the premise and the conclusion are repeating the same trait:
    - PREMISE: any single disease could not kill those 55
    - CONCLUSION: human diseases did not kill those 55

label: Goal
body: Let's look for an answer that says "because no single X could do Y, we can conclude that X's (together) couldn't do Y."

label: Conclusion (So)
body: The disclaimer serves no purpose.

label: Evidence
body:
The only purpose this disclaimer could serve is to provide legal protection for the company.
  - If anything in the e-mail suggests that the client do something illegal, then the disclaimer offers no legal protection.

label: Evaluate
body:
We're trying to prove "serves no purpose" and we are given a rule that allows us to prove "serves no purpose". We just have to establish that the disclaimer provides no legal protection, and then we have proven our conclusion.
  - "Only" and "Only if" are necessary (right side) indicators, whereas "The only" is a sufficient (left side) indicators. That 2nd sentence would look like this, if diagrammed:
  - serves purpose → provides legal protection
  - provides legal protection → serves purpose
  - The 3rd sentence gives us another conditional, signified by "if", which is a sufficient (left side) indicator:
  - email suggests something illegal → provides legal protection

label: Goal
body:
The conclusion gives us this logic path: Disclaimer → serves no purpose
  - The evidence provides this much of the path: suggests something illegal → doesn't provide leg protection → serves no purpose
  - So we'd be anticipating the missing link: Disclaimer → suggests something illegal
  - Let's look for an answer that says that the disclaimer suggests something illegal, but we'll take any answer that allows us to prove that the disclaimer serves no purpose.

label: Conclusion (Thus)
body: Even well-intentioned attempts to resolve the marital problems of friends are usually unjustified.

label: Evidence
body: Well-intentioned attempts are usually ineffectual, thereby fostering resentment among all parties.

label: Evaluate
body:
The judging term we're trying to prove in the Conclusion about well-intentioned attempts is "unjustified", which can be expressed in synonymous language like "bad / should not do / not right".
  - The ammunition we have from the Evidence about well-intentioned attempts is that they're "usually ineffectual and thereby foster resentment among all involved.

label: Goal
body:
So, if we're anticipating the typical "IF premise, THEN conclusion" linking answer that's so common on Principle questions, we'd want something like
  - ineffectual → unjustified
  - or
  - fosters resentment among all parties → unjustified
  - The answer should basically attach something we were told is true of "well-intentioned attempts to resolve others' marital problems" to language that sounds like "unjustified".

label: Conclusion (That claim cannot be true)
body: Authors who write in order to give pleasure can impart the truth of their subject matter.

label: Evidence
body: That would mean that popular books by definition are somewhat untruthful, because if a book is selling well, then it's presumably imparting pleasure, and therefore according to this incorrect principle we would know that those authors were not able to impart the truth of their subject matter.

label: Evaluate
body:
It's fair to say this is in my top 3 least favorite LR problems ever. The argument has so many loose ends and is so incoherent that it's impossible to know what they want you to notice.
  - There's a typical rebuttal assumption here that has to do with the fact that the author wants to argue via the contrapositive of a counterfactual.
  - CONCLUSION: Some people say X, but they're wrong.
  - PREMISE: After all if X were true, then Y would be true.
  - IMPLICIT ASSUMPTION: Y is not true.
  - So there could have been an answer saying that the author assumes that "one cannot determine truthfulness by looking at sales figures".
  - Where this question ultimately ends up going instead is to missing links between term shifts from the conclusion to the evidence.
  - In the conclusion we're talking about "authors who write in order to give pleasure". Are we told anything about such authors in the evidence?
  - No, the closest thing to that is [the book] gave people pleasure. The author must be assuming that "a book that gave people pleasure was written in order to give pleasure".
  - In the conclusion we're talking about "cannot impart the truth of their subject matter". Do we talk about anything like that in the evidence?
  - No, the closest thing to that is some of what is written in the book is not true. The author must be assuming that "if an author is not imparting to readers the truth of the subject matter, then some of what is written in the book is not true".

label: Goal
body: Look for an answer establishing a link the author made between ideas or ruling out some idea that would weaken the argument.

label: Conclusion
body: Most of W&W's new shows for this season will be canceled.

label: Evidence
body: Most of the shows they made for last year got canceled because not enough people watched. Their new shows are all police dramas, and most police dramas have not been popular in recent years.

label: Evaluate
body:
This argument is making a prediction based on some trends, and Assuming Similarities along the way.
  - Since most of W&W's new shows last year got canceled, if we assume that W&W's shows new shows this year are similar, then they will probably get canceled too (if we also assume that audiences' tastes this season are similar to those of last season).
  - And since all of W&W's new shows are police dramas and most police dramas have failed in recent years, if we assume that W&W's police dramas are similar to those failed police dramas of recent years, then they will probably fail too (if we also assume that audiences' appetite for police dramas are similar).

label: Goal
body:
Look for an answer saying
  - W&W's new shows are similar to last year's failed shows
  - W&W's police dramas are similar to the failed police dramas
  - or
  - what audiences wanted last year / in recent years is similar to what audiences want this year

label: Principle
