body: If a corporation obtains money by fraud, then when we punish that corporation, we need to figure out how much they profited off that fraud-money so that our penalty is at least that large financially.

label: Evaluate
body:
The question stem isn't saying to conform to the Principle cited above, rather the principle illustrated above, which indicates that LSAT wants us to do some abstraction.
  - What was this principle basically saying?
  - It was saying that thieves shouldn't be able to profit off stolen money. If we're penalizing these thieves, we should make sure they don't come out with a net financial gain (i.e. if a company steals $10 million and invests it, making $2 million, then our penalty to that company must be to get the $10 million back as well as at least the $2 million they made off that money)

label: Goal
body: Let's get slightly more general with our pre-phrase: If you're punishing someone who did something wrong, the punishment should cancel out whatever gain that person attained by doing the wrong-thing.

body:
```
The television star Markus       I → RA

interviews with newspapers
unless he is given the right
to approve the article
before publication.
```

label: Conclusion
body: It's absurd to say that using GIAPS leads people to develop ineffective presentations. (i.e. using GIAPS doesn't lead to people to develop ineffective presentations)

label: Evaluate
body:
Can't we sometimes blame the tool for bad output? If I'm trying to make you a great cup of coffee, and my only tool is some $15 percolating coffee machine bought at a Wal-Mart 10 years ago, it doesn't matter how good I am at using that tool, you're getting a mediocre cup of coffee with some gross machine aftertaste.
  - Similarly, couldn't this Powerpoint-knockoff, GIAPS, be such a bad tool that there's no way to get a good presentation with it? Maybe all the clip-art is corny, the animations are over the top, and the templates aren't well thought out. Maybe they don't give you enough options for customizing the built-in templates, so you're stuck with what they provide.

label: Goal
body: Look for an answer complaining that "just because something is a tool, that doesn't mean it can't take a share of the blame for bad output".

label: Conclusion (however: rebuttal)
body:
That claim is easily disproven.
  - rephrase: There will be damage to the environment if we allow oil drilling in the Cape Simmons Nature Preserve.

label: Evidence (just look at X)
body: At nearby Alphin Bay, where oil drilling began five years ago, the land is marred by industrial sprawl, drilling platforms, and miles of roads and pipelines.

label: Evaluate
body:
The author is arguing that if we do X (oil drilling) at Cape Simmons, we'll have environmental damage, just like we (supposedly) did at Alphin Bay.
  - There are two big problems with the argument:
    1. Did the author establish that oil drilling led to any environmental damage at Alphin Bay? (Not really, unless industrial sprawl and drilling platforms and roads and pipelines are considered environmental damage. But they're only really ugly aspects of industrial infrastructure. They aren't themselves evidence of damage.)
    2. Did the author make it seem like the situation in Alphin Bay and the one with Cape Simmons are fair to compare?

label: Goal
body:
We'd either want to strengthen this argument by being better convinced that the oil drilling at Alphin led to actual environmental damage.
  - Or we could want an answer to make us feel better about thinking that the situation with Alphin Bay five years ago would be analogous to the proposed situation at Cape Simmons, using modern drilling methods.

label: James's Position
body: James draws a line: community colleges naturally serve community needs, but universities have different primary goals — meaning serving the community isn't a primary university goal.

label: Margaret's Position
body: Margaret rejects that line. She says serving the community is a primary goal of any university. And she adds that the reason people attend a university is the same as the reason they attend a community college: career prep.

label: Anticipate
body: The cleanest disagreement is the headline issue: is serving community educational needs a primary goal of universities? Margaret: yes. James: no.

label: Goal
body: An answer that Margaret affirms and James denies — about whether serving community educational needs is a primary university goal.

label: Given that ...
body: Most people who take a seminar for building organizational skills do become more organized.

label: How can it be that ...
body: Most of them don't become any more efficient.

label: Evaluate / Goal
body:
How can someone be more organized but still just as efficient as before? Well what do we mean by organized and efficient?
  - Organizational skills in the workplace might mean stuff like keeping a detailed calendar, clearing our your inbox, taking notes during meetings.
  - Efficiency, meanwhile, is usually a measurement of how much work is accomplished for a given unit of time.
  - Maybe the answer will just be something like, "all those extra steps to stay organized take time! So even though you spend less time trying to find what you looking for that you don't really get more work done in a given amount of time".

label: Principle
body: If you create an unfair situation → you're obliged to rectify an unfair result

label: Problem
body:
Thimble Corporation created an unfair situation when they distributed some rebate coupons for one of their products and the expiration date was too early.
  - This created the unfair result that some customers believed the rebate offer had already expired.

label: Evaluate
body: According to this principle, Thimble Corporation is "obligated to rectify" the unfair result of having a premature expiration date on their coupons.

label: Goal
body:
It's not clear what would rectify this situation, but presumably customers who would have submitted for a rebate if they didn't think the window of opportunity had already expired should be given a chance to submit for a rebate.
  - In general, we're just looking for an answer saying that Thimble Corporation should rectify (fix) any unfair result of having the wrong expiration date on their rebate coupons.

label: Opposing Evidence
body: The recent biography is by an expert on the history of Elizabethan England.

label: Opposing Conclusion
body: The recent biography does a good job of showing what life would have been like for Shakespeare as a man of that time.

label: Evidence
body: The recent biography does not explain what made Shakespeare different from his contemporaries. (~ED)

label: Conclusion
body: The recent biography of Shakespeare does not explain what is of most interest about him. (~EMI)

label: Evaluate
body: The argument assumes EMI → ED — that what is of most interest about Shakespeare is what made Shakespeare different from his contemporaries.

label: Given
body:
The result of attempting to whip cream in a blender is a thick, velvety substance rather than fluffy whipped cream.
  - This is because a blender's container does not let in enough air to whip cream effectively.
  - Although using a special whipping-cream attachment in a blender can help somewhat, it cannot fully compensate for the container's poor air intake.

label: Conclusion
body: There's good reason to regard their hypothesis as false. (there's good reason to think that life did not evolve extraterrestrially and drift to Earth in spores)

label: Evidence
body: These proponents only have empirical arguments against the competing view that life evolved on Earth. They don't have any evidence in favor of their theory.

label: Evaluate
body:
This seems to commit a version of the famous Unproven vs. Proven False flaw, albeit a much softer one.
  - This author is saying, "There's good reason to regard Theory X as false, since no one has been able to provide positive support for Theory X."
  - Is that a good reason? The fact that no one has provided positive support for the existence of God means that there is good reason to regard the existence of a God as false?
  - We don't treat a lack of evidence as the presence of counterevidence. If we don't have evidence for or against, we should remain agnostic about the truth/falsity.

label: Goal
body: Look for an answer calling out some version of the Unproven vs. Proven False flaw.

label: Conclusion (So)
body: If you child uses VIVVY, you can expect him or her to become a successful university student.

label: Evidence
body: Amy, Matt, and Evelyn were among the first children to use it, and they are successful university students.

label: Evaluate
body:
Parallel Flaw usually gives us argument with a lot of conditionals or quantifiers (which we can diagram), or they give us one of the Top 6 Famous Flaws:
  - Necessary vs. Sufficient
  - Part vs. Whole
  - Ad Hominem
  - Unproven vs. Proven False
  - Causal
  - Sampling
  - This argument could technically be categorized as either of the last two. The Causal flaw is when an author overconfidently assumes one possible explanation for a curious fact, when other possible explanations could exist.
  - Here, our author is assuming that using VIVVY was an important causal factor in these three kids becoming successful university students. But how do we know if VIVVY made any difference? Maybe they also had a lot of after school tutoring. Maybe they studied really hard. The author is taking this one causal possibility and acting like it definitely happened.
  - The other flaw we could complain about is the Sample. Our author is promising every parent that if their child uses VIVVY, they can expect the same thing that happened when Amy, Matt, and Evelyn used it.
  - What if our kids are different from Amy, Matt, and Evelyn?!
  - The argument's sample size is crazy small. Because 3 users went on to be successful university students we should believe that every user will have the same experience?

label: Goal
body: Look for an argument that commits a Sampling flaw (sample size = too small) and/or look for an argument that fails to consider other causal explanations.

label: Activist's Hope (therefore)
body: We can dispense altogether with nuclear power and that we can meet our energy needs in a way that better protects the environment from harm than we presently do.

label: Reason for Activist's Hope
body: We have alternative sources of energy like solar, wind, hydroelectric, and new sludge-power!

label: Evaluate / Goal
body:
The question stem is pretty dense and unusual. Four wrong answers will offer something relevant, when it comes to assessing this "hope" that we can get rid of nuclear power and meet all our energy needs using solar, wind, hydro, and sludge.
  - Since we're not being asked to judge an argument (just the practicability of a certain hope), we probably don't need to spend any energy looking for assumptions or objections.
  - Let's just get rid of four answers that "do the job" ... they raise some issue that could lead to us saying "It's not practical to get rid of nuclear and to rely instead on solar, wind, hydro, and sludge.

label: Given that ...
body: In tropical forests, the tree that is most common is also the one that reproduces the most.

label: How can it be that ...
body: In tropical forests, the tree species that is rarest is the species that survives the longest?

label: Evaluate
body:
It's sort of hard to understand the intended paradox here, but they seemed to be going for the idea that we'd expect the most evolutionarily successful tree species to be,
  - most common
  - best at reproducing
  - best at surviving (live longest)
  - But the length of a species life span isn't really that intertwined with how much it reproduces or how thriving it is. Turtles live 100 years, but they are probably less numerous and reproduce less than squirrels.

label: Goal
body: Let's find an answer that distinguishes the rare tree and explains why it lives longer than these more common trees, that reproduce the most.

label: Conclusion
body: The ad they ran won't attract recurring viewers as well as the ad the producers favored would have.

label: Evidence
body:
The ad they ran totally misrepresents what the show is like.
  - People who tune in to the first episode with false expectations will be unlikely to watch subsequent episodes.

label: Evaluate
body:
This argument has both Comparison issues and a Missing Link. We're given a conditional rule that says: tune in 1st ep w/ false expectations → ~likely keep watch
  - Was it established that people will be tuning into the 1st episode with false expectations?
  - No. The author is just assuming that because the ad grossly misrepresents the show, people will tune in with false expectations.
  - Additionally, say that we stipulate, "Okay, fine, they'll tune in with false expectations and thus be unlikely to keep watching."
  - Would that prove that this ad was less effective at getting recurring viewers than would have been the other ad?
  - Not necessarily -- the author is Assuming a Difference. She's assuming that had they gone with the producers' ad, then viewers wouldn't be coming to the first episode with false expectations.

label: Goal
body:
The missing link: "if add grossly misrepresents, then viewers have false expectations"
  - or
  - the missing part of the comparison: "the other ad didn't grossly misrepresent the show / wouldn't have led to viewers having false expectations".

label: Situation
body:
Sharon has a favorite novelist (X) and a political candidate she's supported for years (Y).
  - She heard that X spoke out against (criticized) Y. It made her think less of X, but it didn't change how she thought about the Y.

label: Evaluate / Goal
body:
Because the paragraph is labeled as a situation, as opposed to an argument / reasoning, we don't need to look for a premise / conclusion breakdown.
  - We just need a principle that matches this situation — one person you like (the novelist) criticizes someone else you like (the politician). you think less of the critic, but your opinion of the criticized stays the same.

label: Conclusion (this shows that)
body: Sparkle Cola elicits a more favorable response from consumers than any of the competing colas tested.

label: Conclusion (Thus)
body: Including large amounts of B vitamins and folic acid in one's diet will likely reduce one's risk of developing Alzheimer's.

label: Evaluate
body:
Given that ... most of the volunteers picked Sparkle as their preference over the other cola they tasted,
  - How can we argue that ... Sparkle does not elicit a more favorable response from consumers than any of the competing colas?
  - The argument is moving from, "Because it was true in the sample, it's true of consumers", so the author is definitely assuming that the sample in this study was big enough, representative enough, unbiased, etc, that it can be trusted as a sample that reflects consumer preferences.
  - But beyond the Sampling concerns, did the author successfully establish that Sparkle elicited a more favorable response from the study volunteers than did any competing cola tested?
  - If Soda X were one of the sodas tested and it was actually the #1 favorable response from these study participants, then how come most participants picked Sparkle as their preference?
  - Well, most participants didn't even get a chance to try Soda X. Only one of the five groups did. Maybe Soda X kicked butt within its group, but Sparkle kicked butt in the other four groups. That could create a situation where most participants ended up picking Sparkle, even though it looks like Soda X is more preferred.
  - If numbers help, suppose there are 20 people in each of the five groups, and let's say this is how the voting went down.
  - Soda V (9) vs. Sparkle (11)
  - Soda W (8) vs. Sparkle (12)
  - Soda X (20) vs. Sparkle (0)
  - Soda Y (5) vs. Sparkle (15)
  - Soda Z (6) vs. Sparkle (14)
  - 52 out of the 100 people (most) said they preferred Sparkle to the competing soda. But if we looked at this table of data, we'd still think that Soda X was the winner. Sparkle beat out the other four sodas, but Soda X demolished Sparkle.

label: Goal
body: Look for an answer discussing the Sampling move or pointing out that even within the study, it's possible that most votes went to Sparkle even though one of the sodas crushed Sparkle in its head to head.

label: Conclusion
body: Watching too much TV can lead people to overestimate the risks that the world poses.

label: Evidence
body: Recent study showed a correlation (people who are X are more likely to be Y) between "thinking you'll be victims of a natural disaster" and "watching an above average amount of TV".

label: Evaluate
body:
Whenever we see correlation language or whenever we feel the author is interpreting the results of a study, we can use our Curious Fact / Explanation template.
  - Curious Fact: Why is there a correlation between watching lots of TV and fearing you'll be victims of a natural disaster?
  - Author's Story: Watching lots of TV leads you to overestimate the risks the world poses (so you over-panic about your likelihood of being killed in a natural disaster).
  - The two pressure points for these arguments:
    - how ELSE could we explain that curious fact?
    - how plausible is the author's explanation?
  - Since this is Weaken, we want to either
    1. Suggest an alternate explanation for why there's a correlation between "lots of TV" and "fear natural disasters"
    or
    2. Hurt the plausibility of the storyline that watching too much TV causes you to overestimate the risks the world poses.
  - A #1 style answer might give us the classic Alternate Explanation for Correlation forms such as
    - Reverse Causality - People who know that natural disasters are coming to their area tend to watch more TV, to get updates about what to do, how to prepare, when to evacuate.
    - Third Factor - People who live in Los Angeles are both threatened by earthquakes and wildfires (explaining the fear of natural disaster) and working in the entertainment industry (explaining the high level of TV watching).
  - A #2 style answer could say something like, "TV shows routinely show the hero improbably avoiding danger, not getting shot, not getting harmed by an explosion, thereby giving the false impression that the world isn't as dangerous as it is."

label: Goal
body: Because it's weaken, we should primarily look for a different way to explain the correlation between "fear of natural disasters" and "watching lots of tv", but we can also stay receptive to answers that hurt the plausibility that "watching lots of tv would lead one to overestimate the dangers of the world".

label: Conclusion
body: If Earth's atmosphere becomes significantly warmer, heavy rains are likely to become more frequent.

label: Evidence
body: If Earth's atmosphere becomes warm, it heats the oceans; water evaporates faster; the water vapor forms clouds more quickly; there's also more moisture in the atmosphere, so there are larger clouds; and larger clouds are more likely to result in heavy rains.

label: Evaluate
body:
Whenever we read Role or Main Conclusion, we prime our brain before reading the paragraph with a reminder that usually the Conclusion will be found earlier than the Evidence (frequently it's the first claim, or it's the first claim after a pivot).
  - Conclusions are supposed to be opinions supported by facts (and sometimes supported by opinions). Everything after the first sentence is a science fact, so it's all disqualified from being a conclusion.
  - Only the first sentence is an opinion, because it's a prediction. Saying what will happen in the future is always implicitly an opinion.
  - Besides being an opinion, we check to see whether our Conclusion is supported by explicit claims.
  - In this case, the first sentence is the Umbrella Claim (pun intended) beneath which all the rest of the ideas go.
  - Everything after the first sentence was a causal chain trying help us see how warmer atmosphere would connect to more frequent heavy rains.

label: Goal
body:
We know the final sentence was part of the Support for the Main Conclusion (everything after the first sentence was support for the conclusion).
  - Whether it was an Intermediate Conclusion or just a Premise, we can wait to litigate. Let's see if any answer choices care to press on that before we commit any mental energy to it. We know it supports the first sentence's main conclusion.

label: Opposing Evidence
body: Most anthropologists do realize that living within the community one is studying affects the community.

label: Evidence
body:
Field studies, which have long been a staple of anthropological research, involve the researcher living within the community being studied.
  - Most anthropologists generally underestimate the extent that their presence affects the community they are studying.

label: Conclusion
body: The usefulness of field studies tends to be overrated by anthropologists.

label: Evidence
body:
```
Juarez thinks that the       ~W → R
sales proposal will be
rejected by the committee
if it is not rewritten before
they see it.
Juarez's opinion is very
reliable on such matters.
The proposal will not be     ~W
rewritten.
```

label: Conclusion
body:
```
Thus, it will probably be     R
rejected by the committee.
```

label: Intermediate Conclusion (these facts suggest)
body: Taiwan in the homeland where Austronesian languages have been spoken longest.

label: Evaluate
body: This argument relies on a conditional rule that someone believes to be true. It supports that rule by testifying to the credibility of the person who believes it to be true. Next it asserts the sufficient condition of the rule is true. Finally, it concludes that the necessary condition is therefore likely to be true.

label: Conclusion
body: Most people who aren't already insured by Popelka would save hundreds of dollars by switching.

label: Evidence
body: In a representative survey, people who have switched to Popelka have saved, on average, hundreds of dollars ($250 / year).

label: Evaluate
body:
This is a Comparison argument, and we're saying "Because X's are saving $250 / year, Y's would save $250 (hundreds of dollars) / year".
  - In order for this argument to work, we have to assume that X's and Y's are relevantly similar. To object to a Comparison argument, we we'd want to think "What if something is meaningfully different between X's and Y's?"
  - What could be different between people who switched to Popelka and people who haven't yet switched to Popelka?
  - It's almost like if you heard this argument: in a large representative survey of people who switched to become Android users reported being happier with their phone. Thus, most people who aren't already on an Android would be happier if they switched.
  - We might object that the important difference between the people who switched to Android and those who haven't, is that the former likes Android phones! Maybe the ones who haven't switched, haven't done so because they have made an accurate comparison between iPhone and Android and prefer, for their needs and tastes, the iPhone.
  - If you survey the people who have switched, it's a self-selecting sample of Android enthusiasts. Similarly, if you survey the people who have saved $250 by switching, you're surveying a self-selecting sample of people who had the most motivation to switch to Popelka. Because they found out they could save $250, they switched. What saved them money might not save other customers money. Maybe they own a motorcycle and a mobile home and for some reason they make out much more cheaply with Popelka, whereas the average consumer would not save much money.

label: Goal
body:
Look for an answer highlighting a potential difference between People who have already switched to Popelka and People who haven't switched.
  - Our objection should help us argue that "Even though most people who've switched saved hundreds, most people who haven't switched wouldn't save hundreds by switching."

label: Conclusion (So)
body: To get clothes really clean in a front-loading machine, you need to use a detergent formulated for front-loaders, not an ordinary powder detergent.

label: Evidence
body: Ordinary power detergents don't dissolve readily in front-loading machines.

label: Evaluate
body:
It sounds like the author cares a lot about whether or not the detergent dissolves readily. What does readily mean? Easily, quickly.
  - The author apparently thinks that to get clothes really clean, it would be bad if your detergent weren't dissolving readily.
  - We might choose to look at the argument more formally. The conclusion involves conditional logic, because it uses the necessary indicator "need". Any conditional statement, X → Y, can be read "X requires Y". Our author is saying:
  - Getting clothes really clean (requires) Using special detergent, not ordinary powder
  - The contrapositive creates this logic path: Use ordinary detergent → Clothes not really clean
  - The evidence does not define any "legal standard" of really clean / not really clean, but it does discuss a fact about using ordinary powder detergent: it doesn't dissolve readily.
  - So the evidence provides this part of the conclusion's logic path: Use ordinary detergent → not dissolve readily
  - The missing assumption completes the logic path: not dissolve readily → clothes not really clean

label: Goal
body:
Look for something saying that it's bad when your detergent doesn't dissolve readily. It impedes your ability to get clothes really clean.
  - The argument also assumes a difference when it comes to the detergent formulated especially for front-loading washers. It assumes that this detergent does dissolve readily (and that it doesn't introduce any new factors that preclude clothes from getting really clean).

label: Given
body:
In marketing their products, drug companies often send gifts to physicians.
  - According to a recent survey, most physicians believe that their own choices when prescribing drugs are not influenced by drug companies' gifts. (P -most→ ~I)
  - The same survey indicates that the majority of physicians believe that most other physicians' prescription choices are influenced by such gifts. (P -most→ ~I)

label: Conclusion
body: This country is not a well-functioning democracy.

label: Evidence
body: This bill (or any similar bill) that most people favor and that does not violate anyone's human rights will not pass into law for many years. The people who would be adversely affected by the bill are very influential.

label: Evaluate
body:
We know we want an answer that helps us to prove "not a well-functioning democracy" (either by telling us it's not a democracy at all or by convincing us that it's not well-functioning)
  - The basis we have for this rule is a bill that
    - most people favor
    - does not violate anyone's basic human rights
    - will not be passed (nor anything similar) for many years
    - would adversely affect influential people
  - A correct answer doesn't need to use all those blips. If we wrote a rule that says "If a bill that most people favor won't pass anytime soon, then it's not a well functioning democracy", then that would be a correct answer. It would successfully prove the conclusion.

label: Goal
body: We need an answer to give us a rule that clearly applies to the bill we've learned about and outputs for us the language of "not a well functioning democracy".

label: Statements — conditionals
body:
Widely available fertilizer → only Macro
  - Long term health for soil → Macro + Micro

label: Statements — causal
body: Raking up glass clippings depletes the Micro from the soil, while letting grass clippings decay does not.

label: Statements — fact
body: Many homeowners regularly add widely available fertilizer in the hopes of obtaining long term health for their soil.

label: Evidence
body: The public square was an important tool of democracy, because it provided a forum for varied citizens to discuss important issues of the day, and now the Internet plays the role of the public square.

label: Goal
body: Pick the most provable claim. Avoid overly strong or specific language; avoid broad, unknown comparisons; avoid commenting on topics that weren't covered.

label: Evaluate
body:
There are a lot of overlapping terms ... commercial (widely available) fertilizers ... long term healthy soil ... macro ... micro.
  - This suggests that there are rules to be chained together or facts to apply these rules to.
  - We know many people are using fertilizers, hoping to get long term soil health. Yet we're told a story that fertilizers only give you half of what you need for soil health (macronutrients). You also need micronutrients, which fertilizers don't provide.
  - Meanwhile, we find out that raking up grass clippings takes the micronutrients out of our lawns.

label: Goal
body: So, it seems like we'd be synthesizing things by saying "These people who are using fertilizer better not rake up their clippings, or else they'll be doing one thing good for healthy soil (giving it macronutrients) but doing something that's bad for healthy soil (robbing it of micronutrients).

label: Evidence
body:
In most industrial waste products that contain the toxic chemical XTX, the concentration of this chemical is approximately 1,000 parts per million.
  - A federal law intended to reduce the harm that can result from the introduction of XTX into the environment permits a company to dispose of these waste products in a dump for hazardous waste, but only if the concentration of XTX is below 500 parts per million.
  - Waste products with concentrations above that level must be destroyed by incineration.

label: Provision
body: Manufacturers may not dilute XTX-containing waste products to bring their concentration of XTX down to a permissible level for dumping.

label: Evaluate
body: The right answer should provide a reason against permitting dilution of XTX-containing waste products.

label: Annette's Only Claim
body: If you wanna persuade the town council to adopt your plan, take them on a trip to visit other towns that have successfully implemented your plan.

label: Does Sefu Diagree?
body:
Well, he kinda has to! Since there's only one claim, Sefu has to be saying that it would NOT be a good idea to take the town council on a trip to visit other towns.
  - He supports that idea by saying, "If they accepted a trip from me, someone who clearly has an interest in their votes, it would give the appearance that I'm bribing them or influencing them in some inappropriate way."

label: Goal
body: Since Annette only makes one claim, Sefu has to be disagreeing with that claim. She thinks that if Sefu wants his plan to be adopted, it would be a good idea to take the town council on a trip to other town, and he thinks it wouldn't be a good idea.

label: Conclusion
body: Eating fish can lower one's cholesterol level.

label: Evidence
body: (1) Two groups were studied. (2) The first group ate a balanced diet including two servings of fish per week; the second ate a similar diet without fish. (3) The first group showed lower cholesterol levels, on average, than the second group. (4) The two groups had displayed similar average cholesterol levels prior to the study.

label: Evaluate
body: The argument relies on a study that compares two groups. To support the conclusion that fish caused the lower cholesterol, the study must rule out the obvious alternative: that the fish group already had lower cholesterol going in. The "similar pre-study cholesterol" claim does exactly that — it eliminates the pre-existing-difference explanation, leaving the dietary difference as the operative variable.

label: Goal
body: Find an answer that captures this role: the claim rules out an alternative explanation for why the fish group ended up with lower cholesterol.

label: Conclusion
body: Fish can lower cholesterol.

label: Evidence
body: Fish-eating group ended with lower cholesterol than the no-fish group. Both groups had similar starting cholesterol.

label: Evaluate
body: The starting-cholesterol claim rules out the alternative that the fish group was already different.

label: Goal
body: Find the answer about ruling out an alternative explanation.

label: Conclusion
body: Eating fish can lower one's cholesterol level.

label: Evidence
body: Two groups were studied. The first group ate a balanced diet including two servings of fish per week. The second group ate a very similar diet, but ate no fish. The first group showed lower cholesterol levels, on average, than the second group. The two groups had displayed similar average cholesterol levels prior to the study.

label: Evaluate
body:
Whenever we read Role or Main Conclusion, we prime our brain before reading the paragraph with a reminder that usually the Conclusion will be found earlier than the Evidence (frequently it's the first claim, or it's the first claim after a pivot).
  - Everything after the first sentence describes the study. Only the first sentence is an opinion/prediction, so it's the Conclusion.
  - The claim about pre-study cholesterol levels closes off the "they were already different" alternative explanation.

label: Goal
body: Look for an answer saying the claim rules out an alternative explanation for the study's result.

label: Conclusion
body: Satnavs save fuel and promote safety.

label: Evidence
body:
Satnavs are a computer voice that announces directions as you drive.
  - When traveling to a new place, drivers with satnavs drove 7% fewer miles per journey than did drivers using paper maps.
  - Fewer miles driven means less fuel consumed, generally.
  - Also, the drivers using satnavs didn't have to take their eyes off the road like the the drivers using paper maps did, so presumably they drove more carefully.

label: Evidence
body:
The intended purpose was to only give passing grades to the students most committed to being science majors.
  - But some of the students who get passing grades are those who are least enthusiastic about science.

label: Setup
body: If two nations have little interaction with each other, then they have little knowledge of another's needs and problems. Sympathy and justice depend largely on understanding the needs and problems of others. In other words, if you don't understand the needs and problems of others, it will be hard to achieve sympathy or justice with them.

label: Director's Explanation
body: It wasn't because it had a couple negative reviews. It's because it was competing with several other films that share the same audience, and it's a pretty small audience.

label: Evaluate
body:
This is a Two-Pronged Conclusion, which means we can strengthen the argument by any answer that helps us argue that satnavs save fuel or one that helps us argue that satnavs promote safety.
  - The argument doesn't have any obvious missing links we need to connect, so we should probably role play The Defense and think about what objections could be made.
  - How could someone argue that "satnavs don't save fuel"?
    - maybe the energy it takes to run the satnav computer is draining fuel, so even though drivers go 7% fewer miles they still end up using at least as much fuel.
    - maybe having a satnav encourages drivers to drive in an inefficient manner (they're determined to beat the "estimated time" on the satnav, so they start speeding a lot, which wastes gas)
  - How could someone argue that "satnavs don't promote safety"?
    - maybe we could argue that the satnav doesn't give the driver much warning before a turn, so the driver has to swerve to get to their exit.
    - maybe the satnav guides people to make more dangerous moves, like trying to make a left out of a residential area with no stoplight onto a busy road.
  - The evidence also only talks about how satnavs compare to paper maps when it comes to traveling to novel destinations. Maybe when you're traveling to familiar destinations, satnavs have no benefits and maybe even make the situation worse?

label: Goal
body: Let's look for an answer that shoots down one of these objections or otherwise makes us feel better about saving gas / being safer when you have a satnav in your car.

label: Situation
body:
You can't get the best out of your employee by threatening them with bad stuff or offering rewards if they do good stuff.
  - Instead, they need to want to do a good job for its own sake.

label: Recommendation
body: A great way to get them to want a job for its own sake is to delegate responsibility to them, especially for decisions that used to be managerial.

label: Goal
body:
The answers look shorter than the stimulus, so we may or may not get the preamble about "You can't get great performance out of someone with threats or rewards".
  - It's more likely that we'll hear the advice for getting them to love something for its own sake.
  - By making someone feel more important / more involved (delegating managerial decisions to them), you can make them more motivated to do a good job for its own sake.

label: Richard's Explicit / Implied Claims
body:
1. A fundamental requirement of art is that it represent
  2. Abstract art fails to represent
  3. Abstract art will eventually be seen as an aberration.
  4. It will be seen as an aberration because it doesn't meet the fundamental requirement of art.

label: Jung-Su's Position on those Claims
body:
1. No comment. Nothing about fundamental requirement.
  2. Disagrees? She says that "makers of abstract art choose to represent the purely formal features of objects.
  3. No comment. She says "whatever others might come to say", as a noncommittal nod to the future. One day others might come to say abstract art is aberration, who knows? What we do know is that today it's not an aberration; it's part of the mainstream.
  4. Since there's no comment on #3, there's definitely no comment on the specific causal mechanism that would lead to #3 coming to pass.

label: Goal
body: It looks like claim 2 is the only area where Jung-Su disagrees. So let's look for an answer about whether or not abstract art represents stuff.

label: Conclusion (Therefore)
body: It's likely that people who regularly inhale the scent of lavender are reducing their incidence of illness by doing so.

label: Evidence
body:
Inhaling the scent of lavender tends to reduce stress.
  - Intense stress can impair the immune system, making one more susceptible to illness.

label: Evaluate
body:
At first this seems like a classic Explain Curious Fact, because the conclusion is making a causal claim. But the evidence isn't some non-causal curious fact like a correlation. The evidence is actually causal itself.
  - Research has shown that inhaling the scent of lavender has measurable effects tending to reduce stress. So most people who inhale lavender will have their stress reduced.
  - We also hear that intense stress can impair the immune system, making one more susceptible to illness. This causal connection is much weaker. We know that some people have stress that impairs their immune system (so presumably reduced stress would be good for their immune system).
  - It seems like the only way to argue that people who regularly inhale the scent of lavender wouldn't have their incidence of illness lowered is if we say, "Yes, their stress is reduced, but their stress wasn't impairing their immune system, so the lavender's stress reduction doesn't have any effect on their immune system."

label: Goal
body: Let's look for an answer saying, "some of these people who regularly inhale lavender are having stress impair their immune system".

label: Conclusion (therefore)
body: The Anderson's real income (adjusted for inflation) must have increased over the last five years.

label: Evidence (since)
body:
Government stats show that real average income for families has risen over the last five years.
  - The Andersen family's income is average for families.

label: Evaluate
body:
This seems to be some sort of mathematical flaw, playing off two different usages of the word "average". Let's flip into objection mode:
  - Given that ... the Anderson's have a family income that is average for families (like if the average family income is $100k, their family income is $100k),
  - and given that ... average income for families has risen over the last five years.
  - How could we still argue that .... the Anderson's income has not increased over the last five years?
  - Well, naturally when we hear "average income for families has risen over the last five years", that does not mean that all families' income has risen. Some have gone up. Some have stayed the same. Some have gone down. But overall, once you average all those stories together, the average has moved up.
  - So we can seemingly just say that the Anderson's weren't lucky enough to be beneficiaries of this recent trend of rising family income. Maybe they also had a family income of $100k five years ago. Maybe they even used to make $180k, and then Mr. Anderson got laid off, and now they're only making $100k.

label: Goal
body: The fact that the Anderson's currently have the average family income doesn't mean that their family income has behaved as "average family income" has over the past five years.

label: Conclusion
body: A stronger economy will probably make it much harder to find day care.

label: Evidence
body: In a stronger economy, many day-care workers will quit to take better-paying jobs in other fields.

label: Evaluate
body:
Since this argument is based on a Prediction, which is an implicit comparison between our Current World and this Hypothetical World, we want to think about what sort of similarities and differences there could be between these two worlds.
  - In the Hypothetical World of stronger economy, the author thinks that one change (many day-care workers quit to take better-paying jobs in other fields) will lead to another change (much harder to find day care).
  - We need to consider what else could change in this hypothetical world that could relate to how hard it is to find day care.
  - The author is assuming the balance between Supply of day care workers and Demand for day care workers will be tilted.
  - He states that the Demand for day care will go up in a stronger economy, as employment increases, and he assumes the overall Supply of day care will go down, since existing day care workers will leave the field.
  - But what if people who weren't in day care before are tempted to join the field of day care?
  - Maybe someone is working at fast food for $10 / hr and then realizes they could do daycare for $15 / hr.
  - As the current $15 / hr day care worker goes off to chase $20 / hr jobs in this stronger economy, there could be other workers or currently unemployed people who are eager to fill these open day care spots.

label: Goal
body: Since the big objection to the author's argument is, "What if, in a stronger economy, there would be people who want to replace all the day-care workers who quit?", the argument needs to assume that "in a stronger economy, we would not be able to find enough people to fill all the day care jobs that were vacated by workers who quit".

label: Information — comparisons (far less / much faster)
body: Ostrich farming requires fewer acres than cattle farming, and ostriches reproduce much faster than cattle.

label: Information — comparison (by contrast)
body:
Start-up requirements for cattle ranching are a large herd of cows, one bull, and at least two acres per cow.
  - Start-up requirements for ostrich farming are two pairs of yearling ostriches and one acre of similar land.

label: Information — comparisons (greater / five times)
body: Start up costs for ostrich farming are greater, but it can bring in as much as five times what cattle ranching does.

label: Evaluate
body:
If you were thinking, "Should I farm cattle or ostriches", ostriches seems to win in almost every category:
  1. you need fewer acres
  2. they reproduce faster
  3. you only need four ostriches an one acre of land to get going
  4. it can bring in 5x the revenue
  - The one downside is that the start-up costs are greater. We might be scratching our heads, thinking, "How are start-up costs greater? Everything sounded simpler and more lucrative with ostrich farming?"
  - It must be really expensive to buy those two pairs of yearling ostriches.
  - After all, when we compare start-up costs for each:
```
CATTLE                          OSTRICHES
one bull + large herd of cows   two pairs (4) yearling ostriches
two acres per cow               one acre of similar land
```
  - We're definitely saving money when it comes to acreage. We only have to pay for one acre of similar (and thus similarly priced) land. For cattle, we need two acres per cow and we start with a large herd of cows (that's definitely at least 10 cows, so at least 20 acres of land).
  - So the only place where ostriches could cost more would be paying for those two pairs of yearlings.

label: Goal
body: Let's look for something playing off these comparisons, being wary of overstating the case (there might be answers making sensational claims about how much better ostrich farming is). Maybe it will have something to do with the "hidden fact" that two pairs of yearlings are apparently pretty pricey to procure.

label: Conclusion
body: The dogs must have been transported from one region to the other by boat (probably during a trading expedition).

label: Evidence (since)
body:
The dogs have never existed in the wild.
  - It would be very unlikely that a rare trait like hairlessness arose two separate times.
  - The vast mountainous jungle separating western Mexico and coastal Peru would have made overland trouble extremely difficult.

label: Evaluate
body:
The author's conclusion is offering an explanation for a curious fact.
  - Curious Fact ... how is it that for several centuries there have been hairless dogs in western Mexico and coastal Peru?
  - Author's Explanation .... the dogs must have been transported from one region to the other by boat.
  - Whenever we see this type of argument we consider 2 things:
    1. can we think of any Alternate Explanation for the curious fact?
    2. how plausible is the Author's Explanation?
  - The author already ruled out a couple possible alternate explanations:
    - the dogs just roam the wild and ended up in both locales
    - the trait of hairlessness just spontaneously arose in two different places
    - the dogs didn't travel overland from one place to another
  - The author doesn't fully rule them out, but makes the 2nd and 3rd ideas there seem very sketchy / unlikely.
  - Are there any alternate explanations that would get the dogs from one place to another that don't involve boat or overland?
  - We can't say by plane, because they have been in both spots for several centuries, so it predates airplane technology.
  - Maybe a hurricane lifted one off the ground in one place and deposited it in the other? Maybe one of them floated on a piece of driftwood (not an actual boat) from one place to the other?
  - How about the plausibility of the author's story? What needs to be true for the boat hypothesis to be plausible? Well we have to assume that one of these dogs would be willing to get on a boat / would be able to survive the journey.

label: Goal
body: Look for an answer that rules out an alternate explanation for how the dogs ended up in both places or that establishes something required for the author's explanation to be plausible.

label: Statements — superlative (oldest)
body: Microdiamonds are the oldest fragment of Earth's early crust that we've identified.

label: Statements — quantitative
body:
Microdiamonds are only 50 microns across and were formed 4.2 billion years ago.
  - The Earth formed 4.5 billion years ago (300 million years prior)

label: Evaluate
body:
There are some Overlapping Ideas (microdiamonds / Earth's crust), but it's not that clear how we would synthesize these statements.
  - We could say stuff like "the oldest fragments of Earth's early crust that we've identified are only 50 microns across".

label: Goal
body: Overall, there's no Conditional / Causal / Pivot wording to guide us in how they want us to synthesize any of these facts, so let's just head to the answers looking for the most provable claim.

label: Conclusion (hence)
body: We should ensure that Internet users have at least as much freedom of expression as did people speaking in the public square.

label: Evaluate
body:
The conclusion is making a recommendation ("should"). Does the evidence define what we should do or have anything normative or evaluative that would match that concept?
  - It sounds like the author places value on the public square, saying it was an important tool of democracy.
  - So if the author is concluding that we should ensure that Internet users have as much freedom of expression as people did in the public square, she must be thinking that freedom of expression is an important part of having the Internet play the same role as the public square did.
  - Maybe she's assuming "you need the same level of freedom of expression in order for the Internet to also be able to provide a forum for disparate citizens to discuss important issues of the day".
  - There's also a wrinkle in this argument in the sense that the author says, "Today, a person with Internet access can ... allow the Internet to play the role once played by the public square". But do Internet users need the Internet to play that role? Or do they have other options for something that could play the role once played by the public square, in which case we don't need to specifically make sure that the Internet is ready to play the role?
  - Does society even need that role to be played? The author seems to assume that we should do what we need to do to make sure something modern can play the role of this "important tool of democracy". What if we're done with democracy?

label: Goal
body: This argument does not lend itself to an obvious prephrase. We know broadly that the author cares about maintaining the important democratic tool of providing a forum for disparate citizens to debate modern issues. And we know that she thinks that for the Internet to be this tool, we should be making sure people have at least as much freedom of expression as they did speaking in the public square.

label: Conclusion (Thus)
body: It's likely that the reasoning power and spatial intuition exercised in chess-playing also contribute to achievement in many other areas of intellectual activity.

label: Evidence
body: In the study of elementary school children who completed an experimental program in which they learn to play chess, most of the children who completed the program soon showed a significant increase in achievement levels in all their schoolwork.

label: Evaluate
body:
Like so many other causal arguments, this argument establishes a correlation in the evidence and then introduces a causal verb (or implicit causal structure) in the conclusion.
  - The evidence provides a before/after correlation: most of the students who completed the chess program soon showed a big uptick in achievement levels in all their schoolwork.
  - The conclusion introduces a causal verb: The reasoning/spatial sense of chess contributes to achievement in other intellectual areas.
  - Since the author is looking at the results of a study / looking at something that changed over time, and then concluding a potential explanation for that data, we can use our Explain Curious Fact mindset:
  - Curious Fact ... Why did most of the kids who went through the chess program have an uptick in schoolwork afterwards?
  - Author's Explanation ... Chess improved their reasoning power / spatial intuition, and those improved faculties allowed them to do better on their schoolwork.

label: Goal
body:
Since this is Weaken, we look for two different types of correct answers (with a strong bias towards the first type):
  1. Could there be some Alternate Explanation for the curious fact? What could be a different reason why the students who went through the chess program generally had an increase in school achievement afterwards?
  2. Could we undermine the plausibility of the Author's Explanation? What could make it seem like chess didn't really improve the kids' reasoning or spatial intuition, or make it seem like even if it did, those improved faculties wouldn't be likely to cause a boost in school achievement.

label: Conclusion
body: Kate must sometimes shop at the local health food store on Wednesdays.

label: Evidence
body:
Kate usually buys guava juice on Wednesdays.
  - The only place you can buy guava juice is the local health food store.

label: Evaluate
body:
This is definitely an airtight argument. It does have some quantified and conditional words (usually / the only / sometimes), so we could try to put it into some algebra.
  - On Wednesdays, Kate usually buys guava → Most Wednesdays, Kate buys guava
  - Only place to buy guava is local health food stores → buys guava → local health food stores
  - Thus, on some Wednesdays, Kate goes to local health food store → Some Wednesdays, Kate shops local health food store
  - It's weird that the conclusion is milder in strength than it could have been. We could have concluded that on "she must usually shop at the local health food store on Wednesdays".
  - What makes the argument work is that we know Kate does something (buy guava on Wed) and we know there's only one way to do that something (shop at local health food store), so that guarantees us that Kate uses that "only one way".

label: Goal
body:
Look for an argument with two premises. One of them should be conditional. The other one should provide a fact that triggers the conditional. The conclusion should involve a (possibly watered-down) inference about the outcome of that conditional.
  - Prem 1: Most/Some A's are B.
  - Prem 2: The only way to be B is to be C.
  - Conc: Thus, Most/Some A's are C.

label: Conclusion
body: It's absurd to think that the new weekly pickup program will be more cost effective because it will lead to a greater volume of recyclables collected each year. (i.e. the new weekly pickup program will not be more cost effective -- either because it won't lead to a greater volume of recyclables collected or because it won't be cost effective for some other reason)

label: Evidence
body: People will put out the same volume of recyclables overall; it will just be spread out over a greater number of pickups.

label: Evaluate
body:
Given that .... people will put out the same volume overall (it will just be a lower amount each week rather than a bigger amount every two weeks)
  - How could we still argue that ... the weekly pickup program would be more cost effective?
  - We'd probably need to hear about other factors involved in doing recyclable pickups that would be more efficient / less costly if we were doing weekly pickups of less stuff, compared to bi-weekly pickups of more stuff.

label: Goal
body: Look for something that helps us argue that making twice the trips to pick up half as much recyclables each time would somehow save money (don't have to hire as many workers? more efficient when it comes to unloading and sorting the recyclables? the trucks get way better mileage when they're only 1/2 loaded?)

label: Conclusion (Hence)
body: Designing intro science courses to serve as proving grounds hasn't served its intended purpose.

label: Evaluate
body:
This conclusion talks about whether or not something is fulfilling the "intended purpose", which was defined at the outset with a conditional rule (only those most committed to being sci majors will get passing grades).
  - That sort of setup suggests that this will be testing a LINKING idea or will be focused on the Idea Math of triggers and outcomes.
  - We have failed our intended purpose if some people who get passing grades are "not most committed to being science majors".
  - We know the premise is about people who get passing grades, despite being "least enthusiastic about science".
  - Does being least enthusiastic about science mean you're not the most committed to being a science major? No, it doesn't. You might be hugely committed to being a science major because your parents are totally forcing you to and don't plan to stand up to them. But that's compatible with being among the "least enthusiastic".

label: Goal
body: The author is assuming that, "These students who are least enthusiastic about science are not most committed to being science majors".

label: Given that ...
body: The ancestors of modern birds and reptiles would have had predators who didn't have the ability to hear hissing sounds,

label: How could it be that ...
body: These ancestors evolved the ability to hiss?

label: Evaluate
body:
This paradox is a little harder than average to find. Usually, the final claim in the paragraph is the Surprising Claim we need to explain. But here, it feels more like the final claim is a background fact, and the surprise comes earlier.
  - The author is convinced that early ancestors of birds and reptiles would have had the ability to hiss, even though their predators wouldn't have been able to hear hissing sounds.

label: Goal
body:
To reconcile this paradox and explain why these ancestors would have evolved hissing behavior, we could go a couple different ways:
  1. Yes, the predators couldn't hear the hissing, but the hissing still worked as a deterrent to predators because _______ .
  or
  2. Yes, the hissing wasn't an effective deterrent against predators because they couldn't hear it, but the hissing still had adaptive value because _______ .

label: Conclusion
body: It was likely the development of cooking that made it possible for humans to support a large brain with a small gut.

label: Evidence
body: Supporting a large brain with a small gut requires getting more calories from less food. Our ancestors developed large brains around the time that they began to control fire. Today, people who choose to eat only raw food have difficulty getting enough calories.

label: Evaluate
body: The conclusion is a causal explanation: cooking made it possible for us to have big brains and small guts. The first piece of evidence is a conditional relationship: Big brain + small gut requires more calories from less food. The second piece of evidence is a temporal correlation: Big brains and controlling fire (which we can pretty reasonably infer is a precondition for cooking) happened around the same time. The last piece of evidence is a control group: those who don't cook food don't get enough calories. But....enough calories for what exactly? Do the raw foodists really not get enough calories to support their big ol' brains? It doesn't specify, which makes this pretty poor evidence.

label: Goal
body: As is the case with all arguments, we can strengthen in a variety of ways. The goal of prediction is not to come up with what the right answer must say, but instead to think through what a right answer might do. We're given a conditional premise: Big brain + small gut requires more calories from less food. If we establish that the only way to satisfy that requirement is to cook your food, this argument looks a whole lot better.

label: Conclusion (so)
body: The increase in Northern Cardinals in Nova Scotia by 2000 is probably due to warmer winters.

label: Evidence
body: The argument is built on the observed change that Northern Cardinals were rare in 1980 but became common by 2000, and we know that winters have gotten warmer from 1980 to 2000.

label: Evaluate
body: This argument follows the "Explain Curious Fact" pattern, where the author provides a causal explanation for a change. *Curious Fact:* How come there are more northern cardinals in NS? *Explanation:* It's cuz the winters there are warmer now.

label: Goal
body: We usually weaken Explain Curious Fact by suggesting an alternate explanation for the curious fact (what could be a *different* reason why there are more northern cardinals in NS?), and sometimes undermining the plausibility of the author's explanation (debunking that warmer winters brought them to NS).

label: Evidence
body: Personality is linked to genes. Genes do not usually change over time.

label: Conclusion
body: So personality does not change over time.

label: Evaluate
body: Whether or not we feel good about articulating an actual objection to this logic, we can feel good about our ability to keep track of repeated concepts (personality, genes, don't change -- all said twice). Premise 1 - X is linked to Y. Premise 2 - Y doesn't change over time. Conclusion - X doesn't change over time.

label: Goal
body: Let's look for something that matches the structure listed above (or something that is similarly vulnerable to an objection like, "Just because two things are linked doesn't mean that if one is the same, the other is the same. Two things could be linked even if one thing is changing and the other thing isn't."

label: Conclusion (So)
body: Brooks will have few supporters in this country.

label: Evidence
body: Brooks was arrested on charges of corruption several years ago, by McFarlane (the military dictator). Brooks is now pardoned and has agreed to join McFarlane's government. Almost all of McFarlane's supporters believe Brooks is guilty of corruption. And almost all of McFarlane's opponents will oppose anyone who agrees to join his government.

label: Implicit Principle
body: We want something like, "Get a weak, manageable sample of something bad now, so that you can be ready for a stronger version of it later and not get yourself in a lot of trouble". i.e. "If you expose yourself to the manageable stress of delivering your work presentation to your friends, then you won't suffer crippling anxiety when it's time to actually face that conference room and deliver your presentation at work."

label: Evaluate
body: Whenever we're evaluating an author's causal hypothesis for a curious fact, we have two different pressure points to consider: 1. Alternate Explanations for that curious fact 2. the plausibility of the author's explanation

label: Evaluate
body: The goal is to prove that Brooks will have few supporters, and the author is trying to do so by arguing via a "Damned if you do, damned if you don't" style of binary. She's trying to make the case that, "If you're A, you don't support Brooks. And if you're not A, you don't support Brooks." M's supporter → think B is guilty of corruption. M's opponent → don't support anyone agreeing to join M's govt (as B has). We want to ask ourselves whether both of those roads end in the idea of "Brooks does not have their support", and then we also want to ask whether those are the only two starting points. The author has established that if you're an opponent of M, then you will oppose Brooks, since she has agreed to join his government. But the author hasn't established that if you're a supporter of M, that you'll oppose B. She's only established that if you're a supporter of M, you think Brooks is guilty of corruption. So there is a Missing Link assumption happening here that, "If you believe Brooks is guilty of corruption, then you won't support her." If we were trying to think of Objections (for the sake of Defender assumptions that would rule them out), we'd be trying to think of ways to argue that even given this evidence, it's possibly that Brooks has many supporters. One possible objection could be, "Maybe most of the country doesn't identify as a supporter or an opponent of M. They're just kind of neutral or ambivalent. We don't know how people who aren't opponents/supporters of M feel about Brooks. The author is sort of assuming a binary, that everyone either supports or opposes M."

label: Goal
body: Look for a link from "If believe guilty of corruption, then don't support" or look for an answer ruling out the possibility that we're failing to consider people in this country who are neither supporters nor opponents.

label: Conclusion (Therefore)
body: If a piece of so-called amber contains a normal-appearing insect, it's more likely to be fake (than would be a piece of so-called amber containing no insect or a not-normal appearing insect).

label: Evidence
body: Forgers create fake amber and often embed small, normal-appearing insects in it.

label: Evaluate
body: The conclusion is saying that a normal-appearing insect inside a supposed piece of amber is a sign that it's probably fake amber. After all, forgers often put normal-appearing insects in their fake amber. If we were trying to object to this argument, we would have to argue that there are way more legitimate pieces of amber with normal-appearing insects in them out there on the market than there are fake pieces with normal-appearing insects in them. Say that in any given year, forgers produce about 1,000 pieces of fake amber with a normal-appearing insect in them. Meanwhile, in any given year, 10,000 pieces of real amber with a normal-appearing insect in them are found. In that marketplace, finding a piece of supposed amber that has a normal-appearing insect in it would not be a sign that it's likely a fake. It could be a fake, but it's 10 times more likely that it's real.

label: Goal
body: We need to rule out this objection. We need the marketplace to contain more examples of fake amber with normal-appearing insects than real amber with normal-appearing insects in it. Or we just need to be more convinced that seeing a normal-appearing insect is a sign that the amber is probably fake.

label: Conclusion (for this reason)
body: Steps should be taken to educate people about the ethical use of the Internet.

label: Evidence
body: People seem to feel more free to harm others through the Internet (such as info theft and hacking) and feel less morally constrained.

label: Evaluate
body: This argument involves a Problem and a Recommended solution. To strengthen this argument, we would want to hear that this recommended solution will actually help to address the problem. Would "educating people about ethical use of the Internet" have any affect on this problem? Would ethical education lead to feeling more morally constrained?

label: Goal
body: Let's look for something like, "If people don't feel morally constrained enough, then they should receive ethical education" or anything else that would strengthen the recommendation the author is offering for this problem.

label: Conclusion (it is clear that)
body: Some residents did switch to phosphate-free detergents.

label: Evidence (since)
body: Phosphate pollution from the municipal wastewater treatment plant decreased significantly in the past year.

label: Evaluate
body: Since the author's conclusion is assuming a causal Explanation for a Curious Fact, we can use our Curious Fact / Explanation mindset. Curious Fact ... why did the phosphate pollution from the treatment plant decrease significantly over the past year? Author's Explanation ... some residents switched to phosphate-free detergents. We, of course, jump into action thinking - could there be some Alternate Explanation for the curious fact? - how plausible is the Author's Explanation?

label: Goal
body: On Evaluate, we're looking for a question that could be answered in some way that would be an Objection. An Objection to this argument would either, suggest an Alternate Explanation for why municipal treatment plants have lower phosphate pollution this year, or undermine the Author's Explanation that some residents have switched to phosphate-free detergents.

label: Conclusion
body: It's unwise for farmers to grow genetically engineered crops.

label: Evidence
body: At any point, a study might come out that freaks people out about one of the genetically engineered crops you use. genetically engineered crops aren't fetching enough profit/revenue to be worth that risk.

label: Evaluate
body: A conclusion should be the Author's Opinion and should be Supported by at least one explicit claim. Here, the word unwise signified Opinion. And if we ask ourselves, "Why is it unwise to grow genetically engineered crops?", the other two claims act like an answer to that question: "because ... your genetically engineered crop is one bad news story from being canceled by scared consumers, and it's not a lucrative enough product to merit that risk."

label: Goal
body: Just go find the Conclusion, buddy! It's your day off. Just find "it is unwise to grow genetically engineered plants", so some equivalent-meaning rephrasing like "I wouldn't grow those crops, if I were you".

label: Doctor's Goal
body: Help a patient to avoid a severe form of a disease.

label: Doctor's Method
body: Give the patient a vaccine with a weakened form of that disease, so that the patient will be better able to resist that pathogen later.

label: Anticipate / Goal
body: We know that the fill in the blank is going to synthesize multiple ideas. There are only two ideas here, so we have to figure out what we get by combining them. Usually the key to synthesis is that two claims have some overlapping idea: in this case, the overlapping concept is knowledge/understanding of another's needs and problems. We can imagine these ideas chaining together to give us something like this sort of chain: if two nations don't interact much, then won't understand other's needs / problems, and so sympathy / justice will be difficult. If we wanted to pretend this was a true conditional, it would look something like this: little interaction → little understanding of needs / problems → no sympathy or justice. In that case, a contrapositive chain would sound like: Sympathy and justice require understanding each other's needs/problems, which requires interacting a lot with each other.

label: Conclusion (clearly)
body: The only effective way to reduce significantly the overall incidence of most cancers and birth defects is to halt industries known to produce these pollutants.

label: Intermediate Conclusion
body: We need to aim at preventing cancers and birth defects.

label: Evidence (since)
body: Most cancers and birth defects are incurable. They have been linked to pollutants in water, where they move up the food chain to people.

label: Evidence (given that)
body: Industries known to produce pollutants are unlikely to comply adequately with strict environmental regulations.

label: Evaluate
body: The move from Premise to Intermediate seems pretty hard to object to. If most cancers and birth defects are incurable, then is it fair to say "we need to aim at preventing them"? Do we have any other options besides trying to prevent them? I guess we could otherwise say, "prevention is unrealistic, but we could realistically try to develop treatments that makes living with these conditions more tolerable". What about the move to the Main Conclusion? Given that ... industries that produce the pollutants linked to cancer and birth defects are unlikely to comply with strict environmental regulations. How could we argue that ... halting these industries isn't the only effective way to get a significant reduction in the incidences of these cancers? I'm not sure specifically what to argue there, but because the conclusion is so restrictive, any other way we can think of to get a significant reduction in these cancers and birth defects will work as an objection to this conclusion.

label: Goal
body: It's a long argument with multiple conclusions, so we should be staying very flexible. But we'd love to find an answer that can help us argue, "we don't need to aim at preventing", or "halting industries that produce these pollutants isn't the only effective way to significantly reduce the incidence of cancers / birth defects".

label: Conclusion
body: Our side will benefit from showing a desire to compromise with the opposition.

label: Evidence
body: If they respond positively, a compromise will be reached. If they don't respond positively, they will be held responsible for the failure to compromise and our side will benefit.

label: Evaluate
body: We have to prove that showing a desire to compromise will "benefit our side", but we're given two different (binary, exhaustive) possibilities for what might happen if we show a desire. To guarantee the conclusion, we need to make sure that our side benefits no matter what. We know that if they don't respond positively, they get blamed and we benefit (it said so explicitly). But we don't know that we benefit if they respond positively. We only know that a compromise will be reached.

label: Goal
body: The only loose end in guaranteeing that we benefit is establishing that "if a compromise is reached, our side will benefit".

label: Conclusion
body: There is harm in promoting a folk remedy that has no effect.

label: Evidence
body: People who are convinced to use an ineffective remedy continue with it for years rather than pursuing conventional treatments that would almost certainly help them.

label: Evaluate
body: We know that the rule we select needs to help us prove that "doing X is harmful" or some equivalent synonym. Why is promoting folk remedies harmful? It's not literally harmful, because the remedy has no effect, but it steers people away from treatments that would probably help. So we're defining "harm" as "directed you away from something that would help".

label: Goal
body: Look for an answer saying something like, "If promoting X causes someone to avoid something that would have been helpful to them, then we can say that promoting X is harmful."

label: Conclusion
body: It's not very convincing to say that the new radio format is popular just because more than 3/4 of the listeners who call in requests say they're pleased.

label: Evidence
body: This would be as un-convincing as determining whether Candidate X is popular by asking only people who are already planning to vote for X.

label: Evaluate
body: The author is pointing out how quizzing people who listen to the radio station is a sampling error. By definition, if they're still listening to the radio station, they must approve of the new format. Similarly (by analogy), if you only asked supporters of a certain candidate whether they approve of that candidate, you would get a really high percentage of people saying they support that candidate.

label: Goal
body: Look for an answer saying the author uses an analogy about political candidates to point out the sampling error with radio listeners.

label: Conclusion
body: People who say that Shakespeare didn't write the plays attributed to him are motivated purely by snobbery.

label: Evidence
body: Shakes was the son of a glove maker, whereas the other potential authors of "his" plays were aristocrats, and many of the people arguing that these other people wrote S's plays are the descendants of these aristocrats.

label: Goal
body: So we have two comparisons we can judge. When it comes to "how long you can be submerged" / "how deep you can dive", dolphins > northern fur seals; elephant seal > Weddell seal. Those don't chain together, because we don't have any way to relate them to each other. So we'll just look for something to contradict one of these two.

label: Albert's Claims
body: 1. Swenson's popular book is a model of poor scholarship. 2. Swenson's popular book argues that sun exposure does not harm skin cells. 3. Swenson's popular book is valuable (despite this) because it's stimulated new research on sun exposure.

label: Evaluate
body: Given this evidence, how could we argue that "people claiming S didn't write all the plays commonly attributed to him are NOT motivated purely by snobbery (they might be motivated partially by snobbery, but they're motivated by something else as well). First of all, are these people even aware that S is the son of a glove maker? They can't be using this against Shakes if they don't know it. Secondly, it says that many of the people claiming S didn't write all the plays are descendants of aristocrats, but that leaves open the possibility that many others claiming the same thing aren't descendants of aristocrats. They might be descendants of lower class people and have no "snobby" motive at all. Finally, it doesn't seem like this argument gives much of a charitable reading of the opponents' position. What is their evidence for thinking Shakespeare didn't write all these plays?

label: Goal
body: Since the conclusion so dismissively says that "these claims are 100% snobbery", we just need any answer that allows us to argue that at least part of this isn't snobbery, it's coming from some other source of evidence or motivation (maybe it's coming from jealously)

label: Comparing the Two Populations
body:
```
              population 1                    population 2
        both tree-dwelling lemurs
        both more nocturnal activity during winter
        live in rain forest             live in deciduous forest
        tree canopy                     many trees
        consistent                      lose leaves
        year round                      during winter
        small winter increase           big winter increase
        in nocturnal activity           in nocturnal activity
```

label: Evaluate / Goal
body: We need to explain how the rainforest lemurs are different from deciduous lemurs, in regards to why the deciduous lemurs have a bigger uptick in nocturnal activity during the winter. Since we were told one difference between the two (year-round canopy vs. lose leaves), we anticipate that the correct answer will "Use that difference to explain this difference". How come the lemurs who live in trees that "lose leaves during winter" are doing "more nocturnal activity" than are the lemurs who live in trees that "still have a full canopy of leaves throughout winter"?

label: Conclusion
body: It is a specious (i.e. faulty) distinction to say that literary fiction should be interpreted while genre fictions should be merely a source of easy pleasure.

label: Intermediate Conclusion (because)
body: No work should be interpreted.

label: Evidence
body: When we evaluate a work principally for its themes and ideas, we cut ourselves off from the work's emotional impact.

label: Evaluate
body: Whenever we read Role or Main Conclusion arguments, we remind ourselves that there's a 90% chance the conclusion will be the first sentence or will be some rebuttal sentiment. This argument begins with an Attribution, "It is common to argue that ...", which would lead us to suspect that a rebuttal is coming, and indeed we do get one after the Pivot (but, yet, however).

label: Goal
body: We're being asked about the role of the final sentence, which was the premise. Let's look for an answer saying that the last sentence is support / evidence / premise for the conclusion that "no work should be interpreted".

label: Principle
body:
```
not criticizing yourself                          shouldn't criticize
for behavior X                    and    →         someone else
not vowing to stop X                               for doing X
```

label: Application
body:
```
Shimada doesn't vow to        →        shouldn't criticize
stop being tardy himself               M for tardiness
```

label: Evaluate
body: Principle-Application questions are dreamy, because they are very self-similar. 1. We're given a rule 2. The application is trying to conclude the right side of the rule 3. Something about the left side of the rule still hasn't been clearly established, and that's our whole job -- figuring out what that is.
