This application is indeed concluding the right side of the rule, shouldn't criticize someone else for [tardiness]. Have we established that "Shimada doesn't criticize himself for being tardy" and that "Shimada does not vow to stop being tardy himself?" Not quite. We only established that Shimada hasn't vowed to stop being tardy himself. Why do we need both? Isn't the rule saying or? It does seem that way at first, but if it were really an or trigger, then saying that Shimada doesn't vow to stop being tardy himself would be sufficient to trigger the rule. If the application were already a correct usage of the rule, then there would be no room for them to ask us a Strengthen question. You can't strengthen something that's already valid. So part of how we'd figure out that the trigger is and, not or, is just by understanding that something has to be missing currently. When you say that something is not X or Y, you're saying ~ (X or Y). This is almost like distributing a -1 in algebra. ~ (X or Y) = ~X and ~Y. Think of a more conversational example: If you are not vaccinated or recovered from covid, then you should wear your mask. When we say "X or Y → Z", we could re-write that as X → Z and Y → Z. When we see, If you are not vaccinated or recovered from covid, then you should wear your mask, if we treated it the same way as the above, we'd get not vaccinated → should wear mask, recovered from covid → should wear mask. That second one doesn't make any sense. If you've had covid and recovered, then you should wear a mask? That's not what we meant. We were saying if you haven't already had and recovered from covid, then you should wear a mask. This trigger, If you are not vaccinated or recovered from covid, is really meaning "If you are not vaccinated or (not) recovered". But the "not" isn't written again there because it's modifying the "vaccinated or recovered". The trigger is saying, "If you're not belonging to the crew of people who are (X or Y), then you should wear your mask." To not belong to that crew means that you have not been vaccinated and have not already recovered from covid. The tl;dr version of that is, when we say "if you're not X or Y", we're saying, "If it is not the case that at least one of these two things is true about you". So we're saying, "If it is the case that neither of these things is true about you".

label: Goal
body: We have half the trigger (hasn't vowed to stop being tardy), but we need the other half of the trigger (doesn't criticize himself for his tardiness).

label: Conclusion
body: Everyone should have access to more than one newspaper.

label: Intermediate Conclusion
body: Some important stories would not be adequately covered if there were only one newspaper.

label: Evidence
body: There are at least two sides to every story. All sides of an important story should be covered, and no newspaper adequately covers all sides of every one of its stories.

label: Does Yvonne Disagree
body: 1. His book is not a model of poor scholarship? No, she never addresses the issue of whether it's good or bad scholarship. 2. His book doesn't argue that sun exposure doesn't harm skin cells? No, she never addresses the contents of his book. 3. His book is not valuable because it's stimulated new research on sun exposure? Yes, this is what she seems to be arguing. She's saying, "Hogwash. You're calling his poorly researched book valuable because of its consequence? Because it's stimulated new research on sun exposure. That's as crazy as saying that a virus is valuable because of its consequence of stimulating epidemiologists".

label: Goal
body: Since Yvonne is taking issue with Albert's 3rd claim, let's look for an answer that addresses whether or not something is valuable. Or if they're trying to be sneakier with wording, "whether or not something that is in itself bad can nonetheless be judged as something good because of the consequences it leads to".

label: Evaluate
body:
The opinion indicator "should" in the first sentence alerts us to the possibility that we have a First Sentence Conclusion. The "for" in the second half of that first sentence shows that we're supporting that initial opinion (F.A.B.S. are the four main support indicators: for, after all, because, since). The "since" at the beginning of the the second sentence paired with the "and" that ropes in the 2nd claim of that sentence, means that the first two ideas of the final sentence are supporting the third idea in the final sentence, which makes that an Intermediate Conclusion.
```
All sides of                                          some imp
important story          No paper can        →        stories would   →   everyone should
should be covered   AND  cover all sides of             not be                have access to
                         all of its stories             adequately             2+ papers
                                                         covered with
                                                         only one
                                                         newspaper
```
We can object to the move from the Premises to the Intermediate Conc, or to the move from the Intermediate to the Main Conc. Let's start with that simpler move, from Intermediate to Main: GIVEN THAT if you only had one paper, some important stories would not be adequately covered. HOW COULD WE SAY it's not the case that everyone should have access to more than one newspaper? We could just say "what's the big deal if some people don't get adequate coverage of important stories? You, author, need to establish the premise that everyone should have access to adequate coverage of important stories." How about the move from Premises to Intermediate Conclusion. GIVEN THAT all sides of an important story should be covered, and that no newspaper can adequately cover all sides of all stories, HOW COULD WE SAY it's possible that if there were only one newspaper, all important stories would be adequately covered? Well, this one is tricky. We might not see the wiggle room until we read the answer choices and it gives us the hint, but the 2nd premise there isn't what it needs to be. It needs to be saying: no newspaper can adequately cover all sides of all important stories. Instead, it says that no paper can adequately cover all sides of all stories. Okay, that's fine. As long as the paper adequately covers all sides of the important stories, we don't care if they only cover one side of some of their unimportant stories. So we've found a way to accept the premises but still argue that one newspaper could adequately cover all important stories.

label: Goal
body: Stay flexible. The answer might speak to this last objection (what if a newspaper were able to cover all sides of all the important stories?) or it might speak to the move to the Main Conclusion (who said that everyone needs to have access to adequate coverage of all important stories?)

label: Statements
body:
```
quantifier (most)
Most Moradco mines           never violated
in Velyena                   enviro regulations
conditional / quantifier (every)
Moradco               →       violated some
gold mine                     enviro regulation
```

label: Evaluate
body: We're given a Most statement and a conditional All statement. In general, Most statements are only interesting as a starting point if you have two most claims about the same group, because then you can prove some overlap. given Most A's are B, these, Most A's are C, we can infer: B and C overlap at least once. But since there aren't two Most claims, the conditional should automatically command our attention. What does a Must Be True question do with a conditional? It either chains it together with other conditionals (there aren't any other conditionals in this two claim paragraph), or we apply this conditional to a fact that was provided, usually via the contrapositive. Does the conditional in the 2nd sentence apply to what's talked about in the 1st sentence? Is there any Overlapping Concept? Yes, both sentences are talking about whether or not something has violated environmental regulations. We know that most of M's mines in Velyena have never violated. And we know that all of M's gold mines have violated. So none of those mines we're talking about in the first sentence are gold mines.

label: Goal
body:
Since the mines being talked about in the first sentence clearly aren't gold mines, since they have never violated an environmental regulation, we can infer that "most of the mines that Moradco operates in the province of Velyena [are not gold mines]". Formally,
```
Most Moradco's           never
mines in Velyena         violated
+
never                →   not one of
violated                  Moradco's gold mines
-------------------------------------------------
Most Moradco's            not one of
mines in Velyena          Moradco's gold mines
```
Like most Must Be True questions that test our ability to apply a conditional rule, you have to contrapose the rule to see how the available fact(s) triggers it.

label: Conclusion
body: Politicians would be more likely to be reelected if they voted against these tariffs on particular products.

label: Evidence
body: Most people oppose tariffs on particular products. These tariffs tend to protect small % of people who work in that industry while hurting everyone else through higher costs.

label: Evaluate
body: This argument is mainly making a move from "Most people oppose position X" to "politicians would be more likely to be reelected if they opposed position X". Intuitively it sounds like opposing an unpopular position would help your reelection chances, but maybe one's reelection chances hinge more on something else. Most people support universal background checks on gun purchases and raising the minimum wage, but that doesn't mean a Republican would be more likely to be reelected by talking about gun control and minimum wage boosts. Most people support tight restrictions on late term abortions, but that doesn't mean a Democrat would be more likely to be reelected by running on tight restrictions for late term abortions. A Republican wouldn't run on gun control, because the vast majority of people who like gun control are Democrats and aren't going to vote for that Republican just because she agrees with them on this issue. A Democrat wouldn't run on restricting abortions because the vast majority of people who oppose abortions are Republicans and aren't going to vote for that Democrat. A stronger argument would say, "If most of a politician's previous voters oppose such tariffs, then they would be more likely to be reelected if they voted against these tariffs." Since reelection basically hinges on getting more of "your voters" to turnout, it's less important whether "most voters oppose X" and more important whether "most of the people who previously voted for you / would consider voting for you oppose X".

label: Goal
body: Look for an answer offering the Missing Link of, "If you vote against something that most people oppose, it improves your chances of reelection", or look for an answer that, when negated, allows us to say that "even though most people oppose tariffs, voting for tariffs could still be the right move for a politician".

label: Information
body:
```
For seals and dolphins,
the longer can            the greater depth
be submerged        →     animal can reach
Dolphins can dive to greater depths than northern fur seals.
elephant seals can stay submerged longer than Weddell seals can.
```

label: Evaluate
body: On a Must Be False question, the correct answer almost always contradicts a conditional provided in the stimulus or an available inference we can make from the stimulus. They didn't give us a conditional, but they gave us a Volume Dial relationship (aka Stepladder / Double-headed Line). The way "the more x, the more y" seems to work is that we can always invert them and say "the less x, the less y", but we usually don't read them backwards (i.e. knowing something is more Y doesn't seem to definitively tell us more X). However, in this context, the first sentence is saying if you listed all the seals and dolphins, the ones who rank higher on the "how long can stay submerged" scale also rank higher on the "how deep an animal can reach" scale. So if you were to read the scale of "Which small/medium marine mammal can reach the lowest point in the water?", who ever is ranked #1 is also #1 on the "which small/medium marine mammal can stay submerged the longest". We're told a head-to-head matchup between dolphins and northern fur seals seals, and one between elephant seals and W seals.

label: Goal
body: Since this is Strengthen, we want an answer to either rule out an Alternate Explanation for why this film had such a small audience during its opening weekend (e.g. "There wasn't a terrible storm that kept people from going to the movies that weekend) or increase the plausibility of the author's explanation (e.g. corroborate the story that the intended audience for this film was split between seeing this film and seeing several other films meant to appeal to the same niche).

label: Conclusion (clearly)
body: Your ad's claim that you provide coverage of the high school's most popular sports is false advertising. (i.e. Your paper does not provide coverage of the high school's most popular sports)

label: Evidence
body: Track gets no coverage, while basketball gets full-page coverage.

label: Intermediate Conclusion (hence)
body: Track is more popular than basketball.

label: Evidence
body: 15% of the students are on the track team, while 5% play basketball.

label: Evaluate
body: Whenever we're doing Flaw questions, we read the paragraph with a special ear for the 10 famous flaws (since the flaw ends up being one of those about 1/3 of the time). Sure enough, we have a famous flaw here. This is the rare bird known as Equivocation, the flaw of using the same term (or concept) in two very different ways. Previous examples have featured talking about maturity, as in how responsible you are, vs. maturity, as in whether you've gone through physical puberty. Or there was one about happiness, as in a prolonged satisfaction with your life, vs. happiness, as in a fleeting moment of pleasure. In this case, the argument is trading on an ambiguity in the term "popular". The newspaper was saying, "We provide coverage of the high school's most popular sports", meaning, "we provide coverage of the sports that are most popular with our readers". The author is interpreting "popular" to mean the sports that are most participated in by students. A lot of questions earlier in an LR section play off our real world common sense, and this is definitely trying to tap into people's awareness that the only high school sports random people in the community are likely to care about are the big spectator sports like football, basketball, baseball.

label: Goal
body: We want to look for an answer calling out the Equivocation flaw (saying that the argument used the term "popular" in two different ways) or an answer that is otherwise spelling out the idea that the newspaper was probably referring to most popular in terms of what its readers want to see, not in terms of what percent of the student body participates in it.

label: Conclusion
body: Joshi is letting campaign contributions influence his vote in city council.

label: Evidence
body: His re-election campaign has gotten the most money from property developers. And his voting record has most favored the interests of property developers.

label: Evaluate
body: When we're doing Flaw and we start to see "bias / self-interest", we probably start to think of the famous Ad Hominem flaw. But this argument is really more of a Curious Fact / Explanation style argument, that will be guilty of the famous Causal Flaw (arriving overconfidently at one possible explanation when there could be alternate explanations). Curious Fact: How come J's voting record favors property developers the most, and his campaign has gotten the most money from property developers? Author's Explanation: The property developers are contributing money to the campaign as a soft bribe for Joshi to enact their agenda via his city council votes. Before the author "clearly" arrives at this possible explanation, he should be thinking whether there are other ways we could explain these same facts. One alternate explanation is that the author kind of has cause and effect backwards: maybe Joshi's pro-development voting habit came first, and once property developers saw that Joshi was their kind of councilperson, they started donating to J's campaign in the hopes that J would be re-elected and keep voting in a pro-development style.

label: Goal
body: Look for an answer pointing out that the author has interpreted these campaign contributions and votes in one possible, cynical way, when there might be a more innocent explanation for them.

label: Statements
body: Some say, "government shouldn't take over failing banks because government doesn't know how to manage a financial institution".

label: Pivot (however)
body: Were they to take over a failing bank, the government wouldn't be managing day-to-day operations, just selecting people to be the bank's new senior management.

label: Analogy
body: We're cool with politicians selecting people to manage the military, even though most politicians don't know who to manage the military, and that's at least as big a responsibility.

label: Evaluate
body: The question stem indicates that we're doing some sort of "soft" Must Be False thing. Some answer will go against what we read; the paragraph will give us reason to reject that answer. On Must Be False, the correct answer usually goes against a conditional idea or goes against some inference we can derive by combining ideas. There isn't any conditional logic in this paragraph, but there is a Pivot word (however) creating tension. Usually, when there's a pivot word, the inference we can derive comes from reconciling what comes after the pivot with what came before. Here, before the pivot, we had people saying the government shouldn't take over failing banks. After the pivot. we get the author seemingly saying, "You're wrong. It's fine for the government to take over a failing bank. It's no weirder than them putting people in charge to run the military."

label: Goal
body: Look for anything that seems to actively go against what the paragraph was saying, possibly something like the original position that the author is rejecting.

label: Conclusion
body: People with a college education are more likely to support maintaining / raising the level of govt. social services than are members of the overall population.

label: Evidence
body: People graduating college are less likely to support reducing the level of govt. social services than are students entering their first year.

label: Goal
body: The correct answer will probably either reward us for connecting the chain by saying "If no experience, can't solve problem", or it will reward us for applying that fact to Outsiders by saying "Sorry, you can't solve these problems".

label: Conclusion
body: These paleobiologist must be mistaken (not all dinosaurs were cold-blooded)

label: Evidence (since)
body: The incidence of flu was much lower during the six months of the campaign than experts had predicted.

label: Evaluate
body: This isn't a Causal conclusion, just statistical. There are two differences between the premise and the conclusion: one says "students entering their first year", the other says "members of the overall population". One says "graduating students", the other says "people with a university education". The argument is like saying, Since people graduating college have been to more countries than have students entering their first year, people who've graduated college have been to more countries than have members of the overall population. Are first year college students fair to compare with the overall population? Are graduating students fair to compare with people who've graduated?

label: Goal
body: Make it seem like first year college students aren't representative of the overall population, or that graduating students aren't representative of people with a university education.

label: Conclusion
body: The claim that this movie will inspire people to act in socially irresponsible ways is untrue and potentially harmful to the moviemaker's reputations.

label: Evidence
body: The claim relies entirely on survey data that has turned out to be deeply flawed.

label: Evaluate
body: This one would be tough to get if we don't know our famous flaws. If an author is saying, "they failed to prove X. there's no proof for X. the argument for X rests on a dubious assumption. the experiment that claimed to prove X turned out to be flawed", or in this case "the claim of X relied on what turned out to be bad survey data", then what is the valid conclusion and what is the flawed conclusion? The valid conclusion to reach is: okay, so we still don't know whether X is true. The flawed conclusion that LSAT authors go to is this: okay, so now we know that X is false. We call this flaw Unproven vs. Proven False (other companies sometimes call it stuff like Absence of Evidence). The movie critics have not successfully proven claim X (that the movie will inspire dangerous behavior). But that doesn't mean that claim X is untrue.

label: Goal
body: Look for an answer saying "just because the data they relied on is bad doesn't mean we get to assume that their claim was false".

label: Statements
body: Most skilled banjo are skilled guitar, but most skilled guitar are not skilled banjo.

label: Evaluate
body:
We know that correct answers on Inference questions want us to synthesize claims, and we only get two claims here. They have a math-y, quantified feel, so we want to think mathematically. The famous Most + Most inference that has been tested throughout the years is this: Most A's are B, Most A's are C, infer: Some B's are C / Some C's are B. But that's not what this is, since the two Most facts are about different groups. This is a new type of Most + Most inference that has now appeared 2 or 3 times on the last twenty tests. Most A's are B, Most B's are ~A, infer: There are more B's than A's. Why is that a valid inference? A little math helps. Let's say there are 9 skilled banjo players in the world. If we say that most of them are skilled at guitar, then at a minimum we have 5 people who are skilled at banjo and guitar. So now we get to the fun part: Could we also have 9 skilled guitar players in the world? If so, 5 of them are skilled at banjo and 4 aren't. But that would contradict our statement that "most skilled guitar players aren't good at banjo." What we have to remember is that the people in this world that are both skilled banjo and skilled guitar are appearing in both of these groups. When we talk about all the skilled banjo players, we'll be counting these 5 people who are good at banjo and guitar. And when we talk about all the skilled guitar players, we'll be counting these 5 people good at both in that tally as well. In order for most skilled guitar players to be bad at banjo, we need at least 11 skilled guitar players: 5 are also skilled at banjo, but the majority, the other 6, are not skilled at banjo. Here it is more graphically:
```
Just Banjo        Banjo and Guitar        Just Guitar
    4                    5                     6
```
9 people are good at banjo. 11 people are good at guitar. 5 people are good at both. When we say that Most A's are B but Most B's are ~A, we're saying that people who are both A and B are a majority of Group A but a minority of Group B. In our example before, there were 5 people good at both banjo and guitar. The statements are saying that these 5 people are a majority of the skilled banjo players, so the max total for banjo would be 9. The statements are saying that these 5 people are a minority of the skilled guitar players, so the min total for guitar would be 11. if you want to see the other example of this, check out Test 80, Section 1, Q22.

label: Goal
body: Look for an answer saying there are more skilled guitarists than skilled banjo players.

label: Conclusion (Hence)
body: The lack of managerial skills and the lack of entrepreneurial ability can each inhibit the development of successful companies.

label: Evidence
body: Entrepreneurial ability is obviously needed to start a successful company.

label: Intermediate Conclusion
body: But even if you succeed in starting a company, you can still fail for lack of managerial skills.

label: Evidence (for instance)
body: You might not adequately analyze market trends, which leads to a failure to manage company growth.

label: Evaluate
body: There are lot of keywords here potentially helping us / confusing us: Obviously = opinion. Opinions are often Conclusions. But the first sentence isn't supported by any idea, so we wouldn't call it a conclusion. Yet = pivot. Pivots frequently introduce the main conclusion on Role and Main Conclusion questions. The idea after Yet does get supported, which we can tell from the fact that it's followed by ... For instance = support indicator. consequently = This can indicate a conclusion or the result of a cause/effect relationship. In this sentence, it appears to be a causal use of consequently, not a reasoning move. Hence = conclusion indicator.

label: Goal
body: We're being asked about a claim that comes right before the word "Hence", so we're guaranteed that this claim plays a supporting role. Other than that, we don't need to be too precise with our prediction.

label: Statements
body:
On Inference questions, we're scanning for Conditional / Causal wording primarily (mathematical and pivot wording, secondarily). 3 conditionals:
```
Universal: attempts at creativity .. are futile
Rule: A's that are B are C                            A and B → C
Attempting creativity + Relevant experience    →       Futile
                                        (negated: ~relevant experience)
-------------
Trigger word: only
Rule: A happens only by B                              A → B
~Really Understand Problems         →       ~Solve problems
--------------
Trigger word: no one
Rule: No one who is A is B                              A → ~B
~Experience         →       ~Really Understand Problems
```
When we have more than one conditional, we check to see whether they chain together (do they have an overlapping term?) The last two both talk about "really understanding problems", so we look for a chain, and it's there.
```
~Experience  →  ~Really Understand Problems  →  ~Solve Problems
```
The first conditional basically gives us the same relationship (without relevant experience → attempt at solution is futile). The other thing we look for with conditionals is a fact we can apply it to. Did they talk about people who lack experience? (or we could trigger the contrapositive if they talked about people who did solve problems) The first sentence told us that outsiders, who by definition lack experience, often think they can bring fresh eyes to a problem that come up with a useful solution. According to our conditional chain, though, these outsiders without experience won't really understand the problem, so they won't be able to solve them.

label: Evidence
body: Some dinosaurs lived in Australia and Alaska, where temperatures drop below freezing. Only warm-blooded animals can live in those temperatures.

label: Evaluate
body: Whenever we're doing Main Conclusion or Role, we read the argument knowing that there's a high tendency the Conclusion will either be the first sentence, or it will be part of some but /yet/ however rebuttal. This one is the latter, signified by "however". The claim we're being asked about it the final claim, which was the 2nd of our two premises.

label: Goal
body: Let's look for some version of "this claim was SUPPORT for the conclusion that at least some dinosaurs were warm blooded".

label: Principle
body:
```
Expressing a true belief             government should
that wouldn't harm people   →        not prevent
generally
```

label: Conclusion
body: The government should not have prevented Calista from expressing her belief [that excessive use of cell phones partly explains the recent uptick in cancer rates].

label: Evaluate
body: The rule has two criterion we need to establish, before we're allowed to conclude the right side (that the govt shouldn't prevent). We got to know 1. true belief 2. expressing it won't harm people generally

label: Goal
body: We want to know 1. it's true that high cell phone use is partly responsible for uptick in cancer 2. expressing that fact won't harm people generally

label: Statements
body:
On Must Be True questions, we're primarily scanning for Conditional words (otherwise math-y or causal ideas). The conditional wording we're hoping to see in this paragraph is "essential" (necessary indicator, Required = Right), "needs" (necessary indicator, Required = Right), "otherwise" (if-not).
```
Learning to read           →       Phonemic
alphabetic language                awareness
Learning to read           →       Learn how sounds
alphabetic language                symbolically represented
~Learn how sounds          →       ~Ability to read
symbolically represented           alphabetic language
```
This third conditional, the "otherwise" one, is essentially the contrapositive of the 2nd conditional. It tells a story about phonemic awareness being the culprit, but it terminates at the idea of ~Learning to read alphabet. So we probably don't need to think hard about that one. The first two conditional ideas don't chain together, but they allow us to say that Learning to Read Alphabet requires two things: phonemic awareness; learn how sounds become letters. Can we apply this conditional to any facts? Did the statements tell us about anyone who Learned to Read Alphabet? Yes, the kids being taught the whole-language method, are learning to read alphabets. So according to our rules, what can we infer about them?

label: Goal
body: The kids being taught the whole-language method must be achieving the two things we know are required in order to learn an alphabet: they're getting phonemic awareness; they're learning how sounds are symbolically represented by means of letters.

label: Curious Fact
body: Pedestrians are more often struck by cars while in a crosswalk than outside of a crosswalk. (why is that?)

label: Explanation
body: When a pedestrian uses a crosswalk, they develop an overly strong sense of security that oncoming cars will honor the signal, so they don't bother to look both ways before crossing.

label: Evaluate
body: Sine the author is offering an explanation for a curious fact, we can undermine it in one of two ways: 1. suggest an Alternate Explanation for the curious fact 2. hurt the plausibility of the Author's explanation. It's much more common on Weaken (and Flaw and Nec Assump and Evaluate) to deal with an alternate explanation. What could be a different way to explain why pedestrians are more often hit while in a crosswalk than outside of a crosswalk? It might just be that people are way more often using a crosswalk than jaywalking through the middle of the street. For example, riding in a car is far more safe than riding in a hang glider, but people more often get injured riding in a car, because billions of people ride in cars and only thousands go hang gliding. Another Alternate Explanation could be that people get hit more frequently in a crosswalk not because the pedestrians are more cocky and cross without looking but because drivers are more reckless and careless around crosswalks (maybe they're checking street signs to see if this is their turn, or they're focused on whether the light is about to turn yellow)

label: Goal
body: Look for an answer that suggests a different explanation for why people are more often struck in a crosswalk than outside of one, or for an answer that makes it less plausible that pedestrians get super cocky when they use a crosswalk and are less likely to look both ways.

label: Conclusion
body: If we find out whether Selena's claim is true, we be able to know whether or not it's possible to have psychic powers.

label: Evidence
body: Selena claims to have psychic powers.

label: Evaluate
body: "Whether or not" is a binary, so the conclusion is saying "Whether we find out that Selena's claim is true or false, it will tell us whether it's possible to have psychic powers." We should think through that binary: If her claim is true, then she does have psychic powers. So that tell us whether it's possible to have psychic powers? Sure. If she has psychic powers, then it's definitely possible to have psychic powers. If her claim is false, then she doesn't have psychic powers. Does that tell us whether it's possible to have psychic powers? Not really. If she doesn't have psychic powers, how does that tell us whether it's possible?

label: Goal
body: We need to patch up what happens if we live in the world where her claim is false and she doesn't have psychic powers. We need an answer to convince us that "If Selena doesn't have psychic powers, then it's impossible to have psychic powers."

label: Background
body: researchers asked leading drug wholesalers who specialize in bulk sales for the current prices of the top 300 drugs,

label: Surprise
body: the prices that the wholesalers provided were 60-80% cheaper than the prices listed for those same drugs in a widely used, independently published pharmaceutical price guidebook?

label: Evaluate / Goal
body: We need to get rid of four answers that help us to explain the mismatch between prices you get from a wholesaler specializing in bulk sales vs. prices you get from the current annual edition of a widely used pharmaceutical price guidebook. These answers should be zeroing in on some salient difference between the two sources.

label: Conclusion (so)
body: Even if the meaning of a given piece of music is the emotion it elicits, this can mean only that music produces the core of a given emotion.

label: Why is it that ...
body: the babblers bark like this?

label: Evidence (for)
body: There are pairs of emotions that have the same core feeling, but can be distinguished from each other only in terms of the social conditions that cause them or the behavior they cause.

label: Intermediate Conclusion (therefore)
body: Music by itself cannot create social conditions or cause human behavior.

label: Evidence
body: Music is merely sound.

label: Evaluate
body: Whenever we do Role and Main Conclusion questions, we expect that 90% of the time the Main Conclusion will appear earlier than at least some of its support. The word "So" attached to the first claim of the 2nd sentence indicates that the 1st sentence is supporting the "So" claim. Thus, the main conclusion can't possibly be the first sentence. The word "for" (FABS: for, after all, because since) indicates support, so we know that the final two claims are there to support the "So" claim that begins the 2nd sentence. Whenever we see a structure like this: X is true. After all, Y is true and thus Z is true. We know that X was the main conclusion, and that the 2nd sentence serves to support X. The "thus" within the 2nd sentence tells us that Y supports Z. Similarly, the "therefore" in the final sentence tells us that "music is merely sound" supports "music by itself creates neither social conditions nor human behavior".

label: Goal
body: They're asking us about the claim that "music is merely sound", which supports an intermediate conclusion, which then supports the main conclusion.

label: Conclusion
body: If the AR3000 is intelligent, then it must have the ability to learn from its mistakes.

label: Evidence
body: For a computer to be intelligent, it must at least one of three qualities: creativity, self-awareness, or ability to learn from mistakes. The AR3000 is not creative or self-aware.

label: Evaluate
body: The argument has two premises, one conditional and one factual. The conditional one says that in order to be a certain thing it's required to have at least one of a set of options. The fact rules out all but one option. The conclusion is a conditional that says "if X is that type of thing, it must have that last option".

label: Goal
body: Premise 1: X → at least one of A,B,C. Premise 2: Thing is not A or B. Conclusion: If Thing is X, then Thing is C.

label: Conclusion (therefore)
body: Dichotomous classifications into mutually exclusive categories should generally be abandoned.

label: Evidence
body: Advances in scientific understanding have shown some long-held dichotomies to be untenable.

label: Evaluate
body: This doesn't quite seem like a Famous Flaw, unless we want to call it Sampling. The main objectionable move seems to be that the evidence establishes that some dichotomies are untenable. But the conclusion is saying that we should generally abandon dichotomies. Just because some of them are unwise, we should get rid of most of them?

label: Goal
body: Let's look for an argument that's saying something like, "Since some X's are bad, we should generally avoid X's."

label: Conclusion
body: One viable way to address the problem of out-of-place sea animals wreaking local ecological havoc would be to dump and refill these ballast tanks in midocean.

label: Evidence (since)
body: Midocean creatures and coastal sea creatures usually can't survive in one another's habitats.

label: Evaluate
body: The argument is concerned that a ship going from New York to London will inadvertently get a bunch of NYC sea life into its ballast tanks, sail across the Atlantic, and then deposit those NYC sea creatures into the coast of London's ecosystem. These NYC sea creatures might be really successful invasive species that can dominate the London coastline, forever changing that habitat (wreaking ecological havoc). The author's solution is to dump these NYC fish in the middle of the Atlantic, and then refill the ballast tanks there with midocean water. Yes, we'll be dropping NYC fish into the middle of the ocean, and yes we'll be sucking up some midocean fish and then dumping them in London, but we're not worried about that. The NYC fish can't survive in a midocean habitat, and the midocean fish can't survive in a coastal habitat (usually). How might we object to this plan? One way seems to just be to point out that "usually" might not be good enough. If a midocean creature can sometimes be dumped into London's coastal ecosystem and proceed to wreak ecological havoc there, then is this really a viable way?

label: Goal
body: The answer is unlikely to be in LINKING form (because this was such a sprawling, real-world paragraph), but that kind of answer would sound something like, If a plan would usually not involve any threat to different habitats, then it is viable. But the answer will probably be phrased in DEFENDING form (ruling out a possible objection). Our usual objections to Plans are that they're not feasible, wouldn't get the cooperation from other parties that the author envisions, would backfire in some way, or don't address the main cause of the problem. So this argument would be assuming stuff like: "This is a feasible idea" / "Ships would be willing to stop mid journey to perform this empty & refill step" / "dumping coastal water midocean or midocean water in coastal habitats would not itself lead to ecological havoc"

label: Conclusion (So)
body: We should just ask respondents to identify the age range that they fall into.

label: Evidence
body: We don't need results that provide employment status figures for every single age.

label: Evaluate
body:
On Principle-Strengthen, we're usually just trying to prephrase a rule that sounds like "If Premise, then Conclusion".
  So in this case,
  "If we don't need results that provide figures for every single age, then we should merely ask for respondents' age range."
  If we wanted to go a little more abstract, we could say,
  "If you don't need a specific data point, then you should just ask for a fuzzy one."

label: Goal
body: Look for a rule whose trigger would apply to our evidence (we don't need results that map to each single age) and whose outcome helps to support our conclusion (we should just ask for age range, not their specific age).

label: Conclusion
body:
That belief cannot be correct.
  rephrase: The ancient city Wilhelm discovered was not the famous Troy, the site of the war described in 'the *Iliad*'.

label: Evidence
body: In 'The *Iliad*', the Trojan War lasted ten years, but the ancient city Wilhelm discovered could not have withstood a siege lasting ten years.

label: Evaluate
body:
This one doesn't seem like a ripe contender for a Missing Link assumption, so let's go into Objection mode instead, and then we can think of Defender assumptions that rule out our objections.
  Given that ... the *Iliad* says the war lasted ten years but this city could not have withstood a war lasting ten years,
  How could we argue that ... this city Wilhelm found was Troy, the site of that war?
  The two premises are irreconcilable. The book says the war was ten years. Reality says this city is too small for a ten year siege.
  Do we have to assume the book is correct about the length of the war? Maybe Homer exaggerated the length for dramatic effect.
  Do we have to assume that in a ten year war, this city was under siege the entire ten years? Maybe this city is the site of the war, but only some of the ten year war was actually "a siege" on this city?

label: Goal
body:
Let's look for an answer ruling out one of these objections, saying something like:
  - Homer's estimate of the 10 year war is accurate
  - if the war were ten years, then this city would have necessarily been under siege that whole time
  The correct answer, when negated, will weaken the argument. In other words, it will allow us to argue that Wilhelm really did discover the Troy, the site of Trojan War.

label: Monroe's Claims
body:
1. The organization's project has been a failure (the project failed to reduce as much as possible the number of homes in the community that lack electricity)
  2. Our stated goal was to reduce as much as possible the number of homes in the community that lack electricity.
  3. The project is over, and approximately 2,000 homes are still without electricity.

label: Wilkerson's Responses
body:
1. Disagrees - She says that the project has not been a failure. It's been a success!
  2. No comment on what the stated goal was.
  3. She implicitly agrees with this. She is acting like the current number is 2,000 (since she thinks they've reduced from 5,000 by 3,000 homes).

label: Evaluate / Goal
body: Since we found an explicit disagreement, we can probably head to the answers looking for an answer that talks about whether or not the project has been a failure or a success.

label: Conclusion
body: There is reason for skepticism about the conclusion that "on average, 50 year olds are more altruistic than 20 year olds."

label: Evidence
body: Many people hesitate to admit that their behavior does not conform to social expectations.

label: Evaluate
body:
There was a study with a Curious Fact (an asymmetric comparison):
  why is it that twice as many 50 year olds as 20 year olds reported that they sometimes give blood?
  The researchers concluded one potential Explanation:
  50 year olds are more altruistic than 20 year olds (obviously assuming that being more altruistic is causing them to be more likely to give blood).
  This author is pushing back against that conclusion by suggesting an Alternate Explanation:
  "maybe it's not that the 50 year olds are more altruistic; maybe they're just lying. They give blood as infrequently as 20 year olds do, but while 20 year olds don't mind admitting to that, 50 year olds feel social pressure to conform to societal expectations, so they were twice as likely to lie and say 'Sure, I give blood! That's what good citizens do, after all, heh, heh'."

label: Goal
body: We're being asked how our author is calling into question the researchers' conclusion. We'll take any answer that seems descriptively true, but we'd probably anticipate language like, "Suggesting an alternate explanation for the observed difference in age groups".

label: Mario's Claims
body:
1. The only rug store in Glendale has gone out of business.
  2. There's little demand for rugs in Glendale.
  3. People planning to open a new business in Glendale should avoid going into the rug-selling business.

label: Renate's Response?
body:
1. Did Renate argue "It's false that to say that Glendale's only rug store went out of business"? That would mean he's either arguing that the store that went out of business wasn't the only rug store in Glendale, or he's arguing that the only rug store in Glendale didn't go out of business..
  He definitely agrees the store is gone. And he never suggests that there is some other rug store still in existence in Glendale. In fact by saying "the market is wide open", he seems to be implying that there's currently no rug store in Glendale. So, if anything, Renate agrees with this claim.
  2. Did Renate argue, "there much demand for rugs in Glendale?"
  Somewhat. By saying "the rug store's closing had little to do with a lack of demand for rugs", he seems to be affirming that there is demand for rugs in Glendale. But more precisely he's just saying that "demand for rugs" was not a primary causal factor in the store's closing.
  3. Did Renate argue, "people planning to open a new business in Glendale should consider getting into the rug-selling business?
  Sure! He's saying, "It wasn't lack of demand for rugs that closed down that store. And now that the store is closed, the next rug store that opens up in Glendale will be the only game in town! The market is up for grabs to the first rug retailer that moves in."

label: Goal
body: Let's look for something dealing with the content of Mario's 3rd claim, whether it would be a good/bad idea to open up a rug store in Glendale right now.

label: Conclusion (this shows that)
body: Even if Neanderthals didn't have language, they could just as well have created their sophisticated tools.

label: Evidence
body:
In an experiment, one group of undergrads was taught how to create a Neanderthal tool using both demonstrations and elaborate verbal explanations. The other group was taught how to use the tool by silent example alone.
  The two groups didn't show any difference in terms of how fast or how well they learned how to use the tool.

label: Evaluate
body:
This is an Anti-Causal conclusion, claiming that possessing language would not have assisted Neanderthals in terms of the sophisticated tools they created.
  The evidence is seeming to show that language didn't make a difference when it came to learning how to use one of the tools Neanderthals used.
  The author seems to assume a missing Link like, "if language doesn't affect the speed or proficiency at which you learn how to use a tool, then it doesn't have a meaningful role in creating the tool".
  We can prime our brain for objections by thinking,
  Given that ... the group that learned by silent example learned just as quickly and just as well as the group that learned by demonstrations and verbal explanations,
  How can we argue that ... Neanderthals could not have created their sophisticated tools just as well if they had no language?
  Were the two groups in the experiment fair to compare, or was the "silent example" group comprised of people who are especially good at learning how to use a tool without verbal explanations?
  Is it possible that you can learn how to use a tool without language being necessary, but creating a sophisticated tool would benefit from language?

label: Statements
body:
```
causal (can produce)
Modest amounts     ⇢   big improvement
of exercise            in cardiovasc health
conditional (need only do X to get Y)
do the equivalent      cardiovasc
of 1/2 hr brisk walking →  health
on most days of week       benefits
```
  causal comparison (more effective)
  More vigorous exercise would get even more cardiovascular health benefits, but the workout doesn't need to be strenuous.

label: Evaluate
body:
We get five claims here. Do any of them combine to yield an inference?
  The paragraph doesn't seem to have any conditional or causal chains. It's more like nuanced exercise advice. We would probably be best served by taking a 2nd (or 3rd) re-read for understanding and nuance and then heading to the answers.

label: Goal
body: Look for the most provable answer (probably with safe, moderate wording) that echoes this idea of relatively light exercise on most days of the week is enough to give someone cardiovascular health benefits.

label: Conclusion
body: Sartore is a better movie reviewer than Kelly.

label: Evidence
body:
A movie review should help readers determine whether or not they are apt to enjoy the movie.
  A person who is likely to enjoy a particular movie is much more likely to realize this by reading a review by Sartore than a review by Kelly.

label: Opposing Point
body: Sartore is more likely to give a movie an unfavorable review than a favorable one.

label: Evaluate
body: The argument is half-finished in proving the conclusion. It has established that those who are likely to enjoy a particular movie will be more likely to realize this by reading Sartore's review. But what about those people who are likely to not-enjoy the movie? They are more important to measure since Sartore's reviews are more often unfavorable.

label: Goal
body: To strengthen this argument find an answer that makes it so that people are more likely to determine that for movies one will not enjoy, one is more likely to learn from a review by Sartore.

label: Statements
body:
There are specially bred aquarium fish who have cool colors and weird shapes.
  They're popular with fish connoisseurs but inferior to ordinary fish.
  causal (hampered by)
  Their weird tails/fins mean they are slower in racing towards food than are ordinary fish, which leads to them being often underfed.
  Most of their babies don't match the exotic features of the parents.

label: Evaluate
body:
In terms of Overlapping Concepts, the exotic aquarium fish were mentioned in each claim, so we could potentially make an inference by synthesizing any two things we know about them.
  f.e.
  These fish have elaborate tails that make them slower in racing towards food
  +
  These fish have babies who don't have their elaborate tails.
  infer: Some fish babies lack a quality that was a survival disadvantage for their parents.

label: Goal
body: It's hard to make a specific prediction here, so let's just look for the most provable answer.

label: Conclusion
body: There are exceptions to the principle that “if one ought to do something, then one can do it”. (i.e. at least sometimes, you ought to do something but can’t do it)

label: Evidence
body: Some promises to meet a friend at a certain time, but they can’t (an unforeseen traffic jam thwarted them).

label: Evaluate
body:
For the author to successfully show a counterexample to the general principle, she must clearly establish a case in which
  a) you ought to do X
  b) you can’t do X
  In her example, have both things been established?
  X = meet someone at a certain time
  It’s established that our person can’t do X (they can’t meet their friend at the agreed-upon time because of the traffic jam).
  Has it been established that our person ought to do X? No. We just know that the friend promised to do X.

label: Goal
body: The author is assuming “if you promised to meet your friend, you ought to do it.”

label: Situation
body: Producing leather and fur is labor intensive, so these materials will tend to be rather expensive.

label: Pivot (But)
body:
As fashion has moved away from these materials, their prices have dropped.
  Meanwhile, as other products (less labor-intensive to produce) have become more fashionable, the price of these materials has risen.

label: Evaluate
body:
When we're doing one of these Proposition / Generalization type question stems, the correct answer is usually a safely worded takeaway that reinforces the Causal Difference-Maker.
  We have causal language in the first sentence: which means that
  So we know that "how labor intensive something is" can affect its price.
  But the covariation we have in the final sentence also suggests a Causal Difference-Maker:
  as leather/fur got less fashionable, the price dropped.
  as other materials got more fashionable, their price rose.

label: Goal
body:
We probably are going to hear something like "how labor intensive the production process is for a given material is not the only factor affecting its price" (aloofly referring to fashion status as another causal factor).
  Trap answers on this type of question are often Too Strong, so look out for stuff like "the price of something depends entirely on how fashionable it is".

label: Evidence
body: In areas of this forest where suppression of forest fires has left the forest unnaturally crowded with immature trees, the tree-eating tussock moth is beneficial.

label: Conclusion
body: Thus, in most of this forest, the outbreak of tree-eating tussock moth should be allowed.

label: Evaluate
body:
After all, _______ ??
  We know the tree-eating TM is beneficial in areas where a no-forest-fire policy has led to lots of immature trees being alive. (Usually forest fires kill off the brush and small trees on the forest floor, whereas older/thicker/taller trees often survive)
  So I guess we need to know that in most of this forest, we've been suppressing fires and now have lots of immature trees filling up the joint.

label: Goal
body: Most of this forest is unnaturally crowded with immature trees?

label: Given that ...
body: The city built a new highway linking several suburbs to the downtown area, in order to relieve traffic.

label: How can it be that ...
body: Since the new highway opened, the average commute time for workers downtown has increased?

label: Conclusion
body: Crows are capable of recognizing threatening people and can even pass their concerns on to other crows.

label: Evaluate / Goal
body:
We thought the new highway would relieve traffic congestion, thereby reducing commute times. But for some people (workers in downtown), the commute has gotten worse.
  So we need to hear something else that's changed with the new highway, that would make commuting slow down for people who work downtown.

label: Conclusion (should = opinion)
body: I should devote all my time to the second one.

label: Evidence
body: It's equal in importance to the first project, the first one is late already, and if I work on the first then I won't finish the second before it's deadline.

label: Evaluate / Goal
body: We need a rule that tells us which project to work on. It should have a trigger that applies to the situation this worker is in, and an outcome that makes it seem like the worker "should devote all their time to the second project".

label: Conclusion (therefore)
body: Secondary school science courses should teach students to evaluate science-based arguments regarding practical issues (instead of, or in addition to abstract science).

label: Evidence
body:
Secondary schools should be teaching skills that are useful for the decisions that adults typically make in their daily lives.
  Abstract science doesn't do that.

label: Evaluate
body:
There's a big New Concept in the Conclusion:
  teaching students to evaluate science-based arguments regarding practical issues.
  Usually when the conclusion introduces a brand new concept, we should be able to articulate what the author is assuming about this new idea.
  Consider the assumption in this argument:
  Joe isn't funny. But the guy that Lisa dates should be funny. Therefore, Lisa should date Fernando, instead of or perhaps in addition to Joe.
  What are we assuming about Fernando? Why are we suggesting that Lisa date him?
  We're assuming that Fernando is funny.
  Similarly, in this argument, we heard:
  Abstract science isn't useful to adults. But what we teach should be useful. Therefore, we should teach students to evaluate science-based arguments regarding practical issues.
  What are we assuming about "learning to evaluate science-based arguments regarding practical issues"?

label: Goal
body: We're assuming that "Learning to evaluate science-based arguments regarding practical issues" is "useful for adults".

label: Evaluate
body:
Most of the time, the two people disagree over an explicit claim. Sometimes, there's nothing explicit and we have to ask ourselves about assumptions. But we can start by taking each of Person 1's claims and asking ourselves if Person 2 tried to go against that idea.
  Did Carl try to argue that
  modernizing the language of premodern plays does not lessen their aesthetic quality?
  No, Carl never talks about aesthetic qualities (what makes them beautiful or artistically worthwhile)
  Did Carl try to argue that
  modernizing the language of premodern plays is not valuable for teaching history?
  Yes, he explicitly says that "modernizing plays is of no use for teaching history".
  Did Carl try to argue that
  modernizing plays does not make them accessible to students who would otherwise never enjoy them? (i.e. is he saying that modernizing doesn't make someone who wasn't likely to see it now be likely to see it?)
  No, Carl doesn't comment at all on whether the potential audience for a premodern play widens / doesn't widen, as a result of modernizing its language.

label: Goal
body:
Since Carl only disagreed with Lyle's 2nd claim, we'll focus our prephrase on that language:
  whether or not modernizing remains valuable for teaching history (because it widens the audience) or whether it is of no value for teaching history (because students can't gain deep knowledge of the past if the play has been modernized).

label: Evidence
body:
```
Most soil has clay              Most A are B
Most soil has sand              Most A are C or D
or organic material
```

label: Conclusion
body:
```
Some soil is clay and sand      Some A are C
and                             and
Some soil is clay and org       Some A are D
```

label: Evaluate
body:
Because we see “most” in one premise and “some” in the conclusion, we want to think of “virtually every” (i.e. “almost all”) as providing us another “most” claim.
  Why? Well, this argument comes close to making the famous and legal “most + most” inference, which looks like this:
```
Most A’s are B
+
Most A’s are C
--------------------
Some B are C
```
  With the ingredients we were provided here, we could have made this inference:
```
Most S’s have C
+
Most S’s have SD or OM
-------------------------------
Some C are (SD or OM)
```
  What the author is doing illegally is thinking he can break that up into two different takeaways: Some C are SD, and Some C are OM.
  Conversationally, the problem with the conclusion is that it’s possible that sand never overlaps with clay, or that organic material never overlaps with clay. It’s not possible that both of them never overlap. At least one of them does need to overlap with clay, but both of them don’t have to.
  If you crave numbers for seeing this flaw, let’s say there are 11 types of soil.
  6 clay, 5 no clay (most soil has clay)
  8 sand, 2 org material, 1 neither (almost all has sand or org material)
  Does there have to be soil that has clay and sand? Yes. 6 + 8 add up to 14, but there are only 11 types of soil, so we know that 3 of them overlap.
  Does there have to be soil that has clay and organic material? No. It’s very possible that the 2 types of soil that have organic material are 2 of the 5 types of soil that don’t have clay.

label: Goal
body:
The cool thing about Parallel Flaw is that we don’t have to thoroughly understand the original argument’s flaw in order to match the argument, when the original argument has conditional or quantified logic.
  We need two Most premises, and one of them needs to have an “or” outcome. The conclusion needs to make two Some claims, one for each member of that “or” outcome.
```
Premise 1: Most A’s are B
Premise 2: Most A’s are C or D
Conclusion: Some A’s are C, and Some A’s are D
```

label: Conclusion (this proves that)
body: The regulation banning PCBs was effective in reducing human exposure to those chemicals.

label: Evidence
body:
The regulation banning PCBs happened in the 1970s.
  In 2005, they measured the levels of toxic chemicals in the bodies of 11 volunteers. Among the subjects tested, younger subjects showed much lower levels of PCB's.

label: Given
body:
Successful stand-up comedians are able to keep the attention of a large audience for a few hours.
  The audience remembers long afterwards what the comedian said.
  In their routines, many comedians make interesting points about serious topics.
  Humor is the means through which comedians are able to accomplish all of this.
  University professors hope to achieve much the same in their lectures.

label: Evaluate
body:
The author's conclusion is offering a causal interpretation of the study's finding, so we can use our Explain Curious Fact framework.
  Curious Fact ... why did the younger subjects have lower levels of PCB's in their bodies than the older subjects did?
  Author's Explanation ... PCBs were banned in the 1970s --> banning PCBs effectively reduced human exposure to those chemicals --> the older subjects (who may have been alive pre-ban) had more exposure to PCBs than the younger subjects did.
  As always, the flaw is that the author is far too certain of one possible explanation. ("This proves that ..")
  And as always, we're supposed to remind the author that there might be other possible ways to explain that data. For example, maybe the younger subjects grew up in countries that never used PCBs. Maybe the livers of younger people are better at processing and expelling PCBs from the bloodstream.

label: Goal
body: Look for an answer complaining that the author is too sure of this one possible causal interpretation.

label: Conclusion
body: Available data on spies are skewed: you can learn a lot about bad spies but very little about good spies.

label: Evidence
body: You only really get data on spies if they're caught, and only bad spies get caught.

label: Evaluate
body:
Although there are some hints at Conditional Logic here because of the "only through" and "never", the conclusion is not trying to derive anything conditionally, so I think I would resist trying to diagram this and think more about the gist-y principle behind it.
  The author is essentially saying that our data set on spies is inherently biased in a certain way based on the nature of collecting data on spies. It's almost like the data we have on spies is a self-selecting sample of data on "bad spies".
  By definition of us having data on you, you're a bad spy.

label: Goal
body:
Because this argument seems to be working more on a conversational level of "unrepresentative sample", I wouldn't be as stringent about forcing the answer choice to have all the same structural similarities.
  I basically want to hear about a situation in which our data is skewed because the nature of how we collect the data makes it very likely that we'll see one subpopulation overrepresented.

label: Conclusion (thus / should)
body: Parents with underage children should be given additional votes to cast on behalf of their underage children in order to achieve fair representation for their families.

label: Evidence
body: These types of families make up much of the population, but because only adults can vote, lawmakers pay little attention to the interests of these families.

label: Evaluate
body:
Most correct answers on questions with Principles in Answers sound like "If Evidence, Then Conclusion" linking ideas.
  But that feels like a weird fit here. We could maybe say that the author is assuming, "if parents can vote on behalf of their kids, then that achieves fair representation".
  This conversation overall involves a Plan / Recommendation. Authors who endorse a plan are usually assuming several things:
  - the plan is feasible
  - people will cooperate with the plan as intended
  - the plan won't backfire
  - the plan addresses the main source of the problem
  It seemed like the author was concerned with the problem that lawmakers in democracies pay too little attention to the interests of families with underage children, because only the adults can vote.
  So the author seems to be assuming that a result of her plan would be that lawmakers would pay more attention to these families.
  Thus, she seems to assume that, "if parents could vote on behalf of their underage kids, then lawmakers would pay more attention to the interests of these families".

label: Goal
body:
Ultimately, it feels hard to know where this one is going. Since the question stem sounds like 1/2 Principle, 1/2 Necessary Assumption, let's look for an answer the author is clearly thinking.
  The correct answer, if negated, should sound like an objection to the Plan or to the reasoning.

label: Conclusion
body: The move to increase editorial staff to avoid factual errors is clearly not working (i.e. there are at least as many factual errors since the increase in editorial staff was enacted).

label: Evidence
body: Compared to its biggest competitor, this paper runs significantly more corrections acknowledging factual errors.

label: Evaluate
body:
This evidence is a Comparison, and the conclusion is Anti-Causal (the new staff is not causing a reduction in factual errors).
  Usually, when we're weakening an Anti-Causal argument, we're saying that the Comparison evidence presented is not a fair comparison (they had different initial reference points / they have different realities that make it unfair to compare along these lines).

label: Goal
body:
We can prephrase any Weaken question by thinking, "Even though [evidence], how could I still argue [anti-conclusion]".
  So, "Even though this paper runs way more corrections acknowledging factual errors than does their biggest competitor, how could we still argue that this paper's move to add editorial staff is helping us to avoid factual errors?"
  But in particular we might look for an answer that makes the Evidence less compelling; some way in which this paper and its biggest competitor are unfair to compare.

label: Given that...
body: Warm-blooded animals need thick skin throughout their lives to maintain body temperature and reduce water loss.

label: How can it be that...
body: Unlike other warm-blooded animals, for the first few weeks after birth the dunnart breathes through its thin skin, which gradually thickens as the dunnart matures inside its mother's pouch.

label: Evaluate
body:
As with many Paradox questions, this one involves a comparison. It compares newborn dunnarts, which have thin skin for the first few weeks after birth, with other warm-blooded animals which need thick skin to survive throughout their entire lives.
  We're being asked to explain how newborn dunnarts manage to survive with such thin skin. It seems like there must be something unique about dunnarts. The stimulus does tell us that a dunnart lives inside its mother's pouch while its skin thickens. It's not too-far fetched to think that living in a pouch might help a thin-skinned newborn dunnart to maintain body temperature and reduce water loss.

label: Goal
body: A correct answer will describe something unique about dunnarts which allows the newborns to survive in spite of their thin skin. Expect an answer to involve living in the mother's pouch, but keep an open mind in case the correct answer brings in some new, unexpected detail which does a good job of explaining the situation. Beware of answers that seem relevant at first glance, but don't actually explain why newborn dunnarts are able to survive.

label: Evaluate
body:
The conclusion indicator "thus" at the end of the argument tells us that the correct answer will be a conclusion supported by the given statements, a conclusion which uses the given statements as evidence. However, the question stem only asks for the answer that "most logically completes the argument." So, the correct answer doesn't need to be an airtight conclusion.
  The evidence describes how successful stand-up comedians keep their audiences engaged. It also contains a statement of causation: "humor is the means through which comedians are able to accomplish all of this." Since university professors want to accomplish the same result in their lectures, it makes sense for the argument to conclude that professors can likewise use humor to achieve that result. This would be a conclusion based on reasoning that a similar cause can produce a similar result.

label: Goal
body: We'll look for an answer which indicates that university professors can use humor in their lectures. Beware of answers that bring in ideas which seem related but actually go beyond the scope of the evidence. Also beware of answers which express unsupported relationships between the concepts in the evidence, and ones that are actually contradicted by the evidence.

label: Evidence
body:
Almost all books that offer management advice are written from the perspective of the CEO.
  Most managers aren't CEOs and don't have the same perspective as CEOs.

label: Conclusion (So)
body: The advice in management books is of limited use for most managers.

label: Evaluate
body:
Taken together, the first two sentences in the argument tell us that almost all books that offer management advice are not written from the perspective that most managers have.
  The conclusion states that the advice in these books is of limited use for most managers. Advice being "of limited use" is a new idea in the conclusion. It's different from the ideas that were mentioned in the evidence. The evidence describes this advice as not being written from the perspective that most managers have.
  For the conclusion to be properly drawn from the evidence, we want the evidence to directly connect to the conclusion. We can do this with statement that says, "if advice is not written from the perspective that most managers have, then that advice is of limited use for most managers."
```
~managers' perspective → of limited use
```

label: Goal
body:
Look for an answer which matches the statement above, connecting the evidence to the conclusion. Since this is a conditional statement, the contrapositive would also be correct:
  "If advice is of more than just limited use for most managers then it will be written from the perspective that most managers have."
```
~of limited use → managers' perspective
```
  Beware of answers which present illegal reversals or illegal negations of this statement and answers which fail to properly connect the evidence to the conclusion.

label: Opposing Evidence
body: A consultant that does business with the city paid for improvements to the mayor's vacation house.

label: Opposing Conclusion (Accusation)
body: The mayor took a bribe.

label: Mayor's Evidence
body: He (the mayor) paid every bill for those improvements that was presented to him.

label: Mayor's Conclusion
body: He did not take a bribe.

label: Evaluate
body:
We're told that the mayor has been accused of taking a bribe, and then given a statement that the mayor makes "in his own defense." We can infer that the mayor is denying the accusation that he took a bribe.
  The mayor is denying this by stating that he paid every bill "that was presented to him." Okay... what if some bills were never presented to the mayor because the consultant paid those bills?
  If the mayor knew the consultant was doing that, the mayors defense is weakened. The consultant would potentially be bribing the mayor with improvements to the vacation house instead of giving the mayor money directly.

label: Goal
body: A correct answer might indicate that this was the situation: the mayor was aware that some bills were never presented to him and were instead paid by the consultant.

label: Conclusion
body:
It looks less likely that "Europe's cold winter climate made mastery of fire a necessity for humans to migrate there".
  i.e. it looks more like "Mastery of fire was not a necessity for human migration to Europe. Humans may have migrated to Europe even before they mastered fire."

label: Evidence
body: The earliest evidence of fire mastery (controlled fire use) in Europe is about 400,000 years ago.

label: Evaluate
body:
There's a big New Term in the conclusion "human migration to Europe". The author must be assuming something about "human migration to Europe".
  Since she thinks saying "the earliest mastery of fire was 400k years ago" makes it more likely that "humans migrated to Europe before they had mastery over fire", she must be assuming that humans migrated to Europe more than 400k years ago.

label: Goal
body: Look for something spelling out that missing connection of how the Premise about fire is even relevant to the claim about "human migration to Europe" in the Conclusion.

label: Conclusion
body: We should not cancel the project to build the space telescope.

label: Evidence
body: If we canceled now, all the money we've spent thus far would be wasted, and the money we've spent is more than the money left we'd have to spend to finish it.

label: Evaluate
body:
We just want to set up an "IF premise, THEN conclusion" bridge idea.
  If all the money would be wasted
  or
  If we've already spent more than the additional we'd have to spend
  then
  should not cancel project

label: Goal
body:
Get rid of any answer that doesn't let you put "shouldn't cancel" on the right side (or some equivalent meaning like "should continue the project").
  Make sure the principle applies to this project and gets us closer to the judgment of "we should keep going / we shouldn't cancel"

label: Statements
body:
Comparative Distinction
  If we leave a screwdriver within reach of different nonhuman primates, there is contrasting behavior:
  - most chimps will examine it, play with it, and then move on to something else.
  - most orangutans will pretend to ignore it at first, and then once no one is looking they might grab the screwdriver and try to dismantle their cage.

label: Evaluate
body: There's not much to put together here. The 1st sentence is already a synthesis of the 2nd and 3rd sentences. It seems like the correct answer will just provide some other derivable claim based on the different reactions chimps and orangutans have to the screwdriver.

label: Evidence
body:
The only employees who should receive bonuses this year are those who were exceptionally productive over the past year.
  Liang works in a division that has failed to meet its productivity goals for the year.

label: Conclusion
body: Liang should not receive a bonus this year.

label: Evaluate
body: The evidence would provide more support for this conclusion if the second premise stated that Liang failed to meet her productivity goals for the year. But we're only told that the division that Liang works in failed to meet its goals. The argument assumes that what is true of the division is also true for Liang. That's not necessarily the case.

label: Goal
body: Look for an answer that describes a Part vs. Whole flaw, an assumption that something must be true of one part (Liang) if it is true of the whole (the division).

label: Conclusion (Thus)
body: (even if information is accurate), the journalist will surely reveal the informant's identity.

label: Evidence (after all)
body:
```
Journalist is ordered
to reveal by judge → will reveal
or her editor
```
  The information concerns safety violations at the power plant.

label: Evaluate
body:
On Sufficient Assumption, we're trying to prove the conclusion. In this case, the conclusion is that a journalist will reveal informant's identity.
  Either the Evidence or the correct answer will thus need to give us some mechanism, some rule that feels like "if xyz is true, then will reveal identity".
  In this case, the Evidence provided that rule.
  If the judge or the editor order the journalist to reveal the identity, the journalist will reveal the identity.
  So if we want to prove that the journalist will reveal the informant's identity, that means our job is to establish that "either the judge or the editor will order the journalist to reveal the identity".
  We could head to the answers with that goal in mind and be fine.
  If we want to be a little more savvy and suss out what the correct answer might sound like, we should make use of the explicit premise (after all), that "the information concerns safety violations at the power plant".
  How could an answer make that fact relevant to our goal, of establishing that the judge/editor will order a reveal?

label: Goal
body:
It seems like the correct answer might say,
  "If the information concerns safety violations at the power plant, then a judge or the editor will order the journalist to reveal her informant's identity."
  But any answer that establishes that the judge or editor will order her to reveal the identity will work for us, because that idea automatically triggers the conclusion, that the journalist will in fact reveal the identity.

label: Principle
body:
if = sufficient
```
Wouldn't be hard to return
a borrowed item on time    should return
and                      → item on time
Person you borrowed from
didn't extend deadline
```

label: Goal
body:
The "if" told us that the trigger was the second half of the statement. We need to be mindful of the "and" because there are two criteria that need to be established before we can conclude that the person "should return the borrowed item on time".
  We should remind ourselves that this rule only has the power to prove you should return an item on time (you can only prove what's on the right side of the arrow), so we can summarily reject any answers trying to prove someone shouldn't.

label: Conclusion
body: Some gas, besides carbon dioxide and lactic acid, is given off my the human arm is attractive to mosquitoes.

label: Evidence
body:
The human arm gives off an array of gases. Two of those gases are carbon dioxide and lactic acid. Each of those gases attracts mosquitoes.
  But if you put a mosquito in complete darkness, and you offer it just carbon dioxide, just lactic acid, the combo of CO2 and lactic acid, or a human arm, the mosquito picks the human arm.

label: Evaluate
body:
Since the author is trying to Solve a Causal Mystery in her conclusion, we can use the Curious Fact / Explanation template.
  Curious Fact
  Why do mosquitoes pick a bare human arm over CO2, lactic acid, or the combo of the two?
  Author's Explanation
  The human arm gives off some other gas that is also attractive to mosquitoes.
  Correct answers always deal with one of these two pressure points:
  1. Alternate Explanations for the Curious Fact
  2. the Plausibility of the Author's Explanation
  Since this is Necessary Assumption, a correct answer will either
  - rule out an Alternate Explanation for why mosquitoes prefer human arms, or
  - provide something that's essential to the plausibility of the Author's Explanation.
  For example
  - mosquitoes are not attracted to human arms because of the smell of blood inside.
  or
  - mosquitoes are attracted to more than two types of gases (essential for the author's explanation to be true)

label: Goal
