body: Look for an answer ruling out an Alternate Explanation for why mosquitoes prefer a human arm to CO2/lactic acid by themselves, or for an answer saying something that would have to be true in order for some third gas to be coming out of a human arm and adding yet another attractive layer for mosquitoes.

label: Given that ...
body: Discovering cobalt, in a 1955 analysis, indicated to people that a certain European painting was made after 1804 (since cobalt blue wasn't used in Europe prior to 1804).

label: How can it be that ...
body: Discovering cobalt, in a 2009 analysis, indicated to people that this painting was produced before 1804?

label: Evaluate
body:
There are probably a few different ways we can resolve a paradox like this. There's a bit of a He Said / She Said to these two different analyses.
  One says, "we found cobalt, so this was made after 1804", and the other says "we found cobalt, and we think this was made before 1804".
  So one way to resolve that tension would just be a storyline that makes either the 1955 or the 2009 analysis seem like they were just wrong / confused.
  But how could they both be right? Maybe the painting was made before 1804 but the cobalt blue was added later?
  Maybe the painting was made before 1804 but the cobalt found on it isn't from cobalt blue paint pigment, but just from some other source of cobalt?

label: Goal
body:
We're probably more likely to be explaining how the 2009 analysis could be correct, but we should stay flexible since there are different ways to resolve this discrepancy.
  I would head to answers thinking, "Given that the cobalt blue pigment wasn't used in Europe before 1804, how could this 2009 analysis find cobalt on the painting but still think the painting came from before 1804?"

label: Conclusion
body: The public evidently heeded the campaign (translation: the public washed their hands frequently and avoided public places when they were experiencing flu symptoms).

label: Evaluate
body:
This argument as a common structure:
  - This policy / this campaign / this plan went into effect
  - Since then / during then, we observed X.
  - Thus, it's clear that X resulted from that policy/plan/campaign.
  These all belong to the broader category of Explain a Curious Fact.
  Curious Fact ... why was the incidence of flu much lower than we predicted it would be during those 6 months?
  Author's Explanation ... people heeded the campaign -> they started washing their hands more frequently / avoiding public places when they had flu symptoms -> this contributed to lower spread of the flu than there would have been otherwise
  We need to consider
  1. Alternate Explanations for the Curious Fact
  2. the Plausibility of the Author's Explanation
  What could be a different reason why the rate of flu was lower than expected? Maybe the predictions were off for some reason. Maybe there were fewer visitors (i.e. germ vectors) to the area than normal during those months. Maybe most workplaces installed better air filtration systems during those months (which helps to cut down on contagious people infecting others in the workplace).
  How would we assess the plausibility of the author's explanation? We would just want any evidence we can get that people were aware of the campaign and started changing their behavior because of it (washed their hands more than they usually would / avoided public places when they felt flu symptoms more than they usually would).

label: Goal
body: Since this is Strengthen, we either need an answer to rule out a different explanation for why the rate of flu was lower than expected, or to boost the plausibility of the story that people started washing their hands and staying home when sick more than before.

label: Conclusion
body: For a meeting to achieve max productivity, it should have a clear time frame and be no more than 30 mins long.

label: Evidence
body:
According to a study, for most meetings ...
  - after 30 min, diminishing returns, and by 60 mins pretty much worthless.
  - most productive meetings were ones with a clearly established time frame.

label: Evaluate
body:
When we do Main Conclusion questions, we know that the conclusion will almost never be in the final sentence. (It's usually the First Sentence or a But/Yet/However rebuttal in the middle)
  However, LSAC hears us test prep companies shouting that pattern from the hilltops, so on some recent tests they've been trying to vary it up a little.
  The one keyword we have available to help us here is the word "then". It's a very infrequently used Conclusion keyword, but it functions much like a "then" in a "if / then" conditional statement.
  All these authors are implicitly thinking, "IF my evidence is true, THEN it proves my conclusion".
  "IF we only get diminishing returns after 30 minutes and IF the most productive meeting have a clear time frame, THEN the most productive meetings would have a clear time frame and go no longer than 30 minutes."
  We always check our conclusions with the Support test. If you think Claim X might be the conclusion, then ask yourself Why should I believe that? and make sure that the argument provides at least one explicit premise to support Claim X.

label: Goal
body: Once we've properly located a conclusion, all the hard stuff is usually done. Now we just go find a meaning match in the answers. So we just want the best meaning match for the final sentence.

label: Statements
body:
Most fad diets - narrow range of nutrients.
  but
  People: vary widely in terms of what nutrients they need.
  (Reconcile what's before/after the pivot ... Infer: most fad diets work work better for some people than for others, since the narrow range of nutrients they prescribe would better match some people's dietary needs than someone else's dietary needs)
  Everyone needs fruits and veggies, which help ward off health problems.
  (infer: maybe it would be good for most fad diets to include fruits and veggies in their range of nutrients suggested, since that's a type of nutrient that doesn't vary widely from person to person. Everyone benefits from those.)

label: Goal
body: Find a safely worded answer, possibly reinforcing the idea that most fad diets are going to work better for some than others, or reinforcing the idea that if you're gonna prescribe a narrow range of nutrients, fruits and veggies would be a good way to go, since everybody needs those.

label: Conclusion
body: If you drink caffeinated coffee, darker roasts will irritate your stomach less than lighter roasts.

label: Evidence
body: Caffeine stimulates the irritating acid in the stomach. But darker roasts have more NMP than lighter roasts, and NMP tends to suppress acid production.

label: Evaluate
body:
Given that darker roasts have more NMP, and NMP suppresses the irritating acid in your stomach, how could we still argue that lighter roasts are easier on your stomach?
  There would to have to be something else different between darker and lighter that tips the scales back in favor of lighter roasts.
  This argument is kind of like a Part vs. Whole argument. Since one part of darker roasts (the higher NMP) is better on your stomach, the author assumes/concludes that darker roasts overall are better on your stomach.

label: Goal
body: Look for an answer that addresses a potential difference between darker and lighter roasts, so that we might be able to argue that lighter roasts are actually easier on your stomach.

label: Statements
body:
It's hard for film historians to figure out typical audience reactions to certain films, especially from the early 20th century.
  Newspaper and magazine reviews fail to provide much insight.
  So do box office figures. They just show whether a film was a financial success or failure. They don't show what audiences found funny, frightening, or moving.

label: Evaluate
body:
Did we see any Conditional, Causal, Mathematical, or Pivot language that would suggest which ideas to combine?
  The closest we have is some anti-causal wording.
  Box office figures don't help us figure out the typical audience reaction to films.
  Newspaper and magazines reviews don't provide much insight into typical audience reaction to films.
  We could potentially derive statements that reinforce that anti-causal relationship:
  - newspaper and magazine reviews don't usually mention the typical audience reaction, and they can't be trusted to reflect the typical audience reaction.
  - box office figures don't indicate typical audience reactions
  - financial success or failure doesn't reveal typical audience response
  The middle sentence seems to have some utility. If we say,
  "A doesn't help determine X. It only shows Y, not Z"
  then we seem to be implying that
  "Y does not help us determine X"
  and that "Z is part of determining X".
  (we already covered "Y doesn't help us determine X" when we said that "financial success or failure doesn't help us determine typical audience reaction")
  (Z is part of determining X)
  - what audiences found funny, frightening, or moving is part of determining the "typical audience response".

label: Goal
body: Hard to know exactly what they're going for because there are several ways to spell out what does and doesn't help us determine typical audience reactions.

label: Conclusion
body: The observed properties of pulsars are consistent with the possibility that some pulsars are filled with quarks.

label: Evidence
body: Based on observations, astronomers think they are balls of neutrons. But if they were filled with quarks, they would have an overall positive charge, which would attract a layer of negatively charged particles that could support a crust of neutrons.

label: Evaluate
body:
This argument is tricky to understand at first. From what astronomers can observe, they think pulsars are balls of neutrons. The author is suggesting an alternate interpretation (she's not insisting on it, just saying that it's also a possible interpretation).
  Her alternate interpretation is essentially, "Sure, sure, we can tell the outer layer is neutrons. But maybe it's not neutrons all the way through. Maybe the inside is actually quarks. If pulsars had a quark-filled center, it's plausible that they would end up covered by a crust of neutrons and so outwardly it would look like a ball of neutrons."
  We're being asked about the claim "the core of a quark-filled pulsar would have a positive charge". That claim was part of the author's attempt to show us how a pulsar filled with quarks would still end up resembling a neutron ball. She was saying, the core of quarks would give a positive charge, which would attract a layer of negatively charged particles, which could support an outer crust of neutrons.
  When we see the word Because preface the claim we're asked about, it means that the claim is either a supporting premise for the other clause of that sentence. Ot it means that the claim describes a causal factor that results in the other clause of that sentence.
  In this case, it seems to make more sense to interpret this as a Causal Because (as opposed to a Reasoning Because).

label: Goal
body:
Look for an answer saying narrowly that this claim helps to explain why a quark-filled pulsar could potentially have an outer crust of neutrons.
  Or look for an answer more broadly saying, "this is part of how the author defends that a quark-filled pulsar would ultimately resemble, from the outside, a ball of neutrons, which shows why the quark-filled pulsar is compatible with observed outer properties".

label: Statements
body:
conditional:
```
close to gas pipeline,
large body water,
new natural gas   and transmission lines
power station   → and
                  in a region where residents
                  won't oppose construction
```
  facts:
  We've got the transmission lines.
  But, we only have transmission lines near three bodies of water, and residents would oppose construction in all those locations.

label: Evaluate
body:
When we're given a Conditional rule, we're often expected to make an inference based on facts that trigger the contrapositive.
  If we're lacking any of those 4 required ingredients, then we can't construct any new natural-gas powered stations.
  It sounds like we're lacking some of those ingredients, since the places that have 3 of the 4 are lacking the last thing, cooperative residents.

label: Goal
body: They seem to want us to say, "We're screwed"? "Can't build any new stations?"

label: Conclusion (this indicates that)
body: Citizens are becoming increasingly disconnected from the political system with each passing generation.

label: Evidence
body: People over 65 vote in the highest percentages while young adults are least likely to vote.

label: Evaluate
body:
The author's evidence presents a Curious Comparison -- why is it that people over 65 have the highest percentage of voting whereas young adults have the lowest percentage of voting?
  His conclusion assumes one possible Causal Explanation -- each new generation is less connected to the political system, so they don't feel as strong an urge to vote.
  We always react to this Curious Fact / Explanation type of argument with the same two pressure points:
  - Alternative Explanations for the curious fact (how else could we explain why higher percentages of older people than younger people vote?)
  - Plausibility of the Author's Explanation (do we have any other evidence that today's generation is less connected to the political system than previous generations were?)
  When we see Curious Fact / Explanation arguments on Flaw, the correct answer is almost always about Alternate Explanations.
  A different way to explain the voting difference between old and young might just be that the old people are retired and can watch cable news all day and have no problem voting on random Tuesdays, whereas young people are busy and have to go to work or have enough of a social life that they don't pay any attention to politics.
  The conclusion isn't saying "as you get older, you get more politically engaged". It's saying, "The Baby Boomers were more politically engaged than Gen X. Gen X is more engaged then Millennials. Millennials are more engaged than Gen Z."

label: Goal
body: Look for an answer complaining that the author failed to consider some alternate explanation for the difference in voting habits.

label: Conclusion
body: The city should block the proposed office complex until they've done an environmental assessment of the marsh's role in maintaining the quality of the city's well water.

label: Evidence
body: The local marsh would need to be drained in order to build the proposed office complex, and marshes often play a crucial role in purifying groundwater.

label: Evaluate
body: We want a conclusion that isn't totally negative, just provisionally negative. The argument should be saying, "Let's not do this ... yet. This action might mess up something really important, and we haven't ascertained yet whether it's gonna mess us up."

label: Goal
body:
Look for an answer containing ingredients something like this:
  - we're considering an action
  - the action involves tampering with a potentially crucial thing
  - thus, let's not take the action until we've better assessed whether this action is going to tamper with the crucial thing.

label: Conclusion
body: Watching a recording of yourself exercising can motivate you to exercise more.

label: Evidence
body: In a study, the people who watched a recording of themselves running on a treadmill reported exercising, on average, 1 more hour per day than the people who instead watched other people run on a treadmill.

label: Goal
body: There must be some utility to this barking that outweighs the fact that the barking usually gives away the presence and position of the babblers, and that explains why it seems to go beyond the point of just warning other babblers so that they can take cover.

label: Evaluate
body:
This is a typical Curious Fact / Explanation kind of setup.
  Curious Fact: How come the ones who saw themselves in the video report exercising more than 1 hr more than those who saw other people exercising?
  Author's Explanation: Watching yourself on video exercising motivates you to exercise more, so these people who watched themselves during the study had new motivation to exercise, increased their exercise regimen, and now average 1 hr more of exercise.
  You'll notice I'm filling in a lot of blanks for the Author. That's a good habit when we're trying to understand the Causal story that they're selling. We always react to Curious Fact arguments with the same two questions:
  How ELSE could we explain the Curious Fact?
  What could help us assess the plausibility of the Author's Story?
  Most correct answers that weaken a Causal argument provide a different way to explain the background data. Why else could the group that watched themselves be exercising 1 hour more? Maybe that group was just already exercising 1 hour more on average. The language of the argument doesn't say that they've increased their amount of exercise. Maybe that group did increase their exercise, but not as the result of this experiment. Maybe a disproportionate number of that group recently hired personal trainers, and that is the reason why they're exercising 1 hour more. Maybe they live in a climate that's more conducive to exercise.
  If we wanted to weaken the plausibility, we could say stuff like, "People are so mortified by how they look when exercising that it makes them want to exercise less" / "in another study, people who exercised in front of a mirror exercised less than people in front of a wall"

label: Goal
body:
Pick an answer that gives us a different way to explain the Curious "1 hr extra" Fact,
  or an answer that undermines the story that watching yourself exercise motivates you to exercise more.

label: Conclusion
body: Convincing people to focus on their personal use of fossil fuels cannot achieve an overall reduction in carbon use.

label: Evidence
body: Even if most people changed their personal use, it wouldn't produce a reduction on the scale we need. Only government policies can produce change on that scale.

label: Evaluate
body:
Given that "only government policies can produce big enough change", how could we argue that "convincing people to focus on their personal use COULD achieve the goal of an overall reduction"?
  Well, the nitpicky objection would be that if the goal is literally just a reduction in carbon use, then if most people reduce their carbon use then there will be an overall reduction. The author is saying, "Yeah, but it won't be reduced enough", but she never stipulated that the goal was "a certain amount of overall reduction in carbon use". So she is assuming, somewhat nonsensically, that "if we don't reduce it enough to produce the needed reductions, then we didn't achieve the goal of an overall reduction."
  But, where I would assume this is actually going is the idea that maybe having individuals change their behavior could trigger governments changing their policies. After all, the government is made up of individuals. Maybe if the citizenry becomes more engaged in conserving carbon use, then their representatives in government will shift policies accordingly.

label: Goal
body: I would look for an answer that rules out our objection: "changing personal behavior would not lead to the government changing its policies".

label: Evidence
body:
There are only two plausible views about where the aesthetic value of a painting lies:
  1. in its purely formal qualities,
  2. in what the painting means.
  There exists no compelling general account of how a painting could derive its value from its purely formal characteristics.

label: Conclusion
body: The aesthetic value of a painting lies in what it means.

label: Evaluate
body:
The basic form of the argument might look valid at first glance:
  Evidence: Either A or B
  Not A
  Conclusion: B
  For the argument to actually follow this pattern, the final premise would need to state that a painting does not derive its value from its purely formal characteristics. The actual premise only states that there is no "compelling general account" of how this could be. This basically means there's no good explanation for it.
  This is very similar to an "Unproven vs. Proven False" flaw. Saying "there is no good way to explain why X is true" is completely different from saying "X is not true." Fun fact: for a very long time, scientists could not explain exactly how anesthesia works. It still worked, and doctors still used it all the time.

label: Goal
body: Look for an answer choice containing an argument that makes this same invalid shift from stating "there is no good way to explain why X is true" to assuming "X is not true."

label: Conclusion
body: A global ban on fossil fuels would be followed by an economic boom, not an economic depression.

label: Evidence
body:
Economic booms ---require--> tech innovations.
  A global ban on fossil fuels would produce tech innovations.

label: Evaluate
body:
This looks like the #1 recurring flaw: Necessary vs. Sufficient.
  We're provided with a conditional rule:
  X must be preceded by Y.
  We're told that Thing A would provide Y.
  And then we illegally reason backwards that Thing A would provide X.

label: Goal
body:
Look for an answer saying, "Just because a requirement of economic booms has been met doesn't mean that we would definitely have an economic boom", or look for an answer pointing out that there may be other things required of an economic boom that wouldn't be present if we were to have a global ban on fossil fuels.
  Also, we could talk about other ramifications of a global ban on fossil fuels that would more likely lead towards depression than growth.

label: Winston's first claim
body:
Nobel rules say that no more than three people can share the same prize.
  Does Sanjay agree with this?
  Yes, implicitly. Sanjay says that "the rules also stipulate something else", which indicates an implicit agreement that the rules do indeed stipulate the thing Winston said.

label: Winston's second claim
body:
Nobel Prizes in science are usually given to recognize particular scientific results.
  Does Sanjay agree with this?
  We have no idea. Nothing he says addresses this.

label: Winston's third claim
body:
Many important results are the work of four or more scientists.
  Does Sanjay agree with this?
  We have no idea. He just talks about some influential scientists dying before their work was fully appreciated.

label: Conclusion (so)
body: There is reason to believe that there may be life on Europa.

label: Evidence
body: The presence of a sea is thought to be a primary factor for the development of life and,

label: Evaluate
body:
It looks like Sanjay agrees with Winston's first explicit claim. What about any implicit claims?
  Well, the thrust of both conversations was that Nobel rules would probably exclude some deserving scientists.
  Winston was like, "rules say a max of 3 people can get an award for the results of their work, but many important results are the work for 4+ scientists."
  Sanjay was like, "rules say you can only give award to someone who's alive, but a some important scientists died before we realized how important their work was".

label: Goal
body: Look for an answer saying "Nobel rules say no more than three can share the same prize", or, more likely, something that sounds like "the Nobel rules end up cheating some people out of getting the award".

label: Conclusion (This suggests that)
body: Most of the people who received the nonprofit letter agreed with their position on the social issue presented.

label: Evidence
body: 283 of the 300 people who responded to the letter agreed with the position.

label: Evaluate
body:
We seem to be looking at one of the Top 10 famous flaws, Sampling.
  We know that most of the respondents agreed with the nonprofit's position on the social issue. The author is trying to conclude that most of the recipients agreed with the position on the social issue.
  So it's a question of whether we think that "people who responded" are a fairly typical cross-section of recipients. Are they a sample from which we can extrapolate general conclusions?
  Our concerns with Samples usually are that the sample is too small (like under 20), the respondents didn't provide truthful responses (out of fear of shame or retaliation), or most commonly that the people who comprise our sample population are self-selecting / biased / skewed / atypical in some way.
  A sample size of 300 out of 5,000 total letters is a pretty respectable size. It could always be more robust with bigger numbers, but anything over 100 is nothing LSAT would ever complain about.
  Are these 300 respondents likely to be an atypical sample of the underlying population of recipients?
  Maybe. This is where our outside common sense comes into play. We might be well aware of "the Yelp phenomenon", the idea that people generally only take the time to write a review if they're really motivated (loved it or hated it), so you see mainly 5-star and 1-star reviews.
  Similarly, it could be that because of the effort it takes to respond to a survey that showed up in your mail, most people wouldn't respond whether they agreed or disagreed. It would mainly be the zealots who write back.

label: Goal
body:
Look for an answer objecting that it's not safe to assume that this sample of 300 respondents is representative of the underlying 5000 recipients, because respondents are a self-selecting group of people who had really strong reactions.
  In general, if a nonprofit you don't agree with mailed you something, you'd pitch it in the recycling bin, thinking "not for me". You probably would only write the organization if you were super aligned with the cause and wanted to get involved. So we could even say that the low response rate overall (only 300 out of 5000) could be evidence that people mostly weren't aligned with that position.

label: Evidence
body:
Tree-ring analysis shows that Europe’s climate underwent extreme fluctuations between 250 A.D. and 550 A.D., a period that encompasses Rome’s decline and fall.
  This highly variable climate surely hurt food production, which made the empire harder to rule and defend.

label: Conclusion
body: An unstable climate was probably a major cause of the fall of the Roman empire.

label: Evaluate
body: The argument establishes a correlation between extreme climatic fluctuations and the fall of the Roman empire and then asserts that the unstable climate was a major cause of the fall of the Roman empire. An answer that strengthens the correlation between the climate and the stability of the Roman empire would support the argument and so too would an answer that rules out an alternative cause of Rome’s decline.

label: Conclusion (Obviously, then)
body:
There are exceptions to the economists' general rule.
  economists' rule: Tendency to purchase is inversely proportional to price.
  Conclusion-translated: Sometimes people's tendency to purchase a given commodity is not inversely proportional to its price
  (i.e. the price rises and more want to buy it, or the price drops and fewer people want to buy it)

label: Evidence
body:
Sure there's an example that fits the economists rule, where price and purchasing were inverted: the price of steel went down, and the amount purchasing went up.
  But, there's a counterexample to the rule, where price and purchasing were aligned: the price of lace went down, and the purchasing of lace went down (if you can't rub it in the poor's face that they can't afford lace, then what's the point?)

label: Evaluate
body:
The arguments on Main Conclusion and Role are intentionally more opaque. They don't want to make finding the conclusion an easy part of the process, because it's the main event on these questions. So any time we're doing Main Conclusion or Role, we're anticipating the conclusion probably won't be at the end with an obvious Therefore / Thus indicator word. But sometimes it will be last, usually on easier ranked problems like this Q4.
  Instead, the Conclusion will usually be one of these two:
  - the first claim in the paragraph
  - a rebuttal
  In this case the conclusion is at the end of the paragraph, and it does have some indicator words, although they're less obvious ones.
  Obviously / evidently / clearly / apparently are frequently used on LSAT to show us an opinion, and of course when we're searching for the Main Conclusion we're searching for the opinion that the author supports.
  Then / consequently / as a result are used to show the terminal end of a chain of thought, i.e. the conclusion of a train of thought.
  This final sentence is the author's rebuttal, so if we're familiar with looking for Rebuttal Conclusions and First Sentence Conclusions on Main Conclusion and Role, we'll hopefully gravitate towards the rebuttal, since the first sentence contained an attribution to "economists".
  The claim we're being asked about is the author's concession to the occasional validity of the economists point of view.
  The four claims here go like this:
  1. Attributed claim
  "according to economists, X"
  2. Author's conceding some validity
  "here's an example about steel that matches X"
  3. Author pivoting into premise
  "Nevertheless, here's a counterexample to X"
  4. Author's rebuttal conclusion
  "Obviously, then, the economists are wrong"

label: Goal
body: They're asking us about #2, so we want something like, "The author is acknowledging that there are some data points that do fit the economists' general rule (even though the rule does not universally hold)."

label: Intermediate Conclusion (this indicates that)
body: There is a warm sea beneath Europa's icy surface

label: Conclusion (so)
body: We should hire Chen.

label: Information
body:
asymmetric comparison (Curious Fact)
  Kuna who were born and live on the islands generally have a low incidence of high blood pressure, whereas Kuna who moved to the mainland don't have this low incidence of high blood pressure.
  asymmetric comparison
  Kuna on the islands typically drink several cups of high-flavonoid cocoa a day, whereas Kuna who live on the mainland don't.

label: Evaluate
body:
This looks ripe for a "One Difference Explains the Other" type inference.
  Suppose we said, "Bob has improved at LSAT much less than Jane has over the course of the three months they've both been studying. Jane, unlike Bob, does mindfulness breathing after every study session."
  Can we prove that the mindfulness breathing is the causal difference-maker that has allowed Jane to improve more than Bob?
  Of course not. But can we support that idea? Yes.
  On Most Supported questions, we're sometimes asked to speculate that Difference 1 explains Difference 2.

label: Goal
body: We would anticipate that "drinking several cups of high-flavonoid cocoa" is a reason that the island Kuna have lower blood pressure than the mainland Kuna.

label: Curious Fact
body: Why do jurors think of evidence as more credible when they see it inside the courtroom vs. outside of a courtroom?

label: Hypothesis
body: Judges prescreen scientific evidence and only allow credible scientific evidence to be presented in the courtroom (so jurors are more likely to trust what they see in a courtroom).

label: Evaluate
body:
We always evaluate Curious Fact / Explanation situations through two prisms:
  1. can we think of an Alternate Explanation for the curious fact?
  What could be a different reason why jurors are more likely to regard evidence as credible when it's presented in a courtroom? (maybe it's because people are wearing suits and sounding like experts / maybe it's because people swear in on a bible before they testify)
  2. how plausible is the Author's Explanation for it?
  What would need to be true for this hypothesis to even make sense? (we would have to assume that jurors are aware that the evidence has been pre-screened for credibility / we have to assume that jurors trust this pre-screening process to filter out dubious stuff / we have to assume a difference, that when people see scientific evidence outside of a courtroom, it hasn't gone through some filtering process to weed out the dubious stuff)

label: Goal
body:
Look for an answer either asking whether or not an Alternate Explanation could be true, or for an answer asking a question that's central to whether or not we'd consider the author's hypothesis plausible.
  One subtle but important feature of the hypothesis is that they're saying the trusting effect is primarily due to the fact that judges prescreen evidence. Because of that word, they're allowing for the idea that other things might also make a difference.
  So an Alternate Explanation here will only weaken if we learn that it is the primary reason why people are more trusting of evidence in the courtroom. Thus, we might be more likely to get a correct answer attacking the plausibility of the Author's Hypothesis.

label: Conclusion (therefore)
body: Sticking with her current platform will allow Whalley to win the election.

label: Evidence
body: If Whalley sticks with her current platform, she'll lose by a few percentage points among under 50 voters, but win by a bigger margin among voters 50 and up.

label: Evaluate
body:
We need to prove that "if Whalley sticks with current platform, she'll win the election", and what we know is that "if she sticks with current platform, she'll win among 50+ voters, while losing by a smaller margin with voters under 50".
  So the answer needs to convince us that "winning among 50+ voters, while losing with voters under 50, is a recipe that guarantees a win in the election."
  We're told that she wins the older crowd by a bigger margin than she loses the younger crowd. Does that guarantee an election win?
  No, not necessarily. Let's pretend it's an election between W and X, and this is how we expect the voting to go:
```
           voting for W    voting for X
50+        60%             40%
under 50   45%             55%
```
  If there were 100 voters under 50 and 100 voters 50 and up, then W would get 105 of the 200 votes, and X would get only 95 votes. So W would win the election.
  But, if there are way more young voters than there are older voters, then you'd rather have the edge with younger voters.
```
           vote for W   vote for X
50+        60%          40%   (100ppl)
18-49      45%          55%   (300ppl)
```
  In this election, W would get 195 of the 400 votes, and X would get 205 votes, so X would win.

label: Goal
body:
The only way that W can lose the election is if there are more younger voters (under 50) than there are older voters.
  If there are an equal number of voters under 50 to those 50 and up, then W wins. If the there are more voters 50 and up than there are under 50, then W wins.

label: Statements (Math-y Pivot)
body:
1880 vs. 2000
  Britain's economy 5x bigger
  but
  Per capita emissions same

label: Goal
body:
Since they're giving us a generalization (similar to a Principle), it might be conditional in nature. If you're violating a conditional, then you provide an example in which the left side is true, but the right side isn't true.
  If, for example, we had a principle like
  "if your economy is 5 times bigger than before, then your per capita emissions will be higher than before",
  this example would be violating it.
  Britain's economy was 5 times bigger,
  but per capita emissions weren't higher.

label: Conclusion
body: When you need a will, a lawyer's expert advice is always worth paying for.

label: Evidence
body:
(When you need a will, getting lawyer's advice is much more expensive than do-it-yourself software, and either method will get you a valid will.)
  But ... you pay extra money to tailor your will to your particular circumstances (similar to how you pay a doctor to get an expertly customized prescription, not just any valid prescription).

label: Evidence
body: Since photos show an area where the icy surface appears to have buckled as a result of turbulent (i.e. warmer, liquid water) is moving beneath.

label: Evaluate
body: There are two conclusion indicators, "this indicates that" and "so". The chain of reasoning they present looks like this: Ice buckling from running water below Europa ⇢ warm sea on Europa ⇢ maybe life on Europa + (warm sea primary factor for dev of life)

label: Opposing Idea
body: When a faculty member's falsification of research was uncovered, the media treated it as evidence of the university's low standards, even though in truth it was a mere case of dishonesty.

label: Evaluate
body:
In terms of Missing Links, it feels like the author is saying, "It's always worth paying for extra customization (for getting a will that's tailored to your particular circumstances)".
  But this argument seems more like it might be going the way of Defending Against Objections. The conclusion is really strong. In every single case where someone needs a will, a lawyer's expert advice is worth paying for?
  This reminds me of whether it's worth getting a tax preparer for one's income tax return. It's not worth it for people who can fill out a 1040 EZ .. they just have their W-2, the standard deduction, and that's pretty much it.
  Similarly, with the medical analogy, is it always worth paying a doctor for customized advice? No. If I'm on my period and have a headache, I'm just going to take some ibuprofen or acetaminophen. I know that both of them are valid prescriptions and that's good enough. I don't need to pay a doctor $150 to get a custom diagnosis, because I have a very straightforward case with a simple diagnosis.
  (This is my most USA culturally biased explanation yet, between 1040 EZ, W2 and paying to go to the doctor!)
  We can imagine that some wills would be so simple and straightforward that the valid will from the do-it yourself software would be good enough.

label: Goal
body: Look for an answer linking "tailoring to particular circumstances" to "always worth the extra money", or an answer ruling out the objection that some people would have simple enough wills that they don't really need to pay for an expert's advice.

label: Evidence
body: conditional (wherever) people indifferent to environment → pollution a problem; conditional (wherever) Pollution → nature's balance is harmed

label: Conclusion
body: conditional (wherever) people indifferent to environment → nature's balanced harmed

label: Evaluate
body: This is probably the most classic recipe for Parallel problems: two conditionals that chain together. In this case, the conclusion just makes the conditional A → C inference. We might have paused wondering if we can chain together the 2nd claim with the 1st claim. Is it fair to say that "where pollution is a problem" there is "pollution"? Of course! How could pollution be a problem if there weren't pollution present?

label: Goal
body: We want a valid argument, with two conditional premises and one conditional conclusion. The premises should chain together (A → B → C) and the conclusion should just give us the A → C connection. Premise 1: A → B. Premise 2: B → C. Conclusion: A → C.

label: Curious Fact
body: Why did mechanism produce so many arguments establishing the superiority of monarchy over other systems of government?

label: Someone Else's Explanation
body: Maybe the principles of mechanism are in tension with democracy (so the principles of mechanism naturally lend themselves to saying that monarchy is better than democracy).

label: Author's Explanation
body: Nah. I bet mechanism works fine with democracy. I bet what happened is that every time a mechanist tried to argue that monarchy was better, the argument would fail (because democracy is actually better), and so someone else would have to come up with a different mechanist argument for why monarch is better.

label: Evaluate
body: Even thought the question stem labels this an "argument", it's not easy to find a classic Conclusion + Support structure. It's more natural to talk about this argument in our Explain Curious Fact framework, because it's all about one possible explanation vs. an alternate explanation for some curious fact. Suppose we say, "Some people think Kevin is crying because he's cutting onions, but it's more likely that the onions aren't bothering him at all and he's really just upset by the UN's new climate change warnings." My conclusion was there was that Kevin is really crying because of the new climate change warnings, but I didn't actually support that with anything. Similarly, this author doesn't give any premise for why we should believe that it's more likely that mechanism supports democracy and that the plurality of mechanist arguments in favor of monarchy are really just an indication that they kept unsuccessfully trying to prove that monarchy was better.

label: Goal
body: We're being asked about the 2nd sentence. We know it's an Opposing idea, because the author follows it with "But it is more likely that ___ ". We will probably see some language saying that this 2nd sentence described "a possible explanation for the first sentence, but an explanation that the author rejected as being less likely than the explanation she favors".

label: Conclusion
body: Ishiko must be a good manager

label: Evidence (since)
body: Ishiko is able to defuse tense situations. Anyone who is able to defuse tense situations must understand people. (infer: Ishiko can understand people) A good manager must understand people and be able to defuse tense situations.

label: Evaluate
body: This argument is functionally the same as this one: A Supreme Court justice must be able to speak in complete sentences and read things written in English. My buddy T-bone can read things written in English and speak in complete sentences. Thus, T-bone must be a Supreme Court justice. There's a big difference between satisfying some necessary requirements for being X and definitely being X. The first sentence doesn't say that the only things a good manager must be able to do is understand people and defuse tense situations. They might also need to be able to enter payroll information into the proper government forms, for example. Does Ishiko know how to do that? We don't know. We are told a couple things required of being a good manager, and we're told that Ishiko meets those requirements. But meeting a couple requirements of being a good manager (or a SCOTUS justice) doesn't prove you are a good manager. The formal name for this flaw is Necessary vs. Sufficient, which just means that the author presented conditional logic in her evidence, but then she tries to apply that conditional rule in backwards or opposite fashion. If she presents a rule that says "X → Y", then the argument will either make the flawed argument that, "Since Ishiko is Y, she must be X" (illegal reversal) or the flawed argument that "Since Ishiko is not X, she must not be Y" (illegal negation). The first premise here looks like this: Good manager → Und ppl and Defuse tense. Then the author argues an illegal reversal: Ishiko can understand people and defuse tense situations. Therefore, she must be a good manager.

label: Goal
body: Look for an answer pointing out the Necessary vs. Sufficient flaw, or one making more conversational objections like, "Maybe there are other requirements of being a good manager that Ishiko doesn't satisfy."

label: Given that ...
body: the babblers' barking gives away their position and that ... the barking continues long after all the other babblers have taken cover

label: Goal
body: We're being asked about the claim that there is a warm sea, so we could call it a Premise, in regards to the conclusion that there may be life on Europa. We can also call it a Conclusion, in regards to the fact that it's supported by photographic evidence of ice buckling. Something that both has support and provides support can be called an Intermediate or Subsidiary Conclusion.

label: Conclusion (too often)
body: Too often, retailers use advertised price cuts to promote their wares.

label: Evidence
body: (Even though consumers love feeling lucky, and promotions of this sort might make them feel lucky,) these promotions cut into profit margins and undermine customer loyalty.

label: Evaluate
body: When we do Main Conclusion we prime our brain to listen for an early Conclusion, since in the vast majority of these, the last idea is Support. The two most common places to find the Conclusion on a Main Conclusion question would be First Sentence, or after a Pivot (like but, yet, however). That helps us pick up on the Opinion indicator "too often" right after the pivot "but", in the second sentence. Is this idea supported? Why does the author think retailers too frequently resort to advertised price cuts? Because, these advertised price cuts cut into profit margins and undermine customer loyalty.

label: Goal
body: We're just looking for an answer that replicates the meaning of "too often they resort to using advertised price cuts to promote their wares". Since that claim has a Pronoun, we should definitely replace the pronoun and think, "Too often retailers use advertised price cuts to promote their wares". We could consider alternate phrasings of the same meaning. What's another way, for example, to say "Eddie, too often you start snacking before dinnertime"? You could say, "Eddie, you should snack less before dinnertime" and that would mean the same thing.

label: Conclusion (should thus)
body: Limiting one's intake of meats, seafood, and other foods rich in iron should reduce one's chance of contracting Parkinson's disease.

label: Evidence (people who are X more likely Y)
body: There's a correlation between diets contain large amount of iron | more likely to get Parkinson's.

label: Evaluate
body: When an author presents a Curious Comparison like a correlation, they will almost always then make some causal assumption about one side causing the other. In this case we can tell the author is assuming that eating diet with lots of iron leads to higher chance of Parkinson's, because her conclusion is acting like avoiding a diet high in iron would help lower chance of Parkinson's. Whenever an author assumes some causal explanation for a curious fact, we react with two different questions: could there be some Alternate Explanation for the curious fact? how plausible is the Author's Explanation?

label: Goal
body: Since this is Strengthen, we want to either rule out a different way to explain why a diet high in iron is correlated with higher Parkinson's risks (i.e. "frequent blows to the head, which is known to increase Parkinson's risks, are not much more likely for people who eat high iron diets than for those who don't") or increase the plausibility that high iron leads to higher Parkinson's risk, or that eating less meat / seafood / iron-rich food would help lower one's Parkinson's risk.

label: Statements
body: Maples (MP candidate) would be a better mayor than Tannett (TP candidate). conditional / comparison: Every member of MP → Better qualified than any member of TP.

label: Evaluate
body: There are two big patterns on Must Be False questions: 1. the correct answer contradicts a conditional (meaning it supplies a data point where the trigger is true but the outcome is false); 2. the correct answer contradicts an inference we can make. Here, there isn't any inference we can make by combining claims, because the 1st sentence is more or less derivable from the conditional rule in the 2nd sentence. And since the second sentence is a conditional, our premonition would be that the correct answer is going to contradict it.

label: Goal
body: Let's look for an answer that makes it seem like some member of the Traditionalist Party could be at least as well qualified as some member of the Modern Party.

label: Conclusion
body: If the maintenance had been done on a different day, I would have gotten to the meeting on time.

label: Evidence
body: Because of the maintenance, I wasn't allowed to park in the parking area directly in front of the building. After finding out that I couldn't park there, it took me 15 minutes to find a spot, which made me a few minutes late.

label: Evaluate
body: The author's conclusion is about a counterfactual ... if they hadn't been doing maintenance that day. So to argue with him, we have to enter that alternative universe and think, how could we argue that in a world where they weren't doing maintenance in front of the building, he still would have been late? We know that he got to the lot around 15 minutes before his meeting (because a 15 min delay in finding a spot made him only a few minutes late). We'd pretty much be trying to think of storylines where arriving to the parking area 15 mins before the meeting isn't long enough. Maybe he still would have needed to cruise around 15 mins to find a spot? Maybe he would get caught in conversation with people and walk into the building? Maybe he never really has access to the front lot (either he's not important enough at the company to have a premier spot or he gets there late enough that the front lot is usually already full).

label: Goal
body: It's hard to know what to predict here. We just know that the author is Assuming a Difference. He's either assuming that if the maintenance hadn't been going on, he would have been able to find a spot in the front lot, or that it would have taken less than 15 minutes to drive around and find a spot.

label: Statements
body: conditionals (must, if): world literature → received and interpreted within your and other national traditions. A work counts as interpreted within a national tradition if it is used as: 1. positive model for development of own tradition, or 2. negative case of bad thing to be avoided in national tradition, or 3. image of radical otherness prompting refinement of tradition.

label: Goal
body: Look for an answer reacting to how ludicrously strong the conclusion is (X influences Y throughout all societies) based on the fact that the evidence considered is an incredibly narrow swath of the human condition (some college students' self-reporting and some personal ads in newspapers).

label: Conclusion (this demonstrates that)
body: The mayor is not an introspective person.

label: (Additional Conclusion?)
body: The new mayor is undeniably bold.

label: Evaluate
body: Yikes, that last monstrosity definitely shouldn't be physically diagrammed on paper. Let's focus on Overlapping Concepts between the first and second sentence. The one thing in both sentences is "interpreted w/in a national tradition". Being considered world literature requires that you're interpreted in your nation's tradition as well as that of others. And there are 3 things that guarantee you'd be interpreted within a national tradition. Are they the only 3 things that get you interpreted within a national tradition? No, not necessarily. But it's heavily insinuated that they are the only 3 things. So it's pretty supportable for us to say that "World literature will usually be at least one of those 3 things".

label: Goal
body: Look for something connecting world literature to those 3 ways of being interpreted as a national tradition. But stay flexible. Ultimately we just want the most provable answer.

label: Conclusion
body: There must be more sociology majors than psychology majors enrolled in Intro to Social Psychology.

label: Evidence
body: Most sociology majors are taking it. Most PSY majors are not taking it.

label: Evaluate
body: Because this argument has conditional/quantified terms, we could potentially get it right without understanding the flaw, as long as we convert it into a symbolic recipe. Most A's are in place X. Most B's are not in place X. Thus, there are more A's than B's in place X. The flaw revolves around the fact that we're making two Most claims, but they're about different groups. You can't really compare such claims without knowing about the relative size of those different groups. For example, let's say at Morris University that there 100 sociology majors and 1000 psychology majors. Most sociology majors are in this class, so at least 51 sociology majors are there. Most psychology majors are not in this class, so at most 499 psychology majors are there. Have I convinced you that this class has more sociology majors than psychology majors? Of course not. There might be way more psychology majors present, if the group of all psychology majors is bigger than the group of all sociology majors.

label: Goal
body: Look for two Most premises, and a conclusion saying one number is bigger than another. Look for something resembling this recipe: Most A's are in place X. Most B's are not in place X. Thus, more A's than B's in place X. Or look for an argument similarly vulnerable to the objection of, "What if one of those groups is much bigger than the other?"

label: Conclusion
body: The film studio will make its money back despite high production costs.

label: Evidence
body: A significant portion of the film's budget is dedicated to developing special effects technology, which can be utilized in future films, reducing the risk of financial loss.

label: Evaluate
body: The author seems to be saying, "Yes the studio is spending on lot on this film, but since part of that money will go towards inventing special FX technology that could be used in other films, they'll still recover their costs." So the author is envisioning that these FX we invent for this film save us money later (the studio pays less than they would to make a future film) or make us money later (some other studio pays us to use our FX technology).

label: Goal
body: Identify an answer choice that raises doubts about the studio's ability to make its money back by exploiting the special effects technology, either by questioning the future utility or marketability of this FX technology.

label: Given that...
body: After a major toll highway introduced a system of electronic toll paying, delays at all of its interchanges declined significantly. Travel time per car trip decreased by an average of 10 percent. Tailpipe pollution for each trip decreased commensurately.

label: How can it be that...
body: The total air pollution from vehicles on that highway did not decrease measurably.

label: Evaluate
body: If we look at all of the changes which occurred after the electronic toll system was introduced, it seems like they would cause the total air pollution to decrease. Why didn't that happen? We know that travel time and tailpipe pollution decreased for each trip. But what if there were significantly more trips? That could result in the total amount of pollution remaining the same.

label: Goal
body: A correct answer might suggest that a greater number of trips were made after the electronic toll system was introduced. Beware of answers which simply reinforce the idea that there was less pollution per trip without explaining why there was no measurable decrease in total air pollution.

label: Evidence
body: Neighborhoods in which people routinely lock their doors have higher burglary rates than neighborhoods in which people do not routinely lock their doors.

label: Conclusion
body: A lack of trust in one's neighbors leads to their lack of respect for the law.

label: Evaluate
body: Based on the second sentence, we know that the third sentence is evidence supporting the claim made in the first sentence. This argument contains a commonly-seen Causal Flaw. It attempts to use a mere correlation to support for a much stronger claim of causation. While the evidence suggests a correlation between locking doors and higher burglary rates, it does not necessarily support the conclusion that a lack of trust in one's neighbors leads to a lack of respect for the law. There could be other factors at play that contribute to higher burglary rates in neighborhoods where people routinely lock their doors. For example, these neighborhoods may be more affluent and have more valuable possessions that make them attractive targets for burglars, regardless of whether or not doors are locked. The argument also assumes that people are locking their doors because they distrust their neighbors, and it assumes that the neighbors are the ones committing the burglaries. It's possible that neither of these things are true.

label: Goal
body: Expect the correct answer to describe a Causal Flaw. If the LSAT wants to be tricky, a correct answer might focus on the difference between people locking their doors and distrusting their neighbors, or the fact that the burglaries might not be the result of the neighbors' lack of respect for the law. Beware of answers which describe other famous flaws which do not actually appear in this argument.

label: Given that...
body: In recent decades, government efforts to fight counterfeiting have been extremely successful, especially efforts to remove counterfeit bills from circulation.

label: How can it be that...
body: Counterfeiters are not finding it at all difficult to get away with passing counterfeit bills to merchants and even banks.

label: Evaluate
body: There seems to be a discrepancy here because it's natural to make an assumption about the government efforts to fight counterfeiting. It's natural to assume that these efforts might involve arresting counterfeiters or otherwise making it harder for them to pass off counterfeit bills. This is a common feature of Paradox questions: there appears to be a paradox because the situation that's described would normally lead us to make certain assumptions. But the first sentence contains a clue which indicates that this assumption might not be accurate: we're told that efforts to "remove counterfeit bills from circulation" have been particularly effective. These efforts seem focused on the bills themselves, not the counterfeiters. How else might the government remove counterfeit bills from circulation if they're not going after the counterfeiters themselves, or preventing counterfeiters from passing counterfeit bills to merchants and banks?

label: Goal
body: A correct answer might explain that the government's efforts are focused on removing counterfeit bills from circulation at some point after the counterfeiters pass them off. Beware of answers that seem related to this situation but don't actually explain the apparent discrepancy.

label: Conclusion (thus)
body:
Scientists can rule out the possibility of finding a civilization as technologically advanced as us that's within 50 light years of distance.
  rephrase: We will not find alien life as sophisticated as us that's within 50 light years.

label: Evidence
body: If such life existed (as advanced as us + within 50 light years), that civilization would have already found evidence of us and could have easily contacted us.

label: Evaluate
body:
The author is trying to make an argument by contrapositive. She's refuting a claim by showing that one of its implications doesn't hold.
```
If X were really true, then Y would be true.
Since Y isn't true,
we can rule out the possibility of X being true.
```
  In this argument, that felt like this:
```
If there were really close/smart aliens, then they would have found evidence of us and could easily contact us.
Since (they haven't found evidence of us / they can't easily contact us)
we can rule out the possibility that there are close/smart aliens.
```
  Thus, the author is missing, or assuming, that second premise, where you factually trigger the contrapositive. If I just say, "If X were true, then Y would be true. So we can rule out the possibility that X is true", then I"m assuming that "Y is not true". This author is assuming that there aren't close/smart aliens who have found evidence of us and could contact us. More conversationally, this argument is saying, "If there were really aliens out there, they would be able to contact us, so we would have heard from them by now." If we accept that "earthlings have not been contacted by aliens yet", does that really prove that there aren't aliens out there with the technology/proximity to contact us? No, we could always argue that there are aliens who are advanced enough and close enough to notice us and be aware of us, but they might choose not to contact us. After all, if they look around at the current state of humanity, they would see a lot of combative imperialism and an inability to take care of the local ecology. Who wants a new friend like that?

label: Goal
body: Look for something like "we haven't been contacted by aliens yet / there aren't aliens who have found evidence of us / they don't currently have the means to contact us but choose not to".

label: Given that...
body: Many traffic lights and street markings were temporarily removed from a heavily traveled street in a major metropolitan area. This street experiences significant volumes of automobile traffic. The number of accidents on the street was expected to increase. The street experienced no reduction in traffic.

label: How can it be that...
body: The number of accidents was greatly reduced.

label: Evaluate
body: Like many Paradox questions, this involves a comparison. After the traffic lights and street markings were removed, the number of accidents was expected to increase compared to when the traffic lights and street markings were present. There's also an element of causation implied here: it's natural to think that a lack of traffic lights and street markings would cause more accidents to occur. There must be some other factor involved which had an even greater impact on the number of accidents, causing them to be greatly reduced. What typically leads to a reduction in the number of accidents on a street? And how might the removal of traffic lights and street signs cause that accident-reducing situation to occur?

label: Goal
body: Expect an answer to describe something that could easily lead to a reduction in the number of accidents, particularly something that might result from the removal of traffic lights and signage. Beware of answers which do the opposite of what we want, describing a situation that could lead to even more accidents.

label: Conclusion
body: Body size influences mating decisions throughout all societies.

label: Evidence (argument rests on)
body: Just look at the self-reports of college-age students, and look at personal advertisements in newspapers for dating partners.

label: Evaluate
body: This argument is presented in a really weird style. We're being told what some people have concluded, and we're being told what sort of evidence they consulted, but there isn't actually any evidentiary claim presented. Like, what were the self-reports of college age students? When they analyzed personal ads for romantic partners, what did they find? We don't get any supporting premises; we only hear where the author got his premise, and so we're apparently supposed to find Flaw with that itself. It's sort of like if we heard, "Some have argued that what kids want most for Christmas is a hula hoop. Their argument rests largely on asking people in nursing homes what they thought would be a kid's #1 Christmas wish." We're supposed to react to the Evidence and say that the flaw is that "you're evidence is looking at a totally inappropriate source". Why would you ask old people what kids want for Christmas? They're going to tell you what a kid in the 1950's wanted for Christmas, not what a modern kid wants. So similarly, if you're trying to figure out whether body size influences mating decisions throughout all societies, then why should we criticize you for asking college students what influences their mating decisions, or for analyzing dating ads in the paper to see what's motivating their dating decisions? Well, it's an incredibly shallow source of evidence, double entendré intended. It's shallow as in way too small a sample. It's bad to extrapolate from what is true among college students and personal ads to what is true "throughout all societies". It's also shallow as in not representative of all mating behavior. College students and people placing hook-up ads in the paper might be more focused on looks, whereas if you looked in more "wholesome" places you'd find people whose partner's body size did not play a meaningful role in their mating decision.

label: Evaluate
body: It's confusing what role to assign to the first sentence. It is an opinion from the author, and it seems to be supported by the second sentence. So it would be fair to call it a conclusion. But it's not really an intermediate conclusion, because it isn't being used to support the conclusion in the final claim. The final claim has Conclusion Indicator wording (this evidence demonstrates this conclusion), so we know we should treat it as a conclusion. Its support is also the 2nd sentence. By contrast, that first claim about "boldness" is undeniable. Sometimes an LSAT author uses a phrase like, "As everybody already knows / As we can all see / It's a given that" and that's sort of supposed to signal to us that the author doesn't feel a need to support this. He thinks it's already something the audience accepts. "The fact that the mayor's assertions are made with utter certainty and confidence demonstrates that the mayor is not an introspective person". The argument is concluding something about whether or not the mayor is "introspective", but the evidence never talks about introspectiveness (the qualify of looking inward and reflecting on your thoughts and actions). All we hear is that the mayor is bold and makes assertions with utter certainty and confidence (the author must be thinking that this lack of self-doubt indicates a lack of self-reflection).

label: Goal
body: Since there is a New Concept in the Conclusion (introspective), we can be 90% or better confident that the correct answer will link "introspective" to the "making assertions with utter certainty and confidence".

label: Conclusion (more likely = opinion)
body: It's more likely that these small humanoid skeletons represent a species of humans that became smaller over time due to environmental pressure (than it is that they are the remains of a human who had a growth disorder).

label: Evidence (X and Y)
body: The skeletons don't fit the pattern of known growth disorders. And there's evidence that on this island that fox and mouse species were also smaller than normal (suggest that there were environmental pressures rewarding smaller bodies).

label: Evaluate
body:
Before we read the argument for any Main Conclusion or Role question, we remind ourselves of the two main styles where they "hide" the conclusion on these questions:
  - First Claim
  - Rebuttal / Pivot
  Here we have an example of the 2nd style. The first claim isn't our author's opinion. In fact, it's an attribution to some other point of view (some scientists believe). That would make us expect some sort of pivot into a rebuttal. The 2nd sentence doesn't use any pivot language, but it is the author rebutting the position in the first sentence. To clinch that this is indeed the conclusion, we need to feel that the author goes on to support the idea that these skeletons are "small species rather than growth disorder". The last two claims are, "doesn't seem like growth disorder, and here's more evidence for small species".

label: Goal
body: Once we've correctly found the conclusion, we've done the hard part. Now we just have to go find an answer that matches the meaning of the 2nd sentence.

label: Conclusion (therefore)
body: The more of Earth's surface is covered with snow and ice, the cooler the global temp is likely to become.

label: Evidence
body: The more sunlight our planet reflects back into space, the cooler the global atmosphere tends to get. Snow and ice reflect more sunlight than ocean or exposed land surfaces do.

label: Evaluate
body: The conclusion is positing a causal idea, the more the surface is covered with snow and ice, the cooler the globe will be, because when the surface is covered with snow and ice it reflects more light back into space, which cools the globe. It seems like a reasonable argument with no glaring flaws. Let's try to debate it. The conclusion is a comparison between our Current World and a world with more of the surface covered by snow/ice. We know one thing that would be different in that world (more sunlight reflected into space). That thing could cool the globe. But what else would be different? Maybe there are other geological processes that affect global temperature, and maybe in a world where more of the surface was covered by snow/ice, those geological processes would be changed in a way that would warm the globe.

label: Goal
body: Since the possible vulnerability of this argument would be "some other change in a more snow-ice-covered world that would have a warming effect", the correct answer might rule out that sort of change. Or maybe it will just give us more reason to believe that in a snowy / icy world, the global temp is cooler.

label: Given Nick's Claims
body:
1. The Pincus family and their construction company have supported our university financially for decades.
  2. The university should not give the contract for building its new library to the family's main competitor.
  3. Doing so would be disloyal to a friend of the university.

label: Evaluate Pedro's Responses
body:
1. no comment
  2. Disagrees
  3. Disagrees (potentially)
  Nick states that the university should not give a building contract to the Pincus family's main competitor. Pedro states that the contract should be awarded to "whatever company makes the most competitive bid." This is their clearest point of disagreement. Neither of them has stated that the Pincus family's competitor made the most competitive bid, but if that ends up being the case then Pedro would give them the contract while Nick would not. Nick says that giving the contract to the Pincus family's competitor "would be disloyal to a friend of the university," while Pedro says that the university is not obliged to give a donor any special privileges. This seems to be a point of disagreement, but there's also some room to argue that Pedro isn't actually disagreeing. Pedro might be saying, "sure, I agree, that could be viewed as disloyal. But we don't owe our donors any loyalty when we're awarding construction contracts."

label: Goal
body: Expect the correct answer to addresses claim #2. An answer that addresses claim #3 instead isn't necessarily wrong, but we're a bit less likely to see that. Beware of answers which describe topics that neither person addressed.

label: Conclusion (Thus)
body: Newer antibiotics are likely to result in an outbreak of diseases caused by drug-resistant bacteria.

label: Evidence
body: Newer antibiotics (like ampicillin) kill a much wider variety of bacteria than penicillin does, and since they make drug companies more money, we could see a situation in which there isn't as much penicillin available and doctors have to prescribe these more powerful antibiotics even when that would otherwise be unnecessary.

label: Evidence (since)
body: Vigilance with respect to academic standards is always necessary

label: Conclusion
body: It's good that standards have become a topic of discussion.

label: Evaluate
body: The blank is prefaced by a Support Indicator, "since" (fabs = for, after all, because, since), so we know we're trying to pick an answer that would support the previous claim. Why would newer antibiotics, which kill a much wider variety of bacteria than penicillin make us more likely to have an outbreak of diseases caused by drug-resistant bacteria? (If we have real-world knowledge about the fear of over-prescribing antibiotics, then we probably understand that the concern is that when you kill off all the bacteria that antibiotics CAN kill, you leave only the bacteria that antibiotics CAN'T kill to survive / thrive / replicate. Soon the dominant strains of bacteria are the ones that resist our drugs.)

label: Goal
body: If we don't already have that anticipated sense of where this is heading, then we just need to look for an idea that connects "newer antibiotics / killing a much wider variety of bacteria" to the emergence of "drug-resistant bacteria".

label: Conclusion (should)
body:
Weingarten's claim should be rejected.
  rephrase: Keeping animals in zoos is not unethical.

label: Evidence
body: Weingarten thinks that zoos involve placing animals in unnatural environments merely for the sake of human amusement. But he sees nothing wrong with owning pets, which involves placing an animal in an unnatural environment merely for human amusement.

label: Evaluate
body:
When we're doing Flaw and we see the argument has a Rebuttal structure, then a few famous flaws should pop on our radar:
  - Ad Hominem (dismissing someone's claim because they are biased or have conflicting behavior)
  - Unproven vs. Proven False (concluding the opposite of someone's claim, just because they failed to prove the claim)
  - Straw Man / Irrelevant Response (misrepresenting the original position or saying something irrelevant to it in the rebuttal)
  This author points out Weingarten's potentially hypocritical premise and therefore concludes that his original claim should be rejected. Did the author offer any positive evidence that "keeping animals in zoos is ethical"? Nope. She just argues, "Since Weingarten's rationale for hating on zoos seems to conflict one of his other beliefs, that must mean that zoos are ethically fine?"

label: Goal
body: It seems like this is a case of Unproven vs. Proven False or Ad Hominem. Maybe Weingarten's argument for zoos being unethical is weak (since he seems inconsistent in terms of objecting to placing animals in unnatural environments for human amusement). But that doesn't mean we've proven that zoos aren't unethical. Maybe there are better arguments to be made for that claim. We could also say, "even if Weingarten is being a bit hypocritical in opposing zoos while accepting pets, who's to say the first belief is wrong and the second is correct? Maybe he's wrong to accept pets. Maybe having pets is also unethical." We could also chip away at the legitimacy of the comparison: "Yes, zoos and pets are both cases in which animals live in unnatural environments for the sake of human amusement. But they're importantly different, because X." Since there are multiple attack strategies, we'll have to stay flexible as we judge these answers.

label: Activist's Conclusion
body: President Z should resign.

label: Activist's Evidence
body: She's unable to govern effectively given the widespread belief that she rigged the election.

label: President Z's Conclusion
body: I must remain in office.

label: President Z's Evidence
body: Given that scandals have forced two presidents to resign over the last decade, if I were to also resign, the rest of the world would see us as a country whose political system is hopelessly unstable.

label: Evaluate
body: How could the activist respond to President Z's premise? Given President Z's concern with what effects her resignation could have on how the world sees this country, how can the activist argue that President Z should still resign? Can he say, "So what if the world sees us as politically unstable. We are. That's the truth. It's okay for the world to see the truth"? He could probably also say, "The world already sees us as politically unstable, given that there's a widespread belief that you rigged the election. So we shouldn't refrain from doing what's right out of concern that we'll start to look politically unhinged. We've already achieved that status. We could probably upgrade the world's impression of our political system if they saw that you, a seemingly illegitimate president, were no longer at the helm."

label: Goal
body: Look for something that addresses Person 2's objection, from the point of view of Person 1. In other words, if we're someone who thinks that President Z should resign, then how can we respond to her notion that "resigning would lead to the world having an unacceptably low opinion of our political system"?

label: Conclusion
body:
It's ridiculous to say that "successful people in business have without exception benefited from a lot of luck on their way to success".
  rephrase: Some people who are successful in business did not benefit from luck on their way to success.

label: Evidence
body: Success requires a lot of hard work.

label: Evaluate
body:
Whenever we're doing Flaw and see that the argument has a Rebuttal structure, we want to be sensitive to a few common flaws relating to Rebuttals
  1. Ad Hominem (dismisses a view by saying the source has a biased interest or a conflicting past)
  2. Unproven vs. Proven True (shows that someone failed to prove X but then erroneously concludes from that that X is false)
  3. Straw Man / Irrelevant Response (the rebuttal doesn't seem to have anything to do with falsifying the original position)
  This feels like #3. Why is the author thinking that it's relevant to object by saying, "Success requires a lot of hard work"? Was the popular book saying that "success doesn't require a lot of hard work"? Not as far as we've heard. So in that sense, this author is responding to a position that his opponent doesn't hold (Straw Man) or is rebutting with something irrelevant. When we're doing Flaw and we see conditional logic wording, we know to look out for the #1 famous Necessary vs. Sufficient flaw, in which the author presents a conditional logic relationship and then interprets it in some illegal reversed or negated fashion. We have a couple conditional logic indicator words here: without exception / requires
  The book says:
  successful in business → benefited from luck
  The author's rebuttal is saying:
  successful in business → lots of hard work
  Those don't conflict, of course. Success in business may require luck AND require lots of hard work.

label: Goal
body: The book was saying, "all successful people have had luck". It suggests that maybe "success requires a lot of luck". But the author is taking this to mean that "success doesn't require anything else". Let's find an answer that speaks to that confusion.

label: Evaluate
body:
When evaluating arguments in LR, we can often pretty much ignore any Opposing Idea that's presented. With question types like Assumption questions, Flaw, Strengthen, and Weaken, once we've identified the evidence and the conclusion we usually focus our attention there. In this question, we need to understand the principle that's illustrated by the argument. The correct answer choice will illustrate the same principle. In this case it helps to keep a more big-picture view, and notice exactly how the evidence and conclusion relate to the opposing idea. Here's how we might describe the argument as a whole:
  "People blamed a situation on X, even though that wasn't the cause. But X is important, so it's good that X is being discussed."
  If we think about the principle being illustrated, we might describe it this way:
  "If something is important then it's good to talk about it, even if if the discussion came up for the wrong reasons."
  A core feature of this principle is the conclusion that it's good for this discussion to happen.

label: Goal
body: We'll look for an answer which matches this same overall pattern. Beware of answers that describe a different type of background scenario / opposing idea, or ones which draw a very different type of conclusion.

label: Conclusion
body: Installing the new street signs is a colossal waste of time and money.
