label: Evidence (since)
body: No one is complaining about the current signs.

label: Evaluate
body: We basically treat Evaluate questions like Weaken questions. We try to think of possible objections and then we look for an answer choice that's asking a question that we could answer in a way that would be a potential objection. Given that ... no one is complaining about the current signs, How could we argue that ... replacing our current street signs with these more readable signs, over the next ten years, is not a colossal waste of time and money? Just because no one is complaining about the signs doesn't mean that the new signs wouldn't be perceived as a huge improvement / upgrade. (I wasn't complaining about our old tea kettle, but when my wife bought me a new one that's better for pour-over coffee, I definitely didn't think it was a waste of money.) The wording of the conclusion is so dramatic, "colossal waste of time and money", that we could also weaken it by speaking to how minimal the outlay of time / money it is. Maybe these street signs were donated by the local sign factory, and the city didn't have to pay for them at all. Maybe the new street signs also have solar panels and can save the city some money on its energy bills.

label: Goal
body: Look for an answer choice posing a question that could be answered in a way that could weaken. Think: which of these can be answered in a way that would allow me to argue that installing these new street signs isn't a colossal waste of time and money?

label: Conclusion (Therefore)
body: Most of the scientists surveyed reject the Minsk Hypothesis (MH).

label: Evidence
body: Most of the scientists surveyed accept Wang's Law (WL), and most of the scientists surveyed know the results of the Brown-Eisler Experiment (BEE). But if you combine BEE with WL, it contradicts MH.

label: Evaluate
body: This seems like a pretty reasonable argument, so I would switch into Find an Objection mode, because I don't see any gap at first: If you accept X and you know Y, and you know that X + Y means that Z is wrong, then don't you believe that Z is wrong? Given that these scientists accept Wang's, and they know the results of B-E, and that Wang's and B-E would collectively contradict Minsk, How could we argue that these scientists do not reject Minsk? There is a language switch from "most of them accept Wang's" to "most of them know the results of B-E". Did we switch verbs because these scientists don't necessarily accept the B-E results? I guess scientists could be aware of results, they could know what B-E reports to have found, without accepting that those results are valid. And then the other wiggle room is that this argument never established that these scientists know that Wang + B-E contradicts Minsk. We can say that "Lois Lane accepts that Superman killed Lex Luther, and she knows that she works next to Clark Kent". Furthermore, "Clark Kent is really Superman!" Does that prove that "Lois Lane knows that she works next to the man who killed Lex Luther?" Nope. We know Lois works next to Lex Luther's killer, but we can't assume that she knows that because we don't know whether Lois knows that Clark Kent is Superman.

label: Goal
body:
We spotted two weak points
  - we need to establish that the scientists accept the results of the B-E experiment (not just that they've heard about the results), and
  - we need to establish that the scientists are aware that combining the B-E results with Wang's Law would contradict Minsk.

label: Conclusion (Thus)
body: Even the most skillful translation will be at best a flawed approximation of the original work.

label: Evidence
body: Every translation is a compromise between two goals that can't be entirely reconciled: you can't be entirely faithful to the meaning of the text while being entirely faithful to the author's style.

label: Evaluate / Goal
body:
On Principle-Strengthen questions, we're generally just looking for a Linking idea that gets us from Evidence to Conclusion. So here that would be something like,
```
If a translation is either not at best a
totally faithful to meaning → flawed
or not totally faithful to style approx.
```

label: Statements
body:
```
causal (encourage)
TV, phones, and ⇢ imprecise, uncritical
other electronic media thinking
conditional (the only = sufficient indicator)
Adequate protection → Critical thinking
against demagogues (requires)
potential conditional (demagogues = universal)
try to exploit people by
Demagogues → presenting emotionally loaded
language as an objective
description of reality
```

label: Evaluate
body:
The correct answer to Must Be False is almost always contradicting a conditional that was provided or contradicting some inference we can make by combining claims. Were there any conditionals provided? Sure, the 2nd and 3rd claims could be thought of as conditionals. Contradicting a conditional means that "the Trigger happens but the Outcome doesn't". So possible answers could be:
  - sometimes you protect against a demagogue, even though you don't have critical thinking
  - sometimes someone is a demagogue, even though they don't used charged language to exploit people
  Are there any available inferences that can be made by combining claims? Sure, the 1st and 2nd claims have an overlapping term, "critical thinking". Electronic media encourages uncritical thinking, and uncritical thinking leaves you vulnerable to demagogues. So there's a causal link between electronic media and susceptibility to demagogues. We could contradict that by saying:
  - the more society X got immersed in electronic media, the more protected they became against demagogues

label: Evidence
body: People with higher than average levels of homocysteine are twice as likely to be diagnosed with Alzheimer's. B vitamins and folic acid convert homocysteine into substances known to have no relation to Alzheimers' disease.

label: Evaluate
body:
Since the evidence is dealing with a correlation (ppl who have trait A are twice as likely to have trait B), while the conclusion includes a causal verb (including large amounts of folic and B vitamins will reduce your risk), we can use our Explain Curious Fact mindset. Curious Fact ... how come people with high homocysteine are twice as likely to have Alzheimer's? Author's Explanation ... the high homocysteine is causing the Alzheimer's. How do we know that the author is thinking that the high homocysteine is causing the Alzheimers? Because the author is saying that by eating more folic acid / B vitamins, you'll break down (i.e. lower) your homocysteine, which will reduce your risk of Alzheimer's. Our job with Explain Curious Fact arguments is to ask these two questions:
  1. What could be an Alternate Explanation for the curious fact?
  2. How plausible is the author's explanation?
  Typically, when there's a correlation between X and Y and then the author assumes that X causes Y, we need to consider alternate explanations like Reverse Causality (Y causes X) or 3rd Factor (Z causes both X and Y). So here alternate explanations could be that having Alzheimer's actually causes your homocysteine to go up, or that some underlying factor (maybe a genetic marker) causes someone to have higher than average homocysteine as well as elevated risk of Alzheimer's.

label: Goal
body: Let's look for an answer that suggests an Alternate Explanation (e.g., the high homocysteine was caused by Alzheimer's), or an answer that otherwise hurts the plausibility that having more folic acid and B vitamins in our system would lead to lower homocysteine which would lead to lower risk of Alzheimer's.

label: Conclusion (implied)
body: This argument claiming that price gouging is efficient fails.

label: Intermediate Conclusion (as a result)
body: Price gouging will not, as they have argued, end up allocating goods to the people with the most need for those goods.

label: Intermediate Conclusion
body: A person's willingness to pay for a pricey item is not proportional to their need for that item.

label: Premise
body: In the real world, no matter how much you need something, you just might not be able to pay as much as others can.

label: Evaluate
body:
Whenever we read Role or Main Conclusion, we prime our brains for arguments that put the conclusion in the very first sentence, or arguments that start with another point of view and then pivot into the author's rebuttal. This was the latter style. When authors rebut some initial position, the conclusion can sometimes be implied. We want to feel these arguments having this sort of chronological structure (usually):
  1. Some people say X
  2. But I, the author, am concluding maybe not X
  3. Here's why (here's my evidence)
  There might be intermediate conclusions within #3, but we don't want to lose sight of the fact that these intermediate conclusions are still serving the purpose of supporting #2, which is the author's rebuttal to #1. Here, we're being asked about "willingness to pay is not proportional to need". This is part of how the author rebuts the economists, so we can say it plays the role of Supporting his rebuttal. But we can also call this claim a Conclusion, because it's supported by the second to last sentence in the paragraph.

label: Goal
body: Look for something saying this claim is part of how the author rebuts the economists, or something saying that this claim is a conclusion supported by the fact that "in the real world, some people just can't pay as much as others".

label: Conclusion (Thus)
body: The prehistoric European cave bears were not exclusively herbivores.

label: Evidence
body: Animals that are not exclusively herbivores (they eat meat) have higher concentrations of heavy nitrogen in their bodily tissues than do animals that are exclusively herbivores. The level of heavy nitrogen in the bones of these prehistoric European cave bears was identical to the levels of heavy nitrogen present in the blood of present-day bears who eat meat.

label: Evaluate
body: The author is interpreting the significance of nitrogen levels in these prehistoric cave bears' bones, so we can use our Explain Curious Fact mindset. Curious Fact ... why does the level of nitrogen in prehistoric cave bears' bone samples match the level of nitrogen in modern meat-eating bears' blood samples? Author's Explanation ... because they were both meat eaters, and eating meat gives you higher concentrations of nitrogen.

label: Goal
body:
Because this is Strengthen, a correct answer could,
  1. rule out an Alternate Explanation for why their nitrogen levels match. maybe these prehistoric European cave bears were strictly herbivores, but there's some other reason why they have as much nitrogen in their bones as modern meat-eating bears have in their blood. an answer that rules-out such a thing makes the author's hypothesis more likely.
  2. increase the plausibility of the Author's Explanation. does any answer give us more reason to think that these prehistoric European cave bears ate meat?

label: Conclusion
body: They are mistaken. (i.e. you would need more than just a computer program that encapsulates the information contained in the human genome to make artificial intelligence)

label: Evidence
body: The operation of the human brain is governed by the interactions of proteins whose structures are encoded in the human genome.

label: Evaluate
body:
The conclusion is about "artificial intelligence" but the evidence doesn't mention this concept at all. That's a big warning that we must be assuming something about artificial intelligence. The author is arguing that having the information contained in the human genome wouldn't be enough to make AI, and the author's big objection to that is that the human brain is governed by "the interactions of proteins". I'm confused by what the author sees as the problem, but I think she's thinking, "even though these crucial proteins' structures are encoded in the human genome, if we had a computer program that had all the information in the human genome, it still wouldn't be able to actually mimic these protein structures, and thus the computer program wouldn't be able to achieve artificial intelligence." Two objections come to mind:
  - who said that the computer program wouldn't be able to model those protein structures somehow?
  - who said that the computer program needs to model those protein structures in order to achieve artificial intelligence?

label: Goal
body: It's hard to predict what the correct answer will do (since they "stole" our best inference), so let's just look for anything we can prove.

label: Goal
body:
If we were as lost as I felt on the first couple reads of this argument, we might at least be able to tell ourselves to look for an answer connecting "artificial intelligence" to these "interactions of proteins". If we're a little more dialed in, we're probably looking for something like
  - computer could not replicate the interactions of proteins
  or
  - computer needs to replicate the interactions of proteins in order to achieve artificial intelligence

label: Information
body: Some advertisers offer consumers a home computer free of charge. (Why?) The computer plays ads while the user is on it, and the computer collects information about the user's browsing patterns and passes that on to advertisers who can then send more targeted ads.

label: causal (because of / result)
body: The advertisers can afford to offer the computers for free because of the increased sales that result from this precise ad-targeting.

label: Evaluate
body:
Whenever we're reading Inference paragraphs, we know our goal is to find any facts that can be combined or synthesized. Specifically, we're looking out for Conditional, Causal, Math-y, or Pivot wording. This paragraph didn't have any of that type of language until the final sentence, which is both Causal and Math-y. In fact, since there are two causal phrases in that last sentence, we could even concoct a little Causal Chain.
```
computer advertisers increased can afford
collects ⇢ receive & ⇢ sales from ⇢ to offer the
browsing send back these users computer
patterns targeted ads for free
```
  Mathematically, we can say that increase in sales is enough to at least offset the cost of providing one of these computers to a consumer.

label: Goal
body: It's hard to predict what the answer will say. We want to look for a safely worded idea that feels derivable from what we read, and most likely it will reflect some aspect of that causal chain we sketched out.

label: Conclusion (so)
body: Speakers who resort to obscenity do not impress their audiences.

label: Evidence
body: Some eloquent speakers impress their audiences. Speakers who resort to obscenity are not eloquent.

label: Evaluate
body:
Since we have repeating symbols (two instances each of "obscenity" / "eloquent" / "impress audiences"), this argument would lend itself to symbolic algebra.
```
P1: Some eloquent speakers impress their audiences.
Some A's are B
P2: Obscene speakers are not eloquent.
C's are not A.
C: Obscene speakers don't impress their audiences.
C's are not B.
```
  We can tell this argument is flawed because it's trying to prove that some people are "not going to impress their audiences", but the argument never provided any way to prove that someone isn't going to impress their audience (it didn't even provide a way to prove that someone is going to impress their audience, but at least it talked about people impressing their audience).

label: Goal
body:
Ultimately, though, if we are able to see the symbolic recipe, we don't really need to possess a conversational understanding of the flaw. Let's just find a similar structure:
```
P1: Some A's are B
P2: C's are not A
C: thus, C's are not B
```

label: Conclusion (therefore)
body: It is wrong for any country to adopt trade policies that are likely to seriously hinder growth in the prosperity of any other country.

label: Evidence
body: Increasing economic prosperity in a country tends to bring political freedom to its inhabitants.

label: Evaluate
body: The overlapping ingredient between the evidence and conclusion is the concept of "prosperity", so we should focus on the link between the language connected to prosperity. From the evidence what we know about prosperity is, "tends to bring political freedom to inhabitants". What we're trying to prove about prosperity is, "shouldn't adopt a trade policy that hinders it".

label: Goal
body:
Let's look for something like "a country shouldn't adopt a policy that would hinder [something that brings political freedom to that country's inhabitants]. If it's more conditional, then we want a Premise to Conclusion move like,
```
If X brings political no country's
freedom to a → trade policy should
country's inhabitants hinder X
```

label: Conclusion (thus)
body: Great works of art are necessarily rare.

label: Evidence
body: No work of art can be great unless both high level of skill and high degree of creativity is combined in its execution. When those two things are combined in the creation of an artwork, the result is great art.

label: Evaluate
body: The New Concept in the Conclusion is the idea that great art is rare. We know what it takes to make great art, so the author must just be assuming that these crucial ingredients are rarely combined.

label: Goal
body: Let's look for something like, "it's rare for an artist who has high skill level and high creativity level to combine both of those in the creation of an artwork".

label: Conclusion
body: By eating Fantastic Flakes every morning, you too will be on the most effective path to physical fitness.

label: Evidence
body:
Regular exercise is the most effective way to become physically fit, and studies show that there's a correlation:
```
adults who eat | | exercise
cereal every day more regularly
```

label: Evaluate
body:
Whenever we see correlations on Flaw, we should be suspicious of the famous Causal flaw.
```
correlation language
X is correlated with Y
X is associated with Y
most X's are Y
X's tend to be Y
... and most commonly,
people who are X are more likely to be Y
```
  When you're told that people who are [cereal eaters] are more likely to be [regular exercisers], you know the author is going to overconfidently conclude that one of those causes the other. In the conclusion, they are assuming that [eating cereal] is having a causal influence on [exercising regularly], because they're selling the idea of cereal as a path to fitness (by way of exercise). Whenever we're presented with a correlation
```
X || Y
```
  and the author concludes X --causes--> Y, consider these two alternate explanations:
  1. Y --causes--> X
  2. Some other factor, Z is really causing X and Y

label: Goal
body: On Flaw, we can just call out the illegal move that the author made from Correlation to Causation. We can raise the possibility of Reverse Causality (#1) or Third Factor (#2). In this case, we also have incredibly loaded language in the Conclusion: the most effective path. We can certainly complain about the fact that the argument in no way justifies that it is better that all alternative paths.

label: Conclusion (hence)
body: Austronesia-speaking people originated in Taiwan and later migrated to other islands.

label: Evidence
body: All subfamilies of Austronesian originated in the same language, which would have been in a single geographic location. 3 of the 4 subfamilies are found only in Taiwan, whereas the fourth is found on islands stretching from Madagascar to the eastern Pacific.

label: Evaluate
body: On Main Conclusion questions, the conclusion is almost always earlier than the evidence, but not this time. The last sentence offers four consecutive claims, and the keywords go like this ... Since claim 1, which means claim 2, these facts suggest that claim 3 and hence, that claim 4. So we can see that 1 -> 2 -> 3 -> 4. The first sentence is a fact, not an opinion, so it couldn't be the Main Conclusion.

label: Goal
body: Let's look for a rephrasing of the final claim, "Austronesian-speaking peoples originated in Taiwan and later migrated to other islands".

label: West's Conclusion
body: Haynes is the worst of our three quality control inspectors.

label: West's Evidence
body: Half of the appliances that were returned to us last year for being defective were inspected by Haynes.

label: Young's Response
body: Yeah, but Haynes does way more than half of the appliances.

label: Evaluate
body: This is a response that's talking about proportionality. All other things being equal, if all three quality control inspectors were equally good at their jobs, then they would each be responsible for 33.3% of the items returned because of defects. They would always be tied in terms of, "which inspector had the most of their items returned for defects". However, let's say they are equally good, but Haynes inspects 50% of the items, Rocco does 25%, and T-Bone does 25%. If it turns out that Haynes is "the inspector who had the most of his items returned for defects", is it fair for Rocco and T-bone to tease him? No, because of course Haynes will have the most items returned. He's inspected twice as many items as those rascals, so he has way more items out there in the world, with his name on it as the quality control inspector. If Haynes inspects 50% of the items, and he's equally good as the other two, then we would expect 50% of the returned items to be from Haynes. If someone does better than their percent, it shows they're better than average. If Rocco inspects 25% of the items but is only responsible for 20% of the returned items, that means that Rocco is outperforming others.

label: Goal
body: Young responds by Introducing a New Consideration, i.e. bringing up important information that makes us see the first person's evidence in a different light. When we were assuming the work was divided 1/3, 1/3, 1/3 among the three inspectors, we would have assumed that each inspector would have inspected 1/3 of the items that got returned. Since Haynes inspected 1/2 of the items returned, he looks like he's doing worse than his fair share. But Young is saying, actually he's doing better than his fair share. He inspects like more than 65% of these items, and he's only responsible for 50% of the returned items.

label: Conclusion/Hypothesis
body: The emotion parents feel while singing to their infants noticeably affects the sound of the singing.

label: Evidence
body: They made recordings of parents singing with / without their infants being present, and then they had psychologists try to guess from just the sound of the recording whether or not infants were present. 80% of the time, the psychologists were able to guess right.

label: Evaluate
body: Since researchers are interpreting the results of a study, we can use our Curious Fact / Explanation mindset. Curious Fact - how is it that psychologists were able to guess right 80% of the time? Author's Explanation - when the parents' infants are present in the room, the emotion the parents feel noticeably affects the sound of the singing. Correct answers will either deal with alternate ways to explain the Curious Fact (maybe the psychologists could hear the babies in the background, when the babies were present) or the plausibility of the Author's Explanation.

label: Goal
body:
Since this is Strengthen, our correct answer needs to either
  - rule out a different way that the psychologists were guessing right 80% of the time
  or
  - increase the plausibility of the author's story that the emotion the parents were feeling when their infants were present was noticeably affecting the sound of the singing.

label: Conclusion
body: To appreciate Shakespeare's work in Richard III, it's irrelevant whether the portrayal was inaccurate or that it was derived by people who didn't like him.

label: Evidence
body: The character in S's work is fascinating and illuminating both aesthetically and morally.

label: Evaluate
body: This argument because with an Attribution (many scholars claim) and then a pivot (But), which is a classic setup for a Rebuttal conclusion. The conclusion is essentially trying to prove that certain claims are irrelevant to appreciating a certain work. So we will definitely want an answer that has language about about whether or not something is "relevant to appreciating" a work. The author's premise is simply that the character is super interesting and illuminating. She's not worried whether the character is historically accurate; she isn't going to let that get in the way of the fact that the character is just super compelling as a character.

label: Goal
body: If we're predicting the classic "If Premise, then Conclusion" type of answer, then we want something like, "If a character is fascinating and illuminating both aesthetically and morally, then it's irrelevant to appreciation whether the portrayal is accurate."

label: Edgar's Claims
body:
1. Some of the pumps supplying water to our region were shut down to protect a small fish species.
  2. It's absurd to inconvenience thousands of people for the sake of something so inconsequential.

label: Rafaela's Responses
body:
1. No comment, but she seems to implicitly agree with this, since she's telling Edgar what she knows about this situation of shutting down the pumps to protect this fish.
  2. She doesn't directly disagree with this, because she isn't saying, "It's not absurd; it's perfectly reasonable to inconvenience thousands for something so inconsequential."

label: Main Conclusion (thus)
body: Letting the government monitor conversations on the Internet would be a setback for democracy.

label: Intermediate Conclusion (therefore)
body: The right to have private, unmonitored conversations is essential to democracy.

label: Evidence
body: Democracy requires that there are no restrictions on the ability of citizens to share their ideas freely without fear of reprisal.

label: Evaluate
body: So since the 2nd speaker isn't disagreeing with any of the explicit claims, we need to think about some of the implicit assumptions the 1st speaker was making. Edgar is assuming that "shutting down some of the pumps" is going to "inconvenience thousands of people". And he's assuming that "this species of small fish" is "something inconsequential". Rafaela seems to be disagreeing with the idea of "inconsequential", because her wording of "a very serious threat" is the best contrast we can find between her and Edgar. However, is Rafaela saying that this fish is a very consequential species, and thus worth taking drastic steps to save? Not really. It sounds like she's saying, "The water professionals are looking at this small fish and thinking, oh crap! If this fish is suffering then that means something in the water is hurting it, and whatever that thing is could potentially hurt humans too, since it could be in our water supply." So it seems like Rafaela might be disagreeing with Edgar's understanding that the pumps are being shut down in order to protect the small fish. She seems to think that the pumps are being shut down in order to investigate the potential pollutant that is threatening this fish and could one day threaten us.

label: Goal
body: Look for something like "whether the pumps are being shut down to protect the fish or to do some investigative work in the hopes of protecting humans".

label: Conclusion
body: Only physiology can analyze whether the organs of an organism are functioning healthily.

label: Evidence
body: Physics and chemistry can't do it, because they can't measure whether a human body is operating "as it should". Physics and chemistry can't analyze whether a machine is successfully working as a whole, because they don't know what it means for the machine to be operating "as it should". Only engineering has language of purpose, of what successful functioning would mean / would look like. (In other words, physics and chemistry can define the nature of things as they are, but they don't have any language to define whether things are successfully working at their purpose, only engineering or physiology can do that).

label: Evaluate
body:
Yikes. This is an all-timer in terms of hard paragraphs to read. In a boring formal sense, any time an author argues like this,
  Only Peter can do thing X. Because Joe and Reggie don't know how to do Y.
  the author would be assuming "You need to know how to do Y in order to do X". the author would also be assuming "Joe and Reggie are the only other two options." So this argument is assuming "you need to be able to ascertain operational principles of the body in order to analyze an organism in terms of its organs' roles in the body's healthy functioning". and it would be assuming "Physics and chemistry are the only other two options besides physiology when it come to potentially analyzing an organism to see if its organs are causing healthy functioning." Because of the word "Similarly", we know that the author is trying to Complete an Analogy, so we want to think about any of the parallels the author is assuming.

label: Goal
body: Look for an answer saying "you need operational principles to analyze an organism in that way", an answer saying "there are not any other options besides physiology, physics, and chemistry that we should be considering", or an answer that feels like it's supplying some idea the author assumed was parallel in both halves of the analogy.

label: Conclusion
body: The hepadnavirus is at least 25 million years old.

label: Evidence
body: Once a hep virus inserts itself into a chromosome, fragments of the virus get passed to all its descendants. A hep virus fragment is found in precisely the same location in a certain chromosome of the junco and the zebra finch, and these two species diverged about 25 million years ago.

label: Evaluate
body:
This argument is hard to understand, let alone critique. The author is assuming that the junco and the finch had a common ancestor (more than 25 million years ago, before the two species diverged), that a hep virus inserted itself into a certain spot of a certain chromosome in this common ancestor, and that this is reason why we now see the junco and the finch having a hep virus fragment in the same spot of the same chromosome. We could use a Curious Fact / Explanation mindset to get through this problem.
  Curious Fact: Why does the junco and finch both have a hep virus fragment in the exact same spot of the same chromosome?
  Author's Explanation: The junco and the finch had a common ancestor; the hep virus inserted itself into the common ancestor and since the hep virus gets passed down to all of an animal's descendants, now the junco and finch both have it.
  We affect these arguments by either
  - discussing alternative explanations for the curious fact
  - affecting the plausibility of the author's explanation
  What could be a different explanation for why the junco and the finch have a hep virus fragment in the same spot? Couldn't it be that it didn't come from some common ancestor, but rather it came from two different ancestors, each of which had the hep virus insert itself into the same spot of the same chromosome?

label: Goal
body:
This answer could come in 3 different flavors:
  - rule out an alternate explanation for how the junco / finch have hep virus in the same spot
  - increase the plausibility that they have it in the same spot because of a common ancestor
  or
  - make it more likely that the hep virus is at least 25 million years old (maybe we find it in the fossils of animals that went extinct 30 million years ago)

label: Statements
body:
The diet of Helio consists entirely of fruit from Physalis plants.
  This fruit doesn't contain linolenic acid.
  pause and infer:
  - The diet of Helio doesn't contain linolenic acid.
  For many other insects, linolenic acid is necessary to growth and maturation.
  pause and infer:
  - The diet of Helio doesn't contain something that is necessary to growth and maturation for many other insects.
  Linolenic acid in (any) insect's diet is necessary for the production of volicitin.
  pause and infer:
  - The diet of Helio means that they aren't going to produce volicitin.
  Most caterpillars have volicitin in their saliva, but Helio doesn't (which we just figured out for ourselves).

label: Evaluate
body: There were like six different claims in there. Normally, with that many claims it becomes pretty unrealistic to try to predict the answer. The first two claims had the overlapping ingredient of "fruit from Physalis". When two claims have an overlapping ingredient, we want to consider whether we can use that to synthesize the other parts, which we did by pausing and articulating to ourselves that "Helio doesn't have linolenic acid". The third claim is about other insects, so it seems more like filler and less likely to be involved in the correct answer. The fourth claim brings it back to all insects (including Helio; caterpillars are insects). Given that we smartly inferred that Helio doesn't have linolenic acid, this fourth claim has the overlapping ingredient of "linolenic acid", allowing us to infer that Helio doesn't produce volicitin. But then it feels like the sixth claim steals that inference from us.

label: Evaluate / Goal
body:
The structure of this paragraph looks like this.
  Claim 1. Therefore, Claim 2. Thus, Claim 3.
  We can see from the "therefore" that claim 2 is supported by claim 1. We can see from the buried "thus" in the last sentence that claim 3 is supported by claim 2. We're being asked about claim 1, so we should be looking for something like Premise / Support.

label: Statements
body:
One way to compare chess-playing programs is to compare how they do with fixed time limits per move.
  If you take a given chess-playing program, give it fixed time limits per move, and then watch it on two different compatible computers, the program will have a better chance of winning (the chess game it's playing) on the faster computer.

label: causal (this is simply because)
body: The faster computer wins because on that computer the program is able to examine more possible moves in the fixed time per move.

label: Evaluate
body: This paragraph is badly written, probably intentionally. The very first sentence is talking about comparing chess program A to chess program B. But the rest of the paragraph has nothing to do with that. The rest of the paragraph is talking about comparing how chess program A does on computer X vs. computer Y. The one piece of signature Inference language (Conditional / Causal / Pivot / Math-y) that sticks out is the Causal Difference-Maker of "this is because". The faster computer can examine more moves and the faster computer has a better chance of winning. One difference explains the other difference. The test-writers want us to see that "being able to examine more possible moves in the allotted time is what's causing the faster computer to have a better chance of winning".

label: Goal
body: Look for an answer potentially reinforcing this causal connection between "examining more possible moves" and "better chance of winning", but ultimately we'll pick whichever answer we can best support.

label: Given that ...
body: Bedding is the main source of exposure to dust mites.

label: Why is it that ...
body: The group whose bedding had a 69% reduction in dust-mite allergens didn't have any symptom reduction?

label: Evaluate / Goal
body:
We just need an answer to give us some way to explain why the group who slept on the special mattresses with less allergen still had allergies just as severe as normal.
  Maybe there's a delayed effect, where someone's allergies are based on their exposure to allergen *weeks ago*. So the week during the study they wouldn't experience relief, but a couple weeks after the study they might?
  Or maybe a 69% reduction just isn't enough of a reduction. Maybe 31% of allergens still being there is enough to trigger a reaction.

label: Conclusion
body: The company's net income from sales of the product must be only half of what it was 5 years ago.

label: Evidence (because)
body:
- 5 yrs ago, 50% of all hair dryers purchased nationwide were Wilson's.
  - Now, only 25% of all hair dryers purchased nationwide are Wilson's.
  - The average net income that Wilson receives per hair dryer has not changed over the last 5 years.

label: Evaluate
body:
This is a very math-y argument, so the flaw is probably related to math. When we see arguments involving percentages, they often involve an illicit switch between percentages and numbers.
  For example, if an author saw that a certain company went from being 40% female to being 50% female, they would assume that there were more females than before. But just because a percentage went up doesn't mean the raw number went up. It could be like this:
  ```
  THEN       NOW
  4 women    4 women
  6 men      4 men
  40% women  50% women
  ```
  In this argument, Wilson went from being 50% of hairdryers sold to 25%. Is the author assuming that since the percentage went down, the raw number went down?
  Yes! And if the raw number did go down, then the conclusion is totally valid.
  If Wilson sold a smaller number of hairdryers last year, compared to five years ago, but they still make the exact same net income (i.e. profit) per hairdryer, then they would be making less net income from that product. Again, let's consider numbers.
  ```
                     5 yrs. ago   Now
  sold nationally    100          100
  % that are Wilson  50%          25%
  # that are Wilson  50           25
  ```
  If they make $10 of profit off each hairdryer, then five years ago they made $500 and now they made $250.
  But let's not play the author's game. How could a smaller percentage not be a smaller number? If the total number of hairdryers sold nationally has doubled, then Wilson would be selling the same number of hairdryers.
  ```
                     5 yrs. ago   Now
  sold nationally    100          200
  % that are Wilson  50%          25%
  # that are Wilson  50           50
  ```
  Now, the author's conclusion is wrong. They sold 50 hair dryers in both cases, so their net income from that product hasn't changed.

label: Goal
body:
In order for the author's conclusion to be valid, we need there to be the same number of hairdryers sold nationally, now vs. 5 yrs ago.
  If that number is different nowadays, then Wilson won't be selling exactly half as many hairdryers and so their profit from hairdryers won't be exactly half of what it was 5 years ago.

label: Conclusion
body: Whether or not one can rightfully call a person's faithfulness a virtue depends in part on the object of that person's faithfulness.

label: Evidence
body: Virtues are supposed to be praiseworthy, but faithfulness isn't always praiseworthy (for example, you could be faithful to hating / resenting someone, and no one would call that virtuous).

label: Evaluate
body:
Whenever we read Main Conclusion or Role, we start by thinking "the Conclusion (on these question types) is almost always earlier than the Evidence. Specifically, it's usually the First Sentence or it's some Rebuttal / Pivot claim that is followed by support."
  If we go into these paragraph thinking, "This first claim has a 45% chance of being the conclusion, so I should try to hear it as though it is", it makes it easier to interpret what's going on.
  Does the first sentence present as though it's our Author's Opinion? Yes, somewhat. It says "rightfully", which is an opinionated term.
  Does the author proceed to try to defend / support that opening claim? Yes, the author gives an example of faithfulness that isn't a virtue, to support his claim that whether or not a certain faithfulness is a virtue depends on other factors.

label: Goal
body: Once we've correctly found the Conclusion, the hard part is done. We're now just picking whatever answer best matches the meaning of the first sentence.

label: Conclusion
body: The proposal to use the money we received from water bills to build new roads instead of a dam is unacceptable.

label: Intermediate Conclusion (thus)
body: A thought of a typical human face must exist in the infants' minds.

label: Evidence
body: The additional charge on water bills was approved with the idea that this additional revenue would go to building a dam.

label: Evaluate
body:
On Strengthen + Principle questions, we're basically just anticipating answers by saying, "If Premise, then Conclusion".
  So here that would sound like this:
  ```
  if the money was being     →  then it's unacceptable
  collected to build a dam      to use it for new roads
  ```

label: Goal
body: Let's look for an answer that's saying we should only use this collected money for the thing we collected it for (building a dam). We shouldn't collect the money for one purpose but then go and use it for some other purpose.

label: Conclusion
body: The leopard magpie moth is danger of extinction.

label: Evidence (since)
body:
- During its caterpillar stage, the leopard magpie moth feeds on a plant called the Natal grass cycad, which laces its body with a toxin that is a deterrent to predators.
  - The Natal grass cycad is now endangered and facing extinction.

label: Evaluate
body:
Since the argument feels more like Comparison / Causal real-world science talk (and less like abstract rules and language math), we should probably think about coming up with an Objection, rather than solving for a Missing Link.
  Given that ... the LM moth uses the cycad to coat itself in a way that turns off predators,
  and that ... the cycad is endangered,
  How can we argue .. the LM moth isn't endangered?
  Maybe it doesn't have as many predators to worry about any more. Some evolutionary adaptations outlive the selection pressure that gave rise to them. Maybe the moths still put the cycad slime on their bodies, even though there are very few predators around to even be deterred. This argument, then, must be assuming that "if the moths didn't have this cycad protection, there would be a significant uptick in threat from predators".
  Similarly, somewhat, maybe the LM moth wouldn't be endangered even if it loses its ability to coat itself in cycad slime because there are simply too many LM moths for any loss to predation to bring the LM moth species to the endangered status. In other words, it's possible that the loss of the cycad species will definitely mean that more LM moths die from predators, but the moth population might be starting at such a populous high number that the lessening effect from increased predation wouldn't ever reduce the moth population to endangered levels.

label: Goal
body:
There are a lot of different directions this answer could go. It could be very literal in its Linking:
  "If some organism uses a species to create a defense mechanism and that species becomes endangered, then the organism becomes endangered".
  It could sound like it's ruling out an Objection:
  "The moth population is not so large that it would thrive even without protection from macrozamin."
  or
  "The moth could not start feeding on a different plant that also produces macrozamin"
  and so on.

label: Opposing Idea
body: Our government has a large budget surplus, which our leaders wish to use to pay down the national debt.

label: Conclusion
body: This [using the surplus to pay down the national debt] makes no sense.

label: Evidence
body: Because of underfunding, our military is inadequate, the infrastructures of our cities are decaying, and our highways are in disrepair. If homeowners used all their money to pay off their mortgages early, while refusing to pay for upkeep of their homes, this would not make them better off financially. The same goes for the country as a whole.

label: Evaluate
body:
This argument follows a common pattern. The first sentence contains an Opposing Idea that the argument will eventually refute. The second sentence contains the argument's conclusion, which is a rebuttal of the idea in that first sentence. Everything that follows this second sentence is evidence supporting the conclusion.
  One challenge in this question is that there aren't any clear premise or conclusion indicators, or even a clear pivot word like "but" in between the Opposing Idea and the Conclusion. We need to read the argument to get a sense for the logical connections between ideas in order to identify the conclusion.
  The big hint here is the way that the first sentence describes a plan—using the budget surplus to pay down the national debt. And then the second sentence sharply refutes that plan: "this makes no sense." This second sentence is definitely an opinion about the first sentence. Together, they follow the common pattern of "Opposing Idea followed by a Conclusion which refutes that idea."
  Everything that follows the conclusion serves as evidence supporting that conclusion. This evidence describes alternative uses for the budget surplus—funding the military and infrastructure. This is followed by an analogy comparing the government to a homeowner. This analogy supports the idea that the government should use the surplus for these alternative uses, just as a homeowner is better off paying for upkeep instead of paying off their mortgage early.

label: Goal
body: Look for an answer stating that using the surplus to pay down the national debt makes no sense.

label: Peraski's Claims
body:
1. Driving gas-guzzling automobiles produces a greater level of pollution than driving smaller cars.
  2. Those of us who drive smaller cars when we could use a bicycle cannot speak out against the use of gas guzzlers.
  3. We would be revealing our hypocrisy.

label: Jackson's Responses
body:
1. No disagreement. In fact, he seems to implicitly agree that gas-guzzlers produce more pollution than smaller cars, since he alludes to "greater sources of pollution"
  2. Disagrees. Peraski said that people who drive small cars can't / shouldn't speak out against gas guzzlers (because they could do even better for the environment if they swapped their small car for a bike). Jackson is saying that people who drive small cars should / can still speak out against gas-guzzlers.
  3. Agrees that it is somewhat hypocritical to complain about emissions if you're still driving a car instead of a bike.

label: Goal
body: In this case, we have an explicit claim that the 2nd speaker disagrees with, so we should be able to head to answers looking for "whether or not someone who drives a small car (or someone who could do more to cut down on pollution) should be complaining about the use of gas guzzlers (or complaining about a worse-form of pollution than the one they use."

label: Given that ....
body: In order for a large abalone to develop from a smaller species, the larger one must spend less energy on finding food and avoiding predators, and more on competition for mates.

label: How can it be that ...
body: The fossil record shows that a species of large abalone developed from a smaller one only after otters began to dominate the local waters (preying on abalone).

label: Goal
body:
To explain the larger one developing, we need to hear about how
  - it spends less energy finding food
  - it spends less energy avoiding predators
  - it spends more energy competing for mates
  The correct answer will have to connect one or more of those to the ascendancy of the otters.
  Like, "once otters moved in, it became easier for abalone to find food / they spent less energy avoiding predators / spent more energy competing for mates"

label: Conclusion
body: Stiff competition can undermine employee performance.

label: Support
body: In situations where one competitor is perceived to be clearly superior, other competitors become anxious and doubt their own ability to perform.

label: Evaluate
body: The term "competition" plays a key role in both statements and represents a link between the evidence and the conclusion.

label: Anticipate
body: The assumption should connect the other two terms from the argument and state that doubting one's ability can undermine one's performance.

label: Statements
body:
- It's been hard to create a database of all the plant species in the scientific record.
  - For hundreds of years, botanists have collected a sample and given it a name (thinking they've discovered a previously undiscovered species), not realizing that the plant had already been discovered and named.
  - And in other cases, we've discovered that we actually should have been counting a handful of plants as different species, rather than several varieties of one species.

label: Evaluate
body:
This question stem looks like a soft Must Be False. On Must Be False the correct answer normally contradicts a conditional statement provided or contradicts an available inference we could have made.
  There are no conditional statements. Are there any available inferences we can get by combining ideas?
  Hmm. The gist of the paragraph is that making a database of all plants is brutal.
  In many cases we were over-recording species (a botanist would file species #978 in the ledger, not realizing it was really a duplicate of species #249 that was found years ago).
  In many cases we were under-recording species (botanists thought that a collection of plants were just varieties of #360 ... 360a, 360b, 360c, for example— instead they really should have been 3 separate species).

label: Goal
body:
Putting those two ideas together, we basically have some sentiment like "when it comes to counting up species, sometimes we overcount, sometimes we undercount".
  I would have no idea what we're looking for. But it needs to actively go against something we read or some understanding we derived from what we read.

label: Conclusion (clearly)
body: The knowledge that their errors were being monitored made the hospital staff more meticulous in carrying out their patient-care duties.

label: Evidence
body: Ever since the hospital instituted a plan to record all staff errors, the rate of patient injuries resulting from such errors has gone down a bunch.

label: Evaluate
body:
There are a lot of copies of this same argument throughout the LSAT canon:
  Premise 1: A policy change was made
  Premise 2: A change has been observed.
  Conclusion: The policy change was the reason
  It might be, "We lowered the speed limit. Since then, highway fatalities are lower. Thus, the speed limit has made people drive more safely"
  or it might be, "I started meditating last Friday. Since then, my Games sections have been going better. Thus, the meditation is helping!"
  But whenever an LSAT author presents a Curious Fact and then concludes something that reveals a Causal Explanation being assumed, then we are supposed to worry about
  1. Alternate Explanations for the Curious Fact
  2. the plausibility of the Author's Explanation
  Here, our curious fact is, "why have injuries due to staff errors gone down" and the causal explanation being assumed is that "we instituted this plan to systematically record such errors. The staff was aware of it and did not want their errors recorded and so has become much more meticulous in carrying out their patient-care duties, which has led to fewer injuries."

label: Goal
body:
Since this is Strengthen, we want to either
  rule out an alternate explanation for the curious fact (e.g. "the incidence of injuries hasn't gone down because we fired Eddie, who was responsible for most of them, or because we just see fewer patients than before)
  or
  increase the plausibility of the author's explanation (e.g. "in the parts of the hospital where they don't record such errors, we haven't seen a reduction in patient injuries")

label: Given that ...
body: Wolves were introduced onto an island to eat up the local moose and thin out the herd,

label: and that ...
body: the wolves prospered in this new environment.

label: How can it be that ...
body: The moose herd continued to grow?

label: Evaluate
body:
Maybe the wolves ate something besides moose. They found an easier food supply to help them sustain and flourish.
  Maybe the wolves ate the moose, but the moose reproduced at a great enough rate that it didn't cause a net reduction.

label: Goal
body:
This paradox could be resolved different ways, but fundamentally they should either be like,
  "The wolves weren't able to eat as many moose as we'd hoped, because X"
  "The wolves didn't choose to eat as many moose as we'd hoped, because Y"
  "The wolves did eat as moose as they could, but that didn't stop the moose population growth, because Z"

label: Main Conclusion (we must conclude)
body: Existing laws acquire legitimacy simply because they are laws.

label: Intermediate Conclusion (Hence)
body: If the purpose of laws is not to contribute to people's happiness, then we have no basis for the evaluation of existing laws.

label: Evidence
body: If the purpose of laws is to contribute to people's happiness, then have a basis for criticizing existing laws as well as proposing new laws.

label: Liang's first claim
body:
When movies show violence as an appropriate way of resolving problems, it increases levels of aggression in viewers.
  Does Sarah agree that condoned violent problem-solving increases aggression in viewers?
  No she disagrees. She says that watching violent characters purges the viewer of such aggression.

label: Liang's second claim
body:
Children's access to movies where violence solves problems should be limited.
  Does Sarah agree that children should be kept from seeing movies where violence solves problems?
  She doesn't talk about it. She says that access to these movies for mature audiences should not be restricted.

label: Evaluate
body:
Since the argument draws two conclusions, we can examine both moves. The move from the 1st claim to the 2nd claim commits the #1 famous flaw Necessary vs. Sufficient, in which the author introduces a conditional statement and then interprets it using illegal backwards or negated logic.
  The first sentence says
  ```
  purpose is happiness → we have a basis
  ```
  The conclusion drawn from that is just an illegal negation.
  ```
  purpose is not happiness → do not have basis
  ```
  The move from the 2nd claim to the 3rd claim is saying, "If we have no basis for evaluating existing laws, then existing laws get their legitimacy simply from being laws".
  We might be able to fight that by saying, "Who says existing laws have legitimacy in the first place?" or " maybe they get their legitimacy from some other arbitrary factor"?

label: Goal
body:
It seems more likely that we're just being tested on the age old Necessary vs. Sufficient flaw and that the bonus conclusion was put in there just as a way to distract us and "hide the ball".
  Whenever we're doing Flaw and see any conditional logic, we should immediately start suspecting an illegal reversal or illegal negation (aka, Necessary vs. Sufficient)

label: Conclusion (so)
body: There is no life on planet P23.

label: Evidence
body:
- In order for life to exist on planet P23, there must be surface water.
  - There's no surface water.

label: Evaluate
body:
This is an argument by contrapositive. There is one premise that gives us a conditional rule,
  ```
  Life → Water
  ```
  Then there is a 2nd premise that says the Outcome of the conditional is not the case.
  Water.
  Then the conclusion correctly says that the Trigger must not be the case.
  Life.

label: Goal
body:
Let's look for something like
  "In order to swim, Pam needs goggles. Pam doesn't have goggles, so Pam can't swim."
  "Entering the club requires shirts and shoes. Eddie isn't wearing a shirt, so Eddie can't enter the club."
  ```
  P1: X → Y (conditional)
  P2: ~Y. (fact)
  C: ~X. (fact)
  ```

label: Sanchez's Claims
body:
1. The 16 new computers that the school bought weren't as expensive as people assume.
  2. It's not true that too much was spent on computers (i.e. an appropriate amount was spent)

label: Merriweather's Responses
body:
1. No comment. She isn't trying to argue that the computers were as expensive as people assume. She deals only with whether they were more/less/comparable to what they were worth.
  2. Disagree. It sounds like Merriweather is nudging towards the idea that "it is true that too much was spent on computer". After all, even though they paid the right price for the computer they bought, they bought a computer that was needlessly elaborate (and thus needlessly pricey).

label: Goal
body:
Since Merriweather disagrees with one of Sanchez's explicit claims, we can just head to the answers with that prephrase in mind. It's possible the correct answer will test one of Sanchez's assumptions, but let's not deal with that until we have to.
  Let's look for "whether or not the school spent more money than they should have on those new computers".

label: Conclusion (so)
body: The figure that 1 in 20,000 commercial flights stray off course while landing is relatively unreliable compared to the figure that 1 in 2 million stray off course.

label: Evidence
body: The 1 in 20,000 figure is based on a partial review of air traffic control tapes, while the 1 in 2,000,000 figure is based on a thorough study of the flight reports required of all commercial pilots.

label: Evaluate
body:
The author is arguing that one figure is more reliable than another figure, because the former is a thorough study and the latter is just a partial review.
  We grant the author that thorough review does sound more reliable than partial review. But is that the only difference between the two figures?
  One of them is air traffic control tapes,
  the other is the flight report of the pilot.
  Do we have a common sense take on which type of data we would find more reliable:
  video tapes of the planes landing, from the air traffic control tower or monitors
  vs.
  a pilot's written report of the flight
  I would trust video evidence over written evidence in most cases. If the video has an unobstructed view of the plane landing, it should be pretty reliable to figure out the rate of stray landings.
  When it comes to the pilot's log, I have no idea how seriously they take that task, how soon after the flight they create this report (maybe it's not for hours and their memory of the flight is shaky), or how honest pilots would be in admitting to a stray landing.

label: Goal
body: Look for an answer saying that, "a partial review of something more trustworthy (like videotape evidence) might still be more reliable than a thorough review of a less trustworthy source (like a pilot's written remarks).

label: Conclusion (So)
body: If you're looking for lake trout in deep temperate lakes while they lakes are still partially iced over in late winter, you should fish in a shallow bay or close to the surface or off a rocky point.

label: Evidence
body:
- In deep temperate lakes, lake trout are found in the coldest water.
  - In winter, the coldest water is at the top. In summer, the coldest water is at the bottom. The change in temperature distribution (the "turnover") occurs in fall and late winter.

label: Evaluate
body:
The conclusion is trying to give trout fishing advice for a particular scenario, one that's kind of ambiguous.
  We know during winter we'd fish close to the surface, because that's where the coldest water and thus the trout would be. During summer, we should fish close to the bottom, because that's where the coldest water and thus the trout will be.
  But what if it's on the borderline between those seasons? If it's late winter and partially iced over, we're right around the "turnover" time, when the cold water switches from being on top to being on bottom.
  Has it already turned over? Should we still be going by winter rules (fish on top) or by summer rule (fish on bottom)? The author's conclusion is saying that we should fish near the top of the lake, so apparently the author thinks the cold water is still on top of the lake.
  note: tons of us are confused by what the conclusion is even saying because of two vocab words. "Eschew" means "to avoid / to reject". And "summer haunts" means "places you hang out in the summer". So the conclusion is conversationally saying, "avoid the places where trout hang out in the summer (i.e. the bottom of the lake) and fish close to the top instead".

label: Goal
body: Let's look for something like, "The author is assuming that the cold water is still on the top of the lake" or "the change in temperature distribution has not yet happened".

label: Evaluate
body:
Usually on Agree questions (which are very rare), the two people fundamentally disagree, and so the correct answer isn't an explicit agreement but rather some underlying background truth or assumption they both accept.
  In this case they clearly diverge on whether watching violence in movies increases aggression or purges aggression.
  But it looks like they'd agree that
  "watching violence in movies can have an effect on our level of aggression".
  Sarah doesn't comment on whether children's access to violent movies should be restricted, but given her belief that watching violence purges us of aggression, we'd have no reason to think she's worried about children seeing these movies. However, she did conclude that "we shouldn't restrict access to mature audiences", so maybe she was saying to Liang, "Fine, I implicitly accept that we should restrict their access to children, but let's not take it too far and restrict their access to older audiences."

label: Goal
body: Ultimately, we will just pick the answer for which we feel like we have the most dual-support, an answer that could be supported if not proved by each paragraph.

label: Conclusion
body: Of the candidates in the race, Thompson is the best to lead this nation.

label: Evidence (for one thing)
body:
- Many agree that anyone who opposes higher taxes will make a better leader than someone who supports higher taxes.
  - Thompson opposes higher taxes whereas the other candidates support them.

label: Evaluate
body:
Yikes, sometimes an argument is so bad, you don't even know where LSAC wants you to begin.
  The conclusion is asking, "who among these candidates is best to lead this nation", picks Thompson, and cites one reason — her position on higher taxes.
  Is that enough? Are we single-issue voters and the one issue we care about is taxes? And a candidate's position on taxes is enough to make them the best one to lead the nation?
  The author hasn't even clearly established that opposing higher taxes is a better position than supporting them — she's only told us that "many would agree" that opposing is better than supporting.
  Well, who are these many people? Why should we listen to them?

label: Goal
body:
It's hard to know what we're going for here. Because choosing a candidate is usually a complex calculus of pros and cons, whereas the author has only offered one lonely pro in favor of voting for Thompson, then we could weaken the argument by learning that Thompson has some disadvantage when it comes to something other than taxes.
  We can also weaken by undermining the position of these "many people who think higher taxes are better".
  I would mainly keep the anti-conclusion in my head,
  "Even though Thompson is the only one opposing taxes, Thompson is not the best one to lead the nation, because ... [answer choice]"

label: Patterson's Conclusion
body: Music probably first arose during the Upper Paleolithic period.

label: Patterson's Evidence
body: Bone flutes from this U.P. period are the earliest evidence for music.

label: Garza's Response
body:
The U.P period was unusual for its intensive use of bone.
  Stuff made of bone can last forever, so we still dig it up archaeologically. Meanwhile, other common instrument materials like wood do not survive well in dug-up ruins.

label: Evaluate
body:
It might take us a bit to process what Garza is saying, but it's crucial we understand the point she's making.
  The fact that her paragraph started with "But" suggests that she is pushing back against Patterson's notion that "music probably arose during the Upper Paleolithic period".
  She isn't proposing a specific alternative period when music arose, but she seems to be questioning how Patterson interprets the evidence.
  Since the earliest archaeological evidence of musical instruments we have are bone flutes from this U.P. period, Patterson assumes that this is when music started.
  But Garza is saying, "Suppose that music began in an earlier period, but they made their instruments out of wood, not bone. After all, wood is commonly used for instruments, and bone isn't. Those fools from the U.P. period were just famously in love with making stuff from bone. Since wood degrades easily, we wouldn't find any of these earlier wooden instruments, even if they existed."
  Her idea is kind of an alternate explanation for why the earliest instruments we've found were made of bone. It's not because humans started with bone instruments; it's because only bone instruments would survive from that long ago.

label: Goal
body:
If we know the typical 8 method answers (analogy, counter/example, ruling out options, implications of logic, distinctions, alternate explanations, overlooked considerations, dubious assumptions), this one seems to feel like calling out a Dubious Assumption or suggesting an Alternate Explanation.
  Look for something like, "Garza points out that Patterson is assuming that bones are not our earliest evidence simply because of their greater durability" or "Garza proposes an alternate explanation for why the earliest instruments we've found are made of bone".

label: Principle
body:
```
  unless (if-not)
  If incompetence performing job X
  job X does not pose a      →  shouldn't be
  plausible threat to human     subject to
  health or safety              license req.
  ```

label: Evaluate
body:
A rule can only justify a conclusion that matches its right side. Here, the right side is "shouldn't be subject to licensing requirement".
  So this rule only has the power to prove a job shouldn't have a licensing requirement. Any answer that is trying to prove a job should is automatically wrong.
  We could contrapose this and have
  ```
  If it should be subject   →  incompetence is
  to licensing                 a threat
  ```
  Thus, technically we could also use this rule to justify a conclusion saying that "incompetence at this job would pose a plausible threat", but Apply the Principle questions have never worked that way in the past.
  Whichever half of the rule sounds more "judgy", more normative or evaluative, should be on the right, because that's the conclusion they'll support.
  In this rule, "should / shouldn't" is the most normative/evaluative language.

label: Goal
body:
1. Check the conclusion first. If it isn't saying "shouldn't have licensing requirement", ditch it (at least on the first pass).
  2. If the conclusion matches the right side of our rule, then we'll see whether the evidence in the answer choice establishes the left side of our rule, that someone being incompetent at doing job X wouldn't be posing a plausible threat to human health or safety.

label: Statements
body:
```
  quantifiers (most)
  Most new cars sold   were purchased by
  Regis Motors         residents of
  last year            Blomenville
  Most new             purchased by   were not sold
  residents of                        by
  Blomenville                         Regis Motors
  math-y comparison
  Regis Motors sold more new cars last year than in any previous year.
  ```

label: Evaluate
body:
On Must Be True questions, we're primarily scanning for Conditional, Quantified, or Causal ideas.
  When we see Quantifiers, we know there are a couple different types of quantity overlap / relationship inferences that LSAT likes to test:
  ```
  All A's are B          Most A's are B
  Some A's are C         Most A's are C
  -------------------    -------------------
  infer: some B's are C  some B's are C
  ```
  Since we were given two Most claims, we should be thinking about that second one, the "Most + Most" inference. However, for that inference to work, we need both Most claims to be about the same group.
  This question is actually testing a more obscure "Most + Most" inference, that has only shown up a couple times (both tests are in the 70s / 80s).
  ```
  Most A's are B
  Most B's are ~A
  -------------------
  infer: more B's than A's
  ```
  Take any two qualities, say "likes cake" and "likes ballet".
  Most people who like ballet like cake, but
  most people who like cake do not like ballet.
  Let's pretend we're in some ballroom that contains people who just like ballet, just like cake, like both, or like neither.
  Let's pretend we have 15 people who like ballet.
  Most of them like cake, so a minimum of 8.
  So we'll say 15 people who like ballet,
  8 of them like cake, 7 of them don't.
  Now let's think about the second fact,
  "Most people who like cake don't like ballet",
  What's the minimum number of cake lovers?
  We already know there are 8 people who like cake and ballet.
  So 8 of the people who like cake also like ballet. But we know most of the people who like cake do not like ballet, so there would have to be at least 9 of them.
  Thus the minimum number of cake lovers in 17.
  We've proven that when we hear
  Most people who like ballet like cake, but
  most people who like cake do not like ballet.
  it tells us that
  there are more cake lovers than ballet lovers.
  I know it's confusing to make it click. Remember, you'll have an easy form you can memorize. You're just trying to understand it so that it's easier to remember and process.
  Here's one more way to talk about it. There is some number of people in the world that like both cake and ballet. Let's use the variable 'x'. There are x people in the world who like both cake and ballet.
  When we say, "Most people who like ballet also like cake", we're saying that those people who like both are a majority of ballet lovers.
  When we say, "Most people who like cake do not like ballet", it means that people who like both cake and ballet (x) are a minority of cake lovers.
  If x is a majority of the ballet group (more than 50%),
  but a minority of the cake group (less than 50%), then that mathematically proves that the cake group is a bigger number.
  ```
  x > 0.50 B
  x < 0.50 C
  0.50 B < x < 0.50 C
  B < x < C
  ```

label: Goal
body:
They seem to be handing us the ingredients for this inference,
  ```
  Most A's are B
  Most B's are ~A
  -------------------
  infer: more B's than A's
  ```
  Most [sold by Regis Motors] are [bought by Blomenville's], but
  Most [bought by Blomenville's] are [not sold by Regis Motors]
  infer: [bought by Blomenville's] > [sold by Regis Motors]
  In other words, more new cars were bought by Blomenville residents than were sold by Regis Motors.

label: Conclusion
body: If the school day started later than 8am, car accidents involving teenagers driving to school could be reduced.

label: Evidence (since, indeed)
body:
- Sleepiness can impair driving ability.
  - Teens tend to wake up around 8am.
  - If teens are made to wake up earlier, they are sleepy.
  - When Granville's high school pushed back its starting time to 830am, the overall number of car accidents involving teen drivers declined in Granville.

label: Evaluate
body:
Well, this is a mouthful to take in. On one hand we have a Comparison situation because the author is proposing a certain Plan (later start time for school day) and predicting a certain Result/Goal (reduce accidents involving teens driving to school).
  We have to consider differences between "Plan World" and "Actual World".
  The author is highlighting one thing that will change, [teens are hopefully less sleepy while driving to school], but we need to consider what other things might change? Maybe the normal rush hour in Granville is from 8am - 9am, so if we are suddenly adding teen drivers to that mix, we're making that hour of driving more dangerous in a way that might actually add more accidents involving teen drivers. LSAT loves to test the idea of a Plan backfiring and making something worse in an unanticipated way. This Plan also assumes that it's feasible for teens to sleep in to 8am, regardless of school start time. Maybe their parents are waking them up by 7am
  Remember, teens don't have to cause the accident. As long as their in an accident with some road-rage morning commuter, it still counts as "an accident involving teenagers".
  There's also a conditional logic element to this answer. If teens are made to wake up earlier than 8, they are sleepy. Our author seems to be assuming a difference, that "if they are made to wake up after 8, they will be less/not sleepy."
  Finally, there's the Interpreting a Curious Fact part of this argument. The author is assuming that the number of car accidents decreased when Granville's high school pushed its start time back is because there was less sleepy driving to school by teens. But maybe there's some alternate explanation for why number of car accidents went down (i.e. a pandemic where everyone has to stay home).

label: Goal
body:
Yikes, so how many pressure points does this argument have?
  - we want to know that if schools pushed back their start times, it would be feasible for teens to wake up later, that they would do so, that they would be less sleepy as a result of doing so, and that changing their drive-to-school times later would not create any new issues that might facilitate more accidents involving teens.
  - additionally, we're in the market for any answers ruling out alternate explanations for why teen accidents declined in Granville or making it more plausible that the change of start time for the high school was the reason.

label: Conclusion (therefore)
body: Lucinda will probably live in Western Hall.

label: Evidence
body:
- Lucinda will be attending National University as an engineering major.
  - At National University, most residents of Western Hall are engineering majors.

label: Evaluate
body:
Given that ... most residents of Western Hall are engineering majors
  and that ... Lucinda is an engineering major
  How could we argue ... Lucinda probably won't live in Western Hall?
  Do most engineering majors life in Western Hall? If not, then there's no reason to think that just because she's an engineering major that she'll probably live in Western Hall.
  Suppose that Eastern Hall has 1000 students and Western Hall has 100 students. Most of the students in both dorms are engineering majors.
  If all you know is that Lucinda is an engineering major, would you conclude that she's probably going to end up in Western Hall? No, it's a safer bet that she lands in Eastern Hall, since there are at least 501 engineering majors there whereas there are only at least 51 engineering majors in Western Hall.
  To make the argument the author wants to make, he needs his Most premise to be reversed. If he had said this, it would be a valid argument:
  Premise 1 - Lucinda is an engineering major
  Premise 2 - Most engineering majors live in Western Hall
  Conclusion - thus, Lucinda will probably live in Western Hall
  The flaw is that his Most premise is backwards. Instead of telling us that Most people with the quality that Lucinda has (engineering major) live in Western, he told us that most people who live in Western have a quality that Lucinda has.

label: Goal
body:
Since we see all these repeating symbols (Lucinda, western hall, national university, and engineering major are all mentioned twice), it makes sense to try to convert this argument into an algebraic recipe.
  Premise1:
  Thing A will be X.
  Lucinda will be engineering major.
  Premise 2:
  Most Y's are X.
  Most Western residents are engineering majors
  Conclusion:
  Therefore, thing A will probably be Y.
  Lucinda will probably be a Western resident.
  In terms of strategizing how we quickly see whether an answer is worth fully reading, let's look to see whether the first half of a Most claim is the backend of the conclusion. (i.e. in the original argument, "residents of Western Hall" was the first half of the Most premise and the second half of the conclusion)

label: Conclusion
body: The supposed epidemic of childhood obesity is a myth.

label: Conclusion (should = opinion)
body: In order to make a big reduction in atmospheric C02, we should capture CO2 and pump it deep into the oceans.

label: Intermediate Conclusion (so)
body: Any C02 pumped deep into the oceans would be trapped there for centuries.

label: Evidence
body: The cool, dense water that's deep in the ocean takes centuries to mix with the warmer water near the surface.

label: Evaluate
body:
Since the argument contained multiple conclusions, we can scrutinize each of the reasoning moves.
  Given that it takes centuries for the cold water at the bottom to mix with the warm water near the surface, does that convince us that any CO2 we pump down there will be trapped for centuries?
  There's definitely a Linking assumption happening,
  ```
  if the cold hasn't    →  then the CO2
  mixed with the warm      is still trapped
  ```
  What about the second reasoning move: if we accepted that the CO2 would be trapped down there for centuries, does that convince us that we should capture CO2 from the atmosphere and pump it deep into the ocean?
  No, I'm not ready to sign-off on that plan yet.
  Does it hurt the ocean wildlife?
  Does it cost too much money?
  Does the pumping process send more CO2 into the atmosphere than the CO2 that gets pumped into the ocean (is there a net savings in atmospheric CO2 ?
  In reality, only that last objection is relevant. The conclusion defines our goal as "substantially reducing CO2 in the atmosphere". So our objections can only be directed at the idea that this plan of pumping CO2 from air to deep-ocean would not result in a substantial reduction in atmospheric CO2.

label: Goal
body: Look for a Linking assumption like, "If cold hasn't mixed with warm, then CO2 still trapped" or look for an answer ruling out an idea that would otherwise make it seem like this plan isn't really going to lead to a big decrease in atmospheric CO2.

label: Conclusion
body: You should use praise and verbal correction to train your dog instead of treats.

label: Evidence (since)
body: Treat-trained dogs will not obey commands unless they are shown a treat, and you cannot always have treats on hand.

label: Evaluate
body:
Ultimately, the argument is suggesting one method over another. That could put us into Weighing Tradeoffs territory, where the correct answer shows that the advantage of one theory outweighs the advantage of another.
  We heard that the advantage of the Treat method is that dogs do quickly learn to do the thing they get a treat for.
  The advantage of the Praise / Verbal method is that you can always supply Praise / verbal correction, whereas you might sometimes be lacking a treat.

label: Goal
body:
Let's look for a conditional answer like, "If one method is available to use in more circumstances, then that method is how you should train your dog".
  Or look for a comparative answer like, "It's more important that your dog training method involves a method of reinforcement that is always on hand then it is that the method can be learned quickly."

label: Conclusion
body: Train your dog with praise and verbal correction instead of treats.

label: Evidence
body: Treat-trained dogs will not obey without a treat in sight, and you cannot always have treats on hand.

label: Evaluate
