body: The author needs a principle that favors training with a stimulus the owner can always provide.

label: Goal
body: Pick the principle that says training should rely on a stimulus the owner can always supply.

label: Conclusion
body: The author wants you to skip treat training and use praise and correction instead.

label: Evidence
body: Why? Because dogs trained with treats only obey when they see one — and you cannot always have a pocket full of treats. Praise and verbal correction, on the other hand, you can always give.

label: Evaluate
body: The hidden idea here is that the right training method is the one that uses a reward or signal the owner can always provide. Without that idea, "you cannot always have treats" does not push us toward praise.

label: Goal
body: Find a principle that lines up with: train your dog using something you can always give.

label: Conclusion (thus)
body: Modern civilizations that continue to rely heavily on irrigation for agriculture are likely to eventually collapse.

label: Evidence
body: The ancient Sumerians relied heavily on irrigation for agriculture and they eventually collapsed, once the irrigation had built up so many toxic salts in the soil that the soil was unable to support crops.

label: Evaluate
body:
This argument relies on a Comparison, assuming that what happened with the Sumerian civilization is likely to happen to similar civilizations (those who use irrigation a lot).
  When we're analyzing Comparisons, the author is usually assuming other similarities or assuming some crucial difference.
  In this case, the author is Assuming Similarities between ancient Sumeria and these modern irrigating cultures.
  She's assuming that the modern cultures will be doing irrigation long enough and intensively enough that they will eventually run into the same problem with toxic salts. (She's also assuming the local soil is similar enough that long-term irrigation could have similar toxic buildup effects).
  And she's assuming that if/when that day of toxic buildup arrives, these modern civilizations don't have a Plan B to save their agriculture / save their civilization.

label: Goal
body: We're probably looking for an answer to provide a Meaningful Difference between these modern civilizations and that of the ancient Sumerians, a difference that would allow us to say that even though they are reliant on irrigation too, we shouldn't consider it likely that this irrigation will one day doom their civilization.

label: Conclusion
body: It's not surprising that we usually don't find mineralized dinosaur bones and dinosaur mud tracks in the same area.

label: Evidence
body: Creatures that scavenged dinosaur carcasses most likely went to mud flats to find food.

label: Goal
body:
Since we have this
  ```
  Some French Literature 206 → Biology 218
  Biology 218 → ~Biology
  major
  ```
  If we added this
  ```
  ~Biology → ~French Literature major
  major
  ```
  We could derive this
  ```
  Some French Literature 206 → ~French Literature major
  ```
  But they might also give it to us in a more conversational style, like "At Tromen University, there are no double-majors."

label: Evaluate
body:
This is one of those arguments that is super hard to understand on a first (or second) read, but if we can figure out the author's intended meaning, then we're actually 90% of the way to our correct answer.
  There are two types of dinosaur fossils, but we don't find them in the same place usually. We either find bones or find footprints in the mud.
  The author has a theory for why we don't find them together, and since our author is trying to explain a puzzling phenomenon, we can use our Curious Fact / Explanation mindset:
  Curious Fact ... why don't we find bones and mud tracks in the same place?
  Author's Explanation ... animals that would scavenge dinosaur carcasses frequented mud flats to find food.
  Again, what?! We need to make sense of causal story the author is telling here. It might help to think about what it would be like if we did find dinosaur bones and mud tracks in the same place:
  It would mean that a dinosaur died in the mud flat. We're generally finding dinosaur bones at the spot where they died (they're too heavy and not-useful for animals to have moved them, so other than weather events like a hurricane or earthquake moving them, they will be found where the dinosaur died).
  So if a dinosaur died in a mud flat, it would definitely leave some footprints in the mud en route to its death scene, right? How come we don't see those final footprints in the mud?
  The author is saying that there were scavenger animals who roamed mud flats looking for food. If they happened upon a dead dinosaur, then they would go to town on its carcass.
  So the author is either thinking that we don't find bones in the mud flats because there were scavengers roaming the mud flats who would perform "clean up duty" and eat the bones.
  Or ... the author is thinking that we don't find muddy dinosaur footprints near the dinosaurs bones, because the footprints of the scavengers that were eating the dinosaurs carcass messed up the dinosaurs mud footprint (kind of like if someone walks through snow, they leave footprints, but if you walk through their footprints, you can't clearly see that person's boot print anymore).

label: Goal
body: Since this is Strengthen, we are most likely adding plausibility to the author's story (i.e. scavengers in the mud flats would have consumed the dinosaur's bones or obscured the dinosaur's footprints), or we might be ruling out an alternate explanation for why bones and mud prints aren't found in the same place.

label: Information
body:
```
  comparisons
  total ounces cat food eaten daily
  canned < dry
  calories per ounce
  canned > dry
  ends with pivot (nonetheless)
  cost per day
  canned > dry
  ```

label: Evaluate
body:
On Inference questions, we're trying to figure out what they want us to synthesize, by looking out for indicators: Conditional, Causal, Pivot, Math-y, or Comparative.
  This paragraph has three Comparisons, and it ends with a Pivot, suggesting that we're supposed to reconcile this last idea with the facts that came before it. It seems like it might be a mathematical inference, since all three comparisons are quantitative in nature.
  If you feed your cat canned cat food, you feed it fewer ounces per day than someone who feeds their cat dry food, but you spend more money per day on your cat food than does someone who feeds their cat dry food.
  If I'm feeding Buffy 5 oz of canned food and paying $1.00 for it, whereas you're feeding Midnight 8 oz of canned food and paying only $0.60 for it, then I'm spending more per ounce than you.
  Can we say who's spending more per calorie?
  No, because we don't know which of our cats is being fed more calories.
  We know that there are more calories in 1 oz of canned food than in 1 oz of dry food, but we don't know whether there's more calories in 5 oz of canned food than in 8 oz of dry food.

label: Goal
body:
The only real definite, derivable idea it seems we have is that owners who feed their cat canned food pay more per ounce of food than do owners who feed their cat dry food.
  But we'll stay flexible for any other answer we could support, in case they're going for something else.

label: Given that ...
body: The reconstruction effort took extraordinary care to return the church to its original form,

label: and that ...
body: the original church had an 18th century baroque organ designed for it

label: and that ...
body: a donor offered to pay the full cost of rebuilding the organ

label: Why is it that ...
body: The foundation built a modern organ instead?

label: Evaluate / Goal
body:
It's real hard to predict the answers to most Paradox questions, and this one seems particularly hard to anticipate.
  We know that the intent was to rebuild the church in its original form. We know the original form had an 18th century baroque organ designed for it. And we know that cost is not an issue (a donor is willing to pay for it).
  So there must be some compelling reason that they don't want to replicate the organ with historical accuracy.
  We just need an answer that helps us understand why having the old style organ would be bad, or why having a modern organ is good, so that we can understand why it was worth departing from their desire at historical accuracy.

label: Evidence (Principle)
body:
A government should reduce taxes on imports if doing so would financially benefit many consumers in its domestic economy. `FBC → RTI`
  There is an exception: [The government] should never reduce import taxes if one or more of its domestic industries would be significantly harmed by the added competition. `HDI → ~RTI`

label: Conclusion
body: The government should not reduce taxes on textile imports. `~RTI`

label: Evaluate
body:
The principle describes a situation where the government should reduce taxes on imports, but describes one exception. If the exception is triggered, the government should not reduce these taxes.
  If we know for a fact that the exception is being triggered, we can properly conclude that the government should not reduce taxes on textile imports.
  If reducing taxes on textile imports will create added competition that harms one or more domestic industries, that triggers the exception.

label: Goal
body: Expect an answer to state that reducing taxes on textile imports will create added competition that harms one or more domestic industries. Beware of answers that trigger the normal situation—benefitting many consumers—and answers that involve tangentially related topics which are not actually connected to the principle.

label: Information
body:
```
  causal (X has contributed to Y)
  Global    ⇢  glaciers / ice   ⇢  rise in global
  warming      sheets melt          sea level
  Global    ⇢  volume of heated ⇢  rise in global
  warming      water increases      sea level
  causal difference-maker (if not for X, less Y)
  artificial reservoirs        reduces the rise
  were built to contain     ⇢  in global sea level
  a great deal of water
  ```

label: Evaluate / Goal
body:
We have three causal connections. They don't quite chain together, but they all relate to rising global sea level.
  Perhaps the correct answer will convey some aspect of the fact that "as global warming worsens, there will be more incentive to build artificial reservoirs". But it's hard to predict. Let's just pick the most provable answer.

label: Conclusion (so)
body: Juan must have entered the contest.

label: Evidence
body:
- Juan has a T-shirt with the new logo.
  - Everyone who entered the contest would receive a T-shirt with the new logo.

label: Evidence
body: Little documentation of his supposed cruelty or outrageous behavior has survived, and what has survived was written by his enemies.

label: Evaluate
body:
Just because Juan has a T-shirt that was given away in this contest, does that prove that Juan entered the contest? No, he might have gotten the T-shirt some other way. Maybe he works at the company and had access to the shirt before the contest even started. Maybe his friend Tara entered the contest and when she got her free shirt she gave it to Juan.
  Whenever we're doing a Flaw question and see conditional logic indicator words (i.e. if, when, any, all, every, each, no, ,only if, only, must, ensures, unless, etc), we should suspect that we're about to see the #1 Famous Flaw: Necessary vs. Sufficient.
  The word "everyone" is a universal, so it's a Sufficient (left side) indicator.
  ```
  entered the contest → received new logo shirt
  ```
  Once an author has provided a conditional relationship in her premises, we look to see if she uses it illegally backwards or in opposite fashion, e.g.
  ```
  X has the new shirt.       X didn't enter contest.
  So X entered contest.      So, X doesn't have shirt
  ```
  Both of these are technically the same flaw. Whether the author illegally negated or reversed the conditional relationship, we can call him out on confusing his Necessary and Sufficient conditions.

label: Goal
body: Look for an answer calling out the Necessary vs. Sufficient flaw or just calling out the fact that there are other possible ways to get that T-shirt.

label: Statements
body:
- Juror often don't understand the technical information involved in expert testimony and thus they're in no position to evaluate it.
  - Experts from both sides often make conflicting claims, while often seeming to both be competent, making it hard for the jury to assess who is more reliable.

label: Evaluate
body:
That was a lot of fuzzy claims that add up to a general gist of, 'Darn — I guess jurors are kind of in a tough position when it comes to expert witness testimony; the witnesses can both seem reliable but say conflicting things, and meanwhile we jurors don't have the technical expertise to know who's right.'
  There aren't any conditionals. There are very wishy-washy quantifiers like "often, often, frequently". There's a little bit of causality in the sense of "lack of technical knowledge causes in ability to evaluate testimony" and in the sense of "thinking both experts seem competent causes jurors to be unable to assess the reliability of the testimony".

label: Goal
body: Hard to predict a specific answer here. We should probably just check out answers and look for the most provable claim we can find.

label: Conclusion (this shows that ...)
body: The criticisms just go to show that the legislation is framed just as it should be.

label: Evidence (since)
body:
- Some the proposed tax reform bill for being too specific and other criticize it for being too vague.
  - One and the same statement cannot be both too specific and too vague.

label: Evaluate
body:
Do we think this is testing Missing Links or Potential Objections?
  The Missing Link language would need to get us to the new language in the Conclusion of "framed as it should be". What kind of rule is the author imagining that shows this bill is "framed as it should be"?
  She would be thinking something like
  ```
  If ... a bill is criticized     then ... it's framed
  by both left and right          as it should be
  political groups
  ```
  ```
  If ... two criticisms           then ... it's framed
  of a bill cannot both           as it should be
  be true
  ```
  But the 2nd one I listed there isn't even quite right. There isn't a premise that says that the two criticisms are mutually exclusive; that's just the implied effect of the actual premise.
  The gap there is really what they might be testing:
  We can agree with the author that "a statement cannot simultaneously be too specific and too vague", but that doesn't mean that the criticisms from the left and right contradict each other. They didn't criticize a statement for being too vague or too specific.
  They criticized legislation. It's certainly possible for the legislation to be both too specific and too vague. Obamacare (the overhaul of the U.S.'s health care system in 2009) was a 2000 page piece of legislation. You can imagine some people criticizing the wording on page 834 as being too vague and people criticizing the wording on page 1329 for being too specific.
  Finally, the author is acting like, "Because these two criticisms (supposedly, in my mind) can't both be true, we must have actually gotten the legislation just right".
  The author is acting like, "Since it can't be the case that both sides are correct, then neither side is correct". But what if one of the sides is correct and the other one is wrong?
  Maybe it's totally valid to say that the legislation is too specific (or to say it's too vague). If that's the case, then why would we agree that "it's framed just as it should be"?

label: Goal
body:
Look for an answer providing a missing link from the Evidence to the wording of "framed as it should be".
  Or, more likely, look for an answer ruling out one of our objections:
  - couldn't the legislation be too specific in some parts and too vague in other parts? Could both criticisms be true?
  - even if we granted that the criticisms were mutually exclusive (can't both be true), couldn't one of them be correct and the other wrong?

label: Conclusion (implied)
body: It's dumb that my company is installing software that blocks access to non-related websites.

label: Evidence
body: They say it's to prevent distractions, but windows and decorations in an office can also distract, and no one is saying people do their best work in a barren, windowless room.

label: Evaluate
body:
This argument does not seem like a good contender for turning into some Algebraic Recipe. It doesn't have any conditional logic or repeating symbols. It doesn't even have an explicit conclusion!
  Our author is rejecting a new policy and telling us that what the stated reason for that policy is (distractions prevent employees from their best work). The argument then attempts to show that this is hypocritical, by pointing to something else that would seem to qualify under that same rationale but somehow isn't thought of that way.

label: Goal
body:
Let's look for something like
  - they're planning to do X
  - they say it's because of rationale Y
  - but Y would apply to Z also, and no one is trying to apply Y in that situation.
  (Even though I'm using algebra loosely here, it's more about the gist of finding a rebuttal argument that feels like, "If you're going to use that logic here, then why aren't you also using it there?")

label: Conclusion
body: Some students taking French Literature 205 are not French Literature majors.

label: Evidence
body:
- Some students taking French Literature 205 are also taking Biology 218.
  - Every student taking Biology 218 is a bio major.

label: Evaluate
body:
This is a weird argument, since the Bio class kind of comes in out of left field, so it's hard to think about how we're going to use that fact to prove our conclusion, that some people are not French-Lit majors.
  We should start by focusing on the parallel between the first premise and the conclusion.
  Conclusion: some French Literature 205 are not French Literature majors.
  Premise: Some French Literature 205 are in Biology 218.
  We can see from this that our logic job is to get from "if you're in Biology 218, then you're not an French Literature major".
  We know one fact about being in Biology 218: "if you're in Biology 218, then you're a bio major".
  So we really need to close the gap between "if you're a bio major, then you're not a French Literature major". (that may seem like a self-justifying truth, but maybe you can be more than one major).

label: Statements
body:
```
  conditionals (must, nothing)
  Literary   →   Reveal something significant
  classic        about the human condition
  Unworthy of  →  Doesn't reveal anything
  serious study    significant about human condition
  ```

label: Evaluate
body:
Our goal in Inference questions is to try to combine 2 or more claims in order to derive some other thought. Here, there are only 2 claims, so we know which two to focus on.
  We otherwise use Overlapping Concepts as a signal about which claims we should try synthesizing. Here, both claims involve the concept of whether or not something "reveals anything significant about the human condition".
  On Must Be True, the most common pattern is to see conditional logic and need to chain it together with other conditional statements, or to have a conditional rule that we can apply to some provided fact.
  Here, both claims are conditional and they have an overlapping ingredient, so it's very likely they chain together. We use the conditional logic indicator words to help ourselves diagram the rules correctly.
  "Must" = introduces the right side of the arrow. "Must" indicates necessity, and the right side is called the necessary condition.
  "Nothing that is A is B" = "No A's are B" = "All A's are ~B"

label: Goal
body:
In order to chain these together we need to contrapose either rule. We end up with this chain.
  ```
  Literary   →  Reveals something  →  worthy
  classic       significant           serious study
  Unworthy      →  Not reveal      →  Not literary
  serious study    significant         classic
  ```
  The correct answer will likely connect the 1st to the 3rd idea. At least one incorrect answer will probably offer us an illegal reversal or negation of these relationships.

label: Conclusion
body: This belief must be abandoned (the T-Rex's big head, long legs, and tiny hands did not develop in order to deal with T-Rex's big size and weight).

label: Evidence
body: We found a skeleton of an earlier dinosaur that had the T-rex features but not the T-rex's big size and weight.

label: Evaluate
body:
This is a confusing argument to even understand at first. It's related to the logic of evolution. Scientists believed that the T-rex combo (big head, big legs, tiny hands) was an adaptation T-rex had to balance out its huge size and weight.
  However, if an earlier dinosaur (i.e. earlier on the evolutionary tree) had the T-rex combo but not the huge size and weight, then it suggests that the T-rex combo of features evolved as some other adaptation.
  This plays off the evolutionary common sense that you probably wouldn't see two very similar sets of physical features that were the result of very different needs. If we know that gills are an adaptation to breathing underwater, and then we find gills on a prehistoric creature, we probably wouldn't put much credence into the idea that "they developed gills as a way to ventilate heat in the desert".
  If we're going to weaken this argument, we need to defend the idea that the T-rex combo of features WAS an adaptation to its big size and weight.
  So the onus is on us to explain away what's going on with this skeleton that seems to have the T-rex features, even though it didn't need an adaptation for big size and weight.

label: Goal
body: Look for an answer that can "make an excuse" for this skeleton that looks like a counterexample, so that we can protect the original notion that T-rex's big head / big legs / small hands was an adaptation to balance out its big size and weight.

label: Conclusion (So)
body: Bliss currently has more viewers than any other program on television.

label: Evidence
body: YXK is the network with the highest overall number of viewers. And Bliss is the #1 show on YXK.

label: Evaluate
body:
We know from real life that the #1 most-watched show on the most-watched network does not have to necessarily be the #1 most-watched show overall. CBS had the highest overall number of viewers, and "Big Bang Theory" was the show on CBS that got the most viewers. But "Big Bang Theory" didn't get as many viewers as "Game of Thrones" on HBO.
  However, we need to abstract this. One thing that can help us is reminding ourselves that Parallel Flaw loves to test the 5 most common famous flaws (Necessary vs. Sufficient, Part vs. Whole, Causal, Unproven vs. Proven False, and Ad Hominem).
  When we notice that the premise and the conclusion are recycling the trait "most viewers", we might suspect Part vs. Whole.
  The network YXK, as a Whole, has more viewers than anything else, but that doesn't mean that Bliss, which is a Part of that network, has more viewers than anything else.

label: Goal
body:
Let's look for an argument that says,
  - This Whole is #1 overall
  - This Part is the #1 within that Whole
  - This Part is #1 overall

label: Principle
body:
```
  only if = necessary indicator, put on Right
  Contract valid → one party accepts
                   legit offer from the other
  if = sufficient indicator, put on Left
  Someone being made
  that offer would reasonably → not legit offer
  assume offer is in jest
  ```

label: Evaluate
body:
It's common to be given two Principles on Apply the Principle questions, but it's very rare the correct answer uses both principles. Each answer ends up being aimed at one rule or the other.
  We want to always arrange our rules so that the "judgy" term is on the right (like good / bad, unjustified / justified, should / should not, etc.).
  So we should contrapose that first rule, to get the judgy concept of valid / invalid on the right.
  ```
  neither party accepts → not valid
  a legit offer from the other contract
  ```
  We might notice that the concept of "legitimate offer" shows up in both rules. Does that allow us to chain those rules together? Yes, here it would!
  We could say something like,
  ```
  someone would not     a legit    not valid
  assume offer      →   offer   →  basis for
  is made in jest                  contract
  ```

label: Goal
body:
Although the answer might chain together both rules, if it's anything like 99% of Apply the Principle, it will use one of these rules. The Evidence part of the correct answer will match the trigger of one of the rules, and the Conclusion part of the answer will match the right side of that rule.
  Here are our two rules:
  ```
  1. Neither party accepts → not valid
  a legit offer from the other contract
  2. Someone being made
  that offer would reasonably → not legit offer
  assume offer is in jest
  ```
  As we look at each answer, we're going to scan for the conclusion. If the conclusion says "not valid", we'll use rule 1. If it says "not legit", we'll use rule 2. If it says anything other than those things, we'll toss it.

label: Conclusion (thus)
body: The ancestors of these iguana must have rafted on floating debris across the Pacific Ocean from the Americas.

label: Main Conclusion
body: There's no cause for alarm that our nation is in decline.

label: Evidence
body:
- These iguanas inhabit several islands near Australia and some related species in the Americas, but nowhere else.
  - These islands were formed after the supercontinent connecting South America and Australia split apart.

label: Evaluate
body:
The author is trying to solve a causal mystery here.
  Curious Fact ... How did we end up with this group of closely related iguana species in the Americas and in the islands of near Australia?
  Author's Explanation ... The ancestor of these iguanas lived on the American/Australian supercontinent. The supercontinent broke apart, and now there's a Pacific Ocean between the Americas and Australia. These islands later formed. Then, some iguanas from the American continent rafted across the Pacific Ocean on floating debris and landed at these islands near Australia, where the iguanas then proliferated into a local species.
  Quite a story, right? Don't skimp on the stage where you're articulating for yourself the causal story that the author is selling. There are often unsaid pieces to that story that we want to get high on our mental radar.

label: Goal
body:
As always, when we want to Weaken an Explain the Curious Fact argument, we go looking primarily for answers that
  - suggest an Alternate Explanation for the Curious Fact (how else could we have ended up with these related iguana species in the Americas / these islands and nowhere else)
  - undermine the plausibility of the Author's Explanation (what would make it seem less plausible that present day iguanas in those near-Australian islands got there by rafting on debris over the Pacific)

label: Conclusion (it must be)
body: The recently discovered tomb, the largest ever found, must be the tomb of Alexander the Great.

label: Intermediate Conclusion (so)
body: Alexander the Great would have had the largest tomb.

label: Intermediate Conclusion
body: Alexander the Great was the greatest Macedonian in history.

label: Evidence (after all)
body: He conquered an empire that stretched from Greece to much of Asia.

label: Evaluate
body:
Since this argument contains a couple Intermediate Conclusions, there are a few different reasoning moves we could impugn:
  Given that ... Alex conquered an empire from Greece to Asia,
  could we argue that ... he wasn't the greatest Macedonian?
  Maybe someone else conquered more. Maybe "amount of land conquered" isn't the most important factor to consider in ranking greatest Macedonians.
  Given that ... he was the greatest Macedonian
  could we argue that ... he wouldn't have had the largest tomb?
  Maybe their culture had a lot of humility surrounding death, and everyone was buried the same way. Maybe Alex was killed in the field of battle and wouldn't have had any tomb.
  Given that ... he would have had the largest tomb,
  could we argue that ... the recently discovered tomb isn't necessarily Alex's tomb?
  Maybe the recently discovered tomb isn't actually the largest tomb, just the largest one found so far. Maybe we'll discover an even bigger tomb someday.

label: Goal
body:
Given that this argument makes multiple reasoning moves, it has multiple vulnerabilities, so we'll have to just scrutinize each answer the way we always can on Flaw:
  1. is this answer descriptively true?
  2. if so, is this a complaint about the logic?

label: Conclusion (Thus)
body: Chu will probably defeat Lewis.

label: Evidence
body: The election is between Chu and Lewis. Chu is a prodevelopment candidate, whereas Lewis favors placing limits on development. Prodevelopment candidates have won in the last six mayoral elections.

label: Evaluate
body: Given that ... prodevelopment candidates have won the last six elections and that ... Chu is more pro-development than Lewis. How could we argue that ... Chu will probably not defeat Lewis? Maybe there's something super toxic about Chu that outweighs the positive that he's more prodevelopment than Lewis. Maybe something has changed in this election cycle that would make the electorate less likely to vote for a prodevelopment candidate. The argument is assuming, "If it was true in the last six elections, it will probably be true again", failing to consider that maybe Past ≠ Present. Maybe it's a total coincidence that the last six winners were prodevelopment. Maybe they won in spite of being pro-development, not because of it.

label: Goal
body: Find any answer that would allow us to diminish the author's evidence or to argue that Chu is not likely to win this election.

label: Evaluate
body: Since Rose only made two claims, we can just ask ourselves which of them Chester seemed to misinterpret. She said: Let's not see Winter Fields. Did Chester misconstrue that one? No. He's correctly processing that. He's saying, "what? You do not want to see that movie? Just based on that review?" She also said: I caught a review in the local paper. Did Chester misconstrue that? Did he think that she meant caught, like a baseball that was thrown in your direction, rather than caught like "read"? No, he seems to think she read a review, not grabbed an airborne review out of the air with her catcher's mitt. Finally, Rose said: It was the worst review I've read in years. Did Chester misconstrue that? Yes. She means by "worst review" = one of the most negative, scathing evaluations of a movie. I haven't seen a movie reviewer hate a movie that much in years. Chester, meanwhile, thinks she means by "worst review" = wow that a poorly executed review by that movie critic. I've seen critics ineptly write a review, but this was the worst I've seen. It was written more poorly then anything I've read in years. How do we know this is his interpretation? It's because he says, "nothing in that paper is particularly well-written". She, of course, was never talking about how well-written the movie review was, so this comment will puzzle her. But he heard her saying, "The review of this movie was so poorly written that I don't think we should see the movie." He's like, "Why does it matter how bad of a writer the movie critic is? Why would that stop you from seeing a movie? By the way, that newspaper sucks overall, so I expect badly written stuff."

label: Goal
body: Look for "worst review".

label: Enrique's Claims
body: 1. The transit authority doesn't have enough money to operate for the next 12 months without cutting service or increasing fares. 2. The federal govt. has so far failed to provide additional funding. 3. The transit authority should keep operating w/o service cuts or fare increases until it runs out of money. 4. One it's run out of money, the federal govt. will provide funding to save it.

label: Warrington's Response
body: Studying classical works is definitely crucial to a liberal arts education, but you don't need a classics department to make that happen. Other departments often engage in that study.

label: Cynthia's Responses
body: 1. no comment. 2. no comment. 3. Disagrees. Cynthia seems to be arguing that the transit authority should not just keep the status quo and let themselves run out of money. 4. Disagrees. Cynthia isn't saying it's impossible that the federal govt. will swoop in and provide funding, but she says it's more probably that it will just let the authority go out of business.

label: Goal
body: Let's look for an answer dealing with claim 3 or claim 4.

label: Conclusion (it must be)
body: Aerobic exercise has a significant beneficial effect on people's health.

label: Evidence (since)
body: Other surveys in addition to one in a leading medical journal in the early 1970s have found that the more frequently people engaged in aerobic exercise, the lower their risk of lung disease tended to be.

label: Evaluate
body: Since the evidence is presenting a Correlation (the more X, the more there tends to be Y) and the conclusion is suddenly moving to Causation (X has a significant beneficial effect on Y), we can use our Explain Curious Fact framework. Curious Fact ... Why do these studies find a correlation between more frequent aerobic exercise and lower risk of lung disease? Author's Explanation ... Aerobic exercise is having a beneficial effect on people's health, thereby causing their risk of lung disease to be lessened. We always evaluate this framework by asking 1. Could there be some Alternate Explanation for the curious fact? 2. How plausible is the Author's Explanation? When we encounter arguments like this one where the author says, "X and Y are correlated. Therefore, X causes Y", we reflexively consider the two alternate explanations that LSAT loves to test: - what if it's Reverse Cause? What if Y causes X? In this case, that means what if having lung disease (or the precursors of lung disease) causes people to not partake of aerobic exercise? - what if there's some 3rd Factor? What if Z causes X and Y? In this case, that means what if there is some causal factor that both explains why someone does a lot of aerobic exercise and explains why they have lower risk of heart disease (or a factor that explains why people don't exercise and do have lower risk of heart disease).

label: Goal
body: On Flaw and Weaken, we're unlikely to see answers that make the author's hypothesis seem implausible. We're much more likely to see answers that deal with the existence of Alternative Explanations for the curious fact. On Flaw, we can simply point out that the author has illegally convinced herself that a correlation indicates a causal relationshp. Or we can raise the possibility of an alternate explanation (such as reverse cause or 3rd factor).

label: Conclusion (they concluded)
body: The genetic defect increases the likelihood of herniated disks.

label: Evidence
body: 5 of 100 people who had disk problems had a defect in gene X. 0 of 100 people who didn't have disk problems had a defect in gene X.

label: Evaluate
body: This argument is a little weird, because 95 of the 100 people who had disk problems did not have any issues with gene X. But the author's thought is that, "If messed up gene X showed up among people with back problems but not among people without back problems, then a messed up gene X must relate to back problems." The author isn't arguing that everyone with back problems has a messed up gene X, just that it increases the likelihood of herniated disks.

label: Goal
body: We can strengthen this by ruling out an alternate explanation for why the 5 (of 200) people who had messed up gene X were all people with herniated disks (i.e. rule out the idea that having a herniated disk can cause gene X to be messed up / rule out the idea that some 3rd factor is causing both a deformed gene X and a herniated back). We can also strengthen this by making it seem more plausible that this genetic defect increases likelihood of a herniated disk (more data points where the defect and the herniated disks go together).

label: Evidence
body:
The only vehicles that have high resale value are those that are well maintained.
```
High Resale → Well Maintained
```

label: Conclusion
body:
Any vehicle that is well maintained has a high resale value.
```
Well Maintained → High Resale
```

label: Evaluate
body: This argument just presents a conditional premise (A → B) and then illegally concludes that the reverse would be true (B → A). (country accent) We call that the famous Necessary vs. Sufficient flaw around these here parts. "the only" is a sufficient indicator that means "put this idea on the LEFT of the arrow". It's more common cousins, "only if" and "only" are necessary indicators that mean "put this idea on the RIGHT side of the arrow". "any" is a sufficient (LEFT side) indicator, just like all other universals (e.g. all, each, every, none)

label: Goal
body: Let's look for an answer that presents a conditional premise and then offers a conclusion that is just the illegal reversal of that conditional rule.

label: Rita's 1st Claim
body: No matter how you look at your survey results, they are misleading. Does Hiro argue that there is a non-misleading way to look at the survey results? Yes! Hiro says that "the relative rates those numbers [on my survey] represent are probably close to being accurate". So we have potentially found the correct answer here, with this first claim.

label: Rita's 2nd Claim
body: People generally lie on surveys of this type. Does Hiro argue that people don't generally lie on surveys of this type? No, he seems to agree with this claim. He says, "I have no doubt that people lie on surveys of this type".

label: Rita's 3rd Claim
body: The numbers you collected are serious underestimates. Does Hiro argue that his numbers aren't serious underestimates? No, he seems to agree because he says, "The raw numbers surely underestimate what I'm trying to measure".

label: Evaluate / Goal
body: If we hadn't found an explicit claim (Rita's 1st) that Hiro was disagreeing with, then we wuld start to fish around for things that Rita was assuming that maybe Hiro disagreed with, but since we already have an explicit contender, we can head to the answers. We're looking for whether or not there's a way to look at these survey results that is not misleading. Or, to put that more in Hiro's language, whether or not the relative rates the underestimated numbers represent still present a fairly accurate picture.

label: Lopez's Conclusion
body: Our university isn't committed to liberal arts.

label: Lopez's Evidence
body: It decided to close the classics department, and the study of classical antiquity has been crucial to the liberal arts since the Renaissance.

label: Evaluate
body: Our job is to characterize the type of rebuttal or response Warrington offered. We can consider the Big 8 repertoire of Method answers (the most common structures they test): - analogy - counter/example for general claim - implications of logic - ruling out alternatives - suggesting alternate explanation - calling out a dubious assumption - raising an overlooked consideration - making a definition or distinction. If we were choosing from this list (we don't need to), we would probably go with "raising an overlooked consideration" or "making a distinction". Warrington is saying to Lopez, "Chill out, dude, they're not getting rid of the study of classical antiquity. It'll still be taught by other departments."

label: Goal
body: Raising the overlooked consideration that the study of classical works will still be done in other departments helps Warrington to make a distinction between "getting rid of the classic department" and "getting rid of the study of classical works". Let's pick any answer that we can match to the text.

label: Decision
body: Ted should not be replaced.

label: Evidence
body: It's obvious to everyone that Ted makes some valuable, unique, and perhaps irreplaceable contributions.

label: Evaluate
body:
Usually for Strengthen-Principle questions, we just predict an "If Premise, then Conclusion" link, so in this case that would be something like
```
if X obviously makes some valuable, unique,
or perhaps irreplaceable contributions
  → then you shouldn't request that X be replaced
```
However, the final claim is prefaced by Nevertheless signaling the tension of Tatiana deciding to keep Ted, given that we were told he does have some deficits in his performance that other coworkers have to work harder to compensate for. When we're doing Strengthen-Principle and we see that the argument is wrestling with a positive and a negative, then the answer will often feel more like it's Weighing Tradeoffs.

label: Goal
body: Look for the linking idea we predicted, or look for something saying the positives of Ted (valuable, unique, possibly irreplaceable contributions) outweigh the negatives (a deficit in performance that other coworkers have to work harder to make up for).

label: Given that ...
body: Camouflage helps some species elude predation

label: How can it be that
body: Some prey species with few or no other adaptations to elude predation have endured for a while with black-and-white coloration that seems unlikely to provide effective camouflage?

label: Evaluate / Goal
body: I'm gonna level with you right away. This is maybe Top 3 of my least favorite problems. I think it's hot garbage from top to bottom. So take this explanation as, "Here's how LSAC might try to explain this", but it does not represent me condoning it. Based on the paragraph I would have been thinking, "Given that these species have coloration that wouldn't provide camouflage, how have they endured for a long time?" And so I would be looking for an answer that explained how they could survive for a long time, given that they have generally ineffective camouflage and few or no other adaptations. But apparently LSAC wanted us to be thinking, "Given that the black-and-white coloration seems unlikely to provide camouflage, how is it that in reality it is providing camouflage?"

label: Statements
body: Saying "I tried to get my work done on time" doesn't actually mean that the person failed to get their work on time, but that is what the speaker is trying to convey. Had they gotten their work done on time, they would have said "I got my work done on time". This is typical of how conversation works.

label: Evaluate
body: This is a very odd Inference stimulus. There don't seem to be any of the usual wording clues that suggest where they might want to go with this (conditional / causal / pivots / math-y stuff). We're basically just hearing that it's typical in conversation for the implied meaning to be different from the literal meaning. Someone who did get their work done on time could also truthfully say, "they tried to get their work done on time", because "to try" means you applied intention and effort, which would clearly be true of anyone who completed their work.

label: Goal
body: Let's just look for a safely-worded claim that can be supported by the fact that "it's typical that we mean something different from what our statements literally convey".

label: Conclusion (clearly)
body: The recently passed highway bill is very unpopular with voters.

label: Evidence (after all)
body: Poll predict that the majority party, which supported the bill's passage, will lose more than a dozen seats in the upcoming election.

label: Evaluate
body: The author is concluding a causal hypothesis for a Curious Fact: why is the majority party expected to lose more than a dozen seats in the upcoming election? He is positing this Explanation: the majority party supported the highway bill's passage, people don't like this bill, they blame the majority party, and they plan to vote out people belonging to the majority party as electoral punishment for this bad bill. Whenever author's are trying to Explain a Curious Fact, we look at two different pressure points: 1. Could there be some Alternate Explanation for why the majority party is expected to lose more than a dozen seats? (maybe there was a census and after re-districting, there aren't as many voting districts that favor that party / maybe the majority party started an unpopular war or caused a recession or botched a pandemic response) 2. How plausible is the Author's Explanation? (did anyone ever express displeasure with the highway bill? are voters aware of it? do voters blame the majority party for it, or was it a bi-partisan measure supported by both parties?)

label: Goal
body: Usually Flaw is much more concerned with the potential for Alternate Explanations. The essence of the famous Causal flaw is that an author is simply too sure of his causal explanation, when other causal explanations could potentially exist.

label: Statements
body: Scanning for Conditional, Math-y, Causal, or Comparative wording, I don't see anything screaming out to me. So I would just take two read-throughs (the 2nd one going slow enough to feel like I understood every claim) and then head to the answers. Every claim is hedged somewhat: - Songwriter's get much of their money from radio play - only a fraction of Songwriter's have hits, even fewer have several - Songwriter's with hits are often asked to write for movies - those Songwriter's sometimes decline. There's a mathematical aspect to how you get paid as a songwriter: - hit song on radio, get paid for each play - hit song from movie on radio, got paid an upfront fee. And there's a causal idea related to this — because of this payment structure, writers of hit songs often decline to write songs for movie sound tracks.

label: Evaluate
body: The only place where I sense a possible synthesis would be when hit songwriters "sometimes" decline to write songs for movie sound tracks, because of the payment structure. They are presumably thinking they'll make less money getting paid up front (for this eventual hit song) than they would if they just released it straight to the radio (where the songwriter is paid for each play). But this feels a little speculative, and this is a Must Be True.

label: Goal
body: With 8 or 9 different claims, there's too much here to have a strong prediction of what the answer will be. So let's just "try on" each answer, asking ourselves whether we could possibly derive this info from only the provided information.

label: Conclusion
body: Robert's debate performance was as good as Britta's.

label: Evidence
body: Sure Britta's command of historical facts was better and so that gave people the impression that Britta won. But we should also consider how reasonable the arguments were, regardless of whether factual support was provided.

label: Evaluate
body: Okay, let's consider how reasonable the arguments were: were Robert's arguments more reasonable? The author seems to be assuming yes. If Robert doesn't have an advantage in that category, then Britta's advantage in the "command of facts" category would make her the winner. The author also has to assume that winning the "reasonableness" category can tie you with someone who won the "command of the facts" category (the fact that each of them would win one category doesn't mean that Robert's performance was as good, if we weight the importance of command of the facts higher than we weight the importance of reasonableness).

label: Goal
body: Look for an answer pointing out the author's assumption that Robert's arguments were more reasonable than Britta's. Or look for a defender answer that sounds like, "Being more factual does not count for more than does being more reasonable, when it comes to judging debate performance".

label: Statements
body:
To create a new kind of atom, we often try to fuse together two existing ones.
  - conditional (must):
```
Fusion of two existing atoms into a new one
  → collide fast enough to overcome electromagnetic force of atoms repelling each other
```
  - pivot (but), conditional (if):
```
they collide super fast → new atom is very hot
```
  - volume dial (the more X, the more Y):
```
the hotter the atom, the greater the chance is immediately splits apart
```

label: Evaluate
body: There are two conditionals that have some overlap (in the sense that both of them are talking about atoms colliding and the energy of the collision). But the symbols there aren't a match, so we can't chain the conditionals together. There's also a big conspicuous pivot: But, so we want to think about how to reconcile what comes before and after that pivot. For two different atoms to fuse together, the collision has to be fast enough to overcome electromagnetic force. But if it's too fast, then the new atom will be super hot and might split apart again into the two constituent atoms.

label: Goal
body: It's hard to predict where this is headed, but we might see an answer saying, "Physicists have to dial in the collision speed to the sweet spot, where it's energetic enough to overcome electromagnetic force but not so energetic that the new atom is super heated and splits apart again.

label: Conclusion
body: I disagree (the fact that Simpson has no background in the oil industry doesn't prove he's not a viable CEO of Pod Oil). In other words, someone with no background in the oil industry could still be a viable candidate for CEO of Pod Oil.

label: Evidence
body: An oil background is no guarantee of success; for example, the last CEO had an oil background and was terrible.

label: Evaluate
body: Galindo's first comment seems to imply that Fremont was thinking that "a background in oil is a guarantee of success". But Fremont certainly never argued that. Fremont is probably thinking "an oil background" is a minimum requirement, not a sufficient guarantee of success.

label: Goal
body: Look for an answer pointing out that Galindo implicitly accuses F of a position that F never espoused (this is called Straw Man), or an answer that says "even if people with backgrounds in oil can still be crappy CEO's, it might still be true that people without backgrounds in oil can't be successful CEO's).

label: Conclusion (hence)
body: Lightning discharge data can sometimes be our only reliable indicator of the altitude of ash clouds.

label: Evidence
body: Weather radar can measure the altitude of ash clouds, but it is not available in all parts of the world. Lightning discharges from an ash cloud can happen once the top of the cloud passes an altitude of 5 km.

label: Evaluate
body: The conclusion has some really strong wording, "our only reliable indicator". Why can't we use anything but lightning discharge data to measure the altitude of ash clouds sometimes? The only thing close to a reason we heard was that weather radar isn't available in all parts of the world. Okay, then we're assuming a few things - lightning discharge data is available in those parts of the world - lightning discharge data is a reliable indicator of altitude (even though it can't measure anything until the ash cloud gets at least 5km high) - no other method is available to measure the altitude of ash clouds (in those areas where weather radar isn't available)

label: Goal
body: Look for one of our anticipated assumptions, or pick an any answer that, if negated, would badly weaken the argument.

label: Statements
body:
conditionals: if (left side)
```
standards committee has quorum → general assembly begins at 6pm
awards committee has quorum → general assembly beings at 7pm
```

label: Evaluate
body:
When we get multiple conditionals, we look to see whether they chain together or get triggered by any available facts. There aren't any facts in this stimulus. Do these two rules have any overlapping ideas? Yes, they both talk about the General Assembly. Would we chain them? Yes, since the outcome of either rule triggers the contrapositive of the other.
```
stnd comm has quorum → gen assem @ 6pm → ~awards comm quorum
```
If the General Assembly begins at 6pm, then it doesn't begin at 7pm, and vice versa. This one could probably be thought of more intuitively, without diagramming. Since these two rules have contradictory outcomes, they certainly can't both happen. It is mutually exclusive that the standards committee and Awards committee have a quorum.

label: Goal
body:
Look for an answer saying
```
standards has quorum → ~awards committee has quorum
awards has quorum → ~standards committee has quorum
```
(remember that it's possible that neither of them have a quorum)

label: Paradox
body: Normally, higher credit score = less default risk. Makes sense — credit scores measure how reliably people pay debts. But for mortgage loans specifically, the very top scorers default more than everyone else. That's the puzzle.

label: Evaluate
body: The credit score isn't suddenly broken — it still predicts well at lower score ranges and for non-mortgage loans. So something must be unique about high-score mortgage borrowers. One natural possibility: lenders treat top-scoring mortgage applicants differently. If the credit score is so high that the lender just stamps "approved" without checking other risk factors (job stability, debt-to-income, savings), then any hidden risks fly under the radar. Those hidden risks then show up as defaults.

label: Goal
body: Find the answer that gives a reason top-scoring mortgage applicants get less scrutiny — letting hidden risks through.

label: Conclusion (So)
body: It appears that we understand the analytical capabilities of our minds much better than we understand our senses.

label: Evidence
body: Computers can defeat chess champions, but cannot see. Computer modeling of reasoning tasks is way easier than computer modeling of sense images.

label: Evaluate
body: The language we're trying to prove in the Conclusion is "we understand X much better than we do Y". We weren't given a rule by which to judge whether we understand one thing better than another, so the correct answer will have to supply us with a rule for why we would understand one thing better than another. The reference to "analytical capabilities" in the conclusion seems intended as a callback to "chess" and "reasoning tasks". The reference to "our senses" seems intended as a callback to "seeing" and "processing of sense images". Why would our author be thinking we understand that first threesome better than we do that second threesome? There are two comparative advantages mentioned: - computer modeling of A is far easier than that of B - computers can beat humans at A but can't accomplish B.

label: Goal
body:
So they've provided us two different launchpads in the Evidence, that can potentially get us to the landing zone in the Conclusion.
```
If computer modeling of A is much easier than computer modeling of B
  → Then we understand A much better than we understand B
```
or
```
If computers can beat humans at A but computers can't even do B
  → Then we understand A much better than we understand B
```

label: Conclusion
body: Aboriginal people in Canada built birchbark canoes 5,000 years ago.

label: Evidence
body: We found tools from 5,000 years ago that are like Aboriginal tools used in recent times to make birchbark canoes. And we found the tools near a river that offered easy access to the all the ingredients of a birchbark canoe.

label: Evaluate
body: Since the author is interpreting the significance behind these found copper tools from 5,000 years ago, we can use our Explain Curious Fact mindset. Curious Fact - what were these 5000 year old tools all about? Author's Explanation - they were used by Aboriginal people to make birchbark canoes. We always evaluate these arguments by asking two questions: - how else could we explain the curious fact? - how plausible is the author's hypothesis? What could be an alternate explanation for these 5,000 year old copper tools? Maybe they were used for something other than canoe-making. Maybe they were used by somebody other than the Aboriginal people. How plausible is the author's story? Pretty good. The Aboriginal people nowadays use tools like these to make birchbark canoes, and the tools were found in an area that had access to all the raw materials for birchbark canoe-making.

label: Goal
body: We're assuming that the Aboriginal people have been making canoes with tools like these for 5,000 years or more (they didn't just recently develop this habit of using these tools to make birchbark canoes). We're assuming that the tools we found were used by people who were from this area, where the raw materials were found. Tough to predict an answer; we can just remind ourselves that the correct answer, if negated, will be an objection to the idea that these tools show us that Aboriginals were making birchbark canoes 5,000 years ago.

label: Conclusion
body: Subsequent instructions on Mesmosis videos are extremely effective.

label: Evidence
body: To be effective, instructions given to the subconscious must be repeated many times.

label: Intermediate Conclusion
body: For the listener, it's as though those subsequent instructions have been repeated 1,000 times.

label: Evidence (because)
body: Once a hypnotic state has been induced, the first instruction given to the listener's subconscious is to experience each subsequent instruction as if it had actually been repeated 1,000 times.

label: Evaluate
body: The 2nd sentence of the argument is a conditional, "X must occur in order for Y to happen". Whenever we see a Flaw question that has a conditional logic premise, we want to immediately be on guard for the #1 Famous Flaw Necessary vs. Sufficient. This rule says: Effective → Repeated Many Times. An argument committing the Nec vs. Suff flaw would proceed to argue via an Illegal Reversal (This thing repeats many times. Thus, it must be effective) or via an Illegal Negation (This thing isn't effective. Thus, it must not repeat many times). This argument does do the former. It attempts to establish that Mesmosis provides instructions that are "repeated" 1,000 times. And it then concludes that those instructions are very effective. So we could definitely bust this author on assuming that a condition required for effectiveness (repeated many times) is also sufficient for effectiveness. But there's another Famous Flaw lurking in here too, the much more rare Self Contradiction, or at least Self-Undermining. We are told that a direction to the subconscious is effective only if it's repeated many times. If it's not repeated many times, then it's not effective. The Mesmosis videos hypnotize someone and then issue an initial command (seemingly only once): interpret each command that follows as though you've heard it 1,000 times. Well according to the author's own provided rule, since the initial command isn't repeated many times, we have no reason to think that it will be effective, so we have no reason to think that people will actually treat subsequent instructions like they've been said 1,000 times.

label: Goal
body: Look for an answer calling out the Necessary vs. Sufficient conflation, or look for an answer calling out the fact that the author's own provided rule undermines the scheme by which these videos are supposed to work.

label: Conclusion
body: Caligula was not a cruel and insane tyrant.

label: Intermediate Conclusion
body: The proportion of children who are obese cannot have gone up much over the last 8 years.

label: Evaluate
body: The two big questions I would have for this author's evidence are 1. How much documentation do you expect to have from the time period of an ancient Roman emperor, or how much do you expect from an emperor if they were cruel and insane? Is it possible that Caligula did crazy mean stuff, but whatever documentation there was has just been lost to the sands of time? Do we have ample documentation of his reign suggesting that he was a normal emperor? If we have almost no documentation of his reign at all, then that doesn't really seem like evidence one way or the other. Is it possible that, were he to be cruel and insane, he might have aggressively prosecuted anyone who was attempting to document his cruelty? 2. The fact that the surviving histories are written by his enemies doesn't mean they're false histories. If Caligula were as cruel and insane as alleged, then wouldn't he have tons of enemies? Thus, it might be that any history from the period (but for that of his most ardent loyalists) is going to sound like, "This Caligula guy was nuts!"

label: Goal
body: We either want to rule out one of these objections or find an answer that supplies more plausibility to the idea that Caligula was not cruel and insane.

label: Given That ...
body: there's a plan to build on land that lies under 5m of water, and there's a local subpopulation of dolphins, who only live in water under 30m of water, and currently live in an area bounded on on side by land and everywhere else by water

label: How Can We Say That ....
body: Building on this land will not reduce the habitat area available to those dolphins?

label: Evaluate / Goal
body: We know the dolphins' habitat area is basically all the stuff less than 30m but not land. This building area is going to claim all of that underwater area that's less than 5m deep. So if we're trying to say that we're not stealing habitat area, we either have to find an answer that says we're balancing out the underwater area we're snatching with some new habitable area for the dolphins, or we need to say that the under 5m parcel of underwater land we're snatching was not really part of the dolphins' habitable area in the first place.

label: Evidence
body:
(conditional: all)
```
Popular television series and groundbreaking → critically acclaimed
```
(fact: not all A's are B = some A's are ~B)
Some popular television series are not critically acclaimed

label: Conclusion
body: Some popular television series are not groundbreaking

label: Evaluate
body:
This is a valid argument. Since there is a conditional and some quantifiers (not all / some) and some repeating ideas (groundbreaking / popular television series / critically acclaimed), we probably want to diagram this.
```
Any A that is B is C.        A and B → C
Not all A's are C.           Some A's are ~C
So, Not all A's are B        Some A's are ~B
```

label: Goal
body: The number one thing to look for is a conditional that has an "and" or a qualifier "Any A that is B". If we find it, the conclusion should be saying "Not all A are B".

label: Evidence
body: Tilapia fillets lack the strong fishy taste that many people find objectionable.

label: Conclusion
body: Eating tilapia fillets is a perfect choice for those who want the benefits of eating fish but do not care for the taste of fish.

label: Evaluate
body: This argument doesn't gift us with any clear premise indicators or conclusion indicators, but we can use the context and content of the statements to understand the role that each statement plays. The first sentence describing what nutritionists recommend looks like a statement of fact. So does the final sentence about the taste of tilapia. The middle sentence contains a value judgement, calling tilapia a "perfect choice." The final sentence also seems to be acting as support for this middle sentence. All of this taken together indicates that the middle sentence is the conclusion. It's useful to notice that the conclusion makes a claim about both taste and the benefits of eating tilapia, but the evidence only discusses the taste of tilapia compared to other fish. We aren't given any evidence about the benefits of eating tilapia compared to other fish. This argument is based on an incomplete comparison. There's no evidence supporting the claim that tilapia provides the same benefit as other fish.

label: Goal
body: A correct answer might highlight the argument's lack of evidence about the benefits of tilapia compared to other fish. But we should keep an open mind, since a correct answer might weaken the argument in a different way that we haven't predicted. Beware of answers that actually strengthen the argument.

label: Conclusion (therefore)
body: It's likely that language developed primarily to facilitate animal domestication.

label: Evidence
body: Domesticating animals is a cooperate activity, and cooperative activities requires a sophisticated means of communication.

label: Evaluate
body: The author's evidence definitely establishes that the evolution of sophisticated language was primarily driven by a need / desire to domesticate animals. But there are presumably other human activities that are also cooperative and would also require sophisticated communication: (agriculture, hunting, building cities, sorting out ethical rules, etc.) Who knows which of those came first or which would be considered the primary reason that language developed?

label: Goal
body: The author seems to be treating one possible thing that could have been the driving force behind developing language as though that thing likely is the primary reason we developed language. Or we could object by saying something besides domesticating animals was the primary / earlier reason we developed language.

label: Conclusion (thus)
body: Using others as a means to one's own ends is not always morally reprehensible or harmful to others.

label: Evidence
body: Many employers treat their employees fairly.

label: Evaluate
body: What a weird, sparse argument. First, let's focus on our burden of proof if we're trying to prove a claim that Doing X is not always Y or Z. To prove this claim, we just need at least one example in which X is done, but neither Y nor Z happen. So this author has to establish - Person A used Person B as a means to A's ends - B was not harmed - this was not morally reprehensible. In the author's example of employers treating employees fairly, has she established any of these things? No.

label: Goal
body: Look for an answer saying, in these cases of employers treating employees fairly, - the employer was using the employee as a means to their ends - the employee was not harmed - this arrangement was not morally reprehensible

label: Intermediate Conclusion (this shows that)
body: The anxious tone of the essays is due to the psychological state of the writers, not the actual condition of the nation.

label: Evidence
body: There are essays that seem to show that our nation is in decline.

label: Evaluate
body: This should strike us as a pretty weird argument. People have written essays offering arguments that seem to show that our nation is in decline. This author is saying, 'We don't need to worry about these essays. There's nothing wrong with our nation. These essays sound alarmist just because the writers are psychologically disturbed." Where's your evidence for that buddy? Why should we just believe that these writers are overly pessimistic alarmists? You're just asking us to take your word for it?

label: Goal
body: Let's look for an answer complaining that this is a totally unfair way to dismiss an argument. If I write an essay showing that our environment is in decline because of global warming, citing the massive loss of over 50% of species, and describing the tens of millions of climate refugees we'll have when the oceans rise a foot or two, can this guy just say, "There's no cause for alarm. Patrick is just an anxious person"? Of course not.

label: Conclusion (probably = Opinion)
body: Eating turmeric probably helps prevent Alzheimer's disease.

label: Evidence (X, furthermore Y)
body: More turmeric per capita is consumed in India than in the rest of the world, and India's rate of Alzheimer's is much lower than the global average. Also, Alzheimer's is characterized by the buildup of amyloid protein plaques in the brain, and studies have found that a compound in turmeric (curcumin) reduces that amyloid plaque buildup.

label: Evaluate
body: Well this argument is already pretty strong! The last sentence gives a Causal Mechanism explanation of how turmeric could plausibly impact Alzheimer's. The 2nd sentence gives us a Correlation to Causation type piece of evidence. There's a strong correlation in India of turmeric consumption and low rate of Alzheimer's, but we don't know for sure that this means one causes the other. We could use our Explain Curious Fact framework: Curious Fact ... Why do people in India have higher than average turmeric consumption and lower than average Alzheimer's? Author's Explanation ... The turmeric consumption is lowering their risk of Alzheimer's, because the curcumin in turmeric reduces the amyloid plaque buildup that characterizes Alzheimer's.

label: Goal
body: We could strengthen this argument by ruling out an Alternate Explanation for why India has a lower rate of Alzheimer's. Or we can strengthen by adding to the plausibility of the author's explanation, that eating turmeric helps to prevent Alzheimer's.

label: Conclusion (Therefore)
body: It's best to let small fires burn.

label: Evidence
body: Relatively frequent, small fires clear out small trees and forest debris, which, if allowed to accumulate, would create the conditions for large, devastating fires.

label: Evaluate
body: When we read the arguments on a Main Conclusion or Role question, we know that 90% of the time the conclusion will be the First Sentence or some Rebuttal / Pivot idea. But here we have the leftover 10% where they just put the conclusion in the final claim and even announce it with a conclusion indicator, Therefore. This argument is still a Rebuttal, so there's also an implicit conclusion going against the original position. Implicit Rebuttal Conclusion: The Forestry Dept is doing its job properly sometimes when they don't extinguish a forest fire as soon as possible. why is that? Because it's best to let small fires burn. why is that? Because frequently small fires just clear out debris and make large, devastating fires less likely.

label: Goal
body: We're being asked about that second to last sentence, which is the author's premise, supporting the conclusion that "it's best to let small fires burn" (which then supports the implicit the conclusion that the Forestry Department may be doing its job properly even if it doesn't put out a forest fire as soon as possible).

label: Gerald's Claims
body: 1. If a consumer doesn't secure their home wifi network, then anyone strolling by is able to access that service with their laptop or smartphone. 2. Such use cannot be considered illegal under current laws. 3. It wouldn't be considered trespassing, just like it wouldn't be considered trespassing to walk by someone's house and enjoy the music you hear coming out of their window.

label: Kendra's Responses
body: 1. No comment. 2. Possible Disagree? She seems to argue that stopping to use someone's wifi could be considered loitering or harassment, both of which can be considered illegal. 3. Definitely disagrees with analogy. She might agree that it's not trespassing, but she doesn't think the hearing music analogy is solid, because it omits the crucial difference that with hearing music you keep strolling whereas with using someone's wifi, you actually stop for a considerable length of time right outside their house.

label: Evaluate / Goal
body: The areas of disagreement are whether or not stopping to use someone's wifi could be considered illegal (like loitering or harassment), as well as whether or not it's fair to compare using someone's wifi to listening to the music that is playing inside their house.

label: Curious Fact
body: How come, over the past 1000 years, plant species native to islands have gone extinct at a much faster rate than those native to mainland regions.

label: Biologists' Explanation
body: Mainland plants have evolved defenses against being eaten by large land mammals, whereas island plants have not, since large land mammals don't show up on islands until after an island is colonized by humans.

label: Evaluate
body: The two pressure points for any Explain Curious Fact argument are 1. Alternate Explanations for the curious fact 2. the Plausibility of the Author's Explanation. We can strengthen such an argument by ruling out an alternative explanation or by increasing the plausibility of the explanation offered by the author. On Strengthen questions (especially those whose question stem asks us to strengthen explanation / hypothesis), the correct answer is much more likely to increase plausibility. The most common form of that type of answer is "Where the cause was absent, the effect was absent" (i.e. No Cause / No Effect data points). The author thinks that "not being exposed to large land mammals until more recent time" caused island plants to go extinct more quickly. So a No Cause / No Effect answer could sound like, "On islands where large land mammals have lived for a long time, the plant species haven't gone extinct as much".

label: Evidence
body: There was only a 1 pound increase in children's average weight over the last 8 years.

label: Goal
body: Let's look for anything that corroborates this idea that islands don't have large land mammals until humans show up. Once humans show up with large land mammals, those land mammals eat the plants into extinction (sooner than the plants can evolve defense mechanisms).

label: Given That ...
body: Music aids memory and that Jokes, like music, elicit an emotional response

label: Why is it That ...
body: Jokes are usually very difficult to remember.

label: Evaluate
body: When we're doing Fill in the Blank (aka Logical Completion), we check to see whether the word prefacing the blank is expecting a Conclusion or a Supporting claim. The blank is prefaced by SINCE, and since/because always indicate supporting claims. That means this could be Strengthen or Paradox, depending on whether we're supporting a Conclusion or a Surprising Idea, respectively. Because the previous claim begins with HOWEVER, we know we're supporting some Surprising Idea.

label: Goal
body: We need a distinction between music and jokes that will allow us to explain how even though music/jokes are similar on one level, there's a reason why music aids memory and jokes don't.

label: Statements
body: TikTok (sorry, can we just call it that?) was the first fingered animal. But having fingers wouldn't have made TikTok stand out as a weirdo, because there were so many variations in species that every fish had some wacky adaptation. However, TikTok's fingers were probably a very important step in animal evolution because later land animals that had fingers probably trace back to TikTok.

label: Evaluate
body: Did we see anything Conditional, Causal, Math-y, or Comparative? We saw some comparative language (and we had a Pivot). TikTok was different in the sense that he had fingers but similar in the sense that he had some unusual variation to him. There's something vaguely causal in the last sentence that makes it seem like TikTok is causally linked to the evolution of fingers in many land animals.

label: Goal
body: This seems like one where I would have little to no idea what they want us to say, so we'll just read it a second time and then go to the answers, being wary of strong language, new concepts, or unknown comparisons.

label: Gabriella's Claims
body: 1. The government has raised interest rates 2. Doing so caused people to borrow less money. 3. Borrowing less money caused less spending. 4. Less spending slowed down the economy

label: Ivan's Responses
body: 1. Implicitly agrees ("the government's action") 2. No comment. Ivan thinks that the government's action did not cause the slowdown, but he doesn't say anything to let us know which part of this causal chain he thinks is off. 3. No comment (same as #2) 4. Ivan implicitly agrees that the economy has slowed down, but thinks that a global slowdown is what caused this country's slowdown.

label: Evaluate
body: Ivan doesn't seem to object to any specific claim Gabriella makes. As he says, he disagrees with her overall analysis. He doesn't think the government's move to raise interest rates is the principal cause of the economic slowdown. She implicitly does, because she lays out a causal chain that starts with the government's raising of interest rates and ends with the economic slowdown.

label: Goal
body: The answer will probably sound like whether the government's action to raise interest rates should be blamed for the recent economic slowdown (vs. whether it was caused by a global slowdown).

label: Statements
body: In a play, Demosthenes starts reading a tablet with a prophecy on it, from an oracle. Demosthenes's buddy can see the amazement on Demosthenes's face and is like, "What is it? What is it?" So, Demosthenes tells his buddy what's up.

label: Evaluate
body: This is an odd question stem, but the idea of , "Based on the paragraph, which of these answers can be most justifiably rejected?" is closest to a Must Be False task. On Must Be False questions, the correct answer usually contradicts a conditional rule or contradicts an available inference. But in the paragraph we read there was no conditional rule and there aren't any obvious inferences that can be made. We could infer stuff like, "What the oracle prophesied was not what Demosthenes was expecting", since we know that Demosthenes reacted with surprise. We could say ""Demosthenes's buddy didn't have a good view of the front of the tablet", since the buddy had to ask "what is it? what is it?" We can infer that "Demosthenes is willing to share some prophetic messages with other people", since Demosthenes shared the news with his buddy.

label: Goal
body: We would have practically no idea what we're looking for. So with each answer, we'll just ask ourselves, "Does the passage seem to contradict this?" If an answer brings up something we never talked about, then it's probably automatically wrong, because we can only contradict stuff we talked about.

label: Conclusion
body: Human emotions must not be physical phenomena.

label: Evidence (since)
body: Human emotions cannot be explained by physics, chemistry, or neurophysiology. Science can't adequately explain emotional phenomena such as feeling frustrated, falling in love, or being moved by a painting.

label: Evaluate
body: Our goal is to prove that X is not a physical phenomena. Has the argument provided any proving mechanism, like "If ____ is true, then it's not a physical phenomenon?" No. So that means the correct answer must be some sort of rule that can output the language or idea of "not a physical phenomenon". We're trying to prove this about human emotions, so what do we know about human emotions? - science can't adequately explain some of them (3 different examples listed) - they can't be explained by physics, chemistry, or neurophysiology

label: Goal
body:
We want an answer that takes something we know to be true about human emotions and says that this proves that human emotions are not physical phenomena. The most predictable answer would sound like,
```
If X can't be explained by phys, chem, or neurophysio
  → X is not a physical phenomenon
```

label: Statements
body: Several T-rex skeletons found in North America have tooth marks from a large carnivore. At that time, T-rex was the only large carnivore.
