(infer: the toothmarks on these T-rex skeletons came from a T-rex) The tooth marks could have resulted only from combat or feeding. (infer: either T-rex 1 was fighting T-rex 2 or eating T-rex 2) It would have been almost impossible to inflict these tooth marks on the skeleton of a live animal. (infer: T-rex 1 was not fighting a live T-rex 2. It was feeding on a dead T-rex 2)

label: Conclusion
body: The Internet will one day gain a humanlike intelligence.

label: Goal
body: Unlike many Most Supported paragraphs, which are a hodge-podge of disorganized facts, this paragraph sort of led us, in order, through several opportunities to stop and combine ideas. So let's look for the most provable answer, but it will probably be something like - Some of these T-rex skeletons we found have tooth marks that were caused by another T-rex that was eating it after it had died.

label: Conclusion
body: The view that poetry cannot be accurately paraphrased is false. (i.e. poetry can be accurately paraphrased)

label: Evidence
body: The critics say a poem can't be paraphrased because a poem itself is the only accurate expression of its meaning. But these critics think that their own paraphrases of poems are accurate.

label: Evaluate
body: It's hard to argue with the idea that the critics are wrong about something, given that they're saying "no poem can be accurately paraphrased" as well as "our paraphrases are accurate". They are definitely contradicting themselves. But the author's conclusion didn't say, "Thus these critics are contradicting themselves". It says their view about whether poetry can be accurately paraphrased is wrong. The author didn't present any evidence for or against the idea that poetry can be accurately paraphrased. She told us that these critics consider their own paraphrases accurate, but we wouldn't accept their opinions as proof that their paraphrases are accurate.

label: Goal
body: This feels kind of like an Unproven vs. Proven False move. The author found a problem with someone's argument (in this case: their other beliefs contradict their conclusion). His conclusion should be like, "Thus their argument seems weird. Thus they contradict themselves." Given a contradiction, "poems can never be accurately paraphrased" + "our own paraphrases are accurate", we know they can't both be right, but we don't know which one is correct. The author is arbitrarily choosing one of those two options.

label: Conclusion (clearly)
body: The tax bill has already created many jobs in this area.

label: Evidence
body: It provided substantial incentives for businesses that move to this area and hire 50 or more employees. Last year, Plastonica qualified for the incentives by opening a new plastics factory that hired 75 employees.

label: Evaluate
body: It doesn't seem like this is testing a Linking idea, because that would be "if Plastonica hired 75 employees, then the bill has create many jobs in this area". We should probably go into debate mode: Given that .. Plastonica qualified for the bill's incentives by opening a new plastics factory that hired 75 employees, How could we argue that ... The bill has not created many jobs in this area. Maybe we could say Plastonica's jobs aren't really in this area? Maybe we could say the bill wasn't the reason that Plastonica opened that factory / it would have done so anyway? We could potentially see this argument in our Explain Curious Fact mindset, with the curious fact being "Why did Plastonica open a new plastics factory with 75 employees" and the author's causal assumption being, "They did so, at least in part, because of this tax incentive". Thus, the author is assuming that Plastonica did not open the new factory "entirely for reason X (not the incentive)". And she has to assume bare minimums when it comes to the plausibility of her explanation, such as "Plastonica was aware that it qualified for the tax incentive when it decided to open the factory here".

label: Goal
body: Look for an answer assuring us that these 75 hired employees represent "jobs in this area", or an answer ruling out the possibility that "something else caused Plastonica to build the factory; the bill's incentives made no difference".

label: Situation
body: 1st move: $0.25 surcharge if you paid for gas with a credit card. Aftermath: the customers were angry. 2nd move: raised the price of gas by $0.25, and then offered a $0.25 discount if you pay by cash. Aftermath: the customers were happier

label: Evaluate
body: Lots of Proposition / Generalization situations deal with a before / after that seems to suggest a Causal Difference-Maker. Why were customers angry with the first system and happy with the second one? It seems like customers are willing to pay whatever price is posted, but if they're suddenly surprised by a surcharge they get angry. Obviously, if cash-paying customers are suddenly surprised by a discount they won't be angry.

label: Goal
body: Look for a safely worded answer reflecting the idea that people paying with credit cards are happier to pay the same price if it's built into the price of gas rather than added as a surcharge.

label: Conclusion (therefore)
body: At least some people who use herbal meds daily should occasionally skip their usual dose for a day or two, to give the body a chance to recuperate.

label: Evidence
body: Even though taking herbal meds over several months is how you get herbal meds to work best, many herbal meds have toxic side effects when taken daily for long periods.

label: Evaluate
body: The author's conclusion is making a recommendation, which is inherently Comparative. When we recommend some approach or tactic, we're assuming the world in which you follow our recommendation will be better than the present world. We can use our Plan / Goal thinking to analyze this argument. The author's Goal is that we harness the value of herbal meds without incurring the toxic downside. The author's Plan is for us to skip a usual dose for a day or two. When authors suggest Plans to achieve a certain Goal, we're typically worried that the Plan isn't feasible, won't work as they're envisioning, or that it will backfire by having some unanticipated consequence.

label: Goal
body: This author seems to assume that "skipping a dose for a day or two" is enough time to "avoid the toxic side effects" of long term herbal med usage (she's assuming that her Plan would actually help with the Goal). But she also has to assume that skipping a usual dose for a day or two would not result in some bad backfire consequence that's at least as bad as the toxic side effects would have been. Maybe, once you've gotten your body acclimated to a certain daily dose of herbal meds, it has a bad reaction when you don't have that substance (like how regular coffee drinkers get bad headaches if they don't have their daily caffeine).

label: Opposing Evidence
body: In one section of the city, food trucks occupy many of the limited metered parking spaces available, thus worsening already bad traffic congestion.

label: Evidence (since)
body: There is plenty of available parking and little traffic congestion in most areas of the city.

label: Conclusion
body: This bill [prohibiting food trucks from parking in metered spaces in any commercially zoned area] should be rejected.

label: Evaluate
body: "Thus" is usually a conclusion indicator, but it's not performing that function here. The second sentence in the argument describes a cause and effect relationship where the food trucks are causing traffic congestion. It's important to recognize the recommendation in the final sentence—"this bill should be rejected." Recommendations like this almost always function as conclusions in LR arguments. And in this case, that recommendation acts more clearly as the conclusion of the argument than the statement about traffic congestion. Food trucks parking in metered spots don't seem to be causing problems in most areas of the city. That seems like a decent reason to reject the proposed bill. But in LSAT LR, it's not enough for the link between the evidence and the conclusion to just be pretty good. We want to notice that the link between evidence and conclusion isn't airtight. We could strengthen this argument by explicitly stating that, if problem caused by an activity does not affect most areas of the city, any bill which would prohibit that activity should be rejected.

label: Goal
body: Look for an answer which states a bill prohibiting an activity should be rejected if the activity does not cause problems in most areas. Beware of answers that bring in irrelevant details which don't actually impact the argument.

label: Michele's Claims
body: 1. It's usually not a good idea for a company to overhaul its databases. 2. The rewards rarely exceed the problems experienced along the way. 3. People considering a database overhaul should think twice before proceeding.

label: Alvaro's Responses
body: 1. Did Alvaro argue that ... usually it is a good idea for a company to overhaul its databases? No, not really. It doesn't seem like Alvaro weighs in on the usually modifier that dictates the truth value of this claim. He doesn't seem to address whether it's a good idea for companies to overhaul databases in most cases. 2. Did Alvaro argue that ... The rewards frequently exceed the problems experienced along the way? Not really. There isn't any discussion of rewards outweighing problem. 3. Did Alvaro argue that ... People considering a database overhaul should not think twice? Yes, kind of. He's definitely countering Michele's advice in her final claim. For her, the best advice for a company considering a database overhaul is to "think twice", which is an expression that means "you probably shouldn't do it". If we say, "I would think twice before emailing your boss while you're drunk", that's another way of saying, "I don't think you should email your boss while you're drunk". So Michele is saying companies should probably avoid overhauling their database, whereas Alvaro is saying "they should feel fine about doing it, as long as they do it the right way."

label: Goal
body: The disconnect seemed to be concentrated around the idea of generic advice about overhauling databases. Michele: "I'd think twice / it's usually not a good idea" Alvaro: "It's fine, just do the job right"

label: Statements
body: People where shown images that usually appeared at the top of the screen but sometimes appeared at the bottom. After each appearance, they were asked to guess where the next image would appear. They were wrong most of the time. All of them said they were basing their guess on a pattern they believed they saw. If they had simply guessed that next image would always appear at the top, they would have been correct most of the time.

label: Evaluate
body: This is a tough one to anticipate. We're usually looking for Conditional / Causal / Quantitative language as a clue for where the answer choice inference may come from, but this paragraph is long and messy. There's a counterfactual conditional in the final sentence, saying that "if they had simply guessed next image will be on top, then they would have been correct most of the time". We know they were basing their guess on a pattern they thought they perceived, so apparently they didn't perceive a pattern of next image is always on top.

label: Goal
body: Because of how long this paragraph is, with five sentences, we should probably just re-read the paragraph one more time for good understanding and then use the answers to guide us. If an answer seems somewhat provable, then we'll research the details in the paragraph.

label: Given That ....
body: The temperature in T is always at least 10 degrees lower than the temperature in C.

label: How Can it Be That ...
body: The average resident of C spends 10 to 20 percent more on winter heating expenses than does the average resident of T.

label: Evaluate / Goal
body: We need four reasons why people in the warmer city (C) are spending more on winter heating expenses, or, equivalently, why people in the colder city (T) are spending less on winter heating expenses. (Since this is about averages, we don't care about real number totals or individual data points.)

label: Conclusion
body:
```
Costs $5 - $18 → used < 10 yrs. old
```

label: Evidence
body:
```
New → costs > $18
≥ 10 yrs old → costs < $5
```

label: Evaluate
body: This conclusion takes the contrapositive of each rule to derive the upper and lower boundary of its conclusion. If it costs < $18, then it's not new (i.e. Used). If it costs > $5, then it's less than 10 yrs old. Thus, if it's between $5 - 18, then it's got to be Used and less than 10 yrs. old.

label: Goal
body: The argument needs to give us two conditional premises. The conclusion's trigger should be the net effect of being "Not outcome 1 + Not outcome 2". The premises' outcomes were → more than $18. → less than $5. And the conclusion's trigger was between $5 and $18. The outcome of the conclusion should combine the negation of the two triggers. The premises' triggers were New →, 10 or more yrs old →. So the conclusion's outcome was Used and less than 10 yrs old

label: Conclusion
body: We're probably finding a higher percentage of tornadoes than we used to.

label: Evidence
body: The number of reported tornadoes per year has doubled since the 1950s. There probably has not been an increase in the number of tornadoes. Our ability to find tornadoes has improved.

label: Evaluate
body: Since we're interpreting the cause of a changing statistic, we can use our Curious Fact / Explanation mindset. Curious Comparison ... why are we reporting twice as many tornadoes per year nowadays, compared to the 1950s? Author's Explanation ... it's not that there are more tornadoes; it's probably that our improved ability to find tornadoes is resulting is our being able to find a higher percentage of them than we used to. To Strengthen this argument we would need to either 1. Rule out an Alternate Explanation for the curious fact or 2. Increase the plausibility of the Author's Explanation

label: Goal
body: So let's look for an answer ruling out some other reason why there are more reported tornadoes (maybe it's way easier to report them than it used to be ... 5 mins online vs. 30 min phone call) or for an answer increasing the plausibility that we're reporting more tornadoes because our ability to find them has improved so we're catching a higher percentage of them than before (this explanation assumes that in the 1950s we were failing to report at least half o the tornadoes that occurred)

label: Conclusion
body: If you only need to clean small areas of uncarpeted floors, a cheap handheld is likely sufficient.

label: Evidence
body: Most cheap handhelds are easy to use and will probably satisfy all your needs for wood / tile floors.

label: Evaluate
body: The "satisfy all your needs" in the premise matches pretty well with the "likely sufficient" in the conclusion. It seems like the biggest vulnerability of this argument is that the sales pitch is directed at wood / tile floors. Maybe there's some other non-carpeted surface we would want to be vacuuming.

label: Goal
body: The answer needs to make us feel better about wood/tile being the main surfaces this vacuum would be used on, making it seem like ease of use is in important factor in buying a vacuum, or ruling out any potential downsides the cheap handheld vacuum might have.

label: Evaluate
body: Like so many proud Parallel Flaw before him, this guy is doing the Necessary vs. Sufficient flaw. We know that ending global warming requires decreased reliance on fossil fuels. One sufficient means of getting less reliance on fossil fuels is if there were economic incentives to develop alternatives. But the author's conclusion is acting like those economic incentives are required.

label: Background
body: Treating tuna with carbon monoxide (as is done to prevent browning) doesn't harm the tuna in any way.

label: Surprising Claim
body: There's a danger that doing this treatment will lead to more people getting sick from eating tuna

label: Evaluation
body: Given that treatment doesn't harm the tuna, How is it that more ppl get sick from eating it. A lot of correct answers to Paradox like to use the "breadcrumbs", the extra details, they included. Since this treatment -> doesn't get brown as it ages, I would imagine this correct answer is going to show us a way that not browning as ages -> more ppl get sick eating

label: Conclusion
body: The descriptive labels "short" and "long" have now outlived their usefulness.

label: Evidence
body: These labels reflect the duration of a GRB's explosion. But we sighted a weird GRB whose duration was long (so it would be labeled "long") but in every other respect it had the properties of one we'd typically label "short".

label: Evaluate
body: Is this one bad data point enough to get rid of these labels? Maybe our measurement of this GRB was just off, and so it didn't fit nicely into our traditional labels because our data on it was skewed. Shouldn't we wait for more data points that defy this classification system before we get rid of it? Since we can make objections such as the above, we could Strengthen the argument with ideas that counter those objections, like "our data on this unusual one is definitely accurate / this isn't just a one-time exception, we expect to find more things like this / we've got a better way to categorize GRBs if we were to get rid of this labeling system". We might also object, "What's the harm in just calling it long, since it did have a long duration?" So we could strengthen the argument by saying, "it would not be cool to just pretend that this is a long GRB."

label: Goal
body: It's hard to know where the correct answer will go with this one. Let's just cue up our mantra of "We should get rid of these labels, because ... [answer choice]."

label: Conclusion
body: A silly person who laughs a little is helped more in their recovery than a stoic person who laughs a lot.

label: Intermediate Conclusion
body: Laugher can aid recovery from illness.

label: Evidence
body: In a study, patients who saw comic videos saw had immune systems that got stronger. Silly people saw bigger immune system gains than did stoic people.

label: Evaluation
body: We have a Correlation to Causality move as we go from Premise to Intermediate Conclusion. Just because the immune systems of the people who watched the video grew stronger doesn't mean that "laughter helps with recovery from illness". First of all, who said anyone was laughing? We just know they watched a comic video. The author is assuming some of them laughed. Secondly, the immune system gain could have been caused by something else (maybe the people who saw the video also got more exercise / also got more sunlight / also had more social interaction). However, the conclusion itself is a random thought. Nowhere in the evidence did we talk about the silly people only laughing a little while the stoic people laughed a lot. It doesn't make any sense where that specific comparison came from.

label: Goal
body: Look for an answer calling out the illicit Correlation vs. Causation assumption, or one calling out the bizarre conclusion comparison that doesn't appear at all in the evidence.

label: Conclusion
body: A male guppy will alter its courting patterns in response to feedback from a female guppy.

label: Evidence
body: Males with more orange on one side than the other were free to vary which side they showed to a female. Females were drawn to those males with more orange showing, and males tended to show the females their more orange side when courting.

label: Goal
body: Find the answer that calls out the reversal: predator -> short OP does not mean short OP -> predator.

label: Evaluate
body: Since the author is interpreting the results of a study and drawing a causal conclusion (X happens in response to Y), we can use our Explain Curious Fact mindset. Curious Fact ... why were the males tending to show the females their more orange side when courting? Author's Explanation ... The male guppy was swimming normally, then noticed that females were drawn to males with more orange showing, and so they altered their courting patterns to highlight more of their orange side.

label: Goal
body: Since this is Strengthen, we have two different options for how the correct answer will work: - rule out an Alternate Explanation of the curious fact (get rid of some other explanation for why males tend to show more of their orange side). - boost the Plausibility of the Author's Explanation (provide more evidence that corroborates the idea that males show more orange in response to feedback from a female. there are lots of ways to do this, but the #1 formula is No Cause, No Effect, i.e. an answer that shows when a male guppy does not get feedback from a female guppy, it does not alter its courting patterns to show more orange).

label: Conclusion (dangerous = opinion)
body: Acting on the basis of the argument that, "if we unilaterally disarm our nukes, it will encourage other countries to reduce theirs, eventually leading to an international agreement on nuclear arms reduction" would be dangerous.

label: Evidence (because)
body: This argument ignores the countries that are presently on the verge of civil wars. Many of these countries have nukes, and we can't rely on them to conform to any international military policy.

label: Evaluate
body: Whenever we do Main Conclusion (or Role), we remind ourselves that the Conclusion shows up, at least 85% of the time, in one of two ways: - it's the very first sentence - it's some pivot / rebuttal idea. The first sentence here is not our author's opinion, so we know it's not the conclusion. But since it's somebody else's opinion, ("some proponents"), it sends a huge warning sign that the author will probably rebut this idea. Sure enough, the 2nd sentence begins with a rebuttal opinion: acting on this argument would be dangerous. The final claims support this opinion.

label: Goal
body: We're looking for the closest meaning match to "Our acting on the basis of this argument would be dangerous". What would be a synonymous way to say the same thing? What does this argument refer to? A synonymous expression would be, "We should not act on the basis of this argument", or "It would be dangerous for us to act on the basis of this argument". But if we substitute the pronoun "this argument" for its referent, we should be looking for something like, "We should not act to disarm our nukes on the basis of the idea that other countries will follow and an international agreement will ensue".

label: Conclusion (that is why)
body: You should insist on receiving LIC's complete course of treatment for whiplash after any accident that involves a fall or a bump on the head.

label: Evidence
body: Whiplash is caused by a sudden sharp motion of the neck. Many types of accidents can produce a sudden sharp motion of the next (a fall, a bump on the head, being shoved from behind, or most commonly an auto accident).

label: Evaluate
body:
Well, this conclusion is completely overstated, but that's pretty common for an Advertisement. They're prone to hyperbole. The conclusion is conditional, since it has the word "any".
```
accident that involves fall or bump of head
  → complete course of treatment for whiplash from LIC
```
To argue with a conditional conclusion, you have to think of a way where the Left side would be true, but the Right wouldn't. How is it possible that we have a fall or bump on the head but we needn't insist on a complete course of treatment for whiplash from LIC? There are a lot of different stories we could tell: - the fall/bump just aren't that bad to merit any medical attention - the fall/bump doesn't actually involve whiplash - the fall/bump involves whiplash, but we don't have health insurance or enough money to pay for LIC's complete course of treatment, so we're going to just YouTube whiplash exercises for free - the fall/bump involves whiplash, and we have means of paying for treatments, but we don't need the complete course of treatment, when just part of it would suffice - the fall/bump involves whiplash, and we have the means of paying, and we need a complete course of treatment, but it doesn't need to be LIC's. Maybe another clinic is more convenient / less expensive / better rated.

label: Goal
body: Look for an answer that presents a way to argue that one might have a fall or bump on the head but not need to get LIC's complete whiplash treatment.

label: Conclusion
body: Development of the trail should proceed

label: Evidence
body: Some people oppose it out of fear that the trails will get littered with food wrappers and other trash, but most trail users will be responsible hikers with great concern for the environment.

label: Evaluation
body: This is vulnerable to several objections: - he's assuming that "hikers with great concern for the environment" don't litter. - he's arguing that "at least 51% of the trail users won't litter", but what about the up to 49% that aren't responsible hikers? Couldn't that still be a significant amount of litter? - even if we reject the argument that the opposition was making, that doesn't mean we've offered positive evidence in favor of the conclusion. One of the famous flaws, Unproven vs. Proven False, is this idea that "just because an argument for X fails doesn't mean we conclude the opposite of X". X should just still be in doubt. Just because an argument that "we shouldn't make these trails" failed doesn't mean that we should conclude that "we should make these trails".

label: Goal
body: Look for the Unproven vs. Proven False answer choice, or an answer that makes the objection that "responsible hikers still litter" or that "the other 49% that aren't irresponsible hikers might still leave a lot of trash"

label: Conclusion
body: These doomsdayers are turning out to be wrong. rephrased: There isn't an imminent and catastrophic shortage of scientists and engineers.

label: Evidence (since)
body: There is little noticeable upward pressure on the salaries of scientists and engineers, and unemployment is as high in these fields as in any other.

label: Background
body:
Geothermal plants get power using heat from underground pools of hot water, which is heated by the surrounding rock.
  It's a more economic way of producing power than conventional, fossil fuel power plants.
  But there are limited areas of the world where such underground hot water and steam can currently be reached by drilling.

label: Contention
body: In the near future, most areas will have access to economical power from geothermal power plants.

label: Evaluate
body: We should take our time to understand the intended meaning / significance of the premises, because (for me at least) it takes asking myself some questions about the real world, to pretend like I'm a grown up who understands that real world. What is upward pressure on salaries? That means that something is driving the salaries up. What drives salaries up or down? Laws could do that, if the minimum wage was raised. But that's more like a mandate, than pressure. What causes downward pressure on prices of retail goods? Competition. If I'm the only gas station in town (like when you drive through Big Sur, California), I can charge $2 / banana, because you don't have any better options. But if there were a rival gas station across the street who charged $1 per banana, that would put some downward pressure on how I price my bananas. Similarly, that gas station can pay its employees minimum wage, if there's no competition for those employees. But if there are only 5 people in town eligible to work at this gas station, and the rival across the street is willing to pay them $20 / hr, then that puts upward pressure on the pay (i.e. salary) that I offer. So labor markets, just like retail markets, operate off principles of supply and demand, and LSAC definitely expects us to have a common sense understanding that low supply or high demand drive up prices. The "doomsayers" were predicting that there was going to be a labor shortage of scientists and engineers. So if you're a science or engineering firm and are looking to hire a scientist or engineer, there are going to be lots of rival firms competing for the same eligible employees. You're going to have to compete with their salary offers, if you hope to lure one of the rare scientist / engineers to work at your company. The author is saying, "Since we're not seeing upward pressure on salaries, I guess that means there isn't a shortage of eligible workers." Why does she mention unemployment being as high as any other field. Why would it matter if unemployment were lower or higher than other fields? If unemployment were low, that means that almost all the scientists / engineers looking for jobs are finding them. If unemployment were high, that would mean there were too many workers looking for jobs (a surplus of eligible science / engineering workers), a labor surplus. The doomsayers who thought there wouldn't be enough scientists / engineers would assume that in this field unemployment would be lower than in others, since firms would be so desperate and labor would be in such short supply that all the eligible workers would find jobs. The author is thinking, "since unemployment is just as high in these fields, it doesn't look like any sort of labor shortage is happening".

label: Goal
body: Because of all the effort it takes to understand this argument, we'd frankly be out of time to dissect the logic. We should probably just head to the answers thinking, "convince me even more that there's no shortage of scientists and engineers".

label: Rhonda's Conclusion
body: You should use your time/energy/money to help others.

label: Rhonda's Evidence
body: People active with charities have richer lives than miserly hermits.

label: Brad's Conclusion
body: Ignore strangers and focus on your relatives/friends

label: Brad's Evidence
body: These people will remember what you did for them and help you when you need it.

label: Evaluation
body: What a weird question task. We need a principle that will help both arguments. So we need to think about where's there's overlap in Brad and Rhonda's conclusion and in their premises. Both conclusions are about where you should focus your time and energy. So the principle should sound something like you should focus your time and energy on xyz. Rhonda wants to focus on others, probably strangers, because she thinks that people involved in charities live richer lives. Brad wants to focus on people we know, because they'll be more likely to repay the favor one day. What do those have in common? Both of them are choosing who to focus on by thinking about what you'll get in return: richer life / help when you need it.

label: Goal
body: It seems like we'll need a principle that sounds something like, "If focusing on this group would potentially give you back something positive in return, do it".

label: Conclusion (therefore)
body: Thrinaxodon was probably warm-blooded.

label: Evidence (for)
body: Its skull suggests it had sensory whiskers. If it had whiskers, Thrinaxadon had hair on other parts of its body, which would have served as insulation. Insulation would be of little use to a cold-blooded animal.

label: Evaluate
body: Usually, on Main Conclusion and Role, they like to avoid putting the Main Conclusion as the final claim, and here the Conclusion is in the final sentence but not the final claim. The support indicator "for" (FABS = for, after all, because, since) tells us the final claim is support. The argument sort of takes this voyage: 1. its skull suggests that it had sensory whiskers 2. so it probably had other body hair 3. that other body hair would serve as insulation 4. insulation is of little use to a cold-blooded animal 5. so it was probably warm blooded

label: Goal
body: We're being asked about something that is part of the Support. The answers might force us to consider whether it's an Intermediate Conclusion or just a Premise, but let's cross that bridge if/when we come to it. We might be able to get our answer just by knowing that this claim being asked about was support for the Main Conclusion that Thrina was probably warm-blooded.

label: Conclusion (therefore)
body: To protect the interests of others, governments are justified in outlawing behavior that puts one's own health at risk.

label: Evidence
body: People who put themselves at risk and injure themselves inevitably impose emotional and financial costs on others.

label: Evaluate
body: If I'm your friend, and I buy a motorcycle, and 3 rad months later I end up in the ER with twenty broken bones, you are going to be emotionally taxed by worrying about me. You may even have to bring me soup. Similarly, society is subsidizing my hospital bills with its tax dollars. So my risk-taking imposed financial and emotional costs on others. The author is saying, "Because of all this, the government should outlaw the riding of motorcycles." That seems like a pretty harsh leap, right? We don't want the government to outlaw any risky behavior that could lead to injury (goodbye, dreams of winning Steeplechase competitions).

label: Goal
body: Let's look for a principle that stands up for our rights to engage in risky behavior with our own bodies. Since this principle is meant to weaken the argument, it should help us argue that "governments shouldn't outlaw risky behaviors."

label: Conclusion
body: It was morally wrong for Sanderson to intentionally withhold from his cousin the fact that he overheard someone say the factory would close.

label: Evidence
body: Making a statement with the intention of misleading is lying. Lying is morally wrong. + Yes, Sanderson didn't actually make a statement, but there's no difference between stating something and failing to state something if they are done with the same intention.

label: Evaluate
body:
All three claims have this "years of specialized training" as an overlapping idea. Do the conditionals chain together?
  No, but if someone doesn't have the specialized training, we'll know two things about them
  - can't be a literature professor
  - don't have ability to judge greatness of lit works
  (A trap answer is probably going to try to make some conditional or over-quantified relationship between those two ideas)
  Since we're told that most of the reading public doesn't have access to this training, we can infer two things ...

label: Evaluation
body: We're trying to conclude that an action is morally wrong, and the author has provided us with the conditional rules we'll be using to try to derive that idea. According to these rules, if you make an intentionally misleading statement, it's lying, which is morally wrong. We know Sanderson didn't make an intentionally misleading statement, but our author is saying that Sanderson intended to mislead by failing to say something (and those are morally equivalent). On a first read, it's hard for me to see the wiggle room here. According to these rules, isn't Sanderson guilty of something morally wrong? If Sanderson's failure to say something was done with the intent to mislead, then he was lying, and so he did something morally wrong. So how can we argue that Sanderson's failure to say something was not done with the intent to mislead? We know that Sanderson was aware that by withholding info, his cousin would assume the factory would remain open. Do we know for a fact that "it's misleading to suggest that the factory will remain open?" We don't. The person that Sanderson overheard is not necessarily right about the factory. If Sanderson knows that random dude who said "the factory is gonna close" is dead wrong about that, then withholding that story from his cousin, and letting his cousin continue to believe that the factory will remain open, is not intentionally misleading. If I overhear an anti-vaxxer saying that "vaccines cause autism" and I refrain from saying that to my cousin, knowing that my cousin will otherwise (continue to) think that vaccines don't cause autism, I'm not intentionally misleading my cousin or lying to her. I'm just protecting her from what I believe is erroneous information.

label: Goal
body: Since the only possible objection to this argument is, "What if Sanderson thinks the factory will remain open / what if Sanderson assumed that person he overheard was wrong?", the correct answer will probably rule out one of those objections. - Sanderson does not think the factory will remain open - Sanderson believed the person he overheard was saying something true

label: Principle
body:
```
Rule 1: Orig ruling not contrary to basic moral values of society
  → judges must follow that first ruling
Rule 2: No precedent + judges views don't contradict broad public opinion
  ←→ abide by own views when deciding
```

label: Evaluation
body: Gross. They gave us two rules, one of which is bi-conditional (signified by "when and only then"). One rule deals with how you judge when there is a precedent. The other deals with how you judge when there isn't a precedent. So as we look through these answers, we'll first check whether we're dealing with a situation in which there is a precedent, in which case we'll use rule 1, or whether it's a situation with no precedent, in which case we would use rule 2.

label: Statements
body: Amusia means "it's hard to tell different melodies apart or to remember simple tunes". In an experiment, they played some shifting pitches to people with amusia (the part about piano is just establishing that these pitches are discernibly different — people w/o amusia can easily hear the difference when someone switches from playing middle C to playing the D key right next to it). The amusia folk could not tell the difference in pitches/tones. But ... they could track the timing of tones and notice differences in timing.

label: Evaluate
body: This seems like a Reconcile the Pivot type setup. We get all this information about people who can't tell the difference between melodies, can't remember simple tunes, can't hear a difference between different tones .... BUT ... they can tell the difference between different timing.

label: Goal
body: It's hard to anticipate how a correct answer here will sound, but it will likely reconcile the fact that people with amusia can detect timing changes with the fact that they can't detect pitch/melody changes.

label: Conclusion
body: There is little of social significance in contemporary novels.

label: Evidence
body:
```
can't experience world from moral perspective of novel's characters
  → can't enter internal world of the novelist's mind
```
In contemporary novels, the (moral) transgressions are just spectacles, not events whose purpose is to be seen as the injustices they are.

label: Evaluate
body: Good Lord, argument, I want to award you some Reddit badge for "Least readable". This is not fun to digest. I'm relying a lot on stopping as I read and saying to myself where this is going / what I'll need to hear. If I said, "There is nothing fun about ferris wheels, because you cannot confuse the body's senses unless you go fast", there are two implicit assumptions there: 1. Ferris wheels don't go fast 2. If you don't confuse the body's senses, it's not fun. Try it on the original first sentence: "There is little of social significance in contemporary novels, because you can't enter internal world of writer's mind unless you experience that world from the moral perspective of the novel's characters". What are the two assumptions? 1. In contemporary novels, you don't experience the world from the moral perspective of the novel's characters. 2. If you don't enter the internal world of the writer's mind, then there is little social significance. The 2nd sentence (yes, shockingly, this is only two sentences) is trying to establish one of these negatives. It's saying "in contemporary novels, X is this, rather than that." We would probably try to match this with #1 above. They're trying to establish that you don't experience the world from the moral perspective of the novel's characters. They say that the transgressions committed (immoral actions) are not events whose purpose is to be seen as the injustices they are.

label: Goal
body: This would make me think we're headed towards, "if moral transgressions aren't presented as events whose purpose is to be seen as the injustices they are, then you won't be able to experience the world of the novel from the moral perspective of the novel's characters." But given how hard this feels, I'd be willing to consider other missing links, and I'm planning to mainly get rid of wrong answers by finding stuff that sounds Too Strong or Out of Scope.

label: Conclusion (hence)
body: The standard recommendations for avoidance of infection by these pathogens must be counterproductive (i.e. the advice being given is actually leading to more infections).

label: Evidence
body: People who precisely follow the recommendations are more likely to contract diseases caused by these pathogens than are people who deviate considerably from them.

label: Goal
body:
... Let's look for what we get when we apply the two conditional rules to the fact in the last sentence:
  Vast majority of the reading public can't be a literature professor.
  Vast majority of the reading public can't judge the greatness of literary works.

label: Conclusion
body:
```
  The characters will not      Action X won't
  be made more realistic.      happen
  ```

label: Evaluate
body: Does the fact that the rule-followers are worse off than the rule-disobeyers show that the rule sucks? This feels a bit like an Anti-Causal type of argument. The author's conclusion is like, "See? These rules don't work. In fact, they probably make stuff worse" (that part makes it slightly causal in the reverse direction). How do we object to Anti-Causal arguments? Usually, we point out that the two groups aren't actually fair to compare, the way the author is doing so. For example, let's say "people who regularly follow seatbelt laws are more likely to get injured in a car crash than are people who regularly drive w/o their seatbelt on". Does that show that seat belts only worsen your chances of getting injured in a car crash? Not necessarily. Maybe the group of people who regularly follow seatbelt laws are a much higher-risk group: they commute every day, on the highway, so they are routinely driving at higher speeds with more likelihood of injury. Meanwhile, maybe the group of people who regularly don't wear their seatbelt live in rural towns and drive 25-35mph on lonely roads. So we could probably object to the author's conclusion here with a similar move.

label: Goal
body: Look for something like, "the author fails to consider that the people who precisely follow the meat recommendations might be a way higher risk group (when it comes to contracting diseases from meat pathogens) than are the people who deviate from the standard recs". This is kind of like the idea that people who are extremely sensitive to getting sick might wash their hands more than others but still get sick more than others (does that show washing hands is counterproductive?)

label: Conclusion (clearly)
body: ~Carriage Books did not publish a nonfiction book last year.

label: Evidence (since)
body: Carriage Books earned a profit on every book it published last year, and no nonfiction book published by Carriage Books has ever earned a profit.

label: Evaluate
body:
After reading the argument on a Parallel question, we have to decide whether we think it would be more effective to make an Algebra Recipe for the argument or to just boil it down to a Principle or Reasoning Pattern. My general rule of thumb is that if there's conditional logic or quantifiers or Overlapping Ideas, then I'll go for Algebra. The first two premises are quantified/conditional logic (no / every). And there are Overlapping Ideas: Carriage Books, nonfiction book, profit, publish are all mentioned at least twice. So if we assign them some variables, we can look at the logic.
```
Premise 1 — No X's from Thing A have ever been Y.
  For Thing A (all time): if X → no Y
Premise 2 — Every Z from Thing A's last year was Y.
  For Thing A (last year): if Z → yes Y
Conclusion — Thing A last year didn't have any Z's that were X
  For Thing A (last year): if Z → not X
```
Since Carriage Books is the common ingredient to all three claims, I would focus more on the movings parts.
```
Nonfiction is never profitable.   N → ~P
Last yr's books were profitable.  Last yr = P
So, last yr's books were fiction. Last yr = ~N
```

label: Goal
body: The form seems to be to provide a very broad conditional (N → ~P), then tell us about something specific (P) that would trigger the contrapositive (P → ~N), and then conclude the outcome of that contrapositive (~N).

label: Statements
body:
conditional / quantifier (all, no)
```
Unemployed artist → sympathetic to social justice
Employed artist → not interested in prospect of great personal fame
```

label: Evaluate
body: Whenever we get a conditional claim on Inference, we ask ourselves two things: 1. Are there any other conditionals to which I could chain this one? 2. Are there any facts to which I could apply this rule? (usually via contrapositive) In this problem, we can tell there are two conditionals. Do they overlap? Is there any common term? (if not, they can't chain) It looks like they're both talking about the concept of whether or not an artist is employed. If we contrapose the first rule, it's saying, "If you're not sympathetic to social justice, then you're not an unemployed artist." Does that mean that you're an employed artist? No, it could just mean that you're not an artist at all. However, if we restrict ourselves to talking about artists, then we would be able to chain these conditionals together. And we have a motivated interest in doing so, since that's how Inference questions with conditionals work. when it comes to artists .... If you're not sympathetic to social justice, then you're not unemployed, which means you are employed, so you are not interested in great fame. by contrapositive, when it comes to artists .. If you're interested in great personal fame then you're not employed, which means you're unemployed, so you're sympathetic to social justice

label: Goal
body: Look for the most provable claim, but the most likely type of answer would combine the two claims by chaining them together, and reward us for seeing the connection between "being interested in fame and being sympathetic to social justice."

label: Conclusion (so)
body: Forster must be the burglar.

label: Evidence
body: The police department has two suspects: Schaeffer and Forster. It's not Schaeffer (he has an ironclad alibi).

label: Evaluate
body:
This argument is attempting to use this reasoning pattern.
```
X is either A or B.
X is not A.
So, X is B.
```
That would be a valid argument. The problem is "the police has two suspects: S and F" is not the same as saying "the burglar was either S or F". This argument is presenting a False Choice. It's acting like S and F are the only two options there are for the burglar, but it never established that they are the only two options. It only established that the police only have those two as suspects. We don't need to assume that the burglar is definitely one of the suspects the police have. We could fight this conclusion by saying, "Maybe Forster also has an ironclad alibi, and the police just don't have the right suspects for the burglary". This author is Assuming a Difference. She's assuming that Forster does not also have an ironclad alibi.

label: Goal
body: Let's look for an argument that tries to present two options, rule out one, and conclude the other. But it should be flawed because it never clearly established that those are the only two options we can possibly consider (they will just be the only two things mentioned).

label: Conclusion
body:
This isn't true.
  *rephrase:* Most university students **do** have interest in philosophical issues.

label: Evidence
body: I often go to university campuses to give talks, and the students at my talks have a deep interest in philosophical issues.

label: Evaluate
body: We could have included the very first idea (that the writers could make the characters more realistic), but that seemed like counterpoint fluff. It could be in the answer or not be there and it won't really affect the logic of how the conclusion is derived.

label: Evaluate
body:
*Given that* ... the students at this philosopher's talks have a deep interest in philosophical issues,
  *How could we argue that* ... most university students don't have interest in philosophical issues?
  We could probably say that the author's sample of student opinion is totally biased!
  Can you imagine if we said, "most university students today hate liberals. After all, I often go to meetings of the campus conservative club, and the students at those meetings hate liberals."
  Well, obviously, if you go to the *conservative* club meeting, they'll hate liberals.
  Just like if you poll people at a philosophy talk, they'll say they like philosophy. If you poll people at a BBQ ribs restaurant, you won't find too many vegetarians.
  Whenever an argument relies on a sample, we worry about whether it's Too Small / Unrepresentative, Biased, or Self-Selecting / Bad Data for some other reason (like the respondents were pressured out of giving honest answers).

label: Goal
body: Let's look for an answer talking about the the Famous Sampling flaw. The philosopher seems to be failing to consider that even though the students at this philosophy talks are interested in philosophy, those students might not be representative of most university students. They might just be the weirdos who like philosophy enough to go attend a talk in their spare time.

label: Conclusion
body: This ancient settlement in eastern North America was occupied at a time when mammoths lived in the area.

label: Evidence
body: We found a fossil bone there, and it had an engraving of a mammoth.

label: Evaluate
body: Okay ... just because the bone had an engraving of a mammoth doesn't mean there were actually mammoths around. My daughters "engrave" pictures of mermaids with their crayons; that doesn't mean that mermaids live in our area.

label: Goal
body:
Look for an answer naming the missing link, "If someone engraved X on a bone, then X was present in their lives", or an answer ruling out an objection:
  for example ...
  - the engraver wasn't just copying picture of mammoths he had seen in cave paintings
  - the engraver wasn't just drawing the picture of an animal which no longer existed but whose description lived on in oral history
  - the bone wasn't just an old bone that made its way to this settlement (in other words, maybe the people lived here 10,000 years ago, but the bone was 15,000 years old)

label: Durham's Claims
body:
1. The mayor will agree to a tax increase
  2. the city council won't agree to her road repair proposal unless she agrees to a tax increase
  3. the road repair proposal is her top priority

label: Espinoza's Reactions
body:
1. Disagrees? She seems to suggest that the mayor will not agree to a tax increase, since she says that "it's more important to the mayor that taxes not increase".
  2. Agrees? She seems to accept the same implicit choice that Durham is offering: you accept the tax increase and get the road repair proposal passed, or you don't accept the tax increase and you don't get the road repair passed.
  3. Disagrees. She does not think the road proposal is the top priority, because she says "it is more important to the mayor that taxes not increase".

label: Goal
body:
Since we have a claim they seem to agree to, we can probably head to the answers and see if we find it. It seems like Espinoza agrees with Durham's 2nd claim:
  if the mayor doesn't agree to a tax increase, then the city council won't let her get her road repair proposal passed.

label: Conclusion (should = opinion)
body: Politicians could persuade more voters with their arguments if they simply followed the scholars in charitably formulating their opponents' positions.

label: Evidence
body: When scholars try to make an opposing position seem as plausible and attractive as possible (when they formulate it as charitably as possible), it makes their argument more persuasive to their colleagues.

label: Evaluate
body:
Since this argument is based on a Comparison, we try to think of salient differences in order to object that the comparison is a shaky one.
  For example, suppose we said, "Marathon runners never run a full marathon as a practice run because it's too depleting. LSAT students should take note: they could fare better if they simply followed the marathon runners' example and didn't take a full practice test."
  We could think of a salient difference: wait a sec, even though taking a full-length LSAT practice is depleting, the recovery time is much faster than for a runner who runs a 26-mile practice run.
  So when it comes to politicians and scholars .... can we think about any salient difference for why the advice of "portray your opponents' arguments as persuasively as possible" would hold for the latter but not for the former?

label: Goal
body: Look for an answer possibly saying that even though presenting opponents' arguments charitably makes scholars look good to their colleagues, it still isn't a good idea for politicians to do (since it would make their political rivals seem more level-headed and worth listening to, which is usually the opposite of a politician's objectives).

label: Conclusion
body: If life functions don't resume following the procedure (in which the heart and brain functions are stopped by drastically reducing patient's body temp), the medical team is technically guilty of manslaughter.

label: Evidence
body: The doctors are deliberately stopping the patient's life functions.

label: Evaluate
body:
There is definitely some cognitive dissonance in agreeing with this argument --- the patients have always given informed consent when this procedure is done, but we're still going to find the medical team guilty of manslaughter if the procedure goes awry?
  It helps, maybe, that the conclusion is just saying the medical team is technically guilty of manslaughter. We're not morally blaming them (the patient wanted them to try this), but the fact that they deliberately stopped life functions and life functions didn't resume apparently fits the technical definition of manslaughter.

label: Goal
body:
We just want a rule that would apply to a medical team doing this test, and that would output the idea that "this is technically manslaughter". Something like,
  ```
  deliberately stop someone's life  → manslaughter
  functions and those don't resume
  ```

```
  Without years        don't have ability to judge
  of specialized   →   greatness of literary
  training             works
  ```

```
  Without years        can't become
  ```

label: Evaluate
body:
This is more of a paradox than an argument. The paragraph does establish that there is reason to want a greater spread of geothermal plants (it's a more economical option for power than are conventional fossil fuel plants).
  But it sounds like the reason it's not already super widespread and popular is that there are only limited areas of the world where we can currently reach those underground hot tubs by drilling.

label: Goal
body:
In order to support the contention that in the near future, most areas will have access to it, we need an answer to tell us that "something pretty big is changing", and that thing should have a common sense tie-in to getting more areas access to geothermal power plants.
  Potentially lots of different things could change for the better to make it more accessible, so we probably don't want to spend time trying to predict; we just want something impactful that's changing so that the future will have more geothermal than the present.

label: Conclusion (should)
body: One should not confuse desire for money with desire for material possessions.

label: Evidence ( ____ . Moreover, ____. )
body:
A lot of what money can buy is not material goods at all.
  And even material goods themselves are usually not wanted for their own sake, but rather for the experiences or activities they make possible.

label: Evaluate
body:
Whenever we're doing Main Conclusion or Role, we read the paragraph with the expectation that the Conclusion will usually occur earlier in the paragraph than the Evidence.
  These questions love to put the conclusion in the opening sentence, or so make it a rebuttal sentiment that follows an attribution to some other view/claim.
  So, priming our brain for such a paragraph, we can see the Opinion Indicator "should" in the opening sentence. Since this opinion isn't attributed to someone else, we assume it's our author's and tentatively nominate this first sentence as our Conclusion.
  As we read on, we're wondering if the author is trying to convince us that "desiring money doesn't necessarily mean desiring possessions".
  Indeed, she is. She provides two examples. They are linked with the word "moreover", which acts just like "and / furthermore". This shows that the author is pairing up multiple ideas that join together to support the conclusion.
  (With the exception of one annoying problem in the 80s'), any time two claims are joined with "and" they are both premises.

label: Goal
body: We're being asked about the first sentence, so we're just looking for an answer to say that it's our Main Conclusion.

label: Conclusion
body: This cannot be true (some of the food at Jason's Restaurant contains products grown with chemical pesticides).

label: Evidence
body: Jason buys the restaurant's produce at Kelly's Grocery, and I've seen workers unloading produce from a MegaFarm truck into that grocery. MegaFarm uses chemical pesticides on all of its crops.

label: Evaluate
body:
The author is assuming that when Jason goes to Kelly's Grocery, he buys some produce from MegaFarm, which has pesticides on it.
  This is the way in which she thinks she's proving that Jason's restaurant uses food with pesticides.
  Do we know that Jason buys MegaFarm produce from Kelly's Grocery?
  No, we were told that Jason does buy the produce for the restaurant from Kelly's, but we don't know that Kelly's exclusively carries MegaFarm produce. Maybe they also have a "farmer's market" produce stand in their produce department, and Jason buys a bunch of organic produce from there.

label: Goal
body: We need a storyline where Jason buys produce from Kelly's, but does not buy the MegaFarm pesticide-laced produce.

label: Setup
body:
There have been a bunch of studies that observed one bird cutting in while another bird is singing a song. It's called song-overlapping -- drowning out your buddy with your own song, right after they started singing a song.
  Researchers see this as an act of aggression.
  The author points out that their only evidence that song-overlapping is an aggressive act is an observation of the behavior of the bird who got their song cut off.
  The author is saying that "if you're measuring an action's intent based off the reaction of the person it's being done to, isn't that pretty speculative and vulnerable to "you'll see whatever it is you're looking for".
  Essentially, the author is saying, "Hey guys. I've heard your theory about song overlapping. But your evidence is just looking at the reactions of the birds whose songs get cut-off, and choosing to interpret it as aggressive. "

label: Goal
body:
So we know what goes in this blank is some sentiment like, "Shut up with your invented aggressive behavior hypothesis, guys."
  But because this is LSAT, you don't expect a full throated rejection. We don't want to act like we know that song-overlapping isn't aggressive (that would be us committing the Unproven vs. Proven False flaw).
  We want a very moderate version of, "your research conclusion is dumb."
  Something like
  - insufficient evidence for your hypothesis to be compelling
  - we shouldn't conclude it's an aggressive behavior based on this evidence

label: Conclusion
body: Any impact there is on election results from the fact that viewers tend to find blinky candidates less appealing in debates is a bad thing.

label: Evidence
body: Blinking a lot is not one of the features that contributes to a candidate's ability to perform well.

label: Evaluate
body: Given that blinking a normal amount isn't something that contributes to a politician's ability to perform well, how can we still argue that it's okay that people tend to discount candidates who blink a lot in debates?

label: Goal
body: Find an answer that makes it seem okay for people to be negatively stereotyping candidates who blink a lot.

label: Conclusion
body:
This isn't true.
  rephrase: The public is not afraid of scientists.

label: Evidence
body: I've been a scientist for decades, and I've never met anyone who is afraid of scientists.

label: Evaluate
body:
In a boring Linking sense, the author's argument assumes that, "If I haven't met someone afraid of scientists in decades as a scientist, then the public is not afraid of scientists".
  But that doesn't sound too much like a realistic answer, so we should consider potential Objections to the argument.
  This is an appeal to a sample of personal experience, and the author's data sample might be small, unrepresentative, or inaccurate.
  Maybe this scientist is in the lab all the time, so they've met very few people over the past few decades. Maybe the people they do meet are atypically within the world of science, and so they are atypically unafraid of scientists.
  Or maybe the people she's been meeting are afraid of scientists, but since she's a scientist they're too afraid of her to admit to her that they're afraid of her.

label: Goal
body:
Let's look for an answer linking the Premise to the Conclusion or for an answer ruling out one of our objections (or any other objection).
  e.g.
  - The scientist does not meet only a handful of people each decade.
  - The people the scientist met are not atypically comfortable around scientists.
  - The people the scientist met were not afraid of scientists but unwilling to admit as much.

label: Conclusion (seems likely that)
body: The earliest flying dinosaurs glided out of trees, rather than lifting off the ground from a running start.

label: Evidence
body: You can glide from a tree with very simple wings, and very simple wings are the middle evolutionary stage between "no wings" and the "large wings" we know the flying dinosaurs ultimately had.

label: Evaluate
body:
The argument assumes a difference. Why does this lady think the first flying dinosaurs probably glided out of trees rather that lifting off the ground?
  You can glide out of trees with simple "early-stage evolution" wings. She must be assuming that you can't lift off the ground to fly with simple "early-stage evolution" wings.

label: Goal
body: We need to find and eliminate four answers that add some plausibility to the idea that the first flying dinosaurs glided out of trees or detract some plausibility from the idea that the first flying dinosaurs did so by flapping they're very simple wings and lifting off from the ground.

label: Conclusion
body: It's wrong to say that "a concern for beauty is a characteristic of all legit art". (i.e. At least some legit art does not have concern for beauty as a characteristic)

label: Evidence
body: Sometimes legit art aims to arouse anger and calls intentionally for real world action.

label: Evaluate
body: We have to get from what we know is a characteristic of some legit art (aims to arouse anger / calls for concrete intervention) to what the conclusion is trying to say is not a characteristic of some legit art (concern for beauty).

label: Goal
body: Look for an answer saying, "If it's trying to arouse anger, then it's not concerned with beauty", or an answer saying, "If it's calling for intervention in the world, then it's not concerned with beauty".

label: Conclusion (clearly = opinion)
body: Children clearly have a reasonably sophisticated understanding of what is real and what is pretend.

label: Evidence
body:
You can ask them which thing is real and which thing is pretend, and they generally get it right.
  Even when you see a kid running away from a dad who's pretending to be a lion, the kid doesn't legitimately think the dad is a lion or else she wouldn't be squealing in delight.

label: Evaluate
body:
Whenever we do Main Conclusion, we know that they have two main tricks for hiding the conclusion from us. The conclusion in 90% of Main Conclusion questions is either
  1. the very first sentence
  2. some Pivot / Rebuttal idea
  So when we read a Main Conclusion paragraph, we read that first sentence thinking there's almost a 50% chance that the very first claim is the Main Conclusion.
  Does this first sentence sound like an opinion coming from our author?
  Yes! It's wearing an Opinion Indicator, "clearly".
  Does the rest of the paragraph seem to be supporting that claim in the first sentence?
  Yes, everything else in this paragraph is helping to support the claim that kids know the difference between real and pretend.

label: Goal
body: Find the answer with the best meaning-match for the first sentence.

label: Conclusion (Therefore / should)
body: Our country should not sign the agreement.

label: Evidence
body: It would reduce economic growth in our country and others.

label: Evaluate
body:
Principle-Justify answers come in a few different forms. The most common form is an "If / Then" linking idea, that gets us from Evidence to Conclusion.
  Here, that would be
  "If reduces econ growth for us and others, should not do it"
  Sometimes the answer is phrased more as a rule-of-thumb that makes the premise sound like the most important consideration when doing whatever the conclusion is talking about.
  Here, that would sound like
  "the government of our country should always try to maximize economic growth"
  The third and most rare kind comes when the paragraph seems to be Weighing Tradeoffs, as this paragraph seems to be doing.
  When it comes to signing this agreement, what are the pros and cons?
  pro - significantly reduces pollution in world's oceans
  con - reduces economic growth for us and others
  We want an answer that tips the scales in the direction the author is leaning, like,
  "maintaining opportunities for economic growth is more important than significantly reducing pollution in the world's oceans".

label: Goal
body:
Let's look for something that sounds like one of our three predictions. It will help us to argue,
  "Even though signing this agreement would reduce pollution in the world's oceans, because it would also reduce economic growth, we should not sign it."

label: Conclusion
body: Taking cold medicine is clearly counterproductive.

label: Evidence
body: In a study, there was a correlation between people who took cold medication and those who had more severe symptoms. (people who were X were more Y than those who weren't)

label: Evaluate
body:
When authors see correlations, they over-eagerly jump to the conclusion that one thing causes the other.
  In this correlation,
  ```
  took cold meds || more severe symptoms
  ```
  which way does this author see causality flowing?
  ```
  took cold meds → more severe symptoms
  ```
  That's why she's saying that taking cold meds is counterproductive (made the cold even worse).
  When we see authors pondering Curious Facts and deciding on their Explanation, we think:
  - could there be some OTHER WAY to explain this curious fact?
  - how plausible is the AUTHOR'S WAY?
  When it comes to correlations, we immediately think of two alternate ways to explain them:
  ```
  curious fact:
  took cold meds || more severe symptoms
  author:
  took cold meds → more severe symptoms
  us:
  took cold meds ← more severe symptoms?
  (reverse causality)
  took cold meds || more severe symptoms
              /
       (third factor?)
  ```
  In this case, reverse causality makes a lot of common sense: if you had mild symptoms, you probably wouldn't be as likely to bother taking cold meds, whereas if you had severe symptoms, you're more likely to seek medicinal relief.

label: Goal
body:
We're kind of looking for a contrapositive structure, but through the lens of an Action / Result.
  X knows that Action A leads to B.
  X doesn't want B.
  So, X won't do A.

label: Goal
body: Look for an answer pointing out the more likely interpretation of that correlation (that the severe symptoms came first, and THAT'S why those people took cold meds), or an answer saying there could be some Third Factor accounting for both (maybe older people are more likely to take meds and more likely to experience bad symptoms), or an answer just calling out the author's illegal inference from a correlation that one of the things is causing the other.

label: Background Claims
body:
Some people hate dealing with ugly truths and resent it when someone's unwanted honesty forces them into confronting these truths.
  Others hate having any information withheld from them, even if it's a painful truth.

label: Setup
body: If someone is in group 1, and they are trying to employ the moral rule to "treat other people as you yourself would want to be treated", then ...

label: Evaluate
body:
People in group 1 don't want to hear or confront the ugly truths. So if a G1 person is trying to "treat people as they want to be treated", then they will refrain from saying an uncomfortable truth to them.
  People in group 2 want to hear every truth, no matter how uncomfortable.
  The setup text doesn't clearly indicate whether this group 1 person will be dealing with other group 1 people or with group 2 people. But if we assume that throughout life we're going to encounter some people from each group, it means that the G1 person will always be withholding the unpleasant truth (because that's how they would like to be treated), even when they deal with a G2 person who doesn't want the truth withheld.

label: Goal
body:
The most interesting tension here is what happens when this G1 person is dealing with a G2. The G1 person wants to avoid confronting unpleasant truths, while the G2 person wants all the truth they can get. So if the G1 person is treating people how they themselves want to be treated, they'll end up withholding unpleasant truths even though the person they're dealing with (a G2) would prefer to hear the unpleasant truth.
  Look for a safely worded answer that addresses this tension.

label: Evidence
body:
```
  Study history → appreciate differences
  Reflect on your civilization → appreciate differences
  ```

label: Conclusion
body:
```
  Study history → Reflect on your civilization
  ```

label: Evaluate
body:
This is a pretty common template for Parallel Flaw (in general, Necessary vs. Sufficient flaws like these are common on Parallel Flaw).
  More commonly, we see
  ```
  A → B
  A → C
  Thus, B → C
  ```
  Here, we're getting
  ```
  A → B
  C → B
  Thus, A → C
  ```
  The hardest part of setting up this one is the novel phrasing of "provided that" to introduce a sufficient condition. If I say "Provided that you drink enough water beforehand, you won't have any trouble with this hike", it would look like
  Drink enough water → Won't have trouble with hike
  Conversationally, here's the problem with the conclusion. If you study history, we know you'll be aware of the differences. But we don't know that if you're aware of the differences that you'll reflect on your own civilization.
  The author tries to go backwards with that conditional.

label: Goal
body:
- Two premises, both conditional, both have the same outcome
  - Conclusion tries to build a conditional between the two triggers

label: Statements
body:
On Must Be True, we're primarily looking out for Conditional or Math-y wording. The last sentence has the conditional word "requires", which is a necessary (right side) indicator.
  Required thing = goes on Right
  ```
  Solving a philosophical → Accepting one of
  paradox                   three things
  ```
  We either have to accept
  1. The conclusion is true
  2. At least one premise is not true, or
  3. The logic isn't valid
  Here's a stupid example of a pseudo-philosophical paradox:
  Applesauce is better than nothing. Nothing is better than getting to hold your newborn baby. Therefore, applesauce is better than getting to hold your newborn baby.
  We know, intuitively, that the conclusion is wrong. Applesauce doesn't beat the first time you cradle your progeny.
  But ... each premise sounds like a true statement. The logic seems solid:
  premise 1: Applesauce > Nothing
  premise 2: Nothing > holding newborn
  conclusion: Applesauce > holding newborn
  In order for us to resolve our cognitive dissonance, we need to either give in and accept the conclusion, or fight it by saying that a premise isn't a valid claim or that we're somehow messing up the logic of combining premises to derive the conclusion.

label: Evaluate
body:
When we have a conditional rule, we look to see if we can chain it to other conditionals, or whether we can apply it to any facts that trigger the rule.
  There aren't any other conditionals, and there isn't a fact where someone has "solved a philosophical paradox", to whom we could apply this rule.

label: Goal
body: So, we should just go to the questions flexibly, and anticipate that the answer will probably make some use of the conditional rule.

label: Conclusion
body: From a sociological perspective, affection plays a similar role in chimp and in human communities.

label: Evidence
body:
Humans are more likely risk danger to save someone they have affection for.
  In chimp communities, chimps who show affection for others are more likely to be saved from danger by other group members than are those who don't show affection.

label: Evaluate
body:
The author is just trying to establish that affection plays a similar role. Let's clarify for ourselves the role in each of chimp/human, to study the similarities and differences.
  In humans, we're more willing to face risks for people we have affection for. If I really like Eddie at the office, I'm more willing to face risks for him than for Stuart, whom I don't really like.
  In chimps, we're more willing to face risks for the gregarious (outgoing, affectionate, life-of-the-party) chimps than for the shy ones. The ones who go around giving out affection, grabbing your arm, giving you big hugs, high fives ... those are the ones we protect. The wallflowers who have closed body language don't get saved.
  The sameness is affection and risking danger to save.
  The difference is that in the human example, the recipient of affection is being saved by others.
  In the chimp example, the giver of affection is being saved by others.

label: Goal
body: Since the author wants to assume these two situations are the same, she must be assuming that the people who give out affection, get back affection. That makes the chimp and human example more fair to compare.

label: Conclusion
body:
This is an overly hasty inference.
  (i.e. the fact that T. Rex was huge and heavy and slow doesn't necessarily mean it wasn't a hunter)

label: Evidence
body: If T. Rex's prey were larger than T. Rex, then the prey would probably be even slower. (So even if T. Rex is slow, as long as it had prey that was even slower, it would be fast enough to hunt down that prey)

label: Evaluate
body:
Like on tons of Main Conclusion and Role questions, the conclusion here is found earlier than the evidence, and as part of a rebuttal.
  COUNTERPOINT It has been argued that ...
  AUTHOR's PIVOT This, however, is [wrong].
  SUPPORT If the prey were slower ...

body: Look for something like Counterpoint, Opposing Position, "the inference the author thinks is unwarranted by the evidence", etc.

label: Conditionals
body:
```
  ~Retributivist
  and → ~Acceptable
  ~Rehabilitationist
  Retributivist
  and → ~Acceptable
  Doesn't use principle
  that punishment = harm
  ```

label: Facts
body: A retributivist theory that punishes extra if it's a repeat offense would go against this principle.

label: Evaluate
body:
The simple Conditional + Fact type inference here would be that the theory they talk about in the last sentence is not acceptable, since it doesn't adhere to the "punishment = harm" principle.
  But my spidey-sense makes me think they are probably going to use the Rehab rule or the fact that there are only two acceptable theories rule, in some way.

label: Given that ...
body: the folktales in almost all cultures are adaptations of the same ancient narratives.

label: How can it be that ...
body: Sociologists study folktales because they provide a means of understanding the distinctive values of a culture?

label: Evaluate / Goal
body:
The tension here is that if the folktales are being adapted from the same ancient narratives, then how would they show off the distinctive values of each culture?
  This is an atypical Paradox question in the sense that the background claim appears last in the paragraph, and the surprising claim appears 1st.
  We can imagine that the correct answer will probably say something about "the way the same narrative can be adapted in different ways is illuminating about the specifics of each culture."

label: Setup Claims
body:
Engineers trying to construct a self-driving robotic car face the challenge of designing a car that avoids common crashes and congestion.
  These problems can also affect fish traveling together in schools.
  But, the principles fish use to navigate in schools ensure that these problems are much less common within schools of fish than among cars on the road.

label: The Blank
body:
Hence .
  Since the blank is prefaced by a conclusion indicator, we want our answer to draw a logical conclusion, like on a Must Be True / Most Supported question.

label: Evaluate
body:
Like many other Fill in the Blank questions, this argument contains an analogy, and the conclusion seems to be inviting us to carry over what we heard about fish schools to what we're saying about robotic cars.
  They both face problems with crashes and congestion.
  The navigation principles fish use help them avoid such events.

label: Goal
body: So let's look for a safely worded answer that sounds like, "Engineers working on self-driving robotic cars might want to consider using navigation principles like fish schools use".

label: Given that ...
body: There are perfectly suitable lakes nearby that are vacant.

label: Why is it that ...
body: More than half the time, loons choose to oust the current occupants of a lake rather than just take over a new one?

label: Evaluate
body:
When two loons return from their winter hideaway and are feeling the itch to breed, they have to claim a vacant lake for themselves or chase away the current occupants of a lake.
  One would think it's easier to claim a vacant lake than to chase away the current occupants of a lake.

label: Goal
body:
So if there are perfectly suitable, vacant lakes nearby, why are loons taking the "harder" route and trying to chase away current occupants of lakes?
  Is there something especially enticing about those lakes (even though others are "suitable", are the other ones worse somehow)?
  Do the loons not realize there are perfectly suitable vacant lakes nearby?
