  Does the conflict of chasing away the previous couple turn these two loons on and get them in the mood to breed? (I'm sure it's not that, but that's a funny correct answer)

label: Conclusion (So)
body: Turning off the air conditioner was the right decision.

label: Evidence
body: Even though my passengers were complaining because it was a hot day, I was driving up a steep hill and if I hadn't turned off the A/C that would have meant either driving more slowly or getting considerably worse fuel economy.

label: Evaluate
body:
Since this argument acknowledges that there was a reason to turn off the A/C and a reason not to turn off the A/C, we could say this falls into the category of Principle-Strengthen questions that are Weighing Tradeoffs.
  Our author ultimately decides that it was correct to turn off the A/C, so he must be assuming that the positives outweighed the negatives.

label: Goal
body:
Look for a comparative answer like, "It's more important to maintain speed / maintain fuel economy than it is to pacify the complaints of your passengers".
  Or maybe we'll see a Missing Link conditional answer like, "If X was required in order to maintain speed / fuel economy, then X was the correct decision".

label: Conclusion
body: Bach is remembered because he was such a prolific (productive) composer, not because he had a high ratio of great songs to mediocre songs.

label: Intermediate Conclusion (so)
body: It was inevitable that some of Bach's songs would be outstanding and thus survive the ages.

label: Evidence
body: He wrote more than a thousand full-fledged compositions.

label: Goal
body: Thus, we should be able to infer something like, "when it comes to the striatum, newly formed neurons never help to heal an injured brain".

label: Evaluate
body:
The author is essentially trying to Solve a Causal Mystery so we can use your Explain Curious Fact mindset.
  Curious Fact ... why is Bach so famous?
  Author's Explanation ... He wasn't better than average at making hits (his ratio of great stuff to mediocre stuff is ordinary). But he was super productive. He wrote more than a thousand songs, so obviously some of those will be timeless hits that make it into civilization's permanent playlist.

label: Goal
body:
Since this is Weaken, we can either suggest an Alternate Explanation for why Bach is famous (maybe he invented a new instrument or a new technique or he had really powerful friends).
  Or we can hurt the Plausibility of the Author's Explanation, by making it seem like Bach is not famous just because he wrote a 1000 songs.

label: Conclusion (Clearly)
body: The two major political parties in this city have become sharply divided on the issues.

label: Evidence (for example)
body: In the last four elections, the parties were separated by less than 1% of the vote.

label: Evaluate
body:
The author is looking at a statistic and interpreting the cause behind it, so we can use our Explain Curious Fact mindset.
  Curious Fact ... how come the parties have been separated by less than 1% of the vote for the last four elections?
  Author's Explanation ... It's because they've become sharply divided on the issues.
  We want to consider these 2 questions:
  1. Could there be some Alternate Explanation for that curious fact?
  2. How plausible is the Author's Explanation?
  In this case, they might meld together more than usual, because one Alternate Explanation for why elections are so close could be that there isn't much difference between the two parties. If Democrats and Republicans were both offering essentially the same position on a lot of issues, then how would a voter choose between them?
  If the parties were sharply divided on issues, for example "Let's take drastic action vs. let's take no action when it comes to climate change", then voters would have a clear choice in terms of whom to vote for, so you wouldn't see a lot of near-ties unless voters themselves were half for drastic action and half for no action.

label: Goal
body: Look for an answer either saying that the author has failed to consider alternate explanations for why the last four elections have been close, or for an answer suggesting that polarized positions would seemingly favor tilted elections.

label: Conclusion
body: The still waters around Shooter's Island serve as a nursery for the juveniles.

label: Evidence
body: Shooter's Island has unusually still waters, and an unusually high percentage of juvenile birds (similar overall number birds).

label: Evaluate
body:
Since the author is interpreting a Curious Fact (anomalies / asymmetries), we can use our Curious Fact / Explanation template.
  Curious Fact
  Why does Shooter's Island have such a high percentage of juvenile birds?
  Author's Explanation
  Because of the super still waters, the local waterbirds must choose to raise their children at Shooter's.
  A correct answer will deal with one of these two pressure points:
  1. an Alternate Explanation for the curious fact
  2. the plausibility of the Author's Explanation
  As yourself,
  "What could be a different reason, besides still water, that Shooter's Island has a lot of juveniles?" (easier hunting for food? better protection from predators? easier place to mate?)
  "What evidence could help corroborate the author's notion that still waters make this a good place for a nursery?" (young waterbirds find it easier to learn to swim and fly in still waters?)

label: Goal
body:
Since this is Strengthen, we either want an answer that
  Rules out a different reason why Shooter's has a high percentage of juveniles
  or
  Helps the author's story that "still waters make for a good nursery" sound more plausible.
  The most common way to Strengthen a Curious Fact is a "No Cause, No Effect" plausibility strengthener. So here that would sound like "where there aren't still waters, you don't see a lot of juveniles"

label: Conclusion (So)
body: If census participation became voluntary, polls designed to discover the opinions of the national population would have less accurate results.

label: Evidence
body:
The accuracy of polling samples is based on census data.
  If the census participation became voluntary, then even fewer people would participate in it.

label: Evaluate
body:
In a straightforward Linking way, the author seems to be assuming, "if fewer people participate in the census, then polls based on census data will be less accurate".
  Why is that a dubious assumption? How could it be that fewer people participate in the census, but polls based on census data are just as accurate?
  if the participation went down evenly across all demographic groups, then the census data would reflect the same relative composition of the country.
  Take one small piece of census data: political party affiliation.
  Say that every person in the country took the census and recorded their political party, and we found out it was like 35% Republican, 35% Democrat, 30% Independent.
  Now say we removed 100,000 data points from the census. What would the political affiliation breakdown look like now?
  We have no idea! It might look exactly the same. If you removed 35,000 Republican respondents, 35,000 Democrat ones, and 30,000 Independent ones, then the resulting pile of data points would still be 35/35/30.
  Meanwhile, if we say "Were the census to become voluntary, almost all Independents would still fill it out, but only half as many Republicans and Democrats would still fill it out", then that will skew the breakdown. It will look like there are more Independent voters than there really are, since they will now be over-represented relative to R's and D's.

label: Goal
body:
The one objection that could tank this argument is if we said, "if you made the census voluntary, and way fewer people participated, but the decreased rate of participation was essentially the same across all demographic groups, then you'd still end up with the same census data, and thus the population samples would still reflect the same breakdown as before."
  Thus, the argument must be assuming that the drop in participation for a voluntary census would not be the same across all demographic groups.

label: Conclusion (so / clearly)
body: Hoitsu's Spring and Autumn Maples is among the most valuable pieces in the collection.

label: Evidence
body:
It will be on display for two weeks only.
  The works that are most sensitive to light and the works that are the most valuable pieces will be on display for two weeks only.

label: Hendry's Claims
body:
1. Most employee strikes should be legally permitted.
  2. University faculty strikes shouldn't be legally permitted.
  3. Faculty strikes harm a university's students.
  4. If a strike would harm the employer's customers, then it shouldn't be legally permitted.

label: Evaluate
body:
Our immediate reaction to this might be, "Wait -- how do you know that Hoitsu's work is one of the most valuable pieces. Couldn't it be one of the ones that are most sensitive to light?
  After all, the first sentence lays out two separate categories of works that will be on display for two weeks only.
  ```
  If most sensitive to light → 2 weeks only
  If most valuable pieces → 2 weeks only
  ```
  It feels like the author looks at the fact that Hoitsu's work will be on display for 2 weeks only and automatically assumes it's from the "valuable" category rather than the "sensitive to light" category.
  But the argument is also making an Illegal Reversal by going from the fact that Hoitsu's work will be on display for 2 weeks only to either of those trigger ideas. It's possible that his work will be on display for 2 weeks only for some other reason we haven't even mentioned yet. The argument never said that these are the only two categories of things that are 2 weeks only displays.

label: Goal
body:
Since there are multiple flaws, the correct answer will probably exhibit both of them. If we wanted to think about this symbolically, we could say:
  ```
  Prem 1: A or B → C
  Prem 2: Thing X is C.
  Conc: Thing X is B.
  ```
  That has both the illegal reversal from the outcome, C, to the trigger. And it also has the arbitrary choice of concluding B, when A would be just as valid a choice.

label: Conclusion
body: 90% of my business clients increased their profits at least tenfold last year.

label: Evidence
body:
Last year, 90% of my clients who made a profit made at least $100k in profit.
  In prior years, not one of these businesses made an annual profit of more than $10k.

label: Evaluate
body:
This argument would be correct if the conclusion had said,
  "90% of my business clients who made a profit last year increased their profits at least tenfold last year."
  The argument's only flaw is that in the Evidence it's talking about
  90% of my profitable clients
  but then in the Conclusion it jumps to talking about
  90% of my clients
  Suppose this marketing agent has 20 clients. Last year 10 of them were profitable and 10 were not profitable.
  The evidence says that 9 of those 10 profitable clients posted $100k in profits after having never done better than $10k.
  So 90% of her profitable clients increased tenfold last year.
  But this is still just 9 out of 20 ... 45% of her clients.

label: Goal
body: Look for an answer complaining that the Evidence was about profitable clients whereas the Conclusion was about all clients.

label: Given that...
body:
Changes in Britain's National Health Service have led many British hospitals to end on-site laundry services for their staff.
  The water in a typical residential washing machine, unlike that in the industrial washing machines used by hospitals, does not reach temperatures high enough to kill the dangerous bacterium Acinetobacter.

label: How can it be that...
body: Hospital officials believe that the discontinuation of the laundry services will not put patients at risk.

label: Evaluate
body:
If on-site laundry services at hospitals are ending, it seems that hospital staff will need to wash their work clothes at home. But residential washing machines aren't going to kill a dangerous bacterium. It seems that this would put patients at risk. Why do hospital officials believe that it won't?
  First, we aren't told that hospital staff will actually use residential machines now. Maybe they'll take their clothes to a laundromat, and maybe washers in laundromats get hot enough to kill the bacterium.
  Maybe hospital staff can do something else at home to kill the bacteria, like using special detergent.
  Also, we have not been told that Acinetobacter actually exists in hospitals. Maybe Acinetobacter is some rare bacterium that only exists at the bottom of the ocean. It might seem absurd for a correct answer to suggest this, but have you met the LSAT?
  All kidding aside, by asking us to "justify the hospital officials' belief," this question assumes that Acinetobacter causes hospital patients to be at risk. A correct answer might challenge this assumption.

label: Goal
body: Look for an answer to suggest an alternative way to kill Acinetobacter. A correct answer might also challenge the idea that Acinetobacter causes any risk for hospital patients.

label: Conclusion
body:
(Such a move is ill-advised)
  Cutting back on book reviews (and replacing them with other features) is an ill-advised move.

label: Evidence
body: It will decrease readership by alienating loyal reading while catering to casual readers who are more likely to watch TV than pick up a newspaper.

label: Evaluate
body:
On Main Conclusion questions, the Conclusion is almost always (but not always) earlier in the paragraph than the support.
  The two main patterns:
  - Conclusion is the very first claim
  - Conclusion feels like a rebuttal
  This one did the second pattern. Newspapers are trying a new strategy and the author rebuts that strategy wit a "Such a move is ill-advised".

label: Goal
body: There's nothing complicated about the backend of Main Conclusion. If we found the right claim, we just go look for a meaning match in the answers: it was an ill-advised move to cut back on book reviews in favor of other features that would interest potential readers.

label: Conclusion (prediction = opinion)
body: There will be more local cases of flu this year than last year.

label: Evidence
body: In addition to the strains of flu that were present last year, a new strain of flu has infected some people this year.

label: Evaluate
body:
The evidence is talking about the number of strains this year vs. last year. The conclusion is talking about the number of cases of the flu.
  So we can tell that the author seems to be assuming,
  "If there are more strains this year, then there will be more cases this year".
  Does that have to be true?
  Not necessarily. There are more strains of Covid now than at the beginning of the pandemic (alpha, delta, omicron, Ba2) but there are fewer cases now than at earlier points in the pandemic. Why? There are more vaccinated and previously-infected people at this point in the pandemic than before.
  Similarly, there might be salient differences this year with the flu. Maybe more people are vaccinated. Maybe tons of people moved away. Maybe people are doing a better job of social distancing / masking / avoiding crowded indoor spaces.

label: Goal
body:
The correct answer needs to convince us of more cases than last year, so that New Concept in the Conclusion should be in the correct answer.
  It should take us from what we know, i.e. "we have more strains than we did last year" and then somehow guarantee that # of cases is also higher.

label: Conclusion
body: Thompson's article is intriguing but ultimately puzzling.

label: Menkin's Responses
body:
1. No Position. Although she says "employee strikes should almost never be legally permitted", that's only if we accept Hendry's principle. We don't know whether Menkin accepts Hendry's principle, so we don't know if Menkin actually thinks that almost no strikes should be legally permitted.
  2. No Position. Menkin never says anything specifically about faculty strikes at a university.
  3. No Position. Menkin never says anything specifically about faculty strikes at a university.
  4. No Position. Menkin just says, "if your principle is correct", so we don't know whether Menkin thinks the principle is or isn't correct.

label: Evaluate
body:
Since the 2nd speaker didn't disagree with any of the 1st speaker's explicit claims, we have to go a level deeper. Is Menkin disagreeing with one of Hendry's assumptions?
  Menkin says that using Hendry's principle would contradict one of the things Hendry's claims.
  Menkin is saying that Hendry's principle contradicts the idea that "most employee strikes should be legally permitted". According to the principle, a strike shouldn't be legally permitted if it would harm the employer's customers.
  ```
  harm customers → shouldn't be permitted
  should be permitted → not harm customers
  ```
  If Hendry thinks that most strikes should be permitted, then he thinks that "most strikes do not harm customers".
  If Menkin thinks that most strikes shouldn't be permitted, then he thinks that "most strikes do harm customer".

label: Goal
body: Let's look for an answer about whether or not most strikes would harm the employer's customers.

label: Conclusion (consequently)
body: Uninformed viewers of dramatic historical films should not regard them as accurate portrayals of historical events.

label: Evidence
body: Most popular historical films are dramatic presentations of historical events, not documentaries. Such presentations cannot present the evidence for the accuracy of what they portray.

label: Evaluate
body: The conclusion cares about whether or not we "should regard X as an accurate portrayal". The reason the author doesn't think we should consider historical films accurate portrayals is that they are not documentaries, they are dramatic presentations, and they cannot present the evidence for the accuracy of what they portray.

label: Goal
body:
The correct answer can potentially use any of the things we know about historical films and then help us link that to "should not regard as accurate".
  - If it's not a documentary, should not regard as accurate portrayal
  - If it's a dramatic presentation of historical events, should not regard as accurate portrayal
  - If the evidence for accuracy can't be presented, should not regard as accurate portrayal

label: Carrillo's Claims
body:
1. Our model strongly supports the conclusion that the first primate developed around 81.5 million years ago.
  2. (implicit): Our model used the number of existing primate species, along with measures of the genetic diversity among these primates and among the primate species.

label: Olson's reaction
body:
1. Your model does not strongly support that conclusion. Your 81.5 million year guess is sheer speculation.
  2. (implicit): I put more faith in our oldest discovered fossils than I do in your statistical model which just used the number of existing primates and the genetic diversity of living and extinct primates.

label: Evaluate
body: This is an unusual Disagree question since the 1st speaker only makes one claim. Lucky for us, that is the claim the 2nd speaker seems to quarrel with, but we have to dial in the language of the disagreement.

label: Goal
body:
It looks like it's "strongly support" vs. "sheer speculation", in regards to this statistical model based on quantity and diversity of primate species.
  Though we could also probably say it's a case of "statistical models based on quantity and diversity of primate species" vs. "known fossil evidence", in regards to which type of data is more trustworthy.

label: Conclusion
body: The communications devices installed in our automobiles are not dangerously distracting to drivers.

label: Evidence
body: Drivers who want to use communications devices are gonna use them either way. Ours are easier to use, and thus safer.

label: Evaluate
body:
Does easier = safer? That makes some sense. But if we're trying to Weaken / Object, we need to think of way to argue that,
  Even Though
  the devices are easier to use
  It Could Still Be True That
  the devices are dangerously distracting to drivers
  What else could be different (besides easier to use) that could help us say that this is a change for the worse?
  I picture people who have their smart phones cleverly mounted on the A/C vent of their car. That seems easier to use than my method -- having my phone just laying in the armrest console or on the passenger seat.
  It's true that I still use my phone regardless, but if I had my phone mounted on my vent I would probably be inclined to use it a lot more. It's so easy to use, why not check Twitter? Why not text Samantha? Why not pull up a YouTube video for the kids shouting in the back seat?
  It's possible that by making something easier to use, it encourages greater use of that thing, and maybe frequent use of a dashboard mounted phone is actually more dangerously distracting to a driver than is occasional use of a less convenient phone on the seat next to you.

label: Goal
body: Look for an answer that allows us to agree with "easier" but lets us still argue that these are dangerously distracting.

label: Background
body: Mosquito larvae are aquatic, so outbreaks of mosquito diseases typically go up after long periods of wet weather.

label: Surprise / Exception
body: If the mosquito breeds in a wetland habitat, then the outbreaks of mosquito diseases tends to go up after a drought.

label: Evaluate / Goal
body: We need something different about mosquitoes who breed in wetlands that would explain why they seem to proliferate after periods of drought.

label: Conclusion (Thus)
body: If public health people emphasized the dangers of a sedentary lifestyle rather than the positive health effects of exercise, then efforts to get the public to exercise regularly would be more successful.

label: Evidence
body:
Efforts that have emphasized the positive health effects of exercise have met with little success.
  Meanwhile, efforts to emphasize the negative health effects of cigarette smoking have been highly successful.

label: Conclusion
body: We shouldn't conclude that volcanic activity caused the sulfur dioxide spike on Venus.

label: Evaluate
body:
This argument has a couple undercurrents, so it'll be tricky to predict exactly where the answer is going.
  On aspect of the argument is a Plan / Recommendation, so we want to consider whether this plan is feasible, whether people would be motivated to cooperate with it, whether it would backfire in some way.
  But another aspect of this argument is Argument by Analogy. The author thinks that "if emphasizing harm worked for cigarettes, it'll work for exercise as well".
  So we could weaken this argument by fighting the Plan ...
  - it's not feasible to emphasize dangers of sedentary
  - it wouldn't motivate people to think about the dangers of sedentary
  - the dangers of sedentary would seem so mild and tolerable that it would backfire and people would think "THAT's the only price I'll pay for not going to the gym?"
  ... or by fighting the Comparison
  - the dangers of smoking are way worse than the dangers of sedentary lifestyle
  - a campaign to emphasize the benefits of quitting smoking would be even more helpful than the successful ones they've done which emphasized the dangers of smoking

label: Goal
body: Look for an answer that seems to match a thought the author definitely had in her mind, or look for something that, when negated, would be a big objection to the argument.

label: Umit's Objection
body: We shouldn't try to replace standard cars with electric cars, in order to reduce urban pollution.

label: Umit's Evidence
body: Electric cars have to be recharged a bunch, so if everyone started driving them it would create more demand for power plant electricity, which is a major source of pollution.

label: Evaluate
body:
Given that
  switching to electric cars would create more demand for power plant electricity, which is a major source of pollution,
  How could we argue that
  replacing regular cars with electric cars would reduce urban pollution?
  Well, there's a Comparison aspect to this argument: we realize that electric cars would still need energy and still cause pollution. We care about whether it would be less / same / more. Umit is just saying it would be major, but that doesn't help us compare.
  So we could counter by saying, "Yes there would be pollution from the increased use of power plants, but that's still less pollution than what we're currently causing by using combustion engine cars."
  But there's also a shift from pollution in the evidence to urban pollution in the conclusion. Maybe there's some way to counter where you say, "Yes there would be more pollution from the increased use of power plants, but there would be less urban pollution", for some reason.

label: Student's Claims
body:
1. It's unfair for the History Department to prohibit students from citing Wikipedia in their research papers because these sources are not peer reviewed.
  2. Students should be allowed to read whatever they wish.
  3. If students aren't allowed to read whatever they with, then it's censorship.

label: Professors's Responses
body:
1. Does she think it is fair to prohibit citing Wikipedia in research papers?
  Yes. She disagrees with the student's first claim. Wikipedia, since it isn't peer reviewed, cannot reasonably be treated as reliable support for any claim.
  2. Does she think students shouldn't be allowed to read whatever they wish?
  No. She explicitly agrees with the student's 2nd claim and says students are allowed to read whatever they like.
  3. Does she think a student could be restricted from reading something they want to, but we wouldn't necessarily call it censorship?
  We have no idea. She never broaches the concept of censorship.

label: Goal
body:
The student made three claims. The professor disagreed with the first, agreed with the second, and had no response to the third.
  Let's look for an answer that sounds like the first claim:
  whether it's fair / unfair for the History Dept to forbid students from citing online encyclopedias in their research papers.

label: Conclusion
body: Our "Doing Business" ranking will probably improve.

label: Evidence
body:
"Doing Business" rankings are based on how easy it is to do business in a given country.
  Since the last "Doing Business" rankings came out, our government has dramatically simplified tax filing for small and midsized businesses.

label: Evaluate
body:
There's a missing link assumption occurring that "simplifying tax filings can make it easier to do business in a country". So we could see a correct answer that just asks that assumption, "Is it generally easier to do business somewhere when the tax system is simplified?"
  But we can also dig into the conclusion ...
  Given that ... we've simplified the tax code since last report,
  How could it be that ... our ranking doesn't go up?
  Well, what about for large businesses? Did we simplify their tax code? Did it get worse? Is it a big part of the "Doing Business" ranking how easy it is for large businesses to do business in a given country?
  Finally, let's say we really did get easier for businesses -- that doesn't necessarily mean we rise in the rankings. It's possible that other businesses above us in the rankings also got easier to work with, thereby maintaining or increasing their superiority over us.
  And it's possible that the next country higher than us in the rankings was so much higher than us that even though we've improved we still haven't eclipsed them.

label: Goal
body:
Look for an answer choice posing a question that could be answered in a way that would weaken the argument.
  In other words, find a question where you could answer it in a way that would help you argue that this business's "Doing Business" ranking is not going to improve in the next issued report.

label: Conclusion
body: Roemer probably doesn't care that her new style of writing is only alienating people with opposing viewpoints.

label: Evidence
body: Her column is just an attempt to please her loyal readers.

label: Evaluate
body:
This one is a TOUGH nut to crack. It's hard to say what exactly was wrong with anything. There also seem to be multiple conclusions.
  BECAUSE she has always had a partisan stance and recently has even started impugning the motives of her opponents, and BECAUSE that style is guaranteed to alienate (rather than change the minds of) her opponents, her column has a polarizing effect?
  That feels like a relatively reasonable argument. If you're alienating opponents and not winning any over, then by definition you are exacerbating polarization.
  The "since" premise keyword in the last sentence makes it seem like LSAT wants us to focus on the reasoning move in that sentence.
  Is it possible that Roehmer's column is just an attempt to please loyal readers, but she is troubled (it is a problem for Roehmer) that her style isn't likely to win over any opponents?
  Sure. Maybe they're testing an Intent vs. Consequences distinction, where the consequence of Roehmer's style is polarization, but the Intent is to please her readers while making arguments that will win over some opponents.

label: Goal
body:
Realistically, most of us are not going to see the actual issue they're going for on a first read, so let's role play that we're just going to the answers thinking, "Maybe Roehmer DOES find it troubling that her column is only alienating opponents."
  (HINT: If you want to try to solve the riddle of what they're going for, it has to do with "impugning motives" and "her column is just an attempt to ... ")

label: Conclusion
body: Fine short story writers are unlikely to become great novelists.

label: Evidence
body:
Fine short story writers have the ability to weave together many small details.
  Novelists must focus on larger matters.
  Only a few writers can do both weave together many small details and focus on larger matters.

label: Evaluate
body:
Because of all the repeating terms (short story writers, novelists, weave together small, focus on larger are all mentioned at least twice), we can probably turn this into algebra to make it easier to compare to answers.
  ```
  Conclusion: A's are unlikely to become B.
  Premise 1: A's are good at X.
  Premise 2: B's need to be good at Y.
  Premise 3: It's unlikely to be good at X and Y
  ```

label: Goal
body:
Look for a conclusion that is saying "A's are unlikely to be B".
  The premises should then tell us a signature quality of A, a signature quality of B, and that those two qualities rarely coincide.

label: Conclusion
body: Each of the proposed regulations would help the economy.

label: Evidence
body: Each of the proposed regulations would reduce the trade deficit, which is so large that it weakens the economy.

label: Evaluate
body:
Given that
  each of the proposed regulations would reduce trade deficit, which is so large that it weakens the economy
  How could we still argue that
  at least one of the regulations would not help the economy?
  Two possible thoughts here:
  1. Maybe the regulations have more than one effect. They reduce the trade deficit (which is a good thing), but maybe they stifle foreign investment (a bad thing). So it's hard to say whether their overall effect is helpful to the economy, just because they definitely do one helpful thing for the economy.
  2. They stressed that the deficit is so large that it weakens the economy. Maybe some of these proposed regulations would reduce the deficit, but not by much. If the economy is weakened by the fact that the trade deficit is so large, then a tiny reduction might not actually impart any help to the economy, because the trade deficit would still be large.

label: Goal
body: Look for an answer talking about other effects of the regulations that would be bad for the economy, or for an answer that says that the reduction they would have on the deficit would not be significant enough to help the economy.

label: Conclusion
body: It's too early to understand the e-book.

label: Evidence
body: New media start by carrying old media's content; e-books are in that phase, so haven't taken final form.

label: Evaluate
body: The argument needs a bridge from "content still borrowed / ultimate form not yet reached" to "can't yet be understood."

label: Goal
body: Find a principle linking understanding a medium to seeing its content evolve.

label: Plato's Evidence
body: Music can manipulate the emotions in harmful ways.

label: Plato's Conclusion
body: Societies need to put restrictions on the music their citizens hear.

label: Ullman's Evidence
body: Musicians seek not to manipulate the emotions but to create beauty.

label: Ullman's Conclusion
body: Plato's argument is misguided.

label: Evaluate
body:
The final sentence in the stimulus follows a common form:
  Premise Indicator - Premise - Comma - Conclusion
  The premise indicator "because" at the beginning of the second sentence is followed by a premise. That premise is followed by a comma, which is followed by the argument's conclusion.
  The pivot indicator "however" also helps us to identify the conclusion. A pivot indicator frequently marks the point where some initial claim or idea comes to an end and the actual argument begins. It also indicates that the actual argument is a rebuttal of the initial claim or idea.
  In this case, Ullman's argument is a rebuttal of Plato's argument.
  Plato's evidence describes something that music is capable of doing—it can manipulate emotions in harmful ways. Notice that Ullman's evidence is about what musicians intend to do: Ullman states that they don't seek to manipulate emotions.
  Ullman's argument is flawed because their evidence addresses a completely different issue than Plato's. Plato could easily say, "look, Ullman, it doesn't matter what musicians seek to do. I'm talking about what music actually does. My argument isn't misguided at all."

label: Goal
body: We'll expect an answer to focus on the difference between Plato's evidence about what music is actually capable of doing and Ullman's objection, which focuses on musician's intentions. This question stem states that a correct answer should describe a possibility that the argument fails to consider, so the correct answer should be worded as an objection to Ullman's reasoning, something that would harm Ullman's argument. Beware of answers that would support Ullman's argument.

label: Conclusion
body: The tax on saturated fat (intended to reduce consumption of unhealthy foods) should not have been repealed so soon.

label: Evidence
body: It was only around for seven months. Apparently, it was having some unintended consequences (people were just traveling to nearby countries to buy the taxed foods).

label: Evaluate
body:
This is a bit weird, because there isn't actually a premise, other than "it's only been around for seven months". The other fact presented is counterevidence — the fact that the plan is backfiring and driving people to buy their unhealthy food from a neighboring country would be a reason to get rid of the tax.
  So, we can't do much to predict the correct answer, other than say, "If it's only been in effect for seven months, then we shouldn't have repealed it so soon."

label: Goal
body: Look for any answer providing a rule that would apply to this tax and would allow us to conclude something like "It was repealed too soon" / "it was premature to repeal it" / "we should have let it stay on the books for longer" / etc.

label: Conclusion (should)
body: We should prohibit this sale (of our domestic iron-mining company FerroMetal to a foreign company).

label: Intermediate Conclusion
body: We need a dependable supply of iron ore.

label: Evidence (since)
body:
Manufacturing is central to our economy.
  If a foreign company buys FerroMetal, we will have no grounds to stop foreign companies from buying other iron-mining companies.
  Then foreigners will control most iron mining, leaving our manufacturers at their mercy.
  Finally, our manufacturers will no longer be able to rely on a domestic supply of iron ore.

label: Evaluate
body:
This argument seems to have a couple intermediate conclusions, as we have a "since X, Y" construction, as well as a "the end result will be" construction. Both of those constructions can be thought of as causal or reasoning, depending on the context.
  With so many ideas, it's hard to know where to begin or how to organize. It might be best to do a second read, claim-by-claim, to think about where it seems to go off the rails / where we'd want to object.
  The first two sentences give us the background and Conclusion, so we know that we will be pretending to inhabit the role of Opposing Counsel and make a case that "We should allow the sale of this domestic iron-mining company to a foreign company".
  Maybe we're lovers of the free market and think that private companies should be allowed to do whatever they wish without government intrusion.
  The 3rd sentence is saying, "since manufacturing is central, we need a reliable supply of iron ore". How does that connect to the conclusion? The author must be thinking that if we sell off a domestic iron mining company to a foreign company, it will threaten our ability to have a reliable supply of iron ore.
  We might already think of objections such as
  - what if we already have plenty of iron ore, or this company is really small and un-impactful, so selling off this company would have no big impact on our supply of iron ore?
  - why is it bad for a foreign company to control a company that mines some of our domestic iron ore? Will they not sell it to us? Won't it still be part of our supply of iron ore?
  The 4th sentence sounds like a really dubious idea in and of itself:
  If we let FerroMetal go to a foreign company, then we will have no grounds to stop other foreign companies from similar purchases?
  You won't? Why not? Why are you so convinced that as soon as you set this precedent, there's no way to put the gene back in the bottle?
  The 5th claim also sounds like a big jump:
  Soon foreigners will control most of the iron mining here.
  Really, soon, most will be under foreign control? Are their tons of foreign firms waiting on the sidelines to pounce as soon as we break the seal by selling FerroMetal?

label: Goal
body:
It's pretty hard to limit our focus here to any one specific objection. The author seems to make a lot of questionable moves that are vulnerable to objections.
  We might do best to remember our Anti-Conclusion perspective, "we don't need to prohibit this sale; it's okay to allow a foreign company to buy FerroMetal" and then deal with answers as they come, once we see what part of this argument they're focused on.

label: Conclusion
body: I stand by my decision to order the dumping of small amounts of chemicals into the local river, even though there's some evidence they may pose health problems.

label: Evidence
body: I fish in the river myself and will continue to do so. And I have no problem if other food manufacturers do what our company does.

label: Evaluate
body:
The author is essentially saying, "it was okay for me to decide that our company would dump some potentially harmful chemicals into the local river".
  Why is it okay?
  1. Golden Rule — I won't object if other companies do the same thing
  2. Put My Money Where My Mouth Is — I'm not afraid of what these chemicals will do to the river, as evidenced by the fact that I love this river and use it and will continue to eat things that come out of it.

label: Goal
body:
Let's look for something like, "If you're okay with other people doing questionable action X, then it's okay for you to do it."
  Or something like, "If you're willing to deal with the potential negative consequences of questionable action X, then it's okay for you do do it."

label: Conclusion (clearly)
body: Attacking an opposing candidate on philosophical grounds in generally more effective than attacking the details of the opponent's policy proposals.

label: Evidence
body: A philosophical attack links an opponent's policy proposals to an overarching ideological scheme, thereby telling a story, providing context, and making the attack emotionally compelling.

label: Evaluate
body:
The conclusion is a comparison between two different strategies, and the author is ultimately trying to say that one strategy is generally more effective than the other.
  The stuff we hear about the supposedly better strategy is that it links an opponent's policies to an overarching ideology, thereby telling a story and providing context, and thereby making the attack emotionally compelling.
  Since there is a chain of causality or reasoning there, we can suspect that LSAT is testing us on where that chain ends.
  Ultimately, we're hearing that attacking on philosophical grounds is more effective because it's emotionally compelling.

label: Goal
body: The most likely answer would be a missing link between "emotionally compelling" and "more effective". But the author is also assuming that "linking to an ideological scheme" is connected to being more effective, and that "telling a story and providing context" is connected to being more effective.

label: Michaela's Conclusion
body: It's a little unfair for doctors to complain about patients doing medical research on the internet.

label: Michaela's Evidence
body: It seems natural that a patient would want to know as much as possible about their condition.

label: Sam's Conclusion
body: It's not unfair for them to complain.

label: Sam's Evidence
body: Doctors (unlike patients, presumably) have undergone years of training. How can you say that a doctor's opinion isn't worth more than an untrained Internet search?

label: Evaluate
body: If I were Michaela, I would be immediately responding, "Whoa, there — I didn't say that! I definitely think a Doctor's opinion is worth more than an untrained person's internet search. I was just saying it's silly for doctors to be mad at patients for doing Internet searches, when it's a natural facet of human behavior to try to seek as much information as possible."

label: Goal
body:
Since Michaela never said "a doctor's opinion is just as valuable as the internet's opinion" and yet Sam is accusing her of having said that, we can say he misinterpreted her remarks to mean that.
  So let's look for something like "a doctor's opinion is not worth more than something an untrained person comes up with from an internet search", or an answer that would sound enough like that that Sam would think he heard that.

label: Given that...
body: People should not feed wild animals because it makes them dependent on humans and less likely to survive on their own.

label: How can this be justified...
body: Bird lovers commonly feed wild birds to attract them to their yards and gardens.

label: Evidence
body: No active volcanoes have been identified on Venus, and the sulfur dioxide spike may just be from a cyclical variation in the chemical composition of Venus's planetary atmosphere (planets are known to have variations).

label: Evaluate / Goal
body: We're looking for a reason to treat the bird lovers' feeding of wild birds as an exception. Is there a reason why these wild birds won't become dependent on humans and less likely to survive on their own? Maybe the bird lovers are only feeding birds that are already dependent on humans. This kind of answer could justify the bird lovers' actions even if we accept the principle.

label: Conclusion
body: The ads sent recently for Ebsen's campaign were evidently testing the ads' potential to influence popular opinion.

label: Evidence
body: They were sent to too few households to be trying to actually influence popular opinion. Also, they covered a wide range of topics, and Ebsen's campaign has spent a bunch of money following up with recipients to gauge their effect.

label: Evaluate
body:
This problem is a modern Bait n' Switch for all the LSAT students savvy enough to know that half the time on Main Conclusion questions, the Conclusion is found attached to some "but / yet / however" rebuttal.
  We always need to verify our Conclusion pick by making sure it passes the Support Test. Does the 2nd sentence have support?
  "the recent ads were sent to too few households to effectively influence popular opinion"
  why should we believe that?
  [crickets]
  A supporting reason for that claim would sound something like, "the mailer only went to 1,000 households, and many studies have shown that it takes at least 10,000 households to have any effect on popular opinion".
  The opinion indicator "evidently" in the 3rd sentence is the one bone they're throwing us to help us find the Main Conclusion.
  Why should we believe that "the ads were just trying to test the potential to influence popular opinion?"
  Because they covered a wide variety of topics and Ebsen's campaign spent lots of money following up with recipients to gauge the effect of the ads.

label: Goal
body:
As always with Main Conclusion questions, the only hard part is finding the Conclusion. If we do that correctly, then picking the correct answer is a straightforward task of finding a meaning match.
  So pick something that means the same thing as "The recent ads sent by Ebsen's campaign were aimed at testing their potential to influence popular opinion".

label: Conclusion (So)
body: The additional promotional money must have been counterproductive, making physicians less willing to receive visits by pharmaceutical sales reps.

label: Evidence
body:
Last year, Big Pharm spent additional money to promote its new drugs.
  The primary way it promotes is by sending sales reps to visit physicians in their offices.
  Two years ago, there was an average of 640 visits per per.
  Last year, each rep made an average of 501 visits.

label: Evaluate
body:
Since the evidence is a Curious Comparison, "two years ago 640 visits per rep vs. last year 501 visits per rep", and since the conclusion is saying something Causal, "the additional promotion [is] making physicians less willing to receive visits", we could use our typical Explain Curious Fact mindset.
  Curious Fact ... why did representatives went from making 640 visits per year to making only 501 visits per year?
  Author's Explanation ... the reps were coming with more promotional energy behind them, they somehow annoyed physicians or changed physicians' behavior in such a way that the physicians started shutting down offers to be visited.
  Often, when we're dealing with Explain Curious Fact arguments, we have to really take our time with the author's explanation and spell out the assumed stages of her causal storyline. She seems to be thinking that with extra promotional money behind them, the sales reps did something extra early on in last year that turned off the physicians. The physicians were like, "Okay, this is too much" and told their receptionists not to schedule any more visits with these annoying sales reps.

label: Goal
body:
Since this is Weaken, we would want to either
  1. suggest an Alternate Explanation for the curious fact
  how else could we explain why it went 640 visits per year to 501 visits per year?
  2. undermine the plausibility of the Author's Explanation
  how could we make it seem like it was not the case that sales reps were too "extra" in the beginning, which turned off physicians and led them to shutdown hosting future visits from sales reps?

label: Conclusion (most likely)
body: The big network of tracks on Malta was probably created by wheeled vehicles eroding these paths.

label: Intermediate Conclusion
body: Even though some people think the tracks were manually cut, the uniformity to the depth of the track is more likely indicative of wheel diameter.

label: Evidence
body: Routes would get used until the the wheel had eroded to a depth that made further vehicle usage impossible.

label: Evaluate
body:
Whenever we're doing Main Conclusion and Role, we remind ourselves prior to reading the paragraph that these questions love to put the Conclusion earlier than the Evidence. We start listening in the first sentence to hear if it's an opinion belonging to the author. If it is, then that's almost always the Conclusion.
  The opinion indicator "most likely" shows us that this first sentence is a speculative opinion. Does our author proceed to try to support this claim? Yes, the rest of the paragraph is trying to defend the idea that these tracks are from wheeled vehicles.
  The two big patterns with Main Conclusion are:
  1. Conclusion is the first sentence
  2. Conclusion is some rebuttal (usually after a but, yet, however)
  So they are trying to use these tendencies against us here by wanting us to zoom in on the Intermediate Conclusion introduced by "However".
  But that conclusion still serves to support the first sentence.

label: Goal
body: Look for something that means the same as the first sentence: the tracks were probably created through erosion from wheeled vehicles going through.

label: Given that ...
body: The goal of reforesting degraded land is to create an area with a multitude of thriving tree species.

label: How can we explain that ..
body: People good at reforesting will do by planting a single fast-growing tree species?

label: Evaluate / Goal
body:
The tension here is between "multitude of species" and "single species". If they're hoping to end up with a variety of species, then why are they planting a single fast-growing species?
  The correct answer needs to help us understand how this single species is a useful step in our long term goal of having a variety of species.

label: Conclusion
body: ProBit is the more reliable computer brand.

label: Evidence
body: An indie computer repair company found that, relative to market share, KRV had the most requests and ProBit had the smallest.

label: Evaluate
body:
The computer service company is thinking, "Wow, KRV is only 20% of the computers sold on the market, but it's like 45% of the service requests we get. Meanwhile, ProBit is 20% of the market, but only 10% of our service requests are for ProBit."
  Since the author is interpreting a statistic, we can use our Curious Fact / Explanation template.
  Curious Fact
  Why is it that a disproportionately small percent of computers serviced by this company are ProBit, whereas a disproportionately high percent of computers served are KRV?
  Author's Story
  ProBit is more reliable than KRV. (ProBit's computers break down less, so their customers don't need to bring their computer into the shop as much as KRV customers do)
  We always think about the same two pressure points:
  - Is there some OTHER WAY to explain the curious fact?
  - How plausible is the AUTHOR'S WAY?
  Since we're doing Weaken, the correct answer is most likely to be an alternate explanation for the curious fact. Why else could it be that ProBit is brought in less frequently?
  - maybe this indie computer company is in part of the country where ProBit users are disproportionately scarce? (i.e. maybe there are more customers that use Apple in the pacific northwest, but more customers that use Microsoft in the south, and this store is in the south).
  - maybe KRV computer owners use their computers way more than ProBit computer owners do (you might drive a more reliable car than your neighbor, but if you drive your car five times as much as she drives hers, you might still end up taking your car in for service more)
  - maybe ProBit is a real entry level computer, and so when your ProBit breaks down, you're more likely to just buy a new one than pay for expensive repairs.

label: Goal
body: Primarily look for an answer suggesting a DIFFERENT WAY to explain why ProBit gets brought in for service less. But stay receptive to an answer that makes it seem less plausible that ProBit is the more reliable (maybe KRV has won awards for "most reliable computer in its class").

label: Given that ...
body: Once science journals started offering all their articles online (in addition to in print), scientists gained access to more journals and easier access to back issues.

label: Why is it that ...
body: This didn't lead to a broader variety of articles being cited; it led to a greater tendency among scientists to cite the same articles as each other?

label: Evaluate / Goal
body:
We would think that if you have access to more journals and to back issues, you'd be exposed to a greater variety of articles and so there'd be a greater variety of citations.
  We need an answer to explain why we're getting greater repetition of citations. It should be something attached to the new reality of being able to search online or something that changed contemporaneously (i.e. at the same time these journals started offering their stuff online, something else also changed that led to greater similarity of citations).

label: Conclusion (we can conclude)
body: The ability of a person to tell whether a human is extroverted just by looking at a neutral picture of them is probably acquired as a result of primate biology.

label: Evidence (since / since)
body:
Humans can also look at a neutral picture of chimp and judge whether that chimp is dominant.
  Humans and chimps are both primates.

label: Evaluate
body:
This argument has a couple layers, so it's hard to know what to focus on. It has some Explain Curious Fact, and it has some Argument by Analogy.
  Curious Fact ... how can humans tell whether a human is extroverted just from a neutral picture?
  Author's Explanation ... primate biology builds that perceptual ability into the primate brain. There are hardwired abilities in the primate brain to detect an extroverted face.
  We could strengthen by ruling out an alternate explanation for how humans can judge "resting extrovert face". Or we could make the author's explanation seem more plausible.
  The other layer here is the way the author seems to connect an ability to recognize dominance in chimps to the ability to recognize extroversion in humans. She's trying to make the case that since we have the ability to recognize X in a human face and Y in a chimp's face, then our ability to recognize X must be a primate thing.
  The reason she's saying "it's a primate thing", rather than just "a human thing", is because she thinks that recognizing X and recognizing Y are somehow part of the same story.
  But are those really related things? Is detecting whether someone is extroverted the same as detecting whether someone is dominant?

label: Goal
body: Let's look for something ruling out an alternate explanation for how humans can detect extroversion in a neutral picture, something increasing the plausibility that the extroversion-detection ability is genetic primate biology, or something making it seem like a human detecting extroversion in a human is connected to a human detecting dominance in a chimp.

label: Conclusion
body: Most old houses on 20th Ave contain more than one apartment.

label: Evidence
body: All the apartments on 20th are in old houses, and there are twice as many apartments as there are old houses.

label: Evaluation
body:
This is very math-y, so using some numbers can maybe help us make sense of it. Let's start with "twice as many apartments as old houses". We'll say there are 10 apartments and 5 old houses.
  All 10 apartments are in those 5 old houses. That's an average of 2 apartments per house, so the author is reasoning that "most of these old houses" have more than one apartment.
  But does an average value have to be true of most data points within a group?
  Can a group of houses have an average of 2 apartments, even if most of those houses have less than 2 apartments?
  Sure. If you want the average value to be unlike most data points in the set, just make a couple data points be total outliers.
  Take any ten people off the street: their average wealth is probably about $50,000. Now add Jeff Bezos and Bill Gates to that group and you have a dozen people with an average wealth of about $10 billion / person. Is it true to say that most of the people in that group have more than $1 billion in wealth? No, only 2 of the 12 do. It's just that their influence skews the average very high.
  Similarly, we could allocate our 10 apartments over five old houses very unevenly:
  House 1: 1 apartment
  House 2: 1 apartment
  House 3: 1 apartment
  House 4: 3 apartments
  House 5: 4 apartments
  It would be true that they have an average of 2 apartments / house, even though most of the houses do not have more than one apartment (only 2 out of 5 have more than one).

label: Goal
body: Look for an answer that calls out this mismatch between "an average" for a group and "something that is true of most members of the group". Or look for an answer raising the specific objection that the apartments might be allocated to the old houses in a very uneven way, such that there are a bunch of apartments found in a minority of the houses, with only 1 or 0 apartments found in the majority of the houses.

label: Evaluation
body:
If we want to argue that the spike in sulfur dioxide is caused by volcanoes, we have a couple possible ways to weaken:
  - we can make it seem like "cyclical variations" is unlikely to be the cause of what we saw. Maybe cyclical variations are known to happen, but they don't spike as dramatically or change as quickly as what we just saw from Venus's short-term spike.
  - we can try to address the "no active volcanoes have been identified" premise, maybe by arguing in an Unproven vs. Proven False style that "just because we haven't found them doesn't mean they aren't there". Maybe we've only ever seen one side of Venus, so there might be active volcanoes "hiding" on part of Venus's surface that we can't get a good look at.

label: Goal
body: Look for something undermining the alternate explanation that it's just a cyclical change in Venus's atmosphere, or for something defending the possibility that it might be volcanoes that are the cause.

label: Statements
body:
```
causal (increasing X increases Y)
more electrical load on the trans line  ⇢  higher temp the line gets
causal (too great an X will cause Y)
too great a load  ⇢  exceeds max temp
causal / comparison (affected by / cools more)
                   COOLER
stronger winds   >   light winds
                   COOLER
blowing across   >   blowing parallel
```

label: Evaluate
body:
We got a whole bunch of causal relationships, so we should ask ourselves whether we can chain those causal ideas together.
  The first two ideas were just saying that as you increase the load, the temperature goes up, and you might actually go beyond the max.
  The last few ideas were about cooling down the line.
  Maybe they're going for something relating to "load heats it up, strong crosswinds cool it down"?

label: Goal
body: Look for something we can support, if not prove, from the causal relationships we were given.

label: Conclusion
body: Sand termite burrowing causes fairy circles to form.

label: Evidence
body: Sand termite colonies were found in every investigated fairy circle.

label: Evaluate
body: The argument leans on a correlation. To strengthen, link the actual damage pattern to termite burrowing.

label: Goal
body: Pick the answer that shows fairy-circle damage is consistent with termite burrowing activity.

label: Evidence
body:
Monroe was elected.
```
Monroe elected  →  fundamental shift in electorate  AND  well-run campaign
```

label: Conclusion
body: One can't avoid the conclusion that there's been a fundamental shift in the sentiments of the electorate.

label: Evaluate
body:
This is a valid argument since they give us a conditional (signified by the certainty of "impossible for X to happen without both Y and Z"). In other words, X requires Y and Z.
  X → Y and Z
  They tell us that the trigger happened (Munroe was elected).
  X.
  From that, we already know that both Y and Z necessarily follow. Their conclusion for some reason only chooses to mention one of those things (still valid).
  Y.

label: Goal
body:
So we know to replicate this we need two premises:
  1. conditional premise (probably with AND in outcome)
  2. factual premise that triggers the conditional premise
  The conclusion
  3. the outcome of the conditional (or part of it)
  It's not necessary for the correct answer to replicate the fact that the conditional had a "Y and Z" outcome, but it probably will, so I would use that as a filtering mechanism on a first pass.
  But the essence of the argument is just
  premise: here's a rule
  premise: here's a fact that triggers the rule.
  conclusion: here's (part of) the outcome of rule.

label: Information
body:
- **Comparison (far more efficient):** Bumblebees are more efficient than Honeybees, when it comes to pollinating cranberries and certain other crops.
  - **Causal Difference-Maker: this is because**
  - **Comparison (broader area / wider variety of species):** Honeybees visit a broader area and visit a wider variety of species

label: Goal
body:
Since there was Causal Difference-Maker language like "This is because", we would assume that the correct answer is going to reinforce the connection between the two things we know about bumblebees and honeybees. It's the ol' One Difference Explains the Other Difference.
  Said from the point of view of bumblebees:
  visiting only a few species over a limited area makes you a more efficient pollinator for certain crops (such as cranberries)
  Said from the point of view of honeybees:
  visiting a wider variety of species over a broader area makes you a less efficient pollinator for certain crops (such as cranberries)

label: Conclusion
body: Total bank lending to companies is less than it was five years ago.

label: Evidence
body:
Total bank lending to small/medium companies is less than it was five years ago.
  When it comes to large companies, there are two categories: the financially strong and not-financially strong.
  For the financially strong large companies, the interest rates banks pay to procure money is higher than the interest rate they can charge these large companies to lend them money.
  For the not-financially strong large companies, banks will not currently lend to them.

label: Evaluation
body:
There's a lot going on in this paragraph, but the most salient supporting claim is that small/medium companies are getting less lending than five years ago. If lending to small/medium companies is down, does that mean lending to companies (overall) is down?
  It depends on how much lending large companies are getting (they're the only missing piece, if all companies are being lumped together as small, medium, or large).
  If banks are also lending less (or the same) to large companies, then total bank lending to companies is definitely lower.
  Does the author tell us how much lending large companies are getting now, compared to five years ago? Nope. So that's the big missing piece of info. But we do have some information about large companies.
  The large companies that aren't financially strong are getting zero lending. So we don't have to worry about them. $0 of lending is definitely less than or equal to what lending they were getting five years ago.
  So the only unknown segment of the "All Companies" pie is large, financially strong companies. If we can establish that they, too, are getting less or equal lending now compared to five years ago, then we will have proven the conclusion.

label: Goal
body: Look for an answer to take the one thing we know about large, financially strong companies (the money that banks can charge these companies for lending to them is less than what the banks have to pay to get the money in the first place) and to use fact to convince us that bank lending to financially strong companies is currently less than or equal to what it was five years ago.

label: Conditionals
body:
```
Kind to someone  →  want them to prosper
Dislike each other  →  can't be fully content in their presence
Don't dislike each other  →  Kind to each other
```

label: Fact
body: Two people who dislike each other may treat each other with respect.

label: Evaluation
body:
On Inference questions, if we get multiple conditionals, we want to ask ourselves if any of them chain together. The idea of "kind" show up twice, giving us this chain:
```
Don't dislike each other  →  Kind to each other  →  Want each other to prosper
```
  The idea of whether or not two people dislike each other also showed up twice. If we contrapose the 2nd rule listed above, we can chain 4 ideas together.
```
Can be fully content  →  Don't dislike each other  →  Kind to each other  →  Want each other to prosper
```
  When it comes to the fact, it overlapped with "two people who dislike each other". We know that they can't be fully content in each other's presence, but they can (not must) treat each other with respect.

label: Goal
body: Look for an answer that contradicts any connection in our conditional chain (provides the trigger, but denies the outcome), or look for an answer that contradicts the idea that respect can coexist with "not fully content in your presence".

label: Evidence
body:
```
1g of aspartame  >  1g of sugar   (Sweeter)
```
  Soda w/ sugar = sweet.

label: Intermediate Conclusion
body:
```
soda w/ aspartame  >  soda w/ sugar   (Sweeter)
```

label: Conclusion
body: Drinking sodas w/ aspartame will cause you to have an extreme preference for sweet things.

label: Evaluation
body:
Because the author draws an Intermediate Conclusion with "so" and then her ultimate conclusion with "Thus", we need to think through both moves here.
  If each gram of aspartame is sweeter than each gram of sugar, does that mean sodas with aspartame are sweeter than sodas with sugar?
  Not necessarily — who said that we're using an equal number of grams? Maybe sodas with aspartame use 3g of aspartame, but sodas with sugar use 20g of sugar.
  What about the next move — if we accepted that aspartame sodas are sweeter, do we have to accept that someone who drinks them will develop a preference for extremely sweetened things?
  Not necessarily — maybe they only like their sodas sweet. maybe the sweetness of their aspartame sodas actually turns them off from other sweetened stuff. maybe they don't even like the sweetness of the aspartame soda but they tolerate it because they have different reasons for wanting to drink that soda.

label: Goal
body:
Premise
  Ingredient 1 has more of property A, per unit, than does Ingredient 2.
  Intermediate Conclusion
  Something with ingredient 1 has more of property A than something with ingredient 2.
  Main Conclusion
  If you have something with ingredient 1, you'll develop a preference for lots of property A.

label: Conclusion
body: Raising our min wage levels would improve overall economic health more than the hiring cutbacks that could result from raising it.

label: Evidence
body: When min wage levels are low (like now), employers would rather hire more people than buy expensive technology that would improve productivity. By hiring workers (who are less productive than that fancy new tech), productivity falls off, and productivity is connected to higher average living standards. Meanwhile, high min wage levels results in higher productivity.

label: Evaluation
body:
Since this is a Comparison between a world in which we have low min wage vs. higher min wage, we are interested in everything that relates to overall economic health in each of those two worlds.
  The author needs there to be more to gain than there is to lose, when we raise the min wage. The current tradeoffs we know about are that with a higher min wage, we would have higher productivity but possibly some people would lose their jobs.

label: Goal
body:
We want an answer to tell us that "the boost we get in higher productivity, leading to higher average living standards, is bigger than the detriment we get from some workers being laid off".
  Or we want any other factor we haven't talked about yet that gets better in a world with higher minimum wage levels (a factor that relates to better overall economic health)

label: Conclusion
body: We need a system for charging people for the use of roads during rush hour.

label: Evidence
body: When something valuable (using roads during rush hour) costs no money, you get overconsumption and long lines (you can see the same thing when there are free ice cream giveaways, and people wait around the block for 45 mins to save $3). If we charged to use roads during rush hour, congestion would abate.

label: Evaluate
body:
This argument winds up with an analogy, just to reach a subsidiary conclusion ( "we learn from this ..." ) that when something valuable costs no money, you get overconsumption and long lines.
  Then the author pivots into her actual suggestion: what is needed.
  You can almost picture this author driving her Range Rover, stuck in traffic, wishing she could pay something to keep the riff-raff away.

label: Goal
body:
They're asking us about that middle sentence that could probably be called an Intermediate Conclusion. It has its own support; "we learn this" claim from the ice cream example. But it's there to support the author's Main Conclusion about charging for rush hour driving.
  But on a first pass, I would just look for anything that sounds like this claim had the role of Supporting the main conclusion.

label: Conclusion
body: The approach Roadwise insurance takes with its ads (ranging from dry and informative to funny and offbeat) is smart.

label: Evidence
body: Even though companies typically strive for uniformity in order to establish brand identity, auto insurance purchasers are a demographically diverse group.

label: Background Ideas
body:
Low self-esteem people will be treated disrespectfully more often than will high self-esteem people. (ouch, that seems like a vicious cycle ... that disrespect will make the low self-esteem people even more low self-esteem?)
  Low self-esteem people are more likely than high self-esteem people to interpret a given way of being treated as disrespectful.

label: Evaluate
body:
We're trying to support a conclusion that's saying, "X should not be allowed to prescribe psychiatric medications", so we know the answer should be a principle that is structured like,
```
if such-and-such is the case  →  should not be allowed to prescribe psychiatric meds
```
  The evidence is all about the fact that clinical psychologists w/o medical degrees haven't had as much medical training / education as have people with medical degrees.

label: Evaluate
body:
Okay, so this is clearly Geico they're talking about, right?
  Strengthen/Weaken questions aren't super likely to test missing links but it seems here like we're missing a link between "If it's a demographically diverse pool of potential customers, then it's smart to have a variety of styles of ads".
  We can flesh out this assumption with its common sense implications:
  - different people will end up liking different ads (maybe the older demographics will appreciate the informative ads and the younger demographics will appreciate the funny/offbeat ads).
  We might also see the correct answer try to establish a difference:
  - most other products (whose ads are more consistent), do not have as demographically diverse a range of potential customers.
  And, of course, we should consider potential objections (what if this ruins Roadwise's chance at having a brand identity? what if some potential customers are attracted to Roadwise based on the ads whose style is a good fit for them but alienated from Roadwise based on the ads whose styles is not a good fit):
  - having a crazy variety of ads does not ruin brand identity / having a crazy variety of ads is their brand identity
  - people are not turned off by the style of Roadwise ads they like the least

label: Goal
body: Keep a flexible mindset and look for something that provides connective tissue between the premise and the conclusion or rules out a potential objection.

label: Given
body:
Researchers put two electrodes in a pool that a dolphin swam in.
  When the dolphin swam near the electrodes, the researchers would sometimes create a weak electric field by activating the electrodes.
  The dolphin would swim away if the electrodes were activated; otherwise it acted normally.
  The researchers then placed a plastic shield over small organs called vibrissal crypts located on the dolphin's snout.
  With the crypts covered, the dolphin no longer swam away when the electrodes were activated.

label: Evaluate / Goal
body:
These statements first describe how a dolphin responded to an electric field when small organs on the dolphin's snout were not covered. It compares that to the way that the dolphin responded when the small organs were covered.
  The dolphin responded differently when the organs were covered. This supports the idea that covering the organs caused the dolphin to respond differently. This in turn supports the idea that these organs allow dolphins to sense electric fields.
  The statements don't prove that there is a causal connection here, but this question only asks for an answer that is most strongly supported.

label: Evidence
body:
Customers who paid in cash at stores and received change were given an extra dollar with their change.
  Few people who received an extra dollar returned it.

label: Conclusion (so)
body: Among those who received an extra dollar, most behaved dishonestly.

label: Evaluate
body:
This argument attempts to explain a curious fact: when people received an extra dollar, why did so few of them return it?
  By claiming that most of these people behaved dishonestly, the argument assumes that nothing else caused these people to keep the extra dollar. There are actually a number of reasonable explanations that have nothing to do with dishonesty. The argument never addresses any of these alternative explanations. Based just on the evidence we're given, there's no way we can be sure that any of these people behaved dishonestly.
  This type of question isn't extremely common in LR, so it's important to clearly understand what the question is asking and what to expect in the answer choices. The answer choices are all questions that can be answered with a short, factual answer. These will often be questions that can be answered with "yes" or "no."
  We need to think about a possible answer to each question, and consider what effect the answer would have on the argument. For example, if the answer to one question is "yes" that might strengthen the argument; however if the answer to that same question is "no" that might weaken the argument.

label: Goal
body: One answer choice will pose a question that has a noticeable impact on the argument. The answer choice which poses that question will be the correct answer choice. The other questions will have much less impact, and possibly even no impact.

label: Dario's Claims
body:
1. The government should continue to grant patents for all new drug compounds.
  2. Patents promote innovation by rewarding pharmaceutical companies for undertaking the costly research needed to develop new drugs.

label: Cynthia's Responses
body:
1. Disagree, at least somewhat. Dario said we should grant patents for all new compounds, but it seems like Cynthia wants to grant patents only for truly innovative ones, not for minor variants of previously existing drugs.
  2. No comment here. Her first sentence almost touches on this subject, but it seems more like she agrees that patents promote innovation and that there's a need to do so.

label: Goal
body:
Since Cynthia seems to disagree with Dario's first explicit claim, we can hope that this is all the correct answer will be testing.
  They would agree that truly innovative drugs should be granted patents.
  But they disagree when it comes to minor variants of previously existing drugs: Cynthia would say patents shouldn't be granted for them (they're not truly innovative) whereas Dario would say they should be granted (all new drug compounds should be).

label: Conclusion (not wrong = opinion)
body: It would not be wrong to perform mining operations on Mars.

label: Evidence
body:
There are only two possible reasons it would be wrong:
  1. because pollution harms ecosystems
  2. because pollution harms human populations
  Mining operations on Mars would cause pollution, but the small human presence needed to run the mining operation would be completely protected from harm.

label: Evaluate
body:
This argument has a form where it lays out the only two ways that X wouldn't be true, rules out those two ways, and then concludes X.
  For example: "Dave would only go to that wedding if there were an open bar or a chocolate fondue fountain. Since there's only a cash bar and the only dessert is key lime pie, Dave will not go that wedding."
  So in this argument, the author needs to rule out that pollution from mining would harm ecosystems and rule out that pollution from mining would harm human populations.
  Did she do both?
  No. She only established that pollution from mining wouldn't harm human populations.

label: Goal
body: So we need our answer to rule out the other one of the "two possible reasons it would be wrong". We need to know that, mining operations on Mars would not harm ecosystems.

label: Goal
body:
So we'll look for something like,
```
if you've only trained for at most a few hundred hours in neuro/phys/pharm  →  should not be allowed to prescribe
```

label: Fill-in-the-blank
body:
Was the second sentence saying that the first sentence wasn't really true: low self-esteem people aren't really treated disrespectfully more often, they're just more likely to interpret treatment as disrespectful?
  No, the first sentence is definitely affirming they are treated disrespectfully more often.
  As an analogy, we might say that younger women are more likely than older women to be treated in some sexist way, but they are also more likely to hear the same comment as being sexist, compared to how older women would hear it.
  So our conclusion needs to tie together the ideas that "X is being persecuted more than Y", but "X is also more likely to interpret something as persecution than is Y".

label: Goal
body:
Let's look for a safely worded answer that maybe sounds like, "low self esteem people are disrespected more than high self-esteem people are, but not as much as they (low self esteem people) think they are".
  I don't really like the latter half of that prediction, though, because who's to say whose interpretation is more correct: the high self-esteem or low self-esteem people's?

label: Conclusion
body: Eradicating the mysis shrimp is preferable to allowing trout fishing.

label: Evidence
body: The shrimp each plankton, which is food for young kokanees, thus the young kokanee are starving to death.

label: Evaluate
body:
The conclusion is saying that This Plan is better than That Plan, so we would expect the evidence to also be comparative — This Plan does X, while That Plan does Y, and X is better than Y.
  The evidence here, though, doesn't mention anything about the plan to allow trout fishing. It just explain the motive for getting rid of the shrimp (they eat the same food source as young kokanees).
  So why does Lopez prefer that plan? We should think about and articulate the differences we have been told about the Trout vs. the Shrimp:
```
TROUT               SHRIMP
eat adult kokanee   eat baby kokanees' food
native              introduced into lake
```
