label: Goal
body:
Because we have those two differences to go off of, we'd anticipate that an answer will say something from the Shrimp column is preferable to something from the Trout column:
  it's better to do something to protect the babies lives than the adults lives
  it's better to get rid of something introduced into the lake than get rid of something native to the lake

label: Evidence
body:
If rational-choice theory is correct, then people act only in ways that they expect will benefit themselves.
```
RCT correct → expect benefit self
```
  Plenty of examples exist of people acting in ways that result in no personal benefit whatsoever.
```
~benefit self
```

label: Conclusion
body:
Rational-choice theory cannot be correct.
```
~RCT correct
```

label: Evaluate
body:
It seems like we can get from the second premise to the conclusion using the contrapositive of the first premise:
```
~benefit self → ~RCT correct
```
  But wait! That's not actually the correct contrapositive. The first premise is about people acting in ways that they expect to benefit from, not ways that they actually benefit from.
  The second premise is about people acting in ways that they actually do not benefit from.
  This argument is assuming that, if someone acts in a way that they do not benefit from, they are acting in a way that they did not expect to benefit from.
```
~benefit self → ~expect benefit self
```
  If you're still not entirely clear about the difference here, think about this: imagine that I invest my life savings in some new cryptocurrency that my ex-girlfriend's cousin's best friend recommends. I might do this because I expect to benefit from the investment. But expecting to benefit is a completely different issue from me actually benefitting from the investment or not.

label: Goal
body: The correct answer is likely to point out this potential difference between an action that is expected to produce a result and an action that does or does not actually produce that result.

label: Given that ...
body: Wind is caused by differences in atmospheric temperature.

label: and that ...
body: Winds on Earth come from the heat of the Sun (causing differences in atmospheric temperature).

label: and that ...
body: the Sun is too far from Jupiter to affect the temperature of its atmosphere.

label: How is it that ...
body: Jupiter has strong winds (stronger than Earth's)?

label: Evaluate / Goal
body: We just need an answer that tells us what causes there to be differences in atmospheric temperature on Jupiter. It will probably be some other source of heat, but maybe there are things besides heat that cause atmospheric temperature differences.

label: Conclusion
body: The number of species that can reproduce through parthenogenesis must be increasing.

label: Evidence
body: We used to think that only a few species could reproduce this way, but recently we've found it in a variety of unexpected cases.

label: Evaluate
body:
Just because we've found more cases of parthenogenesis doesn't mean that there are more and more new species with parthenogenesis than before. Sharks and Komodo dragons have been around for millions of years. So if they're capable of parthenogenesis, then they would have already been included in a proper tally of species that can reproduce through parthenogenesis.
  When we discover more oil in some new well, we don't conclude that the Earth must have more oil than it used to.

label: Goal
body: The author is thinking "why are we discovering more cases of parthenogenesis" (curious fact) and arriving at the causal story of "parthenogenesis is increasing among species", when it's highly possible that an alternate explanation is that we're just discovering more cases of parthenogenesis that already existed, prior to our discovery.

label: Conclusion (should = opinion)
body: Clinical psychologists who don't have medical degrees should no be allowed to prescribe psychiatric medications.

label: Evidence
body: Clinical psychology includes at most a few hundred hours of education in neuroscience, physiology, and pharmacology. Meanwhile, to get a medical degree you must receive years of training in those fields before you're allowed to prescribe psychiatric medications.

label: Conclusion
body:
Those who claim that auto exhaust emissions are a risk to public health are mistaken.
  rephrase: auto exhaust emissions are not a risk to public health.

label: Evidence
body: Over the past 100 years, as auto exhaust emissions increased, every relevant indicator of public health improved dramatically.

label: Evaluate
body:
This conclusion is anti-causal. The author is trying to prove that X does not cause Y, and the evidence is saying that over a certain period of time, X was present and something that sounds like the opposite of Y was occurring.
  It would be sort of like if we said, "Joe's rudeness to customers is not hurting our business. After all, during the last 12 months, as Joe has worked here, every month our revenue and profits have risen."
  One of the two typical objections we make to anti-causal arguments is, "Yes, but it would be even better/worse without that factor".
  Yes, unemployment is still rising, but the stimulus money still did something because unemployment would be even higher without it.
  Yes, COVID cases are still rising, but the vaccine is still helping because they'd be rising even higher without the vaccine.
  Yes, profits and revenue are rising, but Joe's rudeness is still hurting business because our profits/revenue would be even higher if he weren't offending the customers.
  Yes, public health measures dramatically improved over the past century, but they'd be even more positive if we weren't ingesting poisonous auto emissions.

label: Goal
body:
Look for an answer that has this form:
  CONC - X is not causing Y.
  PREM - In the time period where X has been present, stuff has been happening that seems like the opposite of Y.
  And the correct answer should be vulnerable to a similar objection, such as even though things like Y seem to be doing fine in the presence of X, they would be doing even better in the absence of X.
  (even though health indicators seem to be doing fine in the present of auto emissions, they would be doing even better if we weren't breathing in car emissions)

label: Conclusion (so)
body: The fossil does not provide evidence that birds evolved from dinosaurs.

label: Evidence
body:
The fossil is a composite of bones collected from various parts of the discovery site.
  And if the entire fossil is not from a single animal, then it can't serve as evidence that birds evolved from dinosaurs.

label: Evaluate
body:
We're trying to prove that this fossil "does not provide evidence that birds evolved from dinosaurs", so our first question is:
  Did the evidence provide any rule, like
  "If such-and-such, then does not provide evidence"?
  Yes! We have a rule saying,
```
Entire fossil is not from a single animal  →  does not provide evidence birds evolved from dinos
```
  So to prove our conclusion that this fossil doesn't provide evidence, we must establish that "this entire fossil is not from a single animal".
  Do we know anything about this fossil?
  Yes, we know that the fossil is a composite of bones collected from various parts of the discovery site.

label: Goal
body: So, we need to be convinced that, "If it's a composite of bones collected from various parts of the discovery site, then the entire fossil is not from a single animal".

label: Conclusion (so)
body: Justine must have syndrome Q.

label: Evidence (since)
body:
Justine shows positive on this test.
  Whenever a person has syndrome Q, the test shows positive.

label: Evaluate
body:
Any time we're doing a Flaw questions and we see a conditional logic premise (whenever), we have a 90% or better suspicion that they're just testing their #1 famous flaw, Necessary vs. Sufficient.
  The sufficient indicator whenever (just like when, if, any, each, all, every) tells us to put the clause that follows on the left of the arrow, so we get this rule:
```
person tested has syndrome Q → test comes out positive
```
  We would not expect the author to either illegally reverse this rule or negate it.
  REVERSAL
  Bob tested positive. Thus, Bob was syndrome Q.
  NEGATION
  Bob doesn't have syndrome Q. Thus, the test will not come back positive.
  And we see that they did indeed argue via a reversal.

label: Goal
body:
Look for an answer calling out the illegal Necessary vs. Sufficient confusion.
  Or look for an answer making the same objection more conversationally: just because Justine tested positive doesn't guarantee she has Q. Tests sometimes provide false positives, where you think you're pregnant but you're not. You think you have covid, but you don't.
  This test apparently does not have false negatives. If you have Q, the test will say positive. But it's possible this test gives out false positives. You don't have Q, but the test says positive anyway.

label: Statements
body:
- Rock songs used to be limited to 3 minutes to get played on the radio.
  - During that 3 minute era, rockers said, "you're stifling our creativity".
  - When the 3 minute limit was removed, some critics said, "Ah, now rock music has become artistic."
  - *pivot (however) / causal (when X happened, it became Y) / causal (because)*
  - Removing the 3 minute limit led to song structures breaking down and the music becoming aimless.
  - Being derived from certain style of music led to rock music's difficulty in making good songs of extended length.

label: Evaluate
body:
When we read Inference paragraphs, we are hoping to find claims that can be synthesized, usually by finding some Overlapping Information.
  And we read carefully for indicator wording that provides hints about what is being tested:
  - Conditional
  - Causal
  - Mathematical
  - Ends w/ Pivot
  The last sentence is extra juicy here, because it is introduced with a pivot, "however" and contains two causal ideas.
  When the last claim in an Inference paragraph begins with a pivot, it's usually a sign that our job is to reconcile that last idea with what came before it. Most of the time it will create some tension that forces a mathematical inference or triggers the contrapositive of some rule.
  In this case, it's more like a Rebuttal. Some music critics were claiming that, "It wasn't until we got rid of the 3 minute limit that rock music became artistic". In other words, some critics think it was a good thing to remove the 3 minute limit.
  Our author disagrees. She says that removing the 3 minute limit was a bad thing (song structures broke down and the music became aimless).
  The final idea is suggesting, "Based on how rock music evolved, it's not really cut out for doing long songs well".

label: Goal
body: We don't know precisely what to look for, but we can anticipate that it will have the rebuttal vibe of, "Removing the 3 minute limit was a bad thing. Rock music got worse as a result, because it's not well-suited to songs of greater length."

label: Conclusion
body: It's hasty logic to conclude that the recipes compiled by Apicius are a reliable indicator of how wealthy Romans prepared / spiced food.

label: Evidence
body: We don't have other recipes from the same time period to compare these to, and Apicius may have been a weirdo chef, who was atypical from the rest (just as many famous modern chefs are).

label: Anticipate
body: The cleanest pattern in the stimulus is the before-and-after: monkeys went to orchards before, and stopped going once Suzuki put soybeans in their mountain habitat.

label: Evaluate
body:
The author is saying that it's hasty to use Apicius's recipes as a reliable indicator because we don't know whether he's a representative (typical) chef from then or not.
  If we were trying to characterize the author's two pieces of evidence, it might sound something like this:
  - "few other recipes have survived" (the author indicates a sample might not be reliable because it can't be cross-referenced with other samples)
  - "Apicius may have been highly atypical, just like the recipes of notable modern chefs" (the author appeals to an analogy / a modern comparison)

label: Goal
body: Just find an answer choice that descriptively matches the argument.

label: Statements
body:
- *causal difference-maker: "for this reason"*
  - Because normal wood usually disintegrates within a century or two, archaeologists have been unable to find many remains of early wheeled vehicles.
  - *possible inferences:*
    - early wheeled vehicles were made of normal wood.
    - early wheeled vehicles are from more than two centuries ago.
  - *contrast/pivot: "However"*
  - They have found small ceramic models from the same era. They are less susceptible to disintegration.
  - *possible inferences:*
    - ceramics models are not made from wood (that's kind of obvious)
    - ceramic disintegrates more slowly than wood
    - there are ceramic things made more than two centuries ago

label: Goal
body: I wouldn't have a specific prediction here, but it's likely to involve the Causal connector "for this reason", or to involve the contrast-Pivot "however".

label: Conclusion
body: Fish raised in the new hatcheries are more likely to survive after their release than fish raised in traditional hatcheries.

label: Evidence
body:
Traditional ones raise fish in featureless environments, with dull routines.
  New ones raise fish in visually stimulating environments, with non-dull routines.
  As a result, fish released from the new hatcheries are bolder than fish released from the old hatcheries, when it comes to exploring new environments and trying new food.

label: Evaluate / Goal
body: We're mainly looking at an assumption that "if the fish are bolder about exploring new environments and trying new food, then they are more likely to survive after their release".

label: Conclusion
body: A person's mood typically starts out happy in the morning, declines during the day, and improves in the evening.

label: Evidence
body: An analysis of the language in social media messages found that on average the use of positive-mood words is common in the morning, goes down to its lowest midafternoon, then rises sharply through the evening.

label: Evaluate
body:
Since the author is interpreting the results of a study, we can use our Curious Fact / Explanation template.
  Curious Fact
  Why is it that we see more positive words in the morning and evening, and fewer positive words midday, on social media messages?
  Author's Explanation
  People tend to start and end the day in a happy mood, with a decline in mood in between.
  The correct answer to these questions always involves one of two pressure points:
  - an Alternate Explanation for the curious fact
  - affecting the plausibility of the Author's Explanation
  Since we're doing weaken, the #1 tendency is to provide some Other Way to explain why we see more positive words in the morning / evening, less positivity in between.
  Maybe it's not people's moods that change in that cycle, but just the fact that during the day they're at work, so that affects the way they post on social media. Perhaps on a Saturday or Sunday (when not working), they're just as likely to be positive midday.
  Or maybe it's just different people logging in at different times. The people with jobs are only going on social media during morning/evening, and they have positive outlooks. The people logging on midday are jobless and despondent.
  Or maybe midday is just when Russian troll farms are at their most active, seeding social media with intentionally confrontational energy. Yup, I think LSAT is going to talk about Russian troll farms.

label: Goal
body: Look for an answer that provides an Alternate Explanation for why language is happier at the beginning/ending of a day than during the middle of a day, or an answer that hurts the plausibility that people's moods follow a typical U-shaped graph.

label: Conclusion
body: Setting a max wage would protect the country's lowest paid corporate employees from wage cuts.

label: Evidence
body: Setting a max wage would remove one incentive (cutting employee pay in order to boost profits and thus executive salaries) for cutting the wages of the lowest paid employees.

label: Evaluate
body:
The author seems to be assuming a couple things:
  - if you remove an incentive for doing X, people will no longer do it for that reason
  - if you remove an incentive for doing X, there isn't some other incentive that would still be a compelling reason to do X
  Maybe with a max wage law, executives would no longer have the incentive to cut wages for the sake of increasing their own salaries, but they would still have the incentive to cut wages for the sake of increasing profits so that they could flatter their vanity by appearing on the cover of Forbes for their super-profitable business.
  Salary isn't necessarily the only thing motivating wage cuts.

label: Goal
body: Look for an answer ruling out some other reason why executives would want to cut wages, or for an answer that just connects the language of premise to conclusion: "if you remove this incentive, then the executives will stop cutting the wages of the lowest-paid employees".

label: Conclusion (thus)
body: It is likely that consuming large amounts of fat, sugar, or alcohol (things that increase triglyceride levels in blood) is a factor causing heart disease.

label: Evidence
body: Patients with blood triglyceride above 1mg / mL are twice as prone to heart attacks as others.

label: Evaluate
body:
Although this argument is flawed (we aren't justified in being certain that Keeler notified the press), it's still reasonable to suspect Keeler. And the question stem isn't asking for a flawed pattern of reasoning, so we should probably just focus on how the argument works.
  There are two suspects: Greene and Keeler.
  One has a motive: Keeler
  The other has no motive: Greene.
  Thus, it was Keeler.

label: Goal
body:
Let's look for something where they restrict our available options (i.e. "Keeler and Greene were the only ones in a position to talk to the press"), and tell us stuff that makes one option seem much more likely than the other one, (i.e. "Keeler had a motive, Greene did not").
  Then the conclusion should have certain strength ("must have been") as it picks the more likely suspect.

label: Evaluate
body:
Our Conclusion is causal,
  X is a factor causing Y
  and our Evidence was a correlation
  People with trait X are twice as prone to be trait Y
  so we know we're in the world of Explain Curious Fact:
  Curious Fact ... why is there a strong correlation between high blood triglyceride levels and heart attacks?
  Author's Explanation ... the high blood triglyceride is causing the heart attack.
  The author doesn't explicitly say that, but her conclusion implies that she is interpreting this correlation to mean that the blood triglyceride level was a causal factor in the heart attacks. That's why she's arriving at a conclusion that "when you eat large amounts of foods that increase your blood triglyceride level, you're increasing your risk of heart disease".
  Whenever an author interprets a correlation between X and Y to mean that X causes Y, we want to consider two alternate explanations:
  - Reverse Cause (what if Y causes X)
  - Third Factor (what X and Y are both attached to Z)
  Here, that would mean, "What if having heart disease is causing the blood triglyceride to be high"? Or, "what if high blood triglyceride and heart disease are both connected to some other thing (like a genetic condition, or smoking cigarettes, or something)?"

label: Goal
body:
When we're doing Weaken and we come across an Explain Curious Fact type argument, the most typical form for an answer is to suggest an Alternate Explanation for the curious fact. The less typical option is to undermine the plausibility of the story the author is telling.
  So let's primarily look for "a different way to explain the correlation between high blood triglyceride and heart disease", or look for something that hurts the plausibility of the conclusion.
  (We might suspect that the random first sentence is there for some reason. Are they going to use this metabolized fact in the correct answer?)

label: Conclusion
body: Aerobic exercise helps the body handle psychological stress.

label: Evidence
body: In an experiment, the volunteers who were assigned to take aerobics classes had lower measurable stress symptoms following a tough math problem than did the volunteers who were assigned to take a weight-training class.

label: Evaluate
body:
The verb "helps" in the conclusion is Causal. Since the author is making a causal interpretation of a study, we can use our Curious Fact / Explanation mindset.
  Curious Fact
  Why did the people who were assigned aerobics have less stress after the hard math problem than did the people who were assigned weight-training?
  Author's Explanation
  Aerobics helps the body handle psychological stress.
  We can affect these types of arguments in two ways:
  - considering Alternate Explanations for the Curious Fact
  - assessing the plausibility of the Author's Explanation
  What would be some other way to explain these results?
  - maybe the people in the aerobics group just didn't feel as much stress to begin with. Maybe they were were less prone to stress than the aerobics people before the study even started. Maybe the aerobics people were just better at math than the weight-training people, and so the toughness of the math problem wouldn't be as intimidating to them.

label: Goal
body:
Since this is Necessary Assumption, the correct answer will do one of two things:
  - rule out some other way to explain why the aerobics group has less measurable stress
  or
  - say something that is required for the author's explanation to make sense

label: Conclusion
body: Office equipment and furniture are not properly designed to promote workers' health.

label: Evidence
body: There's a higher incidence of lower back injuries among office workers than among people doing work known to place heavy stress on the lower back.

label: Evaluate
body:
There are two issues: one is a move from "higher incidence of lower back injuries" to "not promoting workers' health". We could certainly marshal a counterargument that even if office jobs are worse when it comes to lower backs, they're better when it comes to many other measurements of workers' health.
  The more likely one they're testing is the Curious Fact / Explanation template, which is so common on Strengthen and Weaken.
  Curious Fact: why do office workers get more lower back injuries than people who do stressful back labor?
  Author's Story: the office furniture is terrible for their back and causes the injuries
  We weaken this template by
  - providing some OTHER WAY to explain the curious fact
  - undermining the plausibility of the AUTHOR'S WAY

label: Goal
body:
1. Look for a different way to explain why office workers have a higher rate of lower back injuries than people who do stressful back labor.
  or
  2. A way to undermine the idea that office furniture is causing lower back injuries
  or
  3. A way to argue that offices might be worse for workers' lower backs but still better when it comes to overall health.

label: Conclusion
body: People with degrees are more likely to live in a house with a cat than one with a dog.

label: Evidence
body:
47% of houses with cats have someone with a degree.
  38% of houses with dogs have someone with a degree.

label: Evaluate
body:
The statistics presented in the evidence aren't very useful when it comes to ascertaining what the conclusion is talking about.
  The conclusion wants to know whether there are more people with degrees living in a cat house or a dog house. (Houses with both don't really matter, because they "cancel each other out". If they have both a cat and a dog, then they won't affect the conclusion in either direction)
  Does the evidence tell us whether there are more people with degrees living in a cat house or a dog house?
  No, it just tells us that cat houses are more likely to have a college grad in them than are dog houses. That doesn't mean, however, that there are more college grads living in cat houses than in dog houses, because there could be 100 cat houses and 10,000 dog houses.

label: Goal
body:
There are a lot of different ways to describe the problem here, but essentially the statistics presented don't allow us to make any judgment on the conclusion.
  The premises are about Percent's whereas the conclusion comes down to a raw number comparison. It's expressed in "most likely" language, but the way you would decide whether people with degrees are more likely to live in a cat house vs. a dog house would simply be to ask, "Are there more people with degrees living in cat houses or dog houses"?
  The author's reasoning is that 47% is bigger than 38%, so there must be more people with degrees in cat houses than in dog houses, but those percentages are taken of different totals (47% of cat houses vs. 38% of dog houses), so they're not possible to directly compare.

label: Conclusion (Therefore)
body: It must have been Keeler who notified the press.

label: Evidence
body: Keeler wanted the institute to receive bad publicity. He and Greene were the only ones in a position to tell the press, but Greene had no reason to do so.

label: Given Joe's Claims
body:
1. All vampire stories are based on an absurd set of premises.
  2. According to such stories, every victim of a vampire becomes a vampire.
  3. And [according to such stories] vampires have existed since ancient times and are immortal,
  4. Vampires would by now have almost completely eliminated their prey.

label: Evaluate Maria's Responses
body:
1. no comment
  2. Disagrees
  3. no comment
  4. no comment, possibly disagrees
  The only one of Joe's points that Maria explicitly disagrees with is the idea that every victim of a vampire becomes a vampire. Maria's statements suggest that Maria disagrees with Joe's claim that vampires would by now have almost completely eliminated their prey, but that's not totally certain.

label: Goal
body: Expect the correct answer to addresses claim #2. It's not completely out of the question for a correct answer to address claim #4, but that seems less likely considering Maria's explicit disagreement with claim #2. Beware of answers which focus on other details about which Maria never expressed an opinion.

label: Given that...
body: The salespersons' important work in the central computer database could be easily accessed using portable computers, thereby saving salespersons the effort of lugging their paper files all over the country.

label: How can it be that...
body: Salespersons rarely accessed the database and continued to rely on many paper files, which they had refused to turn over to the staff responsible for creating the database.

label: Evaluate
body:
The stimulus compares the potential benefits of this project to the actual outcome. It seems like scanning the paper documents into a central database would make it easier for the salespersons to do their job. Why didn't they use the database? And why did they refuse to turn paper files over to the staff responsible for creating the database?
  The second question seems like the more important one. An answer to that question could very possibly answer the first question as well. The salespersons might have refused to turn over the files for any number of reasons, but we can imagine a couple of possibilities.
  Maybe there was some kind of office drama going on, and for some reason the salespersons didn't trust the people who were creating the database.
  Maybe the salespersons were worried about their work being automated. Or perhaps they thought that having their important paperwork in a database would make it easier for the company to replace them with other salespersons.
  Or maybe these files were so important to the salespersons that they just worried about the files being lost.

label: Goal
body: Expect a correct answer to focus on the salesperson's refusal to turn over their important files. At the same time, we need to keep an open mind. It's very possible for an answer to suggest something that we haven't thought of. Beware of answers that ignore important aspects of the situation which need to be explained.

label: Evidence (For example, since)
body:
It is illegal to shout "Fire!" in a crowded mall if the only intent is to play a practical joke; the government may ban publication of information about military operations and the identity of undercover agents; and extortion threats and conspiratorial agreements are also criminal acts.
  They [these forms of speech] are all likely to lead directly to serious harm.

label: Conclusion
body: The criminalization of these forms of speech is justified. [The legal right to free speech does not protect all speech.]

label: Evaluate
body:
There are a lot of moving pieces in this argument, but fortunately there are some clues which help us identify the role played by each statement.
  The phrase "for example" at the beginning of the second sentence is generally a premise indicator, and it seems to function that way here. We're getting examples which support the claim in the first sentence. This indicates that the first sentence is a conclusion, and this second sentence provides evidence which supports that conclusion.
  The word "since" in the final sentence is also a common premise indicator. We're seeing another conclusion – premise relationship in this sentence. "The criminalization of these forms of speech is justified," is a conclusion supported by the evidence which comes after the word "since."
  We seem to have two separate conclusions here, but their meaning is very similar. Saying "the criminalization of some forms of speech is justified" is essentially the same as saying, "the legal right to free speech does not protect all speech." If you wondered for a moment if one of these was an intermediate conclusion, that's a good question to ask. But these statements are similar enough for us to say that they're repeating the same idea.

label: Goal
body: The question stem here is a bit odd. It's not explicitly asking for the main conclusion of the argument. It's just asking for an answer that describes what "the politician argues." Since the whole point and purpose of an argument is to present and support the conclusion, this could be the same thing as asking for the politician's conclusion. We'll keep an open mind as we look at the answers, though, just in case one correctly describes the argument in a more general way. Beware of answers that include details which seem relevant but weren't actually discussed in the argument.

label: Conclusion (this tells us)
body: People have become less willing to engage with works of art than they once were.

label: Evidence
body: Nowadays, museum visitors seldom pause to look at a work of art for even a full minute.

label: Evaluate
body:
There is a New Concept in the Conclusion — "less willing to engage with art". Does the argument ever define what it means to be willing to engage with art?
  No. What proxy idea in the evidence seems to be the intended match for "less willing to engage with art"?
  The author is saying that people usually pause and look for less than a minute before moving on. So the author must be assuming a Linking idea that, "If you look for less than a minute, then you're not (fully?) engaging with the work of art.".
  We could also potentially make objections to this argument:
  Given that ... museum visitors usually look for less than a minute before moving on,
  How can we say that ... people are still just as willing to engage with work of art?
  - maybe it's easy to engage in under a minute
  - maybe they're moving on to the next work, not because they're less willing to engage with the work they were looking at, but for some other reason (the museum is crowded and forces them to keep moving without lingering too long at any one place)
  - maybe they've already stared at this art for hours online, engaging with it there. Seeing it in the museum gives them a visceral thrill of seeing the art in person, but they've already engaged with it previously
  - maybe they plan to snap a picture and then blow up that picture on a computer screen at home later and engage with the work of art
  etc.

label: Goal
body:
Look for a Linking idea connecting "people usually spend less than a minute looking" to "less willing to engage".
  Or look for a Defender answer ruling out one of our objections (or something similar).

label: Statements
body:
- *conditional (only = right side)*
```
heavy tapestry appropriate  →  don't need to be laundered frequently
need to be laundered frequently  →  heavy tapestry not appropriate
```
  - *contrast*
  - Swags / balloon valances (which are types of window treatments) do not need to be laundered frequently.
  - All clothing does need to be laundered frequently.

label: Evaluate
body:
Whenever we're given a conditional statement in an Inference stimulus, we ask ourselves two questions:
  1. are there any other conditionals present that I can chain this up with?
  2. are there any facts present to which I can apply this rule? (usually via the contrapositive)
  We got a conditional in the first sentence:
```
heavy tapestry fabric appropriate  →  doesn't need to be laundered frequently
```
  If we wanted to, we could turn the two claims in the second sentence into conditionals:
```
clothing  →  does need frequent laundering
swags or balloon valance  →  does not need freq. laundering
```
  Can we chain those together with the original? The overlapping concept is whether or not something needs to be laundered frequently. We often need to contrapose the rule in order to see how it chains or applies.
  When we look at the contrapositive,
```
Don't need to be laundered frequently  →  heavy tapestry not appropriate
```
  we can see that it could chain up with the Clothing conditional.
```
Clothing  →  does need frequent laundering  →  heavy tapestry inappropriate
```

label: Goal
body: Let's look for an answer like "heavy tapestry fabrics would be inappropriate for any type of clothing (such as skirts / jackets)".

label: Given that ...
body: The new apartments in B-ville increased the supply of available housing, and that increasing the supply of available housing usually leads to lower rents for existing apartments.

label: How can it be that ...
body: Since these new apartments were built, the rents for existing apartments rose.

label: Evaluate / Goal
body:
It's hard to anticipate why these new apartments were an exception to the general trend. We either want an answer that connects with these new apartments and gives us a way to explain increasing rents.
  Or we want an answer that just tells us something else that's changed during the same timeframe that would explain increased rents. The stimulus did provide us with one mechanism for explaining rent increases (a decrease in the supply of available housing).
  Maybe an answer will show us how the new apartments counterintuitively caused a decrease in the supply of available housing.

label: Main Conclusion
body: Politicians often advocate increased overall economic productivity while ignoring its drawbacks.

label: Evidence
body: Attempting to increase the productivity of a corporation means attempting to increase its profitability, which typically leads to a reduction in the number of workers employed by that corporation.

label: Intermediate Conclusion
body: Attempting to increase productivity in the economy as a whole may benefit business owners, but will increase the number of unemployed workers.

label: Evaluate
body:
Strictly speaking, the first sentence appears to be the main conclusion of the argument. "For example" is usually a premise indicator, and the example in the second sentence is being offered as evidence supporting the claim in the first sentence. But we also have the conclusion indicator "thus" at the start of the final sentence, indicating that this is a conclusion supported by evidence in the previous sentence. When we compare this final sentence to the first sentence, the final sentence seems like an intermediate conclusion supporting the more general main conclusion in the first sentence.
  As we start looking for flaws or gaps in the argument, we should notice a gap in between the evidence and the intermediate conclusion. This seems to be where all of the action is in this argument.
  The evidence states that attempting to increase the productivity of a corporation typically leads to a reduction in the number of workers employed by that corporation.
  The intermediate conclusion shifts to a claim about attempting to increase productivity in the economy as a whole, stating that this will increase the number of unemployed workers.
  How exactly is the example of increasing the productivity of a corporation directly relevant to increasing productivity in the economy as a whole? Corporations do play a role in the economy, but at best there seems to be some type of Part vs. Whole flaw happening here. At worst, the argument hasn't made it at all clear how the evidence is supposed to support the conclusion.

label: Goal
body: Look for an answer which highlights the gap between evidence about a corporation and the conclusion about the economy as a whole. There might be other flaws in the argument, and a correct answer could describe one of those flaws, so we'll keep an open mind as we look at the answers. Beware of answers which describe something that doesn't actually happen in the argument.

label: Conclusion
body: A good movie reviewer should be able to give favorable reviews of movies that are not to his or her taste.

label: Evidence
body:
While critics might try to help people appreciate better movies, the function of movie reviewers is to help people determine which movies they might enjoy seeing.
  Movie reviewers' tastes are very different and usually better informed than those of most moviegoers, because they've seen so many movies.

label: Evaluate
body:
Whenever we do Main Conclusion and Role questions, we start by priming our brain with the reminder that the conclusion is almost always earlier than the Supporting ideas.
  So as we read the arguments on these two question types, we're specifically asking ourselves:
  - Is the first sentence the conclusion (#2 most common pattern)?
  - Is there an early attribution and then the author rebuts that idea (#1 most common pattern)?
  When we read this first sentence, does it sound like the author's opinion?
  Sure! It says "should", which is opinionated. If the paragraph starts with an opinion from the author, 99% of the time that's your main conclusion.
  Does the author provide support for why a good movie reviewer should be able to give good reviews of movies they don't like?
  Yes — the job of movie reviewers is to help people figure which movies the people would like, not which movies the reviewer likes. And the reviewer doesn't have the same tastes as most people (because the reviewer has seen so many movies).

label: Goal
body: As long as we correctly find the conclusion, the hard part is done. We just have to find a meaning match for the first sentence, which is our main conclusion.

label: Evidence
body: The brain area that enables one to distinguish the different sounds made by a piano tends to be larger in a highly skilled musician than in someone who has rarely, if ever, played a musical instrument.

label: Conclusion
body: This shows that practicing on, and playing, a musical instrument actually alters brain structure.

label: Evaluate
body:
This is a classic example of a Causal Flaw. As the legendary Steve Irwin would say, "she's a beauty!"
  The evidence describes a correlation—two things that tend to happen together. A certain area of the brain tends to be larger in a highly skilled musician compared to someone who does not play a musical instrument.
  The conclusion then claims that one of these things causes the other. While a correlation is potentially evidence of a causal relationship, by itself a correlation doesn't prove that one thing causes the other. This argument is flawed because it fails to consider alternative possibilities.
  There could be any number of other factors which might cause this area of the brain to be larger in musicians. The actual causal relationship might be the reverse of what the conclusion claims: maybe when this area of the brain is larger than normal, that causes someone to become a skilled musician, or at least it's a partial cause.

label: Goal
body: We'll expect an answer to point out how the argument concludes that a casual relationship exists based solely on evidence of a correlation. A correct answer might suggest that the argument has failed to consider an alternative possibility. Beware of answers that describe flaws which don't occur in this argument.

label: Statements
body:
- *causal (diverts / leaves / because)*
```
Overhearing one-side of a cell-phone conversation  ⇢  Diverts your attention from what you're doing
Hearing only one portion of conversation  ⇢  Constantly trying to guess what other person said
Hearing someone speak abnormally loudly  →  diverts your attention away
```

label: Evaluate
body:
We have three related causal statements. They don't really link up to a causal chain, but they all stem from a related cause.
  You're hearing your friend / loved one talking (abnormally loudly) on the cell-phone. You can only hear their part of the conversation. You're trying to guess what the other person just said or is saying.
  And what does all that cause? It diverts your attention.

label: Goal
body: It's hard to know exactly what the answer will say, but it will seemingly reinforce this causal relationship being stressed that, for multiple reasons, eavesdropping on your friend's cell-phone cause is diverting your attention from whatever you are doing.

label: Conclusion (So)
body: The treatment is probably not actually effective.

label: Evidence
body: All three studies showing the new treatment looked promising had critical methodological flaws.

label: Evaluate
body:
Parallel Flaw usually tests illegal moves with conditionals/quantifiers, or it tests one of the top 6 famous flaws:
  - Necessary vs. Sufficient (illegal conditional moves)
  - overconfident Causal conclusions
  - Part vs. Whole
  - Sampling
  - Ad Hominem
  - Unproven vs. Proven False
  Here, it's doing that last one. The fact that these studies had methodological flaws means they're not super trustworthy as evidence. We shouldn't lean on them as support for the idea that this new treatment is effective.
  The correct conclusion would be, "So, we should not judge the effectiveness of the treatment based on these studies".
  The author, meanwhile, is incorrectly volunteering some pessimism about the effectiveness of the treatment. Where is the author getting any evidence that the treatments aren't effective?
  The fact that these studies aren't good evidence in favor of X does not suddenly mean that they are good evidence against X. They just aren't good evidence.

label: Goal
body: Look for an answer that does something similar Unproven vs. Proven False move. There is an effort to prove X that is flawed or unsuccessful in some way. And the author concludes from this that X is probably wrong / false.

label: Conclusion
body: If computer simulated crash tests become as reliable as actual test crashes, then manufacturers will use far fewer actual test crashes.

label: Evidence
body: The cost of doing computer simulations is lower than paying for actual test crashes.

label: Evaluate
body:
At the heart of this question is a comparison between computer simulated crash tests vs. actual physical ones with cars and dummies and brick walls.
  This argument makes a Prediction, that if computer tests were as reliable as actual tests, then we'd see more computer tests and fewer actual tests based on a Comparison between the two types of tests:
  Computer tests are cheaper than actual tests.
  If you were a car manufacturer deciding whether or not to go with computer tests vs. actual tests, so far you know that they're equally reliable, but computer tests are cheaper. Is there anything else you'd like to find out?
  This is an Incomplete Comparison.
  We know the two options are tied when it comes to reliable information.
  Computer tests win when it comes to how costly.
  But do actual tests have any advantages? Faster turnaround time? Tax incentives? Do they provide some other kind of data that computer tests don't?

label: Goal
body: We want to hear some other way in which computer tests are better than actual tests (or at least, not worse than actual tests). Or we'd like an answer that stressed that 'how costly is it?' is an important part of the decision making process for manufacturers deciding whether to go with computer tests or actual tests.

label: Conclusion
body: We should vote to approve the act.

label: Intermediate Conclusion
body: Her real reason for opposing must not be very persuasive.

label: Intermediate Conclusion
body: She has not revealed her real reason.

label: Evidence
body: She says the act would deter investment, but in the past she's voted for legislation that inhibited investment.

label: Evidence
body:
Were we to believe that, we'd be committed to thinking that what an offender did years ago (i.e. previous offenses) are relevant to how serious their current offense is.
  If previous offenses from years ago were relevant, then almost every other remote consideration would be relevant, which would make it impossible to accurately figure out how serious an offense was so that we can assign a proportionate punishment.

label: Evidence
body: Precognitive means "able to accurately perceive future events", and accurately perceiving future events means "your prediction comes to pass", but some of the supposed precog's predictions do not come to pass.

label: Evaluate
body:
When an author tries to dismiss an argument because the source of the argument either has a biased interest or because the source of the argument has conflicting past behavior, that's the famous flaw known as Ad Hominem.
  This author says, "because in the past you voted for something that inhibited investment, you can't really be worried about inhibiting investment".
  That's flawed thinking for a couple reasons
  - People are allowed to change. People can learn from their mistakes. Maybe this woman has learned that it was a mistake for her in the past to have voted for something that inhibited investment.
  - Deciding to vote for / against something is a complicated calculus. You might vote for something that inhibits investment in spite of the fact that it inhibits investment, because something else outweighs it.
  Any politician who voted for $2 trillion of COVID-relief voted for legislation that will greatly increase the national deficit. Does that mean that any time in the future of they object to legislation because it increases the deficit that we can say, "That must be a bogus reason — after all, you've voted for stuff that increased the deficit before"?
  Of course not. Sometimes you accept a negative part of something because the good / necessary parts outweigh the negative.
  That famous flaw is happening in the move from Premise to Intermediate Conclusion. We have another famous flaw occurring in the move from Intermediate Conclusion to Main Conclusion.
  The author is acting like "since her reason for rejecting the act is bad / invalid / not real, then we should approve the act". But wait a sec — has the author presented any evidence in favor of approving the act?
  Just because the colleague failed to prove the act should be rejected doesn't mean that the author has proven that the act should be approved. This is the famous flaw Unproven vs. Proven False.

label: Goal
body:
Look for an answer calling out the Ad Hominem flaw, saying "just because she's previously supported something that did X doesn't mean she's lying when she says she doesn't like this new thing because it does X."
  Or look for an answer calling out the Unproven vs. Proven False flaw, saying "just because we don't have a good reason for rejecting something doesn't mean that we have a good reason for accepting/embracing something."

label: Setup Information
body:
- *conditional (X will not unless Y)*
```
X requires Y = X → Y
Significantly increasing efficiency  →  comp system requires employees to adopt new ways of working
```
  - *specific fact* - The Ministry's new computer system is built to fit its employees existing ways of working.

label: The Blank (so)
body: We need to draw a logical conclusion, so we think of this like a Most Supported inference question.

label: Evaluate
body:
On Inference, whenever we're given a conditional, we ask ourselves two things:
  1. Am I supposed to be chaining this up with some other conditional?
  2. Am I supposed to be applying this rule to a specific fact?
  The first sentence was conditional, but the second sentence is a specific fact, so we would more likely be doing #2.
  Typically, when we are tested on our ability to apply a conditional to a fact, we have to contrapose the conditional to understand how it applies (or we ask ourselves about what Overlapping Concept is in both the rule and the fact).
  The overlapping concept between the 1st and 2nd sentence is "whether a computer system requires employees to change their ways of working or permits them to continue their existing ways of working".
  When we contrapose the rule from the first sentence, we get:
```
If new computer system doesn't require employees to adopt new ways of working  →  won't signif increase efficiency
```

label: Goal
body:
We were told that the MoT's new computer system does not require employees to adopt new ways (it was custom built to fit their existing ways), so it triggers this conditional and yields this logical conclusion/inference:
  The Ministry of Transportation's new computer system will not significantly increase the ministry's efficiency.
  Let's look for something like that.

label: Evidence
body: For all three of the cars I have owned, I have been unable to get even close to the fuel economy that manufacturers advertise for cars of those makes.

label: Conclusion
body: Manufacturers probably inflate those numbers [fuel economy under normal driving conditions].

label: Evaluate
body:
There are a few possible flaws with this argument. The columnist doesn't tell us whether or not she drove her three cars under the type of "normal driving conditions" that the manufacturers base their numbers on. Maybe the columnist drives her Toyota Corolla like a Formula 1 race car. Maybe her three "cars" were actually pickup trucks that she mostly used to haul cinderblocks and go four-wheeling up in the mountains.
  The core issue here is that the columnist bases her claim solely on the three vehicles she has owned. It's entirely possible that most drivers do get fuel economy that's comparable to the manufacturers' numbers. The columnist's experiences could be different for any number of reasons.

label: Goal
body: Look for an answer to indicate that the argument contains a sample flaw. The evidence is based on too small of a sample to fully support the conclusion.

label: Conclusion
body: If more landlords put electricity meters on individual apartments, so that tenants can be billed for their personal electricity, energy will be conserved as a result.

label: Evidence
body: Presently, tenants who don't have to pay individual electricity bills don't have a financial incentive to conserve electricity.

label: Evaluate
body:
Our author is making a Plan / Prediction and assuming a difference in this new world. He thinks that once people can see their own energy bill and have a financial incentive to use less energy, they will use less energy.
  How could this fail to be true?
  - maybe they're already conserving as much as they can (not because of financial incentives, but because of environmental conscientiousness)
  - maybe they're wealthy enough that even with a financial incentive to use less energy, they choose not to.
  - maybe they would never look at the electricity meters and thus wouldn't really get a sense for how much they were using.

label: Goal
body: Look for an answer suggesting that something doesn't change in the way the author was assuming (i.e. people don't start thinking about their energy usage more and using less as a result), or an answer that otherwise makes it seem like we'll end up using just as much energy under this new plan.

label: Conclusion (unsustainable = opinion)
body: It's not sustainable to think that punishment should be proportional to how serious the offense is and also think that repeat offenders should receive harsher punishments than first-time offenders.

label: Conclusion
body: Organic orchards are likely to be more profitable than conventional orchards in the long run.

label: Evaluate
body:
If this were a Method of reasoning question, then we'd be saying that this author is undermining a position by showing that it's implications, if true, would be untenable.
  The 2nd and 3rd sentence each begin by saying, "If that last thing were true, then THIS thing would be true". And the purpose of tracing out this chain of implications is to demonstrate that if someone believes both that "punishment = proportional to serious of offense" and that "repeat offenders deserve more punishment than first time offenders", then they're committed to the logic that a repeat offender doing action X is a more serious offense than a first time offender doing action X.
  Given that it's the same action, how could the repeat offender's version of doing it be a more serious offense?
  The logic would be that the repeat offenders' past actions make their present offense more serious, and that's where the author sees an impossible outcome, in which we have to assess all of an offender's past actions to determine the seriousness of their present offense.

label: Goal
body: We're being asked about the 2nd sentence, which was one of the three premises. It's the most direct implication the author mentions of the original position that she's refuting. From there, the argument goes through more implications until it hits the brick wall of "impossible" and thus proves her point that the original position was dumb.

label: Conclusion
body: The move from aiming for objectivity to aiming to create stir with partisan reporting is best understood in terms of differing business strategies.

label: Evidence
body:
The new media outlets, who try to create a stir with partisan reporting, need to differentiate themselves in a crowded marketplace.
  The old media outlets, who were aiming for objectivity, needed to avoid offending potential readers.

label: Evaluate
body:
The structure of this argument is that Old vs. New can be explained by Goal 1 vs. Goal 2, which leaves us with two missing links to consider.
  In order for the Old style (objectivity) to satisfy Goal 1 (avoid offending potential readers), the author needs to assume that objectivity is good at avoiding offending potential readers.
  In order for the New style (create stir with open partisanship) to satisfy Goal 2 (differentiate themselves in crowded marketplace), the author needs to assume that creating a stir with openly partisan reporting helps to differentiate a news outlet in a crowded marketplace, i.e. it's not the case that everyone in this crowded marketplace is already doing this create a stir with openly partisan reporting strategy, because then it wouldn't serve the purpose of helping an outlet stick out from the crowd.

label: Goal
body: Look for either of the two missing links we found, or look for an answer ruling out some better explanation for understanding the contrast between Old and New journalistic standards.

label: Statements
body:
- *conditional - ANY / EXCEPT*
```
[might facilitate abuse of power] AND [no compelling reason to do it]  →  shouldn't do it
```
  - *fact* - Keeping govt secrets is a practice that might facilitate abuse of power.
  - (infer-as-we-go: We shouldn't keep govt secrets if there's no compelling reason to do so.)
  - *fact* - Govt officials are sometimes justified in keeping secrets
  - (infer-as-we-go: sometimes they have compelling reasons)
  - *fact* - Too often they keep secrets for insubstantial reasons and enable abuses of power.
  - (infer-as-we-go: they should not have done hat)
  - *conditional - WHEN*
```
Govt officials conceal the fact that they are keeping a secret  →  this practice opens up opportunity for more abuse
```

label: Evaluate
body:
The paragraph ends talking about a practice that "opens up an opportunity for abuse". The paragraph began by talking about a practice that "might facilitate the abuse of power".
  So it seems like we could say that government officials should not undertake the practice of concealing from the public that they are keeping a secret, unless there's a compelling reason to do so.

label: Goal
body: There are so many facts here that I wouldn't try to 'solve' it upfront, since it could go a lot of different directions. We know we have a very useful conditional in the first sentence. It potentially can be applied to some of the actions we then were told about, and maybe it could even be applied to the rule in the final sentence.

label: Conclusion (thus)
body:
The music of these contemporary musicians fails to conform to their theory
  (i.e. the music of these contemporary musicians does have meaning)

label: Evidence
body: These musicians encourage audience acceptance by prefacing their performances with explanations of their intentions (since they realize their approach to music is very weird).

label: Evaluate
body:
"Bereft of" = lacking, devoid of. If we don't know that, we'll struggle to understand what failing to conform with their theory means, although we could make do with thinking, "Okay, we need to prove that these musicians' music is not bereft of meaning."
  Where does the author think he establishes that their music has meaning?
  The closest semantic cousin would be explanation of their intentions. These experimental musicians who are about to play a bunch of weird noises, since to them, 'music is just a series of sounds with no meaning', first tell there audiences a little disclaimer:
  Hey, everyone. Thanks for coming out. We're going to be doing stuff that sounds [smugly] a little different than what you're used to tonight. We believe that music has no meaning and is just a series of sounds, so we want you to listen to what we're doing and accept it via that framework.
  Our author is basically saying, "telling people that your music has no meaning is actually imbuing your music with a meaning".

label: Goal
body:
Look for a linking answer saying "if you're encouraging audiences to accept your music, by explaining to them your intentions, then your music has meaning".
  But we'll take anything that functionally allows us to prove that the music of these musicians does have meaning.
  And if an answer isn't giving us a mechanism to prove that "their music has meaning", then it's functionally worthless to us.

label: Conclusion
body: Evolution does not always optimize survival of an organism.

label: Evidence
body:
Male moose evolved giant antlers as a way to determine the dominant males, for whom the giant antlers provide a survival benefit.
  But those giant antlers make it harder to escape predators, since the antlers can easily get tangled in trees.
  All male moose would be better off with antlers half the current size (for the sake of escaping predators), assuming they could preserve whatever relative size/status advantage they have over their peers.

label: Goal
body: Look for an answer that mirrors the final statement in the argument. Beware of answers that describe other parts of the argument, like premises.

label: Evaluate
body:
On Method questions, the correct answer usually pulls from this list of concepts:
  presents Analogy
  rules out alternate possibilities
  provides (counter)example of general claim
  discusses implications of logic
  calls out dubious assumption
  raises overlooked consideration / distinction
  defines a term
  suggests alternate explanation
  This one seemed to start with a very general claim about evolution and then illustrate it by discussing the case of the male moose.

label: Goal
body: Let's look for something like "providing an example to illustrate a generalization".

label: Conclusion (this suggests that)
body: The bacteria detect red light by monitoring how much energy their chlorophyll is producing.

label: Evidence
body:
The chlorophyll in these bacteria allows them to get more energy from red light than from any other color of night.
  And when you put this bacteria into a tube with different areas lit by different colors, the bacteria all move to the red light district.

label: Evaluate
body:
Since the author is looking at a study / experiment and concluding some causal story, we can think through our Explain Curious Fact lens.
  Curious Fact ... how do these bacteria know to all move to the red light district of the test tube?
  Author's Explanation ... they feel there way there, via chlorophyll-energy (the red light gives them the most chlorophyll energy).
  We always evaluate Explain Curious Fact arguments by thinking
  1. could there be some Alternate Explanation for the curious fact?
  2. how plausible is the Author's Explanation?

label: Goal
body:
Since we're trying to weaken this argument, we either want to
  1. suggest an Alternate Explanation for how/why the bacteria are figuring out where the red light area is, or
  2. undermine the plausibility of the Author's notion that the bacteria can sense how much energy their chlorophyll is producing, and since red provides the most energy they find the red area by seeking the area of most chlorophyll energy.

label: Conclusion (So)
body: We can see that the recently enacted trade agreement represents a series of compromises among the various interest groups that are concerned with it.

label: Evidence (because)
body:
All those groups are clearly unhappy with it,
  and
  if a piece of legislation is the result of negotiation and compromise between competing interest groups, it will not satisfy any of those groups.

label: Evaluate
body:
The first word out of the gate is "If". What does "if" mean to an LSAT student? That's right, it almost always means Conditional Logic (the condition attached to "if" goes on the left of the arrow).
  When we're doing Flaw and we see any Conditional Logic, what should we be thinking?
  We should be on the lookout for the #1 famous flaw of them all, confusing Necessary vs. Sufficient.
  This argument was identical to this one:
  If a person wins the Kentucky state lottery, they will be very wealthy. So, we can see that Bob apparently won the Kentucky state lottery, because he is clearly very wealthy.
  Our conversational objection to this argument would be, "Hey, there could be a ton of different reasons why Bob is wealthy. Sure, winning the KY lottery is one possibility, but we can't be sure that's why Bob is wealthy".
  Our conversational objection to this argument we just read would similarly be, "Hey, there could be a ton of different reasons why the various interest groups are clearly unhappy with this new agreement. Yes, resulting from compromise is one possibility, but we can't be sure that's why they're all unhappy".
  As soon as we see the conditional logic statement offered in the Evidence,
  for example, X → Y
  We listen for the two variations on the Necessary vs. Sufficient flaw (reasoning via an illegal negation or via an illegal reversal).
  We'd expect to hear, "Bob is Y. Thus, Bob is X"
  or, "Bob is not X. Thus, Bob is not Y".
  The conditional we were given was,
```
legislation resulted from compromise between interest groups  →  all the groups will be unsatisfied (unhappy)
```
  Does this argument say, "All the groups are unhappy. Thus, the legislation must have resulted from compromise?"
  Or does it say, "This legislation was not the result of compromise between interest groups. Thus, at least one group will be happy/satisfied."?
  It did the first one. It just tries to hide it with two moves:
  1. They supplied the Conclusion (So) before they supplied the Evidence (Because).
  2. They didn't use a verbatim word match. They're forcing us to see that "unhappy" and "not satisfied" are interchangeable here. They're also forcing us to see that "results from negotiation and compromise between groups" is interchangeable with "represents a series of compromises among the groups".
  In order to see past their shenanigans, we need to be on top of knowing that when we see "If", we're getting conditional logic. And we need to know that when we see conditional logic on Flaw questions, the authors will usually use a conditional rule in some illegal backwards or negated fashion.

label: Goal
body:
Look for the formal answer, saying this author scrambled a condition that is Sufficient to prove that everyone would be unhappy with a condition that is Required in order for everyone to be unhappy.
  Or look for the conversational answer saying, "That's one possible reason they're all unhappy. There might be other reasons, besides negotiation that results in compromise, that could account for why they're all unhappy".

label: Information
body:
- After an accident, they found isotopes of iodine, tellurium, and cesium downwind, but no heavy isotopes.
  - infer: iodine, tellurium, and cesium are not heavy isotopes
  - Those three things either came from (1) spent fuel rods or (2) the plant's core.
  - (1) never has much tellurium in it.
  - (2) would have ejected stuff that included heavy isotopes.
  - infer: both (1) and (2) have a strike against them, if we assume that this three-pack of isotopes traveled as a bunch. The fact that they had tellurium makes (1) seem like it wasn't the source. The fact that they didn't have heavy isotopes makes (2) seem like it wasn't the source.
  - After the accident, steam was released from the plant. It may have been in contact with the core, which contains those three isotopes, and those three isotopes are easily dissolved by steam.

label: Evaluate
body:
What a mouthful! This is a lot to take in, which is why we modeled above some of the self-talk we would be doing while reading it, to try to process where this conversation is headed.
  Even though no one is asking any questions, there appears to be a bit of a causal mystery, because researchers found these isotopes, and then we start hearing, "They either came from X or from Y", which makes it seem like we're trying to figure out which one it came from.
  We know that the tellurium didn't come from the spent fuel rods, but maybe the other two isotopes did?
  We know these three-pack of isotopes didn't eject directly from the core, because if it had then we would have found heavy isotopes in there as well, which we didn't.
  There's a possibility that the three-pack of isotopes came from the core, dissolved into steam, which was then released from the plant and then found by researchers downwind from the plant.
  But that seems pretty speculative.

label: Goal
body: There's so much here that it's hard to make any specific prediction. Let's look for the most supportable answer.

label: Conclusion (Therefore / clearly)
body: Ecology is not being evaluated by means of the criteria used to evaluate the physical sciences.

label: Evidence
body:
If ecology and the physical sciences were evaluated by same criteria, ecology would fail to be successful (it can't be captured by a set of simple laws).
  But ecology is a successful science.

label: Conclusion
body: The plots of these books show that these characters are not precognitive.

label: Goal
body: Find the principle that says: sometimes getting richer at work means enjoying work less.

label: Evaluate
body:
In a very generic sense, this argument just uses contrapositive logic:
  Premise 1: If A were true, then B would be true.
  Premise 2: But B isn't true.
  Conclusion: So A isn't true.
```
If Ecology and physical sciences were evaluated same  →  Ecology not successful science
```
  But, Ecology is successful science.
  Therefore, Ecology and PS not evaluated same.

label: Goal
body:
Before getting too fine-grained, we can head to the answers looking for a simply contrapositive argument. If we see more than one argument matching our desired structure, then we'll look for more nuanced similarities.
  Premise1: If A were true, B would be true.
  Premise2: But B isn't true.
  Conclusion: So A isn't true.

label: Evidence
body:
During the rainy season, bonobos swallow leaves of *Manniophyton fulvum*.
  Ingestion of these leaves facilitates the elimination of gastrointestinal worms.

label: Conclusion
body: Bonobos likely ingest the leaves because of their medicinal properties.

label: Evaluate
body:
This argument is attempting to explain what causes bonobos to eat *M. fulvum* leaves. The evidence describes a correlation between two facts: Fact #1 is that the bonobos eat the leaves. Fact #2 is that the leaves help to eliminate worms inside the body.
  The conclusion jumps to a claim that this medicinal property of eliminating worms is what causes the bonobos to eat the leaves. But there are other, equally plausible reasons for the bonobos to eat the leaves.
  Maybe the leaves taste good. Maybe the bonobos like the rough texture of the leaves. The argument does nothing to rule out these alternatives. We haven't heard from a bonobo food critic or one with a medical degree. So we can't conclude with certainty that the bonobos are eating the leaves because of medicinal properties.

label: Goal
body: Expect an answer to strengthen the argument by either providing more evidence that medicinal properties are causing the bonobos to eat the leaves, or by ruling out an alternative possibility.

label: Conclusion
body: What would contribute the most to safeguarding public health is a reduction in total miles traveled on our roads.

label: Evidence
body: Traveling by car is itself a major risk factor.

label: Evaluate
body:
Whenever we do Main Conclusion or Role, we specifically listen for upside-down arguments, where the Conclusion appears earlier than the Evidence.
  The two dominant patterns on Main Conclusion are that the conclusion is
  - the First Sentence
  or
  - some Pivot / Rebuttal idea
  The first sentence of this argument isn't the author's opinion, so it won't be the conclusion. Instead, it's an attribution:
  Those concerned with X typically focus their efforts on Y.
  That would lead us to anticipate a Pivot / Rebuttal. Sure enough, we get the But to start the 2nd sentence. Is this claim an opinion from our author?
  Yes! She's saying what she thinks would contribute the most to public health.
  Is this claim Supported (as all conclusions must be)?
  Yes, the last sentence is a "fact" that supports it.

label: Goal
body: Look for an answer that captures the meaning of the 2nd sentence. It might take on more language that feels like the Rebuttal: "What would contribute the most to public health isn't auto safety measures but simply a reduction in total miles driven."

label: Conclusion (lamentable = opinion)
body: The arts section of this paper shows a lamentable bias toward movies and against local theatrical productions.

label: Evidence
body: Over the last year alone, the paper has published over five times as many movie reviews as reviews of live plays.

label: Evaluate
body:
The evidence involves a Curious Comparison, and the conclusion is offering an explanation for that asymmetry, so we can use our Explain Curious Fact mindset.
  Curious Fact … How come the paper publishes five times as many movie reviews as reviews of live plays?
  Author's Explanation … The people who run the arts section are biased towards movies. They prefer movies over plays, so they choose to publish more movie reviews because they would rather write about and publish stuff that they like.
  We always ask ourselves
  1. Could there be an Alternate Explanation for the curious fact?
  2. How plausible is the Author's Explanation?

label: Goal
body: We can either hurt the argument by suggesting an Alternate Explanation for why there are five times as many reviews of movies as of live plays (maybe there are way more movies than plays / maybe the readers of the newspaper are five times more interested in movies than in plays), or hurt it by making it seem less plausible that the editors of the arts section prefer movies to plays and thus publish far more reviews of movies than of plays.

label: Background
body: Our university museum possesses several ancient artifacts whose ownership is in dispute.

label: Opposing Idea (Although)
body: The museum has documentation showing that the items were obtained legally.

label: Evidence (Given that)
body:
There is an overriding principle that any important ancient artifact belongs by rights to the nation on whose territory it was discovered.
  An institution is obliged to honor those rights.

label: Conclusion
body: Our museum should return the artifacts.

label: Evaluate
body:
A few clues help us identify the parts of this argument. One of the most helpful ones is the phrase "given that" at the beginning of the final sentence. "Given that" is a premise indicator, and this sentence follows a common pattern:
  Premise Indicator — Premise — Comma — Conclusion
  "Given that" is followed by the premise about an institutions obligation. That statement is followed by a comma, which is followed by the argument's conclusion. It also helps to note that this final statement is a recommendation: "the museum should return the artifacts." A recommendation will commonly be the conclusion of an argument.
  It helps to be sure that nothing else in the argument is a conclusion that we somehow overlooked. The premise we just mentioned speaks of an obligation "to honor those rights." What rights? The ones mentioned in the preceding sentence, the rights a nation has to important artifacts discovered on their territory.
  The word "although" at the beginning of the second sentence is a hint that the conclusion will eventually refute or at least pivot away from this statement. That's exactly what happens: although the museum has documentation showing that the items were obtained legally, our museum should return the artifacts.
  The very first sentence seems like a statement of fact, so it's not likely to be a conclusion. After reading the rest of the statements, it appears to be background information. It provides context, but by itself is not the conclusion.

label: Evaluate
body:
Given That some of their predictions don't come to pass,
  How Can We Still Argue they are correctly portrayed as precognitive?
  Maybe we could say that 90% of the time they're right? If someone were able to predict the future accurately 90% of the time, the fact that they were sometimes wrong wouldn't keep me from saying, "That fool has some precognition."

label: Goal
body: Look for an answer suggesting, "if you make any mistakes, then you're not to be counted as precognitive", or something like "being correct about predictions the vast majority of the time would not be enough to be appropriately called precognitive".

label: Evidence (Since)
body:
Animated films appropriate for children are not threatening.
  New animated films aimed at adults have dark themes such as poverty and despair.

label: Conclusion
body: Such films cannot be considered appropriate for children.

label: Evaluate
body:
Huh. I was going to watch an episode of Love, Death & Robots with my niece. I guess we'll watch Shrek instead.
  There isn't a conclusion indicator in this argument, but the final sentence follows a common form:
  Premise Indicator - Premise - Comma - Conclusion
  The premise indicator "since" is followed by a premise. That premise is followed by a comma, which is followed by the argument's conclusion.
  If we just look at this premise and the conclusion, we can see a missing link. The premise describes new animated films aimed at adults, but doesn't make any claims about them being appropriate or inappropriate for anyone. The conclusion jumps to a claim about these films not being appropriate for children. "Not appropriate for children" is a new idea in the conclusion.
  The conclusion would follow logically if we connect the information in the premise to the new idea in the conclusion with an assumption like this:
  "Films with dark themes are not appropriate for children."
  However, there's a second assumption to consider. The first sentence in the stimulus connects directly to the conclusion: it's about films being appropriate for children. Because it connects directly to the conclusion, we can treat it as a premise. This sentence states that animated films appropriate for children are not threatening. That's a conditional statement:
  ```
  appropriate for kids → ~threatening
  ```
  The contrapositive of this is that threatening films are not appropriate for children.
  ```
  threatening → ~appropriate for kids
  ```
  We already know that new animated films aimed at adults have dark themes. If we assume that "dark themes are threatening," and combine this with the two existing premises, that would also allow the conclusion to follow logically:
  New animated films aimed at adults have dark themes such as poverty and despair.
  Dark themes are threatening.
  Threatening films are not appropriate for children.
  Therefore, new animated films aimed at adults are not appropriate for children.

label: Goal
body: Look for an answer which states that dark themes are not appropriate for children or that dark themes are threatening. Beware of answers that are illegal reversals or illegal negations of one of these assumptions.

label: Conclusion (this shows that)
body: Migrating allows monarch butterflies to avoid these single-celled parasites that can cause deformities that interfere with their flight.

label: Evidence
body: In populations that have not migrated, up to 95% are infected by parasites. In populations that do migrate, less than 15% are infected.

label: Evaluate
body:
The evidence is look at an asymmetric comparison (i.e. a Curious Fact) and concluding a causal interpretation (migrating causes monarchs to avoid these parasites).
  As always, we're supposed to react to this on Flaw primarily by considering Alternative Explanations for the curious fact.
  Whenever the author presents a correlation, "Those who migrate are less likely to be infected by the parasites" and then concludes that the first things causes the second "migration causes them to avoid parasites", we have two alternate explanations we always consider:
  Reverse Cause? (could it be that avoiding parasites allows them to migrate? That could make sense. If you're infected by the parasite, it causes deformities that interfere with flight, so you wouldn't be able to migrate. That would explain why there's a correlation between infected and non-migrating. The infection comes first and prevents the migration!)
  Third Factor? (could there be some 3rd factor we haven't identified yet that both increases the likelihood of migrating and decreases the likelihood of parasite infection?)

label: Goal
body:
