body: Whooping cranes, unlike sandhill cranes, are endangered as a species, and thus the survival of any one whooping crane is much more important to the preservation of its species than the survival of any one sandhill crane is to the preservation of its species.

label: Evaluate
body: The author is arguing that we have a greater duty to protect a whooping crane than a sandhill crane based on two concepts: 1. whooping is endangered / sandhill isn't 2. survival of each whooping is more important to its species' survival than is survival of each sandhill crane.

label: Goal
body: So let's look for an answer saying, "we have a greater duty to protect the lives of members of an endangered species than of non-endangered species". Or look for an answer saying something like, "the more important an individual animal is to the preservation of its species, the greater a duty we have to protect it".

label: Statements
body:
```
conditionals (all, any, only)
one-way street → dedicated bike lane
dedicated bike lane → city buses don't travel
parking allowed → no dedicated bike lane
```
fact: City bus #9 travels the full length of Batchelder Avenue

label: Evaluate
body:
It seems like this is a classic Must Be True where they provide us with a conditional rule and then test our Contrapositive Logic abilities, in applying it to some fact.
  For example, if we were told "Only blond firemen appeared in the calendar" and then told "Mario is a brunette", then we can infer that "Mario did not appear in the calendar".
  Here, we were told that "only neurons that match the most common local type can help heal an injured brain" and then told "in the striatum, the new neurons never match the most common local type (midsized spiny)".

label: Evaluate
body:
Whenever we see conditionals on Inference questions, we're asking ourselves two things: 1. Does this conditional chain to any other conditional? 2. Are there any facts I can apply this conditional to (usually via the contrapositive)? In this case there are three conditionals and they do seem to have overlapping ingredients that could allow them to chain together.
```
                                  no parking allowed
one-way    →    dedicated    →    and
street          bike lane         no city buses
```
The contrapositive chain
```
city bus            no               not a
or            →     dedicated   →    one-way
parking allowed     bike lane        street
```
This contrapositive chain can be applied to the fact we get in the final sentence. If City Bus 9 goes the full length of Batchelder Avenue, then we know that Batchelder Avenue has no dedicated bike lane and is not a one-way street. (We have no idea if parking is or isn't allowed).

label: Goal
body: Look for anything provable, but the most likely answers would maximize the amount of synthesizing we can do: - Batchelder Avenue is not one way - Batchelder Avenue has no dedicated bike lane

label: Conclusion / Recommendation
body: Ecologists should avoid using terms like "invasive species".

label: Evidence
body: Terms like that invoke human cultural standards about fairness and can influence ecologists' opinions of certain organisms before any data is gathered about their impact.

label: Evaluate
body: If an author is saying, "You should avoid doing X, because doing X leads to Y", then the author is assuming the principle that "you should avoid doing things that lead to Y". Here the author is saying, "Ecologists should avoid using terms like invasive species, because those terms are value-laden and bias ecologists to be hatin' on certain organisms before any data's been gathered on their impact."

label: Goal
body: So the author is assuming the principle that, "ecologists should avoid having opinion of organisms before any data is gathered about their impact." But we need our principle to be more generic / abstract, so that it could apply to a different topic. We should look for stuff like: - avoid doing X because doing X would cause you to have a baked-in prejudice before you've even seen the data

label: Conclusion
body: If the company is going to be consistent, then they must give Vernon his job back.

label: Evidence
body: Vernon got (rightfully) fired for unprofessional behavior, but several higher-ranking employees who acted similarly didn't get fired and are even in good standing.

label: Evaluate
body: We might intuitively be offended by this argument and hear ourselves saying, "Wait a sec, the answer is to also fire the offending higher-ranking employees, not to give all of you a pass." If that didn't occur to us, we would try to get there by attacking the conclusion. We would need to argue that "for the sake of consistency, we shouldn't give Vernon his job back or we need't do so, there's some other way to be consistent ..." At that point we might think, "the other way to be consistent would be to fire the other people who should have gotten the same treatment as Vernon.

label: Goal
body: The answer will almost certainly be expressing our sentiment that you don't need to re-hire Vernon to be consistent, you could (and probably should) choose instead to just fire the higher-ranking employees that so far have not been punished.

label: Given that...
body: A company produced a small car that costs much less—but is also much less safe—than any car previously available.

label: How can it be that...
body: Most customers of the new car increased their safety on the roads by buying it.

label: Evaluate / Goal
body:
We're told that this small car is much less safe when compared to other cars, which leads us to believe that the customers of the new car would decrease their safety by driving it. Why have most customers increased their safety?
  Perhaps people who buy this car tend to do something that increases their safety on the roads. Maybe they drive more carefully because they know the car is much less safe.
  We're also told that the car costs much less, so maybe the drivers are doing something with the money they save which increases their safety. Maybe they buy tires more often, so they're less likely to have an accident caused by worn-out tires.
  A correct answer could suggest one of these possibilities, or perhaps some other factor that helps the drivers of these cars increase their safety on the roads.

label: Conclusion (This proves that)
body: Eating bread and meat in the same meal is unhealthy.

label: Evidence
body:
I used to eat fast food burgers almost every day, until I read that eating bread and meat in the same meal interferes with digestion.
  So now I'm eating lean meats, fruits, and vegetables and I feel much better and my cholesterol level and blood pressure are lower.

label: Evaluate
body:
The author is trying to solve the causal mystery of why he feels better on his new diet, so we can use an Explain Curious Fact mindset.
  Curious Fact ... why do I feel better and have lower cholesterol and blood pressure since I switched from daily fast food burgers to a diet of lean meats, fruits, and vegetables?
  Author's Explanation ... It's because I was eating bread and meat in the same meal, which supposedly interferes with digestion, (and thus made me feel worse and caused higher cholesterol and blood pressure)
  When we see this template arise on Flaw, the correct answer is almost always complaining that the author has failed to consider some Alternate Explanation for the curious fact. What could be a different explanation for why he's doing better on the new diet?
  We could say, "It's not because you were combining bread and meat in the same meal. It's because you were eating fast-food almost every day. That stuff is garbage for you, nutritionally."
  We could also say, "the improvement isn't because you stopped combining bread and meat. It's because you started eating really healthy things like fruits and vegetables."

label: Goal
body: Look for an answer complaining that this author has failed to rule out some alternate explanation for his improved condition (or one complaining that this hypothesis isn't a plausible one, since improved digestion might have anything to do with lower cholesterol and blood pressure).

label: Statements
body:
```
conditional (only if)
Newly formed neurons              Can't help
aren't of the type that's    →    to heal an
most common in the area           injured brain
```
  When it comes to the striatum, the most common type of neuron in the area is the midsized spiny neuron. But newly formed neurons there aren't of that type.

label: Evidence
body:
In one scene, he says that a character's furrowed brow indicates inner turmoil and anxiety.
  Later, he says this same character in the same scene is a "self-identified agent", but he begins the article by saying that a "self-identified agent" is incapable of having misgivings or anxiety.

label: Evaluate
body:
Leona is basically saying that this article contradicts itself.
  The stimulus is a pretty dense one to get through. We have a clue in the first sentence that we should be looking for something that is "ultimately puzzling", and then the next two sentences say:
  "in one scene, the author says X. Later, however, the author says Y."
  That pivot is creating the tension that is "ultimately puzzling" (just as pivot words are frequently used on Paradox questions).
  In order to understand why there's tension, we need to make use of the definition of "self-identified" at the end of the paragraph. If we substitute in that definition, then those two sentences we were talking about are really saying,
  "In one scene, the author says X has anxiety. Later, however, the author refers to X as being someone who is incapable of anxiety."

label: Goal
body: Let's look for something like "points out an inherent contradiction between two different things the writer of this article has said".

label: Given that...
body:
In one group of used cars being auctioned, each car's listing included a brief description of its condition.
  In a second group of used cars, the description of each car additionally listed defects of the car.

label: How can it be that...
body: More cars in the second group sold, and cars in the second group fetched higher prices compared to comparable cars in the first group.

label: Evaluate
body:
It would make sense for someone to avoid buying a car if they know that the car has defects. If someone does buy a car with defects, it would make sense for them to want to pay a lower price.
  So why, in this situation, did more of the cars with known defects get sold, and why did they tend to sell for higher prices?
  It's possible that people felt more comfortable buying one of these cars when they knew what defects it had. Maybe they weren't as trusting of used car descriptions that didn't list any defects.
  Maybe the defects that were listed tended to be much more minor and less expensive to fix than the defects that used cars commonly have.

label: Goal
body: We'll expect an answer to explain why buyers viewed knowing about the defects as an advantage, making them more likely to buy the cars and/or willing to pay more.

label: Opposing Idea
body: Linsey has been judged to be a bad songwriter simply because her lyrics typically are disjointed and subjective.

label: Conclusion
body: This judgment [that Linsey is a bad songwriter] is ill founded.

label: Evidence
body: The writings of many modern novelists typically are disjointed and subjective, and yet these novelists are widely held to be good writers.

label: Evaluate
body:
The word "since" in the second sentence helps us see the structure of the argument. The statement that follows "since" is evidence. That evidence supports the conclusion which comes immediately before the word "since."
  It's also helpful to notice that this argument follows a common form. It presents an idea in the first sentence. It then pivots to the conclusion, which refutes the idea in that first sentence.

label: Goal
body: A correct answer might state, "the judgement that Linsey is a bad songwriter is ill founded." We'll keep an eye open for answers that are worded differently but convey the same meaning.

label: Evidence
body: Alternative security options [like fingerprint scanners] remain significantly more expensive to employ [compared to passwords], and they can replace passwords only if they become standard on most of the world's computers.

label: Conclusion
body: Computer passwords are not going to be replaced by other options anytime soon.

label: Evaluate / Goal
body:
The conclusion is about computer passwords not being replaced by other options.
  The evidence states that other options can replace passwords only if they become standard on most computers:
```
replace passwords → standard
```
  The contrapositive of this statement tells us that, if other options do not become standard on most computers, they will not replace passwords:
```
~standard → ~replace passwords
```
  This is a conditional statement. It doesn't actually state that other options are not standard on most computers. If we know that they are not standard, the conclusion follows logically:
```
~standard → ~replace passwords
~standard
Therefore, ~replace passwords
```
  So, a correct answer might state that other security options are not standard on most computers.
  There's also a second path to the conclusion. The evidence states that other options are significantly more expensive to employ. The conclusion follows logically if we assume:
  Any option that is significantly more expensive will not replace passwords.
```
more $ → ~replace passwords
```

label: Conclusion
body:
This refutes those who claim that would-be drunk drivers will not be deterred by the prospect of severe penalties.
  rephrase: Would-be drunk drivers will be deterred by the prospect of severe penalties.

label: Evidence
body: In countries with the most severe penalties for drunk driving, a smaller percentage of drivers have traffic accidents involving alcohol.

label: Evaluate
body:
If we're looking for a safely worded takeaway that combines multiple ideas, it will probably play off the causal sequence of how sketches help designers, and how successive drafts tend to get better.
  We'd be speculating a little, but one idea that would tie them all together is to say something like: as a designer goes from one draft to another, she makes a sketch, which helps her see the flaws or under-conceptualized parts of the design and then fix them.
  But there's no reason the answer needs to tie everything together. We could make a Trait Overlap inference by saying "some designs that turned out well involved sketches of idea during the design process", or "not all designs that turn out well are fully conceptualized on the first draft".

label: Goal
body: Beware strong wording, out of scope ideas, or unknown comparisons. Look for the correct answer to reinforce the fact that sketches are usually the way that designers figure out the way forward with their design.

label: Evidence
body:
We are requiring homeowners to connect to city water services in order to ensure public health and safety.
  We will charge the homeowners a fair market price for the service.
  Our plan will benefit all of the city's residents by increasing city revenue and by making the city a healthier and safer place in which to live.

label: Evaluate
body:
Any time the evidence includes a statistic, study, artifact, or experiment, it's likely that the author's conclusion will announce or assume some causal interpretation of that evidence. We use our Explain Curious Fact mindset for these.
  Curious Fact .... why is there a correlation between countries with severe penalties for drunk driving and lower % of drivers having traffic accidents involving alcohol?
  Author's Explanation ... the harsh penalties scare citizens out of drunk driving.
  As always, we consider the two pressure points of such an argument:
  1. Alternate Explanations for the curious fact
  2. the plausibility of the author's explanation
  Whenever the author presents a correlation between X and Y and concludes/assumes that X causes Y, we reflexively consider two possible alternate explanations:
  - Reverse Cause (maybe Y causes X)
  - 3rd Factor (maybe X and Y are both connected to some other factor Z)
  Here, it doesn't make much sense to say that "Having a lower percentage of drivers involved in alcohol related accidents led to having more severe penalties for drunk driving". So, if we're going to weaken via Alternate Explanation, it will probably be a 3rd factor. For example, maybe the countries with the most severe penalties for drunk driving also happen to have cities that are more walkable / public transportation that is more usable.
  We could say, "the low % of alcohol accidents isn't because of the severe penalties. It's because people can walk or take the bus/train, rather than drive home."

label: Goal
body: It's more common to weaken with an Alternate Explanation, so we'll primarily look for that, but we might otherwise see a correct answer that hurts the plausibility of the idea that "severe penalties are discouraging people from otherwise drunk driving" (f.e. maybe citizens have no idea what the penalties are for drunk driving).

label: Conclusion
body: The schemes where a customer pays a fee to "offset" carbon emissions are almost entirely ineffective.

label: Intermediate Conclusion (so)
body: No carbon emissions are prevented.

label: Evidence
body: The fees get invested in projects that, even though they do reduce carbon emissions, would have happened even without that investment.

label: Evaluate
body:
The buzzword for the main conclusion is "ineffective". Why are these carbon emissions schemes ineffective? Because they're not preventing carbon emissions.
  So maybe the answer will say, "If a carbon offset scheme isn't preventing carbon emissions, then it's almost entirely ineffective." But since that seems like a pretty reasonable move, maybe they're actually wanting us to think about the move from premise to intermediate conclusion.
  The fees people are paying aren't crucial to the projects that receive the fees. Those projects, which do reduce carbon emissions, would have happened even if airline customers hadn't paid a fee to "offset" the carbon emissions of their flight. The fee isn't making a difference, so the author thinks that the fee isn't really preventing any carbon emissions.
  That seems like a bigger, weirder move. Maybe the fee money wasn't crucial for the project to run (in an absolute sense) but it was still helpful in that it increased the project's ability to do its job (relative).

label: Goal
body:
Since the typical form of a correct answer on Strengthen-Principle is "If Evidence, then Conclusion", let's look for something like
```
If these projects would have    then your fee
still operated even without  →  didn't prevent
your fee / donation             any emissions
```
  Or for something like,
```
if you fee didn't        →   then the offset fee is
prevent any emissions        an ineffective scheme
```

label: Conclusion
body: These jumping spiders are defending EFN-producing plants against leaf-eating insects.

label: Evidence
body: Studies show that spiders are attracted to EFN plants way more than to non-EFN plants, and ants that are attracted to EFN-producing plants defend the plants against leaf-eating insects.

label: Evaluate
body:
We might think of this as Curious Fact / Explanation, but it might feel a little weird. If we were asking, "why do the spiders seem more attracted to EFN than to non-EFN", it's not like the Explanation would be "because they're going to defend those plants against leaf-eating insects".
  So it's more about an argument by Analogy.
  Ants are attracted to EFNs and defend it against leaf-eaters.
  Spiders are also attracted to EFN's and thus probably also defend it against leaf-eaters?
  We don't have any reason to believe that these jumping spiders are so charitable. They might be jumping in, sucking up that nectar, and then moving on.

label: Goal
body: We need some reason to believe that spiders are also protecting the plants from leaf-eating insects. It could be anything from "EFN plants won't open up to let you take their nectar unless they recognize you as someone that defends them from leaf-eating insects", to something like "jumping spiders' favorite dessert is leaf-eating insects".

label: Conclusion
body: A professional tailor never blindly follows a pattern, but always adjusts the pattern to fit the wearer exactly.

label: Evidence
body:
```
(unless = if not)
clothing isn't worn by         tailor alters
someone whose measurements  →  the pattern
precisely match the pattern,   to fit person
```

label: Evaluate
body:
This might be the type of Sufficient Assumption argument where we don't really see the missing link, and instead we need to argue the Anti-Conclusion to figure out where there is still wiggle room.
  GIVEN THAT
  a tailor will always adjust a pattern to a wearer, unless the person's measurements exactly match the pattern
  HOW COULD WE ARGUE THAT
  there are at least some cases in which a professional tialor does not adjust the pattern to the wearer exactly?
  It seems like our objection could be, "Well, what if people's measurements match the pattern exactly? In those cases, the tailor can blindly follow the pattern and doesn't need to adjust anything to fit the wearer."

label: Goal
body:
Since this argument is only vulnerable to one objection (what about people whose measurements fit the pattern precisely), the correct answer should be Ruling Out that one possible objection.
  Let's look for something like "people's measurements never match the pattern precisely".

label: Statements
body:
*Causal Difference-Maker (what usually allows)*
  Sketches help us to see the flaws and advantages of a design.
  *Most Claims (typically / tend to)*
  Most good designs are the result of many drafts, and each draft usually is an improvement on the previous one.
  Most of the time, the tentative parts of the sketch help the designer to see the parts of the design they haven't thought sharply enough about yet.

label: Conclusion
body: They [the residents who complain] are wrong [the city has a right to require homeowners to connect to city water services].

label: Evaluate / Goal
body:
A valid argument should explicitly state everything that's required in order for the evidence to completely support the conclusion.
  This argument doesn't explicitly state that:
  If connecting to city water ensures public health and safety then the city has a right to require it;
```
ensures health and safety → right to require
```
  If the city charges homeowners a fair market price for the service then the city has a right to require it;
```
fair price → right to require
```
  or,
  If the plan benefits all of the city's residents by increasing revenue and making the city a healthier and safer place, the city has a right to require it.
```
benefits all residents → right to require
```
  A correct answer is likely to make one or more of these connections.

label: Conclusion
body: The art of still photography can't enable us to understand the world.

label: Evidence
body:
```
Accept the world as it
looks or Don't inquire    →  can't understand
into the world's reality     world
```
  Reality ≠ images. Reality = functions.
```
Doesn't narrate → can't help us understand
```

label: Evaluation
body:
Lots of potholes here, so it's hard to predict which one the answer might fill.
  The art of still photography is a New Term in the Conclusion and thus will almost certainly be in the correct answer.
  We are assuming that still photography does not involve refusing to accept the world as it looks.
  We're assuming that still photography does not involve inquiring into the world's reality.
  We're assuming that still photography only lets us see images, not functions.
  We're assuming that still photography doesn't narrate.

label: Goal
body: Look for one of the four missing links.

label: Conclusion
body: In order to attract additional voters in the northeastern part of my district without alienating other voters, all I need to do is go on record as favoring property tax reform.

label: Evidence
body: In each election in the last ten years, the candidate who supported property tax reform got most of the northeastern votes. In no other part of the district is there any discernible relationship between one's position on property tax reform and votes.

label: Evaluate
body:
There seem to be two potential issues with this argument (both common flaws):
  1. the author is assuming from a correlation between "majority votes in NE" and "pro property tax reform" that the latter helped cause the former. It might just be a coincidence that the candidates who won the NE happened to be pro property tax reform. That might have had nothing to do with why they won the NE.
  2. the author assuming a similarity between the last ten years and now. Just because something was true in the past (being pro property tax reform helped in the NE and had no effect elsewhere) doesn't mean that connection still holds in this cycle. Maybe it won't be as helpful in the NE anymore / maybe it will be damaging in the other parts of the district. The author is overlooking that things may have changed importantly (maybe the previous candidates actually tackled property tax reform, to the satisfaction of the NE, so now they wouldn't want any further reform).

label: Goal
body: Look for an answer calling out the author's Causal Flaw (assuming that because the winning candidate in the NE had a certain position on property tax reform that this position causally influenced their win), or the author's Temporal Flaw (failing to consider that something meaningful may have changed that would alter the pattern of the last ten years).

label: Information
body:
*pseudo-causal (in an effort to X, doing Y)*
  Treating cows with BST is supposed to boost milk production.
  *comparisons*
  BST-treated milk and untreated milk have same nutritional value.
  BST-cows have a greater risk of infection and hence (causal) are more likely to be given antibiotics, which may show up in milk.
  *weak-causal (may be harmful)*
  High levels of these antibiotics may be harmful to humans.
  *pivot (Yet)*
  BST-treated milk and untreated milk are both regularly screened

label: Evaluate
body:
Wow, this is quite a shapeless pile of facts. There are some causal and comparative ideas, but none that chain together or seem to have more emphasis than the others.
  However, the final claim begins with a pivot idea. We know that when Must Be True or Most Supported paragraphs have a final claim that starts with a pivot, usually the correct answer sounds like what you get by Reconciling the Pivot idea with what came before it.
  They had just scared us with the ideas that BST cows get more antibiotics and that antibiotics may show up in milk and may be harmful to humans.
  But then they say that all milk is screened for antibiotics. So ... are we good then?

label: Goal
body: It's hard to predict what the answer will say, so let's just look for the most provable choice we're offered.

label: Conclusion (thus)
body: It is a mistake for universities to cut humanities departments when facing budget shortfalls.

label: Intermediate Conclusion (as a result)
body: Humanities departments subsidize science departments.

label: Intermediate Conclusion
body: Humanities departments bring in more money than they spend (whereas science departments spend more than they bring in).

label: Evidence (because)
body: Teaching and research cost significantly less in humanities than in sciences.

label: Evaluate
body:
We're being asked about the second claim in the paragraph, which is prefaced by a because, so we know it provides support for the other half of the sentence its in.
  The conclusion it provides support for is then supporting the "As a result" conclusion in the 3rd sentence, which is then supporting the "Thus" main conclusion in the final sentence.

label: Goal
body: Let's look for something resembling PREMISE / SUPPORT, and then when it comes to the multiple intermediate conclusions after that, we'll see how much the answer choices force us to care.

label: Conclusion
body: The reason residential architecture changed (fewer high ceilings and thick walls) after WWII is the increased usage of A/C.

label: Evidence
body: Soon after WWII, many builders found that houses with A/C that also lacked the high ceilings and thick walls that were previously used to keep houses cool generally sold well.

label: Principle
body:
"unless" = put the negated version of this idea on the Left side of the arrow.
  (i.e. "if-not")
  If it's not the case that there is some conceivable observation that would refute it, if the theory were wrong, then a theory can't properly be regarded as empirical.
```
No conceivable observation      →   can't consider
that could refute a theory          the theory to be empirical
```

label: Evaluate
body:
The conclusion is this sort of claim: "X is attributable mainly to Y".
  In other words, Y is the main cause of X. Since the author is positing causality in the conclusion, we can use our Curious Fact / Explanation template if we'd like.
  Curious Fact
  Why did residential architecture change after WWII (fewer high ceilings / thick walls)?
  Author's Story
  Builders found that houses that kept cool using A/C, rather than high ceilings / thick walls, were generally selling well (so they made more houses with A/C and fewer with high ceilings / thick walls).
  We can affect these arguments in two ways:
  - some alternative story for why architecture changed
  - something affecting the plausibility of the author's story

label: Goal
body: Since this is Weaken, we would either want a different way to explain why the architecture changed (interior design standards changed? construction styles changed?), or we need to diminish the plausibility of the story where builders look at A/C houses that are selling well and decide to make more of those and less of the kind that has high ceilings / thick walls.

label: Conclusion
body: In the Information Age, a highly literate society will be a democratic one.

label: Evidence
body:
Democracy depends on free choices.
  Free choices require well-reasoned opinions.
  In the Information Age, well-reasoned opinions require reading skills.

label: Evaluate
body:
Whenever we're doing Flaw, if we see any conditional logic, we need to ascertain whether the author is making an illegal Backwards or Opposite move.
  We have three conditional trigger words in the first three claims:
  X depends on Y
  can't have X unless you have Y
  X is essential to Y
  The easiest way to diagram Requirements is to remember that "the Required thing goes on the Right". We can literally read a conditional statement like X → Y as "X requires Y.
```
Democracy → free choices
Free choices → well-reasoned opinions
well-reasoned opinions → reading skills
```
  These all chain together.
```
Democracy → free choices → reasoned opinions → reading skills
```
  The author's conclusion goes
  "if a literate society, then a democratic one",
  in other words
```
reading skills → democracy
```
  We can see this is an illegal Backwards move.

label: Goal
body: We can look for an answer choice describing the famous Necessary vs. Sufficient flaw, or we can look for an answer choice saying, "Hey, undemocratic societies can also be highly literate. You never said that being literate forces a country to be a democracy."

label: Facts
body:
All students live in Pulham or Westerville.
  38% of students take a night class.
  29% of students in W take a night class.

label: Evaluate
body:
We primarily read Inference questions looking for ways to combine ideas using Conditional, Causal, Comparative, or Math-y thinking. This one definitely seems math-y.
  We can infer that more than 38% of Pulham's students a night class, since the average of Pulham and Westerville comes out to be 38%. If W is below that number, than Pulham has to be above that number.
  Suppose all students at a school or girls or boys. If 70% of the boys play soccer and 80% of the girls play soccer, what % of the students at the school play soccer?
  If there were an equal number of boys and girls, it would be 75% of students. But, not knowing whether there's an equal amount, we would just know that the % of students who play soccer is somewhere between 70% and 80%.
  If there are more girls at the school, it would be higher than 75% (the simple average of 70 and 80), because the 80% of girls statistic would have more influence than the 70% of boys statistic. If there were more boys, it would be between 70-75%.
  This is the concept of a weighted average. If you mix a beer that's 5% alcohol with whiskey that's 45% alcohol, the resulting beverage will be somewhere between 5-45% alcohol.

label: Goal
body:
The mathematical inference they're setting up is that since all students come from Pulham or Westerville, and the students at Westerville are lower than the school average for night school (38%), the students at Pulham have to be higher than 38% for night school, in order for the overall average to be 38%.
  If both Pulham and Westerville were lower than 38%, then the school's overall average couldn't be 38%.

label: Evidence
body: The universe has a whole tends towards greater disorder.

label: Conclusion (it follows that)
body: The earth's biosphere is always tending towards greater disorder.

label: Evaluate
body:
This is a Whole to Part flaw.
  When we do Parallel Flaw, we remind ourselves to look out for the most common Famous Flaws:
  - Necessary vs. Sufficient
  - Part vs. Whole
  - Causal
  - Unproven vs. Proven False
  - Ad Hominem
  - Sampling
  That way, when we read "The universe as a whole", it jumps out at us that this could be a Part vs. Whole flaw.
  They never explicitly say "the earth's biosphere is a Part of the universe as a Whole", but that's understood to be common sense.

label: Goal
body:
Premise: - the Whole has Property X
  Conclusion: - some Part of that Whole has Property X

label: Conclusion
body: Consuming turmeric probably slows cognitive decline.

label: Evidence
body:
There was a correlation between eating curries (which have turmeric in them) and higher scores on cognitive-function tests.
  This relationship was strongest for the people in the study of Indian ethnicity.

label: Evaluate
body:
This is a classic Curious Fact / Explanation type argument.
  Curious Fact
  Why is it that the curry-eaters in the study were less likely to have cognitive decline?
  Author's Explanation
  Curry has turmeric, and turmeric apparently slows down cognitive decline.
  We can affect these arguments in two ways:
  - Alternate Explanations for the curious fact
  - evidence affecting the plausibility of the Author's Explanation
  What else could account for the curry-eaters in the study scoring better?
  - they cheated on the test
  - they exercise more
  - they do more things like Sudoku or language learning that preserve mental plasticity
  - there's some OTHER ingredient in curry that's the real difference-maker

label: Goal
body:
Since we're doing Strengthen, we either want an answer to
  Rule Out an alternate explanation for why the curry-eaters had less apparent cognitive decline,
  or we want to Boost the plausibility of the author's explanation, which is that the turmeric in their curry is what's helping them.
  When we're Strengthening a Curious Fact argument, the most common type of answer is to add plausibility to the author's story with a "No Cause / No Effect" answer or a "More Cause / More Effect" answer.

label: Conclusion (Thus)
body: Moral virtue is not among the characteristics that we admire most.

label: Goal
body:
If any of these answers are concluding, "Thus, it is empirical", we can instantly throw them out. Principles can only prove what's on the right side of the arrow.
  If an answer is concluding "this isn't empirical" then we just want to see the answer establish that there's no conceivable observation that could falsify a certain theory.

label: Conclusion
body: I won't be relocating my store to new shopping center. `(~A is not X.)`

label: Evidence
body:
```
My store has two requirements: growth potential and visibility     A → B and C
There are two options for the new shopping center: Maple or West    X is Y or Z.
Maple ≠ visible                                                     Y is ~B.
West ≠ growth potential                                             Z is ~C
```

label: Evaluate
body:
I would think of this in casual terms as:
  This thing has two must-have's .
  There are two options for this thing, but each of them lacks one of the must-have's.
  Thus this thing ain't cool with either of those two options.

label: Goal
body:
Make sure there are two required ingredients.
  Look for two options, each of which fails one of the required ingredients.
  The conclusion should reflect that both options failed.

label: Conclusion (so)
body: Omnicide is the best insecticide for home gardeners, especially gardeners who cannot determine which insects are destroying their plants.

label: Evidence
body: Omnicide kills more species of insects than any other insecticide.

label: Evaluate
body:
Given that ... omnicide kills more species of insects than any other insecticide,
  How could we argue that ... a gardener who isn't sure which insects are destroying their plants should not consider Omnicide the best choice?
  We could say, "It's too expensive / it's terrible for the environment / it kills birds and squirrels and helpful insects likes spiders / it enriches a billionaire we all hate".
  If the author is comparing Omnicide to all other insecticides on the market, then she's assuming that when you weigh all the pros and cons, Omnicide has the best net value.

label: Goal
body: Look for an answer saying something bad about buying Omnicide or something preferable about buying one of its competitors.

label: Conclusion (Thus)
body: Most of the viewers who watched TS on Thursday liked it enough to tune in again on Friday.

label: Evidence
body:
The audience for TS on Thursday was small.
  The audience for TS on Friday was only slightly smaller.

label: Evaluate
body:
You're telling me that a documentary about trains called Train Stories got low ratings?! Yeah, that tracks. [sorry, couldn't resist]
  The author is looking at statistics and interpreting what they mean, so we could use our Explain Curious Fact mindset.
  Why ... did Friday night have pretty much the same small-sized audience that Thursday had?
  Because .. most of the people who watched in on Thursday liked it enough to tune in again.
  We could weaken this argument by providing an Alternate Explanation for the Thu / Fri audience, or by debunking the plausibility of the Author's Explanation.
  Maybe the set of viewers on each night was totally different. 100,000 people came across it while channel flipping on Thursday night, and a different set of 100,000 people came across it while channel flipping on Friday night.
  Maybe it was basically the same audience each night, but not because the people who saw it on Thurs liked it. Maybe they were forced to watch it (it was assigned to them by their train-enthusiast professor / they worked on the show / they had to write an online review of it).

label: Goal
body: Look for an answer ruling out an Alternate Explanation for why Friday had about as many viewers as Thursday, or look for an answer that is required for the Author's Explanation to be plausible (anything that would need to be true in order for the author to be correct in thinking that most of the 1st night's viewers enjoyed the show and tuned in again on Friday).

label: Given that ...
body: Healthy gazelles react to the scary sight of hunters in a truck by running away quickly, using the landscape for concealment.

label: Why is it that ....
body: Healthy gazelles react to the scary sight of a predator (like a lion) by leaping high into the air, drawing the predator's attention and consuming energy that could otherwise be funneled into running away faster?

label: Evaluate / Goal
body:
We either need to hear about some distinction between hunters and animal-predators that makes "use landscape for concealment" appropriate for the former and "stotting - leaping high into the air and drawing attention" appropriate for the latter.
  Or we need to hear what good stotting does. It wouldn't be an adaptation if it only did bad stuff (like drawing the predator's attention and decreasing energy to escape). So it must have some positive attribute to it.

label: Z Motor's Conclusion
body: G Motor should stop running its deceptive minivan commercial.

label: Evidence
body:
The commercial claims that G's minivan has a foldable 3rd row seat and that Z's minivan does not.
  But the new minivan from Z, which recently began arriving at dealers, has a foldable 3rd row seat.

label: G Motor's Conclusion
body: The commercial isn't misleading.

label: Evidence
body: Z dealers are still selling new minivans from the previous model year, which lack a foldable 3rd row.

label: Evaluate
body:
The two companies are fighting over whether or not it's misleading for G's commercial to claim that Z's minivan lacks a foldable 3rd row seat.
  G says it isn't misleading, because Z dealers are still selling new minivans that lack a 3rd row seat.
  Z says it is misleading, because the new Z minivans that are recently arriving at dealerships do have a 3rd row seat.
  The question stem wants a principle accepted by Graham but not by Zahler, so let's look for a principle that would allow Graham to be able to fairly argue that their commercial isn't misleading.

label: Goal
body:
Let's try to find something like,
  "If your dealerships are still selling new models without a certain feature, then it's not misleading to say that your models come without that certain feature."

label: Curious Fact
body: Why did G.b. have a comblike plate inside its beak?

label: Hypothesis
body: G.b., like modern ducks and geese, fed by filtering food from water and mud (using this comblike plate).

label: Evaluate / Goal
body:
To strengthen an Explanation for a Curious Fact, we need to either
  1. rule out an Alternate Explanation
  2. make the Author's Explanation more plausible
  Strengthen questions are more likely to do the 2nd option there.
  So we might see an answer ruling out an alternate explanation for the comblike plate ("it wasn't to prevent them from choking on their food"), but most likely we want to be more convinced that the comblike plate inside G.b.'s beak was used, just as ducks and geese use theirs, to strain out bits of food from water and mud.

label: Statements
body:
```
causal (neutralizes / staves)
Add lime to lakes ⇢ Neutralizes acid ⇢ Avoids some damage and restores some health
conditionals (must, if)
Lime used in lake → Treated periodically w/ more lime (b/c new water carries away lime)
Lake's water replaced more than once / 6 mos → too expensive for liming to be option
```

label: Evaluate / Goal
body: Since this is a (rare) Must Be True EXCEPT and there are four derivable inferences, it feels less advisable to work with these facts up front and try to figure out what can be derived. We're unlikely to figure out all four correct answers ahead of time, so let's head to the answers and find provable stuff.

label: Conclusion (Clearly)
body: Studded snow tires are to blame for the ruts in our city's roads.

label: Evidence
body: There are many places that have as much large truck traffic as we have here and also have similar snowfall, but only the few places that allow studded snow tires have ruts similar to ours.

label: Evaluate
body:
Since the author is trying to solve the causal mystery of what causes the ruts in this city's roads, we can use our Explain Curious Fact mindset:
  Curious Fact ... why do we have ruts in the road?
  Author's Explanation ... it's caused by studded snow tires.
  We evaluate these by considering two things:
  1. Could there be some Alternate Explanation for the curious fact?
  2. How plausible is the Author's Explanation?
  Could there be some different way to explain why the roads have ruts? The argument actually acknowledges and addresses one: what if the ruts are caused by large trucks? The author undermines the plausibility of this explanation by pointing to some Cause w/o Effect data points. There are lots of cities that have large trucks like this city but they don't have ruts.
  The author supports the plausibility of his "studded tire" hypothesis by pointing to No Cause, No Effect data points. The places that don't allow studded snow tires do not have ruts, where as the the few places that do allow studded snow tires do have ruts.

label: Goal
body:
It's a pretty compelling argument already, so it's a little hard to predict an answer. The argument already undermined an alternate explanation and supported the plausibility of the author's explanation.
  But still, the correct answer will do even more:
  - rule out a different Alternate Explanation for the ruts in our roads (or further diminish the plausibility that it could be caused by trucks)
  or, more likely,
  - point to something else that adds even more plausibility to the hypothesis that studded snow tires cause the ruts (maybe the pattern of ruts exactly matches the pattern of studs on the tires, for example)

label: Conclusion
body: Marie will be licensed as an emergency medical technician.

label: Evidence (since)
body:
Marie has a high school diploma and a demonstrated competence in CPR.
  A person who doesn't have a high school diploma and doesn't have demonstrated competence in CPR will not be licensed as an emergency medical technician.

label: Evaluate
body:
Whenever we do Parallel Flaw, we listen a little extra hard for the top 6 famous flaws (Nec vs. Suff, Part vs. Whole, Unproven vs. Proven False, Sampling, Ad Hominem, Causal).
  This argument is committing a Necessary vs. Sufficient flaw, meaning the argument provides a conditional logic premise and then the author interprets it in an illegal reversed or negated fashion. Since the flaw here is related to conditional logic, it makes sense to try to get an abstract recipe for the argument.
```
Conditional Premise
No Diploma or No Comp in CPR → Not be Licensed as EMT     ~A or ~B → ~C
Factual Premise
Mary = Diploma, Comp in CPR                               X is A and B.
Factual Conclusion
Mary = Licensed as EMT                                    X is C.
```

label: Goal
body:
With conditionals, we're never allowed to just "flip the lightswitch" on the ideas. We can say "if you don't have a decent GPA and a decent LSAT score, you won't get into Harvard". That doesn't mean we're saying "if you do have a decent GPA and a decent LSAT score, you will get into Harvard".
  We're looking for this structure
```
Prem 1: ~A or ~B → ~C
Prem 2: X is A and B.
Conc: X is C.
```
  But we could settle for an Illegal Negation, even if it didn't match that exact structure.
  We just need a conditional, and then a Premise to Conclusion move that works by illegally negating that conditional.

label: Conclusion (Thus)
body: If there were a being that was always given whatever it wants immediately, that being could never become intelligent in the practical sense.

label: Evidence
body:
Practical intelligence is the ability to discover means to ends.
  This ability is a skill that does not develop on its own.

label: Evaluate
body:
We're trying to prove that a certain hypothetical being "could never become intelligent in the practical sense".
  Did the argument provide a proving mechanism for that sort of idea? Do we have a rule that says, "If xyz is true, then not intelligent in the practical sense?"
  Yes, the first sentence defines practical intelligence, so we could re-frame it as this rule:
  if you don't have ability to discover means to ends,
  then you don't have practical intelligence.
  So if we're trying prove that a being doesn't have practical intelligence, we need to establish that it doesn't have the ability to discover means to ends, which is a skill that doesn't develop on its own.
  All we know this hypothetical being is that it would be given anything it wants immediately. So the argument is assuming, "If you're given everything you want, the second that you want it, then you'll never be forced to develop the ability to discover means to ends".

label: Goal
body: Let's find an answer convincing us that a being who was always given anything it wants instantly would be a being that never discovers means to ends.

label: Conclusion (this is evidence that)
body: Fluoridation of water does not have a substantial tendency to prevent tooth decay.

label: Evidence
body: In five studies, the US (where water is fluoridated) had higher rates of decayed / missing / filled teeth than did Europe, where water is not fluoridated.

label: Evidence
body: The city raises parking fines AND opens a shiny new parking garage on the same day. Violations drop by half.

label: Evaluate
body:
This argument has an Anti-Causal conclusion. The author is saying that fluoridation doesn't do a certain thing. How would someone object to this? How could someone accept the reports of the five studies but still argue that fluoridation does help prevent tooth decay?
  When we're trying to make anti-causal objections, we're generally making one of two types of claims:
  - hey, those two groups aren't fair to compare
  - hey, it would be even better/worse without this thing
  Someone might object that Europe and the U.S. aren't fair to compare. There are different factors in each place that would impact dental health in children differently. Maybe the tap water in the U.S. rots our teeth, or maybe we drink more soda or do a poorer job flossing / brushing.
  Another way to express this same type of objection is by saying, "Fluoridating the water is helping the American kids to prevent tooth decay. Yes, they have worse rates of dental health than do European kids, but they're only 10% worse. If we took away the fluoridation, the American kids would be 30% worse."

label: Goal
body:
Since this is strengthen, a correct answer could try to eliminate either of these lines of objection: there are not things like bad tap water, sugary sodas, bad brushing habits that make American teeth way worse than European teeth (that make them unfair to compare).
  Or the correct answer might just present new evidence that makes it sound like fluoridation doesn't have much effect on preventing tooth decay.

label: Conclusion (Thus)
body: The lethargy studies do not settle the question of whether fast food is unhealthy.

label: Evidence
body:
Studies show North Americans are getting more lethargic, and from 1970 to 1990, North Americans had a 7x increase in fast food consumption.
  (implied) But that correlation doesn't prove causality. Here's an alternate explanation for why lethargy has been growing: lack of exercise.
  Few lethargic adults do much exercise, and lack of exercise can contribute to lethargy.

label: Evaluate
body:
Over 85% of Main Conclusion and Role questions try to hide the conclusion by making it the very First Sentence, or by attaching it to some Pivot / Rebuttal.
  The first sentence presents as a fact, not an opinion, so it doesn't seem like the Conclusion is our first sentence. The second sentence begins with an Attribution, "One researcher has concluded X".
  We anticipate that our author will be resisting this conclusion. Waiting for that But / Yet / However pivot ... we get it with the second to last sentence.
  But / Yet / However's are what we call the Author's Pivot. They indicate that we're pivoting to the author's argument.
  The author might say
  But [conclusion]. After all, [premise].
  Or the author might say
  But [premise]. Therefore, [conclusion].
  In this case, we see Thus introduces the final claim, so that last claim is our Conclusion.

label: Goal
body:
Once we've correctly located the Conclusion, we often want to rephrase it. If there are any pronouns, we import the idea they refer to. We try to think of a synonymous way of saying the same claim, because correct answers frequently go for a meaning-match, not a word-match.
  The author is saying the lethargy studies don't settle the question of whether fast food is unhealthy. That could be rephrased as, "The fact that lethargy has increased doesn't show that fast food is unhealthy."
  Let's look for the answer that best matches the meaning of the final sentence.

label: Conclusion (So)
body:
Their evidence is inconclusive.
  rephrase: The statistical evidence that people who drink moderate red wine are less likely to have heart disease doesn't show that red wine is the most beneficial alcohol for cardiac benefits.

label: Evidence
body: They have yet to determine what biochemical mechanism would make drinking moderate amounts of red wine different from drinking moderate amounts of other alcohol.

label: Evaluate
body:
In terms of Linking ideas, our author is definitely making some move like this:
```
You can't explain the biochemical         Your evidence that X > Y
mechanism for why X is better than Y   →  is inconclusive
```
  If we shifted more into looking for Objections, we'd be thinking, "Given that the proponents haven't determined a biological mechanism that makes red wine superior to other alcoholic beverages in terms of cardiac benefits, how could we still argue that their evidence is conclusive?"
  Maybe we could just say that the data is so undeniable, that we can tell this is happening even if we can't explain why / how it's happening.

label: Goal
body: Look for an answer establishing the link between "undetermined biochemical mechanism" and "inconclusive evidence", or look for an answer that, if negated, would weaken the argument by letting us argue that this evidence could be conclusive, even though we don't understand the causal mechanism.

label: Conclusion (Thus)
body: Physical objects must be theoretical constructs.

label: Evidence (since)
body: All physical objects are composed purely of mass and energy. Many prominent physicists suggest that energy is merely a theoretical construct, and the theory of relativity says that energy and mass are essentially the same thing.

label: Intermediate Conclusion
body: So mass must be a theoretical construct.

label: Evaluate
body:
Since we're Recycling a Concept, "theoretical construct" appears in the evidence and the conclusion, we should be on high alert for the two Famous Flaws that do that: Sampling and Part vs. Whole.
  This argument is basically saying,
  "Energy and mass are the parts that make up the whole of a physical object. Since energy and mass are each theoretical constructs, that must mean that physical objects are also theoretical constructs."
  That's Part to Whole. Just because the parts (energy and mass) have a certain property (theoretical construct) doesn't mean that the collective whole (physical objects) also has that property.
  There is an intermediate conclusion being drawn by saying, "Since energy is a theoretical construct and since relativity treats mass and energy alike, mass must be a theoretical construct."
  So we could spend some time thinking about that reasoning move, but given that we've found one of the ten Famous Flaws, it would be unlikely if they were testing something other than that.

label: Goal
body: Let's look for an answer describing the Part to Whole flaw, or let's otherwise look for an objection that lets us saying, "Even though physical objects are composed of things that are theoretical constructs, that doesn't mean that physical objects themselves are theoretical constructs".

label: Jones's Conclusion
body: A budget deficit is good for the country's finances.

label: Jones's Premise
body: A budget deficit discourages excessive government spending.

label: Espinosa's Implicit Conclusion
body: A budget deficit is not good for a country's finances.

label: Espinosa's Evidence
body: Governments should be staying out of debt. Saying that debt discourages spending may be true, but it's still poor financial management. We wouldn't say that an individual who reaches their credit card limit has done a good thing for their finances, just because it will discourage excessive spending.

label: Evaluate
body:
Our job is to characterize the type of evidence or reasoning move that the 2nd speaker used. The Big 8 answers on Method are
  - Analogy
  - (Counter)Example of a General Claim
  - Implications of Logic
  - raise an Alternate Explanation
  - Rule Out Competing Options
  - point out Dubious Assumption
  - raise an Overlooked Consideration
  - establish a definition / distinction
  Here we'd be crazy to resist calling this an Analogy, since Espinosa says, "that would be like saying [analogous situation]".

label: Goal
body: Look for any answer that we can match up with Espinosa's response, probably one that emphasizes the analogy she used.

label: Information
body:
```
quantifier (most)
Most cats = like to go out and play when temp > freezing
conditional (unless = if not)
If there is not at least one   →   cat not allowed
member outside                     to go out
conditional (only when = right side)
family members   →   sun is shining
go outside           or hot outside
```

label: Evaluate
body:
Whenever we see a conditional idea in an Inference stimulus, we make it the center of our attention look for two possible moves:
  1. can we chain it up with other conditionals (if any)?
  2. can we apply it to any provided facts (may have to contrapose)?
  Since we noticed two conditional indicators, "unless" and "only when", we should start by figuring out whether they chain together. We may have to contrapose our conditionals to see where they would line up. They need some overlapping claim, and in this case the overlapping idea is whether or not Jamil's family members are outside.
  The easiest way to chain stuff together mentally is to use "X requires Y" language. Any conditional, X → Y, can be read as "X requires Y".
  In order for the cat to be allowed outside, there must be a family member outside. And in order for there to be a family member outside, it has to be sunning or hot (or both).
  We can write that chain of requirements, if we think it will help us maintain a clear image of the chain.
```
Cat allowed   →   some family members   →   sun's shining
outside           are outside               or hot outside
```
  What about the first sentence, the Most claim? Can we apply this rule to that sentence? Are there any overlapping ideas?
  Not really. The concept of "likes to go outside and play" is not the same as "whether the cat is allowed to go outside". And the concept of "when the temperature is above freezing" isn't a good match for ideas like "Sun's shining / hot outside".
  The temperature could be above freezing whether or not the sun is shining, and whether or not it's hot outside.
  We could say that "if hot outside, then temp is above freezing, and thus most cats would like to go outside and play". But it would be pretty awkward to add that on to the chain, because it would build off the "hot outside" half of our Or outcome.
  It's probably more likely that the first sentence just isn't intended to combine with the 2nd and 3rd claims.

label: Goal
body: Look for an answer rewarding us for having assembled that chain of requirements, but pick any answer we can prove from the provided information.

label: Conclusion (should = opinion)
body: We should do no more than issue a simple warning against fishing in the newly restricted areas until we've made a real effort to publicize the new restrictions.

label: Intermediate Conclusion
body: It's unfair to cite people for fishing in the newly restricted areas.

label: Intermediate Conclusion
body: They probably are unaware of the changes in regulations.

label: Evidence (since)
body: Even many of us who are supposed to enforce these changes have not yet been informed of them.

label: Evaluate
body:
The city recently changed the rules on where you can fish. They haven't made a real effort to publicize the new restrictions yet, so the general public probably doesn't know where they're no longer allowed to fish. In fact, even some of the city's enforcement officials haven't yet been informed of all the changes to the rules.
  So the author thinks it would be crazy to walk up to a dude fishing at 7am in the morning and write him a ticket for fishing in an illegal area.
  FISHERMAN: What? I didn't know you can't fish in this area. I've fished here for years.
  OFFICER: Yeah, we recently changed the rules, and this is one of the newly restricted areas.
  FISHERMAN: Well, how was I supposed to know that? Have you publicized these new restrictions? What other areas are newly restricted?
  OFFICER: No, we haven't made a real effort to publicize them yet, and actually I haven't yet been informed about all the new changes so I'm not sure what other areas are newly restricted.
  FISHERMAN: Well, then, again how was I supposed to know? Can't you just let me off with a warning, instead of a citation?

label: Goal
body: We want a principle that will side with the fisherman. Something that sounds like, "If a rule-breaker has not had a fair chance to be informed of the new rule that they're breaking, it makes more sense to give them a warning than to give them a citation / fine."

label: Conclusion (this shows that)
body: The new curriculum has lowered the quality of plumbing instruction.

label: Evidence
body: A survey last year found that only 1/3 of the graduates were able to pass the plumber's certification test (which is well below the national average).

label: Evaluate
body:
We can't really judge the author's Comparative conclusion, which claims that the plumbing instruction is now worse quality than it was before, thanks to the new curriculum.
  In order to compare whether the quality has changed / lowered, we would need some data point from before / after.
  This argument only provides the "after" data point. With the new curriculum in place, only 33% of graduates pass the certification test. What was that percentage "before" the new curriculum was installed?
  If we the grads from this program used to have a 25% passing rate and now have a 33% passing rate, then we'd think the new curriculum is improving the quality.
  The argument tries to compare the 33% rate of Tech Institute's grads to the national average, but that has nothing to with assessing whether T.I. currently is better than T.I. was with the old curriculum.
  Finally, we have a language shift from "what % of grads pass this test" to "what the quality of plumbing instruction" is. Do we really know that this certification test is a good metric of the quality of plumbing instruction? Maybe it's a stupid test, and quality of plumbing instruction should be judged more by how well these plumbers perform out on the job.

label: Goal
body:
Look for an answer complaining about our Incomplete Comparison: is a 33% pass rate better / worse than the pass rate we had with the old curriculum?
  Or look for an answer talking about the dubious idea that this certification test stands as an adequate measurement of what quality of instruction T.I. provides.

label: Conclusion (Therefore)
body: None of the hot spices traditionally used are irreplaceable.

label: Evidence
body: If food is sufficiently spiced, it is impossible to distinguish which ingredient is causing the hot sensation.

label: Evaluate
body:
Whenever we size up an argument on Parallel / Parallel Flaw, we're assessing whether we should try to make an ingredient-by-ingredient algebraic recipe out of the argument, or whether we should try to express its general form in a more gisty way to ourselves.
  The premise here is a conditional, which argues in favor of writing the recipe, but there's only one premise, so it's not like we'll be looking at how premises combine in order to derive the conclusion.
  This one feels like it lends itself more towards a slogan or a principle.
  The conclusion is trying to prove that "none of these things are special / irreplaceable / necessary". Why? Because as long as you do thing X, you wouldn't be able to tell which of those things were used.

label: Goal
body: Let's look for a Conclusion that's saying "none of these Y's are crucial / irreplaceable" and a Premise (most likely conditional) saying, "If you do thing X, you'd never know which Y was the important one."

label: Conclusion (Thus)
body: A business that has increased its reliance on computer technology probably has not improved its productivity growth by doing so.

label: Evidence
body:
Since computer tech became widespread in the 60s and 70s, productivity growth in industrialized nations has dropped.
  And it's dropped the most in industries that rely most heavily on computer technology.

label: Evaluate
body:
This conclusion has an Anti-Causal vibe. It's saying that using more computer tech probably didn't cause your productivity to increase.
  Anti-Causal, just like causal, arguments are interpreting curious background facts.
  Curious Fact ... What does it mean that productivity was dropped since computers came on the scene, dropping the most in computer heavy industries?
  Author's Interpretation ... It means that computer technology isn't good for productivity. Computer technology seems to be hurting these industries that rely most heavily on it.
  Could there be some Alternate Explanation for the curious fact? Maybe the industries that rely most heavily on computer technology have some variables in their industry that limit productivity growth, but those variables aren't directly connected to use of computer technology. (For example, maybe the industries that rely most heavily on computer technology are concentrated in Silicon Valley and Seattle and those cities have tax laws or business atmospheres that limit productivity growth).
  Can we hurt the Plausibility of the author's interpretation? She's assuming that computer tech hasn't been good for businesses who have increased their reliance on computer tech, but maybe there is some evidence that it has?
  There is a Relative vs. Absolute switch happening within the argument that may be tested. The conclusion is about businesses that increased their reliance on computer tech (this could be a small farm that was previously 5% reliant on computers and now is 10% reliant). The evidence is about industries that are most reliant on computer tech. That small farmer is not among that group. So the evidence is potentially about a different group of businesses than the conclusion is.

label: Goal
body:
Look for a way to debunk the author's interpretation of the curious fact (either via an alternate explanation for why computer-reliant industries have had dropping productivity or via something that hurts the plausibility that computer technology has itself been harming productivity),
  or look for a way to argue the Anti-Conclusion, that "Businesses that increased their reliance (like the small farmer) have improved their productivity growth by doing so".

label: Conclusion (Clearly, then)
body:
The complaints are not unfounded.
  rephrase: There is legit reason to believe the complaints.

label: Evidence
body:
Klemke says that the complainants disagree with his widely known political views and they are therefore biased.
  But having different politics is still compatible with being badly treated by his company (different politics in no way prevents you from being badly treated).

label: Evaluate
body:
Whenever we're doing Flaw and we see a Rebuttal style argument, we want to look for the two Top 10 Famous Flaws that deal with rebuttals:
  1. Ad Hominem (dismissing someone's view because the source is biased or because the source has conflicting past behavior)
  2. Unproven vs. Proven False (explaining why one person's attempt to prove X fails, but then illicitly concluding that this shows that X is false)
  #1 is actually what Klemke is doing. He's committing an Ad Hominem flaw by dismissing the views of the complainants simply because they are a biased source (they don't like his politics).
  Our author points out to Klemke that this is a flawed argument. You can't ignore complaints about your roofing company just because the source of the complaints is biased. That's a flawed / inadequate argument.
  But #2 does seem to be what the author is doing. The easiest way to spot Unproven vs. Proven False is to notice that the author's conclusion is the complete opposite of the opponent's conclusion.
  For example:
  Sheila thinks 5G networks cause cancer, but the research paper she found to support that judgment turns out to be forged by a conspiracy theorist. Therefore, 5G networks do not cause cancer.
  The correct, responsible conclusion to draw when someone makes an unsuccessful argument in favor of X is that, "We don't currently know whether X is true." After all, how does this author know that 5G networks don't cause cancer? Does he have evidence to support that claim?

label: Goal
body:
In this argument, Klemke was alleging that "these complaints are unfounded". The author explains to us why Klemke's support for that allegation was flawed and inadequate.
  But the author isn't allowed to go to the opposite side of the spectrum and say, "Clearly, then the complaints are well founded".
  You can't say, "The committee didn't find criminal wrongdoing in Patrick's dealings with Russia. Therefore, Patrick had no criminal wrongdoing in his dealings with Russia."
  Let's look for something describing the illegal Unproven vs. Proven False move, or pointing out that even though Klemke's reason for rejecting the complaints was a bogus one, there still might be a legitimate reason to reject the complaints.

label: Guidelines
body:
```
Installing radiant floor cooling     →   should have radiant
or it's a luxury hotel                   floor heat installed
hotel located in region that tends   →   radiant floor cooling
to have high humidity during summer      system shouldn't be installed
```

label: Goal
body:
We'll start reading each answer by looking for the conclusion.
  If the conclusion says, "we should install heat", we'll look at Guideline 1 and make sure we're either told that it's a luxury hotel or that a radiant floor cooling system is being installed.
  If the conclusion says, "we shouldn't install cool", we'll look at Guideline 2 and make sure that we're told this hotel is in a region where it's usually humid in the summer.
  If the conclusion says anything else (f.e. "shouldn't install heat" / "should install cool"), we'll get rid of without reading the rest of the answer.

label: Evaluate
body:
Whenever we see a conclusion on an Assumption question, it's good to ask ourselves whether the ideas in the conclusion were discussed / defined in the evidence.
  This conclusion is talking about Moral Virtue and What We Admire Most. Are either of those new, or are they both discussed in the evidence?
  The "since" premise talks about What We Admire Most. We most admire whatever characteristics belong to the people whose lives we'd most like to live.
  If you'd love to live Jay-Z's life, then the characteristics Jay-Z has are the ones you admire most. The conclusion is saying that "apparently moral virtue is not among the characteristics we admire most", so in this example the author would be assuming that "moral virtue is not one of Jay-Z's characteristics".
  Did the argument ever talk about Moral Virtue?
  Yes, in the first sentence. The first sentence tells us that the historical figures we find most engaging are usually not the most morally virtuous. If George Washington is one of the historical figures we find most engaging, then he probably wasn't the most morally virtuous.
  Okay, we have a conclusion about Moral Virtue and Most Admire.
  In the evidence, each of those ideas is linked to a 2nd concept:
  Moral Virtue: less likely to be found in historical figures we find most engaging
  Most Admire: the characteristics of people whose lives we'd love to live
  So we can anticipate that the correct answer will be linking those two 2nd concepts.
  It sounds like the author is assuming that the people whose lives we'd love to live the most are the historical figures we find most engaging. That's how she could connect moral virtue and most admire.
  We most admire the traits of the people whose lives we want to live.
  (The people whose lives we want to live are the historical figures we find most engaging).
  The historical figures we find most engaging weren't particularly virtuous.
  So, the traits we most admire don't include being particularly virtuous.

label: Goal
body:
Since this argument involved symbol repetition ("admire most" and "moral virtue" were each deployed twice), it's very high probability this is testing a Linking assumption, and the missing link we found was between
  "people whose lives we most want to live" and "historical figures we find most engaging".

label: Conclusion (Therefore)
body: It is unlikely that life occurred on Mars.

label: Evidence
body:
On Earth, life leads to a change in the ratio of isotope S-34 to S-32.
  A new meteorite that came from Mars shows ratios of these elements found only in terrestrial minerals dating from before the beginning of life on Earth (i.e. the meteorite has the pre-life ratio of 34 to 32)

label: Evaluate
body:
The author is thinking that if Mars had had life, then that life would have converted the S-34 to S-32 ratio. And then if a meteorite came from Mars to Earth, then it would be showing that post-life ratio.
  Since the meteorite that came from Mars showed the pre-life ratio, the author is concluding that there was never life on Mars.
  Given that ... this meteorite has the pre-life ratio we see on Earth
  How could we still argue that ... life did occur on Mars?
  Maybe on Earth biological life changes the ratio, but on Mars it doesn't, so even if there was life it would have still been the same ratio.
  Maybe there was life on some areas of Mars and it changed the isotope ratio in those areas, but this meteorite came from a life-free part of Mars, so it shows the pre-life ratio.

label: Goal
body:
Since this is an EXCEPT, there are going to be four answers that weaken. We aren't going to anticipate all four. We just want to set up our brains to interpret these answers. They fit into either of these sentences:
  "Life did occur on Mars. The reason that meteorite only shows the pre-life ratio is because ...."
  "Yes, the meteorite from Mars had the pre-life isotope ratio. But, it's still likely that life occurred on Mars, because ..."

label: Conclusion (This indicates that)
body: When responding to polls, whether they know it or not, people often portray themselves as they wish to be perceived, not how they actually are.

label: Evidence
body: Last year, in polls, people would say that they were sick of tabloid TV shows, but the ratings of those shows were still super high.

label: Evaluate
body:
The author is interpreting the meaning behind a study/poll, so we could use an Explain Curious Fact mindset.
  Curious Fact … How can it be that tabloid TV has soaring ratings, given that polls say people don't like tabloid TV and are unwilling to watch it?
  Author's Explanation … It's because people responded to those polls the way they want to be seen, not the way they really are. They want to be seen as someone who is above watching trashy tabloid TV. But in reality these people go home and watch the tabloid shows.

label: Goal
body:
Since this is Necessary Assumption, the correct answer could Rule Out an alternate explanation for why there's a gap between the poll and the tv ratings.
  Or it could spell out something required for the author's explanation to be plausible.

label: Conclusion
body: The rise of book megastores in 90s increased sales of best-sellers and decreased sales of less commercial, more literary books.

label: Evidence
body:
1986: 7% of hardcovers sold were best-sellers.
  1996: 14% of hardcovers sold were best-sellers.
  Megastores can offer deeper discounts than indie stores and they offer their biggest discounts on best-selling hardcovers.

label: Evaluate
body:
The author is looking at a Curious Comparison (7% vs. 14%) and trying to explain what caused it in her conclusion, so we can use our Explain Curious Fact mindset.
  Curious Fact ... how come best-sellers went from being 7% of hardcover sales to 14% from 1986 to 1996?
  Author's Explanation ... megabook stores became more popular during that time, offered their biggest discounts on hardcover best-sellers, and thus made more and more of the book buying public choose a best-seller hardcover over a less commercial, more literary hardcover.
  As always, our job is to assess this template by asking,
  - Could there be some Alternate Explanation for the curious fact?
  - How plausible is the Author's Explanation?

label: Goal
body:
Since this is Weaken, we either want to find an answer suggesting a different explanation for why best-sellers went from being 7% of hardcover to 14% of hardcover sales (maybe during that time period best-sellers drastically improved their cover design to make them more alluring, or publishers succeeded in promoting their best-sellers better using billboards and subway ads).
  Or we want an answer hurting the plausibility of the story that more superstores led to more best-sellers being heavily discounted which led to more customers choosing to buy a best-seller over a less commercial, more literary book.

label: Anticipate
body: The strongest pattern here is that the snow monkeys stopped leaving the mountain to raid orchards as soon as Suzuki started providing soybeans in the mountain habitat. The most strongly supported inference will draw on that before-and-after change.

label: Evidence
body: Before food was supplied: monkeys roamed out to apple orchards. After Suzuki provided soybeans in the mountain habitat: monkeys stopped raiding orchards.

label: Goal
body: Find the answer that follows directly from the stimulus — most likely something tying the monkeys' decision to leave the mountain habitat to whether food is available there.

label: Anticipate
body: Monkeys stopped raiding orchards once soybeans were provided in the mountain habitat. The supported inference will tie food availability to where monkeys feed.

label: Evidence
body: That sequence tells us a lot. The monkeys' trips out of the mountains looked like food-seeking — and once food was easy to get at home, the trips stopped.

label: Goal
body: Find the answer that follows from this: the monkeys leave the mountain when food is scarce there, and stay home when it is plentiful.

label: Conclusion
body: Zobel claims Peterson's analytic concepts are wrong and should be rejected.

label: Intermediate Conclusion (thus)
body: It's impossible for a student to make unbiased judgments about the value of the teacher's analytic concepts.

label: Evidence
body: The teacher interprets the actions, dreams, and fantasies of the student in analytic terms, which leads to strong emotional bonds with the teacher that predispose the student to accept the teacher's analytic concepts.

label: Evaluate
body:
