The evidence is about Peterson's students, that they are biased in their assessments. That tells us nothing about whether Peterson's concepts are themselves wrong. Even if every one of her students is hopelessly biased, her concepts could still be correct.
  This is an Unproven vs. Proven False type argument. Zobel is basically showing how the students' faith in Peterson is a faulty way of proving Peterson right (they're too biased to be trusted). But that doesn't mean that Zobel has proven Peterson wrong.

label: Goal
body: Look for an answer saying that Zobel has only established that we should be suspicious of students who say (because of bias) that Peterson's concepts are correct, but has provided no evidence to make us think that Peterson's concepts are wrong.

label: Conclusion
body: Zobel claims Peterson's analytic concepts are wrong and should be rejected.

label: Evidence
body: Peterson's students are biased toward her concepts because of emotional bonds formed during training.

label: Evaluate
body: Bias in students says nothing about whether the concepts themselves are correct.

label: Goal
body: Pick the answer pointing out that Zobel's evidence supports only student bias, not the falsity of the concepts.

label: Conclusion
body: Zobel says Peterson's ideas are wrong.

label: Evidence
body: Her support: Peterson's students get emotionally attached during training and therefore cannot fairly judge her ideas.

label: Evaluate
body:
Watch this carefully — Zobel is talking about students, not the ideas themselves. Even if every student is biased toward Peterson, that does not show Peterson's ideas are wrong. It just shows the students are not in a position to judge.
  Think of it this way: a math teacher's students might worship her too much to judge her work fairly. That has nothing to do with whether her math is right.

label: Goal
body: Find the answer that says Zobel's evidence shows student bias, not the falsity of Peterson's concepts.

label: Conclusion
body: Children lack the moral reasoning skill necessary for their behavior to count as moral.

label: Evidence
body: Children provided unsophisticated verbal responses to hypothetical moral dilemmas.

label: Evaluate
body:
If we were going to try to argue that "children DO have the moral reasoning skill necessary for their behavior to count as moral", how would we respond to the fact that they provided unsophisticated verbal responses to hypothetical moral dilemmas?
  We might say the hypothetical moral dilemmas are dumb / irrelevant / exotic / unlikely to be something a child could weigh in on based on their deficient knowledge of the world (not their moral deficiency).
  We might say that children aren't verbally talented enough to provide a sophisticated verbal response, even though their moral intuitions are still sophisticated. In other words, they aren't responding poorly out of a lack of moral prowess but rather out of a lack of verbal prowess.

label: Goal
body: Look for an answer that gives us a way to argue that kids do have moral reasoning skills or one that allows us to "make an excuse" for kids' poor verbal answers to these hypothetical moral dilemmas.

label: Conclusion
body: Children lack the moral reasoning needed for their behavior to count as moral.

label: Evidence
body: Children's weak verbal responses to *hypothetical* moral dilemmas.

label: Evaluate
body: Hypothetical performance might not reflect actual reasoning ability in real situations.

label: Goal
body: Find an answer showing children reason at a higher level in real moral situations than in hypotheticals.

label: Conclusion (second group)
body: The second group concludes that children don't have enough moral reasoning skill for their behavior to count as moral.

label: Evidence
body: Their evidence is how children performed on hypothetical moral dilemmas — verbal responses to imaginary scenarios. The kids gave unsophisticated answers, so the second group concluded they lack the reasoning skill.

label: Evaluate
body:
Watch the gap. The conclusion is about children's moral reasoning in general. The evidence is performance on a specific kind of test — verbal answers to fake situations. Maybe kids are bad at articulating moral reasoning in the abstract but actually reason carefully when faced with real situations.
  If real-situation reasoning is much better than hypothetical-test reasoning, then the evidence isn't a fair sample of what children can actually do, and the conclusion overreaches.

label: Goal
body: Find an answer showing children do better with real moral situations than with hypothetical ones — making the second group's evidence base too narrow.

label: Conclusion
body: Popular historical awareness is inevitably distorted.

label: Evidence
body: Most people learn history through popular narratives, and those narratives sustain interest by implying that a few famous heroes and notorious villains have shaped all of history.

label: Evaluate
body: The argument moves from "popular narratives imply X" to "popular awareness is distorted." That move only works if the implication itself is distorting — that is, if it is false (or distorting) to suggest a few heroes and villains have shaped all of history.

label: Goal
body: Find the assumption that the implication about heroes and villains is itself distorting. Negate it (the implication is accurate or non-distorting), and the conclusion collapses.

label: Conclusion
body: Popular historical awareness is inevitably distorted.

label: Evidence
body: Popular narratives imply a few heroes and villains shaped all of history.

label: Evaluate
body: The leap requires that the implication itself is distorting.

label: Goal
body: Pick the answer asserting that the heroes-and-villains implication distorts history.

label: Conclusion
body: The historian says popular history awareness is always going to be distorted.

label: Evidence
body: Why? Because most people learn history from books that grab readers by implying a small cast of heroes and villains shaped everything.

label: Evaluate
body: For the argument to work, that implication has to actually *be* distorting. If the heroes-and-villains framing were perfectly accurate, then narratives spreading it would not produce distorted awareness — they would produce accurate awareness.

label: Goal
body: Find the answer that explicitly says the heroes-and-villains implication is distorting. That is the bridge the argument depends on.

label: Given that ...
body: Heart disease incidence is closely related to average fat consumption. *and that* The French consume as much fat as North Americans.

label: How can it be that ...
body: Heart disease occurs half as often among the French as among North Americans?

label: Goal
body: We're going to need some distinction between France and North America to explain why they're not comparable in terms of heart disease. Maybe the French do something good that North Americans don't do that lowers heart disease risk, or the North Americans do something bad that the French don't do that increases heart disease risk.

label: The Paradox
body: Heart disease tracks fat consumption, the French eat as much fat as North Americans, yet have half the heart disease.

label: Evaluate
body: The resolution must explain why current French fat intake has not yet shown up in heart disease rates.

label: Goal
body: Pick the answer that explains a delay between high fat consumption and the appearance of heart disease.

label: The Paradox
body: Two facts that look like they cannot both be true at once: high fat consumption supposedly leads to heart disease, the French eat just as much fat as North Americans, but the French have half the heart disease.

label: Evaluate
body: To resolve a paradox, we don't deny either fact. We find a third fact that lets both be true. The most natural way out: heart disease takes a long time to develop, and the French have only been eating that much fat for a short time. The disease is on its way; it just hasn't shown up yet.

label: Goal
body: Find the answer that introduces a delay — a reason today's heart disease numbers reflect past, not current, fat consumption.

label: Proposition
body: An incentive structure rewards individual participants based on their performance relative to other participants. Each participant's rational response is to do more of the rewarded activity, beyond what they would otherwise do, in order to capture more of the reward. The aggregate result is that everyone overdoes the activity, leading to a worse collective outcome than if no incentive existed.

label: Evaluate
body: The economist describes a competitive incentive that drives participants to take more of an action than is collectively optimal — projects funded externally, where each locality gets more by doing more than other localities — and the systemic outcome is greater overall spending and taxation across the system. The right answer should mirror this dynamic: an incentive based on relative performance, individuals each ramp up their activity, leading to a worse collective outcome.

label: Goal
body: Find an answer where individuals respond to relative-performance incentives by escalating an action beyond what's collectively beneficial, producing a worse aggregate outcome.

label: Proposition
body: Relative-performance incentives push everyone to overdo the rewarded activity, producing worse aggregate outcomes.

label: Goal
body: Find an analogous setup: relative-performance incentive → individuals escalate → collective worse off.

label: The proposition
body:
The economist's point: when you reward people based on how much they do compared to others, each person tries to outdo the others. The result is that everyone overdoes the activity, and collectively things get worse than if no incentive existed.
  In the example, local governments compete to create the most projects, so they all create more projects, and overall spending and taxes go up everywhere — worse outcome than if they'd each just funded their own.

label: Goal
body: Find an answer with the same shape: a competitive incentive (rewards based on doing more than others), each participant ramps up the rewarded activity, the collective ends up worse off than before. Watch out for analogies that miss the "competitive escalation" part — pooling, cooperating, etc., aren't the same dynamic.

label: Conclusion (thus)
body: Non-frightening experiences are at least as memorable as frightening experiences.

label: Evidence
body:
There's a correlation between higher levels of adrenaline and remembering events more clearly.
  Adrenaline is produced in situations involving fear.

label: Goal
body: We want to eliminate the four answer choices that strengthen the idea that the author's proposed method provides better memory retention than does rote memorization.

label: Conclusion
body: Journalistic investigation of political leaders' private lives is detrimental to society.

label: Evidence (and)
body: The practice makes public figures more concerned with mere appearances and makes everyone else cynical about the character of their leaders.

label: Goal
body: Find an answer that must be true based on combining these statements. It will likely address widely emulated people keeping their non-voting private.

label: Evaluate
body:
In this argument, there is a comparative relationship between types of experiences and their memorability, rather than a causal conclusion. The key idea is the correlation between adrenaline and memory. We know that experiences attached to adrenaline are more likely to be remembered.
  Given that producing more adrenaline is associated with better memory and fear produces adrenaline, how could we argue that non-frightening experiences are at least as memorable as frightening experiences?
  One way could be to suggest that other emotions or states, like excitement or pleasure, also raise adrenaline levels. If true, even non-frightening experiences could be memorable due to the same adrenaline boost.
  We could also weaken by saying that there's something ELSE about frightening experiences, like trauma/repression, that makes it less likely that something will be remembered, counteracting the memory boost afforded by adrenaline.

label: Goal
body: Let's find an answer that posits other sources or situations that trigger adrenaline, thereby challenging the assumption that frightening experiences have the inside track to being memorable due to adrenaline, or an answer that tells us there's some component of frightening experiences that actually undermines the ability to remember them.

label: Conclusion
body: Some compounds in soybeans can help humans prevent cancer.

label: Evidence
body: The argument relies on compounds in soybeans, such as isoflavones and sterols, to support the claim. Isoflavones are thought to inhibit estrogen, which allegedly promotes cancer. Similarly, consuming soybeans is said to result in less cholesterol absorption, with an assumption that less cholesterol leads to a reduced cancer risk.

label: Evaluate
body:
The question stem is specifically saying that four answers will weaken the support. So while we might normally head to the answers thinking, "give me four ways to argue that soybeans do not help humans prevent cancer", we can also think about directly attacking the evidence, the support.
  To weaken, we could challenge the effectiveness of estrogen inhibition or cholesterol reduction in reducing cancer risk specifically in humans. Alternatively, evidence showing that soybeans do not significantly impact cancer risk would also weaken the argument.

label: Goal
body: Our goal is to eliminate the four answers that undermine the evidence (or conclusion).

label: Montoya's Conclusion (So / should)
body: Chemical companies should start using ionic liquids in some processes instead of organic solvents.

label: Montoya's Evidence
body: Ionic liquids are less hazardous to workers, generate less pollution, and produce faster reactions with fewer unwanted byproducts.

label: Peterson's Objection
body: Ionic liquids cost many times more than organic solvents, making them impractical to use at the present time.

label: Evaluate
body:
When we're asked to logically counter, we want an answer that responds to the 2nd person's objection in a way that defends the 1st person's conclusion.
  So we're thinking, "GIVEN THAT ionic liquids cost many times more than organic solvents, HOW CAN WE STILL ARGUE that chemical companies should being using ionic liquids instead of organic solvents?"
  The key to defending Montoya's suggestion is to highlight potential ongoing savings or efficiencies that justify the higher cost of ionic liquids, much like investing in a hybrid car to save on fuel costs over time.

label: Goal
body: Our goal is to argue that even though ionic liquids cost more initially, they can still be practical or cost-effective in the long run due to some form of compensatory savings or benefits that offset their expensive upfront costs.

label: Conclusion (this shows that)
body: As the world population grows, aggressive behaviors will increase, including more war and crime.

label: Intermediate Conclusion
body: Overcrowding inclines humans toward aggressive behavior.

label: Evidence
body: People are usually considerate, but become jerks during rush-hour traffic or at crowded sporting events.

label: Evaluate
body:
There is a new term in the conclusion (world population growth) and a repeated term (aggression, which is discussed in the evidence).
  What is the author assuming happens as the world population grows?
  She must think there will be more overcrowding. After all, more people on the same globe does sound like higher density. But will it necessarily create overcrowding?
  If we were trying to weaken this argument, we might say "there is plenty of space to fit more humans, without there being overcrowding. Have you been to Wyoming? It's 99% empty."
  We might also argue that there will be technological innovations that will somehow alleviate aggression, or make things like war / crime less likely.
  So if we're strengthening the argument, we would counter those objections. We would want to believe that more population DOES mean overcrowding, and that new technologies will NOT alleviate these problems.

label: Goal
body: Eliminate the four answers that help tell the story that more people on Earth will lead to more overcrowding, which will lead to more aggression / war / crime.

label: Conclusion (so)
body: The approach of considering the meaning, motivation, and physical/emotional components of words is probably more effective than rote memorization at enhancing memory.

label: Intermediate Conclusion (seems likely that)
body: The argument outlines that engaging with the emotional context, motivation of characters, and physical aspects of delivery may enhance memory.

label: Evidence
body: Actors use emotional, action, and context to learn their lines.

label: Evaluate
body:
The fact that actors use a certain technique to remember their lines isn't great evidence that "this is the superior way to remember things!"
  First of all, maybe the job actors have in memorizing lines is atypical, relative to most things people try to memorize. For example, a geometry student needs to memorize the formula for area of a trapezoid, but they don't need to perform that formula out loud later. They just need to understand it enough to solve for the area of a trapezoid.
  Would something like "area of a trapezoid" even be eligible for the author's method? Is there emotion / meaning / context / physical delivery? Doesn't seem like it.
  If you're memorizing the capital of Nevada, it seems like rote memorization of "Carson City" is more realistic than thinking about the emotion / meaning / context of Carson City.
  Since we need to strengthen, we would want to go against this sort of skepticism. We want rote memorization to sound bad, and we want the author's method to sound accessible / easy / effective / widely applicable.

label: Evaluate
body:
We know when we read the argument on Main Conclusion or Role that we're most likely going to see an upside-down argument, where the conclusion comes earlier and the support comes later. In particular, we listen for First Sentence opinions from the author (usually those would be the Main Conclusion) or early Attributions (usually the conclusion would be a pivot/rebuttal from that idea).
  Here we start with an Attribution, so we'd anticipate a Pivot + Pushback conclusion. We get that with the second sentence. They said the tactic is an effort to improve society. The author is saying, "Well, it's not working. It's detrimental to society".
  She then supports that conclusion with a pair of premises, joined by "and".

label: Goal
body:
We're being asked about the opening claim, which is an Opposing idea.
  Our author isn't exactly refuting it, because it's a statement about what the tactic is attempting to do, and the author's conclusion is about what the tactic is actually doing.
  So we'll need to be more nuanced, like, "It describes a goal that the conclusion argues is not achieved".

label: Conclusion
body: Journalistic investigation of political leaders' private lives is detrimental to society.

label: Evidence
body: The practice makes public figures appearance-driven and makes the public cynical.

label: Evaluate
body: The cited claim is the justification journalists offer for a practice the argument condemns.

label: Goal
body: Pick the answer that calls the cited claim a justification offered for a practice the argument concludes is harmful.

label: Conclusion
body: The author thinks journalistic snooping into politicians' private lives is bad for society.

label: Evidence
body: It makes politicians focus on optics and makes the rest of us cynical about leaders.

label: Evaluate
body: The cited claim is what journalists *say* they are doing — improving society. The author quotes it not to agree with it, but to set it up as the justification before pivoting to the actual consequences.

label: Goal
body: Find the answer that captures: this is the rationale offered for a practice that the argument concludes is actually harmful.

label: Conclusion
body: Average rodent populations will increase in region T in the coming decades.

label: Evidence (since)
body: The argument suggests a chain of causation: air pollution causes global warming, which leads to more frequent El Nino's. More El Ninos cause increased heavy winter rainfall, leading to long periods of sustained rain, which typically increase rodent populations.

label: Evaluate
body: This is a "Weaken" question, and the aim is to find an answer that undermines the prediction made in the conclusion. To weaken the argument, we need to disrupt the causal chain that links global warming and increased El Nino's to more rodents through heavy sustained rain.

label: Goal
body: Identify the answer choice that effectively challenges any part of the causal chain, thus casting doubt on the prediction of increasing rodent populations.

label: Conclusion (therefore)
body: Business historians overestimate the success of past businesses.

label: Evidence
body: Historians tend to study more successful firms when investigating business practices than study unsuccessful firms.

label: Evaluate
body:
The author's logic seems to be that if you study successful businesses more often than unsuccessful ones, it will skew your perception. You'll start thinking most companies are successful, because you spend most of your time looking at Apple and Google.
  But maybe historians are wise enough to study successful ones in order to learn what methods seemed to work, but also look at overall statistics for the number of businesses that succeed vs. fail, when it comes to estimating the success of past businesses.

label: Goal
body: We want an answer that rules out the idea that historians account for the fact that they're mainly looking at successful businesses / that they factor in that potential bias, an answer that supports the connection between "the more you study a certain type of thing, the more you'll overrepresent that thing in your mind", or any other answer that would make it more plausible that they tend to overrate the proportion of businesses that were successful in past eras.

label: Given
body:
- One should not do anything that has the potential to produce serious harm to one’s society.
  - The public actions of celebrities and of people who are widely respected are widely emulated.
  - Some celebrities do not vote.
  - Serious harm befalls a society in which many people refrain from voting.

label: Evaluate
body:
Since this is a Must Be True question, we want to combine statements that are about the same concepts. Does anything show up in more than one statement?
  Statements #2 and #3 are both about celebrities. We're told that celebrities' public actions or inactions are widely emulated, and that some celebrities do not vote. We can conclude that, if celebrities' decisions to not vote were made public, many other people would refrain from voting.
  "Harm" shows up in statements #1 and #4. We're told that one should avoid doing anything that might cause serious harm to one's society, and that serious harm will occur when many people in a society refrain from voting. From these statements, we can conclude that one should not do anything that would cause many people to refrain from voting.
  We can infer an additional recommendation by combining these two conclusions: if celebrities are going to refrain from voting, they should not make the public aware of it.

label: Goal
body: Look for an answer that is absolutely irrefutable. It will probably be derived from combining at least two of the given statements, and maybe more. But it doesn’t have to tie in every statement to be correct. Beware answers that are too strong, bring in out of scope ideas, or express unsupported relationships between the concepts in the stimulus.

label: Given
body: One should not do anything that could produce serious harm to one's society. Celebrities' and widely respected people's public actions are widely emulated. Some celebrities do not vote. Serious harm befalls a society where many people refrain from voting.

label: Evaluate
body: Combining these statements: if celebrities publicly refrain from voting, many people will emulate them, causing serious societal harm. Therefore, widely respected people should not publicly refrain from voting.

label: Given
body: Four puzzle pieces on the table: (1) do not do things that could seriously harm society, (2) celebrities and widely respected people are walking billboards whose public behavior gets copied, (3) some celebrities skip the ballot box, and (4) widespread non-voting is seriously bad for society.

label: Evaluate
body: Snap these pieces together: if a celebrity publicly sits out an election, a herd of admirers will follow suit. Mass non-voting causes serious harm. And doing things that cause serious harm is a no-no. The escape hatch? The word "public." Nobody said celebrities must vote — just that if they are going to skip it, they should keep that to themselves.

label: Goal
body: Find the answer that connects these dots without overreaching. Anything demanding all celebrities vote or applying the rule to everybody goes too far.

label: Evidence (because)
body: *Sonora* was sculpted by Barajas’s assistants, working from three sketches Barajas drew in preparing to create the statue herself.

label: Conclusion
body: The statue probably looks very much like it would have looked if Barajas had lived to complete it.

label: Evaluate
body: The evidence in this argument is pretty flimsy, leaving the argument vulnerable to a host of different objections. Do we know if Barajas’s assistants were skilled enough to sculpt *Sonora* as well as Barajas could herself? Did the sketches provide enough information for the assistants to know how Barajas wanted the completed statue to look? What if Barajas' statues often ended up looking quite different from her sketches?

label: Goal
body: A correct answer might bring up any of these possible objections. But correct answers to Weaken questions don't always match our predictions, so we'll need to keep an open mind and think about how each answer would impact the argument. Watch out for answers that have little impact, if any, or ones that strengthen the argument rather than weakening it.

label: Evidence (because)
body: *Sonora* was sculpted by Barajas's assistants, working from three sketches Barajas drew in preparation.

label: Conclusion
body: The statue probably looks very much like it would have if Barajas had lived to complete it.

label: Evaluate
body: The argument assumes three sketches were sufficient for the assistants to know how Barajas wanted the finished statue to look. If Barajas typically used many more sketches and revised substantially throughout the process, three sketches might represent a very early stage of her vision.

label: Goal
body: Find an answer suggesting the three sketches were insufficient to convey Barajas's final vision, or that the assistants lacked the ability to replicate her work.

label: Evidence (because)
body: Barajas's assistants built *Sonora* using three sketches the artist drew before she died. Three sketches — that is the entire blueprint.

label: Conclusion
body: The statue probably looks like it would have if Barajas had finished it herself.

label: Evaluate
body: Three sketches sounds like a reasonable amount of guidance — until you wonder whether Barajas was the type of artist who drew three sketches and was done planning, or the type who drew fifty sketches and was still changing her mind. If she normally went through dozens of revisions, those three sketches might represent the "rough draft of the rough draft" stage. The assistants would basically be finishing a painting from the artist's napkin doodle.

label: Goal
body: Find the answer that makes those three sketches look woefully inadequate.

label: Given
body:
- There are immediate short-term gains in crop yield from a single application of certain hydrocarbon-based pesticides to fields on which they have not been previously used.
  - Studies have shown clearly that long-term use gradually depresses crop yield from this initially elevated level.

label: Evaluate
body:
The word "although" indicates a concession, and concessions are typically Opposing Ideas. So the first sentence about immediate short-term gains looks like an idea that the conclusion of the argument will contradict.
  “We should conclude that” tells us that whatever fills the blank will be the conclusion, but it also tells us that the statement immediately before this sentence—the statement about long-term use—must be the evidence.

label: Goal
body: We're looking for a conclusion about the use of these pesticides that is based on the fact that they gradually decrease crop yields. This conclusion will probably dampen our enthusiasm about the initial short-term gains. For a Most Strongly Supported question, beware of answers that are too strong for the evidence we're given or any answer with a new idea which might be out of scope.

label: Given
body: First application of certain hydrocarbon-based pesticides produces short-term gains in crop yield on new fields. However, long-term use gradually depresses crop yield from the initially elevated level.

label: Evaluate
body: The concession word "although" introduces the short-term gain, while the main point focuses on long-term decline. The conclusion must follow from the evidence about gradual yield depression.

label: Goal
body: Find a conclusion about pesticide use that is supported by the long-term decline in yields without being too strong. It should acknowledge diminishing returns without claiming the pesticides are entirely harmful.

label: Given
body: These pesticides are the ultimate short-term relationship: great first impression, diminishing returns over time. The first application gives a nice yield boost. Then, with continued use, yields start sliding back down from that high point.

label: Evaluate
body: The "although" at the beginning is LSAT code for "yes, but actually..." The short-term gain is the concession; the long-term decline is the real story. And notice what the evidence does not say — it does not say yields drop below where they started. They drop from the "initially elevated level." So the pesticides might still be helping, just less and less.

label: Goal
body: Find the answer that captures "diminishing returns" without overcommitting to "total waste of money" or "environmental catastrophe."

label: Evidence
body: Our country needs as much capital as possible from overseas investors in order to sustain our economy.

label: Evaluate
body:
There isn't a huge gap in logic between needing as much capital as possible (the evidence) and not wanting any reduction in the existing amount of capital (the intermediate conclusion).
  But there is a significant gap between the intermediate conclusion and the main conclusion. Wanting to avoid any reduction in investments does not automatically support the idea that we should pass laws making it more difficult for investors to remove their capital.
  This main conclusion is a recommendation. Plans and recommendations tend to be vulnerable to a variety of objections, and the correct answer to a Weaken question might focus on any one of them. It helps to think about the kinds of objections that this argument is particularly vulnerable to.
  For example, a recommendation might have the opposite effect. Maybe these laws would discourage investors from making future investments, which would prevent us from acquiring "as much capital as possible." Or there might be some reason why this particular recommendation can't be implemented, or won't be effective. Maybe these types of laws are almost impossible to enforce, and therefore tend to be ineffective.

label: Goal
body: Look for an answer that suggests the recommendation might backfire or be impossible to implement correctly. But, since objections can take many forms, read answers with an open mind. We want to notice if one attacks the recommendation in another way.

label: Evidence
body: Our country needs as much capital as possible from overseas investors to sustain the economy.

label: Intermediate Conclusion (Hence)
body: We cannot afford any reduction in overseas investment capital.

label: Main Conclusion (Therefore)
body: We should pass laws making it much more difficult for overseas investors to remove their capital.

label: Evaluate
body: The main conclusion recommends a specific policy. The gap lies between wanting to keep investment capital and the specific remedy of restrictive laws. Such laws could backfire — if investors cannot easily remove capital, they might not invest in the first place.

label: Goal
body: Find an answer showing the recommended policy would backfire or be counterproductive.

label: Evidence
body: The country is hungry for overseas investment capital. The more the better.

label: Intermediate Conclusion (Hence)
body: So the country really cannot afford to lose any of the capital already invested there.

label: Main Conclusion (Therefore)
body: Solution: trap the money. Pass laws making it nearly impossible for investors to pull their capital out.

label: Evaluate
body: This is the economic equivalent of locking the restaurant doors so diners cannot leave without paying — technically it keeps people inside, but nobody new is going to walk in. If overseas investors hear that their money will be held hostage, they might decide to invest somewhere else entirely. The argument is so focused on keeping existing capital that it ignores the effect on future capital.

label: Goal
body: Find the answer that describes this backfire effect.

label: Opposing Ideas
body: Many people with access to the Internet express a longing for emotional connection to a global human community, which often leads them to use the Internet to learn about other cultures.

label: Conclusion
body: Learning about other cultures probably will not satisfy their longing [for emotional connection].

label: Evidence (for)
body: The Internet is utilized primarily for acquiring information rather than developing feelings of interconnectedness.

label: Evaluate
body: This argument follows a common pattern seen in Main Conclusion questions. It starts with an Opposing Idea, followed by a pivot word. The pivot word is followed by the Conclusion, which is then followed by the Evidence. The pivot word "however" helps us spot that pattern in this argument. Also notice how the statement after "however" is a rebuttal of the statements before "however." The Conclusion of an argument is frequently a rebuttal of an Opposing Idea.

label: Goal
body: Expect the correct answer to state that learning about other cultures will not satisfy a longing for emotional connection.

label: Opposing Ideas
body: Many Internet users long for emotional connection to a global community and use the Internet to learn about other cultures to satisfy this longing.

label: Conclusion
body: Learning about other cultures probably will not satisfy their longing for emotional connection.

label: Evidence (for)
body: The Internet is used primarily for acquiring information rather than developing feelings of interconnectedness.

label: Goal
body: The correct answer should state that learning about other cultures through the Internet will not satisfy a desire for emotional connection.

label: Opposing Ideas
body: People want to feel emotionally connected to the world, so they hop on the Internet and start reading about other cultures. A reasonable strategy, it would seem.

label: Conclusion
body: "However" — the columnist's favorite word for "nice try, but no." Learning about other cultures is probably not going to scratch that emotional itch.

label: Evidence (for)
body: The Internet is basically a giant information vending machine. People want feelings of interconnectedness, but the Internet dispenses facts and data. Ordering an encyclopedia when you wanted a hug.

label: Goal
body: Find the answer that says "cultural learning via the Internet will not satisfy the emotional longing." Not the setup, not the evidence — the actual point.

label: Evidence
body: Democratic societies in which there is widespread discontent more often blame their politicians than they do other powerful figures who are at least as responsible for those societies’ woes.

label: Conclusion
body: This [blaming of politicians] is not primarily because politicians are more familiar to people than are other powerful figures. People blame politicians because they feel that they have more power over politicians than they have over other powerful figures.

label: Evaluate
body: Both of these explanations in the conclusion—politicians being more familiar to people, or the feeling of having more power over politicians—seem equally plausible. Why is one a better explanation than the other?

label: Goal
body: We're looking for a generalization (assumption) indicating that having more power over politicians is more likely to lead us to blame them, or one indicating that being familiar isn't what makes us blame them.

label: Evidence
body: Discontented democratic societies blame politicians more than other equally responsible powerful figures.

label: Conclusion
body: This happens not because politicians are more familiar but because people feel they have more power over politicians than over other powerful figures.

label: Evaluate
body: The argument identifies two possible explanations (familiarity vs. perceived power) and endorses perceived power as the primary one.

label: Goal
body: Find a generalization connecting perceived power over someone to willingness to blame them.

label: Evidence
body: When things go wrong in a democracy, politicians catch most of the flak — even though other powerful people are equally responsible.

label: Conclusion
body: The argument says this is not because politicians are more familiar faces. It is because people in democracies feel they actually have some leverage over politicians. After all, politicians need votes.

label: Evaluate
body: Two suspects are on the board: familiarity and perceived power. The argument eliminates familiarity and pins it on perceived power. The general principle: people are more willing to blame someone they feel they can influence.

label: Goal
body: Find the generalization that captures "perceived power over someone leads to blaming them more."

label: Given
body:
- *contrast:* Mm's generated by cosmic rays just outside Earth's atmosphere travel at speeds approaching the speed of light, **whereas** mm's in the lab are nearly at rest.
  - *math-y contrast:* Time it takes for lab-mm to decay < time it takes for space mm to reach our detection apparatus.
  - *conditional + **implicit fact** that triggers contrapositive:* If mm's traveling through the atmosphere at speeds approaching the speed of light typically decay as fast as lab-mm's, then we should detect only about one one-hundredth of the number **we actually do detect.**

label: Evaluate
body: It's helpful to be clear about the information we've been given and how the different statements connect to one another. We're told that mu mesons—let's just call those MMs—are created just outside of Earth's atmosphere and travel to Earth at close to the speed of light. That's fast. We know something about the speed of MMs created in the laboratory: they're nearly at rest—so, almost not moving. We're told that these resting MMs in the lab typically decay faster than the time it takes for an MM to travel from outside the atmosphere to a detector on Earth. If you notice some connections between these statements, that's great. But there's something very interesting to notice about the fourth sentence. It contains a conditional statement: "If mu mesons traveling through the atmosphere at speeds approaching the speed of light typically decay as fast as they do in the laboratory, then we should detect only about one one-hundredth of the number we actually do detect." This statement is already telling us that the necessary condition—the "then" part—is not true. We are not detecting one one-hundredth of the number we actually do detect. We are detecting the number that we actually do detect. Think about the contrapositive: If we don't detect one one-hundredth of the number that we actually do detect, then MMs traveling through the atmosphere do not decay as fast as they do in the laboratory. The sufficient condition—the "if" part—is automatically triggered. We don't detect one-one hundredth of the number that we actually detect. We detect the number that we actually detect. This means that the necessary condition—the "then" part—must be true. MMs traveling through the atmosphere do not decay as fast as they do in the laboratory. The final sentence in the stimulus, the one we need to complete, mentions MMs "moving at speeds near the speed of light." Those are the ones in the atmosphere. We can expect the rest of this sentence to state that they don't decay as fast as ones in the laboratory.

label: Goal
body: If we can look past the scientific terms and get a handle on the essence of what these statements are telling us, we can make a very good prediction. We expect a correct answer to indicate that MMs traveling through the atmosphere decay more slowly that ones created in the lab.

label: Helpful Tip
body: Don't let the LSAT distract or intimidate you with fancy science terms. You don't need to know what a mu meson is. It's a thing. You don't need to know the exact speed of light. It's fast. We don't even need to know exactly what "decay" means in this context. Whatever it is, we're told it's something that can happen at different speeds. That's all we really need to understand. You could literally replace "decay" with "change color" or "turn into elephants" and still get the correct answer. Try it. The science might not make sense, but the logical connections would stay the same. And we're being tested on our understanding of the logical connections, not the science.

label: Given
body: Atmospheric mu mesons travel near the speed of light; lab mu mesons are nearly at rest. Lab mu mesons decay faster than it takes atmospheric ones to reach detectors. If atmospheric mu mesons decayed as fast as lab ones, we would detect only 1/100 of what we actually detect.

label: Evaluate
body: We detect far more atmospheric mu mesons than the lab decay rate predicts. The contrapositive tells us atmospheric mu mesons must not decay as fast as lab ones.

label: Goal
body: The conclusion should state that mu mesons moving near the speed of light decay more slowly than those at rest.

label: Given
body: Mu mesons from space are speed demons — nearly light speed. Mu mesons in the lab are couch potatoes — barely moving. Lab mu mesons fall apart very quickly. Based on that decay rate, almost none of the space ones should reach Earth. But the detectors catch way more than expected — about 100 times more.

label: Evaluate
body: The stimulus is basically describing time dilation from Einstein's relativity (though no one needs to know that for the LSAT). The math does not add up unless the space mu mesons are living longer than the lab ones. The only difference between them? Speed. The fast ones seem to decay slower. The contrapositive seals it: if they decayed at the lab rate, barely any would be detected. Yet plenty arrive. So they do not decay at the lab rate.

label: Goal
body: The answer should say mu mesons moving fast decay slower than ones sitting still. Do not get intimidated by the physics vocabulary — "mu meson" is just a thing, "decay" is just a process, and speed is the variable.

label: Evidence
body:
The buyer will buy a garment only if it is fashionable and not too expensive for our clientele. The evening dress from the fall collection by Peruka is certainly fashionable, but the dress is far too expensive for our clientele.
```
BG → F and ~TE
F
TE
```

label: Conclusion
body:
The buyer will not buy that dress [garment].
```
~BG
```

label: Conclusion
body: Our most important intellectual skills will be devalued by electronic data-processing technology [similar to the way that the Industrial Revolution decreased the value that society conferred on physical labor].

label: Conclusion
body: Winchester would better meet its residents' needs by closing its small branch libraries and opening one larger, well-supplied library.

label: Evaluate
body:
This is a valid argument. The first premise has two necessary conditions that both must be met in order to buy a garment. One of these necessary conditions will be met but the other will not. Based on this, the conclusion states that the evening dress [a garment] will not be bought. It can also help to look at the contrapositive of the first premise: If a garment is not fashionable or it is too expensive then the buyer will not buy the garment.
```
~F or TE → ~BG
```
The third premise triggers one of these sufficient conditions (TE), so we can conclude that the buyer will not buy this garment (~BG).

label: Goal
body: A correct answer will probably use this same type of contrapositive logic to reach its conclusion. In all likelihood, it will also have the other key features of this original argument: a compound necessary condition in which one item is fulfilled and the other is not.

label: Evidence
body: The buyer will buy a garment only if it is fashionable and not too expensive. The dress is fashionable but too expensive.

label: Conclusion
body: The buyer will not buy the dress.

label: Evaluate
body: Valid reasoning: the first premise has two necessary conditions (fashionable AND not too expensive). One is met, one is not. Via the contrapositive, if either necessary condition is unmet, the garment will not be bought.

label: Goal
body: Match the pattern: compound necessary condition, one met and one unmet, valid denial of the sufficient condition.

label: Evidence
body: The buyer has two non-negotiable requirements: fashionable AND affordable. The dress passes the fashion test with flying colors but spectacularly fails the price test.

label: Conclusion
body: No purchase. If you need both conditions met and one fails, the deal is off.

label: Evaluate
body: This is clean contrapositive logic. Buy -> Fashionable AND Not Expensive. The dress is expensive, so: Expensive -> Not Buy. One out of two is not good enough when the original statement requires both. The correct parallel answer needs to copy this exact blueprint: two requirements, one met, one failed, valid rejection.

label: Goal
body: Find the answer with the same DNA: compound necessary condition, split outcome, valid conclusion.

label: Evidence
body: Psychologists report that children in nine-month schools typically forget a significant amount of schooling during summer breaks.

label: Conclusion (We should conclude)
body: The twelve-month schedule is to be preferred insofar as academic learning is concerned.

label: Intermediate Conclusion
body: [The twelve-month schedule with three month-long breaks] will insure that students will not forget their schooling during their breaks.

label: Evaluate
body: This argument compares one plan [12-month schedule] to another [9-month schedule] and states that the 12-month schedule is preferable. We should consider factors that might have been left out of this comparison. For example, what if a longer, 12-month schedule with three month-long breaks will somehow make students even more forgetful? The argument claims that the 12-month schedule "will insure" that students will not forget their schooling during breaks. But that's a prediction about the future. That's what makes it an intermediate conclusion, not just a premise. It's a claim that might or might not be true. The conclusion is about "academic learning," not just remembering or forgetting. Could the 12-month plan have some unintended negative consequences that would make it worse for learning overall, even if it was better for retention? Comparative arguments frequently overlook these types of potential objections. They'll tell us that one of two options has a certain good quality. Based on that, they'll conclude that this option is better overall. It's a classic example of an "incomplete comparison."

label: Goal
body: A correct answer might describe an objection like the ones we've considered here, pointing out that the argument has "failed to consider" or "overlooked" this possible objection. Beware of answers that describe something which isn't actually happening in the argument, even if it seems related at first glance.

label: Evidence
body: Children in nine-month schools typically forget a significant amount during summer breaks.

label: Conclusion
body: The twelve-month schedule (with three month-long breaks) is preferable for academic learning.

label: Intermediate Conclusion
body: The twelve-month schedule will ensure students do not forget their schooling during breaks.

label: Evaluate
body: The argument assumes the forgetting problem is unique to the nine-month schedule. But students in a twelve-month schedule also have month-long breaks, and might forget schooling during those breaks too.

label: Goal
body: Find the answer describing the flaw of assuming forgetting is only associated with one schedule when it could affect both.

label: Evidence
body: Kids in nine-month schools forget stuff over the summer. Psychologists confirmed it.

label: Intermediate Conclusion
body: A twelve-month schedule with three month-long breaks will definitely prevent forgetting.

label: Conclusion
body: Therefore, the twelve-month schedule is better for learning.

label: Evaluate
body: Hold on — why would three month-long breaks be any different from one three-month break? The argument just assumes the forgetting problem magically disappears with a schedule change, without any evidence about what happens during month-long breaks. Maybe students forget during those too. The argument looked at one schedule, found a problem, and assumed the other schedule is problem-free. That is like declaring your new apartment is quieter than your old one without ever actually visiting it.

label: Goal
body: Find the answer that calls out this one-sided assumption.

label: Evidence
body: The Industrial Revolution decreased the value that society conferred on physical labor because it enabled unskilled workers to quickly produce goods that formerly took skilled craftspeople long periods of time to produce. Computations that once took skilled mathematicians a long time to perform can now be quickly performed by moderately well-trained high school students using computers.

label: Conclusion
body: Therefore Megatherium was probably a predator.

label: Evaluate
body: The argument makes a significant leap by discussing mathematical computations in the evidence and "our most important intellectual skills" in the conclusion. Aren't other types of intellectual skills important? Aren't reading and logical reasoning skills, such as those tested on the LSAT, also important? There might also be important differences between intellectual skills and physical skills, or differences between the Industrial Revolution and our current time, which would prevent us from devaluing intellectual skills.

label: Evidence
body: The Industrial Revolution devalued physical labor by enabling unskilled workers to produce goods that formerly required skilled craftspeople. Similarly, computers now let students perform computations that once required skilled mathematicians.

label: Conclusion
body: Our most important intellectual skills will be devalued by electronic data-processing technology.

label: Evaluate
body: The argument equates mathematical computation with "our most important intellectual skills." But computation is only one type of intellectual skill. Other intellectual skills — critical thinking, reading comprehension, logical reasoning — might not be replicable by computers.

label: Goal
body: Find an answer that breaks the link between computational skills and "most important intellectual skills."

label: Evidence
body: The Industrial Revolution made skilled labor less special because machines let anyone do the job. By the same logic, computers are making math less special because anyone with a laptop can crunch numbers.

label: Conclusion
body: Therefore, the most important intellectual skills are doomed to devaluation.

label: Evaluate
body: Notice the bait and switch: the evidence is about math, but the conclusion is about "the most important intellectual skills." Since when is arithmetic society's most prized intellectual achievement? Reading, reasoning, critical analysis, creative problem-solving — none of these are threatened by the existence of calculators. The argument assumes that because computers can do math, they will devalue everything intellectual. That is quite the leap.

label: Goal
body: Find the answer that says the intellectual skills society values most are not the computational kind.

label: Given that...
body: Wounds become infected because the break in the skin allows bacteria to enter. Infection slows healing. Honey contains significant quantities of bacteria.

label: How can it be that...
body: In a study at a Nigerian hospital, cleaned wounds that were treated with honey healed faster, on average, than both cleaned wounds treated with antibiotic ointment and wounds cleaned but not otherwise treated.

label: Evaluate / Goal
body: We need an answer to explain why the bacteria in the honey isn't causing the wounds to heal more slowly, and why the honey actually speeds healing. Maybe the bacteria in honey is different somehow from the bacteria that normally infects wounds. Or maybe something in honey speeds the healing of wounds to a much greater extent than the bacteria slows healing.

label: Given that...
body: Bacteria in wounds cause infection, which slows healing. Honey contains significant bacteria.

label: How can it be that...
body: Cleaned wounds treated with honey healed faster than wounds treated with antibiotic ointment and wounds only cleaned.

label: Evaluate / Goal
body: We need something that explains both why honey's bacteria does not harm healing and why honey actively speeds healing beyond what ointment achieves.

label: Given that...
body: Bacteria in wounds = bad. Infection = slow healing. Honey = full of bacteria. So honey on wounds should equal disaster, right?

label: How can it be that...
body: Honey-treated wounds healed faster than ointment-treated wounds AND faster than just-cleaned wounds. Honey, the thing full of bacteria, beat the stuff specifically designed to kill bacteria.

label: Evaluate / Goal
body: This is a two-part puzzle: (1) why does honey's bacteria not make things worse? and (2) why does honey make things better than antibiotics? The correct answer needs to handle both. An answer that only explains why honey is not harmful, without explaining why it is better than ointment, only gets halfway there.

label: Evidence
body: Great works of art evoke passionate responses in those who view them. (GW → PR) The work of abstract painter Ezekiel Reilly elicits intensely emotional responses in those who view them. (PR)

label: Conclusion
body: His art is great. (GW)

label: Evaluate
body: In order to draw this conclusion, we must assume that any work of art which elicits a passionate response is a great work. This is an illegal reversal of the first premise. (PR → GW)

label: Evidence
body: Great works of art evoke passionate responses (Great -> Passionate). Reilly's work elicits intensely emotional responses (Passionate).

label: Conclusion
body: Reilly's art is great (Great).

label: Evaluate
body: The argument reverses the conditional. From "great art evokes passion" it concludes "art that evokes passion is great." That is an illegal reversal — treating a necessary condition as sufficient.

label: Goal
body: Find the answer that describes confusing a necessary condition with a sufficient condition.

label: Evidence
body: Great art evokes passion. Reilly's art evokes passion.

label: Conclusion
body: Therefore, Reilly's art is great.

label: Evaluate
body: This is the classic "all dogs are mammals, this animal is a mammal, therefore it is a dog" pattern. Just because great art makes people emotional does not mean everything that makes people emotional is great art. A car alarm evokes intense emotional responses too, but nobody is hanging one in the Louvre. The argument flips the conditional and pretends the necessary condition is sufficient.

label: Goal
body: Find the answer that calls out the necessary-sufficient confusion.

label: Evidence
body: In northern Europe, archaeologists have discovered 400,000-year-old sharpened wooden poles alongside flint cutting implements and the remains of horses. It is normally assumed that Homo sapiens did not inhabit Europe prior to 200,000 years ago.

label: Conclusion
body: This discovery [the sharpened poles, cutting implements, and remains] effectively disproves the widespread belief that the humanlike precursors of Homo sapiens were entirely gatherers and scavengers and did not hunt.

label: Evaluate
body: If we accept the assumption about Homo sapiens (humans) in the second premise, then the sharpened wooden poles and flint cutting implements were probably not made by humans and were likely made by our humanlike ancestors. However, we don't know what the poles and cutting implements were used for. We can't be certain that they were used for hunting, so their existence doesn't necessarily prove or disprove anything.

label: Goal
body: A correct answer might support the idea that the sharpened poles or cutting implements were used for hunting. It could also refute the alternative possibility that they were used for something other than hunting.

label: Evidence
body: 400,000-year-old sharpened wooden poles, flint cutting implements, and horse remains found in northern Europe. Homo sapiens did not inhabit Europe before 200,000 years ago.

label: Conclusion
body: This disproves the belief that humanlike precursors of Homo sapiens were entirely gatherers and scavengers who did not hunt.

label: Evaluate
body: The argument assumes the poles and implements were used for hunting. But they could have been used for other purposes — self-defense, cutting scavenged meat, or transporting carcasses found dead.

label: Goal
body: Find an answer that supports the hunting interpretation by eliminating alternative uses for the tools.

label: Evidence
body: Really old sharpened sticks, flint knives, and dead horses found together in northern Europe — 400,000 years old. Humans were not around yet, so the predecessors made these tools.

label: Conclusion
body: Proof that the precursors hunted, which contradicts the belief they only gathered and scavenged.

label: Evaluate
body: Sharp sticks plus dead horses looks like hunting, but there are other explanations. Maybe the sticks were for poking predators away from dinner. Maybe the cutting tools were for carving up roadkill. Maybe the horses died of natural causes and the precursors just found them. The argument needs help eliminating these alternatives.

label: Goal
body: Find the answer that rules out non-hunting explanations for the tools.

label: Evidence
body: Most taxpayers and their families have few opportunities to use public libraries because they are only open at times when most children are at school and most adults are at work.

label: Conclusion
body: If new taxes supporting the library system are approved, the library hours should be changed to better suit taxpayers and their families.

label: Evaluate
body: This sounds like a reasonable argument, but it's not airtight. There might be ways to make libraries more useful to taxpayers without changing the hours. Additional tax money could be used to improve libraries' web sites and online services, allowing taxpayers to benefit from libraries even when the actual library facilities aren't open. We could pass laws requiring employers and schools to give people time off so they can use the library when it's open. If any of these alternatives occur, the conclusion doesn't necessarily hold up.

label: Goal
body: An ideal correct answer might state that creating any new taxes to support the library system requires giving taxpayers more opportunities to use libraries. (New taxes → more opportunities for taxpayers) Or, it might state that giving taxpayers these opportunities requires changing the library hours. (More opportunities for taxpayers → change hours)

label: Evidence
body: Most taxpayers and their families have few opportunities to use public libraries because libraries are only open when children are at school and adults are at work.

label: Conclusion
body: No new taxes supporting the library system should be approved unless library hours are changed to better suit taxpayers.

label: Evaluate
body: The gap: lacking opportunities to use libraries does not automatically mean new taxes should be conditional on changing hours. We need a principle linking taxpayer access to tax approval.

label: Goal
body: Find a principle stating that new taxes for a public facility require that taxpayers have adequate opportunities to use it.

label: Evidence
body: Libraries are open when nobody can go — kids are at school, adults are at work. Most taxpayers have almost no chance to actually use the library.

label: Conclusion
body: Do not approve new library taxes unless the hours change.

label: Evaluate
body: The argument goes from "taxpayers cannot use this thing" to "taxpayers should not pay more for it unless they can." That seems reasonable, but it relies on an unstated principle: if you are taxing people for a service, they should actually be able to use it.

label: Goal
body: Find the principle that makes tax approval conditional on taxpayer access. Not the other way around.

label: Given
body: The introduction of mass production techniques in modern industrial economies allowed for lower prices because industries could employ fewer workers, many of whom required little training. The lower prices allowed workers to buy goods that they previously would not have been able to afford. But jobs for workers with little training are more vulnerable to elimination than those for more highly trained workers.

label: Evaluate
body: The statements that we're given are the evidence in the argument. The correct answer will be a conclusion that is supported by this evidence. The premises describe a benefit for workers—the ability to buy goods that they previously couldn't afford. But the premises also describe a disadvantage. The workers with little training are at a higher risk for losing their jobs.

label: Goal
body: The correct answer is likely to focus on the disadvantage, or at least state that workers with little training in a modern industrial economy experience a mixed situation with both advantages and disadvantages.

label: Given
body: Mass production allowed lower prices by employing fewer, less-trained workers. Workers could buy previously unaffordable goods. But jobs for less-trained workers are more vulnerable to elimination.

label: Evaluate
body: The same thing that gave workers more purchasing power (fewer jobs requiring less training) also made their employment less secure. A single cause with both a benefit and a drawback.

label: Goal
body: The conclusion should capture this dual nature: a source of purchasing power that also undermines job security.

label: Given
body: Mass production: fewer workers needed, less training required, prices drop. Workers can buy more stuff. But — and here is the catch — jobs for people with less training are easier to eliminate.

label: Evaluate
body: Same cause, opposite effects. Mass production gave workers cheaper goods with one hand and a pink slip with the other. The very thing that put more products on their shelves also put their jobs at risk.

label: Goal
body: Find the answer that captures this bittersweet irony without going overboard in either direction.

label: Evidence
body: Ordinarily, it is only between the ages of six and nine that children begin to understand that animals are independent creatures with their own feelings and needs.

label: Conclusion
body: Most children should not have pets until they are at least six years old.

label: Evaluate
body: Conditional statements are generally about things that must always be true. We don't usually consider something a conditional statement when it merely describes something that "ordinarily" happens or something that happens with "most" people in a group. However, in this case, as long as we remember the words "ordinarily" and "most" in the original argument, we can use conditional statements to better understand the argument. The premise states that most children under age six do not understand that animals are independent creatures with their own feelings and needs. (under 6 → not understand) The conclusion states that most children under six should not have pets. (under 6 → should not have pets)

label: Goal
body: We're looking for an answer which states that anyone who does not understand that animals are independent creatures with their own feelings and needs should not have pets. (not understand → should not have pets) The contrapositive of this would also be correct. (should have pets → understand)

label: Evidence
body: Most children under six do not understand that animals are independent creatures with their own feelings and needs.

label: Conclusion
body: Most children should not have pets until they are at least six.

label: Evaluate
body: We need: not understanding animals' independence -> should not have pets. This bridges the evidence to the conclusion.

label: Goal
body: Find: should have pets -> understands animals are independent (the contrapositive also works).

label: Evidence
body: Kids under six generally do not understand that animals have their own feelings and needs. This awareness usually kicks in between ages six and nine.

label: Conclusion
body: Most kids should not have pets until six.

label: Evaluate
body: The argument goes: kids under six do not understand animals -> kids under six should not have pets. The missing link is obvious: not understanding animals means you should not have pets. Or flipped: having pets requires understanding animals.

label: Goal
body: Find the assumption that says "no understanding of animal independence = no pets for you."

label: Evidence
body: The average tax refund received by taxpayers who use tax preparation services is about 50 percent higher than the average refund received by those who do not.

label: Conclusion
body: If you want a large refund, you should use a tax preparation service.

label: Evaluate
body: The evidence describes a correlation between using a tax preparation service and getting a larger tax refund. The conclusion states that, for those who want a large refund, the preferred option is to use a tax preparation service. There's an underlying assumption that the tax preparation service causes taxpayers to receive a larger refund, but that isn't necessarily the cause. This argument exhibits a Causal Flaw.

label: Evidence
body: Taxpayers who use tax preparation services receive average refunds about 50 percent higher than those who do not use such services.

label: Conclusion
body: If you want a large refund, you should use a tax preparation service.

label: Evaluate
body: The argument treats a correlation (using services correlates with bigger refunds) as causation (using services causes bigger refunds). People with complex finances may both seek professional help and have more deductions — the service does not necessarily create the larger refund.

label: Goal
body: Find the answer choice whose argument has the same structure: a correlation is observed, and from that correlation a causal recommendation is drawn.

label: Evidence
body: People who use tax prep services get bigger refunds on average. A 50 percent bump, no less.

label: Conclusion
body: Want a big refund? Use a tax prep service.

label: Evaluate
body: This is the classic "people who carry umbrellas get rained on more, so carrying an umbrella must cause rain" pattern. People with complicated finances — lots of deductions, investments, side income — are exactly the ones who hire professionals. They would get big refunds anyway because of their tax situation, not because the preparer sprinkled magic dust on the return. The argument sees two things happening together and assumes one causes the other.

label: Goal
body: Find the answer that copies this structure: correlation in the evidence, causal recommendation in the conclusion, confounding variable ignored.

label: Evidence
body: The subjects in an experiment who gestured spoke more quickly and repeated themselves less than those who didn't gesture. (G → SQ and ↓R)

label: Evaluate
body: Predators have short olecranon processes, so anything with a short olecranon process is a predator? That is like saying basketball players are tall, so anyone tall must play basketball. Megatherium might have had fast arms for digging, climbing, or fending off predators. The argument sees one shared trait and jumps to the explanation it likes best without considering alternatives.

label: Conclusion
body: gesturing helps speakers quickly find the phrases they want. (G → QFP) It's worth noting that the conclusion isn't truly a conditional statement. It's similar to one, but it only claims that gesturing helps speakers to find phrases. It doesn't state that gesturing guarantees anything. However, as long as we keep the actual language of the conclusion in mind, diagramming the conclusion as a conditional statement can help us understand the argument.

label: Goal
body: We're looking for an answer which states that when someone speaks quickly or repeats themselves less, this helps them to quickly find the phrases they want. (SQ or ↓R → QFP)

label: Evidence
body: In an experiment, subjects who gestured while describing cartoons spoke more quickly and repeated themselves less than those who did not gesture.

label: Conclusion
body: Gesturing helps speakers quickly find the phrases they want.

label: Evaluate
body: The evidence establishes that gesturing correlates with quicker speech and less repetition. The conclusion claims gesturing helps find phrases quickly. The gap: we need to know that speaking more quickly and repeating less indicates finding phrases quickly.

label: Goal
body: Find an assumption that links "speaking quickly and repeating less" to "finding phrases quickly." Something like: behavior correlated with quicker speech and less repetition helps speakers find phrases.

label: Evidence
body: Scientists told 200 people to describe cartoon action scenes. Half could wave their hands around; half had to keep still. The hand-wavers talked faster and repeated themselves less.

label: Conclusion
body: Gesturing helps you find the words you are looking for.

label: Evaluate
body: The experiment measured talking speed and repetition. The conclusion is about finding phrases. Those are not obviously the same thing. Maybe gesturers just talk faster without actually finding better words. We need something that says "if you talk faster and repeat less, that means you are finding phrases more easily."

label: Goal
body: Find the bridge that connects the measured results (speed, less repetition) to the claimed explanation (finding phrases quickly).

label: Given
body: No new course will be approved for next year's schedule unless a proposal for it has already been received either by this committee or by Dean Wilson. (NCA → PRC or PRDW) Dean Wilson has received only one new course proposal. (PRDW = 1) All of the new course proposals that this committee has received are for upper-level courses. (PRC → UL) Beginning next year, all upper-level courses will have prerequisites. (UL → P)

label: Evaluate
body: We can combine the final two conditional statements to conclude that all of the new course proposals that this committee has received will have prerequisites. (PRC → P)

label: Given
body: No new course is approved unless a proposal was received by the committee or by Dean Wilson. Dean Wilson received only one proposal. All proposals the committee received are for upper-level courses. All upper-level courses will have prerequisites.

label: Evaluate
body: Chain: committee proposals are upper-level, and upper-level courses have prerequisites. So all committee-approved courses will have prerequisites. Dean Wilson has exactly one proposal, which may or may not be upper-level. If more than one new course is approved, at least one must have come through the committee and therefore must have prerequisites.

label: Goal
body: Find an answer that must be true from combining these conditional statements. The key insight is that Dean Wilson can account for at most one non-prerequisite course.

label: Given
body: Four rules: (1) new courses need a proposal from the committee or Dean Wilson, (2) the Dean got exactly one proposal, (3) everything the committee got is upper-level, and (4) upper-level means prerequisites. Chain those last two together: committee courses are upper-level, upper-level means prerequisites, so committee courses have prerequisites.

label: Evaluate
body: Dean Wilson is the wild card — one proposal that could be anything. But the committee is locked down: every course from there gets prerequisites. So if more than one new course gets approved, the extras must go through the committee (the Dean only has one), and committee courses get prerequisites. At least one prerequisite course is guaranteed the moment you have two or more new courses.

label: Goal
body: Find the answer that captures this: more than one new course means at least one has prerequisites.

label: Evidence
body: Predatory mammals generally have short olecranon processes. (predator → short OP (generally)) Megatherium had a short olecranon process. (Meg → short OP)

label: Conclusion
body: In all probability, Megatherium was a predator. (Meg → predator (probably))

label: Evaluate
body: Let's just call Megatherium "Meg" and call the olecranon process "OP." The argument takes evidence about Meg having a short OP and jumps to a conclusion about Meg being a predator. We can reach that conclusion if we know that any extinct mammal with a short OP was probably a predator: (short OP → predator (probably)) But that's a reversal of the first premise: (predator → short OP (generally)) Here's another way of saying this: the evidence doesn't establish that most mammals with a short OP are predators. It's possible that most extinct mammals with short OPs were not predators.

label: Evidence
body: Predatory mammals generally have short olecranon processes because they need to move forelimbs quickly when attacking. Megatherium had a short olecranon process.

label: Conclusion
body: In all probability, Megatherium was a predator.

label: Evaluate
body: The argument reverses the conditional. It establishes: predator -> short olecranon process (generally). From Megatherium having a short olecranon process, it concludes Megatherium was a predator. But many non-predatory mammals could also have short olecranon processes for other reasons.

label: Goal
body: Find the answer that identifies the reversal: the argument fails to consider that most mammals with short olecranon processes might not be predators.

label: Evidence
body: Predators need fast arms, so they generally have short olecranon processes. Megatherium had a short olecranon process.

label: Evidence
body: Something that one is committed to might be either good or bad. Commitment to a relationship that benefits none of the people involved deserves no praise. Often, commitment is nothing more than involvement that has outlasted its original justification.

label: Conclusion
body: All commitments should be seen as morally neutral.

label: Evaluate
body: We can reach this conclusion if we assume that anything which has the capacity to be either good or bad should be seen as morally neutral: (could potentially be connected to good or bad → morally neutral) We can strengthen the argument by making a similar assumption about something that deserves no praise or has outlasted its original justification, since those are also descriptors that the argued applied to "commitments". (some of them deserve no praise → morally neutral) or (often outlasted original justification → morally neutral)

label: Evidence
body: What one is committed to might be good or bad. Commitment to a harmful relationship deserves no praise. Often, commitment is just involvement that has outlasted its justification.

label: Conclusion
body: All commitments should be seen as morally neutral.

label: Evaluate
body: The evidence shows that some commitments are bad or undeserving of praise. The conclusion says all commitments are morally neutral. We need a principle that bridges "some commitments are bad" to "all commitments are morally neutral."

label: Goal
body: Find a principle stating that if any commitments are undeserving of praise (or could be bad), then all commitments should be considered morally neutral.

label: Evidence
body: Commitments can be good or bad. Commitment to a useless relationship deserves no praise. A lot of the time, commitment is just inertia — you stuck around past the point where it made sense.

label: Conclusion
body: All commitments are morally neutral.

label: Evaluate
body: "Some commitments are bad" to "all commitments are neutral" is a big jump. The evidence proves commitment is not always great. The conclusion says commitment is never morally loaded — not good, not bad, just neutral. We need a principle that says something like "if even one commitment is bad, then commitment itself is morally neutral."

label: Goal
body: Find the principle that makes the leap from "some commitments are praiseworthy and some are not" to "commitment as a category is morally neutral."

label: Evidence
body: Few children today spend their free time reading stories.

label: Conclusion
body: Few children today will develop a lifelong interest in literature.

label: Evaluate
body: We can reach this conclusion if we assume that children who do not spend their free time reading stories will not develop a lifelong interest in literature: (~ spend free time reading → ~ lifelong interest in lit)

label: Goal
body: We'll keep our eyes open for an answer containing the statement above or its contrapositive: (lifelong interest in lit → spend free time reading) We can also eliminate any answer that doesn't include the idea of developing a lifelong interest in literature.

label: Evidence
body: Few children today spend their free time reading stories.

label: Conclusion
body: Few children today will develop a lifelong interest in literature.

label: Evaluate
body: The gap: the evidence says few children read, and the conclusion says few will develop a lifelong interest in literature. We need: children who do not read will not develop a lifelong interest in literature. Equivalently: lifelong interest in literature -> reads stories (reading is necessary for developing that interest).

label: Goal
body: Find the answer that makes reading stories a necessary condition for developing a lifelong interest in literature. Look for "only" language establishing reading as a requirement.

label: Evidence
