body: Kids today prefer flashy TV over reading stories. So few of them actually read in their free time.

label: Conclusion
body: Few kids will develop a lifelong love of literature.

label: Evaluate
body: Not reading now means not loving literature later? That is only true if reading stories as a kid is the only way to develop that love. Maybe someone discovers literature in college. Maybe a great teacher sparks interest at age thirty. The argument needs reading during childhood to be a requirement for lifelong literary interest.

label: Goal
body: Find the answer that says reading stories is a necessary condition for developing lifelong literary interest. Look for "only" as the keyword.

label: Evidence
body: The filmmaker's subjects remain unaware of the camera's location and therefore act naturally.

label: Conclusion
body: The filmmaker's documentaries are more worthwhile than other documentaries such as those where people speak directly to the camera.

label: Evaluate
body: The argument shifts from evidence about subjects acting naturally to a conclusion about how worthwhile a documentary is. But there could easily be other factors which influence how worthwhile a documentary is. Maybe the most worthwhile documentaries are about events that impact a large number of people. Maybe those are more worthwhile even if the people who appear in the documentary are speaking directly to the camera and not behaving in a way that's completely natural. We can strengthen this argument by stating that documentaries in which people act naturally are more worthwhile than other documentaries. (act naturally → more worthwhile)

label: Evidence
body: The filmmaker's subjects remain unaware of the camera's location and therefore act naturally, unlike in documentaries where people speak directly to the camera.

label: Conclusion
body: The filmmaker's documentaries are more worthwhile than those in which subjects speak directly to the camera.

label: Evaluate
body: The argument jumps from "subjects act naturally" to "documentaries are more worthwhile." We need a principle linking natural behavior to documentary value.

label: Goal
body: Find a principle stating that documentaries depicting subjects authentically (acting naturally) are more worthwhile than those that do not.

label: Evidence
body: Hidden cameras mean the subjects do not know where the camera is. They act naturally. Meanwhile, in other documentaries, people talk straight to the camera and clearly know they are being filmed.

label: Conclusion
body: Therefore the hidden-camera documentaries are more worthwhile.

label: Evaluate
body: The argument says "my subjects act naturally" and concludes "my documentaries are better." But why does natural behavior make a documentary better? Maybe the most worthwhile documentary is one about an important topic where people speak directly to the camera with prepared, thoughtful statements. The argument needs a principle that says natural = worthwhile.

label: Goal
body: Find the answer that bridges authentic behavior to documentary quality.

label: Evidence
body: Highly profitable corporations can save money by reducing the monitoring done by managers, as long as the employees are given strong incentives to keep working hard.

label: Conclusion
body: Highly profitable corporations can save money by giving their employees expensive bonuses.

label: Evaluate
body: To reach this conclusion about the employees at these particular corporations, we need to assume that there is a relationship between giving them strong incentives to keep working hard and giving them expensive bonuses. We have to assume that these bonuses would motivate them to keep working hard even when the managers aren't watching them closely.

label: Evidence
body: Highly profitable corporations can save money by reducing managers' monitoring time, as long as employees are given strong incentives to keep working hard.

label: Conclusion
body: Highly profitable corporations can save money by giving employees expensive bonuses.

label: Evaluate
body: The evidence says strong incentives can replace monitoring. The conclusion says expensive bonuses achieve this. The gap: we need expensive bonuses to constitute strong incentives for these particular employees to keep working hard.

label: Goal
body: Find the assumption that expensive bonuses are strong incentives for employees at highly profitable corporations where monitoring is reduced.

label: Evidence
body: At highly profitable companies, managers' time is expensive. Monitoring employees eats that time. If you give employees strong incentives to work hard, you can cut the monitoring and save money.

label: Conclusion
body: These companies can save money by handing out expensive bonuses.

label: Evaluate
body: The evidence says "strong incentives" and the conclusion says "expensive bonuses." The argument assumes these are the same thing. But what if the employees at these companies do not care about bonuses? What if the bonuses cost more than the monitoring savings? The argument needs bonuses to actually motivate these specific employees enough to replace supervision.

label: Goal
body: Find the assumption that connects expensive bonuses to strong incentives for employees at these corporations.

label: Evidence
body: Consent forms that medical test subjects fill out before medical tests show that almost all of these subjects accept the risk of receiving ineffective substances.

label: Conclusion
body: This casts doubt on the claim that many test subjects resent being given placebos or resent being given medicines that turn out to be ineffective.

label: Evaluate
body: It's very possible that the test subjects could accept the risk of receiving ineffective substances and then still feel resentment later on. So, the forms that they complete before the tests do not cast doubt on a claim about them feeling resentment at a later time.

label: Evidence
body: Consent forms filled out before medical tests show that almost all subjects accept the risk of receiving ineffective substances.

label: Conclusion
body: This casts doubt on the claim that many test subjects resent being given placebos or ineffective medicines.

label: Evaluate
body: The evidence is about what subjects accept before the tests. The conclusion is about what subjects resent during or after the tests. Accepting a risk in advance does not mean you will not resent the outcome when it actually happens. The argument conflates pre-test acceptance with post-test attitude.

label: Goal
body: Find the answer that identifies the temporal/attitudinal gap: the argument assumes pre-test acceptance means subjects will not later resent the actual outcome.

label: Evidence
body: Before the tests, subjects signed consent forms saying they accept the risk of getting a placebo or ineffective medicine. Almost all of them were fine with it.

label: Conclusion
body: So the claim that many subjects resent getting placebos or ineffective medicines is doubtful.

label: Evaluate
body: Signing a form before the test saying "I accept the risk" is very different from actually getting a sugar pill while your disease gets worse. Someone can accept a coin flip beforehand and still be upset when they lose. The argument assumes that pre-game acceptance translates to post-game contentment, which anyone who has ever lost a bet can tell you is not how emotions work.

label: Goal
body: Find the answer that names this flaw: treating pre-test acceptance of a risk as evidence against post-test resentment about the outcome.

label: Evidence
body: Over the long run, apple orchards that use organic farming methods cost no more to run than, and are just as productive as, apple orchards using conventional methods. Organically grown apples tend to be better tasting.

label: Conclusion
body: Organic orchards are likely to be more profitable than conventional orchards in the long run.

label: Evaluate
body: To reach this conclusion, we need to assume that an orchard which grows apples that taste better is guaranteed to be more profitable. `better tasting → more profitable`. This link is missing from the argument as it's written.

label: Goal
body: We're looking for an answer which makes this missing link more likely to be true. We want more evidence showing that better tasting apples are more profitable.

label: Evidence
body: Organic orchards cost no more to run and are just as productive as conventional orchards. Organically grown apples tend to be better tasting.

label: Evaluate
body: The argument leaps from "better tasting" to "more profitable" without connecting taste to revenue. We need a reason to believe that better flavor translates into higher sales or higher prices.

label: Goal
body: Find an answer that strengthens the link between better taste and greater profitability.

label: Conclusion
body: Organic orchards will out-earn conventional ones in the long run. The organic apples are destined for financial glory.

label: Evidence
body: Organic orchards cost the same to run and produce the same amount. The only edge? The organic apples taste better.

label: Evaluate
body: Costs are equal. Output is equal. So the entire profit argument hangs on taste. But since when does tasting better automatically mean making more money? Plenty of things taste great without being profitable — just ask anyone who has tried to sell homemade jam at a farmers' market. The argument needs a reason to believe that apple buyers actually care enough about flavor to open their wallets wider.

label: Goal
body: Find the answer that connects deliciousness to dollars.

label: Opposing Evidence
body: Banking industry visionaries foresee a bright day in the near future when customers will be able to transact all their financial business by means of computers or telephones from the comfort of their own homes.

label: Conclusion
body: That [transacting all financial business from home by means of computers or telephones] may be more of a paradise for banks than for their customers.

label: Evicence
body: As banks eliminate their branch offices and customer-service employees, customers will have to serve as their own tellers—and pay more transaction fees for their efforts.

label: Goal
body: A correct answer will indicate that conducting financial business from home by computer or telephone is not as beneficial for customers as it is for banks.

label: Conclusion
body: Transacting all financial business from home by computer or telephone may be more of a paradise for banks than for their customers.

label: Evidence
body: As banks eliminate branch offices and customer-service employees, customers will have to serve as their own tellers and pay more transaction fees.

label: Evaluate
body: The first sentence presents an opposing view — banking visionaries see home banking as a bright future. The second sentence pivots with "but" to introduce the author's conclusion. The third sentence provides evidence for that conclusion.

label: Goal
body: Identify the answer that restates the conclusion: home banking benefits banks more than customers.

label: Conclusion
body: Home banking sounds great — for the banks. For customers, not so much. That is the author's actual point.

label: Evidence
body: Banks get to close branches and fire employees. Customers get to do more work and pay more fees for the privilege. Some paradise.

label: Evaluate
body: The structure here is a classic bait-and-switch. Sentence one paints a rosy picture — banking from the couch, the future is now. Then "but" drops like a plot twist, and the author reveals the real winners. Sentence three explains why: banks cut costs while customers pick up the slack. The conclusion is the "but" sentence, not the evidence that follows it.

label: Goal
body: Find the answer that matches "home banking is a better deal for banks than for customers."

label: Bernard's Claims
body:
1. We should not invite Carl to speak at the forum.
  2. Carl's views are clearly false, and worse, dangerous.
  3. To encourage their consideration will not only legitimize them but also help to promulgate them.
  4. We should avoid legitimizing or promulgating Carl's views, since we wish not to support their adoption.

label: Ayla's Responses
body:
1. Disagrees
  2. no comment
  3. Disagrees
  4. no comment, possibly agrees

label: Evaluate
body: Ayla doesn't explicitly state that Carl should be invited to speak at the forum. However, her statements provide support for the idea that she disagrees with Bernard's first claim and believes that Carl should be allowed to speak. Ayla also doesn't explicitly state that that we should avoid legitimizing or promulgating Carl's views and not support their adoption. However, her statements provide some support for the idea that she agrees with Bernard about this. Ayla talks about combating "false views" and about seeing Carl's views for what they are. Bernard states that Carl's views are false. We can infer that Ayla agrees. They appear to disagree about allowing Carl to speak at the forum. Bernard states that Carl should not be invited, but Ayla appears to suggest that it would be best to allow Carl to speak so that people can publicly challenge his views. "Promulgate" means to promote an idea or make it widely known. If you didn't know this when reading Bernard's statements, but had a sense that it might mean "promote" or "spread," that's totally fine.

label: Goal
body: We'll look for an answer that addresses claim #1 or #3.

label: Conclusion
body: Bernard: Carl should not be invited to speak. Ayla: The best way to combat false views is to challenge them publicly.

label: Evidence
body: Bernard argues that allowing Carl to speak would legitimize and promulgate his dangerous views. Ayla argues that public scrutiny will expose Carl's views for what they are.

label: Evaluate
body: Bernard and Ayla agree that Carl's views are false. They disagree about whether allowing public expression of those views is the best way to fight them. Bernard says no — public expression legitimizes. Ayla says yes — public expression allows refutation.

label: Goal
body: Find the answer that captures their disagreement: whether publicly expressing false views is the best way to combat them.

label: Conclusion
body: Bernard: Do not let Carl near a microphone. Ayla: Hand Carl the microphone and let the audience destroy his arguments.

label: Evidence
body: If the branch libraries were closed, then Winchester could afford to open one large library. The large library could carry broader and more current selections [books].

label: Evidence
body: Bernard thinks giving Carl a platform legitimizes his nonsense. Ayla thinks giving Carl a platform lets everyone see the nonsense for what it is. Classic "sunlight is the best disinfectant" versus "do not give bad ideas oxygen" debate.

label: Evaluate
body: They agree on one thing: Carl's views are wrong. They disagree on strategy. Bernard is the "ban him from the conference" camp. Ayla is the "let him speak so we can publicly dismantle his arguments" camp. Neither one thinks Carl is right — they just disagree about the best tactical response to wrongness.

label: Goal
body: Find the answer that nails the actual disagreement: whether letting someone publicly air false views is the best way to fight those views.

label: Principle
body: If someone buys an item, gets all of the use from it they intended to get, and returns it, then they are acting in an unethical way: `buy, use fully, and return → unethical`

label: Evicence in Application
body: James bought an item and later returned it.

label: Conclusion
body: The return was unethical.

label: Evaluate
body: The evidence in the application doesn't state why James returned the video camera. The principle only allows us to conclude that the return was unethical if we have evidence that James got all of the use from the camera that he intended to get.

label: Goal
body: Look for an answer indicating that James got all of the use from the cameral that he intended.

label: Conclusion
body: James's return of the video camera was unethical.

label: Evidence
body: The principle: it is unethical to return an item after getting all intended use from it. James bought a video camera and returned it two weeks later.

label: Evaluate
body: The evidence only says James bought and returned a camera. It does not say he got all his intended use from it. To justify applying the principle, we need evidence that James used the camera for its intended purpose and then returned it.

label: Goal
body: Find an answer showing that James got all the use from the camera that he intended before returning it.

label: Conclusion
body: James returned a video camera and that makes him unethical. The moral police have spoken.

label: Evidence
body: The principle: buying something, using it for everything you planned, and then returning it is wrong. James bought a camera and brought it back two weeks later.

label: Evaluate
body: Hold on — the principle requires that James got all the use he wanted from the camera. The evidence just says he bought it and returned it. Maybe the camera broke. Maybe he changed his mind. Maybe he realized he is not the aspiring filmmaker he thought. Without knowing that James fulfilled his intended purpose, the principle cannot be applied. The answer needs to close this gap.

label: Goal
body: Find the answer that proves James used the camera for exactly what he planned and then returned it — making the return clearly unethical under the principle.

label: Opposing Idea
body: Increased productivity resulting from greater efficiency [by using Taylor's methods] has led to increases in most workers' standards of living.

label: Evidence
body: Taylor's methods have tended to make these workers' jobs routine and repetitive.

label: Conclusion
body: Taylor's methods have robbing their work of some of the intrinsic worth it possessed when it emphasized creativity and talent.

label: Evaluate
body: It's important to notice the leap from "routine and repetitive" in the evidence to the claim in the conclusion about "robbing their work of some of the intrinsic worth it possessed." The argument is making an assumption here. Does making work more routine and repetitive necessarily rob it of intrinsic worth? Intrinsic worth for whom? The workers? "Routine and repetitive" work can be simple and easy. Lots of people don't mind getting paid to do simple, easy work. And we were told that workers' standard of living has increased, so there's no evidence in this argument that workers are being paid poorly for this "routine and repetitive" work. Does the work have less intrinsic worth for the employers? The argument states that greater efficiency has resulted in increased productivity. We don't know if employers have anything to complain about here. Work is not guaranteed to be less worthwhile, for either the workers or their employers, just because the work has become routine and repetitive.

label: Goal
body: A correct answer will be a generalization supporting the idea that, in spite of the benefits of Taylorism—greater productivity and efficiency, and a higher standard of living for workers—the work being done has also become less worthwhile.

label: Conclusion
body: Taylor's methods have robbed workers' jobs of some of their intrinsic worth by making them routine and repetitive.

label: Evidence
body: Taylorism increased productivity and most workers' standards of living, but made jobs routine and repetitive, reducing the creativity and talent previously involved.

label: Evaluate
body: The situation describes a development that produced both a financial benefit (higher standard of living) and a non-financial cost (less rewarding work). A correct generalization will capture this dual-edged quality.

label: Goal
body: Find a general principle that matches: a single development can benefit workers financially while making their work less fulfilling.

label: Conclusion
body: Taylor's efficiency methods sucked the soul out of work. Jobs became repetitive assembly-line tedium, robbing them of the creativity and talent they once required.

label: Evidence
body: On the bright side: workers make more money. On the not-so-bright side: their jobs are now mind-numbingly boring. Taylorism gave workers bigger paychecks and smaller reasons to care about what they do all day.

label: Evaluate
body: This is a classic "good news, bad news" scenario. Good news: higher standard of living. Bad news: the work itself became a creativity-free zone. The correct generalization needs to capture both halves — something that helps workers financially while hurting the quality of their work experience.

label: Evidence
body: Orchids with ants are healthier. Ants store organic matter in orchid roots.

label: Evaluate
body: The conclusion makes a recommendation about building a new library. It does this by introducing a new concept of better meeting residents' needs. A couple of assumptions are required to reach this conclusion. First, the argument assumes that one large library would better meet residents' needs than several smaller ones. We can easily envision a situation where it's convenient for residents to visit the branch libraries that are close to their neighborhoods, while a single main library would be farther away and therefore less accessible. The argument also assumes that a broader and more current selection of books would better meet residents' needs. But people use libraries for many reasons other than borrowing books. Libraries often have computers, study rooms, and meeting rooms that residents can use. Libraries often offer classes and events. And people are likely to borrow older books from libraries, not just current ones.

label: Goal
body: A correct answer is likely to focus on one of these unintended consequences of closing branch libraries and having one large library, a consequence which would prevent one large library from serving residents better than the existing branch libraries.

label: Conclusion
body: Winchester would better meet its residents' needs by closing its small branch libraries and opening one larger, well-supplied library.

label: Evidence
body: Winchester cannot afford to keep branch libraries well-supplied. Closing them would fund one large library with broader and more current book selections.

label: Evaluate
body: The argument assumes a larger library would better meet residents' needs. But "better meeting needs" involves more than book selection — accessibility matters too. If the single library is far from most residents, the improved selection could be offset by reduced convenience.

label: Goal
body: Find an answer that identifies an unintended consequence of consolidating into one library — most likely an accessibility problem.

label: Conclusion
body: Close all the little libraries, build one big one. Problem solved — or so the argument claims.

label: Evidence
body: The branch libraries cannot afford good books. A single large library could. More books, more current titles, happier residents. At least, that is the theory.

label: Evaluate
body: There is a small problem with the "one big library fixes everything" plan: people have to actually get there. Multiple small libraries mean most residents have one nearby. One large library might be a trek for the majority of the town. A library with the world's best book collection does not help anyone who cannot reach it. The argument treats "better books" as the only thing residents need, ignoring the radical concept of convenience.

label: Goal
body: Find the answer that rains on the consolidation parade — most likely by pointing out that the new library would be inconveniently located.

label: Given
body:
- Some recently invented television screens are built out of small tiles seamlessly joined together.
  - Each tile is a separate miniature screen.
  - Television sets with these compound screens are just a few inches thick.
  - For a noncompound screen in a set of this thickness, the larger the screen is, the dimmer it is.
  - However, each tile in a compound screen is small enough to be quite bright.
  - Moreover, an unlimited number of the tiles can be joined together, without making the resulting screen any less bright or the set any thicker.

label: Evaluate
body: The stimulus provides a comparison between noncompound screens and the new, recently invented compound screens. A noncompound screen that is just a few inches thick will get dimmer as it is made larger. However, since each tile in a new compound screen is bright, and an unlimited number of tiles can be joined together without reducing the brightness, it follows that the new compound screens can be made very large without becoming dimmer. Also, joining tiles together doesn't make the new compound screens any thicker, so we can make large, bright compound screens that are still only a few inches thick.

label: Given
body: Compound screens are made of small tiles joined seamlessly. Sets with compound screens are just a few inches thick. For noncompound screens at this thickness, larger means dimmer. Each compound tile is bright, and unlimited tiles can be joined without reducing brightness or increasing thickness.

label: Evaluate
body: Compound screens overcome the size-brightness tradeoff. Since tiles stay bright regardless of quantity and do not add thickness, compound screens can be very large, bright, and thin simultaneously.

label: Goal
body: Find an answer that follows logically from combining these facts.

label: Given
body: TV screens made of tiny bright tiles snapped together. Add more tiles, still bright. Add more tiles, still thin. Noncompound screens get dimmer as they get bigger, but compound screens laugh at that limitation.

label: Evaluate
body: Compound screens can be enormous, bright, and only a few inches thick — the old rules do not apply.

label: Goal
body: Find the answer stating the obvious: thin TVs can now be both large and bright.

label: Intermediate Conclusion
body: For early humans who moved from a hunter-gatherer lifestyle to agriculture, the transition must have been traumatic.

label: Evidence
body: There would have been increased incidence of disease and injury and a more homogeneous diet lacking vital nutrients more easily obtainable from the richly varied diet of hunter-gatherers.

label: Main Conclusion
body: Groups that made the transition were likely motivated by certain benefits that accompany the settled life of the agriculturist, such as opportunities for the accumulation of wealth by those with specialized social roles.

label: Evaluate
body: The statement that is quoted in the question stem is an intermediate conclusion. It is supported by the evidence in the second sentence, and supports the main conclusion in the final sentence.

label: Conclusion
body: Groups that transitioned to agriculture were likely motivated by benefits of settled life, such as wealth accumulation.

label: Evidence
body: The transition was traumatic — increased disease, injury, and a less nutritious diet. Despite these costs, groups still switched.

label: Evaluate
body: The quoted statement is an intermediate conclusion supported by disease/diet evidence, and it supports the main conclusion about motivation by benefits.

label: Goal
body: The quoted statement is a premise that is itself supported by another premise.

label: Conclusion
body: Early humans must have had a compelling reason to switch to farming — the anthropologist suggests the lure of settled-life perks like wealth.

label: Evidence
body: Farming life was objectively worse: more disease, injuries, boring diet. The fact that groups switched despite suffering implies something good was pulling them.

label: Evaluate
body: The "traumatic" claim is the logical middle child — supported by evidence below it, supporting the conclusion above it.

label: Goal
body: Expect the answer to describe it as a claim supported by evidence that also supports the conclusion.

label: Evidence
body: Many of the words used to describe web sites evoke ideas that are usually associated with real estate. The common law of trespass usually applies to cases of encroachment on real estate.

label: Conclusion
body: It is reasonable to extend that law [trespass] to protect against encroachments on property in cyberspace.

label: Evaluate
body: The evidence notes a similarity between web sites and real estate. Many of the same words, like "site" and "visiting" are used when discussing both web sites and real estate. But then the argument gets cheeky. It uses this one similarity, which is pretty superficial, as a basis for claiming that web sites and real estate are similar in another way: the same types of laws should apply to both. When two types of activities happen to use similar terminology, does that necessarily mean that the same types of laws should apply to both? If I drive a car and also use Google Drive on my computer, do I have to obey local traffic laws while sitting at my desk using my laptop? If so, I guess I should put on a seatbelt and get rid of this glass of wine...

label: Conclusion
body: It is reasonable to extend trespass law to protect against encroachments on property in cyberspace.

label: Evidence
body: Web site terminology evokes real estate concepts. Trespass law applies to real estate encroachment.

label: Evaluate
body: The analogy rests solely on shared terminology — a superficial verbal similarity rather than a substantive one.

label: Goal
body: Identify the flaw: treating a merely verbal similarity as a basis for legal analogy.

label: Conclusion
body: Trespass law should apply to the internet. Because they are called "sites" and people "visit" them, just like real estate.

label: Evidence
body: Same words, therefore same laws. That is the entire argument.

label: Evaluate
body: By this logic, since people "drive" Google Drive, a driver's license is needed to use it. Since people "stream" movies, fishing regulations apply. The analogy is built entirely on vocabulary overlap, not on any substantive similarity between web sites and physical property.

label: Goal
body: Find the answer that calls out the verbal-only analogy.

label: Evidence
body: A recent study found that in each of the last ten years, the number of traffic accidents that resulted in death was greater during the day than during the night.

label: Conclusion
body: It is more dangerous for an individual to drive during the day than during the night.

label: Evaluate
body: The evidence contains a comparison between the number of fatal traffic accidents that occur during the day and the number that occur at night. The evidence states that more fatal accidents occur during the day, but it's important to notice that this is only a correlation. Nothing in the evidence indicates what is causing more fatal accidents to occur during the day. The evidence claims that it is more dangerous for "an individual"—meaning anyone—to drive during the day. To reach that conclusion, we need make an assumption about whatever factors are causing more fatal accidents to occur during daytime. We need to assume that those factors will affect everyone who drives during the day. But we haven't been told what is actually causing more fatal accidents to occur during daytime, so we can't be sure that those factors will affect all individuals who drive during the day.

label: Goal
body: An answer choice that strengthens the argument might describe a situation which makes driving more dangerous for everyone, but only occurs during the day, not at night. Since this is an EXCEPT question, we will expect four of the answers to strengthen the argument. The one correct answer will not strengthen the argument. It will either weaken the argument or—more likely—not have any clear impact on the argument.

label: Conclusion
body: It is more dangerous for an individual to drive during the day than at night.

label: Evidence
body: In each of the last ten years, more fatal traffic accidents occurred during the day than at night.

label: Evaluate
body: More total fatal accidents during the day could reflect more drivers, not more per-driver danger. Strengtheners should provide daytime-specific danger factors.

label: Goal
body: Four answers strengthen by providing day-specific risk factors. The correct answer (the exception) will have no clear differential impact between day and night.

label: Conclusion
body: Daytime driving is more dangerous. Hold the headlights.

label: Evidence
body: More fatal accidents happen during the day. That is the entire basis.

label: Evaluate
body: More daytime accidents could just mean more daytime drivers. The argument needs reasons why driving during the day is inherently more dangerous per person, not just busier.

label: Goal
body: Four answers strengthen. One does not. Find the odd one out.

label: Conclusion (it follows that)
body: The sole reason that sexual reproduction has become the rule among both animals and plants is that natural selection has favored some entire species over others.

label: Evidence
body: Planets do not generate light (they only reflect it). There are many celestial objects in this galaxy that are not planets (besides stars).

label: Evidence
body: The evolutionary advantage of sexual reproduction is that it increases the range of genetic variation in a species, which is an advantage for the species as a whole. But an increased range of genetic variation in a species is not advantageous for any individual member of the species.

label: Evaluate
body: The word "however" in the second sentence indicates a pivot from the idea in the first sentence to a different, contrasting idea. In the final sentence, the phrase "it follows that" indicates that this final sentence contains a conclusion, supported by evidence in the previous sentences.

label: Goal
body: The statement quoted by the question stem is in the second sentence of the stimulus, which contains the argument's evidence or premise.

label: Conclusion
body: The sole reason sexual reproduction has become the rule is that natural selection has favored some entire species over others.

label: Evidence
body: Sexual reproduction increases genetic variation, which benefits the species as a whole. But increased genetic variation is not advantageous for any individual member.

label: Evaluate
body: The quoted statement is evidence supporting the conclusion. It establishes that the benefit of sexual reproduction operates at the species level, not the individual level, thereby supporting the conclusion about species-level selection.

label: Goal
body: The quoted statement is a claim offered in support of the conclusion.

label: Conclusion
body: Sexual reproduction won the evolutionary popularity contest because entire species that reproduced sexually beat out species that did not. Species-level natural selection did the work.

label: Evidence
body: Genetic variation from sexual reproduction helps the species, not the individual. If it helped individuals, regular individual-level selection would explain it. Since it does not, the explanation must be at the species level.

label: Evaluate
body: The quoted statement — that genetic variation does not help individuals — is the linchpin. It forces the explanation from the individual level up to the species level.

label: Goal
body: Find the answer that says this statement supports the conclusion.

label: Evidence
body: Making vagrancy illegal means transforming many innocuous everyday occurrences into crimes.

label: Conclusion
body: Vagrancy laws increase crime while purporting to reduce it.

label: Evaluate
body: The argument presents evidence about "transforming many innocuous everyday occurrences into crimes" and then makes a leap to a new concept in the conclusion—increasing crime. The argument doesn't clearly explain what "increase crime" is intended to mean. It's reasonable to think this means that entirely new crimes take place, ones that did not occur before the vagrancy laws were passed. For example, in a certain town there might be 10 cases a month where someone actually trespasses on another person's property, but once vagrancy laws are passed that number jumps to 30 actual instances of trespassing. However, the evidence suggests that something different could be happening. It suggests that actions which were not illegal become illegal once vagrancy laws are passed. This could mean, for example, that napping under a tree in a public park is legal until vagrancy laws make it illegal. The actual number of people who nap under trees might stay exactly the same, or even decrease, but because it is now a crime, there is a sudden increase in the number of people who are arrested or fined for it. The argument doesn't clearly explain the link between innocuous occurrences becoming crimes and an increase in crime. It's not clear what "increase" actually means in this conclusion.

label: Goal
body: A correct answer might point out how the phrase "increase crime" is used in an unclear way. It might point out that the argument doesn't establish a clear link between innocuous occurrences becoming crimes and an actual increase in crime.

label: Conclusion
body: Vagrancy laws increase crime while purporting to reduce it.

label: Evidence
body: Making vagrancy illegal transforms many innocuous everyday occurrences into crimes.

label: Evaluate
body: The conclusion claims vagrancy laws "increase crime," but the evidence only shows that previously legal behaviors are reclassified as crimes. Reclassification is not the same as an actual increase in criminal activity — the same behaviors continue, just with a new legal label.

label: Goal
body: Find the answer that identifies the ambiguity: the argument conflates reclassifying behavior as criminal with an actual increase in criminal activity.

label: Conclusion
body: Vagrancy laws increase crime. Take that, law and order.

label: Evidence
body: Making vagrancy illegal turns previously legal everyday behaviors into crimes.

label: Evaluate
body: Well, technically, yes — if you make sitting on a park bench illegal, you have more "crime" in the sense that more people are now breaking the law. But did crime actually increase? The same people are sitting on the same bench doing the same thing. The only thing that changed is the label. The argument treats relabeling as if it were an actual increase in bad behavior.

label: Goal
body: Find the answer that calls out the sleight of hand: reclassification is not the same as more crime.

label: Evidence
body: The purpose of government is to prevent individuals from injuring others in the pursuit of their own welfare.

label: Conclusion
body: If most individuals take a reasoned approach to getting what they want, the power of government should be less.

label: Evaluate
body: Maybe the ants are helping for a completely different reason. Maybe healthier orchids attract ants. Maybe something else associated with ants is the real hero. The provided explanation is just one possibility.

label: Goal
body: Find a different reason ants and healthy orchids go together.

label: Situation
body: Future overall demand for professors can be predicted with reasonable accuracy from current birth rates.

label: However...
body: The accuracy of predictions of future demand for music professors is lower, and that for jazz studies professors lower still.

label: Evaluate
body: As is sometimes the case in a Necessary Assumption question, this argument contains more than one gap in logic. There are several new concepts in the conclusion that are different from concepts discussed in the evidence. The evidence mentions "injuring others" in the pursuit of our own welfare. The conclusion shifts to "a reasoned approach" to getting what we want. Many people would agree that taking a reasoned approach to something involves not injuring others, but that might not always be true. If someone tries to physically attack me, it might be reasonable for me to injure that person to prevent them from hurting me. This argument assumes that for most people, taking a reasoned approach to getting what we want involves not injuring others in pursuit of our own welfare. The evidence also mentions "the purpose of government," while the conclusion discusses "the power of government." These are different things. The argument assumes that the power of government should be reduced if individuals do not need the government to fulfill its purpose. We can get a sense for the structure of the argument, including the assumptions it makes, by putting it all together like this: Most individuals who take a reasoned approach to getting what they want will not injure others in the pursuit of their own welfare, so they will not need the government to fulfill its purpose. And if most individuals do not need the government to fulfill its purpose, the power of government should be less.

label: Conclusion
body: If most individuals take a reasoned approach to getting what they want, the power of government should be less.

label: Evidence
body: The purpose of government is to prevent individuals from injuring others in pursuit of their own welfare.

label: Evaluate
body: The argument leaps from "injuring others" in the evidence to "a reasoned approach" in the conclusion. It assumes that taking a reasoned approach reduces the likelihood of injuring others.

label: Goal
body: Find a necessary assumption linking "reasoned approach" to "not injuring others."

label: Conclusion
body: If people are reasonable, government can shrink. Less need for the government referee.

label: Evidence
body: Government exists to stop people from hurting each other while pursuing their own interests.

label: Evaluate
body: The magic leap: "reasonable" somehow equals "not hurting people." But history is full of very reasonable people who harmed others quite deliberately in pursuit of their goals. The argument needs to assume that being reasonable means being less injurious.

label: Goal
body: Find the assumption that connects reasonableness to not hurting others.

label: Evidence
body: The best seafood gumbo requires fresh okra.

label: Conclusion
body: If this claim were true [Chris's okra supplier cannot reliably supply fresh okra], then Chris's customers could not count on getting good seafood gumbo.

label: Evaluate
body: The evidence is a conditional statement: `best gumbo → fresh okra`. Using the contrapositive, we can conclude that if we don't have fresh okra, we cannot have the best seafood gumbo: `~ fresh okra → ~ best gumbo`. The argument tries to make a very similar conclusion, but there is an important term shift. The conclusion of this argument is about getting good gumbo, not the best gumbo: `~ fresh okra → ~ good gumbo`. It might be possible to make good seafood gumbo without fresh okra, just not the best seafood gumbo.

label: Conclusion
body: If Chris's okra supplier cannot reliably supply fresh okra, Chris's customers cannot count on getting good seafood gumbo.

label: Evidence
body: The best seafood gumbo requires fresh okra.

label: Evaluate
body: The evidence says fresh okra is needed for the best gumbo. The conclusion shifts to good gumbo. Good gumbo might not require fresh okra — only the best does.

label: Goal
body: Identify the flaw: confusing what is needed for the best gumbo with what is needed for good gumbo.

label: Conclusion
body: No fresh okra, no good gumbo. Or so the food critic claims.

label: Evidence
body: The best gumbo needs fresh okra. But who said anything about the best? The conclusion is about good gumbo. Plenty of things can be good without being the best.

label: Evaluate
body: "Best" and "good" are not the same standard. A restaurant can make perfectly good gumbo without fresh okra — just not the absolute best gumbo. The argument smuggles in a higher standard than what the conclusion actually discusses.

label: Goal
body: Find the answer that catches the best-to-good switch.

label: Curious Fact
body: Why are the ant-hosting orchids of a given species healthier than the orchids that don't host ants?

label: Provided Explanation
body: The ants store organic matter in the orchids' roots, which provides the orchids with additional nutrients, which makes them healthier?

label: Goal
body: Our task is to get an alternate explanation for why there's this correlation between hosting ants and being a healthier orchid. Whenever we're seeking an alternate explanation for a correlation, we consider two things: Reverse Causality — Maybe the orchid's superior health comes first, and that causes ants to shelter there. Third Factor — Maybe some factor that is associated with the presence of ants (for example, a water supply) is also causing those orchids to grow better. It's also possible that we just get an alternate explanation where the ants are the cause of the orchid's health, but not because they're putting extra nutrients in the orchid's roots.

label: Conclusion
body: The organic matter stored by ants provides orchids with additional nutrients, explaining their superior health.

label: Evidence
body: Orchids housing ants are far healthier. Ants store organic matter in orchid roots.

label: Evaluate
body: The provided explanation is that ants' organic matter gives extra nutrients. We need an alternative explanation for the correlation between ants and healthy orchids — perhaps reverse causation, a third factor, or a different causal mechanism.

label: Goal
body: Find an alternative explanation for why orchids with ants are healthier.

label: Conclusion
body: Ants make orchids healthier by depositing nutritious snack packs in their roots. Or so the story goes.

label: Evaluate
body: In this situation we're comparing a prediction about a general group, professors, to a prediction about a subset of that group, music professors. We then compare the prediction about music professors to a prediction about a subset of music professors, namely jazz studies professors. The demand for the overall group can be predicted reasonably well by birth rates. But as we look at each smaller, more specific subset, there's a decrease in the ability to accurately predict demand.

label: Goal
body: We're expecting an answer to state that we have a greater ability to predict something about a general group, with less and less ability to make accurate predictions as we look at specific categories within groups.

label: Situation
body: Future demand for professors can be predicted from birth rates. But predictions for music professors are less accurate, and for jazz studies professors less accurate still.

label: Evaluate
body: As the prediction gets more specific (all professors -> music -> jazz), accuracy decreases. More general predictions are more accurate.

label: Goal
body: Find the principle: more general predictions are more accurate than more specific ones.

label: Situation
body: Birth rates can predict how many professors will be needed. Music professors? Less accurately. Jazz studies professors? Even less. The more you zoom in, the worse the prediction gets.

label: Evaluate
body: General predictions work well because they average out the randomness. Specific predictions are at the mercy of niche trends that birth rates cannot capture.

label: Goal
body: Find the principle that says: bigger picture, better prediction.

label: Evidence
body: People can either fight for anarchy or they can tolerate totalitarian government control. History shows that government control of all facets of human life destroys the spirit, making life miserable. Anarchy allows each individual the freedom to pursue a personal course of happiness.

label: Conclusion
body: People should fight for anarchy.

label: Evaluate
body: "Should" tends to be a strong word on the LSAT. When the conclusion of an argument makes a recommendation, stating what someone "should" do, the evidence is supposed to clearly justify why that is the best course of action. As a general rule, we accept the evidence that we're given in LR questions. However, difficult LR questions will occasionally test our critical thinking skills in a more holistic way. To answer these questions correctly, we need to be flexible and take a big-picture view, rather than mechanically following general rules. Even though we can consider the first sentence of this argument as evidence, it stands out as rather extreme statement. Anarchy and totalitarian government control are extremes at the opposite ends of the spectrum. Most systems of government that exist fall somewhere in between. Is it reasonable to think that anarchy and totalitarian government control are the only two options available? No, it's not. There is a clear false choice flaw baked into this premise, which makes the argument questionable from the start.

label: Conclusion
body: People should fight for anarchy.

label: Evidence
body: People can either fight for anarchy or tolerate totalitarian government control. Totalitarianism destroys the spirit. Anarchy allows freedom to pursue happiness.

label: Evaluate
body: The argument presents a false dichotomy: anarchy and totalitarianism are not the only options. Most political systems fall between these extremes.

label: Goal
body: Identify the false choice flaw.

label: Conclusion
body: Fight for anarchy. That is the recommendation.

label: Evidence
body: The only two options: anarchy or totalitarian oppression. Totalitarianism is terrible. Anarchy is freedom. Therefore: anarchy.

label: Evaluate
body: This is about as false a dichotomy as they come. "Your only choices are no government or the worst possible government" conveniently ignores every form of governance between those two extremes. Most of human civilization operates in the vast middle ground this argument pretends does not exist.

label: Goal
body: Find the false choice flaw.

label: Given that ...
body: Consumer demand for personal computers continues to increase each year.

label: Why is it that ...
body: The retail profit margin on personal computer sales is extremely low compared to that of other high-tech items.

label: Evaluate
body: Since more people want PC's every year, the producers of PC's could theoretically raise their prices and still have buyers, thus we might expect them to have high profit levels. But they don't. Maybe the price is already so high that even though people badly want a PC, if the price were raised any further, lot of people couldn't afford one. Maybe there is a ton of competition in the PC space (whereas there isn't for other high-tech items), since competition keeps prices lower.

label: Goal
body: We need to find four reasons why PC's have a lower profit margin (or why other popular high-tech items have a higher profit margin).

label: Given that...
body: Consumer demand for PCs continues to increase each year.

label: Why is it that...
body: Retail profit margins on PCs are extremely low compared to other popular high-tech items.

label: Evaluate
body: Rising demand usually allows higher prices and profits. Four answers will explain why PC margins remain low despite rising demand. The correct answer (EXCEPT) will not resolve this discrepancy.

label: Goal
body: Find the one answer that does not explain low PC profit margins.

label: Given that...
body: Everyone wants PCs. Demand keeps rising.

label: Why is it that...
body: PC stores barely make money on each sale compared to other tech products.

label: Evaluate
body: High demand usually means fat profits. Something is keeping PC margins thin. Four answers explain what. One does not.

label: Goal
body: Find the odd one out — the answer that does not explain low PC profits.

label: Conclusion
body: It will not be economically feasible to colonize Mars.

label: Evidence
body: If a film is accepted by the festival committee, then one of the distributors attending the festival buys it. `accepted → distributor buys` If a distributor buys a film, the film's financial backers are assured of recouping their investment. `distributor buys → recoup` This film was not accepted by the festival committee. `~accepted`

label: Conclusion
body: This film's financial backers will not recoup their investment. `~recoup`

label: Evaluate
body: By connecting the first two premises, we can conclude that if a film is accepted by the festival committee, the film's financial backers are assured of recouping their investment: `accepted → recoup`. To reach the argument's conclusion, we need to assume that if a film is not accepted by the festival committee, the film's financial backers are not assured of recouping their investment: `~accepted → ~recoup`. This is an illegal negation.

label: Goal
body: We're looking for an argument that makes an assumption which is an illegal negation of the statements given as evidence.

label: Conclusion
body: This film's financial backers will not recoup their investment.

label: Evidence
body: If accepted by the festival committee, a distributor buys the film. If a distributor buys it, backers recoup their investment. This film was not accepted.

label: Evaluate
body: The argument chains two conditionals — accepted leads to distributor buys, which leads to recoup — then negates the first condition and concludes the last condition is also negated. That is an illegal negation. The film could still be bought by a distributor through some other means.

label: Goal
body: Find the answer that commits the same illegal negation: negating the sufficient condition and concluding the necessary condition is negated.

label: Conclusion
body: The film's backers will not get their money back. Case closed, apparently.

label: Evidence
body: Festival acceptance leads to a distributor buying the film, which leads to recouping the investment. This film was not accepted.

label: Evaluate
body: The logic here is like saying "if it rains, the ground gets wet; the ground is wet, so... wait, no — it did not rain, so the ground cannot be wet." The film was not accepted, true. But that does not mean a distributor cannot buy it some other way. The argument illegally negates the sufficient condition and assumes the necessary condition must also be negated. Classic conditional logic error.

label: Goal
body: Find the answer that makes the exact same mistake: chaining two if-then statements, negating the first trigger, and incorrectly concluding the final result is negated.

label: Evidence
body: Business managers who normally drank coffee on a daily basis were given more than their normal amount. The managers got faster at processing new information, but were less able to integrate it with past information when making decisions. Successful management depends more on integrating information than on speed.

label: Conclusion
body: Drinking more coffee than usual impairs overall management ability.

label: Evaluate
body: The evidence compares the speed of processing new information to the ability to integrate information. However, the evidence only compares these two specific factors. We aren't told that these two factors are the only ones that influence a person's success as a manager. Most people would agree that other abilities play an important role in successful management. Drinking more coffee than usual might drastically improve a managers' performance in one of these other areas, like attention to detail. The argument doesn't address this. We don't know if any other abilities were affected, or how. Based on evidence that only discusses those two specific factors, the conclusion makes a significant leap to a claim about overall management ability. We can't draw this conclusion about overall ability when it's very possible that other factors are at least equally as important. Since other factors are likely to be at least equally important, we need to know how coffee affects those factors.

label: Goal
body: A correct answer is likely to rule out the possibility that drinking additional coffee improves other abilities that play an equal or even more important role in overall management ability.

label: Conclusion
body: Drinking more coffee than usual impairs overall management ability.

label: Evidence
body: Managers given extra coffee processed information faster but integrated information with past knowledge worse. Successful management depends more on integration than speed.

label: Evaluate
body: The argument only measures two factors — speed and integration — but concludes about overall management ability. Other factors could be affected by extra coffee in ways that improve overall ability, offsetting the integration loss.

label: Goal
body: Find the assumption that the gains from extra coffee in other areas do not outweigh the integration loss.

label: Conclusion
body: Extra coffee makes you a worse manager overall. Time to switch to decaf, apparently.

label: Evidence
body: Caffeinated managers processed information faster but integrated it worse. And integration matters more than speed for management success.

label: Evaluate
body: The study measured exactly two things: speed and integration. But management involves a lot more than those two skills. Maybe the extra coffee also made managers better at motivating their teams, catching errors, or staying focused in long meetings. The argument assumes that the study captured everything that matters, but it only captured two variables out of potentially dozens.

label: Goal
body: Find the answer that plugs this gap — the one that says the unmeasured benefits of extra coffee do not outweigh the measured cost to integration.

label: Given
body: Moral excellence can be achieved only by repeatedly overcoming inclinations to do the wrong thing. `moral excel → overcome` Overcoming these inclinations is often difficult to do, even for a morally virtuous person. The only way to become a morally virtuous person is through the achievement of moral excellence. `moral virtue → moral excel`

label: Evidence
body: In a study, the vitamin C group had less severe acne. But half the subjects in each group knew which pill they received. Among those who could not tell, there was no difference in acne severity.

label: Evaluate
body: By connecting the final statement to the first statement, we can infer that if someone becomes a morally virtuous person, they have repeatedly overcome inclinations to do the wrong thing. `moral virtue → overcome`. We're also told that overcoming inclinations to do the wrong thing is often difficult to do. From this, we can infer that becoming a morally virtuous person is often difficult to do.

label: Goal
body: Expect the correct answer to involve one of these two inferences that we made by connecting the statements.

label: Given
body: Moral excellence requires repeatedly overcoming inclinations to do wrong. Overcoming these inclinations is often difficult. The only way to become morally virtuous is through moral excellence.

label: Evaluate
body: Chain the conditionals: moral virtue requires moral excellence, which requires repeatedly overcoming inclinations to do wrong. So every morally virtuous person has repeatedly overcome such inclinations — meaning they must have had inclinations to do wrong in the first place.

label: Goal
body: Find the answer that follows logically from connecting these statements.

label: Given
body: To be morally excellent, you have to keep overcoming the urge to do bad things. To be morally virtuous, you have to achieve moral excellence. And overcoming those urges is hard — even for virtuous people.

label: Evaluate
body: Connect the dots: virtuous people achieved moral excellence, which means they repeatedly overcame inclinations to do wrong. You cannot overcome an inclination you never had. So every virtuous person has, at some point, wanted to do the wrong thing. Virtue is not the absence of temptation — it is winning the fight against it.

label: Goal
body: Find the answer that captures this logical consequence: every morally virtuous person has been inclined to do wrong.

label: Conclusion
body: Emotion is not nonrational.

label: Intermediate Conclusion
body: Emotion only seems nonrational way because language lacks the ability to convey adequate conceptions of emotion.

label: Evidence
body: The words we use to refer to emotions name only very general kinds of inner experience, such as excitement / calm / joy, but there is no language for describing just how one joy differs from another.

label: Evaluate
body: Whenever we do Main Conclusion / Role, we listen for Rebuttal/Pivot conclusions (most of them are that style) or First Sentence conclusions (the 2nd most common style). Since this paragraph begins with an Attribution, "Philosophers usually think of emotions as X", we'd be waiting for a Pivot + Pushback, and so when we see "But emotion is not nonrational", we most likely have our rebuttal conclusion. Everything after that is support for the main conclusion. They're asking us about the last sentence, which is hella confusing because it's prefaced by Thus (which usually indicates conclusion) and by "for example" (which always indicates support). How can the last claim be a conclusion and a premise?! We need to remember that premise/conclusion indicator words can also be used to indicate Cause/Effect. "Since I have the flu, I have a fever." / "I have the flu. Thus, I have a fever." That's why we see a Thus in front of this supporting idea. The previous sentence causes this last claim to be true. The fact that we have words for only general emotional states is why we don't have specific words for different types of joy.

label: Goal
body: We know this final claim plays a supporting role, and we know that the main conclusion is "Emotion is not nonrational", that's good enough to head to the answers.

label: Conclusion
body: Emotion is not nonrational — it only seems that way because language cannot adequately convey emotions.

label: Evidence
body: Words for emotions name only general kinds of experience. For example, there is no language for describing how one joy differs from another.

label: Evaluate
body: The statement in the question stem — about one joy not being describable as different from another — is an example supporting the general claim about language's limitations. It is evidence, not the conclusion.

label: Goal
body: Find the answer that correctly identifies this statement as a specific example illustrating the general claim about language, which in turn supports the conclusion.

label: Conclusion
body: Emotions are not nonrational. They just seem that way because the available words are too blunt to capture them properly.

label: Evidence
body: Emotion-words like "joy," "excitement," and "calm" are hopelessly general. Case in point: there is no way to describe how one experience of joy differs from another. The word "joy" covers everything from finding a parking spot to holding a newborn.

label: Evaluate
body: The target statement — no language for distinguishing joys — is a concrete example backing up the general claim. Do not let "thus" fool you into thinking it is the conclusion. "For example" immediately overrides that and confirms it is illustrative evidence. The conclusion is up top: emotions are not nonrational.

label: Goal
body: Find the answer that says this statement is a specific illustration of a general claim, used to support the conclusion.

label: Given
body: Superstring theory is a controversial new theory in physics. Superstring theory is unlike more established physical theories in that it purports to explain the nature and existence of gravity. A major problem with superstring theory is that to test it we would have to build a particle accelerator 100 trillion kilometers long. Another problem is that superstring theory has had no success in adequately explaining why the force of gravity is not stronger or weaker than it is.

label: Evaluate
body: It's interesting that superstring theory is controversial and unlike more established theories. People who study it are probably fun to hang out with. But the statements seem to mainly focus on the goal of superstring theory—to explain the nature and existence of gravity—and on two problems with superstring theory. We would expect an answer to focus on those details.

label: Goal
body: There aren't any clear conditional or quantified statements to link. We'll look for answers that seem closely related to the information we've been given, and watch out for incorrect answers that bring in irrelevant or unsupported details.

label: Given
body: Superstring theory is a controversial new physics theory that, unlike more established theories, claims to explain gravity's nature and existence. Two problems: testing requires a 100-trillion-kilometer accelerator, and it has not adequately explained gravity's strength.

label: Evaluate
body: The stimulus presents facts about superstring theory's goals and shortcomings. The theory aims to explain gravity but cannot explain gravity's strength, which is identified as a "problem." This suggests that failing to account for a force's strength is a deficiency for a theory claiming to explain that force.

label: Goal
body: Find the answer best supported by these facts without going beyond what is stated.

label: Given
body: Superstring theory wants to explain gravity. Big ambition. Two problems: you would need a particle accelerator roughly the diameter of the solar system to test it, and it cannot even explain why gravity is the strength it is.

label: Evaluate
body: The theory says "it can explain gravity" and then cannot explain one of gravity's most basic properties — its strength. And the stimulus calls that a "problem." So apparently, if a theory claims to explain a force, it should be able to account for how strong it is. That seems like a reasonable inference the stimulus is nudging toward.

label: Goal
body: Find the answer that captures this principle: claiming to explain a force but failing to explain its strength is a deficiency.

label: Evidence
body: The number of commercially successful short documentary films is smaller than the number of commercially successful full-length science-fiction films. There are more short documentary films than there are science-fiction films.

label: Conclusion
body: The proportion of full-length science-fiction films that are commercially successful is higher the proportion of short documentary films that are commercially successful.

label: Evaluate
body: It can be helpful to rephrase the statements in this argument as we've done here, hopefully stating them in a clearer way. When dealing with a question like this, we might also take some notes: `# com succ short doc < # com succ FL sci-fi`, `# short doc > # sci-fi`, Therefore, `% com succ FL sci-fi > % com succ short doc`. Notice that the argument starts with evidence based on the number of films of each type, then switches to a conclusion about proportions of films in each type. This could indicate a flaw, but let's not worry about that for a moment. We should also note that the evidence first mentions full-length science-fiction films, then switches to discussing science-fiction films in general.

label: Goal
body: We'll look for answers that contain these same patterns in the evidence and conclusion. We can dig deeper to identify any flaws in this argument so we can match those to the correct answer choice, but let's only do that if we need to.

label: Evidence
body: Fewer short documentary films than full-length science-fiction films are commercially successful. There are more short documentary films than science-fiction films total.

label: Conclusion
body: A higher proportion of full-length science-fiction films than of short documentary films are commercially successful.

label: Evaluate
body: The argument moves from raw numbers to proportions. Also note the shift from "full-length science-fiction films" in the first premise to just "science-fiction films" in the second. The correct answer must match both the reasoning pattern and any term shifts.

label: Goal
body: Find the answer with the same structure: fewer of A than B are X, more A than B exist total, therefore a higher proportion of B than A are X — with a parallel modifier shift.

label: Evidence
body: More sci-fi films succeed commercially than documentaries, but there are more documentaries in total than sci-fi films.

label: Conclusion
body: Therefore, sci-fi films have a higher commercial success rate. Makes sense — fewer successes from a bigger pool means a lower rate.

label: Evaluate
body: The reasoning is straightforward, but watch for the sneaky term shift: "full-length science-fiction films" in one premise becomes just "science-fiction films" in the next. The correct answer needs to match both the numbers-to-proportions logic and this kind of modifier shift.

label: Goal
body: Find the answer that walks the same logical path with the same term shift pattern.

label: Opposing Evidence
body: During a study, a group of subjects receiving vitamin C had less severe acne than did the control group, which received a placebo.

label: Evidence
body: Half of the subjects in each group knew which kind of pill they were given. Among those who could not tell [which pill they were given], no difference in the severity of acne was found between the two groups.

label: Conclusion
body: We can tentatively conclude that vitamin C has no real benefit in reducing the severity of acne.

label: Evaluate
body: Let's make sure that we're clear about what happened to the different groups that are compared in this study. We know that some subjects who received vitamin C had less severe acne than those who received a placebo. Among the subjects who didn't know which kind of pill they were given, there was no difference in the severity of acne. This means that the subjects who received vitamin C and also had less severe acne all knew that they were taking vitamin C, not a placebo. At first, the study seems to show a correlation between taking vitamin C and a reduction in acne. That's evidence—not proof, but evidence—that vitamin C reduces acne. But wait! There's a problem with the study. If people knew which pill they were taking, that could affect the results somehow. From this the argument concludes—at least tentatively—that vitamin C does not help reduce the severity of acne. This looks like an "unproven vs. proven false" flaw. Because this one particular study had a problem, it hasn't necessarily proven that vitamin C helps treat acne. But it's still possible that vitamin C does help treat acne, even if this one study hasn't proven that it does. We can't jump from the details of this one study to a general claim about the benefits of vitamin C.

label: Goal
body: A correct answer might provide evidence that the vitamin C actually did help to reduce subjects' acne, in spite of the apparent problem with the way the study was conducted.

label: Conclusion
body: Vitamin C has no real benefit in reducing acne severity.

label: Evaluate
body: The argument attributes the initial positive results to a placebo-like effect — subjects who knew they were taking vitamin C may have experienced psychological benefits. But this reasoning assumes the two groups started with comparable acne severity. If the vitamin C group had worse acne to begin with, the fact that their acne was less severe during the study is more impressive.

label: Goal
body: Find an answer that undermines the conclusion by suggesting vitamin C actually did help, despite the study's complications.

label: Conclusion
body: Vitamin C does not actually help with acne. The study's positive results were all in people's heads.

label: Evidence
body: The vitamin C group did better overall, but half the subjects knew what they were taking. When you look only at the people who did not know, there was no difference. So the argument chalks it up to placebo effect.

label: Evaluate
body: The argument makes a sneaky assumption: that both groups started with equally bad acne. But what if the vitamin C group had worse acne from the start? Then ending up at the same level as the control group would actually be evidence that vitamin C works — it just brought them down to baseline. The study's design flaw does not automatically mean the vitamin C did nothing.

label: Goal
body: Find the answer that gives a reason to believe vitamin C actually helped, despite the messy study design.

label: Conclusion
body: Many people who simply enjoy listening to popular music do not realize that it has been used to express religious and political messages.

label: Intermediate Conclusion (After all)
body: Popular music has repeatedly been adopted by social movements to express their viewpoints.

label: Evidence (since)
body: [Popular music] has the potential to contribute to the "conversion" of nonmembers to the movement's position, as well as to raise the morale and to express the solidarity of the movement's participants.

label: Evaluate
body: This is a three-layer argument. The phrase "after all" tells us that what follows is support for the sentence before it — so the first sentence is the main conclusion and the "after all" clause is an intermediate conclusion. Within that clause, the word "since" introduces even deeper support — the evidence that feeds into the intermediate conclusion. The chain flows upward: music can convert/raise morale/express solidarity (premise) → social movements have adopted music (intermediate conclusion) → people don't realize music carries these messages (main conclusion). On Main Conclusion questions, identify the claim that everything else supports but that itself supports nothing further.

label: Goal
body: Look for an answer that captures the main conclusion — the first sentence about people not realizing popular music has been used for religious and political messaging. Watch out for answers that restate a premise or the intermediate conclusion instead.

label: Conclusion (Clearly)
body: Smith's proposed ordinance does not even merit consideration.

label: Evidence
body: He's currently proposing a new city ordinance prohibiting "bait-and-switch", but four years ago he owned an appliance store that was famous for its use of bait-and-switch.

label: Evaluate
body: Whenever we're doing Flaw and we see a Rebuttal style argument, we consider the 2 of the 10 Famous Flaws that deal with rebuttals: Ad Hominem - This refers to when an author dismisses an argument because the source of the argument has a biased interest or conflicting past behavior. Unproven vs. Proven False - This refers to when an author argues that "because there's no evidence for X, or because someone's attempt to prove X failed, that shows that X is false". This looks to be an example of Ad Hominem. The author isn't saying that Smith's claim is false, so it couldn't be Unproven vs. Proven False. She's just dismissing his view, saying "it doesn't even merit consideration". And why? Because of Smith's conflicting past behavior. We should never reject someone's suggestion that we do Y just because that person used to say/do the opposite of Y. People and circumstances can change. Maybe there was someone who was really into cryptocurrency when it first came out but now is against it because of how bad its energy demands are for the environment. We can't say, "Don't listen to that crypto-critic. After all, he was way into Bitcoin when it first came out."

label: Goal
body: Look for an answer describing this famous flaw; often it sounds like "the author dismisses an argument because of its source rather than its content". Otherwise, it might be a more specific answer that says, "because Person X did thing A in the past, we shouldn't listen to X's idea to do away with thing A."

label: Conclusion
body: Smith's proposed ordinance prohibiting bait-and-switch does not merit consideration.

label: Evidence
body: Four years ago, Smith owned a store famous for using bait-and-switch tactics.

label: Evaluate
body: The president rejects the ordinance entirely based on who proposed it, not based on any problem with the ordinance itself. This is a textbook ad hominem attack — dismissing a proposal because of its source rather than evaluating its merits.

label: Goal
body: Identify the flaw: attacking the source of the proposal rather than its content.

label: Conclusion
body: The council president's verdict: Smith's anti-bait-and-switch ordinance is not even worth looking at.

label: Evidence
body: Smith used to own a store that was basically the bait-and-switch hall of fame. So, apparently, that disqualifies him from having opinions about bait-and-switch forever.

label: Evaluate
body: This is the logical equivalent of dismissing a former burglar's recommendation to install better locks. Maybe the person is a hypocrite — but the locks would still work. The president is not saying anything is wrong with the ordinance itself. The entire objection is: "Look who is talking!" That is not an argument against the proposal; that is an argument against the proposer. The ordinance could be the best piece of consumer protection legislation ever drafted, and the president would still reject it because Smith wrote it.

label: Goal
body: Spot the answer that calls out this source-versus-content confusion.

label: Conclusion (Thus)
body: These bovines had been domesticated and the people living in the region were no longer exclusively hunter-gatherers.

label: Evidence
body: These bovine were found in a region with humans and no other large mammals. If there had been a natural source of water available to these bovines, then there would have been other large mammals in the area.

label: Evaluate
body:
There is a mini-Inference problem we should do with the two premises. There's a conditional statement:
```
Natural source of → other large mammals
water was available in the area
```
And we are factually told that there are not large mammals in the area. So by contrapositive we know that there was not a natural source of water. The author is thinking that if there were bovines and humans and no other mammals and an unnatural source of water, this sounds like agriculture! It sounds like humans were irrigating water (an unnatural source of water) and domesticating livestock like bovines (bovines are cows / bulls).

label: Goal
body: The argument is making a Linking move that since there wasn't any natural water available to these bovines, they must have been living with humans, so they must have been domesticated. And the author's also assuming that if humans were domesticating cows, then they weren't exclusively nomadic hunter-gatherers. The argument is also making Defender assumptions, such as "there isn't some other reason why we found bovine remains in this area".

label: Conclusion
body: The bovines were domesticated, and the people in the region were no longer exclusively hunter-gatherers.

label: Evidence
body: Bovine remains were found in an arid region. People were there, but no other large mammals. Any natural water sources would have attracted other large mammals.

label: Evaluate
body: The argument reasons: no natural water was available (since other large mammals were absent), yet bovines were present. This implies the bovines got water from humans — meaning they were domesticated. But this only works if wild bovines could not survive without natural water sources, i.e., they need the same water that would attract other mammals.

label: Conclusion
body: These bovines were domesticated, and the locals had graduated from the hunter-gatherer lifestyle.

label: Evidence
