body: Ancient arid Africa. Bovine bones. People around, but zero other large mammals. Any natural water source would have been a large-mammal magnet. So no water means no wild large mammals — but somehow bovines were still there.

label: Evaluate
body: The detective work here is clever: no other large mammals means no natural water, yet bovines were present. Someone must have been keeping those bovines alive — and it was not the rain. But this logic only holds if bovines are the type of animal that would normally need natural water to survive. If bovines could just tough it out in the desert on their own, their presence proves nothing about domestication. The argument is quietly assuming bovines are not some sort of camel-like exception to the large-mammal water rule.

label: Goal
body: Find the answer that plugs this gap: bovines cannot make it without water in the wild, so humans must have been providing it.

label: Given
body: Economists argue that the higher turnover rate of part-time workers shows them to be much more likely to be dissatisfied with their jobs than full-time workers are. Economists also argue that lower-paid, part-time workers threaten to take jobs from full-time employees. But because job efficiency is positively correlated with job satisfaction, companies are unlikely to replace satisfied employees with dissatisfied ones.

label: Evaluate / Goal
body: Since we're told that part-time workers are more likely to be dissatisfied with their jobs than full-time workers, and companies are unlikely to replace satisfied employees with dissatisfied ones, we might conclude that companies are unlikely to replace full-time employees with part-time employees. This suggests that the economists' second claim about part-time workers taking jobs from full-time workers is unlikely to be true. But wait! This is assuming that the economists first claim about part-time workers being dissatisfied is true. We don't actually know that. So, a possible conclusion is that one of the two claims argued by economists is true and the other isn't.

label: Argument Setup
body: Economists claim (1) part-time workers' higher turnover shows greater dissatisfaction, and (2) lower-paid part-timers threaten full-time jobs. Cerrato responds: job efficiency correlates with job satisfaction, so companies are unlikely to replace satisfied employees with dissatisfied ones.

label: Logic
body: Cerrato is using the economists' own dissatisfaction claim against their job-threat claim. If part-timers are dissatisfied, they are less efficient. Companies would not replace efficient, satisfied full-timers with inefficient, dissatisfied part-timers.

label: Goal
body: Complete the conclusion: the blank must follow from Cerrato's reasoning that dissatisfied part-timers will not replace full-timers because they are less efficient.

label: Argument Setup
body: The economists are trying to have it both ways: part-timers are miserable at their jobs, AND they are about to steal all the full-time positions. Cerrato calls the bluff. If part-timers are so unhappy, they are less efficient. And what company is going to fire its happy, productive full-timers to hire unhappy, unproductive part-timers? The economists' own evidence defeats their own conclusion.

label: Logic
body: It is a beautiful judo move: the harder the economists push the "part-timers are dissatisfied" claim, the weaker the "part-timers will take full-time jobs" claim becomes. Dissatisfaction equals inefficiency equals no reason to hire them over the people already doing the job well.

label: Goal
body: The conclusion needs to capture the punchline: the dissatisfied part-timers the economists are worried about are the last people who would replace full-timers.

label: Given that...
body: On the plains where it lives, an individual zebra stands out because of its black-and-white stripes, which contrast with the green or brown of the surrounding vegetation. Zebras are a prey species, and the lions that hunt them can see stripes clearly.

label: How can it be that...
body: Zebras survive with such vivid markings.

label: Evidence
body: All keyboards and most monitors were positioned too high for children, causing craned necks, awkward wrists, and other unhealthy postures. Most computers are installed without considering posture effects.

label: Conclusion
body: Does not matter whether you see a specialist or a general practitioner for physical therapy — your odds are the same either way.

label: Evaluate
body: It seems that the zebra's stripes aren't helping them hide from lions. Instead, the stripes seem to be saying, "hey Simba, check it out! There's a zebra right here! Lunch time!" But wait? Can lions see colors? We're told that the black-and-white stripes stand out against the green or brown of vegetation. Would that matter if lions mostly see in black-and-white or shades of gray? What if a lion can "see stripes clearly," but zebra stripes make the zebras look like part of the background. (Fun note: this might be how a tiger's flashy stripes work. They blend in amazingly well with tall brown grasses.) Maybe the stripes don't prevent a lion from seeing a zebra, but the stripe pattern confuses the lion, making it more difficult for a lion to catch a zebra even if it can see one. (Fun fact: sharks are apparently confused by black-and-white stripes, and less likely to bite something which has that pattern.)

label: Goal
body: A correct answer might indicate that a zebra's stripes do help them hide because of some fact about the vision of lions or other predators. A correct answer might also indicate that the stripes help zebras survive in some way other than by making them hard to see.

label: Paradox
body: Zebras have vivid black-and-white stripes that contrast sharply with the surrounding vegetation. Lions, their predators, can see these stripes clearly. Yet zebras survive as a prey species despite this apparent visibility disadvantage.

label: Goal
body: Find an explanation for how zebras survive despite being highly visible to their predators. The answer must show that the stripes, rather than being a pure disadvantage, provide some survival benefit or that some other factor compensates.

label: Paradox
body: Zebras are nature's most conspicuous dinner option. Black-and-white stripes against green and brown grass? That is basically wearing a neon sign that says "eat me" in lion. And lions can see the stripes perfectly well. Yet somehow zebras are not extinct. How are they pulling this off?

label: Goal
body: Find the answer that explains the zebra's survival magic trick. Something must be offsetting the fact that they look like walking targets.

label: Information
body:
```
comparison (tends to be higher)
(tends to)
Dark honey > light colored honey
ANTI-OXIDANTS
superlative/conditional (most healthful, all)
Most healthful → unusually high
honey       in anti-oxi
pivot (however)
Some strains of honey (from sage nectar) are most healthful but light-colored.
```

label: Evaluate
body: Can we combine any of these facts? The first two claims both talked about anti-oxidants, so it was tempting to think, "Since dark honey as more antioxi's, and since the most healthful are high in antioxi's, maybe the most healthful are dark?" But then the pivot at the end says, "Not so fast -- some of the most healthful is light colored." Because of "most healthful" repeating in the final sentence, we know we can swap in the idea of "unusually high in antioxidants". So we could infer that "some light honey / some honey harvested primarily from sage nectar is unusually high in antioxidants".

label: Goal
body: Let's look for the most provable answer choice.

label: Premises
body: (1) Dark honey tends to have higher antioxidant content than light honey. (2) The most healthful honey strains are all unusually high in antioxidants. (3) Certain sage-nectar strains are among the most healthful yet also among the lightest-colored.

label: Goal
body: Find the answer that must be true (or is most strongly supported) given these premises. The key inference: since sage-nectar strains are among the most healthful, and the most healthful are all unusually high in antioxidants, sage-nectar strains must be unusually high in antioxidants — despite being light-colored.

label: Premises
body: Dark honey: more antioxidants. Most healthful honey: loaded with antioxidants. Sage-nectar honey: among the most healthful AND among the lightest. Wait — light honey with high health value? That breaks the dark-equals-healthy trend.

label: Goal
body: Connect the dots: sage honey is among the most healthful, and the most healthful all have tons of antioxidants. So sage honey must have tons of antioxidants — even though it is light-colored. It is the exception that proves the trend is just a trend, not a rule. Find the answer that captures this inference without going overboard.

label: Conclusion (thus)
body: Children are put at the same risk for repetitive stress injuries as office workers.

label: Intermediate Conclusion (Evidently)
body: Most elementary school computers are installed without consideration of their effect on students' posture.

label: Evidence
body: In a study, all the keyboards and most monitors were placed higher than recommended for children, leading children to sit in ways that encourage craned necks, awkward wrists, and other unhealthy postures.

label: Evaluate
body: The argument makes two conclusions, so we should scrutinize each of those reasoning moves. Given that ... all the keyboards and most monitors were installed in positions higher than what's recommended for kids (giving them bad postures while using the computers), How can we argue ... most elementary school computers are installed with consideration of their effect on posture? We'd have to make up some story for why someone would consider the effect on kids' posture of installing the computers that high but do it anyway. Maybe they hate kids. Maybe they don't want kids to have too much screen time, so they want using a computer to be slightly uncomfortable. Maybe adults also need to use these computers at times, so the computers were installed in a position that tries to balance the needs of both body types. Given that ... most elementary school computers are installed without consideration of their effect on posture, How can we argue ... this does not put children at the same risk for repetitive stress injuries as office workers? We would want to make it seem like the situation with kids is different from the situation with office workers. Presumably, kids don't use the computer for as much time as adults do, so can we really say they're at the "same risk"?

label: Goal
body: Look for an Alternate Explanation for why computers are installed in a non-kid-friendly way, an answer that makes it seem like the computer-installers do consider kids' posture, or an answer that makes it seem like the situation with kids in computer labs is not fair to equate with office workers getting repetitive stress injuries.

label: Conclusion
body: Elementary school computers put children at the same risk for repetitive stress injuries (RSI) as office workers.

label: Evaluate
body: The argument assumes that similar posture problems produce similar injury risks. But the conclusion specifically compares children to office workers — it needs the comparison to hold, not just the posture problems to exist.

label: Goal
body: Find an answer that breaks the link between "same bad posture" and "same injury risk." If something makes children less vulnerable than adults to the same postural problems, the comparison to office workers fails.

label: Conclusion
body: Kids using badly positioned school computers face the same RSI risk as office workers hunched over their keyboards all day.

label: Evidence
body: The study found keyboards and monitors set way too high for children, forcing them into the same kind of pretzel postures that give office workers carpal tunnel and neck problems.

label: Evaluate
body: Same bad posture equals same injury risk? Not necessarily. The argument assumes children's bodies react to postural stress the same way adult bodies do. If there is something about being a kid that makes those awkward postures less dangerous, the whole comparison to office workers collapses.

label: Goal
body: Find the answer that drives a wedge between "same posture" and "same risk" by identifying a relevant biological difference.

label: Given
body: (According to some anthropologists) cultures can most effectively respond to the threat of cultural decay by replacing or abandoning many of their traditions so that other traditions may endure. But each of its traditions is essential to a culture's identity.

label: Evaluate
body: If each of a culture's traditions is essential to a culture's identity, what will happen if a culture replaces or abandons many of their traditions? It seems like this will damage the culture's identity. "Cultural decay" seems like it would be a loss of cultural identity. So, the evidence that we're given seems to indicate that the anthropologists are wrong: replacing or abandoning many traditions so that others may endure is not an effective way to respond to a threat of cultural decay.

label: Goal
body: A correct answer might indicate that this strategy of replacing or abandoning many traditions is not an effective response to the threat of cultural decay, or more generally the strategy is likely to harm a culture.

label: Argument Setup
body: Anthropologists propose that cultures should replace or abandon many traditions so other traditions can survive. The sociologist responds: each tradition is essential to a culture's identity.

label: Logic
body: If every tradition is essential to cultural identity, then abandoning any tradition destroys part of the culture's identity. Abandoning many traditions would not save the culture — it would eliminate it. The "cure" is worse than the disease.

label: Goal
body: Complete the sentence: this strategy will not prevent decay but will instead destroy the culture outright, since every abandoned tradition removes an essential part of what makes the culture what it is.

label: Argument Setup
body: Anthropologists: "To save your culture, throw out a bunch of traditions and keep the rest!" Sociologist: "But every tradition IS the culture."

label: Logic
body: If every tradition is essential, then ripping out "many" of them is not cultural preservation — it is cultural demolition. It is like saying "to save this building, let us tear down most of the load-bearing walls." You will not have a renovated building. You will have a pile of rubble. The strategy designed to prevent decay actually guarantees destruction.

label: Goal
body: The blank needs to deliver the punchline: this strategy will kill the patient rather than cure it.

label: Conclusion (Therefore)
body: A successful legal system prohibits only those few behaviors that citizens find absolute intolerable.

label: Evidence
body: The purpose of laws in a legal system is to deter bad actions by threatening punishment if you perform them, but this only works if people think they're likely to get punished for committing those actions, and the more behaviors that are criminalized, the less likely someone will be caught and punished.

label: Evaluate
body: When we read Role and Main Conclusion we anticipate the conclusion being "hidden" by appearing as the First Sentence or as some Rebuttal / Pivot moment. But this first sentence is not supported, so it can't be a conclusion. And the pivot sentence prefaced by "But" is also not supported, so it can't be a conclusion. Meanwhile, we have a very conspicuous conclusion indicator on the last sentence (we know any time we see so, thus, hence, therefore that it will be a conclusion, even if it's not the main one). But in this case, it's the main conclusion, because the other three ideas combine to get us there. Why do successful legal systems want to limit the number of criminalized actions to the most intolerable ones? Because laws only work as a threat if people think they're likely to be caught and punished, and the more actions we criminalize the less likely people are to be caught / punished.

label: Goal
body: We're being asked about the Role of the first claim. We'd say it's part of the Support for the conclusion in the final sentence.

label: Argument Structure
body: The argument builds a chain: (P1) Laws deter by threatening punishment. (P2) The threat only works if violators believe punishment is likely. (P3) Likelihood of punishment decreases as prohibited acts increase. (C) A successful system prohibits only a few intolerable behaviors.

label: Role of Statement
body: The statement that "the purpose of a law is to deter certain actions by threatening to punish those performing the actions" is the first premise in the chain. It is not the conclusion — it is the starting point from which the argument builds toward the conclusion about limiting prohibited behaviors.

label: Argument Structure
body: The scholar builds a logical domino chain: Laws work by scaring people into compliance. But the scare only works if people think they will actually get caught. And the more things you make illegal, the harder it is to catch anyone. So if you want your legal system to work, keep the rule book short.

label: Role of Statement
body: The statement about law's purpose being deterrence is the first domino — the premise that kicks off the whole chain. It is not the destination; it is the starting point. Everything else builds on top of this foundational claim about what law is for.

label: Evidence
body: In the 14th and 15th centuries, the Swahilis built tombs with big pillars and paneled outsides. Those types of tombs are also super common among the Oromo, who were in contact with Swahili. But no other culture known to have mixed with the Swahili has these types of tombs.

label: Evaluate
body: There is a curious fact — how come both the Oromo and the Swahili both have this style of tomb? The author's causal explanation is that the Oromo invented that style and then influenced the Swahili, who 'copied' that style. We can object that the author is being overconfident in settling on that causal storyline, when there could be other ways to explain it. Maybe the Swahili invented the style and the Oromo copied it from them. Normally, we'd say, "maybe they both copied it from some 3rd culture", but it says that no other culture the Swahili was in contact with had this style of tomb. It could be that both cultures just happened to coincidentally start the same style, without being influenced by each other.

label: Goal
body: The answer will deal with an Alternate Explanation for how Oromo and Swahili both ended up with that distinctive style of tomb, or it will deal with the plausibility of the author's story that the Oromo created the style and then influenced Swahili culture to use the same style.

label: Conclusion
body: Swahili culture was, to some extent, influenced by Oromo culture.

label: Evidence
body: Swahili civilization built tombs with large pillars and paneled facades. The Oromo people have such structures. No other group the Swahili contacted had them.

label: Evaluate
body: The historian assumes the Oromo had these structures before the Swahili did. But the argument only shows both groups share the feature — it does not establish who had it first. The influence could have gone in either direction.

label: Goal
body: Identify the flaw: the argument assumes directionality of influence without establishing which group built the structures first.

label: Conclusion
body: The Swahili got their architectural ideas from the Oromo.

label: Evidence
body: Both groups built the same distinctive tombs, and nobody else the Swahili knew did.

label: Evaluate
body: Okay, so the Swahili and Oromo share a unique building style. But who copied whom? The historian just assumed the arrow points from Oromo to Swahili. What if the Swahili invented the style and the Oromo picked it up? Shared features prove connection, not direction. The historian skipped the crucial "who had it first" question.

label: Goal
body: Spot the answer about the missing temporal evidence — who built these structures first?

label: Conclusion
body: The chorus in a play is not equivalent to the narrator in a novel.

label: Evidence (since)
body: The information introduced by the chorus in a play is sometimes inconsistent with the rest of the information in th eplay.

label: Evaluate
body: This argument is pretty sparse. It's mostly background until we hit the however pivot, and then the author says, "X and Y are not the same, since X does thing A." Okay, so what's being assumed in that case? The author is Assuming a Difference. If she's saying, "the fact that X does thing A proves that X and Y are not the same", she must think that "Y does not do thing A". If I said, "The fact that Max owns a Lebron jersey shows that Max and Karen are not equally fans of Lebron", I would be assuming that "Karen doesn't own a Lebron jersey" (among other things). The author said, "since the chorus introduces inconsistent info, it's not the same as a narrator."

label: Goal
body: So let's look for an answer saying, "narrators do not introduce information in a novel that is inconsistent with the rest of the novel".

label: Conclusion
body: The chorus in a play is not equivalent to the narrator in a novel.

label: Evidence
body: Both chorus and narrator introduce a point of view and contextual information. However, the chorus in a play sometimes provides information inconsistent with the rest of the play.

label: Evaluate
body: The argument uses the chorus's potential inconsistency as the distinguishing factor. But this only works as a differentiator if narrators in novels are NEVER inconsistent. If narrators could also be inconsistent, the inconsistency would not be a meaningful difference.

label: Goal
body: Find the answer that plugs this gap: the narrator in a novel cannot be inconsistent with the rest of the novel, which makes the chorus's potential inconsistency a genuine difference.

label: Conclusion
body: The play's chorus is not the same as a novel's narrator — even though they look similar on paper.

label: Evidence
body: Sure, both do similar jobs: introducing outside perspectives and context. But the chorus sometimes contradicts the rest of the play. And apparently, that makes it fundamentally different from a narrator.

label: Evaluate
body: Wait — does it? The argument uses inconsistency as its trump card for proving non-equivalence. But that only works if narrators are never inconsistent. If novel narrators can also contradict the rest of their story, then the chorus's inconsistency is not special at all — it is just something both do. The argument needs narrators to be the reliable ones for this comparison to hold.

label: Goal
body: Find the answer that says narrators cannot be inconsistent with their novels — which is what makes the chorus's inconsistency a real difference rather than a shared feature.

label: Conclusion
body: This move (moving some of the rare pygmy bears should be moved from their native island to the neighboring island.

label: Intermediate Conclusion
body: This move represents the only viable chance of saving these valuable animals.

label: Evidence (since)
body: The bears risk extinction from the loss of habitat on their native island. The neighboring island is the only place that has a similar habitat.

label: Evaluate
body: We're trying to justify a decision to move bears from their home island to a neighboring island. The motivating concerns are these: 1. their habitat on the home island is disappearing 2. the neighboring island is the only place with a similar habitat 3. moving them is the only chance we have of saving these valuable animals

label: Goal
body: Let's look for answer choices that pair up language from any one (or more) of our supporting concerns with the conclusion's language of "we should do it". For example, "If X's native habitat is disappearing, then we should move X to a place with a similar habitat". "If X is a valuable animal, then we should do whatever is our only viable chance of saving them".

label: Conclusion
body: Some pygmy bears should be moved to a neighboring island.

label: Evidence
body: The bears face extinction from habitat loss. The neighboring island is the only place with similar habitat, making the move the only viable chance of saving them.

label: Goal
body: Find a principle that justifies the reasoning: when a species faces extinction and there is only one viable chance to save it, that option should be pursued.

label: Conclusion
body: Move some pygmy bears to the neighboring island.

label: Evidence
body: They are going extinct. The neighboring island is the only spot with the right habitat. It is their one shot.

label: Goal
body: Find the general principle that says: when a species is about to be wiped out and there is exactly one option to save it, you should take that option. The argument is basically saying "this is the only lifeboat, so get on it."

label: Conclusion (prediction = opinion)
body: Widespread use of encryption software will bring the writing of biographical history virtually to an end.

label: Intermediate Conclusion (so)
body: The most interesting, revealing source material for a biography will be unavailable to historians unless they have the necessary passwords.

label: Evidence
body: When historians write biographical history, their principal sources are often the private correspondence and diaries of the public figure. These confidential writings will more likely be stored as encrypted text in the future, meaning they will be password protected.

label: Evaluate
body: Whenever we do Main Conclusion (or Role), we read the paragraph with a different mindset, because we know that 90% of the time the conclusion is going to be earlier than the evidence. Specifically, the conclusion is usually: - the first sentence, or - some Pivot / Rebuttal sentence. So we read the first sentence, actively asking ourselves, "Is this the Conclusion? Does it sound like the paragraph starts with an opinion from the author?" The first sentence here is a prediction, which is by definition an opinion. Does the author proceed to defend / support that prediction? She does. So we know that the first sentence is the overarching conclusion.

label: Goal
body: We just need a meaning-match for the first sentence.

label: Conclusion
body: The widespread use of encryption software will bring biographical history writing virtually to an end.

label: Evidence
body: Private correspondence and diaries are biographers' principal sources. In the future, most such documents will be encrypted. Historians will not have the necessary passwords, so the most interesting material will be unavailable.

label: Evaluate
body: The first sentence states the main conclusion. Everything that follows provides the causal chain explaining why: encryption leads to inaccessible documents, which leads to the end of biographical history.

label: Conclusion
body: Encryption is going to kill biographical history. Done. Game over for biographers.

label: Evidence
body: Biographers depend on private letters and diaries that eventually become public. But in the future, all those juicy documents will be locked behind passwords that historians will never have. No documents, no biographies.

label: Evaluate
body: The argument is a domino chain: encryption locks documents, locked documents are inaccessible, inaccessible documents mean no biographies. The first sentence announces the grand conclusion; the rest explains the mechanism. Do not confuse the steps in the chain with the final destination.

label: Conclusion (Hence)
body: There are celestial objects in this galaxy that generate light but are not stars.

label: Evidence
body: Stars generate light. Planets do not generate light. There are many other celestial objects in this galaxy that are not planets.

label: Evaluate
body:
This argument is so bad that it's hard to understand what the author is going for. She establishes a difference between stars and planets (the former generates light and the latter doesn't). Then she affirms that there are other celestial objects besides stars and planets. Then she concludes these other objects (or at least some of them) are like stars, rather than like planets, when it comes to generating light. Why? Why wouldn't we just as easily assume that the other objects are like planets and don't generate light? She seems to be assuming that planets are uniquely the celestial objects that don't generate light and that all the other celestial objects do. Her argument could be thought of as an illegal negation:
```
Planet → does not generate light
Some X's are not Planets.
Hence, Some X's do generate light.
```
She's arguing, "if there are other celestial objects that aren't planets, then there are other celestial objects that do generate light", which means she's assuming, "If it's not a planet, then it does generate light".

label: Goal
body: We could potentially call out this Illegal Negation with an answer saying the author is confusing a condition that's sufficient to show you don't generate light (being a planet) with one that's necessary. However, since this question stem prefaced with "fails to consider" they might weaken the Nec vs. Suff error the "conversational" way, where we object to the conditional relationship the author is imagining by saying that the Left side could be true while the Right side is false. This author is imagining that "If it's not a planet, then it generates light". So we can say she fails to consider that something could be the Left side but not the Right side (something could be "not a planet" but not be "something that generates light"). Or we could just complain that the author presents two celestial objects (stars and planets), one that does generate light and one that doesn't. Then she assumes that a 3rd category of celestial objects ("other" celestial objects) belongs in the generating light category, for no apparent reason. The author fails to consider that these other celestial objects could be more like planets than they are like stars, when it comes to light-generating properties.

label: Conclusion
body: There are celestial objects in this galaxy that generate light but are not stars.

label: Evaluate
body: The argument assumes these other non-planet celestial objects must generate light. But perhaps they, like planets, only reflect light or emit no light at all. The argument treats planets as the only category of non-light-generating objects.

label: Goal
body: Find the answer identifying the overlooked possibility that some non-planet celestial objects also fail to generate light.

label: Conclusion
body: Somewhere in this galaxy, there are celestial objects that glow on their own but are not stars. The argument claims to have proven this through pure logic.

label: Evidence
body: Step one: planets are cosmic freeloaders that only reflect light. Step two: there are plenty of other non-planet objects floating around this galaxy besides stars. Therefore — and here is where the magic trick happens — those other objects must be generating light.

label: Evaluate
body: The argument treated "planets" as if they hold the exclusive patent on not generating light. Planets do not generate light, sure. But what about asteroids? Comets? Space rocks? Cosmic dust? The argument saw objects that were not planets and immediately assumed they must be lit up like Christmas trees. That is like saying "fish live in water, and there are animals in the park that are not fish, so those animals must not live in water" — completely ignoring ducks, frogs, and turtles splashing around in the pond.

label: Goal
body: Spot the answer that calls out the argument for assuming planets have a monopoly on not generating light.

label: Conclusion (Hence)
body: Our study suggests that siblings of first-born children will tend to be more adventurous than will the first-borns.

label: Evidence
body: First-born children consistently exhibit less cognitive plasticity than did their siblings. Cognitive plasticity is a willingness to accept new ideas. It's reasonable that those who are open to new ideas will be adventurous in other ways.

label: Evaluate
body: We know from the study that siblings of first-born children exhibit more cognitive plasticity. And we have the author's idea that having more cognitive plasticity will be more adventurous in other ways. So does that prove that younger siblings will tend to be more adventurous? Not totally. Perhaps our capacity for being adventurous is comprised of many factors ... cognitive plasticity might just be one of them.

label: Goal
body: It's hard to say how they'll strengthen this argument, but we can just look for more evidence that younger children (meaning "not the oldest" child) are more adventurous, or more evidence that cognitive plasticity is connected to being adventurous.

label: Conclusion
body: Siblings of first-born children will tend to be more adventurous than first-borns.

label: Evidence
body: A study found first-borns consistently showed less cognitive plasticity (willingness to accept new ideas) than their siblings.

label: Assumption
body: The psychologist bridges from cognitive plasticity to adventurousness with: "It is reasonable to think that those who are open to new ideas will be adventurous in other ways." This link between openness-to-ideas and broader adventurousness is the gap to strengthen.

label: Goal
body: Find evidence that cognitive plasticity actually correlates with adventurousness in non-intellectual domains.

label: Conclusion
body: Later-born siblings are the adventurous ones in the family — more likely to take risks and explore than their cautious, tradition-bound older siblings.

label: Evidence
body: The study found that first-borns are less willing to accept new ideas than their younger siblings. The psychologist then takes a leap: being open to new ideas probably means being adventurous in general.

label: Assumption
body: The psychologist measured one thing (willingness to consider new ideas) and predicted another (adventurous behavior). That is like measuring how much someone likes trying new restaurants and concluding they would probably go skydiving. It is "reasonable to think" the two go together, but reasonable speculation is not evidence. The argument needs something to nail down that connection.

label: Goal
body: Find the answer that provides actual evidence — not just wishful thinking — that people who are open to new ideas also tend to be adventurous in their actions.

label: Given that ...
body: Significant intellectual advances generally occur in cities or countries that have a stable political system.

label: How can it be that ...
body: Plato and Aristotle made unparalleled intellectual progress during a period of great political and social unrest?

label: Evaluate / Goal
body: This isn't really paradoxical, since the general rule in the first sentence is only saying that intellectual advances generally occur in stable political systems. That's not saying that advances only occur in stable political systems. So the fact that Plato and Aristotle are examples of advances that occurred in unstable political systems isn't really contradicting the general rule. It's just an exception. So we should probably understand our task as, "how come Plato and Aristotle were able to make their intellectual advances, despite the unstable political system?" (Maybe they were well-insulated from instability and so within the world of Plato's Academy it still felt like a stable political system)

label: The Paradox
body: Historians find that significant intellectual advances generally require political stability. Yet Plato and Aristotle achieved unparalleled intellectual progress during politically and socially unstable ancient Athens.

label: Goal
body: Find an answer that explains how Plato and Aristotle could have succeeded despite instability — reconciling the counterexample with the general rule rather than eliminating either one.

label: The Paradox
body: Historians say intellectual breakthroughs happen when things are politically calm. Then they turn around and acknowledge that Plato and Aristotle — arguably the greatest intellectual duo in human history — did their best work while Athens was in political chaos. That is like a nutritionist saying candy is terrible for you while admitting that the healthiest person they have ever met eats nothing but Skittles.

label: Goal
body: Find the answer that explains how Plato and Aristotle pulled off their intellectual achievements despite the political turmoil — without destroying the general rule or denying the facts of history.

label: Evidence (because)
body: To colonize Mars, you would have to assemble tremendous quantities of basic materials at the site of the colony. But the costs of transporting such materials through space would be so high.

label: Evaluate
body: We can predict a Linking assumption like, "If the cost of transporting basic materials through space would be super costly, then it won't be economically feasible to colonize Mars". But it's unlikely that this question is testing a Linking idea, since the argument feels more practical and real world. Hence, we should shift to our Objection thinking: Given that ... colonizing requires tons of basic materials at the site of the colony, and that transporting those materials through space would be super high. How could we argue that ... it could be economically feasible to colonize Mars? We can't get around the need for basic materials. Can we get around the cost of transporting those materials through space? What if we send a bunch of 3D printers to Mars and 3D-printed the basic materials there? What if we develop teleportation technology, so we're not transporting the materials through space but rather through some teleportation wormhole? What if we find lots of usable materials on Mars, so we don't have to transport them through space? If we gave up on that line of objection and accepted that the only way to get these needed basic materials to Mars was through expensive transportation through space, is there any way to argue that it would be economically feasible? Maybe tech companies will be so starved for the precious metals that go into computers / phones (which we've nearly exhausted on Earth) that they will be willing to pay for a colony on Mars, so that mining operations on Mars can procure them their precious metals?

label: Goal
body: Look for a Defender answer saying something like, - "We can not just use a 3D printer" - "We can not teleport materials there" - "We can not use the materials we find on Mars" - "There is not so much money to be made by colonizing Mars that companies on Earth would be willing to foot the bill for the expensive cost of transporting basic materials there"

label: Conclusion
body: It will not be economically feasible to colonize Mars.

label: Evidence
body: Establishing a colony requires assembling tremendous quantities of basic materials at the site, and transporting materials through space is extremely expensive.

label: Assumption
body: The argument assumes there is no cheaper alternative to transporting materials from Earth — specifically, that Mars itself cannot supply the necessary basic materials.

label: Goal
body: Find the assumption that, if denied, destroys the argument. If Mars could provide its own materials, the cost-of-transport problem evaporates.

label: Conclusion
body: Sorry, Elon — Mars colonization is not going to work economically.

label: Evidence
body: Building a colony requires mountains of basic materials, and shipping anything through space costs an astronomical amount (pun fully intended). You cannot build a city if you have to FedEx every brick from Earth.

label: Assumption
body: The argument treated Earth as the only Home Depot in the solar system. But what if Mars has its own building supplies? If colonists could mine Martian rocks and use local resources, the whole "transport costs are too high" argument becomes irrelevant. The argument quietly assumes Mars cannot provide what the colony needs.

label: Goal
body: Find the answer that, if you flip it around, wrecks the argument. "Mars CAN supply its own materials" would blow a hole straight through the cost-of-transport reasoning.

label: Conclusion (therefore)
body: The choice between seeing a specialist or a general practitioner for needed PT will not affect one's chances of major improvement.

label: Evidence
body: Among people who received less than six weeks of PT, 31% showed major improvement, whether they were treated by a general practitioner or a by a specialist. Among people who received more PT, again about 50% showed major improvement, regardless of whether they were treated by a general practitioner or by a specialist.

label: Evaluate
body: This conclusion is essentially anti-causal, saying it doesn't make a difference whether you're assigned to a general practitioner or to a specialist. If we were going to argue that it does make a difference which one you're assigned to, then how are we going to explain why people seem to be getting the same rate of major improvement regardless of which type of PT they see? There is a tiny detail that crops up in the conclusion about "necessary physical therapy". The evidence didn't say that the people receiving physical therapy were getting needed physical therapy. Maybe when it's needed, it really makes a difference whether you see a GP vs. a specialist, but the records are distorted by the fact that tons of people get PT when they don't need it. Maybe we're currently doing a great job of assigning people to a GP vs. a specialist based on what their specific situation is, and if we stopped caring about which type of therapist we assigned patients, the 31% and 50% marks would go way down. Conversely, maybe we're currently not doing a great job of assigning people to a GP vs. a specialist based on their specific situation, and if we started caring about which type we assigned patients to, we would do better than 31% and 50% of patients showing major improvement.

label: Goal
body: The author is assuming that if both types of therapist are getting the same percent of their patients to show major improvement, then it doesn't matter whether a patient sees one or the other (for the sake of major improvement). But the author is failing to consider that those current rates of major improvement might change were we to concentrate more or concentrate less on caring about whether patients saw a specialist vs. GP based on their specific needs.

label: Conclusion
body: The choice between a specialist and a general practitioner for physical therapy will not affect one's chances of major improvement.

label: Evidence
body: Patients treated for less than six weeks showed 31% improvement regardless of practitioner type. Patients treated for longer showed 50% improvement regardless of practitioner type.

label: Evaluate
body: The data groups patients by treatment duration and shows equal rates within each group. But this ignores the possibility that specialists and generalists treat different types of patients. If specialists handle harder cases and generalists handle easier ones, equal raw percentages could mask a real advantage for one type of practitioner.

label: Goal
body: Find the flaw: the argument overlooks that the types of patients each practitioner sees might differ, making the raw comparison misleading.

label: Evidence
body: The numbers look identical: 31% improvement for short-term patients with either type of practitioner, 50% for long-term patients with either type. Case closed? Not quite.

label: Evaluate
body: Imagine a heart surgeon and a family doctor both have a 90% patient survival rate. Sounds equal, right? But the heart surgeon is doing open-heart surgery while the family doctor is treating colds. Equal percentages mean nothing if the difficulty of the cases is completely different. The argument looked at matching numbers and declared a draw without asking: are these practitioners even treating the same kinds of patients? If specialists handle the tough cases and generalists handle the easy ones, the "equal" outcomes actually prove specialists are better, not that the choice does not matter.

label: Goal
body: Spot the answer that calls out this apples-to-oranges comparison — the possibility that different practitioners treat different types of conditions.

label: Conclusion (Therefore)
body: We should be able to determine how a star's relative actual brightness correlates with other characteristics by studying stars in the same distant galaxy.

label: Intermediate Conclusion (Thus)
body: If two stars are in the same distant galaxy, any big difference in the apparent brightness of those stars results from differences in how brightly each is actually burning.

label: Evidence
body: If two stars are in the same distant galaxy, their difference in their respective distances from Earth is negligible.

label: Evaluate
body: There are two conclusions here, so we can scrutinize both reasoning moves. The first move is saying that if star X and star Y are both in distant Galaxy A, it doesn't matter is X is 1.21 trillion miles away and Y is 1.22 trillion miles alone. The difference between 1.21 and 1.22 trillion miles is negligible. Two equally bright stars would appear the same from Earth, whether it's 1.21 or 1.22 trillion. So, if we have two such stars and they appear with different brightness, does that have to be based on how brightly each one is burning? Not necessarily. What if one of the stars is hidden by some dust cloud or nebula? That would make it look dimmer than it really is. What if one of the stars ends up having another star right behind it (from our angle of viewing it). If there were another star behind the star we're looking at, in the same direction, then it would add extra brightness. It would make that front-star look brighter than it really is. The second move is saying that "if all differences in brightness indicate differences in how brightly each star is burning, then we can correlate brightness with other characteristics by looking at stars in the same galaxy". That move isn't really that ripe for objections. If the measurement we get for how brightly the stars burn is accurate, then, sure, we can correlate that brightness number with any other numbers we get (f.e. the chemical composition of the stars based on spectral readings).

label: Goal
body: The answer is probably targeting the move from the first sentence to the second, since that move seems to take a big, risky leap. Just because two stars in a distant galaxy are, in practical terms, the "same" distance from Earth, that doesn't necessarily mean we should accept that differences in apparent brightness stem from differences in actual brightness. Is distance really the only factor to consider? There are probably other factors that can also impact apparent brightness. The author is assuming a Linking idea that, "If it's essentially the same distance from Earth and the stars are the same size, they will appear equivalently bright". The author is assuming Defending ideas like, 'There is not some other factor besides distance that could affect the apparent brightness of a star'.

label: Conclusion
body: We should be able to determine how a star's relative actual brightness correlates with other characteristics by studying stars in the same distant galaxy.

label: Evidence
body: Stars in the same distant galaxy are essentially the same distance from Earth, so apparent brightness differences reflect actual brightness differences.

label: Assumption
body: The argument assumes there are stars in distant galaxies that differ in characteristics other than brightness. Without such variation, there would be nothing to correlate brightness with.

label: Goal
body: Find the answer that, if negated, makes the study impossible — no variation in other characteristics means no correlations to discover.

label: Conclusion
body: Want to figure out how a star's brightness relates to its other features? Study stars in the same distant galaxy — problem solved.

label: Evidence
body: The clever insight: stars in the same galaxy are all roughly the same distance from us. So if one looks brighter than another, it actually IS brighter — distance is not tricking us. This eliminates the distance variable and gives us a clean read on actual brightness.

label: Assumption
body: Great, so we can measure brightness accurately. But the conclusion says we can correlate brightness with "other characteristics." What other characteristics? If every star in the galaxy has the exact same size, color, temperature, and composition — if they are all identical except for brightness — there is nothing to correlate. The study needs stars that differ in ways beyond just how bright they are. No variation, no research.

label: Goal
body: Find the assumption that, when flipped, kills the study. "No stars have different other characteristics" means there is literally nothing to study.

label: Given that ...
body: Repressors repress upsetting thoughts and feelings, whereas sensitizers are especially attuned to internal states and freely express distress.

label: Why is it that ...
body: Repressors are less shy and anxious, better tolerate frustration, and have better social skills / grades / self-esteem?

label: Evaluate / Goal
body: It's always hard to predict answers on Paradox questions, but even more so when it's an EXCEPT variation. We want ways to explain how repressing your upsetting feelings is associated with more confidence, less anxiety, better tolerance for frustrations, better social skills, higher grades, more self-esteem. (So many possible targets!) Conversely, we'll also like answers showing why expressing distress leads to the opposite of any of these.

label: The Findings
body: Repressors — people who suppress upsetting thoughts — were found to be less shy and anxious, better at tolerating frustration, and to have superior social skills, higher grades, and greater self-esteem compared to sensitizers.

label: Goal
body: This is an EXCEPT question. Four answers explain why repressors have these superior characteristics. One does NOT. Find the answer that fails to explain any of the repressors' advantages.

label: The Findings
body: The personality test divided students into two camps: repressors (who bury their feelings) and sensitizers (who wear their hearts on their sleeves). And the repressors won at basically everything — less anxious, better social skills, higher grades, better self-esteem. It is like the "just do not think about it" strategy actually works.

label: Goal
body: Four answers explain why repressors have it so good. One does not. Find the odd one out — the answer that does not actually explain any of the repressors' superior characteristics.

label: Conclusion (unlikely = opinion)
body: It's unlikely that nanobes are living things.

label: Intermediate Conclusion
body: Nanobes are probably inanimate artifacts of the microscopic structure of the clay in which they're found.

label: Evidence (because)
body: Nanobes are 1/10 the size of the smallest known bacteria. They are too small to contain a reproductive mechanism, which is a prerequisite for life.

label: Evaluate
body: This feels like a tough one to figure out on our own (we'll need the answers to help), but we can frame the right tension in our brain. Given that .. living things all have a reproductive mechanism, but nanobes are too small to have a reproductive mechanism, How could we still argue that ... nanobes are living things?

label: Goal
body: Let's look for something that helps us say, even though "nanobes are too small to contain a reproductive mechanism" it still could be the case that "nanobes are living things", after all .. [answer choice]. Or, less likely, look for something that hurts the plausibility that nanobes are just inanimate artifacts of the clay's microscopic structure.

label: Conclusion
body: Nanobes are probably not living things — they are likely inanimate artifacts of clay's microscopic structure.

label: Evidence
body: A nanobe is too small to contain a reproductive mechanism, and reproduction is a prerequisite for life.

label: Evaluate
body: The argument assumes that a reproductive mechanism must be contained within a single nanobe. If reproduction could occur through a mechanism external to any individual nanobe — such as collective reproduction — the size limitation would not preclude life.

label: Goal
body: Find an answer that shows how something as small as a nanobe could still be considered alive despite lacking an internal reproductive mechanism.

label: Conclusion
body: These "nanobes" are not alive — they are just weird lumps in the clay. Nothing to see here, certainly nothing living.

label: Evidence
body: The argument says: reproduction is required for life, nanobes are too tiny to hold reproductive machinery, therefore nanobes cannot be alive. It is a tidy little syllogism.

label: Evaluate
body: The argument treated each nanobe as a solo act that needs to carry its own reproductive toolkit. But what if nanobes are more like a band — individually they do not have all the instruments, but together they can play the whole song? The assumption that reproduction must happen inside a single entity is the weak point. If nanobes can team up to reproduce, the size limitation becomes irrelevant.

label: Goal
body: Find the answer that shows reproduction does not require a mechanism crammed into one tiny nanobe.

label: Conclusion (So)
body: Devan is my enemy.

label: Evidence (since)
body: He does not meet any of these basic criteria for friendship (being kind / offering to help / being compassionate).

label: Evaluate
body: How would we object to this conclusion. Given that Devan has never been kind, offered help, or showed compassion, how could we argue that he is not our enemy? Isn't there some middle ground between "not being a friend" and "being an enemy"? Those aren't binary options. It feels like the author is imposing some False Choice that if someone isn't a friend, they must be an enemy. Maybe Devan is just a stranger or just a neutral party, who isn't necessarily for us but isn't against us.

label: Goal
body: Let's look for an argument whose conclusion feels like it's swinging to the opposite pole from what the evidence is talking about. i.e. Jim doesn't meet any of the criteria for "best employee". Thus, he is the worst employee.

label: Conclusion
body: Devan is my enemy.

label: Evidence
body: Devan has not been kind, has not offered help, and has not offered companionship. He fails to meet any basic criteria for friendship.

label: The Flaw
body: The argument assumes that failing to qualify as a friend automatically makes someone an enemy. This is a false dichotomy — there is a middle ground (acquaintance, stranger, indifferent person) between friend and enemy.

label: Goal
body: Find the answer that mirrors this exact structure: failing to meet criteria for Category A, therefore belongs to opposite Category B — ignoring intermediate categories.

label: Conclusion
body: Devan is officially classified as an enemy. Break out the nemesis paperwork.

label: Evidence
body: Devan has not been kind, helpful, or companionable. Zero for three on the friendship checklist. Therefore — enemy.

label: The Flaw
body: This is the "you are either with me or against me" fallacy. Just because someone is not your friend does not make them your enemy. They could be a stranger, an acquaintance, the person who sits two rows behind you in class that you have never spoken to. There is a vast middle ground between "best buddy" and "arch-nemesis," and this argument leapfrogged right over it.

label: Goal
body: Find the answer with the same false dichotomy: something does not qualify for one category, so it must belong to the extreme opposite category. Same leap, same missed middle ground.

label: Conclusion (thus)
body: The discovery of powerful cures for certain high-incidence forms of cancer would probably trigger an increase in behaviors such as smoking and overexposure to sun that are known to increase the risks of such cancers.

label: Evidence
body: Drivers of SUVs correctly believe that they are at less risk of serious injury in an accident, and such drivers therefore tend to drive less carefully than they would in more traditional vehicles.

label: Evaluate
body:
The author is arguing by analogy. If we want, we can lay out the parts to help us articulate any missing ingredients.
```
SUVs                     Cures for Cancer
drivers know their       (people know their
risk of serious injury   risk of dying from
in an accident is low    such cancer is low)
so, the drivers drive    people would smoke
less carefully than      more and not use
they otherwise would     sunscreen, despite
                         the higher cancer risk
```
Since the argument is by analogy and the question stem is asking for an underlying principle, we should probably try to articulate the underlying general idea that operates in both halves of the analogy.

label: Goal
body: Let's look for something like, "If you know you're better protected from the potential downside of risky behavior X, then you're more likely to do X."

label: Conclusion
body: Discovering powerful cancer cures would probably trigger an increase in behaviors like smoking and sun overexposure.

label: Evidence
body: SUV drivers believe they carry lower injury risk, so they drive less carefully than they would in smaller vehicles.

label: The Principle
body: The journalist reasons by analogy: when people believe they are protected from negative consequences, they engage in riskier behavior. SUV safety reduces careful driving; cancer cures would reduce health caution.

label: Goal
body: Find the principle that captures this pattern: protection from consequences of risky behavior leads to increased risky behavior.

label: Conclusion
body: Cure cancer, and people will light up a cigarette to celebrate. That is essentially the journalist's prediction.

label: Evidence
body: SUV drivers know their vehicles are safer in crashes, so they drive like they are invincible. Same logic: if cancer becomes curable, people will stop worrying about behaviors that cause cancer. Why bother with sunscreen if cancer is just a treatable inconvenience?

label: The Principle
body: This is the "seatbelt paradox" — give people safety nets, and they use them as trampolines. When the consequences of bad behavior get defanged, the bad behavior increases. It is moral hazard in action: protect people from results, and they stop caring about causes.

label: Goal
body: Find the principle that says: developing ways to protect people from the consequences of risky behavior will lead to more risky behavior.

label: Conclusion (Thus)
body: Most independent films do not have absolute integrity as works of art.

label: Evidence
body: Indie filmmakers need to make profits, and this affects the artistic decisions made in creating most indie films.

label: Evaluate
body: Like we always do on Sufficient Assumption, once we've found the conclusion we ask ourselves if there's a New Concept in the Conclusion (because, if so, 99% of the time the correct answer will have that new concept). This conclusion is trying to prove that most indie films "do not have absolute integrity". Cool, did they ever define the legal standard for "absolute integrity"? No? Okay, well then our correct answer must be a rule that allows us to prove that concept. What do we know about most indie films? Their artistic decisions are affected by profit considerations.

label: Goal
body: A classic missing link correct answer would sound like, "If artistic decisions made in creating films are affected by the need to make profits, then a film doesn't have absolute integrity as a work of art". They might surprise us with how the trigger is worded, but we're only interested in answers that provide a rule that puts "not absolute integrity" on the right side of the arrow. Naturally, we expect an illegal negation or reversal of this to be a trap answer, and the correct answer will probably write this rule in contrapositive form: "If it does have absolute integrity, then its artistic decisions aren't affected by profit".

label: Conclusion
body: Most independent films do not have absolute integrity as works of art.

label: Evidence
body: All independent filmmakers need to make profits, and this need affects the artistic decisions made in creating most independent films.

label: Gap
body: The argument needs a principle linking profit-affected artistic decisions to the loss of absolute integrity. The evidence establishes that profit needs affect most films' artistic decisions, but it does not explain why that means those films lack absolute integrity.

label: Goal
body: Find the assumption that, when added to the premises, makes the conclusion follow with certainty: if profit affects any artistic decisions, then the work lacks absolute integrity.

label: Conclusion
body: Most indie films do not have absolute artistic integrity. Sorry, Sundance.

label: Evidence
body: Every independent filmmaker needs to make money, and in most cases that profit motive creeps into the artistic decisions. The "I have to actually sell this thing" factor is shaping the art.

label: Gap
body: So profit affects decisions — but why does that kill "absolute integrity"? The argument skipped a step. It needs a principle that says: any whiff of profit motivation in artistic decisions and the work's absolute integrity is gone. Without that bridge, the evidence (profit affects decisions) just hangs there without connecting to the conclusion (no absolute integrity).

label: Goal
body: Find the missing link: if profit needs affected ANY artistic decisions, then absolute integrity is out the window.

label: Evidence
body:
```
If you complete 24
graduate credits
and a thesis in our
department, you
are eligible to
receive a master's
degree.                  24 GC and T → EM
Roger has
completed 24
graduate credits
in our department        24 GC
yet he is not
eligible to receive
a master's degree.       ~EM
So he must not
have finished his
thesis yet.              ~T
```

label: Evaluate
body: The argument has one conditional premise with "and" in the sufficient condition: 24 GC and T → EM. A second premise fulfills one part of the sufficient condition: 24 GC. A third premise states that the necessary condition is not true: ~EM. The conclusion states that the second sufficient condition must not have been met: Therefore, ~T.

label: Goal
body: We should expect a lot of similar-looking answer choices, but only one will match this exact pattern of logic. Others will contain at least one significant difference.

label: Structure
body: If A and B, then C. A is true. C is false. Therefore, B is false.

label: The Logic
body: This is valid reasoning. The conditional states that both A (credits) and B (thesis) are required for C (master's eligibility). Roger has A but not C. By contrapositive: if not-C, then not-A or not-B. Since A is true, not-B must be true — Roger did not complete his thesis.

label: Goal
body: Find the answer with identical structure: a conditional requiring two conjunctive conditions for a result; one condition is met, the result did not occur, so the other condition must not be met.

label: Structure
body: The argument is a logic puzzle. Rule: credits plus thesis equals master's degree eligibility. Roger has the credits but not the eligibility. So the missing piece must be the thesis.

label: The Logic
body: Think of it like a recipe: if you have flour AND eggs, you can make a cake. Roger has flour but no cake. Therefore, Roger must not have eggs. Simple, valid, elegant reasoning by process of elimination.

label: Goal
body: Find the answer that follows the same recipe: two ingredients needed for a result, one ingredient confirmed, result absent, therefore the other ingredient must be missing.

label: Conclusion (Therefore)
body: More rain will probably fall in September than in July.

label: Evidence
body: In the past two years, significantly more rain has fallen in September than in July.

label: Evaluate
body: This isn't a crazy sounding argument. The author is assuming that what's been true in the recent past will probably be true in the near future. For example, "For the past two Christmas's, my neighbor has put a big snowflake over her front door. Therefore, this year she will probably hang a big snowflake over her front door." We know that "just because it was true in past instances, it doesn't have to necessarily be true again in this instance." This argument is more responsible. It's only predicting that it will probably happen again in this instance. But that's still potentially an exaggeration. Maybe something was different about the last two years from this coming year.

label: Goal
body: Look for an answer mentioning the "if it was true before, it'll probably be true again" reasoning move, or an answer pointing out the "maybe this year is importantly different from the previous two years" objection.

label: Conclusion
body: This year in Browning, more rain will probably fall in September than in July.

label: Evidence
body: In the previous two years, significantly more rain fell in September than in July.

label: Evaluate
body: Two years of data is an extremely small sample from which to draw a predictive conclusion about future weather patterns. The argument treats a very short track record as though it establishes a reliable trend.

label: Goal
body: Identify the flaw: generalizing from too few instances to a prediction about the future.

label: Conclusion
body: September will probably out-rain July in Browning this year. Bold call from the two-year weather expert.

label: Evidence
body: It rained more in September than July for the last two years. That is the entire meteorological dataset.

label: Evaluate
body: Two years. That is the foundation for this weather prediction. A coin that lands heads twice in a row does not prove the coin is rigged toward heads. Weather is notoriously variable, and two data points barely qualify as a pattern, let alone a basis for future predictions. Professional meteorologists use decades of data for seasonal forecasts, and even then they hedge their bets. This argument looked at two Septembers and declared a trend.

label: Goal
body: Find the answer that calls out the obvious: you cannot predict the weather from a sample of two.

label: Conclusion (Thus)
body: Schools should not require students to take courses in individual academic disciplines but should instead require them to take interdisciplinary courses.

label: Evidence
body: Most problems in daily life can't be solved most effectively, if at all, by applying knowledge from any single academic discipline in isolation.

label: Evaluate
body: We could spell out the Linking assumption here, If most problems can't be solved most effectively by applying knowledge from any single academic discipline in isolation, then schools shouldn't require students to take classes in single academic disciplines. But it seems more likely that the correct answer will be Defender style, ruling out some objection. GIven that ... most problems in daily life can't be solved best by applying knowledge from any single discipline. How could we still argue that ... schools should require students to take courses in individual disciplines? We could maybe say that solving problems in daily life involves applying knowledge from multiple disciplines, but it's too chaotic and disorganized to learn in that interdisciplinary style in school. Maybe it's better to require courses in individual academic disciplines, and then in daily life when these students face problems, they can just combine things they learned from these separate disciplines.

label: Goal
body: Look for an answer like, "it is not easy to combine things you've learned from individual disciplines in order to face problems in daily life", or an answer linking the premise to the conclusion, or any other answer that, if negated, would hurt the argument.

label: Conclusion
body: Schools should require interdisciplinary courses instead of courses in individual academic disciplines.

label: Evidence
body: Few daily-life problems can be solved most effectively by applying knowledge from a single academic discipline in isolation.

label: Evaluate
body: The argument assumes that interdisciplinary courses will actually equip students to combine knowledge from multiple disciplines. If students in single-discipline courses can already integrate knowledge on their own, the argument weakens. If they cannot, the argument strengthens.

label: Goal
body: Look for an answer complaining about the analogy, probably regarding the fact that while the physician example works for "you don't need to practice what you preach", the logician example seems weirder.

label: Goal
body: Find an answer that bridges the gap between "daily problems require multiple disciplines" and "therefore schools should teach interdisciplinary courses" — ideally by showing that single-discipline courses fail to produce the needed cross-disciplinary competence.

label: Conclusion
body: The educator's prescription: ditch the single-discipline courses and go interdisciplinary.

label: Evidence
body: Real-life problems do not respect departmental boundaries. They require knowledge from multiple fields, so a biology-only or history-only course does not match the demands of actual daily life.

label: Evaluate
body: Fair point about the problems, but there is a missing step. Just because daily life requires combined knowledge does not automatically mean schools need to pre-blend the courses. Maybe students who take separate biology and chemistry courses can still figure out how to combine the knowledge themselves. The argument assumes that course structure determines student capability, but it never proves that connection. A good strengthener will show that students actually cannot make the leap on their own — that taking separate courses leaves them unable to integrate across fields.

label: Goal
body: Find the answer that closes the gap between "life needs multiple disciplines" and "courses should be interdisciplinary."

label: Conclusion
body: It's a mistake to assume figuring out what caused the recession is essential to improving the economy.

label: Evidence (after all)
body: Corrective lenses were an effective treatment for myopia long before the cause was known to be genetic.

label: Evaluate
body:
Whenever we do Main Conclusion, we read the paragraph differently, because we know that instead of putting the conclusion at the end of the paragraph (the most common place), on Main Conclusion and Role we expect the conclusion to be earlier than (at least some of) the supporting ideas. Specifically, 90% of Main Conclusion questions have a conclusion that is
    - the First Sentence
    - a Rebuttal / Pivot idea
    This one did the second. The first sentence is just a fact. There's no support provided to defend the idea that people are hotly debating what caused the current recession. Then we see that magical however and think, "Is this the conclusion? Am I seeing the ol' Rebuttal / Pivot conclusion formula again?" To clinch our suspicion that this 2nd sentence is the Conclusion, we want to see that it's being Supported. The fact that the 3rd sentence begins with one of the four Support Indicators (FABS = for, after all, because, since) tells us that the 2nd sentence was definitely the conclusion.

label: Goal
body: When we have Rebuttal style conclusions, we need to take an extra sec to state our author's position, using the wording of the position she's rebutting. For example, if we hear, "Some people think that ketchup is a vegetable. However, they're wrong", then we need to say that the Conclusion is "Ketchup is not a vegetable". So here the opposing position was that "We need to figure out what caused the current recession in order to improve the economy. It's essential." Our author is saying "No, it's not. That's a mistake. It's not essential. You could improve the economy, even if you didn't figure out what caused the current recession." Let's find the answer that best matches the meaning of the 2nd sentence.

label: Conclusion
body: It is a mistake to assume that answering what caused the current recession is essential to improving the economy.

label: Evidence
body: Corrective lenses effectively treated myopia long before the cause was known to be genetic.

label: Evaluate
body: The analogy supports the idea that solutions can precede understanding of root causes. The main conclusion is the columnist's central prescriptive claim about the recession, not the supporting analogy.

label: Goal
body: Identify the answer that matches the columnist's main claim: knowing the cause of the recession is not a prerequisite for fixing the economy.

label: Conclusion
body: The columnist's big point: stop arguing about what caused the recession and start fixing it, because you do not need to know the cause to find a solution.

label: Evidence
body: Exhibit A: eyeglasses. People were correcting myopia with lenses long before anyone figured out that nearsightedness is genetic. The solution came first, the explanation came later. Same logic should apply to the economy.

label: Evaluate
body: This is a Main Conclusion question, so the job is to separate the argument's central claim from its evidence and background. The myopia example is evidence, the debate about causes is background, and the actual conclusion is the "it is a mistake" claim. The correct answer should paraphrase that central point without going too far or not far enough.

label: Goal
body: Match the columnist's actual conclusion: knowing the cause is not necessary for economic improvement. Dodge the traps that restate the example, overstate the claim, or grab a sub-conclusion.

label: Conclusion
body: There are exceptions to the general rule that you should practice what you preach. rephrase: Sometimes its okay if you don't act in accordance with what they say.

label: Evidence (for instance)
body: Logicians don't need to be logical when they discuss logic, just like physicians don't have to be healthy to discuss health.

label: Evaluate
body: The author is trying to support the idea that sometimes it's okay if you don't practice what you preach. The evidence is an analogy, in which the author is assuming in both cases that it's okay if you don't practice what you preach. It's okay for a doctor to tell her patient to stop smoking cigarettes, even though she herself hasn't been able to quit smoking. It's okay for a logician to be discussing logic, even though they are being illogical as they do so. Any time an argument is based on an Analogy, we should be asking ourselves whether the two things feel fair to compare. In this case, it does seem perfectly fine for a doctor to treat my health conditions, even if they don't live a healthy lifestyle. But it doesn't seem as fine for a logician to be illogical while discussing logic. How will I emerge with a better understanding of logic, if the logician teaches it to me in some illogically? To put it another way, what a physician does outside her clinic to her own body doesn't really affect how she treats people inside her clinic. The former is her life. The latter is her job. But what a logician does within a discussion of logic seems like it is his job, not his life. If he can't be logical while discussing logic, then he's messing up being a logician.

label: Conclusion
body: There are exceptions to the rule that people should practice what they preach — logicians need not be logical in their discussions of logic, just as physicians need not have healthy lifestyles to treat patients.

label: Evidence
body: The argument treats the two cases as parallel: logicians discussing logic and physicians treating patients.

label: Evaluate
body: The analogy is flawed because the two cases are not truly parallel. A logician being illogical in discussions of logic is being incompetent at their core professional activity. A physician having an unhealthy lifestyle is failing in a personal domain unrelated to their professional competence.

label: Goal
body: Find the answer that identifies this disanalogy: being illogical about logic is professional incompetence, while being unhealthy is a personal failing.

label: Conclusion
body: The argument's hot take: just as doctors do not need to be healthy to treat sick people, logicians do not need to be logical when discussing logic. Exceptions to "practice what you preach" exist.

label: Evidence
body: The physician analogy: a doctor with a terrible diet can still diagnose your flu perfectly well. By extension, a logician should get the same pass.

label: Evaluate
body: Wait a second. A doctor eating junk food does not affect their ability to read an X-ray. That is a personal failing separate from their professional skill. But a logician being illogical when discussing logic? That is like a pilot who cannot fly when piloting. The "preaching" and the "practicing" are the same thing for the logician. The argument pretends these are equivalent exceptions, but one is "do as I say, not as I do" and the other is "I literally cannot do my job."

label: Goal
body: Find the answer that spots this broken analogy: illogical logic is incompetence; unhealthy doctoring is not.

label: Conclusion (Therefore)
body: All animal can, in principle, be bred for domesticity.

label: Evidence
body: Domesticated animals have come into existence by breeding only the tamest individuals of a wild species. If you only breed the individuals that show they're tame when they're young, then through successive generations of breeding you will "evolved" a domesticated version of the animal.

label: Evaluate
body: How could the Defense make the case that "Nuh-uh ... not all animals can be bred for domesticity"? They could maybe say that for some species, none of the individuals are tame enough for us to start the selective breeding process. Maybe we're trying to domesticate a hyena, and we go through a litter of hyena babies, but none of them display tameness when young. If they we can't get our hands on multiple tame individuals, then we can't keep breeding tame-with-tame to get ever more tame versions of a hyena.

label: Goal
body: Look for an answer saying "you can't always find some individuals that display tameness when young") or something that helps us argue that the conclusion is too universal, that some animals would not theoretically be eligible for the domestication process.

label: Conclusion
body: All animals can, in principle, be bred for domesticity.

label: Evidence
body: Domesticated animals like dogs were created by selectively breeding the tamest individuals from wild species. Breeding only tame wolves eventually produces dogs.

label: Evaluate
body: The argument assumes every species has some tame individuals to breed from. If a species has no tame members at all, the breeding method cannot even begin.

label: Goal
body: Find an answer that attacks the hidden assumption: that every species has members who display tameness.

label: Conclusion
