body: Audiences' greater pleasure at performances by more famous pianists is fair and gives no cause for cynicism about audiences' ability to distinguish good playing from bad.

label: Evaluate
body: Here is the catch nobody mentions: for tablets from 3300 BC to threaten the Sumerians' crown, the Sumerians cannot have been writing literature way earlier than that. If Sumerian literature dates back to 4000 BC, Egypt showing up at 3300 BC is like arriving at a party two hours late and claiming you were there first. The argument only works if the timeline is tight enough for the Egyptian discovery to actually matter. That unstated timeline assumption is the hidden gear that makes the whole argument turn.

label: Goal
body: Find the answer that, when negated, makes the argument fall apart. The right assumption connects the 3300 BC date to the question of Sumerian primacy.

label: Conclusion (not justified = opinion)
body: The conclusion that ocean warming is a symptom of a more general, global warming caused by human-generated air pollution is far from justified.

label: Evidence (it is known that)
body: There are many natural cycles of ocean temperature changes that last 60 years or more.

label: Evaluate
body:
Whenever we do Main Conclusion (or Role), we remind ourselves that 90% of the time, the conclusion will be the first sentence or it will be a rebuttal.
In this argument, the first case is clearly factual, not the author's opinion, so it's not a First Sentence Conclusion.
And when the second sentence begins with an attribution, "Some scientists claim", we would anticipate a Pivot into a Rebuttal.
Sure enough, we get "However, this conclusion is far from justified". The last sentence provides factual support. We can tell the last claim is factual because it is prefaced by "it is known that".

label: Goal
body:
Since our conclusion has a pronoun, "this conclusion is far from justified", we should take a sec and insert in the specific language the pronoun is referring to, as we did above when we wrote the Conclusion.
We should also limber up our synonym faculties by thinking, "What's another way to say this conclusion is far from justified?" Saying it's incorrect is too strong. It's more like "it's hasty to draw this conclusion / it's prematurely inferred / we don't have strong evidence for this".

label: Conclusion
body: The conclusion that the ocean warming is a symptom of global warming is "far from justified."

label: Evidence
body: There are many known natural cycles that raise and lower ocean temperatures. The warming could be part of one of these cycles.

label: Evaluate
body: The "far from justified" phrase is the main conclusion — an evaluative judgment about evidence quality. Everything else supports it. Do not confuse the acknowledged warming (a background fact) or the natural cycles (a supporting premise) with the conclusion.

label: Conclusion
body: The climatologist plays defense attorney for the ocean: the evidence that warming means global warming? "Far from justified." That is the big claim, the hill they are dying on.

label: Evidence
body: Two things prop up that verdict. First, everyone agrees the ocean got warmer by four degrees — that is not the fight. Second, natural ocean cycles exist that could explain the warming without invoking global warming. The climatologist is basically saying "you have a suspect, but you also have a perfectly good alibi."

label: Evaluate
body: The "far from justified" phrase is the neon sign flashing "MAIN CONCLUSION HERE." Everything else — the warming data, the natural cycles — exists to support that one evaluative judgment. Do not get tricked into picking the warming itself (that is just the setup) or the natural cycles (that is the supporting evidence). And notice: the climatologist is not saying "global warming is fake." They are saying "your evidence is not good enough." That is "not guilty" versus "innocent" — a crucial distinction the LSAT loves to test.

label: Robin's 1st Claim
body:
Archaeologists can study the artifacts left by ancient cultures to determine whether they were nomadic or sedentary.
Is K saying that archaeologists can't derive whether a culture was nomadic or sedentary by its artifacts?
Yes, it does seem like Kendall is pushing back on this idea. He's saying that the artifacts a culture used were a function of availability, not of lifestyle (nomadic vs. sedentary).

label: Robin's 2nd Claim
body:
If artifacts were made to last, rather than to be quickly discarded, then the culture was likely sedentary.
Is K saying that finding durable artifacts doesn't mean that the culture was probably sedentary?
Hmm, not quite? It feels more like Kendall would disagree with an opposite version of that. He would say "if we find artifacts that seem non-durable / discardable, that would not mean the culture was likely nomadic, because it might just be that they were sedentary but only had flimsy materials available to them.
Kendall might agree that "if durable, probably sedentary" but think that "if discardable, probably nomadic" is too much of a leap.

label: Goal
body: Fundamentally, they're arguing about whether you can / can't derive a pretty solid inference about nomadic vs. sedentary lifestyle based on the artifacts left behind by a culture.

label: Robin's Claim
body: Archaeologists can study artifacts to learn about cultures. Durable artifacts indicate a sedentary culture; by extension, non-durable artifacts suggest a nomadic one.

label: Kendall's Claim
body: The materials available in a region — not the culture's lifestyle — determine what kind of artifacts are produced.

label: Evaluate
body: They disagree about whether artifact type reliably indicates a culture's lifestyle. Robin reads lifestyle from artifacts; Kendall reads geography.

label: Robin's Claim
body: Robin looks at a pile of stone tools and pottery and declares: "Sedentary culture. People who wander do not lug rocks around." The bigger inference: artifact type is a lifestyle fingerprint. Durable means settled; flimsy means nomadic.

label: Kendall's Claim
body: Kendall fires back: "Or maybe they just lived near a quarry. People make things out of whatever is lying around, not based on their travel schedule." Artifacts tell you about geography, not lifestyle.

label: Evaluate
body: Robin and Kendall are having the archaeological equivalent of "is it the dress or the lighting?" Same evidence, totally different interpretations. Robin sees lifestyle. Kendall sees geography. The question asks you to pinpoint the exact claim where their views collide — the proposition one would endorse and the other would reject.

label: Conclusion (this means that)
body: We can expect the volume of freight shipped by rail to grow.

label: Evaluate
body:
When we do Main Conclusion (or Role), we expect that about 90% of the time the conclusion will be in the First Sentence or be a Rebuttal. But in either case, we expect the conclusion to arrive earlier than the evidence. An "upside-down argument" in which you hear the conclusion and then hear support.
In this one the conclusion is actually in the middle, sandwiched between premises. It's shown to us via a less common Conclusion indicator phrase, "This means that".
In general, Main Conclusion and Role won't use easy/obvious indicator words like "Therefore, Thus, So" for the main conclusion. They'll use Opinion Indicators (like "probably / evidently / apparently" or just the future-tense, which indicates opinion). Or they might use stuff like "This reveals that, this shows that, this demonstrates that, this means that".

label: Goal
body: The hard part is done. We found the conclusion. Let's just find whatever answer matches the meaning of the 3rd sentence.

label: Conclusion
body: The volume of freight shipped by rail can be expected to grow.

label: Evidence
body: Railroads are automating, which reduces workers and operating costs. Trucking — rail's chief competitor — has no comparable cost reduction ahead.

label: Evaluate
body: This is a chain argument. Automation leads to fewer workers, which leads to lower costs — that's an intermediate conclusion. The competitive advantage over trucking then supports the main conclusion about freight volume growth.

label: Goal
body: Find the claim that everything else supports but that itself supports nothing further in the argument.

label: Conclusion
body: Rail freight volume is going to grow. That's the big prediction — the table-slam moment of this argument.

label: Evidence
body: Railroads are going full robot mode. Fewer workers, lower costs. And trucking? Can't match it. No comparable cost savings on the horizon for the 18-wheelers.

label: Evaluate
body: This argument is a staircase. Step one: robots. Step two: fewer humans. Step three: cheaper operations. Step four: trucks can't keep up. And at the top of the staircase? The prediction that rail freight grows. Every step exists to get us to that top floor. The automation isn't the point. The cost savings aren't the point. The trucking trash-talk isn't the point. They're all steps leading to one destination.

label: Goal
body: Find the answer that captures the top-of-the-staircase prediction. Everything else is just the climb.

label: Information
body:
It used to be that infants who weren't breastfed were fed cow's milk.
Doctors said it should be boiled to sterilize it, thus preventing potentially fatal GI infections in infants.
Once people started boiling their cow's milk, there was an alarming increase of scurvy (caused by vitamin C deficiency) in infants fed boiled cow's milk but not among kids who were breastfed.

label: Evaluate
body: There seems to be a lot of Comparison / Contrast and Causality in this fact set. We have support for thinking that the reason breastfed infants didn't get scurvy is because there is vitamin C in breastmilk. Meanwhile, the infants fed boiled cow's milk got scurvy because either cow's milk doesn't have much vitamin C to begin with or it does but got boiled off.

label: Goal
body: These are pretty speculative inferences to draw, but because it's Most Supported, our answer doesn't have to be bulletproof. They love to have One Difference Explain Another Difference. So it's very likely that they're enticing us to believe that the difference between being breastfed and being fed with boiled cow's milk explains the difference between no scurvy and scurvy.

label: Statements
body: Infants fed boiled cow's milk developed scurvy (vitamin C deficiency) once boiling was widely adopted. Breast-fed infants did not develop scurvy.

label: Evaluate
body: The key variable: boiled cow's milk vs. breast milk. The key outcome: scurvy vs. no scurvy. Since scurvy is caused by vitamin C deficiency, the difference in outcomes points to a difference in vitamin C availability between the two milk sources.

label: Goal
body: Find the inference that follows most directly from these facts without requiring additional assumptions.

label: Statements
body: Historical baby nutrition in a nutshell: doctors said "boil the cow's milk!" to kill germs. It worked for infections, but suddenly babies started getting scurvy — a disease caused by not enough vitamin C. Meanwhile, breast-fed babies were doing just fine. No scurvy for them.

label: Evaluate
body: Two groups, two outcomes. Boiled cow's milk babies: scurvy. Breast-fed babies: no scurvy. Scurvy equals vitamin C deficiency. The math practically does itself — boiled cow's milk must be lower in available vitamin C than breast milk. The boiling probably cooked the vitamin C right out of the cow's milk, while mom's milk kept delivering the goods.

label: Goal
body: Find the answer that stays close to the evidence. No wild leaps, no unsupported quantifiers — just the simple comparison these facts support.

label: Given That
body:
The only way to curb grass and brush fires is rain.
If rain is below normal for an extended period of time, then there are many more such fires.

label: How Can it be That
body: Grass and brush fires cause less financial damage overall during severe drought than during normal rainfall?

label: Evaluate / Goal
body:
To sharpen the paradox a little bit, it seems like we're trying to reconcile this comparison:
```
Severe Drought        vs.   Normal Rain
many more fires             fewer fires
less $ damage               more $ damage
from fires                  from fires
```
So we need a way to explain why fewer fires during rainy times could be causing more financial damage than more fires during drier times.

label: Paradox
body: During droughts there are more grass fires, yet total financial damage is lower than in normal-rainfall years.

label: Evaluate
body: More fires but less total damage means each individual fire must be less destructive during drought. The resolution must explain why drought fires cause less damage per fire.

label: Goal
body: Find a fact that explains how more fires can coexist with less total damage.

label: Paradox
body: More fires, less damage. That seems backwards — like saying "more car accidents but less total repair costs." Something doesn't add up at first glance.

label: Evaluate
body: But think about it this way: what if drought fires are like a bunch of sparklers, while normal-year fires are like bonfires? A hundred sparklers do less total damage than three bonfires. The question is WHY drought fires stay small. The answer almost certainly involves what fires eat — vegetation. Drought means less green stuff to burn, so each fire fizzles out quickly.

label: Goal
body: Find the answer that explains why drought fires individually cause less damage, making the total lower despite the higher count.

label: Conclusion (Thus)
body: The new screening test can prompt dangerous operations that actually are not medically necessary.

label: Evidence
body: The new screening test detects some polyps that turn out not to be malignant, but doctors usually have them surgically removed, which is a dangerous process.

label: Evaluate
body:
The conclusion is very weakly worded; it's only claiming that the new test can prompt a dangerous operation that is not medically necessary.
Do we know that the new test has prompted any "dangerous operations"?
Not yet, but it has the potential to, since it will detect very early polyps, which aren't clearly malignant or benign. Most doctors, not wanting to risk leaving a polyp inside someone in case it turns out to be malignant (i.e. cancerous), will surgically remove the polyp, which is a dangerous process.
So, while we don't know that the new test has already prompted any polyp removal operations, it seems pretty likely that it could. And we know those operations are dangerous because they told us so.
Do we know that the polyp removal surgery was "medically unnecessary"?
Not quite. We're getting the sense that the author thinks, "Hey, if it turns out that this polyp we removed wasn't malignant after all, then that was a medically unnecessary surgery."
But maybe that's too big a leap. Maybe it's medically necessary to remove polyps for other reasons, whether or not they're malignant.

label: Goal
body:
Look for an answer expressing the author's linking move,
"If the polyp wasn't malignant, then the surgery to remove it was medically unnecessary"
or look for an answer ruling out some objection, like
"doctors will not refuse to order any surgeries on the basis of a screening test that detects polyps at such an early stage".

label: Conclusion
body: The screening test can prompt dangerous surgical operations that are not medically necessary.

label: Evidence
body: The test detects polyps of unclear malignancy. Doctors surgically remove them as a precaution. Some turn out nonmalignant.

label: Evaluate
body: The argument leaps from "nonmalignant" to "medically unnecessary." But nonmalignant polyps might still need removal for other reasons. The assumption must bridge this gap.

label: Goal
body: Find the assumption that connects nonmalignant polyps to unnecessary surgery.

label: Conclusion
body: This screening test is leading to unnecessary dangerous surgeries. That's the verdict.

label: Evidence
body: The test finds polyps. Doctors can't tell from the test if they're cancerous, so they cut them out just in case. Some turn out to be harmless. The argument concludes: those harmless-polyp surgeries were unnecessary and dangerous.

label: Evaluate
body: But wait — just because a polyp isn't cancerous doesn't automatically mean removing it was pointless. What if nonmalignant polyps cause other problems? What if they could BECOME malignant later? The argument assumes that "not cancerous" equals "didn't need to come out." That's the gap, and the necessary assumption must fill it.

label: Goal
body: Find the assumption that bridges the leap from "nonmalignant" to "medically unnecessary removal."

label: Conclusion
body: The psychological stress, not the physiological exertion, involved in talking causes one's blood pressure to rise.

label: Evidence
body: Most people's blood pressure rises somewhat when they talk, but introverted people's BP rises even more than extroverted people's, and introverted people are more psychologically stressed when they're talking.

label: Evaluate
body:
The author is presenting a correlation,
```
more psychologically  ||  higher blood
stressed (introverts)     pressure rises
```
Then, like so many brave LSAT authors before her, she assumes that one of those things causes the other.
She thinks that the extra stress is causing the extra blood pressure spike.
We always confront these Curious Fact → Causal Explanation arguments with the same two concerns:
1. Alternate Explanation for the curious fact
2. plausibility of the Author's Explanation

label: Goal
body:
Since this is Strengthen, we want to either
rule out an alternate explanation for the correlation
- f.e., it's not the case that having higher blood pressure is actually causing the extroverted people to feel more stress
or
increase the plausibility of the Author's Explanation
- f.e. when people go from speaking in a more stressful to a less stressful setting, their blood pressure usually falls

label: Conclusion
body: Blood pressure increases during speech result from psychological stress of communication, not physical exertion of speaking.

label: Evidence
body: Most people's BP rises when talking. Introverts experience larger increases than extroverts, and communication is more stressful for introverts.

label: Evaluate
body: The introvert/extrovert difference is evidence for the stress explanation — the physical effort of speaking is similar for both groups, but the psychological stress differs. To strengthen, we need evidence that further isolates communication as the cause while ruling out physical exertion.

label: Goal
body: Find evidence that separates the physical and psychological components of communication to further support the stress explanation.

label: Conclusion
body: Talking to people raises blood pressure because of the STRESS of communication, not the physical workout of flapping your jaw.

label: Evidence
body: Everyone's BP goes up when talking. But introverts' BP goes up MORE. Since talking takes about the same mouth-effort for introverts and extroverts, but talking to people is WAY more stressful for introverts, the stress must be the culprit — not the jaw muscles.

label: Conclusion
body: Parking fines should be raised again to further reduce violations.

label: Evidence
body: It generally holds that the more famous a concert pianist, the greater the pleasure of his or her audience.

label: Evaluate
body: The introvert/extrovert comparison is clever but not bulletproof. Maybe introverts just have more reactive cardiovascular systems. To really nail this down, we need evidence that separates the physical act of speaking from the psychological act of communicating.

label: Goal
body: Find the answer that creates the cleanest possible separation between physical exertion and communication stress — the perfect natural experiment.

label: Conclusion
body: Even if you have to pay more and even if you would never follow through on making a warranty claim if your pan broke, you should only buy a pan that has a warranty.

label: Evidence
body: If offering a warranty meant that a company would need to reimburse a bunch of customers when the product broke, then manufacturers wouldn't offer a warranty.

label: Evaluate
body:
This premise is conditional. By contrapositive, it tells us something we know about every frying pan that offers a warranty.
```
if manufacturers  →  company doesn't think they
offer warranty       will have to reimburse many
```
So our author is saying that we should only buy pans that offer a warranty, because that means the manufacturer isn't worried about having to pay out a bunch of warranty claims.
Our author is assuming that "if they aren't worried about paying out claims, it's because the frying pan is high quality and they don't expect it to break down for a lot of people".
But maybe they're not worried because even though they anticipate many of them breaking, they don't think many customers will have the follow-through to claim the warranty.

label: Goal
body: The answer will give us more reason to buy pans that offer warranties, or it will rule out a possible objection, such as "What if the companies offering warranties are unafraid of having to pay out many claims, not because they trust the product's quality and longevity, but for some other reason?"

label: Conclusion
body: You should buy warranted frying pans even if you'd never seek reimbursement, even if they cost more.

label: Evidence
body: Manufacturers won't offer a warranty if they'd need to reimburse many customers.

label: Evaluate
body: The warranty is treated as a quality signal. But if buyers like you would never seek reimbursement, the warranty costs the manufacturer nothing — so they could warrant bad products freely. The gap: someone must actually use warranties to make them costly for manufacturers.

label: Goal
body: Find the assumption that makes warranties financially risky enough for manufacturers that they only warrant quality products.

label: Conclusion
body: "Buy the warranty pan! Even if you'd never return it!" That's the advice here.

label: Evidence
body: Manufacturers aren't dumb — they won't guarantee junk because they'd lose money replacing it all. So a warranty means quality.

label: Evaluate
body: But here's the catch: if YOU would never use the warranty, and people like you also wouldn't bother, then the manufacturer has nothing to fear. They could slap a warranty on a terrible pan and never pay a dime. The warranty only works as a quality signal if enough people would actually hold the manufacturer accountable. Someone has to be the complainer for the system to work.

label: Goal
body: Find the answer that establishes the warranty as a genuine financial risk for manufacturers of bad products.

label: Conclusion
body: Whenever lawyers engage in obstructive behaviors (such as inflammatory language or badgering witnesses), it's reasonable to doubt whether the eventual verdict is correct.

label: Evidence
body: These obstructive behaviors hinder the jury's effort to reach a correct verdict.

label: Evaluate
body:
They seem to be testing the tension between these two concepts:
"Thing X hinders the effort to reach a correct verdict"
vs.
"Thing X causes us to doubt that a correct verdict was reached".
A strong headwind might hinder my effort to reach the top of Mt. Whitney, but a strong headwind doesn't make it reasonable to doubt my claim that I reached the top of Mt. Whitney.
In other words, yes, these obstructive behaviors make it harder to reach a verdict, but that's different from saying they make it somewhat likely that I'll reach the wrong verdict.

label: Goal
body: Look for an answer saying, "These behaviors might make it harder to reach a verdict, but they don't undermine our trust that if the jury managed to reach a verdict, it was a correct one."

label: Conclusion
body: Whenever lawyers use inflammatory language or badger witnesses, it is reasonable to doubt whether the verdict is correct.

label: Evidence
body: These lawyer behaviors hinder the jury's effort to reach a correct verdict.

label: Evaluate
body: The argument treats the potential to hinder as a guarantee of actual hindrance. To weaken: show that inflammatory behavior does not actually lead to incorrect verdicts in practice.

label: Goal
body: Find evidence that breaks the link between inflammatory lawyer tactics and incorrect verdicts.

label: Conclusion
body: Lawyer yelling in the courtroom? Time to doubt the verdict. That's the argument.

label: Evidence
body: Inflammatory language and witness-badgering mess up the jury's ability to get it right.

label: Evaluate
body: But "can mess things up" isn't the same as "did mess things up." A shark CAN eat you at the beach, but that doesn't mean every swim ends in disaster. The argument assumes that whenever these tactics are present, the verdict is compromised. To weaken it: show that the tactics don't actually work most of the time.

label: Goal
body: Find evidence that courtroom theatrics are all bark and no bite — that they fail to distort verdicts when real evidence is also on the table.

label: Evidence (since)
body:
Global warming has caused permafrost to melt under several arctic villages, forcing all their inhabitants to relocate at great expense.
Pollution from automobiles is a major contributor to global warming.

label: Conclusion (should)
body: The automotive industry should be required to help pay for the villagers' relocation.

label: Evidence
body: When fines for parking violations were raised to help pay for a newly opened parking garage, violations dropped by 50%.

label: Evaluate
body:
The argument gives us evidence about automobiles contributing to a problem, then jumps to a conclusion claiming that the automobile industry should be required to help pay for that problem. This is an incredibly common pattern in Principle Strengthen questions. Regardless of whether or not that recommendation sounds reasonable, logically there is an important missing link in the argument.
For the argument to be valid, we need a premise to actually state that, if pollution from automobiles is a major cause of the village inhabitants needing to relocate, then the automotive industry should be required to help pay for the relocation.
```
autos are a cause → auto industry should pay
```

label: Goal
body: We're looking for an answer to make this missing connection. Since the correct answer only needs to strengthen the argument, it doesn't have to be a precise match for the assumption that we identified, but frequently it will be, so this a great question type to hone your prediction skills. Beware of answers that address a slightly different recommendation, make a recommendation for a different party, or reverse the logic. Eliminate any answer that has "auto industry should pay" as the sufficient condition.

label: Conclusion
body: The automotive industry should help pay for the villagers' relocation costs.

label: Evidence
body: Auto pollution contributes to global warming, which melts permafrost, which forces villagers to relocate at great expense.

label: Evaluate
body: The argument traces a causal chain from the auto industry's product to the villagers' harm and concludes with financial liability. The justifying principle must establish that causing damage through your product creates an obligation to pay.

label: Goal
body: Find the principle that, combined with the facts, logically guarantees the conclusion about the auto industry's financial obligation.

label: Conclusion
body: Car companies should help foot the bill for the villagers' move. That's Mateo's bottom line.

label: Evidence
body: Cars make pollution, pollution heats the planet, the planet melts the permafrost, and the village has to relocate. It's the world's longest game of dominoes, and the auto industry tipped the first one.

label: Evaluate
body: Mateo needs a principle that says: whoever tipped the first domino pays for what the last domino knocked over. Simple causation-to-liability. No escape hatches for "we didn't know" or "we'll try to do better." Just: your product caused damage, you pay.

label: Goal
body: Find the clean, no-loopholes principle that turns product-caused harm into financial responsibility.

label: Conclusion (clearly, then)
body: The company acted fairly in failing to give bonuses to the staff.

label: Evidence
body:
Some people claim the company was unfair, perhaps because they recall that the company promised that if profits were higher than last year's, the staff would get bonuses.
But profits were much smaller than last year's.

label: Evaluate
body:
Whenever we're doing Flaw and the author is rebutting some other position and concluding the polar opposite position, we want to be thinking about the famous Unproven vs. Proven False flaw.
EXAMPLE - Some people claim that cell phones cause cancer. But no scientific study has ever determined this. Thus, cell phones do not cause cancer.
The flaw here is that even though someone else failed to prove that cell phones DO cause cancer, that doesn't mean the author has presented any evidence that proves cell phones DON'T cause cancer.
In this argument, some people claim "the company acted unfairly" in failing to give the staff bonuses. Our author ends up concluding "the company acted fairly", and this is not by presenting positive evidence of her own in favor of this conclusion.
Instead, she's just taking down the argument that (she thinks) was being made in favor of the opposite conclusion.

label: Goal
body:
The author should be responding to the actual reasons these several people offered in defense of their claim that the company was unfair, not speculating that "Perhaps they were basing their claim on X". So an answer might complain about that.
Even if the author is correct, and the people were basing their argument on X, the fact that the author has shown that X is not a valid way to prove "Unfair" doesn't suddenly mean that the author has proven "Fair". This is more in the Unproven vs. Proven False vein.

label: Conclusion
body: Lindsey concludes the company acted fairly in not paying bonuses.

label: Evidence
body: People claimed unfairness, perhaps recalling a promise of bonuses if profits increased. But profits were actually much smaller this year.

label: Evaluate
body: Lindsey disproves one potential reason for the unfairness opinion (large profits) and concludes the opinion itself is wrong. But other valid reasons for unfairness could exist that she never addresses.

label: Goal
body: Find the answer that identifies the flaw of treating one defeated reason as a refutation of the entire opinion.

label: Conclusion
body: Lindsey declares the company acted fairly. Case closed, gavel banged.

label: Evidence
body: People complained about no bonuses. Lindsey says they probably think profits were big — but actually, profits were smaller this year. Therefore: fair!

label: Evaluate
body: Lindsey knocked down ONE reason for the complaint and declared total victory. That's like a restaurant getting one bad review dismissed and claiming all criticism is invalid. Maybe the employees have a dozen reasons to call the decision unfair — contractual promises, tradition, the CEO's new yacht — and Lindsey addressed exactly one. Winning a single battle is not winning the war.

label: Goal
body: Find the answer that nails this specific flaw: treating one undermined reason as a complete refutation of the opinion it supported.

label: Given that
body: It's widely known that rescue squads save the lives of lots of mountain climbers every year.

label: How can it be that
body: A lot of experienced climbers think that the only way to significantly reduce climbing deaths and injuries among climbers is to abolish the rescue squad.

label: Evaluate
body: Two changes happened simultaneously: fines increased AND a new garage opened. The argument credits only the fines for the improvement, ignoring that the garage gave people a legal place to park.

label: Evaluate
body:
Since we know rescue squads save the lives of climbers, how would getting rid of the rescue squad lead to fewer climbing deaths and injuries?
There must something else different in a world without rescue squads that would lead to fewer climbing deaths and injuries. Maybe having a rescue squad emboldens people to take risks they wouldn't otherwise take. It's like if you take away the safety net from a trapeze, a lot fewer people are going to attempt the trapeze, and so maybe you get a net reduction in trapeze injuries.

label: Goal
body: Look for something that would be different in a world without rescue squads, that could help explain fewer climbing deaths and injuries.

label: Paradox
body: Rescue squads save many climbers' lives every year. Yet experienced climbers believe the rising toll of deaths and injuries can be significantly reduced only by completely abolishing rescue squads.

label: Evaluate
body: If rescue squads save lives, abolishing them should cause more deaths — not fewer. Something about the squads' existence must be increasing the total number of casualties more than their rescues reduce it.

label: Goal
body: Find the answer that explains how life-saving rescue squads could paradoxically lead to a higher overall death toll.

label: Paradox
body: Rescue squads are heroes. They save lives. Nobody disputes that. But the people who actually KNOW mountains — experienced climbers — are saying "get rid of them entirely." That sounds insane, like firefighters petitioning to close fire stations.

label: Evaluate
body: The twist is about who shows up when there's a safety net. Imagine a swimming pool with no lifeguard: only strong swimmers jump in. Now post a lifeguard on duty and suddenly every overconfident uncle after three beers is doing cannonballs into the deep end. The lifeguard saves some of them, sure, but the total number of drowning incidents skyrockets. Safety nets don't just catch falling people — they invite people to walk the tightrope.

label: Goal
body: We need the answer that explains how rescue squads create MORE danger than they prevent. Something about their presence must change who decides to climb — and change it dramatically enough to overwhelm the lives they save.

label: Paula
body: There are lots of Earthlike planets out there, so there's probably intelligent life out there, and we should be able to find such life with radio telescopes. Other intelligent life would have basically the same math / physics that humans have. They'd discover the same fundamental forces of the universe and then develop radio communication.

label: Ashley
body: Saying they'd automatically have the same math / physics / radio technology is like saying (absurdly) that they'd have the same legal or political systems we do. All this stuff is a unique extension of the human form and the Earthly environment. Thus, using radio telescopes to find intelligent life would be pointless.

label: Evaluate
body:
I often go claim-by-claim through the first person's statements to see if the 2nd person disagreed with any of the explicit claims.
Here, it seems like Ashley took issue with a couple claims:
- we can expect our radio telescopes to detect signs of such beings
(A would say, "that would be a waste of time and money")
- those smart aliens would have the same math, physics, and radio communication we have.
(A would say, "not necessarily — those are all just outgrowths of our unique physiology")
If we went down to the layer of assumptions, it feels like Paula assumes that "math / physics" are objective properties of the universe that all intelligent life would come to similar conclusions about. Ashley makes those discoveries sound more subjective or contingent on us being us.

label: Goal
body: Look for an answer about whether or not radio telescopes would be likely to detect intelligent life, about whether smart aliens would inevitably find the same (objective) math and physics and technology that we have or whether those things are unique properties of humanity.

label: Paula's Position
body: Earthlike planets probably host intelligent beings. These aliens would share our understanding of math and physics, so they would likely develop radio communication. Radio telescopes can detect their signals.

label: Ashley's Position
body: That is like saying aliens have the same legal and political systems. Science, math, and technology are unique outgrowths of our physiology. Searching with radio telescopes is a waste of time and money.

label: Goal
body: Identify the specific claim that Paula would affirm and Ashley would deny.

label: Paula's Position
body: Paula stands up at the conference and says: "Aliens would totally invent radio! Math is math, physics is physics — any smart civilization figures out radio waves eventually. Let's point our radio telescopes at the sky!"

label: Ashley's Position
body: Ashley grabs the mic: "That is ridiculous. Radio is a HUMAN invention. Our whole science is shaped by our weird human brains. Aliens might communicate with smells, gravity pulses, or interpretive dance for all we know. Spending money listening for alien FM radio is a waste."

label: Goal
body: They agree aliens might exist. They agree aliens would be intelligent. But Paula thinks intelligence naturally leads to radio, while Ashley thinks intelligence could lead anywhere depending on biology. We need the specific proposition where one says yes and the other says no.

label: Conclusion
body: The residents of Sierra should vote in favor of a local tax to fund construction of the proposed road.

label: Evidence
body:
If the proposed road connecting GVAC to Sierra isn't built, then the builders of GVAC won't complete the complex.
Were the complex to be completed, it would strengthen Sierra's economy and that would benefit every Sierra resident.

label: Evaluate
body:
Why does the author think that residents of Sierra should vote in favor of a tax that would fund this proposed road? Ultimately, the author says, because it would benefit every Sierra resident (by making the economy stronger).
Naturally, increasing local taxes would also affect every Sierra resident, so there's an element of weighing tradeoffs going into this recommendation: you should vote to have a new tax imposed because the benefit you'll ultimately get from the stronger economy is worth it?

label: Goal
body: Find the answer that identifies this alternative-cause flaw — the failure to consider that the parking garage, not the fine increase, may explain the drop in violations.

label: Goal
body:
It's hard to predict what ideas they'll pair up in the correct answer choice.
When it comes to Premise facts, we know the proposed road
- is required to complete construction of something that, if constructed, would strengthen the economy / benefit everyone
When it comes to what the Conclusion wants to hear, it's ideas like
- this is a good tax to vote for
- we do want this apartment complex to be completed
- the benefit of the stronger economy would outweigh the harm of the new tax.

label: Conclusion
body: Sierra's residents should vote for a tax increase to fund a new road.

label: Evidence
body: Builders will not complete an apartment complex unless the road is built. The completed complex would strengthen Sierra's economy and thereby benefit every resident.

label: Goal
body: Find the principle that, if accepted, would make the developer's conclusion follow logically from the premises. The gap is between "residents would benefit" and "residents should vote for the tax."

label: Conclusion
body: Vote to raise your own taxes so I can build apartments. That is essentially the developer's pitch.

label: Evidence
body: The logical chain: your taxes pay for a road, I build apartments on that road, apartments boost the economy, economy boosting benefits you. Therefore... hand over your money?

label: Evaluate
body: It is actually a persuasive pitch, but there is a gap big enough to drive an apartment complex through. Just because something benefits you does not automatically mean you should vote to pay for it. Sunshine benefits everyone — should we vote to fund the sun? We need a principle that bridges "you will benefit" to "you should vote yes."

label: Goal
body: Find the general rule that, once accepted, transforms the developer's "this helps you" into an airtight "so you should pay for it." That missing bridge is the whole question.

label: Evidence
body:
If any medieval epistemologists believed claim X, then we'll say "medieval epistemology believed X".
If any medieval epistemologists believed claim X was false, then we'll say "medieval epistemology did not believe X".

label: Conclusion
body: Medieval epistemology should be defined as the epistemological beliefs held by medieval epistemologists.

label: Evidence
body: Medieval epistemology is complex, and scholars have failed to produce a satisfactory definition. This proposed definition would include any belief held by any medieval epistemologist, even contradictory ones.

label: Evaluate
body: The definition is potentially circular: to apply it, you must first identify who the medieval epistemologists were, which may require already knowing what medieval epistemology is.

label: Goal
body: Find the answer that most effectively exposes or exploits this definitional weakness.

label: Conclusion
body: Someone thought they were being clever: "Medieval epistemology is whatever medieval epistemologists believed about epistemology." Sounds neat and tidy, right?

label: Evidence
body: The definition is motivated by frustration. Nobody can agree on what medieval epistemology IS, so this historian says: just look at what the practitioners believed. If they believed it, it counts. Contradictions welcome.

label: Evaluate
body: But here is the problem: to use this definition, you first need to identify the medieval epistemologists. And how do you know who they are unless you already know what medieval epistemology IS? It is the philosophical equivalent of needing work experience to get your first job, but needing a job to get work experience. The definition eats its own tail.

label: Goal
body: We need the answer that best exposes this circular trap — the one that shows why you cannot get the definition off the ground in the first place.

label: Conclusion (Hence)
body: If we want there to be even fewer parking violations, the fines should be raised again.

label: Evidence
body: Six months ago we raised the fines for parking violations, and since then parking violations on our streets have dropped by 50%.

label: Evaluate
body:
A common trope in Logical Reasoning is to say, "Policy change X went into effect. Then thing Y happened. So, apparently policy change X caused thing Y."
It seems here that our author is definitely making that same causal assumption, that the increase in fines is the cause of the 50% drop in parking violations.
The conclusion has implicit causality. When you say, "If you want X, you should do Y", you're implying that Y can bring about X.
This is the classic Explain Curious Fact argument structure, and when it shows up on Flaw, it means that they are usually just testing our awareness that the author has overconfidently arrived at one possible explanation for a curious fact, even though others could exist.

label: Goal
body:
So we might see answers saying, "The author takes for granted that because X was followed by Y, X caused Y" or "the author fails to consider other things could have caused there to be 50% fewer parking violations (a pandemic or storm that led to there being fewer people out and about, or maybe an increase in visibility of meter maids making people worry about whether they still had value left on their meter).
But there's also a prediction aspect to the conclusion, so even if we thought the fines were the causal reason that violations dropped by 50%, we won't necessarily get a further reduction by increasing fines even more. At a certain point, you've already maxed out the disincentive to get a parking violation. Whether it's a $500 or $600 fine, I'm equally determined to not get that ticket.

label: Evaluate
body: That is like starting a diet and a gym membership on the same Monday, losing 20 pounds, and telling everyone "my diet is incredible — I should eat even LESS!" Meanwhile, the gym membership is standing in the corner going "HELLO?! I HELPED TOO!" The argument completely ignores the giant concrete alternative explanation sitting right there with 500 empty parking spaces. Maybe people stopped parking illegally because they finally had somewhere legal to park, not because they were terrified of bigger fines.

label: Goal
body: We need the answer that calls out this blind spot — the failure to consider the garage as the real explanation.

label: Conclusion
body: The fact that some crops are being genetically engineered to produce important drugs raises the possibility that these drugs will end up in the general food supply.

label: Evidence
body: If pollen from a drug-producing crop drifts into a nearby field of ordinary crops of the same species, the pollen could fertilize that ordinary crop and turn it into a drug-producing crop.

label: Evaluate
body:
The author seems to be making a couple assumptions:
1. She thinks that crops being genetically engineered to produce important drugs are the drugs themselves.
Is that right? I thought maybe scientists were bioengineering a crop that has a certain structure or molecule that's used in combination with other ingredients to make the finished product drug, but the plant might not itself be a drug.
Maybe they're bioengineering a special type of wheat crop that has an enzyme that works well with a chemotherapy pill, so the combined drug will be easier on people's stomachs.
While the genetically engineered version of the plant may reach our food supply, will the drug reach our food supply?
2. Is it really a plausible concern that a "drug" plant would cross-pollinate with a non-drug plant and sneak into the food supply?
First of all, are there any non-drug crop X's being grown close enough to a drug crop X for this pollen story to happen? Maybe they don't grow the drug version and the regular version anywhere near each other.
Maybe the drug versions are all grown in greenhouses, where the wind would have no ability to spread the pollen.
Let's say the pollen is spread, do we need to worry that the GMO version would overtake the normal version? What if the GMO stuff is recessive and the normal stuff is dominant genetics. It might be that even if pollen from drug plants blew over to normal plants, the normal plants would win out.
Let's say the pollen is spread, and the drug version of the crop does overtake the regular crops, do we need to worry that those crops will enter the food supply?

label: Goal
body: Look for an answer making it seem like we have less to be worried about, whether that's because the plant isn't "a drug" in and of itself, or because the storyline of it accidentally pollinating and overtaking regular plants before sneaking into our food supply sounds far fetched.

label: Conclusion
body: Drugs from genetically engineered crops will end up in the general food supply.

label: Evidence
body: Pollen from drug-producing crops could drift to ordinary crops, fertilize them, and turn them into drug-producing crops as well.

label: Evaluate
body: The argument assumes that if cross-pollination occurs, the drugs will actually reach the parts of the plant that people eat. If the drugs are produced in non-edible parts, the food supply remains safe even if pollen drift occurs.

label: Goal
body: Find the answer that breaks the causal chain between cross-pollination and food contamination.

label: Conclusion
body: Your breakfast cereal is about to come with a free dose of pharmaceuticals. At least, that is the scary scenario.

label: Evidence
body: Picture a field of corn engineered to grow aspirin. Next door, regular corn destined for your cereal bowl. Wind blows, pollen drifts, and suddenly your Cheerios come with unexpected medication.

label: Evaluate
body: The argument is a biological domino chain: engineered pollen + wind + neighboring crops = drugs in your food. To weaken it, we need to knock over one of those dominoes. Not just say "it is not that bad" or "we could detect it" — we need to show that the chain fundamentally breaks somewhere before drugs end up on your plate.

label: Goal
body: Find the answer that severs the chain between pollen drift and food contamination — ideally at the point where the drugs would need to appear in the parts of the plant people actually eat.

label: Conclusion (Thus)
body:
Some govt employees in Hanson Bldg are computer programmers.
```
some HB are CP   or   HB <--s--> CP
```

label: Evidence
body:
Most ppl in BUN 17 are computer programmers
```
most B17 are CP   or   B17 --m--> CP
```

label: Evaluate
body:
Our 'fill-in-the-blank" is prefaced by the Support Indicator "since", so we know we're supposed to provide Support for the conclusion announced by "thus".
We need to prove that at least one govt. employee in the Hanson Building is a computer programmer, and all we know is that "most members of BUN 17 (all of whom are government employees)" are computer programmers.
Since computer programmers is the overlapping ingredient, we know we need information that ties together the dangling ingredients ...
membership of Bargaining Unit 17
working in the Hanson Building

label: Goal
body:
Since we're trying to prove that some ppl in the Hanson Building are programmers, and we know that a bunch of people in BUN 17 are programmers, we want an answer to put BUN 17 into the Hanson Building.
note: the above is what a normal person would be thinking going to these answer choices. the below is for LSAT Supernerds
When we see Quantifier words like "most" and "some", it triggers our awareness of a certain LSAT game where we use different quantifiers to prove there's some overlap.
for example,
```
Some A's are B
+ All B's are C
=================
Some A's are C
```
The vast majority of Trait Overlap inferences use conditional logic (like "All B are C"), but there's one special inference that doesn't — the most + most.
```
Most A's are B
+ Most A's are C
=================
Some B's are C
```
Since this argument is providing a MOST premise and trying to conclude a SOME idea, we would suspect that we're missing the other MOST idea.
```
Most BUN 17 are programmers      prem
+ Most BUN 17 are Hanson          answer
=================
Some Hanson are programmers      conc
```
p.s. if you want to try another problem just like this, try this one.

label: Conclusion
body: Some government employees who work in the Hanson Building are computer programmers.

label: Evidence
body: Most members of Bargaining Unit 17 are computer programmers.

label: Evaluate
body: There is no connection between BU17 and the Hanson Building. If most BU17 members work in Hanson, then two overlapping "most" statements about the same group guarantee that some Hanson workers are programmers.

label: Goal
body: Find the assumption that, when combined with the premise, makes the conclusion follow with certainty.

label: Conclusion
body: Some people in the Hanson Building are programmers. We need to prove this with certainty.

label: Evidence
body: Most of BU17 are programmers. Great. But right now, BU17 and the Hanson Building are in completely different universes — there is no connection between them.

label: Evaluate
body: Think Venn diagrams. You have got a big BU17 circle, and more than half of it is shaded "programmer." You need some of that shading to land inside the "Hanson Building" circle. The trick: if more than half of BU17 are programmers AND more than half of BU17 work in Hanson, those two halves MUST share members. You cannot fit two groups that each contain more than 50% of the same population into completely separate boxes. Pigeonhole principle wins.

label: Goal
body: Find the answer that forces enough BU17 members into the Hanson Building to guarantee overlap with the programmer majority.

label: Evidence
body:
```
Every Lab in my neighborhood        X → Y
is a well-behaved dog.
Being well behaved requires          Y → Z
that it was trained.
```

label: Conclusion
body:
```
It is training that accounts for     Z causes Y,
well-behaved, not Lab breed          not X*
```

label: Evaluate
body:
Because there are Conditionals / Quantifiers like "Every" and "No", it makes sense to think about diagramming this argument somewhat algebraically.
Also, there are overlapping ideas (well-behaved is in all three claims / training is in two / Labrador is in two), which also argues in favor of an algebraic approach.
Given our strong structural recipe, we might be able to find the correct answer just by matching up those parts. But sometimes we need to think more about why we're objecting to this logic.
How could we argue with the Conclusion?
We know that training is relevant to being well-behaved, since it's identified as a necessary characteristic. But couldn't the DNA of a Labrador also play a role? Maybe the author's conclusion is just messed up because she's saying, "THIS is the cause, not THAT", when we might object, "couldn't they both be causal factors?"

label: Goal
body:
Look for an answer with this structure:
```
P1: Every X is Y
P2: Y requires Z
Conc: Y is due to Z, not to X
```
Or look for an answer whose conclusion is vulnerable to the same type of conversational objection, "couldn't both of them be involved"?

label: Conclusion
body: It is training, not genetic makeup, that accounts for the Labradors' good behavior.

label: Evidence
body: Every Labrador Retriever in the neighborhood is well-behaved. No pet is well-behaved unless it is well trained.

label: Evaluate
body: Training is necessary for good behavior, but that does not make it the only factor. Genetics could also contribute alongside training. The flaw is treating a necessary condition as the sole explanation while dismissing an alternative contributing factor.

label: Goal
body: Find the answer that commits the identical flaw: identifying a necessary condition and using it to exclude an alternative factor as the explanation for an observed outcome.

label: Conclusion
body: "It is the TRAINING, not their Labrador genetics, that makes them good dogs!"

label: Evidence
body: All the Labs in the neighborhood are well-behaved. And no pet can be well-behaved without training. So every good dog was trained. But does that mean training gets ALL the credit?

label: Evaluate
body: Just because every well-behaved dog was trained does not mean training is the ONLY reason they behave well. It is like saying "no one gets a six-pack without exercising, so diet has NOTHING to do with it." Exercise might be necessary, but that does not make it the whole story. The Labs could be well-behaved because of training AND because Labradors are naturally good-natured. The argument spots one required ingredient and declares it the ENTIRE recipe while tossing genetics in the trash.

label: Goal
body: We need the answer that pulls the exact same move: finds a necessary condition, declares it the sole explanation, and dismisses an alternative contributing factor. Same skeleton, same flaw, different nouns.

label: Conclusion
body: The dangers of drinking are greatly exaggerated in the medical press.

label: Evidence
body: The columnist's grandfather drank heavily his entire life and lived to be 95.

label: Evaluate
body: The columnist tries to challenge a general claim about how alcohol shortens lives by citing one person who drank heavily and lived a long life. A single example cannot refute a population-level claim, the claim is about averages and tendencies, not about every individual.

label: Goal
body: Find the answer pointing out that the columnist relies on a single anecdote to attack a general claim.

label: Conclusion (this supports the idea)
body: fMRI can eventually form the basis of an effective lie detector.

label: Evidence
body: When 18 subjects lied about a playing card, fMRI scans showed increased activity in regions of the brain known to be stimulated by stress.

label: Evaluate
body: The evidence tells us that the fMRI picked up on activity in stress-related brain regions. The conclusion is claiming the fMRI is detecting a lie. So we need to assume that activity in these regions clearly signals a lie. The author seems to be thinking, "when you lie, you feel stress. When you feel stress, these regions become active. So if we detect these regions are active, then we've detected that you're lying." But does lying cause stress? If not, this test could provide false negatives, because people would be lying but it wouldn't detect them. And what if other things cause stress, even though the person is telling the truth? Or what if other things besides stress cause these brain regions to light up? If so, this test could provide false positives, because it might look like they're lying even though they aren't.

label: Goal
body: Since we want to weaken, let's look for a way to say that this test wouldn't be reliable. It would provide false negatives or false positives.

label: Evaluate
body: There's a big language shift from the terms of the evidence to the terms of the conclusion. The evidence is talking about how famous a pianist is and how must pleasure the audience feels. The conclusion is talking about good the playing is. We probably want an answer to patch up these missing links. We could interpret this as Explain Curious Fact, where the author is trying to interpret why audiences get more pleasure from more famous musicians. In the author's mind, it's because the pianist is playing better. But maybe the audience just loves seeing someone famous.

label: Goal
body: Look for an answer connecting "more famous, play better" or for an answer connecting "more pleasure, play better". Or let's otherwise look for any answer that suggests that audiences can distinguish good playing from bad playing, or one that rules out the idea that the audience's pleasure comes from some other source besides the quality of playing (such as from the fame of the pianist).

label: Conclusion (clearly then)
body: The cognitive psychologist's definition of intelligence is inadequate. rephrase: Intelligence is not the ability to figure out how things work in order to overcome obstacles.

label: Evidence
body: In a situation where someone acquired an understanding of how things work, we'd say they were intelligent, regardless of whether they acquired that knowledge in order to overcome an obstacle.

label: Evaluate
body: The three most common moves on Method are Analogies, Faulty Implications, and Alternatives. This somewhat has Faulty Implications vibes, because the author is essentially saying: If your definition was correct, then someone who acquired an understanding of how something works just for the sake of learning it (not in order to overcome an obstacle), would not be considered intelligent. However we DO consider those people intelligent. Thus, your definition is wrong.

label: Goal
body: The author is showing that the definition is wrong because it isn't broad enough to encompass cases of intelligence that don't involve overcoming obstacles. Find any answer that says something descriptively true.

label: Conclusion (therefore)
body: The president is mistaken in claiming that academic programs should be tailored to suit student demand. rephrase: Academic programs shouldn't be tailored to suit student demand.

label: Evidence
body: The president supports his claim by saying that, like any business, a university has to satisfy his customers. The author says educating students isn't analogous to providing consumer goods.

label: Evaluate
body: When we're doing Flaw and see that it's a Rebuttal style argument, there are two famous flaws we want to leap to mind: 1. Ad Hominem (discrediting a view on the basis that the SOURCE of the view has an ulterior motive or conflicting past behavior) 2. Unproven vs. Proven False (concluding that someone's claim is wrong on the grounds that they lack evidence to prove it's true or that they made a faulty argument in support of it. This argument is doing the 2nd. The faculty member shows that the president's reasoning for the view is bad — the analogy fails. From "the president's reasons are bad," the faculty member jumps to "the president's conclusion is wrong." That is a leap. A view can be correct even if the particular argument given for it is flawed.

label: Goal
body: Look for an answer getting at this Unproven vs. Proven False flaw.

label: Conclusion
body: It should be illegal to patent an organism's genes.

label: Evidence (for)
body: A person should not be regarded as the inventor of something they merely discovered. Also, exploitation of genetic information for profit is selfish and irresponsible.

label: Evaluate
body: We know that the outcome (right side) of the principle should be something that sounds like "should be illegal to patent". The available ideas for the trigger of the principle are - you discovered it, you didn't invent it - exploiting this is selfish and irresponsible.

label: Goal
body: Let's look for something like "if discovered rather than invented, should be illegal to patent", or something like "if selfish and irresponsible to exploit for profit, should be illegal". But ultimately we just want a rule whose trigger applies to patenting genes and whose outcome helps us say "should be illegal to do it".

label: Conclusion
body: The scholars who say Massachusetts (1690) was the first non-Chinese government to issue paper currency are wrong.

label: Evidence
body: In 1685, New France assigned official value to playing cards and issued them as pay to soldiers, convertible to coin later. So New France did this five years before Massachusetts.

label: Evaluate
body: The scholars' claim is specifically about paper currency. To refute them, the New France case must qualify as paper currency. Playing cards function as currency in the stimulus (assigned value, used to pay soldiers, convertible to coin), but for the conclusion to follow, the playing cards have to also be made of paper. Without that, the New France case might not be a "paper currency" example, and the scholars' claim could survive.

label: Goal
body: Find the assumption that makes the New France playing cards qualify as paper currency — i.e., that the cards were made of paper.

label: Task
body: The uncommon stem makes this question hard to categorize. "Which of the following principles" is common phrasing for both Principle Strengthen and Principle Conform, but "most clearly illustrated by the statements above" is more typical of Proposition / Generalization questions, a subtype of Most Supported. The task for that subtype is to extract a proposition / generalization / principle from the reading, which often feels like articulating the "moral of the story." That will be the task for this question.

label: Given
body: Generally, open discussion of bad and dangerous ideas makes them less appealing. However, even in democracies, certain bad ideas are so attractive that they get more appealing when they are discussed openly.

label: Evaluate
body: Proposition / Generalization questions often revolve around an important pivot word that creates tension in the stimulus. Our job is to find an answer that does the best job articulating that tension. Our first claim is something that is generally true: open discussion lessens the appeal of wrong ideas. After the pivot (however), we get tension in the form of an exception: some bad ideas are so appealing they get more attractive when debated.

label: Goal
body: Look for an answer that articulates that tension. Beware strong language, new ideas, and unsupported relationships. Lean towards the weakest, most provable answer.

label: Opposing Point (some have argued)
body: Once it becomes necessary for us to think about computers in terms of beliefs and desires in order to understand how they function, we can rightly say that computers have beliefs and desires.

label: Evidence (however)
body: We already need to think about what computers believe and desire in order to understand how they function.

label: Intermediate Conclusion (thus)
body: The suggested criterion for ascribing beliefs and desires to computers implies that the computers that exist now have beliefs and desires.

label: Main Conclusion (so)
body: The suggested criterion is obviously flawed.

label: Evaluate
body: The claim in question is part of the Intermediate Conclusion. We know this claim to be a conclusion because of the word thus, and we know it's intermediate because the next sentence begins with the conclusion indicator word so. Since the claim in question is just one part of the intermediate conclusion, we should expect the correct answer to get more granular and describe how that claim works. That's unfortunate in a Role question, but it's to be expected in the Gauntlet where the hardest questions lie! The opposing point is establishes a criterion that, once met, means we can say that computers have beliefs and desires. The evidence is that we've already met that criterion. The intermediate conclusion is that, taken together, the opposing point and the evidence would mean that computers today have beliefs and desires. From this, the author derives their main conclusion: that criterion is obviously bogus. Thus, this argument has classic Rebuttal archetype known as the Reduction to the Absurd: If X was true, it would imply Y. But Y isn't true. So X isn't true either.

label: Goal
body: Look for an answer that acknowledges the Rebuttal and the author's assumption that computers today do not have beliefs and desires.

label: Conclusion
body:
In order for the manufacturer to stay in business, its biggest competitor must stay in business.
stay in ----------------------------→ biggest competitor
business stays in business

label: Evidence
body:
If the biggest competitor went out of business, some specialized suppliers shared by both companies would be bankrupted.
biggest competitor -------------------→ some spec supp
not stay in business shared go bankrupt

label: Evaluate
body:
When we compare our conclusion to our evidence, the overlapping term about the biggest competitor isn't lined up, so we need to either contrapose our evidence or our conclusion (doesn't matter).
If we contrapose the conclusion, we're trying to prove:
biggest comp ---------------------------------→ we not stay
out of business in business
What the evidence provided was
biggest comp ----→ some shared SS
out of business go bankrupt
So the missing piece we need to create the logic path in the conclusion is,
some shared SS --→ we not stay
go bankrupt in business
Those two pieces would combine to give us
"if biggest competitor goes out of business, then we go out of business".

label: Goal
body:
Our answer should be saying, "If some of our shared specialized suppliers go bankrupt, then we still not stay in business",
or its contrapositive, "In order for us to stay in business, our shared specialized suppliers can't go bankrupt".

label: Conclusion
body: Jack's dog must sometimes howl while he is washing it.

label: Evidence
body: Universal premise: the dog howls whenever a train goes by. Particular premise: occasionally a train goes by while Jack is washing the dog.

label: Evaluate
body: Structure: All trains-passing → dog howls. Some washing-events overlap with a train passing. Therefore some washing-events feature howling. The pattern is: all A produce B; some C overlaps with A; therefore some C produces B.

label: Goal
body: Find an answer with the same structure: a universal "all X have property Y," a particular "some Z is X," and a conclusion "some Z has property Y."

label: Given
body: When plants grow fast, they take more CO2 out of the atmosphere than they release. When plants grow very slowly, they release more CO2 than they take out. Any substantial increase in CO2 causes temperatures to increase in the tropics. The bulk of Earth's plants are in the tropics. The more temperatures increase in the tropics, the more slowly, on average, plants there grow.

label: Evaluate
body: All the Causal statements should prompt us to look for opportunities to chain them together. Only claim 1 mentions fast plant growth and taking more CO2 out, so that one won't chain to anything else. Claim 2 tells us that very slow plant growth causes more CO2 to be released. That doesn't necessarily chain to claim 3, because releasing more CO2 doesn't necessarily create a substantial increase, but in cases where it does, it would increase the temperature in the tropics. That chains to the final claim, resulting in slower average plant growth.

label: Goal
body:
Look for an answer that articulates all or part of our Causal Chain:
Very Slow Plant Growth > Releases CO2
Lots more CO2 > Increase Tropic Temps > Slower Ave. Growth of Tropics Plants
Beware answers that are too strong or that ignore important modifiers (substantial increase, very slow growth, etc).

label: Principle
body:
criticism of article appears
in mag where orig published author of orig
or → article should be
criticism appears in another able to respond
magazine and is unfair in mag where criticized

label: Application
body: McFinton should be allowed to publish a response in Speculator's Digest to Wallace's most recent article, because Wallace's article harshly criticizes McFinton's essay on self-deception.

label: Evaluate
body:
The way that all these Principle + Application questions work is that the Application concludes the right side of the principle, but it fails to establish the trigger of the principle.
The application is concluding that McF should be able to respond in Spec Digest to criticism of his article.
But we need to know a couple things:
1. Spec Digest is where Wallace's criticism was published
and then either
2a. McF's orig article was in Spec Digest
or
2b. Wallace's criticism is unfair
If the criticism is unfair, it doesn't matter where McF's article is published.
If McF's article was orig published in Spec Digest, it doesn't matter whether Wallace's criticism is fair or unfair.
For the principle to license a response in Speculator's Digest, McFinton's original essay must have appeared in Speculator's Digest (so that "that magazine" = Speculator's Digest). Then either Wallace's criticism must also have appeared in Speculator's Digest (condition a), or it must have appeared elsewhere and be unfair (condition b).

label: Goal
body: Find an answer that pins down both: McFinton's essay was in Speculator's Digest, and Wallace's criticism was also in Speculator's Digest (or was elsewhere and unfair).
